NAMES.name: angle_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Second inclination angle (β) of the oblique trapezoidal cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap, giving the signed tilt of the beta-side lateral face relative to the directed strap base edge.
NAMES.long:
The oblique trapezoidal cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap is geometrically characterized by two lateral-face inclination angles, alpha (α) and beta (β). The beta angle is the signed inclination of the beta-side lateral face relative to the directed base edge of the trapezoid, complementing [alpha_angle_of_antenna_strap](name:alpha_angle_of_antenna_strap), which describes the inclination of the opposite lateral face.

Together with shape parameters such as [length_of_antenna_strap](name:length_of_antenna_strap) and [height_of_antenna_strap](name:height_of_antenna_strap), the pair of inclination angles (α, β) fully specifies the oblique trapezoidal cross-sectional geometry used to model the conducting strap element in RF antenna simulations. This angle is a fixed mechanical design parameter derived from engineering drawings and does not vary with plasma conditions.

The analogous second-inclination angle for passive structures is [angle_of_passive_loop](name:tilt_angle_of_passive_loop), which encodes the β angle of the passive loop cross-section in the same geometric convention.

NAMES.name: alpha_angle_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Alpha angle is the signed inclination of the alpha-side lateral face of an oblique trapezoidal cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor relative to the directed strap base edge. It complements the beta angle on the opposite lateral face.
NAMES.long:
Alpha angle of an antenna strap is the directed inclination of the alpha-side lateral face of the strap conductor's oblique trapezoidal cross-section. The angle is measured in a local cross-section plane from the directed base edge of the trapezoid to the slanted alpha-side edge; the complementary [beta angle] specifies the opposite lateral face. Together with the strap base length, width, and thickness, it fixes the trapezoidal conductor outline used in antenna geometry models.

The signed inclination can be computed from two unit vectors in the local right-handed cross-section basis $(\hat{u}, \hat{v}, \hat{n})$:

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left[(\hat{u}\times\hat{s}_\alpha)\cdot\hat{n},\ \hat{u}\cdot\hat{s}_\alpha\right]
$$

where $\hat{u}$ is the unit vector along the directed base edge, $\hat{s}_\alpha$ is the unit vector along the alpha-side lateral face from the base edge toward the opposite edge, $\hat{n}$ is the cross-section normal, and $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the directed angle about $\hat{n}$.

In practice, $\alpha$ is specified from the mechanical design geometry or obtained by fitting straight lines to the base edge and alpha-side edge of a surveyed or modeled conductor cross-section. Changing this angle changes the obliqueness of the conductor side wall and therefore the local outline supplied to antenna electromagnetic and structural calculations.

Typical magnitudes for nondegenerate strap trapezoids are about 0.5-2.6 rad. Values near $\pi/2$ rad correspond to an almost rectangular side wall, while values close to 0 or $\pi$ rad would make the side wall nearly parallel to the base and are normally avoided.
NAMES.sign: Positive when rotation from the $+\hat{u}$ base direction to the alpha-side lateral-face direction is counterclockwise when viewed along $+\hat{n}$ in the local right-handed cross-section basis $(\hat{u}, \hat{v}, \hat{n})$.

NAMES.name: angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
NAMES.short: Signed rotation angle of an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror about its mechanical steering axis, measured from the launcher reference orientation and controlling the EC microwave beam injection direction.
NAMES.long:
The mirror angle quantifies the angular position of the steering mirror on an electron-cyclotron launcher, which redirects the millimeter-wave beam along the desired injection path into the plasma. By adjusting this angle, the beam can be directed at different magnetic flux surfaces, enabling localized electron heating or non-inductive current drive at a chosen plasma radius.

The accessible angular range is bounded by the mechanical travel limits of the actuator system: the lower bound is given by [minimum_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:minimum_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and the upper bound by [maximum_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:maximum_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), together defining the full range of injection directions available for the microwave beam. The resulting beam orientation after the mirror reflection is further characterized by angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam, which describes the beam direction in the plane transverse to propagation.

Mirror positioning is achieved through motorized actuators with angular position encoders; real-time feedback enables precise beam aiming during plasma operation. The spatial location of the mirror center is complemented by [radial_centroid_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:radial_centroid_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and [vertical_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:vertical_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), which together define the mirror center position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: area_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Geometric surface area of the neutral beam injector ion-extraction face. It is the total emitting aperture area available for beam formation, independent of the detailed aperture shape.
NAMES.long:
Area of a neutral beam injector is the geometric surface area of the ion-extraction face that is open or emitting for beam formation. For a multi-aperture source, it represents the sum of the contributing aperture areas on the extraction face.

The source area is defined by the surface integral over the emitting extraction surface:

$$
A_\mathrm{src} = \int_{S_\mathrm{ext}} dA
$$

where $S_\mathrm{ext}$ is the emitting portion of the ion-extraction surface, $dA$ is an elemental surface area in m$^2$, and $A_\mathrm{src}$ is the neutral beam injector source area in m$^2$.

In practice, the value is obtained from mechanical design, dimensional metrology, or aperture-pattern geometry. For discrete apertures, the total area may be computed as the sum of the individual open areas; circular and rectangular aperture dimensions are conceptually related to radius_of_aperture and x_width_of_aperture. When converting extraction current density to total extracted current, the relation $I_\mathrm{ext}=\langle j_\mathrm{ext}\rangle A_\mathrm{src}$ uses the area-averaged extraction current density $\langle j_\mathrm{ext}\rangle$ in A m$^{-2}$ and the extracted current $I_\mathrm{ext}$ in A; a nonuniform local current density must instead be integrated over the emitting surface.

Typical emitting areas range from $10^{-3}$-$10^{-1}$ m$^2$ for compact research injectors and about $0.1$-$1$ m$^2$ for large multi-aperture heating injectors, depending on beam power, allowable extraction current density, and source technology.

NAMES.name: beam_area_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Area of the active ion-source emission face of a neutral beam injector. It is defined before downstream neutralization and sets the source cross-section used to normalize extracted beam current density.
NAMES.long:
Beam area of a neutral beam injector is the total active area of the ion-source emission face from which ions are extracted into the accelerator. It describes the source-side geometric cross-section of the charged beam before the neutralizer, not the area of the beam after neutralization or after downstream divergence.

For an emitting surface $S_\mathrm{emit}$, the beam area $A_\mathrm{beam}$ is

$$
A_\mathrm{beam} = \int_{S_\mathrm{emit}} dA
$$

where $dA$ is an element of the active emitting surface. For a multi-aperture or beamlet source, this integral is evaluated over the union of the active emitting apertures or over the effective emitting patches defined by the source model.

The quantity is obtained from the ion-source and extraction-grid geometry, mechanical metrology, or an effective optical model of the source. It is closely related to the source-surface quantity [area_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:beam_area_of_neutral_beam_injector); the `beam_area` wording emphasizes its use as the normalization area for beam extraction, for example the average extracted ion current density $\langle j_i \rangle = I_i/A_\mathrm{beam}$ for total extracted ion current $I_i$.

Typical values for heating neutral beam injectors are about 0.03-1 m^2. Compact diagnostic or test sources may be 10^{-4}-10^{-2} m^2, while large negative-ion heating sources can approach 1-2 m^2.

NAMES.name: capacitance
NAMES.short: Electrical capacitance of a lumped impedance-matching element in an ion cyclotron resonance heating antenna RF tuning circuit. It is the non-negative charge-to-voltage proportionality of that element, not an effective capacitance of the whole antenna or plasma load.
NAMES.long:
Capacitance is the non-negative proportionality between stored electric charge and voltage across a lumped circuit element, expressed in farads. In an ion cyclotron resonance heating RF tuning circuit it describes a physical matching capacitor or equivalent lumped capacitive element, not the effective capacitance of the complete antenna, transmission line, or plasma load.

For sinusoidal phasors proportional to $e^{i\omega t}$, the capacitor impedance is

$$
Z_C = \frac{1}{i 2\pi f C} = -\frac{i}{2\pi f C}
$$

where $C$ is the capacitance in farads, $f$ is the RF frequency in hertz, and $Z_C$ is the complex impedance in ohms. The signed capacitive reactance is therefore $X_C = -1/(2\pi f C)$, while its magnitude is $|X_C| = 1/(2\pi f C)$.

In practice the value is determined from component specifications, calibrated actuator position for variable capacitors, or RF network measurements fitted to a lumped-element circuit model. It governs the reactive part of the matching network and is adjusted to reduce reflected power and match the antenna load during operation.

Typical values for ion cyclotron antenna matching capacitors range from about $10^{-12}$-$10^{-7}$ F, depending on RF frequency, voltage rating, antenna design, and whether the element is a fixed, switched, or continuously tunable capacitor.

NAMES.name: capacitance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Capacitance of a lumped impedance-matching element in an ion cyclotron heating antenna module. It represents the tuner-element capacitance used to adjust the reactive part of the RF matching network, not an effective capacitance of the whole antenna or plasma load.
NAMES.long:
Capacitance of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the capacitance assigned to a specific lumped impedance-matching element in the antenna module RF circuit. It characterizes how that tuner element stores electric energy and changes the reactive impedance seen by the transmission line at the chosen circuit reference plane.

For a simple lossless lumped LC matching branch, the tuning relation between capacitance and resonance frequency is commonly written as:

$$
f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}
$$

where $f_0$ is the resonance frequency in Hz, $L$ is the associated lumped inductance in H, and $C$ is the matching-element capacitance in F. In a driven RF circuit, the same capacitance contributes the ideal capacitive reactance $X_C=-1/(2\pi f C)$ in ohms at drive frequency $f$ in Hz; practical matching networks also include losses, stray reactances, transmission-line transformations, and plasma loading.

The value is normally obtained from the calibrated setting or circuit model of the matching capacitor at the reference plane used for antenna matching. If transmission-line sections or feedthroughs are de-embedded, this quantity denotes the de-embedded capacitance of the specified matching element, rather than the net input capacitance of the complete antenna module.

Typical lumped RF matching-capacitor values for high-power ion cyclotron antenna circuits are hardware-specific but are commonly in the picofarad to nanofarad range, about $10^{-12}$-$10^{-9}$ F. The selected value depends on operating frequency, matching-network topology, antenna loading resistance, and the reference plane used for the circuit representation.

NAMES.name: current_due_to_electron_cyclotron_current_drive
NAMES.short: Net toroidal plasma current driven non-inductively by resonant absorption of electron cyclotron waves, summed over all EC wave sources. The waves drive a parallel current along the magnetic field whose toroidal projection contributes to the conventional toroidal plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Current due to electron cyclotron current drive is the contribution to the conventional toroidal plasma current produced by resonant electron cyclotron wave absorption rather than by transformer induction. The wave selectively modifies the electron momentum distribution along the magnetic field, generating a parallel current density whose toroidal projection adds to the total non-inductive current. This scalar represents the net current summed over all electron cyclotron wave sources in the device.

The net toroidal EC-driven current is the integral of the driven toroidal current density over a poloidal cross-section:

$$
I_{\mathrm{EC}} = \int_{S_p} j_{\phi,\mathrm{EC}} \, dS
$$

where $S_p$ is the plasma poloidal cross-section, $dS$ is its area element, and $j_{\phi,\mathrm{EC}} = j_{\parallel,\mathrm{EC}}\,\mathbf{b}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal component of the EC-driven current density in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height. Here $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{EC}}$ is the field-aligned EC-driven current density and $\mathbf{b}$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field, so the toroidal projection follows from $\mathbf{b}\cdot\hat{\phi}$.

This current is usually inferred from wave absorption and current-drive calculations constrained by injected EC power, launch geometry, magnetic equilibrium, density, and temperature. It is the EC analog of the lower-hybrid and ion-cyclotron driven currents, and contributes to the aggregate non-inductive plasma current; the EC power sustaining it is quantified by the corresponding total absorbed electron cyclotron heating power.

Typical magnitudes span roughly a few kiloamperes for localized current-profile control up to of order a megaampere in high-power scenarios, depending strongly on absorbed power, electron temperature, and deposition geometry. The value approaches zero when EC power is absent, weakly absorbed, or absorbed in a geometry that produces little net driven current.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the EC-driven conventional plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_due_to_ion_cyclotron_current_drive
NAMES.short: Net non-inductive plasma current in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, produced by ion cyclotron wave absorption and integrated over the plasma cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Current due to ion cyclotron current drive is the total non-inductive contribution to plasma current produced by ion cyclotron range waves. It is the toroidal current component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame integrated over the plasma cross-section, representing the boundary-enclosed total rather than the contribution from a single launched toroidal mode. It is the ion-cyclotron contribution to [plasma_current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive](name:plasma_current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive) and the mode-summed counterpart of [per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive](name:per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive).

The total driven current is defined from the ion-cyclotron-driven current density by the cross-sectional current integral used for [toroidal_plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current):

$$
I_{\mathrm{ICCD}} = \int_{S_p} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{ICCD}} \cdot \hat{\phi}\, dS
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{ICCD}}$ is the driven current-density contribution in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $S_p$ is the plasma region in a surface of constant $\phi$, and $dS$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area element in $\mathrm{m^2}$. For an enclosed-current value inside a flux surface, $S_p$ would be restricted to the area inside that surface; for this total-current quantity, $S_p$ is the full plasma cross-section.

In practice, this current is computed from radio-frequency wave propagation and absorption together with a kinetic description of resonant charged particles, minority species, and collisional momentum transfer to the bulk plasma. It can be constrained indirectly by current-balance analysis that separates inductive, bootstrap, ohmic, and other auxiliary-drive contributions, but it is not usually measured as an isolated current. If a current-drive efficiency is quoted separately, a common engineering form is $\eta_{\mathrm{CD}} = I_{\mathrm{ICCD}} n_e R_0 / P_{\mathrm{IC}}$, with units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}\,W^{-1}}$ when $I_{\mathrm{ICCD}}$ is in A, $n_e$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $R_0$ is in m, and $P_{\mathrm{IC}}$ is in W; that efficiency is derived from the current and is not the definition of the current.

Typical absolute magnitudes in present tokamak experiments range from near 0 to $10^5$ A, with optimized phasing or high-power scenarios reaching $10^5-10^6$ A. The signed value and magnitude depend strongly on launched parallel wave-number spectrum, absorption location, species mix, density and temperature, collisionality, and competition with other current sources.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the driven current density flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, counterclockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: current_due_to_lower_hybrid_current_drive
NAMES.short: Lower-hybrid current-drive current is the whole-plasma non-inductive toroidal current produced by lower-hybrid slow waves. It is the lower-hybrid contribution to the total non-inductive plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Lower-hybrid current-drive current is the whole-plasma net toroidal conventional current driven non-inductively by lower-hybrid waves. It is a source-specific contribution to [plasma_current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive](name:plasma_current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive), not an enclosed current or a radial distribution. The underlying wave-particle interaction primarily changes electron momentum along the magnetic field, while this scalar denotes the resulting toroidal current contribution integrated over the plasma.

The scalar current is defined by integrating the lower-hybrid-driven toroidal current-density component over the full plasma cross-section at fixed toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
I_{\mathrm{LHCD}} = \int_{S_p} j_{\phi,\mathrm{LHCD}}(R,Z)\, dR\, dZ
$$

where $j_{\phi,\mathrm{LHCD}}$ is the toroidal component of the lower-hybrid-driven conventional current density and $S_p$ is the entire plasma region in that poloidal cross-section. The area element $dR\,dZ$ gives the integrated current in amperes.

In practice this contribution is not usually measured as an isolated current. It is inferred from current-balance analysis combining the total plasma current, magnetic equilibrium constraints, loop-voltage information, lower-hybrid wave propagation and absorption modeling, and the fast-electron response responsible for the driven current.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. The value is 0 A when no lower-hybrid power is coupled to the plasma; with lower-hybrid current drive it can range from a small correction to a substantial fraction of the total toroidal plasma current, depending on coupled power, wave spectrum, density, temperature, and collisionality.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the driven conventional plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_due_to_neutral_beam_injection
NAMES.short: Non-inductive toroidal plasma current produced by neutral beam injection through directed momentum transfer from fast beam ions to the background plasma during Coulomb-collision thermalization.
NAMES.long:
Current due to neutral beam injection is the neutral-beam contribution to the total non-inductive plasma current, current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive. Injected neutrals are ionized in the plasma, become energetic fast ions, and transfer directed momentum to electrons and ions as they slow down, producing a net driven current.

At a global level, the driven current can be represented as the integral of a local NBI current-drive source density over the confined plasma volume:

$$
I_{\mathrm{NBI}} = \int_{V_p} S_{I,\mathrm{NBI}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{NBI}}$ is the total NBI-driven current, $S_{I,\mathrm{NBI}}$ is the local driven-current source density in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-3}}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $V_p$ is the plasma volume, and $dV$ is a volume element in $\mathrm{m^3}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from neutral-beam deposition, ionization, fast-ion orbit and slowing-down physics, pitch-angle scattering, collisional momentum exchange, and the plasma equilibrium. It depends strongly on the injected and absorbed neutral-beam power, power_due_to_neutral_beam_injection and absorbed_power_of_neutral_beam_injector, as well as beam energy, tangency geometry, fast-ion confinement, electron temperature, density, and trapped-particle fraction.

Typical values range from $1\times10^4$-$1\times10^6$ A in present-day tokamaks, with lower values for weak or poorly aligned beams and values near or above $1\times10^6$ A in large, high-power, high-temperature plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal projection of the driven parallel plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive
NAMES.short: Net non-inductive plasma current generated when resonant absorption of electromagnetic waves transfers directed momentum to charged particles.
NAMES.long:
The current due to wave-driven current drive is the net contribution to plasma current produced by resonant absorption of externally applied electromagnetic waves. It is a wave-driven subset of [current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive](name:current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive) and contributes to [plasma_current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive](name:plasma_current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive): wave-particle interactions such as Landau damping, transit-time magnetic pumping, or cyclotron resonance create an asymmetric velocity-space distribution whose field-aligned current contributes to the net plasma current.

The total current is the surface integral of the wave-driven current density through a poloidal cross-section:

$$
I_{\mathrm{wcd}} = \int_{S_p} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{wcd}} \cdot \hat{\phi}\, dR\, dZ
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{wcd}}$ is the current-density contribution from wave-particle momentum transfer, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal basis vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $S_p$ is the plasma cross-section at fixed $\phi$.

In practice, this current is inferred from absorbed wave power, launch spectrum, deposition location, and equilibrium constraints, often through current-balance analysis that separates ohmic, bootstrap, neutral-beam, and other non-inductive contributions. Specific wave-driven components include [current_due_to_electron_cyclotron_current_drive](name:current_due_to_electron_cyclotron_current_drive) and [current_due_to_lower_hybrid_current_drive](name:current_due_to_lower_hybrid_current_drive); spectra may also be resolved as [per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive](name:per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive).

Typical magnitudes in tokamaks are $10^4$-$10^6$ A. Localized electron-cyclotron drive often produces $10^4$-$10^5$ A, while lower-hybrid or fast-wave drive in large plasmas can contribute $10^5$-$10^6$ A; the value depends mainly on absorbed wave power, plasma density and temperature, magnetic geometry, and launch spectrum.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the driven plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_energy
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated kinetic energy stored in the fast, suprathermal electron population, evaluated from the fast-electron energy density or distribution function over the plasma volume. It excludes the bulk thermal electron energy and is an energy content, not a power or power density.
NAMES.long:
Fast electron energy is the total kinetic energy contained in electrons assigned to the suprathermal population rather than to the bulk thermal electron component. It represents stored energy in the non-thermal electron tail produced by wave heating, current drive, or other acceleration mechanisms.

A common definition is the volume integral of the fast-electron kinetic energy density:

$$
W_{\mathrm{fast},e} = \int_V \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{fast},e}(\mathbf{x})\,dV = \int_V \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{fast}}} (\gamma - 1)m_e c^2 f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v\,dV
$$

where $W_{\mathrm{fast},e}$ is the fast electron energy, $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{fast},e}$ is the fast-electron kinetic energy density in J m$^{-3}$, $f_e$ is the electron distribution function, $\Omega_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the velocity-space region or distribution-function component identified as suprathermal, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\gamma$ is the relativistic factor. In the nonrelativistic limit the kinetic energy factor reduces to $m_e v^2/2$.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating a modeled or reconstructed fast-electron distribution over velocity space and plasma volume. Constraints may come from kinetic wave-particle calculations and from diagnostics sensitive to non-thermal electrons, such as hard x-ray bremsstrahlung, electron cyclotron emission, or synchrotron radiation. It is distinct from fast-electron power density: integrating a power density over volume gives power, while stored energy follows from the accumulated kinetic energy content and changes according to power balance and loss processes.

The value is non-negative and is zero when no fast-electron population is present. Typical global values range from about 10^2-10^6 J in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, depending on injected power, current-drive efficiency, tail confinement, and the energy threshold or model separation used to identify the suprathermal population.

NAMES.name: frequency_of_electron_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Operating microwave frequency of an electron cyclotron heating antenna. It is a non-negative scalar that selects the cyclotron harmonic and constrains where resonance can occur in the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The frequency of an electron cyclotron heating antenna is the electromagnetic wave frequency produced by the antenna for electron cyclotron heating or current drive. It is a non-negative scalar; physically active heating uses $f>0$. The frequency helps select the electron cyclotron harmonic, while the actual absorption location and deposition width also depend on magnetic-field geometry, launch angle, wave polarization, density, temperature, and relativistic and Doppler effects.

In the simple cold, non-relativistic, Doppler-free resonance estimate, the antenna frequency matches an integer harmonic of the local electron cyclotron frequency:

$$
f \simeq n\,\frac{e B}{2\pi m_e}
$$

where $f$ is the antenna frequency in Hz, $n$ is the positive integer harmonic number, $e$ is the elementary charge in C, $B$ is the local magnetic flux density magnitude in T, and $m_e$ is the electron rest mass in kg. More complete resonance calculations include the parallel Doppler shift, relativistic mass correction, finite-temperature effects, and wave propagation constraints.

The frequency is normally set by the microwave source and transmission system and is verified by radio-frequency or millimeter-wave instrumentation. In scenario design it is compared with equilibrium magnetic-field values to identify accessible resonance surfaces, but it should not be interpreted by itself as fixing a unique radial power-deposition location.

Typical electron cyclotron heating frequencies are in the millimeter-wave range, about $3 \times 10^{10}$-$2 \times 10^{11}$ Hz for many magnetic-confinement applications, with the appropriate value set by the magnetic-field strength and chosen harmonic. Related antenna-frequency quantities include [ion cyclotron heating antenna frequency](name:frequency_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and [lower-hybrid antenna frequency](name:frequency_of_lower_hybrid_antenna).

NAMES.name: frequency_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Operating RF frequency of an ion cyclotron resonance heating antenna, which sets the resonance layer position in the plasma and selects the target ion species and harmonic number for cyclotron wave damping.
NAMES.long:
The RF operating frequency of an ICRH antenna determines the spatial location of the ion cyclotron resonance layer and selects the target ion species and harmonic number for wave absorption. Adjusting this frequency steers the deposition layer radially across the plasma cross-section or shifts the heated species between minority and majority heating configurations.

The fundamental resonance condition linking antenna frequency to the local magnetic field is:

$$
\omega = n \, \Omega_{ci} = n \frac{Z_i e B}{m_i}
$$

where $\omega = 2\pi f$ is the angular wave frequency, $n$ is the harmonic number ($n = 1$ for fundamental resonance, $n = 2$ for second harmonic), $Z_i$ is the charge number and $m_i$ is the mass of the resonant ion species, $e$ is the elementary charge, and $B$ is the local magnetic field magnitude at the target layer.

The frequency is set by the RF generator and recorded per antenna module or averaged over modules in a multi-strap launcher. It is combined with equilibrium reconstruction data to determine the resonance layer geometry in the plasma. The antenna [resistance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:resistance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and [capacitance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:capacitance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) are impedance-matched at this operating frequency to maximize power transfer. Strap-to-strap phasing, characterized by [wave_phase_of_antenna_strap](name:wave_phase_of_antenna_strap), is optimized alongside the frequency to shape the launched toroidal wave-number spectrum. The analogous quantity for electron cyclotron systems is [frequency_of_electron_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:frequency_of_electron_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

Typical operating frequencies span 25–120 MHz for major tokamaks; the exact value depends on the target ion species, harmonic number, and on-axis magnetic field strength.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the antenna transmits at the tuned RF operating frequency for ion cyclotron wave injection into the plasma.

NAMES.name: frequency_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: RF carrier frequency at which a lower-hybrid antenna launches waves into the plasma. It is a per-antenna operating parameter that influences wave accessibility, penetration, and current-drive performance together with launcher phasing and launched power.
NAMES.long:
The frequency of a lower-hybrid antenna is the radio-frequency carrier frequency of the electromagnetic wave applied to that antenna. It fixes the temporal oscillation rate of the launched lower-hybrid wave, while the launched refractive-index spectrum is also determined by launcher phasing and geometry.

The antenna frequency is commonly compared with the lower-hybrid resonance using angular frequency:

$$
\omega_\mathrm{RF}=2\pi f_\mathrm{LH,ant}, \qquad \omega_\mathrm{RF} \gtrsim \omega_\mathrm{LH} \approx \frac{\omega_{pi}}{\sqrt{1+\omega_{pe}^2/\omega_{ce}^2}}
$$

where $f_\mathrm{LH,ant}$ is the antenna frequency, $\omega_\mathrm{RF}$ is the launched wave angular frequency in rad s$^{-1}$, $\omega_\mathrm{LH}$ is the lower-hybrid resonance angular frequency, $\omega_{pi}$ and $\omega_{pe}$ are the ion and electron plasma angular frequencies, and $\omega_{ce}$ is the electron cyclotron angular frequency. In more complete cold-plasma accessibility estimates, the required launched parallel refractive index $n_\parallel$ is dimensionless and depends on frequency, density, magnetic field, and ion species.

In practice this frequency is specified by the RF source chain and antenna design, and is checked using RF frequency monitoring such as frequency counters or spectrum analyzers. For modulated or multi-frequency operation, it denotes the carrier or reference frequency associated with the antenna, distinct from the launched power described by [launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and from the summed system power described by [total_launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna). Together with [toroidal_launched_wave_index_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:toroidal_launched_wave_index_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and [poloidal_launched_wave_index_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:poloidal_launched_wave_index_of_lower_hybrid_antenna), it affects the resonant electron velocity range and the efficiency of lower-hybrid current drive.

Typical lower-hybrid current-drive antenna frequencies are about $1\times10^9$-$8\times10^9$ Hz. Representative design frequencies can be near $2.45\times10^9$ Hz or $3.7\times10^9$ Hz, but the selected value is device-, launcher-, and scenario-specific.

NAMES.name: gap_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Perpendicular clearance from the rear surface of an ICRH antenna strap conductor to the conducting wall directly behind it.
NAMES.long:
The gap of an antenna strap is the perpendicular clear distance from the rear surface of an ion-cyclotron-range-of-frequency antenna strap conductor to the conducting wall directly behind it, on the side facing away from the plasma. It is a mechanical clearance that helps set the local electromagnetic coupling between the strap and the back conductor.

In a local parallel-plate approximation, the rear-surface capacitance per unit strap length is estimated by

$$
C' = \frac{\epsilon_0 w_s}{d}
$$

where $C'$ is capacitance per unit strap length in F m$^{-1}$, $\epsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity in F m$^{-1}$, $w_s$ is the effective strap width in m, and $d$ is the antenna-strap gap in m. This approximation neglects fringing fields and nearby conductors, so it gives physical intuition rather than a complete antenna model: increasing $d$ reduces this capacitive coupling, while decreasing $d$ increases it.

The gap is normally obtained from the antenna mechanical design or from dimensional survey of the assembled strap and back conductor. Full RF analyzes use the complete conductor geometry, dielectric environment, and plasma-facing structures, so the gap should be interpreted as one local geometric input rather than as a stand-alone predictor of loading or resonance.

This name denotes the same rear-surface-to-back-wall clearance described by [back_surface_gap_of_antenna_strap](name:back_surface_gap_of_antenna_strap) and distance_of_antenna_strap; the wording here emphasizes the clearance as a gap. It differs from strap body dimensions such as [thickness_of_antenna_strap](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap), [inner_radius_of_antenna_strap](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap), and [outer_radius_of_antenna_strap](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap), which describe the conductor itself rather than the empty space behind it.

Typical values are antenna-design specific and should not be inferred from a universal plasma scaling. They are usually engineering clearances specified in meters, commonly on the millimeter-to-centimeter scale, with the final value constrained by voltage holdoff, mechanical tolerance, cooling layout, and RF-circuit requirements.

NAMES.name: height_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Full vertical height of the rectangular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor element, measured along the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long:
The height of an antenna strap is the full vertical (poloidal) extent of the rectangular cross-section of the current-carrying strap conductor in an ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) antenna system. In ICRH antennas, the strap is the active radiating element that launches electromagnetic waves near the ion cyclotron frequency; its cross-sectional geometry governs current distribution, RF resistance, and coupling efficiency to the plasma.

For a rectangular strap cross-section, the three characteristic dimensions are height (this quantity), [width](name:width_of_antenna_strap) measured along the toroidal direction, and [thickness](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap) perpendicular to the strap plane. Height is measured along the vertical direction $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate. For strap conductors with annular cross-sections, the analogous radial dimensions are the [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap) and [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap) of the conductor.

Typical ICRH strap heights range from a few centimeters to approximately 50 cm depending on antenna design and machine geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: launched_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher
NAMES.short: Net electron cyclotron radio-frequency power crossing from a single launcher into the vacuum vessel, defined as forward minus reflected power at the launcher aperture or reference plane. Evaluated after transmission-line and launcher losses and before any plasma absorption, reflection, or shine-through.
NAMES.long:
Launched power of an electron cyclotron launcher is the net radio-frequency wave power delivered by one electron cyclotron launcher across its launch aperture into the vacuum vessel. It is a boundary power for electron-cyclotron heating and current-drive calculations, defined as the forward power minus the power reflected back at the launcher aperture or reference plane, and before any plasma absorption, reflection from cutoff or resonance regions, wall interaction, or shine-through.

For a launcher represented by one or more launched wave beams, the launcher launched power is the sum of the launched powers of those beams:

$$
P_{\mathrm{EC,launched}}^{\mathrm{launcher}} = \sum_b P_{\mathrm{launched},b}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{launched},b}$ is the launched power of beam $b$ in watts, taken after transmission losses and before plasma interaction. Equivalently, in terms of the directional power components at the reference plane, $P_{\mathrm{EC,launched}}^{\mathrm{launcher}} = P_{\mathrm{forward}} - P_{\mathrm{reflected}}$, with all terms in watts.

This power is typically derived from gyrotron or source output power corrected for transmission-line, window, switch, and launcher losses, or inferred from calibrated radio-frequency power monitors near the launcher. It is commonly used as the input power for ray-tracing or beam-tracing models; subsequent absorbed, reflected, or shine-through power is accounted for separately.

Typical values for a single electron cyclotron launcher are of order $1 \times 10^5$ to $2 \times 10^6$ W in present tokamak systems, with multi-beam or high-power launchers reaching several $10^6$ W.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron cyclotron wave power flows from the launcher into the vacuum vessel.

NAMES.name: length_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Base length of the oblique trapezoidal cross-section used to represent an ICRH antenna strap conductor. It is a reference edge dimension of the conductor section, not the slant height of an inclined side.
NAMES.long:
Length of antenna strap is the reference base dimension of an oblique trapezoidal cross-section used to describe an ion-cyclotron-range-of-frequencies antenna strap conductor. It identifies the straight base edge of the section and should not be interpreted as the sloping side length, slant height, or inclined-face chord.

For an oblique strap section, this length is only one geometric parameter. The full non-rectangular outline also depends on the [width](name:width_of_antenna_strap), [thickness](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap), and inclination angles such as $\alpha$ in [alpha_angle_of_antenna_strap](name:alpha_angle_of_antenna_strap) and $\beta$ in angle_of_antenna_strap. No universal $1/\cos\alpha$ or similar conversion is implied unless the angle reference directions and the selected base edge are specified by the geometric construction.

In practice the value is taken from antenna engineering drawings, CAD geometry, or metrology of the strap conductor as the distance between the endpoints of the chosen base edge of the physical cross-section. It is used with the other strap dimensions and angles in electromagnetic, thermal, and structural models of ICRH antenna conductors.

Typical values are device- and design-dependent, but base lengths for conducting ICRH strap cross-sections commonly lie in the range 0.02-0.5 m, with larger values for high-power antenna straps and smaller values for compact test structures.

NAMES.name: length_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Curvilinear arc length measured along a beam-tracing ray or beam trajectory, used to parameterize propagation from a chosen reference point through vacuum and plasma regions.
NAMES.long:
Length of a beam-tracing beam is the accumulated geometric distance along the modeled ray or beam centerline from a chosen reference point, usually the launch point. It is an arc-length coordinate on the propagation trajectory and is independent of the particular parameter used to integrate the ray equations.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters, the arc length to a point $P$ on the trajectory $\Gamma$ is

$$
\ell(P) = \int_{\Gamma_0}^{P} d\ell' = \int_{\Gamma_0}^{P} \sqrt{dR^2 + R^2 d\phi^2 + dZ^2}
$$

where $\Gamma_0$ is the reference point on the ray, $d\ell'$ is an infinitesimal path length in meters, and the differentials are taken along the same trajectory.

In beam-tracing calculations, this coordinate is computed by integrating the ray path determined by the local dispersion relation and the wave vector $\mathbf{k}$; $\mathbf{k}$ has units of radians per meter, while the angular frequency $\omega$ has units of radians per second. The length coordinate provides the independent distance variable for quantities such as wave-vector components, absorption, and power evolution along the beam.

The physically allowed range is $\ell \ge 0\,\mathrm{m}$, with $\ell = 0\,\mathrm{m}$ at the chosen reference point. There is no device-independent upper bound or universal typical range: the final value is set by the selected trajectory endpoint and may include launch, vacuum, edge, core-plasma, reflection, or cutoff portions of the path.

NAMES.name: maximum_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
NAMES.short: Upper mechanical travel limit for the signed rotation angle of an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror about its movement axis.
NAMES.long:
The maximum angle of an electron-cyclotron launcher mirror is the upper endpoint of the allowed signed rotation interval for the mirror steering actuator. It is referenced to the launcher mirror reference orientation and, together with [minimum_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:minimum_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), bounds the permitted values of the instantaneous [angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror). This is a hardware constraint rather than a plasma quantity.

The admissible mirror rotation is constrained by

$$
\alpha_{\min} \leq \alpha \leq \alpha_{\max}
$$

where $\alpha_{\max}$ is this maximum angle in rad, $\alpha_{\min}$ is the corresponding lower mechanical limit in rad, and $\alpha$ is the instantaneous mirror rotation angle in rad.

The value is established from the launcher mechanical design, actuator travel, clearances, and commissioning calibration. During operation it is used by steering control and protection logic to reject commanded or measured mirror angles outside the allowed interval. The mirror angle affects the launch direction of the electron-cyclotron beam, but the mapping from mirror rotation to beam direction is specific to the launcher optics.

Typical limits are device-specific. For many steerable electron-cyclotron mirrors the allowed excursion is of order 0.1-1 rad from the reference orientation, while narrower or broader ranges can occur depending on actuator geometry and mechanical stops; the signed upper limit must satisfy $\alpha_{\max} \geq \alpha_{\min}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the mirror rotation is counter-clockwise about the movement axis as seen by an observer for whom the positive mirror movement-direction vector points toward the observer.

NAMES.name: neutral_beam_energy
NAMES.subject: neutral_beam
NAMES.short: Kinetic energy per atom of the full-energy injected neutral beam component, inherited from the ion-source acceleration voltage before neutralization. It is not an abundance-weighted average over half- or third-energy molecular-dissociation components.
NAMES.long:
Neutral beam energy is the kinetic energy carried by one atom in the full-energy component of an injected neutral beam. The atom is neutral at injection, but its kinetic energy is set while its charged precursor is accelerated before neutralization. This quantity denotes the full-energy atom value used as the characteristic fast-particle birth energy.

For neutrals produced from an atomic precursor ion, the full-energy value is related to the acceleration voltage by

$$
E_\mathrm{NBI} = \frac{q_\mathrm{acc} V_\mathrm{acc}}{e}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{NBI}$ is expressed in eV, $q_\mathrm{acc}$ is the charge of the precursor ion during acceleration, $V_\mathrm{acc}$ is the acceleration voltage, and $e$ is the elementary charge. The injected neutral atom has zero net charge after neutralization; $q_\mathrm{acc}$ refers only to the charged acceleration stage. For a singly charged atomic precursor, the numerical value of $E_\mathrm{NBI}$ in eV equals $V_\mathrm{acc}$ in volts.

In practice, this energy is set from the accelerator voltage and the selected beam species, and may be checked using beamline spectroscopy, calorimetry, or source voltage and current measurements. If molecular ions are accelerated and then dissociate, their atoms appear as lower-energy spectral components, typically near $E_\mathrm{NBI}/2$ or $E_\mathrm{NBI}/3$ for diatomic or triatomic singly charged precursors. Those components and their fractions describe beam composition; this scalar remains the full-energy atom value, not a mean over all neutral particles.

Typical full-energy values are $2\times10^4$-$1.2\times10^5$ eV for many positive-ion hydrogen or deuterium heating beams, $1\times10^5$-$2\times10^5$ eV for higher-energy systems, and up to about $1\times10^6$ eV for large negative-ion neutral beam systems.

NAMES.name: ordinary_mode_fraction_of_wave_beam
NAMES.short: Dimensionless fraction of launched electron-cyclotron wave-beam power carried by ordinary-mode polarization.
NAMES.long:
The ordinary-mode fraction of a wave beam is the fraction of launched electron-cyclotron power carried by the ordinary cold-plasma eigenpolarization. For propagation perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field, the ordinary mode has its electric field polarized parallel to the magnetic field, while the extraordinary mode has the complementary perpendicular polarization.

The fraction is defined from the launched modal powers:

$$
f_O = \frac{P_O}{P_O + P_X}
$$

where $P_O$ is the launched ordinary-mode power in W and $P_X$ is the launched extraordinary-mode power in W. The denominator is the total launched power in W represented by these two polarization components.

In practice, $f_O$ is computed from the complex wave electric field by projecting the launch polarization onto the ordinary and extraordinary eigenmodes, or inferred from calibrated launcher and polarizer settings. It characterizes the launched polarization state only; absorption and resonance behavior depend additionally on wave frequency, plasma parameters, propagation path, and electron cyclotron harmonic conditions.

Allowed values range from 0 to 1. A value of 0 represents purely extraordinary-mode launch, 1 represents purely ordinary-mode launch, and intermediate values represent mixed launch polarization, with 0.5 corresponding to equal ordinary- and extraordinary-mode launched powers.

NAMES.name: parallel_per_toroidal_mode_current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged parallel current density from wave-driven current drive, resolved per toroidal Fourier mode number, giving the field-aligned driven-current contribution of each harmonic as a radial profile.
NAMES.long:
The flux-surface-averaged parallel (field-aligned) current density attributable to wave-driven current drive for a single toroidal Fourier mode $n_\phi$ describes how each harmonic of the RF wave field contributes to non-inductive current generation as a function of plasma radius. Systems such as electron cyclotron (EC), lower hybrid (LH), and ion cyclotron (IC) heating drive parallel currents by transferring directed momentum to resonant particles; resolving the driven current density by toroidal mode number reveals the modal structure of the deposition profile.

The quantity is the flux-surface average of the mode-resolved parallel current density:

$$
\langle J_\parallel^{(n_\phi)} \rangle = \frac{\langle \mathbf{J}^{(n_\phi)} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle}{\langle B \rangle}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}^{(n_\phi)}$ is the current density from the $n_\phi$-th toroidal mode, $\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic field, and $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes the flux-surface average.

This quantity is computed by ray-tracing, beam-tracing, or full-wave codes that model RF wave propagation and absorption on a flux-surface-resolved radial grid. Integrating over the enclosed plasma cross-section recovers the per-mode driven current [per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive](name:per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive), while summing all modes and integrating radially yields the total [current due to wave-driven current drive](name:current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive). Peak values in tokamak RF scenarios range from $10^4$ to $10^6$ A m$^{-2}$ depending on absorbed power, plasma density, and wave geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave-driven parallel current flows in the same direction as the equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_per_toroidal_mode_electric_field
NAMES.short: Component of a coherent electromagnetic wave's electric field projected along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction and resolved for a single toroidal Fourier mode. It is a mode-resolved electric-field phasor measured in volts per meter; its magnitude gives the field strength and its argument carries the radio-frequency phase. The parallel field drives wave-particle resonances such as Landau damping and transit-time pumping.
NAMES.long:
Parallel per toroidal mode electric field is the component of a coherent electromagnetic-wave electric field directed along the local equilibrium magnetic field, associated with one integer toroidal Fourier mode. It is an electric-field phasor whose unit is volts per meter (equivalently $m^{-1}\cdot V$): its modulus gives the local field strength and its argument gives the radio-frequency phase relative to a stated source and time reference. It is not a dimensionless phase.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius in meters measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in radians increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical height in meters, the instantaneous physical parallel field is reconstructed from the toroidal-mode phasors as:

$$
E_\parallel(R,\phi,Z,t) = \Re\!\left[\sum_n E_{\parallel n}(R,Z)\,\exp\!\left(i(n\phi-\omega t)\right)\right]
$$

where $E_{\parallel n}=\mathbf{E}_n\cdot\hat{b}$ is the complex coefficient for mode $n$, $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the equilibrium magnetic field, $n$ is the integer toroidal mode number, $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency in radians per second, and $t$ is time in seconds. A phase derived from the phasor is $\arg(E_{\parallel n})$ on a branch such as $(-\pi,\pi]$ radians; changing the reference adds a constant phase without altering the field component itself.

The quantity is obtained by decomposing a coherent wave field into toroidal Fourier harmonics and projecting each harmonic onto $\hat{b}$. It is local in the poloidal plane, and the projection along $\hat{b}$ ties its magnitude to the wave-particle interactions that underlie radio-frequency heating and current drive. The associated mode-resolved wave-driven current is described by parallel_per_toroidal_mode_wave_driven_current_density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the real instantaneous electric-field component points in the local magnetic-field direction $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive
NAMES.short: Cumulative toroidal plasma current driven by wave-particle interactions and attributed to a single toroidal Fourier mode. It is enclosed by the flux surface labeled by normalized toroidal flux radius; at the outer closed surface it is that mode contribution to the total wave-driven current.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode current due to wave-driven current drive is the cumulative toroidal plasma current enclosed by a magnetic flux surface and assigned to one toroidal Fourier harmonic of the wave field. The enclosing surface is labeled by the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}, \theta, \phi)$, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with $R$ major radius and $Z$ vertical height. Summing all mode contributions gives the mode-integrated [current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive](name:toroidal_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive) or [toroidal_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive](name:toroidal_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive); evaluated at the outer closed flux surface it gives that harmonic contribution to [toroidal_wave_driven_current](name:toroidal_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive).

The toroidal mode label $n$ follows the wave-field Fourier convention in which the complex amplitude of that harmonic has toroidal phase factor $\exp(i n\phi)$. The enclosed current assigned to that harmonic can be defined from the mode-resolved driven current density by

$$
I_{\mathrm{wd},n}(\rho) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{V(\rho)} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{wd},n}\cdot\nabla\phi\,dV
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{wd},n}$ is in A, $\rho=\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, $V(\rho)$ is the volume inside the flux surface, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{wd},n}$ is the wave-driven current-density contribution in A m$^{-2}$ assigned to mode $n$, $\nabla\phi$ is in m$^{-1}$, and $dV$ is in m$^3$. In an axisymmetric representation this is equivalent to integrating the toroidal component $j_{\phi,\mathrm{wd},n}$ over the poloidal cross-section inside the same flux surface, and the mode-integrated current satisfies $I_\mathrm{wd}(\rho)=\sum_n I_{\mathrm{wd},n}(\rho)$.

Computation normally starts from a wave absorption and wave-particle interaction model that resolves the toroidal Fourier spectrum, then projects or accumulates the driven-current contribution of each harmonic into the enclosed toroidal current. When using parallel_per_toroidal_mode_wave_driven_current_density, note that the related density is a flux-surface-averaged parallel current density; conversion to this current requires the equilibrium magnetic-field pitch and projection from the parallel direction to the toroidal direction before radial accumulation. The per-mode current is generally inferred from modeling constrained by magnetic, kinetic, and RF diagnostics rather than measured directly as an isolated harmonic current.

Typical values are scenario dependent and are best interpreted relative to the mode-integrated wave-driven current at the same radius. Weak or nonresonant harmonics may contribute near 0 A, while a dominant harmonic can be a substantial fraction of the total wave-driven current, with the absolute scale set by the applied wave power, absorption, and current-drive efficiency.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave-driven toroidal current contribution flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_wave_vector_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: The perpendicular wave vector of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the non-negative magnitude of the launched RF wave-vector component perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field. It sets the transverse spatial oscillation scale of the wave in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular wave vector $k_\perp$ is the magnitude of the component of the RF wave vector normal to the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. The perpendicular direction is defined geometrically with respect to the local field unit vector, not as a fixed radial or flux-surface-normal direction. Because this quantity is a magnitude, it is non-negative and has unit $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$.

The defining projection is

$$
k_\perp = \left|\mathbf{k} - (\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right| = \sqrt{|\mathbf{k}|^2 - k_\parallel^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the RF wave vector in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$, and $k_\parallel=\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the parallel wave number in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$.

In practice, $k_\perp$ is obtained from full-wave modeling, ray tracing, or local dispersion analysis of the launched ion-cyclotron-range fast wave. The [antenna frequency](name:frequency_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) sets $\omega=2\pi f$, while strap phasing, represented by quantities such as [wave phase of antenna strap](name:wave_phase_of_antenna_strap), helps determine the launched $k_\parallel$ spectrum. In cold-plasma estimates, the dielectric response depends on species densities, charges, masses, cyclotron frequencies set by the local magnetic-field magnitude, and the RF frequency. If a local dispersion calculation gives negative or complex $k_\perp^2$, the imaginary part represents evanescence or damping rather than a signed perpendicular wave number; a scalar $k_\perp$ refers to the real, non-negative transverse oscillation rate of the propagating branch or to a representative value from the propagating part of the wave field.

Representative ion-cyclotron fast-wave values are commonly of order 10-500 $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, corresponding to perpendicular wavelengths from centimeters to tens of centimeters through $\lambda_\perp=2\pi/k_\perp$. The value depends strongly on plasma composition, density, magnetic field, frequency, and launched parallel wave-number spectrum.

NAMES.name: plasma_absorbed_power_due_to_fusion
NAMES.short: Power deposited in the plasma by charged fusion reaction products as they slow down and thermalize, summed over all active fusion channels.
NAMES.long:
Plasma absorbed power due to fusion is the rate at which energy released by thermonuclear reactions is deposited in the plasma by charged reaction products as they slow down and thermalize. It is an internal self-heating term and excludes fusion energy carried away by products that do not transfer their kinetic energy to the plasma, such as escaping neutrons.

The volume-integrated absorbed fusion power is

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs,fus}} = \int_V q_{\mathrm{fus,ch}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{fus,ch}}$ is the local heating power density from charged fusion products after prompt loss or incomplete deposition is accounted for, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $V$ is the plasma volume. The local term is the sum over all active fusion reaction channels and their charged products; neutron-carried power is a complementary energy channel related to [total_neutron_power](name:total_neutron_power).

In practice this quantity is computed from reaction-rate densities determined by fuel composition, ion temperature, density, and fast-particle distributions, combined with charged-product slowing-down and loss models. It may also be constrained by fusion-product or neutron measurements; converting a reaction rate to absorbed plasma power requires the active reaction channel and the fraction of charged-product energy that thermalizes within the plasma. Applicable channels can include deuterium-tritium, deuterium-deuterium, deuterium-helium-3, tritium-tritium, or other thermonuclear reactions present in the fuel mixture.

Representative values span 0 W in plasmas without appreciable fusion yield, about $10^0$-$10^3$ W in trace-yield conditions, $10^3$-$10^6$ W in high-performance fusion-producing experiments, and $10^6$-$10^8$ W in burning-plasma regimes. The value scales strongly with density, reacting volume, fuel mixture, charged-product confinement, and the temperature dependence of the fusion reactivity.

NAMES.name: poloidal_launched_wave_index_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Poloidal launched wave index of a lower hybrid antenna is the signed dimensionless projection of the launched wave refractive-index vector onto the direction of increasing geometric poloidal angle theta about the antenna reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It equals the poloidal wavenumber divided by the free-space wavenumber and characterizes launch spectral tilt relevant to ray trajectories, current-drive location, and power deposition.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal launched wave index $n_\mathrm{pol}$ is the poloidal component of the lower-hybrid launched refractive-index vector. The geometry is described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. In a fixed-$\phi$ poloidal plane, the geometric poloidal angle $\theta$ is measured about the antenna reference point; increasing $\theta$ follows the local tangent direction $\hat{e}_\theta$ in that plane.

The index is defined by normalizing the poloidal wavenumber component to the free-space wavenumber:

$$
n_\mathrm{pol} = \frac{k_\theta}{k_0} = \frac{c\,k_\theta}{\omega}
$$

where $k_\theta = \mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{e}_\theta$ is the poloidal wavenumber component in m^-1, $k_0=\omega/c$ is the free-space wavenumber in m^-1, $\omega$ is the angular wave frequency in rad s^-1, and $c$ is the speed of light in m s^-1. Together with the [toroidal launched wave index](name:toroidal_launched_wave_index_of_lower_hybrid_antenna), this quantity specifies the directional content of the launched lower-hybrid spectrum.

In practice, $n_\mathrm{pol}$ is specified or computed from the poloidal phasing, waveguide layout, and electromagnetic coupling model of the launcher. It affects how the launched spectrum maps onto the magnetic-field direction and therefore can influence ray trajectories, accessibility, damping location, and driven-current localization.

Typical central values are often near zero, with representative launcher specifications of order $|n_\mathrm{pol}| \lesssim 1$; deliberately tilted or broad spectra can contain components of order a few. These values are dimensionless and should be interpreted as launcher- and spectrum-dependent rather than as universal bounds.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal wavenumber component points in the direction of increasing geometric poloidal angle $\theta$ in the fixed-$\phi$ poloidal plane.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_beam_tracing_point
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at a point on a beam-tracing ray or beam path. It is a dimensional flux-surface label in Wb, distinct from dimensionless normalized poloidal-flux coordinates derived from axis and boundary flux differences.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at a beam-tracing point is the dimensional poloidal magnetic flux value evaluated at the spatial position of a point on a propagated ray or beam path. It labels the magnetic flux surface intersected by that point when an axisymmetric equilibrium description is applicable, but it remains a flux in Wb rather than a normalized radial coordinate.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height, the poloidal magnetic flux can be defined by the vertical magnetic field through a horizontal disk:

$$
\psi(R,Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi$ is in Wb, $R$ and $R'$ are in m, $Z$ is in m, and $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component in T. This disk-integral form fixes the additive reference by taking zero flux at $R=0$ for the disk at height $Z$; if another common additive offset is used for an equilibrium, physical flux differences are unchanged.

In beam-tracing calculations, this quantity is obtained by interpolating the reconstructed or modeled equilibrium flux function to each ray or beam position. It is commonly used to relate wave propagation, absorption, and resonance locations to magnetic surfaces. A corresponding normalized poloidal flux coordinate is dimensionless, for example $\psi_N=(\psi-\psi_\mathrm{axis})/(\psi_\mathrm{boundary}-\psi_\mathrm{axis})$; the dimensional value here must not be confused with that normalized coordinate, and any common additive offset cancels in the normalization.

Typical axis-to-boundary poloidal-flux differences are about 0.1-20 Wb in medium-sized to large tokamaks. Values encountered along a beam path depend on where the trajectory crosses the plasma and on the chosen additive reference for the dimensional flux.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ on the integration disk points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Cumulative power of a given physical channel within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface, obtained by integrating the relevant volumetric power density from the magnetic axis to that surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the radially cumulative power of a physical channel enclosed within the plasma volume bounded by a given magnetic flux surface. It provides the flux-surface-resolved power-balance profile used in transport analyzes, expressing how heating or loss power accumulates from the magnetic axis outward to a specified radial location.

The defining relation integrates the volumetric power density $p_\mathrm{vol}$ of the relevant channel over the enclosed plasma volume:

$$
P(\psi) = \int_{V(\psi)} p_\mathrm{vol} \, dV
$$

where $V(\psi)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the flux surface labeled by the poloidal flux coordinate $\psi$, and the integration runs from the magnetic axis outward.

In practice, $P(\psi)$ is computed by integrating channel-specific deposition profiles derived from wave propagation calculations, beam-particle tracing, or spectroscopic radiation measurements. Species-resolved specializations include [electron power](name:electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface) for net power transferred to the electron population and [ion power](name:ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface) for the ion population; [absorbed wave power] gives the total absorbed auxiliary-heating power, and [radiated power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power) tracks cumulative radiation losses. When the reference surface coincides with the last closed flux surface, the cumulative value equals the corresponding total volume-integrated power expressed by [total plasma deposited power].
NAMES.sign: Positive when the channel transfers net power to the plasma enclosed by the flux surface.

NAMES.name: electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Cumulative net power transferred to electrons within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface. It sums power delivered to fast suprathermal electrons and to the bulk thermal electron population.
NAMES.long:
Electron power at inside flux surface is the cumulative net rate of energy transfer to all electron populations within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface. It is an enclosed-volume quantity: each surface includes all electron power deposition inside it, and the sum of fast and thermal electron components gives the total electron-channel contribution.

The quantity is defined by integrating the flux-surface-averaged net electron power deposition density over enclosed volume, using the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux radius:

$$
P_e(\rho_s) = \int_0^{\rho_s} \left\langle q_e \right\rangle_{\rho} \frac{dV}{d\rho} \, d\rho
$$

where $P_e$ is the enclosed electron power in W, $\rho_s$ labels the bounding flux surface, $\left\langle q_e \right\rangle_{\rho}$ is the flux-surface-averaged net electron power deposition density in W m$^{-3}$, and $dV/d\rho$ is the differential enclosed volume in m$^3$ per unit $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. The derivative $dP_e/d\rho = \left\langle q_e \right\rangle_{\rho} dV/d\rho$ is a power per unit normalized flux radius, not a volumetric density by itself.

In practice, local electron energy-transfer rates are mapped to magnetic flux surfaces from wave absorption, fast-particle slowing down, collisional exchange, or power-balance calculations, then flux-surface averaged and integrated outward from the magnetic axis. The decomposition corresponds to [fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface) for suprathermal electrons plus [thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface) for the bulk thermal electron population; at the outer closed surface it can be compared with [total_electron_power](name:total_electron_deposited_power) when the same source set and plasma volume are used.

Typical enclosed electron powers are 10^4-10^6 W in small or low-power experiments, 10^5-10^7 W for individual electron-heating systems in medium-size tokamaks, and 10^7-10^8 W in high-power or reactor-scale scenarios. For purely deposited auxiliary power, the value generally rises from about 0 W near the magnetic axis to the electron-channel total at the outer closed surface; decreases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ or negative values indicate net electron cooling or transfer of energy from electrons to another channel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net power is transferred to the electron population.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by non-thermal fast electrons inside a specified magnetic flux surface, equal to the enclosed-volume integral of the local fast-electron power-deposition density.
NAMES.long:
Fast-electron power inside a flux surface is the cumulative rate at which coherent-wave energy is absorbed by non-thermal electrons in the plasma volume enclosed by a closed magnetic surface. It represents the fast-electron part of the auxiliary wave-power deposition, distinct from deposition on thermal electrons or ions. The surface label should be an explicitly named flux coordinate, for example $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$ or $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}},\theta,\phi)$, where $\theta$ is a poloidal angle and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with $R$ major radius and $Z$ vertical height.

For a selected flux surface labeled by $\chi_s$, the enclosed fast-electron power is the volume integral

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast}\,e}^{\mathrm{inside}}(\chi_s)=\int_{\Omega_s} p_{\mathrm{fast}\,e}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $\chi$ is the chosen flux-surface label, $\Omega_s$ is the plasma volume enclosed between the magnetic axis and the surface $\chi=\chi_s$, $p_{\mathrm{fast}\,e}$ is the local [fast_electron_power_density](name:fast_electron_power_density) in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, and the result is in W.

In practice this quantity is obtained by integrating a local fast-electron wave-power deposition density over reconstructed magnetic-flux-surface volumes. Together with [thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), it describes how absorbed wave power is partitioned within the electron population; at the outermost closed flux surface it corresponds to the global [fast_electron_power](name:fast_electron_power) for the same absorption definition. The analogous non-thermal ion quantity is [fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface), and all such channels contribute to the overall auxiliary-heating power balance represented by quantities such as [total_electron_power](name:total_electron_deposited_power).

Representative magnitudes range from near 0 W on surfaces enclosing little or no fast-electron absorption to the order of the coupled auxiliary-wave power. Depending on device size and heating scenario, enclosed fast-electron powers can span roughly 10^3-10^7 W, with megawatt-scale values possible when wave absorption is dominated by non-thermal electrons.

NAMES.name: ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by all ion populations — thermal and fast — within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The ion power at inside flux surface is the cumulative rate at which wave energy is deposited into the ion population — spanning both thermal bulk ions and fast (non-thermal) ions — within the plasma volume bounded by a closed magnetic flux surface. It is the ion-channel component of the more general [power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:power_at_inside_flux_surface), separating ion energy absorption from the corresponding electron heating contribution.

The quantity is the volume integral of the total ion wave-power density $p_i(\mathbf{r})$ over the plasma domain $V(\psi)$ enclosed by the flux surface labeled $\psi$:

$$
P_i(\psi) = \int_{V(\psi)} p_i(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $p_i$ is the ion volumetric heating power density in W m$^{-3}$ and $\psi$ is the chosen flux-surface label, such as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$.

The population-resolved breakdown is given by [thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface) for the bulk ion channel and [fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface) for non-thermal beam or fusion-born ions. This cumulative radial profile enables power-balance analysis and is inferred from combining absorbed-power density profiles computed via wave ray-tracing or Monte Carlo beam-deposition codes with equilibrium flux-surface geometry.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by the fast (non-thermal) ion population within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion power at inside flux surface quantifies the running volume integral of RF wave power deposited into the suprathermal (non-thermal) ion population, profiling the radial distribution of enclosed fast-ion wave absorption. It forms the fast-ion component of [ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface), which includes both this quantity and the complementary thermal-ion contribution captured by [thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

The enclosed fast-ion power is defined as:

$$
P_\mathrm{fast}(\psi) = \int_{V(\psi)} Q_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $Q_\mathrm{fast}$ is the volumetric fast-ion wave power deposition density and $V(\psi)$ is the plasma volume enclosed within the flux surface at poloidal flux coordinate $\psi$.

This quantity arises primarily in scenarios such as ion cyclotron resonance heating, where waves resonantly accelerate minority ions to suprathermal energies and sustain a non-Maxwellian tail population. The profile of $P_\mathrm{fast}(\psi)$ accumulates with increasing enclosed volume, saturating at the total fast-ion absorbed power at the last closed flux surface. For the charge-state-resolved counterpart, see [fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface); the local deposition density from which this integral is constructed is given by [fast_ion_power_density](name:fast_ion_power_density).

NAMES.name: ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by ions of a specified charge state within the plasma volume enclosed by a selected magnetic flux surface, spanning both fast-ion and thermal-ion contributions for that charge state.
NAMES.long:
Charge-state-resolved cumulative power delivered by RF or auxiliary waves to the ion component within the plasma volume enclosed by a closed magnetic flux surface. The enclosing surface is labeled by an explicitly chosen flux coordinate such as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, and the integral accumulates all wave power deposited to that ion charge state from the magnetic axis outward to that surface.

The cumulative profile is related to the local charge-state power density $p_\mathrm{ion,state}$ by:

$$
P_\mathrm{ion,state}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_\mathrm{ion,state}(R, Z)\, dV
$$

where $V(\rho)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the flux surface at label $\rho$, and $R$, $Z$ are coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
