This parent generalizes over two population-resolved children: [fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface) for non-thermal ions whose energy distribution departs from Maxwellian, and [thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface) for bulk Maxwellian ions. Summing over all charge states and populations recovers the species-integrated [total_ion_heating_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:total_ion_heating_power_at_inside_flux_surface). The quantity is evaluated from wave-absorption or power-deposition models that resolve plasma species and charge states.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by fast (non-thermal) ions of a specified charge state within the plasma volume enclosed by a selected magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Fast ion state power at an inside flux surface quantifies the net wave energy per unit time deposited in the suprathermal (fast) population of a single specified ion charge state, accumulated over all plasma volume enclosed by a chosen flux surface. It is the fast-ion component of the total ion-state absorbed power [ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface); its thermal-ion counterpart is [thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

The cumulative power is the volume integral of the local fast-ion absorption density $p_{\text{fast},s}$ over the plasma volume enclosed by the flux surface labeled $\rho$:

$$
P_{\text{fast},s}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_{\text{fast},s}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V(\rho)$ is the volume enclosed by the flux surface and $p_{\text{fast},s}$ is the local fast-ion absorbed power density for charge state $s$, the volumetric counterpart [fast_ion_state_power_density](name:fast_ion_state_power_density).

This quantity is computed by RF wave-kinetic or full-wave codes that resolve the resonant energy exchange between the wave field and the non-Maxwellian fast-ion distribution on a per-charge-state basis, as occurs in ICRH minority heating and mode-conversion schemes. Aggregating over all charge states and ion species yields [fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface). The toroidal-mode-resolved complement [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power) decomposes the same cumulative power by toroidal harmonic when the wave field is represented as a Fourier series in toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating
NAMES.short: Net RF wave energy absorbed per unit time by plasma electrons via electron cyclotron resonance from a single ECRH launcher. It is the coupled heating power, distinct from the RF power launched toward or into the vessel.
NAMES.long:
Power due to electron cyclotron heating is the net rate at which RF wave energy from a single electron-cyclotron launcher is absorbed by plasma electrons through cyclotron-resonant interaction. It represents coupled electron heating power, not the launcher output power or the power merely entering the vacuum vessel.

For a launcher-resolved absorbed power density, the total absorbed power is

$$
P_\mathrm{EC} = \int_{V_\mathrm{p}} p_{\mathrm{EC},e}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $P_\mathrm{EC}$ is the absorbed electron-cyclotron heating power in W, $p_{\mathrm{EC},e}$ is the volumetric RF power density deposited in electrons in W m^-3, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, and $V_\mathrm{p}$ is the plasma volume over which the launcher-specific deposition is evaluated.

In practice this quantity is inferred from calibrated launcher power, transmission-line losses, stray-radiation or unabsorbed-power estimates, ray or beam-tracing calculations, and power-balance constraints. It is therefore usually lower than or equal to the corresponding [launched_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher](name:launched_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher), with the difference accounting for propagation, coupling, reflection, shine-through, and other losses not deposited in the plasma electrons.

Typical absorbed powers for one launcher range from about 0.1-2 MW in many present-day experiments, while large multi-megawatt systems can deliver several MW per launcher depending on frequency, injection geometry, plasma density, magnetic field, and optical depth.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net RF wave energy is transferred from the electron-cyclotron wave field to plasma electrons.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_first_orbit_loss
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated non-negative power carried out of the confined fast-ion population by particles whose first guiding-center orbit after birth or acceleration is unconfined. It is reported as a positive loss magnitude and enters fast-ion energy balances with a minus sign.
NAMES.long:
First-orbit loss power is the global energy-removal rate associated with prompt escape of newly born or newly accelerated fast ions before they complete their first guiding-center orbit. A particle is counted only when its loss time after the source event is less than the time for its first complete orbit; particles that survive this cutoff and are lost later are not included. The quantity is a loss from the fast-ion population, not a spatially resolved heat-load distribution on plasma-facing components.

The non-negative loss magnitude can be written as an energy-weighted loss-event rate:

$$
P_{\rm fol} = \int_V \int_0^\infty E_{\rm esc}\, \dot{n}_{\rm fol}^{(1)}(\mathbf{r}, E_{\rm esc})\, dE_{\rm esc}\, dV
$$

where $P_{\rm fol}$ is the first-orbit loss power, $E_{\rm esc}$ is the particle kinetic energy at escape in joules, and $\dot{n}_{\rm fol}^{(1)}$ is the rate density of first-orbit loss events per source volume and per escape-energy interval, with units m^-3 J^-1 s^-1. The superscript $(1)$ denotes the first-orbit classification, $V$ is the source volume over which fast ions are created or accelerated, and using $E_{\rm esc}$ excludes energy already transferred to the background plasma before escape. In a fast-ion energy balance this loss enters as $-P_{\rm fol}$; if charge-exchange loss is treated as a disjoint channel, the combined contribution is $-(P_{\rm fol}+P_{\rm CX})$, where $P_{\rm CX}$ is represented by [fast_ion_power_due_to_charge_exchange](name:fast_ion_power_due_to_charge_exchange).

It is usually computed from orbit-following or Monte Carlo fast-ion transport calculations. Markers are launched from a birth or acceleration distribution, advanced in the magnetic and electric fields, classified by whether they intersect a loss boundary before the first-orbit cutoff, and weighted by their escape energy and source rate. Prompt-loss probes, fast-ion loss detectors, and wall heat-load measurements can constrain the calculation, but the global value is generally inferred from modeling rather than measured directly.

Typical values are 0 W when all prompt orbits are confined. For fast-ion source powers of 10^6-10^7 W, representative modeled losses are often 10^3-10^5 W for well-confined core sources and 10^5-10^6 W when percent-level first-orbit loss fractions occur near the edge or for large orbit widths. The value scales with source power and with the loss fraction set by birth position, pitch angle, particle energy, plasma shape, and the distance between the initial orbit and the material boundary.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating
NAMES.short: Net ion cyclotron resonance heating power absorbed by the plasma from one ICRH launcher. It is the RF wave energy deposition rate in the plasma and is distinct from power launched by the antenna or lost in the RF system.
NAMES.long:
Power due to ion cyclotron heating is the net rate at which radio-frequency wave energy from one ion cyclotron resonance heating launcher is absorbed by the plasma. It includes energy deposited into the plasma bulk through ion-cyclotron, harmonic, electron, and mode-conversion channels, and excludes reflected power and losses in transmission lines, antenna structures, or surrounding material. As a scalar absorbed power, it is not affected by magnetic-field or plasma-current sign conventions.

The launcher-resolved absorbed power is the time rate of absorbed RF energy, equivalently the volume integral of the local RF absorption rate:

$$
P_{\mathrm{ICRH},a} = \frac{dE_{\mathrm{abs},a}}{dt} = \int_{V_p} p_{\mathrm{abs},a}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $a$ labels the launcher, $E_{\mathrm{abs},a}$ is the RF energy absorbed in the plasma from that launcher, $p_{\mathrm{abs},a}$ is the local absorbed power density, and $V_p$ is the plasma volume.

In practice this quantity is obtained from calibrated RF forward and reflected power measurements corrected for transmission and antenna losses, from wave-coupling and absorption calculations, or from plasma power-balance analysis. It differs from the launched antenna power because only the net energy absorbed by the plasma is counted. Summing this quantity over all ICRH launchers gives [total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating); spatially resolved absorption rates integrate to this launcher-resolved scalar value, and time-resolved values follow changes in RF drive, antenna loading, and plasma conditions.

Typical values are $10^5$-$10^7$ W per launcher in present-day tokamak discharges, with high-power systems reaching several $10^7$ W. Values near 0 W occur when the launcher is off, poorly coupled, or when most injected RF power is reflected or lost before absorption.

NAMES.name: power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Electromagnetic wave power associated with a single beam-tracing beam, encompassing both the initial launch power and the net power absorbed by the plasma along the beam trajectory.
NAMES.long:
The electromagnetic power associated with a single coherent-wave beam propagated through the plasma by beam-tracing methods. This quantity spans the full lifecycle of wave energy in a beam: from the power assigned at the launch point to the net power deposited in the plasma species along the propagation path.

The local power flux decreases along the beam arc length $s$ according to

$$
\frac{dP}{ds} = -\alpha(\mathbf{r})\, P(s)
$$

where $\alpha(\mathbf{r})$ is the local wave power absorption coefficient at position $\mathbf{r}$ and $P(s)$ is the beam power at arc length $s$ from the launch point. The value at $s = 0$ corresponds to [initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam), which sets the normalization reference for absorption calculations along the trajectory. The cumulative attenuation integrated over the full path yields [absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam), equal to the initial power minus the residual wave power at the end of the beam.

Beam-tracing calculations for RF heating systems evaluate both the initial power setting and the cumulative deposited power to determine single-pass absorption efficiency and spatial deposition profiles. The beam arc length parameterizing propagation is tracked separately via [length_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:length_of_beam_tracing_beam).

Initial beam powers range from tens of kilowatts to several megawatts per beam depending on the RF system type and number of beams modeled; absorbed fractions approach unity in strongly absorbing core plasmas.

NAMES.name: absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Net coherent-wave power absorbed by the plasma from one beam-tracing beam over its computed trajectory. It is the final path-integrated, species-summed deposited power, equal to the beam power entering the path minus the residual wave power at the end.
NAMES.long:
Absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam is the net coherent-wave power transferred from one traced beam to the plasma over its computed propagation path. It is the final path-integrated total for that single beam, summed over all absorbing species, and is distinct from scenario-level [absorbed power] obtained by summing over beams or launchers.

For a ray arc length $s$ increasing along the direction of wave propagation, the endpoint absorbed power is

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs}} = P_0 - P_{\mathrm{end}} = P_0\left[1 - \exp\left(-2\int_{s_0}^{s_{\mathrm{end}}} \kappa_i^{\mathrm{tot}}(s)\,ds\right)\right]
$$

where $P_0$ is the [launched power] or entering beam power in W, $P_{\mathrm{end}}$ is the residual [power of the beam-tracing beam](name:power_of_beam_tracing_beam) at the end of the path in W, $s_0$ and $s_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the start and end arc-length positions in m, and $\kappa_i^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the species-summed spatial amplitude-damping coefficient along the ray in m^-1. The factor of 2 appears because wave power is proportional to squared wave-field amplitude; positive damping therefore makes the remaining beam power decrease along increasing $s$.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating local absorption along the beam-tracing trajectory using the plasma dielectric response and the wave dispersion relation. Species-resolved channels such as [electron absorbed power](name:electron_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam), [ion absorbed power], and [ion-state absorbed power](name:ion_state_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) may be evaluated separately and summed to recover the total for the beam.

Typical values are bounded by 0 W and the power assigned to the traced beam. They can be near 0 W for weak damping or missed resonance, and can approach the assigned launched or entering power for strongly absorbed paths; in weighted beam-tracing calculations this can span roughly 10^0-10^6 W per traced beam depending on launcher power and beam subdivision.

NAMES.name: ion_state_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by ions of a specified species and charge state along a coherent-wave beam-tracing beam path. It is the charge-state-resolved contribution to the total ion power absorbed from that beam.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam is the net power transferred from a coherent wave beam to ions of one specified species and ionization (charge) state along the traced beam path. It is the charge-state-resolved share of the ion power absorbed from that beam, and summing it over all charge states of a species recovers the species-level ion absorption.

The absorbed power is the integral of the local absorption rate per unit path length over the beam representation:

$$
P_{i,z} = \int_{\mathcal{C}} \frac{dP_{i,z}}{d\ell} \, d\ell
$$

where $\mathcal{C}$ is the traced beam path, $\ell$ is distance along that path in meters, and $dP_{i,z}/d\ell$ is the local net power transferred to ion species $i$ in charge state $z$ per unit path length, expressed in W/m. The integral runs along the beam path used to represent the propagating field, not over the full plasma volume; the corresponding volumetric deposition rates per unit plasma volume are tracked separately.

The quantity is evaluated by beam-tracing models, which extend geometrical optics to include finite beam-width effects by following a Gaussian wave packet through an inhomogeneous plasma. The local transfer follows from the wave field, plasma equilibrium, species composition, charge-state populations, and ion distribution functions, and may arise from any modeled wave-particle damping mechanism rather than only ion-cyclotron resonance. The species and charge state are fixed by the associated ion-state identifier.

Typical per-beam ion-state absorbed power spans a broad range, from near zero on weakly damped paths or for trace charge states up to of order the total coupled beam power for strongly resonant states; the value is bounded above by the available beam power in a passively absorbing plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net wave energy is transferred from the beam to the specified ion charge state.

NAMES.name: power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Net RF power launched from a single ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) antenna into the vacuum vessel, equal to forward power minus reflected power at the antenna reference plane.
NAMES.long:
The power of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the net RF power delivered across the antenna aperture into the vacuum vessel, representing the difference between the forward (incident) and reflected traveling-wave powers at a defined reference plane on the transmission line. It quantifies how effectively the antenna couples RF energy from the generator circuit into the plasma-facing side of the antenna structure.

The net launched power is related to its directional components by:

$$
P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the [forward power](name:forward_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) carried by the incident traveling wave and $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the [reflected power](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) carried by the backward wave, both evaluated at the same reference plane on the feed line.

This quantity is measured using directional couplers installed on the coaxial or waveguide transmission lines feeding each ICRH antenna port. Coupling efficiency depends on plasma edge density, antenna-to-separatrix distance, and operating frequency relative to the local ion cyclotron resonance layer.

Individual ICRH antennas on medium-to-large tokamaks typically launch 1–5 MW; the system-level sum over all antennas is [total_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:total_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna). The analogous per-injector quantity for neutral beam heating is power_of_neutral_beam_injector, and the corresponding ECRH quantity is [launched_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher](name:launched_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher).

NAMES.name: forward_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: The incident RF power traveling from the generator toward the ion cyclotron heating antenna along the transmission line, before any reflection occurs at the antenna-plasma interface.
NAMES.long:
Forward power is the incident traveling-wave RF power propagating from the RF generator toward the ion cyclotron heating antenna along the coaxial transmission line. It represents the total power available at the antenna reference plane before coupling to the plasma, and is the primary input quantity used to compute coupling efficiency together with the returning wave power.

The net power launched into the vacuum vessel is determined by subtracting the reflected wave power:

$$
P_\mathrm{net} = P_\mathrm{fwd} - P_\mathrm{ref}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{fwd}$ is this forward power, $P_\mathrm{ref}$ is the [reflected power of the antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), and $P_\mathrm{net}$ corresponds to the [net launched power](name:power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna). The antenna coupling efficiency is $\eta = (P_\mathrm{fwd} - P_\mathrm{ref}) / P_\mathrm{fwd} = 1 - |\Gamma|^2$, where $\Gamma$ is the voltage reflection coefficient at the antenna aperture.

Forward power is measured using calibrated directional couplers installed on the coaxial transmission line between the RF generator and the antenna strap feed, providing real-time monitoring for power control and antenna protection against excessive reflected power.

Typical forward power levels per ICRH antenna range from 1 to above 10 MW on large tokamaks, with coupling efficiencies between 70% and 95% depending on plasma edge density, strap phasing, and plasma-antenna gap.

NAMES.name: power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Generic RF power at a single lower-hybrid antenna, encompassing the forward, reflected, and launched power components that collectively characterize the wave-power budget at the antenna interface.
NAMES.long:
RF power at a lower hybrid antenna encompasses the distinct power quantities that characterize the wave-power budget at the antenna interface, where RF energy carried by a transmission line is coupled into a phased waveguide array facing the plasma.

The three principal per-antenna power quantities are related by:

$$
P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the [forward power](name:forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) (incident RF power arriving at the antenna input reference plane), $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the [reflected power](name:reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) (the fraction returning toward the transmission line due to impedance mismatch between the waveguide array and the plasma load), and $P_\mathrm{launched}$ is the [launched power](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) (the net power entering the vacuum vessel). Directional couplers installed on the transmission line simultaneously measure both forward and reflected power, from which launched power is derived. System-level aggregates — [total_launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and [total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) — sum these per-antenna values over the full lower hybrid system and quantify, respectively, the total injected and deposited power.

NAMES.name: forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Incident RF power carried by the wave propagating toward a lower hybrid antenna at its input reference plane. It is a per-antenna quantity, not a sum over multiple antennas.
NAMES.long:
Forward power of a lower hybrid antenna is the nonnegative RF power carried by the incident traveling wave at the antenna input reference plane. It represents power propagating from the generator and transmission-line side toward the antenna structure; "forward" specifies this propagation direction rather than a signed power convention. The quantity applies to one antenna, so totals over several antennas are separate quantities.

The launched RF power is the part of the forward power that remains after subtracting the oppositely propagating reflected power:

$$
P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the forward power, $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the reflected power, and $P_\mathrm{launched}$ is the launched power for the same antenna and the same reference plane. If a complex voltage-wave reflection coefficient $\Gamma$ is used, $\Gamma$ is dimensionless and $|\Gamma|^2$ gives the reflected-to-forward power ratio under the corresponding calibration convention.

In practice, forward power is inferred from calibrated RF measurements that separate waves traveling toward and away from the antenna, commonly using directional RF measurements or equivalent network measurements near the antenna input. Corrections may account for transmission-line attenuation, calibration factors, and the chosen reference plane. Forward power can exceed launched power when antenna-plasma mismatch or loading changes produce reflected power.

Typical per-antenna values in lower-hybrid heating or current-drive operation are about $10^5$-$5 \times 10^6$ W, while commissioning, conditioning, or low-power phases can use $10^3$-$10^5$ W.

NAMES.name: launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Net RF power entering the vacuum vessel from a single lower-hybrid antenna, equal to forward power minus reflected power at the antenna aperture.
NAMES.long:
The launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna is the net radio-frequency power injected into the vacuum vessel from one lower-hybrid antenna assembly per unit time. It quantifies the RF energy flux actually available to couple to plasma waves, distinguishing it from the gross input to the antenna system and from the fraction ultimately absorbed by the plasma.

The net launched power is defined as:

$$
P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the [forward power](name:forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) at the antenna aperture and $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the [reflected power](name:reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) returning toward the transmission line. The coupling efficiency is $\eta = P_\mathrm{launched}/P_\mathrm{forward}$, which depends on the match between the antenna wave spectrum and the plasma density at the waveguide mouth.

This quantity is measured by directional couplers on the transmission line feeding each antenna and serves as the primary input to ray-tracing and full-wave calculations for lower hybrid current drive power deposition. Launched powers in current experiments range from tens of kilowatts to several megawatts per antenna.

The gross RF input to the antenna system before accounting for reflections is given by [power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna). The system-level aggregate over all launcher units is captured by [total_launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna), while the fraction deposited in the plasma is tracked by [total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna](name:total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna).

NAMES.name: power_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Non-negative kinetic power launched by a single neutral beam injector into the vacuum vessel, evaluated at the vessel interface before plasma absorption, shine-through, or orbit-loss corrections are applied.
NAMES.long:
Power of a neutral beam injector is the rate at which kinetic energy carried by neutral atoms from one injector is launched into the vacuum vessel. It is a non-negative scalar evaluated before the beam interacts with the plasma, so it excludes subsequent absorption, shine-through, charge-exchange orbit loss, and other plasma-loss corrections.

For an injector whose extracted ions give rise to full-, half-, and one-third-energy neutral components, a common source-current estimate is

$$
P_\mathrm{NBI} = I_\mathrm{ext} V_\mathrm{acc} \left(\eta_1 f_1 + \frac{\eta_2 f_2}{2} + \frac{\eta_3 f_3}{3}\right)
$$

where $P_\mathrm{NBI}$ is the launched neutral power, $I_\mathrm{ext}$ is the extracted ion current in amperes, $V_\mathrm{acc}$ is the acceleration voltage in volts, $f_1$, $f_2$, and $f_3$ are the extracted source current fractions that produce neutrals at $E_0$, $E_0/2$, and $E_0/3$, and $\eta_1$, $\eta_2$, and $\eta_3$ are the corresponding neutralization and beamline-transmission efficiencies. When the reported species fractions are already measured for neutrals delivered to the vessel interface, these efficiency factors are effectively included in those fractions.

In practice, the launched power is obtained from source current and voltage measurements, species-fraction diagnostics, neutralizer and duct transmission estimates, and calorimetry on beam dumps. It is the per-injector quantity whose sum over active injectors contributes to [total_power_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:total_power_of_neutral_beam_injector), and it differs from [absorbed_power_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:absorbed_power_of_neutral_beam_injector), which is evaluated after plasma absorption and loss processes are applied.

Typical launched powers for heating injectors are $1\times10^6$-$5\times10^6$ W per injector in many medium-sized devices and $1\times10^7$-$2\times10^7$ W for high-power systems. Diagnostic neutral beams or low-power commissioning operation may be much lower, about $10^3$-$10^5$ W.

NAMES.name: absorbed_power_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Power from a single neutral beam injector that is absorbed by the plasma. It is the injector launched power after subtracting beam power lost to shine-through and fast-ion first-orbit losses.
NAMES.long:
Absorbed power of a neutral beam injector is the rate at which energy launched by one injector is deposited in the plasma. It excludes the portions of the launched beam power that leave the plasma as neutral-beam shine-through or are lost promptly by fast ions before thermalizing.

A common power balance definition is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs}} = P_{\mathrm{launch}} - P_{\mathrm{shine}} - P_{\mathrm{first\ orbit}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{abs}}$, $P_{\mathrm{launch}}$, $P_{\mathrm{shine}}$, and $P_{\mathrm{first\ orbit}}$ are all powers in W. $P_{\mathrm{shine}}$ is the [power carried through the plasma by un-ionized beam particles](name:power_due_to_neutral_beam_shinethrough), not a particle fraction, and $P_{\mathrm{first\ orbit}}$ is the power carried by newly born fast ions that are lost before depositing their energy in the plasma.

In practice this quantity is estimated from neutral-beam source power, beamline transmission, neutralization efficiency, plasma density and geometry, stopping cross sections, and fast-ion orbit loss modeling. It represents the plasma-deposited part of the injector power budget and is used in heating, current-drive, and energy-confinement analyzes.

The value is non-negative and cannot exceed the launched power of the injector in a physically consistent power balance. Typical absorbed powers are about 0.1-10 MW per injector in many present tokamak experiments, and can reach several tens of MW per injector in large high-power systems, depending on beam energy, plasma density, geometry, and prompt-loss fraction.

NAMES.name: power_of_wave_beam
NAMES.short: Electromagnetic power carried by a single wave beam in an RF or microwave auxiliary heating and current-drive system, abstracting over all stages of the power-delivery chain from launcher to plasma.
NAMES.long:
The power of a wave beam is the total electromagnetic energy flux integrated over the beam cross-section at a defined point in the power-delivery chain of an RF or microwave heating system. It abstracts over the specific power-flow stage — launch, propagation through vacuum, wave–plasma interaction, and residual exit — with child quantities such as [launched_power_of_wave_beam](name:launched_power_of_wave_beam) identifying the particular stage.

The instantaneous beam power relates to the real part of the complex Poynting vector $\mathbf{S}$ integrated over a surface $A$ whose outward normal $\hat{n}$ is aligned with the local propagation direction:

$$
P_\text{beam} = \operatorname{Re} \int_A \mathbf{S} \cdot \hat{n} \, dA, \quad \mathbf{S} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H}^*
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the complex electric-field amplitude, $\mathbf{H}^*$ is the complex conjugate of the magnetic-field amplitude, and the factor $1/2$ applies to peak-amplitude complex phasors. As the beam propagates through plasma, $P_\text{beam}$ decreases along the ray path, with the difference appearing as deposited power; the path-integrated absorbed quantity is described by [absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam).

In practice, beam power is measured at the launcher output by directional couplers or RF calorimetric power meters, with the delivered fraction cross-checked against calorimetric vessel loading or neutron yield scaling. Summed over all actuating beams and heating systems, the aggregate contributes to total_plasma_power.

Typical values range from tens of kilowatts in low-power test-bed experiments to several megawatts per beam element in fusion-class heating systems, depending on actuator type and operational scenario.

NAMES.name: launched_power_of_wave_beam
NAMES.short: Net radio-frequency or microwave power carried by a single wave beam as it enters the vacuum vessel. It is the forward power after transmission losses minus reflected or returned power at the launch reference plane, representing power available for plasma heating or current drive.
NAMES.long:
Launched power of a wave beam is the net electromagnetic power carried by one RF or microwave beam through the launcher aperture into the vacuum vessel. It is evaluated after losses in the transmission and launcher system, but before subsequent propagation losses, wall interception, or plasma absorption inside the vessel.

For a beam crossing a launch surface, the beam-level definition is the net Poynting flux through that surface, equivalently the forward power minus reflected or returned power at the same reference plane:

$$
P_{\mathrm{launched}} = \int_A \langle \mathbf{S} \rangle \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dA = P_{\mathrm{forward}} - P_{\mathrm{reflected}}
$$

where $A$ is the launch aperture or beam reference surface, $\langle \mathbf{S} \rangle$ is the time-averaged electromagnetic Poynting vector, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ points from the launcher into the vessel, and the forward and reflected powers are evaluated for the same beam at that plane.

In practice this quantity is determined from calibrated directional couplers, diode detectors, calorimetry, or power-balance measurements in the transmission line and launcher. Corrections account for source-to-launcher attenuation, beam splitting, imperfect coupling, and reflected power. It is the beam-level analog of net launched RF power used for electron-cyclotron launchers and lower-hybrid antennas; totals are formed separately by summing comparable net launched powers over beams, launchers, or antenna elements.

Typical representative values for an active high-power RF or microwave heating beam are about $1 \times 10^5$-$2 \times 10^6$ W, while inactive or inhibited beams are 0 W. The exact value depends on the source power, transmission efficiency, launcher coupling, pulse timing, and protection limits.

NAMES.name: pressure_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Pressure of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the scalar normal load per unit area associated with antenna module media or interfaces. It denotes absolute thermodynamic pressure for gas or liquid in antenna volumes and nonnegative compressive contact pressure for solid hardware interfaces.
NAMES.long:
Pressure of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the scalar pressure characterizing normal compressive loading in or on an ion cyclotron heating antenna module. For a gas or liquid, it is the absolute thermodynamic pressure of the medium, with zero corresponding to perfect vacuum. For a solid interface, it is the nonnegative compressive contact pressure; tensile normal stress and shear stress are not included.

The shared mechanical interpretation is normal compressive force per unit area:

$$
p = \frac{F_c}{A}
$$

where $p$ is pressure in Pa, $F_c$ is the compressive normal force in N transmitted by the medium or contact, and $A$ is the averaging area in m^2. For a fluid at rest this scalar is the isotropic normal stress on a surface; for hardware contact it is the compressive part of the normal traction averaged over the actual or effective contact area.

Gas or liquid pressure is measured with pressure transducers connected to antenna volumes, feed lines, or cooling circuits; if an instrument reports gage pressure, the reference pressure is added to obtain absolute pressure. Contact pressure is measured by force or contact-pressure sensors, or inferred from known preload, electromagnetic load, and contact area in a mechanical model. The related [gas_pressure_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:gas_pressure_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) is restricted to the neutral-gas thermodynamic component and excludes liquid-coolant and mechanical or interface contact pressure.

Representative values are strongly medium dependent. Neutral-gas absolute pressures, liquid-circuit pressures, and local contact pressures can differ by many orders of magnitude, so no single numerical range is physically meaningful for the combined concept; comparisons should be made within the identified medium or interface and in Pa.

NAMES.name: gas_pressure_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Gas-phase absolute pressure associated with the neutral gas volume of an ion cyclotron heating antenna. It excludes mechanical contact or structural pressure and is nonnegative relative to perfect vacuum.
NAMES.long:
Gas pressure of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the thermodynamic pressure exerted by neutral gas in the antenna-associated vacuum volume. It is the gas component of antenna pressure and excludes mechanical contact pressure, structural stress, or electromagnetic force density. The quantity is an absolute pressure, with zero corresponding to perfect vacuum, not a gage pressure relative to atmospheric pressure.

For a dilute gas close to thermal equilibrium, it may be related to neutral species densities and gas temperatures by the ideal-gas approximation:

$$
p_\mathrm{gas} = \sum_s n_s k_B T_s
$$

where $p_\mathrm{gas}$ is the gas pressure in Pa, $n_s$ is the number density of neutral species $s$ in m^-3, $T_s$ is its gas temperature in K, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant in J K^-1. This relation assumes a dilute gas, known composition, and a representative gas temperature; nonuniform temperature, rarefaction near surfaces, and species-dependent gage sensitivity can make the inferred pressure differ from a simple density measure.

The quantity is normally obtained from absolute vacuum gages or pressure transducers coupled to the antenna region. Capacitance manometers measure absolute pressure directly over their range, while ionization or cold-cathode gages infer pressure from ionization current and require calibration for gas species. RF operation, outgassing, pumping conductance, and gas injection can produce local and transient pressure changes.

Representative values are strongly operating-regime dependent. High-vacuum background pressures near antenna structures are often about $10^{-7}$-$10^{-4}$ Pa; RF conditioning, outgassing, or deliberate gas dosing commonly produces $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}$ Pa, with short poor-vacuum or conditioning transients sometimes approaching $1$ Pa. The physically valid range is $p_\mathrm{gas} \ge 0$; negative values indicate gage offset, subtraction of a reference, or an unconverted gage-pressure convention rather than a physical gas pressure.

NAMES.name: radial_centroid_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the geometric center of an electron cyclotron launcher mirror, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial centroid of an electron cyclotron launcher mirror is the perpendicular distance $R$ of the mirror's geometric center from the machine toroidal symmetry axis, defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is the major radius in meters. Together with [vertical_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:vertical_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), it fully locates the mirror center in the meridional plane, establishing the geometric reference point from which EC beam injection angles and trajectories are computed.

The centroid position in the machine frame combines with the mirror rotation [angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and any mechanical offset_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror to define the complete launch geometry used in ray-tracing and beam-tracing models for electron cyclotron heating and current drive. The local boundary contour of the mirror surface is described separately in the mirror-fixed planar frame via [x1_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:x1_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and [x2_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:x2_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the mirror centroid lies at a finite major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis ($R > 0$), which holds for all physical in-vessel launcher positions.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna_row
NAMES.short: Radial coordinate of the geometric reference point of a lower hybrid antenna row in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. R is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis; this is not a local distance from the antenna mouth.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of a lower hybrid antenna row is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of the row's geometric reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is distance from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height. This coordinate locates the antenna row in the device geometry and is distinct from any local coordinate normal to the antenna mouth or from the electron density at the launching position.

If the same point is expressed in a right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame with $z=Z$ and origin on the machine symmetry axis, its major radius is

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the row reference point.

The coordinate is usually determined from mechanical design data, installation survey, metrology, or geometric reconstruction of the launcher position. The chosen row reference point should be a reproducible physical point, such as the center of the row aperture or another documented launcher reference point, so that radial and vertical row coordinates describe the same physical location.

Typical values are of order the device major radius: about 1-4 m in medium-size tokamaks and about 4-9 m in large tokamaks, with lower hybrid launchers commonly mounted near the low-field-side boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the declared reference position of a neutral beam injector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured as the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate $R$ of a neutral beam injector specifies the major radius of the declared reference position of the injector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$. Paired with [vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector), this coordinate fully locates the injector reference point in the poloidal cross-section and provides the geometric anchor for beam-path tracing and shine-through calculations.

The reference position corresponds to a nominated geometric point on the injector assembly — such as the ion-source face center or beam duct exit plane — with the precise convention established per facility. This coordinate is directly analogous to [radial_coordinate_of_aperture](name:radial_coordinate_of_aperture) for diagnostic apertures and enters the geometric model used to compute the [absorbed_power_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:absorbed_power_of_neutral_beam_injector) deposition profile.

Typical values range from roughly 1 m in compact devices to over 10 m in large-scale tokamaks, with injector ports most commonly located on the outboard midplane where $R$ substantially exceeds the magnetic axis major radius.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference position is displaced from the toroidal symmetry axis in the outward $+\hat{R}$ direction, increasing with perpendicular distance from the axis.

NAMES.name: radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Radial direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector along a beam-tracing ray, equal to the radial component $k_R$ divided by the total wave-vector magnitude $|\mathbf{k}|$.
NAMES.long:
The radial normalized wave vector is the direction cosine of the local wave vector projected onto the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, evaluated at each point along the beam or ray path in beam-tracing calculations. It encodes what fraction of the instantaneous wave propagation direction is oriented radially — outward from or inward toward the machine symmetry axis.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
k_{R,\text{norm}} = \frac{k_R}{|\mathbf{k}|}
$$

where $k_R$ is the [radial wave-vector component](name:radial_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the total wave-vector magnitude. Together with the [toroidal normalized wave vector](name:toroidal_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and the [vertical normalized wave vector](name:vertical_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), this component forms a unit direction vector satisfying $k_{R,\text{norm}}^2 + k_{\phi,\text{norm}}^2 + k_{Z,\text{norm}}^2 = 1$.

In beam-tracing or ray-tracing simulations for RF heating, the normalized wave-vector components track the instantaneous wave propagation direction as the ray refracts through an inhomogeneous magnetized plasma. Values are dimensionless and bounded to the interval $[-1, 1]$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $k_R$ points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, away from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_offset_of_beamlet_group
NAMES.short: Radial displacement of a beamlet group centroid from its nominal reference position within a neutral beam injector, measured along the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radial offset of a beamlet group is the signed displacement of the beamlet-group centroid from its nominal reference position along the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height. The nominal reference position is the unperturbed centroid specified by the injector design geometry or by an alignment datum established for the assembled injector. This offset describes static mechanical or alignment displacement of the group, not the change in beam tangency radius caused by beam steering or tilting.

The radial offset is defined by the difference between the actual and reference centroid major radii:

$$
\Delta R = R_{\mathrm{group}} - R_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{group}}$ is the measured or reconstructed major radius of the beamlet-group centroid and $R_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the nominal reference major radius; both are expressed in meters.

In practice, $R_{\mathrm{group}}$ is obtained from mechanical survey, optical metrology, or beam-based alignment of the apertures or grids that form the beamlet group. The centroid should be formed using the same geometric or intensity-weighted convention used to define $R_{\mathrm{ref}}$, so that the offset isolates a displacement rather than a change of reference definition.

Typical signed offsets for well-aligned injector hardware are about -0.005 to 0.005 m, while commissioning adjustments or deliberately displaced configurations can be about -0.02 to 0.02 m. Larger magnitudes usually indicate a significant alignment error or a configuration intentionally far from the nominal reference.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the beamlet-group centroid is displaced toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Reflected power of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the non-negative RF power carried by the backward-traveling wave from the antenna toward the feed line at a specified reference plane. It quantifies antenna matching and coupling shortfall, but equals forward power minus plasma-coupled power only when losses and reference-plane effects are excluded.
NAMES.long:
Reflected power of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the RF power in the wave traveling back from the antenna load toward the transmission line source. It is reported as a non-negative power-flow magnitude at a specified antenna or feed-line reference plane, not as a signed net power.

At the same reference plane, the reflected power is related to the forward and net powers by the local power balance:

$$
P_{\mathrm{refl}} = P_{\mathrm{fwd}} - P_{\mathrm{net}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{refl}}$, $P_{\mathrm{fwd}}$, and $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ are powers in W; $P_{\mathrm{fwd}}$ is the incident power traveling toward the antenna, and $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ is the net RF power crossing the reference plane toward the antenna-plasma load. Only when losses between the reference plane and the plasma are negligible does $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ approximate the power coupled to the plasma.

In practice, reflected power is obtained from calibrated directional couplers or from a voltage-current traveling-wave decomposition in the antenna feed system. The reference plane should be specified because standing waves, impedance transformations, and transmission-line or antenna losses can change the apparent reflected power measured at different locations.

Typical reflected powers range from near 0 W in well-matched conditions to 10^3-10^6 W in high-power ion-cyclotron operation. Well-matched systems commonly aim for reflected fractions $P_{\mathrm{refl}}/P_{\mathrm{fwd}}$ below about 0.05-0.2, while poor coupling or rapid load changes can produce much larger fractions approaching unity.

NAMES.name: reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: RF power returning from a lower hybrid antenna back toward the transmission line, representing the portion of forward power not coupled into the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Reflected power from a lower hybrid antenna is the component of incident RF power that fails to couple into the plasma and propagates back toward the transmission line source. Poor coupling arises from unfavorable edge plasma density gradients, suboptimal launcher–plasma distance, or antenna phasing conditions that mismatch the slow-wave accessibility window of the lower hybrid wave.

The power reflection coefficient $|\Gamma|^2$ relates reflected power $P_\text{ref}$ to forward power $P_\text{fwd}$:

$$
|\Gamma|^2 = \frac{P_\text{ref}}{P_\text{fwd}}
$$

where $P_\text{fwd}$ is the total power delivered to the antenna from the transmission line. The [launched power](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) into the vacuum vessel is the difference $P_\text{fwd} - P_\text{ref}$, and the [total absorbed power](name:total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) accounts for remaining waveguide and plasma losses. The gross RF input to the antenna system is captured by the parent quantity `power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna`.

Reflected power is monitored in real time using directional couplers embedded in the transmission line feeding the lower hybrid launcher. In well-coupled regimes, $P_\text{ref}/P_\text{fwd}$ is typically below 5–10%; transients such as L–H mode transitions or edge density fluctuations can briefly increase the reflected fraction to 30–50%, triggering protection interlocks. The analogous quantity for ion cyclotron systems is [reflected power of an IC antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

NAMES.name: resistance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Resistive component of the RF loading impedance of an ion cyclotron heating antenna module, setting how much power is transferred from the transmission line into the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The coupling resistance $R_c$ is the real part of the complex RF loading impedance $Z = R_c + jX$ presented by the antenna module to the transmission line, where $X$ is the antenna reactance. It captures both the radiation resistance — power radiated into plasma ion cyclotron waves — and ohmic losses in the antenna conductors themselves.

The RF power $P$ launched from the antenna into the plasma is given by:

$$
P = \frac{1}{2} R_c \, |I_0|^2
$$

where $I_0$ is the peak current amplitude on the antenna strap. This relation makes $R_c$ the central efficiency parameter linking the [antenna current amplitude] to the coupled RF power.

The coupling resistance is determined from transmission-line measurements at the antenna port by extracting the real part of the load impedance from the complex reflection coefficient or from simultaneous forward and reflected power and phase measurements. Its value increases with plasma density and decreasing antenna–plasma gap, and depends on the [operating frequency](name:frequency_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and strap geometry.

In tokamak ICRH systems, values range from approximately 0.5 to 10 ohm depending on plasma conditions, scrape-off layer density, and antenna proximity. Together with the [capacitance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:capacitance_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), it determines the reactive matching condition of the antenna circuit and sets the effective loaded quality factor.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by the bulk thermal electron population within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron power at an inside flux surface quantifies the total rate at which coherent wave energy is absorbed by the bulk (Maxwellian) thermal electron population within the plasma volume bounded by a given flux surface. It represents the radially cumulative wave deposition profile for the thermal electron channel, complementing the fast-electron contribution [fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface) to form the total [electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

The quantity is obtained by integrating the flux-surface-averaged [thermal_electron_power_density](name:thermal_electron_power_density) $p_{\mathrm{th,e}}$ over the enclosed plasma volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th,e}}(\rho) = \int_0^\rho p_{\mathrm{th,e}}(\rho') \frac{dV}{d\rho'} \, d\rho'
$$

where $\rho$ labels the flux surface and $dV/d\rho'$ is the differential volume element per unit radial coordinate.

This profile is computed by RF wave propagation and absorption solvers; the value at the outermost closed flux surface gives the total wave power absorbed by thermal electrons. The analogous quantity for thermal ions is [thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface), and the charge-state-resolved thermal ion analog is [thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by the thermal ion population within the plasma volume enclosed by a specified magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion power at an inside flux surface is the cumulative rate at which wave energy is deposited in the bulk ion population inside the volume enclosed by that magnetic flux surface. It represents thermal-ion heating integrated from the magnetic axis to the chosen surface and excludes direct deposition to electrons and fast ions.

The cumulative power for a flux surface labeled by the dimensionless radial coordinate $\rho$ in a flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ is defined from the local thermal-ion wave-power density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th\,ion}}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_{\mathrm{th\,ion}} \, dV'
$$

where $V(\rho)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the flux surface, $p_{\mathrm{th\,ion}}$ is the local net wave-power density for thermal ions in W m^-3, $dV'$ is a volume element in m^3, and $P_{\mathrm{th\,ion}}$ is the cumulative power.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating wave-power deposition densities from wave propagation and wave-particle absorption modeling over the reconstructed plasma volume. Experimental constraints include injected wave power, coupling losses, ion temperature evolution, species composition, and other heating and transport terms needed to separate thermal-ion absorption from electron or fast-ion channels.

Typical values are near 0 W at the magnetic axis and increase toward the total thermal-ion absorbed wave power at the plasma boundary. Medium-size tokamak discharges commonly have 10^4-10^6 W, while high-power wave-heating scenarios in large devices can reach 10^6-2 x 10^7 W within the outer flux surfaces.
NAMES.sign: Positive when wave energy is transferred to the thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Cumulative radio-frequency wave power absorbed by a specified thermal ion charge state inside the plasma volume enclosed by a selected magnetic flux surface. It is the volume integral of the charge-state-resolved absorbed power density.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion state power at an inside flux surface is the cumulative radio-frequency wave power transferred to one specified thermal ion species and charge state within the volume bounded by that magnetic flux surface. It is the charge-state-resolved contribution to cumulative thermal-ion RF absorption.

The cumulative absorbed power for charge state $z$ of ion species $s$ inside the flux surface labeled by $\rho$ is defined by the volume integral of the local absorbed power density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th},s,z}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_{\mathrm{th},s,z}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th},s,z}$ is in W, $p_{\mathrm{th},s,z}$ is the local RF power density transferred to that thermal ion charge state in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is the differential volume element in m$^3$, and $V(\rho)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the magnetic flux surface labeled by the dimensionless normalized flux-surface coordinate $\rho$.

In practice this quantity is computed from wave propagation and wave-particle interaction models by integrating the charge-state-resolved absorption over nested equilibrium volumes. Summing over all relevant charge states and all thermal ion species gives the total cumulative RF power absorbed by thermal ions inside the same flux surface; summing over charge states for only one species gives the species-resolved contribution.

Typical values for an individual thermal ion charge state range from near 0 W for weakly absorbing states to 10^5-10^7 W when the state is a dominant RF absorber. The value depends on coupled RF power, resonance location, ion composition, charge-state population, temperature, density, and the chosen flux surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net RF energy is transferred from the wave field to the specified thermal ion charge state.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Thickness of an ICRH antenna strap is the full, non-negative depth of the strap conductor cross-section, measured along the local normal to its broad plasma-facing surface. It is a length distinct from the in-plane strap width, height, or length.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of an ICRH antenna strap is the geometric extent of the strap conductor in the direction normal to its broad plasma-facing surface. It is a full separation distance across the conductor cross-section, so it is non-negative and is not an oriented displacement.

For a conductor cross-section $C$ and a dimensionless unit normal vector $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ to the broad plasma-facing surface, the thickness $t$ may be defined by the range of projected positions:

$$
t = \max_{\mathbf{r}\in C}\left(\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\right) - \min_{\mathbf{r}\in C}\left(\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is a position vector with components of length, so each projection $\mathbf{r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ has units of meters. This definition is independent of the arbitrary origin used for $\mathbf{r}$ and returns the complete non-negative depth of the conductor along the local normal direction.

In antenna geometry models, the thickness is taken from the physical strap design or from a simplified cross-section used for electromagnetic and engineering calculations. It helps determine conductor volume, surface placement, self-inductance, resistance, thermal capacity, and the geometric clearance between the strap and neighboring antenna structures. It complements in-plane dimensions such as [width_of_antenna_strap](name:width_of_antenna_strap), [height_of_antenna_strap](name:height_of_antenna_strap), and [length_of_antenna_strap](name:length_of_antenna_strap).

For order-of-magnitude checks, ICRH strap thicknesses are usually millimeter-to-centimeter engineering dimensions, roughly 0.001-0.1 m, but the appropriate value is design-specific and the standard name imposes no universal numerical bounds.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle of an ICRH antenna strap, specifying its angular position around the torus in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle $\phi$ of an ICRH antenna strap is its angular coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from the $+Z$ direction, and $Z$ is the vertical height. This coordinate locates the strap toroidally around the vacuum vessel and, together with $R$ and $Z$, fully reconstructs the 3D outline geometry of the strap for antenna design, electromagnetic modeling, and RF wave coupling calculations.

For the outline contour of a single strap, the variation in $\phi$ across the conductor cross-section is small (typically a few milliradians to tens of milliradians), while the nominal center angle is set by the port location on the machine. ICRH systems on large tokamaks are typically installed at two to six toroidal ports, with strap center angles separated by roughly $2\pi / N$ rad for an $N$-port configuration.

The toroidal angle is determined from engineering design drawings and verified through in-situ metrology surveys of the assembled antenna structure. This quantity follows the same geometric convention used for other conducting components, such as [toroidal_angle_of_coil_conductor_element](name:toroidal_angle_of_coil_conductor_element) and [toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_field_coil). The cross-sectional shape of the strap is further characterized by angular parameters such as [alpha_angle_of_antenna_strap](name:alpha_angle_of_antenna_strap).

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam
NAMES.short: Toroidal steering angle of an electron cyclotron beam, defined by the arc sine of the toroidal wave-vector component divided by the total wave-vector magnitude. It specifies the signed toroidal part of propagation in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of an electron cyclotron beam is the signed steering angle associated with the toroidal component of the beam's local mean wave vector. It measures how much of the propagation direction is along $\hat{\phi}$ rather than within the plane spanned by $R$ and $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The angle is defined from the projection of the wave vector onto the toroidal basis direction:

$$
\alpha_\phi = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{k_\phi}{|\mathbf{k}|}\right)
$$

where $\alpha_\phi$ is the toroidal beam angle, $k_\phi$ is the component of the mean wave vector along $\hat{\phi}$, and $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the total wave-vector magnitude. Both $k_\phi$ and $|\mathbf{k}|$ have units of rad m$^{-1}$, equivalently m$^{-1}$ when radians are treated as dimensionless, so the ratio is dimensionless and $\alpha_\phi$ is in rad.

In practice, this angle is determined from EC launcher geometry, calibrated steering-mirror orientation, or ray and beam-tracing calculations by decomposing the mean wave vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Together with [poloidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam](name:poloidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam), launch position, frequency, and magnetic geometry, it contributes to the parallel refractive index through the local projection $N_\parallel = c\,\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}/\omega$, where $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field, $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency, and $c$ is the speed of light. The toroidal angle controls the $k_\phi$ part of that projection but does not by itself determine $N_\parallel$ because the magnetic-field pitch and the poloidal propagation component also enter; it is complementary to EC beam power, which specifies wave energy flow rather than propagation direction.

Typical values are launcher dependent. The principal-value definition gives a mathematical interval from $-\pi/2$ to $+\pi/2$ rad; EC heating launch is often near zero toroidal angle, while current-drive-oriented launch commonly uses nonzero angles of order a few tenths of a rad. Hardware steering limits and access constraints determine the available range for a given device.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal component of the beam wave vector points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_launching_position
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle of the physical point from which a heating wave or particle beam is launched, measured in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of a launching position is the azimuthal coordinate of the launch point around the toroidal symmetry axis. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a launch point with horizontal Cartesian coordinates $(x_\mathrm{launch}, y_\mathrm{launch})$ in a right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the coordinate can be written as:

$$
\phi_\mathrm{launch} = \operatorname{atan2}(y_\mathrm{launch}, x_\mathrm{launch}) \bmod 2\pi
$$

where the $x$ axis defines the $\phi=0$ direction and $\operatorname{atan2}$ selects the correct quadrant.

In practice, this angle is determined from the surveyed or modeled geometry of the launcher reference point, such as the aperture, antenna phase center, or beam-origin point. It specifies the toroidal location of the source point; separate direction angles or wave-vector components describe the launch orientation.

Typical values span the full toroidal range, most commonly reported as 0-6.283 rad. Fixed launchers usually have values set by port locations, while movable or multiple launch systems may provide several discrete toroidal positions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when angular displacement from the $\phi=0$ direction is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive
NAMES.short: Wave-driven toroidal plasma current enclosed by a magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal current due to wave-driven current drive is the non-inductive toroidal plasma current produced when coherent electromagnetic waves create an asymmetric charged-particle distribution through wave-particle interaction. For a chosen magnetic flux surface, it is the total driven current in the toroidal direction crossing a poloidal cut and enclosed by that surface; at the plasma boundary it corresponds to the global wave-driven toroidal current.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, the enclosed current at a flux surface labeled by poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ is defined by integrating the toroidal component of the wave-driven current density over the enclosed poloidal area:

$$
I_{\phi}^{\mathrm{wave}}(\psi) = \int_{A(\psi)} j_{\phi}^{\mathrm{wave}}(R,Z)\, dR\, dZ
$$

where $A(\psi)$ is the region of the poloidal cross-section inside the $\psi=\mathrm{constant}$ contour at fixed $\phi$, $j_{\phi}^{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the toroidal wave-driven current density in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, and $dR\,dZ$ is the poloidal area element. Here $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux in Wb. If the boundary of $A(\psi)$ is parameterized using flux coordinates $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$, the poloidal angle $\theta$ increases counter-clockwise from the outboard midplane around the magnetic axis in the $(R,Z)$ cross-section drawn with increasing $R$ to the right and increasing $Z$ upward.

The value is obtained by determining the wave-driven current density from wave absorption and kinetic response, projecting the driven current onto $\hat{\phi}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and integrating over the equilibrium flux surface. In experiments it is usually constrained indirectly from changes in total plasma current, loop voltage, magnetic equilibrium, and diagnostics sensitive to the current distribution, with inductive current and other non-inductive sources treated separately.

Typical absolute magnitudes are $1 \times 10^{3}-1 \times 10^{6}$ A in magnetically confined plasmas using radio-frequency current drive; small control actuators may drive $1 \times 10^{3}-1 \times 10^{5}$ A, while high-power scenarios can approach or exceed $1 \times 10^{6}$ A. The magnitude depends on launched wave power, resonance location, plasma density and temperature, magnetic geometry, and current-drive efficiency.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the driven toroidal current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_launched_wave_index_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Toroidal launched wave index for a lower hybrid antenna is the signed dimensionless projection of the launched wave refractive-index vector on the toroidal phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It equals the toroidal wave-vector component divided by the free-space wave number and sets the launched parallel phase velocity relevant to current drive.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal launched wave index $n_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the refractive-index vector of a lower hybrid wave at launch. It is the signed projection on $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. In tokamak lower hybrid launch geometry, this component is commonly used as the launched parallel refractive index controlling the resonant electron parallel velocity.

The quantity is defined by normalizing the physical toroidal wave-vector component by the free-space wave number:

$$
n_\phi = \frac{k_\phi}{k_0} = \frac{c\,k_\phi}{\omega}
$$

where $n_\phi$ is dimensionless, $k_\phi = \mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal projection of the launched wave vector in m$^{-1}$, $k_0$ is the free-space wave number in m$^{-1}$, $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency in rad s$^{-1}$, and $c$ is the speed of light in m s$^{-1}$.

In practice, $n_\phi$ is set by the relative phase and spacing of the powered waveguides or multijunction elements in the lower hybrid launcher. A real launcher produces a finite spectrum of toroidal indices; each spectral component corresponds to a different parallel phase velocity, with larger $|n_\phi|$ resonating with slower electrons and affecting current-drive efficiency and wave accessibility.

Typical lower hybrid current-drive launch spectra have dominant $|n_\phi|$ values of about 1.5-3.5, although values outside this range can be used depending on plasma density, magnetic field, frequency, and launcher phasing. The sign distinguishes launch in the co- or counter-toroidal direction relative to the chosen plasma-current direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the launched wave-vector projection on $\hat{\phi}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_width_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Full edge-to-edge arc length of an ICRH antenna strap conductor measured along the toroidal direction. It is a non-negative geometric width of the current-carrying strap, not a half-width or a signed coordinate difference.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal width of an antenna strap is the full physical arc length between the two toroidally separated edges of the current-carrying strap conductor, measured along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above. It is a non-negative geometric length: not a half-width, not a signed coordinate difference, and distinct from the poloidal height (see [length_of_antenna_strap](name:length_of_antenna_strap)) or the radial thickness ([thickness_of_antenna_strap](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap)) of the strap.

For a strap represented at a characteristic major radius, the toroidal arc length relates to the angular span of the strap edges by

$$
w_\phi = R_\mathrm{strap}\,|\phi_2 - \phi_1|
$$

where $w_\phi$ is the toroidal width in meters, $R_\mathrm{strap}$ is the representative major radius of the strap surface in meters, and $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are the toroidal angles of the two strap edges in radians. The angular span $|\phi_2 - \phi_1|$ is taken as the smaller, physically contiguous separation between the edges, so it never wraps across the $2\pi$ branch cut and always satisfies $0 \le |\phi_2 - \phi_1| \le \pi$ for a single strap.

In practice this width is obtained from antenna mechanical design, survey, or electromagnetic geometry models by measuring the active conductor face from one toroidal edge to the other along the toroidal arc. If the geometry is specified by angular extent, multiplication by the local major radius gives the physical arc length; for curved or tilted straps, a consistent representative radius or surface path should be used. Together with the strap's poloidal length and radial thickness, this dimension sets the finite toroidal aperture of the strap, which influences the launched toroidal wave-number spectrum.

This width complements the orthogonal strap dimensions ([width_of_antenna_strap](name:width_of_antenna_strap), [length_of_antenna_strap](name:length_of_antenna_strap), [thickness_of_antenna_strap](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap)) and the radial placement of the conductor face ([inner_radius_of_antenna_strap](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap), [outer_radius_of_antenna_strap](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap)).

NAMES.name: total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Net RF power deposited into the plasma by the lower hybrid antenna system, aggregated over all individual antennas.
NAMES.long:
The total absorbed power of the lower hybrid antenna system quantifies the net RF energy deposition rate from the LHCD launcher array into the confined plasma, summed over all individual antennas. It is the primary power accounting metric for lower hybrid current drive and supplemental electron heating, governing the wave energy available for driving non-inductive plasma current.

The absorbed power is defined as the volume integral of the local LH wave power deposition density over the plasma volume:

$$
P_\text{abs} = \int_V q_\text{LH}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $q_\text{LH}(\mathbf{r})$ is the volumetric LH wave absorption density at position $\mathbf{r}$ within the plasma volume $V$.

This quantity is distinct from the [total launched power](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna), which represents power entering the vacuum vessel and can exceed the absorbed power by any residual absorption in the edge region or scrape-off layer that does not reach the confined plasma. In practice, the absorbed power is estimated from directional-coupler measurements of the [forward power](name:forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and [reflected power](name:reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) on the high-power RF transmission lines, corrected for resistive dissipation in the launcher structure and waveguide network.

In current LHCD systems on medium-to-large tokamaks, total absorbed power levels range from 1-10 MW.

NAMES.name: total_external_heating_power
NAMES.short: Total non-inductive auxiliary heating power absorbed or deposited in the plasma, combining neutral beam, electron cyclotron, ion cyclotron, lower hybrid, and similar systems. It excludes ohmic inductive heating and source power not coupled to the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Total external heating power is the aggregate non-inductive auxiliary power absorbed or deposited in the plasma. It includes coupled contributions from neutral beam injection and radiofrequency heating systems such as electron cyclotron, ion cyclotron, and lower hybrid heating, and excludes ohmic inductive heating. As a sum of absorbed heating powers, it is non-negative; 0 W indicates that no external auxiliary heating power is coupled to the plasma.

The aggregate power is commonly defined as the sum of the plasma-coupled absorbed powers from the active auxiliary systems:

$$
P_\mathrm{ext} = P_\mathrm{NBI,abs} + P_\mathrm{EC} + P_\mathrm{IC} + P_\mathrm{LH} + \cdots
$$

where $P_\mathrm{NBI,abs}$ is the absorbed neutral-beam power, and $P_\mathrm{EC}$, $P_\mathrm{IC}$, and $P_\mathrm{LH}$ are the plasma-coupled electron-cyclotron, ion-cyclotron, and lower-hybrid powers, respectively.

In practice, each contribution is evaluated with source-specific accounting. Neutral-beam absorbed power is inferred from beam energy and current together with corrections for shine-through, reionization, prompt losses, and fast-ion deposition. Radiofrequency contributions are inferred from launched power corrected for transmission-line, matching, reflection, and coupling losses, together with absorption estimates from diagnostics or wave-deposition modeling. The total should include only power coupled to the plasma, not source inefficiency, unabsorbed radiation, or power lost before reaching the plasma.

Typical values range from 0 W when auxiliary systems are inactive to about $10^5$-$10^7$ W in small and medium experiments, with large high-power scenarios reaching $10^7$-$10^8$ W depending on the active heating mix and plasma conditions.

NAMES.name: total_power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating
NAMES.short: Total radiofrequency power absorbed in the plasma by electron cyclotron heating, summed over all electron cyclotron wave sources. It represents deposited heating power, not launched, transmitted, or reflected power, and is zero or positive.
NAMES.long:
Total power due to electron cyclotron heating is the aggregate rate at which electron cyclotron waves transfer electromagnetic energy to the plasma through resonant interaction with electrons at the cyclotron frequency or its harmonics. It is an absorbed heating power: it counts only the power that is actually deposited in the plasma, excluding power that remains in transmission paths, is reflected, or shines through without absorption.

The total absorbed electron cyclotron heating power is the sum of the absorbed powers from the individual electron cyclotron wave sources:

$$
P_\mathrm{EC} = \sum_{i=1}^{N_\mathrm{EC}} P_{\mathrm{EC},i}
$$

where $N_\mathrm{EC}$ is the number of contributing electron cyclotron wave sources, $P_{\mathrm{EC},i}$ (in W) is the heating power absorbed in the plasma from source $i$, and $P_\mathrm{EC}$ (in W) is the total deposited power. The per-source contribution is reported by [power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating](name:power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating).

In practice this quantity is obtained from power-balance and wave-deposition analysis that combines the launched radiofrequency power with absorption estimates from ray-tracing or beam-tracing calculations, accounting for single-pass absorption efficiency and shine-through losses. It enters the electron energy balance as a heating source term and is therefore closely related to [total_electron_power](name:total_electron_deposited_power).
