Representative integrated values range from a few hundred kilowatts to several megawatts in present-day auxiliary-heated experiments, and reach tens of megawatts in high-power systems, with the exact value depending on source power, coupling efficiency, plasma density and temperature, magnetic field, and the absorption location. The value is zero when no electron cyclotron heating is applied.

NAMES.name: total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating
NAMES.short: Total net radio-frequency power absorbed by the plasma through ion cyclotron resonance heating, summed over all ion-cyclotron launchers or antenna systems. It excludes power that is launched but reflected or lost before coupling to the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Total power due to ion cyclotron heating is the aggregate rate at which radio-frequency electromagnetic energy in the ion-cyclotron frequency range is deposited in the plasma. It includes resonant and mode-converted wave absorption from all active ion-cyclotron launchers or antenna systems, and excludes reflected power and non-plasma losses.

The total absorbed ion-cyclotron heating power is the sum of the absorbed powers from the individual contributing systems:

$$
P_{\mathrm{IC,tot}} = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{IC}}} P_{\mathrm{IC},k}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{IC}}$ is the number of contributing ion-cyclotron launchers or antenna systems, $k$ indexes those systems, and $P_{\mathrm{IC},k}$ is the net power absorbed by the plasma from system $k$ in watts.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from an RF power balance using measurements of forward, reflected, and coupled power together with estimates of transmission-line, matching-network, antenna, and other non-plasma losses when available. It may also be constrained by wave-heating analysis, modulation experiments, or global plasma energy-balance checks; it is not the generator output power or the purely launched RF power.

Typical values are $1\times10^5-1\times10^7$ W in medium-sized tokamak experiments and can reach $2\times10^7-4\times10^7$ W in large high-power ion-cyclotron heating scenarios. The value is zero when no ion-cyclotron RF power is coupled to and absorbed by the plasma.

NAMES.name: total_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: System-level net radio-frequency power launched into the vacuum vessel by all ion-cyclotron heating antennas. It is the sum over antennas of forward power minus reflected power, so it represents launched rather than absorbed heating power.
NAMES.long:
Total power of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna system is the system-level net RF power launched through the antenna array into the vacuum vessel. It is the aggregate of the per-antenna launched powers, distinguishing launched power from the power ultimately absorbed by the plasma, such as [total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating).

The total launched power is defined by summing the net contribution from each antenna:

$$
P_{\mathrm{ICRH,tot}} = \sum_{a=1}^{N_{\mathrm{ant}}} \left(P_{\mathrm{fwd},a} - P_{\mathrm{refl},a}\right)
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{ant}}$ is the number of ion-cyclotron heating antennas, $P_{\mathrm{fwd},a}$ is the forward RF power for antenna $a$, and $P_{\mathrm{refl},a}$ is the corresponding reflected RF power, with all powers expressed in W. The per-antenna net term corresponds to [power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), while the reflected component is represented by [reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

In practice, the forward and reflected RF powers are inferred from calibrated measurements in the antenna feeding system and combined over the active antennas. The value is used as a launched-power input for heating efficiency and power-balance analysis; it should not be interpreted as the absorbed ion-cyclotron heating power, because coupling losses, reflection, edge interactions, and wave absorption determine the fraction deposited in the plasma.

Typical total launched ICRH powers range from about $10^5$-$10^7$ W, depending on antenna configuration, coupling conditions, and device size. High-power tokamak systems commonly operate in the MW range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net RF power flow is from the antenna system into the vacuum vessel.

NAMES.name: total_power_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Aggregate neutral beam injection power carried by all active injector units into the vacuum vessel, evaluated before plasma absorption, shinethrough, charge-exchange, wall, or other downstream losses are applied.
NAMES.long:
Total neutral-beam-injector power is the aggregate rate at which kinetic energy is carried by neutral atoms from all active injector units into the vacuum vessel. It is a launched source power for the neutral beam injection system, distinct from absorbed_power_of_neutral_beam_injector and from net plasma-heating quantities such as power_due_to_neutral_beam_injection.

The total is defined by summing the launched power of each active injector unit:

$$
P_{\mathrm{NBI,total}} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{A}} P_{\mathrm{NBI},k}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{NBI},k}$ is the power_of_neutral_beam_injector for injector unit $k$, and $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of active injector units. The accounting direction is into the vacuum vessel: each term is the kinetic-energy flux delivered across the vessel interface toward the plasma region, and later shinethrough, ionization, charge-exchange, wall, or plasma-absorption losses are not subtracted from this total.

In practice, this quantity is evaluated from injector operating measurements such as acceleration voltage, extracted beam current, neutralization efficiency, species and energy fractions, beamline transmission, and pulse timing, with calorimetry or dedicated beam diagnostics used for calibration. For multi-energy neutral beams, each injector contribution includes the weighted kinetic-energy flux of all neutral species components launched by that injector.

Representative values range from $10^5$-$10^6$ W for small or commissioning injectors to $10^6$-$5 \times 10^7$ W for multi-injector tokamak heating systems; the value is zero when no neutral beam injector is active. It is the neutral-beam analog of aggregate launched-power quantities for other auxiliary heating systems, such as [total_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:total_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) and total_power_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher.

NAMES.name: vertical_angle_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Vertical inclination angle of the central beamlet of a neutral beam injector, measured from the horizontal plane to the beamlet axis.
NAMES.long:
The vertical angle of a neutral beam injector characterizes the elevation of the central beamlet axis with respect to the horizontal plane, encoding the upward or downward tilt component of the beam's injection direction. Together with the toroidal pointing geometry described by angle_of_neutral_beam_injector and the tangency major radius beam_major_radius_of_neutral_beam_injector, this angle fully specifies the 3D trajectory of the central beam axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The angle $\alpha_v$ is the elevation of the central beamlet unit direction vector $\hat{b}$ above the horizontal plane:

$$
\alpha_v = \arcsin\!\left(\hat{b} \cdot \hat{Z}\right)
$$

where $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector and $\hat{b}$ is the unit vector along the central beamlet axis, with $\alpha_v = 0$ for a perfectly horizontal beam and $|\alpha_v| < \pi/2$ for any physical configuration.

This geometric parameter is fixed by the physical design and alignment of the injector unit and its duct orientation, established from engineering design specifications and optical survey measurements. The vertical_width_of_neutral_beam_injector describes the vertical spatial extent of the full beamlet group at the injector aperture, complementing this directional quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the central beamlet is directed upward, in the $+Z$ direction above the horizontal plane.

NAMES.name: vertical_centroid_of_coil_conductor_element
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the geometric centroid of a rectangular coil conductor element cross-section, measured in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical centroid coordinate locates the geometric center of a rectangular coil conductor element cross-section along the $Z$-axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major-radius distance from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

For a rectangular cross-section with lower edge at $Z_\text{min}$ and upper edge at $Z_\text{max}$, the centroid is:

$$
Z_c = \frac{Z_\text{min} + Z_\text{max}}{2}
$$

where $Z_c$ is in meters and coincides with the midpoint between the two horizontal bounding edges of the rectangle.

This geometric parameter is specified in engineering design documentation for coil, antenna, and passive-structure assemblies, and may be confirmed by physical survey measurements before or during machine operation. Paired with the corresponding major-radius centroid, it fully characterizes the planar position of each sub-element within the poloidal cross-section, providing the input required for Biot–Savart magnetic field calculations from individual current-carrying segments. The analogous coordinate for the parent coil conductor is captured by [vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor](name:vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor), the generic conductor cross-section center by [vertical_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section](name:vertical_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section), and the ion cyclotron antenna strap center by [vertical_coordinate_of_antenna_strap](name:vertical_coordinate_of_antenna_strap).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the centroid lies above the machine midplane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the geometric center of an antenna strap in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It locates the strap along the vertical direction and is distinct from the strap height or vertical extent.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of an antenna strap is the $Z$-coordinate of the strap's geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It locates the conducting strap within an ion-cyclotron antenna module for geometric and electromagnetic modeling. This quantity is a center coordinate, not the strap height, vertical span, thickness, or spacing to another strap.

When the strap center is defined as an area centroid of a planar strap face or cross-section, the relevant plane is the local meridional plane at fixed $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
Z_c = \frac{1}{A_\perp}\int_{A_\perp} Z\,dA_\perp
$$

where $Z_c$ is the strap-center vertical coordinate, $A_\perp$ is the area enclosed by the projected strap contour in that local meridional plane, and $dA_\perp$ is its area element. For rectangular, annular, or otherwise symmetric strap descriptions, this coordinate often reduces to the midpoint between the upper and lower $Z$ bounds.

In practice, the value is obtained from mechanical design geometry, metrology, or antenna layout models. It is used with the corresponding radial and toroidal placement of the strap to determine antenna-plasma spacing, near-field phasing geometry, and RF coupling calculations.

Typical values for midplane-mounted ion-cyclotron antenna straps are about -2 to 2 m in medium-sized tokamaks; compact devices may be within -1 to 1 m, while large devices can place strap centers several meters from the vertical origin.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the antenna-strap geometric center lies in the $+Z$ direction from the chosen vertical origin in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_aperture
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of an aperture in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long: The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates the geometric center of an aperture along the direction parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is measured upward from the machine midplane. Apertures appear across a wide range of fusion-relevant hardware — neutral beam injectors, electron cyclotron launcher ports, optical diagnostic slits, and detector entrance windows — and their vertical positions are essential inputs for sight-line reconstruction, ray-tracing, and geometric alignment with plasma-facing components. For a given component, this quantity is paired with the corresponding radial coordinate to fully specify the 2-D cross-sectional location of the aperture center; the analogous quantity for optical elements is [vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element](name:vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element), which follows an identical convention. Aperture center positions are fixed geometric descriptors of the hardware configuration, determined from engineering drawings or in-situ survey measurements and updated only when hardware is modified.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture center lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate Z of a point on a coil conductor, measured in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a coil conductor is the height of a point on the current-carrying conductor relative to the horizontal reference plane used for the device geometry. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity specifies the vertical placement and shape of the conductor independently of the current carried by it.

For a conductor point with position vector $\mathbf{r}$, the vertical coordinate is the projection onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z = \mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice, this coordinate is obtained from engineering geometry, survey metrology, or design models of the conductor path. It is used together with the corresponding radial coordinate and toroidal angle to locate conductor points for electromagnetic, heating, and structural calculations.

Typical values are device dependent. Conductor points are often located within about $-1$-$1$ m of the midplane in compact devices and can extend to several meters above or below the midplane in larger machines.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the conductor point lies in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction, above the horizontal reference plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of an electron cyclotron launcher mirror, measured along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates the geometric center of an EC launcher mirror along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z = 0$ denotes the machine midplane. Together with the major-radius coordinate [radial_centroid_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:radial_centroid_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and the toroidal angle, it fully specifies the three-dimensional position of the mirror center in the machine.

The vertical position is determined by the port assignment in the vacuum vessel and is established during machine assembly or optical survey, with uncertainties of order millimeters. The coordinate serves as a boundary condition for beam-tracing calculations that compute EC wave power deposition and current-drive profiles; small changes in $Z$ shift the injection height and alter which resonance layer the beam intercepts.

EC launchers installed in equatorial ports have mirror $Z$ values near the midplane, while upper-port launchers occupy elevated $Z$ positions depending on machine geometry and plasma shaping requirements. The [angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) parametrizes the mirror rotation that steers the beam poloidally, while the mirror boundary in its local planar frame is described by [x1_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:x1_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) and [x2_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:x2_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror). For an analogous position coordinate of a different heating system, see [vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the mirror center is located above the machine midplane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the reference point used to locate an ion cyclotron heating antenna. It is the Z component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of an ion cyclotron heating antenna is the $Z$ component of the antenna reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The reference point is a defined geometric point for the antenna placement; it is not necessarily a physical endpoint or aperture center unless the antenna geometry defines it that way.

Together with the [major-radius coordinate] and toroidal angle of the same reference point, this quantity specifies the antenna reference-point position in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The same coordinate concept is used for other actuator placement reference points, including lower-hybrid antennas, neutral-beam injectors, and electron-cyclotron launcher mirrors.

In practice, the value is obtained from mechanical design geometry, installation alignment, or survey data for the antenna reference point, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Any uncertainty is usually dominated by the definition of the reference point and by mechanical alignment tolerances rather than by plasma conditions.

Typical values are device- and origin-dependent. For antennas mounted near a machine midplane the coordinate is often close to 0 m, while upper or lower port locations have positive or negative offsets with magnitudes from fractions of a meter to several meters depending on device size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the antenna reference point is displaced in the $+Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the reference point of a lower hybrid antenna in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a lower hybrid antenna is the $Z$ value of the antenna reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It specifies the vertical placement of the launcher reference datum, typically relative to the $Z=0$ midplane of the device geometry.

The coordinate is the $Z$ component assigned to the antenna reference point:

$$
Z_\mathrm{ant} = Z_\mathrm{ref}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{ref}$ is the vertical coordinate of the nominated reference point and $Z_\mathrm{ant}$ is the corresponding lower-hybrid-antenna coordinate.

The reference point is usually a mechanical or geometric datum of the launcher, such as a mounting datum, aperture center, or defined antenna center. It is determined from engineering geometry or installation survey data and, together with the complementary major-radius and toroidal-angle coordinates, fixes the antenna position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Row-specific vertical positions are represented separately by [vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna_row](name:vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna_row).

Typical values are device- and installation-dependent. Midplane launchers often have $Z_\mathrm{ant}$ close to 0 m, while vertically displaced launchers can have offsets of order 0.1-1 m; larger offsets are possible in large devices or for antennas deliberately mounted away from the midplane.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference point lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna_row
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate, in meters, of the geometric reference point of a lower hybrid antenna row in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It locates the row's height relative to the machine equatorial plane and is not the row height or row spacing.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z_\mathrm{row}$ is the height of the specified geometric reference point of a lower hybrid antenna row in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The datum is the row reference point used to locate the row geometry; this coordinate does not describe the physical vertical extent of the row.

For a row reference point with cylindrical coordinates $(R_\mathrm{row}, \phi_\mathrm{row}, Z_\mathrm{row})$, its position may be written as:

$$
\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{row} = R_\mathrm{row}\,\hat{R}(\phi_\mathrm{row}) + Z_\mathrm{row}\,\hat{Z}
$$

where $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are basis vectors of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R_\mathrm{row}$ is the major-radius coordinate, $\phi_\mathrm{row}$ is the toroidal angle coordinate, and $Z_\mathrm{row}$ is the vertical coordinate in meters.

This coordinate is normally obtained from the antenna mechanical geometry, alignment survey, or design model using the same row reference point as the companion major-radius and toroidal-angle coordinates. Together these three coordinates specify the location of the row reference point in space.

There is no device-independent typical range for this coordinate. Rows mounted near the equatorial plane have $Z_\mathrm{row}$ close to $0$ m, while rows placed above or below the midplane take positive or negative values set by the launcher port location and row spacing.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the row reference point lies in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame from the $Z=0$ equatorial plane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Vertical height coordinate Z of the declared reference position of a neutral beam injector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. Z is measured from the machine midplane/equatorial plane along the vertical axis.
NAMES.long:
This is the $Z$ coordinate assigned to the declared reference position of a neutral beam injector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The zero of $Z$ is the machine midplane/equatorial plane, so the coordinate gives the height of that injector reference point above or below the midplane. For an extended injector, this quantity locates only the chosen reference point and does not by itself specify the injector aperture, aiming direction, beam footprint, or full beam geometry.

The vertical coordinate is the projection of the injector reference-point displacement onto the vertical unit vector:

$$
Z_\mathrm{NBI} = \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ is measured from an origin on the machine symmetry axis in the midplane, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice, the value is obtained from the geometry definition, alignment model, or beamline description for the chosen injector reference point and expressed in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame as other machine geometry quantities. Additional coordinates and orientation quantities, such as major radius, toroidal angle, tangency geometry, and beam-axis direction, are required to describe the full neutral-beam injection geometry.

Typical values are facility and reference-point dependent. For injectors whose reference point is near the plasma or port region, signed coordinates commonly fall within -5-5 m; elevated, depressed, or remotely referenced beamlines may lie outside this range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the injector reference point lies above the machine midplane in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: voltage_amplitude
NAMES.short: Peak magnitude of the radio-frequency voltage waveform at an ion-cyclotron antenna module transmission-line feed.
NAMES.long:
Voltage amplitude is the peak magnitude of the RF potential difference between the conductors of an ion-cyclotron antenna module transmission-line feed at a specified reference plane. For a sinusoidal component it is the magnitude of the complex peak voltage phasor, not the RMS value; the RMS value is $V_{\mathrm{amp}}/\sqrt{2}$.

With synchronized peak phasors for voltage and current at the same reference plane, the net time-averaged real power crossing that plane is

$$
P_{\mathrm{net}} = \frac{1}{2} V_{\mathrm{amp}} I_{\mathrm{amp}} \cos(\theta_V-\theta_I)
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ is in W, $V_{\mathrm{amp}}$ is the voltage amplitude in V, $I_{\mathrm{amp}}$ is the current amplitude in A, and $\theta_V$ and $\theta_I$ are voltage and current phases in radians. This relation shows that voltage amplitude and current amplitude alone do not determine RF power; the relative phase is also required.

The amplitude is obtained from calibrated high-voltage RF probes, capacitive dividers, directional couplers, or equivalent transmission-line measurements by extracting the peak phasor at the operating frequency. For reflection analysis, voltage, current, phase, and line-impedance calibration must refer to the same reference plane; forward and reflected powers require a traveling-wave decomposition and are affected by transmission-line losses, matching networks, and probe calibration. Comparisons with [reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) or with forward-minus-reflected power should include only the power balance defined at that reference plane after accounting for intervening losses.

Typical peak amplitudes in high-power ion-cyclotron heating feeds are $5\times10^3$-$5\times10^4$ V; low-power conditioning may be below $10^3$ V, while voltage-standoff limits often keep routine operation below about $8\times10^4$ V.

NAMES.name: wave_frequency
NAMES.short: Temporal frequency of a coherent electromagnetic wave used for plasma auxiliary heating or current drive. Together with magnetic field, density, species, harmonic number, and wave vector, it helps set accessibility and resonance conditions for coupling and absorption.
NAMES.long:
Wave frequency is the number of complete oscillation cycles of a coherent electromagnetic wave per unit time. It is a non-negative scalar physical frequency; any sign assigned to a complex phasor phase or angular frequency is a modeling convention and is not part of this quantity.

For a monochromatic wave with oscillation period $T$ and angular frequency $\omega$, the physical frequency $f$ is

$$
f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{|\omega|}{2\pi}
$$

where $T$ is the period in seconds, $\omega$ is the angular frequency in rad s$^{-1}$, and $f$ is the frequency in Hz.

In auxiliary heating and current-drive applications, the frequency is normally set by the RF or microwave source and verified with frequency counters, spectrum analyzers, or waveguide and transmission-line diagnostics. In wave-propagation and absorption calculations, it enters the dispersion relation and resonance conditions together with magnetic field, plasma density, ion species, harmonic number, launched wave vector, and distribution functions. Frequency helps determine which absorption channels are accessible, such as [fast-electron power](name:fast_electron_power), [thermal-electron power](name:thermal_electron_power), [fast-ion power](name:fast_ion_power), and [thermal-ion power](name:thermal_ion_power), but it does not by itself uniquely determine the absorption location or partition.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. Electron-cyclotron heating and current-drive systems commonly use 20-300 GHz, ion-cyclotron and fast-wave systems use about 10-120 MHz, lower-hybrid current-drive systems use about 1-8 GHz, and helicon or high-harmonic fast-wave schemes may use tens to hundreds of MHz. The selected frequency depends on toroidal magnetic field, plasma density, launched parallel refractive index, ion composition, desired harmonic, launcher constraints, and whether the objective is heating, current drive, or fast-particle interaction.

NAMES.name: wave_phase_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: RF temporal phase angle of the current waveform driving one specified strap of an ion-cyclotron-range heating antenna, referenced to that launcher's phase reference. It is a per-strap quantity; differences between strap phases, not their common value, set the toroidal wave-number spectrum of the launched fast and slow magnetosonic waves.
NAMES.long:
Wave phase of an antenna strap is the temporal phase angle of the RF current waveform driving one identified strap of an ion-cyclotron-range heating launcher, expressed relative to a phase reference common to that launcher. A uniform shift added to every strap of a launcher is an absolute common phase that does not change the coupled spectrum; only the differences between identified straps influence the plasma, shaping the spectral content along the toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

Adopting the time convention in which each strap current varies as $\mathrm{Re}\left[\hat{I}\,e^{-i\omega t}\right]$ with complex phasor $\hat{I} = |\hat{I}|\,e^{i\varphi}$, the strap phase $\varphi$ is the argument of that phasor. For neighboring straps driven with a uniform phase step, the central toroidal wave number selected by the launcher is approximately

$$
k_\phi \simeq \frac{\Delta\varphi}{d}
$$

where $\Delta\varphi = \varphi_{i+1} - \varphi_i$ (in rad) is the phase advance between adjacent straps ordered by increasing $\phi$, $d$ is the toroidal center-to-center strap spacing in meters, and $k_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the launched wave vector in m^-1. Radians are dimensionless, so the relation is dimensionally m^-1 = rad/m. The actual spectrum is broadened by strap geometry, finite phasing errors, nearby conducting structures, and plasma loading.

In practice, strap phases are commanded as RF generator, transmission-line, or matching-network set points and verified from calibrated voltage and current phasors after correcting for cable and feed delays. Phases must be compared only within the same launcher, for the same RF frequency and the same identified strap set, since different launchers may carry independent phase references. The chosen phase pattern realizes the same physical control summarized by the [antenna phasing angle](name:wave_phase_of_antenna_strap) and, together with the strap geometry, fixes the launched [perpendicular wave vector](name:perpendicular_wave_vector_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

Strap phases are periodic modulo $2\pi$ and are commonly reported on $-\pi$ to $\pi$ rad or $0$ to $2\pi$ rad. Representative two-strap patterns include monopole phasing $(0, 0)$ with $\Delta\varphi = 0$ rad for low $|k_\phi|$, dipole phasing $(0, \pi)$ with $\Delta\varphi = \pm\pi$ rad for larger $|k_\phi|$ and minority heating, and traveling-wave or current-drive phasing with $\Delta\varphi = \pm\pi/2$ rad.
NAMES.sign: Positive when, under the $e^{-i\omega t}$ phasor convention, the strap current phasor leads the launcher phase reference, so that a positive strap-to-strap step $\Delta\varphi$ advances the phase from one strap to the next in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: width_of_aperture
NAMES.short: Full edge-to-edge opening distance of a collimating aperture measured along the local X1 direction in the local aperture frame (X1, X2, X3).
NAMES.long:
Aperture width is the full linear extent of a physical opening measured along the local $X_1$ direction. In the local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$, $\\hat{X}_1$ and $\\hat{X}_2$ span the aperture plane and $\\hat{X}_3$ is normal to that plane. This is the same geometric concept as x_width_of_aperture and the neutral-beam-specific [neutral_beam_width_of_aperture](name:neutral_beam_width_of_aperture).

For an aperture region $\\mathcal{A}$, the width can be written as the projected extent of the opening along $\\hat{X}_1$:

$$
w = \\max_{\\mathbf{r} \\in \\mathcal{A}} (\\mathbf{r} \\cdot \\hat{X}_1) - \\min_{\\mathbf{r} \\in \\mathcal{A}} (\\mathbf{r} \\cdot \\hat{X}_1)
$$

where $w$ is the aperture width in meters, $\\mathbf{r}$ is a position vector in meters in the aperture plane measured from any fixed origin, $\\hat{X}_1$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the local $X_1$ direction, and $\\mathcal{A}$ is the transmitting area of the opening.

The width is normally determined from mechanical design geometry, manufacturing drawings, or metrology of the collimating component. For a rectangular aperture it is paired with the orthogonal extent along $X_2$ to define the rectangular opening area. For a circular aperture the related quantity radius_of_aperture is a radius; the corresponding full edge-to-edge width would be the diameter, equal to twice that radius.

Typical values are design-specific rather than set by plasma physics. They should be taken from the aperture geometry of the heating or beamline component; representative engineering scales can range from millimeter-scale beamlet openings to centimeter- or decimeter-scale grouped collimating apertures.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_aperture
NAMES.short: First local transverse coordinate of a neutral-beam injector collimating-aperture outline vertex, measured from the aperture origin in the local aperture-plane Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
The $X_1$ coordinate of an aperture is the signed distance of an outline vertex along the first axis of the local aperture-plane Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame with in-plane basis $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$. The frame origin is the aperture reference point, normally the nominal beam-axis intersection with the aperture plane or the mechanical center used for alignment; $X_1=0$ is the line through that origin parallel to the $X_2$ axis. It is not a coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; it describes transverse position within the injector aperture plane.

Together with [x2_coordinate_of_aperture](name:x2_coordinate_of_aperture), ordered vertices define the closed planar aperture boundary: consecutive vertices lie on adjacent boundary segments, and the final vertex is connected back to the first. The coordinate is determined by projecting each vertex position in the aperture plane onto the $+\hat{X}_1$ axis after the local origin and axis orientation have been established from component geometry and alignment.

Typical neutral-beam collimating apertures have transverse half-widths of 0.01-0.3 m, so individual $X_1$ vertex coordinates commonly span from about -0.3 m to 0.3 m. Small beamlet or mask openings may be at the 0.001-0.02 m scale, while large shaped collimators can approach 0.5 m in full width.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the aperture origin is along the $+X_1$ direction of the local aperture-plane Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
NAMES.short: X1 coordinate of a vertex on the closed outline contour of an electron cyclotron launcher mirror in its element-local planar (X1, X2) Cartesian frame.
NAMES.long:
The electron cyclotron launcher mirror is a steerable reflective element used in ECRH and ECCD systems to direct the gyrotron beam into the plasma at a prescribed injection angle. Its cross-sectional boundary is described by a closed outline contour defined in a local two-dimensional Cartesian frame with orthogonal axes X1 and X2. This coordinate gives the position of each successive vertex of that closed polygon along the X1 axis, fully specifying the mirror shape in the local plane at its reference (unrotated) position.

The local (X1, X2) frame is attached to the mirror at its reference orientation; the relationship of this frame to the machine's right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is determined by the mirror's mounting geometry. Together with [x2_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:x2_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), this coordinate fully defines the 2D mirror outline. The [angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror](name:angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror) describes rotation of the mirror about its movement axis, but the outline vertex coordinates in the local frame remain fixed with respect to that rotation.

Mirror apertures in ECRH systems span roughly 5–20 cm, so X1 outline vertex values cover ranges of that order within the local frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline vertex lies in the positive X1 direction of the element-local Cartesian frame.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Position along X1 of a neutral beam injector source-outline vertex in the beam-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame, referenced to the aperture center.
NAMES.long:
The $X_1$ coordinate of a neutral beam injector source-outline vertex is the signed displacement of that vertex along the first transverse axis of the beam-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. This frame has basis axes $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$ in the source extraction plane, transverse to the nominal beam propagation direction. The origin is the source-aperture center, i.e. the intersection of the nominal beam centerline with the extraction plane.

Together with the [X2 coordinate](name:x2_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector), this quantity defines a vertex of the closed outline of the beam extraction surface. The outline geometry is usually obtained from the source-aperture design or as-built metrology; vertices are normally ordered consistently around the aperture, clockwise or counterclockwise as viewed along the nominal beam direction. A rectangular source outline uses four vertices, while chamfered, rounded, or segmented extraction surfaces may use more.

The local source outline complements global injector-position quantities such as the [vertical coordinate of a neutral beam injector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector), which are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Representative absolute values of $X_1$ for neutral beam source outlines are typically 0.05-0.5 m, depending on source size and whether $X_1$ is aligned with the wider or narrower aperture dimension; large high-power source modules can be larger.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the source-outline vertex is displaced from the local origin in the $+\hat{X}_1$ direction of the beam-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_aperture
NAMES.short: Second local coordinate of a neutral beam injector collimating-aperture outline vertex in the transverse (X1, X2) aperture plane. With the paired first coordinate, it gives the signed in-plane position of a beam-limiting boundary point relative to the aperture origin.
NAMES.long:
The X2 coordinate is the signed scalar component of an aperture-outline vertex along the second axis of the local aperture-plane Cartesian frame $(X_1, X_2)$ with basis $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$. The local origin is the point represented by $x_1=x_2=0$, and all aperture vertices use the same origin and in-plane basis. Paired with [x1_coordinate_of_aperture](name:x1_coordinate_of_aperture), it identifies a point on the boundary of the neutral beam collimating opening.

Given an aperture-plane origin $\mathbf{r}_0$ and unit basis vectors $\hat{X}_1$ and $\hat{X}_2$, the local reconstruction of a vertex position is

$$
\mathbf{r}_v = \mathbf{r}_0 + x_1\hat{X}_1 + x_2\hat{X}_2
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the vertex position in the aperture plane, $x_1$ is the paired first local coordinate, and $x_2$ is this second local coordinate.

Aperture-outline coordinates are specified from the mechanical definition of the collimating aperture or from a measured outline of the hardware. They are used when the beam-limiting opening is represented by explicit boundary vertices rather than by a reduced geometric parameter such as width_of_aperture for a rectangular description or neutral_beam_radius_of_aperture for a circular description.

Values are expressed in meters and may be negative, zero, or positive depending on the vertex location and the chosen local origin. The applicable range is aperture-specific; for an opening centered on the local origin, X2 coordinates span roughly from $-a_2$ to $+a_2$, where $a_2$ is the half-extent of the aperture along $\hat{X}_2$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex is displaced from the local aperture-plane origin in the $+\hat{X}_2$ direction.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
NAMES.short: X2 coordinate of a point on the boundary contour of an electron cyclotron launcher mirror in its local planar (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
The X2 coordinate of an electron cyclotron launcher mirror is the signed in-plane displacement of a boundary-contour point along the second axis of the mirror's local planar Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame with basis $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$. Together with the companion $X_1$ coordinate, it describes the mirror outline relative to the mirror reference point, not the absolute position of the mirror center.

For a contour point with in-plane position vector $\mathbf{r}_\perp$ measured from the mirror reference point, the coordinate is

$$
x_2 = \mathbf{r}_\perp \cdot \hat{X}_2
$$

where $\hat{X}_2$ is the unit vector along the second local planar axis and $x_2$ is measured in meters.

In practice, this coordinate is obtained from the mirror design geometry, metrology, or a fitted boundary model by projecting each outline point onto the local $(X_1, X_2)$ axes. The local outline specifies the mirror aperture or reflecting-surface boundary; placement of the mirror center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame requires separate radial and vertical center coordinates, together with the mirror orientation.

Typical values are set by the mirror size: small steering mirrors often have $x_2$ coordinates within about -0.1-0.1 m, while larger focusing or launcher mirrors may span roughly -0.5-0.5 m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the boundary point is displaced in the $+\hat{X}_2$ direction of the local planar Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Second-axis coordinate of a single neutral beam injector ion-source outline vertex in the beam-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame. It is a signed length coordinate paired with the corresponding X1 coordinate to define the local extraction-grid outline.
NAMES.long:
The $X_2$ coordinate of a neutral beam injector is the signed position of a single vertex of the ion-source outline along the second axis of the beam-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. Together with [x1_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:x1_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector), it specifies the planar outline of the ion-source extraction-grid boundary transverse to the nominal injector beam direction.

The local transverse position of an outline vertex can be written as

$$
\mathbf{r}_\perp = x_1 \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{X_1} + x_2 \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{X_2}
$$

where $x_2$ is this coordinate in meters, $x_1$ is the corresponding first-axis coordinate, and $(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{X_1}, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{X_2})$ are the unit vectors of the beam-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

Values are determined from the injector engineering geometry, such as a design model, survey, or documented extraction-grid outline. Consecutive outline vertices are typically interpreted as connected polygon edges, while the number of vertices and coordinate extent are design-specific. This local outline coordinate is distinct from global injector-placement quantities such as [vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector), which locate the injector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

No universal numerical range applies: typical values are set by the transverse size of the particular ion-source outline and by the chosen local origin, and are reported in meters.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement is along the positive $X_2$ axis of the beam-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Total wave power absorbed by the fast (suprathermal) electron population from a coherent wave, globally integrated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Fast electron power is the volume integral of the local wave energy absorption rate by the non-thermal (suprathermal) electron population, representing the globally integrated fraction of coherent wave energy transferred to electrons whose velocities substantially exceed the bulk thermal velocity.

The defining relation is:

$$
P_\mathrm{fast,e} = \int_V p_\mathrm{fast,e}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $p_\mathrm{fast,e}$ is the [fast electron power density](name:fast_electron_power_density) — the local volumetric wave-energy absorption rate on the suprathermal electron population and $V$ is the total plasma volume.

This quantity is computed from wave-kinetic or quasilinear solvers that partition the electron velocity distribution into thermal and suprathermal components; in electron cyclotron resonance heating scenarios, the fast electron channel captures absorption at harmonic resonances and energy transfer during suprathermal tail formation. The thermally absorbed complement is [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_power); comparing the two characterizes the non-thermal efficiency of a given wave-heating scheme.

Together with [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_power) and [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power), this quantity contributes to absorbed_power — the total wave energy transferred to the plasma per unit time. It enters the electron energy balance as a suprathermal source term within [electron_power](name:electron_power), the all-channel electron energy-balance quantity.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by the fast (non-thermal) electron population from a coherent wave, attributed to a single toroidal Fourier harmonic identified by mode number $n_\phi$.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the contribution to the total absorbed fast-electron wave power from a single toroidal Fourier harmonic of a coherent wave, identified by toroidal mode number $n_\phi$. It decomposes [fast_electron_power](name:fast_electron_power) — the volume-integrated power absorbed by the non-thermal electron population — into individual harmonic contributions.

The summation closure relation is:

$$
P_{\rm fast,e} = \sum_{n_\phi} P_{\rm fast,e}(n_\phi)
$$

where $P_{\rm fast,e}(n_\phi)$ is the power absorbed by fast electrons from the harmonic with toroidal mode number $n_\phi$.

In wave-modeling calculations, the electromagnetic fields of a coherent wave are expanded as a Fourier series in the toroidal angle $\phi$, and the contribution from each harmonic to the fast-electron power balance is evaluated separately using quasilinear diffusion theory applied to the non-thermal electron distribution. Resonant absorption mechanisms — such as electron cyclotron or lower-hybrid resonances — accelerate electrons to suprathermal energies, and the harmonic decomposition reveals which modes dominate this energy transfer. The radially cumulative (inside-flux-surface) variant is [fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), while the local power-density analog per mode is [per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power_density). The equivalent decomposition for the thermal electron population is [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power), and the fast-ion counterpart is [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power).

NAMES.name: fast_electron_power_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: RF wave energy absorption rate per unit volume by the fast, suprathermal electron population. It represents the non-thermal electron channel of wave power deposition.
NAMES.long:
Fast electron power density is the rate per unit volume at which an RF wave deposits energy in the suprathermal electron population. It is a volumetric source term for the fast-electron energy balance; fast denotes the modeled non-thermal part of the electron distribution rather than a universal sharp energy threshold.

For a local point $\mathbf{x}$, a kinetic definition is obtained by taking the particle-energy moment of the wave-driven part of the fast-electron distribution evolution:

$$
p_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{x}) = \int \frac{1}{2} m_e v^2 \, \mathcal{C}_\mathrm{wave}[f_\mathrm{fast}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v$ is particle speed, $f_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-electron distribution function with units $s^3 m^{-6}$, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element with units $m^3 s^{-3}$, and $\mathcal{C}_\mathrm{wave}[f_\mathrm{fast}]$ is the wave-driven contribution to $\partial f_\mathrm{fast}/\partial t$ with units $s^2 m^{-6}$. When the quantity is associated with a flux coordinate $\rho$ such as normalized toroidal flux radius, it denotes the flux-surface average of this local volumetric density, not the cumulative power. The cumulative fast-electron power inside a surface labeled by $\rho$ is related by $P_\mathrm{fast}(<\rho)=\int_{V(\rho)} p_\mathrm{fast}\,dV$, and the corresponding differential volume density is $dP_\mathrm{fast}/dV=(dP_\mathrm{fast}/d\rho)/(dV/d\rho)$.

In practice this quantity is usually inferred from wave-particle absorption calculations constrained by launched RF power, antenna or launcher configuration, magnetic equilibrium, and plasma profiles. Experimental checks can come from global power balance and from diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal electrons, such as non-thermal radiation or energetic-electron emission, but the local partition between thermal and fast-electron channels is generally model dependent.

Representative magnitudes span a wide range because RF deposition can be broad or highly localized. Core values of about $10^3-10^7$ W m$^{-3}$ are typical order-of-magnitude levels for auxiliary heating, with smaller values in weakly absorbing regions and larger peaks possible for strongly localized absorption.
NAMES.sign: Positive when RF wave energy is transferred from the wave field to the fast electron population.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: RF wave energy deposition rate per unit volume into the suprathermal electron population, resolved per toroidal mode number, such that summing over all modes recovers the total fast electron power density.
NAMES.long:
Fast electron power density per toroidal mode is the volumetric rate at which a coherent RF wave deposits energy into the suprathermal (non-thermal) electron population attributed to a single toroidal harmonic of the wave field. The fast electrons are those resonantly accelerated above the bulk thermal velocity through wave-particle interaction, forming a non-Maxwellian energetic tail in the electron distribution function.

The total [fast electron power density](name:fast_electron_power_density) is recovered by summing over all toroidal mode numbers:

$$
P_\mathrm{fast,e}(r) = \sum_{n_\phi} p_\mathrm{fast,e}(r,\, n_\phi)
$$

where $p_\mathrm{fast,e}(r, n_\phi)$ is the power density contribution from toroidal mode number $n_\phi$ and $r$ is the radial coordinate.

The mode-resolved deposition is computed by wave-propagation models — ray-tracing or full-wave solvers equipped with quasilinear diffusion operators — that decompose the RF electric field into toroidal harmonics and evaluate the mode-dependent damping on the fast electron component of the distribution function.

The harmonic structure of fast-electron absorption depends on wave type: electron cyclotron heating concentrates deposition near the fundamental or harmonic cyclotron resonance in a narrow toroidal mode range, while lower-hybrid and ICRH Landau and transit-time damping distribute absorption across a broader toroidal mode spectrum. The fast-ion counterpart is [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power_density), the thermal electron counterpart is [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density), and the mode-resolved total absorbed power density summed over all populations is given by per_toroidal_mode_absorbed_power_density.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total coherent-wave power absorbed by the suprathermal (fast) ion population, integrated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Fast ion power is the volume-integrated rate of energy transfer from a coherent electromagnetic wave to the suprathermal (non-thermal) ion population. It isolates the non-Maxwellian fast-ion channel of wave absorption, complementing [thermal_ion_power](name:thermal_ion_power) and contributing to the species-summed [ion_power](name:ion_power). The dominant physical context is ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH), where minority ions driven to suprathermal energies absorb wave power through quasi-linear wave-particle interaction at the fundamental or harmonic cyclotron resonance.

The power is given by the volume integral of the wave energy source:

$$
P_\mathrm{fast,ion} = \int \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{J}_\mathrm{fast,ion} \, dV
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the RF wave electric field, $\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{fast,ion}$ is the current density carried by the suprathermal ion population, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

This quantity is evaluated by full-wave or ray-tracing RF modeling codes that resolve the fast-ion contribution to the hot-plasma dielectric tensor. The charge-state-resolved counterpart is [fast_ion_state_power](name:fast_ion_state_power), and the spectral decomposition by toroidal mode number is provided by [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power). When summed with [thermal_ion_power](name:thermal_ion_power), [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_power), and [fast_electron_power](name:fast_electron_power), the result recovers the total absorbed_power.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative coherent-wave power absorbed by suprathermal ions inside a flux surface, resolved by toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode fast-ion power is the net rate of energy transfer from a coherent wave to the suprathermal ion population for one toroidal Fourier mode, accumulated over the volume enclosed by a chosen flux surface. Summing over toroidal mode numbers gives the total fast-ion wave power inside that surface, while charge-state-resolved and thermal-species analogs separate the same physical transfer by ion charge state or receiving population.

The cumulative mode-resolved power is defined by integrating the local net power-transfer density for that mode over the enclosed volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},n_\phi}(\psi) = \int_{V(\psi)} q_{\mathrm{fast},n_\phi}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast},n_\phi}$ is the cumulative power in W, $q_{\mathrm{fast},n_\phi}$ is the local net power-transfer density in W m$^{-3}$, $V(\psi)$ is the volume inside the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$. The label $\psi$ may be a magnetic-flux coordinate in Wb or a normalized flux coordinate with unit 1, and $n_\phi$ is a dimensionless integer toroidal mode number defined with respect to the toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

In practice this quantity is computed by decomposing the coherent wave field into toroidal Fourier components and evaluating the wave-particle energy exchange with the modeled fast-ion distribution. The radial cumulative value is obtained by integrating the mode-resolved deposition density inside successive flux surfaces; direct experimental inference usually combines wave coupling information, equilibrium geometry, and fast-ion distribution modeling rather than a single diagnostic measurement. Closely related quantities include [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power), [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power), [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power), and [per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power).

Representative values range from near 0 W for weakly coupled or nonresonant modes to a substantial fraction of the absorbed coherent-wave power for resonant modes. In megawatt-class radio-frequency heating, dominant individual toroidal modes are commonly of order 10^3-10^6 W, with the sum over modes bounded by the net wave power transferred to plasma particles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net energy is transferred from the coherent wave field to the suprathermal ion population.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volumetric rate at which RF waves transfer energy to the nonthermal fast ion population. It represents deposited wave power per unit plasma volume, summed over the relevant fast-ion species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion power density is the volumetric source term for energy deposited by radio-frequency (RF) waves into the nonthermal ion distribution. It is the state-aggregated counterpart of [fast_ion_state_power_density](name:fast_ion_state_power_density) and excludes deposition to thermal ions or fast electrons. Its volume integral gives [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power), while integration inside a chosen flux surface gives [fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

For RF absorption, the local source can be written as the cycle-averaged work done by the RF electric field on the fast-ion current response:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fi}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{a,q} \left\langle \mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{RF}}_{\mathrm{fi},a q}(\mathbf{x},t) \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{RF}}(\mathbf{x},t) \right\rangle_t
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fi}}$ is the fast-ion power density, $a$ labels ion species, $q$ labels charge state, $\mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{RF}}_{\mathrm{fi},a q}$ is the RF current response associated with that fast-ion component, $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{RF}}$ is the RF electric field, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes averaging over the RF period.

In practice this quantity is inferred from wave propagation and quasilinear absorption calculations constrained by magnetic equilibrium, antenna or launcher parameters, and measurements sensitive to the fast-ion distribution. It may also be cross-checked against changes in stored fast-ion energy, neutron or gamma-ray emission, neutral-particle measurements, and global RF power balance.

Representative magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. A useful scale is the absorbed RF power divided by the effective deposition volume: 1 MW deposited over 0.1-10 m$^3$ corresponds to 10$^5$-10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$, while values are near zero where no resonant wave-particle interaction occurs.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from the RF wave field to the fast-ion population.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Absorbed coherent-wave power density deposited in the fast, non-thermal ion population, resolved by toroidal mode number and summed over fast-ion charge states. It quantifies each toroidal harmonic's contribution to volumetric energy transfer from the wave to energetic ions.
NAMES.long:
Absorbed coherent-wave power density per toroidal mode is the rate per unit plasma volume at which one toroidal Fourier harmonic transfers energy to the fast, non-thermal ion population. It is summed over fast-ion charge states; the charge-state-resolved counterpart is [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power_density).

The corresponding volume-integrated per-mode fast-ion power is obtained from the volumetric density:

$$
P_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi) = \int_V p_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi, \mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $p_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi, \mathbf{x})$ is this power density in W m^-3, $P_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi)$ is [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power), $n_\phi$ is the toroidal mode number, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and $V$ is the plasma volume considered. If expressed on a magnetic surface labeled by the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the quantity denotes the flux-surface average of the local volumetric density, still in W m^-3, not a volume-integrated power.

In coherent-wave heating calculations, the wave field is decomposed into toroidal Fourier harmonics and the resonant wave-particle power transfer is evaluated against the fast-ion distribution. The total [fast_ion_power_density](name:fast_ion_power_density) is recovered by summing $p_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi, \mathbf{x})$ over toroidal mode numbers, while $p_\mathrm{fast}(n_\phi, \mathbf{x}) = \sum_q p_{\mathrm{fast},q}(n_\phi, \mathbf{x})$ relates it to the charge-state-resolved density over fast-ion charge states $q$. Integrating the state-resolved densities gives [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power).

Large values occur where a toroidal harmonic has strong wave amplitude, satisfies the relevant resonance condition, and overlaps a substantial fast-ion phase-space density. The absolute scale is highly scenario dependent, so interpretation is usually made by comparing the integrated per-mode power, the absorbing volume, and the distribution of launched toroidal harmonics rather than by using a universal numerical range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when coherent-wave energy is transferred to the fast, non-thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total RF wave power absorbed by the fast (suprathermal) ion population of a specified charge state, volume-integrated over the entire plasma and excluding collisional energy exchange between populations.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion-state power is the total electromagnetic-wave energy per unit time deposited into the fast (suprathermal) ion component of a single, specified ion charge state, integrated over the entire plasma volume. It is the charge-state-resolved fast-ion contribution to [ion_state_power](name:ion_state_power), which also includes the thermal population's absorbed wave power; collisional energy exchange between the fast and thermal ion populations is excluded by definition. Fast ions typically absorb RF energy through direct wave-particle resonance mechanisms such as minority-species fundamental resonance or second-harmonic absorption in ion cyclotron resonance heating schemes.

The quantity is the volume integral of the fast-ion absorbed power density $p_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{r})$ for charge state $s$:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},s} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the total plasma volume and $p_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the local deposition rate given by [fast_ion_state_power_density](name:fast_ion_state_power_density).

In RF wave modeling, the local deposition profile is obtained from quasi-linear wave-particle interaction calculations, then integrated over all flux surfaces. Summing over all charge states of a given ion species recovers [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power), the total fast-ion absorbed wave power without charge-state resolution. The toroidal-mode-resolved cumulative variant is available via [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power).

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Power transferred from a coherent electromagnetic wave to fast ions of a specified ion species and charge state, resolved for one toroidal Fourier mode. For flux-surface-resolved use it is the volume-integrated absorbed power inside the chosen magnetic flux surface; at the outer boundary it is the global mode contribution.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode fast-ion state power is the rate at which a coherent electromagnetic wave transfers energy to the fast, suprathermal population of a specified ion species and charge state for one toroidal Fourier mode. The toroidal mode number is the integer index describing variation with toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. When evaluated on a magnetic flux surface, the quantity is cumulative: it is the absorbed power integrated over the plasma volume enclosed by that surface; evaluated at the outermost closed flux surface or plasma boundary, it is the corresponding global contribution from that toroidal mode.

For a flux surface labeled by a radial flux coordinate $\rho$, the cumulative absorbed power for charge state $q$ and toroidal mode $n$ is commonly defined from the local wave-particle power density as:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},q,n}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_{\mathrm{fast},q,n}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fast},q,n}$ is the local volumetric power density transferred from the coherent wave harmonic with toroidal mode number $n$ to fast ions in charge state $q$, and $V(\rho)$ is the volume enclosed by the flux surface labeled by $\rho$. The outer-boundary value gives the total absorbed power in that ion charge state for mode $n$, and summing over toroidal modes gives the total fast-ion state absorbed wave power.

In practice this quantity is obtained from wave absorption and fast-particle modeling, often using the resonant wave-particle interaction between the wave frequency, the particle parallel motion, and cyclotron harmonics. It may also be constrained by integrated RF power balance and by diagnostics sensitive to fast ions, although the decomposition by toroidal mode is normally a modeled quantity rather than a directly measured observable.

Typical values span a wide range depending on launched RF power, coupling, species concentration, charge state, and resonance location. Weakly absorbed modes may contribute less than $10^3$ W, while dominant modes in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas can deposit $10^5$-$10^7$ W into a particular fast-ion charge state.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Absorbed wave power density deposited on fast (non-thermal) ions in a specified charge state, expressed per unit plasma volume. When averaged over a magnetic flux surface, it is the local radial source whose volume integral gives the cumulative absorbed power for that state.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion state power density is the volumetric rate at which wave energy is transferred to the non-thermal ion population in a specified charge state. It is a charge-state-resolved component of [fast_ion_power_density](name:fast_ion_power_density) and is distinct from heating of the thermal-ion population represented by [thermal_ion_power_density](name:thermal_ion_power_density).

For nested magnetic flux surfaces labeled by a dimensionless radial label $\rho$, the flux-surface-averaged density is

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast},c}(\rho) = \frac{1}{V'(\rho)} \int_{S(\rho)} \frac{q_{\mathrm{fast},c}(\mathbf{x})}{|\nabla \rho|} \, dA
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fast},c}$ is this power density in W m^-3, $c$ denotes the charge state, $q_{\mathrm{fast},c}$ is the local wave-to-fast-ion energy-transfer density in W m^-3, $S(\rho)$ is the magnetic flux surface, $dA$ is the area element in m^2, $|\nabla\rho|$ has units m^-1, and $V'(\rho)$ is the differential volume in m^3 per unit $\rho$. Integrating $p_{\mathrm{fast},c}(\rho)V'(\rho)$ from the magnetic axis to a chosen surface gives [fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:fast_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface) in W.

In practice, this quantity is computed from wave absorption or energy-balance modeling that partitions deposited wave power among ion species, charge states, and thermal or fast components. Inputs typically include wave fields, resonance physics, the fast-ion distribution, charge-state populations, equilibrium geometry, and collisional energy exchange; no particular reconstruction or heating code is implied.

Typical flux-surface-averaged magnitudes are 10^3-10^6 W m^-3 for charge-state-resolved fast-ion wave heating in present tokamaks. Strongly localized resonant absorption can approach 10^7 W m^-3, while regions with little matching fast-ion population are near 0 W m^-3.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from the wave field to fast ions in the specified charge state.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_state_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Absorbed coherent radio-frequency wave power density deposited on the fast, nonthermal ion population of a specified charge state, decomposed by toroidal Fourier mode number. It resolves charge-state-specific fast-ion wave absorption harmonic by harmonic, expressed per unit plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode fast-ion-state power density is the absorbed coherent radio-frequency wave power, per unit plasma volume, deposited on a fast (nonthermal) ion population of a specified charge state and attributed to a single toroidal Fourier harmonic of the wave field. It isolates how much each toroidal mode contributes to the energization of that particular fast-ion charge-state population.

The mode-resolved components sum to the total absorbed power density on that fast-ion charge state:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},s} = \sum_{n} P_{\mathrm{fast},s,n}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast},s,n}$ is this mode-resolved power density for charge state $s$ and toroidal mode number $n$, and $P_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the corresponding total absorbed power density for that charge state, both in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$. Summing instead over all charge states of the species recovers the species-level mode-resolved [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power_density).

The quantity is obtained from coherent-wave absorption calculations that expand the electromagnetic field into toroidal harmonics and evaluate the wave-particle energy exchange with the fast-ion distribution function for each charge state. Resolving by charge state is important in multi-species or impurity-laden plasmas, where distinct charge states absorb on different toroidal harmonics at the same location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net coherent-wave electromagnetic energy is transferred from the wave field to the specified fast-ion charge-state population for that toroidal harmonic.

NAMES.name: left_hand_circularly_polarized_electric_field
NAMES.short: Left-hand circularly polarized electric field is the complex E+ component of a radio-frequency electric field perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field. With the exp(-i omega t) phasor convention, its real field co-rotates with positive-ion gyromotion about the magnetic-field direction.
NAMES.long:
The left-hand circularly polarized electric field $E_+$ is the complex scalar component of a radio-frequency wave electric field perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$. It represents the polarization that co-rotates with positive-ion gyromotion about $\mathbf{B}_0$ and is the ion-cyclotron left-hand component under the phasor convention stated below.

Use a local right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame with $\hat{z}$ parallel to $\mathbf{B}_0$ and perpendicular axes chosen so that $\hat{x} \times \hat{y} = \hat{z}$. For complex amplitudes defined by $\mathbf{E}(t)=\Re\{\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\exp(-i\omega t)\}$, the left-hand component is

$$
E_+ = \frac{\tilde{E}_x + i\tilde{E}_y}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

where $\tilde{E}_x$ and $\tilde{E}_y$ are complex perpendicular electric-field amplitudes in V m^-1, $E_+$ is in V m^-1, $i$ is the imaginary unit, and $\omega$ is the angular frequency. With this convention, a pure real positive $E_+$ rotates from $+\hat{x}$ toward $-\hat{y}$ when viewed along $+\hat{z}$ as time increases, matching positive-ion cyclotron rotation.

In practice, $E_+$ is obtained by determining the complex radio-frequency electric field, projecting it onto the plane perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}_0$, and applying the circular-polarization projection above. Its absolute phase depends on the chosen radio-frequency phase reference, while $|E_+|$, relative phase, and the real and imaginary parts characterize the physically relevant polarization. The complementary component is [right_hand_circularly_polarized_electric_field](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_electric_field); the magnitude, real part, and imaginary part are represented by [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude), [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part), and [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part).

Typical magnitudes in ion-cyclotron-range heating studies are roughly $10^2-10^5$ V m^-1 in the confined plasma and can be larger close to antennas or material boundaries. The complex value has no universal upper bound; values near zero indicate weak left-hand polarization or cancelation of the perpendicular field components.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the zero-phase instantaneous perpendicular electric field of a pure $E_+$ wave points along $+\hat{x}$ and subsequently rotates toward $-\hat{y}$ in the local right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame with $\hat{z}$ parallel to $\mathbf{B}_0$.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_left_hand_circularly_polarized_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex left-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field component for a single toroidal Fourier mode, averaged over a flux surface with power-deposition-density weighting. Its modulus is the amplitude and its argument is the phase; m^-1.V denotes volts per meter.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the complex phasor of the left-hand circularly polarized perpendicular electric-field component for one toroidal mode number $n_\phi$. It has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ (volts per meter), not a fraction or normalized ratio. The modulus is the associated [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field amplitude](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude), and the argument is the phase of the same complex component.

For a power-deposition-weighted flux-surface average at radial flux label $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, the defining value may be written as:

$$
\left\langle E_{+,n_\phi}\right\rangle_p(\rho)=\frac{\int_{\Sigma(\rho)} E_{+,n_\phi}(\mathbf{x})\,p_{\mathrm{dep},n_\phi}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mu_\rho}{\int_{\Sigma(\rho)} p_{\mathrm{dep},n_\phi}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mu_\rho}
$$

where $\Sigma(\rho)$ is the flux surface, $p_{\mathrm{dep},n_\phi}$ is the non-negative power deposition density for that mode in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$, and $d\mu_\rho$ is the positive flux-surface integration measure, with units $\mathrm{m^3}$ per unit radial label for a differential-volume average or $\mathrm{m^2}$ for a surface-area average. The phasor convention is that the physical field is the real part of a complex amplitude multiplying $\exp(i n_\phi\phi-i\omega t)$, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. With $\hat{b}$ along the equilibrium magnetic field, $\hat{e}_1=\nabla\rho/|\nabla\rho|$ outward normal to the flux surface, and $\hat{e}_2=\hat{b}\times\hat{e}_1$, the circular component is $E_+=(E_1+iE_2)/\sqrt{2}$.

In practice the value is obtained from radio-frequency full-wave modeling or reconstruction by Fourier resolving the wave field in toroidal angle, projecting the perpendicular field onto the left-hand circular basis, and applying the power-deposition-density weight. If the denominator of the weighted average is zero or numerically negligible, the weighted field is undefined rather than a zero electric field.

Typical magnitudes of $|\left\langle E_{+,n_\phi}\right\rangle_p|$ in ion-cyclotron-range heating calculations are about $10^2-10^5\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ in regions with appreciable deposited power, with larger local values possible close to antennas. The phase is usually reported on a branch such as $(-\pi,\pi]$ rad and depends on the stated phasor and toroidal-mode convention.
NAMES.sign: Positive when, for the phasor dependence $\exp(i n_\phi\phi-i\omega t)$, a real zero-phase value produces an instantaneous electric field in the $+\hat{e}_1$ direction at $\phi=0$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and $t=0$, with $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{b})$ the local right-handed polarization basis.

NAMES.name: left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude
NAMES.short: Modulus of the complex left-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field phasor. It gives the local strength of the E+ polarization component, the component co-rotating with positive-ion gyromotion and relevant to ion-cyclotron wave interaction.
NAMES.long:
The left-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field amplitude is the magnitude of the complex $E_+$ phasor. In the Stix polarization basis defined perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field, $E_+$ is the component that co-rotates with positive-ion gyromotion and therefore measures the ion-cyclotron-resonant electric-field strength.

The amplitude is defined from the real and imaginary parts of the complex phasor by

$$
|E_+| = \sqrt{\left[\operatorname{Re}(E_+)\right]^2 + \left[\operatorname{Im}(E_+)\right]^2}
$$
