where $E_+$, $\operatorname{Re}(E_+)$, and $\operatorname{Im}(E_+)$ are electric-field quantities in V/m. The modulus is independent of the arbitrary phasor phase and is non-negative.

In full-wave or ray-based ion-cyclotron heating calculations, $|E_+|$ is computed from the solved wave electric field after projection onto the circular polarization basis. When the wave field is expanded in toroidal Fourier harmonics in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height, the same phasor definition applies to each harmonic and may be evaluated in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed $\phi$; in beam- or ray-tracing descriptions it may instead be evaluated along the propagation path.

Typical ion-cyclotron-range wave-field amplitudes in tokamak plasmas are about 10^2-10^4 V/m locally, with larger edge or near-antenna values possible depending on launched power, coupling, density, damping, and resonance location.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_electric_field_amplitude
NAMES.short: Amplitude of the complex RF wave electric-field phasor projected along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. It is the non-negative parallel field strength for a coherent harmonic, independent of the RF phase.
NAMES.long:
The parallel wave electric-field amplitude is the magnitude of the complex RF electric-field phasor projected along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. It characterizes the strength of the wave field parallel to magnetic field lines for a coherent harmonic, not the signed instantaneous electric field. It is the amplitude counterpart of [parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part) and [parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), and the wave analog of [parallel_electric_field](name:parallel_electric_field).

For a coherent harmonic labeled by toroidal mode number $n_\phi$, the defining projection is

$$
E_{\parallel,\mathrm{amp}}(n_\phi) = \left| \tilde{\mathbf{E}}_{n_\phi} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} \right|
$$

where $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}_{n_\phi}$ is the complex electric-field phasor for that harmonic, $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the equilibrium magnetic field, and $n_\phi$ labels variation with toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The modulus removes the RF phase, while the real and imaginary parts retain the phase-resolved phasor components.

In RF wave-heating analysis, this quantity is computed from full-wave, beam-tracing, or ray-tracing solutions by resolving the coherent harmonic, projecting the complex electric field onto $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, and taking the modulus. A local value uses this pointwise projection; a flux-surface representative value for heating studies is obtained by averaging this amplitude over the flux surface with local RF power-deposition density as the weight, so regions contributing most to absorption contribute most strongly to the reported parallel field strength.

The parallel component is important for electron Landau damping and other wave-particle interactions that depend on electric field along the equilibrium magnetic field. For megawatt-class RF heating calculations, representative amplitudes are strongly normalization-dependent but commonly span about $10^2-10^5$ V m$^{-1}$ when scaled to the launched wave power; much smaller values can occur where the parallel projection is symmetry-suppressed.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Power-deposition-weighted flux-surface average of the phase-resolved left-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field phasor for one toroidal mode number. Its phase is referenced to the chosen zero-phase toroidal location and is represented on the (-pi, pi] branch.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the left-hand circularly polarized component of the RF wave electric-field phasor for a single toroidal mode number, averaged over a magnetic flux surface with local absorbed power density as the weight. It describes the non-axisymmetric wave field seen by the plasma and complements the right-hand circular and parallel components needed to reconstruct the wave polarization state.

For toroidal mode number $n$, the weighted flux-surface average is

$$
\overline{E}_{+,n}(\rho)=\frac{\left\langle p_{\mathrm{abs},n}\,E_{+,n}\right\rangle_{\rho}}{\left\langle p_{\mathrm{abs},n}\right\rangle_{\rho}},\qquad E_{+,n}=A_{+,n}\exp(i\varphi_{+,n}),\quad \varphi_{+,n}\in(-\pi,\pi]
$$

where $\rho$ is the explicitly chosen flux-surface label, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rho}$ is a flux-surface average on that surface, $p_{\mathrm{abs},n}$ is the absorbed power density for the same toroidal mode in W m$^{-3}$, $E_{+,n}$ and $\overline{E}_{+,n}$ are electric-field phasors in V m$^{-1}$, $A_{+,n}$ is the local amplitude in V m$^{-1}$, and $\varphi_{+,n}$ is the local phase angle in radians. The toroidal Fourier dependence is referenced to $\phi=0$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and phase angles are reduced to the principal branch $(-\pi,\pi]$.

In practice, this quantity is computed from a full-wave or ray-based RF solution by decomposing the perpendicular electric field into circular polarization components relative to the local magnetic-field direction, selecting one toroidal Fourier harmonic, and applying the absorbed-power weighting on each flux surface. The weighting emphasizes regions where the wave-plasma interaction actually deposits energy, so the result is not a simple geometric average of the field over the surface. The left-hand component is useful for polarization balance, mode conversion, and consistency checks; it should not be identified by itself as the primary ion-cyclotron resonant component without specifying the species, harmonic, propagation direction, and polarization convention.

Typical magnitudes in ion-cyclotron-range heating calculations are about $10^2$-$10^5$ V m$^{-1}$ near the plasma edge and antenna-facing region, and about $10$-$10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ in strongly damped core regions. The phase normally spans the selected branch $(-\pi,\pi]$ and can vary rapidly near cutoffs, mode-conversion layers, and absorption peaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the phasor phase of $\overline{E}_{+,n}$ leads the chosen zero-phase reference after reduction to the $(-\pi,\pi]$ branch.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Amplitude of the right-hand circularly polarized E-minus component of a radio-frequency wave electric field for one toroidal Fourier mode. It is a local electric-field amplitude used to characterize polarization-dependent wave coupling and absorption.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the local amplitude of the $E^-$ component of an oscillatory electromagnetic wave for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic. It isolates the transverse wave-field component with right-hand circular polarization about the equilibrium magnetic-field direction. The quantity is local in the poloidal plane and is not a flux-surface average.

Let the toroidal dependence be expanded in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters. For harmonic $n$, use a local right-handed field-aligned basis $(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \hat{b})$ with $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ and $\hat{e}_1\times\hat{e}_2=\hat{b}$; with wave phasors proportional to $e^{i n\phi-i\omega t}$, the $E^-$ amplitude is:

$$
E_{-,n}(R,Z)=\left|\frac{E_{1,n}(R,Z)-iE_{2,n}(R,Z)}{\sqrt{2}}\right|
$$

where $E_{1,n}$ and $E_{2,n}$ are the complex transverse electric-field components of harmonic $n$, each in V m$^{-1}$; $n$ is the dimensionless toroidal mode number; $\omega$ is angular frequency in rad s$^{-1}$; and $E_{-,n}$ has units V m$^{-1}$. The minus projection $(E_{1,n}-iE_{2,n})/\sqrt{2}$ defines the right-hand circular $E^-$ basis convention, and this quantity is the magnitude of that complex component, not its phase.

In practice, $E_{-,n}$ is usually obtained from frequency-domain wave calculations of the launched antenna spectrum using the equilibrium magnetic field, plasma density, temperature, and species composition. Experimental constraints are indirect and can come from radio-frequency field probes, antenna loading, deposited-power estimates, fast-ion response, and comparison with inferred absorption patterns.

Typical amplitudes in ion-cyclotron-range heating are 10^2-10^4 V m^-1 in the confined plasma and 10^3-10^5 V m^-1 near antennas, edge evanescence regions, or strong resonance layers. Values scale approximately with the square root of launched power for fixed plasma conditions and depend strongly on the toroidal mode spectrum and polarization.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_particle_energy
NAMES.short: Perpendicular fast-particle energy is the non-negative kinetic energy content of the suprathermal particle population associated with motion perpendicular to the local magnetic field. For a gyrotropic fast-particle pressure tensor, it equals the plasma-volume integral of the perpendicular fast-particle pressure.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular fast-particle energy is the volume-integrated kinetic energy of the fast, suprathermal particle population associated with velocity components perpendicular to the local magnetic field. It includes the two perpendicular velocity-space degrees of freedom and excludes the kinetic energy associated with motion parallel to the magnetic field. The value is non-negative and is zero when the plasma volume contains no perpendicular fast-particle pressure.

For a gyrotropic fast-particle pressure tensor, the perpendicular energy is defined by the volume integral of the perpendicular pressure component:

$$
W_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}} = \int_V p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $W_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}$ is in J, $p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [perpendicular fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure) in Pa ($\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$), $dV$ is a volume element in $\mathrm{m^3}$, and $V$ is the plasma volume considered. For the pressure tensor $\mathbf{P}_\mathrm{fast}=p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{b}\mathbf{b})+p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}\mathbf{b}\mathbf{b}$, the total fast-particle energy is $W_\mathrm{fast}=W_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}+W_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}$, with $W_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}=\frac{1}{2}\int_V p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}\,dV$. Thus the isotropic relation $3p/2$ applies to total scalar-pressure energy density, not to the perpendicular component alone.

In practice this quantity is computed from modeled or reconstructed fast-particle distribution functions by taking the perpendicular kinetic-energy moment to obtain $p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}$ and integrating it over the plasma volume. It may include contributions from neutral-beam ions, radio-frequency-heated ions, fusion alpha particles, or other suprathermal species, constrained by fast-particle diagnostics, neutron emission, diamagnetic measurements, and equilibrium pressure balance.

Typical values range from $10^3$-$10^5$ J in low- to moderate-power heated plasmas and $10^5$-$10^7$ J in strongly heated or reactor-scale plasmas. For an isotropic fast-particle distribution, the perpendicular part is about two thirds of the total fast-particle kinetic energy; pitch-angle anisotropy can make this fraction larger or smaller.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Poloidal angle of a beam-tracing ray point, defined geometrically as atan2(Z - Z_axis, R - R_axis) in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It locates the beam in the poloidal plane rather than specifying the propagation direction.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal angle of a beam-tracing beam is the angular position of a ray or beam point in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It is a position coordinate of the beam trace, not a propagation angle or wave-vector pitch, and it complements radial labels such as [poloidal magnetic flux at the same beam-tracing point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_beam_tracing_point).

For a geometric angle centered on the magnetic axis, the defining relation is:

$$
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\left(Z - Z_\mathrm{axis}, R - R_\mathrm{axis}\right)
$$

where $(R,Z)$ is the beam point position, $(R_\mathrm{axis},Z_\mathrm{axis})$ is the magnetic-axis position in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ returns the quadrant-resolved angle from the positive $R$ direction toward positive $Z$. The outboard midplane corresponds to $\theta = 0$.

In beam-tracing calculations, $\theta$ is computed from the propagated ray coordinates or by interpolating an equilibrium coordinate mapping; periodicity is usually handled modulo $2\pi$, with optional unwrapping to keep the trajectory continuous. The coordinate is used to sample equilibrium and wave-plasma quantities along auxiliary-heating beams, including electron-cyclotron and other coherent-wave beam models, and to compare beam position with reference geometry such as the [poloidal angle at a plasma-boundary gap reference point](name:poloidal_angle_at_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point). It should be distinguished from direction-dependent quantities such as the [radial component of normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam].

Typical wrapped values cover 0-6.283 rad: 0 rad on the outboard midplane, about 1.57 rad above the magnetic axis, about 3.14 rad on the inboard side, and about 4.71 rad below the magnetic axis. Unwrapped values can differ by integer multiples of $2\pi$ rad without changing the physical poloidal location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\theta$ increases counterclockwise from the outboard midplane on an $(R,Z)$ poloidal-plane plot with $R$ increasing to the right and $Z$ increasing upward in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam
NAMES.short: Poloidal steering angle of an electron cyclotron beam in the R-Z plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, defined by atan2(-k_Z, -k_R) from the mean wave-vector components. It describes the vertical tilt of the beam relative to inward radial propagation.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal angle of an electron cyclotron beam is the signed steering angle of the beam mean wave vector projected onto the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the vertical tilt of the EC ray or beam relative to an inward radial direction and is used together with launch position and toroidal steering to specify the beam propagation direction.

Using $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ for the quadrant-preserving angle from the positive $x$ axis toward the positive $y$ axis, the poloidal angle is defined by:

$$
\theta_\mathrm{pol} = \operatorname{atan2}(-k_Z, -k_R)
$$

where $k_R$ and $k_Z$ are the radial and vertical components of the beam mean wave vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, typically expressed in rad m$^{-1}$. With this definition, $\theta_\mathrm{pol}$ is measured from the inward radial direction $-\hat{R}$ toward the downward vertical direction $-\hat{Z}$.

In practice this angle is obtained from launcher mirror geometry, steering calibration, or ray and beam tracing that reconstructs the mean wave vector at launch or near resonance. It is interpreted together with quantities such as the [toroidal angle of the electron cyclotron beam](name:toroidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam), [vertical coordinate of the electron cyclotron launcher mirror](name:vertical_coordinate_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror), [toroidal angle of the launching position](name:toroidal_angle_of_launching_position), and [launched power of the electron cyclotron antenna]; the poloidal angle influences the resonance interception and power-deposition location, but those also depend on the magnetic equilibrium, wave frequency, polarization, and plasma profiles.

For near-radial injection the value is close to 0 rad; larger absolute values indicate stronger poloidal tilt. The principal-value output of $\operatorname{atan2}$ lies in the interval $-\pi$ to $\pi$ rad, while the operational steering interval is set by the launcher design and is usually narrower.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the beam direction in the poloidal plane is rotated from the inward radial direction $-\hat{R}$ toward the downward direction $-\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radius_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: A radial distance from the symmetry axis of an ICRH antenna strap conductor to one of its cylindrical boundary surfaces, encompassing both the inner and outer conductor radii of an annular cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The radius of an antenna strap is a geometric length characterizing the cylindrical cross-sectional profile of an ion cyclotron range-of-frequencies (ICRH) antenna strap conductor, measured from the conductor's symmetry axis to a specified boundary surface. For an annular conductor cross-section, two distinct radii are physically relevant and independently defined: the [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap), bounding the hollow interior of the conductor, and the [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap), at the outer conductor wall.

These radial dimensions are geometric input parameters for electromagnetic and mechanical modeling of the ICRH antenna assembly. The conductor wall thickness equals the difference between the outer and inner radii, and together with the [width](name:width_of_antenna_strap) and [thickness](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap) of the strap, the radial boundary values fully specify the cross-sectional geometry used in RF coupling calculations and thermal-mechanical stress analyzes. At typical ICRH frequencies, skin-depth effects confine RF current to a thin surface layer, making the precise radial boundaries relevant to the strap's distributed resistance and inductance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial distance is measured outward from the conductor symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap, measured from the strap conductor axis to the inner cylindrical boundary of the conductor.
NAMES.long:
Inner radius of an antenna strap is the radial distance from the local strap conductor axis to the inner cylindrical surface of an annular strap cross-section. It applies to hollow or tubular ICRH strap conductors; straps with solid rectangular or otherwise non-annular cross-sections do not have this quantity. In a strap-local right-handed cylindrical $(r_s, \varphi_s, z_s)$ frame, $z_s$ follows the strap centerline or long current-carrying direction and $r_s$ is measured perpendicular to that axis.

The inner radius is the distance from the strap axis to the inner wall of the annulus:

$$
r_\mathrm{inner} = \left|\mathbf{x}_\perp - \mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_\perp$ is a point on the inner cylindrical boundary in a cross-section normal to the strap axis, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}$ is the corresponding point on the strap centerline, and both positions are expressed in meters.

This quantity is obtained from antenna mechanical design, CAD geometry, or direct metrology of the conductor cross-section. Together with [outer_radius_of_antenna_strap](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap), it determines the annular conducting area, $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2-r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, and the wall thickness, $r_\mathrm{outer}-r_\mathrm{inner}$, which are important for cooling-channel design, RF current distribution, and impedance modeling at ion-cyclotron frequencies.

Typical ICRH tubular copper strap inner radii are about 0.005-0.03 m, depending on RF power, cooling requirements, and mechanical constraints. Larger high-power antenna conductors may use somewhat larger inner radii to reduce hydraulic resistance and thermal loading.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Outer radial boundary of the annular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor, defining the larger of the two radii that bound the conductor annulus.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius of an ICRH antenna strap is the radial distance from the central axis of the strap conductor to the outer cylindrical surface of the annular cross-section. It marks the external boundary of the conductor material and, together with the [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap), fully specifies the radial extent of the annular conductor.

For an annular cross-section, the radial conductor wall thickness follows $\Delta r = r_\mathrm{out} - r_\mathrm{in}$, where $r_\mathrm{out}$ is the outer radius and $r_\mathrm{in}$ is the inner radius. The nominal centerline radius reported by [radius_of_antenna_strap](name:radius_of_antenna_strap) is the mean $(r_\mathrm{out} + r_\mathrm{in})/2$.

This geometric parameter enters electromagnetic wave-coupling calculations and RF impedance modeling for ion cyclotron resonance heating systems. Together with the [width](name:width_of_antenna_strap), [height](name:height_of_antenna_strap), and [thickness](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap) of the conductor, it provides the complete geometric description needed for antenna strap simulations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured radially outward from the strap conductor axis.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Thermal electron power is the total coherent-wave power absorbed by the bulk thermal electron population, integrated over the plasma volume. It excludes power deposited in fast electrons, ions, or other channels.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron power is the volume-integrated rate at which a coherent electromagnetic wave transfers energy to the bulk thermal electron population. It represents the thermal-electron heating channel of wave absorption and excludes absorption assigned to fast electrons, ions, or other particle populations.

The quantity is defined as the volume integral of the local thermal-electron wave power density:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{th}} = \int_V p_{e,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the total thermal electron power in W, $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the local power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which absorption is evaluated.

In practice this power is inferred from wave-heating power balance, electron energy balance, heating modulation, or wave-absorption calculations constrained by launched power, transmission, reflection, and measured plasma conditions. It is a channel-resolved absorbed power, so consistency with the total absorbed wave power requires summing over all absorbing populations and accounting for unabsorbed or lost wave power.

Typical values range from near 0 W when thermal-electron absorption is weak to 10^4-10^7 W in many wave-heated tokamak plasmas, with values of several 10^7 W possible in high-power heating scenarios. The value depends on launched wave power, coupling efficiency, wave frequency, plasma density and temperature, magnetic configuration, and competing absorption by ions or fast particles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coherent wave transfers net energy to the bulk thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Cumulative wave power absorbed by the thermal electron population from a coherent wave inside a flux surface, resolved per toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long:
The thermal electron power per toroidal mode number quantifies the wave energy deposition rate into the bulk Maxwellian electron population attributed to a single toroidal harmonic $n_\phi$ of a coherent wave's spectrum. When evaluated as a cumulative (volume-integrated) quantity inside a given flux surface, it reveals the radial deposition profile contributed by each toroidal harmonic to thermal electron heating.

The cumulative absorbed power from toroidal mode $n_\phi$ inside the flux surface at normalized radial coordinate $\rho$ is:

$$
P_{\rm th,e}(n_\phi, \rho) = \int_0^\rho p_{\rm th,e}(n_\phi, \rho') \, dV'
$$

where $p_{\rm th,e}(n_\phi, \rho')$ is the [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density) and $dV'$ is the differential plasma volume element.

Summing over all toroidal mode numbers $n_\phi$ recovers the total [thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), whose global limit is the parent quantity [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_power). This quantity is computed from full-wave or ray/beam-tracing models of RF wave propagation and absorption, where quasilinear wave–particle interaction determines how each toroidal harmonic deposits power into the thermal electrons. The analogous mode-resolved quantities for other species are [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power) and [per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_power).
NAMES.sign: Positive when net wave power flows from the coherent wave field into the thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric coherent-wave power density absorbed by the thermal (bulk) electron population. It is the local rate of wave energy deposition into bulk electrons per unit plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron power density is the time-averaged volumetric rate at which a coherent wave transfers energy to the bulk thermal electron population. It represents electron heating by wave absorption, distinct from power deposited directly into ions, fast particles, or other nonthermal populations.

For a monochromatic wave, with physical fields written using peak-amplitude phasors as $\mathbf{E}(t)=\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}e^{-i\omega t}]$ and $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}(t)=\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathrm{th},e}e^{-i\omega t}]$, the cycle-averaged absorbed power density is

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},e}=\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}(t)\cdot\mathbf{E}(t)\right\rangle_t = \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathrm{th},e}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{E}}^{*}\right]
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},e}$ is in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the wave electric field in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},e}$ is the induced current density associated with thermal electrons in A m$^{-2}$, $\omega$ is the angular frequency, $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes an average over a wave period, and $^{*}$ denotes complex conjugation. If rms phasor amplitudes are used instead of peak amplitudes, the factor $1/2$ is omitted.

The cumulative thermal-electron wave power inside a plasma volume is the volume integral of this local density, $P_{\mathrm{th},e}(V)=\int_V p_{\mathrm{th},e}\,dV$. For a volume bounded by a flux surface, this relation connects the local deposition density to [thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

In practice this quantity is computed from wave-field solutions and the electron response used to evaluate absorption, or inferred indirectly by constraining heating models with electron temperature, density, radiated-power, and power-balance measurements. Its spatial distribution depends on wave frequency, polarization, propagation, resonance or damping conditions, and the local electron distribution.

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. Volume-averaged auxiliary wave heating is often of order $10^{4}$-$10^{6}$ W m$^{-3}$, while localized deposition regions can reach $10^{6}$-$10^{8}$ W m$^{-3}$ in high-power heating scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when wave energy is transferred from the coherent wave field to the thermal (bulk) electron population.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Power per unit volume absorbed from a coherent wave by the bulk thermal electron population, resolved by toroidal mode number. It can represent either a local value or a magnetic-surface-averaged value, with the same volumetric normalization.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal electron power density is the coherent-wave power absorbed per unit physical volume by the bulk thermal electron population in a single toroidal harmonic. It may be evaluated as a local volumetric density or as a magnetic-surface-averaged volumetric density; in both cases the quantity represents power density, not total power.

For toroidal mode number $n$, the volumetric definition and the corresponding enclosed power are:

$$
p_{e,n}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{dP_{e,n}}{dV}(\mathbf{x}), \qquad P_{e,n}(V) = \int_V p_{e,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $p_{e,n}$ is this power density in W m$^{-3}$, $P_{e,n}$ is the power in W deposited into thermal electrons by mode number $n$, $V$ is a physical volume, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position, and $dV$ is the volume element. Summing over all represented toroidal mode numbers gives the total thermal-electron absorbed power density, $p_e = \sum_n p_{e,n}$, and integration over an enclosed volume gives the corresponding [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power).

In practice this quantity is computed from wave-field solutions or wave energy-balance models by partitioning absorbed power by receiving species and by toroidal harmonic. It is usually constrained indirectly through electron-temperature evolution, stored-energy changes, and consistency with the launched coherent-wave power rather than measured as a pointwise observable.

Typical per-mode values span about 10$^2$-10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$, depending on launched power, absorption localization, plasma density and temperature, and the number of toroidal modes carrying the wave power. Magnetic-surface-averaged values are generally lower than peak local values when absorption is spatially localized.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net coherent-wave energy is deposited into the bulk thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total RF wave power absorbed by the bulk Maxwellian (thermal) ion population from a coherent wave, volume-integrated over the entire plasma.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion power is the net rate at which a coherent RF wave deposits energy into the bulk Maxwellian ion distribution, integrated over the entire plasma volume. As the thermal ion-channel component of [ion_power](name:ion_power), it isolates wave energy transferred directly to the thermal bulk, distinct from absorption by suprathermal populations captured by [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power).

The absorbed power follows from the volume integral of the wave–plasma energy coupling:

$$
P_{\rm th,i} = \frac{1}{2} \int_V \mathrm{Re}\!\left(\mathbf{J}_{\rm th,i}^* \cdot \mathbf{E}\right) dV
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\rm th,i}$ is the thermal ion current density driven by the coherent wave electric field $\mathbf{E}$, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

Full-wave or ray-tracing codes that incorporate the Maxwellian ion dielectric response (via the plasma dispersion function) are used to evaluate this quantity. Together with [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_power), [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power), and [fast_electron_power](name:fast_electron_power), it partitions absorbed_power across all plasma populations. In ion cyclotron resonance heating, the fraction directed to the thermal bulk versus fast minority ions depends on the resonance harmonic, minority concentration, and wave polarization at the resonance layer. The spatially resolved volumetric deposition per toroidal mode is described by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density).

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative coherent-wave power absorbed by bulk thermal ions inside a flux surface, resolved by toroidal mode number. It is the toroidal-mode spectrum of thermal-ion heating.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal-ion power is the cumulative rate at which a coherent wave transfers energy to the bulk thermal ion population for a single toroidal Fourier mode. The toroidal mode number labels Fourier structure in the toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; it is not a cyclotron resonance harmonic order.

For a closed flux surface labeled by a radial surface label $\rho$, the cumulative power for ion species $i$ and toroidal mode $n$ is the volume integral of the corresponding local absorbed power density:

$$
P_{i,n}(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} p_{i,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{i,n}$ is the cumulative absorbed power in W, $p_{i,n}$ is the [per-toroidal-mode thermal-ion power density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density) in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, and $V(\rho)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the selected flux surface. Summing $P_{i,n}$ over toroidal mode number gives the corresponding [thermal-ion power inside the flux surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface) in W.

This quantity is usually computed from coherent-wave heating calculations by decomposing the wave field or absorbed power density into toroidal Fourier modes and integrating the wave-particle energy transfer over the chosen plasma volume. Experimentally it is inferred indirectly through consistency between wave coupling, ion heating, power balance, and equilibrium or transport analysis rather than measured as a separate direct observable.

Typical per-mode values range from near 0 W for weakly coupled modes to $10^3$-$10^7$ W for strongly absorbed radio-frequency heating in medium and large tokamaks. The sum over modes is bounded by the absorbed wave power available to thermal ions and can vary strongly with species composition, resonance location, wave spectrum, and plasma temperature.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electromagnetic wave energy is absorbed by the bulk thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volumetric absorbed wave power density deposited into the bulk Maxwellian ion population by coherent wave-particle interaction, summed over toroidal modes unless a mode-resolved quantity is specified.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion power density is the local rate per unit volume at which a coherent electromagnetic wave transfers energy to the bulk Maxwellian ion population. It excludes energy deposited directly into fast ions or electrons and represents the total thermal-ion absorption associated with the wave; for a toroidal-mode decomposition, summing the mode-resolved contributions gives this quantity.

The local time-averaged absorption can be written in a quasi-linear Poynting-theorem form as

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},i}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_n \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},i,n}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{E}_n^*(\mathbf{x})\right]
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},i}$ is the thermal ion power density, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode index in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, $\mathbf{E}_n$ is the complex wave electric-field amplitude, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},i,n}$ is the induced current associated with the thermal ion response, $^*$ denotes complex conjugation, and $\mathrm{Re}$ denotes the real part. A positive value corresponds to conversion of wave energy into thermal ion internal energy.

In practice it is computed from coherent-wave fields and the thermal ion dielectric or damping response, including resonant wave-particle interactions, finite-Larmor-radius effects, and the relevant ion composition. Integrating this density over a plasma volume gives the corresponding [thermal_ion_power](name:thermal_ion_power), while integration inside a magnetic flux surface gives [thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface). Charge-state-resolved deposition is represented by [thermal_ion_state_power_density](name:thermal_ion_state_power_density), and toroidal-mode-resolved deposition by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density).

Typical values in RF-heated tokamak plasmas are about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ for broadly distributed thermal-ion absorption, with localized ion-cyclotron resonance layers or strong single-pass damping reaching $10^6$-$10^8$ W m$^{-3}$. Values can be much smaller away from resonant layers or when most wave power is absorbed by electrons or fast ions.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Absorbed coherent-wave power density deposited in bulk thermal ions, resolved by toroidal mode number. It may be local or magnetic-surface averaged under the stated spatial convention; summing modes gives the total thermal-ion absorbed power density.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal-ion power density is the volumetric rate at which one toroidal Fourier component of a coherent wave deposits energy in the bulk thermal ion population. The mode number $n_\phi$ labels variation with toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity can represent either a pointwise deposition density or a flux-surface-averaged density over a thin magnetic-surface shell.

The density is defined as the differential absorbed modal power per unit plasma volume:

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{dP_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}}{dV}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}$ is the coherent-wave power absorbed by bulk thermal ions from toroidal mode $n_\phi$, $dV$ is a plasma volume element, and $\mathbf{x}$ denotes either a spatial position or the magnetic-surface label after averaging. Thus $p_{\mathrm{th},i,n_\phi}$ has units W m$^{-3}$; integrating it over a chosen plasma volume gives [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power), while summing over toroidal modes gives [thermal_ion_power_density](name:thermal_ion_power_density).

In practice this quantity is computed from the mode-resolved wave field and the thermal-ion part of the wave-particle energy balance or dielectric response. For a local convention, the value applies at the specified point; for a flux-surface-averaged convention, it is the shell-volume average whose product with shell volume gives the shell contribution to the absorbed power. The corresponding electron quantities are [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power_density) and, after volume integration, [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_power); ion-state resolution is represented by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density).

Typical magnitudes range from $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in heated plasma cores, with localized resonance or damping regions reaching about $10^7$ W m$^{-3}$ in high-power scenarios and values near zero where the selected toroidal mode is weakly absorbed.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net coherent-wave energy is transferred to the bulk thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total power from a coherent electromagnetic wave absorbed by the thermal bulk ion population in a specified charge state, integrated over the plasma volume and summed over all toroidal mode numbers.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion state power is the net rate at which a coherent electromagnetic wave transfers energy to the thermal, or bulk, ions of one specified ion charge state. It excludes power absorbed by electrons, other ion charge states, and non-thermal energetic-ion populations, and represents the sum over all toroidal mode numbers.

For a mode-decomposed wave field, the total thermal ion state power is defined by the mode-sum volume integral:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q} = \sum_n \int_V p_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q}$ is the total absorbed power for ion species $i$ in charge state $q$, $p_{\mathrm{th},i}^{q,n}$ is the local power-density transfer from toroidal mode number $n$ to that thermal ion state, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which absorption is evaluated. The single-mode contribution corresponds to [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power).

In practice this quantity is computed from wave-field and plasma-response calculations by integrating the deposited power density for the selected ion charge state and summing the mode contributions. It may be constrained experimentally by total launched and coupled wave power, calorimetry or power-balance analysis, and changes in ion temperature, but the charge-state-resolved partition is generally model dependent.

Typical magnitudes for an actively heated thermal ion charge state range from 10^3-10^7 W in present magnetic-confinement experiments, with weakly coupled charge states near 0 W and high-power scenarios reaching 10^7-10^8 W.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from the coherent electromagnetic wave to the thermal ion population of the specified charge state.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by a specified thermal ion species and charge state from one toroidal Fourier harmonic of a coherent wave. It is volume-integrated over the region enclosed by a magnetic flux surface; at the outer boundary it is the global contribution of that mode to charge-state-resolved ion heating.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal ion state power is the coherent-wave power absorbed by the thermal population of a specified ion species and charge state for one toroidal mode number. For an interior magnetic flux surface, it is a cumulative volume integral over the plasma region enclosed by that surface; at the outer boundary it is the total absorbed power for that charge state and mode. The toroidal mode number is the integer harmonic in a Fourier decomposition with respect to the toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For a magnetic flux surface $S$, the cumulative contribution of mode $n$ can be written as

$$
P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(S) = \int_{V(S)} p^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}$ is the absorbed power in W, $p^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}$ is the local absorbed power density in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$, $V(S)$ is the volume enclosed by $S$, $a$ labels the ion species, $z$ labels the charge state, and $n$ is dimensionless. Summing over toroidal mode numbers gives the total charge-state-resolved thermal ion power, $P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z}(S)=\sum_n P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(S)$, while summing over the relevant ion species and charge states gives the aggregate per-mode thermal ion power, $P^{\mathrm{th}}_{\mathrm{i},n}(S)=\sum_{a,z} P^{\mathrm{th}}_{a,z,n}(S)$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from coherent-wave absorption calculations, using local wave fields and thermal ion distribution functions to evaluate the absorbed power density before integrating over the enclosed volume. It may be constrained or checked against global power balance, charge-state composition, and diagnostics sensitive to ion heating, but it is fundamentally a mode-resolved deposition quantity rather than a directly local thermodynamic state variable.

Typical values for an individual charge-state and toroidal-mode contribution range from near 0 W for weakly coupled modes or nonresonant charge states to $10^3$-$10^7$ W in strongly heated plasmas. The sum over modes and charge states is bounded by the coherent-wave power coupled to the plasma and by losses to other particle populations or damping channels.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net wave energy is transferred from the coherent wave field to the specified thermal ion charge state.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric coherent-wave power density absorbed by the thermal (bulk) ion population of a specified charge state, distinguishing bulk-ion heating from fast-particle wave absorption at the same charge state.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the local rate of wave energy deposition per unit plasma volume into the thermal ion population of one specified charge state from a coherent electromagnetic wave, such as an ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) wave. It is the thermal-ion, charge-state-resolved component of the total ion-state power density, separating bulk-ion absorption from the suprathermal contribution captured by [fast_ion_state_power_density](name:fast_ion_state_power_density).

The local absorbed power density for thermal ions in charge state $q$ is:

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},q} = \frac{1}{2} \, \mathrm{Re}\!\left(\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{J}^{*}_{\mathrm{th},q}\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the complex wave electric field amplitude and $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{th},q}$ is the complex current density response of the thermal ions in charge state $q$.

Summing over all charge states of a given species yields the species-level quantity [thermal_ion_power_density](name:thermal_ion_power_density). Volume-integrating over the region enclosed by a given flux surface gives the cumulative absorbed power [thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface](name:thermal_ion_state_power_at_inside_flux_surface), and the toroidal-mode-resolved form is available as [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density). The quantity is computed from full-wave or ray-tracing wave propagation solvers coupled to a kinetic description of the bulk ion distribution.

In ICRH scenarios, bulk thermal-ion absorption power densities near the fundamental or harmonic cyclotron resonance layer reach 0.1–10 MW m$^{-3}$, with the partition between thermal and fast ions depending on the minority heating scheme and local ion temperature.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Absorbed coherent-wave power density deposited on a specified thermal ion charge state, separated by toroidal mode number. It is the volumetric counterpart of per-mode charge-state thermal-ion power; summing over modes gives the total charge-state thermal-ion power density.
NAMES.long:
Per-toroidal-mode thermal ion state power density is the volumetric rate at which a coherent wave deposits energy into a specified charge state of the thermal ion population, resolved by toroidal harmonic. The toroidal mode number $n_\phi$ labels the Fourier harmonic of the wave field in the toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the density counterpart of [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_state_power).

The per-mode deposited power density can be expressed as the wave-period-averaged electromagnetic work done on the charge-state current response by that harmonic:

$$
p_{i,s,n_\phi}(\mathbf{x}) = \left\langle \mathbf{J}_{i,s,n_\phi}(\mathbf{x},t) \cdot \mathbf{E}_{n_\phi}(\mathbf{x},t) \right\rangle_t
$$

where $p_{i,s,n_\phi}$ is in W m^-3, $s$ labels the ion charge state, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{E}_{n_\phi}$ is the electric field of harmonic $n_\phi$ in V m^-1, $\mathbf{J}_{i,s,n_\phi}$ is the associated thermal-ion charge-state current density in A m^-2, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_t$ denotes averaging over the wave period. The total charge-state thermal-ion power density is $p_{i,s}=\sum_{n_\phi} p_{i,s,n_\phi}$; integrating $p_{i,s,n_\phi}$ over a chosen plasma volume gives the corresponding per-mode charge-state thermal-ion power.

In practice, this quantity is computed from coherent-wave field solutions by separating the field into toroidal harmonics, evaluating resonant and collisional damping on the thermal ion distribution for each charge state, and assigning the resulting energy transfer to the local or flux-surface-averaged volumetric source term. Summing over charge states gives the thermal-ion per-mode power density, while analogous source terms describe fast-ion and thermal-electron absorption.

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. Values are near 0 W m^-3 outside absorbing regions and can reach order 10^3-10^7 W m^-3 in localized radio-frequency absorption regions; individual toroidal harmonics are usually smaller than the mode-summed charge-state value.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electromagnetic work by the coherent wave increases the thermal energy of the specified ion charge state.

NAMES.name: wave_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Oscillatory magnetic-field perturbation carried by a coherent electromagnetic wave propagating in a magnetized plasma, as computed in full-wave simulations of RF heating and current-drive systems.
NAMES.long:
The wave magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_w$ is the oscillatory magnetic component of a coherent electromagnetic wave — such as those used in electron cyclotron, ion cyclotron, or lower-hybrid heating and current drive — propagating within a magnetized plasma. It represents a small perturbation superimposed on the much larger equilibrium confinement field $\mathbf{B}_0$ that provides plasma confinement.

In full-wave treatment of plasma-wave interactions, $\mathbf{B}_w$ is related to the wave electric field $\mathbf{E}_w$ through Faraday's induction law:

$$
\mathbf{B}_w = -\frac{1}{i\omega} \nabla \times \mathbf{E}_w
$$

where $\omega$ is the angular wave frequency. The field is decomposed in field-aligned coordinates into three projections: the component parallel to the local equilibrium field (see [parallel_wave_magnetic_field](name:parallel_wave_magnetic_field)), a component normal to the local flux surface, and a binormal component.

Full-wave simulations compute $\mathbf{B}_w$ by solving Maxwell's equations self-consistently with the plasma dielectric tensor on a spatial grid covering the plasma volume. Together with the wave electric field, $\mathbf{B}_w$ determines electromagnetic power flow via the Poynting vector $\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{E}_w \times \mathbf{B}_w / \mu_0$, where $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space; this Poynting flux is closely related to [toroidal_wave_electric_field](name:toroidal_wave_electric_field) for toroidally propagating modes. Typical wave magnetic field amplitudes in RF heating scenarios satisfy $|\mathbf{B}_w| / B_0 \ll 1$, commonly in the range $10^{-4}$–$10^{-2}$ in the plasma core.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Signed scalar projection of the electromagnetic wave magnetic-field perturbation along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. It is a field component in tesla, not a magnitude, RMS amplitude, or unspecified complex phasor; real- or imaginary-part quantities are named explicitly.
NAMES.long:
Parallel wave magnetic field is the field-aligned component of the magnetic perturbation associated with an electromagnetic wave in a magnetized plasma. Parallel means along the local equilibrium magnetic field, not necessarily along the wave vector or any coordinate direction. The quantity is a signed component of the physical perturbation field.

The signed component is defined by projecting the wave magnetic-field perturbation onto the local equilibrium field direction:

$$
B_{\parallel,\mathrm{w}} = \delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{w}} \cdot \hat{b}_0
$$

where $B_{\parallel,\mathrm{w}}$ is in tesla, $\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{w}}$ is the wave magnetic-field perturbation in tesla, and $\hat{b}_0 = \mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$.

Frequency-domain wave fields are often represented by a complex phasor with physical field convention $\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{w}}(t)=\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathrm{w}}\exp(-i\omega t)]$. Under such a convention, explicitly named real-part or imaginary-part quantities refer to components of the phasor; this unqualified quantity denotes the signed physical parallel component and should not be interpreted as $|\tilde{B}_{\parallel,\mathrm{w}}|$, an RMS value, or a polarization-normalized amplitude.

In practice, it is obtained from electromagnetic wave calculations or phase-sensitive magnetic measurements by resolving the perturbation along $\hat{b}_0$ determined from the equilibrium magnetic field. It characterizes field-aligned wave polarization and complements normal magnetic-field projections such as [wave_magnetic_field](name:wave_magnetic_field); analogous electric-field projections include [parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part) and [parallel_electric_field](name:parallel_electric_field).

Representative magnitudes in linear auxiliary-heating wave calculations are often $10^{-7}$-$10^{-3}$ T in the confined plasma, with values scaling with the source or launched-power normalization and potentially larger in near-field regions. Because this is a signed component, it can pass through zero and reverse sign with wave phase or polarization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{w}}$ has a component in the direction of the local equilibrium magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}_0$.

NAMES.name: gyrocenter_frequency
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short: Angular velocity vector of a charged-particle gyrocenter orbit in a magnetized plasma, with toroidal and poloidal components giving the rates of gyrocenter advance in their respective angular coordinates.
NAMES.long:
The gyrocenter frequency vector characterizes how rapidly a charged particle's guiding center advances angularly in the confining magnetic geometry, after averaging over the fast cyclotron gyration to isolate the slower drift and bounce or transit dynamics relevant to transport and stability.

The vector decomposes into two principal angular components. The [toroidal gyrocenter frequency](name:toroidal_gyrocenter_frequency) $\dot{\phi}_{gc} = d\phi_{gc}/dt$ is the rate of change of the gyrocenter toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical height. The [poloidal gyrocenter frequency](name:poloidal_gyrocenter_frequency) $\dot{\theta}_{gc} = d\theta_{gc}/dt$ is the rate of advance in poloidal angle $\theta$ as measured in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho$ is a radial flux-surface label. The two components have qualitatively different characters: passing particles circulate continuously in the poloidal direction, while trapped particles bounce and primarily precess toroidally.

These frequencies are computed in gyrokinetic codes from the guiding-center orbit equations derived from the gyrocenter Hamiltonian, and may be averaged over the particle distribution function to yield population-representative angular velocities. They enter directly into the calculation of resonance conditions for wave-particle interactions and neoclassical transport coefficients.
NAMES.sign: Positive toroidal component when the gyrocenter advances in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$; positive poloidal component when the gyrocenter advances in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_gyrocenter_frequency
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the gyrocenter orbit angular frequency, equal to the signed rate of gyrocenter advance in poloidal angle theta in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
The poloidal gyrocenter frequency is the poloidal component of gyrocenter orbit angular frequency in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. It describes the slow drift-orbit advance of the gyrocenter after the rapid cyclotron gyromotion has been averaged out, and is the poloidal counterpart of [toroidal_gyrocenter_frequency](name:toroidal_gyrocenter_frequency).

The instantaneous frequency is defined by the rate of change of the gyrocenter poloidal angle:

$$
\omega_\theta = \frac{d\theta_\mathrm{gc}}{dt}
$$

where $\theta_\mathrm{gc}$ is the gyrocenter poloidal angle in radians, $t$ is time in seconds, and $\omega_\theta$ has units rad s$^{-1}$.

In kinetic or orbit-following calculations, $d\theta_\mathrm{gc}/dt$ is obtained from the gyrocenter equations of motion using the magnetic geometry and the particle phase-space coordinates. If an ensemble- or distribution-weighted frequency is required, a normalized phase-space average over a region $\Gamma$ may be written inline as $\langle\omega_\theta\rangle_f = \int_\Gamma \dot{\theta}_\mathrm{gc} f\,d\Gamma / \int_\Gamma f\,d\Gamma$, where $f$ is the particle distribution function and $d\Gamma$ is the corresponding phase-space volume element.

Typical magnitudes for thermal ions in magnetically confined plasmas are about $10^3-10^6$ rad s$^{-1}$. Electrons or energetic particles can have larger magnitudes, while the signed value can pass through zero near orbit turning, resonance, or stagnation conditions; the value depends on particle charge, mass, energy, pitch, magnetic-field strength, and flux-surface geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the gyrocenter advances in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_gyrocenter_frequency
NAMES.subject: gyrocenter
NAMES.short: Toroidal gyrocenter frequency is the toroidal component of a charged particle gyrocenter orbit angular frequency. It is the rate of change, or population-averaged rate of change, of toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal gyrocenter frequency is the toroidal component of the angular frequency of a charged particle gyrocenter trajectory after the rapid cyclotron motion has been averaged out. It describes how quickly the gyrocenter advances or precesses around the torus in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. For trapped particles it is commonly interpreted as a toroidal precession frequency; for passing particles it represents the average toroidal advance rate along the orbit.

For a population of gyrocenters, the distribution-weighted toroidal gyrocenter frequency is

$$
\omega_\phi = \left\langle \dot{\phi}_{\mathrm{gc}} \right\rangle_f = \frac{\int f(\mathbf{Z})\,\dot{\phi}_{\mathrm{gc}}(\mathbf{Z})\,d\Gamma}{\int f(\mathbf{Z})\,d\Gamma}
$$

where $f$ is the gyrocenter distribution function, $\mathbf{Z}$ denotes gyrocenter phase-space coordinates, $d\Gamma$ is the phase-space volume element, and $\dot{\phi}_{\mathrm{gc}} = d\phi/dt$ is the toroidal angular velocity along a gyrocenter trajectory, with $\phi$ in radians and $t$ in seconds.

In practice, $\dot{\phi}_{\mathrm{gc}}$ is obtained from the gyrocenter equations of motion using the magnetic geometry, electric field, particle species, charge, energy, pitch, and position. Orbit-following or gyrokinetic calculations may average this rate over bounce, transit, ensemble, or distribution weights depending on the physical population being represented. Together with [poloidal_gyrocenter_frequency](name:poloidal_gyrocenter_frequency), it gives the angular-frequency components associated with the gyrocenter orbit; the combined vector quantity is [gyrocenter_frequency](name:gyrocenter_frequency).

Typical magnitudes span about $10^3-10^6$ rad.s^-1 for thermal-ion gyrocenters in medium-size tokamaks, with trapped-particle toroidal precession often in the $10^3-10^5$ rad.s^-1 range. Passing energetic ions and electrons can have larger toroidal advance rates, reaching $10^6-10^8$ rad.s^-1 depending on energy and magnetic-field strength.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the gyrocenter advances in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Net conventional electric current delivered by the plasma to one divertor target surface, integrated over the wetted strike zone.
NAMES.long:
Current at a divertor target is the net conventional electric current delivered to one divertor target by charged particles crossing the plasma sheath and striking the wetted strike zone. It is a surface-integrated signed charge flux, not a local current density, and represents the per-target contribution to the divertor and wall-current balance.

For a local target surface normal chosen from the plasma toward the material surface, the sheath-edge current integrated over the wetted area can be written as:

$$
I_{\mathrm{div,target}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wet}}} \left(j_{i,n} - j_{e,n}\right)\,dA
$$

where $j_{i,n}$ is the ion conventional-current density normal to the target surface in A m$^{-2}$, $j_{e,n}$ is the magnitude of the electron collection current density normal to the target surface in A m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is the differential target area in m$^2$, and $A_{\mathrm{wet}}$ is the wetted strike-zone area in m$^2$. The resulting integrated current is in A; the electron term is subtracted because electrons moving from the plasma to the target carry conventional current opposite to their particle motion.

The current may be measured with embedded Langmuir probes, segmented target current shunts, or Rogowski-coil arrangements around target structures, and may also be inferred from sheath models using local target plasma conditions such as [electron density at divertor target](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target) and [electron temperature at divertor target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target). It is closely related to deposited divertor power because the same sheath and strike-zone conditions govern both charge and energy fluxes, as represented by [power at divertor target](name:deposited_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_halo_current) and [power of divertor].

For an electrically floating target in steady conditions, the net integrated current is expected to be near 0 A because ion and electron current contributions balance through the sheath. Non-zero values occur with target biasing, transient edge events, current-sharing between conducting structures, or disruption halo-current phases; the single-target value is not the total plasma current $I_p$ but may be assessed relative to $|I_p|$ when evaluating global current closure. No device-independent numerical range is implied, because the magnitude depends strongly on target geometry, electrical connection, plasma regime, and transient scenario.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net conventional current flows from the plasma into the divertor target surface.

NAMES.name: current_of_divertor
NAMES.short: Total net electric current carried by charged particles striking the divertor assembly, summed over all divertor target surfaces. It is positive for conventional current into the material and can be negative when the electron contribution dominates.
NAMES.long:
Current of a divertor is the net electric current delivered to the divertor by incident charged particles. It represents the charge transport associated with ions and electrons striking the plasma-facing divertor targets, summed over all relevant target surfaces.

The net incident current can be expressed as a surface integral of the signed particle charge flux:

$$
I_\mathrm{div} = \int_{A_\mathrm{div}} \sum_s q_s\,\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{mat}\, dA
$$

where $A_\mathrm{div}$ is the union of divertor target surfaces, $q_s$ is the signed charge of species $s$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s$ is the incident particle flux density of that species, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{mat}$ is the local unit normal directed from the plasma-facing side into the material.

In practice this current may be inferred from embedded target current sensors, biased divertor circuits, Langmuir-probe measurements combined with sheath models, or plasma-edge simulations that integrate ion and electron fluxes over the target surfaces. Care is needed to distinguish the net signed current from separate ion and electron current components, which can be much larger before cancelation.

Typical net summed currents are often near 0 A for electrically floating, quasi-ambipolar target conditions. During biased operation, strong sheath asymmetry, detachment transients, or disruption-related wall loading, absolute values from 1-10000 A can occur, with larger values possible in large devices or off-normal events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net conventional current carried by incident charged particles is directed from the plasma into the divertor material.

NAMES.name: current_of_divertor_tile
NAMES.short: Net electric current flowing from the plasma across the electrostatic sheath onto the plasma-facing surface of an individual divertor tile.
NAMES.long:
The current of a divertor tile is the net electric current flowing from the plasma across the electrostatic sheath onto the plasma-facing surface of a single tile. It provides tile-resolved resolution of the current distribution across the divertor strike zone, complementing the target-integrated quantity [current_at_divertor_target](name:current_at_divertor_target).

The tile current integrates the local net sheath current density $j_s$ over the plasma-facing tile area $A_\mathrm{tile}$:

$$
I_\mathrm{tile} = \int_{A_\mathrm{tile}} j_s \, dA
$$

where $j_s$ depends on the local ion saturation current density, the tile-to-plasma sheath potential, and the local [electron temperature at the divertor target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target). Dividing by the tile area, available from [surface_area_of_divertor_tile](name:surface_area_of_divertor_tile), converts this quantity to a mean incident current density.

Tile currents are measured using isolated tile circuits or embedded Langmuir probes whose signals are routed through the mechanical tile support structure, enabling time-resolved acquisition during plasma operation including transient ELM events.

Summing contributions from all tiles on a given target recovers [current_at_divertor_target](name:current_at_divertor_target), and summing over all targets gives [current_of_divertor](name:current_of_divertor). Tile-level current data are used to diagnose thermoelectric current loops, local erosion hot spots, and strike-zone asymmetries driven by 3D magnetic perturbations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net electric current flows from the plasma onto the tile surface.

NAMES.name: density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Local number density of a given plasma species in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target surface; for ionic species the density is summed over all ionization stages, and neutral atoms are excluded.
NAMES.long:
The number density of a plasma species at the divertor target quantifies the local particle count per unit volume in the thin plasma layer immediately upstream of the electrostatic sheath entrance at the plasma-material interface. This parent quantity abstracts over species-specific children covering electrons, fuel ions such as [deuterium_density_at_divertor_target](name:deuterium_density_at_divertor_target), helium ash, low-Z wall materials such as [beryllium_density_at_divertor_target](name:beryllium_density_at_divertor_target), and noble-gas seeding impurities. For all ionic children the density is summed over all positive charge states and excludes neutral atoms; [electron_density_at_divertor_target](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target) is treated as a separate species.

Near-target densities are inferred by Langmuir-probe arrays for the electron species and by spectroscopic line-ratio analysis combined with multi-fluid edge-transport simulations for ion species. Quasi-neutrality provides a cross-species consistency constraint: the sum of species ion densities weighted by their respective charge numbers must equal the local electron density. The [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) aggregates all ion species contributions without charge-state weighting.

Near-target electron densities range from roughly $10^{19}$ to $10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$, increasing from the low-recycling to the high-recycling and detached regimes; individual ion-species densities depend on fuel mix, impurity seeding fraction, and plasma-facing-material composition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when particles of the specified species are present in the plasma at the divertor target.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local non-negative number density of beryllium ions at the divertor target, summed over Be1+ through Be4+ charge states and excluding neutral beryllium atoms.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium density at the divertor target is the local number of beryllium ions per unit volume in the plasma adjacent to the divertor target surface. It is a species-resolved, non-negative scalar density for atomic number 4 and excludes neutral beryllium unless a separate neutral-density quantity is specified.

When individual charge states are not represented separately, the ion density is the sum over the bound-electron charge states of beryllium ions:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{tgt}} = \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{tgt}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{tgt}}$ is the beryllium ion number density at the divertor target, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{tgt}}$ is the partial number density in m$^{-3}$ of ions in charge state Be$^{q+}$, and $q$ is the charge-state index; an ion in charge state $q$ carries charge $+q e$, with $e$ the elementary charge. The neutral state Be$^{0}$ is not included in this sum.

In practice this quantity is inferred from beryllium line emission together with atomic population modeling, from impurity transport modeling constrained by edge and divertor measurements, or from edge-plasma simulations that evolve species-resolved ion densities. It is a beryllium-specific component of the local divertor-target ion population and should be interpreted relative to [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) when assessing impurity concentration.

Typical absolute values are strongly dependent on wall material, erosion and recycling conditions, ionization balance, and divertor plasma state, so no device-independent numerical range is implied by the definition. Under trace-impurity conditions $n_{\mathrm{Be},\mathrm{tgt}}$ is much smaller than the total target ion density; in all cases it is constrained to be non-negative and not larger than the local total ion density. Related beryllium-density quantities include [beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary), [beryllium_density_at_limiter](name:beryllium_density_at_limiter), [volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density), and [line_averaged_beryllium_density](name:line_averaged_beryllium_density).

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Number density of carbon ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target surface, summed over charge states C+ through C6+. Neutral carbon atoms and molecules are excluded unless a neutral-inclusive quantity is explicitly specified.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at a divertor target is the local number density of carbon ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target surface. It is a charge-state-summed impurity ion density, so neutral carbon atoms and molecules are treated as separate species and are not included.

The charge-state-summed carbon ion density is obtained by summing over the ionization stages of carbon:

$$
n_{C,\mathrm{ion}} = \sum_{q=1}^{6} n_{C^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{C,\mathrm{ion}}$ is the total carbon ion density in m^-3, $n_{C^{q+}}$ is the density of carbon ions in charge state $q$ in m^-3, and $q$ is the dimensionless positive ion charge state ranging from $1$ up to the nuclear charge $6$.

This density is commonly inferred from divertor spectroscopy of carbon emission lines combined with local electron density and temperature estimates and a collisional-radiative model, or evolved per charge state in edge-plasma transport calculations and then summed.

Typical values near divertor targets span a wide range depending on plasma-facing material composition, recycling regime, and detachment state, and are generally a fraction of the local total ion density.

NAMES.name: deposited_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_halo_current
NAMES.short: Power deposited on a single divertor target by the halo-current component crossing the target surface. It is the current-driven halo contribution to target loading.
NAMES.long:
Deposited power at a divertor target due to halo current is the rate at which electrical work associated with halo current crossing a single target surface is converted to energy in that target. Halo current denotes current in the edge or scrape-off-layer plasma that closes through conducting plasma-facing structures; this quantity isolates that current-driven contribution from conducted, convected, radiative, neutral, and recombination heat loads.

For a resolved target surface, the deposited halo-current power can be written as the surface integral of normal halo-current density times the local plasma-to-target potential drop:

$$
P_{\mathrm{halo},t} = \int_{A_t} j_{\mathrm{halo},\perp}(\mathbf{r})\,\Delta\Phi_t(\mathbf{r})\,dA
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{halo},t}$ is in W, $A_t$ is the wetted area of the target surface, $j_{\mathrm{halo},\perp}$ is the halo-current density normal to that surface in A m$^{-2}$, positive for conventional current from the plasma into the target, $\Delta\Phi_t = \Phi_{\mathrm{plasma}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the local plasma-to-target potential drop in V, and $dA$ is a surface area element in m$^2$.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by combining the halo-current incident on the target with the relevant potential drop, or by separating the halo-current part from the total current-driven target power. The associated surface-integrated current is the halo-current contribution to [current_at_divertor_target](name:current_at_divertor_target); the corresponding current-driven target power is related to [power_at_divertor_target](name:deposited_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_halo_current), and target contributions combine in divertor power accounting such as power_of_divertor.

Typical values are approximately 0 W when no halo current intercepts the target. During transients with halo current closing through plasma-facing structures, finite values are strongly device-, geometry-, and event-dependent and can range from small corrections to values comparable with the total current-driven power on that target.
NAMES.sign: Positive when conventional halo current crosses from the plasma into the target across a positive plasma-to-target potential drop, so the integrated electrical work deposits net energy in the target material.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target. It is the species-resolved fuel-ion population at the plasma-material interface in deuterium-fueled operation.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density at the divertor target is the local number density of deuterium ions, usually singly ionized $D^+$, in the plasma next to a divertor target surface. It is a species-resolved ion density, distinct from the species-agnostic [density at divertor target](name:density_at_divertor_target) and from [total ion density at divertor target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target), which sums over all ion species present.

For a small volume element adjacent to the target, the deuterium ion density is defined by the local particle population per unit volume:

$$
n_D = \frac{dN_D}{dV}
$$

where $N_D$ is the number of deuterium ions in the volume element $dV$ and $n_D$ is the corresponding number density.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from local divertor plasma measurements and modeling, such as target-region probe analysis, spectroscopic interpretation of deuterium emission, or divertor Thomson scattering when available. The inferred value depends strongly on recycling, ionization balance, cross-field transport, sheath-edge conditions, and whether the divertor is attached, partially detached, or detached.

Typical values are about $10^{18}-10^{20}$ m^-3 in attached divertor conditions and can reach $10^{20}-10^{21}$ m^-3 in high-recycling or detached divertor conditions, depending on fueling, target heat flux, and divertor geometry.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Number density at a divertor target of an effective single ion species representing a deuterium-tritium plasma mixture with mean mass 2.5 amu.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium-tritium density at the divertor target is the number density of the effective DT ion constituent in the plasma adjacent to a divertor target surface. The constituent is a fictitious single species with mean ion mass 2.5 amu, used to represent a combined deuterium-tritium ion population; it is distinct from neutral atomic or molecular density.

When separate deuterium and tritium ion populations are replaced by this effective constituent, the target density represents the combined DT ion population and contributes to the [total ion density at the divertor target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) together with any other ion species and impurities. It is analogous to [deuterium density at the divertor target](name:deuterium_density_at_divertor_target), but for the DT pseudo-species rather than a pure deuterium ion constituent.

Target values are computed directly in edge-plasma models or inferred from target diagnostics through sheath models. A common approximate relation for singly charged ions is the Bohm-sheath ion-saturation current density:

$$
j_{\mathrm{sat}} \simeq e\, n_{\mathrm{DT}}\, c_s
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{sat}}$ is the ion saturation current density in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $e$ is the elementary charge in C, $n_{\mathrm{DT}}$ is the effective DT ion density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, and $c_s$ is the ion sound speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. If $c_s$ is evaluated from electron and ion temperatures, $T_e$ and $T_i$ must be used consistently as temperature energies, commonly in eV with the conversion to joules included in the sound-speed expression.

Typical magnitudes are highly scenario dependent because the target plasma changes with recycling, detachment, magnetic geometry, and strike-point conditions.
