As a broad order-of-magnitude guide for tokamak divertor modeling, effective DT target ion densities may span about $10^{18}-10^{21}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$; this range is contextual rather than a validity bound.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Effective charge (Zeff) of the plasma evaluated at the divertor target, a dimensionless composite indicator of impurity content equal to unity for a pure hydrogen plasma and rising above unity as high-charge impurity species accumulate.
NAMES.long:
The effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ characterizes the multi-species ion composition at the divertor target by weighting each ion species by the square of its charge number, normalized to the electron density. It reflects the local impurity content arising from sputtering of plasma-facing components, deliberate impurity seeding for power exhaust control, and recycling processes at the divertor surface.

The quantity is defined under quasi-neutrality by:

$$
Z_\text{eff} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$ with charge number $Z_s$, and $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$ is the electron number density enforced by quasi-neutrality. High-$Z$ impurities contribute disproportionately: a trace fraction of [iron_density_at_divertor_target](name:iron_density_at_divertor_target) or [argon_density_at_divertor_target](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target) raises $Z_\text{eff}$ far more than an equivalent density of [hydrogen_density_at_divertor_target](name:hydrogen_density_at_divertor_target).

$Z_\text{eff}$ at the divertor is inferred from spectroscopic impurity line emission or from the Bremsstrahlung continuum, whose volumetric emissivity scales as $n_e^2 Z_\text{eff}$. Impurity seeding enhances radiative power dissipation in detachment scenarios, thereby reducing the [peak_power_density_at_divertor_target](name:peak_power_density_at_divertor_target). This is the effective-charge component of the charge_at_divertor_target family.

Typical values range from 1 for a pure hydrogen plasma to 2–8 in seeded or erosion-dominated divertor conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when at least one ion species with nonzero charge number is present in the plasma, as the numerator $\sum_s n_s Z_s^2$ and denominator $n_e$ are both positive under quasi-neutrality, ensuring $Z_\text{eff} \geq 1$.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density in the plasma immediately adjacent to the divertor target surface. It is the downstream scrape-off-layer electron density at the target and is distinct from the electron density at the plasma boundary or separatrix.
NAMES.long:
Electron density at the divertor target is the local number of free electrons per unit volume in the plasma adjacent to the plasma-facing target, usually interpreted as a sheath-entrance or near-target plasma density rather than a property inside the solid surface. It characterizes downstream scrape-off-layer conditions at the material boundary and should not be identified with the separatrix value [electron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:electron_density_at_plasma_boundary), which is evaluated upstream at the plasma boundary.

As a local number density it is defined by

$$
n_{e,t} = \left.\frac{dN_e}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{target}}
$$

where $N_e$ is the number of free electrons in a small plasma volume $V$ adjacent to the target and $n_{e,t}$ is expressed in m$^{-3}$.

In practice, $n_{e,t}$ is obtained from near-target diagnostics and edge-plasma modeling. Flush or embedded Langmuir probes infer it from ion-saturation current using sheath assumptions, effective ion mass, and local electron and ion temperatures; divertor Thomson scattering and spectroscopic analysis can provide independent constraints where available. Reduced two-point scrape-off-layer estimates may infer $n_{e,t}$ from upstream or separatrix conditions and target temperature using quasineutrality and parallel pressure or momentum balance, but the coefficient relating upstream and target quantities depends on ion temperature, Mach number, sheath boundary conditions, volumetric momentum losses, radiation, recycling, and detachment state. Therefore a fixed electron-only pressure-balance factor is not a general definition; in such formulas both $n_{e,t}$ and any upstream density $n_{e,u}$ are electron number densities in m$^{-3}$.

Typical values are about $10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in sheath-limited or attached divertor conditions and $10^{20}$-$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ in high-recycling conditions. During detachment, the near-target density may rise before rollover and then decrease as the ionization front moves away from the target, so the range is strongly dependent on fueling, magnetic geometry, and power exhaust regime.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target. It is summed over the singly ionized and fully stripped (doubly ionized) helium-3 charge states and excludes neutral helium-3 atoms.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 density at the divertor target is the local number density of ionized helium with mass number 3 in the plasma next to the material target surface. It accounts for the helium-3 ion population per unit volume and excludes neutral helium-3 atoms.

Helium-3 has atomic number 2, so its accessible positive charge states are the singly ionized state and the fully stripped doubly ionized state. The ion density is the sum over these two charge states:

$$
n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He},\,\mathrm{ion}} = n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He}^{+}} + n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He}^{2+}}
$$

where $n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He}^{+}}$ is the singly ionized helium-3 density, $n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He}^{2+}}$ is the fully stripped helium-3 density, and $n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He},\,\mathrm{ion}}$ is the total ion density, all in m^-3. The neutral density $n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He}^{0}}$ is not part of this quantity.

In practice this density is inferred from diagnostics or modeling that can distinguish helium-3 from other ion species and separate ionized helium from neutral helium. Common approaches include isotope-resolved spectroscopy interpreted with atomic physics models, mass-sensitive particle measurements where available, and edge or divertor transport analysis tied to local electron density and species composition.

The value is strongly scenario dependent: without deliberate helium-3 fueling it may be negligible or below diagnostic sensitivity, whereas in helium-3 fueled or seeded divertor plasmas it becomes a significant fraction of the local ion inventory.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-4 ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target. It is summed over all helium-4 ionization charge states up to fully ionized helium and excludes neutral helium atoms.
NAMES.long:
Helium-4 density at a divertor target is the local number density of ionized helium-4 in the plasma next to a plasma-facing divertor surface. It represents the charge-state-summed helium-4 ion population at that location, excluding neutral helium atoms, and is relevant to helium ash accumulation and exhaust.

The charge-state-summed density is defined as the sum over ionized charge states:

$$
n_{\mathrm{He4,target}} = \sum_{q=1}^{2} n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He}^{q+},\mathrm{target}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{He4,target}}$ is the helium-4 ion density in m^-3, $q$ is the ion charge state, $q=1$ is singly ionized helium-4, $q=2$ is fully ionized helium-4, and each charge-state density $n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He}^{q+},\mathrm{target}}$ is in m^-3. The neutral state $q=0$ is not included.

In practice this quantity is inferred from measurements and analysis sensitive to helium ion populations near the divertor target, together with local plasma conditions and atomic-physics interpretation. It is commonly compared with upstream or global helium-4 measures such as [helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density), and with the total ion population [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target).

Typical order-of-magnitude values can span $10^{16}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3, from trace helium concentrations to helium-rich divertor conditions. The value depends strongly on helium source rate, ionization balance, recycling, pumping, parallel transport, and divertor plasma density.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen ions evaluated locally in the plasma adjacent to the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogen density at the divertor target is the local number density of hydrogen ions in the plasma immediately adjacent to the target surface. It represents the hydrogen contribution to the ion population that enters the divertor sheath and participates in recycling, ionization balance, and target particle loading.

For an attached sheath-limited target, the hydrogen ion particle flux to the surface is often related to the local density by the Bohm sheath estimate:

$$
\Gamma_H \simeq n_H c_s
$$

where $n_H$ is the hydrogen ion density in m$^{-3}$, $\Gamma_H$ is the hydrogen ion particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $c_s$ is the ion sound speed at the sheath entrance in m s$^{-1}$. In collisional or detached conditions, the same density may require a more detailed treatment of ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and flow between the plasma and the material surface.

This quantity is usually inferred rather than measured directly. Langmuir probes can constrain local electron density and ion saturation current, spectroscopy can constrain hydrogen emission and ionization sources through collisional-radiative analysis, and edge plasma modeling combines these observations with particle-balance assumptions to separate the hydrogen ion contribution from other ion species.

A universal numerical range is not intrinsic to the quantity because divertor target density varies strongly with machine size, fueling, detachment state, impurity seeding, and isotope mix. In hydrogen-dominated, singly ionized target plasma, $n_H$ is typically of the same order as the local [electron density](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target); in mixed-species plasmas it is the hydrogen component of the local [ion density] and is reduced by deuterium, tritium, helium, or impurity dilution.

NAMES.name: ion_fluence_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Cumulative ion particle dose delivered to a divertor target surface over a specified time interval. It is the time integral of the incident normal ion particle flux density, summed over all ion species and charge states, with each ion counted once as a particle.
NAMES.long:
Ion fluence at a divertor target is the cumulative number of ions crossing into a unit area of the plasma-facing target surface during a specified exposure interval. It is a local surface dose summed over all ion species and charge states unless a species-qualified quantity is specified, and each ion is counted once as a particle rather than weighted by charge.

For a target-surface point $\mathbf{x}_s$ and interval $[t_0,t_1]$, the ion fluence $\Phi_\mathrm{ion}$ is defined by:

$$
\Phi_\mathrm{ion}(\mathbf{x}_s; t_0,t_1) = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \sum_{\alpha}\sum_z \Gamma_{\alpha z,\perp}^{\mathrm{inc}}(\mathbf{x}_s,t)\,dt
$$

where $\Phi_\mathrm{ion}$ has unit m^-2, $\Gamma_{\alpha z,\perp}^{\mathrm{inc}}$ is the incident normal particle flux density in m^-2 s^-1 for ion species $\alpha$ and charge state $z$, and $t_0$ and $t_1$ bound the accumulation interval. The value is zero at $t_0$ by convention for that interval, includes only ions incident during the interval, and adds linearly over successive intervals.

In practice, local target fluence is often obtained by time-integrating a measured or reconstructed incident ion flux density. Embedded or surface Langmuir probes can provide an ion saturation current density, but conversion to particle fluence requires assumptions or corrections for effective charge state, collection area, magnetic-field incidence angle, sheath transmission, secondary emission, and the probe interpretation model. Integrated divertor particle-transport calculations or particle balance estimates can also provide the incident flux density when direct measurements are unavailable.

Typical local fluences in present tokamak discharges are about $10^{21}$-$10^{25}$ m^-2 for a single plasma exposure, with the lower end in weakly wetted or detached regions and the upper end near sustained strike-point or high-recycling conditions. Multi-pulse or campaign-integrated exposure of a fixed target location can accumulate $10^{26}$-$10^{30}$ m^-2.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions cross the divertor target surface from the plasma into the material.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Number density of iron ions at the divertor target, summed over all ionization stages, providing a local measure of this high-Z metallic impurity from erosion of iron-containing plasma-facing and structural materials.
NAMES.long:
Iron is a high-Z metallic impurity in fusion plasmas, originating from sputtering and erosion of iron-containing structural components and plasma-facing materials. The iron number density at the divertor target represents the total number of iron ions per unit volume at the divertor target location, aggregated over all ionization states $z = 1, \ldots, 26$.

The combined iron density is defined as:

$$
n_\text{Fe} = \sum_{z=1}^{26} n_{\text{Fe}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\text{Fe}^{z+}}$ is the local density of iron ions in charge state $z$, in m$^{-3}$.

This quantity is a species-resolved component of the broader [density_at_divertor_target](name:density_at_divertor_target), characterizing how much high-Z impurity load reaches the divertor target from the scrape-off layer. Elevated iron concentrations at the divertor target indicate strong erosion or enhanced impurity transport toward the target, and can substantially increase radiated power through iron line emission. The density is inferred from spectroscopic analysis of iron emission lines in the divertor region, combined with collisional-radiative modeling to convert observed line intensities to absolute number densities.

Comparison with [volume_averaged_iron_density](name:volume_averaged_iron_density) reveals the degree of impurity accumulation near the target relative to the bulk plasma, while [iron_density_at_pedestal](name:iron_density_at_pedestal) gives the corresponding local density at the pedestal. Analogous divertor-target densities for other impurity species include [krypton_density_at_divertor_target](name:krypton_density_at_divertor_target), [argon_density_at_divertor_target](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target), and [boron_density_at_divertor_target](name:boron_density_at_divertor_target).

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Number density of krypton ions in the near-target divertor plasma, summed over all krypton charge states unless a specific charge state is identified separately.
NAMES.long:
Krypton density at the divertor target is the local number density of krypton ions in the plasma adjacent to a divertor target. It includes all ionized krypton charge states and excludes neutral krypton atoms unless a neutral density is defined separately. As a number density, it is non-negative.

The charge-state-summed krypton ion density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Kr},t} = \sum_{q=1}^{36} n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+},t}
$$

where $q$ is the krypton charge state, 36 is the atomic number of krypton, and each partial density $n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+},t}$ is in m^-3. The quantity satisfies $0 \le n_{\mathrm{Kr},t}$ and, at a fixed near-target location, is bounded by the part of the [total ion density at the divertor target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) not contributed by non-krypton ion species.

In experiments, this density is inferred mainly from krypton line emission observed near the divertor target, interpreted with collisional-radiative atomic physics using local electron temperature and density. In modeling, it is obtained by summing the charge-state-resolved krypton ion populations from edge, scrape-off-layer, or divertor plasma calculations.

Typical values are 0 m^-3 when krypton is absent or not injected. In seeded divertor scenarios, krypton is usually a trace or minor impurity, so its density is best interpreted as a species fraction of the local [total ion density at the divertor target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target); unusually large fractions indicate impurity accumulation, strong local radiation, or detachment-relevant impurity enrichment. This is the krypton-specific counterpart of the parent [density at divertor target](name:density_at_divertor_target) and is closely related to other seeded noble-gas impurity densities such as [argon density at divertor target](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target) and [xenon density at divertor target](name:xenon_density_at_divertor_target).

NAMES.name: length_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.short: General radial length scale characterizing the spatial variation of a plasma quantity across the scrape-off layer, defined relative to the magnetic separatrix.
NAMES.long:
The scrape-off layer (SOL) is the open-field-line region between the magnetic separatrix and the material wall, where radial length scales quantify how rapidly plasma quantities — heat flux, temperature, density — decay or spread in the direction perpendicular to the separatrix. Specific realizations include the e-folding decay length of a general plasma profile, captured by [decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer), and the Eich-model heat-flux spreading length, captured by heat_length_over_scrape_off_layer.

For a quantity $f$ with exponential radial variation, the characteristic length $\lambda$ is defined by:

$$
f(r) = f_0 \exp\!\left(-\frac{r}{\lambda}\right)
$$

where $r$ is the radial distance from the separatrix measured perpendicular to the flux surface and $f_0$ is the profile value at the separatrix.

These lengths are inferred from radial upstream Thomson scattering or Langmuir probe array profiles, or from divertor target heat-flux profiles unfolded using two-point or Eich-type spreading models. Typical values in medium-sized tokamaks span 1–10 mm, with reactor-scale devices expected at the lower end of this range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the length is measured in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ outward from the separatrix toward the first wall.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Number density of ionized neon immediately adjacent to the divertor target, summed over all neon charge states Ne1+ through Ne10+ and excluding neutral neon atoms.
NAMES.long:
Neon density at the divertor target is the local number density of ionized neon in the plasma directly next to the material target surface. It represents the total population of neon ions over all bound-electron configurations, excluding neutral neon, and is used to quantify impurity content, radiative cooling, and dilution in the divertor plasma.

The total ionized neon density is the sum over neon charge-state densities:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \sum_{q=1}^{10} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}$ is the number density of neon ions with charge $q$ and the upper limit corresponds to fully stripped neon.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity emission measurements combined with atomic-physics modeling, or obtained from edge and divertor plasma simulations that evolve impurity ionization, recombination, radiation, and transport. The ratio to [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) gives the local neon ionic fraction; interpretation is also coupled to local [electron_density_at_divertor_target](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target) and [ion_temperature_at_divertor_target](name:ion_temperature_at_divertor_target).

Typical values range from about $10^{15}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, depending strongly on neon seeding level, divertor detachment state, plasma density, and impurity transport. In trace-seeded attached conditions the value may be far below the main-ion density, while in strongly radiating or detached divertor plasmas it can approach percent-level fractions of the local ion density.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Nitrogen ion number density evaluated at the divertor target.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen ion number density at the divertor target quantifies the local concentration of ionized nitrogen in the plasma immediately adjacent to the divertor plate surface. Nitrogen is commonly seeded as an impurity into the divertor region to enhance radiative power dissipation through atomic line emission, promoting plasma detachment and reducing peak heat loads on the target.

The ion number density $n_\mathrm{N}$ is defined as the zeroth velocity moment of the nitrogen ion velocity distribution:

$$
n_\mathrm{N} = \int f_\mathrm{N}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_\mathrm{N}(\mathbf{v})$ is the nitrogen ion phase-space distribution function and integration is over all velocities $\mathbf{v}$.

This quantity is inferred from optical spectroscopy of nitrogen line emission in the divertor plasma, or from Langmuir probe measurements combined with spectroscopic impurity fraction estimates. It is a key parameter for characterizing impurity seeding scenarios and controlling plasma detachment. Analogous quantities for other seeded impurity species include [neon_density_at_divertor_target](name:neon_density_at_divertor_target), [argon_density_at_divertor_target](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target), [oxygen_density_at_divertor_target](name:oxygen_density_at_divertor_target), and [xenon_density_at_divertor_target](name:xenon_density_at_divertor_target); this quantity is the nitrogen-specific component of the parent [density_at_divertor_target](name:density_at_divertor_target).
NAMES.sign: Positive when nitrogen ions are present at the divertor target.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Local plasma volume number density of oxygen impurity ions adjacent to the divertor target, summed over all ionized oxygen charge states.
NAMES.long:
Oxygen density at the divertor target is the local volume number density of ionized oxygen impurity species in the near-target divertor plasma. It counts oxygen ions by particle number, not by charge density, and excludes neutral oxygen atoms and oxygen retained in or adsorbed on the target material.

The all-charge-state oxygen ion density is defined as the sum of the local charge-state densities:

$$
n_\mathrm{O}^{\mathrm{target}} = \sum_{q=1}^{8} n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{target}}
$$

where $q$ is the oxygen ion charge state, $n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}}^{\mathrm{target}}$ is the local volume number density of oxygen ions in charge state $q$ in m^-3, and $n_\mathrm{O}^{\mathrm{target}}$ is the summed oxygen ion density in m^-3. The neutral state $q=0$ is not included.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from divertor spectroscopy of oxygen emission lines combined with electron temperature, electron density, and collisional-radiative or ionization-balance modeling, or from edge plasma simulations constrained by such measurements. Because different emission lines sample different charge states and plasma conditions, evaluating the all-charge-state sum requires an estimate of the local oxygen charge-state distribution.

Useful value checks are non-negativity and consistency with the local total ion density: $0 \le n_\mathrm{O}^{\mathrm{target}} \le$ [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target). A universal numerical range is not intrinsic to the definition because the value depends strongly on divertor plasma conditions, oxygen sources, and ionization balance; normalized comparisons are often expressed using [oxygen_fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_oxygen_ion_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density). Related oxygen densities at other spatial scopes include [oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density).

NAMES.name: parallel_heat_flux_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Parallel heat flux density incident on a divertor target is the power transported along magnetic field lines toward the target per unit area perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Parallel heat flux at a divertor target is the field-aligned heat-flow density evaluated where scrape-off-layer field lines intersect a plasma-facing target surface. It characterizes how much power is carried along the magnetic field toward the material surface before projection onto the surface normal.

The field-aligned component of the heat-flux vector is

$$
q_\parallel = \mathbf{q}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}$ is the heat-flux vector and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field. The target-normal heat flux is related by a magnetic-incidence projection, commonly $q_n \simeq q_\parallel |\hat{\mathbf{b}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}|$, so $q_\parallel$ is generally larger than the heat flux per unit target surface area when field lines strike the surface at a grazing angle.

In practice it is inferred from divertor target heat-load measurements, such as infrared thermography or embedded calorimetry, combined with surface geometry and magnetic equilibrium reconstruction to de-project the measured target-normal power density along the incident field line. Modeling may compute it from parallel electron and ion conduction, convection, sheath transmission, and volumetric power losses in the scrape-off layer and divertor plasma.

Typical parallel values in present tokamak divertors are about $1\times10^7-1\times10^9$ W m$^{-2}$ during attached or weakly detached operation, with lower values in strongly detached conditions. Because of grazing magnetic incidence, the corresponding target-normal surface heat flux is often smaller by factors of roughly $10-100$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net heat is transported along the incident magnetic-field line from the plasma into the divertor target surface.

NAMES.name: peak_power_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Spatial maximum of the heat flux density deposited on the divertor target surface, equal to the most severe local thermal load per unit area at the point of highest power concentration in the strike zone.
NAMES.long:
The peak power flux density at the divertor target quantifies the maximum local heat load per unit area deposited anywhere on the divertor target surface under a given plasma condition. It is the spatial maximum of the heat flux distribution across the strike zone and governs the thermal stress, erosion rate, and component lifetime of divertor plasma-facing components.

For a heat flux profile $q(\mathbf{x})$ distributed over the target surface, the peak value is:

$$
q_\mathrm{peak} = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S_\mathrm{target}} q(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position on the target surface $S_\mathrm{target}$ and $q$ is the local power per unit area from combined particle and radiation loads.

The spatial heat flux distribution on target tiles is resolved primarily by infrared thermography, with the peak extracted from the measured surface temperature rise and the known surface thermal diffusivity of the tile material. In numerical simulations, the peak is determined as the maximum over the computed deposition profile on the strike zone.

Steady-state peak heat flux values in H-mode operation range from 1-20 MW/m² in present-day devices; reactor design limits for tungsten monoblock divertor components are set near 10 MW/m² for continuous operation, with transient events exceeding steady-state limits by large factors. Analogous peak loads on other plasma-facing surfaces are captured by [peak power density at the limiter](name:peak_power_density_at_limiter), [peak power density at the first wall](name:peak_power_density_at_first_wall), and the device-level [peak power density at the wall](name:peak_power_density_at_wall), while [power at the divertor target due to radiation](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation) quantifies the integrated radiative contribution to the total target heat load.

NAMES.name: power_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Power deposited on a single divertor target by the net electric currents crossing the plasma-sheath interface, carried by ion and electron particle fluxes through the electrostatic sheath and delivered as kinetic and sheath-potential energy.
NAMES.long:
Power at a divertor target is the rate at which charged particles deposit energy on one specified divertor target after crossing the plasma-sheath interface. It is a target-resolved charged-particle power load and excludes radiative, neutral, or purely conductive heat loads unless those contributions are included in the charged-particle heat-flux density being evaluated.

The deposited power is the surface integral of the charged-particle sheath heat-flux density over the material area of that target:

$$
P_t = \int_{A_t} q_{\mathrm{sh}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dA
$$

where $P_t$ is the target power in W, $A_t$ is the target surface area in m^2, $q_{\mathrm{sh}}$ is the charged-particle heat-flux density normal to the target in W m^-2, $\mathbf{x}$ labels position on the target surface, and $dA$ is a surface element in m^2. For non-overlapping targets, the aggregate [power_of_divertor](name:power_of_divertor) is the target sum $P_{\mathrm{div}}=\sum_t P_t$ over the targets included in the divertor definition.

In practice, $P_t$ is obtained by integrating a measured or inferred target heat-flux distribution, commonly from infrared thermography, calorimetry, embedded probes, or edge plasma reconstruction constrained by target measurements. In sheath-physics estimates, $q_{\mathrm{sh}}$ is evaluated from ion and electron particle fluxes $\Gamma_s$ in m^-2 s^-1 and the energy per particle delivered through the sheath; equivalently, species charge-current densities may be written $j_s=Z_s e\Gamma_s$ in A m^-2, where $Z_s$ is charge state and $e$ is the elementary charge in C. A heat-transmission coefficient $\gamma$ is often used as a dimensionless model parameter, with its value depending on sheath assumptions, temperature ratios, secondary-electron emission, collisionality, and magnetic incidence angle; it is not a universal property of the target.

Typical integrated charged-particle power on a single target is about 10^3-10^5 W in small laboratory devices, 10^5-10^7 W in medium and large tokamaks, and can exceed 10^7 W in high-power attached operation. Detached divertor conditions can reduce the charged-particle power reaching the target even when the upstream exhaust power remains large.
NAMES.sign: Positive when charged particles transfer energy from the plasma across the plasma-sheath interface to the divertor target surface.

NAMES.name: neutral_power_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Net power deposited on a single divertor target by incident neutral particles, including contributions from charge-exchange neutrals and volume-recombined ions.
NAMES.long:
Neutral particles reaching the divertor — primarily hydrogen isotopes produced through charge exchange with the edge plasma and through volume recombination — carry both kinetic and potential energy that is released on the target surface upon impact. This quantity gives the net power deposited by all such neutrals on a single divertor target, forming one component of the total per-target heat load alongside the ion and electron contributions.

The net neutral power at the target is the surface integral of the incident neutral energy flux density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{n}} = \int_A \Gamma_{\mathrm{n}}(\mathbf{r})\,\langle E_{\mathrm{n}} \rangle\, dA
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{n}}$ is the incident neutral particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, $\langle E_{\mathrm{n}} \rangle$ is the mean energy per incident neutral in J, and $A$ is the wetted target area in m$^2$.

This quantity is computed from edge transport models that couple fluid plasma equations to Monte Carlo neutral solvers, or estimated by subtracting ion and electron power contributions from calorimetrically measured total heat loads. The neutral power contribution grows most significant under detached divertor conditions, where the recombination front approaches the target and the mechanism quantified by [neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination) dominates. To obtain the neutral power summed over all divertor targets, see [neutral_power_of_divertor](name:neutral_power_of_divertor). The conduction-dominated plasma power channel at the same target is given by [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction).
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles deposit net energy on the target surface, corresponding to power flow directed from the divertor plasma volume toward the target.

NAMES.name: power_at_inner_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Total power deposited on the inner, high-field-side divertor target by all incident energy channels integrated over the wetted strike-zone surface. It represents a surface-integrated load in watts, not a local heat-flux density.
NAMES.long:
Power at the inner divertor target is the total rate at which energy is deposited on the high-field-side divertor target surface. It includes the combined contribution of incident electrons, ions, neutrals, and radiation over the wetted strike-zone area, and represents the integrated thermal load relevant for target heat removal and material limits.

A common definition is the surface integral of the deposited heat-flux density over the wetted inner target area:

$$
P_{\mathrm{inner}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wet,inner}}} q_{\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})\,dA
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{wet,inner}}$ is the part of the inner target receiving plasma or radiative power, $q_{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the total deposited heat-flux density including electron, ion, neutral, and radiative channels, and $dA$ is an element of target surface area.

In practice this power is inferred by integrating measured or modeled target heat-flux distributions from diagnostics such as infrared thermography, calorimetry, embedded thermocouples, and Langmuir-probe measurements, with radiation and neutral contributions estimated from radiation diagnostics or edge-plasma modeling when needed. More specific quantities may isolate a channel, such as [electron power at the inner divertor target](name:electron_power_at_inner_divertor_target), or summarize a time interval, such as [maximum power at the inner divertor target](name:maximum_power_at_inner_divertor_target).

Typical values range from about 10^4-10^6 W in small and medium experiments, 10^6-10^7 W in high-power tokamak operation, and can exceed 10^7 W in reactor-scale scenarios depending on input power, detachment state, radiation fraction, and divertor configuration.

NAMES.name: electron_power_at_inner_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron thermal power deposited on the inner divertor target.
NAMES.long:
Electron power at the inner divertor target is the total rate at which electron thermal energy is deposited on the inner, high-field-side divertor target surface. It is the electron contribution to the deposited target power and is distinct from ion, neutral, radiative, or electromagnetic power contributions.

The deposited electron power is the surface integral of the electron heat-flux density normal to the target and directed into the material:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{inner}} = \int_{A_\mathrm{inner}} q_{e,n}^{\mathrm{dep}} \, dA
$$

where $A_\mathrm{inner}$ is the inner target surface area over which electron heat is deposited, $dA$ is an element of target area in m$^2$, and $q_{e,n}^{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the deposited electron heat-flux density in W m$^{-2}$. If a vector electron heat flux is used, $q_{e,n}^{\mathrm{dep}}$ is its projection onto the unit normal pointing into the target material; only the into-surface electron thermal component is included.

In practice this quantity is obtained by integrating local electron heat-flux estimates over the inner target. Those estimates may come from Langmuir probe measurements with a sheath heat-transmission model, from surface calorimetry or infrared thermography combined with a model that separates the electron channel, or from edge-plasma simulations constrained by divertor diagnostics.

As a deposited power it is reported as a non-negative scalar; 0 W means that no resolved electron thermal power reaches the inner target. Values are strongly device- and scenario-dependent, ranging from near 0 W during highly detached or low-power phases to kilowatt or megawatt scales in powered divertor plasmas. The corresponding outer-target quantity is [electron_power_at_outer_divertor_target](name:electron_power_at_outer_divertor_target), while integrated divertor power balances are described by [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor) and power_of_divertor.

NAMES.name: maximum_power_at_inner_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Maximum power deposited on the inner high-field-side divertor target during a specified time interval. It is a non-negative surface-integrated power in watts, not a local heat-flux density, and supports assessment of target thermal margins.
NAMES.long:
Maximum power at the inner divertor target is the largest total power deposited on the high-field-side divertor target over a specified time interval. It is a non-negative surface integral of deposited heat flux over the wetted target surface, expressed in watts, and is distinct from a local power-flux density expressed in W m^-2.

The maximum deposited power is defined from the time-resolved surface heat-flux distribution as:

$$
P_{\mathrm{inner}}^{\max} = \max_{t \in [t_1,t_2]} \int_{A_{\mathrm{inner}}(t)} q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x}, t)\, dA
$$

where $[t_1,t_2]$ is the time interval of interest, $A_{\mathrm{inner}}(t)$ is the wetted area of the inner divertor target, $dA$ is a surface area element in m^2, and $q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}}$ is the non-negative heat flux deposited through the target surface into the plasma-facing material in W m^-2. The subscript $\perp$ refers to the normal to the material surface; this quantity should not be confused with field-parallel heat flux $q_\parallel$ carried along magnetic field lines before interception by the target.

In practice this quantity is obtained by integrating time-resolved target heat-flux maps inferred from infrared thermography, embedded calorimetry, Langmuir probes, or boundary-plasma power-balance analysis. The definition concerns net power deposited at the target surface and does not require assigning the deposited energy to individual carrier channels; electron, ion, neutral, or radiative contributions may be treated separately when such resolved information is available.

Typical magnitudes are strongly device- and scenario-dependent. Present tokamak discharges commonly span about $10^5-10^7$ W for an individual inner target, with lower values during detached or low-power phases and higher values possible in large, high-power plasmas.

NAMES.name: power_at_outer_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Net power deposited on the outer divertor target, the divertor plate located at larger major radius in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the integral of the net energy flux into the wetted target surface, summed over all energy-deposition mechanisms.
NAMES.long:
Power at the outer divertor target is the net rate at which energy is deposited on the material surface of the outer divertor target, the plate located at the larger major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is an all-mechanism total integrated over the wetted strike-zone area of that single target, not a mechanism-resolved or per-channel contribution.

The deposited power is defined by integrating the local net deposited energy-flux density normal to the target surface over the wetted area:

$$
P_\mathrm{out} = \int_{A_w} q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}} \, dA
$$

where $q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}}$ is the local net deposited energy-flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is a target-surface area element in m$^2$, and $A_w$ is the wetted strike-zone area of the outer target in m$^2$. The flux density $q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}}$ is the net sum of all energy delivered to the surface by the plasma and associated channels arriving at that point.

In experiments this quantity is commonly inferred from infrared thermography of the target tiles, embedded calorimetry, thermocouples, or heat-balance analysis. Langmuir probes, spectroscopy, and edge-plasma modeling can constrain the local flux profile and the underlying deposition channels. This target-specific quantity is distinct from the mechanism-resolved divertor-power quantities, which are aggregated over all divertor targets rather than resolved to the outer target alone.

Typical values are strongly discharge- and device-dependent, spanning roughly $10^3-10^7$ W, with lower values under low-power or strongly detached conditions and higher values under high-power attached or partially detached conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net energy is deposited onto the outer divertor target surface.

NAMES.name: electron_power_at_outer_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Total rate at which the electron population deposits energy on the material outer divertor target.
NAMES.long:
Electron power at the outer divertor target is the total rate at which electrons transfer energy to the material divertor surface on the larger-$R$ side. Here $R$ is major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $Z$ the vertical height. It is a surface-integrated deposited-power quantity, distinct from a local heat-flux density.

For an electron heat-flux density normal to the target surface, the deposited power is

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{outer}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{outer}}} q_{e,n}(\mathbf{x})\, dA
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{outer}}$ is the wetted area of the outer divertor target, $q_{e,n}$ is the electron contribution to the normal heat-flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{x}$ labels position on the material surface, and $dA$ is a surface-area element. The integrand is counted as deposited heat flux when electron energy flows from the plasma into the material target.

In experiments this quantity is inferred by integrating the electron-channel heat flux over the wetted strike-zone area. Target thermography or calorimetry can constrain the total deposited heat flux, while Langmuir probes, spectroscopic constraints, sheath physics, and edge-plasma transport modeling may be used to separate the electron contribution from ion and radiative components. The integration should follow the actual material-surface geometry and include the full wetted area associated with the outer strike zone.

Typical magnitudes span about $10^4$-$10^6$ W in small or low-power tokamak plasmas and about $10^6$-$10^7$ W in medium-size high-heating plasmas; larger high-power scenarios can exceed $10^7$ W. The value depends on input power, radiated power, detachment state, magnetic balance, strike-zone spreading, and inner/outer target power sharing.

NAMES.name: maximum_power_at_outer_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Maximum, over a specified time interval, of the total power deposited on the outer divertor target. The outer target is the divertor target on the larger-major-radius side in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Maximum power at the outer divertor target is the largest value, within a chosen time interval, of the total power deposited on the plasma-facing target surface at larger major radius. The outer target is identified in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity is non-negative because it counts deposited energy flow into the target material.

For a time interval $T$, it is obtained from the local deposited heat-flux density by integrating over the outer target surface and taking the temporal maximum:

$$
P_{\mathrm{max,OT}} = \max_{t \in T} \int_{S_{\mathrm{OT}}} q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{r}, t)\, dA
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{max,OT}}$ is this maximum power, $S_{\mathrm{OT}}$ is the plasma-facing surface of the outer divertor target, $q_{\perp,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{r}, t)$ is the local perpendicular deposited heat-flux density at surface position $\mathbf{r}$ and time $t$, and $dA$ is the surface-area element. The deposited heat-flux density is defined as positive for heat flux into the target surface. The corresponding instantaneous integrated quantity is [power_at_outer_divertor_target](name:power_at_outer_divertor_target).

In practice, the time-dependent outer-target power is inferred from infrared thermography with thermal modeling, embedded calorimetry, probe-based heat-flux estimates, and global power-balance constraints, or computed by integrating modeled loads over the target. Conductive, convective, and radiative contributions are related to [power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction), [power_of_divertor_due_to_convection](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_convection), and [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation). Comparison with [maximum_power_at_inner_divertor_target](name:maximum_power_at_inner_divertor_target) separates larger- and smaller-major-radius divertor loading, while [peak_power_density_at_divertor_target](name:peak_power_density_at_divertor_target) describes the local peak heat-flux density rather than integrated power.

Representative order-of-magnitude maxima are device and scenario dependent: $10^5-10^6$ W in low-power or strongly detached cases, $10^6-10^7$ W in many diverted tokamak scenarios, and $10^7-10^8$ W in large high-heating-power cases. These ranges are indicative rather than definitional; the actual value depends on heating power, radiated fraction, detachment state, strike-point sharing, and wetted area.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_convection
NAMES.short: Power deposited on plasma-facing surfaces by convective plasma particle flux, comprising thermal enthalpy and directed kinetic energy carried by streaming ions and electrons from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Convective power quantifies the energy transported to a plasma-facing surface by the bulk flow of plasma particles — ions, electrons, and neutral species — streaming along open magnetic field lines from the scrape-off layer to bounding material surfaces. It represents the convective channel of the total surface power balance, distinct from the conductive contribution driven by parallel temperature gradients and from radiative deposition.

The local convective heat-flux density summed over particle species $s$ is

$$
q_{\mathrm{conv}} = \sum_s n_s v_{\parallel,s} \left( \frac{\gamma_s}{\gamma_s - 1} k_B T_s + \frac{1}{2} m_s v_{\parallel,s}^2 \right)
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density, $v_{\parallel,s}$ the parallel flow speed, $\gamma_s$ the adiabatic index (5/3 for monatomic species), $T_s$ the temperature, and $m_s$ the particle mass. Integrating $q_{\mathrm{conv}}$ over the wetted surface area yields the total convective power in watts.

In experiments the convective power is inferred from Langmuir-probe measurements of particle flux and sheath-entrance temperature, or decomposed from total calorimetric measurements by subtracting the conductive fraction estimated via two-point model analysis. More specific realizations include [power at a single divertor target due to convection](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection), [convective power summed over all divertor targets](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_convection), and [convective power at the first wall](name:power_at_wall_due_to_convection). The full surface load integrating all channels is characterized by heat_flux_of_plasma_facing_component.

NAMES.name: power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection
NAMES.short: Power deposited on a divertor target by incident plasma particle flow carrying thermal enthalpy and directed kinetic energy. It excludes the conductive heat-flux contribution, so it represents the convective part of the target heat load.
NAMES.long:
Convective power at a divertor target is the rate at which plasma particles flowing into the material surface deliver thermal enthalpy and directed bulk-flow kinetic energy. It is the convective contribution to [power_at_divertor_target](name:deposited_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_halo_current), complements [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction), and may be summed over targets in [power_of_divertor_due_to_convection](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_convection). For an outer target it contributes to quantities such as [power_at_outer_divertor_target](name:power_at_outer_divertor_target).

In a single-ion fluid description, the target-integrated convective power can be written as the surface integral of the incident normal convective energy flux:

$$
P_\mathrm{conv} = \int_A \left[\frac{5}{2}(p_e+p_i) + \frac{1}{2}m_i n_i u_\parallel^2\right] \max\!\left(0,-u_\parallel\,\hat{b}\cdot\hat{n}_\mathrm{in}\right)\,dA
$$

where $A$ is the target surface receiving plasma, $p_e$ and $p_i$ are the local electron and ion thermal pressures at the sheath entrance or equivalent target-facing plasma boundary, $m_i$ and $n_i$ are the ion mass and density, $u_\parallel$ is the plasma flow velocity along the magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$, and $\hat{n}_\mathrm{in}$ is the unit normal directed from the material surface into the plasma. The pressure terms should be in energy density units; if temperatures are expressed in electronvolts, the conversion to pressure includes the elementary charge.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating a modeled or inferred convective heat-flux density over the wetted target surface. Local density, temperature, ion-saturation current, flow, and magnetic-incidence information can constrain the convective term, while infrared thermography or calorimetry usually measure total target heat load; separating convective from conductive power therefore requires a sheath or edge-transport model.

Representative target-integrated values are highly device- and regime-dependent: less than $10^3$ W in small or strongly detached cases, $10^4-10^6$ W in many medium-size diverted tokamak plasmas, and $10^6-10^7$ W or higher during high-power attached operation.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_fusion
NAMES.short: Power due to fusion is the rate at which energy originating in fusion reactions is deposited in, or assigned to, a specified plasma region or material component. It covers fusion-product and secondary nuclear energy deposition only, such as neutron and gamma heating, and excludes non-fusion heat loads.
NAMES.long:
Power due to fusion is the power contribution whose ultimate energy source is nuclear fusion reactions. It is a generic parent quantity for fusion-origin power deposited in particular regions or structures, such as the [divertor fusion deposition power](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_fusion), and is distinct from total thermal, radiative, or particle heat loads not caused by fusion products.

For a specified region or component $\Omega$, the deposited fusion power can be written as the volume integral of the local fusion-origin energy-deposition rate density:

$$
P_\mathrm{fusion,dep} = \int_\Omega S_\mathrm{fusion,dep} \, dV
$$

where $S_\mathrm{fusion,dep}$ is the local power density deposited by fusion reaction products and secondary nuclear radiation, and $dV$ is the volume element of the region or material considered.

In practice this quantity is computed from fusion reaction rates, product energy spectra, and transport or attenuation of fusion neutrons, charged fusion products, and secondary gamma radiation. For material components, nuclear heating calculations account for neutron moderation, scattering, absorption, and gamma production; for plasma regions, charged-particle slowing-down and energy deposition may also contribute.

Typical values range from near 0 W in non-fusing or very low-rate plasmas, through 10^3-10^7 W for localized component nuclear heating in high-performance deuterium-tritium operation, to 10^8-10^9 W for total fusion power in reactor-scale plasmas. The value depends strongly on reaction rate, fuel mixture, geometry, shielding, and the region over which deposition is evaluated.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_radiation
NAMES.short: Net photon power absorbed by a divertor surface or assembly, equal to the incident radiative flux from impurity and hydrogenic plasma emission integrated over the surface area minus the reflected component.
NAMES.long:
Radiative power deposited on divertor plasma-facing surfaces arises from photon emission by impurity and hydrogenic species in the scrape-off layer and divertor volume — primarily line radiation from partially ionized impurity ions, electron-ion bremsstrahlung, and radiative recombination continuum. The net absorbed fraction depends on the incident photon spectrum and the photon reflectivity of the plasma-facing material, which can be non-negligible for metallic first-wall components.

The net radiative power deposited on a surface $S$ is defined as:

$$
P_{\rm rad} = \int_S \bigl(1 - \rho_r(\mathbf{r})\bigr)\, q_{\rm rad}(\mathbf{r})\, dA
$$

where $q_{\rm rad}$ is the incident radiative power flux density and $\rho_r$ is the local photon reflectivity of the surface material at position $\mathbf{r}$.

This parent abstracts over two geometric scopes: [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation) gives the net absorbed radiative power for a single divertor target, while [power_of_divertor_due_to_radiation](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_radiation) sums the net radiative deposition over all divertor targets. In practice, the radiative load is inferred from resistive or photodiode bolometric arrays that integrate broad-spectrum emission, or from spectroscopic line-integrated measurements combined with impurity transport modeling. In detached divertor regimes the radiative component can account for a substantial fraction of the total divertor heat exhaust captured by [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor), whereas in attached high-heat-flux conditions the conducted and convected plasma channels dominate.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_recombination
NAMES.short: Power deposited on plasma-facing materials by recombination processes, encompassing both plasma-ion recombination and surface recombination of neutral atoms, without restriction to a particular surface location.
NAMES.long:
Recombination power is the heat load delivered to plasma-facing materials when ions recover electrons and transition to neutral states, releasing ionization potential energy and residual kinetic energy at or near material surfaces. Two principal channels contribute: sheath-accelerated plasma-ion recombination at target surfaces, and surface recombination of neutral atoms into molecules, which deposits the molecular binding energy directly into the wall or divertor plate material.

The integrated power from recombination events over a wetted area $A$ is:

$$P_\text{rec} = \sum_s \int_A \Gamma_s \, E_s \, dA$$

where $\Gamma_s$ [m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$] is the incident particle flux density for species $s$ and $E_s$ [J] is the energy released per recombination event for that species, including ionization potential and kinetic contributions.

This power channel is intrinsically non-negative and becomes particularly significant in detached and partially detached divertor regimes, where volumetric ion-electron recombination upstream of the strike point redistributes energy deposition away from the target. Location-specific realizations include [power deposited on a single divertor target](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination), the [total over the full divertor assembly](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination), and [power at first-wall surfaces](name:power_at_wall_due_to_recombination). The neutral recombination particle flux produced in these processes is characterized by [neutral_energy_flux_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination).

NAMES.name: power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination
NAMES.short: Total power deposited on a divertor target by recombination processes, summing the plasma-ion and neutral-particle recombination channels at the plasma-material interface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity captures the combined recombination power delivered to a single divertor target, encompassing two physically distinct contributions: energy released when plasma ions recombine at or near the target surface (the plasma channel, quantified by [plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination)) and energy deposited when neutral particles undergo recombination into lower-energy bound states at the material wall (the neutral channel, quantified by [neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination)).

The total recombination power at the target decomposes additively:

$$
P_{\rm rec,target} = P_{\rm rec,plasma} + P_{\rm rec,neutral}
$$

where $P_{\rm rec,plasma}$ is the ion-recombination contribution and $P_{\rm rec,neutral}$ is the neutral-particle recombination contribution, both in W.

This target-localized quantity is a spatial specialization of the volume-integrated [power_due_to_recombination](name:power_due_to_recombination), which integrates recombination power over the full plasma domain. In attached divertor operation, recombination power at the target is a minor fraction of the total heat load; in detached or high-recycling regimes, surface and volumetric recombination become significant energy sinks that reduce the conducted and convected flux reaching the target. It is inferred from edge plasma simulations or from particle flux measurements combined with surface energy-release models, and is non-negative by definition.

NAMES.name: neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Thermal power deposited in a divertor target by neutral atoms, molecules, or fragments that recombine into lower-energy bound states, including molecule formation at the surface. It is the neutral-particle contribution to recombination heat load, distinct from plasma-ion recombination.
NAMES.long:
Neutral recombination power at a divertor target is the thermal energy per unit time deposited in the target material by neutral-particle recombination at the surface or in the near-surface neutral layer. For hydrogenic plasmas, an important example is atomic hydrogen recombining to form molecules; only the fraction of released binding, internal, and kinetic energy that is accommodated by the target contributes to this quantity. This is the neutral-particle channel of recombination heating, distinct from [plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination).

The target-integrated neutral recombination power is obtained by integrating the corresponding heat-flux density over the wetted target area:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rec,n}} = \int_{\mathcal{A}_t} q_{\mathrm{rec,n}} \, dA
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{rec,n}}$ is the neutral recombination power, $q_{\mathrm{rec,n}}$ is the local heat-flux density due only to neutral recombination in W m$^{-2}$, and $\mathcal{A}_t$ is the target area receiving that heat load.

In practice this contribution is estimated from edge plasma-neutral transport and surface-interaction modeling using neutral fluxes, recombination rates, reaction energies, sticking probabilities, and energy-accommodation coefficients. It can be constrained indirectly by divertor calorimetry or infrared thermography together with spectroscopy, neutral-pressure measurements, and gas-balance analysis, but separating it from conduction, radiation, charge exchange, and plasma-ion recombination is generally model-dependent.

Representative values range from nearly 0 W when neutral recombination at the target is weak to about $10^3$-$10^6$ W per target in high-recycling or detached divertor conditions, with strong dependence on device size, neutral density, target temperature, and plasma species. Together with [plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination), it contributes to [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination); summed over divertor targets it corresponds to [neutral_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination) and forms part of [neutral_power_at_divertor_target](name:neutral_power_at_divertor_target) and [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor).
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy from neutral recombination is deposited into the divertor target material.

NAMES.name: power_of_divertor
NAMES.short: Power deposited on all divertor targets by net electric currents crossing the plasma–sheath interface, summed over all target surfaces in the divertor assembly.
NAMES.long:
Net charge currents crossing the plasma sheath transfer electrical power to divertor target surfaces in addition to the kinetic energy carried by streaming particles. For a net current $I_t$ flowing through a sheath potential drop $V_{s,t}$ at target surface $t$, the current-driven deposited power on that target is:

$$
P_t = I_t \, V_{s,t}
$$

where $V_{s,t}$ is the potential difference from the presheath edge to the solid surface, and the sum over all divertor targets yields the quantity reported here. This electrical power channel complements the kinetic heat loads from [parallel thermal conduction](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction), [plasma ion recombination](name:plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination), and [neutral particle deposition](name:neutral_power_of_divertor); the [thermal heat-exhaust component](name:thermal_power_of_divertor) integrates all surface-incident thermal fluxes separately. The net electric current driving this deposition is quantified by [current_of_divertor](name:current_of_divertor).

In practice this quantity is inferred from Langmuir probe or biased-tile measurements of local current density combined with floating-to-wall potential differences. In attached divertor operation the current-driven contribution is typically a minor fraction of the total heat load, but it becomes significant during transient events such as disruptions, where large halo currents traverse divertor surfaces, or in experiments with externally applied target biasing.

NAMES.name: neutral_power_of_divertor
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Net power deposited on all divertor targets by neutral particles, aggregated over all targets in the divertor assembly.
NAMES.long:
Neutral particles — charge-exchange atoms, recycled hydrogen atoms and molecules, and dissociation products — transport energy to divertor target surfaces through thermal accommodation, dissociation, and recombination processes. This quantity aggregates the neutral-particle heat load over all individual divertor targets, capturing the total neutral-particle contribution to the divertor power balance without resolving individual targets or specific interaction processes.

The neutral power deposition arises from both the kinetic energy and the internal (potential) energy carried by neutral particles to the target surface. In attached divertor operation, this channel is typically smaller than the electron and ion heat-flux contributions; in deeply detached regimes, where volumetric recombination is strong and plasma recedes from the target, the neutral component can grow substantially as energy is transported to the surface via neutral atom and molecule flux rather than direct plasma contact. The process-specific subset due to recombination is given by [neutral power of divertor due to recombination](name:neutral_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination), while [neutral power at divertor target](name:neutral_power_at_divertor_target) provides the same physical quantity resolved for an individual target. The electric-current component of the divertor heat load is separately captured by [power of divertor]. This quantity is computed from edge-plasma transport modeling or inferred by decomposing calorimetric measurements of total target heat load into species-resolved channels.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net power is directed from the neutral particles toward the divertor targets.

NAMES.name: power_of_divertor_due_to_convection
NAMES.short: Convective power deposited on the divertor targets, summed over targets, by charged plasma particles flowing along open magnetic field lines. It includes thermal enthalpy and directed kinetic energy carried by incident species into the target surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Convective divertor power is the all-target sum of energy deposited by incident plasma particles rather than by conductive heat flow. It includes the thermal enthalpy and directed kinetic energy carried by ions, electrons, and other charged species through the sheath to material divertor target surfaces. Only energy flux into the material surfaces is included, so this is a non-negative deposited-power magnitude rather than a signed surface-normal flux.

A useful local expression is the surface integral of incident convective energy flux over each target:

$$
P_{\mathrm{conv}} = \sum_k \int_{A_k} \sum_s \Gamma_{s,k}^{\mathrm{inc}} \left(h_{s,k} + \frac{1}{2} m_s u_{\parallel s,k}^2\right)\, dA
$$

where $k$ labels divertor targets, $A_k$ is the wetted target area in $\mathrm{m^2}$, $s$ labels incident charged species, $\Gamma_{s,k}^{\mathrm{inc}}$ is the particle flux density into the target in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, $h_{s,k}$ is the thermal enthalpy per particle in $\mathrm{J}$, $m_s$ is the particle mass in $\mathrm{kg}$, and $u_{\parallel s,k}$ is the directed parallel flow speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The result is in watts.

In practice this quantity is computed from edge plasma transport and sheath models, or inferred from target diagnostics that constrain incident particle fluxes, temperatures, and heat loads. It is distinct from conductive target power [power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction), recombination-related power [plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination](name:plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination), and radiative deposition; the corresponding single-target quantity is [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection).

Typical magnitudes are strongly device and regime dependent and are best interpreted relative to the total divertor thermal power [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor). Values may be near 0 W when detachment, radiation, recombination, or weak particle flux removes most parallel energy before the target, and may become a substantial fraction of the all-target thermal divertor power in attached, particle-flux-dominated conditions.

NAMES.name: power_of_divertor_due_to_fusion
NAMES.short: Nuclear power deposited in the divertor structure through neutron moderation and gamma absorption from fusion reactions, distinct from the plasma thermal load conducted or convected to divertor surfaces along magnetic field lines.
NAMES.long:
In a deuterium-tritium burning plasma, fusion reactions generate 14.1 MeV neutrons carrying approximately 80% of the 17.6 MeV reaction energy per event. These electrically neutral particles stream freely into surrounding structures, and the divertor assembly — comprising plasma-facing targets, support structures, and cooling circuits — absorbs a fraction via elastic and inelastic neutron scattering, radiative capture, and secondary gamma emission. This nuclear heating contribution is structurally and thermally distinct from [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor), which quantifies the plasma heat exhaust deposited at divertor surfaces by conductive and convective transport along open field lines.

The nuclear power deposited in the divertor is the volume integral of the local nuclear heating power density $\dot{q}_{\rm nuc}$ over the divertor assembly:

$$
P_{\rm nuc,div} = \int_{V_{\rm div}} \dot{q}_{\rm nuc}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is position within the divertor volume $V_{\rm div}$, which encompasses all structural and plasma-facing components.

Because neutrons cannot be directly calorimetrically resolved from plasma heat loads during operation, this quantity is computed via neutron transport calculations using divertor geometry and material nuclear cross-section data. It represents a volumetric heat source relevant to divertor coolant system design and structural integrity analysis. Analogous nuclear deposition integrals for breeding zone components are defined by [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer) and [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield); this divertor quantity is a sub-component of the total [power_due_to_fusion](name:power_due_to_fusion).

NAMES.name: power_of_divertor_due_to_radiation
NAMES.short: Total net radiative power deposited on the divertor, summed over all targets, from photon emission by impurity and hydrogenic species during plasma-wall interaction.
NAMES.long:
The total net radiative power deposited on the divertor is the aggregate photon power absorbed across all divertor targets, contributed by line radiation from impurity species (carbon, neon, argon, tungsten, and similar) and hydrogenic Balmer and Lyman continuum emission. The net value equals the total incident radiative flux integrated over all target surfaces minus the fraction reflected by the plasma-facing materials, and is summed over all targets in the divertor assembly.

$$
P_{\mathrm{div,rad}} = \sum_k \int_{A_k} \left(1 - \rho_k\right) F_{\mathrm{rad}}(\mathbf{x})\, dA
$$

where $k$ indexes individual divertor targets, $A_k$ is the wetted surface area of target $k$, $\rho_k$ is the effective surface reflectivity, and $F_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the local incident radiative power flux density in W m$^{-2}$.

This aggregate is inferred from bolometric tomography using fan-array or tangential bolometers that reconstruct the radiated power distribution in the divertor volume, or estimated from integrated impurity spectroscopy combined with impurity transport modeling.

In high-recycling attached conditions, radiative losses to the divertor are a modest fraction of the power crossing the separatrix; in detached or impurity-seeded regimes they can constitute 30–80% of the total divertor heat load, substantially reducing the conducted and convected channels quantified by [power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction) and [power_of_divertor_due_to_convection](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_convection). The per-target counterpart is [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_radiation), and the analogous radiation to the main chamber wall is radiated_power_at_wall.

NAMES.name: power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination
NAMES.short: Total power deposited on all divertor target surfaces by recombination processes, comprising both the plasma-ion and neutral-particle recombination channels summed over the full divertor assembly.
NAMES.long:
Total divertor recombination power is the combined rate at which recombination processes at or near the target surfaces of the divertor assembly release energy into the material, integrated over all targets. It is the divertor-surface counterpart of the volumetric [power_due_to_recombination](name:power_due_to_recombination) and unifies two physically distinct deposition channels:

$$
P_\mathrm{rec,div} = P_\mathrm{rec,div}^\mathrm{plasma} + P_\mathrm{rec,div}^\mathrm{neutral}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{rec,div}^\mathrm{plasma}$ is [plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination](name:plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination), the energy deposited when plasma ions recombine or neutralize at the material surface, and $P_\mathrm{rec,div}^\mathrm{neutral}$ is [neutral_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination), the energy carried by neutral particles undergoing recombination reactions at the plasma-material interface.

This quantity is computed in edge-plasma codes that track ion and neutral fluxes to the targets and apply sheath-energy coefficients along with recombination cross-sections to determine surface deposition. It represents one component of the total divertor heat load alongside conducted, convected, and radiative contributions, and becomes a more prominent fraction of that load in detached or partially detached divertor regimes where volumetric recombination upstream suppresses the ion current reaching the targets.

NAMES.name: neutral_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Thermal power deposited on divertor targets by recombination reactions of neutral particles at the plasma-material interface, summed over all targets. It represents the neutral-surface recombination contribution to the total divertor heat load.
NAMES.long:
Neutral recombination power of the divertor is the heat load delivered to divertor target surfaces when neutral particles undergo recombination reactions that form more tightly bound neutral species, such as atomic hydrogen isotopes forming molecules on a material surface. It is the contribution summed over the divertor targets and excludes heat carried by charged particles or photons unless that energy is deposited through the neutral recombination process at the target.

The integrated divertor contribution can be written as a surface integral over target areas:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rec,n}}^{\mathrm{div}} = \sum_t \int_{A_t} \Gamma_{\mathrm{rec,n}}(\mathbf{x})\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{rec,n}}(\mathbf{x})\,dA
$$

where $A_t$ is the surface area of target $t$, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{rec,n}}$ is the neutral recombination event rate per unit target area in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $\epsilon_{\mathrm{rec,n}}$ is the mean energy deposited at the target per recombination event in J. The effective $\epsilon_{\mathrm{rec,n}}$ is reaction-, species-, and surface-dependent; it may include chemical binding energy released to the surface and kinetic energy accommodated by the material, and is not generally equal to an atomic ionization potential.

In practice this quantity is estimated from a combination of target heat-flux measurements, neutral pressure and spectroscopy constraints, particle-balance analysis, and neutral transport with plasma-surface interaction modeling. The recombination contribution is separated from charged-particle, radiation, and other neutral heat-load channels using reaction rates, recycling coefficients, surface accommodation assumptions, and measured or reconstructed target conditions.

Typical integrated values range from near 0-10^4 W in weakly recycling or attached divertor conditions to 10^4-10^6 W in strongly recycling or detached conditions on present experiments. In larger devices or high-power detached regimes, values of 10^6-10^7 W are possible when neutral recycling and surface recombination make a substantial contribution to the divertor heat balance.

NAMES.name: plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination
NAMES.short: Power deposited on all divertor target surfaces by recombination or neutralization of plasma ions at the material surface. It is the plasma-ion component of the total divertor recombination heat load, complementary to the neutral-particle recombination contribution.
NAMES.long:
Plasma recombination power of a divertor is the rate at which energy is deposited on all target surfaces of that divertor by plasma ions that recombine or neutralize at the material surface. It describes the plasma-ion recombination contribution to the target heat load, distinct from neutral-particle recombination and from conductive heat transport to the targets.

The total divertor recombination heat load is commonly decomposed into plasma-ion and neutral-particle contributions:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rec,div}} = P_{\mathrm{rec,div}}^{\mathrm{plasma}} + P_{\mathrm{rec,div}}^{\mathrm{neutral}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{rec,div}}^{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is this quantity and $P_{\mathrm{rec,div}}^{\mathrm{neutral}}$ is the complementary [neutral recombination contribution](name:neutral_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination). The plasma-ion term can also be obtained by summing the corresponding [target-level plasma-ion recombination powers](name:plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination) over all target surfaces belonging to the divertor.

In practice this power is inferred from divertor power accounting, surface-interaction modeling, and measurements such as target calorimetry, infrared thermography, Langmuir-probe ion fluxes, spectroscopy, and bolometry. Only energy delivered to the material targets by recombination or neutralization of plasma ions is included; radiated power, neutral-particle recombination power, and conductive heat-load components are accounted for separately.

Typical values range from 10^3-10^6 W per divertor in many tokamak discharges. In strongly detached, high-density divertor conditions the contribution can approach 10^6-10^7 W, while in attached low-recycling conditions it may be negligible compared with conductive and convective target heat loads.

NAMES.name: radial_length_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Non-negative span of a divertor target's plasma-facing surface projected onto the major-radius R direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radial length of a divertor target is the non-negative geometric span of the target's plasma-facing surface after projection onto the major-radius coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It characterizes the target dimension in major radius, not the wetted length along the inclined target surface or a distance along magnetic-field lines.

If $S_t$ denotes the plasma-facing target surface, the projected radial length is

$$
L_R = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S_t} R(\mathbf{x}) - \min_{\mathbf{x} \in S_t} R(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $R(\mathbf{x})$ is the major-radius coordinate of point $\mathbf{x}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The result is a span $\Delta R$, so it is independent of whether the target contour is traversed from inner to outer radius or the reverse.

In practice, $L_R$ is obtained from the divertor target contour or surface geometry by selecting the plasma-facing part of the target and taking the difference between the largest and smallest $R$ values.
