For comparison with strike-point quantities, the relevant object is the target major-radius interval $[R_{\min}, R_{\max}]$: major_inner_radius_of_strike_point and major_outer_radius_of_strike_point are coordinates of strike points in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, so they can be tested for lying on or near this interval but are not lengths to be compared directly with $L_R$.

Typical radial spans are 0.02-0.2 m for small or narrow target tiles, 0.1-0.5 m for medium-size tokamak divertor targets, and up to about 1 m in large or strongly extended divertor geometries. The value depends on target inclination, cassette design, baffling, and whether the full plasma-facing target or only an active wetted segment is being characterized.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_divertor_tile
NAMES.short: Geometric surface area of the plasma-facing side of one divertor tile. It is a per-tile area used to convert integrated heat or particle loads on that tile into tile-averaged flux densities.
NAMES.long:
Surface area of a divertor tile is the geometric area of the individual tile face exposed to the scrape-off-layer plasma and recycling neutrals. It is defined per tile, not as an aggregate over a divertor target, cassette, or full divertor, and represents the area used when tile-integrated loads are averaged over that specific component.

For a plasma-facing tile surface $S_\mathrm{tile}$, the area is

$$
A_\mathrm{tile} = \int_{S_\mathrm{tile}} dA
$$

where $A_\mathrm{tile}$ is the tile surface area and $dA$ is the differential element of the actual exposed surface, including geometric shaping, bevels, or curvature when they are part of the plasma-facing face.

The value is normally obtained from engineering geometry, metrology, or a surface mesh of the divertor component. It can be used with an integrated power or particle load on the same tile, for example as $q_\mathrm{tile}=P_\mathrm{tile}/A_\mathrm{tile}$, to form a tile-averaged heat flux density.

Typical divertor-tile surface areas are about $10^{-3}$-$10^{-1}$ m^2, depending on tile size, segmentation, strike-point region coverage, and whether detailed shaped features are included.

NAMES.name: temperature_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Thermal energy per particle of a plasma species in the region immediately adjacent to a divertor target, evaluated at the sheath entrance where the Bohm criterion governs the minimum ion flow velocity.
NAMES.long:
Temperature at the divertor target characterizes the kinetic energy scale of a plasma species in the narrow plasma layer immediately adjacent to the target surface, evaluated at the sheath entrance where ions must satisfy the Bohm condition. This parent quantity abstracts over the species-specific realizations: the electron and ion populations generally carry distinct temperatures and must be treated separately in two-temperature divertor plasma models.

The electron and ion channels differ in how they acquire and exchange energy along the scrape-off layer. [Electron temperature at the divertor target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target) quantifies the energy scale of the electron velocity distribution at the sheath edge, while [ion temperature at the divertor target](name:ion_temperature_at_divertor_target) represents the mean ion thermal energy averaged over species. Equality of the two temperatures requires sufficient collisional energy exchange; departures scale with the electron-ion equilibration time $\tau_{ei}^E \propto T_e^{3/2} / (n_e \ln\Lambda)$, where $n_e$ is the electron density and $\ln\Lambda$ is the Coulomb logarithm. The local [electron density at the divertor target](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target) therefore directly controls the degree of inter-species equilibration.

Electron temperatures at the target are inferred from Langmuir probe current-voltage characteristics; ion temperatures are obtained from spectroscopic line-ratio analysis or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. In attached high-recycling divertor conditions, target electron temperatures typically fall in the range 10-50 eV; partial or full plasma detachment reduces them below about 5 eV. Ion temperatures can exceed electron temperatures in low-collisionality regimes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma species carries finite thermal energy, a condition satisfied by all non-zero-temperature plasma states encountered in tokamak operation.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Kinetic temperature of the electron population in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target surface, typically evaluated at the sheath entrance. It represents the downstream scrape-off-layer electron energy scale at the target, distinct from upstream midplane or generic wall temperatures.
NAMES.long:
Electron temperature at the divertor target is the kinetic temperature characterizing the electron energy distribution in the plasma immediately next to the divertor target surface, usually interpreted at the sheath entrance rather than inside the material or deep within the sheath. It is the downstream scrape-off-layer electron temperature where field-aligned plasma exhaust reaches the divertor plate; this distinguishes it from [electron_temperature_at_midplane](name:electron_temperature_at_midplane), which refers to an upstream location, and from [electron_temperature_at_wall](name:electron_temperature_at_wall), which is not specific to a divertor target.

For an isotropic Maxwellian electron distribution, the electron temperature in eV is related to the mean random kinetic energy per electron by

$$
\langle E_e \rangle = \frac{3}{2}\, e\, T_e
$$

where $\langle E_e \rangle$ is the mean random kinetic energy in joules, $e$ is the elementary charge, and $T_e$ is the electron temperature in eV. Equivalently, if the mean kinetic energy is expressed in eV, $\langle E_e \rangle_\mathrm{eV} = 3T_e/2$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from local divertor measurements such as target Langmuir probe current-voltage characteristics, divertor Thomson scattering, or spectroscopic inference, and may also be estimated from scrape-off-layer transport or two-point modeling constrained by upstream and target conditions. It is commonly interpreted together with [electron_density_at_divertor_target](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target) and [ion_temperature_at_divertor_target](name:ion_temperature_at_divertor_target) when assessing sheath heat transmission, recycling, and divertor detachment state. In strongly non-Maxwellian or rapidly varying conditions, the reported value may represent a diagnostic- or model-dependent effective electron temperature.

Typical values are about 10-100 eV in attached divertor conditions, 2-10 eV in high-recycling regimes, and 0.5-5 eV in detached or strongly cooled divertor plasma. Values below 1 eV can occur in deeply detached recombining plasmas, while transient or weakly cooled target conditions can exceed 100 eV.

NAMES.name: ion_temperature_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Thermal energy per particle of the ion population at the divertor target surface, averaged over ion species and evaluated at the sheath entrance where the Bohm condition applies.
NAMES.long:
Ion temperature at the divertor target is the temperature-equivalent mean thermal energy per ion for ions reaching the divertor target surface. The quantity is conventionally evaluated at the plasma side of the sheath, before sheath acceleration converts ion thermal and directed energy into impact energy at the material surface.

For multiple ion species or charge states, the averaged value is the ion-density-weighted temperature at the sheath entrance:

$$
T_i = \frac{\sum_s n_s T_{i,s}}{\sum_s n_s}
$$

where $T_{i,s}$ is the temperature of ion species or charge state $s$ in eV, $n_s$ is its number density in m^-3, and the denominator is the local total ion density. This weighting represents the mean ion thermal energy per ion in the local plasma population, not a particle-flux-weighted target impact average.

Direct measurement is difficult and is commonly inferred from divertor spectroscopy, retarding-field or probe measurements where sheath models are applicable, or edge-plasma modeling constrained by target density, electron temperature, particle flux, and heat-flux measurements. For context, in a single-effective-ion sheath estimate the ion heat flux is often approximated by $q_i \simeq \gamma_i e n_i c_s T_i$, where $q_i$ is in W m^-2, $\gamma_i$ is a dimensionless ion sheath heat-transmission coefficient, $e$ is the elementary charge converting eV to joules, $n_i$ is the total ion density in m^-3, $T_i$ is this ion temperature in eV, and $c_s \simeq \sqrt{e(T_e+T_i)/m_i}$ for singly charged ions when $T_e$ and $T_i$ are in eV and $m_i$ is in kg.

Typical values are 0.5-5 eV in cold detached or strongly recombining divertors, 5-30 eV in partially detached or attached conditions, and up to 30-100 eV at hot attached targets with strong parallel heat flux.

NAMES.name: total_ion_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Number density of the total ion population at the divertor target, summed over all ionic species and charge states present in the local plasma.
NAMES.long:
The total ion number density at the divertor target is the sum of all positive-ion contributions — fuel ions (hydrogen isotopes), helium ash, and seeded or intrinsic impurities — evaluated locally at the plasma-facing divertor surface. It characterizes the aggregate ion particle concentration in the sheath-entrance region and governs plasma–surface interaction processes including sputtering, recycling, and heat load.

The total ion density $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ is defined as:

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{total}} = \sum_{s} n_{i,s}
$$

where $s$ indexes all ion species and charge states present at the target. By quasi-neutrality, $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ closely approximates the [electron density at the divertor target](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target), with deviations scaling with the mean effective charge of the impurity mixture.

This quantity is measured via Langmuir probe saturation-current analysis at the divertor surface, or derived from edge-transport modeling constrained by spectroscopic observations. In attached and high-recycling regimes, typical values range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$, rising toward the upper end near detachment onset. Species-resolved contributions are available from [deuterium_density_at_divertor_target](name:deuterium_density_at_divertor_target), [neon_density_at_divertor_target](name:neon_density_at_divertor_target), and [carbon_density_at_divertor_target](name:carbon_density_at_divertor_target).
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions are present at the divertor target surface.

NAMES.name: total_ion_power_at_inner_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total power deposited on the inner divertor target by incident ions, summed over all ion species and charge states and integrated over the wetted target surface. It is the ion contribution to the inner-target heat load.
NAMES.long:
Total ion power at the inner divertor target is the surface-integrated rate at which incident ions deposit energy on the inner divertor target. It includes contributions from all ion species and charge states that strike the target and is distinct from electron heat deposition and current-driven electrical power deposition.

A local incident ion energy flux density integrated over the inner target defines the total power:

$$
P_{\mathrm{ion,inner}} = \sum_{s,q} \int_{A_{\mathrm{inner}}} \Gamma_{s,q}^{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf{x})\,\bar{E}_{s,q}^{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf{x})\,dA
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{inner}}$ is the wetted inner divertor target area, $\Gamma_{s,q}^{\mathrm{in}}$ is the incident normal ion particle flux density for species $s$ and charge state $q$ in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, $\bar{E}_{s,q}^{\mathrm{in}}$ is the mean energy delivered per incident ion in J, and $dA$ is a surface element in m$^2$. The product $\Gamma_{s,q}^{\mathrm{in}}\bar{E}_{s,q}^{\mathrm{in}}$ is the local ion power flux density in W m$^{-2}$.

In modeling, this quantity is computed by summing ion energy fluxes to the inner target and integrating over the wetted surface. Experimentally it can be constrained by combining target particle-flux measurements, such as Langmuir-probe ion saturation current interpreted with local plasma conditions, with calorimetry or infrared thermography; separating ion and electron channels generally requires sheath or edge-plasma modeling.

Representative magnitudes are highly scenario dependent: about $10^3$-$10^5$ W in low-power or strongly detached conditions, $10^5$-$10^7$ W in attached high-power operation on present devices, and above $10^7$ W in reactor-scale studies without strong radiative or detachment mitigation. The [maximum_power_at_inner_divertor_target](name:maximum_power_at_inner_divertor_target) describes the corresponding peak local heat-load measure, total_electron_power_at_inner_divertor_target is the electron-channel counterpart, power_of_divertor refers to current-related power deposited on divertor targets, and [current_of_divertor](name:current_of_divertor) is related through the charged-particle flux reaching the targets.

NAMES.name: total_particle_flux_of_divertor_due_to_recycling
NAMES.short: Global rate at which particles are introduced into the plasma by recycling at all divertor targets, including neutral re-emission, molecular release, and ion reflection.
NAMES.long:
Total divertor recycled particle flux is the whole-divertor particle-number source rate produced when particles incident on divertor targets are returned toward the plasma after surface interaction. It includes neutral re-emission, molecular release, and ion reflection from all divertor targets, expressed on a common particle-count basis for the species balance.

The total rate can be written as the surface integral of the recycled flux density over the target surfaces:

$$
\Phi_\mathrm{rec}^\mathrm{div} = \sum_t \int_{S_t} \Gamma_\mathrm{rec}(\mathbf{r}) \, dA
$$

where $S_t$ is the material surface of divertor target $t$, $dA$ is the surface area element, and $\Gamma_\mathrm{rec}$ is the local recycled particle flux density normal to the surface, in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Molecular, atomic, neutral, and ionic channels should be reduced to the same particle inventory before summation; the result is a particle-number rate, not an energy or power flux.

In practice, this rate is inferred from a combination of target particle-flux measurements, divertor spectroscopy, neutral pressure measurements, pump-throughput and gas-balance constraints, and edge plasma/neutral transport modeling. It is the divertor-target recycling counterpart of the more general [surface-emission source rate], while associated energy channels are described separately by quantities such as [plasma power due to recombination](name:plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination) and [neutral power due to recombination](name:neutral_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination).

Typical values are strongly device- and scenario-dependent because the rate scales with incident target particle flux, recycling probability, detached or attached divertor state, and total wetted target area. As order-of-magnitude guidance for tokamak divertor analyzes, whole-divertor recycling rates commonly span about $10^{21}$-$10^{25}$ s^-1, with lower values in smaller or lower-density plasmas and upper-end values in high-density, strongly recycling divertor conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local recycled particle flux density is directed from the divertor target material surface toward the plasma.

NAMES.name: tritium_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Number density of tritium ions in the scrape-off-layer plasma immediately upstream of a divertor target surface.
NAMES.long:
Tritium density at a divertor target is the local number density of ionized atomic tritium in the scrape-off-layer plasma immediately upstream of a material target surface. It excludes neutral tritium atoms and molecules, and is a species-resolved component of the local total ion density at the target.

The local density is the tritium-ion particle count per plasma volume in the infinitesimal-volume limit:

$$
n_T(\mathbf{x}_t) = \lim_{\Delta V \to 0} \frac{\Delta N_T^{\mathrm{ion}}}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n_T$ is the tritium ion number density in m^-3, $\mathbf{x}_t$ denotes a point in the plasma immediately adjacent to the target, $\Delta V$ is a small plasma volume around that point, and $\Delta N_T^{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the number of tritium ions in that volume.

In practice this quantity is inferred from isotope-resolved boundary-plasma analysis, particle-balance modeling, or diagnostics constrained by local electron and ion density measurements when tritium-sensitive measurements are available. It is the divertor-target counterpart of [tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [tritium_density_at_limiter](name:tritium_density_at_limiter), and it relates to the local fuel mixture through ratios such as $n_T/n_i$, where $n_i$ is the total ion density.

The physically allowed range is $0 \le n_T \le n_i$ when $n_i$ includes all local ion species. A tritium-free plasma has $n_T = 0$ m^-3; in a tritium-rich edge plasma the value is set by the local fuel-ion density and tritium fraction, for example $n_T \simeq f_T n_i$ when $f_T$ denotes the tritium ion fraction.

NAMES.name: tungsten_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Number density of tungsten ions at the divertor target, summed over all ionization stages and excluding neutral tungsten atoms.
NAMES.long:
Tungsten (atomic number $Z = 74$) is the primary plasma-facing material in the divertor regions of present-day and next-generation fusion devices, where ion bombardment causes physical sputtering and releases tungsten atoms that rapidly ionize in the scrape-off-layer plasma. The tungsten ion number density at the divertor target quantifies the total local concentration of tungsten ions per unit volume in the plasma immediately adjacent to the strike-zone surface, and is a key component of the broader [density_at_divertor_target](name:density_at_divertor_target) species set.

When charge states are not individually resolved, this quantity represents the sum over all ionization stages:

$$
n_W = \sum_{q=1}^{74} n_{W^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{W^{q+}}$ is the number density of tungsten ions in charge state $q$ at the target location. Neutral tungsten atoms are excluded from this sum.

This quantity is inferred from optical emission spectroscopy of tungsten line radiation, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or impurity transport codes constrained by global particle balance. It characterizes the local impurity source strength at the plasma-material interface and is a key input for assessing core contamination risk, since tungsten fractional concentrations above approximately $10^{-5}$ relative to the electron density can produce intolerable radiated power losses in the confined plasma. The boundary impurity content reaching the separatrix is tracked separately by [tungsten_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:tungsten_density_at_plasma_boundary). Co-seeded impurity densities at the same location, such as [nitrogen_density_at_divertor_target](name:nitrogen_density_at_divertor_target) and [argon_density_at_divertor_target](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target), are routinely compared with this quantity in divertor detachment control studies.

NAMES.name: vertical_length_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Non-negative vertical projection of the divertor target surface in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, equal to the difference between the largest and smallest Z coordinate on the target.
NAMES.long:
Vertical length of a divertor target is the non-negative geometric extent of the target surface projected onto the vertical $Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is a projected height, not the arc length along a tilted or curved target surface.

For a target surface $S_\mathrm{t}$ with vertical coordinate $Z(\mathbf{x})$, the projected vertical length is defined by the range of $Z$ over that surface:

$$
L_Z = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S_\mathrm{t}} Z(\mathbf{x}) - \min_{\mathbf{x} \in S_\mathrm{t}} Z(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ denotes points on the plasma-facing target surface and $Z$ is vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. If the target is represented only by two bounding endpoints and the intervening surface is monotonic in $Z$, this reduces to $L_Z = |Z_2 - Z_1|$.

In practice, this quantity is computed from the surveyed or designed divertor target geometry by identifying the operational target surface and taking the maximum and minimum vertical coordinates over its bounded extent. It is used to characterize how much vertical space the target occupies independently of its radial projection or its surface length.

Typical values range from about 0.05-1 m for compact to medium divertor targets, and can be larger in large devices or vertically extended divertor configurations.

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the surface outline defining the geometric boundary of an individual divertor tile in the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The vertical height component of each point defining the surface outline of a divertor tile within the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate measured from the machine midplane. Paired with the corresponding radial outline coordinate, this quantity fully specifies the cross-sectional geometry of the tile surface in any toroidally axisymmetric representation, enabling computation of wetted surface area, heat-load distribution, and geometric shadowing between adjacent plasma-facing components.

Divertor tile outlines are obtained from engineering or CAD specifications of the first-wall assembly. The geometric boundary of the tile determines which surface elements intercept the scrape-off-layer heat flux in the vicinity of the magnetic strike-point. The outline is also used in optical and infrared camera line-of-sight calculations to monitor tile erosion and thermal response. For the analogous geometry of limiter tiles, see [vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile); for the vacuum vessel boundary, see [vertical_outline_of_vacuum_vessel](name:vertical_outline_of_vacuum_vessel). The center-point location of the divertor target surface is given by [vertical_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:vertical_coordinate_of_divertor_target), which captures a single reference point rather than a full outline contour.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline point is located above the machine midplane, in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: wetted_area_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Surface area of one divertor target over which the deposited heat-flux density is at least one e-folding below its peak on that target. It is a non-negative per-target footprint area; wetted_area_of_divertor is the sum over all target surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The wetted area of a divertor target is the actual plasma-facing surface area on one target plate that receives the main heat-flux footprint, using a threshold one e-folding below the peak deposited heat-flux density on that same target. It is a non-negative scalar surface measure, not an oriented area. The corresponding all-target quantity is the sum over target surfaces, as in [wetted_area_of_divertor](name:wetted_area_of_divertor_target).

A general definition is the surface integral over the parts of the target where the deposited target-surface heat-flux density exceeds the threshold:

$$
A_w = \int_{\mathcal{S}_t} H\!\left(q_t(\mathbf{x}) - \frac{q_{t,\max}}{e}\right)\, dA
$$

where $\mathcal{S}_t$ is the actual target surface, $dA$ is an element of actual surface area, $q_t(\mathbf{x})$ is the deposited heat-flux density crossing into the target surface in W m^-2, $q_{t,\max}$ is its maximum on that target, and $H$ is the Heaviside step function. The threshold is applied to deposited target-surface heat-flux density, not directly to parallel heat flux; if [parallel_heat_flux_at_divertor_target](name:parallel_heat_flux_at_divertor_target) is measured or modeled first, it is converted to deposited surface load using the local field-line incidence before selecting the footprint.

In practice, the footprint is inferred from infrared thermography, calorimetry, embedded temperature sensors, or heat-transport modeling combined with magnetic equilibrium reconstruction and target geometry. For an axisymmetric annular footprint, a common estimate is $A_w \simeq 2\pi R_t w_t$, with $w_t \simeq (\lambda_q f_x + S)/\sin\alpha$; here $R_t$ is the strike-point major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, $\lambda_q$ and $S$ are lengths in meters, $f_x$ is dimensionless flux expansion, and $\alpha$ is the angle between the magnetic-field line and the target surface, so $\alpha=90^\circ$ corresponds to normal incidence and smaller $\alpha$ gives a larger projected footprint. This estimate assumes toroidal symmetry, a slowly varying footprint around the circumference, and nearly constant incidence over the selected region; the surface integral is the defining quantity.

Typical per-target values range from about 0.01-0.3 m^2 in compact and medium-sized tokamaks, 0.1-1 m^2 in larger present devices, and several m^2 in large or deliberately broadened divertor scenarios. The value increases with strike-point circumference, flux expansion, cross-field heat spreading, surface roughness or shaping that increases actual area, and more grazing incidence as defined above. It provides the area scale that connects the spatial footprint to quantities such as [peak_power_density_at_divertor_target](name:peak_power_density_at_divertor_target), without assuming a uniform heat-flux distribution.

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Xenon ion number density in the plasma immediately adjacent to a divertor target, summed over all ionized charge states of elemental xenon and excluding neutral xenon atoms.
NAMES.long:
Xenon density at a divertor target is the local number density of ionized elemental xenon in the boundary plasma next to the target surface. It represents the total population of xenon ions, independent of charge state, and does not include neutral xenon atoms.

When charge-state-resolved densities are available, the elemental xenon ion density is the charge-state sum:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Xe,ion}} = \sum_{q=1}^{54} n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Xe,ion}}$ is the total ionized xenon number density at the divertor target in $m^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{q+}}$ is the number density in xenon charge state $q+$ in $m^{-3}$, and the sum excludes the neutral state $q=0$.

In practice this quantity may be obtained by summing modeled charge-state populations, by interpreting xenon line emission with atomic collisional-radiative data, or from boundary-plasma impurity transport calculations constrained by local diagnostics. It is used to quantify xenon seeding and impurity accumulation near plasma-facing divertor surfaces, where xenon affects radiative cooling and local power balance.

A device-independent numerical range is not intrinsic to the definition. The value is 0 m^-3 when no ionized xenon is present and, in xenon-seeded divertor plasmas, is an experiment-dependent trace-impurity density that can vary by orders of magnitude with seeding rate, divertor temperature, ionization balance, and plasma detachment state.

NAMES.name: peak_power_density_at_wall
NAMES.short: Spatial maximum of the power flux density deposited across all plasma-facing wall surfaces, representing the most severe local thermal load on any wall component of the device.
NAMES.long:
The peak power density at the wall is the spatial maximum of the total incident power flux density over all plasma-facing wall surfaces — encompassing first-wall panels, divertor targets, and limiter tiles — taken as a single global extremum. As the device-level worst-case thermal load, it sets the primary engineering design limit for plasma-facing component materials and machine protection systems.

The defining relation is the spatial extremum of the local surface power flux density $q(\mathbf{s})$:

$$
q_\mathrm{peak} = \max_{\mathbf{s} \in \mathcal{W}} q(\mathbf{s})
$$

where $\mathbf{s}$ denotes position on the full plasma-facing surface set $\mathcal{W}$ and $q$ is the local heat flux in W m$^{-2}$. Location-specific equivalents — [peak_power_density_at_divertor_target](name:peak_power_density_at_divertor_target), [peak_power_density_at_first_wall](name:peak_power_density_at_first_wall), and [peak_power_density_at_limiter](name:peak_power_density_at_limiter) — maximize over their respective sub-surfaces; the more general peak_power_density covers the same concept without a locus qualifier.

Infrared thermography is the primary diagnostic for spatially resolved surface heat flux measurement; the local power flux density is reconstructed from the measured surface temperature transient via the surface heat conduction equation, with emissivity calibration accounting for material surface properties. Embedded thermocouples and calorimetric tiles provide complementary point-wise constraints.

Steady-state peak values range from 0.1–1 MW m$^{-2}$ on main-chamber first-wall panels and 5–20 MW m$^{-2}$ at attached divertor strike zones; transient events such as edge-localized modes and disruptions can drive local peak loading far above these steady-state values.

NAMES.name: power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction
NAMES.short: Thermal power deposited on a single divertor target by conductive plasma heat flow along magnetic field lines. It is the target-surface integral of the conductive heat-flux component into the material, excluding heat carried by convective particle flow.
NAMES.long:
Power at a divertor target due to conduction is the thermal power deposited on one divertor target by electron and ion heat conduction along magnetic field lines in the scrape-off-layer plasma. It represents only the temperature-gradient-driven heat-flow channel and excludes enthalpy and kinetic energy carried to the target by net particle flow, which belongs to [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection).

For a target surface $A_t$, with unit normal $\mathbf{n}_t$ directed from the target material toward the plasma, a surface-integral definition is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cond},t} = -\int_{A_t} \left(q_{\parallel e,\mathrm{cond}} + q_{\parallel i,\mathrm{cond}}\right)\left(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{n}_t\right)\,dA,\qquad q_{\parallel s,\mathrm{cond}} = -\kappa_{\parallel s}\nabla_\parallel T_s,\ s\in\{e,i\}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cond},t}$ is in W; $q_{\parallel e,\mathrm{cond}}$ and $q_{\parallel i,\mathrm{cond}}$ are electron and ion conductive parallel heat-flux densities in W m$^{-2}$; $\mathbf{b}$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field; $dA$ is a target-surface element in m$^2$; $\nabla_\parallel=\mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla$; $T_s$ is the species temperature; and $\kappa_{\parallel s}$ is the species parallel thermal conductivity, in W m$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$ if $T_s$ is expressed in eV. The leading minus sign follows from the chosen normal direction, so heat entering the material from the plasma contributes positively.

In practice, this quantity is computed by integrating separated electron and ion conductive heat-flux channels over the wetted part of a divertor target. It can also be inferred from measured target heat loads when an edge-plasma power-balance model separates conductive heat flow from convective particle-energy transport. Summing this quantity over all divertor targets gives [power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction), and it is one contribution to the broader divertor thermal power balance represented by [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor).

Typical per-target values are highly scenario dependent: an unloaded target is near 0 W, while a wetted strike region in present tokamaks is often in the 10^4-10^7 W range. The value is constrained by the exhaust power entering the scrape-off layer and by how much of that power is dissipated before the field lines intersect the target.

NAMES.name: power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction
NAMES.short: Power transported to all divertor targets via parallel thermal conduction in the scrape-off layer, summed over targets.
NAMES.long:
The total power conducted from the scrape-off layer (SOL) plasma to the divertor represents the conductive channel of the plasma–divertor power exhaust balance, summed over all individual targets. In attached divertor operation, parallel electron and ion thermal conduction along open magnetic field lines is the dominant heat transport mechanism, driven by the temperature gradient between the high-temperature upstream SOL and the cooler target.

The electron conductive heat flux density along a field line follows the Spitzer–Härm relation:

$$
q_{\parallel,e} = -\kappa_0 T_e^{5/2} \nabla_\parallel T_e
$$

where $\kappa_0 \approx 2000$ W m$^{-1}$ eV$^{-7/2}$ is the electron Spitzer conductivity prefactor and $\nabla_\parallel T_e$ is the parallel electron temperature gradient. Integrating over the wetted target area and summing over all divertor targets yields the total conducted power.

Together with [power_of_divertor_due_to_convection](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_convection), this quantity partitions the total plasma heat load reaching the divertor surface; the conductive fraction dominates at high upstream temperatures in attached conditions and diminishes progressively as the plasma approaches detachment, when $T_e$ at the target drops toward the ionization threshold. In detached states, processes such as [plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination](name:plasma_power_of_divertor_due_to_recombination) and volumetric radiation absorb an increasing fraction of the exhaust power before it reaches the targets.

This quantity is assessed from integrated power balance accounting or from multi-fluid SOL transport modeling. Typical values range from 1–10 MW in medium-power present-day devices to tens of MW in high-performance reactor-relevant operations.

NAMES.name: boron_density
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Total number density of elemental boron in the plasma, encompassing neutral boron atoms and all ionization states from B+ through B5+, providing a local or spatially averaged measure of boron impurity concentration.
NAMES.long:
Boron number density quantifies the total number of boron particles — neutral atoms and all ionized charge states — per unit volume of plasma. It is the primary scalar measure of boron impurity content, governing contributions to radiative power losses, dilution of the hydrogenic fuel, and the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$.

The total elemental boron density is the sum over all charge states:

$$
n_\mathrm{B} = \sum_{z=0}^{5} n_\mathrm{B}^{(z)}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{B}^{(z)}$ is the number density of boron in ionization state $z$, with $z = 0$ denoting neutral boron and $z = 5$ the fully stripped B$^{5+}$ ion.

Boron impurity content is inferred experimentally via vacuum ultraviolet spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or soft X-ray tomography. Spatially resolved variants include the [volume-averaged boron density](name:volume_averaged_boron_density), which integrates over the entire confined plasma volume and includes neutrals, and the [line-averaged boron density](name:line_averaged_boron_density), which is the chord-integrated density along a diagnostic line of sight divided by the chord length. The flux-surface-averaged value at the separatrix is captured by the [flux-surface-averaged boron density](name:flux_surface_averaged_boron_density). The dimensionless global boron impurity fraction relative to the electron density is given by [boron_fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_boron_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density).

Typical boron densities in tokamak core plasmas range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, corresponding to impurity concentrations of roughly $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}$ relative to the electron density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when boron atoms or ions are present at the measurement location.

NAMES.name: carbon_density
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Total number density of elemental carbon in the plasma, summed over all charge states from neutral atoms through fully stripped C6+.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density is the total number density of elemental carbon present in the plasma, encompassing neutral carbon atoms and all ionic charge states from singly ionized $C^+$ through fully stripped $C^{6+}$. As a light impurity, carbon dilutes hydrogenic fuel species and contributes to radiative energy losses through line radiation from partially ionized charge states.

The total carbon number density is defined as the charge-state sum:

$$
n_C = \sum_{z=0}^{6} n_{C^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{C^{z+}}$ is the number density of carbon in charge state $z+$, in m$^{-3}$.

Carbon density is inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, which resolves individual charge-state densities, or from passive spectroscopy of carbon line emission analyzed with collisional-radiative models. Spatially resolved forms include [flux_surface_averaged_carbon_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_carbon_density) on closed magnetic surfaces and [volume_averaged_carbon_density](name:volume_averaged_carbon_density) over the confined plasma volume.

Carbon impurity fractions $n_C/n_e$ range from roughly $10^{-4}$ in metallic-wall devices to a few percent in carbon-wall campaigns; [ratio_of_carbon_density_to_electron_density](name:ratio_of_carbon_density_to_electron_density) captures this dimensionless concentration measure. Comparison with [beryllium_density](name:beryllium_density) and [tungsten_density](name:tungsten_density) places carbon in the broader impurity inventory.

NAMES.name: density_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Particle number density of a specified plasma species evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core plasma.
NAMES.long:
The pedestal top marks the shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier where the steep edge density gradient transitions to the flatter confined core plasma. As a parent name, this quantity generalizes over all species-resolved children: electrons as in [electron density at pedestal](name:electron_density_at_pedestal), total ions as in [total ion density at pedestal](name:total_ion_density_at_pedestal), and impurity species such as argon, boron, carbon, and tungsten. For multi-electron impurity species, child names sum over all ionization charge states unless a specific state is indicated.

The number density at the pedestal is the local particle count per unit volume evaluated on the flux surface $\psi_\mathrm{ped}$ identifying the pedestal top:

$$
n_s = \lim_{\Delta V \to 0} \frac{\Delta N_s}{\Delta V}
$$

where $\Delta N_s$ is the count of particles of species $s$ within volume element $\Delta V$ at the pedestal-top flux surface, and $n_s$ is in m$^{-3}$.

Pedestal densities are inferred from high-resolution Thomson scattering, reflectometry, and charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy for impurity ions. The pedestal-top density serves as a key boundary condition for core transport models and constrains peeling-ballooning stability through the pedestal pressure gradient and width.

Typical pedestal-top electron densities range from $0.5 \times 10^{19}$ to $5 \times 10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in current tokamaks; main-ion densities are comparable, while impurity densities are lower by one to several orders of magnitude depending on species and seeding level.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the named species is present at the pedestal location, corresponding to a positive particle count per unit volume.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Number density of argon ions evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core profile.
NAMES.long:
The argon ion number density at the pedestal top quantifies the local concentration of argon impurity ions at the shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. The pedestal top is the radial position where the steep edge-gradient region transitions to the shallower core profile, establishing the inner boundary condition for argon impurity transport into the plasma core and setting the argon inventory available for radiative power exhaust.

The local number density is the zeroth velocity-space moment of the argon ion distribution function $f_{\rm Ar}$:

$$
n_{\rm Ar} = \int f_{\rm Ar}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is the ion velocity. The contribution of pedestal argon to the free electron density is $n_e^{\rm Ar} = \bar{Z}_{\rm Ar} \, n_{\rm Ar}$, where $\bar{Z}_{\rm Ar}$ is the mean ionization state of argon at the pedestal.

Pedestal argon density is typically inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or spectroscopic analysis of argon line emission, supplemented by edge impurity transport modeling. Comparing this value with [argon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:argon_density_at_plasma_boundary) characterizes the argon density gradient across the pedestal, while [argon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis) reflects core accumulation. The analogous quantity for neon seeding is [neon_density_at_pedestal](name:neon_density_at_pedestal). This quantity forms part of the broader [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family describing impurity and main-ion pedestal characterization.

Typical argon pedestal densities in seeded H-mode discharges range from $10^{15}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, several orders of magnitude below the main ion pedestal density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when argon ions populate the pedestal plasma; vanishes in the absence of argon seeding.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local number density of beryllium ions at the H-mode pedestal top. Unless a charge state is specified, it is summed over all beryllium ionization stages.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium density at the pedestal is the local number density of beryllium ions at the top of the H-mode edge pedestal, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier connects to the more weakly varying confined-plasma core. Unless a particular charge state is specified, the quantity includes all ionized beryllium charge states and excludes neutral beryllium atoms. It is the beryllium-specific member of the [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family.

The summed ion density is defined by adding the local densities of the ionized beryllium charge states at the pedestal-top reference position:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}(r_\mathrm{ped})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be,ped}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$ are number densities in m$^{-3}$, $q$ is the positive ion charge state of beryllium, and $r_\mathrm{ped}$ denotes the pedestal-top reference position.

In practice this density is inferred from beryllium line emission using charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy, or collisional-radiative modeling constrained by local electron temperature and electron density. It may also be estimated from impurity transport calculations that balance turbulent diffusion, neoclassical convection, source recycling, and screening at the plasma edge.

Typical pedestal values in tokamak plasmas with beryllium plasma-facing components are $10^{16}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, often corresponding to about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ of the pedestal electron density. Related radial reference quantities include [beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary), [beryllium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:beryllium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis); related pedestal impurity quantities include [oxygen_density_at_pedestal](name:oxygen_density_at_pedestal).

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Number density of boron impurity ions at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core profile.
NAMES.long:
Boron density at the pedestal quantifies the local particle number density of boron ions at the radial shoulder of the steep-gradient edge transport barrier that characterizes H-mode confinement. Boron (atomic number $Z=5$) is a low-Z impurity typically introduced through wall boronization or controlled injection, and its pedestal concentration governs both radiative cooling and the effective plasma charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$.

The contribution of boron to the effective charge is:

$$
Z_\mathrm{eff} = \frac{\sum_k n_k Z_k^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_k$ is the number density of ion species $k$, $Z_k$ is the charge state, and $n_e$ is the electron number density. For fully stripped boron (B$^{5+}$), each boron ion contributes $25/n_e$ to $Z_\mathrm{eff}$, so even trace concentrations measurably elevate the effective charge at the pedestal.

Pedestal boron density is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy targeting boron emission lines or from passive spectroscopy of boron line radiation in the pedestal region. Typical values range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in H-mode pedestals, representing fractional concentrations of order 0.1–5% of the pedestal electron density. As a member of the [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family, this quantity is directly analogous to [carbon_density_at_pedestal](name:carbon_density_at_pedestal) and [argon_density_at_pedestal](name:argon_density_at_pedestal). The radial evolution of the boron impurity content can be traced through [boron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:boron_density_at_magnetic_axis), [boron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:boron_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [boron_density_at_divertor_target](name:boron_density_at_divertor_target).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the boron ion population is finite and non-zero at the pedestal, consistent with particle number density being an intrinsically non-negative scalar.

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Carbon ion number density evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, with charge states summed unless a specific ionization state is named.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at the pedestal is the number of carbon impurity ions per unit volume at the top of the H-mode edge transport barrier, where the steep edge gradients transition toward core plasma conditions. Unless a charge state is explicitly specified, it denotes the total carbon ion density summed over carbon ionization states rather than a charge-state-resolved population.

The total carbon ion density at this location can be written as the sum over carbon charge states:

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{6} \left. n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}} \right|_{\mathrm{ped}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C,ped}}$ and each charge-state density $n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}$ are in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $q$ indexes carbon ions from singly ionized to fully stripped carbon. Neutral carbon atoms are not included in this ion density.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, collisional-radiative modeling, and analysis that identifies the pedestal-top location. If only selected charge states are measured, the total carbon density requires ionization-balance assumptions to account for unobserved charge states.

For orientation, H-mode pedestal carbon ion densities are commonly of order $10^{16}-10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$, typically well below the electron density at the same location. The value is sensitive to wall material, impurity sources, edge screening, and confinement conditions, so comparisons often also use the local ratio $n_{\mathrm{C,ped}}/n_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$.

NAMES.name: density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Number density of a specified plasma species at the plasma boundary, the last closed flux surface geometrically separating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The plasma boundary density is the particle number density of a specified species — electrons, main ions, or impurity ions — evaluated at the last closed flux surface (LCFS), which separates the magnetically confined region from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. This boundary value anchors radial transport equations and couples confined-plasma models to scrape-off-layer physics.

The number density $n_s$ of species $s$ enters the continuity equation

$$
\frac{\partial n_s}{\partial t} = -\nabla \cdot \Gamma_s + S_s
$$

where $\Gamma_s$ is the particle flux of species $s$ and $S_s$ is the net particle source from ionization, recombination, and charge exchange. Evaluating $n_s$ at the separatrix provides the boundary condition shared by both transport domains.

Species-specific instances include [electron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:electron_density_at_plasma_boundary) for the electron population and [krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:krypton_density_at_plasma_boundary) for an injected radiative impurity; see also [deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary) for the fuel pseudo-species. Boundary densities are inferred from edge Thomson scattering, microwave reflectometry, or Langmuir probes near the separatrix, and are also extracted from equilibrium-constrained edge transport reconstructions.

Typical separatrix electron densities in H-mode tokamaks lie in the range $0.5$–$5 \times 10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$; impurity species are several orders of magnitude lower depending on seeding rate and wall material.
NAMES.sign: Positive when particles of the specified species are present at the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Boundary-averaged number density of argon ions on the plasma boundary, represented by the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. Unless a charge state is specified separately, argon ions refers to all ionization stages combined.
NAMES.long:
Argon density at the plasma boundary is the surface-averaged number density of argon ions on the last closed flux surface, also called the separatrix. It provides a boundary-representative measure of argon impurity content, distinct from local poloidal or toroidal variations, and is the argon analog of other impurity boundary densities such as [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary).

The boundary average over the separatrix surface is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar},b} = \left\langle n_{\mathrm{Ar}} \right\rangle_{S_\mathrm{sep}} = \frac{\int_{S_\mathrm{sep}} n_{\mathrm{Ar}}(\mathbf{x})\, dA}{\int_{S_\mathrm{sep}} dA}
$$

where $S_\mathrm{sep}$ is the last closed flux surface, $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local total argon ion number density, and $dA$ is the surface area element. Unless an individual charge state is explicitly specified, $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ denotes the sum over all argon ionization stages.

In experiments, this quantity is inferred from argon line emission using spectroscopic measurements together with electron density, electron temperature, and collisional-radiative or impurity transport modeling. In simulations and equilibrium-edge coupling, it is often computed by averaging the modeled argon density over the separatrix, without assuming that the impurity density is constant on that surface.

Typical values are about $10^{14}-10^{16}$ m^-3 for trace argon concentrations and about $10^{16}-10^{18}$ m^-3 during deliberate radiative seeding, depending on gas injection rate, edge temperature, ionization balance, transport, and plasma size. These values are usually small compared with the total electron or main-ion density at the boundary, but can strongly affect edge radiation because argon is a high-Z impurity.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Number density of beryllium ions at the plasma boundary (last closed flux surface), summed over all ionization stages unless a specific charge state is specified.
NAMES.long:
The beryllium ion number density at the plasma boundary is the total count of beryllium ions per unit volume evaluated at the separatrix, the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined core plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. Beryllium (atomic number $Z = 4$, mass number $A = 9$) is a low-Z metallic impurity that enters the plasma primarily through physical sputtering of beryllium plasma-facing components. Unless a charge-state-resolved quantity is specified, contributions from all ionization stages $\text{Be}^{z+}$ ($z = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$) are included.

The total density at the separatrix is:

$$
n_\text{Be}(r_\text{sep}) = \sum_{z=0}^{4} n_{\text{Be}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\text{Be}^{z+}}$ is the partial density of beryllium ions in the $z$-fold ionized state and $r_\text{sep}$ denotes the separatrix location.

This quantity is inferred from UV and visible spectroscopy of beryllium emission lines, complemented by impurity transport modeling constrained by local electron density and temperature profiles. It forms the outer radial boundary condition for impurity core profiles, linking the central [beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis) to the downstream [beryllium_density_at_divertor_target](name:beryllium_density_at_divertor_target). The pedestal-resolved counterpart [beryllium_density_at_pedestal](name:beryllium_density_at_pedestal) characterizes the steep-gradient region just inside the separatrix, while the species-agnostic parent [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary) provides the general definition applicable to any plasma constituent.
NAMES.sign: Positive when beryllium ions are present at the plasma boundary; number density is intrinsically non-negative as a particle count per unit volume.

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Number density of boron ions at the last closed flux surface, which separates the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Boron (atomic number $Z_B = 5$) is a low-Z impurity introduced into tokamaks through boronization to suppress high-Z metallic impurity influx and limit radiative losses from the confined plasma. The boron ion number density at the plasma boundary is the local concentration of boron ions evaluated at the last closed flux surface, the topological boundary separating closed-field-line confinement from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. It is the boron-specific realization of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary).

The boron ion number density $n_B$ is the zeroth velocity moment of the boron ion phase-space distribution function $f_B$:

$$
n_B = \int f_B(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

evaluated at $\mathbf{x}$ on the separatrix, where $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity. Without accompanying charge-state information, $n_B$ represents the total boron ion density summed over all ionization stages.

Boron concentration at the separatrix is inferred from vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy of boron line emission combined with impurity transport modeling, or from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy when a neutral beam is available. This quantity determines boron's contribution to the local [effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary](name:effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary). Analogous boundary densities for other seeded impurities are provided by [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary); [boron_density_at_divertor_target](name:boron_density_at_divertor_target) gives the companion value further downstream at the divertor plate.

Typical values at the separatrix in boronized tokamaks range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$, decreasing between boronization events as the wall coating erodes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when boron ions are present at the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Number density of carbon impurity ions at the plasma boundary, represented by the last closed flux surface or separatrix. It sums the ion charge states C+ through C6+ and excludes neutral carbon.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at the plasma boundary is the number density of carbon impurity ions evaluated on the last closed flux surface, or on the separatrix in a diverted plasma. It is an impurity-specific ion density and is distinct from the total ion density at the boundary, which includes fuel ions, helium, and all other ion species.

For elemental carbon with nuclear charge $Z_C=6$, the summed ion density is

$$
n_{\mathrm{C},b} = \sum_{z=1}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C}^{z+},b}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C}^{z+},b}$ is the boundary number density of carbon ions with charge state $z$, each density term has units of $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, and the subscript $b$ denotes evaluation at the plasma boundary. Neutral carbon, $\mathrm{C^0}$, is not included in this ion-density sum.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from edge impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements for accessible charge states, and collisional-radiative modeling that maps observed line emission to charge-state densities at the boundary. Equilibrium reconstruction or magnetic-surface identification provides the location of the last closed flux surface used for the boundary evaluation.

Typical summed carbon-ion densities at the plasma boundary are about $10^{15}-10^{18}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ in many tokamak edge plasmas. Values can approach $10^{18}-10^{19}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ in carbon-wall or strong-sputtering conditions, while actively impurity-controlled plasmas may be lower.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core profile.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium ion number density at the pedestal top is the deuterium-specific instantiation of [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal), characterizing the primary hydrogenic fuel species at the shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. The pedestal top marks the radial flux surface where the steep density gradient of the barrier region transitions to the gentler core gradient, and the deuterium density at this location governs fueling efficiency, pressure pedestal height, and edge-localized mode stability.

The number density $n_D$ is the zeroth velocity-space moment of the deuterium ion distribution function $f_D(\mathbf{v})$:

$$
n_D = \int f_D(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_D(\mathbf{v})$ (in m$^{-6}$ s$^3$) is evaluated at the pedestal-top radial location.

The pedestal deuterium density is inferred from edge Thomson scattering systems, charge exchange recombination spectroscopy mapped to the pedestal region, or from fitted profiles combining reflectometry and interferometry data. In DT fuel scenarios, the companion quantity [tritium_density_at_pedestal](name:tritium_density_at_pedestal) provides the tritium ion density at the same radial location, while [deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis) supplies the on-axis reference value for core-to-edge comparison.

Pedestal-top deuterium ion densities in H-mode discharges range from $1 \times 10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ near the L-H power threshold to $5 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in high-density, high-performance scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when deuterium ions are present in the pedestal plasma, consistent with the intrinsic non-negativity of particle number density.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions at the plasma boundary (separatrix), the last closed magnetic flux surface separating confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density at the plasma boundary is the number of deuterium ions per unit volume evaluated on the separatrix, the last closed magnetic flux surface. It is a species-resolved ion density, distinct from electron density and total ion density, and excludes neutral deuterium atoms and molecules. The quantity denotes a separatrix boundary value rather than a divertor target or strike-point density; if a flux-surface average is specified, it is the average of this local separatrix density around the last closed flux surface.

The particle density is the differential deuterium-ion count per volume:

$$
n_D = \frac{dN_D}{dV}
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $dN_D$ is the number of deuterium ions in the differential volume $dV$, and the value is evaluated at the separatrix. In a fully ionized deuterium-dominated edge plasma, quasineutrality often gives $n_e \simeq n_D + \sum_z Z_z n_z$; when impurity and other fuel-ion fractions are small, $n_D \simeq n_e$.

In practice this quantity is inferred by combining diagnostics that measure edge density and species content with an equilibrium estimate of the separatrix location. Thomson scattering can provide the nearby electron density, charge-exchange spectroscopy and passive spectroscopy can constrain ion species fractions, and Langmuir-probe measurements at material surfaces may inform the estimate through edge transport modeling rather than representing the separatrix value directly.

Typical separatrix deuterium ion densities in tokamak plasmas are about $0.1-2 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ in low-density or L-mode operation and $0.5-5 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ in many H-mode plasmas. High-fueling or detached-boundary conditions can approach $1 \times 10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, depending on plasma size, isotope mix, recycling, and confinement regime.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Number density at the H-mode pedestal top of the fictitious single-ion DT pseudo-constituent with atomic mass 2.5 amu, representing deuterium and tritium fuel ions as one constituent.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the ion number density of the DT pseudo-constituent at the H-mode pedestal top. The pseudo-constituent represents the deuterium-tritium fuel mixture as a single ion species with atomic mass 2.5 amu, so the value is a fuel-ion density rather than a resolved deuterium or tritium isotope density.

When the pedestal ion pressure is represented by this pseudo-species and a common ion temperature, the pressure relation is

$$
p_{\mathrm{DT,ped}} = e\, n_{\mathrm{DT,ped}}\, T_{\mathrm{i,ped}}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{DT,ped}}$ is the pedestal ion pressure in Pa, $n_{\mathrm{DT,ped}}$ is this density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $T_{\mathrm{i,ped}}$ is the pedestal ion temperature expressed in eV, and $e$ is the elementary charge converting eV to joules.

In experiments, the pedestal-top density is inferred from edge density measurements such as Thomson scattering, reflectometry, interferometry, and spectroscopic constraints, combined with pedestal fits that identify the top of the steep-gradient region. The DT pseudo-species value may be constructed from the total fuel-ion density, using quasineutrality and isotope-composition information when the individual deuterium and tritium densities are not separately resolved.

Typical H-mode pedestal fuel-ion densities are about $2-10 \times 10^{19}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ in many present tokamak plasmas and may approach $1-2 \times 10^{20}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ in high-density burning-plasma scenarios. The value is generally close to the electron pedestal density after accounting for non-fuel ion impurities and their charge states.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Number density of the fictitious deuterium-tritium pseudo-species (mean atomic mass 2.5 amu) at the plasma boundary, the last closed flux surface separating confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-tritium pseudo-species is a fictitious single-ion plasma constituent with mean atomic mass 2.5 amu, introduced in transport simulations to represent the combined D-T fuel mixture as a single fluid rather than tracking deuterium and tritium separately. The number density $n_{DT,\text{sep}}$ is evaluated at the separatrix — the last closed flux surface bounding the confined plasma — making it the DT-species realization of the more general [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary).

The separatrix density provides an upstream boundary condition for scrape-off-layer transport models and sets fueling depth and recycling source strengths at the plasma edge. It is inferred from edge Thomson scattering or reflectometry measurements combined with equilibrium reconstruction to locate the separatrix position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Typical values in H-mode operation range from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, generally lower than the [deuterium_tritium_density_at_pedestal](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_pedestal) value by a factor of two to four. The corresponding quantity at a limiter contact surface is [deuterium_tritium_density_at_limiter](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_limiter).
NAMES.sign: Positive when deuterium-tritium fuel ions are present at the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: edge_localized_mode_frequency
NAMES.subject: edge_localized_mode
NAMES.short: Repetition rate of edge-localized mode bursts during an ELMing H-mode phase. It quantifies how often pedestal relaxation events occur and sets the cadence, not the size, of transient particle and energy exhaust to the scrape-off layer and divertor.
NAMES.long:
Edge-localized mode frequency is the rate at which discrete ELM bursts occur during an ELMing H-mode phase. It characterizes the temporal spacing of pedestal relaxation events; the energy or particle loss per burst must be specified separately from this rate.

For an analysis window of duration $\Delta t$, the frequency is defined by counting ELM onsets within that window:

$$
f_\mathrm{ELM} = \frac{N_\mathrm{ELM}}{\Delta t} \simeq \frac{1}{\langle \tau_\mathrm{ELM} \rangle}
$$

where $N_\mathrm{ELM}$ is the number of accepted ELM events, $\Delta t$ is measured in seconds, $f_\mathrm{ELM}$ is in Hz ($\mathrm{s}^{-1}$), $\tau_\mathrm{ELM}$ is the time between consecutive ELM onsets in seconds, and $\langle \tau_\mathrm{ELM} \rangle$ is the mean inter-ELM interval over the same window. The reciprocal-interval form is equivalent to the count rate when the same events and boundary treatment are used.

In practice, ELM onsets are identified from correlated transient signatures such as edge light emission, divertor heat-flux pulses, magnetic fluctuations, density bursts, or pedestal profile drops. The averaging window should be chosen so that it is short enough to follow slow discharge evolution but long enough to contain representative events; intervals with no ELMing H-mode, ambiguous compound events, pacing triggers, or deliberately selected ELM classes should be treated by a consistent event-selection rule.

Typical values span about 0.5-1000 Hz. Large, infrequent ELM regimes are often below 10 Hz, many routinely ELMing H-mode plasmas are in the 10-100 Hz range, and small-ELM or actively paced regimes can reach 100-1000 Hz; a value of 0 Hz indicates that no accepted ELM events occurred in the averaging window.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Effective charge (Zeff) at the H-mode pedestal, measuring impurity content through the charge-weighted mean squared ion charge near the edge transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Effective charge at the pedestal is the local plasma effective charge evaluated in the H-mode edge transport barrier. It is a dimensionless measure of impurity content: hydrogenic fuel ions alone give a value close to one, while impurity ions increase the value in proportion to both their density and the square of their charge state.

The effective charge is the electron-density-normalized, charge-squared weighted ion density sum:

$$
Z_\mathrm{eff} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{n_e}
$$

where the sum is over ion species $s$, $n_s$ is the ion density of species $s$ in m^-3, $Z_s$ is its mean ionization state, and $n_e$ is the electron density in m^-3; for a quasineutral plasma, $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$.

Pedestal effective charge is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, visible or soft-X-ray bremsstrahlung, charge-exchange measurements, and edge transport or equilibrium analysis constrained by electron density and temperature. Optically thin bremsstrahlung emissivity scales approximately with $n_e^2 Z_\mathrm{eff} T_e^{1/2}$, making the pedestal value important for radiation, collisionality, resistivity, and bootstrap-current estimates in the edge transport barrier.

Typical pedestal values in H-mode tokamak plasmas are about 1.2-3.5. Values close to 1 indicate a nearly pure hydrogenic plasma, while larger values occur with impurity seeding, enhanced wall influx, or accumulation of high-charge-state impurities.

This quantity complements the generic [effective_charge](name:effective_charge), location-specific values such as [effective_charge_at_magnetic_axis](name:effective_charge_at_magnetic_axis), [effective_charge_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:effective_charge_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [effective_charge_at_limiter](name:effective_charge_at_limiter), and global measures such as [volume_averaged_effective_charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge).

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Effective charge number of the ion mixture at the plasma boundary (separatrix), equal to the charge-squared-weighted sum of ionic densities normalized to electron density.
NAMES.long:
The effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ at the plasma boundary captures the aggregate charge state of all ion species at the last closed flux surface, where the magnetically confined plasma transitions to the open-field-line scrape-off layer. In a pure hydrogenic plasma $Z_\text{eff} = 1$; impurity ions with charge state $Z_i > 1$ raise $Z_\text{eff}$ above unity, increasing resistivity and impurity radiation losses.

$$
Z_\text{eff} = \frac{\sum_i n_i Z_i^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_i$ is the number density of ion species $i$, $Z_i$ is the charge state of species $i$, and $n_e$ is the electron number density, with the sum running over all ion species and charge states present at the boundary.

At the separatrix, $Z_\text{eff}$ is sensitive to plasma-wall interactions, impurity seeding, and edge transport processes that concentrate high-$Z$ ions near the boundary. It governs local Spitzer resistivity ($\eta \propto Z_\text{eff}$) and modifies neoclassical transport coefficients in the edge region. The [electron_pressure_at_plasma_boundary](name:electron_pressure_at_plasma_boundary) and [hydrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:hydrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary) characterize the thermodynamic state at the same boundary location; the analogous pedestal quantity is [effective_charge_at_pedestal](name:effective_charge_at_pedestal). It is inferred from visible bremsstrahlung spectroscopy or from consistency between line-integrated electron density and charge-exchange spectroscopy.

Typical values range from 1 in near-pure hydrogen plasmas to 2–5 in impurity-seeded or metallic-wall discharges.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions are present, as $Z_\text{eff}$ is defined as a ratio of positive-definite charge-weighted ion densities to electron density.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_launching_position
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density in the edge plasma immediately adjacent to a wave launcher aperture or waveguide mouth.
NAMES.long:
Electron density at the launching position is the local number density of free electrons in the plasma that a launched electromagnetic wave first encounters. The launching position denotes the small plasma volume immediately in front of the launcher face, grill, or waveguide mouth, typically in the scrape-off-layer or limiter-shadow region. It is the electron-specific form of density_at_launching_position; unlike a total particle density, it counts free electrons only, and in a quasineutral plasma is approximately balanced by the charge-weighted ion density rather than by neutral density.

A key wave-coupling scale set by this density is the electron plasma angular frequency:

$$
\omega_{pe} = \left(\frac{n_e e^2}{\varepsilon_0 m_e}\right)^{1/2}
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron density in m$^{-3}$, $e$ is the elementary charge in coulombs, $\varepsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity in F m$^{-1}$, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, and $\omega_{pe}$ is in rad s$^{-1}$. For lower-hybrid coupling estimates, $n_e$ also enters the approximate cold-plasma accessibility condition $n_\parallel^2 \ge 1 + \omega_{pe}^2/\omega_{ce}^2$, where $n_\parallel$ is the dimensionless parallel refractive index, $\omega_{ce}=eB/m_e$ is the electron cyclotron angular frequency in rad s$^{-1}$ for magnetic-field magnitude $B$ in tesla, and launched-wave angular frequencies are in rad s$^{-1}$ or equivalently $f=\omega/(2\pi)$ in Hz.

In practice this density is measured or inferred from edge diagnostics viewing the launcher vicinity, such as Langmuir probes, microwave reflectometry, interferometry, or analysis of wave coupling behavior. The reported value should represent the plasma immediately outside the launching structure, not a core density or a distant separatrix value; comparisons with electron_density_at_separatrix and [electron_density_at_limiter](name:electron_density_at_limiter) help distinguish launcher-local conditions from other edge reference locations.

Typical values near wave launchers in tokamak edge plasmas are about $10^{17}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, with lower-hybrid launcher coupling often sensitive in the $10^{17}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ range. The value can vary strongly with gas puffing, recycling from plasma-facing components, launcher-plasma gap, magnetic geometry near the edge, and transient edge events.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density at the H-mode pedestal top, the core-side transition where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core density variation.
NAMES.long:
Electron density at the pedestal is the local [electron density](name:electron_density) at the H-mode pedestal top. The pedestal top is the core-side transition of the edge transport barrier, where the steep edge density gradient connects to the flatter core density variation, and is distinct from the separatrix or scrape-off-layer density.

The quantity is the velocity-space density moment of the electron distribution evaluated at the pedestal-top location:

$$
n_{e,\mathrm{ped}} = n_e(\rho_{\mathrm{ped}}) = \int f_e(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ped}}, \mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $n_e(\rho)$ is electron density as a function of radial flux-surface label $\rho$ in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\rho$ labeling flux surfaces, $\theta$ the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ the toroidal angle. Here $\rho_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is the pedestal-top location, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is a position on that flux surface, $f_e$ is the electron phase-space distribution with SI units $\mathrm{m^{-6}\,s^3}$, and $d^3v$ is a velocity-space volume element with units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-3}}$, giving $n_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$.

In practice, this value is inferred from high-resolution edge density measurements such as Thomson scattering, interferometry, reflectometry, or beam-emission methods, combined with equilibrium mapping to a radial flux label. The pedestal-top location is commonly identified by fitting the radial density variation with a modified hyperbolic tangent or piecewise linear form, or by locating where the [gradient of electron density] changes from the large edge-pedestal value to the smaller core value. Together with [electron temperature at the pedestal top](name:electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top), this quantity determines [electron pressure at the pedestal top]; when $T_e$ is expressed in eV, the pressure relation is $p_{e,\mathrm{ped}} = e\,n_{e,\mathrm{ped}}T_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$, where $e$ is the elementary charge, while $n_e k_B T_e$ applies only when $T_e$ is in kelvin.

Typical pedestal-top electron densities in H-mode tokamaks are $1 \times 10^{19}$-$1 \times 10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$; low-density or small devices can be below this range, while high-performance or reactor-relevant plasmas can approach $2 \times 10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. The value influences edge collisionality, bootstrap current, impurity screening, and peeling-ballooning stability, and generally increases with fueling and confinement quality.

NAMES.name: derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local derivative of electron number density with respect to the normalized poloidal flux coordinate, evaluated at the H-mode pedestal location in the steep edge transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The derivative $dn_e/d\psi_N$ at the pedestal quantifies the radial steepness of the electron density profile across the H-mode transport barrier, where $\psi_N$ is the normalized poloidal flux coordinate increasing from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\left.\frac{dn_e}{d\psi_N}\right|_{\text{pedestal}}
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density and $\psi_N = (\psi - \psi_0)/(\psi_b - \psi_0)$, with $\psi_0$ denoting the poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis and $\psi_b$ its value at the plasma boundary.

This derivative is extracted from profile fits — modified hyperbolic tangent (mtanh) or piecewise-linear models — applied to Thomson scattering or reflectometry measurements parameterized as a function of $\psi_N$. For the maximum gradient over the full pedestal region rather than a single reference point, see [the pedestal-region maximum gradient](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_density_at_pedestal). The analogous derivative for electron pressure is given by [derivative of electron pressure at pedestal](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_pressure_at_pedestal).

Typical magnitudes in H-mode pedestals range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ per unit $\psi_N$, with steeper gradients associated with higher pedestal pressures and stronger edge transport barriers.
