NAMES.sign: Positive when electron density increases with increasing $\psi_N$ (in the radially outward direction toward the plasma boundary); in standard H-mode operation the derivative is negative as density decreases across the pedestal from the confinement interior toward the separatrix.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density at the plasma boundary (separatrix), the last closed flux surface separating confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Electron density at the plasma boundary is the electron number density evaluated on the separatrix, the last closed magnetic flux surface. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, and $Z$ vertical height, this surface separates closed magnetic field lines in the confined plasma from open field lines in the scrape-off layer.

Using the normalized toroidal-flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ as a flux-surface label, the separatrix value is the confined-side limit:

$$
n_{e,\mathrm{sep}} = \lim_{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} \to 1^-} n_e(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}})
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=1$ labels the separatrix. Together with the boundary electron temperature, it determines the boundary electron pressure through the inline relation $p_{e,\mathrm{sep}} = n_{e,\mathrm{sep}} T_{e,\mathrm{sep}}$ when $T_e$ is expressed as an energy per electron.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by mapping edge electron-density measurements onto magnetic flux surfaces from an equilibrium reconstruction. Common inputs include Thomson scattering, reflectometry, and interferometry constrained by fitted pedestal or scrape-off-layer density shapes; the largest uncertainties often come from separatrix position, steep edge gradients, and diagnostic calibration.

Typical values in tokamak H-mode edge plasmas are about $0.3-3 \times 10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, with lower values possible in low-density or limiter-like plasmas and higher values in strongly fueled, high-density discharges.

NAMES.name: electron_density_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number-density baseline on the scrape-off-layer side of an analytic H-mode pedestal fit. It is the fitted offset representing the low-density open-field-line side of the pedestal, distinct from the density at the plasma boundary and from the pedestal-top density.
NAMES.long:
Electron density over the scrape-off layer is the asymptotic baseline electron number density associated with the open-field-line side of an analytic H-mode pedestal representation. It is a fitted offset parameter for the scrape-off-layer side of the density shape, not the density evaluated at a particular location such as the last closed flux surface or the pedestal top.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by fitting an analytic pedestal model to edge electron-density data or to a modeled edge density distribution. Different analytic pedestal forms may use different width, slope, and transition parameters, so the common semantic content is the fitted scrape-off-layer offset, often denoted $n_{e,\mathrm{SOL}}$, rather than any specific formula for the full radial dependence. The separate scrape-off-layer falloff scale is described by electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer, while nearby reference densities include [electron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:electron_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [electron_density_at_pedestal](name:electron_density_at_pedestal).

Typical fitted H-mode tokamak scrape-off-layer density offsets are of order $10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3, depending on fueling, divertor conditions, pedestal collisionality, and how far the fitted interval extends into the open-field-line region. In well-constrained pedestal fits this offset is usually below the pedestal-top density and should be interpreted together with the chosen analytic fit form.

NAMES.name: electron_pressure_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron pressure at the H-mode pedestal reference location, representing the pedestal-height amplitude extracted from a profile fit to the steep-gradient edge transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The H-mode pedestal is a narrow region of strongly suppressed turbulent transport near the plasma boundary, producing a steep gradient in the electron pressure profile between the flat core and the scrape-off layer. The electron pressure at the pedestal characterizes the amplitude of this pressure step and is a primary pedestal-performance figure of merit that, through profile stiffness, strongly influences overall energy confinement.

The pedestal height $p_\mathrm{ped}$ is extracted by fitting the measured electron pressure profile to a modified hyperbolic tangent (mtanh) function:

$$
p_e(\psi_N) = \frac{p_\mathrm{ped}}{2}\left[\tanh\!\left(\frac{\psi_{N,\mathrm{ped}} - \psi_N}{\Delta\psi_N}\right) + 1\right] + p_0
$$

where $\psi_N$ is the normalized poloidal flux coordinate, $\psi_{N,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the pedestal midpoint, $\Delta\psi_N$ is the pedestal half-width, and $p_0$ is the scrape-off-layer baseline captured by [electron_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer](name:electron_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer).

Edge Thomson scattering measurements of electron density and temperature are the primary source for constructing the electron pressure profile from which this pedestal height is derived. Typical pedestal electron pressures span $\sim$1–5 kPa in low-current H-mode discharges and $\sim$20–100 kPa in high-performance H-mode plasmas on large tokamaks. The companion [electron_pressure_at_pedestal_top](name:electron_pressure_at_pedestal) refers to the pressure evaluated explicitly at the core-side top of the pedestal, whereas this name denotes the fit-derived height at the broader pedestal reference location. The radial pressure gradient at this location is described by [derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_pressure_at_pedestal](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_pressure_at_pedestal), and [electron_density_at_pedestal](name:electron_density_at_pedestal) provides the corresponding electron number density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron pressure is positive, as guaranteed for all physical plasma states since kinetic pressure is an intrinsically positive-definite thermodynamic quantity invariant under reversals of the plasma current or toroidal field direction.

NAMES.name: derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_pressure_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local derivative of electron pressure with respect to the normalized poloidal flux coordinate, evaluated at the H-mode pedestal. It describes the radial pressure slope at that pedestal reference location, not an extremum or average over the full pedestal region.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local slope of electron pressure as a function of the normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_N$ at the H-mode pedestal. A large magnitude indicates a sharp edge pressure gradient. It is evaluated at the chosen pedestal reference location and should not be interpreted as the maximum gradient over the pedestal region.

The derivative is defined by differentiating electron pressure with respect to $\psi_N$ and evaluating the result at the pedestal reference position:

$$
\left.\frac{d p_e}{d\psi_N}\right|_{\mathrm{ped}} = \left.\frac{d}{d\psi_N}\left(e\,n_e T_e\right)\right|_{\mathrm{ped}}
$$

where $p_e$ is electron pressure, $\psi_N$ is the normalized poloidal flux coordinate (dimensionless, 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the plasma boundary), $n_e$ is electron density in m$^{-3}$, $T_e$ is electron temperature in eV, and $e$ is the positive elementary charge converting eV to joules. With this temperature convention, $e n_e T_e$ has units of Pa, and the derivative also has units Pa because $\psi_N$ is dimensionless; if $T_e$ is expressed in kelvin instead, the equivalent pressure relation is $p_e=n_e k_B T_e$.

In practice, the value is obtained by mapping electron density and temperature measurements onto $\psi_N$, forming $p_e$, and differentiating a smooth representation of the pedestal variation at the pedestal reference position. The reference position is set by the pedestal characterization method, so this quantity is a local slope rather than a region-wide extremum.

Typical H-mode values expressed per unit $\psi_N$ have outward-gradient magnitudes of $10^4$-$10^6$ Pa; low-performance or broad pedestals can be closer to $10^3$-$10^4$ Pa. For pedestals whose pressure decreases toward the boundary, the numerical value is negative, with magnitude roughly equal to the electron pressure drop across the pedestal divided by its width in $\psi_N$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron pressure increases with increasing normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_N$ from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: electron_pressure_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron thermal pressure evaluated at the plasma boundary (separatrix), where the magnetically confined plasma meets the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The electron pressure at the plasma boundary quantifies the isotropic thermodynamic pressure of the electron population at the last closed flux surface (separatrix), the outermost surface bounding the region of nested, closed magnetic flux and separating confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.

The defining relation is the ideal-gas equation of state:

$$
p_e = n_e k_B T_e
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density and $k_B T_e$ is the electron thermal energy per particle. The boundary value is obtained by evaluating this product at the separatrix. The companion [electron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:electron_density_at_plasma_boundary) provides one factor of this product from independent profile measurements; together they constrain the electron temperature at the boundary.

This boundary pressure is inferred from electron density and temperature profiles measured across the pedestal region — typically by Thomson scattering or electron cyclotron emission — using linear or hyperbolic-tangent functional fits evaluated at the inferred separatrix location. It serves as an essential boundary condition for edge transport and scrape-off layer models, as well as a global summary scalar characterizing the pedestal–SOL interface alongside the parent pressure_at_plasma_boundary.

Typical values in H-mode tokamak discharges range from tens to a few hundred pascals at the separatrix, substantially lower than the pedestal-top electron pressure, which can reach several kilopascals in reactor-relevant conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron population has nonzero temperature and density; as a scalar thermodynamic pressure, this quantity does not change sign under reversal of magnetic field direction or plasma current direction.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron temperature at the top of the H-mode pedestal transport barrier, representing the characteristic pedestal height parameter extracted from analytic fits to the steep-gradient edge profile.
NAMES.long:
The electron pedestal temperature $T_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ characterizes the bulk thermal energy of the electron population at the top of the H-mode edge transport barrier — the high-confinement pedestal formed just inside the separatrix. As a pedestal height parameter, it represents the plateau value of the electron temperature profile above the steep-gradient region, providing a key macroscopic boundary condition that sets the scale of core temperature profiles in H-mode discharges.

The pedestal height is extracted by fitting analytic models — including linear and smooth modified-hyperbolic-tangent forms — to measured edge electron temperature profiles. Each fitting approach yields a value $T_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ corresponding to the temperature at which the steep pedestal gradient transitions to the flatter core region, making $T_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ a robust, fit-model-dependent summary scalar for the pedestal state.

Pedestal electron temperatures in H-mode discharges on mid-scale tokamaks range from approximately 0.3 to 5 keV, increasing with plasma current and auxiliary heating power. Together with the pedestal electron density, $T_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ determines the pedestal electron pressure captured by electron_pressure_at_pedestal. The closely related [electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top) targets the same physical location using an explicit profile-top convention, while [gradient_of_electron_temperature](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top) quantifies the steepness of the transport barrier.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physical plasmas, as electron temperature is a measure of mean thermal kinetic energy per degree of freedom and is intrinsically non-negative.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron temperature at the pedestal top is the fitted pedestal-height value at the radial location where the steep H-mode edge electron-temperature gradient joins the flatter core region. It is an electron kinetic temperature expressed in eV.
NAMES.long:
Electron temperature at the pedestal top is the kinetic temperature of the electron population evaluated at the top, or height, of the H-mode pedestal transport barrier. The pedestal top is the fitted transition location where the steep edge gradient relaxes toward the core region, not a value at the physical plasma boundary or at a particular outboard point.

Using the normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_N$, the pedestal-top temperature is defined as the fitted electron-temperature value at the fitted pedestal-top location:

$$
T_{e,\mathrm{ped}} = T_e(\psi_{N,\mathrm{ped}})
$$

where $T_e(\psi_N)$ is the electron temperature expressed in eV and $\psi_{N,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the fitted pedestal-top coordinate. If another explicitly defined radial flux coordinate is used, such as normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the same quantity is the electron-temperature value evaluated at the corresponding fitted pedestal-top coordinate.

In practice, $T_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ is obtained by fitting edge electron-temperature measurements, commonly from Thomson scattering and sometimes constrained by electron cyclotron emission or other kinetic diagnostics, with a pedestal model such as a modified hyperbolic-tangent shape. The fit returns both the pedestal-top location and the pedestal-height value. When forming an SI electron pressure from this quantity, the eV unit must be converted: $p_{e,\mathrm{ped}} = e\,n_{e,\mathrm{ped}}\,T_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ for density in m^-3, where $e$ is the elementary charge; without the factor $e$, the product has units of eV m^-3 rather than pascal.

Typical pedestal-top electron temperatures range from 100-500 eV in small or low-field H-mode plasmas, 0.5-2 keV in many medium-sized tokamaks, and 2-8 keV in high-performance or large-device pedestals. The value is a key pedestal-height parameter for confinement scaling, edge stability, and pressure-gradient characterization.

NAMES.name: derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Derivative of electron temperature with respect to the normalized poloidal flux coordinate, evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top where the steep edge temperature gradient joins the flatter core region.
NAMES.long:
The pedestal-top electron-temperature flux-coordinate derivative is the local slope of electron temperature with respect to the normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_\mathrm{N}$ at the pedestal top. Here $\psi_\mathrm{N}$ is dimensionless and increases from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last-closed flux surface, and the pedestal top is where the steep H-mode edge temperature gradient joins the flatter core region.

Let $D_{T_e,\mathrm{top}}$ denote this derivative:

$$
D_{T_e,\mathrm{top}} = \left. \frac{\partial T_e}{\partial \psi_\mathrm{N}} \right|_{\mathrm{ped,top}}
$$

where $T_e$ is electron temperature in eV, $\psi_\mathrm{N}$ is the dimensionless normalized poloidal flux coordinate, and the subscript denotes evaluation at the pedestal top. Because $\psi_\mathrm{N}$ is dimensionless, $D_{T_e,\mathrm{top}}$ has units of eV.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by mapping electron-temperature measurements onto $\psi_\mathrm{N}$ using an equilibrium reconstruction, fitting or smoothing the edge temperature variation, and evaluating the derivative at the fitted pedestal-top location. It is distinct from the [maximum pedestal slope](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top), which refers to the steepest-gradient location within the pedestal.

Typical H-mode pedestal-top values are often negative, about $-10^4$ to $-10^2$ eV, because electron temperature usually decreases outward as $\psi_\mathrm{N}$ increases. Weak or broad pedestals may give values close to 0 eV, while very narrow, hot pedestals can reach order $-10^5$ eV.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $T_e$ increases with increasing normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_\mathrm{N}$.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron thermal temperature evaluated locally at the plasma boundary, normally the separatrix where closed magnetic flux surfaces meet the open-field-line scrape-off layer. It is a local confined-edge value, not a flux-surface average.
NAMES.long:
Electron temperature at the plasma boundary is the scalar electron thermal temperature evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface, or separatrix in a diverted plasma. It denotes a local separatrix value on the confined-plasma side; it is not the same as a [flux_surface_averaged_electron_temperature](name:flux_surface_averaged_electron_temperature) unless an explicit flux-surface average has been applied.

For a scalar-temperature description of an isotropic electron distribution, the temperature is related to the mean random kinetic energy per electron at the separatrix by:

$$
\left\langle E_{e,\mathrm{rand}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{sep}} = \frac{3}{2}\,e\,T_{e,\mathrm{sep}}
$$

where $\left\langle E_{e,\mathrm{rand}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is in joules, $e$ is the elementary charge, and $T_{e,\mathrm{sep}}$ is this temperature in eV. The related boundary electron pressure is $p_{e,\mathrm{sep}} = n_{e,\mathrm{sep}} e T_{e,\mathrm{sep}}$, where $n_{e,\mathrm{sep}}$ is the [electron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:electron_density_at_plasma_boundary) in m^-3 and $p_{e,\mathrm{sep}}$ is in pascals.

The boundary location is identified from the magnetic equilibrium as the separatrix in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. In practice, the value is commonly obtained by evaluating an edge electron-temperature fit at the separatrix, often constrained by spatially resolved Thomson scattering and, in colder boundary plasmas, by probe or spectroscopic measurements. It characterizes the upstream edge thermal condition adjacent to the temperature_over_scrape_off_layer, and it is generally lower than the [electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top) while being physically distinct from the [electron_temperature_at_divertor_target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target).

Representative tokamak separatrix electron temperatures are of order 10-300 eV. L-mode plasmas are often around 10-100 eV, while H-mode plasmas with strong edge pedestals commonly reach tens to a few hundred eV, depending on plasma current, heating power, density, and divertor conditions.

NAMES.name: energy_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.short: Fick's-law coefficient relating the diffusive thermal energy flux of a plasma constituent to its local temperature gradient, serving as the species-agnostic parent abstraction over electron, ion, and neutral population specializations.
NAMES.long:
The energy diffusion coefficient characterizes gradient-driven thermal energy transport for any plasma constituent — electrons, ions, or neutrals — by specifying the proportionality between the diffusive heat flux and the local temperature gradient in the Fick's-law sense. It is the thermal-energy channel of the general diffusion_coefficient, which governs particle, momentum, and energy transport alike, and it is distinct from convective or $E \times B$ contributions to the total heat flux.

The defining relation for the diffusive energy flux $\mathbf{Q}_\mathrm{diff}$ of a given constituent is:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_\mathrm{diff} = -D_E \, \nabla T
$$

where $D_E$ is the energy diffusion coefficient and $\nabla T$ is the temperature gradient of that constituent. In a magnetized plasma $D_E$ is strongly anisotropic; radial cross-field values govern energy confinement while values along field lines are orders of magnitude larger.

Species-resolved children include [electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient) for the electron population and [ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient) for the total ion population aggregated over all charge states; neutral-particle transport is handled by analogous neutral specializations. The effective diffusivity that combines diffusive and convective contributions is tracked separately by energy_effective_diffusivity.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_boron_density
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Number density of boron ions averaged over the last closed flux surface (separatrix) at the plasma boundary, summed over all ionization states and excluding neutral boron atoms. It quantifies the boundary boron impurity content as a particle density.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged boron density is the number density of boron ions averaged over the last closed flux surface (separatrix) at the plasma boundary. The boron population is counted by nuclei in ionic charge states only, so neutral boron atoms are excluded. It is the flux-surface-averaged counterpart of [boron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:boron_density_at_plasma_boundary) and can be compared with [flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density) to characterize the boundary boron fraction.

In magnetic flux coordinates $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$, where $\psi$ labels nested toroidal flux surfaces, $\theta$ is a poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, the boundary value is the closed-surface limit of the Jacobian-weighted flux-surface average:

$$
\left\langle n_\mathrm{B} \right\rangle_\mathrm{LCFS} = \lim_{\psi \to \psi_b} \frac{\int_0^{2\pi} n_\mathrm{B}(\psi, \theta)\, J(\psi, \theta)\, d\theta}{\int_0^{2\pi} J(\psi, \theta)\, d\theta}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{B}$ is the local boron ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ summed over all charge states, $\psi_b$ is the flux value at the last closed flux surface, and $J$ (in $\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{T}$ for $(\psi, \theta)$) is the coordinate-space Jacobian that supplies the flux-surface-average weighting measure rather than a simple arithmetic average over poloidal angle. Near an X point the separatrix value is interpreted as a limit from neighboring closed flux surfaces.

The quantity is inferred from edge impurity emission spectroscopy combined with charge-state-resolved collisional-radiative and impurity-transport modeling, mapped to the plasma boundary through equilibrium reconstruction. Because each boron ion is counted once regardless of charge state, this is a particle density and carries no charge-squared weighting; charge-state populations are required separately to evaluate charge density, radiated power, or effective-charge contributions.

Unlike the present quantity, [volume_averaged_boron_density](name:volume_averaged_boron_density) averages over the entire confined plasma volume and, depending on definition, may include neutral boron. Boundary boron densities depend strongly on wall conditioning, boronization, and edge transport, and are typically small relative to the boundary total ion density.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_carbon_density
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the total elemental carbon number density on a closed magnetic surface. The local carbon density is summed over all charge states from neutral carbon to fully stripped carbon before averaging.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged carbon density is the mean total elemental carbon number density on a closed magnetic flux surface. The local carbon density is summed over all charge states from neutral carbon through fully stripped carbon before averaging, matching the charge-state scope of [volume_averaged_carbon_density](name:volume_averaged_carbon_density) and [line_averaged_carbon_density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density) while using a magnetic-surface average.

For an axisymmetric closed surface labeled by the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, the flux-surface average over the closed poloidal contour is

$$
\langle n_C \rangle_\psi = \frac{\oint_\psi n_C(R,Z)\, R\, dl / |\nabla\psi|}{\oint_\psi R\, dl / |\nabla\psi|}
$$

where $n_C = \sum_{q=0}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C},q}$ is the total carbon density, $n_{\mathrm{C},0}$ is neutral carbon, and $n_{\mathrm{C},6}$ is fully stripped carbon. The contour lies in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height; $dl$ is the arc-length element in meters, $\psi$ is in webers, and $|\nabla\psi|$ is in Wb m$^{-1}$. The denominator normalizes the geometric weighting so the result retains units of m$^{-3}$.

In practice, local charge-state densities are estimated from impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination measurements when available, collisional-radiative modeling, and particle-balance constraints for weakly observed charge states. A magnetic equilibrium maps those local estimates to the same closed flux surfaces used for [flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density), and the charge-state sum is formed consistently before applying the average.

Representative edge-plasma values are commonly $10^{16}-10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ in carbon-wall or carbon-seeded conditions, with smaller values possible in low-carbon metal-wall plasmas and larger transient values during sputtering or injection events. Comparison with [ratio_of_carbon_density_to_electron_density](name:ratio_of_carbon_density_to_electron_density) expresses the carbon burden relative to electrons, while [carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis) gives the corresponding central local value. The analogous [flux_surface_averaged_iron_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_iron_density) applies the same magnetic-surface average to iron.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_electron_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density averaged over the last closed flux surface at the plasma boundary. It represents the separatrix density as the limiting flux-surface average from the confined plasma side.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged electron density at the plasma boundary is the electron number density averaged over the separatrix, or last closed flux surface. Because the separatrix is the boundary between closed magnetic surfaces and open scrape-off-layer field lines, the quantity is interpreted as the limit of the closed-surface average taken from inside the confined plasma.

The separatrix value is defined from the flux-surface average of the electron density as the closed magnetic surface approaches the separatrix:

$$
\langle n_e \rangle_{\mathrm{sep}} = \lim_{\psi \to \psi_{\mathrm{sep}}^-} \frac{\oint_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} n_e \, dS / |\nabla\psi|}{\oint_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} dS / |\nabla\psi|}
$$

where $n_e$ is the local electron number density in m^-3, $\psi$ is a poloidal magnetic flux label, $\psi_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is its value at the separatrix, $dS$ is the surface-area element on a closed magnetic surface, and $|\nabla\psi|$ accounts for the differential volume between neighboring flux surfaces. The weighting is therefore a volume-shell weighting of the flux-surface average, not a measure of field-line spacing.

In practice this quantity is inferred by combining edge density measurements, such as Thomson scattering, interferometry, reflectometry, or Langmuir-probe information, with an equilibrium reconstruction that identifies the last closed flux surface. Because diagnostics rarely sample the mathematical separatrix exactly, the value is usually obtained by fitting or mapping measurements to flux coordinates and extrapolating or interpolating to the separatrix from the confined-plasma side.

Typical values in tokamak plasmas are about $0.1-5 \times 10^{19}$ m^-3, with lower values in low-density limiter-like or detached-edge conditions and higher values in high-density H-mode or reactor-relevant edge plasmas. The value depends strongly on fueling, recycling, pedestal conditions, and divertor or scrape-off-layer transport.

NAMES.name: gradient_of_radial_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Core-side derivative of electron number density with respect to normalized poloidal flux at the H-mode pedestal, representing the density slope just inside the steep pedestal region.
NAMES.long:
The gradient of radial electron density is the derivative of electron number density with respect to the normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_N$, evaluated on the core-side branch of an H-mode pedestal density fit. It characterizes the gentler radial variation just inside the steep pedestal layer and is distinct from the maximum pedestal density gradient gradient_of_electron_density.

The core-side pedestal slope is defined by evaluating the derivative of the fitted electron density $n_e$ at the core-side pedestal location $\psi_{N,\mathrm{core}}$:

$$
G_{n_e,\mathrm{core}} = \left.\frac{d n_e}{d\psi_N}\right|_{\psi_N = \psi_{N,\mathrm{core}}}
$$

where $G_{n_e,\mathrm{core}}$ is this quantity, $n_e$ is electron number density, and $\psi_N$ is the normalized poloidal flux coordinate. Because $\psi_N$ is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as electron number density.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by fitting edge electron density measurements with a pedestal representation and taking the derivative of that fitted function on the core side of the pedestal. The value should not be interpreted as the steepest pedestal slope; that maximum-gradient quantity is usually larger in magnitude and located within the narrow pedestal transition region.

Typical H-mode core-side values are often negative, with magnitudes about $10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3 for weakly varying or moderately sloped density, and occasionally approaching $10^{21}$ m^-3 in strongly shaped or high-density pedestals. Values near zero indicate an almost flat core-side density variation over the fitted interval.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron number density increases with increasing normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_N$.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep edge transport barrier joins the flatter confined-plasma density region.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 density at the pedestal is the local number density of ions of the stable mass-3 helium isotope evaluated at the pedestal top. The pedestal top is the inner edge of the steep-gradient edge transport barrier, so this quantity characterizes the helium-3 content entering the confined plasma from the edge region.

The local pedestal value may be defined by the particle-number density of helium-3 ions in a small volume centered on the pedestal-top location:

$$
n_{^3\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ped}} = \left.\frac{dN_{^3\mathrm{He}}}{dV}\right|_{\mathrm{ped}}
$$

where $N_{^3\mathrm{He}}$ is the number of helium-3 ions in volume $V$, and the subscript $\mathrm{ped}$ denotes evaluation at the pedestal top.

In practice it is obtained from an edge or pedestal density reconstruction combined with an estimate of the helium-3 isotope fraction. That fraction may come from fuel accounting, isotope-sensitive spectroscopy or neutral analysis where available, and transport or particle-balance modeling; the result is usually interpreted together with quasineutrality and the densities of the main ion species.

Typical values are highly scenario dependent. In plasmas without intentional helium-3 fueling, the pedestal helium-3 density is usually a trace component, often below routine quantification or below about $10^{16}$-$10^{18}$ m^-3. In helium-3 minority or fueled scenarios, a pedestal isotope fraction of about 0.1-10% of an ion pedestal density near $10^{19}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3 corresponds to roughly $10^{16}$-$10^{19}$ m^-3.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions (the stable helium isotope with mass number 3) evaluated at the plasma boundary, the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 ($^3$He) is the stable helium isotope with two protons and one neutron (mass number 3, charge number 2). This quantity gives the number of $^3$He ions per unit volume evaluated at the plasma boundary, defined as the last closed flux surface (separatrix) that divides the closed-field-line confined region from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. It is the helium-3 specialization of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary).

Helium-3 enters tokamak plasmas either as a minority heating species in ion cyclotron resonance heating schemes, where a small $^3$He fraction resonates efficiently with the ICRH wave, or as a fuel ion in D-$^3$He burn scenarios. In both cases, the boundary density is a key parameter for edge particle balance and fuel-purity assessment. Boundary values are inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy using $^3$He spectral lines or from edge transport modeling constrained by particle flux boundary conditions.

Typical $^3$He boundary densities in minority-heating scenarios lie in the range $10^{16}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, well below the separatrix electron density of $10^{19}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$. The corresponding core value is captured by [helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis), the pedestal-top value by [helium_3_density_at_pedestal](name:helium_3_density_at_pedestal), and the downstream target value by [helium_3_density_at_divertor_target](name:helium_3_density_at_divertor_target), together forming a complete radial survey of $^3$He ion density from core to divertor.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-4 ions evaluated at the pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier transitions toward the flatter core plasma.
NAMES.long:
Helium-4 density at the pedestal is the local number density of helium-4 ions evaluated at the pedestal top. In deuterium-tritium plasmas this species includes thermalized alpha-particle ash, while in other plasmas it may also represent helium introduced for fueling, wall conditioning, or impurity studies.

The pedestal value is the local helium-4 ion number density evaluated at the pedestal-top location:

$$
n_{\mathrm{He4,ped}} = n_{\mathrm{He4}}\big|_{\mathrm{ped}} = \lim_{\Delta V \to 0} \frac{\Delta N_{\mathrm{He4}}}{\Delta V}
$$

where $\Delta N_{\mathrm{He4}}$ is the number of helium-4 ions contained in a small volume $\Delta V$ around the pedestal-top location, and $\Delta V$ is expressed in m^3 so that $n_{\mathrm{He4,ped}}$ is in m^-3.

The pedestal top is identified from the break between the steep-gradient edge region and the flatter core-side behavior of edge plasma quantities. The helium-4 density there may be inferred from helium-sensitive spectroscopy or charge-exchange measurements when available, and is often constrained together with other ion densities by quasineutrality, transport analysis, and particle-balance modeling.

Physical values are non-negative: $n_{\mathrm{He4,ped}} \ge 0$. Representative values can range from effectively 0 m^-3 in plasmas with no helium source to trace or minority-ion levels in helium-seeded or deuterium-tritium plasmas, commonly spanning about 10^15-10^19 m^-3 depending on helium production, external injection, confinement, and exhaust.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-4 ions evaluated on the plasma boundary, the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Helium-4 density at the plasma boundary is the number density of ions whose nuclei are the isotope $^{4}\mathrm{He}$, evaluated on the last closed flux surface. The plasma boundary is the separatrix between the closed-field-line region and the scrape-off layer. The quantity is non-negative and is a species density, not a charge density.

Using a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ with normalized radial label $\rho$ chosen so that the plasma boundary is at $\rho=1$, the local boundary value is

$$
n_{^{4}\mathrm{He},b} = n_{^{4}\mathrm{He}}(\rho=1)
$$

where $n_{^{4}\mathrm{He}}$ is the helium-4 ion number density field and the subscript $b$ denotes evaluation at the boundary. This definition specifies boundary evaluation only; it does not by itself imply a flux-surface average over $(\theta,\phi)$. If an averaged boundary value is used, that averaging is an additional reduction of the local boundary density.

In practice the value is obtained by evaluating a species-resolved edge plasma model or reconstruction at the separatrix, often constrained by spectroscopic, charge-exchange, divertor, or edge-profile measurements when available. In a fully ionized plasma, helium-4 is typically present as $\mathrm{He}^{2+}$, so its electron-density contribution is $2 n_{^{4}\mathrm{He}}$; charge-state effects should be treated consistently when partial ionization is important near the edge.

Typical values can range from near 0 m^-3 when helium-4 is absent or weakly retained to about $10^{16}$-$10^{19}$ m^-3 in plasmas with helium ash, helium fueling, or dedicated helium operation. The upper range is limited by the local edge electron density and the helium concentration.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Hydrogen (protium) ion number density evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogen density at pedestal is the local number density of protium ions at the pedestal top of an H-mode plasma. The pedestal top is the inner edge of the steep-gradient edge transport barrier, where the edge density gradient relaxes toward the core plasma behavior.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from edge density measurements together with ion-species composition information and an identification of the pedestal-top location. It represents the protium ion contribution only; deuterium, tritium, and impurity ions are separate species contributions to the total ion population.

Representative values are scenario dependent. In majority-hydrogen H-mode plasmas, pedestal-top protium ion densities are commonly of order $1-10 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$; in mixed-isotope or trace-hydrogen plasmas they can be substantially lower depending on fueling, isotope mix, and edge transport.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen (protium) ions at the plasma boundary, the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogen ion number density at the plasma boundary is the count of protium (H+) ions per unit volume at the separatrix, the last closed flux surface (LCFS) that bounds magnetically confined plasma against the open-field-line scrape-off layer. As the hydrogen-specific instance of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary), it characterizes the local protium population at the edge transport boundary, governing ionization balance, recycling flux, and neutral penetration depth.

The boundary value is obtained as the flux-surface average of the local hydrogen ion density over the LCFS:

$$
n_H^{\rm sep} = \frac{1}{S_{\rm LCFS}} \oint_{\rm LCFS} n_H \, dS
$$

where $S_{\rm LCFS}$ is the total area of the last closed flux surface and $n_H$ is the local hydrogen ion number density on the surface.

This quantity is inferred from edge Thomson scattering, Balmer-series hydrogen spectroscopy (H$\alpha$ emission), or Langmuir-probe measurements combined with ionization-balance modeling in edge fluid codes.

In deuterium-dominated discharges, protium (hydrogen-1) is a minority main-ion species due to wall outgassing; separatrix hydrogen ion densities lie in the range $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, rising toward $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in hydrogen-fueled or heavy-recycling scenarios. The analogous density for the dominant fuel isotope is [deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary), while heavier impurity boundary densities include [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary).

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion average temperature at the pedestal top is the density-weighted temperature of all ion species and charge states evaluated at the core-side shoulder of the H-mode pedestal. The pedestal top is distinct from the pedestal foot near the separatrix and scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Ion average temperature at the pedestal top is the ion_average_temperature evaluated at the core-side shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. Moving outward from the plasma center, this location marks the transition from the central plasma to the steep-gradient pedestal region; it is distinct from the pedestal foot on the separatrix and scrape-off-layer side.

For ion populations indexed by $j$, where each population corresponds to a species and charge state, the pedestal-top average is commonly defined as a density-weighted mean:

$$
\langle T_i \rangle_{\mathrm{top}} = \frac{\sum_j n_{j,\mathrm{top}} T_{j,\mathrm{top}}}{\sum_j n_{j,\mathrm{top}}}
$$

where $T_{j,\mathrm{top}}$ is the temperature of ion population $j$ in eV, $n_{j,\mathrm{top}}$ is its number density in m^-3, and the subscript $\mathrm{top}$ denotes evaluation at the pedestal-top radial location. If the value is used to estimate SI ion thermal pressure, the eV-valued temperature must be converted by the elementary charge: $p_i = e\,n_i\langle T_i\rangle_{\mathrm{top}}$, with $n_i = \sum_j n_{j,\mathrm{top}}$.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from edge ion-temperature measurements such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, neutral-particle analysis, or integrated kinetic analysis, combined with an identification of the pedestal-top location from the measured radial variation of temperature, density, or pressure. When only impurity-ion temperatures are measured, main-ion temperature estimates require collisional equilibration or transport assumptions.

Typical pedestal-top ion average temperatures range from 100-1000 eV in smaller or moderate-performance H-mode plasmas and from 1000-5000 eV in large, high-performance H-mode plasmas. The value varies with heating power, pedestal density, isotope mix, collisionality, and edge-localized-mode phase.

NAMES.name: ion_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Diffusion coefficient for total ion particle transport in a magnetized plasma, relating the ion particle flux to the local ion number density gradient across field-aligned and poloidal directions.
NAMES.long:
Ion diffusivity quantifies gradient-driven (Fickian) transport of the total ion population in a magnetized plasma, relating the ion particle flux to the ion number density gradient. Strong magnetic confinement makes ion transport intrinsically anisotropic, so the diffusivity is a directional quantity whose magnitude differs by orders of magnitude between field-aligned and cross-field directions.

The diffusive ion particle flux $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i$ is governed by Fick's law:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i = -\mathbf{D}_i \cdot \nabla n_i
$$

where $\mathbf{D}_i$ is the ion diffusivity tensor and $n_i$ is the local total ion number density in m$^{-3}$. The physically resolved projections of this tensor are the [parallel ion diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_diffusivity), which characterizes field-aligned transport governed by collisional dynamics and can exceed cross-field values by many orders of magnitude, and the [poloidal ion diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_diffusivity), which captures transport along the poloidal direction in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ where $\rho$ is a radial flux label, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

Ion diffusivity is inferred from experimental density profiles by fitting gradient-flux relationships, or computed from neoclassical theory and turbulence simulations. Anomalous (turbulence-driven) contributions typically dominate over neoclassical values in the core and pedestal. Typical cross-field values range from $10^{-2}$ to $1\;\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$ in the confined core, increasing sharply toward the scrape-off layer. The analogous quantity for the electron population is [electron diffusivity](name:electron_diffusivity).

NAMES.name: iron_density
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Total number density of iron impurity ions in the plasma, summed over all ionization states from singly to fully ionized iron (atomic number Z = 26).
NAMES.long:
Iron density is the total number density of iron ions present in the plasma, aggregated over all charge states from Fe$^{1+}$ through Fe$^{26+}$ (atomic number $Z = 26$). It characterizes the iron impurity content without resolving the per-charge-state distribution, and may refer to a local point value or a spatially averaged quantity depending on the sampling convention.

The total iron ion number density $n_\mathrm{Fe}$ is defined as:

$$
n_\mathrm{Fe} = \sum_{z=1}^{26} n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{z+}}$ is the number density of iron in charge state $z$.

Iron enters confined plasmas primarily through physical sputtering of high-$Z$ plasma-facing components. Spectroscopic measurements in the vacuum-ultraviolet and soft X-ray ranges resolve individual charge-state emission lines; the total iron density is reconstructed by summing ionization-state-resolved densities derived from ionization balance calculations.

This general quantity is concretized by spatial-sampling variants: [flux_surface_averaged_iron_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_iron_density) averages the local density over a magnetic flux surface, [line_averaged_iron_density](name:line_averaged_iron_density) represents a chord-integrated value divided by path length, and [volume_averaged_iron_density](name:volume_averaged_iron_density) integrates over the full plasma volume. Position-specific forms are available at key radial locations such as [iron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:iron_density_at_magnetic_axis), [iron_density_at_pedestal](name:iron_density_at_pedestal), and [iron_density_at_limiter](name:iron_density_at_limiter).
NAMES.sign: Positive when iron ions are present in the sampled plasma volume; the quantity is intrinsically non-negative as a particle number density.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_iron_density
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the total iron impurity ion number density, summed over all iron ionization states. It represents the density assigned to a magnetic flux surface after averaging local variation around that surface, not a statement that iron is spatially uniform there.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged iron density is the average of the total iron impurity ion number density on a magnetic flux surface. The total iron density is summed over all iron ionization states. It is a representative density for the surface and does not imply that the local iron density is uniform on that surface.

The flux-surface average can be written using a poloidal magnetic flux label $\psi$:

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Fe}}\rangle_{\psi} = \frac{\int_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} n_{\mathrm{Fe}}\, dA/|\nabla\psi|}{\int_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} dA/|\nabla\psi|}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Fe}}$ is the local total iron ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{Fe}}=\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}$ over iron ionization states $q$, $dA$ is a surface-area element in $\mathrm{m}^2$, and $|\nabla\psi|$ is in $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}$ when $\psi$ is in $\mathrm{Wb}$. The weighting corresponds to averaging over the thin volume between neighboring flux surfaces.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by combining an equilibrium reconstruction that supplies the magnetic flux surfaces with local or modeled iron charge-state densities. These densities may be inferred from extreme-ultraviolet, x-ray, or visible line emission with collisional-radiative modeling, and may be constrained by impurity transport, radiation, electron density, and electron temperature measurements. Strong edge gradients and localized sources can make the local iron density vary strongly on a surface, so the flux-surface average should be interpreted as an averaged abundance rather than a local value.

Typical values for trace iron contamination are $10^{12}-10^{16}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ in confined plasmas. During strong wall influx, impurity accumulation, disruptions, or deliberate impurity injection, edge or separatrix averages can reach $10^{17}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ or higher.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Charge-state-summed number density of iron impurity ions at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep edge transport barrier joins the flatter confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
Iron density at the pedestal is the total number density of iron impurity ions on the pedestal-top flux surface. It is summed over all ionized charge states of iron and is non-negative as a particle number density. The pedestal top is the shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier, often identified consistently with quantities such as [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal), electron_density_at_pedestal_top, and [electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top).

The charge-state-summed pedestal density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Fe,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{26} n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}(\rho_\mathrm{ped})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Fe,ped}}$ is the total iron ion density at the pedestal top in m$^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}$ is the density of iron ions with charge state $q+$ in m$^{-3}$, and $\rho_\mathrm{ped}$ denotes the pedestal-top flux surface.

Iron is a high-Z metallic impurity commonly produced by sputtering or erosion of steel components, ferritic materials, and other iron-containing plasma-facing structures. At the pedestal, iron can contribute strongly to line radiation and bremsstrahlung losses, so this local density is important for interpreting pedestal energy balance, impurity screening, and edge confinement degradation. It complements [volume_averaged_iron_density](name:volume_averaged_iron_density), [iron_density_at_divertor_target](name:iron_density_at_divertor_target), and [iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

In practice, the pedestal iron density is inferred from spectroscopic measurements of selected iron emission lines, typically in the vacuum ultraviolet, soft X-ray, or charge-exchange wavelength ranges, together with collisional-radiative or ionization-balance modeling to recover the total charge-state-summed density. The pedestal-top location is usually obtained from fitted edge profiles, commonly near the transition between the steepest-gradient pedestal region and the flatter core plasma.

Representative pedestal values are highly device-, wall-condition-, and scenario-dependent: clean discharges may have about $10^{12}$-$10^{14}$ m$^{-3}$, while stronger metallic source conditions or impurity-accumulation phases can reach $10^{15}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$. Related seeded-impurity pedestal densities include [nitrogen_density_at_pedestal](name:nitrogen_density_at_pedestal) and [argon_density_at_pedestal](name:argon_density_at_pedestal).

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Number density of iron impurity ions summed over all ionization stages, evaluated at the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Iron (atomic number $Z = 26$) is a metallic impurity that can enter the plasma from iron-containing plasma-facing components or structural materials. At the plasma boundary — the last closed flux surface between the confined core and the open-field-line scrape-off layer — this density characterizes the iron impurity concentration at the innermost edge of the scrape-off layer and serves as a boundary condition for edge impurity transport modeling.

Unless a specific charge state is stated, the density sums over all ionization stages:

$$
n_\mathrm{Fe} = \sum_{q=1}^{26} n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}$ is the partial number density of iron ions in charge state $q^+$.

The boundary iron density can be inferred from VUV or soft X-ray spectroscopy of iron line emission or from impurity transport simulations constrained by edge diagnostics. Elevated concentrations at the plasma boundary signal strong metallic impurity sourcing from plasma-facing components and can lead to significant radiative cooling and hydrogenic fuel dilution. The species-agnostic parent concept is defined by [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary); the iron impurity distribution inside the separatrix is further characterized at the pedestal by [iron_density_at_pedestal](name:iron_density_at_pedestal) and at the divertor plate by [iron_density_at_divertor_target](name:iron_density_at_divertor_target). The analogous boundary density for another seeded impurity species is given by [nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary).

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Number density of krypton ions at the H-mode pedestal top, summed over all ionization states. The pedestal top is the core-side end of the steep edge transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Krypton density at the pedestal is the local elemental krypton ion number density evaluated at the pedestal top, the core-side end of the steep H-mode edge transport barrier. It represents the total krypton ion population at that location rather than the density of a single charge state.

The quantity is the charge-state sum of charge-resolved krypton ion densities at the pedestal top:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Kr,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}} n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+},\mathrm{ped}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Kr,ped}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{q+},\mathrm{ped}}$ are number densities in m^-3, $q$ is the dimensionless ion charge state, and $Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}=36$ is the dimensionless nuclear charge of krypton.

The pedestal-top location is identified from the transition between the steep edge transport-barrier region and the flatter core plasma. Charge-state-resolved krypton densities are inferred from spectroscopic constraints combined with atomic physics, ionization-balance, or impurity-transport modeling; the summed density removes dependence on which individual krypton charge states dominate locally.

Because krypton is usually used as a trace radiating impurity, its pedestal density is strongly scenario dependent and is commonly interpreted together with the local electron density or krypton concentration rather than by a universal absolute range.

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Number density of ionized lithium at the H-mode pedestal top, equal to the local sum over Li+, Li2+, and Li3+ charge states. Neutral lithium atoms are excluded, so the quantity is non-negative and expressed per cubic meter.
NAMES.long:
Lithium density at the pedestal is the local number density of ionized lithium evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier transitions toward the flatter core plasma. It includes the lithium ion charge states Li$^+$, Li$^{2+}$, and Li$^{3+}$, and excludes neutral lithium atoms, lithium molecules, and wall-bound lithium. The value is a local pedestal-top density, not an average over the pedestal region.

The pedestal-top lithium-ion density is defined by the charge-state sum:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Li,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{3} n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}\big|_{\mathrm{ped}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}\big|_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is the local number density of lithium ions with charge state $q+$ at the pedestal top. The neutral density $n_{\mathrm{Li}^0}$ is not included in this sum.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from lithium-sensitive spectroscopy, charge-exchange or emission analysis where available, and impurity transport or collisional-radiative modeling constrained by local electron density and temperature. The pedestal-top location is usually identified from steep-gradient-region structure in measured or reconstructed edge plasma quantities, then the lithium charge-state densities are evaluated at that location.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. In plasmas without an active lithium source the value may be zero or below diagnostic detectability, while lithium-conditioned or lithium-injected plasmas often remain in a trace-impurity range of about $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ at the pedestal top; higher local values can occur during strong transient injection.

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Number density of ionized lithium impurity at the plasma boundary, identified with the separatrix. It is summed over Li+, Li2+, and Li3+ charge states, excludes neutral lithium, and is a non-negative scalar in m^-3.
NAMES.long:
Lithium density at the plasma boundary is the number density of ionized lithium impurity at the separatrix, the interface between closed magnetic flux surfaces and open scrape-off-layer field lines. It includes all ionized lithium charge states, Li$^+$ through Li$^{3+}$, and excludes neutral lithium. As a particle number density, it is non-negative and has unit m$^{-3}$.

The charge-state-summed lithium ion density is defined by:

$$
n_\mathrm{Li} = \sum_{q=1}^{3} n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Li}$ is the total ionized lithium number density in m$^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{Li}^{q+}}$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$ of lithium ions with charge state $q$, and $q=1,2,3$ for lithium. Neutral lithium, $\mathrm{Li}^0$, is not included.

Boundary lithium ion density is inferred from edge impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements when available, atomic-physics modeling, and consistency with separatrix electron density and temperature. When represented as a single boundary scalar, it denotes a representative separatrix value; it should not be interpreted as necessarily flux-surface averaged unless the quantity is explicitly identified as flux-surface averaged, as in [flux_surface_averaged_electron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_electron_density_at_plasma_boundary).

Typical separatrix lithium ion densities are often trace levels of about $10^{14}$-$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$, but active lithium injection, evaporation, or strong lithium wall sources can raise values toward $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$. These values are usually small compared with [total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary) and the corresponding electron density, but they can still affect edge radiation and [effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary](name:effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary). The concept is analogous to other impurity boundary densities such as [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary).

NAMES.name: momentum_coefficient
NAMES.short: Dimensionless coefficient that scales the collisionless free-streaming upper bound on momentum-flux density in multi-fluid edge plasma transport closures, capping the flux magnitude while leaving its sign direction unchanged.
NAMES.long:
In multi-fluid edge plasma transport models, gradient-driven diffusive closures can produce momentum-flux densities that exceed the physically realizable collisionless free-streaming limit in steep-gradient regions such as the scrape-off layer and divertor. A flux-limiter coefficient $\alpha_m$ is introduced to bound the effective flux: the limited momentum-flux density magnitude cannot exceed $\alpha_m$ times a free-streaming reference scale, while the sign follows the underlying diffusive flux direction.

The limited momentum-flux density $\Pi^{\mathrm{lim}}$ is formed by the harmonic-mean combination:

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{lim}} = \frac{\alpha_m \, \Pi^{\mathrm{FS}} \cdot \Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}}{|\Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}| + \alpha_m \, \Pi^{\mathrm{FS}}}
$$

where $\Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the collisional diffusive momentum-flux estimate, $\Pi^{\mathrm{FS}} = m n v_{\mathrm{th}}^2$ is the free-streaming scale with $m$ the particle mass, $n$ the number density, and $v_{\mathrm{th}}$ the thermal speed. When $|\Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}| \gg \alpha_m \Pi^{\mathrm{FS}}$ the flux saturates at $\pm \alpha_m \Pi^{\mathrm{FS}}$; when $|\Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}| \ll \alpha_m \Pi^{\mathrm{FS}}$ the diffusive value is recovered unchanged.

Specializations target individual projection directions, such as [parallel_momentum_coefficient](name:parallel_momentum_coefficient) for field-aligned transport, and individual particle populations, such as [ion_state_momentum_coefficient](name:ion_state_momentum_coefficient) for specific ion charge states or [parallel_neutral_state_momentum_coefficient](name:parallel_neutral_state_momentum_coefficient) for neutral-particle parallel transport. The coefficient is intrinsically non-negative; values in the range 0.1–1 are common in edge-plasma simulations, selected by calibration against experimental separatrix and divertor data.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Neon ion number density at the H-mode pedestal top, summed over all ionization charge states of the neon element. It is a non-negative elemental impurity density at the transition from the steep edge transport barrier to the flatter core plasma.
NAMES.long:
The neon density at the pedestal is the total number density of neon ions at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier joins the more weakly varying confined plasma. It is an elemental impurity density: ions in different neon charge states contribute to the same total. As a number density, it is non-negative and has units of $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

The charge-state-summed elemental density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ne,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{Z_\mathrm{Ne}} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+},\mathrm{ped}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ne,ped}}$ is the neon ion number density at the pedestal top in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+},\mathrm{ped}}$ is the number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ of neon ions with charge state $q+$ at the pedestal top, and $Z_\mathrm{Ne}=10$ is the nuclear charge of neon.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by summing resolved charge-state densities, or by inferring the elemental neon content from impurity measurements together with a pedestal-top location determined from plasma profiles and equilibrium information. It is commonly interpreted relative to [electron_density_at_pedestal](name:electron_density_at_pedestal) or main_ion_density_at_pedestal, for example through the concentration $n_{\mathrm{Ne,ped}}/n_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$, because neon is usually a trace or minor impurity rather than the dominant ion species.

Typical values are strongly scenario-dependent, especially in plasmas with deliberate neon seeding for edge radiation control. No device-independent absolute range is implied by the definition; the physically useful scale is usually the neon concentration relative to the local pedestal electron or main-ion density.

This quantity is the neon counterpart of pedestal impurity densities such as [nitrogen_density_at_pedestal](name:nitrogen_density_at_pedestal), [oxygen_density_at_pedestal](name:oxygen_density_at_pedestal), and [xenon_density_at_pedestal](name:xenon_density_at_pedestal). The same elemental neon density evaluated at an internal transport barrier is represented by [neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Number density of neon ions at the plasma boundary (separatrix), the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The neon impurity density at the plasma boundary quantifies the concentration of neon ions at the separatrix, which marks the transition between the nested closed flux surfaces of the confined plasma and the open-field-line scrape-off layer. Neon (atomic number $Z = 10$) is a widely used medium-Z seeding species whose partially stripped ionization states radiate efficiently in the edge region and divertor, contributing to radiative power exhaust and reducing peak heat loads on plasma-facing components.

The separatrix neon density $n_\mathrm{Ne}$ provides a key boundary condition for impurity transport models linking the core plasma to the exhaust region. It complements [neon_density_at_divertor_target](name:neon_density_at_divertor_target) in constraining the neon distribution between the separatrix and the divertor target, and belongs to the same species-resolved family as [nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary), [xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary), all components of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary).

Boundary neon density is measured or inferred through charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, emission spectroscopy from helium-like or hydrogen-like neon charge states, or estimated from integrated power balance coupled with edge transport modeling. The reported value is often a flux-surface average over the separatrix contour.

In neon-seeded experiments, separatrix densities range from roughly $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, scaling with the gas injection throughput and local edge transport properties.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neon ions are present at a nonzero concentration at the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: neutral_momentum_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Dimensionless vector flux-limiter coefficient that scales the free-streaming upper bound on neutral-particle momentum-flux density component-by-component in edge-plasma transport closures.
NAMES.long:
The neutral momentum coefficient is the neutral-particle specialization of the general [momentum_coefficient](name:momentum_coefficient) vector, providing one dimensionless limiter factor per spatial direction for neutral momentum transport in multi-fluid edge plasma models. Each directional component independently bounds the corresponding neutral momentum flux density, preventing unphysical exceedance of the free-streaming limit when the neutral mean free path is large relative to macroscopic gradient scales.

The component $\alpha_\alpha$ in direction $\hat{e}_\alpha$ is defined as the ratio of the modeled flux to its free-streaming upper bound:

$$
\alpha_\alpha = \frac{\Pi_\alpha}{\Pi_\alpha^{\rm free}}
$$

where $\Pi_\alpha$ is the modeled neutral momentum flux density in direction $\hat{e}_\alpha$ and $\Pi_\alpha^{\rm free} = m_n n_n u_\alpha^{\rm free}$ is the free-streaming estimate, with $m_n$ the neutral particle mass, $n_n$ the neutral number density, and $u_\alpha^{\rm free}$ the direction-$\alpha$ free-streaming reference speed. The constraint $\alpha_\alpha \in [0, 1]$ ensures the closure preserves the sign of the momentum flux while bounding its magnitude. The field-aligned component is analogous to [parallel_neutral_state_momentum_coefficient](name:parallel_neutral_state_momentum_coefficient), which resolves the same quantity by internal neutral state.

Components are computed within edge-plasma transport closures as a function of local collisionality; values near 1 characterize the collision-dominated limit, while values near 0 indicate strongly free-streaming conditions where the limiter actively constrains the flux.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral momentum flux in the corresponding direction is in the same sense as the free-streaming estimate along the respective axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame or along the magnetic-field direction.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of nitrogen impurity ions at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier transitions to the flatter core plasma.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen density at the pedestal is the total number density of nitrogen impurity ions at the pedestal top of an H-mode plasma. Unless a charge state is specified separately, it represents the sum over all nitrogen ionization states at the location where the steep edge transport barrier joins the core plasma.

The density is the zeroth velocity moment of the nitrogen ion distribution functions at the pedestal-top position:

$$
n_{\mathrm{N,ped}} = \sum_q \int f_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ped}},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{N,ped}}$ is in m^-3, $q$ indexes nitrogen ionization charge states, $f_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}}$ is the phase-space distribution function with units m^-6 s^3, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is the pedestal-top position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m/s, and $d^3v$ has units m^3 s^-3. For a single resolved charge state, the summation is omitted.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination measurements when available, and collisional-radiative modeling, often constrained by local electron density and temperature at the pedestal top. The pedestal top is identified from the transition between the steep edge gradient region and the core plasma, commonly using fitted electron pressure, density, or temperature behavior.

Representative pedestal nitrogen densities span roughly 10^16-10^19 m^-3, depending strongly on nitrogen seeding level, edge transport, ionization balance, and plasma size. Trace or unseeded conditions are usually toward the lower end, while actively seeded H-mode plasmas can reach the upper part of this range locally.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of nitrogen impurity ions evaluated at the plasma boundary (separatrix), representing the impurity concentration at the last closed flux surface separating confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen ion number density at the plasma boundary quantifies the concentration of nitrogen impurity ions at the separatrix — the last closed flux surface demarcating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. This is the nitrogen-species instantiation of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). Nitrogen is routinely injected into tokamaks as a controlled impurity to enhance radiative dissipation of exhaust power and reduce peak heat loads at divertor targets.

The boundary value reflects the balance between impurity sources (gas injection, ionization of recycled neutrals) and outward transport through the scrape-off layer. Its magnitude relative to the main-ion density influences the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ and the radiated power fraction at the plasma edge. The toroidal flow of nitrogen at the same location is separately captured by [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

The quantity is inferred from spectroscopic measurements of nitrogen line emission in the edge and divertor regions combined with collisional-radiative modeling, or from fluid impurity transport simulations constrained by bolometric data. Typical values range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on the nitrogen injection rate and edge plasma density. Analogous separatrix densities for other impurity species include [neon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:neon_density_at_plasma_boundary), [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive definite, as number density is a particle count per unit volume and does not change sign under any coordinate transformation.

NAMES.name: normalized_electron_collisionality_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of the electron collision frequency to the trapped-electron bounce frequency evaluated at the pressure pedestal top.
NAMES.long:
Normalized electron collisionality at the pedestal top measures how rapidly Coulomb collisions scatter electrons compared with the bounce motion of trapped electrons at the top of the H-mode pressure pedestal. It is a local dimensionless neoclassical parameter: values much smaller than unity indicate weakly collisional trapped-electron motion, while values near or above unity indicate that collisions significantly modify trapped-particle dynamics.

A common neoclassical estimate is:

$$
\nu^*_e = \frac{q R \nu_{ei}}{v_{\mathrm{th},e} \epsilon^{3/2}}
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor, $R$ is major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\nu_{ei}$ is the local electron-ion collision frequency, $v_{\mathrm{th},e}$ is the electron thermal speed, and $\epsilon$ is the local inverse aspect ratio of the flux surface. The thermal speed is commonly taken as $v_{\mathrm{th},e}=\sqrt{2T_e/m_e}$ when $T_e$ is expressed as an energy, so the ratio can also be read as $\nu_{ei}$ divided by an effective trapped-electron bounce frequency $v_{\mathrm{th},e}\epsilon^{3/2}/(qR)$.

In practice this quantity is computed by evaluating the local density, temperature, safety factor, major radius, and flux-surface geometry at the pressure pedestal top, then using them to calculate $\nu_{ei}$ and the bounce-frequency normalization. The pedestal-top location is typically identified from fits to the edge pressure or density and temperature gradients, while magnetic geometry is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction.

Representative pedestal-top values are dimensionless and commonly range from well below unity to order 10, depending mainly on electron temperature, density, size, safety factor, and aspect ratio. Hot, low-density pedestals tend toward lower $\nu^*_e$, whereas cooler or denser pedestals tend toward higher values.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial coordinate of the H-mode pedestal, defined as the normalized poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at the pedestal's flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal magnetic flux coordinate $\psi_N$ maps the equilibrium poloidal flux function $\psi$ to the interval $[0, 1]$ by subtracting the on-axis value and dividing by the flux range from axis to boundary. Evaluated at the pedestal, it provides a dimensionless, device-independent label for the radial location of the H-mode edge transport barrier.

The defining relation is:

$$
\psi_N = \frac{\psi - \psi_0}{\psi_b - \psi_0}
$$

where $\psi_0$ is [the poloidal flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), $\psi_b$ is its value at the last closed flux surface, and $\psi$ is the flux at the flux surface of interest. The pedestal center in this coordinate marks the inflection point of the steep-gradient region; combined with the pedestal [full width], it fully characterizes the radial extent and location of the barrier.

In H-mode operation, the pedestal position is found in the range $\psi_N \approx 0.88$–$0.99$, with the exact value depending on plasma shaping, current, and heating power. It is extracted from analytic fits to edge profiles of electron density, temperature, or pressure using methods such as modified hyperbolic-tangent or piecewise-linear models. The companion quantity [poloidal magnetic flux at the pedestal](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_pedestal) gives the corresponding absolute flux value without normalization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pedestal flux surface lies outside the magnetic axis, so that $\psi > \psi_0$.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Oxygen impurity ion number density at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core profile.
NAMES.long:
The oxygen ion number density at the pedestal top characterizes the volumetric concentration of oxygen impurities within the H-mode edge transport barrier. Oxygen (atomic number $Z = 8$) enters tokamak plasmas primarily through plasma-wall interactions and recycling; at the pedestal, its local density contributes to fuel dilution, radiative heat losses, and the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$.

The quantity $n_\mathrm{O}$ represents the total oxygen ion number density summed over all ionization charge states at the pedestal-top flux surface. At pedestal electron temperatures of 0.3–1 keV, oxygen approaches full ionization, predominantly occupying the $\mathrm{O}^{7+}$ and $\mathrm{O}^{8+}$ charge states. This is the oxygen-specific member of the [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family, using the same pedestal-top evaluation convention as [neon_density_at_pedestal](name:neon_density_at_pedestal), [carbon_density_at_pedestal](name:carbon_density_at_pedestal), and [nitrogen_density_at_pedestal](name:nitrogen_density_at_pedestal).

Oxygen pedestal density is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or from impurity transport modeling constrained by soft X-ray and visible spectroscopy data. Typical values in current tokamak experiments range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, representing a trace level relative to the main ion pedestal density. The associated fluid velocity at the pedestal is captured by [toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen ions are present at the pedestal location.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged number density of oxygen impurity ions at the plasma boundary, defined by the last closed flux surface separating the confined plasma from the scrape-off layer. It represents the sum over oxygen ion charge states, not neutral oxygen.
NAMES.long:
