Oxygen density at the plasma boundary is the elemental number density of ionized oxygen on the last closed flux surface, taken as a flux-surface average over that boundary. It is one impurity-species contribution to [total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary); the quantity counts oxygen ions as particles and is not charge-weighted.

The total oxygen ion density at the boundary is obtained by summing charge-state-resolved oxygen ion densities and applying the boundary flux-surface average:

$$
n_{\mathrm{O},b} = \left\langle \sum_{q=1}^{8} n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{LCFS}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{O}^{q+}}$ is the number density of oxygen ions with charge $q e$, $q=1$ to $8$ spans singly ionized through fully stripped oxygen, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ denotes the flux-surface average over the last closed flux surface, normally understood as the closed-surface limit approaching the separatrix.

In practice this density is inferred from impurity spectroscopy combined with electron temperature, electron density, ionization balance, and impurity transport modeling. Line emission constrains charge states with bound electrons, while the fully stripped contribution is inferred indirectly from ionization balance or recombination-related information.

Typical boundary oxygen ion densities are highly scenario dependent. In tokamak edge analyzes oxygen is usually a trace impurity, with representative values around 10^14-10^18 m^-3, and should be interpreted relative to the local total ion and electron densities.

NAMES.name: parallel_electric_field_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Parallel electric field at the plasma boundary is the signed component of the electric field along the local magnetic field direction, evaluated on the last closed flux surface or separatrix. It is a local boundary quantity, not a flux-surface average.
NAMES.long:
Parallel electric field at the plasma boundary is the local scalar projection of the electric field onto the magnetic-field direction at the last closed flux surface or separatrix. It characterizes field-aligned electric acceleration in the edge plasma and is distinct from a flux-surface-averaged parallel electric field.

The local projection is defined by:

$$
E_\parallel = \mathbf{E}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \frac{\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in tesla, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the local magnetic field, and $E_\parallel$ is in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred by combining the local magnetic-field direction at the plasma boundary with an electric-field estimate from equilibrium evolution, loop-voltage constraints, electrostatic-potential measurements, or edge transport modeling. The definition uses the physical electric field itself; decompositions into inductive and electrostatic parts are method dependent and should not change the projected value when the same physical field is used.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. In quiescent edge conditions the local parallel component is often near zero or much smaller than perpendicular electric fields; during current ramp phases, resistive edge conditions, or transient boundary evolution, representative magnitudes can be about $0.01-1\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, with larger values possible in strongly driven events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric field has a component in the direction of the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: parallel_electron_particle_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Parallel electron particle convection velocity is the signed advective coefficient multiplying electron density in the electron particle flux along the magnetic field. It represents the convective streaming part of parallel electron transport, distinct from diffusion driven by density gradients.
NAMES.long:
Parallel electron particle convection velocity is the signed component of the effective electron particle advection velocity parallel to the magnetic field. In edge plasma transport closures, it is the coefficient that multiplies electron density in the convective part of the [parallel_electron_particle_flux](name:parallel_electron_particle_flux), separate from diffusive transport caused by parallel density gradients.

A common local convection-diffusion decomposition of the parallel electron particle flux is

$$
\Gamma_{e,\parallel} = n_e v_{e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}} - D_{e,\parallel}\nabla_{\parallel} n_e
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\parallel}$ is the electron particle flux density along the magnetic field, $n_e$ is the electron density, $v_{e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the parallel electron particle convection velocity, $D_{e,\parallel}$ is the parallel electron particle diffusivity, and $\nabla_{\parallel}=\hat{b}\cdot\nabla$ with $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

This quantity is usually obtained as an effective transport coefficient in fluid, drift-fluid, or kinetic edge plasma modeling rather than measured directly. It can be constrained by combining measurements or estimates of electron density, parallel particle flux, sheath losses, recycling sources, and collisional friction with a chosen transport closure.

Typical effective values in scrape-off-layer and divertor-edge conditions are $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s^-1, with smaller values near flow stagnation regions and larger values on open field lines with strong parallel losses. Near absorbing material boundaries, sheath physics constrains the net ambipolar particle flux; the fitted electron convective coefficient may be comparable to ion-sound-flow scales but is not itself the Bohm criterion.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convective electron particle velocity is directed along $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: parallel_flux_surface_averaged_electric_field_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged parallel electric field at the plasma boundary, defined as the separatrix average of the electric-field and magnetic-field dot product divided by the signed reference toroidal field in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is not an average of the local unit-vector projection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the separatrix flux-surface average of $\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{B}$ has the same sign as the signed reference toroidal magnetic field $B_0$, with $B_0$ positive for toroidal magnetic field in the direction of increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_heat_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: The effective velocity at which bulk ion thermal energy is advected along magnetic field lines in the edge plasma, used as a transport coefficient in the parallel ion energy equation.
NAMES.long:
The parallel ion heat convection velocity is the field-aligned component of the effective velocity governing convective ion thermal-energy transport in the edge plasma. It represents the aggregate ion population over all charge states, in contrast to the per-charge-state quantity parallel_effective_ion_state_energy_convection_velocity, which resolves a single ionization level.

In the ion energy equation, the parallel convective heat flux density is:

$$
q_{\parallel,i}^{\text{conv}} = \frac{5}{2}\, n_i T_i\, v_{\parallel,\text{heat}}^{i}
$$

where $n_i$ is the total ion number density, $T_i$ is the ion temperature, and $v_{\parallel,\text{heat}}^{i}$ is this convection velocity. The prefactor $5/2$ reflects the enthalpy content per particle for a monatomic ideal gas.

This quantity is computed from edge plasma fluid transport models solving the ion energy equation in the scrape-off layer and divertor regions. Values range from order $10^2$ m/s in low-density far-SOL regions to near the ion acoustic speed ($\sim 10^4$–$10^5$ m/s) approaching divertor target plates, depending on local ion density and temperature.

The parent quantity ion_heat_convection_velocity defines the full vector; the parallel component dominates along open field lines where parallel transport greatly exceeds cross-field transport. The analogous transport coefficient for parallel momentum is [parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity](name:parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion heat convection is directed along the local magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_species_particle_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral_species
NAMES.short: Parallel particle diffusivity for neutral species in edge plasma. It parameterizes density-gradient-driven neutral transport along the local magnetic-field direction in reduced transport models.
NAMES.long:
Parallel neutral species particle diffusivity is the scalar coefficient that sets the strength of neutral-density smoothing along the local magnetic-field direction in a diffusive edge-plasma transport model. Although neutral particles are not magnetized, the magnetic-field direction is often used as a reference direction because neutral sources, ionization, and charge exchange are coupled to the surrounding magnetized plasma.

In a Fick's-law closure, the parallel neutral particle flux is modeled as:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,0} = -D_{\parallel,0}\,\nabla_{\parallel} n_0
$$

where $\Gamma_{\parallel,0}$ is the neutral particle flux along the magnetic field in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $D_{\parallel,0}$ is this diffusivity, $n_0$ is the neutral species density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $\nabla_{\parallel} n_0 = \hat{b}\cdot\nabla n_0$ is the density gradient along $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-4}$. Components of $\mathbf{B}$ may be expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. The minus sign means that the modeled flux is down the neutral-density gradient; if $n_0$ decreases in the $+\hat{b}$ direction, $\Gamma_{\parallel,0}$ is positive along $+\hat{b}$.

The coefficient is normally not a direct diagnostic observable. It is prescribed in transport calculations or inferred by adjusting a neutral model to reproduce neutral-density-sensitive observations such as Balmer-line emission, neutral pressure, recycling fluxes, or charge-exchange signals. Estimates may also be based on an effective random-walk form involving a neutral thermal speed and an effective mean free path or loss time, but kinetic neutral models may replace this diffusion approximation entirely.

Typical effective values are strongly model and regime dependent. In reduced edge-plasma calculations, order-of-magnitude values often span 0.1-10^4 m^2.s^-1; cold, dense divertor regions tend toward the lower part of this range, while more transparent scrape-off-layer or main-chamber regions may require larger effective values when diffusion is used to mimic long mean-free-path neutral motion.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Effective field-line-parallel convection velocity for total momentum transport in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
Parallel total momentum convection velocity is the effective speed along a magnetic field line that transports the total parallel momentum density. It represents the advective coefficient for the combined momentum variable in an edge-plasma momentum balance, not necessarily the measured parallel flow of any single species.

The defining relation for the convective part of the total parallel momentum flux is:

$$
\Gamma_{P_\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}} = P_\parallel\, v_{\parallel,\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{P_\parallel}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective flux density of total parallel momentum in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $P_\parallel$ is the total parallel momentum density in kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $v_{\parallel,\mathrm{conv}}$ is this effective convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$.

In practice this coefficient is obtained from edge fluid or kinetic-fluid momentum closures, or computed as the ratio of convective momentum flux to total parallel momentum density where that density is nonzero. In a simple single-fluid closure it is usually close to the center-of-mass parallel flow velocity; in multi-species, neutral-coupled, or reduced transport closures it can differ from ion or neutral parallel flow velocities because it is the coefficient that advects total momentum. The cross-field analog is [radial effective momentum convection velocity], and species-resolved analogs include [parallel ion momentum convection velocity](name:parallel_ion_momentum_convection_velocity) and [parallel neutral momentum convection velocity].

Typical values in scrape-off-layer and divertor momentum balances are about $10^2-10^5$ m s$^{-1}$, spanning slow recirculating plasma or neutral flows up to ion-sound-order parallel advection. This range applies to the velocity coefficient itself, because it multiplies a momentum density to produce a convective momentum flux.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the field-line-parallel convection velocity points in the direction of the local magnetic field vector.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of electron thermal pressure at the pedestal top to the magnetic pressure associated with the local high-field-side poloidal magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal electron beta at the pedestal top high-field side is the electron thermal pressure at the pedestal top normalized to the magnetic pressure of the local poloidal magnetic field on the inboard side of the same pedestal-top flux surface. The high-field side is the smaller-major-radius side in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining relation is:

$$
\beta_{p,e,\mathrm{ped,HFS}} = \frac{2\mu_0 p_{e,\mathrm{ped}}}{B_{\mathrm{pol,HFS}}^2}
$$

where $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space, $p_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the electron pressure at the pedestal top, and $B_{\mathrm{pol,HFS}}$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic-field component at the high-field-side pedestal-top location. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame this poloidal magnitude is the magnitude of the field component in the $(R, Z)$ plane, excluding the toroidal component. Because the field enters as a squared magnitude, reversing the poloidal-field direction does not change this beta.

In practice, $p_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ is obtained from pedestal fits or edge-profile analysis, commonly from electron density and temperature through $p_e = n_e T_e$ when $T_e$ is expressed as an energy. The magnetic-field factor is evaluated from an equilibrium reconstruction at the high-field-side intersection of the pedestal-top flux surface, not at the low-field-side intersection. This is the same pressure normalization concept as the low-field-side counterpart, but with $B_{\mathrm{pol}}$ evaluated on the inboard side; local flux expansion, shaping, and magnetic-axis displacement can make the high-field-side poloidal field differ substantially from the low-field-side value.

Typical values are about 0.01-2 in tokamak pedestal analyzes. For fixed pedestal-top pressure, a smaller high-field-side poloidal-field magnitude gives a larger value, so high-field-side and low-field-side poloidal electron beta values should not be assumed equal.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Dimensionless local ratio of pedestal-top electron pressure to poloidal magnetic pressure, evaluated using the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude at the low-field-side outer-midplane point of the pedestal-top flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal electron beta at the pedestal-top low-field side is a local measure of how strongly the electron pressure at the top of the H-mode pedestal competes with the poloidal magnetic pressure. The low-field-side evaluation point is the outboard midplane location on the pedestal-top flux surface, usually the largest-major-radius point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is defined as the electron pressure divided by the poloidal magnetic pressure at that low-field-side point:

$$
\beta_{e,\mathrm{pol,LFS}} = \frac{2\mu_0 p_{e,\mathrm{ped}}}{B_{\mathrm{pol,LFS}}^2}
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the electron pressure at the pedestal top, $B_{\mathrm{pol,LFS}}$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field at the low-field-side pedestal-top location, and $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability.

In practice, $p_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ is inferred from pedestal fits to measured electron density and temperature, often using edge Thomson-scattering data together with equilibrium mapping. The poloidal field magnitude is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction at the outboard-midplane intersection of the pedestal-top flux surface. This local quantity should not be confused with global poloidal beta, which uses a volume-averaged plasma pressure rather than pedestal-top electron pressure.

For a fixed enclosed toroidal plasma current, simple large-aspect-ratio estimates give $B_\mathrm{pol} \sim \mu_0 I_p/(2\pi R)$, so the larger-$R$ low-field side often has a smaller poloidal-field magnitude than the high-field side. Because the beta scales as $1/B_\mathrm{pol}^2$, the low-field-side value is commonly larger than the corresponding high-field-side value.

Typical H-mode pedestal-top values are about 0.05-2, with values near or above unity indicating that local electron pressure is comparable to or exceeds the local poloidal magnetic pressure.

NAMES.name: poloidal_flux_surface_averaged_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of electron kinetic pressure to flux-surface-averaged poloidal magnetic pressure, evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal electron beta using the flux-surface-averaged poloidal field quantifies the electron pressure balance against the poloidal confining field at the outer edge of the H-mode transport barrier. Using the flux-surface average of the poloidal magnetic field removes the poloidally asymmetric variation between the high-field and low-field sides, providing a single representative value per flux surface at the pedestal top.

The defining relation is:

$$
\beta_{p,e}^{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{2\mu_0 \, p_e}{\langle B_\theta \rangle_{\mathrm{fs}}^2}
$$

where $p_e$ is the electron kinetic pressure at the pedestal top, $\langle B_\theta \rangle_{\mathrm{fs}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged poloidal magnetic field at the same flux surface — see poloidal_flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_at_pedestal_top — and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H m$^{-1}$ is the permeability of free space.

Values are inferred from pedestal profile analysis, combining electron temperature and density fits (modified hyperbolic tangent or linear functions applied to Thomson scattering data) with equilibrium magnetic field reconstruction for the poloidal field. Typical values in H-mode pedestals range from 0.05 to 0.5 across current tokamaks.

The flux-surface-average normalization distinguishes this quantity from [poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side](name:poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side), which evaluates $B_\theta$ at the high-field-side midplane, and from [poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top](name:poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side), which uses the poloidal field at a specific poloidal location. The total-species analog is beta_at_pedestal_top.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective poloidal diffusion coefficient for total ion particle transport in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi), relating the down-gradient poloidal ion particle flux to the metric-scaled gradient of ion number density.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion diffusivity is an effective transport coefficient for total ion particle diffusion tangent to magnetic flux surfaces. In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, it relates the poloidal component of the total ion particle flux to the local gradient of total ion number density. The coefficient represents the aggregate ion population rather than a single ion charge state.

For a diffusive closure of the poloidal ion particle flux, the coefficient $D_{i,\theta}$ is defined by Fick's law using the metric-scaled poloidal gradient:

$$
\Gamma_{i,\theta}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{i,\theta}\,\frac{1}{h_\theta}\frac{\partial n_i}{\partial \theta}
$$

where $\Gamma_{i,\theta}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive poloidal total-ion particle flux, $n_i$ is total ion number density, and $h_\theta = |\partial \mathbf{x}/\partial\theta|$ is the poloidal metric scale factor at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$. The metric-scaled density gradient has dimensions of density per meter, so multiplication by $D_{i,\theta}$ gives a particle flux.

In practice, $D_{i,\theta}$ is inferred by fitting particle-balance or edge-transport equations to measured or reconstructed density evolution, source distributions, and ion flux constraints. It can include unresolved turbulent mixing, collisional diffusion, charge-exchange effects, and geometry-dependent averaging; convective pinches and parallel losses should be represented separately when the model permits, otherwise the fitted value is an effective closure coefficient.

Typical effective values in edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas are 0.01-5 m^2.s^-1, with strongly turbulent or transient cases reaching around 10 m^2.s^-1. Values near or above 1 m^2.s^-1 are usually larger than purely neoclassical estimates and indicate anomalous transport or compensation for unresolved physics.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diffusive poloidal ion particle flux is down the metric-scaled gradient of $n_i$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$; equivalently, a decrease of $n_i$ with increasing $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$ gives a flux in the $+\theta$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux at the H-mode pressure pedestal top location, providing a dimensional flux-surface label for the edge pedestal.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the pedestal is the value of the poloidal flux function on the flux surface identified as the H-mode pressure pedestal top. This surface is the radial location assigned to the core-side top of the steep edge pedestal region; it is distinct from the pedestal center or maximum-gradient surface unless a particular pedestal analysis explicitly defines those surfaces to coincide.

In a right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters, the full poloidal magnetic flux at a point on the pedestal-top surface may be written as the horizontal-disk integral of the vertical magnetic field:

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{ped}} = \int_0^{R_{\mathrm{ped}}} B_Z(R', Z_{\mathrm{ped}})\, 2\pi R'\, dR'
$$

where $(R_{\mathrm{ped}}, Z_{\mathrm{ped}})$ is any point on the pedestal-top flux surface, $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component in tesla, and $\psi_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is in Wb. The lower integration limit fixes the additive reference to zero flux for the zero-radius disk on the toroidal symmetry axis; adding a constant offset to the flux function would shift this absolute value but not flux differences between surfaces.

In practice, an equilibrium reconstruction provides $\psi(R,Z)$, while pedestal analysis of edge pressure or its components determines the pedestal-top radial location. The pedestal flux is obtained by evaluating the equilibrium flux on that flux surface, rather than by assuming the surface is the pedestal center or the point of maximum pressure gradient.

Typical absolute values, using a consistent additive reference, are about 0.1-5 Wb in small and medium tokamaks and 5-50 Wb in large high-current tokamaks. Because the pedestal top lies close to the outer confined plasma boundary, $\psi_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is usually near the boundary poloidal flux, with the pedestal-to-boundary flux interval much smaller than the axis-to-boundary flux span.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ on the horizontal integration disk points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_momentum_coefficient
NAMES.short: Dimensionless momentum-flux-density limiter that scales the collisionless free-streaming bound for gradient-driven poloidal momentum transport. It caps the modeled poloidal momentum-flux density while leaving its direction set by the underlying transport closure.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal momentum coefficient is a dimensionless flux-limiter parameter for gradient-driven momentum transport in the poloidal direction on a magnetic surface. It scales the collisionless free-streaming bound used to limit the modeled poloidal momentum-flux density, so the coefficient controls the allowed magnitude rather than the sign of the flux.

A common limiter form constrains the poloidal momentum-flux density for species or population $s$ by

$$
|\Pi_{\theta,s}| \le \alpha_{\theta,s}\,\Pi_{\mathrm{fs},s}, \qquad \Pi_{\mathrm{fs},s} \sim m_s n_s v_{\mathrm{th},s}^{2}
$$

where $\Pi_{\theta,s}$ is the poloidal momentum-flux density in kg m^-1 s^-2, $\alpha_{\theta,s}$ is the poloidal momentum coefficient, $\Pi_{\mathrm{fs},s}$ is the selected free-streaming momentum-flux-density estimate in kg m^-1 s^-2, $m_s$ is particle mass, $n_s$ is number density, and $v_{\mathrm{th},s}$ is thermal speed. The index $\theta$ denotes the poloidal direction in a chosen flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$; factors of order unity in the free-streaming estimate are closure-dependent. Because the limiter is applied to $|\Pi_{\theta,s}|$, the sign of the limited flux follows the underlying diffusive or reference momentum flux.

The coefficient is specified as a transport-model closure parameter rather than measured directly. It is used to prevent a diffusion approximation from producing momentum-flux densities larger than a collisionless population could carry across the same direction, especially in low-collisionality edge-plasma regimes where unbounded gradient-driven diffusion can overestimate transport.

Typical model choices are non-negative fractions not exceeding order unity. Smaller values impose a stronger cap on poloidal momentum transport, while values near unity allow momentum-flux densities comparable to the chosen free-streaming estimate.

Conceptually related limiters include the [parallel momentum coefficient](name:parallel_momentum_coefficient) and [toroidal momentum coefficient](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum_coefficient) for other directional momentum-flux-density limits, and energy-flux limiters such as the [total ion energy coefficient].

NAMES.name: poloidal_particle_diffusivity
NAMES.short: Effective particle diffusion coefficient for transport along the poloidal direction in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi). It relates particle flux in the direction of increasing poloidal angle to the metric-scaled gradient of particle number density for a generic particle population.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal particle diffusivity $D_\mathrm{pol}$ is an effective scalar transport coefficient for particle mixing along the poloidal direction in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. It applies to a generic particle population and represents the net effect of collisional, turbulent, or modeled unresolved transport along increasing or decreasing $\theta$.

The local Fick-law closure for the poloidal particle flux density is

$$
\Gamma_\theta = -D_\mathrm{pol}\,\nabla_\theta n
$$

where $\Gamma_\theta$ is the particle flux density along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $D_\mathrm{pol}$ is in $\mathrm{m}^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $n$ is the particle number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $\nabla_\theta n$ is the physical component of $\nabla n$ along increasing $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$. For an orthogonal metric this component is $h_\theta^{-1}\partial n/\partial\theta$, where $h_\theta$ is the poloidal arc-length scale factor. For $D_\mathrm{pol} > 0$, the minus sign gives down-gradient transport: flux in the direction of increasing $\theta$ occurs when density decreases with increasing $\theta$.

This coefficient is usually prescribed or inferred in edge particle-balance and transport calculations rather than measured directly. It may be adjusted to reproduce measured density evolution, particle balance, or poloidal density asymmetries, and its interpretation should follow the particle population being modeled; species-resolved counterparts are used when electron, ion, or ion-state transport must be distinguished.

Typical prescribed edge-plasma values are model-dependent and are commonly of order 0.01-10 m^2.s^-1 for anomalous particle mixing. Reduced closures or effective neutral-particle treatments may use values up to about 100 m^2.s^-1, while values near zero represent negligible poloidal diffusive mixing. A passive diffusion coefficient is normally non-negative; negative values would represent an anti-diffusive closure rather than ordinary diffusion.

NAMES.name: pressure_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.short: Thermal pressure of a plasma constituent or neutral-gas population in the open-field-line scrape-off layer, the region between the last closed flux surface and the material plasma-facing components.
NAMES.long:
The scrape-off layer (SOL) is the open-field-line region extending from the last closed flux surface to the material plasma-facing components, where local pressure governs energy and particle exhaust, neutral recycling, ionization balance, and the onset of divertor detachment. This parent name generalizes over species-resolved SOL pressure quantities: [electron pressure over the scrape-off layer](name:electron_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer) represents the electron partial pressure and additionally anchors the pressure baseline offset in H-mode pedestal profile fits, while [neutral pressure over the scrape-off layer](name:neutral_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer) characterizes the neutral gas inventory affecting recycling, pumping balance, and detachment control.

For any thermally equilibrated species $s$, the scalar thermal pressure satisfies:

$$
p_s = n_s k_B T_s
$$

where $n_s$ is the species number density and $T_s$ is its temperature in energy units.

SOL pressure is inferred from a combination of diagnostics: Langmuir probes provide local electron pressure at plasma-facing surfaces from saturation current and electron temperature; neutral gas pressure gages directly measure gas pressure in the divertor pumping region; Thomson scattering resolves electron density and temperature profiles from which electron pressure is derived. The characteristic radial scale over which pressure falls from the separatrix outward is described by the [decay length over the scrape-off layer](name:decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer).

NAMES.name: electron_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron pressure associated with the scrape-off-layer baseline of an H-mode pedestal fit. It is the offset level outside the last closed flux surface against which the pedestal rise is measured.
NAMES.long:
Electron pressure over the scrape-off layer is the scalar electron pressure assigned to the low-pressure baseline of an H-mode pedestal fit. It is the asymptotic value approached outside the last closed flux surface and provides the reference level for the pedestal rise toward electron_pressure_at_pedestal and electron_pressure_at_pedestal_top. It is the electron contribution to the more general [pressure_over_scrape_off_layer](name:pressure_over_scrape_off_layer).

The baseline is commonly obtained as the constant offset in a modified-tanh representation of the electron-pressure variation across the pedestal:

$$
p_e(\rho) = p_{\mathrm{SOL}} + \frac{p_{\mathrm{ped}} - p_{\mathrm{SOL}}}{2}\left[1 - \tanh\!\left(\frac{\rho-\rho_{\mathrm{ped}}}{\Delta/2}\right)\right]
$$

where $p_e(\rho)$ is the electron pressure, $p_{\mathrm{SOL}}$ is this scrape-off-layer offset, $p_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is the pedestal-side pressure level, $\rho$ is an outward-increasing flux-surface label such as $\rho_{\psi_N}=\sqrt{\psi_N}$ in flux coordinates $(\rho_{\psi_N},\theta,\phi)$, $\rho_{\mathrm{ped}}$ is the center of the transition, and $\Delta/2$ is the half-width parameter of the steep-gradient region.

In practice, the value is inferred by forming electron pressure from electron density and temperature measurements, then fitting the radial dependence over a region spanning the pedestal and the near scrape-off layer. When $\rho_{\psi_N}$ is used, $\rho_{\psi_N}=1$ denotes the last closed flux surface and larger values lie in the scrape-off layer; related fitted fall-off behavior may be summarized by electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer.

Typical fitted offsets in H-mode edge analyzes are about 10-1000 Pa, with cold or low-density scrape-off layers near the lower end and high-density, high-power plasmas reaching higher values. They are normally well below electron_pressure_at_pedestal_top, often a few percent to a few tens of percent of that value.

NAMES.name: neutral_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged scalar thermal pressure of neutral atoms and molecules in the scrape-off layer, the open-field-line region outside the last closed flux surface. It characterizes the neutral inventory relevant to recycling, pumping balance, ionization, and divertor detachment.
NAMES.long:
Neutral pressure over the scrape-off layer is the volume average of the scalar translational pressure carried by neutral atoms and molecules in the open-field-line region outside the last closed flux surface. In toroidal geometry, this region is described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity is the neutral-gas contribution to the edge pressure balance and is distinct from charged-particle pressures such as [electron_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer](name:electron_pressure_over_scrape_off_layer).

For an ideal neutral gas mixture, the volume-averaged pressure is

$$
p_{n,\mathrm{SOL}} = \frac{1}{V_{\mathrm{SOL}}}\int_{V_{\mathrm{SOL}}} \sum_a n_a(\mathbf{x}) k_\mathrm{B} T_a(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{SOL}}$ is the scrape-off-layer volume, $a$ indexes neutral species, $n_a$ is the neutral density, $T_a$ is the neutral translational temperature in K, and $k_\mathrm{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant. If a neutral temperature is expressed in eV, the factor $k_\mathrm{B}T_a$ is replaced by the corresponding energy obtained by multiplying by the elementary charge.

In practice this pressure is inferred from calibrated neutral gas diagnostics such as ionization gages, Penning gages, capacitance gages, gas-balance measurements, and spectroscopy constrained by neutral transport modeling. A true volume average requires combining local pressure or density estimates with the spatial distribution of neutrals across the SOL, divertor, and recycling regions, accounting for wall pumping, fueling, molecular species, and ionization losses.

Typical volume-averaged values range from about $10^{-3}$-$10$ Pa in attached edge plasmas and from about $1$-$100$ Pa in high-recycling or detached divertor conditions. Local gage pressures near pumping ducts or divertor targets can differ substantially from the SOL volume average because neutral density is highly nonuniform.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_particle_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective radial cross-field diffusivity for total ion particle transport in the edge plasma, where total ion density is the unweighted sum over charged ion species and charge states. It relates outward particle flux density across magnetic flux surfaces to the negative outward gradient of total ion density.
NAMES.long:
Radial ion particle diffusivity is an effective transport coefficient for cross-field diffusion of the total charged-ion particle population normal to magnetic flux surfaces in the edge plasma. The associated total ion density is the unweighted particle-density sum over charged ion species and charge states, consistent with [flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density), so ions are counted as particles rather than weighted by charge or mass.

In a local diffusive closure, the radial ion particle flux density is written in Fick-law form:

$$
\Gamma_{i,r} = -D_{i,r}\,\frac{\partial n_i}{\partial r}
$$

where $\Gamma_{i,r}$ is the diffusive ion particle flux density in m^-2.s^-1 and is taken positive outward across magnetic flux surfaces, $D_{i,r}$ is this radial ion particle diffusivity in m^2.s^-1, $n_i = \sum_\alpha n_\alpha$ is the total charged-ion density in m^-3 with $\alpha$ labeling charged ion species and charge states, and $r$ is an outward radial distance in m measured normal to the flux surfaces. With this convention, a density that decreases outward gives a positive outward diffusive flux.

This coefficient is used in particle-balance and edge-transport models as an effective representation of unresolved cross-field mixing. It may include collisional, turbulent, and model-reduction effects, so it should be interpreted as a transport-model coefficient rather than as a universal material property. Charge-state-resolved particle transport is described by related quantities such as [radial_ion_state_particle_flux](name:radial_ion_state_particle_flux).

Typical magnitudes are scenario- and model-dependent rather than universal; values are reported in m^2.s^-1 and should be compared only for the same radial coordinate definition, source terms, and transport closure. The coefficient is normally non-negative, and larger values correspond to stronger outward diffusive particle transport for a given outward density gradient.

NAMES.name: radial_momentum_coefficient
NAMES.short: Dimensionless, non-negative flux-limiter coefficient for transport of momentum along the major-radius direction R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It scales the collisionless free-streaming upper bound on the radial momentum-flux density, capping how large the modeled radial momentum flux may become; the inward or outward sign is carried by the underlying momentum flux, not by this coefficient.
NAMES.long:
The radial momentum coefficient $C_R$ is a dimensionless flux-limiter factor for transport of momentum along the major-radius direction $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is a non-negative magnitude limiter: it scales the collisionless free-streaming upper bound on the radial momentum-flux density, so that diffusive transport closures cannot drive an unphysically large flux in steep-gradient edge regions. The inward or outward sign of the transported momentum is carried by the underlying momentum flux, not by this coefficient.

The limiter caps the modeled radial momentum-flux density at a fraction of the collisionless free-streaming upper bound:

$$
\left|\Pi_R\right| \le C_R \, \Pi_{\mathrm{fs},R}, \qquad \Pi_{\mathrm{fs},R} \sim n_s m_s v_{\mathrm{th},s} \left|u_s\right|
$$

where $\Pi_R$ is the radial momentum-flux density, $C_R$ is the dimensionless coefficient, and $\Pi_{\mathrm{fs},R}$ is the collisionless free-streaming momentum-flux-density scale. For species $s$, $n_s$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$, $m_s$ is the particle mass in kg, $v_{\mathrm{th},s}$ is the thermal speed in m s$^{-1}$, and $u_s$ is the flow-velocity component being transported in m s$^{-1}$; the product has units kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, equivalent to Pa.

The coefficient is a user-specified model parameter assigned prior to a transport simulation rather than a quantity inferred from diagnostics. It may be set separately for ion, neutral, or total momentum transport and is often tuned via sensitivity studies to keep diffusive closures within physically plausible collisionless limits.

Typical values lie between 0 and 1. Values much smaller than unity impose a strong limiter that strongly suppresses radial momentum transport, while values of order unity allow the flux to approach the selected free-streaming upper bound.

NAMES.name: radial_plasma_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.short: Effective radial diffusion coefficient for cross-field transport of ion-fluid momentum in the edge plasma. It aggregates the momentum carried by all ion species and charge states into a single transport parameter, rather than resolving it per species or charge state.
NAMES.long:
Radial plasma momentum diffusion coefficient is the scalar coefficient that relates the radial (cross-field) diffusive flux of ion-fluid momentum to the radial gradient of momentum density in the edge plasma. It is an aggregate quantity summed over all ion species and charge states; electron inertial momentum is usually negligible in these ion-dominated edge regimes and is not included. It complements the species- and charge-state-resolved [radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity).

In a Fickian transport closure, the radial diffusive flux of a momentum component is proportional to the radial gradient of the corresponding aggregate momentum density:

$$
\Gamma_j = -D \, \frac{\partial \mathcal{P}_j}{\partial r_\perp}
$$

where $D$ is the radial plasma momentum diffusion coefficient, $\Gamma_j$ is the radial flux of the $j$-th momentum component in kg m^-1 s^-2, $r_\perp$ is the distance measured outward normal to flux surfaces in m, and $\mathcal{P}_j = \sum_{a,z} m_a\, n_{a,z}\, u_{a,z,j}$ is the aggregate ion momentum density in kg m^-2 s^-1, with $m_a$ the ion mass in kg, $n_{a,z}$ the number density of charge state $z$ of species $a$ in m^-3, and $u_{a,z,j}$ the corresponding fluid-velocity component in m s^-1. The leading minus sign means a positive coefficient drives momentum down its gradient, from regions of higher toward lower momentum density.

The coefficient is typically inferred as an effective transport parameter from edge momentum-balance analysis, measured ion flows and rotation shear, and comparisons with collisional, neoclassical, or turbulence-based transport estimates. It is the aggregate momentum counterpart to the aggregate energy and particle transport coefficients radial_total_energy_diffusion_coefficient and [radial_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_particle_diffusivity), and pairs with the convective term radial_ion_effective_momentum_convection_velocity in diffusion-convection closures.

Representative effective edge-plasma values used in transport modeling are of order 0.01-10 m^2 s^-1, with smaller values where diffusive coupling is weak and larger values in regions of strong turbulent or externally driven momentum redistribution. This range is indicative and not a physical bound.

NAMES.name: radiated_power_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic power radiated from the open field-line scrape-off layer plasma by all species and emission channels combined.
NAMES.long:
The radiated power over the scrape-off layer is the total electromagnetic power emitted by plasma occupying the open field-line region between the magnetic separatrix and the first wall or divertor structures. Contributions arise from line radiation of impurity ions (both intrinsic and deliberately seeded species such as argon or neon), hydrogen isotope resonance emission, bremsstrahlung, and radiative recombination, integrated over the full SOL volume.

The total SOL radiated power is the volume integral of the local emissivity:

$$
P_\mathrm{rad,SOL} = \int_\mathrm{SOL} \varepsilon_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $\varepsilon_\mathrm{rad} = n_e \sum_z n_z L_z(T_e, n_e)$, with $n_e$ the electron number density, $n_z$ the density of radiating species $z$, and $L_z$ the temperature- and density-dependent cooling function for species $z$.

It is measured via resistive or photodiode bolometer arrays, with the spatial distribution recovered by tomographic inversion. Alternatively, it is inferred from global power balance by subtracting the conducted and convected power reaching the divertor targets from the total power crossing the separatrix given by total_lost_power_at_plasma_boundary.

A high SOL radiated power fraction $f_\mathrm{rad} = P_\mathrm{rad,SOL} / P_\mathrm{SOL}$ is the primary control target in reactor-relevant divertor detachment scenarios, as it disperses the power load before it reaches solid surfaces. The residual non-radiated heat governs the radial heat-flux profiles characterized by the [electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) and [ion_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:ion_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer). This quantity is the radiated sub-component of power_over_scrape_off_layer.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_active_limiter_point
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle, in radians, of the active limiter point: the point where the plasma boundary contacts the limiter surface. It is measured in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, with phi increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above +Z.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of the active limiter point is the azimuthal coordinate of the plasma-boundary contact point on a limiter surface. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\phi$ is the angle about the toroidal symmetry axis.

For a contact point with Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ in the right-handed $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the toroidal angle is defined by

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x)
$$

where $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angular displacement from the chosen $+x$ reference direction to the point's projection in the horizontal plane. The angle $\phi$ is measured in radians; because radians are dimensionless, the canonical unit may be written as $1$.

In practice, this quantity is computed from the three-dimensional location assigned to the active plasma-limiter contact point by projecting that point onto the horizontal plane and evaluating its azimuth. The definition is purely geometric and does not depend on a particular reconstruction code or diagnostic method.

Typical reported values lie in a $2\pi$ interval, most commonly $0-2\pi$ rad or equivalently $-\pi$ to $\pi$ rad depending on angle wrapping. Values differing by $2\pi$ rad represent the same physical toroidal direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\phi$ increases in the counter-clockwise toroidal direction when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_argon_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of argon impurity bulk flow velocity evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, a key quantity for determining the pedestal radial electric field through the impurity force balance.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity of argon ions at the pedestal top quantifies the $\hat{\phi}$-directed bulk flow of this impurity species within the steep-gradient edge transport barrier of H-mode plasmas. Alongside [toroidal nitrogen velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal tungsten velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_pedestal), it enables species-resolved comparison of impurity momentum transport in the pedestal region.

The toroidal velocity component $v_\phi^{\rm Ar}$ enters the radial force balance for argon ions:

$$
E_r = v_\phi^{\rm Ar} B_\theta - v_\theta^{\rm Ar} B_\phi + \frac{1}{Z_{\rm Ar} e n_{\rm Ar}} \frac{dp_{\rm Ar}}{dr}
$$

where $E_r$ is the radial electric field, $B_\theta$ and $B_\phi$ are the poloidal and toroidal magnetic field components, $v_\theta^{\rm Ar}$ is the argon poloidal velocity, $Z_{\rm Ar}$ is the mean ionization state of argon, $n_{\rm Ar}$ is the argon number density (see [argon density at the pedestal](name:argon_density_at_pedestal)), and $p_{\rm Ar}$ is the argon pressure.

Argon toroidal velocity at the pedestal is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), which detects the Doppler shift of argon emission lines excited by neutral beam injection in the pedestal region. The full radial profile of argon rotation is built from this pedestal value together with the counterpart quantities [at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [at the internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the argon flow points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Local toroidal component of the argon ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the last closed flux surface (separatrix). This is the pointwise boundary value, not a flux-surface average; for the averaged counterpart see the flux-surface-averaged variant.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal argon velocity at the plasma boundary is the local projection of the argon impurity ion bulk velocity onto the toroidal direction at the last closed flux surface (separatrix) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity denotes a local value on the separatrix; a flux-surface-averaged boundary velocity is a separate concept.

The toroidal component is obtained by projecting the argon bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the argon ion bulk velocity (in m·s$^{-1}$) and $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The velocity is primarily measured using charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), which resolves the Doppler shift of argon emission lines produced by charge exchange with injected neutral beams. Passive edge spectroscopy of argon lines can also provide local estimates when combined with equilibrium reconstruction of the separatrix location. The measurement is local in the sense that it applies to the argon population at a given poloidal and toroidal position on the boundary; poloidal variation is expected and not removed by this definition.

Typical toroidal argon velocities at the separatrix range from a few km·s$^{-1}$ in low-momentum ohmic plasmas to several tens of km·s$^{-1}$ in strongly beam-heated discharges. The sign reflects the direction of edge rotation and can be either co- or counter-current depending on momentum input.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the argon bulk flow projects in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, i.e., counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

NAMES.name: toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of beryllium impurity ion velocity at the H-mode pedestal, where the steep electron pressure gradient defines the edge transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity of beryllium ions at the pedestal is the projection of the beryllium impurity ion fluid velocity onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, evaluated at the pedestal location.

The defining projection is:

$$
v_{\phi}^{\rm Be} = \mathbf{v}_{\rm Be} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\rm Be}$ is the beryllium ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Toroidal impurity rotation is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), in which the Doppler shift of Be emission lines at the pedestal chord positions yields the local toroidal velocity. The pedestal's steep pressure gradient and associated radial electric field well can drive strong toroidal velocity shear, contributing to turbulence suppression at the edge transport barrier. Toroidal velocities at the pedestal range from near-zero in low-momentum-input plasmas to tens of km/s in discharges with strong neutral-beam injection. Position-resolved analogs are available via [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) and [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis); the analogous quantity for tritium at the same location is [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\phi}^{\rm Be}$ is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the beryllium impurity ion bulk flow velocity at the plasma boundary, summed over all ionization stages and averaged over the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component of the beryllium impurity ion bulk flow velocity at the plasma boundary quantifies the azimuthal rotation of beryllium ions at the last closed flux surface, which separates the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. This quantity encompasses all beryllium ionization stages (Be$^+$ through Be$^{4+}$) and represents the flux-surface-averaged toroidal impurity flow at the separatrix.

The toroidal velocity is defined as the projection of the charge-state-averaged beryllium ion fluid velocity onto the toroidal direction:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Be}} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Be} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Be}$ is the charge-state-averaged beryllium ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Beryllium toroidal rotation at the plasma boundary is inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), which resolves the Doppler shift of emission lines produced during charge-transfer reactions between beryllium ions and diagnostic neutral beam atoms. This measurement constrains edge impurity momentum transport and toroidal rotation profiles near the separatrix.

Toroidal impurity velocities at the plasma boundary span approximately $-10^5$ to $+10^5$ m/s in tokamak plasmas, with sign and magnitude governed by plasma current direction, auxiliary heating power, and external toroidal momentum injection. The pedestal-top value is given by [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_pedestal), and the on-axis value by [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis); the associated impurity density at this location is characterized by [beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the beryllium ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the carbon impurity ion fluid velocity evaluated at the pedestal top, the steep-gradient transport barrier just inside the separatrix in H-mode plasmas.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal carbon velocity at the pedestal top quantifies the $\phi$-component of the carbon impurity ion fluid velocity at the top of the H-mode transport barrier, where the steep pressure-gradient region transitions to the flatter core profile. Carbon (typically fully stripped C$^{6+}$ in hot plasmas) provides a widely used spectroscopic tracer for plasma toroidal rotation because inter-species Coulomb collisions couple impurity and main-ion momenta on the neoclassical timescale.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as:

$$
v_\phi = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS): a neutral beam excites carbon ions in the pedestal region, and the resulting Doppler-shifted C VI emission line encodes the line-of-sight velocity component. Spatial resolution is set by the beam geometry and viewing configuration. Typical pedestal-top values range from a few km/s up to tens of km/s depending on plasma current, heating scheme, and device size. The analogous carbon velocity at other radial locations includes [toroidal carbon velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [at the internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). The hydrogen-isotope counterpart in the pedestal region is [toroidal hydrogen velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the carbon ion flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the carbon impurity ion bulk flow velocity at the plasma boundary, resolved in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the local value at the last-closed flux surface, not a flux-surface average.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal carbon velocity at the plasma boundary is the component of the carbon impurity ion bulk flow along the toroidal direction at the last-closed flux surface or separatrix. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity denotes a local boundary value; the corresponding flux-surface-averaged quantity is [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

The local toroidal component is defined by projecting the carbon bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi}^{\mathrm{C}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}} \cdot \hat{\phi} = R\Omega_{\mathrm{C}}
$$

where $v_{\phi}^{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon toroidal velocity in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon ion bulk velocity in m.s^-1, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, $R$ is the major radius in m, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon toroidal angular rotation frequency in s^-1.

In practice, this velocity is commonly inferred from Doppler shifts of carbon spectral lines, often using charge-exchange or passive edge spectroscopy, after correcting for viewing geometry and projecting the measured line-of-sight velocity onto the toroidal direction. The plasma boundary location is usually supplied by magnetic equilibrium reconstruction, and the measured or modeled velocity is mapped to the last-closed flux surface. When only an average over the boundary flux surface is intended, the flux-surface-averaged standard name should be used instead.

Typical absolute values at the plasma boundary are of order $10^3-5 \times 10^4$ m.s^-1 in tokamak edge plasmas. Values can be close to zero in weakly rotating conditions and can approach $10^5$ m.s^-1 in plasmas with strong external torque or steep edge rotation gradients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the carbon ion flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal velocity of the fictitious DT single-species (atomic mass 2.5 amu) at the H-mode pedestal, used in simulations treating the deuterium-tritium fuel as a single ion fluid.
NAMES.long:
The fictitious DT species is a single-fluid representation of the deuterium-tritium fuel mixture, assigned an atomic mass of 2.5 amu (the arithmetic mean of deuterium mass 2 and tritium mass 3), and treated as a single ion population in transport and gyrokinetic simulations. The toroidal velocity of this species at the pedestal quantifies the bulk toroidal rotation of the fuel ions within the steep-gradient edge transport barrier characteristic of H-mode plasmas.

The toroidal component is the projection of the DT ion fluid velocity onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
v_\phi = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{DT} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{DT}$ is the DT ion fluid velocity vector.

Toroidal rotation at the pedestal contributes to the $E \times B$ shear layer that suppresses turbulent transport and sustains the H-mode confinement barrier. Ion toroidal velocities are inferred from Doppler shifts in charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) emission lines on trace impurity species and corrected to the DT fuel population via neoclassical offsets. This pedestal evaluation belongs to a spatial family that includes [toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier); the resolved deuterium counterpart at the same location is [toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity for the effective deuterium-tritium single-species approximation with atomic mass 2.5 amu, evaluated at the last closed flux surface. It is the projection along the phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where phi increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above +Z.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal deuterium-tritium velocity at the plasma boundary is the component of the effective DT bulk flow tangent to the toroidal direction at the last closed flux surface. The effective species represents deuterium and tritium as a single ion population with atomic mass 2.5 amu. The right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame uses $R$ as major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ as toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ as vertical height.

The toroidal component is defined by projecting the effective DT bulk velocity vector onto the toroidal basis direction at the plasma boundary:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{DT}}^{\mathrm{bdry}} = \left. \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{DT}}(R,\phi,Z) \cdot \hat{\phi} \right|_{\mathrm{LCFS}}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{DT}}^{\mathrm{bdry}}$ and $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{DT}}$ are velocities in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless toroidal unit vector, LCFS denotes the last closed flux surface, $R$ and $Z$ are coordinate values in meters, and $\phi$ is in radians.

In transport modeling this quantity is obtained from the effective DT ion momentum balance or velocity field and evaluated, or interpolated, to the last closed flux surface. When related to measurements, edge ion flow information is commonly inferred from spectroscopic Doppler shifts together with a model that maps the observed ion flow to the effective DT species representation.

Typical edge toroidal ion flow magnitudes near the last closed flux surface are about $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s^-1, with smaller values possible in weakly rotating plasmas and larger values during strong external momentum input or strong edge electric-field shear. The signed value may be positive or negative depending on the toroidal flow direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal component of the effective deuterium-tritium bulk velocity points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the deuterium ion fluid velocity evaluated at the H-mode pedestal, defined as the projection of the deuterium flow along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal deuterium velocity at the pedestal is the toroidal component of the deuterium ion fluid velocity evaluated in the steep-gradient edge region that forms the H-mode pedestal. It represents the projection of the species flow along the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The component is defined by projecting the local deuterium fluid velocity onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi,D,\mathrm{ped}} = \mathbf{v}_{D,\mathrm{ped}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{D,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the deuterium ion fluid velocity at the pedestal in m.s^-1, $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and $v_{\phi,D,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the toroidal component in m.s^-1.

In practice this quantity is inferred from spectroscopic ion Doppler measurements, momentum-balance analysis, or edge transport interpretation. Measurements often involve impurity-ion rotation and require physics assumptions to relate the observed species to deuterium, including collisional coupling, neoclassical effects, and radial electric-field constraints; the pedestal location is identified from the local steep-gradient edge region.

Typical pedestal toroidal deuterium velocities are strongly scenario dependent. Many edge analyzes find values from near 0 to several $10^4$ m.s^-1 in magnitude, while plasmas with strong external torque or large intrinsic rotation can approach order $10^5$ m.s^-1; either sign is possible depending on the rotation direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium ion fluid velocity at the pedestal points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the deuterium ion bulk flow velocity at the last closed flux surface. It is the projection along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal deuterium velocity at the plasma boundary is the toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity of deuterium ions evaluated on the last closed flux surface. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The boundary value is the projection of the deuterium bulk velocity onto the local toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{D,\phi,b} = \mathbf{v}_D(\mathbf{x}_b,t) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{D,\phi,b}$ is the toroidal deuterium velocity at the boundary in m s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{v}_D$ is the deuterium ion bulk velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the last closed flux surface with $R$ and $Z$ in meters and $\phi$ in radians, $t$ is time, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$.

In practice this quantity is inferred by evaluating or reconstructing the deuterium flow field at the plasma boundary and projecting it onto $\hat{\phi}$. It may be constrained by ion-flow spectroscopy, edge diagnostics where applicable, and equilibrium or transport interpretation that maps measured velocities to the last closed flux surface; it is a boundary toroidal component and is distinct from a flux-surface average.

Typical boundary toroidal deuterium velocities in tokamak plasmas are often within $-5\times10^4$ to $5\times10^4$ m s$^{-1}$, with magnitudes approaching $1\times10^5$ m s$^{-1}$ in strongly momentum-driven or rapidly rotating edge conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium bulk flow at the plasma boundary has a toroidal component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal component of the carbon impurity ion bulk velocity at the plasma boundary, resolved in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents impurity-ion flow on the last closed flux surface, distinct from main-ion flow.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal flux-surface-averaged carbon velocity at the plasma boundary is the flux-surface average of the toroidal component of the carbon impurity ion bulk velocity on the last closed flux surface. The toroidal component is resolved along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This impurity flow is distinct from main-ion flow, even when carbon spectroscopy is used as a tracer for plasma rotation.

For an axisymmetric boundary flux surface, the flux-surface average is commonly written with the poloidal-field Jacobian weighting:

$$
\left\langle v_{\phi,\mathrm{C}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{LCFS}} = \frac{\oint_{\mathrm{LCFS}} v_{\phi,\mathrm{C}}\, dl / B_p}{\oint_{\mathrm{LCFS}} dl / B_p}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{C}}$ is the local toroidal carbon velocity, $dl$ is poloidal arc length along the last closed flux surface, and $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude. It is the boundary flux-surface average corresponding to the local quantity [toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

In practice, this quantity is usually inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy of carbon emission, often from C VI lines, combined with an equilibrium reconstruction to locate the emitting region relative to the boundary. When measurements do not cover the full poloidal contour, the average may be obtained by fitting or interpolating local toroidal velocities before applying the flux-surface weighting. Related species-resolved averages describe analogous impurity or main-ion toroidal flows, such as deuterium, oxygen, neon, and tungsten boundary velocities.

Typical separatrix carbon toroidal velocities are of order -5e4 to 5e4 m.s^-1 in many ohmic, RF-heated, or moderately beam-heated plasmas. Strong external momentum input or steep edge rotation gradients can produce absolute magnitudes around 1e5-2e5 m.s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the carbon impurity bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_tritium_velocity
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the local contravariant toroidal bulk-flow component of a modeled deuterium-tritium composite ion species with mass 2.5 amu. The component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, and positive values point toward increasing toroidal angle phi.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal flux-surface averaged deuterium-tritium velocity is the flux-surface average of the local contravariant toroidal bulk-flow component of a modeled DT composite ion species. The composite species represents deuterium and tritium as one ion fluid with effective mass 2.5 amu, and the toroidal component is the signed component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity has dimensions of velocity, with unit m.s^-1.

The flux-surface average can be written as

$$
\langle v_{\phi,\mathrm{DT}} \rangle_\psi = \frac{\oint_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} v_{\phi,\mathrm{DT}} \, d\ell / B_p}{\oint_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} d\ell / B_p}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{DT}}$ is the local DT toroidal velocity component in m.s^-1, associated with the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude; and $d\ell$ is the non-negative arc-length element along the closed poloidal contour of the flux surface. The contour orientation does not enter this scalar average because the weighting uses $d\ell$ and the magnitude $B_p$. Here “toroidal” identifies the local $\phi$ component of the bulk-flow vector, not a projection of motion in a poloidal cross-section.

For the composite DT species, the value is most often computed or inferred in a single-ion-fluid representation of the fuel mixture. Spectroscopic or charge-exchange measurements can constrain the underlying ion-flow physics, but comparison with this composite velocity normally requires the model assumption that maps separate species flows to the 2.5 amu DT fluid. The same 2.5 amu convention applies to DT quantities on any selected flux surface, including a plasma-boundary flux surface; the selected surface changes the averaging domain, not the composite-species definition. This quantity is the toroidal component of flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_tritium_velocity and uses the same composite-species convention as [flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density). Related toroidal velocity quantities include [toroidal_ion_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity), [toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), and [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

In edge and near-boundary tokamak conditions, flux-surface averaged toroidal ion-flow magnitudes are commonly 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1. Values can be near zero or change sign when momentum input, radial electric-field shear, collisionality, or neoclassical and turbulent transport alter the balance of toroidal momentum.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the averaged DT toroidal bulk-flow component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal component of deuterium ion bulk-flow velocity at the plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-surface average, on the plasma boundary or separatrix, of the deuterium ion bulk-flow velocity component in the toroidal direction. The toroidal component is the projection of the deuterium flow velocity onto $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the net boundary toroidal rotation of the deuterium ion population after poloidal variation around the boundary surface has been averaged out.

A compact definition is:

$$
V_{\phi,D}^{\mathrm{FS},b} = \left\langle v_{\phi,D} \right\rangle_{\psi=\psi_b}
$$

where $V_{\phi,D}^{\mathrm{FS},b}$ is the boundary flux-surface-averaged deuterium toroidal velocity in m.s^-1, $v_{\phi,D}$ is the local deuterium toroidal bulk-flow velocity in m.s^-1, $\psi_b$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux value at the plasma boundary, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi=\psi_b}$ denotes the flux-surface average over that boundary surface.

Experimentally, this quantity may be inferred from spectroscopic measurements of deuterium flow near the separatrix, combined with magnetic-equilibrium geometry to map local measurements to the boundary surface. In transport modeling it is the boundary-surface representative value of deuterium toroidal rotation, distinct from the local [toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). It is directly comparable with species analogs such as [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_helium_3_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), and [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

Representative edge values are strongly discharge-dependent and are often near zero to a few $10^4$ m.s^-1 in magnitude; stronger external momentum input or edge radial-electric-field shear can produce values of order $10^5$ m.s^-1. The signed value can be positive or negative depending on the direction of toroidal deuterium flow.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium ion bulk flow is directed along $+\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_iron_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal component of the iron impurity ion bulk flow velocity at the plasma boundary (last closed flux surface).
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component of the iron impurity bulk flow velocity, averaged over the magnetic flux surface coinciding with the plasma boundary, characterizes the net toroidal rotation of iron ions at the last closed flux surface. The flux-surface average eliminates poloidal asymmetries in the local velocity distribution, providing a single scalar representative of the toroidal impurity flow at the edge.

The flux-surface average of a quantity $f$ on a given flux surface is defined as:

$$
\langle f \rangle = \frac{\oint f \, dl_p / B_p}{\oint dl_p / B_p}
$$

where $l_p$ is the poloidal arc length along the flux-surface contour and $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field magnitude. Iron ($Z = 26$) is a high-$Z$ metallic impurity that enters the confined plasma through sputtering of plasma-facing components; its toroidal rotation at the boundary reflects edge momentum transport and neoclassical impurity flow physics.

This quantity is measured via charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, exploiting Doppler shifts of iron charge-state emission lines recorded along multiple poloidal viewing chords; the flux-surface-averaged value is then reconstructed from multi-chord data.
