In deuterium-tritium H-mode operation, representative pedestal-top tritium densities are about $10^{18}-5 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$, depending on total pedestal density, dilution by impurities and other fuel ions, and the tritium fraction.

NAMES.name: tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Number density of tritium ions at the plasma boundary (separatrix), the last closed magnetic flux surface separating the confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Tritium density at the plasma boundary is the local number density of tritium ions evaluated on the separatrix. It characterizes the tritium component of the ion population at the outer edge of the closed-field-line plasma and is non-negative by definition.

Using the normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_N$, with $\psi_N=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\psi_N=1$ at the separatrix, the boundary value is

$$
n_{\mathrm{T},b} = n_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi_N=1)
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{T},b}$ is the tritium ion density at the plasma boundary in m^-3 and $n_{\mathrm{T}}$ is the tritium ion density as a function of $\psi_N$, also in m^-3.

In practice this quantity is obtained by identifying the separatrix from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction and evaluating or extrapolating the tritium ion density to that surface. The isotope-resolved value is commonly constrained from the total edge density together with an assumed, modeled, or independently inferred tritium fraction, rather than from the separatrix location alone.

Typical values range from 0 m^-3 in plasmas without tritium to about 10^18-10^20 m^-3 in deuterium-tritium edge plasmas, depending on the total separatrix density and isotope mix. Values below zero are unphysical for a number density.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged number density of tritium ions at the plasma boundary (separatrix).
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged tritium density at the plasma boundary is the average tritium ion number density over the last closed flux surface, also called the separatrix. It represents a single scalar boundary value after averaging local variations around that magnetic surface. The density counts ionized tritium nuclei, summed over tritium ion charge states if such states are distinguished, and excludes neutral tritium atoms and tritium-bearing molecules such as $T_2$ and DT.

The flux-surface average at the boundary poloidal-flux surface is defined by the weighted surface integral:

$$
\langle n_T \rangle_{\psi_b} = \frac{\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} n_T \, dS / |\nabla \psi|}{\oint_{\psi=\psi_b} dS / |\nabla \psi|}
$$

where $n_T$ is the local tritium ion number density in m^-3, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $\psi_b$ is the value of $\psi$ at the plasma boundary, $dS$ is a surface-area element in m^2, and $|\nabla\psi|$ has units Wb m^-1. The factor $1/|\nabla\psi|$ is the geometric weighting associated with integration over a magnetic flux surface in toroidal geometry.

In practice, this quantity is computed by mapping local or modeled tritium ion density values onto a reconstructed boundary flux surface and carrying out the flux-surface average. Tritium ion density may be constrained by isotope-resolved edge spectroscopy, neutral-particle measurements, fueling and recycling balance, and quasi-neutrality together with ion-composition modeling. The resulting boundary value is commonly used as an edge condition for fuel-ion transport, isotope balance, and scrape-off-layer coupling calculations.

Typical values are 0 m^-3 in plasmas without tritium fueling. In deuterium-tritium edge plasmas, representative separatrix values are about $1 \times 10^{18}$-$1 \times 10^{20}$ m^-3, depending on isotope fraction, fueling, recycling, confinement regime, and the total separatrix density.

NAMES.name: tungsten_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged tungsten ion number density at the H-mode pedestal top, summed over all ionization stages W1+ through W74+ and excluding neutral tungsten atoms.
NAMES.long:
Tungsten density at the pedestal is the total number density of ionized tungsten on the flux surface identified with the top of the H-mode pedestal. The pedestal top is the inner edge of the steep edge pressure-gradient region, where pedestal profiles connect to the core plasma. Neutral tungsten atoms are not included.

The charge-state-summed pedestal density is defined by summing all positive tungsten ionization stages:

$$
n_{\mathrm{W,ped}} = \sum_{q=1}^{74} \left\langle n_{\mathrm{W}^{q+}} \right\rangle_{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=\rho_{\mathrm{ped}}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{W}^{q+}}$ is the number density of tungsten ions with charge $q$, 74 is the atomic number of tungsten, $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes a flux-surface average, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the flux coordinate normalized toroidal flux radius, and $\rho_{\mathrm{ped}}$ labels the pedestal-top flux surface.

In practice this quantity is obtained by evaluating an impurity-density reconstruction or radial impurity profile at the pedestal top. The pedestal location is commonly identified from electron pressure, density, or temperature gradients, while tungsten densities are constrained by visible, VUV, and soft-X-ray spectroscopy, bolometry or tomography, charge-exchange measurements where applicable, and collisional-radiative modeling of the charge-state distribution.

Typical values in present H-mode tokamak plasmas are about $10^{13}-10^{16}$ m^-3 in well-controlled conditions. Strong tungsten influx or poor impurity screening can raise pedestal values toward $10^{17}$ m^-3 or above; even small fractions relative to the electron density can produce substantial radiative losses because tungsten is a high-$Z$ impurity.

NAMES.name: tungsten_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Separatrix-averaged number density of ionized tungsten at the plasma boundary, summed over charge states W1+ through W74+. Neutral tungsten atoms are excluded.
NAMES.long:
Tungsten density at the plasma boundary is the charge-state-summed number density of tungsten ions on the last-closed flux surface or separatrix. It includes ionized tungsten charge states only, $W^{q+}$ with $q=1,\ldots,74$, and excludes neutral tungsten atoms $W^0$.

A flux-surface average on the last-closed flux surface may be written as:

$$
n_{W,\mathrm{sep}} = \frac{\oint_{\mathrm{LCFS}} \left(\sum_{q=1}^{74} n_{W^{q+}}\right) B_p^{-1} \, dl}{\oint_{\mathrm{LCFS}} B_p^{-1} \, dl}
$$

where $n_{W^{q+}}$ is the number density of tungsten ions in charge state $q$ in m^-3, $dl$ is the poloidal arc-length element in m along the last-closed flux surface, and $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude in T. The $B_p^{-1}$ weighting gives the usual magnetic-flux-surface average rather than a simple geometric contour average.

This quantity is typically inferred from edge impurity modeling constrained by spectroscopy, bolometry, charge-exchange measurements where available, and equilibrium reconstruction of the separatrix geometry. It characterizes the tungsten ion content entering or residing at the confined-plasma boundary and is commonly compared with core, pedestal, divertor-target, and volume-averaged tungsten densities to assess impurity screening and transport.

Typical values vary strongly with wall material, auxiliary heating, edge conditions, and impurity control. In tungsten-wall tokamaks, separatrix-averaged ionized tungsten densities are often in the range 10^10-10^15 m^-3, with transient events or poorly screened conditions producing larger excursions.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_neutral_species_density
NAMES.subject: neutral_species
NAMES.short: Volume average of the number density of neutral particles over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged neutral species density quantifies the mean number density of neutral atoms and molecules within the plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface (LCFS). Neutrals arise from edge recycling at plasma-facing walls, gas injection, and charge-exchange reactions, and their inventory affects ionization balance, fueling efficiency, and momentum exchange between the plasma and neutral background.

The volume average is defined as:

$$
\langle n_0 \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_0(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_0(\mathbf{r})$ is the local neutral number density at position $\mathbf{r}$ and $V$ is the volume enclosed by the LCFS.

This global scalar condenses the spatially resolved neutral_species_density profile into a single quantity well suited for particle balance analysis and for monitoring the neutral inventory during plasma initiation and ramp-up. It is typically estimated from spectroscopic line emission or neutral pressure gage measurements combined with ionization balance modeling. As the neutral counterpart to [volume_averaged_total_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_density), it contributes to total particle inventory alongside the ion and electron populations described by total_electron_ion_neutral_particle_number_density.

NAMES.name: vorticity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Signed field-parallel component of the curl of the diamagnetic drift velocity for a plasma species or effective fluid. It measures rotation of the pressure-gradient-driven cross-field drift and is distinct from radial, poloidal, and toroidal vorticity components.
NAMES.long:
Vorticity due to diamagnetic drift is the signed field-parallel scalar component of the curl of the diamagnetic drift velocity. It represents local rotation of the pressure-gradient-driven cross-field drift about the magnetic-field direction for the species or effective fluid whose pressure gradient defines the drift. It is related to [parallel_vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity), [toroidal_vorticity](name:toroidal_vorticity), [poloidal_vorticity](name:poloidal_vorticity), and [radial_vorticity](name:radial_vorticity), but it identifies the diamagnetic-drift contribution rather than the total vorticity component.

The field-parallel scalar is defined by projecting the curl of the diamagnetic drift velocity onto the local magnetic-field direction:

$$
\omega_{\mathrm{dia},s} = \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \left(\nabla \times \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},s}\right)
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},s}$ is the diamagnetic drift velocity of species $s$. For a scalar-pressure fluid, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},s} = \mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_s /(q_s n_s |\mathbf{B}|^2)$, with $p_s$ the pressure, $n_s$ the number density, and $q_s$ the signed particle charge; electron and ion contributions therefore have opposite drift directions for the same pressure gradient.

In practice this quantity is evaluated from pressure and density gradients together with the magnetic-field geometry, followed by spatial differentiation of the diamagnetic drift velocity and projection along $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$. It is sensitive to pressure-gradient length scale, magnetic-shear and curvature effects, and numerical smoothing because it contains derivatives of a drift velocity that is itself gradient-driven.

Typical magnitudes in tokamak edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas are 10^4-10^6 s^-1 in broad-gradient regions and 10^5-10^7 s^-1 in steep pedestal or filamentary structures. Values can pass through zero where the pressure gradient or its curvature is weak, and the sign may reverse across pressure-gradient extrema or when the magnetic-field direction is reversed.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\nabla \times \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},s}$ points along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Xenon ion number density evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core pressure profile.
NAMES.long:
Xenon impurity ion number density at the pedestal top characterizes the local concentration of xenon at the shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. As a heavy noble gas with atomic number $Z = 54$, xenon contributes substantially to the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ and radiative power losses even at trace concentrations, making its pedestal value a key diagnostic of impurity accumulation, pedestal stability, and impurity transport modeling.

The pedestal top is the radial location $\rho_\mathrm{ped}$ at which the steep-gradient barrier region joins the gentler core density profile. The xenon pedestal density $n_\mathrm{Xe,ped}$ is the value of the ion number density profile at that reference position:

$$
n_\mathrm{Xe,ped} = n_\mathrm{Xe}(\rho_\mathrm{ped})
$$

where $\rho_\mathrm{ped}$ is determined from the electron temperature or pressure profile pedestal fit, and $n_\mathrm{Xe}$ is the total xenon ion density summed over all ionization stages unless individual charge states are specified separately.

Xenon is introduced into fusion plasmas for controlled radiative seeding to reduce divertor heat loads, for ELM suppression, and in disruption mitigation scenarios. Pedestal xenon density is typically inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or soft X-ray emission spectroscopy, with the pedestal location identified from Thomson scattering or reflectometry profiles. This quantity is part of the [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family; analogous pedestal densities for lighter noble gas seeding species include [neon_density_at_pedestal](name:neon_density_at_pedestal) and [argon_density_at_pedestal](name:argon_density_at_pedestal). For xenon density at other plasma reference locations see [xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon ions are present at the pedestal top.

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Number density of xenon ions at the plasma boundary (last closed flux surface), setting the outer boundary condition for xenon impurity transport between the confined plasma and the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Xenon ($Z = 54$) is a heavy noble-gas impurity that is either deliberately seeded into the edge plasma for radiative power exhaust mitigation or present as a trace contaminant. The xenon ion number density at the plasma boundary is the local ion number density $n_{\rm Xe}$ evaluated at the last closed flux surface — the magnetic separatrix separating field-line-closed confinement from the open-field-line scrape-off layer — constituting the outer boundary condition for core impurity transport calculations. Unless a specific ionization stage is resolved separately, it is summed over all charge states Xe$^{1+}$ through Xe$^{54+}$.

This boundary value connects the core inventory, quantified by [volume_averaged_xenon_density](name:volume_averaged_xenon_density) and [line_averaged_xenon_density](name:line_averaged_xenon_density), to scrape-off-layer impurity balance. The analogous on-axis value is [xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis), while xenon_fraction expresses the xenon ion content relative to electrons. The boundary density is inferred from passive spectroscopy of high-charge-state line emission near the separatrix or from two-dimensional edge transport modeling benchmarked to spectroscopic line-ratios. The parent quantity [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary) defines the general species-agnostic framework.

Typical separatrix xenon densities in seeded tokamak discharges range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on seeding rate and plasma conditions; trace-impurity backgrounds may be two to three orders of magnitude lower.
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon ions are present at the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: bulk_plasma_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift_magnitude
NAMES.short: Scalar magnitude of the bulk plasma velocity component associated with diamagnetic drift. It represents the speed of the pressure-gradient-driven drift of the bulk fluid perpendicular to the magnetic field, independent of the drift direction.
NAMES.long:
Bulk plasma velocity due to diamagnetic drift magnitude is the norm of the bulk-fluid velocity component associated with diamagnetic drift. Diamagnetic drift is a fluid drift caused by pressure gradients perpendicular to the magnetic field; for a bulk plasma quantity, the contributing species flows must be combined rather than treated as a single-species test-particle drift. The magnitude discards the orientation of the corresponding vector quantity bulk_plasma_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift.

In a multi-species fluid description, the mass-weighted bulk diamagnetic speed may be written as:

$$
v_{\mathrm{dia,bulk}} = \left|\frac{\sum_s m_s\,\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p_s /(q_s B^2)}{\sum_s m_s n_s}\right|
$$

where the sum is over species $s$, $m_s$ is species mass in kg, $q_s$ is species charge in C, $n_s$ is density in m$^{-3}$, $p_s$ is pressure in Pa, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $B=|\mathbf{B}|$, and $v_{\mathrm{dia,bulk}}$ is in m.s$^{-1}$. This expression shows that ion and electron diamagnetic contributions have opposite charge dependence and that the bulk result depends on the chosen fluid averaging.

In practice this quantity is computed from the diamagnetic component of a fluid momentum decomposition, or from pressure-gradient, density, species-composition, and magnetic-field information. It is usually inferred from reconstructed or modeled edge plasma states rather than measured directly as an isolated velocity component.

Typical edge-plasma values are often 10$^2$-10$^4$ m.s$^{-1}$, with the largest values occurring where pressure gradients are steep and the magnetic field or density is relatively low. Weaker-gradient regions can have values below this range.

NAMES.name: coulomb_logarithm_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Coulomb logarithm evaluated at the H-mode pressure pedestal top, characterizing Debye screening of binary Coulomb collisions in the pedestal plasma.
NAMES.long:
The Coulomb logarithm at the pedestal top is the value of the plasma Coulomb logarithm evaluated at the radial location marking the top of the H-mode pressure pedestal. It measures the logarithmic separation between long-range Debye shielding and the shortest effective collision impact parameter, and is a key factor in collisional transport estimates near the edge transport barrier.

The Coulomb logarithm is defined by the ratio of maximum to minimum effective impact parameters:

$$
\ln\Lambda = \ln\left(\frac{\lambda_D}{b_{\min}}\right)
$$

where $\lambda_D$ is the Debye length in meters and $b_{\min}$ is the minimum effective impact parameter in meters, usually taken as the larger of the classical distance of closest approach and the quantum de Broglie wavelength for the relevant colliding species.

In practice this quantity is computed from local pedestal-top plasma conditions, primarily electron temperature and electron density, after identifying the pedestal top from fitted edge pressure or kinetic profiles. It is used as an input to collision frequencies, resistivity estimates, neoclassical transport coefficients, and derived quantities such as [normalized_electron_collisionality_at_pedestal_top](name:normalized_electron_collisionality_at_pedestal_top).

Typical pedestal-top values in tokamak H-mode plasmas are about 15-20 for electron temperatures of roughly 200-1000 eV and electron densities of about $10^{19}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3, with weak logarithmic dependence on the local plasma parameters.

NAMES.name: decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.short: Radial e-folding scale over which a plasma quantity — heat flux, particle density, or temperature — decreases exponentially with distance from the separatrix into the open-field-line scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The decay length over the scrape-off layer (SOL) is the radial e-folding scale over which a plasma quantity decreases exponentially with increasing distance from the magnetic separatrix into the open-field-line region between the separatrix and the material wall. It is the abstract parent of a family of species- and transport-channel-specific lengths, including [heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) and electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer, and is itself a specialization of [length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:length_over_scrape_off_layer) restricted to exponentially decaying profiles.

The e-folding length $\lambda$ is defined by the exponential fit to the radial profile:

$$
f(r) = f_0 \exp\!\left(-\frac{r}{\lambda}\right)
$$

where $r$ is the radial distance measured outward from the separatrix in the direction perpendicular to the magnetic field and $f_0$ is the value of the decaying quantity at the separatrix.

SOL decay lengths are inferred from midplane Langmuir probe traversals, edge Thomson scattering measurements, or divertor target heat-flux distributions mapped back to the upstream midplane along field lines. Typical heat-channel decay lengths in H-mode tokamak plasmas lie in the range 1–10 mm, while particle density e-folding lengths are generally larger at 10–50 mm, reflecting the differing cross-field transport coefficients for energy and particles.

NAMES.name: electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Positive radial e-folding length of electron number density in the scrape-off layer, defined as the inverse magnitude of the outward logarithmic radial gradient. It measures how rapidly electron density falls with distance outside the confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
Electron decay length in the scrape-off layer is the positive e-folding length for the falloff of electron number density with outward distance across the scrape-off layer. It characterizes the radial width of the electron-density decay region; a larger value means a more gradual decrease of density outside the confined plasma.

For a local outward distance coordinate $x$, the decay length is defined by the inverse magnitude of the logarithmic density gradient:

$$
\lambda_{n_e} = \left|\frac{d\ln n_e}{dx}\right|^{-1} = \frac{n_e}{\left|d n_e/dx\right|}
$$

where $n_e$ is electron number density in $m^{-3}$, $x$ is outward distance in m across the scrape-off layer, and $\lambda_{n_e}$ is the decay length in m. The absolute value makes the quantity non-negative for the usual outward density decrease and for local gradients of either sign.

In practice, $\lambda_{n_e}$ is obtained by fitting or differentiating electron-density measurements in the scrape-off layer, commonly using Langmuir probes, Thomson scattering, reflectometry, or equilibrium-mapped edge measurements over a specified radial interval. It is conceptually equivalent to [radial_electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) when the decay direction is the outward radial direction; the explicitly radial name is useful when distinguishing this scale from parallel, poloidal, or other directional decay lengths.

Typical values in tokamak scrape-off-layer analyzes are about 0.001-0.05 m, depending on plasma conditions, magnetic geometry, density, fueling, recycling, and the radial interval used for the fit.

NAMES.name: heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.short: Radial e-folding decay length of the heat flux profile in the scrape-off layer, without specifying the electron or ion heat channel.
NAMES.long:
The heat decay length in the scrape-off layer (SOL) is the radial distance over which the heat flux profile falls to $1/e$ of its value at the separatrix, characterizing the spatial scale of heat exhaust across the open-field-line region. This parent quantity leaves the contributing heat channel unspecified, generalizing over both the electron and ion contributions captured by its species-resolved children.

The decay length is formally defined as the inverse of the magnitude of the logarithmic radial gradient of the heat flux $q$:

$$
\lambda_q = \left| \frac{\partial \ln q}{\partial r} \right|^{-1}
$$

where $r$ is the radial coordinate measured outward from the separatrix into the SOL. The species-specific children [electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) and [ion_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:ion_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) resolve this quantity into the electron and ion heat channels, respectively; users requiring species resolution should reference those names directly.

The heat decay length is inferred from infrared thermography of the divertor target, which images the radial heat load footprint, or from radially distributed Langmuir probe arrays in the SOL. Typical midplane-mapped values in H-mode tokamak plasmas span 1–10 mm.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the heat flux decreases with increasing radial distance outward from the separatrix toward the first wall.

NAMES.name: electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial e-folding decay length of electron heat flux in the scrape-off layer, equal to the inverse magnitude of its logarithmic radial gradient.
NAMES.long:
The electron heat decay length over the scrape-off layer is the radial e-folding distance over which the electron heat flux decreases outside the last closed flux surface. It quantifies how narrowly the electron heat channel is localized in the scrape-off layer; smaller values correspond to a steeper radial falloff.

For a local outward radial coordinate $r$, the decay length is defined from the logarithmic radial gradient of the electron heat flux:

$$
\lambda_{q_e} = \left|\frac{q_e}{d q_e / dr}\right| = \left|\frac{d \ln q_e}{dr}\right|^{-1}
$$

where $q_e(r)$ is the electron heat flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $r$ is the outward radial distance in m, and $\lambda_{q_e}$ is in m. The absolute value makes the decay length non-negative; for an outwardly decreasing heat flux, $d q_e / dr < 0$.

In practice, $\lambda_{q_e}$ is obtained by fitting an exponential falloff of the electron heat flux as a function of a consistently defined radial coordinate, or by evaluating the local logarithmic gradient from measurements or edge-plasma transport calculations. If distances are mapped between locations, such as from a target surface to an outer-midplane radial coordinate, the geometric mapping should be treated consistently with the heat-flux definition.

Typical values in tokamak scrape-off layers are of order millimeters to centimeters, approximately 0.001-0.05 m, with the value depending on confinement regime, collisionality, connection length, and magnetic geometry.

NAMES.name: ion_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Radial e-folding decay length of the ion heat flux in the scrape-off layer, equal to the inverse magnitude of its outward logarithmic radial gradient. It is non-negative by definition and characterizes how rapidly ion heat exhaust falls away from the separatrix.
NAMES.long:
The ion heat decay length over the scrape-off layer is the radial e-folding scale over which the ion heat flux decreases outside the confined plasma. It characterizes the width of the ion heat exhaust channel and complements the electron-channel quantity [electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer) in determining the overall heat-exhaust fall-off described by [heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer).

The local decay length is the inverse magnitude of the outward logarithmic gradient of the ion heat flux:

$$
\lambda_{q_i} = \left|\frac{\partial \ln q_i}{\partial r_\perp}\right|^{-1}
$$

where $q_i(r_\perp)$ is the positive ion heat-flux density in W m^-2, $r_\perp$ is distance in meters measured locally outward from the separatrix approximately normal to magnetic flux surfaces, and $\lambda_{q_i}$ is in meters. For an exponential dependence $q_i \propto \exp(-r_\perp/\lambda_{q_i})$, the ion heat flux decreases by a factor $e$ over one decay length.

In practice, this quantity is inferred by fitting or differentiating the radial dependence of ion heat-flux estimates in the scrape-off layer. Those estimates may come from target heat measurements, probe-based ion energy and particle flux measurements, edge power balance, or transport modeling with magnetic mapping between divertor and upstream locations. It is distinct from ion temperature decay lengths such as radial_average_ion_temperature_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer and ion_average_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer, because it describes heat-flux fall-off rather than temperature fall-off.

Typical magnitudes in present tokamak scrape-off layers are on the order of 0.001-0.03 m, ranging from millimeter-scale widths in narrow high-confinement conditions to centimeter-scale widths in broader low-confinement or high-collisionality conditions. The value depends on plasma density, power crossing the separatrix, magnetic geometry, collisionality, and whether the quoted location is upstream or mapped to the divertor target.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial e-folding scale length of the thermal electron temperature in the scrape-off layer. It is the positive inverse magnitude of the outward logarithmic radial gradient of the thermal electron temperature.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron decay length over the scrape-off layer is the characteristic distance over which the thermal electron temperature falls by a factor of $e$ outside the last closed flux surface. It describes the local radial steepness of $T_e$ in the open-field-line region and is a positive scale length, not a signed gradient.

For a local radial coordinate $r$ measured outward from the separatrix along the normal to magnetic flux surfaces into the scrape-off layer, an exponential falloff is represented by:

$$
T_e(r) \simeq T_{e,\mathrm{sep}} \exp\left[-\frac{r-r_{\mathrm{sep}}}{\lambda_{T_e}}\right], \qquad \lambda_{T_e} = \left|\frac{d\ln T_e}{dr}\right|^{-1}
$$

where $T_e$ is the thermal electron temperature in eV, $T_{e,\mathrm{sep}}$ is its separatrix value, $r_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is the separatrix location on the same outward radial coordinate, and $\lambda_{T_e}$ is the thermal electron temperature decay length.

In practice, $\lambda_{T_e}$ is obtained by fitting an exponential or local logarithmic-gradient model to scrape-off-layer electron temperature measurements or reconstructed edge profiles. The radial coordinate is usually interpreted locally at a specified poloidal location, such as the outboard midplane or divertor-mapped upstream location, because flux expansion and magnetic geometry can make the apparent decay length location dependent.

Typical values in tokamak scrape-off layers are about 0.002-0.05 m, with shorter lengths in high-confinement, high-power-density conditions and longer lengths in cooler, lower-power, or more weakly magnetized edge plasmas.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short: Heat-viscosity diamagnetic current density is the signed scalar projection of the electric current density driven by heat-viscous stress onto the local direction perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the poloidal-flux gradient.
NAMES.long:
Heat-viscosity diamagnetic current density is the diamagnetic component of the electric current density produced by heat-viscous stress in a magnetized edge plasma. It is the signed coefficient of the heat-viscosity current vector along the local direction perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the poloidal-flux gradient.

The scalar projection is

$$
j_{\mathrm{dia,hv}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{dia,hv}}$ is this scalar component in A m^-2, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}$ is the heat-viscosity electric-current-density vector in A m^-2, and $\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the dimensionless positive local diamagnetic unit direction satisfying $\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\mathbf B=0$ and $\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\nabla\psi=0$. Here $\mathbf B$ is magnetic flux density in T, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, and $\nabla\psi$ has units Wb m^-1. If $|\mathbf B|=0$ or the transverse direction defined by $\mathbf B$ and $\nabla\psi$ is degenerate, the diamagnetic projection is not physically defined and should not be interpreted as a true zero.

The vector $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}$ is generally obtained from edge transport modeling rather than direct measurement. In fluid closures, the divergence of the heat-viscous stress tensor $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{\mathrm{hv}}$ contributes a force density to charged-particle momentum balance; schematically, this force-density contribution is balanced by the corresponding term in $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}\times\mathbf B$ together with electric-field, pressure-gradient, inertia, and collisional terms. After the vector current contribution is computed, this quantity is formed by projection onto $\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{dia}}$.

Other projections of the same heat-viscosity electric-current contribution include [parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), [radial_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), [poloidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), [toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and [vertical_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity). The same diamagnetic projection geometry is used for [diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity). The related [parallel_heat_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) concerns heat-current transport associated with viscosity rather than electric-current density.

No device-independent numerical range is implied by this closure component. Its magnitude depends on the heat-viscous closure, collisionality, local gradients, magnetic geometry, and edge region, and it may vanish in models that omit heat-viscous current terms; it is usually interpreted by comparison with [current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) or with neighboring perpendicular current components.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}$ has a component in the positive local diamagnetic direction $\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{dia}}$.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction
NAMES.short: Component of the ion-neutral-friction current density projected onto the local diamagnetic direction. It quantifies the friction-driven current from ion-neutral momentum exchange along that direction.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic current density due to ion-neutral friction is the scalar projection, onto the local ion-diamagnetic direction, of the electric current density associated with momentum exchange between plasma ions and neutral particles. It represents the part of the friction-driven drift current perpendicular to the magnetic field and complements projections such as [parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), [poloidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), where the toroidal projection is along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

For a single ion species, the force-drift projection can be written as:

$$
j_{\mathrm{dia},in} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{R}_{in}\times\mathbf{B}}{B^2}\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}, \qquad \mathbf{R}_{in}=m_i n_i \nu_{in}(\mathbf{u}_n-\mathbf{u}_i)
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{dia},in}$ is the diamagnetic ion-neutral-friction current density in A m^-2, $\mathbf{R}_{in}$ is the ion-neutral friction force density in N m^-3, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $B=|\mathbf{B}|$, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the dimensionless unit vector along $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p_i$, with $p_i$ the ion pressure in Pa. In the friction model, $m_i$ is the ion mass in kg, $n_i$ is the ion density in m^-3, $\nu_{in}$ is an effective ion-neutral momentum-exchange frequency in s^-1, and $\mathbf{u}_i$ and $\mathbf{u}_n$ are ion and neutral flow velocities in m s^-1. For multiple ion species, the force density is summed over species before projection.

This quantity is usually computed from edge plasma and neutral-particle models using charge-exchange, elastic-scattering, ionization, and recombination momentum exchange rates, together with measured or reconstructed density, temperature, flow, and magnetic-field information. Direct measurement is uncommon; it is typically constrained through momentum balance, current balance, and comparisons with spectroscopy, neutral pressure measurements, probe data, and magnetic equilibrium information.

Typical absolute magnitudes in the edge and scrape-off layer are about 0.1-1000 A m^-2, depending strongly on neutral density, ion flow speed, magnetic-field strength, and recycling conditions. In dense divertor or strong gas-puffing conditions, localized values can approach 10000 A m^-2, while in low-neutral regions the contribution may be negligible compared with other current-density components.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the friction-driven current density has a component in the direction of $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p_i$.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the combined deuterium-tritium fuel ion number density. Deuterium and tritium are treated as a single pseudo-species with effective mass 2.5 amu, which assumes equal deuterium and tritium number densities.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged deuterium-tritium density is the mean fuel-ion number density on a magnetic flux surface when deuterium and tritium are represented together as one ion pseudo-species. The fixed effective mass of 2.5 amu is valid for an equal-number-density mixture of deuterium and tritium; the pseudo-species density is the combined deuterium plus tritium ion number density.

For an axisymmetric closed flux surface labeled by poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, the flux-surface average is commonly written as:

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{DT} \rangle_\psi = \frac{\oint_\psi n_\mathrm{DT} \, dl / B_p}{\oint_\psi dl / B_p}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{DT} = n_D + n_T$ is the combined fuel-ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ with the equal-mixture constraint $n_D = n_T$, $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the deuterium and tritium ion densities in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $dl$ is the poloidal contour length element in m, and $B_p$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field in T. The contour integral is taken around the intersection of the flux surface with a poloidal plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

In practice this quantity is obtained from equilibrium and transport or edge-plasma calculations by evaluating the local deuterium and tritium ion densities on the reconstructed magnetic surface and applying the flux-surface metric weighting. It is appropriate only when the DT pseudo-species approximation is intended; unequal isotope mixtures should be represented by separate deuterium and tritium density quantities.

Typical edge and separatrix flux-surface averages in tokamak plasmas are about $1 \times 10^{18}$-$1 \times 10^{20}$ $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, depending on fueling, pumping, confinement regime, and detachment state. Core-adjacent surfaces in high-performance plasmas may approach a few $10^{20}$ $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron temperature averaged over a magnetic flux surface using flux-surface-average weighting, giving the thermodynamic temperature associated with that surface after poloidal and toroidal variations are removed.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged electron temperature is the electron temperature averaged over one magnetic surface labeled by the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$. It describes the thermodynamic temperature of the electron population associated with that surface, not the total electron thermal energy content.

The flux-surface average of electron temperature is defined by the surface-element weighting appropriate to a magnetic-flux label:

$$
\langle T_e \rangle_\psi = \frac{\int_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} T_e\, dS / |\nabla \psi|}{\int_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} dS / |\nabla \psi|}
$$

where $T_e$ is the local electron temperature in eV, $dS$ is a surface element in m^2 on the magnetic surface, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux label in Wb, and $|\nabla\psi|$ is in Wb m^-1. In an axisymmetric equilibrium this is equivalently a poloidal-contour average weighted by $dl/B_p$, where $dl$ is distance along the poloidal contour and $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude.

In practice, the quantity is obtained by mapping local electron-temperature measurements or model results onto reconstructed magnetic surfaces and applying the flux-surface-average weighting. At the separatrix it gives the limiting closed-surface value used to characterize the boundary between confined plasma and the scrape-off layer, but the definition applies to any closed flux surface. It differs from [volume_averaged_electron_temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature), which averages over a finite plasma volume, and from [electron_temperature_at_divertor_target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target), which is a local material-surface temperature on open field lines.

Typical edge and separatrix values are 10-300 eV in many L-mode and detached-boundary conditions, while H-mode pedestal surfaces can reach 100-2000 eV. Hot core flux surfaces in high-performance plasmas can have flux-surface-averaged electron temperatures of 1000-20000 eV.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_shear
NAMES.short: Flux-surface value of magnetic shear, describing how the safety factor changes with normalized toroidal flux radius on a magnetic flux surface. When the safety factor is a flux function, it is the representative surface value, not an independent average of a local pointwise shear.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged magnetic shear is the magnetic shear assigned to an entire magnetic flux surface, quantifying the radial variation of field-line pitch through the safety factor. It is the flux-surface counterpart of [magnetic_shear](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal); when the safety factor is constant on a flux surface, no separate local-shear averaging model is implied.

The value on a surface labeled by normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is defined by:

$$
s_{\mathrm{fs}}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}) = \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}{q(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}})} \frac{d q}{d \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $s_{\mathrm{fs}}$ is the flux-surface value of magnetic shear, $q$ is the [safety factor](name:safety_factor), and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ labels the flux surface, with $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}=1$ at the last-closed flux surface.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from an equilibrium description by evaluating the radial derivative of $q(\rho_{\mathrm{tor}})$ at the chosen surface, such as a separatrix, pedestal, or internal-transport-barrier location. It is sensitive to the local radial variation of $q$, so uncertainty is largest where the safety-factor variation is weakly constrained or changes rapidly.

Typical dimensionless values are of order unity to several in many tokamak equilibria. Values near zero indicate a locally flat safety-factor variation, negative values indicate reversed magnetic shear, and larger positive values can occur in steep-gradient edge or separatrix regions.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the aggregate ion number density, formed by summing the number densities of all charged ion species and charge states without charge weighting. Neutral atoms and molecules are excluded, so it represents ion particle density rather than charge density.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface-averaged total ion density is the magnetic-surface mean of the local aggregate ion number density. The local aggregate is an unweighted particle-density sum over all charged ion species and ionization states; neutral atoms and molecules are excluded, and no multiplication by charge state is applied.

For a magnetic flux surface labeled by poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, the flux-surface average can be written as

$$
\langle n_{i,\mathrm{tot}} \rangle_\psi = \frac{\int_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} \left(\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{z\ge 1} n_{\alpha z}\right)\, dS/|\nabla\psi|}{\int_{\psi=\mathrm{const}} dS/|\nabla\psi|}
$$

where $\psi$ is in Wb, $dS$ is a surface-area element in m^2, $|\nabla\psi|$ is in Wb m^-1, $n_{\alpha z}$ is the number density in m^-3 of ion species $\alpha$ in charged ionization state $z$, and the sums include only charged states with $z \ge 1$. The factor $dS/|\nabla\psi|$ gives the volume weighting of a thin shell between neighboring flux surfaces, and the resulting average has units m^-3.

In practice this quantity is obtained by combining an equilibrium geometry with local or modeled ion composition, summing the charged ion particle densities on each flux surface before averaging. Electron density and quasineutrality constrain a charge-weighted ion sum, so composition information is needed to recover the unweighted total ion particle density; neutral-density contributions are not included.

Typical edge-plasma values in magnetic-confinement devices are about $10^{18}-10^{20}$ m^-3, depending on fueling, confinement regime, impurity content, and radial location relative to the confined edge and boundary region.

NAMES.name: gradient_of_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Signed derivative of electron pressure with respect to normalized poloidal magnetic flux, evaluated at the H-mode pedestal location of greatest absolute pressure steepness. The selection uses the largest magnitude of the derivative, while the reported value retains its algebraic sign.
NAMES.long:
The gradient of electron pressure is the signed slope of [electron_pressure](name:electron_pressure) with respect to the normalized poloidal magnetic flux coordinate $\psi_N$ in the H-mode pedestal. It is evaluated at the pedestal location where the absolute value of that slope is greatest, so a steep outward pressure drop is selected by magnitude but reported with its negative sign.

The defining value is

$$
G_{p_e} = \left.\frac{d p_e}{d\psi_N}\right|_{\psi_N=\psi_*}, \qquad \psi_* = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\psi_N \in \mathrm{pedestal}} \left|\frac{d p_e}{d\psi_N}\right|
$$

where $p_e$ is electron pressure, $\psi_N$ is normalized poloidal magnetic flux increasing from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface, and $\psi_*$ is the pedestal location of maximum absolute slope. Electron pressure is $p_e=n_e k_B T_e$ when $T_e$ is thermodynamic temperature in K, equivalently $p_e=n_e e T_e$ when $T_e$ is reported in eV; $n_e$ is electron density in m$^{-3}$, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $e$ is the elementary charge.

In practice this quantity is obtained by fitting the radial dependence of electron pressure across the pedestal, often from electron density and temperature measurements such as Thomson scattering, and then differentiating the fitted function with respect to $\psi_N$. Modified hyperbolic-tangent and piecewise-linear fits are common ways to locate the steepest pedestal segment. This normalized-flux derivative complements [gradient_of_electron_temperature](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top) and gradient_of_electron_density, and differs from [gradient_of_radial_electron_pressure](name:derivative_with_respect_to_normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_electron_pressure_at_pedestal), which is a spatial derivative requiring a local conversion between $\psi_N$ and a chosen radial distance.

Typical signed values are usually negative in ordinary H-mode pedestals. Absolute magnitudes are about $10^4$-$10^6$ Pa in present tokamaks; small or low-pressure pedestals can be near $10^3$ Pa, while high-performance pedestals can reach several $10^6$ Pa.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron pressure increases as the normalized poloidal magnetic flux coordinate $\psi_N$ increases from the magnetic axis toward the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Dimensionless magnetic shear — the normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius — evaluated at the H-mode pedestal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear quantifies the spatial variation of field-line helicity across nested flux surfaces, controlling the stability of MHD and drift-wave modes. Evaluated at the pedestal — the steep pressure-gradient transport barrier characteristic of H-mode confinement — it enters directly into peeling-ballooning stability criteria governing edge-localized modes and sets constraints on the maximum achievable pedestal pressure.

The pedestal magnetic shear is defined as:

$$
s = \frac{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}{q} \frac{dq}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor}}
$$

where $q$ is the local safety factor and $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the separatrix. This is the scalar pedestal-locus counterpart of the radial profile [magnetic_shear](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal), and is analogous in structure to [magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis) evaluated on axis and [magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier) evaluated at internal barriers.

Pedestal magnetic shear is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction, combining external magnetic measurements with internal profile constraints such as motional Stark effect polarimetry or pressure-profile data. In conventional H-mode pedestals, $s$ spans 1–5, reflecting the rapid increase in $q$ across the narrow pedestal width; reversed-shear configurations can yield negative values near the pedestal foot.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $q$ increases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$, corresponding to outward-increasing field-line helicity toward the plasma edge.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless magnetic shear at the last closed flux surface, equal to the normalized radial derivative of the safety factor with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear at the plasma boundary is the value of magnetic shear on the last closed flux surface. It quantifies how rapidly the magnetic field-line pitch, represented by the [safety factor](name:safety_factor), changes with normalized toroidal flux radius at the edge of the confined plasma.

The boundary value is defined by evaluating the magnetic-shear expression at the outer end of the normalized toroidal flux radius:

$$
s_b = \left. \frac{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}{q}\frac{dq}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor}} \right|_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}=1}
$$

where $s_b$ is the dimensionless magnetic shear at the plasma boundary, $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux radius with $\rho_\mathrm{tor}=1$ on the last closed flux surface, and $q$ is the dimensionless safety factor.

In practice this quantity is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction or magnetic-geometry model by fitting or differentiating $q(\rho_\mathrm{tor})$ near the boundary. Because it depends on a radial derivative, it is sensitive to edge resolution, separatrix location, and smoothing of the reconstructed safety-factor variation.

Typical tokamak edge values are about 2-10 in conventional H-mode equilibria, with values near 1-5 often found in weaker-shear edge conditions and larger values possible in strongly shaped or high edge-current-gradient plasmas. Values near zero indicate weak radial variation of field-line pitch, while negative values occur when $q$ decreases outward with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal
NAMES.short: Radial flux-surface location of the H-mode pedestal, expressed by the normalized poloidal flux coordinate. It identifies the position of the edge transport barrier relative to the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal is the value of the flux coordinate $\psi_N$ at the characteristic radial location of the H-mode pedestal or edge transport barrier. It specifies where the pedestal sits between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface; the associated normalized_width_of_pedestal gives the pedestal extent in the same coordinate.

The normalized poloidal flux coordinate is defined by normalizing the poloidal magnetic flux to its magnetic-axis and last-closed-flux-surface values:

$$
\psi_N = \frac{\psi - \psi_\mathrm{axis}}{\psi_\mathrm{LCFS} - \psi_\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the flux surface of interest, $\psi_\mathrm{axis}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and $\psi_\mathrm{LCFS}$ is its value at the last closed flux surface. With this definition, $\psi_N = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\psi_N = 1$ at the last closed flux surface.

In practice, the pedestal position is obtained by mapping edge measurements of density, temperature, or pressure onto equilibrium flux surfaces and locating the characteristic pedestal center or transition position from the resulting radial variation. Different physical channels and fitting choices can give slightly different pedestal positions, so the quantity should be interpreted as the location associated with the specified pedestal observable.

In H-mode plasmas the pedestal position is usually close to the plasma edge, typically $\psi_N = 0.90$-$1.05$, with many pedestal centers lying around $0.95$-$1.00$. Values below 1 are inside the last closed flux surface, while values slightly above 1 can occur when the inferred transition extends into the near scrape-off-layer region or when the fitted midpoint lies just outside the separatrix.

NAMES.name: parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the heat-viscosity-driven current density, obtained by projecting that current-density vector onto the local magnetic-field direction.
NAMES.long:
Parallel current density due to heat viscosity is the field-aligned scalar component of the current density associated with heat-viscosity transport effects. It represents the part of this signed electric current density that flows along, or opposite to, the local magnetic field direction.

The component is defined by projection onto the magnetic-field unit vector:

$$
j_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{hv}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}} = \frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}$ is the heat-viscosity-driven current-density vector in A m^-2, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector in T, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude in T, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the local magnetic field.

This quantity is usually computed in edge-plasma transport or fluid modeling by first evaluating the heat-viscosity current-density vector and then taking its projection along $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$. It is not normally measured as a separate diagnostic observable, but may contribute to modeled current balance, parallel closure currents, sheath-connected current paths, and comparisons with magnetic or electric-current constraints.

Representative signed values in edge-plasma applications are often near zero where heat-viscosity effects are weak, with typical modeled ranges from -10^3 to 10^3 A m^-2 and localized excursions up to about -10^4 to 10^4 A m^-2 in steep-gradient or strongly driven regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the heat-viscosity-driven current density is directed along the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_diamagnetic_current_density
NAMES.short: Field-aligned component of the diamagnetic current density, projected onto the local magnetic field direction in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The parallel diamagnetic current density is the projection of the total [diamagnetic_current_density](name:diamagnetic_current_density) onto the local magnetic field direction at each point in the edge plasma. The diamagnetic current arises from the gyration of magnetized particles in a pressure-gradient field; in an isotropic ideal plasma, $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} = (\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p)/B^2$ is purely perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$, so its parallel component vanishes in that limit. In more complete descriptions including pressure anisotropy, finite Larmor radius corrections, or the inhomogeneous magnetic geometry of the tokamak edge, a field-aligned component emerges and must be tracked separately.

The parallel projection is defined as:

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{dia}} = \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} \cdot \hat{b}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia}$ is the diamagnetic current density vector and $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field of magnitude $B$.

In edge plasma current decompositions, this component is closely related to [parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), which encodes the same physical mechanism through the explicit drift formalism. The toroidal_diamagnetic_current_density provides the complementary geometric projection of the same vector field onto the toroidal direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of the local magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$.

NAMES.name: parallel_energy_diffusivity
NAMES.short: Field-line-aligned effective diffusivity in a Fick-law closure for neutral thermal-energy transport. It multiplies the parallel gradient of neutral energy density to give the diffusive neutral energy flux along magnetic field lines.
NAMES.long:
Parallel energy diffusivity is the component of an effective neutral thermal-energy diffusivity tensor aligned with the local magnetic field. It represents unresolved collisional, kinetic, or turbulent processes that spread neutral thermal energy along field lines in edge plasmas.

The diffusive closure for the parallel neutral thermal-energy flux is

$$
q_{E,\parallel} = -D^E_\parallel \, \nabla_\parallel u_n
$$

where $q_{E,\parallel}$ is the parallel diffusive thermal-energy flux density, $D^E_\parallel$ is this diffusivity, $u_n$ is the neutral thermal energy density, and $\nabla_\parallel = \hat{b}\cdot\nabla$ is the derivative along the magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$. The minus sign fixes the Fick-law flux convention: for positive $D^E_\parallel$, energy flows from larger to smaller $u_n$ along the chosen field-line direction. If the closure is instead written using neutral temperature, the temperature must be treated as an energy per particle, or an explicit conversion factor such as $k_B$ must be included for temperature in kelvin.

This coefficient is usually not measured directly. It is inferred from neutral transport modeling, collisional mean-free-path estimates, kinetic or fluid closures, and comparison with observables such as neutral pressure, spectroscopic emission, ionization patterns, and energy loading of plasma-facing surfaces.

Typical effective values in edge-plasma applications span about 0.1-10^4 m^2.s^-1. Cold, highly collisional divertor neutrals often use values near 0.1-10 m^2.s^-1, while weakly collisional atoms or molecules with long mean free paths can require 10^2-10^4 m^2.s^-1.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_charge_state_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Parallel ion charge-state diffusivity is the Fickian coefficient relating the density gradient of a specified ion charge state to its diffusive particle flux along magnetic field lines. A positive value drives particle flux down the field-aligned density gradient.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion charge-state diffusivity is the effective particle diffusion coefficient along magnetic field lines for ions in a specified charge state. It describes only the diffusive part of charge-state-resolved parallel transport, distinct from separately modeled advection, sources, ionization, recombination, or force-driven terms.

The diffusive contribution to the associated parallel particle flux is defined by Fick's law along the magnetic field:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,z}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\parallel,z}\,\nabla_{\parallel} n_z
$$

where $z$ labels the ion charge state, $\Gamma_{\parallel,z}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive part of the [parallel ion state particle flux](name:parallel_ion_state_particle_flux) in m^-2.s^-1, $D_{\parallel,z}$ is the parallel ion charge-state diffusivity in m^2.s^-1, $n_z$ is the ion charge-state density in m^-3, and $\nabla_{\parallel}=\hat{b}\cdot\nabla$ is the derivative along the unit magnetic-field direction $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$. With positive $D_{\parallel,z}$, the diffusive flux is opposite to a positive field-aligned density gradient.

In practice this coefficient is prescribed by a transport closure or inferred by comparing density gradients with estimates of the field-aligned particle flux in charge-state-resolved edge plasma modeling. It is an effective coefficient: any physics not represented explicitly in the flux equation is included only insofar as it changes the multiplier of the parallel density-gradient term.

Typical values are highly model dependent. Edge-plasma applications commonly use values from 1-10^5 m^2.s^-1, often much larger than perpendicular diffusivities, while 0 m^2.s^-1 represents the absence of an explicit Fickian parallel diffusion term for that charge state.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_state_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the effective convective velocity used for particle transport of a specified ion charge state in the edge plasma. It is a transport coefficient along the local magnetic-field direction and need not equal the bulk ion fluid velocity.
NAMES.long:
The parallel ion-state convection velocity is the coefficient multiplying the density of one ion charge state in the convective part of its parallel particle transport. It describes transport along the local magnetic-field direction in the edge plasma and is an effective balance-equation coefficient, not necessarily the literal mean fluid velocity of that ion state.

A common particle-flux decomposition defines the named quantity as:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,s} = n_s v_{\parallel,s}^{\mathrm{conv}} + \Gamma_{\parallel,s}^{\mathrm{nonconv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\parallel,s}$ is the total parallel particle flux of charge state $s$ along $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, $n_s$ is the charge-state density, $v_{\parallel,s}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is this effective convection velocity, and $\Gamma_{\parallel,s}^{\mathrm{nonconv}}$ contains diffusive, drift-ordering, turbulent, and source-related contributions that are not represented as density times a convective coefficient. Equivalently, where $n_s$ is nonzero, the effective coefficient is the residual parallel flux per particle after those nonconvective contributions have been separated; it can differ from the bulk ion fluid parallel velocity.

In practice it is obtained from charge-state particle-balance analysis or transport modeling using density evolution, parallel flux constraints, and atomic source terms such as ionization, recombination, charge exchange, neutral fueling, and recycling. Direct charge-state-resolved parallel flux measurements are uncommon, so the coefficient is usually constrained by a combination of spectroscopy, edge or divertor probes, and consistency with modeled sources and sinks. The same effective-coefficient interpretation underlies related radial convection-velocity quantities such as [radial_ion_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_convection_velocity) and [radial_ion_state_effective_momentum_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity).

Typical signed values in the confined edge are about $-10^4$ to $10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, while scrape-off-layer and divertor values often reach $-10^5$ to $10^5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Magnitudes comparable to a fraction of the local ion sound speed are common near material boundaries or strong source regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convective particle flux for the ion charge state is directed along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_state_momentum
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Parallel ion state momentum is the component, along the local magnetic-field direction, of the momentum source term for a specified ion species and charge state in an edge plasma. It has unit kg m^-1 s^-2 and represents addition or removal of that state's parallel momentum.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion state momentum is the signed projection of a charge-state-resolved ion momentum source term along the local magnetic-field direction. It applies to one ion species and one ion charge state, and has unit $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, the same dimensional unit as pressure or momentum flux.

The signed parallel projection is defined by:

$$
S_{p,\parallel}^{(a,q)} = \mathbf{S}_p^{(a,q)} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $S_{p,\parallel}^{(a,q)}$ is the parallel momentum source term for ion species $a$ and charge state $q$ with unit $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{S}_p^{(a,q)}$ is the corresponding vector momentum source term with the same unit, $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the local magnetic field, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field measured in tesla.

In practice this quantity is usually inferred or computed as part of a momentum balance for the selected ion state rather than measured directly. Contributing mechanisms can include ion-neutral momentum exchange, charge exchange, ionization and recombination momentum transfer, collisional friction, and externally applied momentum sources. Complementary projections of the same charge-state-resolved ion momentum source are represented by [poloidal_ion_state_momentum](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum), [toroidal_ion_state_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum), and radial_ion_state_momentum.

Typical absolute magnitudes are strongly case dependent: they range from near $0\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ where net parallel momentum transfer cancels to values comparable with local edge ion pressure $p_i$ or dynamic momentum-flux scales such as $m_i n_i u_\parallel^2$, where $m_i$, $n_i$, and $u_\parallel$ are ion mass, ion density, and parallel flow speed. The relevant scale can vary by orders of magnitude between weak-source edge regions and localized divertor or recycling regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the momentum source acts in the direction of the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Signed field-parallel particle flux density for a single ion charge state. It is the total charge-state particle flux density projected onto the local magnetic-field direction, giving the net number of ions crossing a unit area per unit time along the field.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion state particle flux is the signed particle flux density of a specified ion charge state projected onto the local magnetic-field direction. It quantifies net transport of that charge-state population along magnetic field lines, including any convective, diffusive, drift, or source-driven contributions included in the total particle flux density.

The defining projection is

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,i,k} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,k} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,k}$ is the total particle flux density of ion species $i$ in charge state $k$ in m^-2.s^-1, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{b}} = \boldsymbol{B}/|\boldsymbol{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field. For a purely convective contribution, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,k} = n_{i,k}\boldsymbol{v}_{i,k}$, so the field-parallel part is $n_{i,k} v_{\parallel,i,k}$, where $n_{i,k}$ is the charge-state density in m^-3 and $v_{\parallel,i,k}$ is the field-parallel velocity in m.s^-1.

In edge plasma analysis, this quantity is usually obtained from transport or kinetic calculations by projecting the charge-state-resolved particle flux onto $\hat{\boldsymbol{b}}$. Experimentally, it may be inferred indirectly from combinations of density, flow, spectroscopy, probe measurements, and magnetic geometry, with charge-state separation provided by atomic physics modeling or charge-state-resolved diagnostics.

Typical absolute values in the scrape-off layer and divertor range from 10^20-10^24 m^-2.s^-1, with the largest values near sheath entrances and high-recycling divertor regions. Weakly populated charge states, detached conditions, or near-stagnation regions can have much smaller values, and the signed flux may pass through zero where the field-parallel flow reverses.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the charge-state particle flux is directed along the local magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_momentum
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the aggregate neutral momentum source term, summed over all neutral states and projected along the local magnetic-field direction.
NAMES.long:
Parallel neutral momentum is the signed field-aligned component of the neutral momentum source term for the combined neutral population. It represents the net momentum loading of neutrals along the local magnetic field after summing contributions from all included neutral atomic, molecular, or excited states.

The aggregate state sum and parallel projection can be written as:

$$
S_{\parallel n} = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathcal{N}} \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \mathbf{S}_{n,\alpha}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}} = \frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $\mathcal{N}$ is the set of neutral states, $\mathbf{S}_{n,\alpha}$ is the momentum-source vector for neutral state $\alpha$ with unit kg m^-1 s^-2, $S_{\parallel n}$ is the aggregate scalar with the same unit, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is dimensionless, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field with unit T. The unit kg m^-1 s^-2 is equivalent to N m^-2, so this quantity has the dimensions of a stress or momentum-flux contribution in a momentum balance.

In practice it is computed from neutral momentum-exchange processes such as ionization, recombination, charge exchange, elastic scattering, molecular reactions, recycling, or neutral injection, without assuming that any one process is dominant. Conceptually related quantities include the full [neutral_momentum](name:neutral_momentum) source vector, the aggregate [toroidal_neutral_momentum](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum) component, the state-resolved [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum) component, the ion-state analog [parallel_ion_state_momentum](name:parallel_ion_state_momentum), and the transport quantity [parallel_neutral_momentum_flux](name:parallel_neutral_momentum_flux).

Typical magnitudes are highly case-dependent: values are often zero or negligible where the neutral density or net parallel exchange is small, while active edge, scrape-off-layer, divertor, recycling, or gas-puff regions can span many orders of magnitude. As an order-of-magnitude edge-plasma scale, nonzero absolute values may lie roughly in the range $10^{-6}$-$10^2$ kg m^-1 s^-2, but they should be interpreted relative to local pressure, momentum-flux, and paired plasma-neutral exchange terms rather than as a universal bound.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the source deposits momentum into the neutral population in the direction of $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, the local magnetic-field direction.

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_state_momentum_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Dimensionless flux-limiter coefficient that multiplies the field-aligned reference momentum-flux density for a neutral state in edge-plasma fluid transport. It changes the magnitude of the modeled parallel neutral momentum transport without defining its direction.
NAMES.long:
The parallel neutral-state momentum coefficient is a dimensionless flux-limiter multiplier for the component of neutral momentum transport resolved along the local magnetic-field direction. It applies to a specified neutral state and modifies the magnitude of a reference field-aligned momentum-flux density used by a fluid closure; the coefficient itself does not carry a direction.

A common closure interpretation is that the limited momentum-flux density is obtained by multiplying the reference value by this coefficient:

$$
\Pi_{\parallel,n}^{\mathrm{lim}} = C_{\parallel,n}^{\mathrm{mom}}\,\Pi_{\parallel,n}^{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $C_{\parallel,n}^{\mathrm{mom}}$ is this coefficient, $n$ labels the neutral state, and $\Pi_{\parallel,n}^{\mathrm{lim}}$ and $\Pi_{\parallel,n}^{\mathrm{ref}}$ are the limited and reference parallel momentum-flux densities, both with units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$. The reference momentum-flux density is the signed value supplied by the un-limited closure, such as a free-streaming, convective, or diffusive estimate, before this multiplier is applied.

The coefficient is normally specified by the transport model or inferred by calibration against kinetic neutral calculations and experimental constraints on edge density, pressure, and flow behavior. It is used to keep a fluid neutral momentum closure within a physically plausible range when mean-free paths become comparable to edge scale lengths.

Typical values are 0-1. A value of 0 suppresses the reference parallel momentum flux, while 1 leaves it unchanged; values greater than 1 represent model-specific enhancement rather than flux limiting. Negative values are generally outside the physical domain because they reverse the reference momentum-flux density instead of limiting it.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_ion_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Parallel effective convection velocity for total ion energy transport in edge plasma. It is the signed field-aligned speed associated with the convective part of the total ion energy flux.
NAMES.long:
Parallel total ion energy convection velocity is the signed effective field-aligned speed that multiplies a total ion energy density to give the convective part of the parallel ion-energy flux density. It represents advection of the ion energy variable used in an edge-plasma transport model and need not be identical to the bulk ion particle velocity.

The defining relation is the flux-density ratio:

$$
v_{\parallel,E_i}^{\mathrm{conv}} = \frac{q_{\parallel,E_i}^{\mathrm{conv}}}{\mathcal{E}_i}
$$

where $q_{\parallel,E_i}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the signed parallel convective flux density of total ion energy in W.m^-2 and $\mathcal{E}_i$ is the total ion energy density in J.m^-3, so the ratio has units m.s^-1. The denominator must be consistent with the energy variable used by the transport model; for a thermal-ion contribution, $T_i$ is treated as energy per ion, so $3 n_i T_i/2$ is in J.m^-3 when $T_i$ is in joules, while $3 n_i e T_i/2$ is used when the numerical temperature is in eV.

In practice, this velocity is specified by a transport closure or recovered from modeled energy flux density and energy density. It is the field-aligned analog of [radial_total_ion_effective_energy_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity), with the direction taken along magnetic field lines rather than across magnetic surfaces. Because enthalpy factors, species sums, or other closure choices may be included in either the flux or energy variable, values should be compared only when the same total-ion-energy definition is used.

Typical values are model dependent rather than universal. Magnitudes may be near 0 m.s^-1 when explicit parallel energy convection is absent and can range up to the local field-aligned transport-speed scale, often order 10^2-10^5 m.s^-1 in edge-plasma modeling; the chosen value should be interpreted with the same energy-density convention used in the defining ratio.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convection of total ion energy is along the local magnetic-field direction $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: plasma_momentum_flux
NAMES.short: Momentum-current vector carried by the plasma across an oriented surface per unit area. It is the contraction of the plasma momentum-flux tensor with the surface normal and includes convective flow, isotropic pressure, and viscous or turbulent stress contributions.
NAMES.long:
Plasma momentum flux is the vector flux of bulk plasma linear momentum through an oriented surface per unit area. It represents the traction-like momentum current obtained by applying the rank-2 plasma momentum-flux tensor to the surface unit normal; its direction gives the component of momentum being transported, while the chosen normal defines the surface through which transport is evaluated.

For a single-fluid plasma, the momentum-current vector through a surface with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is commonly written as

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{p}(\hat{\mathbf{n}}) = \left(\rho_m\,\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{u} + p\,\mathbf{I} + \boldsymbol{\pi}\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{p}$ has units of kg.m^-1.s^-2, $\rho_m$ is the plasma mass density in kg.m^-3, $\mathbf{u}$ is the bulk plasma velocity in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{u}$ is the dyadic convective momentum transport, $p$ is the scalar plasma pressure in Pa, $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity tensor, $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ is the viscous or turbulent stress tensor in Pa, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is a dimensionless unit normal. Contracting the rank-2 tensor with one unit normal yields a vector, not a scalar; scalar directional fluxes are obtained by an additional projection, as in [parallel_plasma_momentum_flux](name:parallel_plasma_momentum_flux).

In edge and scrape-off-layer plasma modeling this quantity is usually computed from fluid moments, kinetic closures, or turbulence simulations rather than measured directly. Components are often resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height; neutral analogs such as [toroidal_neutral_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_flux) describe momentum transport by neutral particles rather than by the charged plasma fluid.
