Values near zero are common where counteracting processes or nearly equal toroidal neutral and plasma flows cancel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral momentum-source vector points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_state_momentum
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Area-normalized toroidal momentum source acting on a specified neutral state in the edge plasma, projected along the phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal neutral state momentum is the toroidal component of the area-normalized linear momentum source acting on a specified neutral state in the edge plasma. It represents the rate per unit area at which interactions add or remove neutral momentum along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Unlike [toroidal_neutral_momentum](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum), it is resolved by neutral state rather than summed over all neutral states.

For a surface element, the area-normalized toroidal projection can be written as:

$$
S_{\phi,q}^{\mathrm{n}} = \hat{\phi} \cdot \mathbf{S}_{q}^{\mathrm{n}} = \hat{\phi} \cdot \frac{1}{A}\frac{d\mathbf{P}_{q}^{\mathrm{n}}}{dt}
$$

where $S_{\phi,q}^{\mathrm{n}}$ is the toroidal neutral-state momentum source in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, $\mathbf{S}_{q}^{\mathrm{n}}$ is the area-normalized vector momentum source for neutral state $q$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $A$ is the surface area in $\mathrm{m^2}$, $t$ is time in $\mathrm{s}$, and $\mathbf{P}_{q}^{\mathrm{n}}$ is the linear momentum in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ transferred to that neutral state.

This quantity is usually obtained from neutral and edge-plasma source calculations rather than from a direct measurement of toroidal neutral force. The contributing terms depend on the physics model and species represented; common momentum-transfer mechanisms include charge exchange, ionization, recombination, scattering, and recycling at material surfaces. Spectroscopy, neutral-pressure measurements, recycling observations, and plasma-background diagnostics can constrain the inputs used to compute the state-resolved source.

Typical magnitudes are highly localized and model dependent. Values may be close to $0\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ where toroidal momentum transfer is weak or balanced between processes, while order-of-magnitude edge estimates in active recycling or charge-exchange regions can span roughly $10^{-4}-10^{2}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ depending on neutral flux, toroidal velocity difference, interaction rates, and the chosen area normalization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net momentum source acts in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the momentum diffusion coefficient for neutral particles in a specified state. It parameterizes diffusive transport of neutral momentum along the toroidal direction.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal neutral-state momentum diffusion coefficient is the effective diffusion coefficient associated with transport of neutral-particle momentum along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the momentum-transport counterpart of [toroidal neutral-state diffusivity](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity), with the transported quantity being neutral momentum rather than particle density or another scalar moment.

For a local Fick-law closure, the projected toroidal diffusive momentum flux is commonly written as:

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{p,\phi} = -D_{p,\phi}\,\nabla_\phi p_n = -D_{p,\phi}\,\frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial p_n}{\partial \phi}
$$

where $D_{p,\phi}$ is the toroidal momentum diffusion coefficient in $m^2.s^{-1}$, $p_n$ is the neutral-state momentum density of the transported momentum component in $kg.m^{-2}.s^{-1}$, $R$ is in $m$, $\phi$ is in radians, and $\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{p,\phi}$ is the toroidal diffusive momentum flux density in $kg.m^{-1}.s^{-2}$. A positive $\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{p,\phi}$ denotes transport in the direction of increasing $\phi$; for positive $D_{p,\phi}$ the diffusive flux opposes the toroidal gradient of $p_n$.

This coefficient is usually not measured directly. It is inferred or prescribed in neutral momentum-balance models from kinetic neutral transport, momentum-exchange collision rates, closure fits, or reduced transport assumptions; when neutral mean free paths are comparable to plasma-gradient scale lengths, it should be interpreted as an effective local parameter rather than a fundamental material property.

Typical effective values in edge and scrape-off-layer neutral transport modeling span about $0.01-100\ m^2.s^{-1}$, with smaller values in dense, highly collisional recycling regions and values of $10^2-10^3\ m^2.s^{-1}$ possible in coarse-grained or weakly collisional closures.

NAMES.name: vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z-direction) component of the electric current density driven by frictional momentum exchange between plasma ions and background neutral particles in the edge or divertor plasma.
NAMES.long:
The vertical component of [current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction) is the projection of the ion-neutral friction current density vector onto the $\hat{Z}$ axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is the coordinate perpendicular to the tokamak midplane. In partially ionized edge and divertor plasmas, collisions between the ion fluid and background neutrals produce a frictional force that drives charge flow in all spatial directions, including the vertical.

The component is defined as

$$
j_Z^{\rm in} = \mathbf{j}_{\rm in} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\rm in}$ is the full ion-neutral friction current density vector, arising from momentum exchange between the ion fluid and neutrals at a rate governed by the ion-neutral collision frequency $\nu_{in}$, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector.

This component is obtained from edge and divertor plasma transport simulations that resolve neutral fluid dynamics in the scrape-off layer and divertor volume. The vertical direction gains significance where recycled neutrals stream vertically from plasma-facing surfaces, making the vertical ion-neutral coupling non-negligible. Together with the [radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), [poloidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction) siblings, it fully specifies the ion-neutral friction current density vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion-neutral friction current density flows in the $+Z$ direction, toward increasing vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_ion_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Vertical component of the effective convection velocity that advects ion momentum in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is defined per ion species without resolving charge states.
NAMES.long:
The vertical ion momentum convection velocity is the $Z$ component of an effective transport velocity for advective ion-momentum transport in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It applies to an ion species as a whole, without separating individual charge states.

The convective contribution to the vertical flux of an ion momentum density is written as

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{conv}}_{i,Z} = M_i V^{\mathrm{conv}}_{i,Z}
$$

where $V^{\mathrm{conv}}_{i,Z}$ is the vertical ion momentum convection velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $M_i$ is the transported ion momentum density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and $\Pi^{\mathrm{conv}}_{i,Z}$ is the corresponding vertical convective momentum flux in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

In practice this effective velocity is obtained from momentum-transport analysis by isolating the advective part of the ion momentum flux and dividing by the associated ion momentum density. It is a transport coefficient for momentum convection and need not be identical to the ion fluid velocity component.

Typical values are strongly case-dependent and may be positive, negative, or close to zero; they are interpreted in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ relative to the local vertical momentum flux balance rather than by a universal device-independent range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convection carries ion momentum toward increasing vertical height $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_total_current_density
NAMES.short: Vertical total current density is the Z component of the total electric current density vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the net conventional charge flux per unit area in the vertical direction after summing all resolved species and transport contributions.
NAMES.long:
The vertical total current density is the component along the vertical basis direction of the total electric current density vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It represents the net conventional positive charge flux per unit area carried vertically after all contributing species and current-driving mechanisms are summed, so cancelations can make the total smaller than individual partial contributions.

The component is defined by projecting the total current density vector onto the vertical unit vector:

$$
j_{Z,\mathrm{tot}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ and $j_{Z,\mathrm{tot}}$ are in A m^-2, and $\hat{Z}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the vertical direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. For particle flows, a species contribution has the form $q_s n_s \mathbf{u}_s$, where $q_s$ is charge, $n_s$ is number density, and $\mathbf{u}_s$ is flow velocity, yielding A m^-2.

In practice this quantity is usually inferred from modeling rather than measured directly. Edge-plasma and MHD descriptions compute it by summing resolved vertical contributions from particle motion, pressure-gradient, collisional-friction, inertial, neutral-friction, anomalous, and other transport terms; examples of related partial terms include [vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction) and vertical_anomalous_current_density. Magnetic-field constraints may use the full Maxwell-Ampere relation including displacement current; the simpler magnetoquasistatic curl-to-current estimate is an approximation valid when displacement current is negligible.

Typical edge and scrape-off-layer values of $|j_{Z,\mathrm{tot}}|$ are often 1-10^4 A m^-2, with localized sheath-connected structures, steep-gradient regions, or strong transient events reaching 10^4-10^5 A m^-2. Values near zero are also common where upward and downward partial currents nearly cancel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total conventional current density points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged translational kinetic temperature of a specified neutral species or neutral state over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. When multiple neutral states are treated together, the local neutral temperature is the particle-density-weighted translational temperature of the included neutral population.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged neutral temperature is the geometric volume average of the local neutral translational kinetic temperature over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. The local quantity being averaged is the [neutral temperature](name:neutral_state_temperature) for the specified neutral species or state; if several neutral states are grouped, it represents the particle-density-weighted local temperature of the included neutral population. As a thermodynamic temperature it is non-negative, with zero corresponding only to the idealized limit of no translational kinetic energy.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle T_n \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} \int_{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} T_n(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $T_n(\mathbf{x})$ is the local neutral temperature in eV, $dV$ is a differential volume element in m^3, and $V_\mathrm{LCFS}$ is the volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface in m^3. The resulting average $\langle T_n \rangle_V$ is expressed in eV.

In practice, local neutral temperatures may be inferred from Doppler broadening of neutral spectral lines, from kinetic neutral transport calculations, or from coupled plasma-neutral models constrained by measurements. The volume average is then obtained by integrating that local temperature over the closed-flux-surface plasma volume.

Representative neutral translational temperatures in magnetic-confinement plasmas range from about 0.03-1 eV for cold or warm gas populations to several eV when faster neutral components contribute. The LCFS-volume average depends strongly on neutral penetration, species composition, and the definition of the neutral states included in the averaged population.

NAMES.name: faraday_angle
NAMES.short: Signed rotation angle of the plane of linear polarization of an electromagnetic probe beam after propagation through a magnetized plasma. It is produced by Faraday circular birefringence and is proportional to wavelength squared times the line integral of electron density multiplied by the magnetic-field component along the beam path.
NAMES.long:
Faraday angle is the signed change in orientation of a linearly polarized electromagnetic wave after it traverses a magnetized plasma. The rotation arises because the left- and right-circularly polarized components of the wave have different refractive indices in the presence of a magnetic field component along the beam path. Since a linear polarization plane is physically unchanged by a rotation of $\pi$, reported angles may be phase-unwrapped when rotations exceed this periodicity.

For a cold plasma away from wave resonances, the single-pass Faraday angle is commonly approximated by:

$$
\chi_F = C_F \lambda^2 \int_{\mathcal{L}} n_e(l)\,B_\parallel(l)\,dl
$$

where $\chi_F$ is the Faraday angle, $C_F \simeq 2.63 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{T}^{-1}$ in SI units, $\lambda$ is the vacuum wavelength, $n_e$ is the electron number density, $l$ is distance along the beam path $\mathcal{L}$, and $B_\parallel = \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{k}$ is the magnetic-field component along the propagation direction $\hat{k}$.

Faraday angle is measured by polarimetry, using the change between the injected and received linear polarization states of a probing beam. It is computed in forward models by integrating density and magnetic-field information along the optical path, with corrections for refraction, multiple passes, window rotations, and calibration offsets when they are significant.

Typical absolute values in magnetically confined plasmas range from 0.01-5 rad for far-infrared or submillimeter polarimetry, depending strongly on wavelength, path length, density, and magnetic-field strength. Low-density plasmas or short chords can give milliradian rotations, while long paths through dense, high-field plasmas can produce rotations of several radians.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the emergent polarization plane is rotated counter-clockwise relative to the incident plane as viewed looking along the beam propagation direction.

NAMES.name: frequency_of_diagnostic_antenna
NAMES.short: Temporal frequency of the electromagnetic wave to which a diagnostic antenna channel transmits, receives, or is tuned. It sets the wave interaction scale; for some diagnostics it helps infer resonance, cutoff, or phase-shift locations, but it does not by itself specify a plasma position.
NAMES.long:
Frequency of a diagnostic antenna is the non-negative temporal oscillation rate of the electromagnetic field selected by a transmitting or receiving diagnostic channel. It identifies the spectral component used by the diagnostic and is distinct from a plasma characteristic frequency, although it is often compared with characteristic frequencies such as cutoff, plasma, or cyclotron frequencies.

The temporal frequency $f$ is related to angular frequency $\omega$ by:

$$
f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}
$$

where $f$ is in hertz and $\omega$ is in radians per second. In vacuum the corresponding wavelength is $c/f$, where $c$ is the speed of light in meters per second.

In practice, the frequency is set by the transmitter synthesizer, local oscillator, receiver filter, or channel passband. Reflectometry and refractometry use one or more probe frequencies and interpret the measured phase, amplitude, or reflection behavior through the plasma dispersion relation; a cutoff or phase-shift location also depends on density, magnetic field, launch geometry, polarization, and propagation effects. For electron cyclotron emission diagnostics, a channel frequency is compared with the electron cyclotron resonance condition; in the nonrelativistic, zero-Doppler limit $f \simeq s e B/(2\pi m_e)$, where $s$ is the harmonic number, $e$ is the elementary charge in coulombs, $B$ is magnetic-field strength in tesla, and $m_e$ is the electron mass in kilograms. This comparison can help localize emission, but the antenna frequency alone is not a universal radial coordinate.

Typical diagnostic antenna frequencies in magnetized fusion experiments range from about $10^6-10^{12}$ Hz depending on the diagnostic. Microwave reflectometry and refractometry commonly use about $10^{10}-2 \times 10^{11}$ Hz, while electron cyclotron emission channels often use about $5 \times 10^{10}-10^{12}$ Hz. The appropriate range is determined by the target density, magnetic-field strength, propagation accessibility, and hardware bandwidth.

NAMES.name: launched_wave_duration
NAMES.short: Elapsed time for one complete swept-frequency launch of a probing electromagnetic wave, from the beginning of the sweep to its end.
NAMES.long:
Launched wave duration is the elapsed time over which a probing electromagnetic wave is emitted while completing one frequency sweep. It describes the time span of the swept launch itself, independent of how the received signal is analyzed.

For a single sweep, the duration is the difference between the end and start times of the launched frequency ramp:

$$
\Delta t_{\mathrm{sw}} = t_{\mathrm{end}} - t_{\mathrm{start}}
$$

where $\Delta t_{\mathrm{sw}}$ is the launched wave duration in seconds, $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ is the time at which the sweep begins, and $t_{\mathrm{end}}$ is the time at which the sweep ends.

In swept-frequency reflectometry or refractometry, this duration is determined from the launch timing waveform or from the timing markers that delimit one sweep. The corresponding frequency evolution during the same interval is described by [launched_wave_frequency](name:launched_wave_frequency). This quantity represents the same sweep-duration concept as [launched_duration](name:launched_wave_duration), with the wording emphasizing the emitted probing wave.

Typical values are diagnostic- and operating-mode dependent, because the selected sweep duration must cover the desired frequency span while providing the required temporal sampling of the plasma evolution.

NAMES.name: length_of_electron_cyclotron_beam
NAMES.short: Curvilinear arc length measured along the propagation path of an electron cyclotron beam-tracing ray. It parameterizes position along the wave trajectory and can be evaluated at any point along the beam path through the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Length of an electron cyclotron beam is the accumulated curvilinear distance along the beam-tracing ray from a chosen launch or reference point to a point on the propagation path. It is a path coordinate for the wave trajectory, not the straight-line distance between endpoints, and it can be evaluated at any point reached by the traced beam.

For a ray position vector $\mathbf{r}(s)$ parameterized by an arbitrary monotonic ray parameter $s$, the arc length $\ell$ is defined by the line integral along the path:

$$
\ell(s) = \int_{s_0}^{s} \left|\frac{d\mathbf{r}}{ds'}\right|\,ds'
$$

where $\ell$ is the arc length in meters, $\mathbf{r}$ is the ray position in meters, $s_0$ is the launch or reference value of the ray parameter, and $s'$ is the integration variable. If the ray is parameterized by physical time $t$ in seconds, the equivalent differential relation is $d\ell = |\mathbf{v}_g|\,dt$, where $\mathbf{v}_g = \partial\omega/\partial\mathbf{k}$ is the group velocity in meters per second, $\omega$ is angular frequency in radians per second, and $\mathbf{k}$ is the wave vector in radians per meter.

In beam-tracing calculations, this quantity is computed by integrating incremental path segments along the numerically traced ray or beam centerline. It is used to locate absorption, emission, refraction, or diagnostic weighting along the electron cyclotron wave path without assuming that the path is straight.

Typical values range from about 0.1-10 m in laboratory magnetic-confinement devices, depending on launcher position, viewing geometry, plasma size, and the amount of refraction along the trajectory.

NAMES.name: length_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short: Total non-negative arclength of the optical fiber used by a Fiber Optic Current Sensor, measured along the fiber centerline. It sets the optical propagation length and scales the accumulated Faraday rotation, while the spatial trajectory of the winding determines which magnetic-field line integral is sampled.
NAMES.long:
Length of a Fiber Optic Current Sensor fiber is the total arclength of the sensing optical fiber centerline between the defined optical endpoints. It is a non-negative geometric length and does not by itself define the magnetic-field integration path; the full path requires the fiber trajectory, for example coordinates $R(s)$, $\phi(s)$, and $Z(s)$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The arclength is defined from the fiber centerline curve $\mathbf{r}(u)$ as:

$$
L = \int_{u_0}^{u_1} \left|\frac{d\mathbf{r}}{du}\right|\,du
$$

where $L$ is the fiber length in meters, $\mathbf{r}$ is the centerline position in meters, and $u$ is any monotonic parameter along the fiber. The Faraday rotation measured by the sensor is governed more generally by the line integral $\Phi_F = \int_\Gamma V\,\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{l}$, where $\Phi_F$ is the optical rotation in radians, $V$ is the [Verdet constant](name:verdet_constant_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor) in rad T$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in tesla, and $d\mathbf{l}$ is the oriented fiber path element in meters.

In practice, the length is obtained from fiber manufacture records, installation metrology, optical time-domain measurements, or by integrating the surveyed centerline of the installed winding. Related geometric quantities describe parts of the trajectory or optical setup, such as the [vertical outline](name:vertical_outline_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor), which constrains vertical positions of outline points, and the [initial angle], which specifies an azimuthal reference for the spun fiber rather than the total path length. The [spun wavelength] characterizes the twist period along this same length.

Typical installed sensing-fiber lengths are 10-100 m for compact or partial windings and 50-300 m for full-vessel tokamak installations, depending on vessel size, number of turns, routing allowances, and lead-in fiber included in the sensing path.

NAMES.name: parallel_normalized_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Dimensionless signed fraction of the beam power flow parallel to the local magnetic field along a beam-tracing ray path, normalized to the initial launched power. It is based on the time-averaged wave power flow; positive values indicate local propagation along the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The parallel normalized power of a beam-tracing beam is the field-aligned component of the beam power flow divided by the initial launched power. It describes how much of the surviving wave power is transported along the local magnetic field direction at each point on the ray path, with the sign retained.

For an arc-length coordinate $s$ along the beam path, the quantity is defined by

$$
p_{\parallel,\mathrm{norm}}(s) = \frac{\mathbf{P}(s) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}(s)}{P_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{P}(s)$ is the time-averaged beam power-flow vector obtained from the electromagnetic Poynting flux integrated over the local beam cross-section and has unit W, $P_0$ is the initial launched power and has unit W, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}(s)=\mathbf{B}(s)/|\mathbf{B}(s)|$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the local magnetic field.

In beam tracing, this quantity is computed from the ray direction, wave amplitude or wave-action evolution, and the local magnetic-field direction. Absorption, mode conversion, or other power-loss mechanisms reduce the magnitude as the beam propagates; the sign is evaluated locally throughout propagation relative to $\hat{\mathbf{b}}(s)$, not fixed by the initial launch direction. It complements the perpendicular normalized power by separating field-aligned and cross-field transport of the time-averaged wave power.

Typical values are between -1 and 1 for passive propagation without gain. Values near 1 indicate power flow nearly parallel to the local magnetic field, values near -1 indicate power flow nearly antiparallel to it, and values near 0 indicate predominantly perpendicular power flow or a strongly attenuated beam.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the time-averaged beam power flow at the evaluated point has a component in the direction of the local magnetic field.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_normalized_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Non-negative fraction of the beam power-flow vector lying in the plane perpendicular to the local magnetic field, normalized to the initial launch power. It is a magnitude, not a signed projection onto a chosen perpendicular direction.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular normalized power of a beam-tracing beam is the magnitude of the beam power flow across the local magnetic-field direction, divided by the initial launched beam power. The perpendicular direction is the plane normal to the local magnetic field, so this scalar does not choose or encode a signed direction within that plane.

A dimensionally consistent definition uses the beam power-flow vector, not a Poynting flux density:

$$
p_{\perp,N}(s) = \frac{P_\perp(s)}{P_0} = \frac{\left|\mathbf{P}(s) - \left[\mathbf{P}(s)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}(s)\right]\hat{\mathbf{b}}(s)\right|}{P_0}
$$

where $s$ parameterizes position along the ray path, $\mathbf{P}(s)$ is the local beam power-flow vector integrated over the beam cross-section, $P_0$ is the initial launch power, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field. Both $\mathbf{P}$ and $P_0$ represent powers in W, making $p_{\perp,N}$ dimensionless.

In beam tracing, this quantity is computed from the local group-velocity or power-flow direction together with the remaining beam power after absorption, emission, or gain processes included in the model. It is used to distinguish cross-field transport of wave energy from power flow along the magnetic field.

Typical values range from 0-1 in passive calculations normalized to the launched power. Values near 0 indicate propagation nearly along the magnetic field, while values near the local normalized remaining beam power indicate predominantly cross-field propagation; values above 1 require net amplification or a source term in the modeled beam power.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_wave_vector_magnitude
NAMES.short: Magnitude of the wave vector component perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field, setting the cross-field spatial scale of wave-plasma coupling and turbulent density fluctuation backscattering.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular wave vector magnitude $k_\perp$ is the modulus of the wave propagation vector projected onto the plane perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$. It governs the cross-field spatial periodicity of the wave and is fundamental to both electromagnetic wave propagation calculations and fluctuation turbulence diagnostics. This scalar quantity is the magnitude of perpendicular_wave_vector.

$$
k_\perp = |\mathbf{k} - (\mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{b})\hat{b}|
$$

where $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}_0 / |\mathbf{B}_0|$ is the unit vector along the equilibrium magnetic field and $\mathbf{k}$ is the full wave vector.

In Doppler reflectometry, the Bragg backscattering condition selects density fluctuations at $k_\perp \approx 2 k_0 \sin\theta$, where $k_0 = \omega/c$ is the vacuum wavenumber and $\theta$ is the beam tilt angle. The doppler_frequency shift of the backscattered signal is proportional to $k_\perp$ times the perpendicular plasma flow velocity, enabling turbulence wavenumber spectra to be resolved across the spectral_frequency grid. In wave beam tracing, $k_\perp$ characterizes the cross-field propagation scale relevant for finite Larmor radius effects and mode conversion, complementing the field-aligned scale encoded in the [parallel_refractive_index](name:parallel_refractive_index).

Typical values in Doppler reflectometry range from a few to several hundred m$^{-1}$, probing turbulent density fluctuations from the plasma minor-radius scale down toward the ion gyroradius.

NAMES.name: plasma_frequency_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Local electron plasma frequency at the diagnostic measurement position, set by the electron number density through the cold-plasma oscillation frequency. In reflectometry it equals the ordinary-mode cutoff frequency at the reflection layer; for extraordinary-mode operation it is the density-dependent plasma-frequency component inferred from the cutoff condition.
NAMES.long:
Electron plasma frequency at a measurement position is the local natural oscillation frequency of electrons about a quasi-neutral ion background, with ions effectively fixed on the electron time scale. It is a specialized form of frequency_at_measurement_position in which the frequency is determined by local electron density and fundamental constants.

The electron plasma frequency is defined by

$$
f_{pe} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{n_e e^2}{\varepsilon_0 m_e}}
$$

where $n_e$ is the local electron number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$ is the elementary charge, $\varepsilon_0=8.854\,187\,8128\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}$ is the vacuum permittivity, and $m_e=9.109\,383\,7015\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$ is the electron mass. The reported value is the cycles-per-second frequency in Hz; for harmonic fields written as $\mathrm{Re}\{\tilde{A}\exp(-i\omega t)\}$, $\omega=2\pi f_{pe}$, and the opposite exponential convention gives the same frequency.

In ordinary-mode (O-mode) reflectometry, the cold-plasma cutoff layer is the location where the probing [frequency_of_diagnostic_antenna](name:frequency_of_diagnostic_antenna) equals $f_{pe}$, so the local density follows from $n_e=(2\pi f_{pe})^2\varepsilon_0 m_e/e^2$. In extraordinary-mode (X-mode) reflectometry, cutoff frequencies also depend on electron cyclotron frequency and propagation geometry; in that case this quantity is the density-dependent plasma frequency inferred at the reflection layer from the appropriate dispersion relation, not the full X-mode cutoff frequency.

Typical values in magnetic-confinement plasmas are $2\times10^{10}-3\times10^{11}$ Hz, corresponding approximately to electron densities from $5\times10^{18}$ to $1\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$. At $n_e=1\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $f_{pe}\approx9.0\times10^{10}$ Hz.

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_suprathermal_electron_angle_at_measurement_position
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Poloidal angular shift of the ECE measurement position caused by suprathermal electrons, relative to the thermal-emission position.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed poloidal-angle component of the displacement between the nominal thermal-electron ECE emission position and the apparent measurement position when suprathermal electrons contribute to the emission. The poloidal angle $\theta$ is measured around the magnetic axis in a constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $\theta=0$ at the outboard midplane and $\theta$ increasing from larger $R$ toward $+Z$. It isolates the suprathermal-electron contribution rather than a generic viewing or equilibrium-position correction.

The additive correction to the poloidal coordinate of the assigned measurement position is represented by:

$$
\theta_\mathrm{meas} = \theta_\mathrm{th} + \Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}
$$

where $\theta_\mathrm{meas}$ is the corrected poloidal angle of the measurement position, $\theta_\mathrm{th}$ is the poloidal angle inferred for the thermal-emission position, and $\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}$ is this quantity; all three angular quantities are measured in radians.

The correction is normally obtained by comparing the localization of ECE emission for a thermal-electron population with the localization obtained when the suprathermal electron population is included, using the viewing geometry and magnetic equilibrium. This name refers to the diagnostic measurement position; the related poloidal_suprathermal_electron_perturbed_angle_of_ece_channel_emission_position applies specifically to the ECE-channel emission position, while poloidal_perturbed_angle_at_measurement_position denotes the corresponding generic poloidal perturbation without specifying suprathermal electrons as the cause.

There is no device-independent typical range for this signed angular offset. It is zero when suprathermal-electron effects are absent or negligible, and its magnitude depends on the suprathermal distribution, optical depth, observing frequency, harmonic, viewing geometry, and equilibrium.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}$ shifts the assigned measurement position in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$, defined from the outboard midplane toward $+Z$ in a constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Radial (major-radius) component of the local wave vector along the beam tracing ray path.
NAMES.long:
The wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ characterizes the local spatial frequency and propagation direction of an electromagnetic wave at each point along a beam tracing ray. Its radial component $k_R = \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{R}$ quantifies how rapidly the wave phase advances in the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the wave vector decomposes as:

$$
\mathbf{k} = k_R \hat{R} + k_\phi \hat{\phi} + k_Z \hat{Z}
$$

where $k_\phi = n_\phi / R$ with $n_\phi$ the toroidal mode number and $R$ the major radius in meters, and $k_Z$ is the [vertical wave vector component](name:vertical_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam). Together with [toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), these three components fully specify the local wave propagation geometry consistent with the local dispersion relation $D(\mathbf{k}, \omega, \mathbf{x}) = 0$.

This component is computed by beam tracing along the ray path for electron cyclotron heating, current drive, and electron cyclotron emission diagnostic beams. For electron cyclotron waves near 170 GHz, the vacuum wavenumber $|\mathbf{k}_0| = \omega/c$ is approximately 3600 m$^{-1}$; in-plasma values of $k_R$ vary along the ray according to plasma geometry and the local dispersion relation.

The dimensionless counterpart [radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) gives the direction cosine $k_R / |\mathbf{k}|$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial wave vector component points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radiative_temperature
NAMES.short: Radiative temperature is the brightness temperature obtained by converting electron cyclotron emission intensity measured by an ECE radiometer channel to an equivalent blackbody temperature. It approaches the local electron temperature at the resonant layer when the selected polarization and propagation path are optically thick.
NAMES.long:
Radiative temperature is the equivalent blackbody temperature associated with the electron cyclotron emission received by a radiometer channel. It represents the emitted microwave brightness, not necessarily the kinetic [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature), because finite optical depth, polarization coupling, reflections, and absorption along the propagation path can make the detected brightness differ from the local thermal value.

For spectral radiance expressed in the Rayleigh-Jeans convention, the energy-equivalent radiative temperature is

$$
T_\mathrm{rad} = \frac{c^2 I_\nu}{2\nu^2 e}
$$

where $I_\nu$ is the calibrated spectral radiance at frequency $\nu$, $c$ is the speed of light, and $e$ is the elementary charge. The result $T_\mathrm{rad}$ is in eV; the corresponding thermodynamic temperature in kelvin is $eT_\mathrm{rad}/k_B$, where $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant. Polarization-specific measurements fold the X-mode or O-mode response, mode purity, and coupling efficiency into the calibrated radiance used in this definition.

In practice, radiative temperature is obtained from absolutely calibrated radiometer power after correction for receiver gain, offsets, electronic noise, background emission, filter bandwidth, antenna pattern, and the channel spectral response. Forward calculations use polarized radiative transfer for the selected ordinary or extraordinary mode, including emission, absorption, optical depth, relativistic broadening, harmonic overlap, and possible mode coupling. The channel frequency maps to electron-cyclotron harmonic layers set by the local magnetic-field strength; in tokamak geometry this often corresponds to a major-radius location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is measured from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height.

Typical thermal ECE radiative temperatures are about 100-1000 eV for cooler edge or pedestal sightlines and 1000-20000 eV for hot core sightlines, with higher values possible in high-performance plasmas. When the plasma is optically thick, $T_\mathrm{rad}$ is a close proxy for local electron temperature and may be compared with [electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](name:electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) or [radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](name:radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) for central channels. In optically thin regions or channels affected by polarization mismatch, mode conversion, or wall reflections, the measured radiative temperature can be substantially lower than the local electron temperature.

NAMES.name: refractive_index
NAMES.short: Dimensionless refractive-index vector of an electromagnetic wave in plasma, equal to the local wave vector divided by the vacuum wave number k0 = omega/c.
NAMES.long:
The refractive-index vector $\mathbf{N}$ specifies the local phase-gradient direction and normalized wavelength of an electromagnetic wave in a plasma. It is the wave vector scaled by the vacuum wave number, so its magnitude gives the refractive index of the propagating branch when the wave vector is real.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathbf{N} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{k_0} = \frac{c\,\mathbf{k}}{\omega}
$$

where $\mathbf{N}$ is dimensionless, $\mathbf{k}$ is the local wave vector in m$^{-1}$, $k_0=\omega/c$ is the vacuum wave number in m$^{-1}$, $\omega$ is the angular frequency in rad s$^{-1}$, and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum in m s$^{-1}$. Relative to the magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, the linked components are the [parallel refractive index](name:parallel_refractive_index) $N_\parallel=\mathbf{N}\cdot\hat{b}$ and the [perpendicular refractive index](name:perpendicular_refractive_index) $N_\perp=|\mathbf{N}\times\hat{b}|$.

In ray-tracing and beam-tracing descriptions, $\mathbf{N}$ is obtained from the local electromagnetic dispersion relation and evolves along the trajectory together with position. Where a dispersion branch is propagating, $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{N}$ are real; near cutoffs or in evanescent regions the relevant dispersion root can make one or more components of $\mathbf{k}$ complex, with the imaginary part describing spatial attenuation.

Typical values are dimensionless. In vacuum $|\mathbf{N}|=1$; in weakly dispersive propagating plasma waves $|\mathbf{N}|$ is usually of order unity, while individual components such as $N_\parallel$ may be much smaller than one or may become larger depending on launch angle, plasma density, magnetic field, and the selected wave branch.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a component of $\mathbf{N}$ has the same sign as the corresponding component of the wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ in the chosen basis.

NAMES.name: parallel_refractive_index
NAMES.short: Projection of the refractive-index vector onto the local equilibrium magnetic field direction, equal to the wave vector component parallel to the magnetic field normalized by the vacuum wave number.
NAMES.long:
The parallel refractive index $N_\parallel$ is the component of the refractive-index vector $\mathbf{N} = \mathbf{k}/k_0$ projected along the local equilibrium magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, where $k_0 = \omega/c$ is the vacuum wave number at angular frequency $\omega$ and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. It governs the phase velocity of a wave along the field line and controls parallel resonance effects including Landau damping and transit-time magnetic pumping.

The defining relation is:

$$
N_\parallel = \mathbf{N} \cdot \hat{b} = \frac{\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{B}}{k_0 |\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the local wave vector and $\mathbf{B}$ is the background magnetic field.

Together with [perpendicular_refractive_index](name:perpendicular_refractive_index), $N_\parallel$ fully decomposes the parent [refractive_index](name:refractive_index) vector into its field-aligned and cross-field components. In beam-tracing or ray-tracing calculations, $N_\parallel$ is evaluated at each point along the ray path; for lower hybrid current drive it is a primary launch parameter controlled by the phasing between antenna straps, and for electron cyclotron emission diagnostics it determines the Doppler shift of the resonance layer.

For lower hybrid waves, $N_\parallel$ at launch lies in the range 1.5–3.5 to satisfy the wave accessibility condition in the core plasma. For nearly perpendicular electron cyclotron beams, $|N_\parallel|$ is well below unity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave vector projected onto the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ points in the same direction as $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_refractive_index
NAMES.short: Component of the refractive-index vector perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field, evaluated at each point along a beam or ray tracing path in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular refractive index $N_\perp$ is the magnitude of the component of the refractive-index vector $\mathbf{N} = \mathbf{k}/k_0$ (where $\mathbf{k}$ is the local wave vector and $k_0 = \omega/c$ is the vacuum wave number) that lies perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field direction $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$. Together with the [parallel refractive index](name:parallel_refractive_index) $N_\parallel$, it fully characterizes the field-aligned decomposition of wave propagation geometry in a magnetized plasma.

The two components satisfy the identity:

$$
N_\perp^2 + N_\parallel^2 = |\mathbf{N}|^2
$$

where $N_\parallel = \mathbf{N} \cdot \hat{b}$ and $N_\perp = |\mathbf{N} - N_\parallel \hat{b}|$. For a cold magnetized plasma, the Appleton-Hartree dispersion relation constrains the allowed pairs $(N_\parallel, N_\perp)$ for each propagating normal mode; cutoff surfaces occur where $N_\perp \to 0$ and mark wave reflection or mode-conversion layers, while cyclotron resonances correspond to $N_\perp \to \infty$.

$N_\perp$ is evaluated at each step along beam or ray tracing trajectories and enters directly into calculations of single-pass absorption, mode conversion efficiency, and wave accessibility for electron cyclotron heating, current drive, and emission diagnostics. Typical values for electron cyclotron beams in the plasma core range from near zero at cutoff layers to approximately 1–3 for O-mode and X-mode propagation, depending on wave frequency, local electron density, and magnetic field strength.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the refractive-index vector has a non-zero component perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field direction $\hat{b}$; $N_\perp$ is non-negative by construction as it represents the magnitude of a vector projection.

NAMES.name: tilt_angle_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Tilt angle of the elliptical beam-spot cross-section for a beam-tracing wave beam. It is measured in the plane normal to propagation, from e1 toward e2 in the local right-handed beam frame (e1, e2, e_parallel), where e_parallel follows the beam direction.
NAMES.long:
The tilt angle of a beam-tracing beam is the orientation of the principal axes of the elliptical beam-spot cross-section in the plane perpendicular to the local propagation direction. It specifies how the spot ellipse is rotated relative to the transverse axes of the local right-handed beam frame $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{e}_\parallel)$, with $\hat{e}_\parallel$ along the beam direction. It is the beam-tracing specialization of the more general [tilt_angle_of_wave_beam](name:tilt_angle_of_beam_tracing_beam) and should be interpreted together with the transverse spot sizes.

If the beam spot is represented by the symmetric transverse second-moment matrix $\Sigma$ in the basis $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2)$, the tilt angle $\alpha$ of the major principal axis is obtained by diagonalizing that matrix:

$$
\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(2\Sigma_{12},\,\Sigma_{11}-\Sigma_{22}\right)
$$

where $\Sigma_{11}$ and $\Sigma_{22}$ are the second moments along $\hat{e}_1$ and $\hat{e}_2$, $\Sigma_{12}$ is the cross moment, and $\operatorname{atan2}$ selects the correct quadrant. Equivalently, $\tan(2\alpha)=2\Sigma_{12}/(\Sigma_{11}-\Sigma_{22})$ when the denominator is nonzero; the orthogonal principal axis is at $\alpha+\pi/2$.

In beam-tracing or Gaussian-optics calculations, the spot matrix is propagated with the beam through optical elements and plasma, and the tilt is computed from the eigenvectors of that matrix at each location. Near launch or reception, it can also be inferred from fitted beam patterns or optical design parameters. The angle becomes poorly conditioned when the two spot sizes are nearly equal, because a circular spot has no unique orientation.

Typical values are reported modulo $\pi$, commonly in the interval $-\pi/2$ to $\pi/2$ rad. Well-aligned beams often have $|\alpha| < 0.2$ rad near launch, while astigmatic optics, oblique propagation, or strong refraction can produce rotations of order $0.5-1.5$ rad.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the major principal axis of the beam-spot ellipse is rotated from $\hat{e}_1$ toward $\hat{e}_2$ in the local right-handed beam frame $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{e}_\parallel)$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Toroidal direction cosine of the local electromagnetic wave vector along a beam-tracing ray, equal to the toroidal wave vector component divided by the total wave vector magnitude.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal normalized wave vector component is the projection of the unit wave vector onto the geometric toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$, quantifying the fraction of the wave's phase advance occurring in the toroidal direction at each point along a beam-tracing path. It characterizes the propagation geometry of electromagnetic waves in magnetized plasma and enters the local dispersion relation governing wave accessibility and resonance conditions.

The defining relation is:

$$
k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{k_\phi}{|\mathbf{k}|}
$$

where $k_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the wave vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the total wave vector magnitude. The three normalized direction cosines satisfy $k_{R,\mathrm{norm}}^2 + k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}}^2 + k_{Z,\mathrm{norm}}^2 = 1$, linking this component to the [radial normalized wave vector](name:radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and the [vertical normalized wave vector](name:vertical_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam). The unnormalized toroidal component is available as the [toroidal wave vector of beam tracing beam](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam).

This quantity is computed by beam-tracing or ray-tracing solvers integrating the geometric-optics equations for RF or ECE wave propagation in inhomogeneous magnetized plasma. It governs polarization selection at cyclotron harmonic layers and mode-conversion regions along the beam path.

Values are bounded by $-1 \leq k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} \leq 1$. For beams launched near-perpendicular to the magnetic field the toroidal direction cosine is near zero; oblique launches into the plasma yield larger magnitudes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal wave vector component $k_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Physical toroidal component of the electromagnetic wave vector along a beam-tracing ray, defined by projection onto the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It determines, but is not identical to, the toroidal refractive-index component through the wave frequency.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the physical component of the electromagnetic wave vector along the toroidal unit direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It describes the local toroidal phase advance per unit length of the propagating wave and is one component of the full ray wave vector.

The component is defined by projecting the local wave vector onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
k_\phi = \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the local electromagnetic wave vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. The corresponding normalized toroidal refractive-index component is $N_\phi = c k_\phi / \omega$, where $c$ is the speed of light in m s$^{-1}$ and $\omega$ is the angular wave frequency in rad s$^{-1}$.

In beam tracing, $k_\phi$ is computed from the ray or beam solution of the electromagnetic dispersion relation and evolves as the ray refracts through spatially varying plasma and magnetic-field conditions. This quantity is the physical orthonormal toroidal component, not the canonical phase-gradient component conjugate to the toroidal angle; the associated canonical quantity is $R k_\phi$, and in an axisymmetric medium it is $R k_\phi$, not $k_\phi$ alone, that may be conserved along a ray.

Typical electron-cyclotron and ECE beam-tracing values are about $10^1$-$10^3$ m$^{-1}$, with values of a few $10^3$ m$^{-1}$ possible for 100-200 GHz waves with strong toroidal steering. There is no fixed universal bound independent of frequency and plasma dispersion, but as a physical projection it satisfies $|k_\phi| \le |\mathbf{k}|$ locally.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave vector component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: twist_period_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short: Positive length along a spun optical fiber over which the effective birefringent axes complete one full helical turn. It is the optical-axis twist pitch used in FOCS polarization modeling, distinct from the nominal manufacturing spun period.
NAMES.long:
The twist period $L_t$ is the positive arc length along a spun optical fiber over which the effective birefringent axes rotate by one full turn. It characterizes the helical pitch of the optical-axis orientation that helps average linear birefringence in a Fiber Optic Current Sensor, without by itself determining the Faraday responsivity.

For a signed angular twist rate $\tau$, the twist period is defined by the full-turn length:

$$
L_t = \frac{2\pi}{|\tau|}
$$

where $L_t$ is the twist period in m and $\tau = d\alpha/ds$ is the signed rate of change of the effective optical-axis angle $\\alpha$ with fiber arc length $s$, in rad m$^{-1}$. The absolute value makes $L_t$ a non-negative period; handedness is carried by the signed twist rate or by the initial twist phase, not by the period itself.

The twist period may be obtained from a characterized fiber specification or from polarimetric or optical-reflectometry measurements that resolve the rotation of the birefringent axes along the fiber. It is conceptually distinct from the [spun period], which denotes the imposed manufacturing spin modulation period; $L_t$ denotes the effective optical-axis period used in the polarization model. Its influence is interpreted together with the [linear polarization beat length], the [initial twist phase](name:initial_twist_phase_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor), the Verdet constant, and the optical path length.

Values are reported as positive lengths in meters. For birefringence averaging, designs are commonly assessed by comparing $L_t$ with the linear polarization beat length, often seeking a twist period substantially shorter than that beat length; the numerical value is fiber- and fabrication-specific rather than universal.

NAMES.name: verdet_constant_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short: Signed magneto-optic coefficient of the optical fiber in a fiber-optic current sensor. It relates Faraday polarization rotation to the magnetic-field component parallel to the oriented optical path per unit path length.
NAMES.long:
The Verdet constant is the local magneto-optic coefficient of an optical fiber material. It quantifies how strongly the component of magnetic field along the light path rotates the plane of polarization as light propagates, and it depends on fiber material, optical wavelength, temperature, and installation-dependent stress or birefringence effects.

For an oriented fiber path, the Faraday rotation is described by the line integral

$$
\Delta \chi = \int_C V(s)\,\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}(s))\cdot\hat{\mathbf{t}}(s)\,ds
$$

where $\Delta \chi$ is the net polarization rotation in radians, $C$ is the oriented optical path, $s$ is arc length in meters, $\hat{\mathbf{t}}(s)$ is the unit tangent in the positive path direction, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in tesla, and $V(s)$ is the Verdet constant in m^-1.rad.T^-1. For a uniform fiber and field component, $V$ is the rotation per unit path length per unit magnetic-field component parallel to the path.

In a fiber-optic current sensor, the integral is evaluated along the actual optical path, including all winding turns around the conductor or plasma current. Each turn contributes with the sign set by its path orientation. When $V$ is effectively uniform and the fiber forms $N$ closed turns linking the measured current, the line integral may be reduced using Ampere's law to $\Delta \chi \approx V\mu_0 N I$, where $\mu_0$ is the magnetic permeability of free space and $I$ is the linked current; practical systems usually determine an effective calibrated value for the installed fiber, wavelength, and operating conditions.

Typical values for silica-based optical fibers are of order 0.1-10 m^-1.rad.T^-1, with larger or smaller values possible for other glass compositions, wavelengths, and temperatures. The calibrated value for the specific fiber and optical wavelength is normally used for current reconstruction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a magnetic-field component parallel to the positive optical path rotates the optical polarization in the positive sense about the propagation direction, with positive rotation defined by the right-hand rule.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_antenna
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a diagnostic antenna in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates the geometric center of a diagnostic antenna along the machine symmetry axis within the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height, both in meters, with the nominal midplane at $Z = 0$.

This coordinate, together with the corresponding major radius, specifies the spatial position from which electromagnetic wave diagnostics launch or receive signals. Applications include reflectometer emission and detection channels, electron cyclotron emission receivers, and X-ray and UV spectrometer optical components. Beam-tracing and ray-tracing algorithms use the antenna center position as the boundary condition for the launch or detection point of the propagating wave. The analogous geometric reference for related diagnostic hardware is captured by [vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture), [vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element](name:vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element), and [vertical_coordinate_of_antenna_strap](name:vertical_coordinate_of_antenna_strap).

Values span the full height range of the machine port system; in medium-sized tokamaks this is approximately $-2$ to $+2$ m depending on port access geometry and the plasma region targeted by the diagnostic.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the antenna center is located above the device midplane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field_at_wall
NAMES.short: Signed, local Z-directed part of the magnetic field at a specified vacuum-vessel wall position, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame where Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Vertical magnetic field at the wall is the signed local component of the magnetic-field vector along the vertical basis direction at a specified point on the vacuum-vessel wall. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters.

The defining projection is

$$
B_Z(R, \phi, Z) = \mathbf{B}(R, \phi, Z) \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector and $B_Z$ is its vertical component, both expressed in tesla; $\hat{Z}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing vertical height.

In practice, this local scalar may be obtained from wall magnetic diagnostics, magnetic-field reconstruction, or electromagnetic modeling at the specified wall position. The position is interpreted geometrically in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and may be related to coordinates such as the [vertical coordinate of measurement position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position). This quantity itself does not define a closed contour, a path integral, or an enclosed-current sign convention.

The value can be positive, negative, or zero because it is a component of the total field rather than a magnitude. Its scale is strongly device-, discharge-, and location-dependent, reflecting the local superposition of plasma current, external coils, induced currents, and non-axisymmetric perturbations; no universal numerical wall-field range is intrinsic to the quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ points in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector along the vertical Z-direction, equal to k_Z divided by the total wave-vector magnitude, evaluated pointwise along a beam-tracing ray path.
NAMES.long:
The normalized vertical wave vector component is the direction cosine of the local electromagnetic wave propagation direction projected onto the vertical $Z$-axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, computed pointwise along a beam-tracing or ray-tracing path. It encodes the fraction of the propagation direction aligned with the vertical direction at each position along the ray.

The defining relation is:

$$
k_{Z,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{k_Z}{|\mathbf{k}|}
$$

where $k_Z$ is the [vertical wave vector component](name:vertical_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the total wave-vector magnitude. Together with [radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and [toroidal_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:toroidal_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), it fully specifies the unit propagation direction in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, satisfying $k_{R,\mathrm{norm}}^2 + k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}}^2 + k_{Z,\mathrm{norm}}^2 = 1$.

This quantity is computed during beam-tracing or ray-tracing simulations for RF wave propagation and ECE diagnostics, where the Hamiltonian ray equations simultaneously advance the spatial position and wave vector along the ray. The normalized form characterizes the instantaneous propagation direction independently of the local wave number magnitude.

As a direction cosine, values are bounded to $[-1, 1]$. Values near zero indicate nearly horizontal propagation, while values near $\pm 1$ correspond to strongly oblique launch geometries or wave turning near a vertical reflection layer.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $k_Z$ points in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: The Z-direction component of the wave vector along the beam tracing ray path, quantifying the spatial frequency of the electromagnetic wave in the vertical direction at each point of propagation.
NAMES.long:
The vertical wave vector component $k_Z$ is the projection of the wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ onto the vertical axis $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Together with the radial and toroidal components, it fully specifies the local propagation direction of an electromagnetic wave at each point along a beam tracing trajectory.

The component is defined as:

$$
k_Z = \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector and $|\mathbf{k}| = 2\pi n / \lambda_0$, with $n$ the local refractive index and $\lambda_0$ the free-space wavelength. During beam tracing, $k_Z$ evolves according to the ray equation $dk_Z/ds = -\partial D/\partial Z$, where $D(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{k})$ is the plasma dispersion relation and $s$ is the arc length along the ray.

Beam tracing is applied in electron cyclotron heating and current drive analysis and in electron cyclotron emission diagnostics. All three cylindrical wave vector components are propagated together to track refraction and mode conversion through the inhomogeneous magnetized plasma.

For electron cyclotron waves at frequencies of 100–170 GHz, $|k_Z|$ typically ranges from zero to order $10^3$ m$^{-1}$, varying continuously as the ray refracts. The direction cosine form is given by the [vertical normalized wave vector](name:vertical_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) ($k_Z / |\mathbf{k}|$). The complementary cylindrical components are the [radial wave vector](name:radial_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and the [toroidal wave vector](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $k_Z$ points in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_diagnostic_antenna
NAMES.short: Raw voltage reported by an electron-cyclotron-emission diagnostic antenna channel before calibration to radiation temperature. It is measured relative to an electronics reference and can include receiver gain, detector response, baseline offset, and readout polarity, so it is not by itself a strictly proportional measure of received power.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a diagnostic antenna is the uncalibrated electrical readout of an electron-cyclotron-emission radiometer channel associated with a receiving antenna band. It is the voltage after the receiver, detector, and readout electronics, measured relative to an electronics reference, before conversion to a calibrated radiation temperature.

The channel affine calibration to [radiative_temperature](name:radiative_temperature) is written as:

$$
T_{\mathrm{rad}} = a_V\,(V - V_{\mathrm{ref}}) + T_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V$ is the raw channel voltage in volts, $V_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the electronics reference or baseline voltage in volts, $a_V$ is the channel calibration coefficient in temperature units per volt, and $T_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is an additive temperature offset in the same unit as $T_{\mathrm{rad}}$.

In a heterodyne radiometer, this quantity denotes the detected video-bandwidth voltage formed after microwave mixing, intermediate-frequency filtering, and detection; in a direct-detection radiometer, it denotes the detector video voltage. It is not the microwave electric-field waveform at the antenna terminals. Interpreting the calibrated signal as a local electron temperature also requires the calibrated [frequency_of_diagnostic_antenna](name:frequency_of_diagnostic_antenna), the relevant cyclotron harmonic and polarization, viewing geometry, magnetic-field information along the line of sight, and an assessment that the emission is sufficiently optically thick.

Typical magnitudes for detected ECE video outputs are instrument dependent and are often about 0.001-1 V during normal operation. Offsets, receiver gain, detector type, bandwidth, and digitizer scaling can shift the recorded baseline or full-scale value outside this range, so the calibrated temperature relation carries the physical interpretation rather than the raw voltage alone.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the channel readout, with its assigned electronics polarity, is above the electronics reference level.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: Calibrated peak amplitude of the narrow-band microwave voltage at a reflectometer antenna terminal or electrical reference plane. It is a generic terminal quantity, not necessarily the isolated plasma-reflected component.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a reflectometer antenna is the calibrated peak amplitude of the narrow-band microwave voltage at the antenna terminal or another specified electrical reference plane. As a generic terminal quantity it can include launched-wave leakage, plasma-reflected or scattered signal, antenna coupling, standing-wave effects, and receiver response unless the reflected component has been separated explicitly. This distinguishes it from [reflected_voltage_of_reflectometer_antenna](name:reflected_voltage_of_reflectometer_antenna) and reflected_wave_voltage_of_reflectometer_antenna_amplitude, which refer specifically to reflected-wave quantities.

For a narrow-band signal represented by a complex voltage phasor, the antenna voltage is the phasor peak magnitude:

$$
v(t) = \Re\{\tilde V(t)\,e^{-i\omega_0 t}\}, \qquad V_\mathrm{ant}(t) = |\tilde V(t)|
$$

where $v(t)$ is the real microwave voltage waveform, $\tilde V(t)$ is the slowly varying complex voltage phasor at the reference plane, $\omega_0$ is the carrier angular frequency, and $V_\mathrm{ant}$ is the reported voltage amplitude. For a pure sinusoid, the corresponding RMS value would be $V_\mathrm{ant}/\sqrt{2}$; the quantity defined here follows the peak-amplitude convention used for RF voltage amplitude.

In practice the voltage is obtained from a homodyne or heterodyne reflectometer receiver by down-converting the microwave carrier, calibrating gain and attenuation, and forming the amplitude from the in-phase and quadrature components, commonly as $|\tilde V|=\sqrt{I^2+Q^2}$ after calibration. Interpreting this voltage as a plasma-reflected signal requires additional separation or normalization, such as directional coupling, background subtraction, reference measurements, or complex reflection-coefficient calibration. By itself it is not a cutoff position, density measurement, or reflection coefficient.

Typical calibrated amplitudes are strongly receiver dependent. Usable processed signal levels are often about $10^{-4}$-$1$ V at an electrical reference plane, while antenna-plane values can differ substantially because of cable loss, coupling, attenuation, and receiver gain.

NAMES.name: wave_phase_of_wave_beam
NAMES.short: Angular phase of the complex envelope of a probing wave beam at a specified point along its propagation path. Its absolute zero is set by a chosen phase reference; only phase differences, such as a launch-referenced phase shift, are directly observable.
NAMES.long:
Wave phase of a wave beam is the angular argument of the beam's complex signal envelope. It is an angular quantity modulo one full cycle, with an arbitrary zero set by the chosen phase reference, and should be distinguished from a launch-referenced phase difference or from an unwrapped continuous phase trace.

The eikonal accumulation of beam phase along a ray or beam centerline can be represented by:

$$
\phi_\mathrm{beam}(s)=\phi_\mathrm{ref}+\int_{s_\mathrm{ref}}^{s} k_s(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\phi_\mathrm{beam}$ and $\phi_\mathrm{ref}$ are phases in rad, $s$ and $\ell$ are path lengths in m, and $k_s$ is the component of the local wave vector along the propagation path in rad m$^{-1}$. Equivalently, $k_s$ may be written as $k_0 n_\mathrm{eff}$, where $k_0$ is the vacuum wave number in rad m$^{-1}$ and $n_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective refractive index along the beam path.

In interferometry and refractometry, receivers generally determine a phase relative to a launch signal or local oscillator rather than an absolute phase with a universal zero. When the reference is the launched wave phase, the observable is the launch-referenced phase difference $\Delta\phi_\mathrm{launch}=\phi_\mathrm{beam}-\phi_\mathrm{launch}$, represented by [difference_of_wave_phase_and_launched_wave_phase_of_wave_beam](name:wave_phase_of_wave_beam). Measured phases are often wrapped modulo $2\pi$; an unwrapped or fringe-jump-corrected phase is a continuous branch obtained by adding integer multiples of $2\pi$ rad and is a representation of the same angular phase evolution.

Typical reported wrapped phases lie within a chosen $2\pi$ rad interval, commonly $-\pi$ to $\pi$ rad or $0$ to $2\pi$ rad. Unwrapped accumulated phase has no universal range: useful excursions can be fractions of a radian for weak perturbations or many $2\pi$ rad cycles for long paths, high frequency, or strongly refracting plasmas. Conversion from phase to line-integrated plasma properties requires the wave frequency, polarization, propagation path, and refractive-index model.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the complex envelope, written as $A=|A|\exp(i\phi)$, is rotated counterclockwise from the chosen phase reference in the complex plane.

NAMES.name: width_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: Full aperture width of a reflectometer antenna along one transverse dimension of the local orthogonal (X1, X2) antenna frame, applicable when the aperture is described by a rectangular geometry.
NAMES.long:
The width characterizes the physical extent of a reflectometer antenna aperture along one of the two transverse axes of the local orthogonal (X1, X2) frame used to describe the antenna geometry. It applies to both emission and detection antennas in reflectometry diagnostics and is defined when the aperture shape is rectangular; a companion dimension specifies the orthogonal transverse extent.

For a rectangular aperture, the width $d$ along each transverse axis governs the far-field beam divergence, with the diffraction half-angle scaling as $\theta \approx \lambda / d$, where $\lambda$ is the probing wavelength. Larger apertures produce more collimated beams and sharper spatial localization of the reflection layer along the probing path. The aperture geometry is complemented by the outline vertex coordinates [x1_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna](name:x1_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna) and [x2_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna](name:x2_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna), which define the full aperture shape. The analogous quantity for optical focusing elements is [optical_element_width](name:optical_element_width).

This is a fixed hardware parameter set by the physical waveguide or horn antenna dimensions at the diagnostic port. It is used in beam characterization models to compute antenna radiation patterns and to assess spatial resolution for density profile or fluctuation measurements. Typical aperture widths for fusion microwave reflectometer antennas range from about 1–20 cm, depending on the probing frequency band (typically 15–150 GHz) and the waveguide standard employed.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physically realizable apertures; the width is a non-negative spatial extent that does not depend on the orientation of the ambient coordinate system.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: Positions of the reflectometer antenna aperture outline vertices along the X1 axis of the local (X1, X2) orthogonal coordinate frame.
NAMES.long:
The X1 coordinate positions define the vertices of the aperture polygon of a reflectometer antenna projected onto the first axis of the local orthogonal (X1, X2) frame attached to the antenna element. Together with [x2_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna](name:x2_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna), the X1 coordinates fully characterize the two-dimensional cross-sectional shape of the emission or detection aperture for both profile and fluctuation reflectometer channels.

Reflectometers probe plasma electron density by transmitting microwaves that reflect from density cutoff layers; the detailed aperture outline described by the X1 vertex positions determines the launched beam pattern and influences diffraction modeling in wave propagation calculations. The [width_of_reflectometer_antenna](name:width_of_reflectometer_antenna) provides a scalar summary of the aperture extent derived from the full polygon geometry.

The outline is specified as an ordered polygon in the (X1, X2) plane, with the number of vertices chosen to represent non-rectangular aperture shapes. Typical aperture dimensions for fusion-relevant reflectometer antennas span a few centimeters to several tens of centimeters, depending on operating frequency and the required beam directivity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex position lies in the positive X1 direction from the local frame origin.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: X2-axis coordinate of a reflectometer antenna aperture-outline vertex in the local aperture frame, paired with the corresponding X1 coordinate to locate a point on the emitting or receiving aperture boundary.
NAMES.long:
The X2 coordinate of a reflectometer antenna is the signed in-plane offset of an aperture-outline vertex along the second transverse axis of the local antenna aperture frame. The local frame is the right-handed frame $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2, \hat{n})$, where $\hat{X}_1$ and $\hat{X}_2$ span the aperture plane and $\hat{n}$ is the aperture normal.

For an outline vertex indexed by $j$, the physical point on the aperture boundary is represented by

$$
\mathbf{r}_j = \mathbf{r}_0 + X_{1,j}\hat{X}_1 + X_{2,j}\hat{X}_2
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the antenna aperture reference point, $X_{1,j}$ is the paired coordinate along $\hat{X}_1$, and $X_{2,j}$ is this coordinate along $\hat{X}_2$, all expressed in meters. The ordered vertices $(X_{1,j}, X_{2,j})$ trace the aperture boundary; neighboring vertices define boundary segments, and the last vertex connects back to the first unless the closing vertex is repeated explicitly.

In practice, this coordinate is obtained from the antenna mechanical definition, design model, survey, or metrology of the emitting or receiving aperture. It is used with the paired X1 coordinate to define irregular horn, waveguide, or quasi-optical aperture outlines for reflectometry beam and coupling calculations.

Typical absolute values are set by the physical aperture size: millimeter-scale values for small waveguide openings, about 0.01-0.1 m for many horn or quasi-optical apertures, and occasionally up to a few tenths of a meter for large launch or collection optics.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture vertex is displaced from the local antenna-frame origin in the $+\hat{X}_2$ direction.

NAMES.name: electron_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by the electron population from a single coherent beam-tracing beam, representing the electron contribution to total path-integrated wave energy deposition.
NAMES.long:
The electron absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam is the total wave power transferred from a single traced coherent electromagnetic beam to the electron population over its computed propagation path. It represents the electron contribution to wave energy deposition and sums with the ion species contributions — ion_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam and [ion_state_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:ion_state_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) — to give the species-summed [absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam).

The path-integrated electron absorbed power is determined by the local electron damping coefficient $\alpha_e(s)$ and the evolving beam power $P(s)$:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{abs}} = \int_{\mathrm{path}} 2\,\alpha_e(s)\,P(s)\,ds
$$

where $s$ is the arc length along the ray and $\alpha_e$ derives from the electron contribution to the anti-Hermitian part of the plasma dielectric tensor. For electron cyclotron resonance heating and ECE diagnostics, $\alpha_e$ peaks near the resonance layer where the wave frequency satisfies $\omega = n\,\Omega_{ce}$, with $\Omega_{ce} = eB/m_e$ the local electron cyclotron frequency and $n$ a harmonic integer.

This quantity is computed by beam-tracing solvers that propagate ray equations through a plasma equilibrium and evaluate the electron dielectric response at each point along the path.
