The ratio $P_{e,\mathrm{abs}} / P_0$ — where $P_0$ is the [initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) — characterizes single-pass absorption efficiency, which approaches unity in strongly absorbing scenarios such as fundamental or second-harmonic electron cyclotron resonance heating.

NAMES.name: initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Electromagnetic wave power assigned to a beam-tracing beam at its launch point. It sets the reference power from which electron and ion absorption losses are evaluated along the beam propagation path.
NAMES.long:
Initial power of a beam-tracing beam is the electromagnetic wave power carried by the beam at the start of the propagation calculation, before attenuation by plasma absorption. It is a normalization reference for the remaining beam power and for absorbed-power channels, including electron absorption and ion absorption by species or charge state.

For single-pass attenuation along the beam path, the remaining beam power is commonly modeled as

$$
P(s) = P_0 \exp\left[-\int_0^s \alpha_\mathrm{tot}(s')\,ds'\right]
$$

where $P_0$ is the initial beam power in W, $P(s)$ is the beam power in W after distance $s$, $s$ is path length in m measured from the launch point along the direction of propagation, and $\alpha_\mathrm{tot}$ is the total absorption coefficient in m^-1. Equivalently, with $s$ increasing along propagation, positive absorption gives $dP/ds = -\alpha_\mathrm{tot}P$; the total absorbed fraction is obtained from all absorption channels together, not from the electron channel alone unless ion absorption is negligible.

In practice, this quantity may be set by source calibration, receiver/antenna normalization, optical throughput modeling, or a chosen reference value for a linear beam-tracing calculation. Absorbed powers are then computed relative to this initial value and partitioned among electrons, bulk ions, and ion charge-state channels according to the wave-plasma absorption model.

Typical values depend strongly on the application: normalized diagnostic calculations often use 1 W, calibrated passive or probing diagnostics can correspond to much smaller or larger effective powers, and actively launched microwave diagnostic beams may use 1-100000 W.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density averaged along a representative chord through the plasma, equal to the line-integrated electron density divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged electron density $\bar{n}_e$ is the local [electron_density](name:electron_density) $n_e$ integrated along a straight diagnostic chord through the plasma cross-section and divided by the chord length $L$. It condenses the spatially-resolved density profile to a single line-of-sight scalar proportional to the total electron content along the chord, serving as a standard global density measure for confinement scaling and density feedback control.

The defining relation is:

$$
\bar{n}_e = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_e(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $\ell$ is the coordinate along the chord and $L$ is the chord length.

Interferometers — microwave, far-infrared, or visible-laser systems — measure a phase shift $\Delta\phi$ proportional to $\int n_e \, d\ell$; dividing by $L$ and the spectral_calibration_factor_of_interferometer_beam yields $\bar{n}_e$. Multi-wavelength systems combine two or more channels for dispersion-based absolute phase determination.

Typical values span $10^{18}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in ohmic and L-mode discharges, rising to $\sim 10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ near the density limit. The greenwald_fraction normalizes $\bar{n}_e$ by the Greenwald limit to yield a dimensionless confinement-regime indicator. The chord-averaged analog for ion content is [line_averaged_total_ion_density](name:line_averaged_total_ion_density), and [line_averaged_electron_temperature](name:line_averaged_electron_temperature) provides the corresponding temperature scalar.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate evaluated at the magnetic axis. It is the non-negative radial flux-surface label based on toroidal magnetic flux and is exactly zero at the axis because that reference location has no toroidal flux interval relative to itself.
NAMES.long:
The [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) at the magnetic axis is the value of the dimensionless radial flux-surface label on the magnetic-axis reference line of a toroidal equilibrium. It is zero by definition because the magnetic axis is the inner reference for closed flux surfaces, so no finite toroidal-flux interval lies between the axis and itself. In flux coordinates $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$, the poloidal angle $\theta$ is singular at the magnetic axis, but the radial coordinate has the well-defined limiting value $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = 0$.

The normalized coordinate is defined using the non-negative square root of the toroidal-flux fraction between the magnetic-axis and boundary reference values:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi - \Phi_0}{\Phi_b - \Phi_0}}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the toroidal magnetic flux in Wb on the flux surface being labeled, $\Phi_0$ is the magnetic-axis reference value in Wb, and $\Phi_b$ is the boundary reference value in Wb at the last closed flux surface. At the magnetic axis $\Phi = \Phi_0$, so $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = 0$.

This value is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction rather than measured as an independent observable. In diagnostic mapping, it serves as the radial origin and a consistency check for measurement locations assigned close to the plasma center; off-axis locations are described by quantities such as [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position). It is the dimensionless axis counterpart of the dimensional [toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis), while the outer normalization is set by the boundary reference related to [toroidal_flux_radius_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_radius_at_plasma_boundary).

The physical value at the magnetic axis is exactly 0. For closed flux surfaces, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ spans 0-1 from the magnetic axis to the last closed flux surface; diagnostic positions near, but not exactly on, the axis may be assigned small nonzero values because of finite spatial resolution and equilibrium-reconstruction uncertainty.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial flux-surface label based on normalized toroidal magnetic flux, evaluated at the physical position sampled by a diagnostic measurement. It identifies the corresponding nested flux surface, with 0 at the magnetic axis and approximately 1 at the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a measurement position is the dimensionless radial label assigned to the point or localized region sampled by a diagnostic measurement. It is derived from the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by nested magnetic flux surfaces, with the origin at the magnetic axis and the outer normalization reference at the plasma boundary or last closed flux surface.

The coordinate is defined from the toroidal flux difference between the flux surface through the measurement position and the magnetic-axis flux:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_m) = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_m - \Phi_0}{\Phi_b - \Phi_0}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_m$ is the measurement position, $\Phi_m$ is the toroidal magnetic flux in Wb of the flux surface passing through that position, $\Phi_0$ is the magnetic-axis toroidal flux in Wb, and $\Phi_b$ is the boundary toroidal flux in Wb. The square root makes this a nonnegative radial coordinate; for a valid nested-flux-surface mapping the numerator and denominator have the same flux orientation, so the ratio is nonnegative and increases outward from the magnetic axis.

In practice, the value is obtained by combining the diagnostic measurement geometry with an equilibrium reconstruction that maps the sampled position to a flux surface. For measurements with finite spatial extent, the value represents the effective or representative measurement position used in the diagnostic interpretation, rather than a property of the diagnostic signal itself.

Typical values for measurements inside the confined plasma are 0-1, with values near 0 corresponding to the core, 0.2-0.8 to the plasma interior, and 0.8-1 to the edge region near the last closed flux surface. Values greater than 1 can occur for positions mapped outside the last closed flux surface or when an equilibrium mapping is extrapolated beyond the confined region.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Poloidal angle of a diagnostic measurement position in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. The zero direction is outward major radius +R from the magnetic axis, and positive angles increase clockwise when viewed from the +phi direction.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal angle of a measurement position is the angular coordinate of that point about the magnetic axis in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It identifies where around the magnetic axis a diagnostic samples, separate from any radial coordinate or absolute position coordinates.

For a measurement position $(R_\mathrm{m},Z_\mathrm{m})$ and magnetic-axis position $(R_\mathrm{ax},Z_\mathrm{ax})$ in that cross-section, the clockwise-positive angle from the outward radial direction can be written as:

$$
\theta \equiv \operatorname{atan2}(Z_\mathrm{ax}-Z_\mathrm{m},\, R_\mathrm{m}-R_\mathrm{ax}) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{m}$ and $Z_\mathrm{m}$ are the measurement-position major radius and vertical height in meters, $R_\mathrm{ax}$ and $Z_\mathrm{ax}$ are the magnetic-axis major radius and vertical height in meters, and $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ returns a quadrant-resolved angle in radians. Values that differ by $2\pi n$ with integer $n$ represent the same physical direction; the branch, such as $(-\pi,\pi]$ or $[0,2\pi)$, is a representation choice rather than part of the physical definition.

In practice this angle is computed from the reconstructed measurement position and magnetic-axis location, or from an equivalent ray, beam, or scattering-point geometry for electromagnetic-wave diagnostics. It is commonly used together with measurement-position major radius, vertical height, or a radial flux coordinate to describe the diagnostic sampling location without implying a unique spatial position by the angle alone.

A full poloidal coverage spans any interval of length $2\pi$ rad. With the convention above, outboard-midplane positions have $\theta$ near 0 rad, lower positions have $\theta$ near $+1.57$ rad, upper positions have $\theta$ near $-1.57$ rad, and inboard-midplane positions lie near $\pm 3.14$ rad depending on the chosen branch.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the angular displacement from the outward radial $+R$ direction toward the measurement position is clockwise in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame when viewed from the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction.

NAMES.name: radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Radiative temperature at the magnetic axis is the blackbody-equivalent brightness temperature of electron cyclotron emission from the resonance layer closest to the magnetic axis. In optically thick thermal emission, it is a central electron-temperature proxy reported as an energy-equivalent temperature in electronvolts.
NAMES.long:
Radiative temperature at the magnetic axis is the blackbody-equivalent brightness temperature assigned to the electron cyclotron emission resonance layer nearest the magnetic axis. It is a property of the radiation field rather than necessarily a thermodynamic temperature, but in optically thick thermal conditions it approaches the local [electron_temperature](name:electron_temperature) and is closely related to [temperature_at_magnetic_axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis).

In the Rayleigh-Jeans limit relevant to microwave electron cyclotron emission, the energy-equivalent radiation temperature is defined from spectral radiance by:

$$
T_\mathrm{rad} = \frac{c^2 I_f}{2 f^2 e}
$$

where $I_f$ is the spectral radiance per unit frequency and solid angle at frequency $f$, $c$ is the speed of light, and $e$ is the elementary charge. The value is expressed in electronvolts; equivalently, $e T_\mathrm{rad}=k_B T_K$, where $T_K$ is the brightness temperature in kelvin and $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant.

In practice, this quantity is obtained from calibrated electron cyclotron emission radiometry by mapping each observing frequency and polarization to a cyclotron resonance layer using the magnetic field and equilibrium, then selecting the channel whose layer is closest to the magnetic axis. The second-harmonic extraordinary mode is often optically thick in the core of tokamak plasmas and therefore gives the most direct central electron-temperature estimate; ordinary-mode channels may also be used, with greater sensitivity to optical depth and polarization purity.

Important uncertainties come from absolute radiometric calibration, receiver bandwidth, resonance-position mapping, relativistic and Doppler broadening, refraction, wall reflections, and possible nonthermal electron emission. When the optical depth is not large, $T_\mathrm{rad}$ is an emissivity- and absorption-weighted brightness temperature rather than the local electron temperature, so it can differ substantially from the true central electron thermal energy.

Typical central values are 500-3000 eV in ohmic or low-confinement tokamak plasmas and 2000-20000 eV in high-performance H-mode plasmas, with larger or burning-plasma scenarios potentially exceeding 20000 eV.

NAMES.name: wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex vector phasor of the electric field of an electromagnetic wave propagating in a magnetized plasma. It encodes the local field amplitude, phase, and polarization state from which the real time-dependent electric field is recovered.
NAMES.long:
The wave electric field $\mathbf{E}_w$ is the complex vector phasor representing the electric oscillation of an electromagnetic wave in a magnetized plasma. It contains the relative amplitudes and phases of the vector components, so it determines whether the wave is linearly, elliptically, or circularly polarized and how much field is parallel or perpendicular to the background magnetic field.

Using the negative-time-harmonic phasor convention, in which the physical field is obtained by multiplying the phasor by $\exp(-i\omega t)$ and taking the real part, a homogeneous cold-plasma normal mode satisfies:

$$
\left[n^2\left(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\hat{\mathbf{k}}-\mathbf{I}\right)+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}(\omega,\mathbf{B}_0)\right]\cdot\mathbf{E}_w=\mathbf{0}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}_w$ has units V m^-1, $n=c|\mathbf{k}|/\omega$ is the dimensionless [refractive index](name:refractive_index), $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum in m s^-1, $\mathbf{k}=|\mathbf{k}|\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ is the wave vector in m^-1, $\omega$ is the angular frequency in rad s^-1, $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity tensor, $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ is the dimensionless plasma dielectric tensor, and $\mathbf{B}_0$ is the background magnetic field in T. Nonzero solutions determine the allowed dispersion and polarization.

Components of $\mathbf{E}_w$ must be interpreted with the basis used for the vector. In a right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis the components are projections on $\hat{x}$, $\hat{y}$, and $\hat{z}$; in a right-handed field-aligned $(\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \hat{b}_0)$ basis, where $\hat{b}_0=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ and $\hat{e}_1\times\hat{e}_2=\hat{b}_0$, the parallel projection gives the complex quantity whose parts are represented by [parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part) and [parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part). The transverse projections may be combined as $E_\pm=(\mathbf{E}_w\cdot\hat{e}_1\pm i\mathbf{E}_w\cdot\hat{e}_2)/\sqrt{2}$; these circular components are related to [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude) and [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field).

Wave electric fields are usually computed from antenna launching models, cold- or hot-plasma full-wave calculations, ray tracing with polarization evolution, or local dispersion calculations normalized to launched power. Measurements infer them indirectly from calibrated edge probes, microwave polarimetry, reflectometry, scattering, or absorbed-power and current-drive constraints; phase and polarization are often determined more robustly than absolute local amplitude.

Typical phasor magnitudes are strongly power-normalization dependent. Weak probing waves can be 10^-1-10^2 V m^-1, while RF and microwave heating or current-drive fields are often 10^3-10^5 V m^-1 for local power fluxes of about 0.01-10 MW m^-2; evanescent layers, resonances, and near-antenna regions can fall outside these ranges.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a real component of $\mathbf{E}_w$ points along the corresponding positive basis vector, such as $+\hat{x}$, $+\hat{y}$, or $+\hat{z}$ in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis.

NAMES.name: left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex phasor of the left-hand circularly polarized component of the wave electric field along a beam-tracing path. It is the E+ projection in the local transverse basis (x, y, b), with x cross y in the b direction and b parallel to the local background magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field, $E_+$, is the complex phasor obtained by projecting the transverse wave electric-field vector onto the circular polarization that follows positive-ion gyration about the local background magnetic field. It represents the rotating electric-field component relevant for ion-cyclotron resonant coupling, while actual damping and species heating also depend on resonance location, wave frequency, composition, and the plasma dielectric response.

In the local orthonormal triad $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{b})$ with $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$, $\hat{x}\perp\hat{b}$, $\hat{y}\perp\hat{b}$, and $\hat{x}\times\hat{y}=\hat{b}$, the phasor is defined by

$$
E_+ = \frac{E_x + iE_y}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

where $E_x$ and $E_y$ are the complex phasor components of the transverse wave electric field along $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$, $i$ is the imaginary unit, and $E_+$, $E_x$, and $E_y$ have unit $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. The physical time-dependent field is recovered with the convention $\operatorname{Re}[(E_x\hat{x}+E_y\hat{y})\exp(-i\omega t)]$, where $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency. With the complementary right-hand component $E_-=(E_x-iE_y)/\sqrt{2}$, the transverse phasor is reconstructed as $E_x=(E_+ + E_-)/\sqrt{2}$ and $E_y=-i(E_+ - E_-)/\sqrt{2}$; the real and imaginary quadratures are [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part) and [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), and the envelope is [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude).

Along a beam-tracing ray, $E_+$ is computed by solving the wave propagation equations using the cold- or warm-plasma dielectric response, expressing the resulting [wave_electric_field](name:wave_electric_field) in the local basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{b})$, and applying the circular-polarization projection. It is usually a derived complex quantity rather than a directly measured observable; boundary conditions may come from antenna, launcher, or polarization-sensitive diagnostic information.

Typical magnitudes depend strongly on launched power, focusing, absorption, and normalization, but values of about $10^1$-$10^5\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ are common in radio-frequency wave-heating calculations. The ratio $|E_+|/|E_-|$ and the relative phase between the two circular components characterize the polarization ellipticity and influence resonant absorption, but they do not by themselves determine preferential ion-species heating.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the real amplitude of a purely left-hand, zero-phase phasor makes the physical electric field point along $+\hat{x}$ at $t=0$ and rotate from $+\hat{x}$ toward $-\hat{y}$ about $+\hat{b}$ in the local orthonormal basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{b})$ with $\hat{x}\times\hat{y}=\hat{b}$.

NAMES.name: left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the E+ left-hand circular wave electric-field projection onto the polarization basis perpendicular to the local magnetic field along a beam-tracing ray path. It is a signed phasor component; together with the E- and parallel components it determines local wave polarization and coupling, not the field modulus.
NAMES.long:
The left-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field real part is the in-phase component of the complex scalar coefficient $E_+$ obtained by projecting the wave electric-field phasor onto the normalized left-hand circular basis perpendicular to the local background magnetic field. It describes phase and polarization state, so it can be positive, negative, or zero and should not be confused with the non-negative modulus $|E_+|$.

Let $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ be the local magnetic-field direction and choose an orthonormal transverse triad $(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2,\hat{\mathbf{b}})$ with $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1\times\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2=\hat{\mathbf{b}}$. With the phasor convention $\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r},t)=\operatorname{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}(\mathbf{r})\exp(-i\omega t)]$ and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_+=(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1+i\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2)/\sqrt{2}$, this quantity is defined by

$$
E_{+,\mathrm{re}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\hat{\mathbf{e}}_+^{\,*}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\right]
$$

where $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}$ is the complex electric-field phasor, the star denotes complex conjugation in the Hermitian projection, and $E_{+,\mathrm{re}}$ has the electric-field unit $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. The companion coefficient $E_-$ uses $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_-=(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1-i\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2)/\sqrt{2}$ for the opposite circular polarization.

In beam-tracing and ray-tracing calculations, the local wave polarization is propagated along the ray and then decomposed into left-hand circular, right-hand circular, and parallel components with respect to $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$. The complete local phasor in this basis is reconstructed as $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}=E_+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_+ + E_-\hat{\mathbf{e}}_- + E_\parallel\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, using the real and imaginary parts of $E_+$, $E_-$, and $E_\parallel$; relevant sibling quantities include [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part), and [parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part).

Absolute numerical values are normalization-dependent because a phasor may be scaled to launched power, unit power, or a local eigenvector normalization. In a fixed SI normalization, $E_{+,\mathrm{re}}$ lies between $-|E_+|$ and $+|E_+|$ in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$; values near zero indicate either weak left-hand circular content or a quadrature phase relative to the chosen phasor reference, while values comparable to $|E_+|$ indicate an almost purely in-phase left-hand component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference-phase left-hand circularly polarized phasor corresponds, for $E_-=E_\parallel=0$, to an electric field pointing along $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ while subsequently rotating toward $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ about $+\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ under the $\exp(-i\omega t)$ time dependence.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex scalar phasor of the oscillatory (time-harmonic) wave electric field projected onto the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. Its modulus gives the magnitude of the parallel component and its argument gives the phase relative to the chosen time convention.
NAMES.long:
The parallel wave electric field is the component of a time-harmonic wave electric-field phasor resolved along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. As a complex scalar it carries both the magnitude and the phase of the parallel oscillation: its modulus is the parallel phasor magnitude and its argument is the phase relative to a fixed time-harmonic reference.

The projection is defined by

$$
E_{\parallel} = \hat{b} \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{E}}
$$

where $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}$ is the complex wave electric-field phasor in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$. The complex phasor is reconstructed from its in-phase and quadrature parts as $E_{\parallel} = \mathrm{Re}[E_{\parallel}] + i\,\mathrm{Im}[E_{\parallel}]$, held respectively by [parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part) and [parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part). If the physical field is written as $\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\exp(-i\omega t)]$, the real and imaginary parts are the in-phase and quadrature amplitudes; adopting the opposite time convention complex-conjugates the phasor describing the same physical field.

In practice $E_{\parallel}$ is obtained by projecting a measured, reconstructed, or beam/ray-traced complex wave electric field onto the local magnetic-field direction. It vanishes only where the electric-field phasor is exactly orthogonal to $\hat{b}$; a wave vector perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}_0$ does not by itself force $E_{\parallel}=0$, because the wave polarization can still retain a field component along the magnetic field.

Magnitudes span a very wide range that depends strongly on wave frequency, launched power, coupling efficiency, and plasma location: weak diagnostic or probing fields are small, while radio-frequency heating and current-drive fields can be locally much larger. Quantitative values should be taken from the specific scenario rather than assumed.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the in-phase component of the wave electric-field phasor points along the local equilibrium magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary quadrature coefficient of the complex wave electric field projected along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction for a beam or ray path. It is the quadrature counterpart of parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part and, with that real part, determines the complex parallel field amplitude and phase; it is not the field magnitude.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the parallel wave electric field is the quadrature coefficient of a monochromatic complex electric-field phasor after projection onto the direction of the local equilibrium magnetic field. It is one scalar component of the complex parallel polarization; together with the [parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part) it determines the phase and the [parallel_wave_electric_field_amplitude](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_amplitude), but it is not itself the magnitude.

Using a phasor convention with time dependence $\exp(-i\omega t)$, the complex parallel electric field is decomposed as

$$
\tilde{E}_\parallel = \tilde{\mathbf{E}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}} = E_{\parallel,\mathrm{r}} + i E_{\parallel,\mathrm{i}}, \qquad \mathbf{E}(t)=\operatorname{Re}\!\left[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}e^{-i\omega t}\right]
$$

where $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}$ is the complex wave electric-field phasor, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$, $\omega$ is the angular frequency, $i$ is the imaginary unit, $E_{\parallel,\mathrm{r}}$ is the real parallel coefficient, and $E_{\parallel,\mathrm{i}}$ is this quantity. Both scalar coefficients have units of V m$^{-1}$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from wave-propagation, beam-tracing, ray-tracing, or full-wave polarization calculations by projecting the computed complex electric-field phasor onto $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ along the propagation trajectory. It is used with the real parallel coefficient to reconstruct the complex longitudinal polarization; analogous transverse quadrature coefficients include the [left-hand](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part) and [right-hand](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part) circularly polarized wave electric-field imaginary parts, whose corresponding real parts are also required to reconstruct the full complex circular-basis polarization.

There is no universal numerical range independent of wave normalization, launch power, propagation model, and absorption. For a specified parallel amplitude $A_\parallel$, the physically allowed range is $-A_\parallel$ to $+A_\parallel$ in V m$^{-1}$; values are near zero when the chosen phasor phase makes the parallel component nearly real, and the parallel component is often small for nearly transverse electromagnetic propagation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\operatorname{Im}(\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})>0$ for $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ directed along the local equilibrium magnetic field and the phasor time dependence $\mathbf{E}(t)=\operatorname{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}e^{-i\omega t}]$.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Real, in-phase coefficient of the complex wave electric-field phasor projected along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. Together with the imaginary part, it specifies the signed parallel polarization relevant to resonant wave-particle interactions.
NAMES.long:
The real part of the parallel wave electric field is the in-phase scalar component of a complex wave electric-field phasor along the local equilibrium magnetic field. It is one quadrature of the complex parallel field; the complementary quadrature is [parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part).

The scalar phasor component is defined by projecting the complex wave electric-field phasor onto the unit vector along the equilibrium magnetic field:

$$
E_{\parallel,r} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\mathbf{E}_w \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}\right),\qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}} = \frac{\mathbf{B}_0}{|\mathbf{B}_0|}
$$

where $E_{\parallel,r}$ is this quantity, $\mathbf{E}_w$ is the complex wave electric-field phasor, $\mathbf{B}_0$ is the equilibrium magnetic field, and all electric-field quantities are measured in V m$^{-1}$. The full complex scalar is $E_\parallel = E_{\parallel,r} + iE_{\parallel,i}$, where $E_{\parallel,i}$ is the companion imaginary part. The associated real time-domain field is interpreted as $\operatorname{Re}\{E_\parallel e^{-i\omega t}\}$, so $E_{\parallel,r}$ is the component in phase with the selected phasor reference.

This quantity is computed in wave, ray, or beam-tracing calculations from the local complex polarization state and the equilibrium magnetic-field direction. It is physically important because parallel electric fields couple directly to charged-particle motion along magnetic field lines, contributing to resonant energy exchange such as Landau damping and current drive; it should therefore be interpreted together with the companion imaginary part and with transverse polarization components such as [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part) and [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part).

Typical magnitudes are normalization-dependent because the absolute phasor scale is set by the chosen wave-power or field-amplitude normalization. Relative to the local total wave-field amplitude $|\mathbf{E}_w|$, the signed real part is bounded between $-|\mathbf{E}_w|$ and $+|\mathbf{E}_w|$; it is often small for predominantly transverse electromagnetic polarization and can become comparable to $|\mathbf{E}_w|$ for waves with strong longitudinal or electrostatic character. For a reference normalization $|\mathbf{E}_w|=1$ V m$^{-1}$, the corresponding signed range is from $-1$ to $+1$ V m$^{-1}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the in-phase vector component represented by $E_{\parallel,r}$ points along $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ rather than opposite to the equilibrium magnetic-field direction, with the phasor decomposition $E_\parallel=E_{\parallel,r}+iE_{\parallel,i}$.

NAMES.name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex phasor of the right-hand circularly polarized (E-minus) component of the wave electric field, projected onto the circular polarization basis constructed from the transverse plane perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the E-minus component of the transverse wave electric field in a magnetized plasma, obtained by projecting the full [wave electric field](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field) phasor onto the right-hand circular polarization basis. In the local orthonormal frame $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{b})$, where $\hat{b}$ is the unit vector along the equilibrium magnetic field and $\hat{x} \times \hat{y} = \hat{b}$, the component is defined as

$$
E_- = E_x - i E_y
$$

where $E_x$ and $E_y$ are the complex transverse Cartesian components of the wave electric field phasor.

The full complex phasor encodes both amplitude and phase. Its real and imaginary quadrature components are individually given by [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part) and [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), while the nonnegative modulus $|E_-|$ is provided by [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude). The complementary left-hand circular component (E+) is documented under [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field). In ion-cyclotron-range-of-frequencies heating, the relative magnitude of $E_-$ characterizes the right-hand polarization fraction of the wave and governs coupling to electron-cyclotron and right-hand-cutoff resonances along the wave propagation path.

NAMES.name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the right-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field phasor. It is the quadrature component of the E-minus polarization and, together with the real part, determines the amplitude and phase of that complex field component.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the quadrature coefficient of the complex scalar phasor for the E-minus polarization component. This component describes the part of the transverse wave electric field that has right-hand circular polarization about the local background magnetic-field direction $\hat{b}$. It is meaningful only together with the corresponding [real part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part), because the two components jointly specify the complex phase.

The right-hand circular component is defined by projecting the complex wave electric-field phasor onto the right-hand circular polarization basis:

$$
E_-(s) = \mathbf{e}_-^*(s) \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{E}}(s) = E_{-,r}(s) + i\,E_{-,i}(s)
$$

where $s$ is distance along the ray or beam path, $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}$ is the complex wave electric-field phasor, $\mathbf{e}_-$ is the right-hand circular polarization unit vector about $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$, the superscript $*$ denotes complex conjugation, $E_{-,r}$ is the real part, $E_{-,i}$ is this imaginary part, and $i$ is the imaginary unit. The phasor is interpreted with the harmonic time dependence $\operatorname{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\exp(-i\omega t)]$; no particular spatial phase factor along the ray is required by this definition. The electric-field unit is volts per meter, equivalently $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ or $\mathrm{m^{-1}\,V}$.

In electromagnetic wave and beam-tracing calculations, the full wave field is commonly decomposed into right-hand circular, left-hand circular, and field-aligned polarization components relative to $\hat{b}$. This quantity is computed from the complex field solution by applying the circular-basis projection at each point of interest, and it is used with [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field), [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), and [parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part) to characterize the polarization state relevant to wave-plasma coupling.

No universal absolute range applies, because the value scales with wave power, focusing, propagation normalization, and the chosen phase reference. It may be zero when the E-minus component is purely real or absent, and otherwise its magnitude can be comparable to the [right-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field amplitude](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude); the amplitude and phase are obtained from the real and imaginary parts through $|E_-|=\sqrt{E_{-,r}^2+E_{-,i}^2}$ and $\arg(E_-)=\operatorname{atan2}(E_{-,i},E_{-,r})$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $E_{-,i}$ is the positive $+i$ quadrature coefficient in $E_- = E_{-,r} + iE_{-,i}$ for the right-hand circular polarization basis about $\hat{b}$ with physical time dependence $\operatorname{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\exp(-i\omega t)]$.

NAMES.name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Real, in-phase component of the complex right-hand circularly polarized electric-field phasor of an electromagnetic wave. Together with the imaginary component, it specifies the phase and amplitude of the E-minus polarization that couples to the right-hand wave branch in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The real part of the right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the in-phase quadrature of the complex $E^-$ phasor. $E^-$ is the component of the transverse electric-field phasor that rotates in the electron-cyclotron sense about the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction and couples to the right-hand electromagnetic wave branch in a magnetized plasma.

With the physical field represented as $\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf E}\exp(-i\omega t)]$, and using a local right-handed orthonormal polarization basis $(\hat{\mathbf e}_1,\hat{\mathbf e}_2,\hat{\mathbf b})$ with $\hat{\mathbf e}_1\times\hat{\mathbf e}_2=\hat{\mathbf b}$ and $\hat{\mathbf b}$ along the local equilibrium magnetic field, the right-hand circular component is defined by:

$$
E^- = \tilde{\mathbf E}_\perp \cdot \hat{\mathbf e}_-^{*} = E^-_\mathrm{R} + i E^-_\mathrm{I}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf e}_- = \frac{\hat{\mathbf e}_1 - i\hat{\mathbf e}_2}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

where $\tilde{\mathbf E}_\perp$ is the transverse electric-field phasor, $\hat{\mathbf e}_-^{*}$ is the complex-conjugate projection vector, $E^-_\mathrm{R}$ is this real part, and $E^-_\mathrm{I}$ is the quadrature component [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part). All electric-field quantities in this relation are in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. The corresponding [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude) is $|E^-|=\sqrt{(E^-_\mathrm{R})^2+(E^-_\mathrm{I})^2}$, and the phase is determined by the two quadratures.

This quantity is computed by decomposing a complex wave electric-field solution from full-wave, ray-tracing, or beam-tracing analysis into circular polarization components. Together with the left-hand circular counterpart [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part) and the parallel component [parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part), it characterizes the local polarization state relevant to absorption, emission, and mode coupling in magnetized plasmas.

Typical absolute amplitudes of right-hand circular electric-field components are about $10^3$-$10^6\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ for externally launched microwave or RF heating waves, depending on launched power, focusing, and propagation. The signed real part can range from $-|E^-|$ to $+|E^-|$; passive emission calculations or normalized polarization calculations may have much smaller absolute scaling while retaining the same phase and polarization meaning.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the in-phase right-hand circular component gives an electric-field contribution along $+\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ at the phasor reference phase for the convention $\mathrm{Re}[\tilde{\mathbf E}\exp(-i\omega t)]$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Signed toroidal component of the wave electric field at a point, equal to the projection of the local wave electric-field vector onto the toroidal unit direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. Its unit m^-1.V is equivalent to volts per meter.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal wave electric field is the component of an oscillatory electric field along the toroidal direction. It describes the signed projection of the local wave electric-field vector onto $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The component is defined by projecting the wave electric-field vector onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
E_\phi(\mathbf{x}, t) = \mathbf{E}_\mathrm{wave}(\mathbf{x}, t) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{wave}$ is the local wave electric field and $\hat{\phi}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. For harmonic waves the same projection applies to a phase-referenced phasor or amplitude; the physical dimension is volts per meter, written here as m^-1.V.

In practice this quantity may be obtained from electromagnetic-wave modeling, probe measurements where available, or spectroscopic inference of wave-induced Stark effects. In polarization-resolved spectroscopy, fits to line positions, widths, intensities, and polarization-dependent Stark components can constrain the local oscillatory electric-field vector, which is then projected onto $\hat{\phi}$ using the viewing geometry and magnetic-field geometry.

Typical radio-frequency or lower-hybrid wave-field amplitudes range from about 10^2-10^5 m^-1.V in plasma-facing or edge regions, with locally stronger fields near launch structures sometimes approaching 10^6 m^-1.V and weaker fields in poorly coupled or far-field regions falling below 10^2 m^-1.V.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the real toroidal component of the wave electric field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex phasor component of the electromagnetic-wave electric field projected onto the vertical Z direction at the measurement position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents the signed vertical polarization component, not an instantaneous field value.
NAMES.long:
The vertical wave electric field $E_Z$ is the complex phasor component of an electromagnetic-wave electric-field vector along $\hat{Z}$, the vertical basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is a coordinate projection, not a separate wave mode; together with [radial_wave_electric_field](name:radial_wave_electric_field) and [toroidal_wave_electric_field](name:toroidal_wave_electric_field), it describes the polarization of [wave_electric_field](name:wave_electric_field) in that frame.

The component is defined by the scalar projection of the complex wave electric-field phasor onto the vertical basis vector:

$$
E_Z = \mathbf{E}_w \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}_w$ is the complex wave electric-field phasor in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $\hat{Z}$ is a dimensionless unit vector, and $E_Z$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. The phasor represents time dependence as $\exp(-i\omega t)$, so the observable vertical field is $\operatorname{Re}[E_Z\exp(-i\omega t)]$; the real and imaginary parts of $E_Z$ are the in-phase and quadrature vertical components.

In practice, $E_Z$ is obtained by determining the complex wave electric-field vector from diagnostic measurements or electromagnetic-wave modeling and then projecting it onto $\hat{Z}$. The definition is independent of wave branch: for a lower-hybrid, electron-cyclotron, ion-cyclotron, or other electromagnetic wave, it is the vertical component of that same wave phasor. Parallel components such as [parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part) instead project onto the magnetic-field direction, while circularly polarized components use a rotating polarization basis.

No branch-independent absolute range is intrinsic to this component; amplitudes depend on launched power, plasma conditions, position, and diagnostic calibration. The value may be zero for a purely horizontal electric-field polarization and may approach $|\mathbf{E}_w|$ when the wave electric field is predominantly vertical; the ratio $|E_Z|/|\mathbf{E}_w|$ lies between 0 and 1 when the orthonormal cylindrical components are complete.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a real-valued phasor coefficient for this component, such as its real or imaginary part, represents an electric-field vector contribution in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_wave_beam
NAMES.short: Vacuum wavelength of a probing electromagnetic wave beam, the spatial period corresponding to one complete cycle of its field phase.
NAMES.long:
The wavelength of a wave beam is the vacuum spatial period of the probing electromagnetic field along its propagation direction. It refers to the incident or launch radiation itself, not to the detection-side spectral coordinate used to label measured scattered or emitted light, such as [spectral_wavelength](name:spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element).

For a monochromatic component in vacuum, the defining relation is

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{c_0}{f}
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is the vacuum wavelength in meters, $c_0$ is the speed of light in vacuum in meters per second, and $f$ is the wave frequency in hertz ($\mathrm{s}^{-1}$). If angular frequency $\omega$ is used, $f = \omega/(2\pi)$.

In practice, the wavelength is set by the electromagnetic source, for example a laser line or microwave oscillator, and may be determined from the source frequency or by spectroscopic calibration. For finite-bandwidth or pulsed beams, the quoted value is usually the central vacuum wavelength. Plasma propagation changes the local wavelength through the refractive index, but this quantity remains the vacuum reference wavelength used to specify the launched beam.

The wavelength enters diagnostic sensitivity and calibration. In cold-plasma interferometry, the magnitude of the plasma phase shift relative to vacuum scales as $\lambda_0 \int n_e\,dl$, linking this quantity to the spectral_calibration_factor_of_interferometer_beam; in polarimetry, Faraday rotation scales as $\lambda_0^2 \int n_e B_\parallel\,dl$, where $n_e$ is electron number density, $B_\parallel$ is the magnetic-field component along the beam path, and $l$ is path length. In Thomson scattering, the probe wavelength sets the spectral location of the scattered signal and affects the scattering geometry and calibration.

Typical values are $5.32 \times 10^{-7}$ m and $1.064 \times 10^{-6}$ m for common Thomson-scattering lasers, $1.06 \times 10^{-5}$ m for CO2 interferometers, $1 \times 10^{-4}$-$1 \times 10^{-3}$ m for far-infrared interferometry or polarimetry, and $1 \times 10^{-3}$-$1 \times 10^{-2}$ m for millimeter-wave systems.

NAMES.name: current_density
NAMES.short: Electric current density is the vector charge flux per unit area in the plasma, equal to the sum of charge-weighted mean flows over all charged species and encompassing inductive, neoclassical, wave-driven, and kinetic contributions.
NAMES.long:
Electric current density $\mathbf{J}$ characterizes the net charge transport per unit area at every point in the plasma, unifying contributions from all current-carrying mechanisms across the thermal and suprathermal particle populations with a single vector field.

The fundamental relation connecting $\mathbf{J}$ to the magnetic field is given by Ampere's law:

$$
\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field vector and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space. The microscopic definition is $\mathbf{J} = \sum_s q_s n_s \mathbf{u}_s$, where $q_s$, $n_s$, and $\mathbf{u}_s$ are the charge, number density, and mean flow velocity of species $s$ respectively.

As a parent quantity, $\mathbf{J}$ subsumes contributions from physically distinct mechanisms: [fast current density] carried by energetic suprathermal particles, [flux-surface-averaged current density] describing the equilibrium distribution over nested toroidal surfaces, pressure-gradient-driven bootstrap and diamagnetic currents, and wave-driven contributions. The full vector decomposes into toroidal, poloidal, radial, vertical, and field-parallel projections that govern axisymmetric force balance and Grad-Shafranov source terms. In tokamak core plasmas, parallel current densities are typically $10^5$–$10^7$ A m$^{-2}$, scaling with total plasma current divided by poloidal cross-sectional area.

The total current density is reconstructed from external magnetic measurements through equilibrium analysis, or assembled from individual contributions computed by kinetic transport and fluid models.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the conventional current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: current_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Net toroidal electrical current circulating in a passive conducting structure, induced by time-varying magnetic flux from the plasma, active coils, and neighboring conducting structures rather than by an external power supply.
NAMES.long:
Current of a passive structure is the net toroidal conduction current circulating in an electrically conducting component that is not driven by an external current supply. It is induced by time-varying magnetic flux from the plasma current, active poloidal-field coils, and neighboring conducting structures, and it couples back to the magnetic equilibrium through mutual inductance.

Using the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the net toroidal current is the cross-sectional integral of current density through a cut surface of the conducting path:

$$
I_\mathrm{passive} = \int_S \mathbf{J}\cdot\hat{\phi}\, dS
$$

where $I_\mathrm{passive}$ is the passive-structure current, $S$ is a cross-section of the connected conductor normal to the toroidal direction, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $dS$ is an area element in $\mathrm{m^2}$, and $\hat{\phi}$ points toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

In lumped circuit models this current is often evolved with $L\,dI_\mathrm{passive}/dt + R\,I_\mathrm{passive} = -d\Phi_\mathrm{ext}/dt$, where $L$ is self-inductance in H, $R$ is electrical resistance in Ω, and $\Phi_\mathrm{ext}$ is the linked magnetic flux from plasma, active coils, and other conductors in Wb. The characteristic resistive decay time is $\tau = L/R$; for multiple coupled structures, inductance and resistance matrices replace the single $L$ and $R$. For loop elements, this resistance is closely related to [resistance_of_passive_loop](name:resistance_of_passive_loop).

The value may be measured by diagnostics that encircle or magnetically couple to the conducting element, such as Rogowski coils, flux loops, or magnetic probes, and may also be inferred by equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic measurements and conductor circuit equations. Isolated passive loops are described by [current_of_passive_loop](name:current_of_passive_loop), while vessel elements are represented by quantities such as [toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel](name:toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel); the driving plasma current is [toroidal_plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current).

Typical magnitudes are device- and event-dependent: individual passive elements during slowly varying equilibria are commonly treated on the order of $10^0-10^4$ A, while larger connected structures or rapid flux changes can produce substantially larger transient currents. The appropriate range is set by the linked flux-change rate, resistance, inductance, and electromagnetic coupling geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Electric current carried by a single discrete plasma-filament element in an axisymmetric filamentary representation of the distributed plasma current.
NAMES.long:
In the filamentary model of an axisymmetric plasma, the spatially distributed plasma current is represented as an array of discrete annular current-carrying elements, each called a filament. The current of each element is its individual contribution to the net toroidal plasma current, and the ensemble of filament currents constitutes a discrete model of the plasma current density distribution across the poloidal cross-section.

The total plasma current $I_p$ is recovered by summing the contributions from all filament elements:

$$
I_p = \sum_k I_k
$$

where $I_k$ is the current of the $k$-th filament element and the sum runs over all elements in the filamentary array.

Filament currents are determined during equilibrium reconstruction or electromagnetic circuit-equation integration, treating the plasma as a collection of discrete current sources. Each filament element is fully characterized by its current together with its geometric descriptors — including area_of_plasma_filament, [inner_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament), and [outer_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament) — which together define the local current-density contribution. The analogous quantity for the conducting vessel structure is [toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel](name:toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: current_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed conductor current carried by a poloidal-field coil winding. It is the electrical current in amperes through the winding conductor, distinct from the ampere-turn product obtained by multiplying by the number of turns.
NAMES.long:
Current of a poloidal-field coil is the signed electrical current carried by the coil winding conductor. For a multi-turn winding, this quantity is the conductor current $I_\mathrm{PF}$, while the magnetomotive ampere-turn product is $N I_\mathrm{PF}$, where $N$ is the number of turns.

The vacuum poloidal-flux contribution of a coil can be written, for a field point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system where $R$ is major radius in meters and $Z$ is vertical height in meters, as

$$
\psi_\mathrm{coil}(R,Z) = M_\mathrm{coil}(R,Z) I_\mathrm{PF}
$$

where $\psi_\mathrm{coil}$ is in Wb, $I_\mathrm{PF}$ is in A, and $M_\mathrm{coil}$ is the mutual inductance in Wb/A between the modeled coil winding and the flux surface label at $(R,Z)$. When $M_\mathrm{coil}$ is defined per conductor current, it includes the winding turn count and the finite coil cross-section represented by the coil model; if a per-turn Green-function response is used instead, the factor $N I_\mathrm{PF}$ appears explicitly.

In practice, poloidal-field coil currents are measured with electrical current transducers in the coil circuits and may also be estimated or constrained during equilibrium reconstruction. These currents determine the externally applied poloidal magnetic-field and flux contributions used for plasma position, boundary, and shape control, together with plasma current and currents in passive conducting structures.

Representative values are strongly device- and coil-dependent, ranging from kA-scale currents in smaller or auxiliary poloidal-field coils to several tens of kA in large shaping or vertical-field coils.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the conventional current in the winding flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Number density of free electrons per unit volume in the plasma, encompassing both bulk thermal and non-thermal (fast or suprathermal) electron populations.
NAMES.long:
The electron density $n_e$ quantifies the number of free electrons per unit volume at a given point in the plasma and is a fundamental scalar of plasma state, entering directly into fluid, kinetic, and transport equations governing plasma behavior.

In a quasi-neutral plasma, $n_e$ is constrained by charge neutrality:

$$
n_e \approx \sum_s Z_s \, n_s
$$

where $Z_s$ is the charge number and $n_s$ the number density of ion species $s$, with the sum extending over all ion species. Departures from quasi-neutrality are confined to length scales of order the Debye length $\lambda_D$.

Thomson scattering measures $n_e$ locally from the total intensity of incoherently scattered laser light; interferometry and reflectometry provide line-integrated or cutoff-layer measurements; and Langmuir probes at the plasma boundary infer $n_e$ from the ion saturation current. Together these diagnostics span the full radial range from core to scrape-off layer.

Core electron densities in H-mode tokamaks lie in the range $1$–$20 \times 10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, falling to $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in the scrape-off layer. The bulk thermal component alone is captured by [thermal_electron_density](name:thermal_electron_density), the non-thermal component by [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density), and the plasma-volume average by [volume_averaged_electron_density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density).

NAMES.name: elongation_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of the vertical to horizontal semi-axis of each nested magnetic flux surface, parameterizing the poloidal elongation of plasma shape as a function of the flux label.
NAMES.long:
The elongation $\kappa$ of a flux surface is a dimensionless measure of how vertically stretched the poloidal cross-section of a nested toroidal magnetic surface is relative to its horizontal extent. A value of $\kappa = 1$ denotes a circular cross-section, while $\kappa > 1$ characterizes the vertically elongated shapes used in modern tokamaks to improve MHD stability and energy confinement.

The defining relation is:

$$
\kappa = \frac{b}{a}
$$

where $b$ is the vertical semi-axis (half-height measured from the geometric center of the surface) and $a$ is the horizontal semi-axis (half-width) of the flux surface in the poloidal cross-section.

The elongation profile is derived from MHD equilibrium reconstruction by extracting the geometric shape parameters of each nested flux surface obtained from the Grad-Shafranov solution, parameterized as a function of the poloidal flux coordinate $\psi$ across the minor radius. The radial variation of $\kappa$ is captured by [radial_derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface](name:radial_derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface). Complementary poloidal shape descriptors include [lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), which characterizes the poloidal corner geometry, and [area_of_flux_surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface), which gives the total enclosed cross-sectional area.

Typical values rise from $\kappa \approx 1.0$ near the magnetic axis to $\kappa \approx 1.5$–$2.0$ at the plasma boundary in shaped tokamak discharges; ITER is designed for a boundary elongation near $\kappa = 1.85$.

NAMES.name: elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of the plasma boundary vertical half-height to its minor radius, quantifying the overall vertical elongation of the plasma cross-sectional shape at the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The elongation $\kappa$ is a global dimensionless shape parameter characterizing the vertical-to-horizontal aspect ratio of the plasma cross-section at the plasma boundary. It enters directly into MHD stability criteria, the Troyon beta limit, and confinement scaling relations, making it one of the primary descriptors of plasma shaping alongside triangularity.

The defining relation is:

$$
\kappa = \frac{b}{a}
$$

where $b$ is the vertical half-height of the plasma boundary (half the total poloidal extent between the uppermost and lowermost boundary points) and $a$ is the plasma minor radius (half the horizontal full width at the midplane).

The quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the closed poloidal boundary contour to external magnetic measurements and internal pressure or current profiles. The boundary extremal coordinates determine $b$ and $a$ directly.

A circular cross-section corresponds to $\kappa = 1$. Modern shaped tokamaks typically operate in the range $\kappa = 1.5$–$2.0$; strongly elongated configurations approach $\kappa \approx 1.8$–$2.0$. Higher elongation increases plasma volume at fixed minor radius and improves the MHD beta limit, but at the cost of reduced vertical stability requiring active position control.

When up-down asymmetry is significant, this global parameter decomposes into [upper elongation](name:upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary) and [lower elongation], each measuring the half-boundary contribution. The radial variation of elongation across nested flux surfaces is captured by [elongation_of_flux_surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface).

NAMES.name: external_loop_voltage
NAMES.short: Electromotive-force contribution to the total loop voltage from the time variation of externally generated poloidal magnetic flux, produced by driven central-solenoid and poloidal-field circuits and by induced currents in conducting passive structures.
NAMES.long:
External loop voltage is the inductive contribution to the total loop voltage associated with changes in poloidal magnetic flux generated by currents outside the plasma. The external sources include driven central-solenoid and poloidal-field coil circuits, as well as induced currents in conducting passive structures; the plasma self-flux contribution is excluded.

For a single plasma-representative value, it is defined as the time derivative of the signed plasma-current-weighted average of the external poloidal flux over the plasma cross-section:

$$
V_\mathrm{ext}(t) = \frac{d}{dt}\left[\frac{\int_{\Omega_p(t)} \psi_\mathrm{ext}(R,Z,t)\, j_\phi(R,Z,t)\, dR\,dZ}{\int_{\Omega_p(t)} j_\phi(R,Z,t)\, dR\,dZ}\right]
$$

where $V_\mathrm{ext}$ is the external loop voltage, $\psi_\mathrm{ext}$ is the signed poloidal magnetic flux produced by non-plasma currents, $\Omega_p$ is the plasma cross-section in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $j_\phi$ is the toroidal plasma current density. The weighting uses the signed differential plasma current $dI_p = j_\phi\,dR\,dZ$, so this is a current-weighted cross-sectional average rather than an unweighted geometric or flux-surface average.

In practice, this quantity is obtained from magnetic-equilibrium and circuit reconstructions by decomposing the poloidal flux into contributions from driven coils, conducting passive structures, and plasma current. Passive-structure currents are generally inferred through electromagnetic response models constrained by magnetic measurements, and their contribution can lag the driven coil-current waveforms.

Typical values are highly scenario and device dependent. The external loop voltage is near 0 V when external and passive-structure currents are steady, and it can become either positive or negative during current ramp-up, ramp-down, coil waveform changes, or passive-current decay; it is usually interpreted relative to the total loop voltage and other inductive or resistive voltage components rather than by a universal numerical range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the signed plasma-current-weighted average of $\psi_\mathrm{ext}$ increases with time, with positive $\psi_\mathrm{ext}$ corresponding to external vertical magnetic field through the horizontal integration disk pointing in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: gap_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Signed geometric distance from a specified measurement location to the plasma boundary, represented by the last closed flux surface or separatrix. It is zero on the boundary, positive on the scrape-off-layer side, and negative inside the confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
Gap at the plasma boundary is the signed shortest distance from a specified point to the nearest point on the last closed flux surface or separatrix. It measures the point's geometric offset from the confined plasma edge and is zero when the point lies on that boundary.

Using position vectors expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the signed gap $g$ is defined as the minimum Euclidean distance to the plasma-boundary surface $\Gamma_b$:

$$
g = \sigma \min_{\mathbf{x}_b \in \Gamma_b} \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_m - \mathbf{x}_b \right\rVert
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_m$ is the measurement position, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is a point on the plasma-boundary surface, and $\sigma$ assigns the outside or inside sign. For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the same definition is commonly evaluated as the minimum distance to the separatrix curve in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame at the relevant toroidal angle $\phi$.

The quantity is computed by combining the measurement-point geometry with an equilibrium reconstruction of the last closed flux surface or separatrix. If a flux-surface label such as normalized poloidal flux $\psi_N$ is used operationally, that label must first be mapped to a specified geometric distance, for example an outboard-midplane radial distance, rather than treated as a distance by itself.

Typical near-edge values have absolute magnitudes from about $10^{-3}$-$10^{-1}$ m, with embedded or reciprocating edge measurements often within a few centimeters of the separatrix. Larger magnitudes can occur for points well inside the confined plasma or far into the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the measurement point lies outside the last closed flux surface on the scrape-off-layer side of the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: height_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section of a discrete plasma current-carrying filament element, measured parallel to the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
In the filamentary model of plasma current distribution used for equilibrium reconstruction, the plasma current is represented by a set of discrete elements, each assigned a cross-sectional geometry. When the cross-section is modeled as a rectangle, the height defines the full vertical extent of that rectangle measured along the $Z$ axis of the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate.

For a rectangular filament element with height $h$ and horizontal width $w$, the rectangular cross-sectional area is $A = h \times w$, which is consistent with area_of_plasma_filament. The height is specified alongside [width_of_plasma_filament](name:width_of_plasma_filament) to fully characterize the rectangular geometry; for annular cross-sections, the radial bounds are instead described by [inner_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament) and [outer_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament).

The height is a fixed geometric input parameter assigned when constructing the filamentary current model, with its value chosen to resolve the spatial scale of interest in the current distribution. Typical values range from a few centimeters to tens of centimeters depending on the resolution requirements of the equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical extent of the filament cross-section is measured in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: internal_inductance
NAMES.short: Dimensionless measure of plasma current profile peaking, defined as the volume-integrated squared poloidal magnetic field normalized by the square of the total plasma current and the reference major radius.
NAMES.long:
The internal inductance $l_i$ is a dimensionless global equilibrium parameter that characterizes the shape of the plasma current density profile. A broadly distributed current results in a lower $l_i$ (near 0.5 for a circular cross-section with uniform current), while a strongly peaked profile raises it toward 2. This quantity enters vertical stability analysis and the plasma–coil circuit equations relating the resistive loop voltage to the time-evolving current distribution.

The $l_{i,3}$ definition relates $l_i$ to the volume integral of the squared poloidal magnetic field:

$$
l_{i,3} = \frac{2}{R_0 \mu_0^2 I_p^2} \int B_p^2 \, dV
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius of the geometric axis, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $I_p$ is the total plasma current, $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field magnitude, and the integral is taken over the plasma volume.

The internal inductance is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements, or estimated from the resistive diffusion evolution of the current profile during ramp-up and flat-top phases. In H-mode flat-top conditions, $l_i$ lies in the range 0.7–1.2; sawtooth-free operation and current ramp-up can drive values toward 2. The [total plasma inductance] $L_p$ combines $l_i$ with the external inductance contribution to give the total inductive impedance of the plasma circuit.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any current-carrying plasma, since $l_{i,3}$ is proportional to $\int B_p^2 \, dV$, which is intrinsically non-negative.

NAMES.name: length_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Arc length of the plasma boundary in a fixed-toroidal-angle poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the perimeter of the last closed magnetic-flux-surface contour.
NAMES.long:
Length of the plasma boundary is the total arc length of the closed contour formed by the last closed magnetic flux surface in a fixed-toroidal-angle poloidal cross-section. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; this quantity is computed from the contour in the $(R,Z)$ cross-section at constant $\phi$. It is independent of whether the contour is traversed clockwise or counter-clockwise.

For a smooth boundary represented by a parameter $\lambda$ that traces the closed contour once, the poloidal boundary length is

$$
L_\mathrm{pol} = \int_0^1 \sqrt{\left(\frac{dR}{d\lambda}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dZ}{d\lambda}\right)^2}\, d\lambda
$$

where $R(\lambda)$ and $Z(\lambda)$ are the contour coordinates in meters and $\lambda$ is dimensionless. For a circular boundary of minor radius $a$ in meters, this reduces to $L_\mathrm{pol}=2\pi a$.

The contour is obtained from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction by identifying the separatrix in diverted plasmas or the limiting last closed flux surface in limited plasmas, then integrating the arc element around that closed curve. This length complements other boundary-geometry measures such as area_of_plasma_boundary, [volume_of_plasma_boundary](name:volume_of_flux_surface), [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary), and [triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary); elongation, triangularity, and X-point shaping generally increase the perimeter relative to a circular contour with the same minor radius.

Representative values scale directly with plasma minor radius and shaping. As geometric scale checks, a circular contour with $a=0.3-2$ m has $L_\mathrm{pol}\approx 2-13$ m, while elongated or diverted contours of comparable minor radius are typically larger by tens of percent.

NAMES.name: lower_elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Ratio of the lower boundary half-height to the plasma minor radius, describing the vertical elongation of the plasma cross-section below the geometric axis.
NAMES.long:
The lower elongation $\kappa_{\rm lower}$ is a dimensionless shape parameter quantifying the vertical extent of the lower half of the plasma boundary cross-section relative to the plasma minor radius, complementing [upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary) for up-down asymmetric plasma shaping.

The defining relation is:

$$
\kappa_{\rm lower} = \frac{Z_{\rm axis} - Z_{\rm lower}}{a}
$$

where $Z_{\rm axis}$ is the vertical coordinate of the plasma geometric axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $Z_{\rm lower}$ is the vertical coordinate of the lowermost point of the boundary contour, and $a$ is the plasma minor radius.

When $\kappa_{\rm lower}$ differs from [upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary), the plasma has up-down asymmetric shaping, which is characteristic of single-null divertor configurations with the X-point in the lower divertor. The global [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) captures the overall vertical half-height ratio for symmetric boundaries, but $\kappa_{\rm lower}$ and its upper counterpart together fully characterize asymmetric boundary shapes relevant to MHD stability and confinement modeling. Typical values range from 1.0 in near-circular lower halves to approximately 2.0 in strongly shaped H-mode plasmas. The quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the boundary contour in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane using external magnetic measurements.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lowermost point of the plasma boundary contour lies below the geometric axis, i.e., $Z_{\rm lower} < Z_{\rm axis}$.

NAMES.name: magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Total local magnetic field vector in a magnetically confined plasma, formed by superposition of contributions from external coil systems and plasma-current-generated fields.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$ represents the total local magnetic field at each point in a magnetically confined plasma, combining the dominant toroidal component provided by toroidal field coils with the poloidal component arising from plasma current and poloidal field coils, together with any non-axisymmetric perturbations from error fields or applied resonant magnetic perturbations. The [toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) isolates the externally driven toroidal contribution, while [toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field) captures the toroidally varying non-axisymmetric part.

The field satisfies the solenoidal constraint $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0$ everywhere and, in the presence of plasma currents $\mathbf{j}$, obeys Ampère's law:

$$
\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \, \mathbf{j}
$$

where $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H m$^{-1}$ is the permeability of free space and $\mathbf{j}$ is the total current density in A m$^{-2}$.

The field is reconstructed from external magnetics diagnostics — flux loops, Rogowski coils, and pick-up coils — supplemented where available by in-vessel probe measurements. The ratio of plasma kinetic pressure to local magnetic pressure defines beta, a key dimensionless stability parameter derived from $|\mathbf{B}|$.

On-axis total field magnitudes span 1–6 T in present-day tokamaks, with the toroidal component dominant and the poloidal component typically 10–100 times smaller.
NAMES.sign: Positive when each component points in the positive direction of the corresponding axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — outward for the radial component, in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ for the toroidal component, and upward ($+Z$) for the vertical component.

NAMES.name: magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Family of magnetic flux quantities in tokamak equilibrium, spanning poloidal and toroidal projections and contributions from external coils, resistive dissipation, and plasma diamagnetism.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic flux is the surface integral of the magnetic field over a bounded area, quantifying the total field lines threading a specified surface. In tokamak equilibrium, the vector quantity encompasses several physically distinct components: [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) threading horizontal disks centered on the toroidal symmetry axis serves as the canonical radial flux-surface coordinate, while [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) threads the poloidal cross-section enclosed by each flux surface and increases monotonically outward from the magnetic axis.

The defining surface integral is:

$$
\Phi = \int_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector and $d\mathbf{A}$ is the oriented area element of the bounding surface $S$.

Beyond the geometric poloidal and toroidal projections, the equilibrium flux budget includes contributions from external coil systems such as the central solenoid and poloidal-field coils, and flux consumed by resistive dissipation within the plasma. The [poloidal current weighted average external magnetic flux](name:poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux) is one such derived quantity combining external-source flux with current weighting.
