Flux quantities are measured by saddle loops, flux loops, and diamagnetic loops distributed around the vacuum vessel, and are reconstructed from equilibrium solvers that invert the Grad-Shafranov equation in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the enclosed magnetic flux is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear
NAMES.short: Normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius, quantifying the radial rate of change of magnetic field-line helicity across nested flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear $s$ measures how rapidly the pitch of nested magnetic field lines changes across flux surfaces and is a fundamental parameter governing magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) stability and cross-field turbulent transport. It distinguishes conventional positive-shear configurations, which suppress certain interchange modes, from reversed-shear configurations, which can suppress ion-temperature-gradient turbulence.

The defining relation is:

$$
s = \frac{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}{q} \frac{dq}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor}}
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor and $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius running from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface. An equivalent minor-radius form is $s = (r/q)(dq/dr)$ where $r$ is the local minor radius.

Magnetic shear is computed from equilibrium reconstructions by evaluating the logarithmic derivative of the reconstructed safety factor profile with respect to the radial flux label. In conventional H-mode scenarios, $s$ rises from near zero on axis to approximately 2–5 near the edge; in reversed-shear advanced scenarios, $s$ is negative (typically $-1$ to $-2$) in the core. The on-axis limit is given by [magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis), the pedestal value by [magnetic_shear_at_pedestal](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal), and the flux-surface-averaged form by [flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_shear](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_shear).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the safety factor $q$ increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Dimensionless magnetic shear at the magnetic axis, defined as the limiting normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius. For a smooth finite-q equilibrium this axis limit is zero.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear at the magnetic axis is the axis limiting value of local magnetic shear, describing how rapidly the safety factor changes as one moves outward from the magnetic axis in normalized toroidal flux radius. It is a dimensionless local equilibrium quantity, not a finite-radius average.

The defining value is the one-sided radial limit of local magnetic shear:

$$
s_\mathrm{axis} = \lim_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}\to 0^+} \frac{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}{q(\rho_\mathrm{tor})}\frac{d q}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor}}
$$

where $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, a dimensionless radial coordinate with value 0 at the magnetic axis and value 1 at the plasma boundary, and $q(\rho_\mathrm{tor})$ is the safety factor. Since both $q$ and $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ are dimensionless, $s_\mathrm{axis}$ has unit 1.

In equilibrium analysis it is obtained from the reconstructed radial dependence of $q$ by fitting or differentiating near the magnetic axis and taking the limiting expression above. For regular equilibria with finite $q$ at the axis, the factor $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ makes the exact limit vanish; the curvature of $q$ controls how quickly magnetic shear rises away from the axis, not a finite physical on-axis shear. Negative or positive shear associated with reversed-shear configurations occurs at finite radius, while the smooth on-axis limit remains zero.

The typical physical value is 0 for smooth finite-q tokamak equilibria. Numerical evaluations may show small residual absolute values, commonly 0-0.1 depending on radial resolution, smoothing, and whether a finite-radius point was used instead of the mathematical limit; larger magnitudes usually indicate extrapolation or loss of near-axis regularity.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Maximum value of the total magnetic field magnitude on a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface. It is a non-negative scalar that characterizes the strongest field encountered on that surface.
NAMES.long:
Maximum magnetic field magnitude is the largest value of $|\mathbf{B}|$ over a single nested toroidal magnetic flux surface. It is paired with [minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude) and, together with that minimum, characterizes the magnetic-field variation experienced by guiding-center orbits on the surface.

For a surface labeled by poloidal flux $\psi$, the quantity is defined by

$$
B_{\max}(\psi) = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S(\psi)} \left|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})\right|
$$

where $S(\psi)$ is the magnetic flux surface with label $\psi$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field vector, and both $|\mathbf{B}|$ and $B_{\max}$ are measured in T.

In equilibrium analysis it is computed by evaluating the full magnetic field magnitude on each flux surface and taking the surface maximum, usually with interpolation between reconstructed equilibrium points. In axisymmetric tokamaks the maximum often occurs toward the inboard, higher-field side because the toroidal field usually increases there, but this location is not part of the definition and can be affected by shaping and poloidal-field contributions.

For trapped-passing physics, $B_{\max}$ gives the largest field strength a particle must access to circulate around the surface. For a particle with kinetic energy $E$ and magnetic moment $\mu$, full access to the surface requires $\mu B_{\max} < E$; equality gives the trapped-passing boundary, while $\mu B_{\max} > E$ implies reflection before the particle reaches the highest-field region.

Typical values are about 1-8 T in many present tokamak plasmas and can exceed 10 T in compact high-field devices; low-field or spherical tokamak plasmas can be below 1 T. The value depends mainly on external toroidal field strength, plasma geometry, and the poloidal-field contribution.

NAMES.name: minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Smallest value of total magnetic field magnitude on each nested toroidal flux surface, used in determining the magnetic trapping condition for charged particles in bounce motion.
NAMES.long:
The minimum magnetic field magnitude $B_\mathrm{min}(\psi)$ is the smallest value of $|\mathbf{B}|$ over all points on the flux surface labeled by poloidal flux $\psi$. In tokamaks with a dominant toroidal field satisfying $B_\phi \propto 1/R$, the minimum occurs near the outboard (low-field-side) midplane, where the major radius $R$ reaches its largest value on the flux surface.

The ratio $B_\mathrm{min}/B_\mathrm{max}$ governs magnetic trapping of charged particles bouncing along field lines. A particle with normalized parallel velocity $\xi = v_\parallel/v$ is magnetically trapped when

$$
\xi^2 < 1 - \frac{B_\mathrm{min}}{B_\mathrm{max}}
$$

where $v_\parallel$ is the velocity component along the magnetic field and $v$ is the total particle speed. The resulting trapped particle fraction enters neoclassical transport coefficients, bootstrap current models, and bounce-averaged kinetic equations.

$B_\mathrm{min}$ is obtained from MHD equilibrium reconstruction by minimizing the total field strength $|\mathbf{B}(\psi, \theta)|$ over the poloidal angle $\theta$ on each flux surface. Together with [maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude) and flux_surface_average_magnetic_field, it fully characterizes the field-strength variation on a flux surface that is relevant for classifying particle orbits.

NAMES.name: minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Half the difference between the maximum and minimum major radii of the plasma boundary contour, giving the characteristic radial half-width of the outermost closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The minor radius $a$ of the plasma boundary is a fundamental geometric length quantifying the radial half-extent of the outermost closed flux surface. Together with the [major radius of the plasma boundary], it sets the first-order cross-sectional size and determines the plasma aspect ratio.

The minor radius is defined from the extremal major radii of the boundary outline in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
a = \frac{R_{\max} - R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum values of the major radius $R$ along the closed poloidal boundary contour.

The minor radius is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements — flux loops and poloidal field probes — supplemented by internal constraints from motional Stark effect polarimetry or pressure-profile data. It also serves directly as a position-control reference in plasma shape control.

Values range from 0.2–0.3 m in small tokamaks to ~2 m in large high-current devices. The inverse aspect ratio $\epsilon = a / R_0$ (where $R_0$ is the major radius on axis) underpins dimensionless confinement scalings, and derived shape descriptors such as [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) and the [poloidal boundary perimeter](name:length_of_plasma_boundary) are both normalized by $a$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_{\max} > R_{\min}$ along the boundary contour in the $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Non-axisymmetric part of the vacuum magnetic field vector, obtained by removing the toroidally averaged component, representing toroidally varying perturbations such as error fields, resonant magnetic perturbations, and finite coil geometry effects.
NAMES.long:
The non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the vector magnetic induction formed by subtracting the axisymmetric (toroidally averaged) component from the total vacuum magnetic field, retaining only the part that varies with toroidal angle $\phi$. It encompasses both intrinsic error fields arising from coil misalignment and discrete conductor geometry, and deliberately applied perturbation fields from coil systems used in resonant magnetic perturbation (RMP) experiments targeting edge-localized mode suppression.

The decomposition into non-axisymmetric and axisymmetric parts is defined as:

$$
\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{na}(R,\phi,Z) = \mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}(R,\phi,Z) - \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}(R,\phi',Z)\,d\phi'
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the total vacuum magnetic field and the integral extracts its toroidal average. The vector is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$.

The field is computed by Biot-Savart integration over each conductor's geometry followed by subtraction of the axisymmetric component; it represents the vacuum perturbation only and does not include plasma shielding or amplification, which require magnetohydrodynamic or kinetic modeling. The individual cylindrical components are [radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), [toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), and [vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field). The normal projection onto prescribed control surfaces is given by non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field_at_control_surface, commonly used as an equilibrium reconstruction constraint.

Typical perturbation amplitudes at the plasma boundary range from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-2}$ T, with deliberately applied RMP systems at the upper end and residual intrinsic error fields around $10^{-4}$ T for well-corrected devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when each cylindrical component points in the direction of its respective basis vector, $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: normalized_minor_radius_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless minor-radius label of a magnetic flux surface. It is half the difference between the surface's maximum and minimum major radii, divided by a specified positive reference length L_ref.
NAMES.long:
The normalized minor radius of a flux surface is a geometric radial coordinate based on the inboard-to-outboard extent of that surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It labels how far the surface lies from the magnetic axis by using the surface half-width in major radius, normalized by a separately specified positive reference length.

The defining relation is

$$
r_{\mathrm{minor,norm}} = \frac{R_{\max} - R_{\min}}{2 L_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum major radii of the flux surface in meters, and $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference length in meters used for the normalization. The reference length is part of the normalization definition and must be stated consistently; for a whole-plasma radial coordinate it is commonly the minor radius of a reference boundary flux surface, so the boundary value is approximately 1, whereas other modeling contexts may choose a different positive reference length.

In practice the quantity is computed from an equilibrium flux surface by finding the extrema of $R$ on the closed surface or on its poloidal cross-section in an axisymmetric equilibrium. It is a geometric flux-surface label and should be distinguished from flux-based radial coordinates such as the toroidal flux radius, which are derived from enclosed magnetic flux rather than from the major-radius half-width.

Typical values are 0 at the magnetic axis, about 0.1-0.9 for core to near-edge flux surfaces when $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the boundary minor radius, and approximately 1 at the reference boundary surface. Values greater than 1 can occur if the chosen reference length is smaller than the surface minor radius or if surfaces outside the reference boundary are considered.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless normalized poloidal magnetic flux evaluated on the flux surface selected as the plasma boundary. It is near unity when that surface coincides with, or lies close to, the outer reference flux surface such as the last-closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Normalized poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the value of the normalized poloidal magnetic-flux function on the flux surface selected to represent the plasma boundary. It identifies that boundary relative to the magnetic-axis flux and an outer reference flux, which is often the last-closed flux surface or separatrix.

The normalized boundary value is defined by evaluating the normalized poloidal flux on the selected boundary surface:

$$
\psi_{N,\mathrm{b}} = \left. \frac{\psi - \psi_0}{\psi_\mathrm{ref} - \psi_0} \right|_{\psi=\psi_\mathrm{b}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $\psi_0$ is the magnetic-axis value in Wb, $\psi_\mathrm{b}$ is the poloidal flux on the selected plasma-boundary flux surface in Wb, and $\psi_\mathrm{ref}$ is the outer reference flux in Wb used for normalization. If the selected boundary is itself the normalization reference, then $\psi_{N,\mathrm{b}}=1$.

In practice this value is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating the normalized poloidal-flux label on the reconstructed boundary contour or on the flux surface prescribed as the fixed boundary. This is the normalized flux value $\psi_N$ itself; it should not be confused with the square-root radial flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{pol}=\sqrt{\psi_N}$ represented by [normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).

Typical values are close to 1 for boundaries chosen near the outer reference flux surface. With $\psi_N=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\psi_N=1$ at the reference boundary, values from 0 to 1 label closed flux surfaces between those two surfaces, and the selected plasma boundary has value 1 when it coincides with the reference boundary.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial flux-surface label defined as the square root of the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by a flux surface normalized to its value at the last closed flux surface, spanning 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ is a dimensionless radial label identifying nested magnetic flux surfaces in an axisymmetric toroidal equilibrium. It equals zero at the magnetic axis and unity at the last closed flux surface (LCFS), providing a monotonically increasing coordinate that spans the entire confined plasma region.

The defining relation is:

$$
\rho_{\rm tor,norm} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\rm tor}}{\Phi_{\rm tor,b}}}
$$

where $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed within a given flux surface and $\Phi_{\rm tor,b}$ is the toroidal flux at the plasma boundary.

The coordinate is obtained from magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium reconstruction by integrating the toroidal magnetic field over poloidal cross-sections of increasing enclosed area. Because it is rooted in toroidal rather than poloidal flux, it is the natural abscissa for radial transport calculations and differs from the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) except in special limiting geometries. Specific physics events are located by their value of this coordinate; for example, [the minimum-safety-factor surface](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor) corresponds to a well-defined $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ that shifts with plasma current profile.

The coordinate spans $[0, 1]$ for all confined flux surfaces. In H-mode discharges the steep-gradient pedestal region typically spans $\rho_{\rm tor,norm} \approx 0.85$–$0.95$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic flux $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ enclosed by the flux surface is directed in the same toroidal sense as the flux at the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial flux-surface label of a toroidal current-density constraint position, equal to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate evaluated at that position. It is 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a constraint position is the dimensionless radial label of the flux surface on which a toroidal current-density constraint is applied. It is the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) evaluated at that constraint position, with the magnetic axis mapped to 0 and the plasma boundary mapped to 1.

The coordinate is defined from the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed between the magnetic axis and the flux surface containing the constraint position:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_b}}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by that flux surface in Wb, $\Phi_b$ is the corresponding boundary value in Wb, and the non-negative square root is used.

In equilibrium reconstruction, this quantity specifies where a toroidal current-density constraint is located in radial flux space. It is computed by identifying the flux surface associated with the constraint position and evaluating the normalized toroidal flux radius there; no diagnostic-specific projection mechanism is implied.

Typical values for constraints on closed flux surfaces lie in the range 0-1. Values near 0 correspond to constraints close to the magnetic axis, while values near 1 correspond to constraints close to the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial position of the minimum-safety-factor surface, expressed as the normalized toroidal flux coordinate rho_tor_norm, ranging from zero at the magnetic axis to unity at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,N}}$ evaluated at the minimum safety factor surface identifies the dimensionless radial location of the $q_{\min}$ surface within the plasma. This coordinate ranges from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary, so its value distinguishes centrally located $q_{\min}$ surfaces (near-axis, values close to 0) from off-axis surfaces characteristic of reversed-shear plasmas (values in the range 0.3–0.7).

The [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) is defined as:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,N}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}}}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by a given flux surface and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$ is the total toroidal magnetic flux within the plasma boundary. This quantity is the value of $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,N}}$ at the flux surface that globally minimizes $q(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,N}})$.

The location of $q_{\min}$ is extracted from equilibrium reconstruction combining external magnetic measurements with internal diagnostics such as motional Stark effect or polarimetry to resolve the $q$-profile shape. In conventional H-mode plasmas with monotonically increasing $q$-profiles, $q_{\min}$ lies near the magnetic axis and this coordinate approaches 0; in reversed-shear advanced-tokamak scenarios it is off-axis with values in the range 0.3–0.7. The analogous poloidal-flux-based label for the same surface is given by [normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor), while the corresponding location for the $q = 1$ sawtooth inversion surface is [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed within the minimum safety factor surface has the same sign as the boundary toroidal flux, which holds for all physically realizable nested-flux-surface equilibria.

NAMES.name: parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Flux-surface averaged current density parallel to the local magnetic field, evaluated on the magnetic surface at the constraint point's normalized toroidal flux radius.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface averaged parallel current density at a constraint position is the average, over a closed magnetic flux surface, of the local current density projected along the local magnetic-field direction. The constraint position is labeled by the flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, the normalized toroidal flux radius, with 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface.

For a constraint at $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm},c}$, the volume-based flux-surface average is

$$
\langle j_\parallel \rangle(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm},c}) =
\frac{\oint_{\psi=\psi_c} \mathbf{j}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}} \, dS/|\nabla\psi|}
{\oint_{\psi=\psi_c} dS/|\nabla\psi|}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}$ is the current-density vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, $dS$ is a surface element on the magnetic surface, $\psi_c$ is the poloidal magnetic flux labeling the same surface as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm},c}$, and the $dS/|\nabla\psi|$ weighting is the volume-derivative form of a flux-surface average. No reference magnetic field $B_0$ (a magnetic flux density in tesla) enters this definition; in particular, it is not the field-weighted quantity $\langle\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\rangle/B_0$.

In practice the value is computed from an axisymmetric equilibrium by evaluating the reconstructed $\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ on the flux surface selected by $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm},c}$ and carrying out the flux-surface average. Constraint values can come from consistency with magnetic measurements, polarimetry or motional Stark effect information, kinetic pressure and density information, and current-drive or transport modeling; comparison is made at the same flux coordinate.

Typical magnitudes in tokamak equilibrium reconstructions are $10^4-5 \times 10^6$ A m^-2; values near the magnetic axis in high-current plasmas often reach $0.5-5 \times 10^6$ A m^-2, while edge constraints can be much smaller and may change sign if local current is driven opposite to the magnetic field.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux-surface averaged projection of the current density is along the local magnetic-field direction, so $\langle\mathbf{j}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}\rangle > 0$.

NAMES.name: plasma_current
NAMES.short: Net electric current of the plasma column, obtained by integrating toroidal current density over the poloidal cross-section; the primary global parameter governing poloidal field strength and MHD stability.
NAMES.long:
The plasma current $I_p$ is the net toroidal electric current of the plasma column, obtained by integrating the toroidal [current density](name:current_density) $j_\phi$ over the entire poloidal cross-sectional area bounded by the last closed flux surface.

$$
I_p = \iint_{\mathcal{S}} j_\phi \, dA
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the current density and $\mathcal{S}$ is the full poloidal cross-section enclosed by the plasma boundary.

$I_p$ sets the amplitude of the poloidal magnetic field and, together with the toroidal field, determines the safety factor profile that governs MHD stability and energy confinement. It incorporates contributions from ohmic induction, pressure-gradient-driven bootstrap current, and all non-inductive current-drive mechanisms. It is measured directly by Rogowski coils or fiber-optic current sensors exploiting the Faraday magneto-optic effect, and may also be inferred from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic flux loops and field probes. The purely toroidal projection is reported as [toroidal total plasma current](name:toroidal_plasma_current). Typical values range from a few hundred kA in compact devices to 15 MA in large-scale fusion experiments.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: plasma_pressure
NAMES.short: Isotropic scalar pressure of the plasma fluid in a continuum description, serving as the parent concept for both the bulk thermal equilibrium pressure and first-order perturbative pressure deviations in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
Plasma pressure in the fluid (MHD) description is the isotropic part of the pressure tensor, entering the radial force balance $\nabla p = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$, where $\mathbf{j}$ is the current density and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field. This parent abstracts over two physically distinct realizations: [thermal_plasma_pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure), which sums the kinetic contributions from bulk thermal electron and ion populations while excluding fast or suprathermal particles, and [perturbed_plasma_pressure](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure), which represents the complex-amplitude linear eigenfunction $\delta p$ arising in stability analysis about a magnetohydrostatic equilibrium.

In the thermal regime the pressure is given by the equation of state:

$$
p = n_e k_B T_e + \sum_i n_i k_B T_i
$$

where $n_e$ and $n_i$ are the electron and ion number densities, $T_e$ and $T_i$ are their respective temperatures, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant. In linear MHD stability analysis the equilibrium profile $p_0$ is perturbed as $p = p_0 + \delta p$, where $\delta p$ is the pressure eigenfunction resolved per toroidal Fourier mode.

Pressure profiles are inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by enforcing the radial force-balance constraint against magnetic diagnostic data and a finite set of kinetic pressure measurements. The volume integral of the thermal pressure, scaled by $3/2$, yields the stored thermal energy [thermal_plasma_energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), while a pointwise sum of electron and ion contributions is captured by [total_thermal_pressure](name:total_thermal_pressure).

NAMES.name: plasma_resistance
NAMES.short: Effective non-negative electrical resistance of the plasma column, defined as the volume-integrated ohmic dissipation power divided by the square of the total plasma current. It represents the resistive part of the plasma circuit response, distinct from inductive voltage associated with changing current or magnetic stored energy.
NAMES.long:
Plasma resistance is the effective scalar resistance associated with collisional ohmic dissipation in the conducting plasma column. It is a non-negative quantity for positive ohmic dissipation and characterizes how strongly the plasma converts current-driven electrical work into heat, separately from inductive effects described by total_plasma_inductance.

The effective resistance is defined from the ohmic power dissipated in the plasma:

$$
R_\mathrm{plasma} = \frac{\int_{V_p} \mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{J}\,dV}{I_p^2} = \frac{P_\Omega}{I_p^2}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{plasma}$ is in ohm, $V_p$ is the plasma volume, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{J}$ is the current density in A m$^{-2}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, $P_\Omega$ is the volume-integrated ohmic heating power in W, and $I_p$ is the total plasma current in A. When a circuit representation is used, this corresponds to the resistive voltage component divided by $I_p$ for nonzero current; it should not be identified with the total loop voltage unless inductive and other non-resistive voltage contributions have been removed.

In equilibrium and transport analysis, plasma resistance is computed from reconstructed current density together with an electrical resistivity or parallel conductivity model, or inferred from the resistive component of the plasma voltage balance. Its time integral is related to resistive magnetic-flux consumption, represented by poloidal_accumulated_resistive_magnetic_flux, while the inductive part of the voltage balance is associated with changes in current and magnetic energy through total_plasma_inductance.

Typical values in tokamak plasmas are about 0.01-10 microohm, decreasing strongly as electron temperature rises and increasing with effective ion charge and collisionality. Cold startup, ramp-down, or low-temperature edge-dominated conditions can have substantially larger effective resistance than hot flattop conditions.

NAMES.name: polarization_angle_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Motional Stark effect polarization angle evaluated at a discrete spatial location designated as a measurement constraint in tokamak equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.long:
The polarization angle at a constraint position is the angle of linear polarization of Stark-split Balmer-alpha emission from fast neutral beam ions traversing the plasma, evaluated at a discrete spatial site where this measurement serves as an input constraint in equilibrium reconstruction. The motional Stark effect (MSE) diagnostic exploits the Lorentz electric field experienced by injected beam neutrals to align the polarization plane of the emitted light in a direction encoding the local magnetic-field pitch angle.

The MSE polarization angle $\gamma$ is related to the local magnetic field components by:

$$
\tan(\gamma) = \frac{B_Z}{A_1 B_R + A_2 B_\phi}
$$

where $B_Z$ is the vertical field component, $B_R$ is the radial field component, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal field component, and $A_1$, $A_2$ are dimensionless geometric weighting factors determined by the beam trajectory and sightline orientation.

During equilibrium reconstruction, the measured value at each constraint position is compared against the corresponding reconstructed [polarization_angle](name:polarization_angle_at_constraint_position) to form residuals that enter the least-squares cost functional. The motional_stark_radiance provides complementary spectral intensity data from the same beam-emission event. MSE polarization angles in conventional-aspect-ratio tokamak configurations span a few degrees to roughly 20 degrees, varying with local field pitch, beam geometry, and viewing-sightline angle.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle
NAMES.short: Geometric poloidal angle identifying position around a magnetic flux-surface cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is measured from the outboard midplane about the surface's geometric center and is distinct from a straight-field-line poloidal angle.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal angle is the geometric angular coordinate of a point on a surface of constant [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) around the poloidal cross-section. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, with zero at the outboard low-field-side midplane relative to the flux-surface center. This quantity is the geometric poloidal angle, not a [straight-field-line poloidal angle].

For a point on a closed flux-surface contour at fixed $\phi$, let $(R_c,Z_c)$ be the geometric center of that same contour. A definite construction is

$$
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(Z_c - Z,\; R - R_c)
$$

where $\theta$ is the poloidal angle in radians, $R$ and $Z$ are the point coordinates in meters, $R_c$ and $Z_c$ are center coordinates in meters, and $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ is the quadrant-aware arctangent. Here the center is defined from the contour extrema as $R_c=(R_\mathrm{out}+R_\mathrm{in})/2$ and $Z_c=(Z_\mathrm{top}+Z_\mathrm{bottom})/2$, with all extrema measured in meters in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

In equilibrium analysis, the angle is computed by reconstructing or specifying a flux-surface contour, determining its geometric center, and applying the construction above to points on that contour. A [straight-field-line poloidal angle] requires a separate remapping chosen so magnetic field lines satisfy $d\phi/d\theta^* = q(\psi)$, where $\phi$ and $\theta^*$ are angles in radians, $q$ is the dimensionless [safety factor](name:safety_factor), and $\psi$ labels the flux surface.

Because it is periodic, values differing by $2\pi n$ for integer $n$ identify the same geometric direction from the chosen center. A single poloidal circuit spans $2\pi$ rad; common branch choices include $(-\pi,\pi]$ rad and $[0,2\pi)$ rad, while unwrapped coordinates may extend beyond these intervals.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the angle increases from the outboard midplane toward decreasing $Z$ at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_beta
NAMES.short: Poloidal beta is the dimensionless ratio of total plasma pressure content to the magnetic-pressure scale of the poloidal field generated by the toroidal plasma current. It measures the pressure contribution to equilibrium force balance relative to the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal beta, $\beta_p$, is a global equilibrium measure of plasma pressure normalized to the magnetic-pressure scale associated with the plasma-current-driven poloidal magnetic field. It is used to compare pressure loading with the current needed to confine the plasma and is closely connected to Shafranov shift, bootstrap-current fraction, and equilibrium stability limits.

The common volume-integral definition is:

$$
\beta_p = \frac{4 \int p \, dV}{R_0 \, \mu_0 \, I_p^2}
$$

where $p$ is the total kinetic plasma pressure in pascals, $dV$ is the volume element in cubic meters, $R_0$ is a reference major radius in meters measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space in H/m, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current in amperes. The squared current makes $\beta_p$ insensitive to the sign of $I_p$; unlike [toroidal beta], which is normalized to toroidal-field magnetic pressure, $\beta_p$ is normalized to the poloidal-field energy scale set by [plasma current](name:toroidal_plasma_current).

In practice, $\beta_p$ is computed by integrating [plasma pressure](name:plasma_pressure) over reconstructed flux-surface volumes, with pressure obtained from density and temperature measurements such as Thomson scattering, interferometry, electron-cyclotron emission, and charge-exchange spectroscopy. Magnetic equilibrium analysis can also constrain $\beta_p$ through the Shafranov shift and external poloidal-field measurements. In large-aspect-ratio ordering, external magnetic constraints often involve a combined pressure and current-profile term such as $\beta_p + l_i/2$, where $l_i$ is the internal inductance, so $\beta_p$ and current-profile information are not always independently determined by magnetic measurements alone.

Typical values are about 0.1-0.5 in Ohmic or L-mode plasmas and 0.3-1.5 in H-mode plasmas. Advanced high-bootstrap-current scenarios often target $\beta_p > 1$; the bootstrap-current fraction scales approximately with $\epsilon^{1/2}\beta_p$, where $\epsilon = a/R_0$ is the inverse aspect ratio.

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short: Diamagnetic function equal to the product of major radius and toroidal magnetic field, constant on each nested magnetic flux surface in an axisymmetric ideal-MHD equilibrium and one of the two free flux-function profiles entering the Grad-Shafranov equation.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal current function $F(\psi) = R B_\phi$ is the product of the major radius $R$ (distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame) and the toroidal magnetic field component $B_\phi$. In axisymmetric ideal-MHD equilibrium, the solenoidal condition $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} = 0$ combined with axisymmetry forces $F$ to be constant on each nested poloidal flux surface, making it a function solely of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$.

The profile $F(\psi)$ is one of the two free functions of the Grad-Shafranov equation governing axisymmetric magnetohydrostatic equilibrium:

$$
\Delta^* \psi = -\mu_0 R^2 \frac{dp}{d\psi} - F \frac{dF}{d\psi}
$$

where $\Delta^*$ is the elliptic Shafranov differential operator, $p(\psi)$ is the pressure flux function, and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space. The product $F \, dF/d\psi$ constitutes the toroidal-field-gradient source term and is represented explicitly by the [associated product quantity](name:product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_poloidal_current_function). In vacuum, $F$ reduces to the constant [vacuum poloidal current function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function) $F_\mathrm{vac} = R B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$.

The $F(\psi)$ profile is recovered through equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements, optionally supplemented by internal diagnostic constraints such as motional Stark effect polarimetry or q-profile data. Typical magnitudes range from approximately 1 to 35 m·T across present-day tokamaks, scaling approximately as $R_0 B_{\phi,0}$ where $R_0$ is the reference major radius and $B_{\phi,0}$ is the on-axis toroidal field strength.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Average poloidal magnetic flux produced by circuits external to the plasma (central solenoid, poloidal-field coils, in-vessel coils, passive structures, and eddy currents), with the average taken over the plasma poloidal cross-section weighted by the local toroidal current density. The plasma self-flux is excluded.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux generated by all conductors external to the plasma, averaged over the plasma cross-section using the local toroidal current density as the weighting function. External sources comprise the central solenoid, poloidal-field coils, in-vessel coils, passive conducting structures, and induced eddy currents; the flux produced by the plasma current itself is not included. The qualifier refers to the poloidal magnetic flux being current-weighted by the toroidal current density, not to a poloidal-current weighting.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the average over a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system is defined as the toroidal-current-density-weighted integral of the external flux divided by the total plasma current:

$$
\langle \psi_\mathrm{ext} \rangle = \frac{\int_{\Omega_p} \psi_\mathrm{ext}(R,Z)\, j_\phi(R,Z)\, dR\, dZ}{I_p}
$$

where $\Omega_p$ is the plasma poloidal cross-section in the $(R,Z)$ plane, $R$ is the major radius in meters, $Z$ is the vertical height in meters, $\psi_\mathrm{ext}$ is the external poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal current-density component in A m$^{-2}$, and $I_p = \int_{\Omega_p} j_\phi\, dR\, dZ$ is the signed total plasma current in A. The quantity is meaningful only when $I_p$ is nonzero.

In practice it is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating the poloidal flux contribution of all external circuits across the plasma cross-section and combining it with the reconstructed toroidal current-density distribution. It characterizes how externally produced flux links the current-carrying plasma region and is used in flux-consumption and loop-voltage analyzes; its time derivative is the externally driven contribution to the loop voltage seen by the plasma current channel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the external-circuit vertical magnetic field threading the horizontal flux disks that define $\psi_\mathrm{ext}$ points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Signed projection of the poloidal magnetic field at a specified constraint position onto the local poloidal sensitive direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic field at a constraint position is the signed component of the magnetic field in the meridional $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, evaluated at a specified spatial point. It is a direction-resolved form of poloidal_magnetic_field: the [radial_magnetic_field](name:radial_magnetic_field) and vertical component contribute to it, while the [toroidal_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field) is excluded.

The defining projection is

$$
B_{\mathrm{pol},c} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pol}}(R_c,\phi_c,Z_c)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{\mathrm{pol},c} = B_R(R_c,\phi_c,Z_c)s_R + B_Z(R_c,\phi_c,Z_c)s_Z
$$

where $(R_c,\phi_c,Z_c)$ is the constraint position, with $R_c$ and $Z_c$ in meters and $\phi_c$ in radians; $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pol}}=B_R\hat{R}+B_Z\hat{Z}$ is the local poloidal magnetic-field vector in tesla; and $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{\mathrm{pol},c}=s_R\hat{R}+s_Z\hat{Z}$ is the dimensionless unit vector defining the positive local sensitive direction in the poloidal plane. For axisymmetric equilibria the field components do not depend on $\phi_c$, but the point and the sensitive direction still define the signed scalar value.

In equilibrium calculations, $B_R$ and $B_Z$ may be obtained from a poloidal magnetic-flux function $\psi(R,Z)$. The relations $B_R=-(1/R)\partial\psi/\partial Z$ and $B_Z=(1/R)\partial\psi/\partial R$ assume the Grad-Shafranov flux normalization in which $\psi$ is the poloidal flux per radian, commonly reported in Wb because the radian is dimensionless; if a full $2\pi$ flux convention is used, the corresponding $1/(2\pi R)$ factor must be included. Only derivatives of $\psi$ enter, so an additive reference such as [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) does not change the field.

The quantity is obtained by evaluating a magnetic-field model at the constraint position and projecting it onto the specified sensitive direction, or by calibrating a local magnetic probe whose orientation defines that direction. Calibration sets the scale in tesla and the positive orientation, while geometric alignment determines the coefficients $s_R$ and $s_Z$.

Representative absolute magnitudes for tokamak wall or near-wall magnetic constraints are strongly device- and position-dependent, often spanning roughly 0.001-0.3 T. The value depends on distance from plasma and coils, enclosed toroidal current, plasma shape, and the chosen sensitive direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local poloidal magnetic field points along the chosen local poloidal sensitive direction at the constraint position.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Total magnetic flux threading a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis, serving as the canonical radial coordinate for labeling nested flux surfaces in axisymmetric plasma equilibria.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ is the total magnetic flux threading a horizontal disk of major radius $R$, centered on the toroidal symmetry axis at height $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Because $\psi$ is constant on each nested magnetic-flux surface in an axisymmetric equilibrium, it provides the natural radial coordinate for plasma profiles and equilibrium analysis, ranging from [the magnetic-axis value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) to the last-closed-flux-surface boundary.

The defining integral is:

$$
\psi(R, Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R', Z) \, 2\pi R' \, dR'
$$

where $B_Z$ is the vertical component of the magnetic field and $R'$ integrates from the symmetry axis to major radius $R$. In MHD equilibrium, $\psi$ satisfies the Grad-Shafranov equation and all equilibrium quantities — plasma pressure $p(\psi)$ and the toroidal-field function $F(\psi) = R B_\phi$ — are functions of $\psi$ alone. The [gradient of the poloidal flux](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux) determines the local poloidal-field strength, and the [time derivative](name:time_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux) is related to the inductive electric field by Faraday's law.

Evaluated at specific flux surfaces, $\psi$ serves as a coordinate label; sampled values such as [the pedestal value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_pedestal) provide reference points for normalized flux coordinates. The profile is recovered from external magnetic measurements — flux loop signals, pickup coil voltages, and Rogowski-integrated coil currents — through MHD equilibrium reconstruction, supplemented by internal constraints from motional Stark effect polarimetry where available.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net vertical magnetic field $B_Z$ threading the horizontal integration disk points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated on a specified closed magnetic flux surface in an axisymmetric equilibrium. It is constant over that surface and labels its radial position between the magnetic axis and the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at a flux surface is the value of the equilibrium flux function on one specified closed magnetic surface. In an axisymmetric equilibrium, nested surfaces of constant poloidal magnetic flux provide the natural radial labeling of the confined plasma between the magnetic axis and the plasma boundary.

Using the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, a flux-surface value can be defined by evaluating the disk flux at any point $(R_s, Z_s)$ on that surface:

$$
\psi_s = \psi(R_s, Z_s) = \int_0^{R_s} B_Z(R', Z_s)\, 2\pi R'\, dR'
$$

where $\psi_s$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the selected surface in Wb, $R'$ and $R_s$ are major radii in m, $Z_s$ is vertical position in m, and $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component in T. The disk is centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and lies in the horizontal plane $Z=Z_s$.

The disk integral fixes one possible additive reference by assigning zero flux at $R=0$ for that height. Equilibrium flux functions are otherwise meaningful only up to a common additive constant: the same offset must be used for $\psi_s$, the [magnetic-axis value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and the [plasma-boundary value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary). With this common reference, the normalized poloidal flux is $(\psi_s-\psi_0)/(\psi_b-\psi_0)$, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and to the [boundary normalization](name:normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) at the plasma boundary.

In practice, $\psi_s$ is obtained from an axisymmetric equilibrium reconstruction or forward equilibrium calculation. The selected surface is identified as a contour of the reconstructed poloidal magnetic flux function; because the flux is constant on that contour, the evaluated value is independent of which point on the surface is used, within reconstruction accuracy.

Because the additive constant is arbitrary, the meaningful scale is usually a flux difference. Typical absolute differences $|\psi_s-\psi_0|$ are about 0.01-1 Wb in small tokamaks and 1-20 Wb in medium to large tokamaks, depending on the selected surface, plasma current, magnetic field strength, and plasma shape.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ on the horizontal integration disk points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the value of the equilibrium flux function at the innermost closed-flux-surface point where its gradient vanishes. It provides the inner reference for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis, $\psi_0$, is the value of the equilibrium poloidal-flux function at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the nested closed-flux-surface family where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It is an extremal reference value for radial flux labeling; the absolute offset of $\psi$ is gage dependent, so physically meaningful radial labels use flux differences such as $\psi - \psi_0$.

The dimensionless normalized poloidal flux coordinate anchored at the axis is commonly defined by:

$$
\psi_N = \frac{\psi - \psi_0}{\psi_b - \psi_0}
$$

where $\psi_N$ is dimensionless, $\psi$ is the local poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $\psi_0$ is the magnetic-axis value in Wb, and $\psi_b$ is the plasma-boundary value in Wb from [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary). With this normalization, $\psi_N = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\psi_N = 1$ at the plasma boundary, matching [normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary).

Equilibrium reconstruction obtains $\psi_0$ by locating the extremum of the reconstructed poloidal-flux map inside the last closed flux surface. The same axis reference is used when interpreting flux values at internal features such as an [internal transport barrier](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_internal_transport_barrier), a [secondary separatrix](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_secondary_separatrix), or a pedestal position expressed by [normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).

Because an additive gage can be chosen for $\psi$, a universal absolute range for $\psi_0$ is not physically meaningful; many equilibria set the axis value to 0 Wb. The physically relevant separation $|\psi_b - \psi_0|$ is often 0.1-10 Wb in small and medium tokamaks and 10-100 Wb in large high-current plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\psi$ increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux on the closed flux surface where the safety factor profile attains its minimum value. It is a dimensional flux given in webers that labels that surface, not the dimensionless normalized flux coordinate of the same surface.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor is the value of the poloidal magnetic flux on the closed flux surface where the safety factor profile reaches its minimum. It provides an absolute, dimensional flux label (in webers) for that surface, as opposed to the dimensionless normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the same surface.

The quantity is defined by selecting the flux surface that minimizes the safety factor and reading off its poloidal flux:

$$
\psi_{q_{\min}} = \psi(\chi_\ast), \qquad \chi_\ast \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\chi \in \mathcal{D}} q(\chi)
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $q$ is the dimensionless safety factor, $\chi$ is any monotonic label ordering the nested closed flux surfaces of the domain $\mathcal{D}$, and $\chi_\ast$ labels a surface on which $q = q_\mathrm{min}$. The argmin form makes no assumption that the minimum is an interior extremum: it may occur at the magnetic axis, at an interior surface, or near the plasma boundary. The poloidal flux itself is the magnetic flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis, $\psi(R,Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'$, and is defined only up to an arbitrary additive gage constant; only flux differences (for example relative to the magnetic axis or boundary) are physically meaningful.

In practice the quantity is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating $q$ over the nested closed flux surfaces, identifying the surface that attains $q_\mathrm{min}$, and interpolating the corresponding $\psi$ value. The same surface can be expressed in dimensionless form by [normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor) via a normalization such as $\psi_N = (\psi - \psi_\mathrm{axis})/(\psi_\mathrm{boundary} - \psi_\mathrm{axis})$, where $\psi_\mathrm{axis}$ and $\psi_\mathrm{boundary}$ are the magnetic-axis and boundary fluxes; this removes the gage ambiguity inherent in the dimensional value.

Typical magnitudes scale with device size, plasma current, toroidal field, and the gage chosen for $\psi$, so absolute values are reported as flux differences from the magnetic axis. Monotonic-shear equilibria place the minimum at or near the magnetic axis, while reversed-shear configurations move it to mid-radius or farther out.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux through the enclosed horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis is oriented along $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the value of the axisymmetric equilibrium flux function on the last closed flux surface. It is paired with the magnetic-axis flux to define normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary, denoted $\psi_b$, is the value of the equilibrium poloidal-flux function on the last closed flux surface (LCFS), the outermost closed magnetic surface enclosing confined plasma. In diverted configurations the LCFS passes through an X-point; in limited configurations it contacts the limiter. This boundary value is the outer endpoint paired with [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) for flux-coordinate normalization.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the poloidal magnetic flux at a boundary point can be written as the flux of the vertical magnetic-field component through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system:

$$
\psi_b = \int_0^{R_b} B_Z(R', Z_b)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component in tesla, $R_b$ and $Z_b$ are the coordinates of a point on the LCFS, and $R'$ is the integration radius. In an exact axisymmetric equilibrium, $\psi$ is constant on the LCFS, so any point on that surface gives the same boundary value; the resulting $\psi_b$ is in webers.

This quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by determining the poloidal-flux function and locating its outermost closed contour. Together with the axis value $\psi_0$, it defines the [normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) through the endpoint relation $\psi_N=(\psi-\psi_0)/(\psi_b-\psi_0)$, so that the magnetic axis maps to 0 and the plasma boundary maps to 1.

Typical absolute magnitudes are 0.1-5 Wb in small to medium tokamaks and several to tens of Wb in large, high-current devices, depending mainly on plasma current, toroidal magnetic field, and plasma size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ on the horizontal integration disk is directed in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_secondary_separatrix
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux at the secondary separatrix is the value of the equilibrium poloidal flux function on the flux surface that passes through the secondary X-point. It distinguishes the secondary separatrix from the primary separatrix in double-null, near-double-null, or snowflake magnetic topologies.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the secondary separatrix, denoted $\psi_\mathrm{sec}$, is the value of the equilibrium poloidal flux function on the flux surface passing through the secondary X-point. The secondary X-point is a saddle of $\psi$ distinct from the primary X-point. Flux differences relative to the magnetic axis, plasma boundary, or primary separatrix carry the physical information because the absolute value of $\psi$ includes an arbitrary additive reference.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters, radial differences of the flux function at fixed $Z$ are determined by the vertical magnetic field:

$$
\psi(R_2,Z)-\psi(R_1,Z) = \int_{R_1}^{R_2} B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi$ is in Wb, $R_1$, $R_2$, and $R'$ are major radii in meters, and $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component in tesla. This relation fixes flux differences; an additive reference such as the [magnetic-axis value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) is chosen separately.

In practice, $\psi_\mathrm{sec}$ is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction or magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium calculation by locating X-points as saddle points of $\psi$ in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. After the primary X-point and associated [plasma-boundary flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) are identified, the distinct secondary saddle gives the secondary separatrix value. In an exactly balanced double-null configuration, the primary and secondary separatrix flux values coincide; otherwise their difference is the flux width of the inter-separatrix region. The related [normalized boundary flux label](name:normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) is formed from the magnetic-axis and boundary flux values, and the secondary separatrix can be compared using the same normalization.

Typical reported values are strongly affected by device size and by the chosen additive reference. With the magnetic-axis value used as the zero reference, separatrix flux values are commonly of the order of the axis-to-boundary flux span, about 0.1-100 Wb across tokamak-scale equilibria; the primary-secondary separation in near-balanced configurations is usually much smaller than that span.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical magnetic field contributing to a positive radial flux increment is directed along $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at the physical attachment point of a flux-loop sensor. It is the local value of the equilibrium flux function at that position, using the same additive reference offset as the global poloidal-flux definition.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment point is the value of the equilibrium [poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) function at the physical point where a flux-loop conductor is fixed to the vessel or support structure. For axisymmetric interpretation, the flux function is independent of toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, so the point value is determined by major radius and vertical height. The absolute value is meaningful only with the same additive reference offset as the equilibrium flux function; flux differences relative to the magnetic axis or another reference surface are independent of that offset.

The point value is the evaluation of the flux function at the sensor attachment coordinates:

$$
\psi_\mathrm{sensor} = \psi(R_s, Z_s)
$$

where $\psi_\mathrm{sensor}$ is the sensor-attachment-point poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $\psi(R,Z)$ is the equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $R_s$ is the attachment-point major radius in m, and $Z_s$ is the attachment-point vertical height in m, all in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Flux loops measure the voltage induced by a changing magnetic flux; time integration with calibration gives a flux signal that can be compared with the local equilibrium value at the attachment point. This localized interpretation assumes that the loop geometry and the axisymmetric equilibrium allow the measured signal to be represented by a point evaluation; the corresponding whole-loop observable is described by [poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux). When the attachment point is associated with a reconstructed flux contour, the value can also be related to [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface).

Typical absolute values depend strongly on device size, plasma current, toroidal field, sensor location, and the chosen reference offset. Flux differences relevant to vessel-mounted loops are commonly 0.01-5 Wb in small and medium devices and 1-50 Wb in large tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\psi$ increases outward from the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short: Product F dF/dpsi of the poloidal current function F = R B_phi, with R and B_phi defined in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, and its derivative with respect to poloidal magnetic flux psi. It is the toroidal-field-gradient contribution to the flux-function source in the Grad-Shafranov equation.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is $F\,dF/d\psi$, the product of the poloidal current function and its derivative with respect to the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$. In an axisymmetric equilibrium, $F=R B_\phi$ is a flux-surface function representing the toroidal magnetic-field contribution in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The product measures how the toroidal-field contribution changes between magnetic flux surfaces.

The defining relation is

$$
Q_F(\psi) = F(\psi)\frac{dF}{d\psi}
$$

where $Q_F$ denotes this quantity, $F=R B_\phi$ has units $\mathrm{m\,T}$, $R$ is major radius in $\mathrm{m}$, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component in $\mathrm{T}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux in $\mathrm{Wb}$, $dF/d\psi$ has units $\mathrm{m\,T\,Wb^{-1}}$, and $Q_F$ has units $\mathrm{m^2\,T^2\,Wb^{-1}}$. Equivalently, $Q_F=(1/2)d(F^2)/d\psi$.

In the SI Grad-Shafranov force-balance equation, $F\,dF/d\psi$ appears alongside the pressure-gradient contribution $\mu_0 R^2 dp/d\psi$ in $\Delta^*\psi = -\mu_0 R^2 dp/d\psi - F\,dF/d\psi$, where $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $p$ is scalar pressure, and $\Delta^*$ is the Grad-Shafranov elliptic operator. Through $\mu_0 R j_\phi=-\Delta^*\psi$, these terms determine the $R$-weighted toroidal current density $Rj_\phi$; this magnetic term is therefore related to, but not identical to, the direct toroidal-current source quantity.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by reconstructing an axisymmetric equilibrium, representing $F$ as a smooth function of $\psi$ on nested magnetic surfaces, and differentiating with respect to $\psi$. Because numerical differentiation can amplify noise, smoothing and consistency with the reconstructed pressure gradient and toroidal current density are important when interpreting it.

Typical values are close to 0 m^2.T^2.Wb^-1 when $F$ is nearly constant across the confined plasma. Medium-size tokamak equilibria often have absolute values of 0.01-5 m^2.T^2.Wb^-1, while high-field or strong-gradient cases can reach 10-50 m^2.T^2.Wb^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $F^2=(R B_\phi)^2$ increases with increasing poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) coordinate of the active limiter contact point, where the outermost closed flux surface of a limited plasma makes tangential contact with the limiter surface.
NAMES.long:
The active limiter point is the specific location on the limiter surface where the last closed flux surface of a limited plasma makes tangential contact with the physical wall. The radial coordinate $R_{\rm lim}$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to that contact point, measured in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ increases outward from the symmetry axis.

In limited plasma configurations, this coordinate defines the radial extent of the confined plasma region and serves as a primary geometric constraint in equilibrium reconstruction. Reconstruction procedures reconcile external magnetic measurements with the known limiter geometry to identify the tangency point of the last closed flux surface on the limiter.

Typical values range from 0.5 m to 8 m across current and planned tokamak devices, spanning the full scale from small research machines to ITER-class reactors. The [radial_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point](name:radial_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point) gives the major radius of the nearest wall location for gap calculations, while [gap_at_plasma_boundary](name:gap_at_plasma_boundary) expresses the signed separation between the plasma boundary and the wall at prescribed reference points.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_{\rm lim}$ is measured radially outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the $+\hat{R}$ direction.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_current_center
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) of the plasma current centroid, defined as the first moment of the toroidal current density distribution over the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate of the current center identifies the major radius at which the plasma toroidal current density is effectively concentrated, treating the distributed toroidal current as a weighted ensemble whose centroid is obtained from the first spatial moment of $j_\phi$ over the poloidal cross-section.

The current center major radius is formally defined as:

$$
R_{\mathrm{cc}} = \frac{\iint j_\phi(R, Z)\, R\, dR\, dZ}{\iint j_\phi(R, Z)\, dR\, dZ}
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma current density and the integrals span the confined plasma cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis.

This global scalar is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic diagnostics, and is sensitive to the radial peaking and any off-axis structure of the current profile. It is conceptually distinct from the [radial coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), which is located at the extremum of the poloidal flux function, and from the [radial coordinate of the geometric axis](name:radial_coordinate_of_geometric_axis), which is determined purely by the plasma boundary shape. In conventional H-mode discharges the current center lies close to the magnetic axis, but can shift outward during off-axis current drive or inward during peaked current profiles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current centroid is located at a nonzero major radius $R$ from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_dr_dz_zero_point
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the point on a plasma boundary or flux surface where dR/dZ = 0, locating the inboard or outboard midplane extremity of the contour in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long:
The dR/dZ = 0 point marks the poloidal location on a plasma boundary or flux-surface contour in the poloidal cross-section where the boundary tangent is vertical — equivalently, where the major radius $R$ reaches a local extremum as the height $Z$ varies along the contour. For a convex, simply connected tokamak boundary, two such points exist per flux surface: the outboard (maximum $R$) and inboard (minimum $R$) extremes, both situated near the magnetic midplane.

The defining geometric condition is

$$\left.\frac{dR}{dZ}\right|_{\text{contour}} = 0$$

where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle.

This coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by numerically locating the $R$ extremum on the reconstructed last-closed flux surface or separatrix contour. It provides a compact boundary-shape descriptor complementary to the X-point geometry described by [radial_coordinate_of_x_point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point), and is geometrically paired with its vertical counterpart [vertical_coordinate_of_dr_dz_zero_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_dr_dz_zero_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the dR/dZ = 0 point lies at a positive major radius measured outward from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, which is satisfied everywhere in the plasma-accessible region where $R > 0$.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the plasma geometric axis, defined as the midpoint between the maximum and minimum radial extents of the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The geometric axis of the plasma cross-section marks the horizontal center of the outermost closed flux surface boundary, providing a fundamental reference for characterizing plasma shape and radial position. It is distinct from the [magnetic axis](name:radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), which is the point of extremal poloidal magnetic flux; the separation between the two radial positions quantifies the Shafranov shift, an inward displacement of the flux surfaces toward the high-field side driven by finite plasma pressure and toroidal current.

The radial coordinate of the geometric axis is defined using the plasma boundary extrema:

$$
R_{\rm geom} = \frac{R_{\rm max} + R_{\rm min}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\rm max}$ and $R_{\rm min}$ are the outermost and innermost major radii of the plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ measured from the toroidal symmetry axis.

This coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by tracing the plasma boundary contour or separatrix. Typical values range from 1.5–3.5 m for medium-sized tokamaks and approach 6 m for large devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_{\rm geom}$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; major radius coordinates are non-negative for any physical plasma location.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Major radius R of the magnetic axis, the singular point in the poloidal cross-section where the poloidal magnetic field vanishes and all nested magnetic flux surfaces converge.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic axis is the topological center of the nested magnetic flux surfaces in the plasma — the unique locus in the poloidal cross-section where the poloidal magnetic field $B_p = 0$ and the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ attains its on-axis extremum. The radial coordinate $R_\mathrm{axis}$ locates this axis along the major-radial direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.

This coordinate enters the definition of the plasma minor radius $a$ and the inverse aspect ratio $\epsilon = a / R_\mathrm{axis}$, where $a$ is the plasma half-width. It differs from the [geometric axis major radius](name:radial_coordinate_of_geometric_axis) $R_\mathrm{geom} = (R_\mathrm{max} + R_\mathrm{min})/2$; the outward displacement $R_\mathrm{axis} - R_\mathrm{geom}$ is the Shafranov shift, which is positive under finite plasma pressure. The [radial coordinate of the X-point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point) is a related equilibrium position marker defined at the poloidal-field null on the separatrix rather than at the flux-surface center.

The magnetic axis position is determined from equilibrium reconstruction, combining external magnetic measurements with pressure and current profile information. Typical values range from about 0.6 m in small tokamaks to approximately 1.65 m in JET-scale devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_\mathrm{axis}$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, as holds for all physical plasma configurations.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Major radius R of a magnetic strike point, where the plasma separatrix intersects a divertor target or first-wall surface in the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
A strike point is the location in the poloidal cross-section where the plasma separatrix — or, in double-null and snowflake configurations, the secondary separatrix — contacts a material target surface such as a divertor tile or limiter wall. Its major-radius coordinate $R$ is measured perpendicularly from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R > 0$ by construction.

The radial position of the strike point governs the spatial distribution of the parallel heat flux deposited on the divertor target and is central to power exhaust management. The separatrix is the flux surface threading the magnetic X-point; the strike point is where this surface meets the first-wall geometry. For reference, the [radial_coordinate_of_x_point](name:radial_coordinate_of_x_point) locates the null of the poloidal field from which the separatrix originates, while the [radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis](name:radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis) marks the innermost reference. In double-null configurations, primary and secondary separatrices produce distinct inner and outer strike points whose $R$ coordinates differ and whose relative positions affect the heat-load sharing between divertor legs.

The strike-point radial coordinate is inferred during equilibrium reconstruction, with constraints supplied by Langmuir probe signals, infrared thermography of divertor tiles, or other plasma-facing-component diagnostics that detect the plasma-wall contact location. It also serves as a real-time position-control target during divertor operation.

Typical major-radius values range from approximately 1.0–1.5 m on the inner divertor to 1.8–2.5 m on the outer divertor in medium-sized tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ is directed outward from the toroidal symmetry axis, consistent with all major-radius coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Major radius R coordinate of the magnetic X-point, the null of the poloidal magnetic field at which the separatrix forms and the confined plasma meets the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The X-point is the location in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane where the poloidal magnetic field vanishes, creating the degenerate separatrix topology that separates the closed-field-line confined plasma region from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. Its radial coordinate $R_X$ is the major-radius distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to this null, measured in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is the horizontal distance from the machine symmetry axis.

The null condition defining the X-point is:

$$
\left.\nabla\psi\right|_{(R_X,\, Z_X)} = 0
$$

where $\psi(R, Z)$ is the poloidal magnetic flux function and $Z_X$ is the companion vertical X-point coordinate.

The X-point location is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic diagnostics including flux loops, Rogowski coils, and magnetic pickup probes. The X-point radial position is displaced from the [radial coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:radial_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis) by an amount that reflects the poloidal asymmetry of the diverted plasma configuration; in single-null geometries, $R_X$ shifts inboard or outboard depending on the divertor target orientation and plasma shaping. The [current center radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate_of_current_center) provides a complementary moment-based measure of the current distribution centroid, distinct from the X-point null.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the X-point lies outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Projection of the magnetic field vector onto the outward major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, forming the radial part of the poloidal field in tokamak geometry.
NAMES.long:
The radial magnetic field $B_R = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{R}$ is the component of the magnetic induction resolved along $\hat{R}$, the unit vector pointing away from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In an axisymmetric tokamak equilibrium, $B_R$ is entirely a poloidal-field quantity and is generally much smaller in magnitude than the dominant toroidal component; it encodes information about flux-surface shape and poloidal field structure.

In axisymmetric equilibrium, $B_R$ is related to the poloidal magnetic flux function $\psi(R, Z)$ by:

$$
B_R = -\frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial Z}
$$

where $R$ is the major radius in meters and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate in meters. Together with $B_Z = \frac{1}{R}\partial\psi/\partial R$, this satisfies the solenoidal constraint $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0$ in axisymmetric form. The companion [parallel_magnetic_field](name:parallel_magnetic_field) gives the field-aligned projection, while [radial_magnetic_vector_potential](name:radial_magnetic_vector_potential) provides the corresponding vector-potential component in the same radial direction.

$B_R$ is obtained by differentiating the reconstructed poloidal flux on a computational grid, or evaluated directly on generalized geometry description grids for complex wall and boundary regions. Magnitudes in the core plasma are typically 0.001–0.1 T, increasing near the X-point and divertor where the poloidal field changes direction rapidly.
