NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_R$ points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, away from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Radial component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the magnetic-flux-density-equivalent magnetization of an iron core segment. It equals the permeability of free space times the textbook radial magnetization component, so it is expressed in tesla rather than amperes per meter.
NAMES.long:
Radial magnetization of an iron core segment is the radial component of the segment magnetization vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height. The documented quantity is the magnetic-flux-density-equivalent component, equal to the permeability of free space times the textbook magnetization component, so it is expressed in tesla rather than amperes per meter.

The conversion from the textbook material magnetization to this iron-core quantity is

$$
M_R = \mu_0\,\mathbf{M}\cdot\hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{M}$ is the material magnetization vector in A/m, $\hat{R}$ is the outward radial unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m/A is the permeability of free space.

In equilibrium analysis, this quantity is inferred from magnetic measurements together with a ferromagnetic model of the iron core. The segment model treats the magnetization as uniform within each iron segment, while the fitted value can depend on nonlinear permeability, hysteresis, remanent magnetization, demagnetization effects, and the approach to magnetic saturation.

Typical values range from near 0 T in weakly magnetized or demagnetized regions to about 1.5-2.2 T in magnitude near saturation in soft iron. The radial component may be much smaller than the total magnetization if the material is magnetized mainly in another direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetization vector has a component in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, outward from the toroidal symmetry axis, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Radial (R) component of the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic field in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, representing toroidally non-uniform perturbations from error fields, resonant magnetic perturbations, and finite coil effects.
NAMES.long:
The radial non-axisymmetric magnetic field $B_R^{\rm na}$ is the $\hat{R}$-projection of the vacuum magnetic-field perturbation that breaks toroidal symmetry, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. Physical sources include geometric imperfections in coil placement (error fields), current-lead feeds, and deliberately applied non-axisymmetric coil currents such as resonant magnetic perturbations (RMPs) used for ELM suppression and error-field correction.

The field is defined by subtracting the toroidally averaged axisymmetric radial component from the full three-dimensional vacuum radial field:

$$
B_R^{\rm na}(R, \phi, Z) = B_R(R, \phi, Z) - \langle B_R \rangle_\phi(R, Z)
$$

where $\langle B_R \rangle_\phi$ denotes the average over toroidal angle $\phi$ at fixed $(R, Z)$.

This component is computed from three-dimensional vacuum field calculations using Biot-Savart integration over all non-axisymmetric coil elements, and evaluated on spatial field maps or at control surface points for error-field identification and feedback-correction algorithms. Together with [vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field) and [toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), it provides the complete cylindrical decomposition of the non-axisymmetric vacuum field; non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field_at_control_surface gives the corresponding surface-normal projection. Typical perturbation amplitudes for RMP and error-field applications range from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-2}$ T in medium- to large-scale tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_R$ points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, away from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: rotational_transform
NAMES.short: Rotational transform is the average poloidal winding of a magnetic field line for each toroidal circuit on a magnetic flux surface. It is dimensionless and equals the inverse of the safety factor.
NAMES.long:
Rotational transform $\iota$ characterizes the helical pitch of magnetic field lines on a magnetic flux surface. It gives the average number of poloidal turns made by a field line during one toroidal turn and is related to the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) by $\iota = 1/q$.

In straight-field-line flux coordinates $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$, where $\psi$ labels the flux surface, $\theta$ is a poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height, the field-line equation is:

$$
\frac{d\theta}{d\phi} = \iota(\psi)
$$

where $d\theta/d\phi$ is evaluated along a magnetic field line on the flux surface labeled by $\psi$. Rational values such as $\iota = m/n$ mark surfaces where a field line closes after $n$ toroidal circuits and $m$ poloidal circuits, making them important for resonant magnetic perturbations and island formation.

In tokamak equilibria, rotational transform is obtained from magnetic equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements and, when available, internal constraints on magnetic pitch. In stellarators and other three-dimensional configurations, it is commonly computed from equilibrium calculations or magnetic field-line tracing.

Typical magnitudes in tokamak plasmas range from about 0.2-1, with edge values near $\iota = 0.2$-$0.33$ corresponding to $q = 3$-$5$. Stellarator configurations commonly use values around 0.3-1.5, depending on magnetic geometry and the intended avoidance or placement of low-order rational surfaces.

NAMES.name: squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient for nested magnetic flux surfaces, measuring corner deviation from a reference ellipse; positive values indicate a boxy super-elliptical shape and negative values a concave diamond-like shape.
NAMES.long:
The squareness of a flux surface is a dimensionless geometric shape parameter, following Luce (Plasma Phys. Control. Fusion 55, 095009, 2013), that characterizes the corner geometry of nested poloidal cross-sections. The coefficient $\zeta$ quantifies the deviation of each quadrant of the flux-surface contour from a co-centered reference ellipse: $\zeta > 0$ corresponds to a super-elliptical (boxy) corner that bulges outward relative to the reference ellipse, while $\zeta < 0$ characterizes a sub-elliptical (diamond-like or concave) corner.

Resolved by machine side, this general quantity separates into [inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), capturing the high-field-side (inboard) corners, and [outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), capturing the low-field-side (outboard) corners. A finer decomposition into four independent quadrant coefficients is available through dedicated names such as [upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface).

Squareness profiles are determined from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting a parameterized boundary shape to magnetic diagnostic measurements. Typical magnitudes range from approximately $-0.5$ to $+0.5$ in tokamak operation; the sign and spatial distribution of corner squareness influence edge stability margins and divertor geometry. The quantity complements [elongation_of_flux_surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface) and the general coefficient_of_flux_surface in the complete parameterization of nested flux-surface geometry.

NAMES.name: inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient quantifying how much the high-field-side (inner) corners of a nested magnetic flux surface deviate from a reference ellipse; positive values indicate a boxier corner, negative values a more diamond-like or indented corner.
NAMES.long:
The inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how much the high-field-side (inboard, smaller major radius) corners of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface depart from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the inboard counterpart within the [squareness_of_flux_surface](name:squareness_of_flux_surface) family, complementing the outboard variants [upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface). This parent quantity abstracts over the quadrant-resolved coefficients [upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), which independently describe the upper and lower high-field-side corners.

The coefficient $\zeta$ enters the parametric flux-surface shape model as an additional harmonic beyond elongation $\kappa$ and triangularity $\delta$, evaluated at the high-field-side corners of the poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. A value of zero recovers the reference ellipse precisely; deviations capture corner shaping not expressible through $\kappa$ and $\delta$ alone.

The inner squareness is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting closed flux-surface contours to a multi-parameter shape model. Asymmetry between upper and lower inner quadrants can arise in vertically asymmetric or diverted configurations, motivating the quadrant-resolved child quantities.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the high-field-side corner of the flux-surface cross-section extends outward beyond the reference ellipse (boxy shape); negative when the corner is indented inward relative to the reference ellipse (diamond-like shape).

NAMES.name: lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce squareness coefficient zeta_li for the lower high-field-side quadrant of a nested magnetic flux surface, relative to a reference ellipse with the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation. It quantifies the quadrant's non-elliptical flattening, boxiness, or indentation.
NAMES.long:
Lower inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce coefficient $\zeta_\mathrm{li}$ for the quadrant that is both on the high-field side and below the flux-surface center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The qualifier lower is relative to the surface center, not to an absolute condition such as $Z<0$. The reference shape is an ellipse with the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation as the flux surface; the coefficient measures the residual non-elliptical deformation of that quadrant.

In the Luce quadrant construction, the signed departure from the reference ellipse may be written as

$$
\Delta_\perp(\theta) = a\,\zeta_\mathrm{li}\,\sin^2(2\theta)
$$

where $\Delta_\perp(\theta)$ is the normal displacement from the reference ellipse to the flux surface in meters, positive along the outward normal of the ellipse, $a$ is the horizontal half-width in meters, $\zeta_\mathrm{li}$ is dimensionless, and $\theta$ is a dimensionless parametric segment angle in radians. For the lower-inner segment, $\theta$ runs from the inner midplane point to the lower vertical extremum; the reference ellipse has center $(R_c,Z_c)$ in meters, horizontal half-width $a$ in meters, and dimensionless elongation $\kappa$, and may be written on this segment as $R_\mathrm{ell}=R_c-a\cos\theta$ and $Z_\mathrm{ell}=Z_c-\kappa a\sin\theta$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. A zero coefficient corresponds to an exactly elliptical lower-inner quadrant for this reference ellipse.

The coefficient is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction by tracing the selected nested flux surface, determining its center, horizontal half-width, and elongation, constructing the reference ellipse, and fitting the Luce form over only the lower-inner segment. It separates local boxiness or indentation of the lower high-field-side quadrant from global elongation and triangularity.

Typical values are close to 0 for nearly elliptical core surfaces, commonly within -0.1 to 0.1. Strongly shaped edge or boundary surfaces often lie within -0.3 to 0.3, with larger magnitudes indicating pronounced local squaring or indentation.

NAMES.name: outer_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce squareness coefficient for the outboard corners of nested magnetic flux surfaces, measuring departure from a co-centered reference ellipse; abstracts over both upper-outer and lower-outer quadrants in the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The outer squareness of a flux surface is the Luce (2013) dimensionless shape coefficient that quantifies how much the outboard (low-field-side, larger-$R$) corners of a poloidal cross-section deviate from a reference ellipse sharing the same geometric center, horizontal half-width, and elongation. It is a component of the [squareness_of_flux_surface](name:squareness_of_flux_surface) family, restricted to the outer ($R > R_\text{geo}$) portion of the cross-section defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Because a flux surface has two outboard corners — one above and one below the magnetic midplane — this quantity generalizes over both: in up-down symmetric equilibria the upper-outer and lower-outer values coincide, whereas in asymmetric configurations (such as single-null divertor plasmas) they differ and are resolved individually as [upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface). The squareness is evaluated at a reference corner angle of approximately $45°$ within each outer quadrant, measuring the signed displacement of the actual flux-surface contour from the reference ellipse normalized by the local ellipse scale.

Outer squareness is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting an analytic shape parameterization to magnetic diagnostic data and extracting the Luce shape coefficients. It complements [upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), which characterize the inboard (high-field-side) corners. Typical magnitudes in H-mode tokamak plasmas satisfy $|\zeta_o| \lesssim 0.2$, with positive values corresponding to box-like protrusions beyond the reference ellipse and negative values to inward-indented, star-shaped cross-sections.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outboard corner of the flux surface extends beyond the reference ellipse (box-like cross-section), and negative when the corner is indented inward relative to the reference ellipse (diamond-like or star-shaped cross-section).

NAMES.name: lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce squareness coefficient for the lower outer quadrant of each flux surface, measuring the deviation of that corner from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation.
NAMES.long:
The lower outer squareness $\zeta_{lo}$ is the quadrant-specific Luce (2013) shape parameter describing how the lower outboard corner of a poloidal flux-surface cross-section departs from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width $a$, and elongation $\kappa$. As one of four independent corner squareness coefficients, it captures asymmetries — both up-down and in-out — that a single symmetric squareness value cannot resolve.

In the Luce parametric form, the lower outer quadrant shape is governed by:

$$
Z(\theta) = Z_0 + a\,\kappa\sin\!\bigl(\theta + \zeta_{lo}\sin 2\theta\bigr)
$$

where $\theta \in (-\pi/2,\,0)$ parameterizes the lower outer quadrant, $Z_0$ is the geometric center height of the flux surface, $a$ is the horizontal minor half-width, and $\kappa$ is the local [elongation_of_flux_surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). Setting $\zeta_{lo} = 0$ recovers a pure ellipse in that quadrant.

This quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the Luce parametric contour to each nested flux surface computed from magnetics and internal measurements. At the outermost closed flux surface the value reduces to [lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary). The upper-outer analog is [upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), the lower inner counterpart is [lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), and the up-down symmetric outer combination is [outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower outer corner of the flux-surface cross-section bulges outward beyond the reference ellipse, increasing the cross-sectional area of the lower outer quadrant relative to the elliptic baseline.

NAMES.name: squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce squareness coefficient for the plasma boundary, measuring the signed departure of the boundary corners from the reference ellipse defined by the elongation and triangularity shape parameters.
NAMES.long:
The squareness of the plasma boundary is a dimensionless Luce shape coefficient that quantifies how much the corners of the poloidal cross-section depart from the reference ellipse parameterized by size, [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary), and triangularity. A positive value indicates corners that bulge outward beyond the reference ellipse, giving a more rectangular cross-section; a negative value indicates corners that indent inward, producing a more rounded, over-elliptic shape. This general quantity subsumes the [inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) characterizing the high-field-side boundary and the [outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) characterizing the low-field-side corners.

In the Luce boundary parameterization, the squareness $\zeta$ enters as the coefficient of a $\sin(2\theta)$ angular distortion term in the poloidal angle mapping:

$$
\theta_b(\theta) = \theta + \arcsin(\delta)\sin\theta + \zeta\sin(2\theta)
$$

where $\theta$ is the poloidal parameter angle, $\delta$ is the triangularity, and $\theta_b$ is the effective angle determining the boundary coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height. The $\sin(2\theta)$ factor peaks at the corner positions ($\theta = \pi/4, 3\pi/4, 5\pi/4, 7\pi/4$), concentrating the squareness effect at the corners while leaving the outboard midplane and top/bottom extrema unaffected.

The squareness is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the parametric boundary form to measured plasma shape data; quadrant-resolved values are accessible as [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) and [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary). Typical values in shaped tokamak plasmas range from approximately $-0.5$ to $+0.5$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma boundary corner regions lie outside the reference ellipse defined by the elongation and triangularity, corresponding to a more rectangularly squared cross-sectional shape.

NAMES.name: inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce squareness parameter for the inboard (high-field-side) plasma boundary, measuring the departure of the inner corners from the reference ellipse set by minor radius, elongation, and triangularity; parent of the upper-inner and lower-inner quadrant components.
NAMES.long:
The inner squareness of the plasma boundary is the dimensionless Luce shape coefficient quantifying how much the inboard (smaller major-radius) portion of the last-closed flux surface deviates from the reference ellipse determined by the boundary minor radius, the inner-side elongation, and the inner-side triangularity. It is the high-field-side counterpart to the outer squareness and serves as the parent quantity encompassing the quadrant-specific [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) (above-midplane, inboard) and [lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) (below-midplane, inboard).

In the Luce higher-order boundary parameterization, the inboard boundary contour in a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is described by a $\sin(2\theta)$ correction to the standard elliptical shape:

$$
R(\theta) = R_0 - a\cos\!\bigl(\theta + \arcsin(\delta_{\mathrm{i}})\sin\theta - \zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\sin(2\theta)\bigr)
$$

where $R_0$ is the major radius of the magnetic axis, $a$ is the boundary minor radius, $\delta_{\mathrm{i}}$ is the inner triangularity, $\theta$ is the poloidal parametric angle, and $\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}$ is the inner squareness. An analogous form $Z(\theta) = a\kappa_{\mathrm{i}}\sin(\theta + \zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\sin(2\theta))$ governs the vertical extent with inner elongation $\kappa_{\mathrm{i}}$.

This parameter is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the Luce boundary representation to the geometry of the last-closed flux surface. It extends [squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:squareness_of_plasma_boundary) and complements [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) for complete higher-order boundary characterization. Typical values of $\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}$ lie in the range $-0.5$ to $0.5$ for conventional tokamak configurations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the inboard boundary corners are more rectangular than the reference ellipse; negative when the corners are more pointed (diamond-like).

NAMES.name: lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless shape parameter quantifying the deviation of the lower inner quadrant of the plasma cross-section from a reference ellipse, as part of the higher-order Luce boundary parameterization.
NAMES.long:
The lower inner squareness $\zeta_{LI}$ characterizes how much the plasma boundary in the lower inner quadrant — below the equatorial plane and on the high-field inboard side — departs from the reference ellipse defined by the plasma elongation $\kappa$ and triangularity $\delta$. It is a higher-order geometric shape descriptor that refines the plasma boundary representation beyond what elongation and triangularity alone can capture.

In the Luce boundary-shape framework, the plasma cross-section is divided into four quadrants, each assigned an independent squareness coefficient $\zeta$ to represent up-down and inner-outer asymmetries. A value of zero indicates that the boundary in the lower inner quadrant coincides exactly with the local reference ellipse; positive values indicate the boundary extends beyond the ellipse (producing a squarer, more rectangular profile in that quadrant), while negative values indicate the boundary lies inward of the ellipse (a more rounded profile).

This coefficient is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the reconstructed plasma boundary contour — derived primarily from magnetic diagnostics and boundary position measurements — to the higher-order shape parameterization. It is the lower-half counterpart of [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), and together with [lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) and [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), provides the complete quadrant-resolved squareness description of the plasma boundary, complementing the [inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) aggregate.

Typical values in diverted tokamak plasmas range from approximately $-0.4$ to $0.4$, with the sign and magnitude sensitive to X-point position, divertor geometry, and poloidal field coil configuration.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower inner quadrant of the plasma boundary extends outward beyond the reference ellipse, producing a squarer cross-section profile in that region.

NAMES.name: outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient measuring how both outboard (low-field-side) corners of the plasma boundary depart from the reference ellipse defined by minor radius, elongation, and triangularity.
NAMES.long:
The outer squareness of the plasma boundary is the Luce (2013) dimensionless shape coefficient characterizing how the low-field-side (large-$R$) corners of the last-closed flux surface poloidal cross-section depart from the reference ellipse defined by the boundary minor radius $a$, elongation $\kappa$, and triangularity $\delta$. It is the parent quantity for [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) and [lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), which resolve the upper-outboard and lower-outboard corner contributions separately.

A positive outer squareness indicates the outboard corners of the plasma cross-section lie outside the reference ellipse (a more rectangular boundary), while a negative value indicates inward concavity at the outboard corners. The outer squareness is particularly sensitive to X-point geometry and the configuration of low-field-side shaping coils, making it relevant to heat-load distribution and edge stability.

Outer squareness is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the poloidal boundary contour $\{R(\xi), Z(\xi)\}$, where $\xi$ is a poloidal parameter, to external magnetic measurements and internal constraints. The global single-coefficient summary is provided by [squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:squareness_of_plasma_boundary), while the high-field-side corner contributions are captured by [lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) and [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outer boundary corner lies outside the reference ellipse at the corner poloidal angle, i.e., the outboard boundary is displaced toward larger minor radius relative to the inscribed ellipse in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Shape parameter for the lower outer quadrant of the plasma cross-section boundary measuring its deviation from an inscribed ellipse, following the Luce (2013) four-corner squareness decomposition.
NAMES.long:
The lower outer squareness $\zeta_{lo}$ is one of four corner-specific shape parameters in the Luce (2013) plasma boundary parameterization, describing how much the lower outer quadrant of the plasma cross-section boundary deviates from an inscribed ellipse with the same elongation and triangularity. The lower outer quadrant spans the outboard lower region of the cross-section, characterized by increasing major radius $R$ and decreasing height $Z$ from the geometric midplane.

In the Luce framework the boundary near each corner is locally fitted by a superellipse whose exponent $n_{lo}$ controls the corner curvature:

$$
\zeta_{lo} = 1 - \frac{2}{n_{lo}}
$$

where $n_{lo} = 2$ corresponds to a pure ellipse ($\zeta_{lo} = 0$), $n_{lo} > 2$ produces more rectangular corners ($\zeta_{lo} > 0$), and $n_{lo} < 2$ produces more rounded corners ($\zeta_{lo} < 0$). The squareness parameters capture fourth-order boundary shaping effects that are independent of elongation and triangularity.

The squareness parameters are obtained from equilibrium reconstructions by fitting the reconstructed last-closed flux surface or separatrix boundary contour. They are particularly relevant for diverted configurations where divertor geometry shapes the lower boundary region.

Typical values of $\zeta_{lo}$ in tokamak plasmas range from approximately $-0.3$ to $+0.3$. Together with [lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), and [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), it completes the four-corner boundary shape decomposition; the parent quantity [outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) describes outer-quadrant squareness without the upper/lower distinction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower outer quadrant of the boundary protrudes further outward than the ellipse inscribed at the same elongation and triangularity.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Total geometric surface area of a closed toroidal magnetic flux surface, computed by revolving the poloidal boundary contour through the full $2\pi$ toroidal angle around the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The surface area of a magnetic flux surface is the total area of the two-dimensional toroidal shell swept out when a closed poloidal flux contour is revolved through the full toroidal angle. It characterizes the geometric extent of each nested flux surface and enters flux-surface-averaged transport equations as a weighting factor relating cross-field particle and energy fluxes to radial gradients along the flux coordinate.

For an axisymmetric magnetic equilibrium, the surface area of the flux surface at poloidal flux label $\psi$ is:

$$
S(\psi) = 2\pi \oint_{\psi} R \, d\ell_p
$$

where $R$ is the major radius (distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame) and $d\ell_p$ is the arc-length element along the closed poloidal contour at constant $\psi$.

The surface area profile is obtained from magnetic equilibrium reconstruction, which determines the flux-surface geometry across the plasma cross-section as a function of the flux label. This quantity is geometrically distinct from the [cross-sectional area of a flux surface], which is the poloidal area enclosed by the contour rather than the revolving-surface area. The full radial profile of this quantity shares the same physical concept as [area_of_flux_surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface), and its value at the outermost closed flux surface equals flux_surface_area_at_plasma_boundary.

Surface area increases monotonically from near zero at the magnetic axis to a maximum at the plasma boundary, reaching tens of square meters in medium-sized tokamaks and several hundred square meters in large high-field devices.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Full thickness of a rectangular plasma filament cross-section, measured along the in-plane direction normal to the filament's central segment. It is the transverse side length of the rectangle, complementing the tangential length measured along the segment.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of a plasma filament is the full transverse extent of a rectangular (thick-line) filament cross-section, measured in the local plane of the element along the direction normal to the filament's central segment. The central segment lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the local tangential-normal basis is defined within that plane: the tangential direction follows the central segment while the normal direction is the in-plane perpendicular. It is a full side length, not a half-width.

For a rectangular filament cross-section, the cross-sectional area is the product of the two full local side lengths:

$$
A_\mathrm{fil} = L_\mathrm{tan}\, t
$$

where $A_\mathrm{fil}$ is the filament cross-sectional area in $\mathrm{m}^2$, $L_\mathrm{tan}$ is the [tangential length](name:thickness_of_plasma_filament) in $\mathrm{m}$, and $t$ is the thickness in $\mathrm{m}$. When the local tangential and normal directions align with the cylindrical axes, the thickness coincides with either the [width](name:width_of_plasma_filament) (radial $R$-direction extent) or the [height](name:height_of_plasma_filament) (vertical $Z$-direction extent) of the same rectangular cross-section.

In equilibrium filament descriptions, the thickness is set by the chosen local geometric representation of a discrete current-carrying plasma element. For a thick-line element it is specified directly as the rectangle side perpendicular to the central segment.

The value is a non-negative geometric length governed by the spatial resolution and local size of the filament representation. No universal device-independent numerical range applies; it should be interpreted relative to the associated tangential length and to neighboring filament spacing.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_control_surface
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle phi coordinate of points on the control surface used for non-axisymmetric magnetic field analysis, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle $\phi$ identifies the azimuthal position of sample points on the control surface within the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the machine symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. The control surface is a geometric reference surface employed in studies of non-axisymmetric magnetic field distributions — for example, to evaluate boundary conditions or to perform surface integrals of perturbed field components in three-dimensional equilibrium analysis. Each point on the surface is fully specified by its $(R, \phi, Z)$ triplet; this quantity carries the $\phi$ component of that triplet, related to Cartesian coordinates by $x = R\cos\phi$ and $y = R\sin\phi$.

Values span $[0, 2\pi)$ rad for a full toroidal circuit, though a particular control surface may cover only a restricted toroidal arc. The analogous coordinate for diagnostic settings is [toroidal_angle_of_measurement_position](name:toroidal_angle_of_measurement_position), and the same coordinate applied to EC launcher geometry appears as [toroidal_angle_of_launching_position](name:toroidal_angle_of_launching_position).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\phi$ increases in the counter-clockwise direction viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle phi of a generic measurement position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, locating sensors, beams, and diagnostic elements at their installed angular positions around the torus.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle $\phi$ of a measurement position is the angular coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame that locates a diagnostic sensor, beam origin, antenna element, or hardware component at its installed angular position around the device symmetry axis, where $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. It relates to horizontal Cartesian coordinates by $\phi = \arctan(y/x)$, with $\phi = 0$ fixed by the facility reference direction.

This coordinate applies across a wide range of measurement and hardware contexts — including neutron detector apertures, Thomson scattering laser entry points, NBI beamlet group positions, reflectometer channels, charge-exchange spectrometer apertures, and antenna modules — wherever the full angular location of a generic measurement point must be specified in three-dimensional geometry. It is the generic-position variant of the $\phi$-coordinate family; more specific counterparts include [toroidal_angle_of_along_line_of_sight](name:toroidal_angle_of_along_line_of_sight) for diagnostic line-of-sight defining points, [toroidal_angle_of_antenna_strap](name:toroidal_angle_of_antenna_strap) for ICRH antenna strap positions, and [toroidal_angle_of_coil_conductor_element](name:toroidal_angle_of_coil_conductor_element) for coil conductor element geometry.

Values span 0 to $2\pi$ rad for positions distributed around the full torus; diagnostics installed at a single port occupy a narrow angular range at their installation angle, while symmetric systems may provide several evenly spaced values of $\phi$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\phi$ increases in the counter-clockwise direction when viewed from above along the $+\hat{Z}$ axis.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density
NAMES.short: Toroidal projection of the total electric current density onto the geometric toroidal direction, aggregating all inductive, bootstrap, wave-driven, and inertial current contributions at every point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal current density $j_\phi = \mathbf{J} \cdot \hat{\phi}$ is the $\hat{\phi}$-projection of the total [current_density](name:current_density) vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical height. It represents the net signed rate of charge transport per unit cross-sectional area in the toroidal direction, encompassing every contributing mechanism — ohmic induction, bootstrap, wave-driven, diamagnetic, and inertial — without attribution to any single process.

In axisymmetric MHD equilibrium, $j_\phi$ is related to the poloidal magnetic field through Ampere's law:

$$
\mu_0 j_\phi = \frac{\partial B_R}{\partial Z} - \frac{\partial B_Z}{\partial R}
$$

where $B_R$ and $B_Z$ are the radial and vertical components of the magnetic field in the $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H m$^{-1}$ is the permeability of free space.

The total toroidal current density profile is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by combining external magnetics measurements with internal diagnostics such as motional Stark effect polarimetry. It can also be computed directly from fluid or kinetic simulations. Mechanism-specific contributions such as [toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction) sum to the total quantity defined here.

Peak core values in tokamak H-mode plasmas range from $10^5$ to $10^7$ A m$^{-2}$, peaking on the magnetic axis and decreasing toward the separatrix; edge and wall regions carry substantially lower values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_radius
NAMES.short: Radial flux-surface coordinate equal to the square root of the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux divided by pi times the reference vacuum toroidal field, approximating the effective minor radius of a flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux radius $\rho_{tor}$ is a dimensional radial coordinate labeling nested magnetic flux surfaces in a tokamak equilibrium. It is constructed from the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by a given surface rather than from a purely geometric distance, making it a magnetic coordinate that faithfully reflects the flux-surface topology even in strongly shaped or diverted plasmas. It increases monotonically from zero at the magnetic axis to the effective plasma minor radius at the last closed flux surface.

The defining relation is:

$$
\rho_{tor} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{tor}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\Phi_{tor}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the flux surface and $B_0$ is the reference vacuum toroidal field evaluated at the magnetic axis. In the limit of circular cross-section plasmas, $\rho_{tor}$ converges to the geometric minor radius $r$.

$\rho_{tor}$ is computed from equilibrium reconstruction by integrating the toroidal field component over the poloidal cross-section of each nested flux surface. It serves as the standard radial grid axis for one-dimensional equilibrium profiles, transport analysis, and wave propagation calculations across the plasma volume. The dimensionless counterpart [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) is obtained by dividing $\rho_{tor}$ by its value at the last closed flux surface. The underlying enclosed flux is [toroidal_magnetic_flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux).

For medium-sized tokamaks, $\rho_{tor}$ spans from 0 m at the magnetic axis to approximately 1–2 m at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux $\Phi_{tor}$ and the reference vacuum toroidal field $B_0$ share the same sign, ensuring the square-root argument is non-negative and $\rho_{tor} \geq 0$ throughout the confined plasma.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_radius_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Boundary toroidal flux radius rho_tor = sqrt(Phi_tor/(pi B0)) is the non-negative square-root radius associated with the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the plasma boundary. It provides an effective minor-radius scale for the outermost closed magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal flux radius at the plasma boundary is the radial flux label obtained from the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the selected boundary flux surface. It gives a non-negative effective minor-radius scale for the outermost closed magnetic flux surface or separatrix, rather than a purely geometric distance.

The boundary value is defined by normalizing the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux to the reference toroidal magnetic field:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor},b} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}$ is the [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), $B_0$ is the reference toroidal magnetic field used for the flux-radius normalization, and the flux and field are taken consistently so that the ratio is non-negative.

This quantity is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating the toroidal flux enclosed by the boundary flux surface and applying the flux-radius normalization. It sets the outer radial scale for coordinates such as the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). For a large-aspect-ratio circular plasma with nearly uniform toroidal field it is close to the geometric minor radius, while finite aspect ratio, shaping, and toroidal-field variation make it an effective flux radius rather than an exact geometric radius.

Typical values are about 0.2-1 m in small tokamaks, 0.5-2 m in medium and large tokamaks, and can exceed 2 m in reactor-scale equilibria.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Toroidal flux radius evaluated at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal flux radius at the magnetic axis is the value of the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ on the central magnetic flux surface. The coordinate is a non-negative, minor-radius-like label constructed from the toroidal magnetic flux interval between the magnetic axis and a flux surface; at the magnetic axis that interval is zero.

For a flux surface, the toroidal flux radius is defined by

$$
\rho_\mathrm{tor} = \sqrt{\frac{|\Delta \Phi_\mathrm{tor}|}{\pi |B_0|}}
$$

where $\Delta \Phi_\mathrm{tor}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux difference between the magnetic axis and the flux surface, and $B_0$ is the reference toroidal magnetic field magnitude used for the normalization. The absolute-value form states the radius convention explicitly: equivalently, a signed flux difference and signed reference field may be used only when their ratio is non-negative.

In equilibrium reconstruction, this quantity is obtained by identifying the magnetic axis and evaluating the toroidal-flux-radius coordinate on that flux surface. Numerically it should be exactly zero; small nonzero values indicate interpolation tolerance, finite grid resolution, or an inconsistent choice of flux origin.

Typical value: 0 m for all equilibria. The allowed range of $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is non-negative, $\rho_\mathrm{tor} \ge 0$, and the magnetic-axis value is the inner endpoint of that range.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the toroidal component of plasma current density evaluated on the magnetic surface selected by an equilibrium reconstruction constraint point. The selected surface is identified by the constraint point's normalized toroidal flux radius, making this the constrained-location counterpart of the unconstrained radial distribution of flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal flux-surface-averaged current density at a constraint position is the Jacobian-weighted flux-surface average of the toroidal component of plasma current density, evaluated on the single magnetic surface picked out by an equilibrium reconstruction constraint point. That surface is identified by its normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the radial constraint label, so this quantity is a single-point evaluation of the corresponding radial equilibrium quantity rather than its full radial dependence.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium in flux coordinates $(\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}, \theta, \phi)$, the defining average on the constraint surface $\rho_c$ is

$$
\left\langle j_\phi \right\rangle(\rho_c) = \frac{\displaystyle\oint j_\phi(\rho_c,\theta)\,J(\rho_c,\theta)\,d\theta}{\displaystyle\oint J(\rho_c,\theta)\,d\theta}
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of current density in A.m^-2 in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $\theta$ is the geometric poloidal angle in radians, $J$ is the coordinate Jacobian of the flux coordinates, and the closed integrals run over one full poloidal circuit ($\theta$ from $0$ to $2\pi$) at fixed $\rho_c$. The denominator $\oint J\,d\theta$ supplies the normalization, so the result is the Jacobian-weighted equilibrium flux-surface average and not an unweighted geometric surface-area average; the $2\pi$ poloidal circuit cancels between numerator and denominator.

In equilibrium reconstruction, this value is obtained by evaluating the reconstructed current-density distribution on the flux surface identified by the constraint label and applying the same Jacobian-weighted average used for the radial equilibrium quantity. The constrained value is compared against an inferred or prescribed toroidal-current-density constraint; inferred values rest on magnetic measurements together with diagnostics sensitive to the internal current distribution. The unconstrained radial dependence is described by [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_current_density](name:toroidal_current_density), and the field-aligned counterpart at the same point is [parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_at_constraint_position](name:parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_at_constraint_position).

Typical signed magnitudes in tokamak equilibria reach the order of $10^6$ A.m^-2 in the high-current core and fall toward $10^4$-$10^5$ A.m^-2 near the edge, with hollow or locally reversed values possible in advanced or off-axis current-drive scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal current density points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the total magnetic field vector along the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. Positive when pointing in the direction of increasing toroidal angle φ (counter‑clockwise when viewed from above). Includes contributions from toroidal field coils and plasma currents in the equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic field is the component of the total [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field) along the toroidal basis direction $\hat{\phi}$ in the right‑handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is the dominant magnetic field component in tokamak geometry and is generated by the external toroidal‑field coils as well as by plasma currents (diamagnetic and paramagnetic responses) that modify the vacuum field in equilibrium.

In an axisymmetric magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium, the toroidal field is related to the poloidal‑current function $F(\psi)$ by the Grad–Shafranov equation:

$$
B_\phi(R,Z) = \frac{F(\psi(R,Z))}{R}
$$

where $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic field, $R$ is the major radius, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux labeling the flux surface, and $F = R B_\phi$ has units of T·m. On a given flux surface $F$ is constant; the $1/R$ factor gives the characteristic variation across the plasma cross section.

The total toroidal field is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction that solves the Grad–Shafranov equation using magnetic probe measurements, flux loops, and information on the toroidal‑field coil currents. The vacuum contribution alone is described by [toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field), while the value on the magnetic axis is given by [toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis).

Typical magnitudes range from about 0.1 T in small or low‑field experiments to several tesla in conventional tokamaks, with higher values in high‑field devices such as spherical tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right‑handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the total magnetic field at the magnetic axis, evaluated as the projection onto the positive toroidal-angle direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It includes both vacuum toroidal-field-coil and equilibrium plasma-current contributions.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed toroidal component of the total magnetic field evaluated at the location where the poloidal magnetic flux has its magnetic-axis value. It is the on-axis value of [toroidal_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), not the vacuum reference field represented by [toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field).

In an axisymmetric equilibrium, the toroidal component is commonly expressed through the poloidal-current function $F(\psi)=R B_\phi$:

$$
B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{B}(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis}) \cdot \hat{\phi} = \frac{F(\psi_0)}{R_\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field in T, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R_\mathrm{axis}$ is the major radius of the magnetic axis in m, $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ is its vertical height in m, $\psi_0$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis in Wb, and $F(\psi)$ has units T m.

The value is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction by locating the magnetic axis and evaluating the reconstructed total field there, either by projecting $\mathbf{B}$ onto $\hat{\phi}$ or by using $F(\psi_0)/R_\mathrm{axis}$. Because the toroidal field usually dominates the total magnetic-field magnitude near the axis, its absolute value is often used as an approximate reference for cyclotron frequencies and Larmor radii; exact gyrofrequency estimates use the magnitude of the full magnetic field rather than this signed component alone.

Representative absolute values in tokamak equilibria are of order 0.1-10 T, with low-field or spherical tokamak operation often below 1 T, many conventional devices around 1-6 T, and high-field operation reaching larger values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the on-axis toroidal magnetic-field component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a given flux surface, increasing monotonically from zero at the magnetic axis and used as a natural radial flux-surface label in equilibrium analysis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic flux $\Phi_{tor}$ is the total flux of the toroidal magnetic field threading the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a closed magnetic flux surface. In an axisymmetric equilibrium, $\Phi_{tor}$ increases monotonically from zero at the magnetic axis to its maximum at the plasma boundary, making it one of the two fundamental flux-surface labels alongside the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$.

The defining integral over the poloidal cross-sectional area $S_{\rm pol}$ bounded by the flux surface is:

$$
\Phi_{tor} = \int_{S_{\rm pol}} B_\phi \, dA
$$

where $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic field component in T and $dA$ is the area element of the poloidal half-plane in m². The safety factor relates the two canonical flux coordinates through $q = d\Phi_{tor}/d\psi$, linking the toroidal flux to the flux-surface geometry characterized by [flux_surface_area](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface).

In equilibrium reconstruction, $\Phi_{tor}$ profiles are computed from the Grad–Shafranov solution and tabulated as a function of normalized radial coordinates across nested flux surfaces. Typical boundary values span a few to tens of Wb in current tokamaks, with larger values for higher-field machines. The [toroidal_diamagnetic_magnetic_flux_at_inside_flux_surface](name:toroidal_diamagnetic_magnetic_flux_at_inside_flux_surface) isolates the portion of this flux arising from plasma diamagnetism.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Total toroidal magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by the plasma boundary, including externally produced toroidal field and the contribution associated with plasma poloidal currents.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the net flux of toroidal magnetic field through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by the last-closed flux surface. It is the boundary value used to normalize toroidal-flux radial coordinates and is complementary to [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which refers to flux through a horizontal disk rather than through a poloidal cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height, the boundary toroidal flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b} = \int_{A_b} B_\phi(R,Z)\, dR\, dZ = \int_{A_b} \frac{F(\psi(R,Z))}{R}\, dR\, dZ
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux in Wb, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component in T, $F=R B_\phi$ is the poloidal-current function in T m, $\psi$ is the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux label, $R$ and $Z$ are in m, and $A_b$ is the boundary-enclosed poloidal area in m^2 at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$.

The value is computed from an axisymmetric equilibrium by integrating the reconstructed toroidal magnetic field over the region inside the plasma boundary. The reconstructed field generally contains the externally imposed vacuum toroidal-field contribution and the plasma-current contribution represented through $F(\psi)$; the quantity is therefore an integral flux associated with the boundary, not a local boundary condition.

Typical absolute magnitudes scale approximately as $\langle B_\phi\rangle A_b$: compact or medium tokamaks are often in the 0.1-10 Wb range, while large high-field plasmas can be 10-100 Wb or more depending on toroidal field strength and boundary area.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net toroidal magnetic field threading the plasma-boundary cross-section points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic field, defined as its projection along the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the toroidal component of the vacuum magnetic field that varies with toroidal angle and is not part of the axisymmetric equilibrium field. It is a local component of the perturbation field in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, not a projection onto a material or control-surface normal.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ satisfying $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$, the non-axisymmetric magnetic field is decomposed as:

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}(R, \phi, Z) = B_R(R, \phi, Z)\,\hat{R} + B_\phi(R, \phi, Z)\,\hat{\phi} + B_Z(R, \phi, Z)\,\hat{Z}
$$

where $B_\phi$ is the toroidal component described here, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}$, $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are measured in T, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in m, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in rad increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height in m.

The quantity is computed from vacuum magnetic-field models for non-axisymmetric perturbation coils, error-field sources, and passive conducting structures, or inferred by combining magnetic measurements with a field model and removing the toroidally averaged axisymmetric contribution. On a control surface, $B_\phi$ is still the tangent toroidal component; the surface-normal non-axisymmetric field is the separate projection $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}} \cdot \hat{n}$ and generally differs from $B_\phi$.

Representative magnitudes are device- and location-dependent because the vacuum perturbation depends on coil currents, source geometry, and distance from the conductors. In tokamak perturbation studies, $|B_\phi|$ is commonly in the range $10^{-6}-10^{-2}$ T and is often quoted as $|B_\phi|/B_0$, where $B_0$ is the magnitude of the reference axisymmetric toroidal magnetic field in T; perturbative cases usually have $|B_\phi|/B_0 \ll 1$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the non-axisymmetric magnetic-field component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_plasma_current
NAMES.short: Net toroidal electric current carried by the plasma, equal to the integral of the toroidal current density over the poloidal plasma cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal plasma current $I_p$ is the net electric current flowing in the toroidal $\hat{\phi}$ direction, integrated over the full poloidal cross-section of the plasma column. It is a primary global parameter governing poloidal magnetic field generation, MHD equilibrium, plasma confinement, and stability thresholds including the Kruskal-Shafranov $q = 1$ condition.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
I_p = \iint_{\mathcal{S}} j_\phi \, dA
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the current density, $dA$ is the area element, and $\mathcal{S}$ is the poloidal cross-section of the plasma.

$I_p$ is measured by Rogowski coils encircling the torus, or inferred from flux-loop and magnetic-pickup-coil arrays as a primary constraint in equilibrium reconstruction. The closely related [toroidal_total_plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current) explicitly labels this as the total aggregated current. It should be distinguished from [current_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:current_of_toroidal_field_coil), which drives the external vacuum toroidal field, and from [current_of_plasma_filament](name:current_of_plasma_filament), which represents current in discrete plasma filament elements.

Typical values range from a few hundred kA in small research tokamaks to approximately 15 MA in ITER-class reactors, scaling roughly with the product of toroidal field strength and minor radius.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless shaping parameter measuring the inward displacement of the vertical extrema of a nested toroidal flux surface relative to its geometric center, normalized by the flux-surface minor radius.
NAMES.long:
The triangularity $\delta$ of a magnetic flux surface is a dimensionless plasma shaping parameter quantifying the degree to which the flux-surface poloidal cross-section is displaced toward a D-shaped or triangular form. It is defined via the major-radius offset of the upper and lower vertical extrema from the flux-surface geometric center, normalized by the minor radius, and constitutes one of the primary degrees of freedom in plasma shape optimization for confinement and MHD stability.

For a flux surface with geometric center $R_{geo} = (R_{out} + R_{in})/2$, minor radius $a = (R_{out} - R_{in})/2$, and major radius $R_{ext}$ at a vertical extremum, the triangularity is:

$$
\delta = \frac{R_{geo} - R_{ext}}{a}
$$

where $R_{out}$ and $R_{in}$ are the outboard and inboard midplane radii of the flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The general triangularity is the average of the [upper](name:upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface) and [lower](name:lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface) components evaluated at their respective vertical extrema.

The triangularity profile as a function of the flux-surface label is derived from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting magnetic field measurements to the inferred flux-surface geometry. Together with [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), it specifies the leading-order departure of the cross-section from an ellipse; higher-order deformations are captured by squareness parameters such as [lower inner squareness](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface).

Typical values at the last closed flux surface range from $|\delta| \approx 0.3$–$0.5$ in standard H-mode operation; strongly shaped devices may reach $|\delta| \approx 0.6$–$0.8$. The triangularity decreases monotonically toward zero at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical extrema of the flux surface are displaced toward smaller major radius $R$ relative to the geometric center $R_{geo}$, corresponding to a conventional D-shaped cross-section.

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless shaping parameter measuring the inward horizontal displacement of the lower vertical extremum of a nested toroidal flux surface, normalized by the flux-surface minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity of a flux surface quantifies how far the lower part of the poloidal cross-section is shifted inward relative to the magnetic axis. It separates up-down asymmetric shaping from the corresponding upper triangularity; for an up-down symmetric surface the upper and lower triangularities are equal, and an unsplit triangularity is commonly represented by that common value or by an average of the two.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the lower triangularity is defined by

$$
\delta_\mathrm{lower} = \frac{R_\mathrm{axis} - R_\mathrm{lower}}{a}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{axis}$ is the major radius of the magnetic axis, $R_\mathrm{lower}$ is the major radius of the point on the flux surface with the lowest vertical position $Z$, and $a = (R_\mathrm{out} - R_\mathrm{in})/2$ is the minor radius of the same flux surface determined from its outermost and innermost midplane intersections.

It is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction or analytic flux-surface description by locating the magnetic axis, tracing the chosen closed flux contour, finding its lower vertical extremum, and normalizing the horizontal displacement by the contour minor radius. Positive values correspond to the lower extremum lying at smaller major radius than the magnetic axis, while negative values indicate an outward-shifted lower extremum.

Typical values range from about -0.4 to 0.8. Conventional positive-triangularity tokamak plasmas often have values around 0.2-0.6 near the outer flux surfaces, nearly circular surfaces have values close to 0, and negative-triangularity configurations have values below 0.

NAMES.name: triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Average triangularity (δ) of the plasma boundary, measuring the mean inward radial displacement of the poloidal cross-section extrema relative to the geometric center normalized by the plasma minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Triangularity is a dimensionless shape parameter quantifying the deviation of the plasma poloidal cross-section from an ellipse. The average triangularity $\delta$ is the arithmetic mean of the upper and lower directional components, defined at the topmost and bottommost points of the last closed flux surface. Together with [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary), it is a primary descriptor of plasma shape governing MHD stability margins, bootstrap current fraction, and confinement quality.

The average triangularity is defined as:

$$
\delta = \frac{\delta_U + \delta_L}{2}
$$

where $\delta_U$ is the [upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) and $\delta_L$ is the [lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary). Each directional component is $(R_\mathrm{geo} - R_\mathrm{ext})/a$, where $R_\mathrm{geo} = (R_\mathrm{max} + R_\mathrm{min})/2$ is the major radius of the geometric center, $R_\mathrm{ext}$ is the major radius at the respective poloidal extremum, and $a = (R_\mathrm{max} - R_\mathrm{min})/2$ is the plasma minor radius.

Equilibrium reconstruction determines $\delta$ from the fitted boundary contour constrained by external magnetic measurements. Typical values are $\delta \approx 0.2$–$0.5$ in standard H-mode configurations and can approach 0.7 or higher in strongly shaped divertor geometries; reverse-triangularity discharges have $\delta < 0$. For asymmetric equilibria, [outer_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) and [inner_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:inner_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) provide the low-field-side and high-field-side decompositions respectively.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal extrema of the plasma boundary are displaced radially inward (toward smaller major radius $R$) relative to the plasma geometric center.

NAMES.name: inner_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: High-field-side triangularity of the plasma boundary, measuring the inboard boundary extrema relative to the plasma geometric center and minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Inner triangularity is the high-field-side component of the triangular deformation of the plasma separatrix. In a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height, it quantifies the inboard displacement of the triangularity-defining boundary extremum relative to the plasma geometric center. It complements [outer_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) and the single averaged [triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary).

For an extremum-based separatrix shape description, the inner triangularity is commonly written as the normalized radial displacement

$$
\delta_{\mathrm{inner}} = \frac{R_{\mathrm{geo}} - R_{\mathrm{tri,in}}}{a}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{geo}}$ is the major radius of the plasma geometric center in meters, $R_{\mathrm{tri,in}}$ is the major radius of the high-field-side separatrix extremum or fitted boundary point used to define the inner triangularity in meters, and $a$ is the boundary minor radius in meters. The result is dimensionless; values greater than zero correspond to an inboard triangularity point at smaller $R$ than the geometric center, while values less than zero correspond to the opposite displacement.

Inner triangularity is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction or a fitted separatrix contour by determining the geometric center, the boundary minor radius, and the high-field-side boundary extremum used by the chosen shape definition. It is often interpreted together with [minor_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:minor_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), [outer_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), and [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) because these parameters jointly describe the noncircular shape of the plasma cross-section.

Typical reported magnitudes are of order a few tenths. Values near 0 indicate weak triangular shaping of the inboard side, while larger absolute values indicate stronger high-field-side indentation or anti-indentation; the realized range depends on device geometry, divertor configuration, and the operational scenario.

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Lower triangularity is a dimensionless shape parameter for the lower half of the plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It is the inward displacement of the boundary point at minimum Z relative to the geometric center, normalized by half the maximum-minus-minimum R extent.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity $\delta_{\rm lower}$ quantifies triangular shaping of the lower half of the plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It compares the major radius of the lower boundary extremum with the geometric center constructed from the inboard and outboard radial extrema of the same boundary.

The geometric definition uses the boundary minor-radius normalization:

$$
\delta_{\rm lower} = \frac{R_0 - R_{\rm low}}{a}, \qquad R_0 = \frac{R_{\rm out}+R_{\rm in}}{2}, \qquad a = \frac{R_{\rm out}-R_{\rm in}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\rm low}$ is the major radius in meters at the minimum-$Z$ point of the boundary, $R_{\rm in}$ and $R_{\rm out}$ are the minimum and maximum boundary major radii in meters, $R_0$ is the geometric-center major radius in meters, and $a$ is the [minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary](name:minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary) in meters. This construction makes inward lower shaping, $R_{\rm low}<R_0$, positive and outward lower shaping negative.

It is computed from an equilibrium boundary contour by locating the inboard, outboard, and lower vertical extrema and applying the geometric construction above. The lower value can differ from [upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) in vertically asymmetric, single-null, or double-null configurations, while [minor_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:minor_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) denotes a related but distinct boundary-shape measure.

Typical values are order-unity dimensionless numbers: nearly circular or weakly shaped lower boundaries are close to 0, positive-triangularity tokamak plasmas commonly lie around 0.2-0.6, and reverse-triangularity lower shaping is negative.

NAMES.name: outer_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless low-field-side triangularity of the separatrix, representing the mean inward radial indentation of the upper and lower outboard shoulders relative to the plasma geometric center, normalized by the horizontal minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Outer triangularity of the plasma boundary is a dimensionless measure of the low-field-side triangular indentation of the separatrix in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It combines the upper and lower shoulder displacements into one outboard shape parameter, so it is distinct from choosing either upper or lower triangularity alone.

For a boundary contour with geometric center $R_{\mathrm{geo}}$ and horizontal minor radius $a$, the outer triangularity is defined as the arithmetic mean of the upper and lower normalized radial displacements:

$$
\delta_{\mathrm{outer}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{R_{\mathrm{geo}} - R_{\mathrm{upper}}}{a} + \frac{R_{\mathrm{geo}} - R_{\mathrm{lower}}}{a}\right)
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{upper}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{lower}}$ are the $R$ coordinates of the upper and lower vertical extrema of the same separatrix contour, $R_{\mathrm{geo}}=(R_{\mathrm{out}}+R_{\mathrm{in}})/2$, and $a=(R_{\mathrm{out}}-R_{\mathrm{in}})/2$ with $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{in}}$ the maximum and minimum $R$ values of the contour. The two normalized displacements are combined by averaging; they are not alternative definitions of this scalar.

In practice, this quantity is obtained from an equilibrium boundary reconstruction or a fitted separatrix contour by identifying the inboard and outboard radial extrema, locating the upper and lower vertical turning points, and averaging their normalized radial offsets. Boundary smoothing and the treatment of X-point neighborhoods can affect the extracted extrema, so consistent contour processing is important when comparing cases.

Typical values are near 0 for nearly circular cross-sections, about 0.2-0.5 for many conventionally D-shaped tokamak plasmas, and can be negative for inverse or outward-flared triangularity. Values above about 0.6 represent strongly shaped boundaries.

NAMES.name: upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Ratio of the vertical distance from the plasma cross-section geometric axis to the topmost boundary point to the minor radius, capturing vertical elongation of the upper half of the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The upper elongation $\kappa_u$ is a dimensionless shape parameter quantifying how far the upper half of the plasma boundary extends vertically relative to the minor radius. Unlike the full-boundary [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary), which represents the overall vertical-to-horizontal aspect ratio of the cross-section, $\kappa_u$ isolates the upper-half geometry and is sensitive to up-down asymmetries induced by, for example, a single-null divertor configuration.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\kappa_u = \frac{Z_{\max} - Z_{\rm geo}}{a}
$$

where $Z_{\max}$ is the vertical coordinate of the topmost point of the plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $Z_{\rm geo}$ is the vertical coordinate of the geometric axis of the poloidal cross-section, and $a$ is the plasma minor radius.

This parameter is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by identifying the outermost closed flux surface or the specified plasma boundary contour and computing the ratio from the upper vertical extremum. The companion quantity [lower_elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_elongation_of_plasma_boundary) measures the analogous shape of the lower half; differences between the two reflect up-down asymmetry in the plasma cross-section. In conventional single-null diverted H-mode plasmas, $\kappa_u$ falls in the range 1.2–1.9.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the topmost point of the plasma boundary lies above the geometric axis of the cross-section.

NAMES.name: upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce (2013) squareness coefficient for the upper-inner, high-field-side quadrant (smaller major radius, positive vertical height) of a nested magnetic flux surface. It measures the deviation of that quadrant from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation; zero recovers the ellipse, positive values give a boxier corner and negative values a more diamond-like corner.
NAMES.long:
Upper-inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce shape coefficient that describes how the upper, high-field-side quadrant (smaller major radius $R$, positive vertical height $Z$) of a nested magnetic flux surface departs from a reference ellipse. The reference ellipse for that quadrant shares the same geometric center, the same horizontal half-width (minor radius $a$), and the same elongation $\kappa$ as the local flux surface, so the coefficient isolates the corner curvature alone. It is the upper-inner quadrant component of [inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface).

In the four-quadrant parameterization of Luce (PPCF 55, 2013), the vertical coordinate of the upper-inner segment of the surface, expressed in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height, follows:

$$
Z(\theta) = a\,\kappa\,\sin\!\bigl(\theta + \zeta_{ui}\,\sin(2\theta)\bigr)
$$

where $a$ is the local minor radius (horizontal half-width), $\kappa$ is the local elongation, $\theta$ is the geometric poloidal angle measured in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section, and $\zeta_{ui}$ is the upper-inner squareness coefficient. The upper-inner quadrant is the segment running from the top of the surface to the inner (high-field-side) midplane. Setting $\zeta_{ui} = 0$ recovers the reference ellipse exactly; positive values produce a more rectangular, box-like corner, while negative values yield a concave, diamond-like corner.

The coefficient is obtained from an equilibrium flux-surface contour by first determining the surface center, minor radius, and elongation, then fitting the Luce parameterization on the upper-inner segment alone. Across nested surfaces it varies smoothly from the magnetic axis to the boundary, where it connects continuously to [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary).

Values are small in magnitude near the axis, where surfaces are nearly elliptical, and grow toward the edge of shaped equilibria; strongly shaped cases produce the largest magnitudes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the upper-inner corner of the flux surface protrudes outward beyond the reference ellipse, giving a more rectangular poloidal cross-section.

NAMES.name: upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient for the upper outboard quadrant of each nested flux surface, measuring the departure of that corner from a reference ellipse with the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation.
NAMES.long:
The upper outer squareness $\zeta_{uo}$ is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient for the upper outboard ($+Z$, large-$R$) corner of each nested magnetic flux surface, measuring how much that quadrant departs from a reference ellipse sharing the same geometric center, horizontal half-width, and elongation. It is one of four quadrant-resolved squareness parameters — alongside the [lower outer squareness](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), [upper inner squareness](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), and [lower inner squareness](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) — extending the standard elongation-triangularity shape description to higher order.
