In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the flux-surface boundary in the upper outer quadrant is described by the Luce parameterization as:

$$
R = R_\mathrm{geo} + a\cos\!\bigl(\theta + \delta_{uo}\sin\theta + \zeta_{uo}\sin 2\theta\bigr)
$$

with $Z = Z_\mathrm{geo} + \kappa\, a\sin\theta$, where $R_\mathrm{geo}$ and $Z_\mathrm{geo}$ are the coordinates of the flux-surface geometric center, $a$ is the minor radius, $\kappa$ is the elongation, $\delta_{uo}$ is the upper outer triangularity, and $\theta \in [0, \pi/2]$ is the geometric poloidal angle spanning the upper outboard quadrant.

Values near zero indicate an approximately elliptic corner; positive values are characteristic of D-shaped cross-sections with a squared-off outboard corner, while negative values correspond to a more concave or helmet-shaped upper outer region. The coefficient is extracted from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting computed flux-surface contours to the Luce parameterization in the upper outboard region. The symmetric combination of upper and lower outer quadrant values constitutes the aggregate [outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), and the value at the outermost flux surface corresponds to [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the upper outer corner of the flux surface protrudes beyond the reference ellipse, giving the cross-section a more rectangular (D-shaped) outboard corner.

NAMES.name: upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce shape parameter for the upper outboard corner of the plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system. It measures how the positive-Z, large-R boundary quadrant departs from the reference ellipse set by the boundary radius, upper elongation, and upper triangularity.
NAMES.long:
Upper outer squareness of the plasma boundary quantifies the non-elliptical shaping of the outboard, positive-$Z$ quadrant of the last-closed flux surface or separatrix. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the upper outer quadrant lies at larger $R$ than the radial center and above the vertical center. Positive values in the Luce convention make this quadrant fuller and squarer relative to the reference ellipse, while negative values make it more chamfered or indented.

A full Luce parameterization for the upper outer boundary quadrant is

$$
\begin{aligned}
R(\theta) &= R_0 + a\cos\left[\theta + \sin^{-1}(\delta_u)\sin\theta - \zeta_{UO}\sin(2\theta)\right],\\
Z(\theta) &= Z_0 + \kappa_u a\sin\left[\theta + \zeta_{UO}\sin(2\theta)\right],\qquad 0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $\zeta_{UO}$ is the upper outer squareness, $\theta=0$ is the outboard midplane point, and $\theta=\pi/2$ is the top point. $R_0=(R_{out}+R_{in})/2$ is the radial center, $a=(R_{out}-R_{in})/2$ is the boundary minor radius, $Z_0$ is the vertical center used for the boundary shape description, $\kappa_u=(Z_{top}-Z_0)/a$ is the upper elongation, and $\delta_u=(R_0-R_{top})/a$ is the upper triangularity. For small $|\zeta_{UO}|$, the effect is locally proportional to $\sin 2\theta$, but the parameter is defined by the full angular distortion rather than by a single midpoint displacement.

The quantity is obtained from an equilibrium boundary contour by identifying the radial and vertical extrema, fixing the associated radius, center, elongation, and triangularity, and fitting the upper-outboard segment to the Luce form. The analogous flux-surface quantity, [upper outer squareness of a flux surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), applies the same shape concept to an interior magnetic surface rather than to the plasma boundary.

Values near 0 correspond to an approximately elliptical upper outer quadrant. In shaped tokamak equilibria, typical absolute values are a few hundredths to a few tenths, commonly about 0.02-0.2, with strongly squared boundaries sometimes approaching 0.3.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless upper-half triangularity of a flux surface, defined by the inward major-radius displacement of the point at maximum vertical height from the surface horizontal mid-radius, normalized by the minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Upper triangularity of a flux surface quantifies the D-shape asymmetry of the upper half of a closed magnetic surface in a poloidal cross-section. It isolates the position of the topmost point relative to the same surface's horizontal mid-radius, so it distinguishes upper-half shaping from lower-half triangularity and from elongation.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the upper triangularity is defined by

$$
\delta_\mathrm{upper} = \frac{R_0 - R_\mathrm{top}}{a}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{top}$ is the major radius of the point with maximum $Z$ on the flux surface, $R_0=(R_\mathrm{out}+R_\mathrm{in})/2$ is the horizontal mid-radius of that surface, and $a=(R_\mathrm{out}-R_\mathrm{in})/2$ is its minor radius. The lengths $R_\mathrm{top}$, $R_0$, $R_\mathrm{out}$, $R_\mathrm{in}$, and $a$ are in meters, while $\delta_\mathrm{upper}$ is dimensionless; $R_\mathrm{out}$ and $R_\mathrm{in}$ are the maximum and minimum major radii of the same flux surface.

It is computed from an equilibrium flux contour or an analytic flux-surface shape by locating the horizontal radial extrema and the upper vertical extremum of the contour. Together with lower triangularity, elongation, and squareness parameters, it describes poloidal shaping and up-down asymmetry of nested flux surfaces.

Typical values in tokamak equilibrium descriptions are commonly between about -0.6 and 0.6. Values near zero indicate that the upper extremum lies close to the horizontal mid-radius, positive values indicate an inward-shifted upper point, and negative values indicate an outward-shifted upper point.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless parameter measuring how far the uppermost point of the plasma boundary is displaced radially inward relative to the plasma geometric center, normalized to the minor radius, capturing the triangular deviation of the upper half of the cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The upper triangularity $\delta_u$ characterizes the poloidal asymmetry of the upper portion of the plasma cross-section. It quantifies how far the uppermost point of the plasma boundary is displaced toward the high-field side relative to the plasma geometric center, and is a key shaping parameter governing MHD stability, pedestal formation, and divertor heat-load distribution in shaped tokamak discharges.

The upper triangularity is defined geometrically as:

$$
\delta_u = \frac{R_0 - R_{top}}{a}
$$

where $R_0$ is the major radius of the plasma geometric center (midpoint between maximum and minimum major radius on the horizontal midplane), $R_{top}$ is the major radius of the uppermost point of the plasma boundary, and $a$ is the plasma minor radius.

Together with [lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), $\delta_u$ captures up-down asymmetry in plasma shape that is characteristic of single-null divertor configurations, where the half facing the divertor typically exhibits higher triangularity. Their mean approximates the overall [triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary). Typical H-mode values range from 0.2 to 0.7 in standard tokamak operation. For finer resolution of the upper boundary geometry, $\delta_u$ is complemented by the [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) and [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) parameters. Upper triangularity is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetics and boundary identification diagnostics.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the uppermost point of the plasma boundary lies at smaller major radius than the plasma geometric center, displaced toward the high-field side.

NAMES.name: vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Magnetic-field vector produced exclusively by external coil currents, satisfying the curl-free condition throughout the plasma volume in the absence of any plasma currents.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the magnetic-field vector that exists throughout the plasma region when no plasma is present, arising entirely from the external coil system — toroidal field coils, poloidal field coils, and correction coils. It is the vacuum-limit component of the full equilibrium [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field), against which the plasma-current contribution is superposed to yield the total equilibrium field.

The absence of free currents in the vacuum region constrains $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ to satisfy

$$
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} = \mathbf{0}
$$

so that $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} = -\mu_0 \nabla \phi_m$, where $\phi_m$ is a scalar magnetic potential and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space. The field also satisfies $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} = 0$. In practice it is evaluated via Biot-Savart integration over the coil current distribution or by solving Laplace's equation for $\phi_m$ with coil-boundary conditions.

The vector is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical height. The [toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) component dominates in tokamak geometry and varies roughly as $1/R$; the poloidal components, governed by the poloidal coil configuration, are typically one to two orders of magnitude smaller.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal component $B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the vacuum magnetic field evaluated at the reference major radius, produced solely by the external coil system in the absence of any plasma currents.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum toroidal magnetic field $B_0$ is the $\hat{\phi}$-projection of the [vacuum_magnetic_field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field) evaluated at a fixed [reference major radius](name:reference_major_radius) $R_0$. It captures the toroidal field contribution from the external coil system — primarily the toroidal field coils — with no plasma-current contribution included.

For an ideal current-free axisymmetric configuration the vacuum toroidal field follows a $1/R$ profile:

$$
B_\phi^{\rm vac}(R) = \frac{R_0 B_0}{R}
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius and $B_0 \equiv B_\phi^{\rm vac}(R_0)$. The product $R_0 B_0$ is invariant across radial position and serves as the primary magnetic normalization parameter used throughout equilibrium reconstruction, stability analysis, and flux-coordinate definitions.

The value of $B_0$ is inferred from the electrical current in the toroidal field coil system via a calibrated coil-current-to-field relationship, or confirmed by in-vessel magnetic probes under vacuum conditions. It enters the definition of the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor} = \sqrt{\Phi_{\rm tor}/(\pi B_0)}$, linking it directly to [toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis), and normalizes current densities used across core and edge plasma analysis. It also differs from the flux_surface_average_magnetic_field in that the latter includes plasma diamagnetic and paramagnetic modifications. Typical values at the reference radius range from 1 T in small devices to 5–6 T in large high-field machines.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the active limiter point, the location where a limited plasma boundary contacts the limiter, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the active limiter point is the $Z$ component of the point where a limited plasma boundary is in contact with the material limiter. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters.

If the active limiter contact point is denoted $P_\mathrm{AL}=(R_\mathrm{AL}, \phi_\mathrm{AL}, Z_\mathrm{AL})$, its vertical coordinate is

$$
z_\mathrm{AL}=Z_\mathrm{AL}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{AL}$ is the point's major radius in meters, $\phi_\mathrm{AL}$ is its toroidal angle in radians, and $Z_\mathrm{AL}$ is its vertical height in meters.

In equilibrium analysis, the active limiter point is identified from the contact between the reconstructed plasma boundary and the limiter geometry for a limited configuration. This coordinate is the vertical companion of major_radius_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point; related vertical coordinates include [vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary), [vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point), and [vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).

Typical values are device dependent and commonly lie between -2 m and 2 m in medium-sized tokamaks, with larger vertical excursions possible in elongated or vertically shifted plasmas. The value depends on the chosen vertical origin of the device coordinate definition and on which limiter element is contacted.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the active limiter point lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the first-wall point geometrically nearest to the plasma boundary or separatrix, measured upward from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the closest wall point is the $Z$ value of the point on the first wall that minimizes the geometric distance to the plasma boundary or separatrix. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $Z$ is vertical height measured upward from the machine midplane, and this quantity identifies only the vertical component of that nearest wall location.

For a first-wall contour $\Gamma_w$ and a plasma boundary or separatrix contour $\Gamma_p$ in the same poloidal $(R, Z)$ cross-section, the closest wall point $q_*=(R_*,Z_*)$ is defined by the Euclidean poloidal-plane distance:

$$
q_* = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{q \in \Gamma_w}\; \min_{p \in \Gamma_p} \sqrt{(R_q - R_p)^2 + (Z_q - Z_p)^2}
$$

where $q=(R_q,Z_q)$ is a point on the first wall and $p=(R_p,Z_p)$ is a point on the plasma boundary or separatrix. The documented quantity is $Z_*$. If more than one wall point has exactly the same minimum distance, the geometric definition alone does not determine a unique point and an additional tie-breaking convention is required.

In practice, this coordinate is computed from a reconstructed plasma boundary or separatrix and a first-wall contour expressed in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, usually by interpolation and a nearest-distance search in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane. Together with the corresponding [major radius of the closest wall point], it specifies the poloidal location of the nearest wall point; by itself it gives only the vertical height.

Typical values are bounded by the vertical extent of the first wall. For a wall extending from $Z_{\min}$ to $Z_{\max}$, the coordinate lies between those limits in m; values near $0$ m indicate a closest point near the machine midplane, positive values indicate the upper side, and negative values indicate the lower side.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wall point lies in the $+Z$ direction, above the machine midplane, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate locating a point at which a physical quantity is imposed as a constraint during equilibrium reconstruction, measured in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ specifies the height of a position at which a physical quantity — such as the parallel current density $j_\parallel$, safety factor $q$, toroidal current density $j_\phi$, or pressure $p$ — is prescribed as a constraint during equilibrium reconstruction. It is measured in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is the height along the machine symmetry axis, with $Z = 0$ conventionally at the machine equatorial plane.

Together with the companion major-radius coordinate, $Z$ fully locates each constraint point in the poloidal cross-section. Equilibrium solvers minimize the mismatch between the MHD equilibrium solution and the constrained physical quantities at their specified $(R, Z)$ positions, making accurate constraint-point coordinates essential metadata for interpreting which plasma-profile measurements drive the reconstruction. The analogous coordinate for diagnostic measurement positions is given by [vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position).

In medium-to-large tokamaks the vertical extent of the confined plasma region spans roughly $-2$ to $+2$ m, with $Z = 0$ at the midplane.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the constraint position lies above the machine equatorial plane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_control_surface
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the control surface in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, identifying the height of the boundary surface used to evaluate the normal component of non-axisymmetric magnetic fields.
NAMES.long:
The control surface is a geometric boundary — typically a closed toroidal surface enclosing the plasma — at which the normal component of the non-axisymmetric magnetic field is evaluated. Its vertical coordinate identifies the height of each surface point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. Together with the corresponding major-radius coordinate, the $Z$ coordinate fully specifies the poloidal cross-sectional location of any control-surface point.

Control surfaces are employed in non-axisymmetric magnetostatics, error-field analysis, and resonant magnetic perturbation studies. The surface geometry is prescribed, and the normal magnetic flux through each area element is then computed from the field values and the local surface-normal vector; the $Z$ coordinate of each surface point enters both the geometric specification of the surface and the projection of normal-field couplings between external coil perturbations and the plasma interior.

This coordinate belongs to the same geometric family as [vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and [vertical_coordinate_of_beam_tracing_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_beam_tracing_point), all giving the $Z$ position of a specified geometric locus. For medium to large tokamaks, control-surface $Z$ values typically range from approximately $-3$ m to $+3$ m, spanning the full vertical extent of the plasma cross-section.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the control surface point lies above the device midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_current_center
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the plasma current center, defined as the toroidal current-density-weighted centroid of the plasma current distribution in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the current center is the $Z$ position of the centroid of the toroidal plasma current distribution in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the effective vertical location of the net plasma current in the poloidal cross-section.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the current center is defined by the signed toroidal current-density-weighted centroid:

$$
Z_\mathrm{cc} = \frac{\int_\Omega Z\, j_\phi(R,Z)\, dA}{\int_\Omega j_\phi(R,Z)\, dA}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{cc}$ is the vertical coordinate of the current center in m, $Z$ is vertical height in m, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal current density in A m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is the poloidal area element in m$^2$, and $\Omega$ is the current-carrying plasma cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The denominator is the total signed toroidal plasma current.

In practice, this quantity is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction or model that provides the toroidal current-density distribution. It is useful for describing vertical plasma position control because it tracks the centroid of the current channel rather than a purely geometric boundary center.

Typical values are near the magnetic or geometric midplane. In many medium-size tokamaks, vertical offsets are commonly within about $\pm 0.3$ m, while large or strongly shaped plasmas can have offsets approaching about $\pm 1$ m depending on the chosen $Z=0$ reference plane and operating scenario.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current-density-weighted centroid lies in the $+Z$ direction from the $Z=0$ reference plane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_dr_dz_zero_point
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate, measured from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of a selected plasma-boundary or separatrix point where major radius has zero slope with respect to vertical height. The point marks an inner or outer radial extremum of the boundary shape.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a $dR/dZ=0$ point is the scalar $Z_0$ of a selected point on the plasma boundary or separatrix where the contour reaches a radial extremum in a poloidal cross-section. It is measured from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Let $R_b(Z)$ represent the local branch of the boundary contour near the selected radial extremum. The defining condition is:

$$
\left.\frac{dR_b}{dZ}\right|_{Z=Z_0} = 0
$$

where $Z_0$ is the documented vertical coordinate in meters, $R_b$ is the boundary major radius in meters expressed as a function of the vertical coordinate $Z$ in meters, and the derivative is evaluated on the selected branch. If both the high-field-side and low-field-side branches satisfy this condition, the relevant solution is the one associated with the intended radial extremum; it should be interpreted together with the companion major-radius coordinate or an explicit inner/outer branch specification.

In equilibrium analysis, $Z_0$ is obtained by tracing or interpolating the plasma boundary or separatrix in a fixed-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and solving for zeros of $dR_b/dZ$. The value is used with boundary-shape quantities such as the boundary major radius and minor radius to characterize radial extrema and vertical displacement of the plasma shape.

Typical values are machine-size dependent and lie within the vertical extent of the boundary. Midplane-centered, up-down symmetric equilibria commonly give $Z_0$ close to 0 m for radial extrema, while vertically shifted or asymmetric equilibria can give signed values from less than 0.01 m in magnitude to several m in large devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the selected point lies in the $+Z$ direction from the machine midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the plasma geometric axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured upward from the machine midplane. It is the arithmetic midpoint between the maximum and minimum vertical positions of the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the geometric axis is the $Z$ location halfway between the uppermost and lowermost points of the last closed flux surface. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height measured upward from the machine midplane. This is an extrema-based midpoint, not a vertical centroid or area-weighted center of the boundary.

The quantity is defined from the vertical extrema of the plasma boundary:

$$
Z_\mathrm{geom} = \frac{Z_\mathrm{max} + Z_\mathrm{min}}{2}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{max}$ and $Z_\mathrm{min}$ are the maximum and minimum boundary vertical coordinates in meters, and $Z_\mathrm{geom}$ is the vertical coordinate of the geometric axis.

In practice, $Z_\mathrm{geom}$ is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction after identifying the last closed flux surface or separatrix and finding its upper and lower vertical extrema. It is complementary to the radial geometric-axis coordinate and can differ from the [vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), especially in shaped or vertically displaced plasmas.

Typical values are near 0 m for plasmas centered on the machine midplane, often within -0.5 m to 0.5 m in medium-size tokamaks. Larger devices or deliberately vertically shifted equilibria can have values of order several meters.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the geometric axis lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the magnetic axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where the magnetic axis is the innermost degenerate flux surface at which the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis is the $Z$ position of the innermost degenerate magnetic flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The magnetic axis is the point in an axisymmetric poloidal cross-section about which closed magnetic surfaces are nested; it is distinct from the geometric center of the plasma boundary and from X-point locations.

The magnetic-axis location $(R_0,Z_0)$ is identified by the stationary point of the poloidal magnetic flux:

$$
\nabla_{R,Z}\psi(R_0,Z_0) = 0
$$

where $\psi$ is [poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) in Wb, $\nabla_{R,Z}$ is the gradient in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R_0$ is the major radius of the magnetic axis, and $Z_0$ is this vertical coordinate. The associated flux value is [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), which provides the inner reference for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.

In practice, this coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by locating the extremum of $\psi$ inside the last closed flux surface, constrained by magnetic measurements and, where available, kinetic or imaging information. It is used to quantify vertical plasma displacement and to compare magnetic-axis position with quantities such as the geometric-axis height and X-point height.

Typical values are near 0 m when the $Z$ origin is the device midplane and the plasma is vertically centered. Controlled offsets are often within -0.05-0.05 m in small and medium tokamaks and within -0.2-0.2 m in larger devices, while vertically shifted scenarios can reach order -1-1 m depending on the chosen origin and plasma size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic axis lies in the $+Z$ direction relative to the coordinate origin in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Vertical height coordinate of points on the plasma boundary contour in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where Z is measured upward from the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate gives the $Z$ component of each point tracing the plasma boundary contour — the outermost closed flux surface in limited configurations or the separatrix in diverted configurations — in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is the vertical height from the machine midplane and $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis.

Together with the corresponding radial coordinate, these $Z$ values fully define the poloidal cross-sectional shape of the plasma boundary, which governs geometric descriptors such as [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) and the proximity of the plasma to the first wall, as characterized by [vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point). In diverted plasmas the boundary follows the separatrix through the X-point region, whose vertical position is described by [vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point).

The boundary outline is derived from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements and flux loop data. Typical $Z$ values span from approximately $-a\kappa$ to $+a\kappa$, where $a$ is the minor radius and $\kappa$ is the elongation; for medium and large tokamaks this corresponds to a range of roughly $\pm 1$ to $\pm 3$ m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the boundary point lies above the machine midplane, in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point
NAMES.short: Height above the machine midplane of the reference point from which a plasma boundary gap is defined, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ of the reference point anchoring a plasma boundary gap, defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is the height measured upward along the machine symmetry axis. Plasma boundary gaps quantify the clearance between the plasma separatrix (or last closed flux surface) and the first wall or limiter; each gap is anchored at a pre-defined geometric reference point, and this coordinate specifies its vertical location within the poloidal cross-section.

In equilibrium analysis and position control, gap reference points are fixed as part of the machine geometry configuration. The actual gap distance along the specified direction is given by gap_at_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point, while the general scalar separation from the reference point to the boundary is captured by distance_of_plasma_boundary_gap. The vertical position of the plasma boundary itself is described by [vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary), and the analogous coordinate for the geometrically nearest wall point by [vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point).

For medium-to-large tokamaks, gap reference points span the poloidal cross-section, with $Z$ values ranging from roughly $-3$ to $+3$ m depending on machine size and the placement of position-control gaps at inner, outer, upper, and lower vessel locations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference point lies above the tokamak midplane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the primary X-point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the primary X-point is the $Z$ position of the main saddle point of the poloidal magnetic flux that forms the separatrix in an axisymmetric equilibrium. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The primary X-point position $(R_X,Z_X)$ is the saddle point at which the poloidal-flux gradient in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane vanishes:

$$
\nabla_{R,Z}\psi(R_X,Z_X)=\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial R},\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial Z}\right)_{(R_X,Z_X)}=(0,0)
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux in webers, $R$ and $Z$ are measured in meters, and $(R_X,Z_X)$ are the radial and vertical coordinates of the null in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. For an axisymmetric equilibrium with total poloidal flux $\psi$, $B_R=-(2\pi R)^{-1}\partial\psi/\partial Z$ and $B_Z=(2\pi R)^{-1}\partial\psi/\partial R$, so this condition is equivalent to vanishing radial and vertical components of the poloidal magnetic field at the X-point. The point is an X-point rather than a magnetic axis because the flux surface has saddle topology there.

The coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by locating the primary saddle of $\psi$ after fitting or interpolating the reconstructed flux map. Constraints may come from magnetic probes, flux loops, coil currents, kinetic pressure information, and boundary diagnostics; the reported value depends on the selected separatrix when several magnetic nulls exist.

Typical values should be assessed relative to the chosen vertical origin rather than as a universal device-independent range. With an origin near the machine midplane, a lower primary X-point has negative $Z_X$ and an upper primary X-point has positive $Z_X$; the magnitude is normally of order the plasma minor radius and lies within the modeled vessel and separatrix vertical extent.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the primary X-point lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame relative to the chosen vertical origin.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the secondary X-point, the poloidal magnetic null that anchors the secondary separatrix in double-null and snowflake divertor configurations.
NAMES.long:
The secondary X-point is a poloidal magnetic null at which both components of the poloidal magnetic field vanish and the secondary separatrix topology is established. It arises in advanced divertor configurations — double-null, snowflake, and related geometries — where a second separatrix surface exists, directly influencing power exhaust and particle control. The vertical coordinate $Z$ of this null locates it in the poloidal cross-section within the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the height measured from the geometric midplane.

Null points of the poloidal field are saddle points of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi(R, Z)$, satisfying

$$
\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial Z} = 0
$$

where the secondary X-point is the solution located outside the primary separatrix. Equilibrium reconstruction determines $\psi(R, Z)$ and identifies all saddle points numerically to extract this coordinate.

In symmetric double-null configurations the secondary X-point lies near the negative of the primary X-point $Z$-value; in asymmetric or snow-flake geometries its height depends on plasma shape and coil currents. The [vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point) provides the companion coordinate for the dominant null, while [vertical_coordinate_of_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point) documents the generic single-null case.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the secondary X-point lies above the geometric midplane, i.e., $Z > 0$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the strike point, the location where the plasma separatrix intersects a divertor target plate or limiter surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long:
The strike point is the intersection of the plasma separatrix — the outermost closed magnetic flux surface boundary — with a plasma-facing component, typically a divertor target plate. In a diverted tokamak configuration, separatrix field lines originate at the poloidal magnetic null, the [X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point), and terminate at the divertor surface. The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates this termination in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is directed vertically along the symmetry axis.

The strike-point position is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by intersecting the traced separatrix contour — derived from the reconstructed poloidal flux distribution — with the known device geometry. Both the primary and secondary separatrices can yield associated strike-point positions, corresponding to different divertor target plates in single-null and double-null configurations.

In standard single-null and double-null divertor configurations, strike points are positioned at $|Z|$ values of order $0.5$–$2.0$ m from the geometric midplane, reflecting the vertical depth of the divertor chamber and strongly depending on device size and plasma shaping.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the strike point lies in the $+Z$ direction, above the tokamak geometric midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the X-point, the poloidal magnetic null point at which the separatrix forms, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The X-point is a magnetic null in the poloidal cross-section where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ vanishes, causing adjoining flux surfaces to merge and form the separatrix that separates confined plasma from the scrape-off layer. Its vertical position $Z_X$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is a fundamental geometric parameter of divertor configurations.

The X-point location satisfies the simultaneous first-order null conditions on $\psi(R, Z)$:

$$
\left.\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R}\right|_{(R_X,\,Z_X)} = \left.\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial Z}\right|_{(R_X,\,Z_X)} = 0
$$

where $R_X$ is the major-radius position and $Z_X$ is the vertical position, both in meters.

The vertical coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by solving the Grad-Shafranov equation and locating saddle points of $\psi(R, Z)$, constrained by external magnetic measurements. Measured position estimates from real-time magnetics diagnostics may also serve as direct constraints in the reconstruction fit.

In lower single-null configurations $Z_X$ is negative (below the midplane), while upper single-null configurations yield positive $Z_X$; typical magnitudes lie in the range 0.5–2.0 m for medium-to-large tokamaks. When both X-points are present in double-null equilibria, their vertical coordinates are captured by [vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point) and [vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the X-point lies above the geometric midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Z component of the magnetic field vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where Z is vertical height. It includes contributions from plasma currents, external coil systems, and any non-axisymmetric field perturbations.
NAMES.long:
The vertical magnetic field $B_Z$ is the projection of the [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field) vector onto the vertical unit direction $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is one component of the poloidal magnetic field in axisymmetric equilibria, and it may also include toroidally varying contributions; the non-axisymmetric part is represented by [vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field). The same component evaluated at material boundary locations is [vertical_magnetic_field_at_wall](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_wall).

In an axisymmetric equilibrium, $B_Z$ is related to the radial derivative of the [poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) function $\psi(R, Z)$:

$$
B_Z = \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R}
$$

where $R$ is major radius in meters, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux per radian. Axis and boundary reference values such as [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_boundary set flux-surface normalization, while the local derivative of $\psi$ determines the vertical magnetic-field component.

$B_Z$ is computed in equilibrium reconstruction from magnetic measurements, plasma-current constraints, and, when available, internal magnetic-field constraints such as motional Stark effect polarimetry. It can also be obtained directly from magnetic-field calculations by projecting the vector field onto $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Representative values are highly device- and location-dependent. In tokamak plasma regions, $|B_Z|$ is commonly much smaller than the toroidal magnetic field, often in the range $10^{-3}$-$10^{-1}$ T, with larger local values possible near strong poloidal-field coils, divertor regions, or X-point shaping fields.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Vertical component of an iron-core segment's magnetization in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, taken to be uniform within the segment. The quantity is mu0 times M_Z, so it is expressed in tesla rather than amperes per meter.
NAMES.long:
Vertical magnetization of an iron-core segment is the component along the $Z$ direction of the volume-averaged magnetization vector $\mathbf{M}$ within a discrete ferromagnetic iron-core segment, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Each segment is treated as having a single uniform magnetization, so this quantity is one scalar per segment. The physical magnetization is magnetic dipole moment per unit volume (units A m$^{-1}$); the value reported here is scaled by the permeability of free space so that it carries units of tesla.

The reported vertical component is the scaled quantity

$$
\mathcal{M}_Z = \mu_0 M_Z
$$

where $\mathcal{M}_Z$ is in T, $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space ($4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m A$^{-1}$), and $M_Z$ is the $Z$ component of $\mathbf{M}$ in A m$^{-1}$. In macroscopic magnetostatics the magnetization enters through the constitutive relation $\mathbf{B} = \mu_0(\mathbf{H} + \mathbf{M})$, where the magnetic flux density $\mathbf{B}$ is in T and the magnetic field intensity $\mathbf{H}$ and the magnetization $\mathbf{M}$ are both in A m$^{-1}$.

In equilibrium analysis this component is generally inferred from external magnetic measurements together with a magnetic model of the iron structure rather than measured directly within the material. Its magnitude and sign are governed by the local field, the segment geometry, and the nonlinear iron $B$-$H$ response including magnetic saturation and hysteresis. The companion radial component is given by [radial_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment](name:radial_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment), and the associated field response is described by magnetic_field_of_iron_core_segment.

For soft-iron cores the scaled magnetization saturates near the material's saturation flux density, so magnitudes of order a few tesla represent an effective upper bound, with smaller magnitudes typical in unsaturated operation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetization component points in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Vertical component of the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic field in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the signed Z-directed part of toroidally varying perturbation fields such as error fields and resonant magnetic perturbations.
NAMES.long:
Vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the $Z$ component of the toroidally varying part of a vacuum magnetic field in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the upward or downward component of perturbation fields that break toroidal symmetry, excluding the axisymmetric equilibrium contribution.

The component projection is defined by

$$
B_Z^{\mathrm{NA}}(R,\phi,Z) = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}(R,\phi,Z) \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $B_Z^{\mathrm{NA}}$ is the vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field in tesla, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}$ is the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic-field vector in tesla, $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector, $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters. In current-free vacuum regions this perturbation field satisfies $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}} = 0$ and, away from coil conductors, $\nabla \times \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}} = 0$.

Together with the [radial non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field) and [toroidal non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), this quantity completes the cylindrical component decomposition of $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The related [vertical magnetic field at wall](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_wall) is also a $Z$-component field, but refers to the total or relevant magnetic field at the wall rather than specifically to the toroidally varying vacuum perturbation.

It is commonly computed from Biot-Savart integration over non-axisymmetric coil currents or from vacuum magnetic-field calculations, and may be compared with magnetic-probe measurements after accounting for probe orientation and location. The quantity is evaluated at physical locations of interest to characterize error fields, resonant magnetic perturbations, and their coupling to the plasma boundary or surrounding structures.

Typical magnitudes are strongly device-, coil-current-, and location-dependent. The value is zero for a purely axisymmetric vacuum field and is usually interpreted in tesla or as a fraction of the local equilibrium magnetic field rather than by a universal numerical range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z^{\mathrm{NA}}$ points in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_velocity_at_current_center
NAMES.short: Vertical velocity of the plasma-current centroid, equal to the time derivative of its Z coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical velocity at the current center is the rate of change of the vertical coordinate of the plasma-current centroid. The current center is the centroid of the toroidal plasma current density in a poloidal cross-section, with coordinates defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the velocity associated with vertical_position_at_current_center and is complementary to radial_velocity_at_current_center.

The current-density-weighted definition can be written as:

$$
v_Z^{cc} = \frac{d}{dt}\left[\frac{\int_{\Omega_p} Z\, j_\phi(R,Z,t)\, dR\, dZ}{\int_{\Omega_p} j_\phi(R,Z,t)\, dR\, dZ}\right]
$$

where $v_Z^{cc}$ is the vertical velocity of the current center, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma current density, $\Omega_p$ is the plasma region in the poloidal cross-section, and the denominator is the total toroidal [plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current) through that cross-section.

In practice, the current-center position is obtained from an equilibrium solution or reconstruction of the toroidal current density distribution, and the velocity is computed from its time evolution, usually with smoothing or filtering because time differentiation amplifies noise. The quantity characterizes vertical motion of the current channel, which is especially important for position control and vertical-displacement dynamics in elongated plasmas. Unlike [toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity), it describes the motion of the current-density centroid rather than mass-weighted bulk plasma flow.

Typical values are close to 0 m.s^-1 in a stationary or well-controlled equilibrium, because the current centroid is not translating vertically on average. During vertical transients the magnitude is device- and scenario-dependent and can become much larger than the controlled-state value, so universal numerical limits are not physically meaningful.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current centroid moves in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: volume_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Volume enclosed by a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface, increasing monotonically from zero at the magnetic axis to the total plasma volume at the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The volume of a flux surface quantifies the total three-dimensional region enclosed within a closed toroidal magnetic surface on which magnetic field lines lie. In an axisymmetric equilibrium, these nested surfaces are labeled by the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, and $V(\psi)$ increases monotonically from zero at the magnetic axis to its maximum at the last closed flux surface.

For an axisymmetric plasma in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the enclosed volume follows from revolving the poloidal cross-section about the toroidal symmetry axis:

$$
V(\psi) = 2\pi \int_{\mathcal{A}(\psi)} R \, dR \, dZ
$$

where $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis and $\mathcal{A}(\psi)$ is the poloidal area enclosed by the flux contour at $\psi$.

The volume profile is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction, which derives the flux surface geometry $\psi(R, Z)$ from external magnetic measurements augmented by internal diagnostics. It serves as the primary geometric metric in flux-surface-averaged transport equations: the differential $dV/d\psi$ acts as a volume element enabling conversion between flux coordinates and physical space. The companion quantities [surface_area_of_flux_surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface) and [cross_section_of_flux_surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface) give the total surface area and the poloidal cross-sectional area of the same flux surface.

Typical enclosed volumes range from negligible values near the magnetic axis to tens of cubic meters for medium-sized tokamaks and several hundred cubic meters for reactor-scale devices at the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all non-degenerate closed flux surfaces; the volume is zero only at the magnetic axis and increases monotonically outward to the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: major_radius
NAMES.short: Perpendicular distance from the machine's toroidal symmetry axis to a point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, used as the fundamental radial coordinate in equilibrium grids, MHD geometry, and device cross-section calculations.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the machine's toroidal symmetry axis to a given spatial point, measured in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$ and $Z$ is the vertical height. It is the primary radial coordinate of axisymmetric plasma geometry, entering metric factors in cylindrical differential operators, the ion gyroradius $\rho_i = m_i v_{\perp} / (Z_i e B)$, and the geometric weighting of current and pressure distributions.

In axisymmetric equilibrium, the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi(R, Z)$ satisfies the Grad-Shafranov equation:

$$
R\frac{\partial}{\partial R}\!\left(\frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial R}\right) + \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial Z^2} = -\mu_0 R^2\frac{dp}{d\psi} - F\frac{dF}{d\psi}
$$

where $p(\psi)$ is the plasma kinetic pressure, $F(\psi) = RB_\phi$ is the poloidal current function, and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space. Coordinate grids in $R$ are constructed for equilibrium reconstruction, MHD linear stability analysis, and the geometric description of device structures including halo-current wall boundaries and injector positions.

The [flux-surface-averaged major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius) provides the flux-surface mean of $R$, weighted by the inverse poloidal field strength, and is used in transport modeling. The quantity major_radius_of_geometric_axis specializes $R$ to the plasma geometric center, and major_radius_of_strike_point gives $R$ at the divertor heat-load footprint. Typical values span roughly 0.3–1.5 m on the high-field side to 1.5–6 m at the outer midplane for present-day tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the direction of increasing $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_major_radius
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the major radius coordinate R on each nested magnetic flux surface, yielding the mean distance from the toroidal symmetry axis weighted by the inverse poloidal field strength.
NAMES.long:
The flux-surface averaged major radius $\langle R \rangle$ is the mean value of the cylindrical major radius coordinate $R$ over a closed toroidal magnetic flux surface, weighted by the local inverse poloidal magnetic field magnitude. It belongs to the family of geometric metric coefficients (sometimes denoted $gm8$ in neoclassical transport literature) that enter the flux-surface-averaged forms of transport and equilibrium equations, and is the flux-surface-averaging transformation of the parent quantity [major_radius](name:major_radius).

The defining expression is:

$$
\langle R \rangle = \frac{\oint R \, \frac{dl}{B_p}}{\oint \frac{dl}{B_p}}
$$

where $l$ is the poloidal arc length along the flux surface and $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field magnitude, with integrals taken over one complete poloidal circuit. Because $B_p$ is smaller on the outboard low-field side, field lines dwell longer there, and $\langle R \rangle$ is shifted toward larger $R$ relative to a simple geometric centroid; it lies between the inner_major_radius_of_flux_surface and the outer_major_radius_of_flux_surface.

This coefficient is computed directly from the magnetic geometry obtained in equilibrium reconstruction, and is closely related to flux_surface_average_magnetic_field and flux_surface_averaged_curvature, which are derived from the same surface-averaging procedure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the $+\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: reference_major_radius
NAMES.short: Fixed major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system at which the vacuum toroidal magnetic field is specified. It is a non-negative geometric radius; the sign of the toroidal field is carried by the associated field value, not by the radius.
NAMES.long:
Reference major radius $R_0$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system at which the [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) value $B_0$ is defined. It is a geometric distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and is therefore non-negative; it does not carry the sign of the magnetic field.

For an axisymmetric vacuum toroidal field in a current-free region, the toroidal field scales inversely with major radius:

$$
B_\phi^\mathrm{vac}(R) = B_0\,\frac{R_0}{R}
$$

where $B_\phi^\mathrm{vac}(R)$ is the toroidal vacuum magnetic-field component in tesla at major radius $R$ in meters, $B_0$ is the signed toroidal vacuum magnetic field in tesla at $R_0$, and $R_0$ is the reference major radius in meters. The factor $R_0/R$ is positive; the field direction is determined by the sign of $B_0$.

In practice, $R_0$ is specified from the device geometry or equilibrium reference setup rather than measured by an independent diagnostic. It identifies where $B_0$ is quoted, and quantities that use the same vacuum-field reference, including flux-radius definitions such as [toroidal flux radius of the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis), should use a consistent $B_0$ and $R_0$ pair.

Representative tokamak values are about 0.3-7 m, ranging from compact or spherical devices to large conventional devices; the appropriate value is facility and configuration dependent.

NAMES.name: minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Minimum safety factor is the lowest signed value attained by the safety-factor function q across closed magnetic flux surfaces. It is the value of the minimum, not the flux-surface location, and is used to assess access to low-order rational-q MHD thresholds.
NAMES.long:
Minimum safety factor is the global minimum value of the signed safety factor on the nested closed magnetic flux surfaces. The safety factor on a surface is the field-line pitch, equal to the toroidal angle advance per poloidal circuit in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity is the scalar value of that minimum; the corresponding surface location is represented by [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor).

The minimum is defined by taking the minimum of the safety-factor function over the closed-surface domain:

$$
q_{\min} = \min_{0 \le \rho \le 1} q(\rho)
$$

where $\rho$ is a dimensionless monotonic flux-surface label normalized to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface, $q(\rho)$ is the signed safety factor (dimensionless), and $q_{\min}$ is dimensionless. The result is independent of the particular monotonic label used, provided the same set of closed flux surfaces is covered.

In practice, $q_{\min}$ is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction by computing $q$ on closed flux surfaces from the magnetic-field geometry and locating the global minimum, with interpolation between evaluated surfaces when needed. Magnetic measurements constrain the reconstruction, and kinetic or polarimetric constraints may improve the inferred current density and field-line pitch. The related point value [safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95](name:safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95) samples $q$ near the edge rather than taking a global minimum.

Typical tokamak values are about 0.7-2.5 for conventional or weakly reversed-shear plasmas. Values near 1 are important for internal-kink and sawtooth thresholds; crossing low-order rational values such as $3/2$ or $2$ can mark changes in resonant surfaces relevant to tearing and other MHD modes. Advanced or high-safety-factor scenarios may have $q_{\min}$ above 2.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle $\theta$ increases in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Normalized poloidal flux coordinate evaluated on the flux surface where the safety factor reaches its global minimum within the confined plasma. It gives the radial flux-surface location of the minimum-q surface on the 0-to-1 poloidal-flux scale.
NAMES.long:
Normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor is the value of the normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_N$ on the flux surface where the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) $q$ is globally smallest inside the last-closed flux surface. It locates the minimum-$q$ surface relative to the magnetic axis and plasma boundary, independent of the dimensional scale of [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux).

The quantity is defined by minimizing the safety factor as a function of normalized poloidal flux coordinate and applying the axis-to-boundary normalization of poloidal magnetic flux:

$$
\psi_{N,q_{\min}} = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \le \psi_N \le 1} q(\psi_N), \qquad
\psi_N = \frac{\psi - \psi_\mathrm{axis}}{\psi_\mathrm{b} - \psi_\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $\psi_{N,q_{\min}}$ is the coordinate of the minimum-safety-factor surface, $q(\psi_N)$ is the safety factor on a closed flux surface, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux of that surface, $\psi_\mathrm{axis}$ is the value at the magnetic axis, and $\psi_\mathrm{b}$ is the value at the plasma boundary. The minimization is over closed flux surfaces in the confined plasma; if several surfaces share the same minimum value, the arg-min is mathematically non-unique.

In practice this coordinate is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating the safety-factor radial behavior on nested closed flux surfaces, identifying the global minimum, and converting the corresponding surface to $\psi_N$. The corresponding dimensional flux on the same surface is [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor); a toroidal-flux-radius analog is [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor).

Typical values lie in the interval 0-1. Values near 0 indicate that the minimum safety factor is on or very close to the magnetic axis, while values around 0.2-0.6 are common for reversed-shear or otherwise non-monotonic equilibria with an off-axis minimum; values approaching 1 indicate a minimum near the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radius_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Curvature radius of an arc-of-circle segment used to represent the cross-sectional contour of a plasma current filament; it is the non-negative radius of the circle from which the arc is drawn.
NAMES.long:
Radius of a plasma filament segment is the curvature radius of one circular arc in an idealized cross-sectional contour of a current-carrying plasma filament. It is the non-negative distance from every point on that arc to its center of curvature; smaller values correspond to sharper boundary bending, while a straight segment is the limiting case of infinite radius.

For a circular segment, the arc length is related to the curvature radius by:

$$
\ell = R_c |\Delta\alpha|
$$

where $\ell$ is the arc length in meters, $R_c$ is the curvature radius in meters, and $\Delta\alpha$ is the signed central angle subtended by the arc in radians, treated as dimensionless in the product.

This quantity is usually specified or fitted as part of a piecewise geometric approximation to a filament cross-section for equilibrium and electromagnetic calculations, rather than measured directly by a diagnostic. Together with [width_of_plasma_filament](name:width_of_plasma_filament), [height_of_plasma_filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament), and the general radius, it helps define the idealized filament geometry; it is conceptually analogous to [radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:radius_of_iron_core_segment) and [radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) for other piecewise circular contours.

Finite curved segments require $R_c > 0$ and normally have values comparable to, or larger than, the local contour scale. Typical practical values range from 0.001-1 m, with millimeter-to-centimeter radii representing rounded corners in compact filament models and decimeter-to-meter radii representing gently curved, large-scale contours.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a plasma current-carrying filament element, marking the boundary between the hollow central region and the conducting annular zone.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius $r_\mathrm{inner}$ specifies the radial position of the inner wall of an annular plasma filament cross-section, defining the boundary between the hollow (non-current-carrying) core and the conducting annular region. In filamentary models of distributed plasma current, individual elements may be assigned annular geometries bounded at the outer wall by [outer_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament) $r_\mathrm{outer}$, with current flowing only in the region $r_\mathrm{inner} \leq r \leq r_\mathrm{outer}$.

The conducting cross-sectional area of the annular element is:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2 \right)
$$

where $A$ is the geometric cross-sectional area corresponding to area_of_plasma_filament. A valid annular geometry requires $0 \leq r_\mathrm{inner} < r_\mathrm{outer}$; setting $r_\mathrm{inner} = 0$ recovers a solid circular cross-section with no hollow core.

This parameter is a geometric input to the filamentary discretization of the plasma current distribution and is always specified alongside [outer_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament). For rectangular filament cross-sections the analogous spatial parameters are [height_of_plasma_filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament) and [width_of_plasma_filament](name:width_of_plasma_filament).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the inner boundary of the annular cross-section is measured outward from the local geometric center of the filament element.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a discrete plasma current-carrying filament element, marking the external radial boundary of the hollow-disk geometry.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius defines the external boundary of an annular cross-section when a plasma current filament element is represented as a hollow cylinder. Together with [inner_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament), it fully characterizes the annular geometry, which contrasts with the rectangular cross-section model parametrized by [height_of_plasma_filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament) and [width_of_plasma_filament](name:width_of_plasma_filament).

For an annular cross-section, the cross-sectional area relates to both radii by:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is this outer radius, $r_\mathrm{inner}$ is the inner radius, and $A$ is the area_of_plasma_filament.

The outer radius is specified as input geometry when constructing discrete filamentary representations of plasma current distributions used in equilibrium reconstruction and mutual-inductance computations. The constraint $r_\mathrm{outer} > r_\mathrm{inner} \geq 0$ must be satisfied to define a valid non-degenerate annular region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as a radial distance from the cross-section center to the outer boundary, satisfying $r_\mathrm{outer} > r_\mathrm{inner} \geq 0$.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Safety factor at the magnetic axis is the limiting value of the field-line pitch on the innermost closed magnetic flux surface, where the poloidal magnetic-flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Safety factor at the magnetic axis, often denoted $q_0$ or $q_\mathrm{axis}$, is the on-axis limit of the safety factor $q$. The safety factor expresses the field-line pitch on a closed magnetic flux surface: the number of toroidal turns made by a magnetic field line per poloidal circuit.

For nested closed flux surfaces, the on-axis value can be defined from the flux-surface safety factor as

$$
q_0 = \lim_{\psi \to \psi_\mathrm{axis}} \frac{d\Phi_\mathrm{tor}}{d\psi}
$$

where $\Phi_\mathrm{tor}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux in Wb, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, and $\psi_\mathrm{axis}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis.

In practice, $q_0$ is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating the reconstructed flux geometry and current distribution near the magnetic axis, then taking the innermost closed-flux-surface limit. It is sensitive to the central current density and is therefore less directly constrained by external magnetic measurements than edge or volume-integrated equilibrium quantities.

Typical dimensionless values in tokamak equilibria are of order unity to several, rather than being fixed by a universal bound. Values close to low-order rational numbers, especially near one, are important for core magnetohydrodynamic stability.
NAMES.sign: Positive when magnetic field lines advance in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ for an advance in the positive poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$, with $\phi$ increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95
NAMES.short: Safety factor evaluated on the closed flux surface where normalized poloidal magnetic flux is 0.95, commonly called q95.
NAMES.long:
Safety factor at normalized poloidal magnetic flux equal to 0.95, commonly denoted $q_{95}$, is the value of the safety factor on the closed flux surface whose flux coordinate $\psi_N$ is 0.95. It measures how many toroidal turns a magnetic field line makes per poloidal turn near the plasma edge, while remaining inside the separatrix where X-point geometry can make the boundary value more sensitive. It is an edge-near complement to [safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary](name:safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95) and [safety_factor_at_pedestal](name:safety_factor_at_pedestal).

Using the safety-factor function as a function of normalized poloidal magnetic flux, the defining relation is

$$
q_{95} = q(\psi_N = 0.95) = \left.\frac{d\Phi_\mathrm{tor}}{d\psi}\right|_{\psi_N=0.95}
$$

where $\Phi_\mathrm{tor}$ is toroidal magnetic flux, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux, and $\psi_N$ is normalized poloidal magnetic flux, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the boundary of closed flux surfaces. The derivative is dimensionless because both fluxes are measured in webers.

In practice, $q_{95}$ is obtained from an axisymmetric magnetic equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic diagnostics and, when available, pressure and current-distribution information. The reconstruction determines the relevant closed flux surface and the flux functions; $q(\psi_N)$ is then evaluated or interpolated at $\psi_N=0.95$.

Typical tokamak values are about 2-8; H-mode and baseline scenarios often lie around 3-6, while low-current or high-safety-factor scenarios can exceed 8. Values close to low-order rational numbers, especially near 2 or 3, are important for global kink, tearing, and edge-stability limits.
NAMES.sign: Positive when, moving outward across neighboring closed flux surfaces at $\psi_N=0.95$, the signed toroidal magnetic flux changes in the same sense as the signed poloidal magnetic flux.

NAMES.name: toroidal_total_current_density
NAMES.short: Toroidal projection of the total current density, aggregating ohmic, bootstrap, and all externally driven contributions over all plasma species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal total current density is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the aggregated current density vector [total_current_density](name:total_current_density), which sums ohmic, bootstrap, and externally driven currents over all plasma species and charge states. It is the dominant current-density component in tokamak operation because the plasma current flows primarily in the toroidal direction.

The defining projection is:

$$
j_\phi = \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{total} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{total}$ is the net current density aggregated over all mechanisms and species.

In magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium, $j_\phi$ is the source term in the Grad-Shafranov equation governing the poloidal flux distribution. It may be decomposed into partial contributions such as [toroidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density](name:toroidal_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density) or mechanism-specific components like [toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity). The orthogonal counterpart is [poloidal_current_density](name:poloidal_current_density). The closely related [toroidal_current_density](name:toroidal_current_density) names the same projection when no explicit aggregation qualifier is needed.

Typical core values span 0.1–5 MA m$^{-2}$ in medium-sized tokamaks, with the profile peaking on axis and decreasing toward the separatrix.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $j_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: area_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Non-negative effective sensing area of a flux loop diagnostic. It combines the loop aperture, number of turns, and calibration factors relating magnetic flux threading the loop to the spatially averaged magnetic-field component normal to the loop aperture.
NAMES.long:
The effective area of a flux loop is the non-negative field-to-flux sensitivity factor of the sensor. It represents the aperture area, winding count, and calibration corrections that make the total linked magnetic flux equivalent to a spatially averaged normal magnetic field over an effective aperture.

The defining relation is

$$
A_\mathrm{eff} = \frac{\Phi}{\bar{B}_n}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the signed magnetic flux threading the loop in Wb, $\bar{B}_n$ is the spatial average of the magnetic-field component normal to the loop aperture in T, and $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective area in m$^2$. For a specified loop normal and terminal polarity, Faraday's law gives the flux-loop voltage as $V = -d\Phi/dt = -A_\mathrm{eff}\,d\bar{B}_n/dt$ when $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is constant; reversing the winding direction or terminal polarity reverses the signs of $V$ and $\Phi$ but not the non-negative area.

The effective area is obtained from the constructed winding geometry or from calibration in a known applied magnetic field. It is the flux-loop analog of the sensitivity area used for [area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), while [area_of_rogowski_coil](name:area_of_rogowski_coil) describes coupling to enclosed current rather than linked magnetic flux. It is used with [voltage_of_flux_loop](name:voltage_of_flux_loop) or time-integrated voltage to infer [poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) or an equivalent averaged field.

Typical values span several orders of magnitude. Compact local or saddle-loop sensors may have effective areas around $10^{-3}$-$10^{-1}$ m$^2$, while large multi-turn or vessel-encircling loops in major-radius-scale devices can have effective areas of order 1-100 m$^2$.

NAMES.name: area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Cross-sectional area of each turn of a poloidal magnetic field probe coil, which together with the turn count determines the effective flux-sensing area of the pickup coil.
NAMES.long:
The cross-sectional area of each individual turn of a poloidal magnetic field probe coil is the geometric enclosed area of the wire loop in the plane perpendicular to the probe's sensitive axis. Combined with the number of turns $N$, it determines the total effective flux-sensing area $NA$ that links induced voltage to the local magnetic field component.

The induced terminal voltage follows Faraday's induction law:

$$
V = -N A \frac{dB_n}{dt}
$$

where $V$ is the terminal voltage, $N$ is the turn count, $A$ is the cross-sectional area per turn, and $B_n$ is the magnetic field component normal to the coil plane. Integrating the [voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) signal and dividing by $NA$ recovers the local poloidal field time trace.

The area is established during probe fabrication and verified by calibration in a known applied field. It plays the same fundamental role for the poloidal sensing channel as [area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) plays for the toroidal channel. Typical values for tokamak pickup coils range from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-4}$ m², reflecting a balance between sensitivity and spatial resolution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as the geometric cross-section of the coil loop enclosed by the windings in the plane perpendicular to the probe's sensitive axis.

NAMES.name: area_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short: Effective cross-sectional area linked by the turns of a Rogowski coil. It is the flux-coupling area per turn that, together with winding turn density, sets the voltage sensitivity to a time-varying enclosed current.
NAMES.long:
Area of a Rogowski coil is the effective cross-sectional area linked by its sensing winding. It represents the flux-coupling area per turn for the magnetic field generated by current enclosed by the closed coil. In a real coil it is a calibrated effective quantity that includes finite winding pitch, cross-section variation, and placement tolerances.

For an ideal uniformly wound Rogowski coil that fully encloses the primary conductor, the current recovered from the coil voltage is

$$
I(t)-I(t_0) = \frac{1}{\mu_0 n A}\int_{t_0}^{t} V_R(t')\,dt'
$$

where $A$ is the Rogowski-coil area, $n$ is the winding turn density in turns per meter along the closed winding path, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, and $V_R$ is the [Rogowski-coil voltage] after applying the chosen terminal polarity and integrator calibration. Equivalently, the ideal differential sensitivity is $V_R = \mu_0 n A\,dI/dt$ for the same polarity convention.

In practice, $A$ may be estimated from mechanical dimensions for simple windings, but precision use normally determines it by calibration with a known pulsed current. The ideal relation assumes uniform turn density, a nonmagnetic core, complete enclosure of the measured current, negligible pickup from external fields, and a return conductor routed along the coil centerline so it does not form an additional single-turn pickup loop. The [major radius of the Rogowski coil] helps set the mean winding path length used to convert total turns to turn density.

Typical effective areas for installed Rogowski coils are about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ m$^2$ (1-100 cm$^2$), with compact in-vessel coils near the lower end and large air-core or calibration coils near the upper end. The overall current sensitivity is set by the product $\mu_0 n A$, so coils with the same area can produce different voltage signals if their winding densities differ.

NAMES.name: area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Cross-sectional area of each turn of a toroidal magnetic field probe coil, which together with the number of turns sets the total effective flux pickup area for converting induced voltage to the toroidal magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The cross-sectional area of a single winding turn of a toroidal magnetic field probe determines how much toroidal magnetic flux threads each loop of the coil.
