The product of this area with the turn count gives the total effective pickup area that governs the coil's voltage response to changes in the toroidal field component $B_\phi$.

The induced terminal voltage follows Faraday's law:

$$
V = -N A \frac{dB_\phi}{dt}
$$

where $V$ is the [terminal voltage](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), $N$ is the algebraic turn count (see [count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe)), $A$ is the per-turn cross-sectional area, and $B_\phi$ is the local toroidal magnetic field component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The area is determined from the coil's physical dimensions during fabrication or verified by laboratory calibration; time-integrating the measured voltage and dividing by $NA$ recovers the absolute field $B_\phi$. The corresponding quantity for poloidal pickup coils is [area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).

Typical single-turn cross-sectional areas in tokamak magnetics diagnostics range from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$ m$^2$, depending on probe dimensions and required sensitivity.

NAMES.name: breakdown_stray_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Magnitude of the residual magnetic field at the plasma position during the breakdown phase of plasma initiation. It quantifies the all-direction stray field from imperfect cancelation of external coil fields that can impede electron avalanche formation.
NAMES.long:
Breakdown stray magnetic field magnitude is the scalar magnitude of the residual magnetic field present at the plasma position during the initial electron-avalanche phase. It is the breakdown-specific form of [stray_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:breakdown_stray_magnetic_field_magnitude) and includes residual field in all spatial directions, not only the poloidal component.

For a stray-field vector $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{stray}$ with components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the magnitude is

$$
B_\mathrm{stray} = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are the radial, toroidal, and vertical components of $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{stray}$, all expressed in tesla; $B_\mathrm{stray}$ is also reported in tesla.

In practice this quantity is estimated from magnetic-field calculations for the breakdown scenario, including external-coil currents and relevant residual or induced fields. It may be constrained or checked using magnetic measurements when suitable diagnostics and timing are available, but the definition is the local magnetic-field magnitude at the intended breakdown location.

Optimized breakdown conditions commonly require residual fields at the millitesla scale, for example about 0.001-0.005 T in many tokamak scenarios. This range is device- and scenario-dependent rather than a universal acceptance criterion, because the tolerable stray field also depends on electric field, neutral pressure, vessel size, connection length, toroidal field, and pre-ionization conditions; poorly nulled configurations can reach several millitesla to tens of millitesla.

NAMES.name: count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Number of turns in a toroidal magnetic-field probe coil; the sign indicates whether the winding and terminal polarity give a signed area normal in the direction of increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The signed turn count of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the number of conductor turns linked by the probe aperture, including the orientation imposed by the winding sense and the chosen terminal polarity. Its magnitude multiplies the magnetic flux coupled into the coil, while its sign records whether the coil's signed area normal corresponds to the positive or negative $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The electromagnetic calibration follows the flux-linkage form of Faraday's law:

$$
V = -\frac{d\Lambda}{dt}, \qquad \Lambda = N\Phi_+ = N\int_{S_+} \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}_+ \simeq N A B_\phi
$$

where $V$ is the open-circuit [terminal voltage](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) in volts, $\Lambda$ is the flux linkage in webers, $N$ is this signed turn count, $\Phi_+$ is the flux through a reference turn, and $d\mathbf{S}_+$ is the vector area element in square meters with normal chosen along increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The approximation uses the effective [probe area](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) $A$ in m$^2$ and a locally uniform toroidal magnetic-field component $B_\phi$ in tesla.

The magnitude of $N$ is assigned from winding records and checked by magnetic calibration with a known time-varying $B_\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The sign is determined from the documented terminal polarity and the right-hand rule for the coil winding; calibration verifies it by comparing the measured terminal-voltage polarity with that predicted by Faraday's law. The [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) specifies the sensitive-axis orientation, and the [probe length](name:length_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) characterizes finite spatial sampling rather than multiplying the flux pickup factor $N A$.

Typical magnitudes are 1-10 turns for high-bandwidth probes and 10-500 turns for higher-sensitivity or low-noise coils. Larger magnitude increases induced voltage for a given $dB_\phi/dt$ but generally increases winding resistance, self-inductance, and capacitance, so the selected count reflects a trade-off between sensitivity and frequency response.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the winding and terminal polarity define a signed area normal pointing in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis_magnitude
NAMES.short: Euclidean norm of the total magnetic field vector evaluated at the magnetic axis, where the poloidal flux reaches its extremum and poloidal field components vanish in an axisymmetric equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic axis is the unique interior point where the poloidal flux function $\psi$ attains its extremum, defining the center of the nested flux-surface topology. In an axisymmetric equilibrium, the poloidal field components vanish there by symmetry, so the field magnitude is dominated by the toroidal contribution.

The on-axis field magnitude is defined as:

$$
B_0 = |\mathbf{B}|_{\rm axis} = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2}\bigg|_{R=R_{\rm axis},\, Z=Z_{\rm axis}}
$$

where $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are the radial, toroidal, and vertical components of $\mathbf{B}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, evaluated at the axis position $(R_{\rm axis}, Z_{\rm axis})$.

This quantity serves as the conventional reference field $B_0$ for normalizing plasma parameters, and is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction combining external magnetic diagnostics with pressure profile constraints. Its value closely tracks [toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis) because the poloidal field contribution is negligible at the axis. Typical on-axis values range from 1–6 T in medium to large tokamaks; the corresponding flux-surface extremal counterparts are [maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude) and [minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude).

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Major radius R coordinate of a flux loop diagnostic position, giving the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the loop center in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate $R$ gives the position of a flux loop diagnostic in the major-radius direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis. Flux loops are closed conducting loops whose terminal voltage obeys Faraday's law, $V = -d\Psi/dt$, where $\Psi$ is the total poloidal magnetic flux enclosed by the loop; the loop's $(R, Z)$ position is essential for mapping the measured flux to the equilibrium geometry during reconstruction. Typical major-radius positions for flux loops span from values near the inner wall to the outer vacuum vessel structure, covering roughly 0.5–12 m across current and planned tokamak devices.

The radial position is obtained from engineering survey data or the design geometry of the magnetic diagnostic assembly and is treated as a fixed calibration parameter for each measurement campaign. Together with the [terminal loop voltage](name:voltage_of_flux_loop) and the [effective sensing area](name:area_of_flux_loop), this coordinate fully characterizes the spatial contribution of each flux loop to the equilibrium constraint set. The identical spatial registration convention is used for the [radial coordinate of a poloidal magnetic field probe](name:radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign: Positive when directed away from the toroidal symmetry axis in the direction of increasing $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Major radius R coordinate of the physical location of a poloidal magnetic field probe in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate $R$ gives the major-radius position of a poloidal magnetic field probe, measured from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

Poloidal magnetic field probes are distributed around the poloidal cross-section of the vessel to sample the local poloidal field component; their radial positions span from the inboard wall to the outboard wall and are established by physical survey of the installed hardware. Together with [radial_coordinate_of_flux_loop](name:radial_coordinate_of_flux_loop) and [radial_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:radial_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), this value maps the complete primary magnetics diagnostic array onto the poloidal cross-section for equilibrium reconstruction. The [area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and [voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) characterize the flux-sensing area and measured signal of the same probe at this radial location.

Typical values range from roughly 0.5-2 m for compact devices to 4-10 m for large tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured outward from the machine symmetry axis in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Major radius R coordinate of the physical location of a toroidal magnetic field probe in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis to the probe center.
NAMES.long:
The radial position of a toroidal magnetic field probe specifies how far the sensing coil is located from the machine symmetry axis, measured along the major radial direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height.

Together with the [vertical coordinate](name:vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) and the [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), this coordinate fully determines the three-dimensional position of the probe in the device. These three coordinates enter directly into equilibrium reconstruction algorithms, which weight magnetic field measurements by their geometric location relative to the plasma column. The analogous coordinate for poloidal-field sensing coils is the [radial coordinate of a poloidal magnetic field probe](name:radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).

The coordinate is obtained from engineering survey data or computer-aided design models of the diagnostic hardware. Typical values range from approximately 1 m at the inner wall to 10 m at the outer wall for large-scale devices, with medium-sized tokamaks spanning roughly 1.5–5 m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe position is displaced outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the $+\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle of a magnetic-field probe is the signed tilt of the coil sensitive axis out of the local poloidal plane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It specifies the toroidal component of the unit sensitivity direction used to project the local magnetic field onto the measured component.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal angle of a magnetic-field probe is the signed angle between the probe sensitive axis and its projection onto the local poloidal plane. The local poloidal plane is spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The angle is commonly represented on the principal branch $-\pi/2 \leq \alpha \leq \pi/2$, with $\alpha=0$ for a sensitive axis lying in the local poloidal plane.

The local magnetic-field component measured along the sensitive axis is obtained from the angular projection:

$$
\hat{n}=\cos\alpha\,\hat{p}+\sin\alpha\,\hat{\phi}, \qquad B_n=\mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{n}=\cos\alpha\,B_{p,\mathrm{loc}}+\sin\alpha\,B_\phi
$$

where $\alpha$ is the toroidal angle, $\hat{n}$ is the unit sensitive-axis direction, $\hat{p}$ is the unit projection of $\hat{n}$ onto the local poloidal plane, $B_n$ is the field component sensed by the probe, $B_{p,\mathrm{loc}}=(B_R\hat{R}+B_Z\hat{Z})\cdot\hat{p}$ is the local scalar projection of the poloidal magnetic field onto $\hat{p}$, and $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component. Thus a zero toroidal angle means the probe responds to the local poloidal-field projection selected by its in-plane orientation, not to all poloidal components simultaneously.

The angle is determined from probe design geometry, mechanical metrology, installation survey, or magnetic calibration. For an induction coil, it enters the conversion from coil voltage to field through the projected component, for example with the voltage proportional to $-N A_\mathrm{eff}\,dB_n/dt$ for $N$ turns and effective area $A_\mathrm{eff}$. A major-radius coordinate $R$ fixes only distance from the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame; it does not by itself specify the full probe location or the sensitive-axis projection direction $\hat{p}$.

For probes intended to measure poloidal magnetic field, $|\alpha|$ is usually small, often 0-0.1 rad after alignment and calibration. Deliberately oblique installations or constrained mounting geometries may use 0.1-0.5 rad, while values approaching $\pm\pi/2$ rad correspond to an axis that is predominantly toroidal-field sensitive.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the sensitive axis is tilted from its projection in the local poloidal plane toward the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle of the horizontal projection of a toroidal magnetic field probe's sensitive-axis normal vector, defining the probe's azimuthal orientation in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle $\phi_\mathrm{probe}$ specifies the azimuthal orientation of a toroidal magnetic field probe's sensitive axis, defined as the angle of the horizontal projection of the probe's normal vector measured from the outward major-radius direction $+\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$.

Together with the poloidal orientation angle, this quantity fully determines the three-dimensional pointing direction of the pickup coil, which is essential for correctly projecting the raw inductive voltage signal onto the toroidal field component during signal interpretation. The analogous orientation angle for non-type-specific magnetic probes is captured by [toroidal_angle_of_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_magnetic_field_probe).

The value is determined from mechanical design drawings and installation surveys of the magnetics diagnostic system. Combined with the major_radius_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe and [vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), it fully localizes the probe in three-dimensional space. For probes distributed around the machine, values span the range $0$ to $2\pi$ rad.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the horizontal projection of the probe's normal vector points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of a flux loop diagnostic in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, giving the height of the loop above or below the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates a flux loop diagnostic along the direction parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ increases upward from the geometric midplane. Together with the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate_of_flux_loop) $R$, it fixes the poloidal-plane position of the loop, which is essential for mapping the induced voltage signal to the local poloidal magnetic flux distribution used in equilibrium reconstruction.

The $Z$ coordinate is determined during installation by precision engineering surveys and is fixed hardware metadata characterizing the diagnostic geometry. Knowing the full $(R, Z)$ position enables forward-model calculations of the expected flux threading each loop for a given equilibrium, which are compared against [measured voltage signals](name:voltage_of_flux_loop) integrated over time; the [effective sensing area](name:area_of_flux_loop) must also be known to complete this calibration.

Typical $Z$ values span from the machine midplane ($Z = 0$) to $\pm 1$–$\pm 4$ m in medium to large tokamaks, placing flux loops on the inboard wall, outboard wall, and top or bottom regions of the vacuum vessel. The analogous vertical-position quantity for Rogowski coil diagnostics is [vertical coordinate of the Rogowski coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux loop position is located above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of a poloidal magnetic field probe in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measuring the probe's height relative to the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates a poloidal magnetic field probe along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ increases upward from the machine midplane.

Poloidal field probes measure the poloidal component of the magnetic field and are deployed around the vacuum vessel to support equilibrium reconstruction; their precise spatial position is essential because the poloidal field pattern sensitively reflects the plasma current distribution. Together with [radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), the $Z$ coordinate fully defines the probe location in the poloidal cross-section. The analogous coordinate for toroidal probes is given by [vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), and the equivalent geometry for flux loop diagnostics is described by [vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop](name:vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop).

Probe positions are established by mechanical survey during installation or from engineering drawings, with positional uncertainties of order 1 mm or less for precision installations. Values range from approximately $-2$ m to $+2$ m in medium-sized tokamaks, and up to several meters in larger devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe position is above the machine midplane, in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the Rogowski coil position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured along the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The vertical Z coordinate locates the Rogowski coil along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ measures height above the $Z = 0$ reference plane. Together with the major radius given by [radial_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil](name:radial_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil), it fully specifies the coil's position in a poloidal cross-section, which is required to associate the enclosed-current measurement with the correct plasma geometry and to provide geometric inputs for magnetic equilibrium reconstruction.

This coordinate is a fixed geometric parameter established from engineering metrology of the installed coil. The same vertical-coordinate convention is applied to [vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop](name:vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop) and [vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor](name:vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor) across the magnetic diagnostics family.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coil is located above the $Z = 0$ reference plane, in the upward direction along the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the toroidal magnetic field probe position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, giving the probe's height relative to the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates a toroidal magnetic field probe along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ increases upward from the machine midplane and $R$ is the perpendicular distance from that axis.

Together with the major-radius coordinate [radial_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:radial_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) and the azimuthal orientation [toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), this value fully specifies the three-dimensional position of the probe within the vacuum vessel. Probe positions are established from engineering drawings and verified by in-vessel survey or photogrammetry during installation and maintenance campaigns. The analogous vertical coordinate for the poloidal probe is given by [vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), which follows the same frame convention. Typical values span the vertical extent of the vacuum vessel, ranging from approximately $-2$ to $+2$ m in medium-sized tokamaks, with symmetric upper and lower probe arrays straddling the midplane.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe is located above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of an outline point defining the geometric boundary of a Fiber Optic Current Sensor in a poloidal cross-section, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame where Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline of a Fiber Optic Current Sensor is the $Z$ coordinate of an indexed point on the sensor's geometric boundary in a poloidal cross-section. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height.

For outline vertex $i$, the vertical coordinate is paired with the corresponding major-radius coordinate to define the point in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
P_i = (R_i, Z_i)
$$

where $P_i$ is the outline vertex, $R_i$ is the companion [major-radius outline coordinate], and $Z_i$ is this vertical outline quantity.

In practice, $Z_i$ is obtained from the sensor design geometry, mechanical survey, or alignment model using the same vertical datum as the companion $R_i$ coordinates. The paired coordinates trace the sensor boundary used to locate the fiber optic current sensor relative to surrounding hardware and magnetic-field geometry.

No device-independent numeric range applies; values are expressed in meters and are bounded by the vertical extent and reference plane of the installed sensor geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline point is displaced in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame relative to the chosen $Z=0$ reference plane.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Voltage of a flux loop is the direct, unintegrated terminal voltage measured across the sensor. It is induced by the time rate of change of the oriented magnetic flux threading the loop and is related to that flux by Faraday's law.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a flux loop is the signed terminal potential difference produced when the magnetic flux linked by a conducting loop changes in time. It is the direct, unintegrated sensor output: the measured voltage itself, before conversion to magnetic flux by time integration, offset removal, or calibration.

For an oriented surface $S$ bounded by the loop, the flux-loop voltage is defined by Faraday's law:

$$
V(t) = -\frac{d\Phi(t)}{dt}, \qquad \Phi(t)=\int_S \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x},t)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dA
$$

where $V$ is the terminal voltage in volts, $t$ is time in seconds, $\Phi$ is the oriented magnetic flux in webers, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic flux density in tesla, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen unit normal to the surface, and $dA$ is an area element in square meters. The chosen $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ defines positive flux; the corresponding positive circulation around the loop is given by the right-hand rule, and reversing $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ or swapping the terminal polarity reverses the reported sign.

The voltage is measured with a high-impedance differential input across the two loop terminals so that the sensor minimally loads the induced electromotive force. Recovering flux requires choosing the polarity and an integration constant: with the equation's polarity, $\Phi(t)=\Phi(t_0)-\int_{t_0}^{t} V(t')\,dt'$, where $t_0$ is the reference time and $\Phi(t_0)$ is the integration constant. For equilibrium or shape constraints, this integrated flux may be used as a local constraint on [poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_sensor_attachment_point); the [area of the flux loop](name:area_of_flux_loop) sets the scale for converting a flux change to an average normal-field change.

The magnitude scales with linked area and field slew rate, approximately as $|V|\sim A_\mathrm{eff}|dB_n/dt|$ for a nearly uniform normal field over effective area $A_\mathrm{eff}$, where $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is in square meters and $B_n$ is the magnetic field component along $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ in tesla. Representative operating amplitudes are often 10^-3-10 V, but near-zero values occur during slowly varying field intervals and larger voltages can occur for large loops or rapid magnetic changes; the usable range is normally set by sensor area, bandwidth, and digitizer range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the designated positive terminal is at higher electric potential than the designated negative terminal; with the chosen loop normal defining positive magnetic flux by the right-hand rule, this corresponds through $V=-d\Phi/dt$ to a decreasing positive flux through the loop.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Terminal voltage induced at the terminals of a poloidal magnetic field probe coil by the time variation of the local poloidal magnetic field component threading the coil windings.
NAMES.long:
The terminal voltage of a poloidal magnetic field probe is the raw inductive electrical signal generated when the poloidal magnetic field component at the sensor location changes with time. It is the primary electrical observable from which the local poloidal field is derived during post-processing.

For a coil with $N$ turns and effective cross-sectional area $A$ per turn, Faraday's law gives:

$$
V = -N A \frac{dB_p}{dt}
$$

where $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field component along the probe's sensitive axis, $N$ is the algebraic turn count encoding the winding direction, and $A$ is the effective [area of each turn](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).

The raw voltage is time-integrated in post-processing to recover the instantaneous $B_p$, with corrections for resistive losses and signal drift. Arrays of poloidal field probes distributed around the vacuum vessel provide the boundary field measurements essential for equilibrium reconstruction and real-time plasma shape control. The directly analogous signal for probes oriented to sense the toroidal field is [voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe); the complement for flux-enclosed measurements is [voltage_of_flux_loop](name:voltage_of_flux_loop). The probe's spatial location entering the field derivation is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux threading the coil in the direction of the probe's positive sensitive-axis normal is decreasing with time.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Terminal voltage of a toroidal magnetic field probe coil, induced by the time variation of the local toroidal magnetic field component threading the coil windings.
NAMES.long:
A toroidal magnetic field probe is a pickup coil wound to sense the toroidal component of the magnetic field at a specific location. The terminal voltage is the raw inductive signal produced as the local toroidal field $B_\phi$ evolves in time.

The coil voltage follows from Faraday's law of induction:

$$
V = -N A \frac{dB_\phi}{dt}
$$

where $N$ is the number of turns and $A$ is the effective cross-sectional area per turn. Time-integrating the voltage signal and dividing by the coil sensitivity $NA$ recovers the local toroidal field value; the geometric parameters are provided by [count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) and [area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

Probes are mounted on the vacuum vessel wall or plasma-facing surfaces and sampled on fast analog-to-digital converters to capture the full temporal evolution of the toroidal field. The analogous measurement for the poloidal field component is given by [voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $dB_\phi/dt > 0$ for a coil wound in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Alpha angle of an iron core segment is the first signed inclination of an oblique trapezoidal or parallelogram cross-section. It is measured in the poloidal R-Z cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame from the outward major-radius direction to the slanted alpha-side direction.
NAMES.long:
The alpha angle $\alpha$ is the first inclination angle used to parameterize an oblique trapezoidal or parallelogram cross-section of an iron core segment. The cross-section is taken in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It defines the orientation of the slanted side associated with [major_length_of_iron_core_segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment), complementary to the other inclined side length [length_of_iron_core_segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment).

For an $\alpha$-inclined side, the unit tangent in the cross-section is

$$
\hat{t}_{\alpha} = \cos\alpha\,\hat{R} + \sin\alpha\,\hat{Z}
$$

where $\hat{t}_{\alpha}$ is the tangent along the alpha-side, $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the major-radius and vertical basis vectors of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, and $\alpha$ is in radians. A side of length $L_{\alpha}$ then gives in-plane displacements $\Delta R=L_{\alpha}\cos\alpha$ and $\Delta Z=L_{\alpha}\sin\alpha$, which fixes the vertices and face normals used in geometric, magnetic, and structural calculations.

In practice, $\alpha$ is obtained from engineering drawings, CAD geometry, or the coordinates of the endpoints of the slanted side in the local $R$-$Z$ cross-section. If the two endpoints are known, the same convention is recovered with $\alpha=\operatorname{atan2}(Z_2-Z_1,R_2-R_1)$, with $R$ and $Z$ in meters and the angular branch chosen consistently with the segment geometry.

There is no universal device-independent design range. The full angular branch is commonly interpreted over about $-3.14$-$3.14$ rad; reference orientations are $0$ rad for an outward radial side, $1.57$ rad for a vertical upward side, and about $3.14$ rad or $-3.14$ rad for an inward radial side. Nearly rectangular cross-sections have $\alpha$ close to one of these reference orientations, while tapered iron-core segments use design-specific offsets.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the alpha-side tangent is rotated counter-clockwise from the outward $+\hat{R}$ direction toward $+\hat{Z}$ in an $R$-to-the-right, $Z$-up drawing of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: area_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Area of the conducting cross-section of a passive conducting loop element, measured in a plane perpendicular to the local current path; for an annular loop cross-section it is the area between the inner and outer conductor boundaries.
NAMES.long:
Area of a passive loop is the cross-sectional area of solid conducting material in a passive conducting loop element, evaluated in a plane normal to the local current path. It is a geometric property of the conductor and is non-negative; for fixed material properties and path length, a larger area reduces the electrical resistance of a uniform conductor model.

For an annular passive-loop cross-section defined by an inner radius $r_i$ and an outer radius $r_o$, the area is

$$
A = \pi\left(r_o^2 - r_i^2\right)
$$

where $A$ is the cross-sectional area in m$^2$, and $r_i$ and $r_o$ are the [inner](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and [outer](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop) radii in m measured from the annulus center to the conducting boundaries.

In practice, $A$ is computed from the engineering geometry of the passive conductor cross-section. For non-annular or simplified sections it is the area of the bounded conducting region normal to the current path; rectangular approximations use the product of a geometric width and height, while other parameterizations may use a thickness together with the relevant cross-section dimensions. In electromagnetic circuit models, the relation $R = \rho \ell/A$ applies only for an idealized uniform conductor of resistivity $\rho$ in $\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$, path length $\ell$ in m, and uniform current distribution.

There is no device-independent typical numerical range for this quantity: values depend on the size and category of the passive structure being represented. Physically meaningful values are positive and should be consistent with the associated radii, width, height, or thickness used to describe the same conductor cross-section.

NAMES.name: area_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Cross-sectional area of an individual conductor element of a poloidal field coil.
NAMES.long:
The area of a poloidal field coil element is the geometric cross-sectional area of the conducting material assigned to one conductor element. It is a non-negative engineering geometry quantity that sets the conversion between element current and average current density and contributes to electromagnetic force, thermal, and structural calculations.

For an arbitrary cross-section, the area is the surface measure of the conductor region:

$$
A = \int_{\mathcal{S}} dS
$$

where $\mathcal{S}$ is the conductor cross-section and $A$ is the resulting area. For common parameterizations, a rectangular element has $A = w t$, where $w$ is the [width](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) and $t$ is the [thickness](name:thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil), while an annular element has $A = \pi(r_{\rm out}^2-r_{\rm in}^2)$, where $r_{\rm out}$ and $r_{\rm in}$ are the [outer](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [inner](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) radii.

In practice this area is obtained from the conductor design geometry, manufacturing drawings, or surveyed coil dimensions. For polygonal cross-sections it is computed from the closed boundary of the conductor region; for composite conductors the effective conducting area may be distinguished from the total structural envelope when evaluating the engineering average current density $J = I/A$, where $J$ is in A m$^{-2}$, $I$ is the element current in A, and $A$ is in m$^2$.

Typical values range from $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ m$^2$ for small trim or auxiliary poloidal-field conductors to $10^{-2}$-$1$ m$^2$ for large poloidal-field and central-solenoid conductor elements, depending on current, cooling, insulation, and structural requirements.

NAMES.name: area_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Cross-sectional area enclosed by a toroidal field coil conductor in the plane normal to the coil centerline. It is the geometric area used with coil current to estimate average engineering current density and support electromagnetic and structural engineering estimates.
NAMES.long:
Area of a toroidal field coil conductor is the area enclosed by the conductor cross-section in the plane perpendicular to the local coil centerline. In a local Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, the cross-section lies in the normal-binormal plane spanned by $(\hat{n}, \hat{b})$; it complements the [width](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil) and [height](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil) of the toroidal field coil conductor.

For a closed polygonal contour with vertices $(u_i, v_i)$ in the normal-binormal plane, where $u$ is distance along $\hat{n}$ and $v$ is distance along $\hat{b}$, the area is commonly evaluated using the shoelace formula:

$$
A = \frac{1}{2}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(u_i v_{i+1} - u_{i+1} v_i\right)\right|,\quad (u_{N+1},v_{N+1})=(u_1,v_1)
$$

where $A$ is the conductor cross-sectional area, $N$ is the number of contour vertices, and $u_i$ and $v_i$ are measured in meters. The absolute value removes dependence on whether the contour is traversed clockwise or counter-clockwise in the local cross-section plane.

The area is obtained from the conductor geometry, a design drawing, a CAD model, or direct dimensional metrology. For a rectangular cross-section, $A$ is approximately the product of the normal and binormal extents; for circular or annular sections, the corresponding circular area is used with any represented voids subtracted. In engineering estimates the average current density is often approximated as $J_\mathrm{eng}=I/A$, with $I$ in A and $J_\mathrm{eng}$ in A m$^{-2}$; for composite, hollow, or cable-in-conduit conductors, the current and area must refer to the same physical material region.

Typical values span about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}$ m$^2$. Small normal-conducting research coils may use conductors near $10^{-4}$-$10^{-3}$ m$^2$, superconducting cable-in-conduit conductors are often $10^{-3}$-$10^{-2}$ m$^2$, and large aggregate winding-pack or busbar-like conductors can approach $10^{-2}$-$10^{-1}$ m$^2$ depending on design and cooling requirements.

NAMES.name: binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of a correction-coil conductor cross-section vertex along the binormal direction of the local Frenet-Serret (tangent, normal, binormal) frame. Paired with the normal coordinate, it specifies the conductor outline in the plane perpendicular to the coil centerline.
NAMES.long:
The binormal coordinate is the signed displacement of a vertex on a correction-coil conductor cross-section along the binormal direction of the local Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$. Together with the paired [normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil), it defines the conductor outline in the cross-section plane perpendicular to the local coil centerline.

In the Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, $\hat{t}$ is tangent to the conductor centerline, $\hat{n}$ is the principal normal toward the local center of curvature, and $\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}$ completes the right-handed orthonormal triad. For a closed polygonal outline, the binormal and normal vertex coordinates describe the external geometric boundary used for electromagnetic spacing and structural envelope calculations. Unless separate quantities describe voids, cooling channels, insulation layers, or subcomponents, the outline represents the gross conductor cross-section rather than a net conducting-material area.

The coordinates are usually obtained from engineering drawings, CAD geometry, or coil-design models by projecting each cross-section vertex onto $\hat{b}$ in the local $(\hat{n}, \hat{b})$ plane. For rectangular or nearly rectangular conductors, the spread of binormal coordinates corresponds to one transverse conductor dimension and is interpreted consistently with [height_of_correction_coil](name:height_of_correction_coil) and [width_of_correction_coil](name:width_of_correction_coil); the analogous quantity for toroidal-field coils is [binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil).

Typical absolute coordinate values are 0.005-0.1 m for compact in-vessel correction coils and 0.05-0.3 m for larger external correction coils. When the cross-section origin is placed on the conductor centerline, the largest positive and negative binormal coordinates are typically about half of the corresponding transverse conductor size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement is in the $+\hat{b}$ direction of the local Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$.

NAMES.name: binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Coordinate of the toroidal field coil conductor cross-section outline vertices along the binormal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame, measuring each polygon vertex's displacement in the binormal direction perpendicular to the conductor centerline.
NAMES.long:
The binormal coordinate locates each vertex of the polygonal cross-section outline of a toroidal field coil conductor along the binormal direction $\hat{b}$ of the local Frenet-Serret frame. In this frame, the unit tangent $\hat{t}$ follows the conductor centerline, the principal normal $\hat{n}$ points toward the center of curvature of the conductor path, and the binormal vector is defined as

$$
\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}
$$

forming a right-handed orthonormal triad $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, with the cross-section lying in the $(\hat{n}, \hat{b})$ plane.

Together with the [normal coordinate], the binormal coordinate fully specifies the 2D polygonal shape of the conductor cross-section perpendicular to the conductor path. The total span in the binormal direction for a rectangular conductor equals the [height of the toroidal field coil]. This framing is also used for non-axisymmetric coils; see [binormal coordinate of correction coil] for the analogous quantity.

These coordinates are derived from engineering design data and are used in electromagnetic and structural analyzes of TF coils, where the precise cross-section shape affects current density distribution, self-inductance, and mechanical stress. Typical TF conductor cross-section dimensions range from a few centimeters to tens of centimeters in each local direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coordinate is in the direction of $\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}$, where $\hat{t}$ is the unit tangent along the conductor centerline and $\hat{n}$ is the principal normal directed toward the center of curvature.

NAMES.name: count_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Number of discrete toroidal field coil modules in the confinement device, excluding conductor turns within each module.
NAMES.long:
The count of toroidal field coils is the integer total of discrete coil modules arranged around the device to produce the dominant toroidal magnetic field. It counts coil modules, not individual conductor turns, pancakes, or strands within a module, and is a fixed engineering design parameter for the magnet system.

For an axisymmetric tokamak with uniformly spaced toroidal field coils, this count sets the rotational periodicity of the coil set. If the count is $N_\mathrm{TF}$, one geometric sector spans $2\pi/N_\mathrm{TF}$ in toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. The finite number and detailed shape of the coils determine the toroidal-field ripple spectrum and can affect fast-ion confinement and periodic heat-load patterns.

The count is obtained from the device magnet design by identifying the mechanically distinct toroidal field coil modules in the full torus. It is used together with geometric coil properties such as [cross-sectional area](name:area_of_toroidal_field_coil), [conductor width](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil), and [major-radius position] when characterizing the toroidal field system. In stellarators and heliotrons, comparable coil counts usually refer to separate modular, helical, or planar coil families rather than to tokamak-style toroidal field coils.

Typical tokamak values are 12-20 toroidal field coils, with many medium and large devices using 16-18 coils. Smaller or specialized devices may use fewer coils, while increasing the count generally reduces the angular spacing between coils and changes the high-toroidal-mode content of the ripple field.

NAMES.name: current_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Electrical current driven through a non-axisymmetric correction coil. It is a signed circuit quantity whose waveform sets the amplitude and phase of the coil magnetic perturbation.
NAMES.long:
Current of a correction coil is the signed electric current driven through an active non-axisymmetric coil. It is a commanded circuit quantity, distinct from [current_of_passive_loop](name:current_of_passive_loop), which is induced by electromagnetic coupling rather than directly driven.

In a lumped single-coil circuit model, the current is related to the applied coil voltage by:

$$
V(t) = R I(t) + L \frac{dI}{dt}
$$

where $I(t)$ is the correction-coil current in amperes, $V(t)$ is the applied [voltage_of_correction_coil](name:voltage_of_correction_coil) in volts, $R$ is the [resistance_of_correction_coil](name:resistance_of_correction_coil) in ohms, and $L$ is the coil self-inductance in henries. Detailed circuit models may also include mutual inductance, eddy-current coupling, and plasma response terms.

In practice, $I(t)$ is set by the coil power supply and measured with calibrated current transducers such as Rogowski coils, DC current transformers, or Hall sensors. Together with the coil winding geometry, it determines the amplitude and phase of the imposed non-axisymmetric magnetic perturbation; the analogous active axisymmetric coil quantity is [current_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:current_of_poloidal_field_coil).

Typical values range from 10-10^4 A, depending on coil size, number of turns, cooling, and operating scenario. Small trim or error-field correction coils may operate below 100 A, while resonant magnetic perturbation coil systems commonly use 10^3-10^4 A per powered circuit.
NAMES.sign: Positive when charge flows through the coil in the defined winding direction from its reference start terminal to its reference end terminal.

NAMES.name: current_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Electric current induced in a passive axisymmetric conducting loop by time-varying magnetic flux linked from the plasma, active coils, and neighboring conducting structures.
NAMES.long:
Current of a passive loop is the toroidal electric current that flows in an electrically conducting, axisymmetric loop without an applied power supply. It is an eddy current driven by time-varying magnetic flux linked by the loop, including contributions from the plasma, active poloidal-field coils, and other conducting structures.

For a lumped passive circuit $k$, Faraday's law and Ohm's law give

$$
R_k I_k + \frac{d}{dt}\left(L_k I_k + \sum_{j \ne k} M^{pp}_{kj} I_j + \sum_a M^{pa}_{ka} I_a + \Psi^{\mathrm{plasma}}_k\right) = 0
$$

where $I_k$, $I_j$, and $I_a$ are currents in A, $R_k$ is the [resistance_of_passive_loop](name:resistance_of_passive_loop) in $\Omega$, $L_k$ is the loop self-inductance in H, $M^{pp}_{kj}$ and $M^{pa}_{ka}$ are mutual inductances in H to other passive loops and active coils, and $\Psi^{\mathrm{plasma}}_k$ is the plasma-linked magnetic flux in Wb. The resistive drop $R_k I_k$ and the inductive electromotive force are the circuit terms associated with the voltage_of_passive_loop; with no applied source, their closed-loop sum is zero.

Passive-loop current is measured with Rogowski coils encircling the conductor or inferred from magnetic sensor data constrained by a coupled circuit model. In modeling, it is solved together with plasma and active-coil currents using geometry-dependent inductances and conductor properties such as [resistivity_of_passive_structure](name:resistivity_of_passive_structure); finite resistance dissipates the eddy current over a decay time $\tau = L_k/R_k$, while mutual coupling determines how strongly the loop opposes changes in linked flux.

Representative magnitudes are 1-10^4 A for small loops and routine coil transients; 10^4-10^5 A can occur in low-resistance vessel, shell, or stabilizing-loop circuits during rapid plasma-current changes or disruptions. Decay times range from milliseconds for thin components to hundreds of milliseconds for massive high-conductivity structures.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the loop current flows in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, i.e. increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with $R$ major radius and $Z$ vertical height.

NAMES.name: current_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed conventional current carried by a toroidal-field coil winding.
NAMES.long:
Current of a toroidal-field coil is the signed conventional electric current carried by one toroidal-field coil winding or conductor path. It is an individual coil-circuit current; the magnetic effect of a coil set is determined by the signed ampere-turns obtained from all coil currents and turn counts.

For an ideal toroidal winding, the vacuum toroidal magnetic field at reference major radius $R_0$ is approximated by Ampere's law:

$$
B_\phi(R_0) \simeq \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi R_0}\sum_j N_j I_j
$$

where $B_\phi$ is the toroidal component of magnetic field in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $N_j$ is the number of turns in coil $j$, $I_j$ is the current of that coil winding, and the sum is the total linked ampere-turns. Detailed vacuum-field calculations use the actual coil geometry through Biot-Savart integration or equivalent magnetic modeling rather than this idealized estimate.

The current is measured with power-supply and coil-circuit instrumentation such as DC current transducers, Rogowski coils, Hall sensors, or calibrated shunts. Series-connected toroidal-field coils usually share one current, whereas independently supplied coil modules can carry distinct signed currents; circuit modeling combines this quantity with coil voltage, resistance, and inductance.

Typical coil currents are 1,000-20,000 A in small or medium resistive systems, 10,000-50,000 A in large resistive systems, and 10,000-80,000 A in superconducting toroidal-field circuits. The relevant magnetic scale is often the product of current and turn count, so designs trade current against number of turns for a required toroidal field.
NAMES.sign: Positive when conventional current in the winding is oriented so that its contribution to the toroidal magnetic field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Fast neutron flux incident on the inboard side of a non-axisymmetric correction coil, used to assess radiation exposure and predict material degradation of coil components.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutrons produced predominantly by deuterium-tritium fusion reactions scatter through plasma-facing and structural components and irradiate the conductors of non-axisymmetric correction coils. The fast neutron flux quantifies the number of energetic neutrons crossing a unit area of the coil's inboard surface per unit time, with the inboard face experiencing the highest neutron loading due to its relative proximity to the plasma.

The threshold-integrated fast neutron flux is defined as:

$$
\Phi_{\rm fast} = \int_{E \geq E_{\rm th}} \phi(E) \, dE
$$

where $\phi(E)$ is the differential neutron flux spectrum (m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$), $E$ is neutron kinetic energy, and $E_{\rm th}$ is a threshold energy (commonly 0.1 MeV or 1 MeV) defining the fast-neutron energy range.

This quantity is computed from neutron transport calculations using the device three-dimensional geometry and the predicted fusion neutron source rate; results are validated against threshold-detector or activation-foil measurements placed near accessible coil positions. Time-integrating this flux over an operational pulse yields the neutron fluence, which governs displacement damage in conductor insulation and structural materials. The analogous quantity for the main toroidal field coil is [fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil); for direct detector measurements see [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector).

NAMES.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Fast neutron flux incident on the inboard side of a toroidal field coil, providing a measure of radiation exposure relevant to material activation, radiation damage, and conductor insulation lifetime assessment.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutron flux at a toroidal field coil quantifies the number of energetic neutrons crossing unit area per unit time at the inboard-facing surface of the coil structure. In deuterium-tritium burning plasmas, 14.1 MeV fusion neutrons are the dominant source; these are attenuated and scattered by the blanket and shield, but a residual fast population reaches the coil and constitutes the primary radiation load on the superconducting windings and their organic insulation.

The quantity is the energy-integrated fluence rate above a fast-neutron threshold:

$$
\Phi_n = \int_{E_\mathrm{th}}^{\infty} \Phi(E)\, dE
$$

where $\Phi(E)$, in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$, is the differential neutron flux spectrum and $E_\mathrm{th}$ is the fast-neutron energy threshold adopted in the transport model.

This flux drives radiation damage processes including atomic displacement damage in conductor structural materials, helium bubble formation, and degradation of organic insulation resins — all of which set operational lifetime limits for the coil. It is assessed using Monte Carlo or deterministic neutron transport codes, validated against activation foil and threshold detector measurements. The analogous quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is [fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed electromagnetic force on an individual poloidal field coil, formed from radial and vertical Lorentz force components, used to define structural load limits and engineering bounds for coil system design.
NAMES.long:
The force on a poloidal field coil arises from the Lorentz interaction between the energized coil conductors and the total magnetic field contributed by the plasma current and all electromagnets in the device. It is a signed scalar representing a projection or combination of force components resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with radial contributions along $\hat{R}$ (increasing major radius) and vertical contributions along $\hat{Z}$.

The net electromagnetic force along a given direction is obtained by integrating the Lorentz body force over the conductor volume:

$$
F = \int_V (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{n} \, dV
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the current density in the conductor, $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field, and $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector of the projection direction. This force scalar underlies the engineering bounds expressed by [maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), which set the upper and lower structural limits used in coil system design and scenario optimization. For spatially resolved component forces, see [radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil); for the global coil-system resultants, see [radial_force](name:radial_force) and vertical_force.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical force component is directed upward along $+Z$ and the radial force component is directed outward along increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: height_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Full height of the rectangular cross-section of a correction-coil conductor along the binormal axis of the local Frenet-Serret (tangent, normal, binormal) frame.
NAMES.long:
The height of a correction coil is the full transverse extent of a rectangular conductor cross-section along the binormal basis vector $\hat{b}$ of the local Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$ attached to the conductor centerline. It is the dimension perpendicular to the normal-direction width and is meaningful when the conductor cross-section is represented as rectangular.

For a rectangular cross-section, the complementary width $w$ is measured along $\hat{n}$ and the height $h$ is measured along $\hat{b}$. Their product gives the cross-sectional area $A = w h$, where $h$ and $w$ are in meters and $A$ is in square meters. For a conductor carrying current $I$ in amperes, a simple average engineering current density is $J_\mathrm{eng} = I/A$ in A m^-2, before any corrections for insulation, cooling channels, or nonconducting structural material.

In design and metrology, the height is obtained by resolving the rectangular cross-section onto the $\hat{b}$ direction of the local Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$ along the conductor centerline. The associated local coordinates are described by [binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil) and [normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil), while the perpendicular rectangular dimension is [width_of_correction_coil](name:width_of_correction_coil).

Representative values for correction-coil conductor or winding-pack heights are 0.01-0.2 m for compact internal or edge coils and 0.05-0.5 m for larger external coils. The selected value depends on required ampere-turns, current density limits, cooling layout, insulation thickness, and mechanical support requirements.

NAMES.name: height_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section of an iron core segment, defining the vertical extent of the segment geometry used in electromagnetic modeling of the tokamak transformer core.
NAMES.long:
The height of an iron core segment is the total vertical dimension of the rectangular cross-section in the axisymmetric representation of the ferromagnetic transformer core used to drive poloidal flux in a tokamak. In the thick-line approximation, each core segment is modeled with a rectangular cross-section; this quantity measures its extent along the $Z$ axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate.

The rectangular cross-section area $A$ entering the magnetic reluctance calculation is:

$$
A = h \cdot w
$$

where $h$ is the height and $w$ is the [width](name:width_of_iron_core_segment). The reluctance follows $\mathcal{R} = l\,/\,(\mu_r \mu_0 A)$, where $l$ is the path length along the segment, $\mu_r$ is the relative permeability of the iron, and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H m$^{-1}$ is the permeability of free space.

The segment geometry — including this height, the [width_of_iron_core_segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment), and the [thickness_of_iron_core_segment](name:thickness_of_iron_core_segment) — is derived from engineering drawings of the tokamak magnetic circuit and provided as input to field and equilibrium reconstruction models. For segments with annular cross-sections, the complementary radial dimensions [inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment) and [outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment) apply instead.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical extent is measured from the lower boundary to the upper boundary of the cross-section in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: height_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Vertical full height of a rectangular cross-section element of a passive conducting structure, measured along Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Height of passive structure is the full vertical extent of a rectangular cross-section passive conducting element. It is measured parallel to $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity is a geometric length and is non-negative.

For a rectangular cross-section whose sides are aligned with the $R$ and $Z$ directions, the cross-sectional area is related to height and width by:

$$
A = h w
$$

where $h$ is the vertical height in meters, $w$ is the horizontal [width of the passive structure](name:width_of_passive_structure) in meters, and $A$ is the rectangular cross-sectional area in square meters.

In practice, this height is obtained from engineering geometry, survey data, or geometric reconstruction of the passive conductor boundary as the separation between the lower and upper faces of the rectangular cross-section. It applies specifically to rectangular cross-sections; annular or shell-like passive-loop descriptions are better characterized by quantities such as [inner radius of passive loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and [thickness of passive loop](name:thickness_of_passive_loop).

Typical values range from 0.01-1 m. Small segmented passive conductors may have heights of a few centimeters, while large vessel-integrated or stabilizing conducting structures can have vertical extents of several tenths of a meter or more.

NAMES.name: height_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section of a poloidal field coil conductor element, measured parallel to Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The height of a poloidal field coil conductor element is the full vertical extent of its rectangular cross-section. It is measured parallel to the $Z$ axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a rectangular cross-section, the height is the difference between the upper and lower vertical boundaries:

$$
h = Z_{\max} - Z_{\min}
$$

where $h$ is the coil height, and $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum vertical coordinates of the conductor cross-section boundary.

This dimension is obtained from coil engineering geometry, drawings, or electromagnetic models. Together with the radial [width of a poloidal field coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil), it defines the rectangular cross-section; for a solid rectangle, their product gives the [area of a poloidal field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil). The related [thickness of a poloidal field coil](name:thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil) describes a separate conductor or winding-pack extent when that dimension is distinguished.

Typical values range from 0.05-0.5 m for small correction or shaping coils and about 0.2-2 m for large equilibrium-field coils, depending on current capacity, mechanical support, and available space.

NAMES.name: height_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Full geometric height of a rectangular toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section measured along the binormal direction of the local right-handed Frenet-Serret frame. It is a gross external envelope dimension, not a net current-carrying material thickness.
NAMES.long:
The height of a toroidal field coil conductor cross-section is the full geometric extent of a rectangular conductor envelope measured along the binormal direction $\hat{b}$ of the local right-handed Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$ attached to the conductor centerline. Together with the complementary [width_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil), measured along $\hat{n}$, it specifies the rectangular external cross-section used for coil geometry and engineering calculations.

For a rectangular conductor envelope, the gross cross-sectional area is related to height and width by:

$$
A_\mathrm{env} = w h
$$

where $h$ is this height, $w$ is the corresponding rectangular width, and $A_\mathrm{env}$ is the gross envelope area of the modeled conductor cross-section.

In practice this dimension is taken from engineering drawings, manufacturing specifications, or a geometric model of the toroidal field coil conductor. It represents the outer envelope of the modeled conductor cross-section and should not be interpreted as the net thickness of current-carrying material; internal subdivision into strands, stabilizer, jacket, coolant channels, insulation, or voids is accounted for separately unless those regions are explicitly included in the chosen conductor envelope. For non-rectangular conductor shapes, polygonal outline quantities such as [binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil) provide the detailed shape description.

Typical gross heights are about 0.02-0.2 m for individual cable-in-conduit or busbar-like toroidal field coil conductors, and about 0.2-1.5 m when the modeled conductor represents a larger homogenized winding-pack block. The appropriate value depends on machine size, number of turns, conductor technology, and the level of geometric homogenization used in the coil model.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a non-axisymmetric correction coil conductor, defining the bore size of the hollow conductor or winding pack.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius defines the bore boundary of the annular cross-section used to model a correction coil conductor or winding pack. Together with the outer radius given by radius_of_correction_coil, it fully specifies the hollow circular geometry, with conductor material occupying the annular region between $r_{\rm in}$ (this quantity) and $r_{\rm out}$.

The cross-sectional area enclosed by the conductor annulus is

$$
A = \pi \left( r_{\rm out}^2 - r_{\rm in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_{\rm out}$ is the outer radius and $r_{\rm in}$ is the inner radius, both in meters.

This parameter enters electromagnetic and structural models of non-axisymmetric coils used for error field correction or ELM suppression. The [area_of_correction_coil](name:area_of_correction_coil) is computed directly from the inner and outer radii. An analogous bore parameter for poloidal field coils is given by [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as a radial distance from the conductor bore axis to the inner conducting surface.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular conductor cross-section of a toroidal field coil. It is the non-negative distance from the annulus center to the bore-side boundary of the conducting material.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius $r_\mathrm{inner}$ is the distance from the center of an annular toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section to the inner boundary of the conducting material. It describes the radius of the central opening of the annulus and is defined only for hollow, annular conductor cross-sections, with $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} < r_\mathrm{outer}$.

For an annular conductor, the conducting cross-sectional area is related to the inner and outer radii by:

$$
A = \pi\left(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2\right)
$$

where $A$ is the conducting area, $r_\mathrm{inner}$ is the inner radius in meters, and $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the outer radius in meters. The paired quantity $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is represented by outer_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil.

This radius is specified from the mechanical design of the toroidal field coil conductor or inferred from cross-section drawings and manufacturing data. Together with the outer radius, it determines the amount of conducting material, the available cooling or insulation space in the central opening, and derived engineering quantities such as average current density.

Typical values range from 0 m for a solid conductor treated as the limiting case to about 0.01-0.5 m for large annular conductors, depending on coil scale, conductor technology, cooling-channel layout, and structural design.

NAMES.name: length_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Non-negative Euclidean length of the beta-angle-inclined side of an oblique parallelogram iron-core segment, measured in the poloidal R-Z plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. The side is referenced to the vertical Z direction; its inclination is set by the beta angle.
NAMES.long:
Length of an iron-core segment is the non-negative Euclidean size of the beta-inclined side of an oblique parallelogram cross-section. The geometry is interpreted in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height. The beta side is referenced to the $+Z$ vertical direction: the beta angle specifies the inclination of that side in the $R$-$Z$ plane, toward increasing $R$ for a positive beta angle.

For two vertices on the same beta-inclined side, the length is the Euclidean distance between their coordinates in the poloidal cross-section:

$$
L_\beta = \sqrt{(R_2 - R_1)^2 + (Z_2 - Z_1)^2}
$$

where $L_\beta$ is this side length, $(R_1, Z_1)$ and $(R_2, Z_2)$ are the endpoint coordinates, $R$ is major radius, and $Z$ is vertical height. The endpoint ordering does not affect $L_\beta$; the beta-angle convention selects which pair of opposite sides of the parallelogram is being measured.

The quantity is normally derived from the geometric specification of the iron core, such as CAD vertices, mechanical drawings, or survey points. A complete oblique-parallelogram parameterization requires this beta-side length together with the complementary major length or other side length, the alpha and beta angle conventions, and a position reference such as a center or corner; the length alone does not determine the full cross-section.

Typical values for magnetic-system iron-core segments range from 0.05-10 m. Small shaping inserts or chamfer-like pieces can be below 0.5 m, while large transformer limbs and yoke segments are commonly 1-10 m.

NAMES.name: length_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Non-negative Euclidean length of the beta-side inclined edge of an oblique parallelogram cross-section of a passive conducting structure element, measured in the poloidal R-Z plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The beta-side length is the geometric length of one inclined edge of an oblique parallelogram cross-section representing a passive conducting structure element. It is a non-negative scalar Euclidean distance in a constant-$\phi$ poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

For endpoints $(R_1,Z_1)$ and $(R_2,Z_2)$ of the beta-side edge in that poloidal plane, the length is

$$
L_\beta = \sqrt{(R_2-R_1)^2 + (Z_2-Z_1)^2}
$$

where $L_\beta$ is the beta-side length and the coordinate differences are measured between the two edge endpoints.

In practice this quantity is obtained from engineering geometry, CAD-derived cross-section descriptions, or simplified electromagnetic models of passive conductors. Together with the complementary side length, inclination angle, and thickness, it fixes the oblique cross-section used to compute conductor area, resistance, mutual inductance, and induced-current response.

Typical values for individual passive-structure elements range from 0.01-1 m, depending on device size and the geometric discretization of vessel, shell, plate, or stabilizing conductor components. Very fine segmented models may use lengths below 0.01 m, while large structural plates can have edge lengths of order 1-2 m.

NAMES.name: major_length_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Euclidean length of the parallelogram side inclined at the alpha angle in an axisymmetric ferritic element's oblique parallelogram cross-section, measured in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The major length of a ferritic element is the Euclidean length of the pair of opposite sides inclined by the alpha angle in an oblique parallelogram cross-section. The cross-section is defined in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height; rotating this cross-section about the symmetry axis represents an axisymmetric ferritic body. This is a geometric size parameter, not a magnetic permeability or field-strength quantity.

For endpoints $(R_1, Z_1)$ and $(R_2, Z_2)$ of one alpha-inclined side, the length is

$$
L_\alpha = \sqrt{(R_2 - R_1)^2 + (Z_2 - Z_1)^2}
$$

where $L_\alpha$ is the major length, and $R_i$ and $Z_i$ are the endpoint coordinates in meters in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The corresponding edge orientation is given by the [alpha angle of the ferritic element], measured from the outward $R$ direction.

The value is obtained from the engineering geometry or reconstructed geometric model by identifying the two vertices connected by the alpha-inclined edge. Together with minor_length_of_ferritic_element, [width_of_ferritic_element](name:width_of_ferritic_element), and alpha_angle_of_ferritic_element, it helps specify the size and orientation of the ferritic material region used in electromagnetic modeling. The analogous geometric parameter for iron-core segment models is [major_length_of_iron_core_segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment).

Typical values range from 0.02-0.3 m for small ferritic inserts or tiles, 0.3-2 m for passive magnetic shields and vessel-adjacent ferritic structures, and 2-10 m for large axisymmetric return-yoke or iron-core-like elements represented by a coarse oblique parallelogram model.

NAMES.name: major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Length of the parallelogram side inclined at the alpha angle from the major-radius direction, defining the alpha-edge of the oblique cross-section of a poloidal field coil.
NAMES.long:
In the oblique parallelogram model of a poloidal field coil cross-section, the full shape in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane is described by two inclined side lengths and their respective angles from the outward major-radius direction $+\hat{R}$. The major length $L_\alpha$ is the Euclidean length of the side whose orientation is inclined at the alpha angle from $+\hat{R}$, complementing the beta-side length given by [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For a parallelogram cross-section with alpha-side $L_\alpha$, beta-side $L_\beta$, and interior angle $\theta$ between the two sides, the cross-sectional area satisfies:

$$
A = L_\alpha \, L_\beta \, \sin\theta
$$

where $\theta$ is set by the combination of the alpha and beta inclination angles.

This side length, together with [radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil), fully parameterizes the oblique cross-section and enters coil flux and inductance calculations. The same alpha-side naming convention is used for iron core segments in [major_length_of_iron_core_segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment) and for individual conductor elements in major_length_of_coil_conductor_element.
NAMES.sign: Positive as a geometric side length in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane; this quantity is invariant under reversal of plasma current or toroidal field direction.

NAMES.name: maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Upper bound on a signed electromagnetic force resultant for poloidal-field coils, with the resultant and its sign defined by the weights in one row of the force-combination matrix.
NAMES.long:
Maximum force of a poloidal-field coil is the upper allowable value of a signed electromagnetic force resultant acting on the poloidal-field coil system. Each row of the force-combination matrix defines one such resultant by weighting independent products of coil currents; this quantity is the upper bound for that row. Together with [minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), it defines the admissible signed force interval for the matrix-defined load.

The force resultant for row $k$ of the force-combination matrix is constrained by the maximum limit:

$$
F_k = \sum_j C_{kj} G_j \le F_{k,\max}
$$

where $F_k$ is the $k$-th [force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil) and $F_{k,\max}$ is its maximum limit, both in N. The index $j$ runs over the matrix columns, each representing an independent coil-current product $G_j$ such as $I_m I_n$; $G_j$ has dimensions of current squared when currents are in A. The coefficient $C_{kj}$ is the signed force weight for that product, with units $\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{A}^{-2}$ for currents in A, so each term $C_{kj}G_j$ has units N.
