The limit is normally selected from allowable mechanical loads or scenario-design constraints and used when evaluating candidate coil currents. The same matrix formalism can describe radial loads along $R$ or vertical loads along $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, as in [radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), or aggregate resultants such as [radial_total_maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_total_maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil). If no finite upper ceiling is imposed for a particular row, the absence of a bound means that row does not constrain the force from above.

No device-independent numerical range is intrinsic to this quantity. Finite values are real numbers in N determined by the selected load combination and allowable-load model; their scale follows the electromagnetic force coefficients and the square of the relevant coil currents, and may differ between radial $R$, vertical $Z$, and aggregate load constraints in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the force resultant computed from the corresponding row of the force-combination matrix is positive, i.e. when the weighted sum of the signed coil-current products specified by that row is positive.

NAMES.name: minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Lower engineering limit on a signed net electromagnetic force formed from poloidal field coil force components in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is a hard constraint for axisymmetric PF coil-system design and scenario optimization.
NAMES.long:
Minimum force of a poloidal field coil system is the lower engineering bound on a signed net electromagnetic force formed from individual poloidal-field-coil force components. It constrains axisymmetric coil-system design and scenario optimization by excluding coil-current waveforms or plasma scenarios that would exceed allowable mechanical loading in the negative limiting sense. The force components are resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius outward from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For the $i$-th force constraint, acceptable operating states satisfy:

$$
\mathbf{c}_i \cdot \mathbf{F} \ge F_{\min,i}
$$

where $\mathbf{F}$ is the vector of electromagnetic force components on the poloidal field coils in N, $\mathbf{c}_i$ is the dimensionless vector of weighting coefficients that defines the signed force combination, and $F_{\min,i}$ is the minimum permitted value in N. If no finite lower bound is imposed for a particular combination, the lower constraint is mathematically absent rather than represented by a mechanical force value.

The actual signed combination is the [force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil). It is typically computed from electromagnetic equilibrium or coil-design models by integrating $\mathbf{J}\times\mathbf{B}$ loads over conductor volumes, or equivalently by evaluating mutual forces between current-carrying circuits and surrounding magnetic fields. The lower bound is set from structural allowables for winding packs, casings, supports, insulation, and fatigue margins, and is used together with [maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) to define the admissible force interval for each signed combination.

Typical absolute magnitudes of finite lower limits are 10^5-10^8 N for medium-sized PF coil systems and can approach 10^9 N in very large devices or for aggregate load combinations. The signed value may be negative, zero, or positive depending on the chosen combination-matrix weights and on whether the limiting sense is inward, outward, downward, or upward.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the limiting force corresponds to a weighted electromagnetic-force resultant in the sense selected by positive weighting coefficients: $+\hat{R}$ for outward radial components, $+\hat{\phi}$ for increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and $+\hat{Z}$ for upward vertical components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; negative weighting coefficients reverse the selected sense.

NAMES.name: normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Coordinate of the correction-coil conductor cross-section outline vertices along the normal axis of the local Frenet–Serret frame.
NAMES.long:
The normal coordinate locates each vertex of the polygonal outline bounding a correction-coil conductor cross-section along the principal normal basis vector $\hat{n}$ of the Frenet–Serret moving frame. In that frame, $\hat{t}$ is the unit tangent along the conductor centerline, $\hat{n}$ points toward the instantaneous center of curvature, and $\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}$ is the binormal. Paired with the complementary [binormal coordinate](name:binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil), the two coordinates fully specify each outline vertex in the plane perpendicular to the centerline.

For an outline vertex at position $\mathbf{r}$ relative to the centerline reference point $\mathbf{r}_0$, the normal coordinate is:

$$
n = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{n}
$$

where $\hat{n}$ is the Frenet–Serret principal normal unit vector at the corresponding centerline location.

The outline vertices are defined from engineering drawings or CAD models of the correction-coil winding pack. The closed polygon formed by the normal and binormal vertex pairs encloses the [cross-sectional area](name:area_of_correction_coil) of the conductor. The analogous quantity for toroidal field coils is [normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement is in the direction of the principal normal $\hat{n}$, pointing toward the center of curvature of the conductor centerline.

NAMES.name: normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Coordinate along the normal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame for a toroidal field coil conductor cross-section, measuring each outline vertex's displacement perpendicular to both the conductor centerline and the binormal direction.
NAMES.long:
The normal coordinate specifies the position of each vertex of the toroidal field coil conductor cross-section outline polygon along the principal normal axis $\hat{N}$ of the local Frenet-Serret frame. Together with the [binormal coordinate](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil), it fully describes the 2D polygonal shape of the conductor cross-section in the plane perpendicular to the conductor centerline.

At any point along the conductor path, the Frenet-Serret frame is defined by the unit tangent $\hat{T}$ (along the centerline), the principal normal $\hat{N}$ (perpendicular to $\hat{T}$ in the plane of curvature), and the binormal $\hat{B} = \hat{T} \times \hat{N}$. The normal coordinate of an outline vertex is:

$$
s_N = \mathbf{r}_v \cdot \hat{N}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the displacement vector from the local centerline point to the vertex in meters, and $\hat{N}$ is the dimensionless unit normal vector.

The complete set of normal and binormal coordinate pairs for all outline vertices defines the conductor cross-section polygon, which determines conductor area, current density distribution, and electromagnetic force calculations on the coil. The analogous quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is [normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil).

Typical TF coil conductor cross-sections in large tokamaks span a few centimeters to tens of centimeters, placing vertex coordinates in the range of roughly $-0.1$ to $0.1$ m relative to the conductor centerline.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement is in the direction of the Frenet-Serret normal vector $\hat{N}$.

NAMES.name: radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: First inclination angle (alpha) of the oblique parallelogram or trapezoidal cross-section of a poloidal field coil element, measured in the poloidal plane from the outward major-radius direction.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal field coil conductors are frequently designed with non-rectangular cross-sections modeled as parallelograms or trapezoids in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The radial angle $\alpha$ defines the inclination of one pair of parallel sides (the alpha-sides) relative to the outward major-radius direction $+\hat{R}$, characterizing how much the conductor winding departs from a purely radial orientation.

The oblique cross-section is fully parameterized by two inclination angles and two side lengths. The radial angle $\alpha$ pairs with the [vertical angle](name:vertical_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil) $\beta$ — measured from the vertical $+\hat{Z}$ direction — to define both side orientations, while [major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil) give the corresponding alpha-side and beta-side lengths.

This angle is a fixed geometric design parameter derived from coil engineering drawings and used in computing cross-sectional area, mutual inductance, and electromagnetic force distributions in poloidal field coil systems. The analogous first inclination angle for iron core segments is described by [alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment](name:alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the alpha-side of the cross-section is inclined counter-clockwise from $+\hat{R}$ (toward $+\hat{Z}$) in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane.

NAMES.name: radial_force
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic force on the poloidal-field coil system resolved along increasing major radius R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where Z is vertical height. It equals the sum of the radial force components on the individual poloidal-field coils.
NAMES.long:
Radial force is the net electromagnetic force component acting on the poloidal-field coil system in the direction of major radius. It represents the aggregate radial Lorentz load over all active poloidal-field coils, complementary to the axial component described by vertical_force.

The radial component can be written as the radial projection of the Lorentz force density integrated over the coil conductors, equivalently as a sum over individual coil contributions:

$$
F_R = \int_{V_{\mathrm{PF}}} (\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\, dV = \sum_k F_{R,k}
$$

where $F_R$ and each $F_{R,k}$ are forces in N, $V_{\mathrm{PF}}$ is the conducting volume of the poloidal-field coil system, $\mathbf{j}$ is current density in A m^-2, $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic flux density in T, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the outward radial unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The term $F_{R,k}$ is the [radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) for coil $k$.

This quantity is usually computed from electromagnetic models using the coil current distribution, conductor geometry, and magnetic field at the coil locations. It may also be obtained by summing the evaluated radial forces of the individual poloidal-field coils.

Typical absolute magnitudes are strongly device and scenario dependent: small experimental coil systems may have radial forces of order $10^3$-$10^5$ N, while medium and large tokamak poloidal-field systems commonly reach $10^6$-$10^8$ N. Values should be interpreted relative to the mechanical limits defined for the specific coil system.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the force is directed toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Radial component of the electromagnetic Lorentz force acting on an individual poloidal field coil, positive in the direction of increasing major radius.
NAMES.long:
The radial force on a poloidal field coil is the $\hat{R}$ component of the integrated Lorentz body force on the conductor, arising from the interaction of the coil current with the total magnetic field produced by the plasma, the central solenoid, and all other coils in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It represents the net mechanical loading pushing the coil radially toward or away from the machine symmetry axis under a given plasma scenario.

The defining relation is:

$$
F_R = \hat{R} \cdot \oint I \, d\boldsymbol{\ell} \times \mathbf{B}
$$

where $I$ is the coil current, $d\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is the vectorial conductor path element, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field at the conductor location.

In practice, $F_R$ is computed from electromagnetic modeling of the coil-plasma system or inferred from equilibrium reconstruction combined with coil-current measurements. It is a primary structural loading parameter governing coil support structure design, machine assembly tolerances, and operational limits. For large tokamaks, individual PF coil radial forces can range from a few MN to several hundred MN depending on coil geometry, current, and plasma scenario. The companion quantity [vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) captures the $Z$-direction loading on the same coil, while [radial_force](name:radial_force) gives the system-level sum over the full PF coil assembly.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the force is directed in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Radial component of the magnetic field evaluated at the centroid of a ferritic element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial magnetic field at a ferritic element centroid is the component of the local magnetic flux density projected onto the outward major-radius direction at the element's geometric center. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius measured outward from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The component is defined by the projection of the magnetic field vector onto the local radial unit vector:

$$
B_R(\mathbf{x}_c) = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}_c) \cdot \hat{R}(\mathbf{x}_c)
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_c$ is the ferritic element centroid, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic flux density vector with components in T, $B_R$ is its radial component in T, and $\hat{R}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $R$.

In practice, this quantity is obtained from magnetic-field calculations or equilibrium/electromagnetic reconstructions evaluated at the ferritic element centroid, including contributions from external coils, plasma current, induced currents, and magnetized materials as appropriate. It is relevant to ferritic response modeling, but magnetization is determined through the magnetic field intensity $\mathbf{H}$ in A/m and the material constitutive relation for magnetization $\mathbf{M}$ in A/m, rather than by $B_R$ alone.

Typical absolute values $|B_R|$ near ferritic structures are often 1e-4-1 T, depending on proximity to coils, plasma current, geometry, and magnetic shielding. Local values can approach several T in regions close to strong sources or highly magnetized ferromagnetic material.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local magnetic field component points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_magnetization_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Radial component of the magnetization vector of a ferritic element, projecting the local magnetic polarization along the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Magnetization is the volumetric density of magnetic dipole moments within a material. For ferromagnetic structural components — such as ferritic inserts positioned within the tokamak vessel — the confinement magnetic field induces a local magnetization vector $\mathbf{M}$ whose projection onto the outward major-radius direction defines the radial component $M_R$.

$$
M_R = \mathbf{M} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector pointing in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The magnetization state of ferritic elements is obtained from nonlinear electromagnetic models that couple the permeability of the ferritic material to the local applied magnetic field. Together with [toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element](name:toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element) and [vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element](name:vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element), this radial component fully characterizes the magnetization vector in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The field perturbations induced by the magnetized elements can be evaluated at each element's geometric center via quantities such as [radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid](name:radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $M_R$ points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, away from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Minimum allowed value of the signed weighted radial-force combination for a poloidal field coil set. It is the lower structural bound applied to a selected radial loading mode of the coils.
NAMES.long:
Radial minimum force of a poloidal field coil set is the lower allowable value of a signed weighted combination of radial electromagnetic forces on the axisymmetric coils. The radial direction refers to the major-radius coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; the sign of the combined loading mode is defined by the selected force-combination weights, not by a universal inward or outward convention.

The lower-bound constraint is

$$
F_{\mathrm{rad}}^{\mathrm{comb}} = \sum_{j=1}^{N_{\mathrm{coil}}} w_j F_{R,j}, \qquad F_{\mathrm{rad}}^{\mathrm{comb}} \ge F_{\mathrm{rad,min}}
$$

where $F_{\mathrm{rad}}^{\mathrm{comb}}$ is the signed combined radial force in N, $F_{R,j}$ is the radial electromagnetic force assigned to coil $j$ in N, $w_j$ is the dimensionless combination weight for that coil, $N_{\mathrm{coil}}$ is the number of coils included in the combination, and $F_{\mathrm{rad,min}}$ is this minimum allowable value in N. Different choices of $w_j$ represent different mechanically relevant load modes, such as a single-coil limit, a group load, or a differential load between coil groups.

In practice the individual coil forces are computed from coil currents and magnetic fields using the Lorentz force density or an equivalent magnetic-energy derivative, then combined with the prescribed weights from the structural constraint set. The limit is normally established from engineering analysis of coil supports, cases, and attachments, and is used to reject operating points whose radial loading would exceed the allowed lower bound.

Typical magnitudes of lower radial-force limits are strongly machine-specific: small devices may use bounds of order 10^4-10^6 N, medium-sized tokamaks often use 10^6-10^8 N, and large superconducting systems can use 10^8-10^9 N for the most demanding load combinations. The signed stored value may be negative or positive depending on the selected combination weights and the allowable load interval.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the weighted combination $\sum_j w_j F_{R,j}$ is positive for the selected radial-force combination weights.

NAMES.name: radial_offset_of_conductor_cross_section
NAMES.short: Signed radial displacement of a contour point on a coil conductor cross-section outline, measured relative to the cross-section's reference point along the major-radius direction.
NAMES.long:
The radial offset of a conductor cross-section is the signed displacement of a contour point on the conductor outline in the major-radius ($R$) direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, measured relative to a designated reference point for that cross-section. Together with corresponding vertical and toroidal-angle offsets from the same reference, this quantity fully parameterizes the conductor cross-section shape in the plane perpendicular to the local conductor axis.

The absolute major-radius coordinate $R_i$ of the $i$-th contour point is recovered from:

$$
R_i = R_\mathrm{ref} + \Delta r_i
$$

where $R_\mathrm{ref}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the cross-section reference point and $\Delta r_i$ is the radial offset of the $i$-th contour vertex.

The contour-point description is used in electromagnetic and structural design calculations, where the precise conductor cross-sectional shape affects current-density distribution, net Lorentz force, and mutual inductance between turns. Compare with [radial_outline_of_coil_conductor_element](name:radial_outline_of_coil_conductor_element), which gives the absolute major-radius coordinate of an outline point rather than a displacement from a reference, and with [binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil), which characterizes cross-section vertices in the local Frenet-Serret frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the contour point lies at a larger major radius $R$ than the reference point.

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_coil_conductor_element
NAMES.short: Absolute, non-negative major-radius coordinate R of an outline point, including an arc start point, on the cross-sectional contour of a coil conductor element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial outline of a coil conductor element is the major-radius component $R$ of a point on the element's cross-sectional contour at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$. It is an absolute, non-negative distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, not a signed local offset from a conductor reference point.

The major radius is related to horizontal Cartesian coordinates by:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are horizontal distances in meters in a right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame with origin on the toroidal symmetry axis and $z$ parallel to the vertical $Z$ direction; $R$ is in meters. The accompanying vertical outline coordinate $Z$ is the vertical height in meters in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice, outline coordinates are obtained from engineering geometry, CAD models, or surveyed conductor contours and then expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. For a contour represented using circular arcs, an $R$ value locates an outline construction point such as an arc start point; the corresponding $Z$ value gives its vertical position, while separate arc parameters determine the curved segment between construction points.

This quantity is closely related to major_radius_of_coil_conductor_element, which describes a characteristic major-radius coordinate of the same type of conductor element. It is also analogous to [radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil) and uses the same major-radius geometry as major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil.

Typical values are device-specific non-negative lengths measured in meters and lie at the major radii occupied by the conductor outline. Within a single conductor cross-section, variations among outline points are usually set by the conductor's radial width rather than by the full device size, so no universal numerical range is implied by the quantity.

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of a point on the poloidal cross-sectional outline of a poloidal-field coil conductor in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the absolute non-negative distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to that outline point.
NAMES.long:
Radial outline of a poloidal-field coil is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of a point on the conductor boundary in a poloidal cross-section. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is the non-negative distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height; for an axisymmetric coil, the same poloidal outline is swept around the toroidal direction $\phi$. Together with the [vertical outline of a poloidal-field coil], it locates the boundary point; a circular contour segment may also require a separate [curvature radius].

This quantity is determined from the physical conductor envelope in an $(R, Z)$ poloidal section and is used to define the coil boundary for geometric field, force, and inductance calculations. It is a boundary coordinate, not the curvature radius of an outline segment and not a central or reference radius of the whole coil.

Typical values range from about 0.5-3 m for compact or inboard poloidal-field coils to 3-12 m for large outboard coils, depending on device size and coil placement. Valid values are non-negative because $R$ is an absolute distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_total_maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Upper allowable bound on a signed linear combination of radial electromagnetic forces across an axisymmetric poloidal field coil system. It is used as a mechanical integrity constraint for coil-current scenarios and machine protection.
NAMES.long:
Radial total maximum force of a poloidal field coil system is the upper allowable bound on a signed linear combination of the radial electromagnetic forces acting on the coils. The radial direction is the major-radius direction $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the bound represents a mechanical integrity constraint for the coil support structure.

The constraint is commonly expressed as a weighted-force inequality:

$$
F_{R,\mathrm{comb}} = \sum_i w_i F_{R,i} \le F_{R,\mathrm{max}}
$$

where $F_{R,\mathrm{comb}}$ is the signed combined radial force in N, $w_i$ is a dimensionless linear-combination weight, $F_{R,i}$ is the individual radial force on coil $i$ in N, and $F_{R,\mathrm{max}}$ is the maximum allowable bound in N. Each $F_{R,i}$ is obtained by integrating the Lorentz force density $\mathbf{J}_i \times \mathbf{B}$ over the coil conductor and projecting onto $R$, where $\mathbf{J}_i$ is current density in A m^-2 and $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic flux density in T.

This limit is evaluated from electromagnetic load calculations using the coil currents, conductor geometry, and magnetic field from the full coil and plasma configuration. The resulting force combination is compared with structural margins from support design, stress analysis, preload assumptions, and protection requirements.

Typical allowable magnitudes are highly machine-dependent: small devices may have limits of order 10^5-10^6 N, medium and large tokamaks often use 10^6-10^8 N, and reactor-scale coil systems can exceed 10^8 N. The appropriate value depends on coil size, support stiffness, load sharing, disruption assumptions, and the chosen linear-combination weights.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the defining weighted sum is positive under the specified linear-combination weights, taking each individual radial force as positive toward increasing $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radius_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Cylindrical radial coordinate R of the geometric point used to locate a ferritic element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured as distance from the toroidal symmetry axis. It is a generic radial position, not an inner or outer boundary of an annular cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Radius of a ferritic element is the cylindrical radial coordinate $R$ of the geometric point used to locate that element in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height. It specifies a position in the poloidal plane and is not the element's annular thickness; for the radial bounds of an annular cross-section use [inner_radius_of_ferritic_element](name:inner_radius_of_ferritic_element) and [outer_radius_of_ferritic_element](name:outer_radius_of_ferritic_element), and when the point is specifically an outline vertex use major_radius_of_ferritic_element.

For the same point expressed in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis with $\hat{z}$ vertical, the cylindrical radius is

$$
R_f = \sqrt{x_f^2 + y_f^2}
$$

where $x_f$ and $y_f$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the ferritic-element point in meters and $R_f$ is its radial distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in meters.

In practice this coordinate is taken from the geometric description of the ferritic component, such as engineering design geometry, magnetic-model geometry, or survey-derived component positions.

Typical values are machine-size dependent, generally falling in the 0.2-15 m range across tokamak magnetic-field systems, within the radial envelope occupied by the ferritic structures.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Inner radial boundary of the annular cross-section of a ferritic element in the axisymmetric equivalent geometry, defining the bore of the annulus centered at a reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius specifies the hollow bore of the annular cross-section used to represent a ferritic element in the axisymmetric thick-line equivalent geometry. Ferritic elements are ferromagnetic inserts employed in some fusion devices to reduce toroidal magnetic-field ripple; each element is modeled as an axisymmetric body whose cross-section is an annulus centered at a reference point $(R_0, Z_0)$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height.

For an annular cross-section with inner radius $r_\mathrm{in}$ and outer radius $r_\mathrm{out}$, the enclosed area is

$$
A = \pi\bigl(r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2\bigr)
$$

with the geometric constraint $0 \leq r_\mathrm{in} < r_\mathrm{out}$. The inner radius is a design parameter supplied directly to the geometry model and is not inferred from in-situ measurements. Together with [outer_radius_of_ferritic_element](name:outer_radius_of_ferritic_element), it fully characterizes the radial extent of the annular cross-section, while the overall radial placement of the element is given by [radius_of_ferritic_element](name:radius_of_ferritic_element). The analogous quantity for iron core segments is [inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment).
NAMES.sign: Positive as a non-negative radial distance from the annulus center to the inner surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R \geq 0$.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Outer major-radius boundary of an annular representation of a ferritic element in an axisymmetric equivalent geometry. It is the maximum R extent of the ferritic annulus in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius of a ferritic element is the largest major-radius coordinate occupied by the annular cross-section used to represent magnetically permeable material in an axisymmetric equivalent geometry. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height; this quantity defines the radially outward boundary of the annulus.

For an annular ferritic region $\Omega_f$ represented in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane, the outer radius is

$$
R_{\mathrm{outer}} = \max_{(R,Z)\in\Omega_f} R
$$

where $\Omega_f$ is the cross-section assigned to the ferritic material and $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The value is usually obtained from engineering geometry, computer-aided design models, or simplified axisymmetric models of ferritic inserts, cores, shields, or other magnetic structures. Together with the corresponding inner radius, it sets the radial thickness and placement of the annular magnetic material used in equilibrium and magnetic-field calculations.

Typical values are device- and component-dependent: compact ferritic inserts may have outer radii of 0.2-2 m, while larger ferritic structures in medium to large tokamaks may extend to 2-10 m. The value is non-negative by geometry and must exceed the corresponding inner radius for a finite annular thickness.

NAMES.name: radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Non-negative curvature radius of an arc-of-circle segment representing the boundary of an iron-core segment in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative curvature radius of a circular-arc element used to describe the segment boundary in a poloidal cross-section. The cross-section is the $(R, Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The radius specifies the size of the local circular arc, not its position, endpoint, sweep angle, or traversal orientation.

For a circular arc, the radius $r$ is the reciprocal of the magnitude of the local curvature $\kappa$:

$$
r = \frac{1}{|\kappa|}
$$

where $r$ is the curvature radius in m and $\kappa$ is the signed planar curvature in m$^{-1}$. The absolute value makes the radius non-negative; the limiting case $|\kappa| \to 0$ corresponds to an uncurved boundary element with $r \to \infty$.

In practice, this quantity is obtained from the geometric description of the iron-core cross-section, for example from engineering drawings, computer-aided design boundaries, or a fitted piecewise-circular representation of the contour. A complete arc also requires geometric information beyond the radius, such as a start point in the $(R, Z)$ plane and either an endpoint, a sweep angle, or an orientation convention that fixes which part of the circle is used.

Typical values are set by the scale and detailed shaping of the iron-core segment rather than by a universal material property. They are non-negative lengths comparable to the local geometric feature size of the represented boundary.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Inner radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative distance from the center or central axis of an annular cross-section to its inner ferromagnetic boundary. It defines the hollow bore and must be smaller than the corresponding outer radius.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius of an iron-core segment is the radius of the inner boundary of an annular ferromagnetic cross-section. It identifies the boundary between the hollow region and the iron material, and together with [outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment) fixes the annular geometry of the segment.

For a circular annulus, the defining distance is

$$
r_\mathrm{inner} = \left|\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{inner} - \mathbf{x}_0\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_0$ is the center of the annular cross-section, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{inner}$ is any point on the circular inner ferromagnetic boundary, and the resulting radius is measured in meters. A physically valid annulus satisfies $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} < r_\mathrm{outer}$, where $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the outer radius in meters; the corresponding iron cross-sectional area is $A = \pi\left(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2\right)$.

This radius is used when constructing geometric and electromagnetic representations of iron-core segments. Increasing the inner radius reduces the flux-conducting iron area for a fixed outer radius, thereby affecting magnetic reluctance, possible saturation, and mass distribution. Non-annular segment cross-sections are more naturally described by [width_of_iron_core_segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment) and [height_of_iron_core_segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment).

Typical values are strongly device- and design-dependent. In tokamak iron-core models they are usually engineering-scale lengths, from about 0.1-5 m, with compact or local annular segments toward the lower end and large central-core or return-yoke elements toward the upper end.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Non-negative radial distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the outer boundary of an annular iron-core segment. Together with the inner radius, it fixes the radial extent of the hollow circular cross section.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative major-radius distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the outer boundary of an annular iron region. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Together with [inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment), it defines the radial span of the annular segment used to represent the iron transformer core.

For an ideal annular segment, the outer radius is the largest major-radius coordinate occupied by the segment material:

$$
R_\mathrm{out} = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in \Omega_\mathrm{seg}} R(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\Omega_\mathrm{seg}$ is the material region of the annular iron-core segment and $R(\mathbf{x})$ is the major-radius coordinate of point $\mathbf{x}$. The radial wall thickness is $R_\mathrm{out} - R_\mathrm{in}$, with $R_\mathrm{out} > R_\mathrm{in} \ge 0$ for a physically valid hollow annulus.

This quantity is usually taken from engineering geometry, survey data, or a simplified magnetic-circuit representation of the iron core. It determines the outer radial reach of high-permeability material and therefore affects estimates of iron volume, magnetic reluctance, flux linkage, and saturation in equilibrium or magnetic-field modeling. For rectangular iron-core segment descriptions, related geometric extents are [width_of_iron_core_segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment) and [height_of_iron_core_segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment).

Typical values range from about 1-5 m in small and medium tokamaks and about 5-15 m in large devices, depending on the size and placement of the transformer yoke. The difference between outer and inner radii is commonly 0.1-2 m for annular iron-core elements.

NAMES.name: radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Radial dimension of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element, abstracting over the specific inner and outer conductor boundaries used in electromagnetic and resistive circuit modeling.
NAMES.long:
A passive conducting loop element has a toroidal geometry with an annular cross-section; the radial extent of this annulus is characterized by its inner and outer boundaries. This parent quantity abstracts over both the [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), the distance from the annulus center to the inner conducting surface, and the [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop), which defines the outer radial boundary of the annulus.

The cross-sectional area used in resistance and inductance calculations follows from

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_\mathrm{outer}$ and $r_\mathrm{inner}$ are the outer and inner radii in meters. The conductor wall thickness $\delta r = r_\mathrm{outer} - r_\mathrm{inner}$ and the [area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop) both derive directly from these two boundary values.

Passive loop radii are taken from engineering design specifications or as-built conductor surveys, and feed into electromagnetic circuit models for passive stabilization and eddy-current analysis. In fusion devices, passive loop cross-sectional radii range from a few millimeters for thin stabilizing shells to several centimeters for heavier current-carrying elements.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element. It is the distance from the annulus center to the inner conducting boundary and, with the outer radius, sets the conductor thickness used in electromagnetic and resistive calculations.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius of a passive loop is the radius of the hole or excluded central region in an annular conductor cross-section. Together with the [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop), it defines the conducting material thickness of the loop element and affects its resistance, inductance, and eddy-current response.

For an ideal annular cross-section, the conducting area is related to the inner and outer radii by:

$$
A = \pi\left(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2\right)
$$

where $A$ is the conducting cross-sectional area, $r_\mathrm{inner}$ is the inner radius, and $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the corresponding outer radius.

The value is determined from the mechanical geometry of the passive conducting structure, such as a vacuum-vessel segment, stabilizing plate, shell, or other closed conducting loop. It is used in reduced electromagnetic models to compute the conductor area, resistance, mutual inductance, and induced eddy currents. The closely related [inner radius of a passive structure](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) describes the same geometric concept for passive conducting structures more generally.

Typical values range from 0.001-0.1 m for small annular conductor features and from 0.01-1 m for large vessel or support-structure elements, depending on the device scale and the level of geometric simplification.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element, defining the outer radial boundary of the annulus geometry used in electromagnetic modeling.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius defines the radial extent of the outer boundary of the annular (hollow circular) cross-section of a passive conducting loop element, such as a vacuum vessel segment or other passive toroidal conductor. Together with [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), it fully parameterizes the annular cross-section geometry used in electromagnetic circuit models to compute eddy-current responses, self-inductances, and resistances.

The cross-sectional area of the annulus is:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_{\rm out}^2 - r_{\rm in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_{\rm out}$ is the outer radius and $r_{\rm in}$ is the correspondent [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), both in m. This area enters directly into resistance and inductance estimates of the passive loop element under the thin-shell approximation.

Geometry parameters are obtained from engineering drawings or CAD models of the passive conductor assembly. Typical values range from a few centimeters for small conducting ribs to approximately 0.5 m for large vacuum vessel sectors, depending on device scale. The [outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) is the analogous quantity for active poloidal field coil conductors.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as a radial distance from the geometric center of the annular cross-section outward to the conductor's outer boundary.

NAMES.name: radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Non-negative curvature radius of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour of a poloidal field coil. The contour lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Radius of a poloidal-field-coil arc is the non-negative circle radius of a single circular segment of the coil cross-sectional contour, taken in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The conductor or winding-pack boundary is approximated by connected circular arcs, and this quantity sets the local radius of curvature of one such arc.

For a circular contour segment, the curvature radius $\rho$ (in m) is the inverse magnitude of the planar curvature $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) of the boundary curve in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section:

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{|\kappa|}
$$

where a finite physical arc has $\rho > 0$, and as $\rho$ grows the segment approaches a straight line ($\kappa \to 0$). Each arc is anchored by a start point in the poloidal plane: its major-radius coordinate is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil and its vertical coordinate by [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); both together with $\rho$ are needed to locate and shape one arc, with the end of each arc coinciding with the start of the next.

The value is determined from the designed circular-arc contour, from CAD geometry, or by fitting circular arcs to surveyed boundary points. Small radii represent tightly rounded corners and compact winding-pack features, while larger radii represent gently curved coil sides; the magnitude scales with coil aperture, winding-pack dimensions, and mechanical-clearance requirements. An analogous arc-of-circle convention applies to iron core segment boundaries via [radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:radius_of_iron_core_segment).

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a poloidal field coil, defining the size of the conductor bore in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius is the smaller of the two radial dimensions characterizing the annular conductor cross-section of a poloidal field coil, measured from the center of the annulus to its inner conducting boundary in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical height.

Together with [outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and the annulus center position, the inner radius completely specifies the annular cross-section geometry required for electromagnetic calculations including inductance and field-map computations. The annular cross-sectional area relates to both radii via:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_\mathrm{in}$ is the inner radius and $r_\mathrm{out}$ is the outer radius; this area corresponds to [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil). The physical constraint $0 \le r_\mathrm{in} < r_\mathrm{out}$ must hold; when $r_\mathrm{in} = 0$ the annular cross-section degenerates to a solid disk.

The inner radius is taken directly from engineering design specifications and serves as a geometric input to electromagnetic and structural modeling of PF coil systems. The analogous quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is [inner_radius_of_correction_coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the inner conductor boundary is displaced radially outward from the annulus center, as measured in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a poloidal field coil conductor element, defining the radial outer boundary of the conductor geometry.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius defines the outward radial extent of the annular cross-section used to model a poloidal field coil conductor element. Together with the [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and the coil center position in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane, it fully specifies the annular geometry required for electromagnetic calculations such as mutual inductance and Biot-Savart field evaluation.

The annular cross-sectional area $A$ is:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_\mathrm{out}$ is the outer radius and $r_\mathrm{in}$ is the [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil). This [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) enters directly into current density and inductance calculations.

For PF coil conductors in medium-to-large fusion devices, outer radii range from a few centimeters to approximately 0.3-0.5 m, depending on the conductor bundle size and design current.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outer boundary lies at a greater radial distance from the annulus center than the inner boundary, as required for a physically valid annular cross-section.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Electrical resistance of a non-axisymmetric correction coil conductor, determining the ohmic power dissipation and static voltage drop across the coil terminals.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a correction coil characterizes the DC ohmic resistance of the conductor winding, governing resistive power dissipation and the steady-state voltage-current relationship in the coil circuit. Correction coils are non-axisymmetric coils that apply three-dimensional magnetic perturbations for ELM suppression, error field correction, or resonant magnetic perturbation experiments.

The ohmic power dissipated in the coil is:

$$
P_{\rm ohm} = I^2 R
$$

where $I$ is the [current through the coil](name:current_of_correction_coil) and $R$ is the resistance. The corresponding [terminal voltage](name:voltage_of_correction_coil) satisfies $V = IR$ under DC conditions; at finite frequency an inductive contribution adds to the impedance, but the resistive component captured here determines steady-state dissipation and thermal loading on the coil support structure.

Resistance is determined from conductor material resistivity (which varies with temperature), conductor cross-sectional area, and total winding path length, or measured directly by a DC voltage-current sweep at the coil terminals.

Values for correction coils in large tokamaks range from a few milliohms to several ohms, depending on conductor dimensions and winding geometry. The analogous quantity for toroidal field coils is [resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil).

NAMES.name: resistance_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a passive conducting loop, which together with its self-inductance sets the L/R time constant governing eddy-current decay during plasma transients.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a passive conducting loop quantifies the ohmic opposition to current flow in an axisymmetric conductor that is inductively coupled to the plasma but not connected to an external power supply. Passive loops carry eddy currents induced by changes in plasma current or equilibrium position, and their resistance governs how quickly those induced currents decay.

The resistance $R$ and self-inductance $L$ together determine the characteristic decay time constant:

$$
\tau = \frac{L}{R}
$$

where $\tau$ is the e-folding time for eddy-current decay, $L$ is the self-inductance, and $R$ is this resistance. A smaller resistance extends $\tau$, prolonging the stabilizing influence of the eddy currents during vertical displacement events or plasma disruptions.

For a loop of uniform cross-section, $R = \rho \ell / A$, where $\rho$ is the material resistivity (see [resistivity_of_passive_structure](name:resistivity_of_passive_structure)), $\ell$ is the mean conductor path length, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area determined by [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop). Values range from sub-milliohm for low-resistivity conductors to tens of milliohms for higher-resistivity materials, depending on geometry. This quantity follows the established resistance-of-object pattern alongside [resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil) and [resistance_of_correction_coil](name:resistance_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a poloidal field coil winding. It relates coil current to resistive voltage drop and Joule heating at the specified operating state.
NAMES.long:
Resistance of a poloidal field coil is the effective series ohmic resistance of the coil winding at its operating state. It represents conversion of electrical energy into heat in the conductor, joints, and other series elements included in the coil definition, and it sets the resistive part of the terminal voltage demand.

In a lumped circuit model for coil $k$, the terminal-voltage balance is commonly written after choosing branch-current and terminal-voltage reference directions:

$$
V_k = R_k I_k + L_k \frac{dI_k}{dt} + \sum_{j \ne k} \epsilon_{kj} M_{kj} \frac{dI_j}{dt}
$$

where $V_k$ is the terminal voltage in V, $R_k$ is the coil resistance in ohm, $I_k$ and $I_j$ are currents in A, $L_k$ is self-inductance in H, $M_{kj}$ is mutual inductance in H, $dI/dt$ is in A/s, $j$ labels coupled circuits or conductors, and $\epsilon_{kj}$ is a dimensionless factor equal to $+1$ or $-1$ for the chosen mutual-reference orientation. The equation assumes the passive reference for the resistive drop, with $V_k$ positive as a voltage drop along the chosen positive $I_k$ direction; reversing a current reference or terminal-voltage polarity changes the algebraic signs of the inductive and mutual terms consistently, but does not change the non-negative value of $R_k$.

The value is computed from conductor material resistivity, winding length, cross-sectional area, cooling state, and the temperature distribution of the winding. It may be measured by four-terminal DC injection or inferred from slow current ramps after subtracting inductive and mutual voltage contributions. For normal-conducting coils the resistance increases with temperature; for superconducting coils the effective series resistance depends on whether joints, current-sharing regions, or quench behavior are included in the coil model.

Typical effective resistances are $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}$ ohm for large normal-conducting poloidal field coils and $10^{-3}$-1 ohm for smaller shaping or laboratory coils. Superconducting poloidal field windings in steady superconducting operation are often represented as 0-$10^{-6}$ ohm effective series resistance when only persistent or joint losses are included; during current sharing or a quench, the apparent resistance can rise to $10^{-4}$-1 ohm and becomes strongly time dependent.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a toroidal field coil conductor, determining resistive power dissipation and voltage drop during coil operation.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a toroidal field coil is the ohmic impedance of its conductor winding at a given temperature and operational state, governing how the coil dissipates energy and sustains a voltage drop when carrying current.

The resistive power deposited in the coil is defined by:

$$
P_\mathrm{ohm} = I^2 R_\mathrm{TF}
$$

where $I$ is the coil current and $R_\mathrm{TF}$ is the coil resistance. The resistance depends on conductor geometry and material electrical resistivity $\rho_e$ through $R_\mathrm{TF} = \rho_e L / A_c$, where $L$ is the total conductor length and $A_c$ is the conductor cross-sectional area.

Coil resistance is determined by direct four-wire (Kelvin) electrical measurements or from conductor material properties and geometry as a function of temperature. For superconducting TF coils operated below the critical temperature, the effective resistance is negligible; for normal-conducting (resistive) TF coils, values range from a few milliohms to tens of milliohms depending on device scale and conductor material.

The resistive voltage drop $V_R = I \cdot R_\mathrm{TF}$ contributes to the total terminal voltage captured by [voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil). Analogous quantities for other coil systems include [resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [resistance_of_correction_coil](name:resistance_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Intrinsic electrical resistivity of the material forming a passive conducting structure. It is an effective isotropic, nonnegative scalar material property that relates local current density to electric field, independent of the conductor's geometry, and is distinct from the structure's total electrical resistance.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistivity of a passive conducting structure is the intrinsic, effective isotropic scalar material property that relates current density to electric field and quantifies how strongly the material opposes electrical conduction. It applies to non-driven conductors such as vacuum-vessel shells, passive stabilizing plates, blanket modules, and support structures, and unlike the total resistance it does not depend on the conductor's path length or cross-sectional area. As a material property it is nonnegative.

The resistivity enters the local form of Ohm's law relating electric field to current density:

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho \, \mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field, $\mathbf{J}$ is the current density, and $\rho$ is the resistivity in ohm meter. Its reciprocal is the electrical conductivity, $\sigma = 1/\rho$. For a uniform circuit element of effective current-path length $L$ and cross-sectional area $A$, the lumped resistance follows as $R = \rho L / A$, the quantity that enters circuit models directly.

Resistivity is usually taken from material specifications, temperature-dependent material databases, or direct electrical measurements such as four-terminal resistance tests on representative samples. In passive-conductor models it is combined with geometry to compute each element resistance, which sets the inductive eddy-current decay time $\tau = L/R$ ($L$ being the element self-inductance) governing how rapidly induced currents decay following a change in external flux linkage during transient electromagnetic events.

Typical room-temperature values are about $1.7 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$ for high-conductivity copper, $2.5\text{-}5 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$ for copper alloys, $2.7 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$ for aluminum, and $6\text{-}8 \times 10^{-7}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$ for austenitic stainless steels. Heating to several hundred degrees Celsius can raise copper resistivity by roughly a factor of 2-3 and stainless-steel resistivity by about 20-50%, depending on alloy and temperature history.

NAMES.name: saturated_permeability_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Absolute tangent permeability assigned to the saturated high-field branch of a ferritic element's nonlinear B-H characteristic. It is the finite-field slope used after magnetization is mostly saturated, not the strict infinite-field limit of the material.
NAMES.long:
Saturated permeability $\mu_\mathrm{sat}$ is the absolute scalar permeability assigned to the high-field saturated branch of a ferritic material model. It represents the residual slope of the nonlinear $B$-$H$ characteristic after the magnetization has largely approached its saturation value. As a scalar, it assumes an isotropic or isotropized material response for the ferritic element.

The saturated permeability is defined as the tangent slope of the saturated branch, or in practice as the slope of a linear fit over the selected high-field interval:

$$
\mu_\mathrm{sat} = \left.\frac{dB}{dH}\right|_\mathrm{saturated\ branch} \approx \frac{\Delta B}{\Delta H}
$$

where $B$ is magnetic flux density in tesla, $H$ is magnetic field strength in A m$^{-1}$, and $\Delta B/\Delta H$ is evaluated only over the chosen saturated-field interval. This is a tangent or fit-slope permeability, not the secant ratio $B/H$ unless a particular material model defines the fitted high-field line through the origin. For an ideal fully saturated material with constant magnetization, the collinear SI relation is $B=\mu_0(H+M_\mathrm{sat})$, so the limiting tangent slope tends to $\mu_0$ while the offset $\mu_0 M_\mathrm{sat}$ remains.

The value is obtained from measured or specified $B$-$H$ curves by selecting the branch beyond the knee of the magnetization curve and fitting its local slope. It is used together with the general field-dependent permeability_of_ferritic_element and B-H characteristic quantities such as magnetic_field_of_iron_core_segment to model nonlinear ferritic inserts or steel structures. The resulting magnetization may be resolved into components such as [radial_magnetization_of_ferritic_element](name:radial_magnetization_of_ferritic_element), [toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element](name:toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element), and [vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element](name:vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For soft ferromagnetic steels near saturation, $\mu_\mathrm{sat}/\mu_0$ commonly ranges from 2-100 over a finite high-field fitting interval, corresponding to about $2.5 \times 10^{-6}$-$1.3 \times 10^{-4}$ H m$^{-1}$. Values depend on alloy composition, temperature, mechanical processing, magnetic history, and the selected field interval; at sufficiently large field the ideal tangent limit approaches $\mu_0 = 1.26 \times 10^{-6}$ H m$^{-1}$.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Bulk conductor temperature of an individual poloidal field coil.
NAMES.long:
Bulk conductor temperature of a poloidal field coil is the representative thermodynamic temperature of the current-carrying winding material for one physically distinct PF coil. It determines temperature-dependent resistance in normal conductors and the thermal margin and allowable current density in superconducting windings.

When internal temperature gradients are small, or when a single engineering temperature is required, the bulk value is commonly interpreted as a conductor-volume average:

$$
T_\mathrm{PF} = \frac{1}{V_c}\int_{V_c} T(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $T_\mathrm{PF}$ is the bulk coil temperature, $T(\mathbf{x})$ is the local conductor temperature, and $V_c$ is the volume of current-carrying conductor. In current-limit characterization, this temperature is an independent variable in relations such as $I_\max(T_\mathrm{PF}, B)$ or $J_c(T_\mathrm{PF}, B)$, where $B$ is magnetic flux density in tesla and $J_c$ is an allowable or critical current density in A m^-2.

The temperature may be measured by embedded resistance thermometers, thermocouples, cryogenic temperature sensors, or inferred from conductor resistance and thermal models. Each value refers to a named or otherwise physically identified PF winding, such as a particular shaping, vertical-field, divertor-control, or central-solenoid module when that module is part of the poloidal-field coil system.

Typical values are strongly design dependent: cryogenic superconducting windings are often operated in the range of a few K to several tens of K, while normal-conducting copper coils are commonly near 290-400 K during operation, with pulse heating and cooling conditions setting the detailed value.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Face-to-face distance across an iron-core segment measured normal to its centerline; a non-negative transverse size of the segment cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of an iron-core segment is the face-to-face distance across the segment measured along the local normal to its centerline; it is a non-negative geometric length. In a local right-handed segment basis $(\hat{s}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, $\hat{s}$ is tangent to the centerline, $\hat{n}$ is the transverse thickness direction, and $\hat{b}$ completes the triad. For axisymmetric poloidal-plane descriptions, $\hat{s}$ and $\hat{n}$ lie in the $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a rectangular cross-section normal to the centerline, the thickness sets the area together with the segment width:

$$
A_\perp = t\,w
$$

where $A_\perp$ is the cross-sectional area in m^2, $t$ is the segment thickness in m, and $w$ is the [width of the iron-core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment) in m.

Thickness is obtained from engineering drawings, surveys, or magnetic-circuit geometry by taking the separation of the two bounding faces along $\hat{n}$. In electromagnetic calculations, increasing thickness increases cross-sectional area, reduces magnetic reluctance, and lowers the magnetic flux density for a given total flux, helping to avoid iron saturation.

Typical values are about 0.05-0.5 m for small pole-piece or local insert segments, 0.5-2 m for medium transformer-core limbs or return-yoke pieces, and 2-5 m for very large iron-core sectors. The selected value depends on required flux, allowable saturation, mechanical clearance, and segmentation.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Non-negative perpendicular distance across a passive conducting loop element in its poloidal cross-section, measured between the two parallel bounding sides. It is the thickness dimension paired with loop cross-section length and inclination to define the conductor geometry.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of a passive loop is the non-negative shortest distance through the conducting material in a constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is measured normal to the pair of parallel bounding sides of an oblique trapezoidal, parallelogram, or thick-line rectangular approximation, complementing the [length of the passive loop](name:major_length_of_conductor_cross_section) and the cross-section inclination angle.

For two parallel bounding sides, the thickness $d$ is the perpendicular separation between them:

$$
d = \left|\left(\mathbf{r}_b - \mathbf{r}_a\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_\perp\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_a$ and $\mathbf{r}_b$ are any points on the two opposite sides in the same cross-section, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\perp$ is the unit vector normal to those sides within that plane. The absolute value reflects that thickness is a geometric size, not an oriented displacement.

In practice, $d$ is obtained from mechanical drawings, CAD geometry, surveys, or simplified passive-structure models. Together with [length_of_passive_loop](name:major_length_of_conductor_cross_section) and the inclination angle, it fixes the cross-section used to compute [area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop); for rectangular and parallelogram approximations the area is $d$ times the complementary base length, while for a trapezoid it is $d$ times the mean parallel-side length.

Typical values are 0.003-0.02 m for thin liners or vessel panels, 0.02-0.15 m for passive stabilizing plates and shells, and up to about 0.3 m for massive passive conductor blocks.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Thickness of a poloidal field coil is the full conductor-package cross-sectional extent measured normal to the coil reference centerline in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height. It is distinct from radial width and vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of a poloidal field coil is the face-to-face size of the coil conductor package measured along the direction normal to the coil reference centerline in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is a local transverse dimension of the winding pack or conductor envelope, not necessarily the same as the radial width along $R$ or the vertical height along $Z$.

For a coil cross-section with boundary points $\mathbf{x}$ and a unit normal $\hat{n}$ in the poloidal plane, the thickness $t$ may be written as the full projected extent of the cross-section:

$$
t = \max_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{n}) - \min_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{n})
$$

where $\hat{n}$ is perpendicular to the local coil reference centerline and the extrema are taken over the gross conductor-package cross-section.

The value is obtained from the engineering geometry of the poloidal field coil winding pack or conductor package. Unless a more specific quantity states otherwise, it denotes the gross physical envelope assigned to the coil package, including insulation, stabilizer, casing, or internal voids that are part of that envelope; it is not the net area of electrically conducting material alone. Together with complementary dimensions such as [width_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), it determines the geometric cross-section used to compute quantities such as [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil).

Typical values range from 0.05-0.5 m for small or medium experimental coils and about 0.2-1.5 m for large tokamak poloidal-field winding packs; very large superconducting coil packages can have thicknesses of order 2 m or more.

NAMES.name: tilt_angle_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Tilt angle of the directed reference axis for the oblique cross-section of a passive conducting loop element. It is measured in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, with zero along +R and positive rotation from +R toward +Z.
NAMES.long:
The tilt angle of a passive conducting loop is the orientation of the directed reference axis used to describe an oblique cross-section, such as a parallelogram or trapezoid, in the poloidal plane. The reference axis is the cross-section side or side-family direction associated with the oblique tilt parameter, not the toroidal direction of the loop itself.

Let $\hat{e}_\beta$ be the unit vector along this directed cross-section reference axis in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The tilt angle $\beta$ is defined by

$$
\beta = \operatorname{atan2}(\hat{e}_\beta \cdot \hat{Z},\, \hat{e}_\beta \cdot \hat{R})
$$

where $\hat{R}$ is the outward major-radius basis vector and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical basis vector. Thus $\beta=0$ corresponds to a reference axis parallel to $+R$, and the principal branch is usually taken as $-\pi < \beta \le \pi$; angles differing by $2\pi$ describe the same directed orientation.

In practice the angle is obtained from engineering geometry, a CAD description, or a reconstructed polygonal outline of the passive conductor cross-section. It is distinct from the overall toroidal placement angle of a loop and from other oblique-shape angles that may describe a second side inclination or another local edge direction.

Typical values are near 0 rad for cross-section axes approximately radial, around $\pm 1.57$ rad for nearly vertical axes, and commonly within about -0.8-0.8 rad for mildly skewed passive-conductor elements.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the directed cross-section reference axis is rotated counter-clockwise from the $+R$ direction toward the $+Z$ direction in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: tilt_angle_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Tilt angle of a plasma filament is the signed inclination of the oblique side of a parallelogram cross-section in a poloidal section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is measured counterclockwise from the upward vertical +Z direction in an R-Z plot with R increasing to the right.
NAMES.long:
The tilt angle of a plasma filament is the signed geometric inclination of the oblique side of a parallelogram cross-section used to represent an extended filamentary plasma current element. The angle is defined in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a unit vector $\mathbf{u}=u_R\hat{R}+u_Z\hat{Z}$ along the oblique side in that cross-section, the angle $\beta$ can be written as:

$$
\beta = \operatorname{atan2}(-u_R, u_Z)
$$

where $u_R$ and $u_Z$ are the radial and vertical components of the side direction. This gives $\beta=0$ for an upward vertical side, $\beta=+\pi/2$ for a side pointing toward decreasing $R$, and $\beta=-\pi/2$ for a side pointing toward increasing $R$.

In practice, the tilt is obtained from the prescribed or reconstructed filament geometry by fitting or selecting the oblique side vector of the parallelogram cross-section in the $(R,Z)$ plane. Together with related geometric parameters such as [length of plasma filament](name:thickness_of_plasma_filament), [tangential length of plasma filament](name:thickness_of_plasma_filament), and [thickness of plasma filament](name:thickness_of_plasma_filament), it fixes the shape and orientation of the finite current element used in magnetic-field calculations.

Typical values are often kept within the principal interval $-\pi/2$ to $+\pi/2$ rad for non-overturned cross-sections. Nearly vertical filaments have values close to $0$ rad, while strongly slanted cross-sections may approach magnitudes of about $1.57$ rad.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the oblique side is rotated counterclockwise from the upward vertical $+Z$ direction in an $(R,Z)$ plot of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with $R$ increasing to the right.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_coil_conductor_element
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle of a coil conductor element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It gives the element's azimuthal location about the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of a coil conductor element is the azimuthal coordinate of a geometric point on that element in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It locates the point around the toroidal symmetry axis relative to the facility-defined $\phi=0$ radial half-plane. Because it is an angular coordinate, values separated by a full turn represent the same physical direction.

Given Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ of the same point in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ frame, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$ and the $+\hat{x}$ direction lying in the $\phi=0$ half-plane, the toroidal angle is defined by:

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x)
$$

where $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from $+\hat{x}$ to the horizontal projection of the point. In this definition the principal branch is $(-\pi,\pi]$; an equivalent representative on $[0,2\pi)$ is obtained by adding $2\pi$ to negative principal values.

In practice, this angle is computed from coil-design geometry, survey geometry, or transformed Cartesian coordinates of points used to describe the conductor element, such as endpoints, center points, or interpolation points. A common zero reference and branch should be used consistently, and angles may be unwrapped only to follow a continuous conductor without artificial jumps at the branch cut. This absolute cylindrical coordinate is distinct from the [toroidal angle of a conductor cross-section](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_field_coil), which is a relative orientation angle referenced to a local cross-section reference point or direction.

Typical representative values span a full torus: -3.14-3.14 rad on the $(-\pi,\pi]$ branch, or 0-6.28 rad on the $[0,2\pi)$ branch. In devices with $N$ repeated coil sectors, corresponding element locations are often separated by about $2\pi/N$ rad.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial direction from the toroidal symmetry axis to the conductor-element point is rotated from the $\phi=0$ half-plane toward increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle coordinate of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section contour point, expressed relative to the cross-section reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is used with major radius and vertical height to locate the contour point.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross section is the angular coordinate of a conductor-contour point measured relative to a designated reference point on that cross section. It is the toroidal component of the point location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For contour point $i$, the relative toroidal angle is defined as the difference between the point and reference toroidal coordinates:

$$
\phi_{\mathrm{rel},i} = \phi_i - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\phi_i$ is the toroidal coordinate of the contour point, $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the toroidal coordinate of the reference point, and $\phi_{\mathrm{rel},i}$ is expressed in radians. Because toroidal angle is periodic, values that differ by $2\pi n$, with integer $n$, represent the same toroidal direction; the physical definition does not impose a device-independent wrapping interval.

In practice, this coordinate is computed from the engineered conductor geometry by evaluating the toroidal coordinate of each contour point and subtracting the reference-point toroidal coordinate. Together with the radial coordinate major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil and vertical height [height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil), it locates the contour point in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The corresponding generic conductor quantity is [toroidal_angle_of_conductor_cross_section](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_field_coil).

Typical numerical values are design-specific and depend on the chosen reference point and conductor cross-section geometry. The relevant universal scale is the angular periodicity $2\pi$ rad, so the values should be interpreted as relative toroidal coordinates rather than as absolute toroidal positions of the coil.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the contour point is displaced from the reference point in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the magnetic field evaluated at the geometric centroid of each ferritic in-vessel element, giving the local phi-direction field strength experienced by the ferromagnetic material.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic field at a ferritic element centroid is the projection of the total magnetic field vector onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ at the geometric center of a ferromagnetic in-vessel structural component. Ferritic elements are ferromagnetic inserts installed inside the vacuum vessel; the field value at their centroid provides a representative local field for each discrete element in thin-shell or equivalent-circuit magnetic models of ferromagnetic in-vessel hardware.

The toroidal component is defined by:

$$
B_\phi = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$
