The $x$ coordinate of a sensor attachment point is the signed horizontal position component of the mechanical point at which a sensor or its mount is fixed to a device component. It is defined in a right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$; $+\hat{z}$ is vertical and parallel to $+\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The origin lies on the toroidal symmetry axis at the machine midplane, so $z=0$ and $Z=0$ denote the midplane.

Relative to the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the horizontal Cartesian component is

$$
x = R \cos\phi
$$

where $R$ is major radius in meters and $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians; $\phi=0$ lies along $+\hat{x}$ and increasing $\phi$ points toward $+\hat{y}$ when viewed from $+\hat{z}$.

Together with the [y coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and the [vertical coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), this quantity specifies the mechanical attachment location. In practice it is obtained from engineering design geometry or from alignment surveys using coordinate-measuring equipment, laser trackers, photogrammetry, or optical metrology of the installed sensor and mount. The attachment point is a mechanical reference point, not necessarily the sensitive volume, viewing aperture, or line-of-sight origin of the sensor.

Typical values are set by device size and by whether the sensor is mounted inside the vessel, on the vessel wall, or on external support structures. Compact devices often fall within $\pm 2$ m, medium-sized devices within $\pm 5$ m, and large devices or external diagnostic supports can reach $\pm 15$ m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the attachment point is displaced from the Cartesian origin in the $+\hat{x}$ direction.

NAMES.name: x_direction_unit_vector
NAMES.short: X-axis projection of a direction unit vector encoding the spatial orientation of a device or sensor in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The x component of the [direction_unit_vector](name:direction_unit_vector) gives the projection of a hardware device's pointing direction onto the $\hat{x}$ axis of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame, where $\hat{z}$ coincides with the vertical $+Z$ direction and the azimuthal origin $\phi = 0$ is defined by facility convention.

For a unit vector $\hat{d}$ specifying device orientation, the three Cartesian components satisfy the unit-norm identity:

$$
d_x^2 + d_y^2 + d_z^2 = 1
$$

where $d_x$ is this quantity, $d_y$ is the [y_direction_unit_vector](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge_sensor), and $d_z$ is the [vertical_direction_unit_vector](name:vertical_direction_unit_vector). This constraint restricts the valid range to $d_x \in [-1, 1]$, with $|d_x| = 1$ only when the device points purely along the $\pm x$ axis.

This component is determined from mechanical installation geometry — precision survey measurements or engineering alignment procedures — rather than from plasma diagnostics. It applies to a broad class of hardware components including sensors, cameras, injector nozzles, and launcher mirrors whose spatial pointing must be registered in a common Cartesian frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the direction vector has a component in the $+x$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short: Y coordinate of the point where a sensor is physically attached to a device component, in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) machine frame.
NAMES.long:
The $y$ coordinate of a sensor attachment point specifies the location along the $y$ axis of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ machine frame at which a sensor is physically mounted to a structural component, where $\hat{z}$ is the vertical axis and $\phi = 0$ is defined by the facility convention.

Together with [x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and [vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), this coordinate fully determines the three-dimensional position of the mechanical attachment point in the machine reference frame. Attachment point coordinates are established from engineering drawings or direct metrology surveys of the as-built device; accurate knowledge of these positions is essential for relating sensor signals to plasma geometry and for alignment corrections in field or current reconstructions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the attachment point lies in the $+\hat{y}$ direction from the machine Cartesian origin.

NAMES.name: y_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge_sensor
NAMES.short: Y component of the unit vector defining the orientation of a strain gage sensor, resolved in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The y direction unit-vector component of a strain gage sensor is the projection of the sensor's oriented measurement axis onto the $\hat{y}$ basis direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. It describes orientation only; it is not a strain value and does not by itself transform a scalar strain reading into a vector deformation.

For a sensor direction unit vector $\hat{u}$, the component is defined by the projection onto $\hat{y}$:

$$
u_y = \hat{u} \cdot \hat{y}
$$

where $u_y$ is the y component, $\hat{u}$ is the unit vector along the strain gage measurement direction, and $\hat{y}$ is the y-axis unit basis vector in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

In practice, this component is obtained from the sensor installation geometry, calibration survey, or mechanical design model. Together with the corresponding x and z components, it specifies the axis along which the strain gage is sensitive, enabling comparison of sensor orientation with structural geometry and applied-load directions.

Typical values lie between -1 and 1. A value of 1 means the sensor direction is aligned with $+\hat{y}$, 0 means it has no y component, and -1 means it is aligned with $-\hat{y}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the strain gage sensor direction has a component along the $+\hat{y}$ axis of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis.

NAMES.name: electrostatic_potential_at_midplane
NAMES.short: Electrostatic potential of the plasma evaluated at the equatorial midplane, providing the local plasma potential reference in the boundary plasma and scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
The electrostatic potential $V_p$ at the midplane is the local electric potential of the unperturbed plasma, setting the reference against which sheath voltages, probe biases, and radial electric fields are measured in the boundary region. It is distinct from the [floating electrostatic potential](name:floating_electrostatic_potential), which is the potential at which a probe draws zero net current; the two differ by a sheath correction proportional to the local electron temperature.

The plasma–floating potential difference follows:

$$
\Delta V = V_p - V_f \approx \frac{k_B T_e}{e}\,\Lambda
$$

where $k_B T_e / e$ is the electron temperature expressed as a voltage, and $\Lambda = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(m_i / 2\pi m_e)$ is a dimensionless sheath factor of order 2–3 for hydrogen-isotope plasmas ($m_i$ is the ion mass and $m_e$ the electron mass).

In practice, $V_p$ at the midplane is inferred from Langmuir probe I–V characteristics collected during radial plunges through the scrape-off layer; it is identified at the knee of the electron-saturation branch or estimated by adding the sheath correction to the floating potential using the co-located [electron_temperature_at_midplane](name:electron_temperature_at_midplane). The `midplane` locus is unqualified, but in diverted tokamak configurations the probe traverse most commonly samples the outboard equatorial plane.

Typical SOL values range from a few to approximately 50 V above machine ground, consistently positive with respect to the [electrostatic_potential_at_wall](name:electrostatic_potential_at_wall) due to the ambipolar sheath constraint.

NAMES.name: electrostatic_potential_at_wall
NAMES.short: Local plasma electrostatic potential immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing wall, relative to the chosen electrical reference. It is distinct from the material wall voltage, floating potential, and any applied wall bias.
NAMES.long:
Electrostatic potential at wall is the voltage-valued scalar potential of the quasineutral plasma just outside the sheath adjacent to a plasma-facing surface. It is the plasma-side reference for sheath potential drops and near-wall electric fields, not the electrical potential of the solid wall material itself.

In the electrostatic approximation, the electric field is related to the scalar potential by

$$
\mathbf{E} = -\nabla \Phi
$$

where $\Phi$ is the electrostatic potential in volts and $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field in volts per meter. Only potential differences are physically meaningful; changing the electrical reference shifts $\Phi$ by a constant without changing $\mathbf{E}$.

In practice this quantity is commonly inferred from a near-wall Langmuir-probe current-voltage characteristic, sheath analysis, or an edge-plasma reconstruction tied to a specified electrical reference. It differs from [floating electrostatic potential](name:floating_electrostatic_potential), which is the potential of an electrically isolated probe or surface when the net collected current is zero, and from [electrostatic potential at midplane](name:electrostatic_potential_at_midplane), which refers to the local plasma potential at a different position. A grounded or biased wall can have a material voltage that differs from the adjacent plasma potential by the sheath voltage drop.

Typical values are strongly reference- and regime-dependent. In many low-temperature boundary-plasma measurements relative to a grounded vessel, values are of order a few volts to several tens of volts, with larger offsets possible near biased components, strong emission, or hotter edge conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local plasma potential at the wall is above the chosen electrical reference potential.

NAMES.name: floating_electrostatic_potential
NAMES.short: Electrostatic potential acquired by an electrically isolated probe or surface when the net plasma current to it is zero.
NAMES.long:
Floating electrostatic potential is the potential acquired by an electrically isolated material surface in contact with a plasma when the total collected current vanishes. It is usually displaced from the local plasma potential by a sheath drop governed mainly by electron temperature, ion mass, collecting geometry, and surface emission.

The defining condition for the floating potential $V_f$ is zero net current to the surface:

$$
I_\mathrm{i}(V_f) + I_\mathrm{e}(V_f) = 0
$$

where $I_\mathrm{i}$ is the ion current and $I_\mathrm{e}$ is the electron current collected by the surface at potential $V_f$. For a Maxwellian plasma with ions collected near ion saturation, $V_f$ is commonly below the plasma potential $V_p$ by a few electron-temperature volts; equivalently, $V_p - V_f$ is often about $2.5-4$ times $T_e$ when $T_e$ is expressed in eV, with the coefficient depending on ion species, effective collection area, magnetic-field incidence, and secondary-electron emission.

Floating potential is measured directly with a high-impedance connection to an isolated Langmuir-probe electrode or inferred from the zero-current crossing of a probe current-voltage characteristic. Interpretation requires care because RF pickup, sheath expansion, temperature fluctuations, surface condition, and emitted electrons can shift the measured value relative to the local plasma potential.

Typical values relative to grounded conducting structures are often -80 to -5 V in limiter and scrape-off-layer edge conditions, while divertor, strongly biased, or RF-perturbed regions can reach about -200 to +50 V. The range is not universal because the value follows both the local plasma potential and the electron-temperature-dependent sheath drop.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the floating surface potential is above the chosen electrical reference potential.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local number density of beryllium impurity ions per unit plasma volume, summed over all ionization states from singly ionized to fully stripped (Be1+ through Be4+), excluding neutral beryllium atoms.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium (atomic number $Z = 4$) enters the plasma primarily through sputtering or evaporation from beryllium first-wall surfaces. The local beryllium ion number density $n_\mathrm{Be}$ aggregates contributions from all four charged ionization stages:

$$
n_\mathrm{Be} = \sum_{z=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{z+}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in charge state $z+$, with $z$ running from 1 (singly ionized) to 4 (fully stripped). Neutral beryllium atoms are excluded from this sum.

Beryllium impurity content is inferred from passive spectroscopy of beryllium emission lines or from active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, with spatially resolved profiles reconstructed by tomographic inversion of chord-integrated measurements. Spatially averaged representations include [line_averaged_beryllium_density](name:line_averaged_beryllium_density) along a diagnostic chord and [volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density) integrated over the confined plasma volume. The relative impurity abundance with respect to the electron population is characterized by the [ratio_of_beryllium_density_to_electron_density](name:ratio_of_beryllium_density_to_electron_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when beryllium ions are present in the plasma volume.

NAMES.name: diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Full linear width of a circular diagnostic aperture at the entrance pupil, equal to twice the aperture radius and determining the solid-angle light-collection acceptance of the diagnostic channel.
NAMES.long:
The diameter of a diagnostic aperture is the full chord across the circular opening at the entrance pupil of the optical collection system. It is geometrically related to the [radius_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) by $d = 2r$, and it directly governs the solid angle subtended at a given distance from the plasma emission region, setting the total light throughput and therefore the signal-to-noise balance of the diagnostic.

The solid angle $\Omega$ subtended by a circular aperture of diameter $d$ at perpendicular distance $L$ from the emission region is:

$$
\Omega \approx \frac{\pi d^2}{4 L^2}
$$

where $d$ is the aperture diameter and $L$ is the line-of-sight distance from the plasma to the aperture plane.

This geometric parameter characterizes the entrance cone of spectroscopic diagnostics, including charge exchange recombination spectroscopy channels where the aperture diameter limits angular acceptance and spatial resolution. Typical values in fusion diagnostic systems range from a few millimeters to several centimeters depending on the required étendue and spatial selectivity of the measurement.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as the full chord through the aperture center in the plane of the entrance pupil.

NAMES.name: difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Signed difference between the motional-Stark-shifted wavelength of a fast neutral-beam spectral emission line and the field-free reference wavelength of the same transition. It is the wavelength correction produced by the Lorentz electric field experienced by beam atoms moving through the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed wavelength difference between a fast neutral-beam spectral line after motional Stark shifting and the field-free reference wavelength of the same atomic transition. It isolates the displacement caused by the Lorentz electric field in the rest frame of the fast beam atom, distinct from Doppler shifts, Zeeman splitting, and instrumental wavelength offsets.

For a selected spectral transition and Stark component, the linear Stark approximation gives the difference as:

$$
\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{MS} = \lambda_\mathrm{MS} - \lambda_\mathrm{ref} = S_\ell |\mathbf{E}_L|, \qquad \mathbf{E}_L = \mathbf{v}_b \times \mathbf{B}
$$

where $\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{MS}$, $\lambda_\mathrm{MS}$, and $\lambda_\mathrm{ref}$ are wavelengths in meters; $\lambda_\mathrm{MS}$ is the motional-Stark-shifted wavelength; $\lambda_\mathrm{ref}$ is the field-free reference wavelength; $S_\ell$ is the signed linear Stark coefficient for the specified line component in $\mathrm{m^2\,V^{-1}}$; $\mathbf{E}_L$ is the Lorentz electric field in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$; $\mathbf{v}_b$ is the fast neutral beam velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic flux density in tesla.

In beam emission spectroscopy and charge-exchange spectral analysis, this difference is computed from the local magnetic field, beam velocity, viewing geometry, and transition-specific Stark coefficients, or inferred by fitting resolved Stark components in the measured spectrum. It is used as a wavelength correction for the same spectral line to which the reference wavelength applies.

Typical absolute values for deuterium Balmer-alpha emission near a 656 nm reference wavelength are about $1\times10^{-10}$-$2\times10^{-9}$ m in medium to large tokamaks, depending mainly on beam energy, magnetic field strength, and the selected Stark component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the motional-Stark-shifted wavelength is greater than the field-free reference wavelength of the same spectral transition.

NAMES.name: efficiency_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Detection efficiency of a neutron detector is the probability that a neutron incident on the sensitive detector surface, with energy in the selected band, produces a registered count event.
NAMES.long:
Detection efficiency of a neutron detector is a dimensionless probability for converting an incident neutron into an accepted count. It includes detector-physics and acquisition effects such as neutron conversion reactions, moderation, scintillation or ionization yield, thresholds, dead-time corrections when included in the calibration, and event-selection cuts.

For incident neutron kinetic energy $E$ and an accepted energy interval bounded by $E_{\min}$ and $E_{\max}$, the efficiency is defined as the registered fraction of incident neutrons:

$$
\eta(E; E_{\min}, E_{\max}) = \frac{N_{\mathrm{registered}}(E; E_{\min}, E_{\max})}{N_{\mathrm{incident}}(E)}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{incident}}$ is the number of neutrons incident on the sensitive detector surface, $N_{\mathrm{registered}}$ is the number producing accepted count events in the selected band, and $E$, $E_{\min}$, and $E_{\max}$ are neutron kinetic energies in eV, often reported in MeV for fusion neutrons.

Efficiencies are measured using calibrated neutron fields or inferred from particle-transport and detector-response modeling validated by calibration data. The quantity is conditional on the detector-surface incidence described by [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector): for a uniform surface flux $\Phi_n(E)$ over active area $A$, the count-rate contribution is approximately $\int \Phi_n(E) A \eta(E)\,dE$, with angular and spatial dependence included when needed. Inferring plasma emission or source emissivity additionally requires the source-to-detector response represented by neutron_coefficient_of_neutron_detector; efficiency alone does not include plasma-to-detector transport, solid angle, shielding, or collimator transmission.

Values are bounded by 0-1. In fusion-neutron diagnostics, effective efficiencies after thresholds and event selection are often 1e-6-1e-1 for collimated fast-neutron measurements; compact scintillators or moderated thermal-neutron counters can reach 0.01-0.8 in favorable energy bands, while narrow spectrometer bands may be lower.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_radiance_of_spectral_line_due_to_charge_exchange
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight photon radiance of a selected spectral line emitted by fast ions after charge exchange with neutral beam atoms. It is the path-integrated spectral-line emissivity through the beam-plasma overlap and is non-negative.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion charge-exchange spectral-line radiance is the photon radiance of a specified atomic transition emitted after fast ions capture electrons from beam neutrals and radiatively decay. It is integrated along the viewing path over the region where fast ions, neutrals, and the diagnostic sightline overlap, and over the selected spectral line rather than per unit wavelength. As a photon-counting radiance, physical values are non-negative.

The defining relation is the line integral of the local spectral-line emissivity along the viewing path:

$$
\mathcal{R}_{\ell} = \int_{\mathrm{LOS}} \varepsilon_{\ell}^{\mathrm{FICX}}(\mathbf{r}, \hat{\mathbf{n}})\, dl
$$

where $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ is the radiance of transition $\ell$, $l$ is distance along the line of sight, $\mathbf{r}$ is position on that path, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the viewing direction, and $\varepsilon_{\ell}^{\mathrm{FICX}}$ is the local photon emissivity for that line in m^-3.s^-1.sr^-1. The path integration gives units of m^-2.s^-1.sr^-1.

In practice it is obtained from absolutely calibrated active charge-exchange spectroscopy after correcting for instrument throughput, viewing solid angle, background light, and spectral-line fitting. The local emissivity is governed by a velocity-space convolution of the fast-ion distribution with the neutral density and relative-speed-dependent charge-exchange or excitation rate coefficients, multiplied by the appropriate radiative branching probability and the line-shape or Doppler selection of the observation.

Typical calibrated line radiances span about 10^13-10^18 m^-2.s^-1.sr^-1, depending on fast-ion density, beam neutral density, path length through the beam-plasma overlap, transition strength, and viewing geometry. Values approach zero outside the active neutral-beam overlap; negative fitted values, if reported after background subtraction, represent measurement uncertainty rather than a physical radiance.

NAMES.name: height_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Full extent of the neutron detector aperture in the second local coordinate direction (X2), specifying one transverse dimension of a rectangular detector opening.
NAMES.long:
The height of a neutron detector specifies the aperture dimension along the second axis of the detector-local Cartesian $(X1, X2)$ coordinate frame, where $X2$ is oriented perpendicular to both the line-of-sight direction and the $X1$ axis. This quantity applies to rectangular aperture geometries and, paired with [width_of_neutron_detector](name:width_of_neutron_detector) measured along the $X1$ axis, fully defines the two-dimensional rectangular aperture opening.

The aperture height enters the computation of geometric detector acceptance: for a rectangular aperture the effective acceptance area is the product of the height ($X2$) and width ($X1$) dimensions, which scales the solid angle subtended by the detector and directly affects the inferred [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector). The aggregate quantity [surface_area_of_neutron_detector](name:surface_area_of_neutron_detector) is derived from these geometric parameters.

In fusion neutron diagnostics, detector aperture heights range from a few millimeters to a few centimeters, chosen to balance spatial resolution against counting-rate requirements.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture height is measured in the positive $X2$ direction of the detector-local coordinate frame.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Local number density of helium-3 ions per unit plasma volume, summed over all ionization states from singly ionized to fully stripped and excluding neutral helium-3 atoms.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 density is the local number density of ionized helium-3 nuclei in the plasma. It includes both singly ionized $^3\mathrm{He}^{+}$ and fully stripped $^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}$ ions, while excluding neutral helium-3 atoms.

The total helium-3 ion density is the sum over the two possible ion charge states:

$$
n_{^3\mathrm{He}} = \sum_{q=1}^{2} n_{^3\mathrm{He},q}
$$

where $n_{^3\mathrm{He}}$ is the total helium-3 ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $n_{^3\mathrm{He},q}$ is the density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ of helium-3 ions with charge state $q$, $q=1$ denotes singly ionized helium-3, and $q=2$ denotes fully stripped helium-3.

In practice, helium-3 density can be inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, passive helium spectroscopy, neutral-particle measurements, or integrated particle-balance analysis. Interpretation usually requires collisional-radiative modeling and knowledge of the ionization balance; in hot plasma cores helium-3 is typically dominated by the fully stripped charge state, while singly ionized helium-3 is more important in cooler edge regions.

Typical local densities range from $10^{17}$-$10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ for trace or minority helium-3 populations, and can reach $10^{19}$-$10^{20}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ when helium-3 is a major fuel or dilution species. The corresponding fraction relative to electron density depends on fueling, isotope mix, wall recycling, and transport.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Local number density of helium-4 ions per unit plasma volume, the principal measure of fusion ash concentration in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas.
NAMES.long:
The helium-4 ion number density $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ quantifies the local concentration of ${}^4\text{He}$ nuclei at a given point in the plasma. At fusion-relevant temperatures (several keV), helium-4 is fully stripped to He$^{2+}$, and in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas it accumulates as the primary fusion ash product of the reaction ${}^2\text{H} + {}^3\text{H} \rightarrow {}^4\text{He} + n$; its buildup dilutes the fuel and reduces the fusion reaction rate if not exhausted by the divertor system.

The time evolution of $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is governed by the particle continuity equation

$$
\frac{\partial n_{{}^4\text{He}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{{}^4\text{He}} = S_{{}^4\text{He}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the helium-4 particle flux and $S_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the volumetric source rate from fusion reactions and ionization of recycled helium neutrals at the plasma edge.

The helium-4 density is measured primarily via charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, where injected neutral beam atoms undergo charge exchange with He$^{2+}$ ions to produce line emission from excited helium atoms; passive spectroscopy of edge recycling emission provides a complementary approach. Chord-averaged and volume-averaged forms are provided by [line_averaged_helium_4_density](name:line_averaged_helium_4_density) and [volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density) respectively, while [helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary) gives the boundary value.

In D-T burning plasmas, central He-4 densities are in the range $10^{18}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, with the helium-to-electron density ratio — captured by [fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_helium_4_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density) — kept below approximately 5-10% in steady state to avoid excessive fuel dilution.

NAMES.name: krypton_density
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Local number density of krypton impurity summed over all ionization states, giving the total krypton particle concentration per unit plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The krypton number density is the volumetric concentration of krypton impurity at a given point in the plasma, encompassing all ionization states from neutral krypton Kr$^0$ through fully stripped Kr$^{36+}$. It is the primary local measure of krypton seeding level and the parent quantity from which spatially averaged forms are derived.

The total krypton particle density $n_\mathrm{Kr}$ at a given location is defined as:

$$
n_\mathrm{Kr} = \sum_{q=0}^{36} n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}$ is the number density of krypton ions in charge state $q$. The [chord-averaged form](name:line_averaged_krypton_density) integrates this local quantity along a line of sight, while [volume_averaged_krypton_density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density) provides a global mean. The concentration relative to electron density is tracked by krypton_fraction, and the pedestal-region value by [krypton_density_at_pedestal](name:krypton_density_at_pedestal).

Krypton (atomic number $Z=36$) is injected as a high-$Z$ seeding gas for radiative power exhaust and divertor detachment control. Its local density is inferred from passive spectroscopy of charge-state emission lines, active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or tomographic inversion of multi-chord line-integrated measurements. Typical seeded-discharge values in tokamak edge and divertor regions range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, corresponding to 0.01–1% of the local electron density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when krypton particles are present in the plasma volume element.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_beryllium_density
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Chord-average of the beryllium ion number density along a diagnostic line of sight, equal to the path integral of the local beryllium density divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged beryllium ion number density quantifies the mean beryllium ion content along a plasma diagnostic chord, normalized by chord length. It is the chord-integrated analog of the local [beryllium_density](name:beryllium_density) and is the most directly accessible measure of beryllium impurity concentration from line-of-sight diagnostics.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\bar{n}_{Be} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_{Be}(l) \, dl
$$

where $n_{Be}(l)$ is the local beryllium ion number density at path coordinate $l$ along the chord and $L$ is the total chord length.

Inferred from passive spectroscopy of beryllium emission lines by inverting chord-integrated emission intensities using atomic emissivity coefficients; the result aggregates contributions from all beryllium ionization states present along the chord. The [volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density) provides a complementary global volume average, while [beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis) gives the local on-axis value.
NAMES.sign: Positive when beryllium ions populate the measurement chord.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_helium_3_density
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Line-averaged helium-3 density is the chord-length average of the local charged helium-3 ion number density. It sums singly ionized and fully stripped helium-3 ions, excludes neutral helium-3 atoms, and is independent of deuterium or tritium background densities except through separately defined composition fractions.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged helium-3 density is the mean charged helium-3 ion number density along a specified sightline through the plasma. The local density being averaged includes $^3\mathrm{He}^{+}$ and $^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}$ ions and excludes neutral $^3\mathrm{He}$ atoms.

The chord average is defined by integrating the local charged helium-3 ion density along the path and dividing by the chord length:

$$
\bar{n}_{{}^3\mathrm{He},i} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L \left[n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{+}}(s) + n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}}(s)\right] \, ds
$$

where $s$ is distance along the chord, $L$ is the total chord length, $n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{+}}$ is the singly ionized helium-3 density, and $n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}}$ is the fully stripped helium-3 density. Deuterium and tritium background densities do not enter this path integral; they only affect related composition quantities such as a helium-3 fraction.

In practice this quantity is inferred from diagnostics or analysis methods that determine the helium-3 ion concentration along a line of sight, often combined with independent density measurements. Isotope-sensitive spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements, neutral-particle analysis, or reconstructed species-density distributions can provide the local or path-integrated helium-3 contribution.

Typical line-averaged helium-3 densities are $10^{16}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ for trace or minority-species operation in tokamaks. In plasmas using helium-3 as a substantial fuel component, values can approach $10^{19}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on total density and mixture fraction.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_helium_4_density
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Chord-averaged helium-4 ion number density, equal to the path integral of the local helium-4 density divided by the measurement chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged helium-4 density gives the spatial mean of the local [helium_4_density](name:helium_4_density) along a diagnostic chord through the plasma. As the principal ash product of deuterium-tritium fusion, helium-4 accumulates in the plasma core and its line-integrated concentration must be monitored to prevent fuel dilution and degradation of energy confinement.

The chord average is defined as:

$$
\bar{n}_{\mathrm{He4}} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_{\mathrm{He4}}(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{He4}}(\ell)$ is the local helium-4 ion number density at position $\ell$ along the chord (in m$^{-3}$) and $L$ is the total chord length in m.

This quantity is a natural output of line-integrated optical diagnostics such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy and helium spectral-line emission measurements, prior to any spatial inversion. It complements [volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density), which integrates over the full plasma volume, and is directly analogous to [line_averaged_helium_3_density](name:line_averaged_helium_3_density) for the lighter helium isotope. Typical values in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas range from $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on fusion power and helium exhaust efficiency.
NAMES.sign: Positive when helium-4 ions occupy the measurement chord at finite density; number density is orientation-independent and cannot take negative values.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_krypton_density
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Chord-average of the krypton number density, equal to the path integral of the local krypton particle density divided by the measurement chord length.
NAMES.long:
Krypton ($Z = 36$) is a noble-gas impurity that may be seeded into fusion plasmas for edge radiative cooling and power exhaust control. The line-averaged krypton density $\bar{n}_\mathrm{Kr}$ gives the krypton particle concentration averaged along a measurement chord, providing a line-of-sight integrated measure of impurity content rather than a local point value.

The defining relation is:

$$
\bar{n}_\mathrm{Kr} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_\mathrm{Kr}(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Kr}(\ell)$ is the local krypton number density at position $\ell$ along the chord and $L$ is the total chord length in meters.

This quantity is typically inferred from chord-integrated optical or vacuum-ultraviolet emission spectroscopy of krypton line radiation, combined with emissivity modeling along the line of sight. It provides a path-integrated measure complementary to the local [krypton_density](name:krypton_density) and to the global [volume_averaged_krypton_density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density). For comparison, [line_averaged_argon_density](name:line_averaged_argon_density) follows the same chord-average definition for argon seeding. Local concentrations at specific plasma regions are captured by [krypton_density_at_pedestal](name:krypton_density_at_pedestal) and [krypton_density_at_limiter](name:krypton_density_at_limiter).

Typical line-averaged krypton densities in power-exhaust seeding scenarios range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on seeding rate and plasma confinement regime.
NAMES.sign: Positive when krypton particles are present along the measurement chord, consistent with the intrinsically non-negative character of particle number density.

NAMES.name: lithium_density
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Number density of lithium impurity ions per unit plasma volume, summed over all ionization states from singly ionized to fully stripped, excluding neutral lithium atoms.
NAMES.long:
Lithium impurity ion number density quantifies the concentration of ionized lithium (atomic number $Z = 3$) within the plasma, summing contributions from all charge states $\text{Li}^{1+}$, $\text{Li}^{2+}$, and $\text{Li}^{3+}$ while excluding neutral lithium atoms. This total is related to the partial charge-state densities by

$$
n_\text{Li} = \sum_{z=1}^{3} n_{\text{Li}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\text{Li}^{z+}}$ is the local number density of lithium ions in charge state $z+$.

Lithium impurity concentrations are measured locally via charge exchange recombination spectroscopy or inferred from spectroscopic inversion of lithium-line emission; spatially averaged forms include [line_averaged_lithium_density](name:line_averaged_lithium_density), obtained by integrating along a diagnostic chord, and [volume_averaged_lithium_density](name:volume_averaged_lithium_density), which characterizes global impurity content within the confined plasma volume. Lithium is introduced into fusion devices through wall conditioning, pellet injection, or gas puffing, and its concentration influences impurity radiation losses and fuel dilution. The ratio of lithium ion density to electron density is tracked by lithium_fraction, which indicates the impurity burden on plasma performance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when lithium ions are present in the plasma; this quantity is non-negative by physical definition.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_lithium_density
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Path-length average of the lithium impurity ion number density along a diagnostic line of sight. It sums all ionized lithium charge states and excludes neutral lithium.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged lithium density is the path-length average of the lithium impurity ion number density along a specified line of sight. The local lithium ion density is the sum over ionized lithium charge states, $n_{\mathrm{Li,ion}} = n_{\mathrm{Li}^+} + n_{\mathrm{Li}^{2+}} + n_{\mathrm{Li}^{3+}}$, and excludes neutral lithium atoms.

For a chord of length $L$, the line average is defined by

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Li}} \rangle_{\mathrm{line}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_{\mathrm{Li,ion}}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\ell$ is distance along the line of sight in meters, $L$ is the chord length in meters, $n_{\mathrm{Li,ion}}$ is the local summed ionized-lithium density in m^-3, and $\langle n_{\mathrm{Li}} \rangle_{\mathrm{line}}$ is in m^-3.

In practice, this quantity may be inferred from a line-integrated lithium-sensitive measurement divided by the relevant chord length, or computed by integrating a reconstructed local lithium ion density along the same path. It provides a bulk chord measure of lithium impurity content and does not by itself resolve where along the line of sight the lithium ions are located.

The value is non-negative and is typically interpreted relative to electron density or to other impurity densities, because lithium content depends strongly on wall conditioning, fueling, transport, and plasma scenario. No universal numerical range is implied by the definition.

NAMES.name: lower_energy
NAMES.short: Minimum neutron energy threshold that defines the low-energy edge of a detector energy band; neutrons below this threshold are excluded from that spectral interval.
NAMES.long:
Lower energy is the minimum neutron energy included in a neutron detector energy band. It defines the low-energy edge of the interval paired with the corresponding [upper-energy threshold](name:neutron_maximum_energy_of_neutron_detector); neutrons below this edge are outside that band, while neutrons within the interval may be registered according to the detector response.

For a sharp nominal energy band, a dimensionally complete band counting-rate model uses an effective energy-dependent acceptance:

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{band}} = \int_{E_{\mathrm{low}}}^{E_{\mathrm{high}}} \Phi_E(E)\, \mathcal{G}(E)\, dE
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{band}}$ is the detector counting rate in s$^{-1}$, $E$, $E_{\mathrm{low}}$, and $E_{\mathrm{high}}$ are neutron energies in eV, $\Phi_E(E)$ is the differential directional neutron flux at the detector in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$, $\mathcal{G}(E)$ is the effective detector acceptance in m$^2$ sr including active area, geometric acceptance, transmission, and [detection efficiency](name:efficiency_of_neutron_detector), and $dE$ is an energy interval in eV. The physical constraints are $E_{\mathrm{low}} \ge 0$ and, for a nonempty band, $E_{\mathrm{low}} < E_{\mathrm{high}}$.

In practice, the lower threshold is determined by detector hardware settings, pulse-height or time-of-flight calibration, response-matrix definitions, and analysis selections used to assign events to spectral intervals. Because real detectors have finite energy resolution, the threshold is often a nominal band edge rather than an abrupt step in registration probability.

Typical values in fusion neutron diagnostics span about $10^3$-$2 \times 10^7$ eV. Bands used around D-D neutrons near $2.45 \times 10^6$ eV or D-T neutrons near $1.41 \times 10^7$ eV may have narrow separations of $10^3$-$10^6$ eV for spectroscopy or broader thresholds across $10^5$-$10^7$ eV for rate-oriented measurements.

NAMES.name: neutral_beam_mass
NAMES.subject: neutral_beam
NAMES.short: Atomic mass per particle of the injected neutral beam species, identifying the beam composition for diagnostic applications such as beam emission spectroscopy and charge exchange recombination spectroscopy.
NAMES.long:
The neutral beam mass specifies the atomic mass of the injected neutral beam particle on a per-atom basis. This property identifies the beam species and is an essential input for modeling spectroscopic observables — including Doppler line shapes and Lorentz-field motional Stark effects — in beam emission spectroscopy (BES) and charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS).

This quantity is a fixed hardware parameter determined by the choice of injected gas species. In fusion diagnostic applications the beam species is a hydrogen isotope; typical masses are 1 u (hydrogen), 2 u (deuterium), or 3 u (tritium), with deuterium the most widely used owing to its favorable penetration depth and clear spectral separation from plasma impurity lines.

Together with neutral_beam_charge and [neutral_beam_energy](name:neutral_beam_energy), this mass fully characterizes the diagnostic beam species for spectral modeling. The analogous per-particle mass of the observed fast ion population detected via charge exchange emission is [fast_ion_mass](name:ion_atomic_mass), while the general ionic species mass is [ion_mass](name:ion_atomic_mass).

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Fusion-neutron number flux incident on the active surface of a neutron detector, expressed as the number of neutrons crossing unit detector area per unit time.
NAMES.long:
Neutron flux of a neutron detector is the incident fusion-neutron number flux through the detector's active surface. It is a surface rate density for neutrons entering the detector, distinct from both the total plasma neutron emission rate and the detector count rate.

Using a local right-handed detector-surface frame $(\hat{u}, \hat{v}, \hat{n})$, where $\hat{u}$ and $\hat{v}$ are tangent to the active surface and $\hat{n}$ points from the plasma-facing front face into the sensitive volume, the surface-averaged incident neutron flux is

$$
\Phi_n = \frac{1}{A}\int_A \int_{\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{n} > 0} (\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{n})\, f_n(\mathbf{x}_s,\mathbf{v})\, d^3v\, dA
$$

where $\Phi_n$ is the neutron flux, $A$ is the active detector surface area, $\mathbf{x}_s$ is a point on that surface, $\mathbf{v}$ is neutron velocity, and $f_n$ is the neutron phase-space density at the surface. The condition $\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{n} > 0$ selects neutrons crossing the front face toward the sensitive volume.

In practice this quantity is inferred from the neutron count rate after corrections such as background subtraction, dead-time correction, attenuation, scattering, collimation, and the detector response to neutron energy and angle. For a simple calibrated response coefficient $C_n$, an area-averaged estimate may be written inline as $\Phi_n \simeq \dot{N}_\mathrm{det}/(A_\mathrm{eff} C_n)$, where $\dot{N}_\mathrm{det}$ is the neutron count rate and $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective detector area. Fusion-neutron spectra are commonly dominated by 2.45 MeV neutrons from deuterium-deuterium reactions or 14.1 MeV neutrons from deuterium-tritium reactions, with broadening and scattering depending on plasma and surrounding material conditions.

Typical incident fluxes at neutron detectors range from about 10^4-10^17 m^-2 s^-1, spanning low-yield or heavily shielded measurements through high-yield deuterium-tritium operation. The value at a particular detector depends strongly on plasma neutron source strength, viewing geometry, distance, shielding, collimation, and detector calibration.

NAMES.name: neutron_lower_energy
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Minimum neutron kinetic energy threshold defining the low-energy edge of a detector energy band, below which neutrons are excluded from energy-resolved counting.
NAMES.long:
The lower neutron energy defines the minimum kinetic energy at which a neutron is accepted into a given measurement band, establishing the low-energy discrimination boundary for energy-resolved neutron flux and spectroscopy diagnostics. It is the lower bound on the spectral variable described by [neutron_energy](name:neutron_energy), which spans the full range of kinetic energies of fusion-born and transported neutrons.

Together with the corresponding upper_energy bound, this threshold partitions the neutron energy spectrum into discrete detection intervals. The band structure enables separation of neutrons born in different fusion reactions: DD fusion produces neutrons with characteristic birth energies near 2.45 MeV, while DT fusion produces neutrons near 14.1 MeV, so band thresholds are chosen to bracket these peaks and isolate their contributions to measured count rates.

The threshold value is determined by the detector's hardware or software discrimination settings — pulse-height discriminators, time-of-flight gates, or digital threshold filters — and is fixed for a given experimental configuration. It is a required input for converting raw count rates into absolute neutron fluxes using the detector response described by the [efficiency_of_neutron_detector](name:efficiency_of_neutron_detector). The analogous bound for photon-based diagnostics is [lower_photon_energy](name:lower_photon_energy).

NAMES.name: neutron_maximum_energy_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Maximum neutron energy threshold of a neutron detector energy band.
NAMES.long:
Maximum neutron energy of a neutron detector is the upper kinetic-energy threshold of a detector energy band. Together with the corresponding minimum neutron energy, it defines the neutron-energy interval associated with that band.

The detector band is represented by the allowed neutron kinetic energies:

$$
E_\mathrm{lower} \le E_n \le E_\mathrm{upper}
$$

where $E_n$ is the neutron kinetic energy in eV, $E_\mathrm{lower}$ is the minimum neutron energy threshold in eV, and $E_\mathrm{upper}$ is this maximum neutron energy threshold in eV. By definition $E_\mathrm{upper}$ is non-negative and must satisfy $E_\mathrm{upper} \ge E_\mathrm{lower}$.

The threshold is determined by the detector response model, hardware settings, filters, moderators, time-of-flight selection, or the calibrated energy binning used to interpret neutron counts. It is a band definition rather than the measured energy of an individual neutron.

Typical upper thresholds for fusion neutron diagnostics range from about $10^5$-$2 \times 10^7$ eV for fast-neutron measurements. Bands centered on D-D and D-T fusion neutrons are commonly placed around the 2.45 MeV and 14.1 MeV neutron features, respectively, with upper thresholds chosen according to the desired bandwidth and detector resolution.

NAMES.name: neutron_rate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Number of individual neutron detection events registered per unit time by a neutron detector operating in pulse-counting mode.
NAMES.long:
Neutron rate of a neutron detector is the count rate of resolved neutron-induced pulses recorded by the detector. It is a detector response quantity, not the total neutron emission rate of the plasma source and not the incident neutron flux at the detector location.

The rate is defined from the cumulative number of accepted neutron detection events:

$$
R_n(t) = \frac{dN_\mathrm{det}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $R_n(t)$ is the neutron detection rate and $N_\mathrm{det}(t)$ is the cumulative number of neutron events that pass the detector pulse-height, timing, and discrimination criteria.

In practice, the rate is obtained by counting pulses in a finite time bin and dividing by the bin duration, with corrections as needed for dead time, background, pile-up, and neutron-gamma discrimination. For a given neutron field it depends on detector efficiency, active area or volume, shielding, collimation, and the neutron energy and angular response; at high rates, unresolved pile-up can make pulse counting unreliable and motivate current-mode or other integrating operation.

Typical pulse-counting rates range from about 10^0-10^7 s^-1, depending on detector type, distance from the plasma, shielding, and fusion power. Rates above roughly 10^6-10^7 s^-1 often require careful dead-time correction or a change of operating mode.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Local number density of all nitrogen nuclei per unit plasma volume, summed over all ionization states from neutral nitrogen through fully stripped ions.
NAMES.long:
Local number density of all nitrogen nuclei per unit plasma volume, totaling contributions from every ionization state of the species.

The total nitrogen density is the sum over all charge states:

$$
n_N = \sum_{z=0}^{7} n_{N^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{N^{z+}}$ is the number density of nitrogen ions in charge state $z+$, with $z = 0$ for neutral nitrogen and $z = 7$ for fully stripped N$^{7+}$ (atomic number $Z_N = 7$).

Nitrogen is commonly seeded into fusion plasmas as a radiative impurity to dissipate excess divertor heat flux; the local $n_N$ directly determines the radiative cooling power and the nitrogen contribution to the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$. It is inferred from vacuum-ultraviolet or extreme-ultraviolet emission spectroscopy analyzed with collisional-radiative models, or from active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy.

During active nitrogen seeding, core concentrations in present-day tokamaks range from $10^{17}$ to $5 \times 10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, with elevated values near the plasma edge. The [line-averaged nitrogen density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density) and [volume-averaged nitrogen density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density) provide chord-integrated and globally averaged measures of the nitrogen particle inventory; [nitrogen_fraction](name:nitrogen_fraction) normalizes $n_N$ to the electron density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when nitrogen nuclei are present in the plasma volume.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Line-averaged number density of nitrogen nuclei along a plasma diagnostic chord, summed over all ionization states. It equals the path integral of the local nitrogen density divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged nitrogen density is the chord-average of the local nitrogen number density sampled along a diagnostic line of sight. The nitrogen density includes nitrogen nuclei in all ionization states, so different charge states contribute according to their local abundance along the chord.

For a chord path $\Gamma$, the line-averaged nitrogen density is defined by:

$$
\langle n_N \rangle_L = \frac{1}{L}\int_{\Gamma} n_N(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $n_N(\ell)$ is the local nitrogen number density in m^-3, summed over all ionization states, $\ell$ is arclength along the chord in meters, and $L=\int_{\Gamma}d\ell$ is the chord length in meters over the sampled plasma region.

In practice this quantity is inferred from diagnostics and analysis methods that constrain nitrogen content along a line of sight, often using spectroscopic signals, atomic physics modeling, plasma background parameters, and the known viewing geometry. Because many measurements are sensitive to emissivity or to particular charge-state populations rather than directly to total nitrogen density, the conversion to all-ionization-state nitrogen density is model dependent and is not simply a geometric division of a raw signal by chord length.

Typical line-averaged nitrogen densities in tokamak plasmas range from about 1e15-1e18 m^-3 for trace-seeded conditions and can reach 1e19 m^-3 in strongly seeded or detached-edge regimes, depending on fueling, impurity seeding rate, transport, and ionization balance.

NAMES.name: nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Number density of target nuclei in a neutron detector converter material for the nuclear species involved in the neutron-induced detection reaction.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear density of a neutron detector converter is the number of target atomic nuclei per unit volume of converter material for the nuclear species that participates in the neutron-induced detection reaction. It is a material-and-composition property, distinct from converter volume or neutron flux, and sets the number of reaction centers available to incident neutrons.

For a converter made from one or more compounds or phases $c$, the target-nucleus density can be computed from the bulk material density and composition as:

$$
n_i = \rho_m N_A \sum_c f_c \frac{\nu_{i,c} a_{i,c}}{M_c}
$$

where $n_i$ is the target nuclear density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\rho_m$ is the bulk mass density of the converter material in $\mathrm{kg\,m}^{-3}$, $N_A$ is Avogadro's constant in $\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$, $f_c$ is the dimensionless mass fraction of compound or phase $c$, $M_c$ is its molar mass in $\mathrm{kg\,mol}^{-1}$, $\nu_{i,c}$ is the number of atoms of the relevant parent element per formula unit, and $a_{i,c}$ is the dimensionless isotopic abundance or enrichment of target isotope $i$. For a pure elemental or pure isotopic converter this reduces to the familiar single-component density relation.

In practice this quantity is derived from material specifications, density measurements, stoichiometry, isotopic assay, enrichment certificates, and corrections for porosity or inactive binder fraction when those affect the active converter volume. In response calculations it is combined with the microscopic reaction cross section and the converter-level neutron flux, such as neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector_converter; this is the flux at or within the converter and is distinct from a detector-level incident or averaged [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector).

Typical dense solid converter materials have total atomic densities of about $10^{28}-10^{29}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$. Target isotope densities are commonly $10^{26}-10^{29}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ depending on stoichiometry, enrichment, and loading, while gas or low-density converter media can be much lower, around $10^{20}-10^{25}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Total number density of oxygen atoms and ions across all charge states, from neutral to fully stripped, giving the local oxygen impurity concentration at a point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The local oxygen number density $n_\mathrm{O}$ quantifies the total concentration of oxygen impurity per unit plasma volume, encompassing neutral atomic oxygen and all ionic charge states up to fully stripped O$^{8+}$. Oxygen is a ubiquitous low-Z impurity in fusion devices, entering through wall outgassing and vessel conditioning; it contributes to radiative power losses and dilutes the hydrogenic fuel inventory.

The total oxygen density is defined as the sum over all ionization states:

$$
n_\mathrm{O} = \sum_{Z=0}^{8} n_{\mathrm{O}^{Z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{O}^{Z+}}$ is the number density of oxygen in charge state $Z^+$, with $Z$ ranging from 0 (neutral) to 8 (fully stripped).

The local density is inferred from passive extreme-ultraviolet spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and soft X-ray emission tomography. Spatially averaged forms include [line_averaged_oxygen_density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density) (chord integral divided by chord length) and [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) (integral over the plasma volume). The dimensionless [oxygen_fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_oxygen_ion_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density) relates this local density to the electron density as an impurity concentration measure.

In well-conditioned fusion plasmas the core oxygen density is a small fraction of the electron density; edge concentrations of $10^{15}$–$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ are representative of limiter and divertor configurations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen atoms or ions are present in the plasma volume element.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_oxygen_density
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight average of the total oxygen impurity number density, encompassing all charge states from neutral to fully stripped, divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged oxygen density is the chord-mean of the local oxygen number density—summed over all charge states from neutral O$^0$ through fully stripped O$^{8+}$—along a measurement path through the plasma. It characterizes the mean impurity concentration of oxygen along a given line of sight and is directly related to the local [oxygen_density](name:oxygen_density) integrated along the chord.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_O \rangle_\ell = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_O(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_O(\ell)$ is the local oxygen number density at position $\ell$ along the chord and $L$ is the chord length in m.

Line-averaged impurity densities are extracted from chord-integrated spectroscopic measurements of oxygen emission lines combined with ionization balance models. Passive spectroscopy of ultraviolet oxygen transitions or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy of helium-like and hydrogen-like oxygen lines provides the chord-integrated signal from which the line-averaged density is inferred. As a chord-averaged observable, spatial resolution is inherently limited, and tomographic inversion or profile modeling is required to recover local distributions.

Oxygen is a low-concentration impurity in fusion plasmas under normal operating conditions; line-averaged values fall several orders of magnitude below the electron density, with representative ranges of $10^{15}$–$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on wall conditioning and impurity seeding. The [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) provides the plasma-volume–weighted counterpart, while analogous chord-averaged densities for other impurity species include [line_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density) and [line_averaged_carbon_density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen impurity particles are present along the measurement chord at nonzero concentration.

NAMES.name: solid_angle_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Solid angle subtended by a neutron detector aperture at a neutron emission point, or the volume-averaged value over a finite source region. It is a nonnegative geometric acceptance in steradians, separate from detector efficiency or material response.
NAMES.long:
Solid angle of a neutron detector is the apparent angular size of its accepting aperture as seen from where neutrons are emitted. When one value represents a finite source region, it is the volume average of the pointwise solid angle over that region. It is a non-negative geometric acceptance and does not include intrinsic detector efficiency, neutron conversion probability, attenuation, or scattering.

The pointwise solid angle for an unobstructed aperture is the surface integral of the visible projected area divided by squared distance:

$$
\Omega(\mathbf{x}) = \int_S \frac{\max\left[0,\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{y})\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})\right]}{|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}|^3}\,dA(\mathbf{y})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the emission point, $\mathbf{y}$ is a point on the transmitting aperture surface $S$, $dA$ is an aperture area element, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ points toward the side from which neutrons are accepted. The $\max$ operation enforces a non-negative projection: aperture elements facing away from the emission point contribute zero. For a small flat aperture of area $A$ at distance $d$ and incidence angle $\alpha$, this reduces to $\Omega \simeq A\max(0,\cos\alpha)/d^2$; for isotropic emission, the purely geometric intercepted fraction is $\Omega/(4\pi)$ before applying any efficiency or transport factors.

For a finite source region $V$ with physical volume $|V|$, the averaged value is $\langle\Omega\rangle_V=|V|^{-1}\int_V\Omega(\mathbf{x})\,dV$. This average lies between the minimum and maximum pointwise solid angles within the region and is bounded by the full-sphere value, $0 \le \langle\Omega\rangle_V \le 4\pi$. It is computed from the measured aperture, collimator, and line-of-sight geometry using analytic formulas for simple apertures or numerical surface integration and ray tracing for finite openings and partial visibility.

Typical values are $10^{-6}$-$10^{-3}$ sr for narrow collimated neutron viewing channels and $10^{-3}$-$10^{-1}$ sr for nearby or wide-aperture views. Values approaching 1 sr require a very large or very close accepting aperture; no physical aperture can exceed $4\pi$ sr as seen from an emission point.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Total geometric area of the neutron detector's neutron-sensitive active surface, excluding passive housing, shielding, supports, and electronics. For segmented or curved detectors it is the sum or integral of the active surface area, not a projected area or solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Surface area of a neutron detector is the unsigned geometric area of the detector surface that can register or convert incident neutrons. It refers to active neutron-sensitive material or the active entrance face coupled to that material, and excludes passive structures such as housings, shielding, supports, cables, and electronics.

For an active surface $S$, the area $A$ is defined by integrating the local surface element over the active region:

$$
A = \int_S dA
$$

where $dA$ is the differential geometric surface area element. For a detector made of multiple active patches, $A$ is the sum of the patch areas; for a flat circular or rectangular face it reduces to the usual geometric face area.

This quantity is commonly determined from mechanical drawings, aperture definitions, metrology, or manufacturer specifications of the neutron-sensitive face. In count-rate estimates for a uniform mono-directional neutron flux normally incident on a flat active face, an approximate relation is $C \approx \Phi A \epsilon$, where $C$ is count rate in s$^{-1}$, $\Phi$ is neutron flux in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ at the detector face, and $\epsilon$ is the detection efficiency. For oblique incidence, the effective projected area includes angular factors such as $\cos\alpha$ or a measured angular response; collimator width, aperture shape, and solid angle are separate geometric quantities and should not be inferred from area alone.

Typical active surface areas range from $10^{-6}$-$10^{-4}$ m$^2$ for small diamond, silicon, or compact scintillator detectors, $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ m$^2$ for common scintillator or proportional-counter faces, and up to about $10^{-1}$ m$^2$ for large moderated or extended detector assemblies.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Calibrated thermodynamic temperature, in kelvin, representing the thermal state of a neutron detector assembly or its neutron-conversion element. It is the temperature used to characterize detector response, not the raw temperature-sensor voltage.
NAMES.long:
Temperature of a neutron detector is the calibrated thermodynamic temperature representing the thermal state of the detector assembly, housing, electronics-adjacent sensor location, or neutron-to-charged-particle converter element. The reported quantity is an absolute temperature in kelvin and is therefore non-negative; it is distinct from a raw sensor output such as [voltage_of_temperature_sensor](name:voltage_of_temperature_sensor).

When the detector temperature is spatially non-uniform or measured by several sensors, the scalar value should represent the location or thermal component most relevant to the detector response, such as the converter material or the sensor thermally coupled to the active detector module. If several readings are combined, the value is normally a calibrated representative temperature, for example an average or response-weighted estimate, with the choice determined by the detector calibration model.

In practice the temperature is obtained from thermistors, resistance temperature detectors, thermocouples, semiconductor sensors, or similar devices attached to the detector body, converter, or local electronics package. The calibrated temperature is used to monitor gain stability, temperature-dependent efficiency, electronic noise, and time-dependent corrections applied to neutron count-rate or signal measurements such as [voltage_of_neutron_detector](name:voltage_of_neutron_detector) and [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector).

Representative operating values for room-temperature neutron detector systems are often about 280-330 K. Detectors with active heating, cooling, in-vessel placement, or thermally isolated converter elements may operate outside this range, and transient heating during a discharge can produce smaller time-dependent excursions around the local baseline.

NAMES.name: toroidal_plasma_momentum_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Local density of toroidal angular momentum of the plasma at a diagnostic measurement position, equal to the major-radius lever arm times the total toroidal linear momentum density. The total includes electrons and all ion species.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal plasma momentum at a measurement position is the local density of angular momentum about the toroidal symmetry axis. It is the major-radius lever arm multiplying the toroidal component of the total plasma linear momentum density at the sampled point, including electrons and all ion species.

For a measurement point $\mathbf{x}_m$, the quantity is defined by

$$
\ell_\phi(\mathbf{x}_m) = R_m \sum_{s \in \{e,\mathrm{ions}\}} n_s(\mathbf{x}_m)\,m_s\,V_{\phi,s}(\mathbf{x}_m)
$$

where $R_m$ is the major radius of the measurement point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $n_s$ is the number density of species $s$, $m_s$ is its particle mass, and $V_{\phi,s}$ is its toroidal linear velocity component. The factor $R_m$ converts toroidal linear momentum density to angular momentum density about the symmetry axis, giving units of $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

In charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, the ion contribution is commonly inferred from Doppler shifts of impurity emission together with geometry, density, and species-composition information. Main-ion and electron contributions may be measured, inferred, or modeled; the electron term is included in the total definition but is usually small because of the electron mass.

Typical magnitudes range from $10^{-4}$ to $1\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ in tokamak plasmas, depending mainly on density, major radius, ion mass, and toroidal rotation speed. Strongly beam-driven or rapidly rotating plasmas can reach several $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ locally, while weakly rotating plasmas may be close to zero.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total toroidal linear momentum density points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_beam_tracing_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of a discrete point along the wave-beam ray path in a beam-tracing model of electromagnetic wave propagation, giving the height above the machine equatorial plane.
NAMES.long: The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates a beam-tracing point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the height above the machine equatorial plane. In beam-tracing models used to follow the propagation of radio-frequency and microwave waves through a magnetized plasma — including electron cyclotron, lower hybrid, and ion cyclotron scenarios — the wave-beam trajectory is discretized into successive spatially resolved points; this quantity specifies the vertical component of each such point's position. Together with the major-radius and toroidal angle coordinates of the same beam-tracing point, it fully determines the three-dimensional location of the ray within the plasma volume, and it is used alongside local wave-vector quantities such as [radial_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:radial_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) to evaluate wave absorption and current-drive profiles. The beam energy deposited along the trajectory may also be referenced through [wave_beam_energy](name:wave_beam_energy). Typical values fall within the vertical extent of the plasma cross-section, ranging from approximately -2 m to +2 m in current mid-size tokamaks and proportionally larger in reactor-scale devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the beam-tracing point lies above the machine equatorial plane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_launching_position
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the physical launching position where a diagnostic viewing ray, emitted probing beam, or antenna path begins in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It gives the launch height Z relative to the coordinate origin.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a launching position is the $Z$ component of the physical point from which a diagnostic line of sight, emitted probing beam, or antenna-launched path is initiated. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This coordinate complements the radial and toroidal coordinates of the same launch point to locate the starting point of a ray or beam in space. More specific quantities may be used when the object is specialized, such as the vertical position of a neutral-beam injector, a diagnostic aperture, or a point along a beam-tracing trajectory; this name denotes the generic launch point itself.

The value is obtained from the known instrument geometry and its alignment with respect to the machine coordinate origin. It is normally treated as a geometric configuration quantity, while changes in movable launchers or steering systems are represented by the corresponding updated launch geometry.

Typical values are set by the vertical extent of the vessel and diagnostic access ports. In medium-sized tokamaks they commonly lie in the range -2-2 m, while larger devices may have launch heights extending to several meters above or below the midplane.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the launching position lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Vertical height coordinate Z of a neutron detector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured from the horizontal midplane of the machine.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ specifies the position of a neutron detector along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height measured from the geometric midplane.

Together with the [major-radius coordinate], this quantity fully locates the detector in the poloidal cross-section, determining the chord geometry through the plasma and the emission region sampled. The transverse aperture dimensions are separately characterized by [width_of_neutron_detector](name:width_of_neutron_detector) and [height_of_neutron_detector](name:height_of_neutron_detector).

The coordinate is established from engineering survey data or design drawings of the diagnostic port geometry and enters the line-of-sight integrals used in neutron emission tomography and absolute neutron yield calibration. The same vertical-coordinate convention is applied to [vertical_coordinate_of_bolometer](name:vertical_coordinate_of_bolometer) and [vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector), ensuring geometric consistency across diagnostic systems. Typical $Z$ values range from approximately $-2$ m to $+2$ m in medium-sized tokamaks, depending on machine height and port allocation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector is located above the geometric midplane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Instantaneous or sampled raw electrical output voltage of a neutron detector module, measured relative to its electronics reference or baseline before pulse extraction, filtering, calibration, or conversion to neutron rate.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a neutron detector is the signed electrical potential difference produced at the detector output at a specified instant or sample of the raw waveform. It represents the direct analog signal relative to an electronics reference level or baseline, not a calibrated neutron flux, count rate, pulse height, or integrated charge.

For an output node with electric potential $\Phi_\mathrm{out}(t)$ and a reference or baseline potential $\Phi_\mathrm{ref}(t)$, the raw detector voltage is defined by:

$$
V_\mathrm{raw}(t) = \Phi_\mathrm{out}(t) - \Phi_\mathrm{ref}(t)
$$

where $t$ is the sampling time, $\Phi_\mathrm{out}$ is the detector or front-end electronics output potential, and $\Phi_\mathrm{ref}$ is the chosen electronics ground, bias reference, or estimated baseline.

In practice this quantity is obtained from the uncalibrated detector readout before pulse finding, shaping correction, pile-up rejection, energy calibration, efficiency correction, or conversion to neutron rate. For pulsed detectors it is the waveform sample value; derived quantities such as pulse maximum, pulse integral, or discriminator counts should be treated separately.

Typical raw amplitudes range from 1e-3-10 V depending on detector type, biasing, preamplifier gain, termination, and neutron intensity. Baseline fluctuations and electronic noise are often in the 1e-4-1e-2 V range, while large pulses may approach the dynamic range or saturation limit of the acquisition electronics.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector output potential is above the chosen electronics reference or baseline potential.

NAMES.name: peak_voltage_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Peak voltage of a neutron detector is the baseline-referenced pulse height of the processed detector signal, evaluated at the pulse extremum after applying the channel pulse-polarity convention. It represents the voltage amplitude assigned to an individual detector response.
NAMES.long:
Peak voltage of a neutron detector is the pulse height assigned to the processed voltage waveform from a detector module. It is referenced to the local pre-pulse baseline and uses the channel pulse-polarity convention, so it is not simply the raw algebraic maximum of the unprocessed waveform or an absolute value over the full record.

For a pulse-search window, the baseline-referenced peak voltage can be written as the maximum polarity-corrected excursion:

$$
V_{\mathrm{peak}} = \max_{t \in W}\left[p\left(V_{\mathrm{proc}}(t)-V_{\mathrm{base}}\right)\right]
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{peak}}$, $V_{\mathrm{proc}}(t)$, and $V_{\mathrm{base}}$ are in volts, $W$ is the time window associated with the pulse, and $p$ is the pulse-polarity factor: $p=+1$ for positive-going processed pulses and $p=-1$ for negative-going processed pulses.

In practice, the digitized detector output is conditioned by shaping, filtering, or other signal-processing steps before the peak is found. The baseline is usually estimated from pre-pulse samples or a nearby quiet interval, and pulse pileup, saturation, and electronic noise determine whether the extracted peak is reliable. This quantity is distinct from the instantaneous [detector voltage](name:voltage_of_neutron_detector), which denotes the voltage signal itself before the peak-height reduction.

Representative processed pulse heights are strongly instrument-dependent, but neutron detector electronics commonly report values from about 0.001-5 V for resolved pulses. Values near the noise floor are threshold-dependent, while values approaching the acquisition full scale may indicate saturation rather than a proportional neutron response.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pulse excursion is in the channel's configured pulse-polarity direction relative to the local baseline; for a positive-going channel this means the processed voltage at the pulse peak exceeds the baseline, and for a negative-going channel it means it is below the baseline before polarity correction.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_temperature_sensor
NAMES.short: Electrical potential difference output by a temperature sensor that monitors the thermal environment of a neutron detector module. It is the sensor signal measured relative to a designated electronics reference, normally before conversion to calibrated temperature.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a temperature sensor is the electrical potential difference generated by, or produced from, the sensor element and read by the acquisition electronics as the thermal-monitor signal for a neutron detector module. It is an electrical signal in volts, not a temperature; conversion to detector or sensor temperature requires the applicable calibration, baseline, and electronics gain information.

The temperature calibration is commonly represented as a mapping from the corrected sensor voltage:

$$
T_s = f_\mathrm{cal}\!\left(\frac{V_s - V_0}{G}\right)
$$
