where $T_s$ is the inferred sensor temperature, $V_s$ is this measured voltage, $V_0$ is the voltage offset or baseline associated with the reference condition and readout chain, $G$ is the dimensionless electronics gain, and $f_\mathrm{cal}$ is the calibration function for the sensor type. For a locally linear calibration, the sensitivity $S_T = dV/dT$ has units of V/K and is distinct from the voltage value $V_s$ itself.

In practice the voltage is obtained by digitizing the potential difference between the sensor signal terminal and the electronics reference or return terminal. The sensor may be a thermocouple, resistance thermometer, thermistor, or integrated temperature monitor, with appropriate excitation, cold-junction compensation, amplification, filtering, and offset correction applied according to the measurement chain.

Typical recorded voltages depend strongly on sensor type and conditioning. Unamplified thermocouple signals are commonly in the $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ V range over practical temperature excursions, with sensitivities of order $10^{-5}$-$10^{-4}$ V/K; conditioned resistive or semiconductor temperature channels are often scaled to about $0$-$5$ V or $-10$-$10$ V. These voltage ranges should not be interpreted as temperature sensitivities unless a calibration slope in V/K is specified.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the sensor signal terminal is at higher electric potential than the designated electronics reference or return terminal.

NAMES.name: volume_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Physical volume occupied by the converter material in a neutron detector. It excludes inactive supports, housings, and voids unless they are part of the neutron-converting medium.
NAMES.long:
Converter volume is the physical volume occupied by material that produces the detectable secondary signal from incident neutrons, such as a gas fill, scintillator, fission deposit, or neutron-converting coating. It is a geometrical property of the active converter medium, distinct from its nuclear number density or reaction rate per unit volume.

The converter volume is defined by integrating over the region occupied by the active converter material:

$$
V_\mathrm{conv} = \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{conv}} d^3x
$$

where $\Omega_\mathrm{conv}$ is the physical region containing converter material and $d^3x$ is the local volume element.

In practice, $V_\mathrm{conv}$ is obtained from the detector geometry: the measured or specified dimensions of gas cells, scintillator blocks, converter foils, coatings, or deposits. For segmented or multilayer converters, the total volume is the sum over active converter regions; for porous, patterned, or partially filled media, only the fraction actually occupied by converter material is included. For thin coatings, the volume is often computed as active coated area times effective converter thickness.

Representative values are highly detector-dependent: thin fission or boron/lithium coatings can be about $10^{-11}$-$10^{-7}$ m$^3$, compact solid scintillator converters about $10^{-7}$-$10^{-4}$ m$^3$, and gas-filled converter regions about $10^{-5}$-$10^{-2}$ m$^3$. The detection probability also depends on the [nuclear number density](name:nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter) and microscopic cross sections, while the local conversion rate is represented by the [nuclear reaction rate per unit volume](name:nuclear_rate_of_neutron_detector_converter).

NAMES.name: wave_beam_energy
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic energy carried by a coherent wave-beam pulse through a specified transverse beam cross-section at a specified position along its propagation path. It is the time integral of the instantaneous beam power at that location over the pulse duration.
NAMES.long:
Wave-beam energy is the electromagnetic pulse energy transported by a coherent beam through a chosen transverse surface at a specified location along the beam path. It is a pulse-integrated quantity in joules, distinct from instantaneous or time-averaged beam power in watts. Because absorption, scattering, reflection, or optical losses can change the beam energy along the path, the location of the evaluated cross-section is part of the physical definition.

For a pulse crossing a transverse surface labeled by path position $s$, the beam energy is defined by the time integral of the instantaneous beam power through that surface:

$$
E_\mathrm{beam}(s) = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} P_\mathrm{beam}(s,t)\,dt
$$

where $P_\mathrm{beam}(s,t)$ is the electromagnetic power crossing the specified surface, $t_1$ and $t_2$ bound the pulse, and $s$ labels position along the beam centerline. Energy in joules equals power in watts integrated over time, so this quantity should not be confused with absorbed or deposited power, which describes a rate of energy transfer.

In practice, wave-beam energy is measured with calibrated energy meters, photodiodes combined with pulse-shape calibration, calorimeters, or inferred from independently calibrated optical diagnostics. Comparing energies at two positions gives the pulse transmission $T = E_\mathrm{out}/E_\mathrm{in}$, while the energy loss $E_\mathrm{in}-E_\mathrm{out}$ may include plasma absorption, scattering, reflection, aperture clipping, and optical attenuation.

Typical values depend strongly on the diagnostic and source technology. Thomson-scattering laser pulses commonly carry about 0.1-10 J per pulse, while smaller alignment or probe beams may be in the 10^-6-10^-2 J range and high-energy pulsed laser systems can exceed 10 J.

NAMES.name: wave_beam_energy_at_launching_position
NAMES.short: Energy carried by a wave beam pulse at the position where it is launched into the experimental region, before interaction with the plasma or other target medium. It is the incident pulse energy at that reference position.
NAMES.long:
Wave-beam energy at launching position is the total electromagnetic energy carried by a single launched wave-beam pulse at the launch reference position, before absorption, scattering, or other interaction in the experimental region. It is a nonnegative pulse-integrated quantity and is the launch-position specialization of [wave_beam_energy](name:wave_beam_energy).

The launch-position pulse energy is the time integral of the beam power crossing the launch reference surface during the pulse:

$$
E_\mathrm{in} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} P_\mathrm{in}(t)\,dt
$$

where $E_\mathrm{in}$ is the launch-position energy in joules, $P_\mathrm{in}(t)$ is the instantaneous beam power in watts at that position, and $t_1$ and $t_2$ are the pulse start and end times in seconds. If the beam is described by an intensity distribution, $P_\mathrm{in}(t)$ is the area integral of that intensity over the beam cross-section at the launch reference surface.

In practice, the quantity is measured with a calibrated energy meter, calorimeter, fast photodiode with known response, or a monitored pick-off of the launched beam. Measurements are corrected for known transmission and attenuation between the monitor and the launch reference position. Together with [wavelength_of_wave_beam](name:wavelength_of_wave_beam), the energy gives photon number for a monochromatic beam, for example $N_\gamma = E_\mathrm{in}\lambda/(hc)$; photon flux also requires the pulse duration, and photon-flux density requires both pulse duration and beam area.

The physical range is $E_\mathrm{in} \ge 0$ J. Operational diagnostic pulses are commonly $10^{-3}$-10 J: millijoule-scale for weak probing or alignment pulses and 0.1-5 J for many pulsed laser scattering systems, with larger systems reaching tens of joules.

NAMES.name: wavelength
NAMES.short: Vacuum optical wavelength used as the spectral sampling coordinate for a Thomson scattering polychromator detection band. It identifies where the channel or filter spectral response is evaluated when modeling scattered light for electron-temperature inference.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength is the spatial period of an optical electromagnetic wave, expressed here as vacuum wavelength. In a Thomson scattering polychromator, it is the spectral coordinate used to evaluate filter transmission, detector efficiency, and the scattered-light spectrum within a detection band.

For a monochromatic wave in vacuum, wavelength is related to optical frequency by

$$
\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}
$$

where $\lambda$ is the vacuum wavelength in meters, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum in meters per second, and $\nu$ is the optical frequency in hertz.

In practice, wavelength values are obtained from optical calibration of filters, spectrometers, or polychromator channels and are used when integrating the product of the Thomson-scattered spectrum and the channel spectral response. If a calibration is specified in air or another medium, it should be converted to vacuum wavelength using the refractive index, for example $\lambda_\mathrm{vac} = n\lambda_\mathrm{medium}$ with dimensionless refractive index $n$. Several wavelength values may be chosen to represent one detection band; the number of sampling positions is an instrumentation and numerical-integration choice rather than a separate physical convention.

Typical optical wavelengths relevant to Thomson scattering diagnostics lie from about $0.3\times10^{-6}$ m to $2.0\times10^{-6}$ m. Common laser wavelengths include approximately $1.064\times10^{-6}$ m for Nd:YAG systems and $6.94\times10^{-7}$ m for ruby systems, with polychromator detection bands selected around the laser wavelength and its thermally broadened scattered spectrum.

NAMES.name: width_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Full width of a rectangular neutron detector aperture along the first local coordinate direction (X1), defining the collimation boundary on that transverse axis.
NAMES.long:
The width of a neutron detector specifies the full linear extent of its rectangular aperture along the first transverse local coordinate direction, X1, of the detector assembly. This geometric parameter governs the collimation acceptance in the X1 direction and is defined only when the aperture cross-section is rectangular.

Together with [height_of_neutron_detector](name:height_of_neutron_detector), which gives the corresponding aperture extent along the orthogonal X2 local coordinate, these two dimensions fully characterize the rectangular aperture geometry. Their product yields the total aperture area captured by [surface_area_of_neutron_detector](name:surface_area_of_neutron_detector), which enters the solid-angle computation and flux normalization underpinning the measured [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector). The spatial location of the detector in the machine frame is described by major_radius_of_neutron_detector and [vertical_coordinate_of_neutron_detector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutron_detector).

Typical aperture widths in tokamak neutron diagnostics range from a few millimeters to several centimeters, balancing spatial resolution against counting-rate requirements and detection efficiency.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture extent is measured from the lower X1 boundary to the upper X1 boundary of the detector geometry.

NAMES.name: width_of_wave_beam
NAMES.short: Width of a wave beam is a transverse linear size of its field or intensity envelope measured perpendicular to the propagation direction. For an elliptical beam, the convention must distinguish a center-to-contour semi-axis from a full-width measure such as FWHM.
NAMES.long:
The width of a wave beam is a linear measure of the transverse extent of the beam envelope in the plane normal to the local propagation direction. It describes one direction across the beam spot, not the enclosed cross-sectional area, and its numerical value depends on the stated intensity-contour or beam-edge convention.

For an elliptical contour described by principal semi-axis widths, the enclosed area is related to the two widths by

$$
A = \pi w_1 w_2
$$

where $A$ is the enclosed beam area in $\mathrm{m^2}$ and $w_1$ and $w_2$ are centerline-to-contour semi-axis widths in m for the same contour. This relation does not apply directly to full-width quantities such as FWHM unless they are first converted to the corresponding semi-axis widths; for example, a full width across an ellipse gives a semi-axis equal to one half of that full width.

Beam width is determined from optical or microwave beam measurements such as camera imaging, knife-edge scans, moving-wire scans, or from ray and beam propagation calculations. Together with [tilt_angle_of_wave_beam](name:tilt_angle_of_beam_tracing_beam), it can specify the orientation and size of an elliptical spot, while [area_of_wave_beam](name:width_of_wave_beam) describes the total enclosed cross-section. In diagnostic applications, beam width contributes to spatial resolution, but the final resolution also depends on collection geometry, scattering volume, refraction, diffraction, and signal integration.

Typical values range from $1 \times 10^{-4}$-$5 \times 10^{-3}$ m for tightly focused optical laser waists, $1 \times 10^{-3}$-$3 \times 10^{-2}$ m for broader optical or millimeter-wave diagnostic beams, and $1 \times 10^{-2}$-$2 \times 10^{-1}$ m for lower-frequency microwave or RF beams and launcher spots.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Coordinate of a neutron detector or aperture outline vertex along the X1 axis of the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame with basis (X1-hat, X2-hat). Together with the matching X2 coordinate, it defines the boundary of the detector sensitive face or aperture.
NAMES.long:
The $x_1$ coordinate of a neutron detector is the signed local-position coordinate of one outline vertex along the $X_1$ axis of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame with unit basis $(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_1, \hat{\mathbf{X}}_2)$. Paired with the corresponding [x2 coordinate](name:x2_coordinate_of_neutron_detector), it defines the planar boundary of the detector sensitive face, collimator opening, or aperture.

The coordinate is the scalar projection of the displacement from the local origin to the outline vertex onto the first local basis direction:

$$
x_{1,i} = (\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{X}}_1
$$

where $i$ labels a vertex, $x_{1,i}$ is the coordinate in meters, $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the vertex position, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the per-detector local origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{X}}_1$ is the unit vector along the $+X_1$ axis of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

In practice, the outline vertices are obtained from the mechanical design, survey, or alignment model of the neutron detector, collimator, or aperture. The per-detector origin is fixed at the reference point where the nominal sightline intersects the detector or aperture plane; when no sightline is defined, it is fixed at the chosen geometric center of the sensitive face or opening. The vertex index $i$ labels successive points around the boundary polygon, with neighboring indices defining boundary segments and the final vertex connecting back to the first; the same ordering applies to the paired $x_2$ coordinate.

Typical values are -0.05-0.05 m for small collimator apertures, -0.5-0.5 m for compact detector faces, and up to about -1-1 m for large neutron-camera or shielding-aperture outlines, measured relative to the detector-local origin.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the detector-local origin has a positive projection along the $+X_1$ direction of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate along the X2 axis of a vertex on the neutron detector boundary in the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame, defining the detector's cross-sectional outline.
NAMES.long: The X2 coordinate, together with [x1_coordinate_of_neutron_detector](name:x1_coordinate_of_neutron_detector), traces the irregular polygonal boundary of the neutron detector element in its detector-local planar Cartesian $(X1, X2)$ frame. This local frame is rigidly attached to the detector's physical orientation and position, and is distinct from the machine cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; the relationship between the two frames is determined by the detector mounting geometry. The complete ordered sequence of $(X1, X2)$ vertex pairs defines the detector's active area or aperture cross-section, which enters computations of detection solid angle, geometric efficiency, and neutron-emission synthetic diagnostics. The analogous coordinate for hard X-ray detectors follows the same convention as [x2_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector](name:x2_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector), and the soft X-ray analog is [x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector](name:x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex lies in the positive X2 direction of the detector-local Cartesian $(X1, X2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: xenon_density
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Number density of xenon ions at a given point in the plasma, summed over all ionization states from singly ionized through fully stripped xenon, excluding neutral xenon atoms.
NAMES.long:
Xenon is a high-$Z$ noble-gas impurity (atomic number $Z_\mathrm{Xe} = 54$) introduced into fusion plasmas for radiative-mantle experiments, impurity-transport studies, and disruption mitigation. The xenon ion number density $n_\mathrm{Xe}$ quantifies the local concentration of all charged xenon species and enters the plasma effective charge through $Z_\mathrm{eff} = \sum_i Z_i^2 n_i / n_e$, where $n_i$ is the partial density of ion species $i$ and $n_e$ is the electron density.

The total xenon ion density is the sum over all ionic charge states:

$$
n_\mathrm{Xe} = \sum_{z=1}^{54} n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{z+}}$ is the partial number density of xenon ions carrying charge $ze$. The charge-state distribution is determined by coronal equilibrium or collisional-radiative modeling at the local electron temperature and density.

The xenon density profile is inferred from vacuum-ultraviolet or soft-X-ray line emission via spectroscopy and tomographic inversion, or from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy using neutral-beam injection. Spatially resolved forms include [xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis) at the innermost flux surface and [xenon_density_at_pedestal](name:xenon_density_at_pedestal) in the edge transport barrier, while [volume_averaged_xenon_density](name:volume_averaged_xenon_density) provides the global impurity content figure of merit. The dimensionless impurity fraction relative to electron density is given by xenon_fraction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ionized xenon is present in the plasma.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_xenon_density
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Line-averaged number density of xenon ions along a chord through the plasma, obtained by dividing the path integral of the local xenon ion density by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged xenon ion number density is the chord-path mean of the local [xenon_density](name:xenon_density), which sums all charged xenon ionization states from Xe$^{1+}$ through Xe$^{54+}$, normalized by the measurement chord length through the plasma.

The defining relation is:

$$
\bar{n}_\mathrm{Xe} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_\mathrm{Xe}(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Xe}(\ell)$ is the local xenon ion number density at arc-length position $\ell$ along the chord and $L$ is the total chord length.

This quantity is inferred from line-integrated emission diagnostics sensitive to xenon spectral lines — including soft X-ray arrays and visible-range spectrometers — combined with knowledge of the chord geometry. The [volume_averaged_xenon_density](name:volume_averaged_xenon_density) provides the spatial mean over the full plasma volume, and [xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis) captures the on-axis value. The analogous chord-averaged quantity for argon is documented as [line_averaged_argon_density](name:line_averaged_argon_density).

In trace impurity transport experiments, xenon concentrations yield $\bar{n}_\mathrm{Xe} \sim 10^{14}$–$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$; during disruption-mitigation massive gas injection or shattered-pellet scenarios, values can reach $10^{17}$–$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon ions are present along the measurement chord.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_atomic_number
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Nuclear proton count of the fast ion species detected in charge exchange spectroscopy, uniquely identifying the element independently of its ionization state.
NAMES.long:
The fast ion atomic number $Z_n$ is the number of protons in the nucleus of the energetic (non-thermal) ion species observed via Fast Ion Charge eXchange (FICX) spectroscopy. As an intrinsic nuclear property, $Z_n$ is invariant with respect to ionization state and unambiguously identifies the element: $Z_n = 1$ for hydrogen isotopes (deuterium, tritium), $Z_n = 2$ for helium (alpha particles), $Z_n = 6$ for carbon, and $Z_n = 74$ for tungsten.

This quantity is the fast-ion-population counterpart of [ion_atomic_number](name:ion_atomic_number), which gives the same nuclear property for a general ion species. It is physically distinct from [fast_ion_charge](name:fast_ion_atomic_number), which specifies the ionic charge state $Z_\text{ion}$ — the net charge arising from electron removal — and which can vary for the same element at different ionization conditions. Together with [fast_ion_mass](name:ion_atomic_mass), the atomic number fully characterizes the fast ion species entering the spectral interpretation of FICX emission.

In charge exchange diagnostics, the fast ion species is identified prior to line inversion; $Z_n$ is an integer-valued input parameter rather than a derived measurement, taking values from 1 (hydrogenic fast ions in D-T plasmas) to the atomic number of the heaviest injected impurity species.

NAMES.name: fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless composition fraction of a specified constituent within a neutron detector converter material. The precise basis of the fraction is defined by the more specific child quantity, such as an atomic fraction, rather than being fixed by this parent concept.
NAMES.long:
Fraction of neutron detector converter describes how much of a specified constituent contributes to the total converter material composition. It is a generic dimensionless composition measure: the denominator and numerator may be based on the basis specified by the child standard name, such as atom count for [atomic fraction of neutron detector converter](name:atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter).

A generic composition fraction for constituent $k$ can be written as

$$
f_k = \frac{q_k}{\sum_j q_j}
$$

where $q_k$ is the amount of constituent $k$ measured on the relevant basis, and the sum runs over all constituents included in the converter material on the same basis. For the atomic-fraction child, $q_j$ is an atom count; other specialized children would define a different basis if introduced.

The quantity is used to characterize the material that converts incident neutrons into detectable secondary particles. It is determined from material specification, isotope enrichment data, fabrication records, or compositional analysis methods such as spectroscopy or mass analysis, depending on the required accuracy and the fraction basis.

Typical values lie between 0 and 1. A dominant or enriched neutron-sensitive constituent may have values around 0.5-1, while minor constituents, dopants, residual impurities, or isotopic contaminants may range from less than 1e-6 to 0.1.

NAMES.name: atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Atomic fraction characterizing the composition of a neutron detector converter, the material that transforms incident neutrons into detectable secondary charged particles.
NAMES.long:
A neutron detector converter is a material placed within or adjacent to the active detection medium to transform incident neutrons — electrically neutral particles that interact weakly with most matter — into secondary charged particles (alpha particles, protons, or tritons) that produce measurable ionization or scintillation signals. The compositional fractions of the converter govern the macroscopic neutron absorption cross-section and hence the detection sensitivity for a given neutron energy range.

The most diagnostically specific instance of this quantity is the target atomic fraction, which gives the share of converter atoms that are the reactive nuclei for the neutron-capture or neutron-scattering channel of interest. For boron-based converters this corresponds to the B-10 enrichment fraction; for helium-3 proportional detectors it is the He-3 purity. Converter fractions are dimensionless and bounded between 0 and 1, with values close to unity for highly enriched materials used in high-sensitivity fusion diagnostics.

Converter composition fractions are manufacturing parameters determined from isotopic enrichment specifications and chemical analysis of the converter material. They enter the detector response model alongside the [efficiency_of_neutron_detector](name:efficiency_of_neutron_detector) to relate measured count rates to absolute neutron fluxes during fusion plasma diagnostics.

NAMES.name: target_atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Fraction of all atoms in a neutron detector converter material that are the nuclear target species for the primary neutron-induced detection reaction. It is a dimensionless composition factor that includes stoichiometry and isotopic enrichment.
NAMES.long:
Target atomic fraction of a neutron detector converter is the fraction of all atoms in the converter material that are atoms of the nuclear target species. The target species is the isotope that participates in the primary neutron-induced detection reaction, such as $^6\mathrm{Li}$ in a lithium converter or $^{10}\mathrm{B}$ in a boron converter.

For a representative amount of converter material, the fraction is defined by the atom-count ratio:

$$
f_t = \frac{N_t}{N_\mathrm{tot}}
$$

where $N_t$ is the dimensionless count of target atoms, $N_\mathrm{tot}$ is the dimensionless count of all atoms in the same material amount, and $f_t$ is a dimensionless fraction with unit 1. The admissible range is $0 \le f_t \le 1$.

In practice, this quantity is computed from the converter composition, stoichiometry, and isotopic enrichment, or determined from material assay or manufacturer specifications. It scales the available target atom density and therefore affects the normalized converter response per emitted source neutron represented by [nuclear_rate_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:nuclear_rate_of_neutron_detector_converter); an absolute reaction count rate also depends on neutron fluence or source strength.

Typical values span 0-1. Elemental converter layers enriched in the target isotope can approach 0.9-1, while natural elemental boron has $f_t \approx 0.199$ for $^{10}\mathrm{B}$. In stoichiometric compounds the denominator includes non-target atoms: for fully $^6\mathrm{Li}$ lithium fluoride, $f_t = 0.5$, and for 95% $^6\mathrm{Li}$-enriched lithium fluoride, $f_t \approx 0.475$.

NAMES.name: nuclear_target_atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Fraction of atoms in the neutron detector converter material that belong to the nuclear target species responsible for the primary neutron-induced detection reaction.
NAMES.long:
The nuclear target atomic fraction specifies what proportion of the total atoms present in the neutron detector converter are of the isotopic species that participates in the primary neutron detection reaction (for example, neutron capture or fission). Converter materials exploit specific target nuclei that interact with incident neutrons to produce detectable secondary charged particles; the converter's intrinsic efficiency and absolute response are set directly by how many such target atoms exist within the active volume.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\rm target} = \frac{N_{\rm target}}{N_{\rm total}}
$$

where $N_{\rm target}$ is the number of target nuclear species atoms and $N_{\rm total}$ is the total atom count in the converter.

This fraction enters the calculation of the total reactive nucleus inventory together with the [nuclear number density](name:nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter) and the [converter volume](name:volume_of_neutron_detector_converter), and it scales the [nuclear reaction rate per unit volume](name:nuclear_rate_of_neutron_detector_converter) proportionally. Converters fabricated from isotopically enriched materials have values approaching 1, while natural-abundance converter materials may exhibit significantly lower fractions depending on the isotope's natural abundance. The [normalized atomic count](name:nuclear_target_atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter) provides a complementary dimensionless measure of the reactive nucleus inventory integrated over the full detector assembly.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_argon_density
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Line-averaged number density of argon ions along a chord through the plasma, obtained by dividing the path integral of the local argon ion density by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged argon density is the chord-averaged number density of argon ions along a line of sight through the plasma. The local argon ion density is understood as the sum over argon ionization stages, so the line average represents the effective argon ion content sampled by the chord.

The line average is defined by normalizing the line-integrated density by the chord length through the plasma:

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Ar}} \rangle_L = \frac{1}{L}\int_{\mathrm{chord}} n_{\mathrm{Ar}}(l)\,dl
$$

where $l$ is distance along the chord in meters, $L$ is the chord length through the plasma in meters, and $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}(l)$ is the local argon ion number density in $m^{-3}$. The integral has units of $m^{-2}$, and division by $L$ gives a line-averaged density in $m^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is obtained by first converting calibrated diagnostic signals to an argon density line integral, using the appropriate atomic physics, instrument response, and plasma-parameter modeling for the measurement. Raw brightness, spectral intensity, or other chord-integrated signals are not themselves line-averaged density; they must be interpreted as or transformed into $\int n_{\mathrm{Ar}} dl$ before normalization by the effective chord length.

Typical values are about $10^{14}-10^{16}\ m^{-3}$ for trace argon concentrations, $10^{16}-10^{18}\ m^{-3}$ during deliberate argon seeding or impurity transport studies, and can approach $10^{19}\ m^{-3}$ transiently during strong gas injection or disruption-mitigation scenarios.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_boron_density
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Line-averaged number density of boron ions along a diagnostic chord, obtained by dividing the path integral of the local boron ion density by the chord length. Unless a charge state is specified separately, it represents the sum over boron ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged boron density is the chord average of the local boron ion number density along a specified line of sight. It characterizes the boron impurity content sampled by that chord rather than a local point value. Unless a charge state is specified separately, the local boron density represents the sum over boron ionization states, excluding neutral boron.

For a chord of length $L$, the line average is defined by the path integral of the local boron ion density along arc length $l$:

$$
\bar{n}_B = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_B(l)\,dl
$$

where $\bar{n}_B$ is the line-averaged boron density in m^-3, $n_B(l)$ is the local boron ion density in m^-3, $l$ is distance along the chord in m, and $L$ is the total chord length in m. For charge-state-unresolved measurements, $n_B$ is interpreted as the sum of the densities of the boron ionization states included in the plasma model.

In practice this quantity is inferred from line-integrated spectroscopic information, such as absolutely calibrated boron line emission or charge-exchange recombination signals. The conversion from measured photons to boron density requires geometry, calibration, relevant atomic rate coefficients, local electron temperature and density information, and a collisional-radiative or ionization-balance model; tomographic or forward-modeling methods may be used when spatial variation along the chord is important.

Typical line-averaged boron densities in magnetically confined plasmas are about 10^15-10^18 m^-3, depending on wall conditioning, impurity sources, plasma density, and transport. Values may be lower in clean core plasmas and transiently higher near strong boron sources or during impurity injection.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_carbon_density
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Line-averaged carbon density is the total carbon number density, including neutral carbon through fully stripped C6+, averaged along a diagnostic line of sight. It equals the path integral of the summed local carbon charge-state densities divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged carbon density quantifies the carbon impurity content sampled by a diagnostic chord. It is the chord average of the total local carbon number density, where total carbon includes neutral carbon and all ionization states through fully stripped carbon.

The line average is defined by integrating the charge-state-summed carbon density along the chord:

$$
\bar{n}_C = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L \left[n_{\mathrm{C^0}}(l) + \sum_{q=1}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}(l)\right] \, dl
$$

where $\bar{n}_C$ is the line-averaged carbon density, $L$ is the chord length in meters, $l$ is distance along the line of sight in meters, $n_{\mathrm{C^0}}(l)$ is the local neutral carbon density in m^-3, and $n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}(l)$ is the local density in m^-3 of carbon with charge state $q$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from passive impurity spectroscopy, active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or related line-emission measurements. The inference uses calibrated brightnesses together with viewing geometry, electron density and temperature, charge-state balance, and atomic rate coefficients to estimate the path-integrated total carbon density before division by the chord length.

Typical line-averaged carbon densities are about $10^{17}-10^{18}$ m^-3 in plasmas with carbon plasma-facing components, and can be lower in devices with non-carbon walls or strong impurity screening. The same chord-averaging concept is used for [line_averaged_electron_density](name:line_averaged_electron_density) and impurity analogs such as [line_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density) and [line_averaged_iron_density](name:line_averaged_iron_density); [volume_averaged_carbon_density](name:volume_averaged_carbon_density) is the corresponding volume average of the same total carbon density.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_deuterium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Chord-average of the deuterium ion number density along a diagnostic line of sight, equal to the path integral of the local deuterium density divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged deuterium ion number density gives the mean deuterium particle density along a diagnostic chord through the plasma, providing a chord-path-weighted scalar measure of absolute deuterium content distinct from the isotopic fraction described by [volume_averaged_deuterium_fraction](name:ratio_of_deuterium_density_to_electron_density).

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\bar{n}_D = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_D(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_D(\ell)$ is the local deuterium ion number density in m$^{-3}$ at chord position $\ell$ and $L$ is the total chord length in m.

It is typically inferred from interferometric phase-shift measurements combined with isotope-resolved spectroscopy sensitive to deuterium Balmer emission. It complements the volume-based [volume_averaged_deuterium_density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_density) and analogous chord-averaged fuel densities such as [line_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:line_averaged_hydrogen_density) for protium and [line_averaged_helium_4_density](name:line_averaged_helium_4_density) for helium-4.

Typical values range from $5 \times 10^{18}$ to $5 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in tokamak deuterium plasmas, scaling with the line-averaged electron density and the deuterium fuel fraction of the isotopic mix.
NAMES.sign: Positive when deuterium ions are present in the plasma along the measurement chord.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Chord-averaged number density of the combined deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species. It is the line integral of the local DT density along a diagnostic chord divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged deuterium-tritium density is the chord average of the local number density assigned to the combined DT fuel-ion pseudo-species. The DT pseudo-species represents the deuterium-tritium fuel population as a single effective ion component; when separate deuterium and tritium densities are resolved, the corresponding combined density is commonly formed from their sum.

For a chord $\mathcal{C}$ of length $L$, the line-averaged DT density is defined by

$$
\langle n_{DT} \rangle_{\mathcal{C}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_{\mathcal{C}} n_{DT}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $n_{DT}(\ell)$ is the local combined DT ion number density at path-length position $\ell$ along the chord, and $L=\int_{\mathcal{C}} d\ell$ is the total chord length through the sampled plasma region.

In experiments this quantity is generally inferred rather than measured directly as a species-resolved line integral. Line-integrated electron-density diagnostics provide the total plasma content along the chord, while isotope composition and fuel dilution are constrained using spectroscopy, neutral-particle measurements, neutron emission, charge-exchange measurements, and transport or equilibrium modeling. In simulations it is obtained by integrating the modeled local DT pseudo-species density along the chosen chord.

Typical values in magnetically confined DT plasmas are about $0.1-2 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with lower values in low-density or strongly diluted plasmas and values approaching $2-3 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in high-density reactor-relevant scenarios.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_effective_charge
NAMES.short: Line-averaged effective ion charge Zeff of the plasma, obtained as the chord-path integral of the local effective charge divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged effective charge characterizes the mean impurity content of the plasma as sampled along a diagnostic line of sight. The local [effective charge](name:effective_charge) $Z_\text{eff}$ is defined as $Z_\text{eff} = \sum_i n_i Z_i^2 / n_e$, where $n_i$ is the number density of ion species $i$, $Z_i$ is the integer charge number of species $i$, and $n_e$ is the electron number density; deviations above unity indicate the presence of impurity ions heavier than hydrogen.

The line average integrates the local effective charge along a chord of length $L$:

$$
\langle Z_\text{eff} \rangle_L = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L Z_\text{eff}(l) \, dl
$$

where $l$ is the coordinate along the chord.

This quantity is inferred from visible or near-ultraviolet bremsstrahlung continuum emission along a chord, whose emissivity scales as $\varepsilon \propto n_e^2 Z_\text{eff} T_e^{-1/2}$, where $T_e$ is the electron temperature; combining this signal with a simultaneous line-integrated electron density measurement yields $\langle Z_\text{eff} \rangle_L$ without requiring assumed spatial profile shapes. In a pure deuterium plasma $Z_\text{eff} = 1$; with typical light impurity content in reactor-relevant tokamak operation values of 1.5–3 are common, while heavy impurity seeding scenarios can yield values of 4–6. This chord-averaged quantity complements [volume_averaged_effective_charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge), which weights by the full plasma volume, and differs from [effective_charge_at_limiter](name:effective_charge_at_limiter), which is a boundary-localized evaluation.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any plasma with nonzero electron density, since $Z_\text{eff}$ equals the ratio of the charge-weighted ion density second moment to $n_e$, both of which are positive-definite quantities.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron temperature averaged along a diagnostic chord through the plasma, equal to the path integral of the local electron temperature divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged electron temperature collapses the radial [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature) profile into a single chord-weighted scalar, providing a global measure of plasma electron thermal content that depends on the diagnostic viewing geometry.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle T_e \rangle_L = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L T_e(s) \, ds
$$

where $T_e(s)$ is the local electron temperature at position $s$ along the chord and $L$ is the total chord length.

This quantity is obtained by numerically integrating temperature profile measurements from multi-channel diagnostics such as Thomson scattering or electron cyclotron emission along the chord and normalizing to the chord length. Unlike the [volume_averaged_electron_temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature), it is sensitive to the specific chord geometry rather than reflecting a global plasma volume moment; unlike the [flux_surface_averaged_electron_temperature](name:flux_surface_averaged_electron_temperature), it does not follow flux-surface topology, making its value dependent on the viewing angle and line-of-sight position relative to the plasma cross-section.

Typical values for a core-viewing chord in H-mode tokamak plasmas range from 1-5 keV; edge-chord geometries yield values of 0.1-1 keV.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron population has finite thermal kinetic energy, consistent with temperature being a non-negative measure of the mean thermal energy per particle.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_hydrogen_density
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight average of the hydrogen ion number density over a specified chord through the plasma. It represents the path-length-normalized hydrogen ion content, not neutral hydrogen density and not electron density.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged hydrogen density is the path-length average of the local hydrogen ion number density along a chosen chord through the plasma. Hydrogen density here denotes the density of hydrogen ions, excluding neutral hydrogen atoms and excluding electrons.

For a chord $C$ of averaging length $L$, the line average is defined by

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{H} \rangle_C = \frac{1}{L}\int_C n_\mathrm{H}(l)\,dl
$$

where $n_\mathrm{H}(l)$ is the local hydrogen ion number density at path-length coordinate $l$, and $L = \int_C dl$ is the chord length over which the average is taken.

This quantity is generally inferred from a combination of constraints rather than measured directly by interferometric phase shift alone. Interferometry primarily constrains line-integrated electron density; hydrogen ion density is separated from electron density using quasineutrality together with composition information from spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements, impurity modeling, particle balance, or transport analysis. In a nearly pure singly ionized hydrogen plasma it can be close to the line-averaged electron density, while impurity dilution, multiple ion species, and neutral populations make the hydrogen ion density distinct.

Typical line-averaged hydrogen ion densities in magnetically confined plasmas range from $10^{18}$-$10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, with lower values in weakly fueled or edge-dominated conditions and higher values in high-density core plasmas.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_iron_density
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Chord-average of the iron impurity ion number density, equal to the path integral of the local iron density divided by the chord length, summed over all ionization states.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged iron density $\bar{n}_\mathrm{Fe}$ is the path-length-weighted average of the local iron impurity ion number density along a diagnostic chord, covering all ionization states from singly ionized to fully stripped iron. It provides a spatially integrated measure of iron contamination that is directly accessible to line-integrated spectroscopic diagnostics without requiring tomographic inversion of a local profile.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\bar{n}_\mathrm{Fe} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_\mathrm{Fe}(l) \, dl
$$

where $l$ is the coordinate along the line of sight and $L$ is the total chord length traversing the plasma. This chord average relates directly to the parent local quantity [iron_density](name:iron_density), which gives the volumetric concentration at each spatial point. In contrast, [volume_averaged_iron_density](name:volume_averaged_iron_density) weights contributions by plasma volume element rather than by chord path length.

Iron enters magnetically confined plasmas primarily through sputtering and erosion of plasma-facing components, and elevated concentrations lead to significant radiative power losses. The line-averaged value is inferred from passive spectroscopy of iron line emission in the visible or vacuum ultraviolet range combined with ionization equilibrium modeling, or from impurity charge exchange spectroscopy on selected iron charge states. Typical line-averaged values range from $10^{14}$ to $10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on iron source strength, impurity transport, and plasma conditions. The iron_fraction provides a related dimensionless indicator of iron contamination normalized to electron density, while [line_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density) is a sibling quantity measured by the same chord-averaging technique for a lighter impurity species.
NAMES.sign: Positive when iron ions are present along the measurement chord.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight average of the total ion number density, summed over all ion species, obtained by dividing the path integral of the local ion density by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged total ion density is the chord-mean ion particle concentration measured along a diagnostic line of sight of length $L$. The local total ion density at each point along the chord is the sum of number densities of all ion species present in the plasma, and the line average collapses this spatial profile to a single scalar characterizing the bulk ion inventory of the plasma along that chord.

The defining relation is:

$$
\bar{n}_{i,\text{tot}} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L \sum_s n_s(l) \, dl
$$

where $n_s(l)$ is the local number density of ion species $s$ at path coordinate $l$ (in m), the sum runs over all ion species, and $L$ is the chord length in m.

In practice, far-infrared or microwave multi-chord interferometers measure the line-integrated electron density; the total ion line density is then recovered by applying quasi-neutrality ($\sum_s Z_s n_s \approx n_e$, where $Z_s$ is the charge state of species $s$) together with spectroscopic estimates of impurity content. The result is closely related to, but physically distinct from, the electron line density, differing by the effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ weighting.

Typical values in tokamak discharges span from $\sim 10^{18}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in low-density L-mode operations to $\sim 10^{21}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in high-density or pellet-fueled H-mode plasmas. The companion quantity [volume_averaged_total_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_density) provides a flux-surface rather than chord-based global measure; species-resolved contributions are accessible from names such as [line_averaged_carbon_density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density) and [line_averaged_oxygen_density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density).

NAMES.name: line_averaged_tritium_density
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Tritium ion number density averaged along a measurement chord, computed as the path integral of local tritium density divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged tritium density is the chord average of the local tritium ion number density through a plasma. It gives a path-weighted measure of the tritium fuel-species content along the chosen sight line, without resolving variation along that line.

For a chord parameterized by path length $\ell$, the line average is defined by:

$$
\langle n_T \rangle_L = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_T(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $n_T(\ell)$ is the local tritium ion number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\ell$ is distance along the chord in meters, $L$ is the chord length in meters, and $\langle n_T \rangle_L$ is in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

In practice, this quantity may be obtained by combining line-integrated density information with independent constraints on isotope composition; the diagnostic combination depends on plasma conditions and available measurements. It is conceptually analogous to [line_averaged_electron_density](name:line_averaged_electron_density), but refers only to tritium ions rather than all electrons.

Typical values in deuterium-tritium plasmas are about $0.1-8 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$, depending on total fuel density, tritium fraction, chord geometry, and radial density variation. The value is non-negative and is zero for a chord containing no tritium ions. For related tritium-density measures, compare with [volume_averaged_tritium_density](name:volume_averaged_tritium_density) and [tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis).

NAMES.name: motional_stark_radiance_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Photon radiance of a single identified Stark-split spectral line component from neutral beam atoms moving through the plasma magnetic field, measured per unit area perpendicular to the viewing direction and per unit solid angle integrated over the wavelength interval of that component.
NAMES.long:
The motional Stark effect (MSE) arises when neutral beam atoms injected into the plasma experience a Lorentz electric field due to their motion through the confining magnetic field. This field Stark-splits the beam emission — most commonly the hydrogen or deuterium Balmer-alpha transition — into a multiplet of $\pi$ and $\sigma$ components at characteristic wavelength displacements from the field-free line center. This quantity gives the photon radiance of one identified component of that multiplet, wavelength-integrated over the assigned spectral interval, as defined by the parent concept [radiance_at_spectral_line](name:radiance_at_spectral_line).

The Lorentz electric field driving the Stark splitting is:

$$
\mathbf{E}_L = \mathbf{v}_b \times \mathbf{B}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_b$ is the beam atom velocity vector and $\mathbf{B}$ is the local plasma magnetic field. The magnitude of $\mathbf{E}_L$ sets the wavelength splitting between Stark components, and the intensity ratio between $\pi$ and $\sigma$ components encodes the local magnetic field pitch angle, making per-component radiance the primary observable in MSE-based field reconstruction.

In practice, narrow-band optical filters or polychromators isolate individual $\pi$ or $\sigma$ components along one or more viewing chords intercepting the beam injection volume. The wavelength shift of an identified Stark component from the unperturbed transition is characterized by the [Stark-shifted minus reference wavelength difference](name:difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line). The line-of-sight path integral of the local MSE emissivity yields the related quantity [line_integrated_motional_stark_radiance_at_spectral_line](name:line_integrated_motional_stark_radiance_at_spectral_line), while [motional_stark_radiance](name:motional_stark_radiance_at_spectral_line) captures the aggregate calibrated spectral radiance without resolving individual Stark components.

NAMES.name: total_ion_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Density-weighted effective temperature of the combined thermal ion population at a plasma location, aggregated over all thermal ion species and charge states into a single scalar.
NAMES.long:
The total ion temperature is the single scalar temperature that characterizes the entire thermal ion population at a plasma location by aggregating contributions from every ionic species and charge state through a density weighting. It is the multi-species generalization of [ion_temperature](name:ion_temperature), constructed so that the product with the [total_thermal_ion_density](name:total_thermal_ion_density) recovers the [total_thermal_ion_pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure) through the thermal equation of state.

The defining relation is a density-weighted species average:

$$
T_{i,\text{tot}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s T_s}{\sum_s n_s}
$$

where $s$ runs over all thermal ion species and charge states, $n_s$ is the local number density and $T_s$ is the kinetic temperature of species $s$, both evaluated at the same plasma location.

In practice this quantity is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, which resolves individual species temperatures and densities; the aggregate total follows by density weighting. Typical core values in tokamak plasmas range from 1 to 20 keV. Spatially integrated variants include [line_averaged_total_ion_temperature](name:line_averaged_total_ion_temperature), which averages along a diagnostic chord, and [volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature), which serves as a global ion energy-confinement metric.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any thermalized ion population, as kinetic temperature is an intrinsically non-negative quantity.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_total_ion_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Chord-length average of the total ion temperature along a diagnostic line of sight through the plasma. The local total ion temperature is the density-weighted effective temperature of all thermal ion species and charge states combined.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged total ion temperature is the path integral of the local total ion temperature divided by the chord length through the plasma. It characterizes the ion thermal energy per particle sampled by that line of sight, not a volume-averaged or whole-plasma temperature.

For a chord coordinate $\ell$, the line average is defined by

$$
\langle T_{i,\mathrm{tot}} \rangle_\ell = \frac{1}{L}\int_{\ell_0}^{\ell_1} T_{i,\mathrm{tot}}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\ell$ is distance along the line of sight in meters, $L=\ell_1-\ell_0$ is the averaged chord length in meters, and both $T_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ and $\langle T_{i,\mathrm{tot}} \rangle_\ell$ are in eV. The local total ion temperature is $T_{i,\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_s n_s T_{i,s}/\sum_s n_s$, where $n_s$ is the density in m^-3 and $T_{i,s}$ is the temperature in eV of thermal ion species or charge state $s$. With temperatures expressed in eV, the corresponding ion thermal pressure is $p_i=e\sum_s n_s T_{i,s}=e n_{i,\mathrm{tot}}T_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$, where $e$ is the elementary charge and converts eV per particle to joules per particle.

In practice this quantity may be inferred from line-integrated or chord-sampled ion-temperature diagnostics such as charge-exchange spectroscopy, Doppler broadening measurements, neutron spectroscopy, or model-assisted diagnostic inversions. Diagnostic response, emissivity weighting, and viewing geometry can affect the inferred chord representative value, but the semantic quantity is the chord-length average of the density-weighted total thermal ion temperature.

Physically valid values are non-negative. Typical line-averaged ion temperatures range from about 10-500 eV in cold edge or scrape-off-layer-dominated chords, 500-5000 eV in many auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, and 5000-30000 eV in high-performance or fusion-grade plasmas.

NAMES.name: accumulated_ammonia_count
NAMES.subject: ammonia
NAMES.short: Accumulated ammonia count is the total NH3 injected into the plasma vessel since plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each ammonia molecule contributes 10 equivalent electrons, equal to the total number of electrons in neutral NH3.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated ammonia count is the time-integrated amount of ammonia gas injected into the plasma vessel after plasma breakdown, represented as an equivalent-electron count rather than as a molecule count or particle inventory. For neutral ammonia, each $\mathrm{NH_3}$ molecule contains 10 electrons: 7 from nitrogen and 1 from each of the 3 hydrogen atoms.

The equivalent-electron count is related to the injected molecular amount by:

$$
N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{NH_3}}(t) = 10 \int_{t_\mathrm{bd}}^{t} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{NH_3}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{NH_3}}$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{NH_3}}$ is the ammonia molecular injection rate, and $t_\mathrm{bd}$ is the plasma breakdown time. The factor 10 is stoichiometric and does not imply that the molecule is fully ionized at the point of injection.

In practice, this quantity is computed from calibrated gas-injection valve commands, flow-meter signals, reservoir pressure drops, or gas-box models, with corrections for line conductance, temperature, and valve response where available. It is an injected-source measure and may differ from the number of ammonia-derived particles that enter the confined plasma because of wall retention, dissociation, pumping, and edge neutral transport.

Typical values depend strongly on device size and gas-injection purpose. Small diagnostic or impurity-seeding puffs may correspond to about $10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ equivalent electrons, while larger fueling or disruption-mitigation injections can reach $10^{21}$-$10^{23}$ equivalent electrons.

NAMES.name: accumulated_ammonia_deuterated_count
NAMES.subject: ammonia_deuterated
NAMES.short: Accumulated deuterated ammonia (ND3) introduced after plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each neutral ND3 molecule contributes 10 equivalent electrons: 7 from nitrogen and 1 from each of the three deuterium atoms.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated deuterated ammonia count is the cumulative amount of neutral ND3 gas injected after plasma breakdown, expressed as the number of electrons associated with those neutral molecules in complete ionization accounting. It tracks delivered deuterated-ammonia inventory, not net plasma electron density or electric charge, and is the deuterated-isotopologue counterpart of [accumulated_ammonia_count](name:accumulated_ammonia_count).

The conversion from molecular injection to equivalent-electron count is

$$
N_\mathrm{eq}(t) = 10 \int_{t_\mathrm{bd}}^{t} \Gamma_{\mathrm{ND}_3}(t')\, dt'
$$

where $N_\mathrm{eq}$ is a dimensionless equivalent-electron count, $t_\mathrm{bd}$ is the plasma-breakdown time, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{ND}_3}$ is the neutral ND3 molecular injection rate in molecules per second. The factor 10 is the neutral-molecule electron inventory, $7+1+1+1$, from nitrogen plus three deuterium atoms.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating a calibrated ND3 molecular flow rate, commonly inferred from gas-injection hardware such as mass-flow controllers, pulsed valves, plenum pressure and temperature evolution, and calibrated line conductance. The accumulation starts at breakdown, increases during ND3 delivery, and remains unchanged when no deuterated ammonia is injected.

Typical values are strongly device- and scenario-dependent. Small calibrated impurity puffs may correspond to $10^{18}-10^{21}$ equivalent electrons, routine radiative-seeding injections to $10^{21}-10^{23}$ equivalent electrons, and large cooling or mitigation injections to $10^{23}-10^{25}$ equivalent electrons or higher.

NAMES.name: accumulated_argon_count
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Cumulative count of argon delivered by gas injection since plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron inventory. The count increases by 18 for each argon atom, using the atomic number of argon.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated argon count is the time-integrated amount of argon delivered by gas injection after plasma breakdown, represented as a dimensionless equivalent-electron inventory. It counts injected argon atoms with a weighting equal to the argon atomic number, so one argon atom contributes 18 count units. This is an injected inventory measure, not a measure of free electrons, plasma content, retained argon, or ionization state.

The accumulated count is defined by integrating the argon atom injection rate from breakdown time:

$$
N_{\mathrm{Ar,eq}}(t) = 18 \int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{Ar}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{Ar,eq}}$ is the dimensionless equivalent-electron argon count, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the argon atom injection rate in atoms per second, $t$ is time in seconds, and $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma-breakdown time in seconds. Argon introduced before breakdown belongs to the prefill contribution represented by argon_count, not to this accumulated post-breakdown quantity.

In practice, the injection rate is obtained from calibrated gas-valve systems, reservoir pressure drops, conductance models, or mass-flow measurements, and then integrated from the breakdown reference time. Because this quantity represents delivered gas, it is not decremented by subsequent ionization, radiation, pumping, exhaust, wall retention, or redistribution within the vessel. It is analogous to [accumulated_neon_count](name:accumulated_neon_count) and [accumulated_xenon_count](name:accumulated_xenon_count), with the numerical weighting set by the atomic number of each species, and can contribute to a total injected-particle inventory such as [accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection).

Typical values are about $10^{19}$-$10^{22}$ count units for routine argon puffs or impurity seeding, corresponding to roughly $6 \times 10^{17}$-$6 \times 10^{20}$ argon atoms. Larger disruption-mitigation injections can reach about $10^{22}$-$10^{24}$ count units, depending on the valve system, reservoir pressure, and mitigation strategy.

NAMES.name: accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Cumulative carbon injected by gas injection after plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count with six counts per carbon atom.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated carbon count due to gas injection is the running total of carbon introduced after plasma breakdown by gas injection, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each injected carbon atom contributes 6 to the dimensionless count, corresponding to the atomic number of carbon, so the value is non-negative and increases only when carbon-bearing gas is injected.

The accumulated equivalent-electron count is related to the carbon atom source rate by

$$
N_{C,\mathrm{acc}}(t) = 6 \int_{t_\mathrm{bd}}^{t} \Gamma_{C,\mathrm{gas}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{C,\mathrm{acc}}$ is the accumulated dimensionless equivalent-electron count, $t_\mathrm{bd}$ is the plasma-breakdown time, $t$ and $t'$ are times in seconds, and $\Gamma_{C,\mathrm{gas}}$ is the injected carbon atom rate in atoms per second. The corresponding physical number of injected carbon atoms is $N_{C,\mathrm{acc}}/6$.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating calibrated gas-injection flow rates from breakdown onward, converting molecular flow to carbon atom flow using the gas stoichiometry, and applying the factor of 6. It is the time integral of [carbon_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:carbon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) and excludes the pre-breakdown inventory represented by [carbon_initial_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:carbon_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection).

Typical values are 0 for pulses without deliberate carbon-bearing gas injection and about $10^{18}$-$10^{22}$ for trace or impurity-gas injection cases, depending on injected gas species, calibrated valve throughput, and injection duration.

NAMES.name: accumulated_deuterated_methane_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: deuterated_methane
NAMES.short: Cumulative deuterated methane (CD4) admitted by gas injection after plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each CD4 molecule contributes 10 equivalent electrons: 6 from carbon and 1 from each of the four deuterium atoms.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated deuterated methane count due to gas injection is the time-integrated dose of neutral deuterated methane, $\mathrm{CD}_4$, admitted into the plasma vessel after plasma breakdown, expressed as a dimensionless equivalent-electron count. The factor of 10 comes from the electron content of a neutral $\mathrm{CD}_4$ molecule: 6 electrons from the carbon atom (atomic number $Z = 6$) and 1 from each of the four deuterium atoms (atomic number $Z = 1$). Gas present in the vessel before breakdown, such as prefill gas, is excluded unless it is actively injected during the post-breakdown interval.

The accumulated equivalent-electron count is defined by integrating the molecular injection rate from the breakdown time $t_\mathrm{bd}$ to time $t$:

$$
N_{\mathrm{CD}_4,e}(t) = 10 \int_{t_\mathrm{bd}}^{t} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{CD}_4}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{CD}_4,e}$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $t_\mathrm{bd}$ is the plasma-breakdown time, and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{CD}_4}$ is the neutral $\mathrm{CD}_4$ molecular injection rate in molecules per second. By construction the quantity is non-decreasing in time and resets to zero at each new plasma breakdown, so it tracks the running total over a single discharge. It is the time-accumulated form of deuterated_methane_count_due_to_gas_injection.

In practice this quantity is inferred from calibrated gas-injection diagnostics such as valve flow calibrations, reservoir pressure and temperature evolution (PVT), commanded valve-opening histories, or downstream mass-flow measurements. The measured molecular dose is converted to equivalent electrons by multiplying the number of injected $\mathrm{CD}_4$ molecules by 10. The equivalent-electron convention enables direct comparison and summation across injected species, with the carbon contribution feeding [accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection), the deuterium contribution feeding [deuterium_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:deuterium_count_due_to_gas_injection), and the molecule contributing to [accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection).

Molecular injection rates for gas-injection valves typically span $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ molecules per second during active puffing. Integrated over a discharge, accumulated values range from about $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ equivalent electrons for small diagnostic or impurity-seeding puffs, rising to $10^{21}$-$10^{23}$ equivalent electrons for larger cumulative doses.

NAMES.name: accumulated_ethane_count
NAMES.subject: ethane
NAMES.short: Cumulative ethane (C2H6) gas injection since plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count where each ethane molecule contributes 18 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated ethane count tracks the time-integrated amount of ethane (C2H6) gas injected into the plasma vessel since plasma breakdown, expressed as a dimensionless equivalent-electron count. Each ethane molecule consists of two carbon atoms (atomic number $Z_C = 6$) and six hydrogen atoms (atomic number $Z_H = 1$), contributing $2 \times 6 + 6 \times 1 = 18$ equivalent electrons per molecule, so the accumulated count $N_{\rm acc}$ and the total number of injected molecules $N_{\rm mol}$ are related by:

$$
N_{\rm acc} = 18 \, N_{\rm mol}
$$

where $N_{\rm mol}$ is the number of ethane molecules delivered since plasma breakdown.

The accumulated count is obtained by integrating the instantaneous ethane injection rate from the moment of plasma breakdown. It provides a direct measure of the combined carbon and hydrogen impurity load introduced via ethane injection over the discharge. This quantity complements [ethane_prefill_count](name:ethane_prefill_count), which covers only the prefill phase preceding breakdown. Related hydrocarbon injection counts include [accumulated_propane_count](name:accumulated_propane_count) (C3H8, 26 electrons per molecule) and [ethylene_count](name:accumulated_ethylene_count) (C2H4, 16 electrons per molecule).
NAMES.sign: Positive when ethane gas is injected into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: accumulated_helium_3_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Time-integrated helium-3 inventory added by gas injection since plasma breakdown, represented as an equivalent-electron count. Each helium-3 atom contributes 2 equivalent electrons because its atomic number is Z = 2.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated helium-3 count due to gas injection is the total amount of helium-3 introduced after plasma breakdown by gas injection, expressed as a dimensionless equivalent-electron count. The equivalent-electron convention weights each neutral helium-3 atom by its atomic number, so one injected helium-3 atom contributes two counts.

The accumulated equivalent-electron count is defined from the injected helium-3 atomic source rate:

$$
N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{^{3}\mathrm{He}}(t) = 2 \int_{t_\mathrm{bd}}^{t} \Gamma_{^{3}\mathrm{He}}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{^{3}\mathrm{He}}$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $t_\mathrm{bd}$ is the plasma-breakdown time, and $\Gamma_{^{3}\mathrm{He}}$ is the helium-3 atom injection rate in atoms/s. The factor 2 is the helium atomic number and converts atoms to equivalent electrons.

In practice this quantity is computed from calibrated gas-injection measurements such as valve flow calibrations, pressure-volume-temperature accounting, or mass-flow controller signals, with isotope-specific calibration for helium-3 when available. It represents gas injected after breakdown and is distinct from any prefill inventory present before the plasma is formed.

Typical accumulated values are about $10^{18}-10^{21}$ equivalent electrons for trace or minority helium-3 puffs, and can reach $10^{22}-10^{23}$ equivalent electrons in large devices or long pulses with deliberate helium-3 fueling.

NAMES.name: accumulated_helium_3_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Cumulative number of helium-3 atoms introduced by gas injection during the prefill phase, reported as an equivalent electron count. Each helium-3 atom contributes two equivalent electrons because its atomic number is 2.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated helium-3 prefill count due to gas injection is the total amount of helium-3 admitted by gas valves before plasma breakdown, reported as an electron-equivalent particle count. It is an accounting convention for particle inventory: each neutral helium-3 atom contributes two equivalent electrons, but the gas need not be ionized during the prefill phase.

The electron-equivalent prefill count is obtained by integrating the helium-3 atomic injection rate over the prefill interval:

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq,prefill}}(^{3}\mathrm{He}) = 2 \int_{t_{\mathrm{start}}}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}} \dot{N}_{^{3}\mathrm{He}}(t)\,dt
$$

where $\dot{N}_{^{3}\mathrm{He}}(t)$ is the helium-3 atomic injection rate in atoms s$^{-1}$, $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ is the start time of helium-3 prefill, $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the breakdown time or end of the prefill phase in seconds, and the factor 2 converts atoms to equivalent electrons. The resulting count is dimensionless.

In practice this quantity is inferred from calibrated gas-valve flow, reservoir depletion, pressure-rise measurements, or gas-balance analysis integrated over the prefill interval. It counts the amount introduced by injection, not the amount retained in the vessel after pumping, wall adsorption, or ionization. It is closely related to [helium_3_initial_count](name:accumulated_helium_3_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection), is the prefill contribution to [accumulated_helium_3_count](name:accumulated_helium_3_count_due_to_gas_injection), and is the helium-3 counterpart of [accumulated_helium_4_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection).

Typical values are $10^{19}$-$10^{22}$ equivalent electrons for small to medium devices and can approach $10^{23}$ equivalent electrons in large-volume machines or high-minority-fraction helium-3 prefills. These counts correspond to half as many injected helium-3 atoms and are often chosen to set the initial minority concentration for ion-cyclotron-resonance-heating scenarios.

NAMES.name: accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Time-integrated count of helium-4 atoms from gas injection accumulated since plasma breakdown, expressed in equivalent electrons, where each helium-4 atom contributes 2 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated helium-4 gas injection count is the time-integrated total of helium-4 delivered via gas injection over the full discharge, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Unlike the phase-restricted quantity [accumulated_helium_4_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection), this quantity accumulates contributions from all injection phases — prefill, flat-top fueling, and ramp-down — and represents the total helium-4 gas throughput for the entire pulse, making it the discharge-level integral of helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection.

The cumulative count is defined as:

$$
N_\text{acc}(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{He}_4}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He}_4}$ is the instantaneous equivalent-electron injection rate and $t_0$ marks plasma breakdown. Since helium-4 has atomic number $Z = 2$, each atom contributes 2 equivalent electrons; the atomic particle count is therefore this value divided by 2. This equivalent-electron convention is shared across the gas-injection count family, including [accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection) and [accumulated_argon_count](name:accumulated_argon_count), enabling uniform cross-species fueling accounting.

The accumulated count is obtained by integrating calibrated gas-valve flow signals over time and is used for helium inventory management, fueling budget analysis, and helium-ash simulation studies.
NAMES.sign: Positive when helium-4 is injected into the plasma vessel, increasing the accumulated equivalent-electron count.

NAMES.name: accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Cumulative count of hydrogen atoms delivered by gas injection after plasma breakdown, expressed in equivalent electrons; hydrogen's atomic number Z = 1 means each atom contributes one equivalent electron.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated hydrogen count due to gas injection is the time-integrated number of hydrogen atoms introduced into the plasma vessel by gas injection systems after plasma breakdown. Because hydrogen has atomic number $Z_H = 1$, the equivalent-electron count equals the atom count directly, unlike heavier species such as the analogous [accumulated carbon count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection), which multiplies by $Z = 6$.

The defining relation for equivalent-electron counting is:

$$
N_\mathrm{eq} = Z \cdot N_\mathrm{atoms}
$$

where $N_\mathrm{atoms}$ is the number of injected atoms of the species and $Z$ is its atomic number. For hydrogen, $Z_H = 1$, so $N_\mathrm{eq} = N_\mathrm{atoms}$.

This quantity is obtained by integrating the gas valve flow rate over time from plasma breakdown onward. The [accumulated hydrogen prefill count](name:accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count) records the hydrogen contributed during the pre-breakdown prefill phase; the two together account for the full hydrogen gas inventory. Analogous counts for other injected species — such as [accumulated nitrogen count](name:accumulated_nitrogen_count) and [deuterium count due to gas injection](name:deuterium_count_due_to_gas_injection) — follow the same equivalent-electron convention, scaled by the respective atomic number.
NAMES.sign: Positive when hydrogen atoms have been injected after plasma breakdown.

NAMES.name: accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Cumulative count of hydrogen atoms introduced by gas injection during the plasma prefill phase prior to breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count with one count per hydrogen atom.
NAMES.long:
The prefill phase occurs before plasma breakdown, during which hydrogen gas is introduced into the vacuum vessel to establish the initial neutral density required for plasma initiation. This quantity accumulates the total hydrogen gas inventory across the entire prefill phase, with each hydrogen atom contributing one unit to the count, consistent with hydrogen's atomic number $Z_H = 1$.

The equivalent-electron convention expresses multi-species gas inventories on a common dimensionless scale by weighting each injected atom's contribution by its atomic number $Z$:

$$
N_{\rm eq} = Z \cdot N_{\rm atoms}
$$

where $N_{\rm atoms}$ is the total number of injected atoms over the prefill interval. For hydrogen ($Z_H = 1$), the equivalent-electron count equals the raw atom count. This convention enables direct comparison across prefill species: for example, [accumulated helium-4 prefill count](name:accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection) weights each helium-4 atom by $Z = 2$, while [accumulated lithium prefill count](name:accumulated_lithium_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection) uses $Z = 3$.

The quantity is inferred from upstream pressure sensors and calibrated valve conductance integrated over the prefill interval, or from mass-flow controllers. The post-breakdown hydrogen inventory is tracked separately by [accumulated hydrogen count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection), which resets at plasma breakdown.
NAMES.sign: Positive when hydrogen gas flows into the vacuum vessel during the prefill phase, incrementing the accumulated atom count.

NAMES.name: accumulated_krypton_count
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Cumulative number of krypton atoms injected into the machine since plasma breakdown, expressed in equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated krypton count is the running total of krypton atoms introduced since plasma breakdown, converted to an electron-equivalent basis where each krypton atom contributes $Z_{\rm Kr} = 36$ electron equivalents when fully stripped of its bound electrons.

The quantity is obtained by integrating the instantaneous injection rate $\dot{N}_{\rm Kr}$ over time from the moment of plasma breakdown $t_0$:

$$
N_{\rm Kr,eq} = Z_{\rm Kr} \int_{t_0}^{t} \dot{N}_{\rm Kr}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $Z_{\rm Kr} = 36$ is the atomic number of krypton and $\dot{N}_{\rm Kr}$ is in atoms per second. This is distinct from the prefill-phase contribution captured by [krypton_prefill_count](name:krypton_prefill_count), which records only the gas load introduced before breakdown.
