Krypton serves as a heavy radiative seed impurity for power exhaust management and as a disruption mitigation agent; the cumulative injection inventory is therefore essential for interpreting bolometric radiated-power fractions and spectroscopic charge-state distributions throughout the discharge. Analogous running totals are defined for other injected species, including [accumulated_neon_count](name:accumulated_neon_count) and [accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection).
NAMES.sign: Positive when krypton has been cumulatively injected into the plasma since breakdown.

NAMES.name: accumulated_lithium_count
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Cumulative amount of lithium supplied by gas injection after plasma breakdown, reported as an equivalent-electron count. Each lithium atom contributes 3 equivalent electrons, so the value is three times the injected lithium atom count over the post-breakdown interval.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated lithium count is the cumulative lithium supplied by gas injection after plasma breakdown, converted to an equivalent-electron count using the lithium atomic number 3. It excludes lithium present before breakdown or introduced by other sources unless those sources are part of the gas-injection flow being integrated. The corresponding accumulated lithium atom count, comparable to lithium_count when that quantity represents an inventory or prefill amount, is one third of this value.

The accumulated equivalent-electron count at time $t$ is defined by integrating the lithium atom injection rate from breakdown to that time:

$$
N_{\mathrm{Li,eqe}}(t) = 3 \int_{t_\mathrm{bd}}^{t} \Gamma_{\mathrm{Li}}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{Li,eqe}}$ is the accumulated lithium count expressed as equivalent electrons, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{Li}}$ is the neutral lithium atom flow rate delivered by gas injection in atoms/s, $t'$ is the integration time in seconds, $t_\mathrm{bd}$ is the plasma-breakdown time, and the factor 3 is the atomic number of lithium.

In practice this quantity is computed by time-integrating calibrated gas-injection throughput, valve-command, pressure-drop, or mass-flow measurements after conversion to a lithium atom flow rate. Corrections may account for valve response, conductance of the injection line, reservoir temperature, and uncertainty in the fraction of commanded material that enters the plasma chamber.

Typical values depend strongly on device size and seeding scenario. Small experiments may accumulate about $10^{17}-10^{19}$ lithium atoms, corresponding to $3 \times 10^{17}-3 \times 10^{19}$ equivalent electrons, while deliberate injection in medium or large tokamak discharges can reach about $10^{19}-10^{21}$ lithium atoms, corresponding to $3 \times 10^{19}-3 \times 10^{21}$ equivalent electrons.

NAMES.name: accumulated_lithium_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Accumulated count of lithium introduced by gas injection during the prefill phase, expressed as a dimensionless equivalent-electron count. Each lithium atom contributes three count units from its atomic number.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated lithium prefill count is the total lithium delivered by gas injection before plasma breakdown, converted to an equivalent-electron bookkeeping count. It includes only the prefill interval and is distinct from the post-breakdown accumulated lithium inventory represented by [accumulated_lithium_count](name:accumulated_lithium_count).

The count is defined by integrating the lithium atom injection rate over the prefill window:

$$
N_{\mathrm{Li,eq}} = 3 \int_{t_{\mathrm{start}}}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}} \frac{dN_{\mathrm{Li}}}{dt} \, dt
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{Li,eq}}$ is the dimensionless equivalent-electron count, $dN_{\mathrm{Li}}/dt$ is the lithium atom injection rate in atoms per second, $N_{\mathrm{Li}}$ counts lithium atoms rather than equivalent electrons, $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ is the start of the prefill interval, and $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the time of plasma breakdown. The factor 3 is lithium's atomic number, so one injected lithium atom contributes three equivalent-electron count units. For non-negative flow rates and $t_{\mathrm{bd}} \ge t_{\mathrm{start}}$, the accumulated count is non-negative.

In practice, the prefill inventory is inferred from calibrated gas-injection flow measurements, reservoir conditions, valve timing, or particle-throughput calibrations integrated over the pre-breakdown interval. The same equivalent-electron convention is used for related prefill species inventories such as [accumulated_helium_4_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection), [accumulated_helium_3_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_helium_3_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection), and [accumulated_oxygen_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_oxygen_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection).

Typical values for lithium prefill are often about 10^16-10^21 in dimensionless equivalent-electron count, depending on the gas-injection system, valve duration, requested conditioning dose, and discharge preparation scenario.

NAMES.name: accumulated_methane_carbon_13_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: methane_carbon_13
NAMES.short: Cumulative equivalent-electron count for carbon-13-labeled methane injected after plasma breakdown. Each 13CH4 molecule contributes 10 equivalent electrons, using atomic number 6 for carbon and 1 for each of the four hydrogen atoms.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated carbon-13 methane count due to gas injection is the running equivalent-electron count associated with neutral ${}^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4$ molecules admitted after plasma breakdown. The carbon isotope label identifies the injected tracer species, while the electron-budget conversion is the same as for ordinary methane because ${}^{12}\mathrm{C}$ and ${}^{13}\mathrm{C}$ have the same nuclear charge. The accumulation starts from zero at plasma breakdown and remains constant during intervals with no ${}^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4$ injection.

The accumulation at time $t$ is defined from the molecular injection rate by:

$$
N_\mathrm{acc}(t) = 10 \int_{t_\mathrm{bd}}^{t} \dot{n}_{{}^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $N_\mathrm{acc}$ is the dimensionless equivalent-electron count, $t_\mathrm{bd}$ is the plasma-breakdown time in seconds, $t$ and $t'$ are times in seconds, and $\dot{n}_{{}^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4}$ is the calibrated molecular injection rate in molecules per second. The factor $10 = Z_\mathrm{C} + 4 Z_\mathrm{H}$ uses $Z_\mathrm{C}=6$ for carbon and $Z_\mathrm{H}=1$ for each hydrogen atom.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating calibrated gas-valve or mass-flow measurements over the discharge, with corrections for valve conductance, reservoir pressure, gas temperature, and isotopic purity when needed. It is an isotope-resolved component of [accumulated_gas_count](name:accumulated_methane_carbon_13_count_due_to_gas_injection) and is directly comparable with accumulated_methane_count_due_to_gas_injection, [accumulated_deuterated_methane_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_deuterated_methane_count_due_to_gas_injection), [accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection), and [accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection) in particle and wall-retention accounting.

Typical accumulated values for small ${}^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4$ tracer puffs are $10^{17}$-$10^{20}$ equivalent electrons per discharge. Larger calibration, fueling, or wall-conditioning injections can reach $10^{20}$-$10^{22}$ equivalent electrons; the corresponding number of injected ${}^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4$ molecules is one tenth of the equivalent-electron count.

NAMES.name: accumulated_neon_count
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Cumulative number of neon atoms from gas injection accumulated since plasma breakdown, expressed in equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated neon count is the running temporal integral of the neon gas injection rate from plasma breakdown onward, giving the total neon inventory delivered to the plasma vessel over the discharge. Each injected neon atom contributes to the tally in equivalent-electron units — the raw particle count scaled by the neon atomic number $Z_\mathrm{Ne} = 10$ — enabling direct comparison with other injected fuel and impurity species.

The defining integral is:

$$
N_\mathrm{acc}(t) = Z_\mathrm{Ne} \int_{t_0}^{t} \dot{n}_\mathrm{Ne}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $\dot{n}_\mathrm{Ne}$ is the instantaneous neon injection rate in atoms per second, $t_0$ is the time of plasma breakdown, and $Z_\mathrm{Ne} = 10$ is the neon atomic number.

This quantity is determined from calibrated gas valve flow measurements integrated temporally throughout the discharge. It is particularly relevant in impurity seeding and disruption mitigation experiments where the cumulative neon dose governs radiated power fractions and pedestal stability.

The parent neon_count provides phase-specific or instantaneous counts; [neon_prefill_count](name:neon_prefill_count) covers the pre-breakdown injection phase exclusively. Analogous accumulated quantities for other injected species include [accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection) and [accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection).
NAMES.sign: Positive when neon gas is injected, so the accumulated count increases monotonically from zero at plasma breakdown.

NAMES.name: accumulated_nitrogen_count
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Cumulative nitrogen gas injection since plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count where each nitrogen atom contributes 7 equivalent electrons equal to its atomic number.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated nitrogen count tracks the total nitrogen atoms delivered by gas injection from plasma breakdown onward, weighted by the atomic number of nitrogen ($Z_N = 7$) to produce a dimensionless equivalent-electron count. This convention reflects the electron inventory that would result from complete ionization of all injected nitrogen and places different injected species on a common quantitative footing shared across the gas-injection monitoring family.

The count is defined as:

$$
C_N = Z_N \, N_N = 7 \, N_N
$$

where $N_N$ is the cumulative number of nitrogen atoms delivered since plasma breakdown and $Z_N = 7$ is the atomic number of nitrogen. The count integrates contributions from each gas valve pulse throughout the discharge and increases monotonically from breakdown.

Nitrogen is regularly injected in fusion devices for divertor detachment seeding, radiative power dissipation, and disruption mitigation. The equivalent-electron count is inferred from gas valve actuation signals integrated against calibrated throughput curves from the moment of plasma breakdown. Typical values span from $10^{20}$ equivalent electrons for trace impurity seeding to $10^{24}$ in massive gas injection scenarios. The analogous count for argon is provided by [accumulated_argon_count](name:accumulated_argon_count) using $Z = 18$, the hydrogen reference uses $Z = 1$ per atom in [accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection), and the prefill-only nitrogen inventory is tracked separately by [nitrogen_prefill_count](name:nitrogen_prefill_count).
NAMES.sign: Positive when nitrogen atoms have been cumulatively injected into the plasma vessel after plasma breakdown onset.

NAMES.name: accumulated_oxygen_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Cumulative post-breakdown oxygen delivered by gas injection, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each oxygen atom contributes 8 counts, so the value is 8 times the injected oxygen atom inventory.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated oxygen count due to gas injection is the cumulative amount of oxygen introduced after plasma breakdown, expressed in equivalent electrons rather than oxygen atoms. It provides a charge-normalized impurity inventory: one oxygen atom contributes 8 counts because the atomic number of oxygen is 8.

The equivalent-electron count $N_\mathrm{eq}$ is defined from the injected oxygen atom inventory $N_\mathrm{O}$ by:

$$
N_\mathrm{eq} = Z_\mathrm{O} N_\mathrm{O}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{O}=8$ is the atomic number of oxygen and $N_\mathrm{O}$ is the cumulative number of oxygen atoms injected after plasma breakdown.

In practice, the quantity is computed from calibrated gas-injection flow rates integrated over time, with molecular composition accounted for when oxygen is injected as $\mathrm{O}_2$ or in another oxygen-bearing gas. The accumulation starts from zero at breakdown and increases as additional oxygen is delivered; it excludes oxygen present in the prefill inventory. The simpler [oxygen_count](name:accumulated_oxygen_count_due_to_gas_injection) denotes an oxygen gas count in the same equivalent-electron representation, while [accumulated_oxygen_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_oxygen_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection) refers to the corresponding pre-breakdown contribution.

Typical accumulated values range from about $10^{18}-10^{22}$ equivalent-electron counts for small impurity puffs to stronger radiative seeding phases, with larger values possible in long pulses or large devices.

NAMES.name: accumulated_oxygen_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Cumulative oxygen gas introduced during the prefill phase by gas injection, expressed as an equivalent-electron count where each oxygen atom contributes 8 count units equal to its atomic number.
NAMES.long:
The prefill phase precedes plasma breakdown, during which controlled gas injection establishes an initial neutral gas background in the vessel. This quantity accumulates the total oxygen inventory delivered during that phase, representing each oxygen atom as 8 equivalent electrons equal to the atomic number $Z_\mathrm{O} = 8$.

The equivalent-electron inventory is defined as:

$$
N_\mathrm{eq} = Z_\mathrm{O} \cdot N_\mathrm{O}
$$

where $N_\mathrm{O}$ is the total number of oxygen atoms injected during the prefill interval and $Z_\mathrm{O} = 8$ is the atomic number of oxygen.

The count is inferred from calibrated gas injection valve records integrated over the prefill interval, from the start of the prefill phase through plasma breakdown. It is the accumulated component of oxygen_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection and follows the same equivalent-electron convention applied to helium-3 in [accumulated_helium_3_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_helium_3_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection) and to lithium in [accumulated_lithium_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_lithium_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection). Post-breakdown oxygen injection is tracked separately by [oxygen_count](name:accumulated_oxygen_count_due_to_gas_injection).

NAMES.name: accumulated_particle_count_at_pellet_path_due_to_pellet_injection
NAMES.short: Cumulative number of particles ablated from an injected pellet between the pellet-path entry point and a specified position along its trajectory. It is a nondecreasing count representing the integrated release of pellet material along the path.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated particle count at a pellet path is the total number of pellet-material particles released by ablation from the path entry point up to a specified position on the trajectory. It starts near zero at entry and increases as material is released, reaching the ablated inventory for that pellet at the stopping point or final tracked position.

The path coordinate $s$ is arc length measured in meters from the pellet-path entry point, with $s=0$ at entry and increasing in the direction of pellet motion. The accumulated count is the line integral of the particle-count gradient along the path:

$$
N_\mathrm{abl}(s) = \int_0^s \Gamma_N(s') \, ds'
$$

where $N_\mathrm{abl}$ is the dimensionless particle count, $\Gamma_N=dN_\mathrm{abl}/ds$ is the number of ablated particles per unit path length with unit m^-1, and $s'$ is arc length in meters. If an ablation model provides a time rate $\dot{N}$ in s^-1, the corresponding path gradient is $\Gamma_N=\dot{N}/v_\mathrm{pel}$ for pellet speed $v_\mathrm{pel}$ in m s^-1.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by tracking the pellet trajectory and integrating a local ablation source that depends on pellet composition, size, speed, and local plasma conditions such as temperature and density. It can also be constrained experimentally using combinations of fast imaging, spectroscopy, interferometry, and particle inventory balance. The closely related [accumulated_particle_count_of_pellet_path](name:accumulated_particle_count_at_pellet_path_due_to_pellet_injection) denotes the same cumulative-count concept for the pellet path.

Typical final accumulated counts range from about $10^{17}$-$10^{20}$ particles for small diagnostic or shallow fueling pellets, $10^{20}$-$10^{22}$ particles for routine fueling pellets, and up to about $10^{23}$ particles for large or shattered pellets used for rapid fueling or mitigation.

NAMES.name: accumulated_particle_gas_count_at_inlet_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Cumulative count of neutral gas particles delivered through a specified gas injection inlet since plasma breakdown. It resets for each new breakdown event and increases as calibrated gas throughput is injected.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the accumulated number of neutral gas particles delivered through one gas injection inlet during a discharge, counted from the plasma breakdown event. It is a dimensionless particle count: the unit is 1 because it counts particles rather than measuring a dimensional amount. The value resets at each new breakdown event and is normally nondecreasing while gas is injected through that inlet.

The accumulated inlet count is the time integral of the instantaneous particle delivery rate through the same inlet:

$$
N_\mathrm{inlet}(t) = \int_{t_\mathrm{bd}}^{t} \dot{N}_\mathrm{inlet}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $N_\mathrm{inlet}(t)$ is the accumulated particle count, $t_\mathrm{bd}$ is the breakdown time, and $\dot{N}_\mathrm{inlet}$ is the instantaneous neutral-particle delivery rate through the inlet.

In practice, the count is computed from gas-valve commands, calibrated valve flow curves, plenum or upstream pressure measurements, gas species, temperature assumptions, and conductance models that convert throughput to particle rate. Summing corresponding inlet quantities gives location-group totals such as lower, upper, or midplane gas injection totals, and summing over all gas injection inlets gives the total accumulated gas particle count for the discharge.

Typical accumulated values for a single inlet are about $10^{19}$-$10^{23}$ particles per discharge, depending on pulse length, valve size, gas species, fueling scenario, and whether the inlet is used for small prefill/puffing corrections or sustained density control.

NAMES.name: accumulated_propane_count
NAMES.subject: propane
NAMES.short: Accumulated propane count is the time-integrated amount of injected propane after plasma breakdown, converted to the number of electrons contained in the corresponding neutral propane molecules. One propane molecule contributes 26 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated propane count is the cumulative amount of propane gas injected after plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. It is an atomic-accounting quantity: a neutral propane molecule, $\mathrm{C_3H_8}$, contains 26 electrons, so the value is 26 times the number of injected propane molecules rather than a direct measurement of plasma electrons.

The count at time $t$ can be defined from the molecular injection rate:

$$
N_{\mathrm{C_3H_8,eq}}(t) = 26 \int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t} \Phi_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{C_3H_8,eq}}$ is dimensionless, $\Phi_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}$ is the propane molecular flow rate in molecules s$^{-1}$, $t$, $t'$, and the breakdown time $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ are in seconds, and $26 = 3\times6 + 8\times1$ is the number of bound electrons in one neutral propane molecule.

In practice, the value is computed by integrating a calibrated propane flow over the interval beginning at plasma breakdown. If the available flow is molar, in mol s$^{-1}$, it is first multiplied by Avogadro's constant to obtain molecules s$^{-1}$; if it is given as a gas throughput or volume flow, it is converted to molecule rate using the relevant gas calibration before applying the electron-count conversion. The quantity complements [propane_prefill_count](name:propane_prefill_count) for pre-breakdown inventory and is analogous to [accumulated_ethane_count](name:accumulated_ethane_count) for another hydrocarbon species.

Typical values are 0 when no propane is injected, about $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ for small trace or impurity-seeding puffs, and up to $10^{22}$-$10^{23}$ for larger or longer injections. These values represent injected inventory; they do not by themselves specify the retained amount, ionization fraction, or resulting plasma electron density.

NAMES.name: accumulated_silane_count
NAMES.subject: silane
NAMES.short: Accumulated silane gas injection since plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated silane count is the time-integrated amount of silane, SiH4, injected into the plasma after breakdown. The count is dimensionless and uses an equivalent-electron convention: one SiH4 molecule corresponds to 18 equivalent electrons, from silicon with atomic number 14 and four hydrogen atoms with atomic number 1.

The accumulated count at time $t$ is defined from the silane source rate by

$$
N_{\mathrm{SiH_4,acc}}(t) = \int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH_4,eq}}(t')\,dt' = 18\int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH_4,mol}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{SiH_4,acc}}$ is the accumulated dimensionless equivalent-electron count, $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma-breakdown time in seconds, $t'$ is time in seconds, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH_4,eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron source rate in s^-1, and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH_4,mol}}$ is the molecular silane injection rate in molecules per second. The factor 18 is a counting convention for the injected molecular species, not a statement that neutral SiH4 supplies free electrons before dissociation or ionization.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating the calibrated [silane source rate](name:silane_source_rate) from plasma breakdown onward. Gas present as vessel prefill or static inventory before breakdown is excluded; only deliberately injected silane during the plasma discharge contributes.

Typical values are 0 for discharges without silane injection. When silane is deliberately puffed for wall conditioning or impurity seeding, accumulated values are often about 10^18-10^22 in the dimensionless equivalent-electron count, depending on pulse duration, valve calibration, and injection recipe.

NAMES.name: accumulated_total_gas_count_at_midplane_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Cumulative total number of gas particles injected from all valves located near the equatorial midplane since plasma breakdown.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the running total of gas particles delivered from all injection valves positioned near the equatorial midplane, accumulated from the moment of plasma breakdown onward. It aggregates contributions from all midplane valves regardless of injected species or individual valve identity, providing a single integrated measure of total midplane fueling inventory over the course of a discharge.

The accumulated count $N_\text{mid}$ is obtained by integrating the total midplane injection rate $\dot{N}_\text{mid}(t')$ over time:

$$
N_\text{mid}(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} \dot{N}_\text{mid}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $t_0$ is the time of plasma breakdown and $\dot{N}_\text{mid}$ is the combined instantaneous particle flux from all midplane gas injection valves.

The count is derived from gas injection valve diagnostics — flow meters or pressure gages calibrated in particles per unit time — integrated from plasma breakdown. This midplane-specific total complements the spatially resolved siblings accumulated_total_lower_gas_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection and accumulated_total_upper_gas_particle_count_at_inlet_due_to_gas_injection, which distinguish upper and lower valve groups. For the machine-wide total across all injection positions, see [accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection).

NAMES.name: accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Cumulative number of particles delivered by gas injection since plasma breakdown, summed over all injected species and converted to an equivalent-electron count. The count resets at each new plasma breakdown event and is non-decreasing within a discharge while injection continues.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated total particle count due to gas injection is the time-integrated amount of neutral gas delivered after plasma breakdown, summed over all injection systems and injected species. Each species is weighted by the number of electrons carried by one neutral injected particle when fully ionized, so the result is a dimensionless equivalent-electron count rather than a molecule count alone. The accumulator is reset to zero at each new plasma breakdown event.

The accumulated count can be written as the species-weighted time integral of the injection rates:

$$
N_{\mathrm{tot}}(t) = \sum_s Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}} \int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t} \Gamma_s(t') \, dt'
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the dimensionless equivalent-electron count, $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma-breakdown time, $\Gamma_s$ is the neutral-particle injection rate of species $s$ in $s^{-1}$, and $Z_s^{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the number of bound electrons in one neutral injected particle of species $s$ when fully ionized. With non-negative injection rates the value is monotonic between resets and remains constant between gas pulses.

In practice, this quantity is computed by integrating calibrated gas-valve throughput, flow-meter measurements, or reconstructed injected particle rates over time, then applying the species weights before summing. It uses the same equivalent-electron normalization as [accumulated_total_gas_count](name:accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection), while specifically identifying the contribution from gas injection. If injector groups are reported separately, accumulated_total_lower_gas_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection and accumulated_total_upper_gas_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection are partial sums whose total equals the vessel-wide value when the partition covers all gas injectors.

Typical accumulated values are $10^{20}$-$10^{23}$ equivalent electrons for small or short-pulse experiments and $10^{22}$-$10^{25}$ equivalent electrons for larger tokamak discharges, depending on fueling rate, pulse duration, gas species, and whether large pre-programmed gas puffs are included. Short diagnostic or impurity puffs can contribute smaller increments, often $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ equivalent electrons.

NAMES.name: accumulated_tritium_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Cumulative number of tritium atoms delivered by gas injection since plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count where each tritium atom corresponds to one equivalent electron.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated tritium count due to gas injection is the running total of tritium ($^3\mathrm{H}$) atoms introduced to the plasma vessel through gas injection valves, accumulated continuously from plasma breakdown onward. The quantity is dimensionless, representing each injected atom as an equivalent-electron contribution scaled by its atomic number.

For tritium, whose atomic number is $Z = 1$, the equivalent-electron inventory equals the raw atom count directly:

$$
N_\mathrm{eq} = Z \cdot N_\mathrm{atoms} = N_\mathrm{atoms}
$$

where $N_\mathrm{atoms}$ is the total number of tritium atoms injected after breakdown. The equivalent-electron convention provides a species-independent basis for comparing injected particle inventories — for higher-$Z$ species such as argon ($Z = 18$), the multiplier is correspondingly larger.

This is the time-integrated form of tritium_count_due_to_gas_injection, accumulating monotonically as gas is puffed after breakdown. Tritium introduced before breakdown is tracked separately as [tritium_prefill_count](name:tritium_prefill_count). The deuterium analog in the same equivalent-electron framework is [deuterium_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:deuterium_count_due_to_gas_injection).

NAMES.name: accumulated_xenon_count
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Cumulative number of xenon atoms from gas injection accumulated since plasma breakdown, expressed in equivalent electrons, where each xenon atom contributes 54 equivalent electrons corresponding to its atomic number Z = 54.
NAMES.long:
The accumulated xenon count tracks the total xenon atoms introduced by gas injection from plasma breakdown onward, expressed as a dimensionless equivalent-electron tally in which each neutral xenon atom contributes 54 counts equal to its atomic number $Z_{\mathrm{Xe}} = 54$.

The defining integral is:

$$
N_{\mathrm{Xe,eq}}(t) = 54 \int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t} \frac{dN_{\mathrm{Xe}}}{dt'} \, dt'
$$

where $dN_{\mathrm{Xe}}/dt'$ is the instantaneous xenon injection rate in atoms s$^{-1}$, $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the time of plasma breakdown in s, and $N_{\mathrm{Xe,eq}}$ is dimensionless. The prefill xenon inventory prior to breakdown is excluded from this integral and is tracked separately by [accumulated_xenon_prefill_count](name:accumulated_xenon_prefill_count).

The instantaneous injection rate contributing to this integral is characterized by [xenon_source_rate](name:xenon_source_rate). Xenon is employed as a high-$Z$ impurity in disruption mitigation and radiative cooling experiments; in massive gas injection scenarios the equivalent-electron count can reach $10^{23}$–$10^{24}$. For lighter noble gas comparisons, see [accumulated_neon_count](name:accumulated_neon_count) ($Z = 10$) and [accumulated_krypton_count](name:accumulated_krypton_count) ($Z = 36$).
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon gas is injected into the vessel after plasma breakdown, incrementing the cumulative count.

NAMES.name: accumulated_xenon_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Accumulated xenon prefill count is the end-of-prefill neutral xenon inventory expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each xenon atom contributes 54 to the dimensionless count.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated xenon prefill count is the scalar final value of the xenon gas dose introduced during the plasma prefill interval, expressed as an equivalent-electron count rather than as a count of neutral atoms. The conversion uses the xenon atomic number, so each neutral xenon atom contributes 54 equivalent electrons to the dimensionless count with unit 1.

The end-of-prefill count is defined from the integrated neutral xenon atom flow over the prefill time window:

$$
N_{\mathrm{Xe,prefill}}^{\mathrm{eq}}(t_{\mathrm{end}}) = 54\,N_{\mathrm{Xe,prefill}}(t_{\mathrm{end}}) = 54 \int_{t_{\mathrm{start}}}^{t_{\mathrm{end}}} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{Xe}}(t)\,dt
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{Xe,prefill}}^{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{Xe,prefill}}$ is the accumulated number of xenon atoms, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Xe}}$ is the neutral xenon atom flow rate in atoms per second, $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ is the start of prefill injection, and $t_{\mathrm{end}}$ is the end of the prefill interval, usually before plasma breakdown.

In practice the value is computed by integrating a calibrated xenon gas-flow or inventory estimate over the prefill interval. It is an accumulated final-time dose, not an instantaneous flow rate, and is the xenon-specific prefill analog of [accumulated_xenon_count](name:accumulated_xenon_count) when restricted to the prefill phase.

Typical values are highly device- and scenario-dependent because prefill dosing depends on vessel volume, pumping, gas-valve calibration, and the intended initial neutral composition; the standard name therefore specifies the counting convention rather than a universal numerical range.

NAMES.name: ammonia_deuterated_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: ammonia_deuterated
NAMES.short: Equivalent-electron count of deuterated ammonia (ND3) accumulated during the plasma prefill phase, with each ND3 molecule contributing 10 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
The prefill equivalent-electron count for deuterated ammonia (ND3) quantifies the total ND3 inventory introduced into the vessel before plasma breakdown, using the same equivalent-electron bookkeeping adopted across the prefill gas inventory family. This enables direct comparison of different gas species on a common electron-count basis regardless of molecular mass.

The count is defined by multiplying the number of delivered ND3 molecules by the total electron count of one neutral ND3 molecule:

$$
C = 10 \, N_{\mathrm{ND_3}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{ND_3}}$ is the number of injected molecules; the factor 10 arises from the atomic number of nitrogen ($Z_N = 7$) plus three deuterium atoms ($3 \times Z_D = 3 \times 1 = 3$). Note that NH3 and ND3 carry the same equivalent-electron factor because deuterium and protium share atomic number $Z = 1$.

The value is derived from gas injection flow records integrated over the prefill phase, ending at plasma breakdown. The analogous count for standard ammonia is [ammonia_prefill_count](name:ammonia_prefill_count), while post-breakdown ND3 accumulation is tracked by [accumulated_ammonia_deuterated_count](name:accumulated_ammonia_deuterated_count). The same equivalent-electron convention governs [accumulated_xenon_prefill_count](name:accumulated_xenon_prefill_count) and the broader prefill inventory family.
NAMES.sign: Positive when deuterated ammonia gas has been injected during the prefill phase.

NAMES.name: ammonia_deuterated_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ammonia_deuterated
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate at which deuterated ammonia (ND3) molecules are introduced into the plasma vessel by gas injection.
NAMES.long:
Deuterated ammonia (ND3) delivers both nitrogen impurity and deuterium fuel to the plasma in a single injection stream, with each molecule contributing one nitrogen atom ($Z_N = 7$) and three deuterium atoms ($Z_D = 1$). This dual-function character makes ND3 injection relevant to radiative mantle formation, edge cooling, and isotope fueling studies.

The source rate $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{ND_3}}$ is the time derivative of the cumulative injected molecule count:

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{ND_3}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{ND_3}}}{dt}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{ND_3}}$ is the total number of ND3 molecules introduced since the reference time. The time-integrated equivalent-electron inventory is tracked by [accumulated deuterated ammonia count](name:accumulated_ammonia_deuterated_count), where each ND3 molecule contributes 10 equivalent electrons: 7 from nitrogen and 3 from the three deuterium atoms. The deuterium fueling contribution from ND3 is three times this rate and should be combined with other deuterium sources when using [deuterium source rate due to injection](name:deuterium_source_rate_due_to_injection).

The rate is inferred from fast gas-valve diagnostics, calibrated using reference-volume pressure drops and gas conductance models. Typical injection rates range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{21}$ molecules per second for steady-state impurity seeding, rising to $10^{22}$ molecules per second or higher during massive gas injection for disruption mitigation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ND3 molecules flow into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: ammonia_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: ammonia
NAMES.short: Accumulated ammonia gas injected during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count.
NAMES.long:
Ammonia prefill count is the accumulated amount of NH$_3$ introduced before plasma breakdown, expressed as the number of bound electrons carried by the injected neutral molecules. The convention uses the full stoichiometric electron content of ammonia, not the instantaneous ionization state of the gas.

For a number of injected ammonia molecules $N_{\mathrm{NH_3}}$, the equivalent-electron count is

$$
N_{e,\mathrm{eq}} = 10\,N_{\mathrm{NH_3}}
$$

where the factor 10 is the total electron count of one neutral NH$_3$ molecule: 7 from nitrogen and 3 from hydrogen.

In practice this quantity is computed from the time-integrated ammonia gas throughput during the prefill interval, using calibrated valve, pressure, flow, or reservoir-depletion measurements to infer the number of NH$_3$ molecules delivered. It is specific to the prefill phase and is conceptually distinct from an accumulated ammonia count over a longer or differently defined injection interval.

Typical values are strongly device and scenario dependent. Small conditioning or trace-species prefills may be around $10^{19}$-$10^{21}$ equivalent electrons, while larger dedicated molecular-gas prefills can reach $10^{22}$-$10^{23}$ equivalent electrons or more.

NAMES.name: argon_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Accumulated number of argon atoms injected as gas during the prefill phase before plasma breakdown, represented as an equivalent-electron count with 18 count units per argon atom. The quantity is dimensionless and refers to introduced gas, not the retained, ionized, or pumped inventory.
NAMES.long:
Argon prefill count is the accumulated amount of argon introduced as gas before plasma breakdown, represented in equivalent-electron counting units. This is a dimensionless convention in which one neutral argon atom contributes 18 count units, equal to the atomic number of argon.

The conversion from physical atom count to equivalent-electron count is

$$
N_{\mathrm{Ar,eq}} = 18\,N_{\mathrm{Ar}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the number of argon atoms injected during the prefill phase and $N_{\mathrm{Ar,eq}}$ is the corresponding dimensionless equivalent-electron count.

In practice this quantity is computed from calibrated gas-valve throughput, pressure-volume inventory, or other gas-accounting measurements integrated over the pre-breakdown prefill interval. It describes the source amount introduced into the vessel and does not correct for subsequent pumping, ionization, charge state evolution, wall retention, recycling, or the amount remaining in the plasma after breakdown.

Typical argon prefill values in medium-size experiments are about $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ equivalent-electron count units, corresponding to approximately $6 \times 10^{16}$-$6 \times 10^{19}$ argon atoms. Larger radiative or disruption-mitigation gas injections may extend above this range, depending on vessel volume, valve throughput, and operating scenario.

NAMES.name: beryllium_source_rate
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Electron-equivalent rate at which beryllium contributes to the plasma particle source balance. It uses the same electron-counting convention as other species source rates; the corresponding beryllium nucleus rate depends on the assumed electron yield or charge state.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium source rate is the electron-equivalent contribution of beryllium to the plasma particle balance. It counts the electron source credited to beryllium under the chosen charge-state accounting, so it can be compared directly with electron-equivalent source quantities such as [total_electron_source_rate](name:total_electron_source_rate) and [electron_source_rate_due_to_surface_emission](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_surface_emission). It is not an unqualified neutral-atom or nucleus throughput.

The conversion from beryllium nucleus accounting to the electron-equivalent rate is

$$
S_\mathrm{Be} = \sum_k y_{e,k}\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Be},k}
$$

where $S_\mathrm{Be}$ is the beryllium source rate in s^-1, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Be},k}$ is the beryllium nucleus source rate for channel $k$ in s^-1, and $y_{e,k}$ is the dimensionless number of electrons credited per beryllium nucleus for that channel. The value $y_{e,k}=4$ applies only when each beryllium nucleus is counted as fully ionized to $\mathrm{Be}^{4+}$; other effective yields may be used for partial ionization, charge-state-resolved accounting, or model-specific penetration assumptions.

In practice, this rate is obtained from the source accounting used for beryllium: calibrated material-injection or inventory data, spectroscopy-constrained impurity influx estimates, erosion or material-balance models, or integrated particle-balance calculations. Comparisons with neighboring species quantities such as [xenon_source_rate](name:xenon_source_rate) should be made in electron-equivalent units; comparison of nucleus rates requires dividing by the adopted electron yield.

Absolute values scale with plasma size, operating scenario, source mechanism, and the yield convention, so no universal device-independent absolute range exists. A useful scale is the fraction $f_\mathrm{Be}=S_\mathrm{Be}/S_e$ relative to a total electron source rate $S_e$: for orientation, $f_\mathrm{Be}=10^{-6}-10^{-3}$ of $S_e=10^{20}-10^{24}$ s^-1 corresponds to $S_\mathrm{Be}=10^{14}-10^{21}$ s^-1. Deliberate material introduction, transient erosion, or different charge-state accounting can give values outside this range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when beryllium processes produce a net increase in the plasma electron particle balance.

NAMES.name: carbon_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Number of carbon atoms injected as gas during the plasma prefill phase, expressed in equivalent electrons using six count units per carbon atom.
NAMES.long:
Carbon prefill count due to gas injection is the dimensionless equivalent-electron inventory assigned to carbon atoms delivered by gas injection before plasma breakdown. It is a counting convention: each carbon atom contributes six count units because carbon has atomic number 6, independent of whether or when the atom is actually ionized.

The prefill equivalent-electron count is defined from the carbon atom flux delivered during the prefill interval:

$$
N_{\mathrm{C,prefill}} = 6 \int_{t_{\mathrm{start}}}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}} \Phi_{\mathrm{C}}(t)\,dt = 6\,N_{\mathrm{C,prefill}}^{\mathrm{atoms}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{C,prefill}}$ is the carbon prefill equivalent-electron count in dimensionless count units, $\Phi_{\mathrm{C}}(t)$ is the carbon atom flow rate in atoms per second, $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ is the start of the prefill gas delivery interval, $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma-breakdown time, and $N_{\mathrm{C,prefill}}^{\mathrm{atoms}}$ is the number of carbon atoms delivered in the same interval, also as a dimensionless count.

In practice this quantity is inferred from calibrated gas-injection valve commands, pressure-rise measurements, gas-line conductance models, or mass-flow diagnostics, converted from injected carbon-bearing gas molecules to carbon atoms and then multiplied by the six-count-per-carbon-atom convention. It is the carbon contribution to the total prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection and is closely related to [carbon_initial_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:carbon_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection), which represents the same initial carbon inventory convention. Carbon injected after plasma breakdown belongs to the post-breakdown counterpart [accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection), not to this prefill count.

Typical values depend strongly on vessel volume, wall conditioning, gas species, and fueling strategy. Equivalent-electron counts may be negligible when no carbon-bearing prefill gas is used, while intentional carbon-bearing prefill can produce about 10^18-10^22 count units in medium-sized magnetic-confinement devices.

NAMES.name: coolant_pressure
NAMES.short: Absolute static pressure of the coolant working fluid at a component port, characterizing the mechanical load and thermodynamic state of the fluid interface between connected plant-system components.
NAMES.long:
Coolant pressure is the absolute static pressure of the coolant working fluid at a component port or fluid interface. It is an isotropic scalar measure of the normal compressive loading exerted by the fluid, excluding dynamic pressure associated with bulk flow velocity.

The mechanical definition of static pressure is the normal force per unit area in the infinitesimal limit:

$$
p = \lim_{\Delta A \to 0} \frac{\Delta F_n}{\Delta A}
$$

where $p$ is the absolute pressure in Pa, $\Delta F_n$ is the compressive normal force in N exerted by the fluid on a surface element, and $\Delta A$ is the surface area in m$^2$.

Coolant pressure is measured with calibrated absolute or gage pressure transducers, with gage readings converted to absolute pressure by adding the local reference pressure. In thermal-hydraulic calculations it is combined with [coolant temperature](name:coolant_temperature) and [coolant flow] through an equation of state or property table; for a single-phase control volume in local thermodynamic equilibrium it enters the enthalpy relation $h = u + p/\rho$, where $h$ and $u$ are specific enthalpy and internal energy in J kg$^{-1}$ and $\rho$ is density in kg m$^{-3}$. Location-specific boundary conditions include [coolant pressure at the cooling circuit inlet](name:coolant_pressure_at_cooling_circuit_inlet), often interpreted together with [coolant temperature at inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet) and [coolant temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet).

Typical absolute pressures span about $10^5$-$10^6$ Pa for near-atmospheric auxiliary water or gas circuits, $10^6$-$10^7$ Pa for many pressurized gas coolant loops, and $10^7$-$2 \times 10^7$ Pa for high-pressure water coolant circuits. The applicable range depends on coolant species, phase margin, pump head, heat-exchanger design, and component pressure limits.

NAMES.name: coolant_temperature
NAMES.short: Absolute thermodynamic temperature of the coolant or working fluid at an inlet or outlet port of a balance-of-plant power conversion component. It characterizes the fluid thermal state at that connection point for heat-balance and cycle-performance calculations.
NAMES.long:
Coolant temperature is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of the working fluid at a component connection point in a plant power-conversion or heat-transport system. It is a local state variable of the fluid stream and may refer to either an inlet or an outlet port unless a more specific standard name identifies the locus.

For a steady single-phase stream with approximately constant heat capacity, the temperature change across a component is related to transferred thermal power by the calorimetric balance:

$$
\dot{Q} = \dot{m} c_p \left(T_\mathrm{out} - T_\mathrm{in}\right)
$$

where $\dot{Q}$ is the thermal power transferred to the fluid, $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $c_p$ is the specific heat capacity at constant pressure, and $T_\mathrm{in}$ and $T_\mathrm{out}$ are the inlet and outlet coolant temperatures.

In practice, coolant temperature is measured with temperature sensors such as resistance thermometers, thermocouples, or process transmitters installed in the fluid stream or thermowell near the port. It is used together with coolant pressure and flow to determine fluid enthalpy, heat removal, component efficiency, and thermodynamic cycle state points. For outlet-specific quantities, use [coolant_temperature_at_outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet).

Typical values are about 293-363 K for low-temperature water cooling circuits, about 553-613 K for pressurized-water heat-transfer loops, and about 523-823 K for helium or other high-temperature gas coolant systems. The applicable range depends strongly on coolant type, pressure, component function, and operating regime.

NAMES.name: count_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Total discrete particle inventory of a pellet, encompassing both the individual atom count of the pellet material and the propellant gas-molecule count carried with the pellet.
NAMES.long: The count of a pellet captures the total discrete particle inventory attributable to one injected pellet, abstracting over both its solid material constituents and its gas-phase payload. The [atomic count](name:atomic_count_of_pellet) tallies every individual atom present in the pellet, counting each atom once regardless of whether the propellant material is monatomic, diatomic, or molecular in form. The [gas count] enumerates the propellant gas molecules carried with the pellet, representing the gas-phase component of the overall particle inventory. Together these two child quantities partition the total pellet particle inventory and are applied in pellet fueling efficiency analysis, particle balance accounting, and ablation modeling for pellet injection systems.

NAMES.name: atomic_count_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Total number of individual atoms in a pellet, with each atom counted once regardless of whether the propellant material is monatomic, diatomic, or molecular in form.
NAMES.long:
The atomic count of a pellet is the total discrete number of atoms present throughout the entire pellet body, tallied individually without regard to the molecular or bonding state of the constituent propellant material. A diatomic fuel such as D$_2$ (frozen deuterium) contributes two atoms per molecule; monatomic species contribute one atom per particle. This whole-pellet total differs from spatially resolved counterparts such as [outer_atomic_count_of_pellet](name:outer_atomic_count_of_pellet), and extends the general atom-counting convention of [count_of_pellet](name:count_of_pellet).

The atomic count $N_\mathrm{at}$ relates to the number of propellant molecules $N_\mathrm{mol}$ by:

$$
N_\mathrm{at} = \nu \, N_\mathrm{mol}
$$

where $\nu$ is the number of atoms per molecule of the propellant species (for example, $\nu = 2$ for D$_2$ or DT, and $\nu = 1$ for a monatomic noble gas).

The count is determined from the pellet geometry combined with the atomic number density of the solid propellant at cryogenic storage temperature, or from pellet mass measured immediately before injection. Fueling and disruption-mitigation pellets for large tokamaks contain on the order of $10^{21}$–$10^{23}$ atoms. The [normalized_atomic_count_of_pellet](name:normalized_atomic_count_of_pellet) expresses this total scaled against a reference count for nondimensional comparison across pellet types or injection scenarios.

NAMES.name: core_atomic_count_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Total number of atomic nuclei in the innermost core layer of a composite pellet, counted regardless of molecular bonding, phase, or species. For a core-outer partition, it complements the outer atomic count so their sum gives the whole-pellet atomic inventory.
NAMES.long:
Core atomic count is the total number of atomic nuclei contained in the innermost core material of a composite pellet. It is an inventory, not a density: molecular bonding, phase, and ionization state do not change the count. In a two-region pellet decomposition it complements the [outer atomic count](name:outer_atomic_count_of_pellet); with additional regions, the whole-pellet inventory is the sum over all regions.

The general definition is the volume integral of total atomic-nuclei number density over the core volume:

$$
N_\mathrm{core} = \int_{V_\mathrm{core}} n_\mathrm{atom}(\mathbf{x})\,dV = \int_{V_\mathrm{core}} \sum_s n_s(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $N_\mathrm{core}$ is the dimensionless count, $V_\mathrm{core}$ is the physical volume occupied by the core, $n_\mathrm{atom}$ is the total atomic-nuclei number density in m^-3, and $n_s$ is the number density in m^-3 of atomic species or isotope $s$. The species sum must be performed for mixtures; for example, deuterium and tritium nuclei in a mixed hydrogenic core are counted separately, and each molecule contributes one count per atomic nucleus. For a spatially uniform total atomic density the expression reduces to $N_\mathrm{core}=n_\mathrm{atom}V_\mathrm{core}$, but that product is valid only after all species contributions have been included.

In practice, the count is computed from the core geometry and material composition using solid, liquid, or cryogenic number densities, with corrections for porosity, voids, temperature, or graded composition when relevant. It can also be inferred from the measured core mass and isotopic or elemental fractions by converting mass to numbers of nuclei using molar masses and stoichiometric coefficients.

Typical values for fusion fueling or disruption-mitigation pellets are about 10^19-10^23 counted atomic nuclei in the core layer. Small tracer or dopant cores may contain 10^16-10^19 nuclei, while millimeter-scale hydrogenic cores commonly contain 10^20-10^22 nuclei.

NAMES.name: density_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Number density of atoms of a specified species in the condensed pellet material. For layered, mixed, or fragmented pellets, it denotes the species atom count per material volume for the relevant material region or its volume average, not the density of gas molecules.
NAMES.long:
Density of pellet is the number of atoms, or nuclei, of a specified chemical species per unit volume of condensed pellet material. For molecular pellet materials such as $\mathrm{D}_2$, this is an atom-count density: the deuterium density counts deuterium atoms, not $\mathrm{D}_2$ molecules. In layered, mixed, or fragmented material it may represent the local species density in a material region or a volume-averaged species density over the selected condensed-material volume.

For a uniform material, or for a volume average over a specified condensed-material volume, the relation to the species atom inventory is

$$
n_a = \frac{N_a}{V}
$$

where $n_a$ is the species atom density, $N_a$ is the number of atoms of species $a$ as a dimensionless count, and $V$ is the condensed-material volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$. If inferred from mass density, the relation $n_a = \rho_{m,a} N_A / M_a$ uses the species partial mass density $\rho_{m,a}$, or the total mass density only for a pure species, with molar mass $M_a$ and Avogadro constant $N_A$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from pellet composition, mass, dimensions, phase, and material equation-of-state data, or from imaging and reconstruction of the occupied condensed volume after layering or fragmentation. For fragmented pellets, the relevant volume is the material volume of the fragments; voids between separated pieces are not included unless an envelope-averaged density is explicitly intended.

Typical atom-count densities for cryogenic hydrogen-isotope, noble-gas, or impurity pellets are about $10^{28}$-$10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Partial species densities in mixtures or porous material are reduced according to stoichiometry, composition fraction, and porosity.

NAMES.name: core_density_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Number density of a constituent atomic species in the inner core layer of a pellet used by a shattered-pellet injector.
NAMES.long:
Core density of pellet is the number density of a specified atomic species within the pellet's inner core layer. It represents how many atoms of that species are present per unit volume of the core material and is non-negative by physical definition.

The density is defined by the species population in the core divided by the core volume:

$$
n_{s,\mathrm{core}} = \frac{N_{s,\mathrm{core}}}{V_\mathrm{core}}
$$

where $n_{s,\mathrm{core}}$ is the core species number density in m$^{-3}$, $N_{s,\mathrm{core}}$ is the number of atoms of species $s$ in the core and is dimensionless, and $V_\mathrm{core}$ is the core volume in m$^3$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from the specified pellet composition and core geometry, or equivalently from the total core species inventory normalized by the core volume. It is species-resolved: different atomic constituents of the same core can have different values.

No device-independent typical numerical range is implied by the standard name alone; values depend on the chosen pellet material, mixture, and core volume.

NAMES.name: deuterium_count_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Cumulative number of deuterium atoms delivered by gas injection after plasma breakdown, expressed as equivalent electrons. Each deuterium atom contributes one count; deuterium introduced during the prefill phase is excluded.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium count due to gas injection is the accumulated amount of deuterium delivered by gas puffing or valve injection after plasma breakdown. It is expressed as an equivalent-electron particle count: because deuterium has atomic number one, each injected neutral deuterium atom contributes one count. Deuterium supplied before breakdown belongs to [deuterium_prefill_count](name:deuterium_prefill_count) rather than this quantity.

The accumulated count is the time integral of the deuterium injection source rate from the breakdown time to the time of interest:

$$
N_D^\mathrm{inj}(t) = \int_{t_\mathrm{bd}}^{t} \dot{N}_D^\mathrm{inj}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $N_D^\mathrm{inj}$ is the accumulated deuterium equivalent-electron count with unit $1$, $t_\mathrm{bd}$ is the plasma breakdown time in s, $t$ and $t'$ are times in s, and $\dot{N}_D^\mathrm{inj}$ is the [deuterium source rate due to injection](name:deuterium_source_rate_due_to_injection) in atoms/s, equivalently counts/s for deuterium.

In practice, the count is computed by integrating calibrated deuterium gas flow rates from injection valves, gas lines, or plenum pressure changes, with corrections for gas temperature, isotopic purity, valve calibration, and molecular composition when relevant. Contributions from all deuterium injection paths are summed, while prefill inventory and non-gas fueling sources are kept separate.

Typical accumulated values are dimensionless counts of about $10^{20}$-$10^{23}$ for short or medium tokamak pulses, and can reach $10^{24}$-$10^{25}$ in large-device or long-pulse operation depending on fueling demand, plasma density, and discharge duration.

NAMES.name: deuterium_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Accumulated deuterium introduced by gas injection during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Because deuterium has atomic charge Z = 1, each deuterium atom contributes one count; deuterium from wall recycling, neutral beams, pellets, or later fueling is excluded.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium prefill count is the accumulated amount of deuterium introduced as neutral gas before plasma breakdown, expressed as the number of electrons that would be supplied by complete ionization. For deuterium, the atomic charge is $Z_D = 1$, so the equivalent-electron count is numerically equal to the number of injected deuterium atoms. The quantity is limited to the prefill gas-injection phase and excludes deuterium supplied later by fueling, wall recycling, pellets, or neutral beam injection.

The accumulated count is obtained by integrating the injected atomic deuterium rate over the prefill interval:

$$
N_{D,\mathrm{prefill}} = \int_{t_\mathrm{start}}^{t_\mathrm{end}} Z_D\,\dot{N}_D(t)\,dt
$$

where $N_{D,\mathrm{prefill}}$ is the deuterium prefill count, $Z_D = 1$ is the deuterium atomic charge, $\dot{N}_D(t)$ is the atomic deuterium injection rate in atoms s$^{-1}$, and $t_\mathrm{start}$ and $t_\mathrm{end}$ are the start and end times of the prefill interval in s. If the measured gas throughput is a molecular $D_2$ rate, the corresponding atomic rate is twice the molecular rate.

In practice this quantity is computed from calibrated gas-valve commands, mass-flow measurements, pressure-drop calibrations, or reservoir inventory changes, with corrections for line volume, gas temperature, valve conductance, and species purity when needed. It represents the requested or delivered neutral-gas inventory before breakdown, not the amount that remains confined after ionization.

Typical prefill inventories are about $10^{20}-10^{23}$ equivalent-electron counts in small and medium tokamaks, and may approach $10^{24}$ in large devices or high-pressure prefill scenarios.

NAMES.name: efficiency_of_plant_system
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio quantifying how effectively a plant system converts input power or energy into a specified useful output, abstracting over thermal and net efficiency definitions.
NAMES.long:
The efficiency of a plant system is a dimensionless performance metric expressing the fraction of input power or energy that the plant converts into a specified useful output. The exact physical scope depends on the efficiency type applied: [thermal efficiency](name:thermal_efficiency_of_plant_system) characterizes heat-to-work conversion across all thermodynamic conversion stages, while [net efficiency](name:net_efficiency_of_plant_system) accounts for the signed ratio of exported electrical power to total plant electrical consumption including recirculating power.

The general defining relation takes the form:

$$
\eta = \frac{W_\text{out}}{W_\text{in}}
$$

where $W_\text{out}$ is the useful output (work, exported electrical power, or heat converted to work) and $W_\text{in}$ is the total input power or energy over the same operating interval.

Efficiency is evaluated from calorimetric heat-flow surveys, electrical generation meters, and auxiliary power consumption measurements across all plant subsystems. For fusion facilities, thermal conversion efficiencies in steam-cycle plants lie in the range 30–45%, and net electrical efficiencies are further reduced by recirculating power fractions for heating, current drive, and cooling systems.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plant system delivers net useful output, so that $W_\text{out} > 0$.

NAMES.name: electron_source_rate_at_pellet_path_due_to_pellet_injection
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron-equivalent source rate at a specified position along an injected pellet trajectory, produced by ablation and ionization of pellet material. It is charge-weighted by the number of free electrons ultimately contributed and is a non-negative path-position rate in s^-1, not a source per meter.
NAMES.long:
The electron source rate at a pellet path position is the local, charge-weighted electron-equivalent production rate caused by ablation and ionization of injected pellet material. It is the path-resolved counterpart of the total [electron_source_rate_due_to_injection](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_injection) and differs from electron_density_of_pellet_path, which describes local electron concentration rather than production rate.

For distance $ell$ along the pellet trajectory and time $t$, the electron-equivalent source rate can be written as a charge-weighted sum over ablated pellet constituents:

$$
S_e(\ell,t) = \sum_a Z_a^\mathrm{eff}(\ell,t)\,\dot{N}_a(\ell,t)
$$

where $S_e$ is the electron source rate at that path position in s^-1, $\ell$ is distance along the pellet trajectory in meters, $t$ is time in seconds, $\dot{N}_a$ is the ablation or ionization rate of constituent $a$ at that same position in s^-1, and $Z_a^\mathrm{eff}$ is the dimensionless number of free electrons ultimately contributed per ablated constituent. For fully ionized deuterium or tritium atoms, $Z_a^\mathrm{eff}=1$; mixtures, impurities, molecules, or partially ionized material use the appropriate effective charge weighting.

In practice this quantity is computed from pellet ablation and ionization models using the pellet trajectory, speed, size, composition, and local plasma conditions, and may be constrained by fast imaging, line radiation, microwave or interferometric measurements, and post-injection density evolution. Its unit s^-1 denotes a rate at a path position, not a line source per meter; an event-integrated contribution over a small path segment is obtained by combining the rate with the pellet transit time through that segment, for example $S_e\,\Delta \ell / v_p$ when the pellet speed is $v_p$.

The value is non-negative and is zero where no pellet material is being ablated or ionized. For cryogenic hydrogen-isotope fueling pellets, active-path values commonly span about 10^21-10^25 s^-1, with small pacing pellets or weak edge ablation below this range and large or high-Z pellets reaching about 10^25-10^27 s^-1. Magnitudes depend strongly on pellet size, speed, material, plasma density, and plasma temperature.

NAMES.name: ethane_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: ethane
NAMES.short: Accumulated ethane gas injected during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each C2H6 molecule contributes 18 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
Ethane prefill count is the accumulated amount of ethane introduced before plasma initiation, expressed as the number of electrons that would be supplied if the injected molecules were fully ionized. The quantity represents the ethane contribution to the initial neutral inventory in an equivalent-electron convention.

The conversion from injected ethane molecules to equivalent-electron count is:

$$
N_{e,\mathrm{eq}} = 18\,N_{\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_6}
$$

where $N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}$ is the ethane prefill count, a dimensionless count of equivalent electrons, and $N_{\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_6}$ is the accumulated number of injected ethane molecules, a dimensionless molecule count. The factor 18 is the total nuclear charge of one ethane molecule: two carbon atoms with charge 6 each plus six hydrogen atoms with charge 1 each.

In practice, the value is obtained from calibrated gas-delivery accounting over the defined prefill interval and converted from delivered molecular amount to equivalent-electron count. It should include ethane delivered for the prefill phase only, not later gas injection used for fueling, impurity control, or other discharge phases.

Typical values are strongly device- and scenario-dependent. They may be zero when ethane is not used for prefill, while intentional nonzero prefill amounts can span roughly $10^{19}$-$10^{23}$ equivalent electrons in small to medium devices and scale upward with vessel volume, target fill pressure, and delivered gas inventory.

NAMES.name: ethane_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ethane
NAMES.short: Instantaneous ethane gas injection rate delivered to the plasma vessel, expressed as the equivalent number of bound electrons carried by the neutral C2H6 molecules per second. For ethane, each molecule contributes 18 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
Ethane source rate is the instantaneous neutral-gas delivery rate of ethane to the plasma vessel expressed as an equivalent-electron rate. The equivalent-electron convention weights each injected $\mathrm{C_2H_6}$ molecule by the total number of bound electrons in the neutral molecule, so that different molecular gas feeds can be compared on a common particle-count basis.

For ethane, the conversion from molecular injection rate to equivalent-electron source rate is

$$
\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{eq}} = 18\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{C_2H_6}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{C_2H_6}}$ is the injected ethane molecule rate and the factor 18 comes from two carbon atoms with 6 electrons each plus six hydrogen atoms with 1 electron each.

In practice, the molecular injection rate is inferred from calibrated gas-valve flow measurements, pressure-drop measurements, or mass-flow-controller signals, then converted to the equivalent-electron rate using the molecular stoichiometry. The value represents gas supplied by the injection system, not the fraction that is ionized, dissociated, retained, or pumped after entering the vessel.

Typical values depend strongly on valve calibration, pulse duration, and experimental purpose. Small diagnostic or conditioning puffs may correspond to about $10^{19}$-$10^{21}$ s$^{-1}$ in equivalent electrons, while larger fueling or seeding pulses can reach $10^{21}$-$10^{23}$ s$^{-1}$ for short intervals.

NAMES.name: ethylene_count
NAMES.subject: ethylene
NAMES.short: Cumulative ethylene (C2H4) gas injection since plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count where each ethylene molecule contributes 16 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
Cumulative ethylene (C2H4) delivered by gas injection since plasma breakdown, expressed as a dimensionless equivalent-electron count. Each neutral ethylene molecule contributes 16 equivalent electrons, reflecting two carbon atoms at atomic number $Z = 6$ and four hydrogen atoms at $Z = 1$.

The equivalent-electron count $N_\mathrm{eq}$ for an injected number of ethylene molecules $N_\mathrm{mol}$ is:

$$
N_\mathrm{eq} = 16 \, N_\mathrm{mol}
$$

where the factor $16 = 2 \times 6 + 4 \times 1$ is the total bound-electron inventory of a neutral C$_2$H$_4$ molecule. The count accumulates from the moment of plasma breakdown and resets between discharges, providing a measure of the total electron inventory introduced via ethylene injection. It complements hydrocarbon siblings such as [accumulated_ethane_count](name:accumulated_ethane_count) and contributes to the cross-species total captured by [accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection)
NAMES.sign: Positive when ethylene gas has been injected into the vessel since plasma breakdown.

NAMES.name: accumulated_ethylene_count
NAMES.subject: ethylene
NAMES.short: Cumulative ethylene (C2H4) gas injection since plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count where each ethylene molecule contributes 16 equivalent electrons (2 carbon atoms at Z = 6 each, 4 hydrogen atoms at Z = 1 each).
NAMES.long:
Ethylene (C2H4) is a two-carbon hydrocarbon molecule in which each molecule contributes 2 carbon atoms (atomic number $Z_C = 6$) and 4 hydrogen atoms ($Z_H = 1$), yielding 16 equivalent electrons per molecule.

The accumulated equivalent-electron count is defined by:

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = 16 \int_{t_{\mathrm{bd}}}^{t} \frac{dN_{\mathrm{C_2H_4}}}{dt'} \, dt'
$$

where $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the time of plasma breakdown and $dN_{\mathrm{C_2H_4}}/dt$ is the instantaneous ethylene injection rate in molecules per second.

The integral runs from plasma breakdown onward, excluding any prefill contribution. The quantity is inferred from calibrated gas-valve flow measurements and tracks the hydrocarbon-based electron inventory added to the plasma, relevant to impurity seeding and disruption mitigation experiments. Closely related hydrocarbon counts include [accumulated_ethane_count](name:accumulated_ethane_count) (C2H6, 18 equivalent electrons per molecule) and [accumulated_propane_count](name:accumulated_propane_count) (C3H8, 26 equivalent electrons per molecule). For the species-summed inventory across all injected gasses, see [accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_total_particle_count_due_to_gas_injection).

NAMES.name: ethylene_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: ethylene
NAMES.short: Cumulative neutral ethylene (C2H4) introduced during the prefill gas-loading phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each C2H4 molecule contributes 16 bound atomic electrons: 12 from two carbon atoms and 4 from four hydrogen atoms.
NAMES.long:
Ethylene prefill count is the cumulative amount of neutral ethylene introduced during the prefill gas-loading interval before plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. The equivalent-electron convention counts the bound atomic electrons in each neutral molecule; for ethylene, two carbon atoms with atomic number 6 and four hydrogen atoms with atomic number 1 give 16 electrons per C2H4 molecule.

For a molecular injection rate over the prefill interval, the count is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{prefill}} = \int_{t_0}^{t_b} 16\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C_2H_4}}(t)\,dt
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C_2H_4}}(t)$ is the neutral ethylene molecular injection rate in molecules per second, $t_0$ is the start of the prefill interval, $t_b$ is the breakdown time or end of prefill, and $N_{\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{prefill}}$ is a dimensionless equivalent-electron count. Equivalently, if $N_{\mathrm{C_2H_4}}$ molecules are injected during prefill, the count is $16 N_{\mathrm{C_2H_4}}$.

In practice the molecular amount is inferred from calibrated gas-flow or valve-throughput measurements, reservoir pressure changes, or gas-inventory accounting, with conversion to molecule number using the gas equation of state. This quantity is restricted to the prefill interval and is distinct from [accumulated_ethylene_count](name:accumulated_ethylene_count), which tracks ethylene accumulated from plasma breakdown onward. It follows the same equivalent-electron accounting idea used for other injected-species inventory counts such as [accumulated_helium_4_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection), [accumulated_lithium_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_lithium_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection), and [carbon_initial_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:carbon_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection).

Typical prefill magnitudes are about $10^{19}$-$10^{23}$ equivalent electrons, corresponding to roughly $6 \times 10^{17}$-$6 \times 10^{21}$ ethylene molecules. The value depends on vessel volume, target prefill pressure, gas-line calibration, and the duration of the prefill injection.

NAMES.name: ethylene_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ethylene
NAMES.short: Instantaneous injection rate of ethylene (C2H4) gas into the plasma vessel, expressed as equivalent electrons per second with each molecule counted as 16 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
Ethylene (C2H4) is a two-carbon, four-hydrogen molecule used as a gaseous source of both carbon and hydrogen in plasma fueling and wall-conditioning experiments. The source rate is the instantaneous equivalent-electron delivery rate to the plasma vessel, where each molecule is assigned 16 equivalent electrons based on the total atomic electron inventory of the molecular formula.

The equivalent-electron rate $\dot{N}_\mathrm{eq}$ relates to the molecular injection rate $\dot{N}_\mathrm{C_2H_4}$ by

$$
\dot{N}_\mathrm{eq} = 16\,\dot{N}_\mathrm{C_2H_4}
$$

where the factor $16 = 2Z_\mathrm{C} + 4Z_\mathrm{H}$, with $Z_\mathrm{C} = 6$ the carbon atomic number and $Z_\mathrm{H} = 1$ the hydrogen atomic number.

The injection rate is inferred from valve conductance calibrations and upstream pressure measurements. Its time-integral gives the [accumulated ethylene count](name:accumulated_ethylene_count), which tracks the total equivalent-electron inventory delivered since plasma breakdown. Related molecular and atomic injection rates include [silane_source_rate](name:silane_source_rate) for SiH4 and [hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) for atomic hydrogen delivery.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ethylene gas flows from the injection system into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: krypton_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Equivalent electrons from krypton injected during the prefill phase; it is 36 times the number of krypton atoms delivered and is not the raw atom count.
NAMES.long:
Krypton prefill count is a bookkeeping measure of the neutral krypton inventory introduced before plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. It converts the number of krypton atoms delivered during the prefill phase into the number of electrons those atoms would contain if fully counted by atomic number, enabling comparison with other species inventories.

The equivalent-electron count is defined from the injected krypton atom count as:

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq,e}}^{\mathrm{Kr,prefill}} = Z_{\mathrm{Kr}} N_{\mathrm{Kr,prefill}} = 36 N_{\mathrm{Kr,prefill}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{Kr,prefill}}$ is the number of krypton atoms injected during the prefill phase and $Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}=36$ is the atomic number of krypton. Both $N_{\mathrm{eq,e}}^{\mathrm{Kr,prefill}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{Kr,prefill}}$ are dimensionless counts.

In practice, $N_{\mathrm{Kr,prefill}}$ is obtained by integrating a calibrated krypton flow over the prefill time interval. For particle flow $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ in atoms s$^{-1}$, $N_{\mathrm{Kr,prefill}}=\int \dot{N}_{\mathrm{Kr}}(t)\,dt$; for molar flow $\dot{n}_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ in mol s$^{-1}$, $N_{\mathrm{Kr,prefill}}=N_A\int \dot{n}_{\mathrm{Kr}}(t)\,dt$; and for gas throughput $Q$ in Pa m$^3$ s$^{-1}$ at gas temperature $T$ in K, the ideal-gas estimate is $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Kr}}\approx Q/(k_B T)$, where $N_A$ is Avogadro's constant and $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant. The same equivalent-electron inventory convention is used for related prefill or gas-injection quantities such as [argon_prefill_count](name:argon_prefill_count), [neon_prefill_count](name:neon_prefill_count), [tritium_prefill_count](name:tritium_prefill_count), [accumulated_xenon_prefill_count](name:accumulated_xenon_prefill_count), [accumulated_helium_4_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection), and [carbon_initial_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:carbon_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection); [accumulated_krypton_count](name:accumulated_krypton_count) denotes the krypton inventory accumulated beyond the prefill-only interval.

Typical values are strongly device- and recipe-dependent. Trace or calibration prefills may be about $10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ equivalent electrons, while larger high-atomic-number gas puffs can reach $10^{21}$-$10^{24}$ equivalent electrons, corresponding to approximately $3\times10^{16}$-$3\times10^{22}$ krypton atoms after division by 36.

NAMES.name: length_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Axial length of the intact cylindrical pellet before injection or shattering, measured end to end along the pellet symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Pellet length is the end-to-end axial extent of an intact cylindrical pellet before injection or shattering. It specifies the pellet geometry together with the pellet diameter and is independent of the later fragment distribution produced during shattering.

For an ideal right circular cylindrical pellet, the geometric volume is related to length and diameter by:

$$
V = \frac{\pi}{4} d^2 L
$$

where $V$ is the initial pellet volume in m$^3$, $d$ is the pellet diameter in m, and $L$ is the pellet length in m. This volume characterizes the initial geometry; the delivered material inventory also depends on pellet density, composition, shape fidelity, and losses or changes during injection, shattering, ablation, and transport.

In practice, pellet length is determined from the fabrication or injector geometry and may be checked by mechanical, optical, or cryogenic metrology before launch. It is used with diameter to estimate initial pellet volume and, when combined with material density and isotopic or impurity composition, the initial mass and particle content.

Typical lengths for cryogenic pellets used in shattered pellet injection are about 0.003-0.05 m, depending on injector bore, pellet material, and disruption-mitigation requirements.

NAMES.name: maximum_gas_flow
NAMES.short: Operational upper limit on pressure-weighted gas throughput through a gas injection valve, expressed as gas pressure times volumetric flow rate in the injection direction.
NAMES.long:
Maximum gas flow $Q_{\max}$ is the upper engineering limit on pressure-weighted volumetric gas throughput deliverable by a gas injection valve.
