It bounds the instantaneous gas_flow in the positive injection direction and, together with [minimum_gas_flow](name:minimum_gas_flow), defines the usable valve throughput range.

The pressure-throughput limit is defined from the product of gas pressure and volumetric flow rate over the allowed operating states of the valve:

$$
Q_{\max} = \max_{\mathrm{allowed}} \left(p\,\dot{V}\right)
$$

where $p$ is the gas pressure in Pa at the specified reference section, $\dot{V}$ is the volumetric flow rate in m$^3$ s$^{-1}$ for the same gas state, and $Q_{\max}$ is in Pa m$^3$ s$^{-1}$.

The value is usually obtained from valve specifications, calibrated flow-bench measurements, or pressure-decay tests under specified gas species, temperature, and upstream/downstream pressure conditions. It is a pressure-throughput limit, not directly a particle source rate: for an ideal gas at gas temperature $T_g$, the molecule rate is $\dot{N}=Q/(k_B T_g)$ and the molar rate is $\dot{n}=Q/(R T_g)$, so comparison with total_upper_source_rate requires the gas temperature and composition.

Typical maximum throughputs range from $0.01-10\ \mathrm{Pa\,m^3\,s^{-1}}$ for small fueling or impurity-seeding valves, $10-10^3\ \mathrm{Pa\,m^3\,s^{-1}}$ for high-capacity gas puffing valves, and $10^3-10^6\ \mathrm{Pa\,m^3\,s^{-1}}$ for fast disruption-mitigation injection systems.
NAMES.sign: Positive when gas is transported from the upstream supply side of the valve toward the injection outlet.

NAMES.name: methane_carbon_13_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: methane_carbon_13
NAMES.short: Equivalent-electron count of carbon-13-labeled methane injected during the prefill phase before plasma breakdown.
NAMES.long:
Methane-carbon-13 prefill count is the total amount of $^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4$ introduced before plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each neutral $^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4$ molecule contributes 10 equivalent electrons: 6 from the carbon-13 atom and 4 from the hydrogen atoms.

The equivalent-electron count is obtained from the accumulated molecular amount over the prefill interval:

$$
N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4,\mathrm{prefill}} = 10\,N_{^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4,\mathrm{prefill}} = 10\int_{t_0}^{t_\mathrm{bd}} \dot{N}_{^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4}(t)\,dt
$$

where $N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4,\mathrm{prefill}}$ is the equivalent-electron count with unit 1, $N_{^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4,\mathrm{prefill}}$ is the accumulated molecular count with unit 1, $\dot{N}_{^{13}\mathrm{CH}_4}$ is the molecular injection rate, $t_0$ is the start of the prefill interval, and $t_\mathrm{bd}$ is the plasma-breakdown time.

In practice this quantity is computed from calibrated gas-valve throughput, reservoir pressure drop, or mass-flow measurements integrated over the prefill interval and then multiplied by the factor 10. It is used to compare isotopically labeled methane fueling or wall-conditioning doses on the same equivalent-electron basis as other prefill gasses.

Typical values range from 0 to $10^{23}$ in small and medium devices, depending on vessel volume, requested prefill pressure, gas species mix, and the fraction of methane that is carbon-13 labeled.

NAMES.name: methane_carbon_13_source_rate
NAMES.subject: methane_carbon_13
NAMES.short: Instantaneous injection rate of carbon-13-labeled methane (13CH4) into the plasma vessel, expressed as an equivalent-electron rate where each molecule contributes 10 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
Carbon-13-labeled methane (13CH4) is deployed as a controlled tracer gas for erosion and carbon transport studies in fusion devices, because the stable 13C isotope can be discriminated spectroscopically from the naturally occurring 12C background. The equivalent-electron weighting assigns a factor of 10 to each injected 13CH4 molecule, reflecting the total electron count of the neutral species: atomic number $Z = 6$ for carbon plus $Z = 1$ for each of the four hydrogen atoms.

The instantaneous equivalent-electron source rate $\dot{S}$ accumulates over time to give the total equivalent-electron inventory:

$$
N(t) = \int_0^t \dot{S}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $N(t)$ is the cumulative equivalent-electron count tracked by [accumulated 13CH4 injection](name:accumulated_methane_carbon_13_count_due_to_gas_injection).

The rate is inferred from upstream reservoir pressure and valve conductance measurements. For comprehensive carbon gas accounting, this quantity complements [carbon_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:carbon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection), which sums contributions from all carbon-bearing gas species.
NAMES.sign: Positive when 13CH4 gas flows from the injection system into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: methane_source_rate
NAMES.subject: methane
NAMES.short: Instantaneous molecular source rate of methane (CH4) delivered to the plasma vessel by gas injection systems, expressed as CH4 molecules per second. It is not an electron-equivalent rate; under complete ionization, one methane molecule corresponds to ten electron-equivalent particles.
NAMES.long:
Methane source rate is the instantaneous number of CH4 molecules introduced into the plasma vessel per unit time by gas injection. It is a molecular flow rate: one count corresponds to one methane molecule entering the vessel, independent of later dissociation, ionization, pumping, recycling, or wall retention.

For a cumulative methane molecule count $N_{\mathrm{CH}_4}(t)$, the rate $S_{\mathrm{CH}_4}(t)$ is defined by:

$$
S_{\mathrm{CH}_4}(t) = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{CH}_4}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $t$ is time in seconds and $N_{\mathrm{CH}_4}(t)$ is the cumulative number of methane molecules delivered over the chosen accounting interval. Integrating $S_{\mathrm{CH}_4}$ between two times gives the number of methane molecules delivered during that interval, not necessarily a retained inventory in the plasma.

Each methane molecule contains one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. If the delivered methane is converted to constituent atom rates, the associated carbon atom rate is $S_C = S_{\mathrm{CH}_4}$ and the associated hydrogen atom rate is $S_H = 4S_{\mathrm{CH}_4}$, linking this quantity to [carbon_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:carbon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) and [hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection). If an electron-equivalent source rate is required using atomic numbers, complete ionization gives $S_{e,\mathrm{eq}} = (Z_C + 4Z_H)S_{\mathrm{CH}_4} = 10S_{\mathrm{CH}_4}$ with $Z_C=6$ and $Z_H=1$; that is a derived convention, not the methane molecular rate itself.

In practice this rate is computed from calibrated gas-injection throughput, valve timing, reservoir pressure and temperature, mass-flow-controller calibration, and gas composition. A pressure-volume throughput can be converted to a molecular rate using the ideal-gas relation with the local gas temperature; corrections may be needed for line conductance, valve response, calibration-gas differences, and back-pressure near the injection point.

Typical methane puff rates in fusion experiments are about $10^{17}$-$10^{21}$ s^-1. Short diagnostic tracer puffs often lie near the lower end of this range, while stronger impurity-seeding, wall-conditioning, or disruption-mitigation-related injections can approach $10^{21}$-$10^{22}$ s^-1 depending on the injector and pulse duration.

NAMES.name: minimum_gas_flow
NAMES.short: Minimum gas flow is the smallest pressure-volume gas throughput that a gas injection valve can reliably deliver. It is the lower bound of the controllable flow range.
NAMES.long:
Minimum gas flow is the lower reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It is a static hardware capability that bounds the same physical quantity represented by gas_flow, while [maximum_gas_flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) gives the corresponding upper limit.

The underlying pressure-volume gas throughput is defined by

$$
Q = p\,\dot{V}
$$

where $Q$ is the gas throughput in $\mathrm{Pa\,m^3\,s^{-1}}$, $p$ is the gas pressure in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\dot{V}$ is the volumetric flow rate in $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$. The minimum gas flow is the calibrated lower reliable value of $Q$ for the valve, not a particle source rate; for an ideal gas, an approximate molecular source rate is $\dot{N}=Q/(k_B T_g)$, where $T_g$ is the gas temperature and $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant.

In practice this limit is obtained from factory qualification, bench calibration, or in-system flow calibration by identifying the smallest command or valve opening that gives reproducible throughput within the required tolerance. It is used in fueling, wall-conditioning, density-control, and disruption-mitigation gas systems to determine the smallest controllable gas puff and, together with the maximum flow, the valve turndown ratio.

Typical minimum reliable flows range from about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}\ \mathrm{Pa\,m^3\,s^{-1}}$ for fine metering or leak valves, $10^{-2}$-$10^{1}\ \mathrm{Pa\,m^3\,s^{-1}}$ for general fueling valves, and can be higher for large fast-injection or disruption-mitigation valves. The applicable value is strongly dependent on valve design, gas species, upstream pressure, pulse duration, and calibration tolerance.

NAMES.name: molecular_neutral_species_flow_at_outlet
NAMES.subject: neutral_species
NAMES.short: Throughput of a molecular neutral species at a gas pumping duct outlet, equal to the volumetric pumping speed at the outlet multiplied by the outlet partial pressure of that species.
NAMES.long:
Molecular neutral species flow at an outlet is the pressure-weighted gas throughput of one molecular neutral species crossing the outlet of a pumping duct. It represents the exhaust rate in vacuum-engineering units and is specific to the species partial pressure, not the total gas pressure when multiple species are present.

The outlet throughput is defined by the product of local pumping speed and species partial pressure at the outlet:

$$
Q_{s,\mathrm{out}} = S_{\mathrm{out}}\,p_{s,\mathrm{out}}
$$

where $Q_{s,\mathrm{out}}$ is the molecular neutral species throughput, $S_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the volumetric pumping speed at the duct outlet, and $p_{s,\mathrm{out}}$ is the outlet partial pressure of species $s$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from calibrated pumping speed, conductance modeling, and pressure or residual-gas measurements near the duct outlet. For an ideal gas at temperature $T$, the corresponding particle flow is $\dot{N}_s = Q_{s,\mathrm{out}}/(k_B T)$ and the molar flow is $\dot{n}_s = Q_{s,\mathrm{out}}/(R T)$.

Typical values range from about 0.01-100 Pa m^3 s^-1 for individual molecular species in fusion-vacuum pumping systems, with larger transient or high-throughput exhaust cases reaching 100-1000 Pa m^3 s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the molecular neutral species is extracted through the duct outlet in the pumping direction away from the vessel.

NAMES.name: neon_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Total number of neon atoms injected as gas during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an electron-equivalent count using the 10 bound electrons of neutral neon.
NAMES.long:
Neon prefill count is the total amount of neon gas introduced before plasma breakdown or current initiation, represented as an electron-equivalent particle count. It is species resolved and prefill-only: it excludes neon injected after breakdown and excludes other gas species used for fueling, wall conditioning, or radiative control.

The electron-equivalent normalization is defined from the injected neutral-neon atom count:

$$
N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{Ne,prefill}} = Z_{\mathrm{Ne}}\,N_{\mathrm{atom}}^{\mathrm{Ne,prefill}}
$$

where $N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{Ne,prefill}}$ is the neon prefill count, $N_{\mathrm{atom}}^{\mathrm{Ne,prefill}}$ is the number of injected neon atoms during the prefill interval, and $Z_{\mathrm{Ne}}=10$ is the atomic number of neon. This convention is an accounting normalization based on neutral atomic composition; it is not a statement that the gas is fully ionized during the prefill phase.

In practice, the injected atom count is obtained from calibrated gas-injection measurements such as valve throughput, pressure-volume-temperature accounting, or mass-flow integration over the prefill time window. The electron-equivalent count allows gas quantities for different species to be compared on a common atomic-electron basis while preserving the species identity.

Typical values are scenario and device dependent. Neon prefill may be zero when not used; nonzero values in tokamak applications can span roughly $10^{18}$-$10^{22}$ electron-equivalent counts, with larger values possible for large vacuum volumes or deliberately high-quantity gas-puff scenarios.

NAMES.name: neon_source_rate
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Instantaneous injection rate of neon gas into the plasma vessel, expressed in equivalent electrons per second.
NAMES.long: The neon source rate quantifies the instantaneous rate at which neon gas is introduced into the plasma vessel through gas injection systems. Each neon atom (atomic number $Z = 10$) contributes 10 equivalent electrons to the count, so the source rate equals 10 times the atomic injection rate expressed in atoms per second. Neon seeding is widely applied in fusion devices to control edge radiation and protect plasma-facing components from excessive heat loads, and is also employed in disruption mitigation scenarios requiring rapid radiative cooling. The source rate is inferred from calibrated flow controllers or gas injection valve diagnostics, with values ranging from $10^{20}$ to $10^{23}$ s$^{-1}$ depending on the seeding scenario. Integrating this rate over time yields the [accumulated neon count](name:accumulated_neon_count). Analogous injection rates for other species include [nitrogen_source_rate](name:nitrogen_source_rate) and [oxygen_source_rate](name:oxygen_source_rate), which follow the same equivalent-electron convention.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neon gas is being injected into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: net_efficiency_of_plant_system
NAMES.short: Net efficiency of a plant system is the dimensionless ratio of signed net electrical power exported by the plant to the total electrical power consumed by plant subsystems over the same operating interval.
NAMES.long:
Net efficiency of a plant system characterizes plant-level electrical gain by comparing signed net electrical export with the electrical power consumed by plant subsystems inside the chosen accounting boundary. It is a dimensionless ratio, so the numerator and denominator should refer to the same operating interval and accounting boundary.

The net plant efficiency is defined from signed net electrical power and plant electrical consumption:

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{net,plant}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{net}}}{P_{\mathrm{plant}}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{net}}$ is the [net electrical power of the plant system](name:net_power_of_plant_system) in W and $P_{\mathrm{plant}}$ is the [electrical power consumed by the plant system](name:net_absorbed_power_of_plant_system) in W. The denominator is the positive sum of included internal electrical loads, commonly represented inline as $P_{\mathrm{plant}} = \sum_i P_{\mathrm{cons},i}$ over plant subsystems such as heating and current drive, cryogenic cooling, pumping, control systems, and other auxiliaries as applicable.

The quantity is computed from plant-level electrical accounting, using time-averaged powers or interval-integrated energies divided over the same duration. Unlike [thermal efficiency of a plant system](name:thermal_efficiency_of_plant_system), which relates electrical generation to thermal input, net efficiency includes the effect of recirculating electrical loads and therefore measures net electrical gain relative to internal electrical consumption.

Representative values are negative during net-importing intervals, 0 at net electrical break-even, between 0 and 1 when net export is positive but smaller than internal consumption, and greater than 1 when net export exceeds internal consumption. No universal numerical range applies because the value depends on the plant boundary, operating phase, auxiliary loads, and averaging interval.
NAMES.sign: Positive when signed net electrical power is exported from the plant to an external electrical network or load.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Nitrogen prefill count is the accumulated amount of nitrogen injected during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as a dimensionless equivalent-electron count. Each nitrogen atom contributes 7 count units; molecular nitrogen N2 contributes 14 through its two constituent nitrogen atoms.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen prefill count quantifies the externally injected nitrogen delivered during the plasma prefill interval, expressed in equivalent-electron count units. The quantity counts nitrogen nuclei, not gas molecules: molecular nitrogen contributes through its two constituent nitrogen atoms.

Using the equivalent-electron convention, the count is

$$
C_\mathrm{N} = Z_\mathrm{N} N_\mathrm{N}
$$

where $C_\mathrm{N}$ is the nitrogen prefill count in dimensionless count units, $N_\mathrm{N}$ is the dimensionless number of nitrogen atoms injected, and $Z_\mathrm{N}=7$ is the dimensionless atomic number of nitrogen. For molecular nitrogen, $N_\mathrm{N}=2N_{\mathrm{N}_2}$, so each $\mathrm{N}_2$ molecule contributes 14 count units.

In practice, this quantity is computed from the calibrated nitrogen throughput during the prefill time window, using mass-flow-controller data, valve conductance calibrations, or reservoir pressure-drop measurements. It includes only externally commanded nitrogen injection during prefill, typically before breakdown or before the explicitly defined end of the prefill interval; it excludes nitrogen from wall recycling, desorption, neutral beams, pellets, and gas injection occurring after the prefill phase.

Typical trace nitrogen prefill values are about $10^{17}$-$10^{21}$ dimensionless count units, while large devices or deliberately nitrogen-rich prefill scenarios can reach $10^{21}$-$10^{23}$. As a scale reference, a $1\,\mathrm{Pa\,m^3}$ dose of $\mathrm{N}_2$ at 300 K contains about $2.4\times10^{20}$ molecules and corresponds to about $3.4\times10^{21}$ nitrogen prefill count units.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_source_rate
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Instantaneous neutral nitrogen gas injection rate into the plasma vessel, reported as an electron-equivalent particle rate. For molecular nitrogen N2, the value is 14 times the molecular flow rate because each molecule contains 14 electrons.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen source rate is the rate at which neutral nitrogen gas is introduced into the plasma vessel, expressed as an electron-equivalent particle rate. The convention is molecular nitrogen, so each injected N2 molecule contributes the equivalent of 14 electrons before any dissociation or ionization processes are considered.

The electron-equivalent rate is related to the molecular nitrogen flow rate by:

$$
S_{\mathrm{N},e} = 14\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{N}_2}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{N},e}$ is the nitrogen source rate in electron-equivalent s^-1 and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{N}_2}$ is the molecular N2 flow rate in molecules s^-1. Equivalently, a quoted electron-equivalent rate may be converted back to molecular flow as $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{N}_2}=S_{\mathrm{N},e}/14$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from calibrated gas-delivery measurements such as mass-flow calibration, valve conductance calibration, pressure-rise measurements, or gas-balance calculations. It represents the neutral gas admitted through the vessel boundary, not the subsequent local ionization, radiation, or impurity transport response inside the plasma.

Typical nitrogen injection rates used for impurity seeding are about 10^18-10^22 s^-1 in electron-equivalent units, with 0 s^-1 corresponding to no nitrogen injection and larger transient rates possible in large devices or short gas puffs. Physically valid values are finite and non-negative; if a molecular N2 flow is reported instead, its numerical value is smaller by a factor of 14.

NAMES.name: normalized_atomic_count_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Dimensionless pellet propellant-gas atom inventory equal to the physical number of atoms divided by 10^20. It counts atoms, not gas entities: a diatomic molecule contributes two atoms and a monatomic atom contributes one.
NAMES.long:
Normalized atomic count of a pellet is the total number of atoms in the pellet gas load expressed in units of $10^{20}$ atoms. It is an atom inventory rather than a molecule inventory, so molecular species are converted to their constituent atoms before summing.

For a mixture of gas species or molecular forms, the normalized atomic count is

$$
N_{\mathrm{atom},n} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{atom}}}{10^{20}} = \frac{1}{10^{20}} \sum_s A_s N_s
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{atom},n}$ is dimensionless, $N_{\mathrm{atom}}$ is the physical atom count, $N_s$ is the count of gas entities of species or molecular form $s$, and $A_s$ is the atomicity in atoms per entity. The denominator represents $10^{20}$ atoms, so $N_{\mathrm{atom},n}=1$ corresponds to $10^{20}$ atoms.

In practice this quantity is computed from the gas amount, pellet composition, injection calibration, or pressure-volume-temperature estimates using an appropriate equation of state. For molecular gasses, the measured molecule count is multiplied by atomicity before normalization; for mixtures, all components are summed after this conversion.

The physical range is $0 \le N_{\mathrm{atom},n} < \infty$. A value of 0 indicates no atoms in the counted gas load, and values greater than 1 are allowed because the normalization is a scale factor, not a fraction or probability. Device-independent numerical ranges are not implied because pellet inventories depend strongly on pellet size, species, and injection scenario.

NAMES.name: outer_atomic_count_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Total number of atoms contained in the outer shell layer of a composite pellet. It counts atomic nuclei in that layer independent of molecular binding and complements the inner-core inventory in the whole-pellet atom count.
NAMES.long:
Outer atomic count of a pellet is the total inventory of atomic nuclei contained in the pellet's outer shell layer. It is an unnormalized count: molecules, compounds, or mixtures are converted to their constituent atoms before summation, so one D$_2$ molecule contributes two atoms. Together with the [core atomic count of a pellet](name:core_atomic_count_of_pellet), it contributes to the total [atomic count of a pellet](name:atomic_count_of_pellet) and may be used to form a [normalized atomic count of a pellet](name:normalized_atomic_count_of_pellet).

For a shell volume $V_\mathrm{outer}$ with local atomic number density $n_\mathrm{atom}$, the count is

$$
N_\mathrm{outer} = \int_{V_\mathrm{outer}} n_\mathrm{atom}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $N_\mathrm{outer}$ is the outer-shell atom count, $n_\mathrm{atom}$ is the total number density of atoms after accounting for molecular stoichiometry and species composition, and $\mathbf{x}$ labels position within the shell material.

In practice, the count is computed from the shell geometry, material density, isotopic or elemental composition, and molecular formula of the pellet material. For multi-species shells, each component contributes according to its molar or atomic fraction; for example, molecular deuterium is counted by atoms rather than by molecules. The related [density of pellet](name:core_density_of_pellet) helps determine the number density used in the inventory calculation.

Typical values range from about $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ atoms for small fueling or tracer shell payloads and about $10^{21}$-$10^{23}$ atoms for large mitigation pellets, depending on pellet size, shell thickness, material density, and composition.

NAMES.name: oxygen_source_rate
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate at which oxygen gas is injected into the plasma vessel, expressed as the equivalent number of bound electrons carried by the injected oxygen atoms or molecules per second.
NAMES.long:
Oxygen source rate is the instantaneous input of oxygen gas into the plasma vessel, expressed as an equivalent-electron rate. The equivalent-electron convention counts eight electrons per oxygen atom, so the quantity tracks the injected oxygen inventory on the same counting basis as total neutral-gas injection rates rather than the instantaneous plasma electron source after ionization.

The relation between the equivalent-electron source rate and the injected neutral oxygen flow is

$$
S_\mathrm{O} = 8\,\dot{N}_\mathrm{O} = 16\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{O}_2} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{O},e}}{dt}
$$

where $S_\mathrm{O}$ is the oxygen source rate in equivalent electrons per second, $\dot{N}_\mathrm{O}$ is the rate of injected oxygen atoms, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{O}_2}$ is the rate of injected oxygen molecules, and $N_{\mathrm{O},e}$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count. For mixed atomic and molecular gas, contributions are summed with eight equivalent electrons per oxygen nucleus.

In practice, $S_\mathrm{O}$ is computed from calibrated gas-handling signals such as mass-flow-controller demand, reservoir pressure drop, or piezoelectric valve opening together with gas temperature and conductance calibration. Its time integral gives [accumulated_oxygen_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_oxygen_count_due_to_gas_injection), and it contributes to the aggregate [electron_source_rate_due_to_injection](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_injection) along with other injected species such as [hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection), [nitrogen_source_rate](name:nitrogen_source_rate), and [neon_source_rate](name:neon_source_rate). Oxygen injection is commonly used for impurity seeding, radiative-power control, radiative mantle formation, and divertor detachment studies; the subsequent ionization balance is a plasma response, not part of this injection-rate definition.

Typical controlled oxygen injection rates are about $10^{19}-10^{22}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in equivalent-electron units. Small calibration puffs or wall-conditioning flows can be below $10^{19}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$, while large impurity puffs in high-density plasmas may approach or exceed $10^{22}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_pellet_path
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at a point on a pellet injection path. It provides the flux-surface label used to relate pellet ablation or deposition to the magnetic equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
At a pellet injection path point, poloidal magnetic flux is the value of the equilibrium poloidal-flux function at the pellet position. It identifies the magnetic flux surface intersected by the pellet and relates local ablation, ionization, and deposited material to the surrounding equilibrium geometry.

Using a path coordinate $\ell$ along the pellet trajectory in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the value along the trajectory is

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{pellet}}(\ell) = \psi\!\left(R(\ell), Z(\ell)\right)
$$

where $\psi(R,Z)$ is the equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux function and $\psi_{\mathrm{pellet}}$ has unit Wb. For an axisymmetric equilibrium, $\psi$ is independent of $\phi$; $\phi(\ell)$, represented by toroidal_angle_of_along_pellet_path, locates the same path point toroidally.

In practice this quantity is computed by combining a reconstructed magnetic equilibrium with the pellet trajectory inferred from injector geometry, timing, and observations of pellet emission or ablation. Interpolation of $\psi(R,Z)$ to the trajectory point converts ablation versus distance or time into a flux-surface coordinate for deposition analysis.

Typical values are comparable to equilibrium poloidal flux values: the difference between the magnetic-axis value and the plasma-boundary value is often 0.1-10 Wb in tokamaks, and may be larger in high-current devices. Along a pellet path, the values usually span only the portion of this interval traversed before complete ablation or exit from the confined plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic field crossing a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis has positive net flux in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: power_of_plant_subsystem
NAMES.short: Real electrical power drawn by an individual plant subsystem during operation. It is the subsystem-level contribution to plant auxiliary load accounting and system-level electrical power balances.
NAMES.long:
Power of a plant subsystem is the real electrical power drawn by one defined subsystem while carrying out its operational function. It represents active electrical load rather than reactive or apparent power, and it is used to attribute auxiliary demand within plant electrical power balances.

For an accounting boundary containing $N$ subsystems, the corresponding system load is the sum of the subsystem loads:

$$
P_\mathrm{system} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} P_{\mathrm{subsystem},i}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{system}$ is the system real power in W, $P_{\mathrm{subsystem},i}$ is the real power drawn by subsystem $i$ in W, and $N$ is the dimensionless number of subsystems included in the accounting boundary. The aggregate system quantity is [power_of_plant_system](name:net_absorbed_power_of_plant_system); summing over plant systems gives [total_power_of_plant_system](name:total_power_of_plant_system), while [absorbed_power_of_plant_system](name:net_absorbed_power_of_plant_system) is the closely related system-level absorbed electrical load.

Subsystem power is measured with calibrated active-power meters, energy monitors on subsystem electrical feeds, or control-system estimates based on voltage, current, and power factor. Time averaging should match the plant power-balance interval, and shared services such as cooling, vacuum support, or control infrastructure should be allocated consistently to avoid double counting or omission.

Typical subsystem loads span about $10^3-10^8$ W. Small instrumentation, control, or auxiliary-service subsystems may draw $10^3-10^5$ W; pumps, local cooling loops, drives, and medium auxiliary equipment commonly draw $10^5-10^7$ W; major pulsed or continuous plant subsystems such as cryogenic, heating, current-drive, magnet-power, or large thermal-management equipment can reach $10^7-10^8$ W depending on operating phase.

NAMES.name: power_of_plant_system
NAMES.short: Real electrical power drawn by an individual plant system during operation, evaluated at the system electrical boundary. It is a load-oriented demand quantity; net plant-system power uses generated minus consumed accounting.
NAMES.long:
Power of a plant system is the real electrical power crossing the electrical boundary of one plant system, with consumption represented as draw from the plant electrical supply. It describes electrical demand at a system level, not thermal power, apparent power, reactive power, or accumulated energy.

For boundary accounting with a load-positive convention, the system power is defined as consumed real electrical power minus generated real electrical power within the same system boundary:

$$
P_\mathrm{system} = P_\mathrm{consumed} - P_\mathrm{generated} = \sum_{j=1}^{N} P_{\mathrm{subsystem},j}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{system}$ is this plant-system power, $P_\mathrm{consumed}$ is the real electrical power imported by loads in the system, $P_\mathrm{generated}$ is the real electrical power exported by generators belonging to the system, and $P_{\mathrm{subsystem},j}$ are [power_of_plant_subsystem](name:power_of_plant_subsystem) values using the same sign convention for the $N$ included subsystems. Internal electrical transfers between subsystems cancel in the system total. The corresponding [net_power_of_plant_system](name:net_power_of_plant_system) follows generated-minus-consumed accounting, so for the same boundary and scope $P_\mathrm{net}=P_\mathrm{generated}-P_\mathrm{consumed}=-P_\mathrm{system}$.

In practice, this quantity is obtained from electrical metering, power-converter telemetry, or a sum of subsystem feeder powers over a consistently defined system boundary. For AC supplies it is the real power from phase-wise voltage-current measurements averaged over the electrical cycle; for DC supplies it is the signed voltage-current product. Summing $P_\mathrm{system}$ over a selected set of consuming systems gives that set's load-positive electrical demand only; plant net electric output requires generated and consumed terms to be combined with consistent accounting boundaries.

Typical operating magnitudes are highly system dependent: instrumentation and control systems may draw $10^0-10^4$ W, medium auxiliary systems $10^4-10^6$ W, and large pumps, compressors, power supplies, or power-conversion systems $10^6-10^8$ W. Values can be near zero in standby or off states, and may become negative for a system exporting more electrical power than it consumes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when real electrical power flows from the plant electrical supply into the plant system across the system boundary.

NAMES.name: absorbed_power_of_plant_system
NAMES.short: Real electrical power crossing a plant-system boundary into the plant system. It is the absorbed, incoming component of the plant-system electrical power balance, distinct from generated, returned, or net power.
NAMES.long:
Absorbed power of a plant system is the real electrical power delivered across the plant-system boundary into that system. It specializes [power_of_plant_system](name:power_of_plant_system) by selecting the incoming electrical boundary-power component before any combination with generated, returned, or net power. It is not the same as internal consumption or dissipation, because storage, conversion, and later export can occur inside the boundary.

The instantaneous absorbed electrical power is the time derivative of the cumulative incoming electrical energy:

$$
P_\mathrm{abs}(t) = \frac{dE_{\mathrm{elec,in}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{abs}$ is absorbed power in W, $E_{\mathrm{elec,in}}$ is cumulative electrical energy delivered into the plant system in J, and $t$ is time in s.

In practice, absorbed power is obtained from electrical metering at the supply connections of the plant system. Terminal voltages and currents are combined as real power, summed over all relevant feeds, and averaged over an AC cycle or power-electronics switching interval when needed. Reactive power is excluded, and electrical power flowing out of the system boundary belongs to generated, returned, or net-power accounting rather than to positive absorbed power.

Typical values range from 1-10^3 W for small control or instrumentation plant systems, 10^3-10^6 W for pumps and auxiliary services, and 10^6-10^8 W for major heating, cryogenic, pulsed-power, or magnet-support plant systems; short transients in large facilities can approach 10^9 W.
NAMES.sign: Positive when real electrical power crosses the plant-system boundary into the plant system from an external electrical connection.

NAMES.name: net_absorbed_power_of_plant_system
NAMES.short: Net electrical power absorbed by a plant system, defined as the system's electrical consumption minus electrical power generated locally within the same system boundary.
NAMES.long:
Net absorbed electrical power is the net electrical import of a plant system across its defined electrical boundary. It is positive for an overall electrical load and negative for a system that produces more electrical power locally than it consumes internally.

The defining balance is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{net,abs}} = P_{\mathrm{consumed}} - P_{\mathrm{local,gen}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{consumed}}$ is the total electrical power used by equipment within the system boundary and $P_{\mathrm{local,gen}}$ is the electrical power generated within that same boundary.

In practice this quantity is obtained from electrical metering, plant power-balance calculations, or supervisory control estimates at the system boundary. It differs conceptually from a net electrical output quantity: this name represents net import required to operate the system, while net output represents export available from the system under its own accounting definition.

Typical values for individual plant systems range from $10^3$-$10^8$ W, depending on the size and operating state of loads such as pumps, cryogenic equipment, power supplies, auxiliaries, and control systems. Large pulsed or high-power subsystems may transiently approach $10^8$-$10^9$ W, while a locally generating subsystem can have a negative value.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plant system absorbs electrical power across its electrical boundary, so total electrical consumption exceeds electrical power generated locally within the same system boundary.

NAMES.name: net_power_of_plant_system
NAMES.short: Net electrical power of a plant system, equal to generated electrical power minus internal operational electrical consumption within the same system boundary.
NAMES.long:
Net electrical power of a plant system is the algebraic electrical power delivered by that system after subtracting the electrical power it consumes for its own operation. It indicates whether the chosen system boundary is a net source or net sink of electricity at a given operating condition.

For a defined plant-system boundary, the net power is

$$
P_\mathrm{net} = P_\mathrm{elec,gen} - P_\mathrm{elec,cons}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{net}$, $P_\mathrm{elec,gen}$, and $P_\mathrm{elec,cons}$ are electrical powers in W evaluated over the same time interval. $P_\mathrm{elec,gen}$ is the electrical power produced within the boundary, such as generator-terminal or power-conversion output, and $P_\mathrm{elec,cons}$ is the operational electrical power drawn by equipment inside the same boundary.

In practice, this quantity is computed from electrical metering or plant power-accounting models by summing generation feeds and subtracting allocated internal loads such as pumps, compressors, cryogenic equipment, control systems, power-conversion auxiliaries, and other parasitic consumers. The system boundary must be applied consistently: loads outside the boundary are excluded, while recirculating power and auxiliary loads inside the boundary are included. During startup, shutdown, standby, or operation of systems without local generation, the net power can be negative.

Typical values depend strongly on the boundary. Purely consuming plant systems are often about -1e3 to -1e8 W, large balance-of-plant or power-conversion systems can range from near 0 W to 1e9 W, and whole-plant net electrical output for power-plant-scale devices is commonly of order 1e8-2e9 W. Values near 0 W indicate that internal electrical consumption nearly balances local electrical generation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the system exports electrical power across its boundary after subtracting internal operational consumption.

NAMES.name: prefill_gas_pressure
NAMES.short: Neutral gas pressure in the vessel during the prefill phase, which sets the ionization conditions for electron avalanche breakdown at plasma startup via the Townsend mechanism.
NAMES.long:
The prefill gas pressure is the neutral gas pressure established in the vacuum vessel before plasma breakdown during the startup phase. A controlled amount of working gas is admitted to bring the vessel to a target pressure that optimizes the electron avalanche threshold for the available loop voltage.

The Townsend ionization model relates the gas pressure to the avalanche breakdown condition through the first Townsend ionization coefficient:

$$
\alpha = A \, p \, \exp\!\left(-\frac{B \, p}{E}\right)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the number of ionizations per unit path length, $p$ is the prefill gas pressure, $E$ is the applied electric field, and $A$ and $B$ are gas-species constants. Breakdown is achieved when $\alpha d \geq \ln(1 + 1/\gamma)$, where $d$ is the path length and $\gamma$ is the secondary electron emission coefficient, so the prefill gas pressure directly controls the loop voltage required for plasma initiation.

Vessel pressure during the prefill phase is measured by calibrated ionization gages or Penning gages and regulated through mass-flow-controlled gas injection valves. This quantity is closely related to [prefill_pressure](name:prefill_gas_pressure), which captures the same physical pressure in the specific context of the Townsend electric field calculation.

Typical prefill pressures in tokamak startup range from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-1}$ Pa, with the optimal working point set by the Paschen curve minimum for the injected gas species.

NAMES.name: pressure_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Gas pressure inside the vacuum tank of a lower hybrid antenna.
NAMES.long:
Gas pressure of a lower hybrid antenna is the scalar pressure of residual neutral gas in the antenna vacuum tank or waveguide enclosure. It characterizes the local vacuum state relevant to RF voltage holdoff, antenna conditioning, and operational safety.

For a uniform gas inventory, pressure is related to the amount of gas by the ideal-gas relation:

$$
pV = N k_B T
$$

where $p$ is gas pressure in Pa, $V$ is tank volume in m$^3$, $N$ is the number of neutral molecules, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant in J K$^{-1}$, and $T$ is gas temperature in K.

The pressure is normally inferred from vacuum instrumentation connected to the antenna tank or nearby pumping manifold. The indicated value can depend on gage calibration, gas composition, and conductance between the measurement point and the enclosed antenna volume. Operating limits and interlock thresholds are device dependent and are set by the antenna design, RF conditioning state, and local protection strategy.

Representative lower-hybrid antenna vacuum-tank pressures during prepared RF operation are commonly in the high-vacuum range, about $10^{-6}$-$10^{-3}$ Pa. Higher values may occur during conditioning, outgassing, leaks, or abnormal vacuum events.

The analogous antenna-vacuum quantity for ion-cyclotron systems is [gas_pressure_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:gas_pressure_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

NAMES.name: propane_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: propane
NAMES.short: Total propane (C3H8) introduced during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count using 26 electrons per propane molecule.
NAMES.long:
Propane prefill count is the accumulated amount of propane introduced before plasma breakdown, expressed on an equivalent-electron basis. A propane molecule, C$_3$H$_8$, contains $3 \times 6 + 8 \times 1 = 26$ electrons, so each injected molecule contributes 26 to this count.

The accumulated prefill count is defined from the propane molecular flow integrated over the prefill interval:

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}} = 26\,N_{\mathrm{mol}} = 26 \int_{t_{\mathrm{start}}}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{mol}}(t)\,dt
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the dimensionless equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{mol}}$ is the dimensionless count of propane molecules injected during prefill, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{mol}}$ is the propane molecular flow rate in molecules s$^{-1}$, and $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ are the prefill start time and breakdown time in seconds.

In practice, the value is obtained from the propane gas-injection accounting over the prefill interval, using the inferred or measured molecular throughput and the gas-species conversion factor. It contributes to the total prefill inventory [prefill_count](name:accumulated_lithium_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection) and is directly comparable with other prefill gas counts because all are expressed on the same equivalent-electron scale.

The physical range is $N_{\mathrm{eq}} \ge 0$, with $N_{\mathrm{eq}} = 0$ when no propane is introduced during prefill. No universal numerical range is implied: values depend strongly on vessel volume, prefill pressure target, gas-line calibration, and pulse scenario, and may vary by many orders of magnitude between devices and operating regimes.

NAMES.name: propane_source_rate
NAMES.subject: propane
NAMES.short: Instantaneous propane (C3H8) injection source rate into the plasma vessel, expressed as equivalent electrons per second rather than as molecule or atom counts.
NAMES.long:
Propane source rate is the rate at which neutral propane, $\mathrm{C_3H_8}$, is supplied to the plasma vessel using the electron-equivalent gas-source convention. It counts the number of bound electrons carried by the injected neutral molecules per unit time, so one propane molecule contributes 26 equivalent electrons.

The electron-equivalent rate is related to the molecular propane throughput by:

$$
\dot{N}_e^{(\mathrm{C_3H_8})} = 26\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{C_3H_8}}$ is the molecular injection rate and $26 = 3\times6 + 8\times1$ is the total nuclear charge, or neutral-electron count, of one propane molecule. This convention differs from a molecular rate, which would be smaller by a factor of 26, and from an atom-counting rate, which would count 11 neutral atoms per molecule rather than their electron inventory.

In practice the rate is computed from calibrated gas throughput measurements, valve flow models, reservoir pressure and temperature evolution, or mass-flow-controller signals, with conversion from molecular flow to electron-equivalent flow using the factor above. The electron-equivalent convention allows direct comparison with other gas source rates such as hydrogenic fueling and impurity-gas injection.

Typical propane injection rates are strongly scenario-dependent. Trace or diagnostic puffs are commonly of order $10^{19}-10^{21}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ in electron-equivalent units, while larger short impurity or wall-conditioning injections can reach $10^{22}-10^{23}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when propane is injected into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: radial_velocity_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Major-radius component of the shattered pellet center-of-mass velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radial velocity of a pellet is the component of the pellet center-of-mass velocity along the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It quantifies motion of the pellet material center of mass toward or away from the symmetry axis, separate from toroidal and vertical motion.

The radial component is obtained by projecting the center-of-mass velocity onto the local radial basis vector:

$$
v_R = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $v_R$ is the radial velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm}$ is the pellet center-of-mass velocity with components in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $R$. Together with [toroidal_velocity_of_pellet](name:toroidal_velocity_of_pellet) and [vertical_velocity_of_pellet](name:vertical_velocity_of_pellet), it specifies the pellet velocity components in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice, $v_R$ is computed from the time derivative of the pellet center-of-mass position, or from a specified launch speed and injection direction, followed by projection onto $\hat{R}$. For shattered-pellet applications, the same definition applies when the tracked center of mass represents the pellet material after fragmentation.

Typical pellet injection speeds in magnetic-confinement devices are about 100-1000 m s^-1. The radial component may be near 0 m s^-1 for nearly toroidal or vertical launch and may reach magnitudes of 100-1000 m s^-1 for predominantly radial launch; signed values depend on whether the motion is inward or outward in major radius.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pellet center of mass moves in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, toward increasing major radius $R$ and away from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: shattered_pellet_fragment_density
NAMES.subject: shattered_pellet_fragment
NAMES.short: Number density of a specified atomic species within an individual fragment produced by a shattered pellet injector.
NAMES.long:
Shattered pellet fragment density is the species-resolved number of atoms of a given species per unit physical volume of a single condensed fragment. It describes the material composition of the fragment before substantial ablation or expansion, and differs from the density of the ablated gas or plasma formed later.

For species $s$ in a fragment of volume $V_f$, the density is defined by

$$
n_s = \frac{N_s}{V_f}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of species $s$, $N_s$ is the number of atoms of that species in the fragment, and $V_f$ is the physical fragment volume.

In practice, this quantity is usually inferred from the pellet material composition, condensed-phase mass density, and the assigned or reconstructed fragment volume. For mixed-material pellets, each species component is determined from the mixture fraction; the sum over species gives the total atomic number density. Fragment-to-fragment variation can arise from nonuniform composition, porosity, cracks, coatings, thermal state, and partial vaporization during shattering.

Typical condensed hydrogen-isotope and noble-gas pellet materials have atomic number densities of about $2 \times 10^{28}$-$8 \times 10^{28}$ m^-3. Pure deuterium, tritium, or deuterium-tritium fragments are commonly a few $10^{28}$ m^-3, while minority dopants or mixed-species components can be lower in proportion to their atomic fraction.

NAMES.name: shattered_pellet_fragment_volume
NAMES.subject: shattered_pellet_fragment
NAMES.short: Volume of a single solid fragment produced by shattered pellet injection. It characterizes the fragment size distribution and contributes, together with material density, shape, and plasma conditions, to fragment ablation and material delivery.
NAMES.long:
Shattered pellet fragment volume is the physical volume occupied by one solid piece formed when a cryogenic pellet is broken before injection into the plasma. It is a geometric size measure for an individual fragment, not the total volume of the fragment cloud, and is used to characterize the fragment size distribution produced by the shattering process.

For a fragment represented by an equivalent sphere of diameter $d_
obreak\mathrm{eq}$, the fragment volume $V_f$ is

$$
V_f = \frac{\pi}{6} d_\mathrm{eq}^3
$$

where $V_f$ is the fragment volume in m$^3$ and $d_\mathrm{eq}$ is the diameter in m of a sphere with the same volume. For irregular fragments, $d_\mathrm{eq}$ is a convenient size parameter rather than a statement that the fragment is spherical.

In practice, fragment volume may be estimated from calibrated images of the shattered pellet plume, from assumed fragment-shape models, or from a mass estimate divided by the solid material density. It is closely related to the parent [diameter_of_pellet](name:diameter_of_pellet) and to material-density quantities such as [core_density_of_pellet](name:core_density_of_pellet). Combined with fragment velocity and ablation modeling, it helps determine the time-dependent material source represented by quantities such as [radial_velocity_of_pellet](name:radial_velocity_of_pellet) and atomic_source_rate_of_pellet.

Representative fragment volumes in shattered-pellet studies are often in the approximate range $10^{-12}$-$10^{-7}$ m$^3$, corresponding to sub-millimeter through several-millimeter equivalent spherical diameters. The range depends strongly on pellet size, material, shatter-tube geometry, and the fragment-size distribution assumed or measured for a particular injector.

NAMES.name: silane_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: silane
NAMES.short: Accumulated equivalent-electron count of silane (SiH4) gas injected during the prefill phase before plasma breakdown, where each SiH4 molecule contributes 18 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
The silane prefill count is the dimensionless total of silane (SiH4) gas introduced into the plasma vessel during the prefill phase — before plasma breakdown — expressed using the equivalent-electron convention in which each atom contributes a weight equal to its atomic number.

Each SiH4 molecule contributes 18 equivalent electrons: 14 from the silicon nucleus ($Z_\mathrm{Si} = 14$) and 1 from each of the four hydrogen atoms ($Z_\mathrm{H} = 1$):

$$
C_{\mathrm{SiH_4}} = Z_\mathrm{Si} + 4\,Z_\mathrm{H} = 14 + 4 = 18
$$

where $N_\mathrm{mol}$ is the number of SiH4 molecules injected before breakdown, giving a total prefill count of $18\,N_\mathrm{mol}$.

The prefill phase precedes plasma ignition and is used to condition the vessel or establish a neutral-gas background. The accumulated count records all injection events within that window, giving a species-resolved inventory of silicon and hydrogen introduced before breakdown. The corresponding post-breakdown tally is provided by [accumulated_silane_count](name:accumulated_silane_count), and the instantaneous injection rate is tracked by [silane_source_rate](name:silane_source_rate). Analogous prefill counts for other species include [accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count](name:accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count) and [nitrogen_prefill_count](name:nitrogen_prefill_count).
NAMES.sign: Positive when silane gas is injected into the vessel during the prefill phase.

NAMES.name: silane_source_rate
NAMES.subject: silane
NAMES.short: Instantaneous injection rate of silane (SiH4) gas into the plasma vessel, expressed in equivalent electrons per second.
NAMES.long:
Silane ($\mathrm{SiH_4}$, silicon tetrahydride) is a silicon-bearing compound injected as a controlled impurity source in plasma experiments. The source rate quantifies the instantaneous rate of silane introduction expressed as an equivalent-electron flux, where each $\mathrm{SiH_4}$ molecule contributes the combined atomic numbers of its constituent atoms.

Each silane molecule carries $Z_\mathrm{Si} + 4\,Z_\mathrm{H} = 14 + 4 = 18$ equivalent electrons. The equivalent-electron rate $\dot{N}_\mathrm{eq}$ relates to the molecular injection flux $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH_4}}$ by:

$$
\dot{N}_\mathrm{eq} = 18 \, \dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH_4}}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{Si} = 14$ is the atomic number of silicon, $Z_\mathrm{H} = 1$ is the atomic number of hydrogen, and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{SiH_4}}$ is the molecular injection rate in molecules per second.

The instantaneous rate is inferred from calibrated gas-valve systems monitoring flow at the injection manifold. Integrating this rate over the plasma discharge from breakdown gives the [accumulated silane count](name:accumulated_silane_count), which tracks the total equivalent-electron inventory of silane introduced during a discharge. Analogous rate quantities for other injected species include [xenon_source_rate](name:xenon_source_rate) and [nitrogen_source_rate](name:nitrogen_source_rate).
NAMES.sign: Positive when silane gas is being injected into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Instantaneous equivalent-electron source rate delivered to the plasma vessel by gas injection systems, where each injected atom contributes Z equivalent electrons per second according to its atomic number.
NAMES.long:
The source rate due to gas injection characterizes the instantaneous rate at which neutral gas is admitted to the plasma vessel by gas injection hardware, expressed as an equivalent-electron count rate. Every injected atom of atomic number $Z$ contributes $Z$ equivalent electrons per second to the total inventory rate, providing a unified accounting framework across species of differing nuclear charge.

The defining relation for a single injected species is:

$$
\dot{S} = Z \cdot \dot{N}_{\mathrm{atoms}}
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{atoms}}$ is the raw atomic delivery rate in atoms per second and $Z$ is the atomic number of the injected species. For simultaneous multi-species injection, contributions are summed over all active species.

This rate is inferred from calibrated mass-flow controllers or upstream pressure-rise measurements on the gas supply plumbing. It is the instantaneous time derivative of the corresponding accumulated equivalent-electron inventories, such as [accumulated_argon_count](name:accumulated_argon_count) or [accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection). The nearest-peer quantity gas_particle_source_rate_over_vessel_due_to_gas_injection provides the vessel-integrated analog expressed in raw gas-phase particles rather than equivalent electrons.
NAMES.sign: Positive when gas is being delivered into the vessel at a nonzero rate, increasing the equivalent-electron particle inventory.

NAMES.name: argon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Instantaneous argon gas injection source rate expressed as equivalent electrons per second; the actual argon atom injection rate is multiplied by 18, the atomic number of argon.
NAMES.long:
Argon source rate due to gas injection is the instantaneous rate at which neutral argon is supplied by a gas injection system, expressed in equivalent electrons per second. The equivalent-electron convention weights each argon atom by its atomic number, so one injected argon atom contributes 18 equivalent electrons for bookkeeping of particle throughput and impurity fueling.

The equivalent-electron source rate is related to the physical argon atom injection rate by:

$$
S_{\mathrm{Ar,eq}} = 18\,\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Ar}}}{dt}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{Ar,eq}}$ is the argon source rate in equivalent electrons per second, $N_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the number of injected argon atoms, and $dN_{\mathrm{Ar}}/dt$ is the atomic injection rate in atoms per second. The corresponding atomic rate is therefore $S_{\mathrm{Ar,eq}}/18$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from calibrated gas-flow measurements, valve commands combined with conductance models, reservoir pressure decay, or mass-flow controller signals. It represents the delivered source from the injection hardware, not the fraction that is ionized, confined, or retained in the plasma.

Typical impurity-seeding values are about $10^{20}$-$10^{23}$ s^-1 in equivalent-electron units, depending on device size and seeding scenario. Short high-throughput argon injection pulses used for rapid radiative cooling or disruption mitigation can reach about $10^{24}$-$10^{26}$ s^-1 for brief intervals, while the value is zero when no argon is being delivered.

NAMES.name: carbon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Instantaneous electron-equivalent carbon source from gas injection. Each injected carbon atom contributes six source counts, so this rate is six times the raw carbon-atom delivery rate and is consistent with accumulated carbon source-count accounting.
NAMES.long:
Carbon source rate due to gas injection is the instantaneous electron-equivalent particle source associated with carbon introduced by gas injection. It uses full-ionization electron-yield accounting: each carbon atom contributes six counts, independent of its later charge-state evolution, so it differs from the raw carbon-atom delivery rate.

Let $\Gamma_C^{\mathrm{atom}}$ denote the raw carbon-atom delivery rate and $N_C^{\mathrm{eq}}$ the accumulated electron-equivalent carbon count. The defining relation is:

$$
S_C = 6\,\Gamma_C^{\mathrm{atom}} = \frac{dN_C^{\mathrm{eq}}}{dt}
$$

where $S_C$ is the carbon source rate due to gas injection, the factor 6 is the nuclear charge of carbon, and $N_C^{\mathrm{eq}}$ is counted in electron-equivalent source counts. The raw rate $\Gamma_C^{\mathrm{atom}}$ corresponds to [carbon_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:carbon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection), while the time integral of $S_C$ gives changes in [accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_carbon_count_due_to_gas_injection) in the same equivalent-count convention.

In practice, the raw carbon-atom rate is inferred from calibrated gas-flow measurements, pressure-volume calibrations, or valve models together with the gas composition. For molecular injections such as methane or carbon monoxide, the raw carbon-atom rate counts the number of carbon atoms per molecule, then the source rate is obtained by multiplying by six. Ionization timing, transport, and the instantaneous charge-state distribution in the plasma do not change this bookkeeping factor.

Values are zero when no carbon-containing gas is injected. Diagnostic or trace impurity puffs commonly give 10^17-10^20 s^-1 in electron-equivalent counts, while stronger impurity dosing or conditioning pulses can reach 10^21-10^22 s^-1; the corresponding raw carbon-atom delivery rate is smaller by a factor of six.

NAMES.name: helium_3_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate of helium-3 atom delivery into the plasma vessel by gas injection, where each He-3 atom counts as two equivalent electrons due to its atomic number Z = 2.
NAMES.long:
The helium-3 source rate due to gas injection is the instantaneous equivalent-electron count rate for helium-3 ($^3$He, $Z = 2$) delivered by external gas injection systems into the plasma vessel. In the equivalent-electron counting convention, each injected helium-3 atom contributes 2 count units to the rate, so the reported value equals twice the physical atom delivery rate.

The equivalent-electron rate $\dot{N}_{\text{He-3}}$ is the time derivative of the cumulative helium-3 inventory:

$$
\dot{N}_{\text{He-3}} = \frac{d N_{\text{He-3}}}{dt}
$$

where $N_{\text{He-3}}$ is the [accumulated helium-3 count since plasma breakdown](name:accumulated_helium_3_count_due_to_gas_injection).

The injection rate is inferred from calibrated gas feed diagnostics such as piezoelectric or solenoid valves with integrated flow metering. Helium-3 is employed for minority-species ion cyclotron heating, specialized fueling experiments, and impurity studies requiring a light noble gas. The analogous hydrogen rate is [hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection), and the species-summed total across all injected gasses is given by [source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:source_rate_due_to_gas_injection).
NAMES.sign: Positive when helium-3 gas is being delivered into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: helium_4_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate of helium-4 atom delivery into the plasma vessel by gas injection, where each He-4 atom with atomic number Z = 2 contributes two equivalent electrons to particle inventory accounting.
NAMES.long:
The helium-4 source rate due to gas injection quantifies the instantaneous number of $^4$He atoms introduced per unit time into the plasma vessel through externally controlled gas injection valves. Helium-4, comprising two protons and two neutrons, is used in fusion devices for plasma heating studies, alpha-particle ash simulation, and wall conditioning scenarios.

The source rate $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4}}$ is the time derivative of the cumulative helium-4 atom count tracked by [accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:accumulated_helium_4_count_due_to_gas_injection):

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4}} = \frac{d N_{\mathrm{He4}}}{dt}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{He4}}$ is the total helium-4 atom count since plasma breakdown. For electron-equivalent particle accounting, the contribution to the total inventory rate is $Z\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4}} = 2\dot{N}_{\mathrm{He4}}$, reflecting helium's atomic number. This species-resolved rate is one component of the total [source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) summed over all injected species, and is directly analogous to [helium_3_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:helium_3_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) for the lighter helium isotope.

The rate is determined from calibrated mass-flow controllers or conductance-based gas metering on the injection lines. Typical values range from $10^{20}$ to $10^{22}$ s$^{-1}$ for seeding and fueling applications in present-day tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when helium-4 gas is actively flowing into the plasma vessel, increasing the helium-4 atom inventory.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Source rate of hydrogen atoms supplied into the plasma by gas injection. Because hydrogen has unit atomic number, each injected hydrogen atom also counts as one electron-equivalent particle per second.
NAMES.long:
The hydrogen source rate due to gas injection is the instantaneous rate at which hydrogen atoms are supplied toward the plasma by a gas-injection system. It is counted as hydrogen atoms per second; because neutral hydrogen has atomic number $Z_\mathrm{H}=1$, the same numerical value is also the electron-equivalent particle source rate before ionization.

The rate is the time derivative of the cumulative injected hydrogen count, with molecular gas throughput converted by stoichiometry:

$$
S_{\mathrm{H,gas}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{H,gas}}}{dt} = \sum_k \nu_{\mathrm{H},k}\,\Phi_k
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{H,gas}}$ is the hydrogen source rate in s$^{-1}$, $N_{\mathrm{H,gas}}$ is the accumulated injected hydrogen atom count, $\Phi_k$ is the injected molecular throughput of gas component $k$ in s$^{-1}$, and $\nu_{\mathrm{H},k}$ is the number of hydrogen atoms in each molecule of component $k$. For example, one atomic H particle gives $\nu_{\mathrm{H}}=1$, while one H$_2$ molecule gives $\nu_{\mathrm{H},\mathrm{H}_2}=2$ and therefore contributes two hydrogen atoms, or two electron-equivalent particles.

In practice this rate is obtained from calibrated gas valves, mass-flow controllers, reservoir pressure-drop measurements, or line-throughput calibrations, followed by conversion from molecular flow to atom rate. The quantity is the hydrogen-species contribution to the total gas-injection source rate and is time-integrated to obtain the accumulated injected hydrogen count.

Typical values range from about $10^{19}$-$10^{23}$ s$^{-1}$ in tokamak operation, with lower values used for small puffs, wall conditioning, or edge-density control, and higher values used for strong fueling in larger plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when hydrogen gas is supplied from the gas-injection system into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: krypton_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Instantaneous krypton gas injection rate into the plasma vessel, expressed in equivalent electrons per second. Each neutral krypton atom contributes 36 equivalent electrons according to its nuclear charge.
NAMES.long:
Krypton source rate due to gas injection is the rate at which krypton atoms are introduced into the plasma vessel by a gas injection system, expressed with equivalent-electron weighting. This charge-weighted convention counts one neutral krypton atom as 36 equivalent electrons, allowing krypton injection to be compared with other particle sources in balance calculations.

The equivalent-electron krypton source rate is related to the physical krypton atom injection rate by:

$$
S_{\mathrm{Kr}} = Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Kr}} = 36\,\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Kr}}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the krypton source rate in equivalent electrons per second, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the neutral krypton atom injection rate in atoms per second, and $Z_{\mathrm{Kr}} = 36$ is the atomic number of krypton.

In practice this quantity is computed from calibrated gas-valve, piezo-valve, or mass-flow-controller throughput using gas species, plenum pressure, temperature, valve conductance, and timing response. The weighting is based on nuclear charge and does not imply that the injected atoms are fully ionized at the injection location.

Representative controlled krypton seeding rates are about $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ s^-1 in equivalent-electron units, corresponding to roughly $3 \times 10^{16}$-$3 \times 10^{19}$ krypton atoms per second. Short high-throughput puffs may exceed this range depending on the fueling hardware and experiment scenario.
NAMES.sign: Positive when krypton is injected into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: lithium_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Instantaneous lithium gas-injection source rate into the plasma vessel, expressed as equivalent electrons per second. Because lithium has atomic number 3, one injected neutral lithium atom contributes three equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
Lithium source rate due to gas injection is the instantaneous rate at which a lithium gas-feed source delivers lithium into the plasma vessel, expressed using the equivalent-electron counting convention. It is the lithium-species contribution to the total [source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:source_rate_due_to_gas_injection); analogous species-resolved quantities include [hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) and [helium_3_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:helium_3_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection). Lithium gas injection may be used for wall conditioning, impurity control, or plasma-facing-component surface treatment.

The equivalent-electron source rate is related to the atomic lithium flow rate by the lithium atomic number:

$$
S_{\mathrm{Li,eq}} = Z_{\mathrm{Li}}\,\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Li,atoms}}}{dt}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{Li,eq}}$ is the lithium equivalent-electron source rate in s$^{-1}$, $Z_{\mathrm{Li}} = 3$ is the dimensionless atomic number of lithium, and $dN_{\mathrm{Li,atoms}}/dt$ is the neutral lithium atom delivery rate in atoms s$^{-1}$. The time integral of $S_{\mathrm{Li,eq}}$ gives the accumulated equivalent-electron lithium delivery, corresponding to [accumulated_lithium_count](name:accumulated_lithium_count) when that cumulative quantity is used.

The rate is commonly inferred from calibrated gas-valve flow measurements, mass-flow controllers, or the time evolution of plenum pressure and temperature upstream of the injection valve. Converting an atomic or molecular lithium flow to this quantity requires applying the equivalent-electron factor for the number of lithium atoms delivered.

Typical lithium gas-injection source rates span about $10^{18}$-$10^{22}$ s$^{-1}$ in equivalent-electron units, depending on valve conductance, pulse duration, conditioning scenario, and whether the injection is a small perturbative puff or a stronger wall-treatment flow.
NAMES.sign: Positive when lithium gas flows into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: source_rate_due_to_injection
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate at which particles are supplied to the plasma by active injection systems, equal to the time derivative of the cumulative injected particle inventory across all injected species.
NAMES.long:
The source rate due to injection quantifies the instantaneous particle supply from externally controlled injection hardware — gas valves, neutral beam injectors, pellet launchers — entering the plasma or vessel. It serves as the externally applied source term in the particle balance equation and abstracts over species-resolved formulations such as [deuterium_source_rate_due_to_injection](name:deuterium_source_rate_due_to_injection), which tallies atomic injection in atoms per second, and electron-equivalent formulations such as [electron_source_rate_due_to_injection](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_injection), which weights each injected species $s$ by its nuclear charge number $Z_s$ to represent the ionizable electron inventory it can contribute.

The rate is the time derivative of the cumulative injected count $N(t)$:

$$
\dot{N}(t) = \frac{dN}{dt}
$$

where $N$ represents either a raw atomic count or an electron-equivalent inventory depending on the specific formulation. It is inferred from calibrated gas valve throughput and flow-meter readings or from pellet injection timing corrected for delivery efficiency. Closely related quantities are particle_source_rate_over_vessel_due_to_gas_injection and source_rate_due_to_pellet_injection, which distinguish delivery mechanism. Typical values span $10^{20}$–$10^{23}$ s$^{-1}$ for gas injection in medium-to-large tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when particles flow from the injection system into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: deuterium_source_rate_due_to_injection
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate at which deuterium is supplied to the plasma by active injection systems. Deuterium is a Z=1 isotope, so the deuterium particle rate is numerically equal to the equivalent-electron source rate: one delivered deuterium nucleus counts as one.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium source rate due to injection is the instantaneous number of deuterium nuclei delivered per unit time by active fueling systems such as gas valves or pellet injectors. It is a species-resolved particle source: molecular deuterium is counted after dissociation, so one $\mathrm{D}_2$ molecule contributes two deuterium nuclei. Because deuterium has charge number $Z=1$, this particle count is also the equivalent-electron count that would result after full ionization.

The rate is the time derivative of the cumulative deuterium inventory delivered by the included injection systems:

$$
S_D^{\mathrm{inj}}(t) = \frac{dN_D^{\mathrm{inj}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $S_D^{\mathrm{inj}}$ is the deuterium injection source rate and $N_D^{\mathrm{inj}}$ is the cumulative number of injected deuterium nuclei, counted in equivalent-electron units for this $Z=1$ isotope.

In practice the quantity is computed from calibrated gas throughput, valve timing, reservoir conditions, pellet mass, pellet repetition rate, or other metered injector information, with isotope fractions and molecular composition converted to deuterium nuclei. It describes the material supplied by the injector, not the fraction that is ionized, confined, recycled from surfaces, or retained by the plasma. A gas-only cumulative count, such as [deuterium_count_due_to_gas_injection](name:deuterium_count_due_to_gas_injection), is the integral of only the gas-injection subset and must not include pellet or other non-gas contributions.

Typical time-averaged rates are about $10^{19}$-$10^{22}$ s^-1 for gas fueling in medium and large magnetic-confinement devices. Pellet events can give short apparent rates of about $10^{22}$-$10^{24}$ s^-1 when the pellet inventory is divided by the delivery interval.

NAMES.name: electron_source_rate_due_to_injection
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Instantaneous electron-equivalent source rate supplied by plasma injection systems. It is the sum over injected atomic species of nuclear charge number times the atomic injection rate, representing the electron inventory that the injected material can contribute after ionization.
NAMES.long:
Electron source rate due to injection is the electron-equivalent particle rate delivered to the plasma or vessel by fueling or material injection systems. It counts the number of electrons per second associated with the injected atoms after ionization, and is used for particle inventory and density-control accounting rather than as a local ionization-rate density.

For a mixture of injected atomic species, the rate is defined by

$$
\dot{N}_{e,\mathrm{inj}} = \sum_s Z_s\,\dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{inj}}
$$

where $\dot{N}_{e,\mathrm{inj}}$ is the electron-equivalent injection rate, $s$ indexes the injected atomic species, $Z_s$ is the nuclear charge number of species $s$, and $\dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{inj}}$ is its atomic injection rate. Molecular flows are converted to atomic rates before applying the sum; for example, each injected $\mathrm{D}_2$ molecule contributes two deuterium atoms and therefore two electron equivalents after complete ionization.

In practice this quantity is computed from calibrated gas-valve throughput, pellet or compact-toroid particle content, or other injector flow measurements combined with the specified species composition. It may represent a single injector, a subsystem, or the total injected electron-equivalent rate, depending on the physical scope being described.

Typical values span about $10^{19}$-$10^{23}$ s$^{-1}$ for ordinary gas fueling valves in present-day tokamaks. Short high-throughput events such as massive gas injection or pellet injection can reach about $10^{22}$-$10^{25}$ s$^{-1}$ for brief intervals.

NAMES.name: thermal_efficiency_of_plant_system
NAMES.short: Fraction of total thermal power supplied to the whole plant heat-conversion system that becomes gross useful electrical output. Equivalently, one minus the ratio of rejected thermal power to thermal power input, evaluated over the same plant boundary and time interval.
NAMES.long:
Thermal efficiency of the plant system is the dimensionless fraction of thermal power supplied to all plant heat-conversion stages that is converted into gross useful electrical output. It is an aggregate plant-level heat-balance quantity, not the efficiency of a single component or thermodynamic cycle.

The plant thermal efficiency is defined from the steady or time-averaged power balance:

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{th,plant}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{el,gross}}}{P_{\mathrm{th,in}}} = 1 - \frac{P_{\mathrm{th,reject}}}{P_{\mathrm{th,in}}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th,in}}$ is the total positive thermal power supplied to the heat-conversion system in W, $P_{\mathrm{th,reject}}$ is the total positive thermal power rejected to heat sinks in W, and $P_{\mathrm{el,gross}}$ is the gross electrical power generated in W before subtraction of plant auxiliary electrical consumption. The definition is valid only for a consistent plant boundary and averaging interval with $P_{\mathrm{th,in}} > 0$; for a closed steady-state heat balance without unaccounted energy storage, $0 \le \eta_{\mathrm{th,plant}} \le 1$.

In practice, this efficiency is computed by summing thermal power flows across the chosen plant boundary and through all thermal conversion stages. Thermal power entering the conversion system is counted as heat input, while thermal power discharged to condensers, coolers, exhaust streams, or the environment is counted as rejected heat; signed component-port thermal powers must therefore be oriented consistently before forming the aggregate sums.

Typical values are 0.25-0.45 for steam Rankine plant concepts, 0.35-0.50 for high-temperature advanced cycles, and up to about 0.60 for idealized or highly optimized high-temperature conversion systems. Values outside 0-1 usually indicate inconsistent boundaries, transient energy storage, sign errors in heat-flow accounting, or that the quantity is not being evaluated as a closed plant thermal balance.

NAMES.name: thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket
NAMES.short: Total non-nuclear thermal power deposited on the tritium breeding blanket, integrated over the relevant blanket-facing area. It represents plasma-facing heat loads and excludes volumetric neutron and gamma heating within the blanket material.
NAMES.long:
Thermal power of the breeder blanket is the total rate at which non-nuclear heat is deposited on or transferred into the tritium breeding blanket from plasma-facing thermal loads.
