It is an integrated power over the relevant blanket-facing area, not a heat flux density, and is distinct from volumetric neutron and gamma heating represented by [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket).

For a surface heat-load representation, the integrated thermal power is defined by the area integral of the local non-nuclear heat flux entering the blanket:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th,bb}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{bb}}} q_{\mathrm{th}} \, dA
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{th,bb}}$ is the integrated blanket thermal power in W, $A_{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the blanket-facing area in m^2, $q_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the local non-nuclear heat flux density in W m^-2, and $dA$ is the surface element in m^2.

In plant energy accounting this quantity is usually obtained from thermal-load modeling, radiation transport to plasma-facing surfaces, neutral and charged-particle heat-transfer estimates when applicable, or calorimetric heat-balance measurements in test modules. Radiative contributions may be related to [incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), while total and layer-resolved nuclear contributions should be treated separately using [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket) and [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer).

Typical integrated non-nuclear blanket thermal powers in reactor studies are of order 10^6-10^8 W, depending on plasma radiation distribution, exposed blanket area, divertor shielding, and first-wall or blanket module design. Volumetric nuclear heating can be larger in power-producing blankets and should not be inferred from this quantity alone.
NAMES.sign: Positive when thermal energy is deposited in the breeder blanket.

NAMES.name: toroidal_velocity_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the shattered-pellet center-of-mass velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal velocity of a pellet is the component of its center-of-mass velocity tangent to circles of constant $R$ and $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes motion around the torus rather than radial motion in $R$ or vertical motion in $Z$.

It is defined by projecting the pellet center-of-mass velocity vector onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_\phi = \mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is the pellet center-of-mass velocity vector in m.s^-1, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, and $v_\phi$ is the toroidal component in m.s^-1.

In practice, $v_\phi$ is specified from the intended pellet trajectory or inferred from time-resolved center-of-mass positions by differentiating the toroidal position and projecting the resulting velocity onto $\hat{\phi}$. For a shattered pellet, the center of mass is the mass-weighted center of the represented pellet material or fragment ensemble.

Representative absolute values are 0-500 m.s^-1 for many pellet-injection applications; near-radial launches can have $|v_\phi|$ close to 0, while oblique launches can have toroidal components of tens to several hundred m.s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pellet center of mass moves in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: total_gas_source_rate_at_midplane_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Total gas injection rate from valves located near the equatorial midplane of the vacuum vessel, expressed as the number of neutral gas particles supplied per unit time. It is the midplane contribution to the overall gas source from externally actuated injection valves.
NAMES.long:
The total gas source rate at midplane due to gas injection is the instantaneous number of neutral gas particles delivered per unit time by all gas injection valves located near the vessel equatorial midplane. It represents the midplane valve contribution to the externally supplied gas source before subsequent transport, ionization, recycling, or pumping processes modify the neutral population.

For the set of midplane injection valves, the total rate is the sum of the individual valve particle throughputs:

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{mid}}^{\mathrm{gas\,inj}} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{mid}}} \dot{N}_k
$$

where $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{mid}}^{\mathrm{gas\,inj}}$ is the total midplane gas injection source rate, $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{mid}}$ is the set of valves assigned to the midplane region, and $\dot{N}_k$ is the particle throughput of valve $k$ in s^-1.

In practice, each valve rate is obtained from calibrated gas throughput measurements or inferred from valve conductance, opening command, gas species, upstream pressure, downstream pressure, and gas temperature. Time integration of this rate gives the corresponding accumulated injected particle count for the midplane valves, while sums over upper, midplane, and lower valve groups give broader total gas source rates.

Typical tokamak midplane gas injection rates are about 10^19-10^22 s^-1. Small diagnostic puffs or edge perturbation pulses are often near 10^19-10^20 s^-1, whereas routine fueling or strong feedback-controlled fueling can reach 10^21-10^22 s^-1.

NAMES.name: total_lower_gas_source_rate_of_vacuum_vessel_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Total particle injection rate from gas valves in the lower region of the vacuum vessel.
NAMES.long:
The total lower gas source rate is the combined rate at which particles are introduced into the vacuum vessel by gas injection valves located near the lower wall or lower poloidal region. It represents the lower-region contribution to externally supplied neutral fueling.

The rate is defined as the sum of the particle source rates from all lower-region gas injection valves:

$$
\dot{N}_\mathrm{lower} = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{lower}} \dot{N}_i
$$

where $\dot{N}_\mathrm{lower}$ is the total lower gas source rate and $\dot{N}_i$ is the particle injection rate from the $i$-th lower-region valve, both in s$^{-1}$.

In practice, the individual valve rates are obtained by converting calibrated gas throughput to particle rate using the injected gas species and molecular or atomic content. The quantity is useful for comparing lower-region fueling with midplane or upper-region fueling and for identifying poloidal asymmetries in neutral particle sources. The corresponding time integral is the accumulated lower gas particle count.

Typical values range from $10^{20}$-$10^{23}$ s$^{-1}$ in tokamak gas fueling, depending on device size, injected species, valve configuration, and fueling scenario.

NAMES.name: total_particle_source_rate_at_wall_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Total gas-puff particle source rate at the wall is the aggregate rate at which wall gas-injection valves introduce particles, summed over all included injection ports and species. It contributes to the global particle balance.
NAMES.long:
The total particle source rate at the wall due to gas injection is the combined gas-puff influx from wall-mounted injection valves, expressed as the number of injected particles per unit time. It is an external fueling source for particle-balance calculations and represents the aggregate over the selected wall ports and gas species.

If $\dot{N}_{s,v}^{\mathrm{gas}}(t)$ is the particle source rate from valve $v$ for species $s$, after any molecular throughput has been converted to the counted particle basis, the total rate is

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{tot,wall}}^{\mathrm{gas}}(t) = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{wall}}} \dot{N}_{s,v}^{\mathrm{gas}}(t)
$$

where $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of included particle species and $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the set of wall gas-injection valves. For molecular gasses, stoichiometric factors are applied before summing when the balance is expressed in atomic, neutral-particle, or electron-equivalent counts.

In practice this rate is obtained from calibrated valve commands, plenum pressure and temperature, gas species, conductance models, or direct flow-meter measurements. Its time integral over a fueling interval gives the corresponding accumulated injected particle count, while the instantaneous per-source contribution is conceptually related to a gas source rate at the wall.

Typical values range from 10^19-10^22 s^-1 for steady or moderately pulsed gas puffing in small and medium tokamaks, and can reach 10^22-10^24 s^-1 during high-throughput fueling transients or in larger devices. The rate is zero when no gas-injection valves are open and can vary rapidly with valve timing and plenum conditions.

NAMES.name: total_power_of_plant_system
NAMES.short: Aggregate electrical power consumed by all plant systems during operation. It represents the total auxiliary electrical load of the plant, summed over individual plant-system consumption terms.
NAMES.long:
Total plant-system power is the aggregate electrical load required to operate all auxiliary plant systems. It includes electrical consumption by systems such as pumps, cryogenics, heating and current-drive auxiliaries, tritium processing, cooling, control, and other balance-of-plant services when those systems are drawing power.

The total is defined as the sum of the consumed electrical power of each plant system:

$$
P_{\mathrm{plant,total}} = \sum_i P_{\mathrm{plant},i}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{plant,total}}$ is the total plant-system electrical consumption in W, $P_{\mathrm{plant},i}$ is the electrical power consumed by plant system $i$ in W, and the sum extends over all plant systems included in the plant operating boundary. Each term is treated as a positive electrical load; this quantity is not a signed net export or generation term.

In practice, the quantity is computed from electrical metering, plant control signals, or design-point power budgets for the contributing systems. Time averaging should be chosen consistently with the plant operating state being represented, because pulsed operation, recirculating power, standby loads, and transient actuator demands can change the aggregate load substantially.

Typical values range from 1-100 MW for large experimental facilities and from 100-1000 MW for power-plant studies, depending strongly on heating and current-drive demand, cryogenic load, coolant pumping power, and balance-of-plant design.

NAMES.name: total_thermal_coolant_absorbed_power_at_wall
NAMES.short: Total thermal power transferred from plasma-facing wall structures to the active coolant circuits, integrating heat-load contributions from all cooled plasma-facing surfaces including the first wall, divertor, and limiter tiles.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the aggregate rate at which thermal energy is extracted from plasma-facing wall structures by the active cooling circuits. It encompasses heat deposited by plasma particle bombardment, charge-exchange neutrals, radiation, and nuclear heating that is conducted through the wall material and subsequently removed by the coolant, representing the primary thermal energy removal pathway from the plasma-facing components.

In calorimetric practice, this power is inferred from the coolant enthalpy rise across each cooling circuit:

$$
P_{\rm cool} = \sum_i \dot{m}_i \, c_{p,i} \, (T_{{\rm out},i} - T_{{\rm in},i})
$$

where $\dot{m}_i$ is the coolant mass flow rate through circuit $i$, $c_{p,i}$ is the specific heat capacity of the coolant fluid, and $T_{{\rm out},i}$ and $T_{{\rm in},i}$ are the outlet and inlet temperatures of that circuit.

In steady-state operation, this value closely tracks the total plasma-origin heat load described by [plasma_deposited_power_at_wall](name:plasma_deposited_power_at_wall), with discrepancies arising from nuclear wall heating, eddy-current losses, and transient thermal storage in wall structures. It is a key thermal-hydraulic parameter for assessing plasma-facing component load limits and validating cooling system performance against the incident heat load captured by total_deposited_plasma_power_at_wall. Typical magnitudes range from a few to tens of megawatts in current research tokamaks and are projected to reach several hundred megawatts in reactor-class devices.

NAMES.name: total_thermal_power_at_inlet
NAMES.short: Gross thermal power delivered to the heat-input side of a power conversion cycle in a fusion power plant. It is the total recoverable heat entering the cycle before thermal-to-electric conversion, as opposed to the rejected heat or the net electrical output.
NAMES.long:
Total thermal power at the inlet is the gross heat rate carried into the power conversion cycle by the working and coolant fluids, before any thermal-to-electric conversion. It is the heat-input reference against which rejected heat and thermal conversion efficiency are balanced, and is the counterpart of the [total thermal power at the outlet](name:total_thermal_power_at_outlet), which carries the rejected heat to the cold sink.

The inlet thermal power is the sum, over all coolant and working-fluid streams feeding the cycle, of mass flow rate multiplied by the enthalpy rise relative to the cycle's cold-return state:

$$
P_\mathrm{th,in} = \sum_i \dot{m}_i \left( h_{i,\mathrm{in}} - h_{i,\mathrm{ref}} \right)
$$

where $\dot{m}_i$ is the mass flow rate of stream $i$ in kg/s, $h_{i,\mathrm{in}}$ is its specific enthalpy at the cycle inlet in J/kg, and $h_{i,\mathrm{ref}}$ is the specific enthalpy of the corresponding cold return state in J/kg. The thermal conversion efficiency follows inline as $\eta_\mathrm{th} = (P_\mathrm{th,in} - P_\mathrm{th,out})/P_\mathrm{th,in}$, where $P_\mathrm{th,out}$ is the heat rejected from the cycle.

In practice this quantity is obtained from a steady-state plant heat balance or calorimetrically from measured coolant mass flow rates and enthalpy changes across the heat exchangers that feed the conversion cycle. The per-stream contributions correspond to the [thermal power of plant component ports](name:thermal_power_of_plant_component_port) summed over the inlet ports of the conversion cycle.

For reactor-scale plants the inlet thermal power is of the order of one to several gigawatts, with the precise value set by the heat sources coupled to the cycle and the plant design.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net heat flows into the power conversion cycle.

NAMES.name: total_thermal_power_at_outlet
NAMES.short: Total waste-heat power rejected from the power-conversion cycle to the environment rather than converted into useful electrical output.
NAMES.long:
Total thermal power at the outlet is the rate at which a power-conversion cycle rejects heat to its low-temperature sink. It represents the waste-heat load that must be removed by condensers, cooling water systems, dry coolers, cooling towers, or other heat-rejection equipment after useful electrical work has been extracted.

For a steady power-conversion cycle, the first-law power balance is:

$$
P_\mathrm{out} = P_\mathrm{in} - P_\mathrm{net}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{out}$ is the rejected thermal power in W, $P_\mathrm{in}$ is the [total thermal power at the inlet](name:total_thermal_power_at_inlet) in W, and $P_\mathrm{net}$ is the net useful electrical power delivered by the conversion system in W. The thermal efficiency is $\eta = P_\mathrm{net}/P_\mathrm{in}$, so the rejected fraction is $P_\mathrm{out}/P_\mathrm{in} = 1 - \eta$; for a heat engine operating between hot and cold reservoirs, $\eta$ is limited by the reservoir temperatures through the second law of thermodynamics.

In practice this quantity is obtained from a plant-level energy balance, from calorimetry of the heat-sink stream, or from both. Calorimetric estimates use measured coolant mass flow rate and enthalpy rise across the heat-rejection equipment, while electrical metering provides the net work term needed to close the cycle balance.

For reactor-scale fusion power-plant studies, thermal efficiencies of about 30-40% imply rejected heat loads of about 60-70% of the inlet thermal power. Commercial-scale cases with several hundred MW of net electrical output typically reject about 1-3 GW of thermal power, depending on cycle efficiency, auxiliary loads, and heat-sink temperature.

NAMES.name: tritium_prefill_count
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Accumulated number of tritium atoms injected as gas during the plasma prefill phase, expressed in equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
The tritium prefill count records the total number of tritium atoms ($^3_1\text{H}$, charge number $Z = 1$) delivered to the vessel as neutral gas during the prefill phase — the period from the start of gas injection up to plasma breakdown. Because tritium is a hydrogen isotope with $Z = 1$, the equivalent-electron count equals the raw atom count directly.

The prefill phase establishes the initial neutral gas background required for reproducible plasma initiation; the tritium component is particularly relevant in deuterium-tritium operations, where it contributes to the initial fuel mix and breakdown conditions. The count is accumulated from calibrated gas injection valve signals integrated over the duration of the prefill phase. For multi-species prefill scenarios, the total electron-equivalent inventory is $\sum_s Z_s N_s$, where $Z_s$ is the charge number and $N_s$ the atom count for species $s$.

This quantity complements [deuterium_prefill_count](name:deuterium_prefill_count), [neon_prefill_count](name:neon_prefill_count), and [krypton_prefill_count](name:krypton_prefill_count), which together with this name characterize the full multi-species neutral gas inventory available at breakdown; the aggregate is captured by [prefill_count](name:accumulated_lithium_prefill_count_due_to_gas_injection).
NAMES.sign: Positive when tritium atoms have been injected into the vessel during the prefill phase.

NAMES.name: tritium_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Instantaneous source rate of tritium atoms supplied to the plasma by gas injection.
NAMES.long:
Tritium source rate due to gas injection is the instantaneous rate at which neutral gas injection delivers tritium atoms, equivalently tritium nuclei carried by injected neutrals, into the plasma particle source. It is the tritium-species component of the gas-injection particle source and counts atoms rather than injected molecules.

It is the time derivative of the accumulated tritium atom count delivered by gas injection:

$$
S_T^{\mathrm{GI}}(t) = \frac{dN_T^{\mathrm{GI}}}{dt}
$$

where $S_T^{\mathrm{GI}}$ is the tritium source rate in s$^{-1}$, $N_T^{\mathrm{GI}}$ is the accumulated number of tritium atoms delivered by gas injection as a dimensionless count, and $t$ is time in seconds. Conversely, the tritium atom count delivered over any chosen time interval is the time integral of this rate over that interval.

In practice this rate is computed from calibrated gas throughput, valve actuation history, reservoir pressure and temperature changes, or particle-balance estimates, with corrections for delivery-line inventory and composition when needed. If the metered quantity is a molecular flow, it must be converted to a tritium atom flow: one $\mathrm{T}_2$ molecule contributes two tritium atoms, one $\mathrm{DT}$ or $\mathrm{HT}$ molecule contributes one tritium atom, and mixtures are summed with the corresponding stoichiometric weights.

No single device-independent range applies, because the value depends on machine size, pulse scenario, tritium fraction, and whether tritium is used as a trace species or main fuel. The rate is 0 s$^{-1}$ when tritium gas injection is disabled; trace injections are often about $10^{17}$-$10^{20}$ s$^{-1}$, while main-fueling gas injection in large deuterium-tritium plasmas can be about $10^{20}$-$10^{22}$ s$^{-1}$ or higher in reactor-scale systems.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_pellet_path_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of a point on a pellet injection trajectory in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured relative to the tokamak equatorial plane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a pellet path point is the $Z$ position of a specified point on a pellet injection trajectory. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters measured relative to the tokamak equatorial plane. Together with the [major radius] and [toroidal angle], it specifies the spatial location of the path point.

Values are usually obtained from injector and guide-tube geometry, alignment surveys, trajectory modeling, or reconstruction of the pellet path when direct position observations are available. The coordinate describes the geometry of the path point and does not by itself specify pellet speed, mass, fragmentation, ablation rate, or time of flight.

For paths crossing the confined plasma, $Z$ is commonly within -1 to 1 m in medium-sized tokamaks and can span about -3 to 3 m in large tokamaks. Points near injectors or external launch structures can lie farther from the equatorial plane, depending on the device geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the path point lies above the tokamak equatorial plane in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_shattering_position
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the point where a pellet is shattered in a shattered pellet injection system, measured along the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
In a shattered pellet injection (SPI) system, a solid pellet is fractured into fragments at a prescribed shattering position before the debris enters the plasma. The vertical coordinate $Z$ identifies the height of this shattering event in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ increases upward along the machine symmetry axis.

Together with the radial companion major_radius_of_pellet_path_point, this $Z$ coordinate fully specifies the poloidal location of fragment formation, directly influencing the spatial distribution of the ablating pellet cloud and the resulting material deposition profile in the plasma. The [vertical_coordinate_of_pellet](name:vertical_coordinate_of_pellet_path_point) gives the instantaneous $Z$ position of the intact pellet along its trajectory before impact.

The shattering position is a fixed geometric property of the injector assembly, set by the guide tube termination and barrel exit geometry; it is determined by mechanical survey of the injection system relative to the machine coordinate origin. Typical $Z$ values range from approximately $-2$ m to $+2$ m in medium-sized tokamaks, depending on the injection port location and whether the system targets midplane, upper, or lower regions of the vessel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the shattering position lies above the machine equatorial plane, in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_velocity_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Z component of the shattered pellet center-of-mass velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical velocity of a pellet is the $Z$ component $v_Z$ of the center-of-mass velocity of a shattered pellet or its fragment cloud. It describes motion parallel to the vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Together with [radial velocity of the pellet](name:radial_velocity_of_pellet) and [toroidal velocity of the pellet](name:toroidal_velocity_of_pellet), it forms the cylindrical component representation of the pellet translational velocity.

The pellet center-of-mass velocity decomposes in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame as:

$$
\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{pellet} = v_R \hat{R} + v_\phi \hat{\phi} + v_Z \hat{Z}
$$

where $v_R$, $v_\phi$, and $v_Z$ are the radial, toroidal, and vertical velocity components, all in m.s^-1, and $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ are the corresponding unit vectors.

In practice, $v_Z$ is obtained from the time derivative of the pellet or fragment-cloud center-of-mass position, or from a reconstructed trajectory and launch geometry. For a fragment cloud, the center-of-mass velocity represents the mass-weighted translational motion of the cloud rather than the motion of any individual fragment.

Typical values are configuration- and trajectory-dependent and are reported in m.s^-1. For a given pellet speed $|\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{pellet}|$, the component satisfies $-|\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{pellet}| \le v_Z \le |\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{pellet}|$; it may be near zero for nearly horizontal trajectories or comparable to the total speed for strongly inclined trajectories.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pellet center of mass moves in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: xenon_source_rate
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Instantaneous injection rate of xenon gas into the plasma vessel, where each xenon atom is counted as Z = 54 equivalent electrons.
NAMES.long:
The xenon source rate quantifies the instantaneous flux of xenon gas delivered to the plasma vessel by gas injection systems. Xenon (atomic number Z = 54) is a heavy noble gas used as a high-radiating impurity for plasma control, impurity seeding, and disruption mitigation in fusion devices.

The equivalent-electron rate $\dot{N}_\mathrm{Xe}$ is obtained by weighting the instantaneous atom injection rate by xenon's atomic number:

$$
\dot{N}_\mathrm{Xe} = 54 \cdot \dot{n}_\mathrm{Xe}
$$

where $\dot{n}_\mathrm{Xe}$ is the xenon atom flux in atoms s$^{-1}$ and 54 is the atomic number of xenon.

The injection rate is inferred from valve conductance and upstream gas pressure measurements. Integrating over time yields the cumulative xenon inventory. The [krypton_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:krypton_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) follows the same equivalent-electron convention for the neighboring noble gas krypton, while [electron_source_rate_due_to_injection](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_injection) aggregates equivalent-electron contributions across all injected species.
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon gas flows from the injection system into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: thermal_power_of_divertor
NAMES.short: Total heat-exhaust power deposited on the plasma-facing surfaces of the divertor system. It is the surface integral of the local thermal heat flux over divertor targets and included divertor components, excluding main-wall loads and distinct electrical-current power.
NAMES.long:
Thermal power of the divertor is the total rate at which plasma exhaust energy is deposited as heat on the divertor system. The relevant integration surface is the plasma-facing boundary of the divertor system, including divertor targets and any other divertor components included in the thermal-load definition, but excluding main-wall surfaces. This quantity represents the thermal heat-exhaust load; it is distinct from divertor power associated specifically with electric currents.

For a specified divertor surface set, the total thermal power is the surface integral of the deposited thermal heat-flux density:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th,div}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{div}}} q_{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dA
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{div}}$ is the selected plasma-facing divertor surface, $q_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the local thermal heat-flux density deposited into that surface in W m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is the surface element in m$^2$, and $P_{\mathrm{th,div}}$ is in W. If the divertor is treated as a set of components or targets, the same quantity is the sum of this integral over those components.

In practice it is inferred by integrating mapped divertor heat-flux measurements from infrared thermography, embedded calorimetry, thermocouples, probes, or radiation and neutral-exhaust analysis, often constrained by global power balance. Modeling estimates compute the same surface-integrated thermal deposition from parallel transport, cross-field spreading, volumetric radiation, charge-exchange neutrals, and plasma-surface interaction physics.

Typical values are strongly device and scenario dependent: small or medium experiments may deposit about $10^5$-$10^7$ W on the divertor, large tokamak scenarios about $10^7$-$10^8$ W, and reactor or power-plant designs can require exhaust handling at about $10^8$-$10^9$ W. The distribution over the wetted area is often as important as the total, because material limits are governed by local heat flux as well as integrated power.
NAMES.sign: Positive when thermal energy is deposited into the divertor system from the plasma.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_at_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point
NAMES.short: Angle in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame that specifies the direction used for a plasma boundary gap distance from its reference point. It is measured clockwise from the outward radial (+R) direction.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal angle at a plasma boundary gap reference point is the orientation of the line along which the associated [plasma boundary gap distance] is evaluated. The angle lies in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height; $\alpha_\mathrm{gap}=0$ points in the outward radial $+\hat{R}$ direction.

The reported angle $\alpha_\mathrm{gap}$, in radians, defines the unit direction vector for the gap measurement as

$$
\hat{\mathbf{g}} = \cos(\alpha_\mathrm{gap})\,\hat{R} - \sin(\alpha_\mathrm{gap})\,\hat{Z}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{g}}$ is the unit vector along the specified gap direction, and $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the local radial and vertical basis vectors of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

In practice this angle is chosen from the position-control geometry or computed from the direction vector between the gap reference point and the intended boundary-intersection direction in the poloidal cross-section. It specifies only the direction; the companion gap quantity gives the distance along that direction from the reference point.

Typical values may be represented over $-\pi$ to $\pi$ rad or equivalently over $0$ to $2\pi$ rad, with angles differing by $2\pi$ rad describing the same direction. Common reference directions include $0$ rad for outward radial, $\pi/2$ rad for downward, $\pi$ rad for inward radial, and $3\pi/2$ rad or $-\pi/2$ rad for upward.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the gap direction is rotated clockwise from $+\hat{R}$ toward $-\hat{Z}$ in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: density_at_limiter
NAMES.short: Local particle number density of any plasma species evaluated in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to the plasma-facing limiter surface, on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance.
NAMES.long:
Number density of a specified plasma species — electrons, fuel ions, or impurity ions — evaluated at the plasma-limiter interface on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance. The limiter terminates open magnetic field lines in the scrape-off layer (SOL), and this boundary density sets the particle source for both the confining plasma and for wall-material interactions including sputtering, recycling, and impurity release.

The macroscopic number density is related to the velocity distribution function $f_s$ of species $s$ by:

$$
n_s = \int f_s(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where the integral is taken over all velocities at the evaluation point immediately adjacent to the limiter.

Quasineutrality at the sheath entrance couples the [electron_density_at_limiter](name:electron_density_at_limiter) to the charge-weighted sum of ion densities, $n_e \approx \sum_s Z_s n_s$, where $Z_s$ is the ion charge number of species $s$. The charge-state-summed ion total is given by [total_ion_density_at_limiter](name:total_ion_density_at_limiter), while impurity species such as [carbon_density_at_limiter](name:carbon_density_at_limiter) and [oxygen_density_at_limiter](name:oxygen_density_at_limiter) contribute to the local effective charge. The analogous family at divertor target surfaces is [density_at_divertor_target](name:density_at_divertor_target).

This density is measured by Langmuir probes embedded in or flush-mounted near the limiter, or inferred from edge spectroscopy combined with ionization balance modeling. Typical boundary plasma densities at limiter surfaces span $10^{17}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on species, heating power, and plasma configuration.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local plasma contains particles of the specified species at the evaluation point adjacent to the limiter.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Argon ion number density immediately adjacent to a limiter material surface, evaluated in the boundary plasma at the plasma-limiter contact. It represents the local concentration of ionized argon impurity at the plasma-wall interface.
NAMES.long:
Argon density at the limiter is the number density of ionized argon in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a material limiter surface. The evaluation point is the plasma-facing sheath-edge region at the plasma-limiter contact, not inside the solid limiter and not a core, pedestal, or flux-surface-averaged value.

For an argon impurity population resolved by charge state, the local ion density is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar,lim}} = \lim_{\Delta V \to 0} \frac{1}{\Delta V}\sum_{q=1}^{18} \Delta N_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}
$$

where $q$ is the argon charge state, $\Delta N_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+}}$ is the number of argon ions in charge state $q$ within a small plasma sampling volume adjacent to the limiter, and $\Delta V$ is that volume in m$^3$, giving $n_{\mathrm{Ar,lim}}$ in m$^{-3}$. Neutral argon atoms are not included in this ion density.

In practice this quantity is obtained from boundary-plasma and impurity-transport modeling, or inferred from argon line emission using collisional-radiative modeling together with local electron density and temperature. It is governed by parallel transport to the limiter, ionization and recombination balance, recycling and impurity source rates, and radiative cooling in the scrape-off-layer plasma near the limiter.

Typical values for trace argon seeding near limiter contact are about $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$. Strong local impurity sources or highly radiating edge conditions can produce values approaching $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, while unseeded plasmas may be below spectroscopic detectability.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local number density of charged beryllium ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter surface, summed over all charged ionization states. Neutral beryllium atoms are not included.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium density at a limiter is the local total number density of charged beryllium ions in the plasma immediately next to a limiter material surface. It is an impurity ion density for beryllium charge states and excludes neutral beryllium atoms, molecules, dust, and beryllium bound in the solid wall.

The total charged beryllium ion density is the sum over the charged ionization states of beryllium:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be,lim}} = \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{lim}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be,lim}}$ is the total charged beryllium ion density in m^-3, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{lim}}$ is the number density in m^-3 of beryllium ions with charge $q e$, and $q=1,\ldots,4$ for beryllium.

In practice, this density may be evaluated by summing charge-state densities in a boundary-plasma or impurity-transport calculation, or inferred from charge-state-sensitive spectroscopic observations together with an atomic population model and local plasma parameters. The definition is independent of the method used to obtain the charge-state densities.

As a number density, its physically allowed range is $n_{\mathrm{Be,lim}} \ge 0$ m^-3. A value of 0 m^-3 means that no charged beryllium ions are present at the limiter location within the sensitivity of the model or measurement; finite values are often interpreted relative to the local electron density or main-ion density because absolute magnitudes depend strongly on local boundary-plasma conditions and discharge phase.

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Charge-state-summed boron ion number density immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface.
NAMES.long:
Boron density at the limiter is the local number density of boron ions in the plasma volume immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter, where open scrape-off-layer field lines intersect a material boundary. Unless a single charge state is specified, it is the charge-state-summed boron ion population and is the boron-resolved component of [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter).

For a representative small plasma volume next to the limiter, the localized density $n_{B,\mathrm{lim}}$ is the boron ion count per unit volume:

$$
n_{B,\mathrm{lim}} = \frac{N_B}{V}
$$

where $N_B$ is the number of boron ions in the sampled volume and $V$ is that volume in m$^3$, giving $n_{B,\mathrm{lim}}$ in m$^{-3}$. Because fully stripped boron carries charge $Z_B = 5$, its contribution to the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff} = \sum_k n_k Z_k^2 / n_e$ is large relative to its number fraction, so even sub-percent boron concentrations affect plasma resistivity and the radiated power budget.

This quantity is inferred from edge impurity emission spectroscopy combined with collisional-radiative or atomic-rate modeling, from active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or from scrape-off-layer transport calculations constrained by limiter source estimates. The limiter value refers to the plasma-side impurity density adjacent to the material surface, not to boron bound within the solid limiter material.

Typical limiter-adjacent boron densities depend strongly on wall conditioning, limiter material history, plasma density, erosion source strength, and ionization balance. Trace impurity values in edge modeling are often roughly $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, while localized transient sources, boron injection, or freshly boronized surfaces can produce values outside this range.

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Unweighted number density of ionized carbon in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter, summed over all carbon ionization stages. It excludes neutral carbon atoms and does not weight charge states by charge or mass.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at a limiter is the local number density of carbon impurity ions in the boundary plasma next to a limiter surface. It is an unweighted sum over ionized carbon charge states and excludes neutral carbon atoms.

The charge-state-summed ion density is defined by:

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,ion}} = \sum_{q=1}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}$ is the number density of carbon ions with charge state $q$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $n_{\mathrm{C,ion}}$ is also in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$. The sum runs over ionized carbon from $\mathrm{C}^+$ through fully stripped $\mathrm{C}^{6+}$; neutral carbon $\mathrm{C}^0$ is not included.

In practice this quantity is obtained from local impurity charge-state populations in boundary-plasma modeling, or constrained experimentally using carbon line emission together with electron density, electron temperature, and collisional-radiative modeling. It is sensitive to local impurity sources, ionization balance, transport, and the plasma conditions adjacent to the limiter.

No device-independent typical range is implied by the definition. Values are non-negative, reported in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and should be interpreted relative to the local edge plasma density and carbon impurity fraction for the discharge being considered.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions in the plasma-side boundary layer immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface, evaluated near the plasma-sheath interface.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density at a limiter is the local number density of deuterium ions, usually $D^+$, on the plasma side of the sheath adjacent to a limiter surface. It is the species-resolved deuterium contribution to the edge ion population, not necessarily the total ion density when several ion species are present.

For sheath-limited contact, a common boundary estimate relates the partial deuterium ion flux to the sheath-edge density through the Bohm relation:

$$
\Gamma_D \simeq n_D c_s
$$

where $n_D$ is this density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $\Gamma_D$ is the species-resolved deuterium particle flux to the limiter in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and $c_s$ is the ion-acoustic speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For singly ionized deuterium, $c_s$ is commonly estimated from local electron and ion temperatures, for example $c_s \approx [e(T_e+\gamma_i T_i)/m_D]^{1/2}$ when $T_e$ and $T_i$ are in eV; $e$ is the elementary charge, $m_D$ is the deuterium ion mass, and $\gamma_i$ is an ion heat-capacity factor.

In practice this quantity is inferred from edge diagnostics near the limiter, such as probe measurements combined with sheath models, spectroscopic analysis with collisional-radiative modeling, or edge plasma simulations constrained by density and recycling measurements. Its value is sensitive to parallel transport along open field lines, local ionization and recombination, neutral recycling from the limiter surface, and the degree to which deuterium is diluted by other ion species.

Typical limiter-adjacent deuterium ion densities are about $10^{18}-10^{19}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ in many tokamak scrape-off-layer conditions, with broader operating ranges of roughly $10^{17}-10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ depending on plasma current, fueling, recycling, and proximity to high-density or detached boundary regimes.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Number density of the fictitious deuterium-tritium fuel pseudo-species in the plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter surface. The pseudo-species represents an equimolar DT mixture as one ion constituent with effective mass about 2.5 atomic mass units.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium-tritium density at a limiter is the local number density of the fictitious DT fuel pseudo-species on the plasma side of a plasma-facing limiter surface. The pseudo-species represents an equimolar mixture of deuterium and tritium as one ion constituent with effective mass about 2.5 atomic mass units, distinct from separately tracked deuterium or tritium densities.

The local limiter value is defined by evaluating the DT pseudo-species density at the plasma-facing limiter boundary:

$$
n_{\mathrm{DT,lim}} = \left. n_{\mathrm{DT}} \right|_{\text{plasma side of limiter}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{DT}}$ is the local pseudo-species number density and the vertical bar denotes evaluation immediately outside the limiter material, normally near the sheath entrance. Both quantities have unit m^-3. When comparing with a resolved-isotope description, the equimolar pseudo-species corresponds to the total fuel-ion density $n_D+n_T$ with $n_D \simeq n_T$.

This quantity is the DT-fuel component of [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter). It may be inferred from edge density measurements combined with species-fraction information, or computed from edge, scrape-off-layer, and plasma-wall interaction models at the limiter contact region. In limiter-bounded plasmas it is closely related to [deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary), while [deuterium_tritium_density_at_divertor_target](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_divertor_target) describes the analogous pseudo-species density at a divertor target.

Representative near-limiter DT pseudo-species densities in tokamak edge plasmas are often about 10^17-10^19 m^-3, varying strongly with fueling, recycling, edge temperature, confinement regime, and whether the plasma boundary is limiter- or divertor-defined.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_limiter
NAMES.short: Effective charge number of the ion mixture in the boundary plasma at the limiter, quantifying the degree of impurity contamination at this plasma-facing surface.
NAMES.long:
The effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ at the limiter is the charge-squared-weighted average ion charge of the plasma species in the scrape-off layer immediately adjacent to the limiter surface. It captures the aggregate effect of all impurity species on plasma resistivity and radiation behavior without resolving individual impurity charge states.

The quantity is defined by

$$
Z_\text{eff} = \frac{\sum_i n_i Z_i^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_i$ is the number density of ion species $i$ with integer charge number $Z_i$, and $n_e = \sum_i n_i Z_i$ is the electron density enforced by quasi-neutrality. For a pure hydrogen-isotope plasma, $Z_\text{eff} = 1$; impurity ions with $Z_i > 1$ raise the value above unity.

At the limiter, $Z_\text{eff}$ is typically elevated compared to the core because sputtered wall material and recycled impurities concentrate near the plasma-facing surface. Typical values range from 1.5 to 4 in limiter-configuration plasmas, depending on the wall material (beryllium, carbon, or tungsten) and fueling conditions. This local value complements [effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary](name:effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary) and [effective_charge_at_divertor_target](name:effective_charge_at_divertor_target), which quantify $Z_\text{eff}$ at other boundary reference locations. It is inferred from the ratio of total Bremsstrahlung emissivity to the square of the electron density integrated along lines of sight through the boundary plasma, or from spectroscopic resolution of individual impurity charge states.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any plasma consisting of positively charged ions and electrons satisfying quasi-neutral balance.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density in the plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter surface, evaluated on the plasma side near the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance. It characterizes scrape-off-layer plasma contacting the limiter, not the separatrix density at the confined-plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
Electron density at a limiter is the local number of free electrons per unit volume in the plasma immediately upstream of a limiter material surface. It describes the scrape-off-layer or edge plasma that intersects the limiter and helps determine local sheath behavior, recycling, and particle fluxes. It is distinct from electron density at the plasma boundary, which refers to the separatrix between confined plasma and the scrape-off layer.

The local electron number density is defined by the electron population contained in a small volume element:

$$
n_e = \frac{dN_e}{dV}
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron density, $N_e$ is the dimensionless number of electrons, and $V$ is volume in m$^3$.

In practice this quantity may be obtained from limiter or edge Langmuir-probe analysis, from spectroscopic or microwave diagnostics with suitable spatial localization, or from edge plasma modeling constrained by measurements. If inferred from ion-saturation current or sheath-transmission relations, the result depends on assumptions about sheath physics, electron temperature, ion species, magnetic incidence angle, and probe geometry; such relations are diagnostic models and are not the definition of the density.

Physically valid values satisfy $n_e \ge 0$. Typical limiter-adjacent scrape-off-layer densities are about $10^{17}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with lower values in tenuous far-SOL conditions and higher values near strong plasma-wall contact, high fueling, or detached or highly recycling edge conditions.

NAMES.name: electron_source_rate_due_to_surface_emission
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Rate at which material released from plasma-facing surfaces by recycling, outgassing, and physical or chemical sputtering supplies electrons to the plasma after ionization, summed over all emitting surfaces and weighted by the number of electrons each released species contributes. It is the electron-equivalent surface-emission source and is non-negative by construction.
NAMES.long:
Electron source rate due to surface emission is the wall-emission contribution to the global electron particle balance: the number of electron-equivalent particles supplied to the plasma per unit time by material released from plasma-facing surfaces. Surface emission collects all release channels \fed by plasma-surface interaction, including recycling (prompt return of incident plasma ions as neutrals), outgassing (delayed release of retained fuel from the wall bulk), and physical and chemical sputtering of wall material. Each emitted atom, molecule, or impurity is weighted by the number of electrons it contributes once ionized, so the quantity is an all-species, all-surface electron source. It is the electron-specific form of source_rate_due_to_surface_emission and one component of [total_electron_source_rate](name:total_electron_source_rate); the corresponding electron loss to the wall is the separate incident channel total_incident_electron_particle_flux_at_wall.

The global rate is obtained by integrating the emitted particle flux density over all plasma-facing surface area, with each released species weighted by its electron yield on full ionization:

$$
S_e = \int_{A_\mathrm{pf}} \sum_{s} Z_s \, \Gamma_{s}^{\mathrm{emit}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dA
$$

where $A_\mathrm{pf}$ is the total plasma-facing surface area, $\Gamma_{s}^{\mathrm{emit}}$ is the emitted particle flux density of released species $s$ (atoms, molecules, or impurity species) in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, $Z_s$ is the number of electrons that species $s$ liberates when fully ionized in the plasma, $\mathbf{x}$ labels position on the surface, and $S_e$ is in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The species sum aggregates fuel and impurity contributions; for pure hydrogenic recycling $Z_s$ reduces to the number of nuclei per emitted neutral.

In practice the rate is inferred from particle-balance analysis combining plasma density evolution with fueling and pumping data, from neutral pressure and spectroscopy measurements, from wall outgassing and recycling-coefficient estimates, and from edge-plasma or neutral-transport modeling. The calculation should include material emitted from all limiters, divertor targets, first-wall panels, and other plasma-facing components that returns toward the plasma.

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent, often ranging from roughly $10^{20}$ to $10^{24}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and increasing with plasma density, recycling fraction, and impurity production. The value approaches zero when surfaces are not releasing material into the plasma and is largest under high-recycling divertor conditions in large, strongly fueled discharges.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local electron temperature at the plasma-wall interface on the plasma-facing side of a limiter, where open scrape-off-layer field lines terminate on material surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Electron temperature at the limiter is the local temperature of the electron population on the plasma-facing side of a limiter surface, at the plasma-wall interface where open scrape-off-layer magnetic field lines intersect material structures. It characterizes the electron thermal energy available for sheath formation, recycling, and plasma-surface interaction, and is not the temperature of the solid limiter.

For an isotropic Maxwellian, or a scalar moment-equivalent electron distribution, the value expressed in electronvolts is related to the random kinetic energy per electron by:

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3e}\left\langle \frac{1}{2} m_e |\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_e|^2 \right\rangle
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $\mathbf{v}$ is the electron velocity in $m\,s^{-1}$, $\mathbf{u}_e$ is the local mean electron flow velocity in $m\,s^{-1}$, angle brackets denote an average over the local electron velocity distribution at the limiter-side plasma, and $e$ is the elementary-charge energy conversion factor in $J\,eV^{-1}$. The kinetic-energy moment is in joules, so division by $e$ gives $T_e$ in eV; for non-Maxwellian distributions the reported scalar value is an effective or moment temperature.

In experiments, this quantity is commonly inferred from Langmuir-probe current-voltage characteristics at or near the limiter surface, local edge spectroscopy, Thomson scattering where spatial access is available, or scrape-off-layer modeling constrained by edge and wall measurements. Probe and sheath interpretations usually assume a quasineutral sheath-edge plasma, a specified electron energy distribution, and corrections for magnetic-field incidence angle, collisionality, secondary electron emission, and surface conditions. When combined with [electron density at the limiter](name:electron_density_at_limiter), derived quantities must convert eV to joules; for example, the electron pressure estimate $p_e = e n_e T_e$ uses $n_e$ in $m^{-3}$, $T_e$ in eV, $e$ in $J\,eV^{-1}$, and gives $p_e$ in Pa. Sheath heat-flux or sound-speed estimates additionally require explicit assumptions for ion mass, charge state, ion temperature, sheath transmission coefficients, and the electron distribution.

Typical limiter-side electron temperatures are 1-5 eV in cold, strongly recycling edge plasmas, 5-50 eV in many attached limiter scrape-off-layer conditions, and 50-200 eV in hot near-limiter or transient high-power phases. The appropriate value can vary strongly over a few millimeters near the material surface because of parallel heat conduction, recycling neutrals, sheath physics, and impurity radiation.

NAMES.name: energy_flux_at_wall
NAMES.short: Total energy flux density incident on a plasma-facing wall surface, equal to the sum of contributing particle, photon, and electromagnetic power fluxes per unit area.
NAMES.long:
Energy flux at the wall is the local power per unit area delivered to a plasma-facing surface by plasma, neutral, radiative, and electromagnetic processes. It represents the aggregate wall heat-loading density; integrating it over a surface gives the corresponding [plasma_deposited_power_at_wall](name:plasma_deposited_power_at_wall), while its maximum over a surface is related to [peak_power_density_at_wall](name:peak_power_density_at_wall).

The total wall energy flux density is the area density of deposited power and may be decomposed into resolved physical channels:

$$
q_\mathrm{wall}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{dP_\mathrm{wall}}{dA}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} q_c(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $q_\mathrm{wall}$ is the total energy flux density at wall position $\mathbf{x}$, $P_\mathrm{wall}$ is the power crossing into a surface element of area $dA$, and $q_c$ is the contribution from channel $c$, such as charged particles, neutral atoms, photons, recombination energy, or inductive electromagnetic heating.

In practice this quantity is estimated from edge-plasma and wall-interaction modeling, from heat-transfer inversion of infrared thermography, calorimetry, thermocouples, or embedded sensors, and from diagnostic constraints on radiated and particle power. Care is needed to distinguish local surface loading from area-integrated power and from material temperature response, which also depends on thermal properties, geometry, and exposure time.

Typical values range from 10^2-10^5 W m^-2 on weakly loaded main-chamber wall regions, 10^5-10^7 W m^-2 on limiter or divertor target regions during sustained plasma contact, and can exceed 10^7 W m^-2 for short transient events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net energy crosses the plasma-facing surface from the plasma side into the wall material.

NAMES.name: electron_energy_flux_at_wall
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Kinetic energy flux density carried by electrons emitted from a plasma-facing wall surface into the adjacent plasma or vacuum region. It quantifies the surface-emitted component of electron energy transport, arising from secondary, backscattered, thermionic, or photo-emission processes, and is distinct from the incident electron power arriving at the wall from the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Electron energy flux at the wall is the kinetic energy flux density transported away from a plasma-facing material surface by the emitted electron population. Emitted electrons originate from secondary electron emission, backscattering, thermionic emission, or photoemission, and this quantity captures the energy these electrons carry across the surface into the adjacent plasma or vacuum region.

For an emitted electron velocity distribution at the surface, the flux density is the first kinetic-energy moment of the outgoing electrons:

$$
q_{e,\mathrm{emit}} = \int_{\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_w>0} \tfrac{1}{2} m_e v^2 \, (\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_w) \, f_{e,\mathrm{emit}}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v = \Gamma_{e,\mathrm{emit}} \, \langle E_k \rangle_\Gamma
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v$ is the electron speed, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_w$ is the unit surface normal pointing from the material into the plasma-facing region, and $f_{e,\mathrm{emit}}$ is the emitted electron velocity distribution function (units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$, i.e. number density per unit velocity-space volume). $\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{emit}}$ is the outward emitted electron particle flux density in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and $\langle E_k \rangle_\Gamma$ is the flux-weighted mean kinetic energy per emitted electron; if expressed in eV it must be multiplied by the elementary charge to obtain joules.

This quantity is obtained from surface-emission models, sheath or kinetic plasma-wall calculations, or from diagnostics that infer the emitted electron current together with the emitted-electron energy spectrum. The flux-weighted mean energy weights each electron by its normal velocity component, so electrons crossing the surface more nearly along the normal contribute more strongly than electrons with the same energy moving nearly tangentially. The emitted flux enters the surface energy balance as a cooling term for the wall, partially offsetting the incident electron and ion energy loads.

Typical magnitudes are strongly model-dependent, governed by the emission yield, the emitted-electron energy spectrum, the surface temperature and material, and the local sheath potential. The value is generally a fraction of the incident electron energy flux and rises sharply when strong secondary or thermionic emission is active on hot, intensely loaded divertor surfaces.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the emitted electron kinetic energy flows across the wall surface along the outward normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_w$, from the material into the plasma-facing region.

NAMES.name: energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_eddy_current
NAMES.short: Energy flux density crossing the plasma-facing wall surface due to Joule heating by eddy currents induced in conducting structures. It represents the portion of internally deposited Ohmic power that is transported back to the surface and emitted toward the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Energy flux at the wall due to eddy current is the thermal power per unit wall area that reaches the plasma-facing surface after eddy-current Joule heating inside conducting wall material. Time-varying magnetic fields induce currents in the wall; their Ohmic dissipation deposits power within the solid, while this quantity describes only the emitted surface flux directed toward the plasma.

The volumetric source that feeds this surface emission is the local Ohmic dissipation from the induced current density:

$$
p_\mathrm{eddy} = \frac{|\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{eddy}|^2}{\sigma_w}
$$

where $p_\mathrm{eddy}$ is the volumetric power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{eddy}$ is the eddy-current density in A m$^{-2}$, and $\sigma_w$ is the wall electrical conductivity in S m$^{-1}$. The corresponding surface energy flux density depends on the spatial distribution of this source, the wall geometry, thermal conductivity, heat capacity, and the timescale over which heat diffuses to the plasma-facing surface.

In practice, the quantity is computed from electromagnetic and thermal analyzes of conducting wall structures during magnetic transients such as disruptions, current quenches, vertical displacement events, or rapid control-coil field changes. It may be inferred by combining reconstructed or modeled eddy-current distributions with a heat-transfer calculation that maps internal Ohmic deposition to heat flux at the surface.

Typical values are near zero during steady conditions when magnetic fields vary slowly. During fast transients, localized emitted fluxes can be 10^3-10^6 W m$^{-2}$, with higher short-duration peaks possible near highly conducting structures or geometric current-concentration regions.

This quantity is part of the wall energy balance together with radiative loading, particle energy fluxes, and total Ohmic dissipation in wall structures. It is distinct from the total [power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation](name:power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation), because only the portion transported to and emitted from the plasma-facing surface contributes to this surface flux density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when thermal energy is emitted from the wall surface toward the plasma.

NAMES.name: energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_radiation
NAMES.short: Incident radiative energy flux density at a plasma-facing wall is the photon power crossing onto the material surface per unit area. It counts arriving radiation before absorption, reflection, or re-emission, so it is not by itself the net heat deposited in the wall.
NAMES.long:
Energy flux at wall due to radiation is the local incident photon power per unit wall area arriving at a plasma-facing material surface. It includes radiative transport from plasma emission processes such as line radiation, bremsstrahlung, and synchrotron emission, but excludes the subsequent material response. It is a radiative contribution to [energy_flux_at_wall](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_eddy_current); its wall-integrated counterpart is related to radiated_power_at_wall, and its largest local value contributes to [peak_power_density_at_wall](name:peak_power_density_at_wall).

The incident radiative flux density can be written as an integral of incoming spectral radiance over frequency and solid angle:

$$
q_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_0^\infty \int_{\hat{s}\cdot\hat{n}<0} I_\nu(\mathbf{x},\hat{s})\,[-\hat{s}\cdot\hat{n}]\,d\Omega\,d\nu
$$

where $q_\mathrm{rad}$ is this quantity in W m^-2, $\mathbf{x}$ is a point on the wall, $I_\nu$ is the incoming spectral radiance in W m^-2 sr^-1 Hz^-1, $\hat{s}$ is the photon propagation direction, $\hat{n}$ is the unit normal pointing from the wall material into the plasma-facing vacuum, $d\Omega$ is a solid-angle element in steradians, and $d\nu$ is a frequency interval in hertz. The factor $[-\hat{s}\cdot\hat{n}]$ is the projected-area cosine for rays crossing from the plasma-facing side into the material.

In practice this quantity is computed from radiation-transport or view-factor calculations using plasma emissivity, wall geometry, opacity, and shadowing. Measurements such as bolometry can constrain the total radiated power, but the local incident wall distribution depends on the assumed radiation source distribution and geometric transport model. Net absorbed or deposited radiative heat flux additionally requires material optical properties and emitted or reflected radiation terms.

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. Area-averaged incident radiative wall loads in tokamak wall-load studies are often assessed on scales of 10^3-10^5 W m^-2, while localized divertor or first-wall peaks in high-power radiating scenarios may reach 10^5-10^6 W m^-2; these ranges are representative engineering scales rather than universal limits.
NAMES.sign: Positive when photon energy crosses the wall surface from the plasma-facing vacuum side into the material.

NAMES.name: energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination
NAMES.short: Aggregate energy flux density deposited on a plasma-facing wall by recombination processes, summed over all incident particle species, charge states, and recombination channels.
NAMES.long:
Recombination energy flux at the wall is the power per unit wall area deposited by plasma particles undergoing neutralization or electron-ion recombination at or near a plasma-facing surface, accumulated across all ion species, charge states, and recombination pathways. When a multiply-charged ion captures successive electrons and recombines, each step releases ionization potential energy plus residual kinetic energy; this aggregate quantity collects those contributions into a single heat-load density at the material surface.

The total recombination heat flux density is the sum over all contributing species and charge states:

$$
q_\mathrm{rec} = \sum_{s,\,z} \Gamma_{s,z}(w)\,E_\mathrm{rec}(s,z)
$$

where $\Gamma_{s,z}(w)$ is the particle flux density incident on the wall for species $s$ in charge state $z$, and $E_\mathrm{rec}(s,z)$ is the energy released per recombination event, including ionization potential and kinetic energy contributions.

The aggregate can be decomposed into species- and charge-state-resolved contributions. Neutral recombination products leaving the surface are tracked by [neutral_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination) and [neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination). The complementary radiative contribution to wall heat loading is captured by [energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_radiation](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_radiation), and the total deposited surface power integrated over the full wall area appears in deposited_power_at_wall.

NAMES.name: flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission
NAMES.short: General flux density of any quantity (e.g., particles, energy, momentum) emitted from a plasma-facing wall surface due to surface emission processes. This serves as a parent category for specific flux components such as energy flux.
NAMES.long:
Flux density at a plasma-facing wall surface due to surface emission processes represents the rate of transfer of a physical quantity per unit area from the wall into the plasma. Surface emission encompasses phenomena such as sputtering, desorption, thermal evaporation, photon emission, and secondary electron emission, each contributing a flux of particles and energy. The total flux can be decomposed into specific channels: particle flux (number of emitted particles per unit area per second), energy flux (kinetic and potential energy carried by emitted species per unit area per second), and momentum flux (momentum transfer per unit area per second).

This quantity is a general abstraction; concrete measurements or calculations refer to one of the component fluxes. For example, the child standard name [energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission) captures the energy channel specifically.

In practice, the flux is estimated from plasma-facing material diagnostics (e.g., Langmuir probes, spectroscopic measurements of atomic line emission, calorimetry) or from plasma-wall interaction modeling codes. Typical values for the energy flux density in the scrape-off layer of a tokamak range from 0.1 to 10 MW/m², depending on the plasma scenario and wall material. Particle flux densities vary from 10²² to 10²⁴ m⁻²s⁻¹.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net flux is directed outward from the wall surface into the plasma.

NAMES.name: energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission
NAMES.short: Total energy flux density at a plasma-facing wall surface due to surface emission processes, encompassing kinetic and potential energy carried by emitted particles and photons.
NAMES.long:
Surface emission at the plasma-facing wall encompasses secondary electron emission, neutral and ion sputtering, particle reflection, and photon emission stimulated by plasma–wall interactions. Each emission channel carries energy away from the wall surface, and this quantity represents their aggregate energy flux per unit area. It is the energy-channel specialization of [flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission](name:flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission), which spans multiple transported quantities at the wall interface.

The total emitted energy flux $Q_\mathrm{em}$ is expressed by summing over all surface-emitted species $s$ the energy-weighted flux of particles leaving the surface:

$$
Q_\mathrm{em} = \sum_s \int E_s \, f_s(E_s) \, v_{\perp,s} \, dE_s
$$

where $E_s$ is the energy of emitted species $s$, $f_s$ is its energy distribution function, and $v_{\perp,s}$ is the wall-normal velocity component. The kinetic contribution alone is resolved separately as [kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission](name:kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_surface_emission).

Contextualizing this emission flux against the incident plasma heat flux quantifies the effective energy reflection coefficient of the plasma-facing surface, a key parameter for thermal design of wall components. The net deposited power density derives from the difference between the incident and emitted energy fluxes and connects to aggregate quantities such as [energy_flux_at_wall](name:energy_flux_at_wall) and [plasma_deposited_power_at_wall](name:plasma_deposited_power_at_wall).

NAMES.name: flux_due_to_recombination
NAMES.short: Surface-normal particle flux density arising from recombination of plasma ions and electrons into neutral atoms or molecules. It quantifies the rate at which plasma particles are removed from the confined region through recombination across a specified surface, such as a material boundary or a flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Recombination-driven particle flux density is the surface-normal flux of plasma particles that recombine, typically at a plasma-facing surface or across an arbitrary reference surface. It measures the rate per unit area at which ions and electrons combine to form neutral atoms or molecules, thereby removing particles from the plasma volume.

The defining kinetic expression relates the recombination flux density to the velocity distribution of recombined particles emerging from the surface:

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{rec}} = \int (\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{n})\, f_{\mathrm{rec}}(\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $\hat{n}$ is the unit normal vector of the surface, $f_{\mathrm{rec}}(\mathbf{v})$ is the velocity distribution function of recombined particles (atoms or molecules) leaving the surface, and integration is over the outgoing half-space. When recombination is purely surface-mediated, the flux is often approximated as the product of the incident ion flux density and a recombination coefficient $R_{\mathrm{rec}}$.

In practice, the recombination flux is inferred from Langmuir probe measurements of the incident ion flux combined with spectroscopic determination of neutral densities or from particle-balance analysis in scrape-off layer modeling. For volume recombination, it may be derived from rate coefficients and local plasma conditions.

Typical magnitudes at divertor targets in attached conditions range from $10^{21}$ to $10^{23}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, decreasing under detached regimes to $10^{20}$--$10^{22}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. Volume recombination fluxes across flux surfaces are typically several orders lower.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the particle flux due to recombination is directed outward from the plasma (i.e., away from the confined region towards a material surface or across an enclosing boundary).

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 density at a limiter is the number of ionized helium-3 nuclei per unit volume in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface. It quantifies the local minority-isotope ion population participating in recycling, fueling balance, sheath physics, and plasma-wall interactions at the limiter.

For a helium-3 ion distribution function, the density is the zeroth velocity moment evaluated at a limiter-adjacent plasma location:

$$
n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}(\mathbf{x}_\ell) = \int f_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}(\mathbf{x}_\ell, \mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_\ell$ denotes a point in the plasma immediately next to the limiter surface, $\mathbf{v}$ is ion velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$, and $f_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}$ has units m$^{-6}$ s$^3$, giving $n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}$ in m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is usually estimated from edge-plasma analysis and boundary modeling rather than measured as a direct local ion density at the material surface. Estimates may combine local plasma density and temperature, ionization and recombination balance, limiter recycling sources, isotope-resolved fueling or exhaust information, and diagnostic constraints such as helium line emission when available.

Typical trace-minority helium-3 densities near a limiter can span roughly 10$^{16}$-10$^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, depending strongly on helium-3 fueling rate, confinement, ionization state, scrape-off-layer transport, and recycling at the limiter. Values can be substantially different in dedicated helium-3 operation or in plasmas with weak local helium-3 sources.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-4 ions in the boundary plasma immediately outside a limiter surface, evaluated on the plasma side of the sheath or presheath.
NAMES.long:
Helium-4 density at a limiter is the local number density of helium-4 ions in the boundary plasma immediately outside the limiter material surface. The value is evaluated on the plasma side of the sheath or presheath at the limiter contact region, not inside the solid material or in neutral gas retained at the surface.

For a point on the limiter surface, the kinetic definition is the velocity-space integral of the helium-4 ion distribution taken as a plasma-side surface limit:

$$
n_{\mathrm{He4,lim}}(\mathbf{x}_w) = \lim_{\ell \to 0^+} \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} f_{\mathrm{He4}}(\mathbf{x}_w + \ell \hat{\mathbf{n}}_p, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{He4}}$ is the velocity distribution function for helium-4 ions, summed over charge states if they are not resolved separately, $\mathbf{x}_w$ is a point on the limiter surface, and $n_{\mathrm{He4,lim}}$ has units $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$. The local right-handed surface basis is $(\hat{\mathbf{t}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{t}}_2,\hat{\mathbf{n}}_p)$ with $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_1 \times \hat{\mathbf{t}}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{n}}_p$; $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_p$ points from the material into the plasma and $\ell$ is distance along that normal.

This quantity is the helium-4 isotope contribution to the local ion population at the limiter. In a quasineutral boundary plasma, [electron_density_at_limiter](name:electron_density_at_limiter) is balanced to leading order by the charge-weighted sum of ion densities, so helium-4 contributes $Z n_{\mathrm{He4,lim}}$ for a single dominant charge state $Z$, or $\sum_Z Z n_{\mathrm{He4,lim}}^{(Z)}$ when multiple helium charge states coexist. The unweighted isotope density contributes to [total_ion_density_at_limiter](name:total_ion_density_at_limiter) and to [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter).

The value is usually inferred rather than directly counted. General methods include localized or line-integrated helium line-emission spectroscopy interpreted with collisional-radiative modeling, probe-constrained boundary-plasma analysis, particle-balance estimates using helium sources and recycling, and boundary-plasma modeling constrained by electron density and temperature measurements.

Typical values are about $10^{16}-10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ when helium-4 is a trace, minority, or fusion-ash species near a limiter. In helium-fueled or strongly recycling plasmas, the value can become a substantial fraction of the local total ion density, whose boundary values are commonly $10^{17}-10^{20}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen (protium) ions in the boundary plasma adjacent to a limiter surface. It characterizes the local ion population interacting with the plasma-facing limiter material.
NAMES.long:
Hydrogen density at a limiter is the local number density of hydrogen ions in the boundary plasma next to a limiter surface. It describes the plasma population available for particle flux, recycling, charge exchange, and plasma-material interaction at the limiter location, without implying a universal relation to upstream or pedestal densities.

As a number density, it is defined by the local particle content per unit volume:

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}^+} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{H}^+}}{dV}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{H}^+}$ is the number of hydrogen ions in a small plasma volume $V$ near the limiter. The value is non-negative and is expressed in $m^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from boundary-plasma diagnostics and modeling, such as Langmuir probes, spectroscopic measurements combined with collisional-radiative interpretation, or edge plasma simulations constrained by measurements. Its value depends on local ionization, recycling from the limiter, cross-field transport, magnetic connection length, plasma fueling, and the limiter geometry.

Typical values in tokamak boundary plasmas are about $10^{17}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with lower values in tenuous scrape-off-layer conditions and higher values near dense, strongly recycling limiter plasmas.

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion average temperature at a limiter is the density-weighted temperature of the boundary-plasma ion population adjacent to a limiter surface, averaged over all ion species and their charge states.
NAMES.long:
Ion average temperature at a limiter is the local thermal temperature of ions in the boundary plasma adjacent to a limiter surface. It represents the mixture-averaged ion thermal energy near the plasma-wall interface and includes all contributing ion species and ionization states.

A common definition is the density-weighted average over species and charge states:

$$
T_{i,\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\sum_s \sum_z n_{s,z} T_{i,s,z}}{\sum_s \sum_z n_{s,z}}
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species, $z$ indexes charge states, $n_{s,z}$ is the local number density of ions in charge state $z$ of species $s$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $T_{i,s,z}$ is the corresponding ion temperature in eV. The resulting $T_{i,\mathrm{avg}}$ is in eV; if charge states are not separately resolved, the same expression applies using the available effective species populations and temperatures.

In practice, this quantity is obtained from boundary-plasma measurements, edge modeling, or a combination of both at a location representative of the limiter interaction region. It is a plasma ion temperature, not a material surface temperature, and may correspond to the ion population approaching the sheath when the limiter directly intersects open magnetic field lines.
