The [ratio of tungsten density to electron density](name:ratio_of_tungsten_density_to_electron_density) is the standard dimensionless measure of tungsten contamination, while the [volume-averaged tungsten density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density) characterizes the total confined tungsten inventory. In experiments, $n_W$ is inferred from spectroscopic measurement of tungsten line emission — typically in the vacuum ultraviolet or soft X-ray spectral range — combined with atomic data for the charge-state distribution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when tungsten ions are present in the plasma region of interest.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_tungsten_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless concentration ratio of tungsten ion number density to electron number density in a plasma. The tungsten density is summed over ionized tungsten charge states and excludes neutral tungsten atoms.
NAMES.long:
Ratio of tungsten density to electron density is a dimensionless impurity concentration comparing the total number density of tungsten ions with the free-electron number density. The tungsten density counts tungsten nuclei in ionized charge states, summed over charge state, and excludes neutral tungsten atoms. It is not charge weighted, so it is not the fraction of the electron population supplied by tungsten ions.

The ratio is defined as:

$$
c_W = \frac{n_W}{n_e} = \frac{\sum_{z=1}^{74} n_{\mathrm{W}^{z+}}}{n_e}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{W}^{z+}}$ is the number density of tungsten ions in charge state $z$, $n_W$ is the total ionized tungsten number density, and $n_e$ is the free-electron number density. The lower limit excludes neutral tungsten $\mathrm{W}^0$; if all densities are expressed in the same number-density unit, the ratio has unit 1. The quantity is meaningful where $n_e>0$ and is non-negative for physical number densities.

In practice, $n_W$ is inferred from plasma composition analysis constrained by tungsten radiation and charge-state information, while $n_e$ is obtained from electron-density measurements or kinetic reconstructions. The numerator and denominator should refer to the same plasma region or averaging operation when the ratio is interpreted as a regional concentration.

Representative core-plasma values in tungsten-containing devices are often $10^{-6}$-$10^{-4}$. Local values near strong tungsten sources or in colder boundary regions can be higher, for example $10^{-4}$-$10^{-3}$, depending on source strength, ionization balance, and plasma conditions.

NAMES.name: tungsten_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Tungsten ion number density in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter surface at the plasma-limiter contact.
NAMES.long:
Tungsten density at a limiter is the local number density of tungsten ions in the boundary plasma immediately next to a limiter surface. It characterizes how much tungsten released from the limiter is present in the plasma-facing region before dilution, ionization, and transport redistribute it elsewhere.

When charge states are resolved, the total tungsten ion density at the limiter is the sum over ionization stages:

$$
n_{\mathrm{W,lim}} = \sum_{z=1}^{74} n_{\mathrm{W}^{z+},\mathrm{lim}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{W}^{z+},\mathrm{lim}}$ is the number density in m^-3 of tungsten ions with charge $z$ adjacent to the limiter, and 74 is the atomic number of tungsten. Neutral tungsten is not included in this ion density.

In practice this quantity is estimated from edge impurity diagnostics and boundary-plasma modeling, for example by combining spectroscopic line emission, local plasma conditions, atomic data, and transport or source estimates. It is closely related to tungsten density at other plasma locations, but can be more directly affected by local sputtering, prompt redeposition, sheath conditions, and near-surface plasma parameters.

Typical values are highly device- and discharge-dependent. Trace tungsten conditions may give about $10^{10}-10^{14}$ m^-3 near a limiter, while strong local sputtering or transient impurity release can raise the boundary value to about $10^{15}-10^{17}$ m^-3.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a diagnostic aperture in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured upward from the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates the center of a diagnostic aperture along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ increases upward from the geometric midplane. Diagnostic apertures are the physical openings in detector housings, filter assemblies, crystal-spectrometer cameras, and other optical benches through which plasma emission passes; their geometric centers define the reference point from which lines of sight, solid angles, and etendue are computed for each diagnostic channel.

Together with the corresponding major-radius $R$ and toroidal angle $\phi$, this coordinate fully specifies the aperture center in three dimensions. The analogous coordinate for a generic aperture is [vertical_coordinate_of_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_aperture), while [vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element](name:vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element) covers the broader class of optical components and [vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position) covers general sensor locations.

On present-day medium and large tokamaks, diagnostic apertures range from the lower divertor region (Z near -2 m) to the machine top (Z near +2 m); port-mounted apertures near the midplane have |Z| less than approximately 0.5 m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture center lies above the geometric midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the divertor target surface center in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the divertor target is the $Z$ component of the geometric center of the target surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It locates the hardware surface as a geometric reference and is distinct from the vertical position of a plasma strike point on that surface.

For a finite divertor target surface $S_t$, the surface-center coordinate is the area centroid of that surface:

$$
Z_t = \frac{1}{A_t}\int_{S_t} Z(\mathbf{x})\,dA, \qquad A_t = \int_{S_t} dA
$$

where $Z_t$ is the target-center vertical coordinate, $A_t$ is the target-surface area, $dA$ is the surface area element, and $Z(\mathbf{x})$ is the vertical height of point $\mathbf{x}$ on the target surface.

In practice this coordinate is computed from the defined target geometry, for example from an engineering surface model, metrology description, or calibrated diagnostic geometry. For a mesh representation, the integral is evaluated as an area-weighted average of the mesh-element center $Z$ coordinates. The corresponding horizontal or transverse coordinates are described by [x_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:x_coordinate_of_divertor_target) and [y_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:y_coordinate_of_divertor_target), while inner and outer strike-location quantities refer to different physical points on the divertor.

Typical values are machine-size and vertical-origin dependent. In lower-single-null tokamaks the target surface center commonly has $Z<0$, often about 0.5-3 m below the magnetic-axis or midplane region in medium to large devices; upper-divertor targets have comparable positive values, and compact devices can have magnitudes of about 0.1-1 m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the divertor target surface center lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of an optical element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured from the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ specifies the height of the geometric center of an optical element along the symmetry axis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the upward vertical height. Optical elements include mirrors, lenses, optical fibers, beam splitters, and windows deployed in visible-light cameras, infrared cameras, and spectrometers used for plasma diagnostics.

This position is established from engineering metrology, alignment surveys, or installation records and is used together with the major radius and toroidal angle to reconstruct complete sight-line or ray-tracing geometries. The vertical center coordinate is geometrically analogous to [vertical_coordinate_of_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_aperture) and [vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture), which describe the corresponding position for other components along the same observation path.

Typical values span approximately $-3$ to $+3$ m in medium-sized tokamaks, measured relative to the machine midplane at $Z = 0$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the optical element center is located above the machine midplane, in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: X coordinate of the center of a diagnostic aperture, measured along the x axis in a right-handed camera Cartesian frame with basis (x, y, z). It locates the aperture laterally relative to the chosen camera-frame origin.
NAMES.long:
The x coordinate of a diagnostic aperture is the signed lateral position of the aperture center relative to the origin of a right-handed camera Cartesian frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$. It specifies one component of the aperture center location used to define viewing geometry, optical alignment, and line-of-sight calculations.

The coordinate is the projection of the aperture-center displacement onto the camera-frame x basis direction:

$$
x_\mathrm{ap} = (\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ap} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{x}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ap}$ is the aperture-center position, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the origin of the camera Cartesian frame, and $\hat{x}$ is the unit vector along its x axis.

In practice, this coordinate is determined from mechanical design drawings, metrology, optical calibration, or camera alignment procedures. Together with the corresponding y and z coordinates, it fixes the aperture center used to construct rays or fields of view for diagnostics such as infrared cameras, visible cameras, bolometry, or spectroscopy systems.

Typical values depend on the chosen camera origin and optical layout. For compact in-vessel or port-mounted diagnostics, offsets are often in the range -0.5-0.5 m, while larger external optical assemblies may have offsets of order -2-2 m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture center is displaced from the camera-frame origin in the $+\hat{x}$ direction of the right-handed camera Cartesian frame with basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$.

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Cartesian x coordinate of the divertor target surface center in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame. The +x direction is the horizontal direction corresponding to toroidal angle phi = 0, and z is vertical.
NAMES.long:
The x coordinate of a divertor target is the signed horizontal Cartesian coordinate of the geometric center of the target surface, expressed relative to an origin on the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis. The $+\hat{x}$ direction is the horizontal reference direction at toroidal angle $\phi=0$, and $\hat{z}$ is vertical. The coordinate itself does not identify which physical target is meant; inner, outer, upper, lower, or other target identity is specified by the associated divertor geometry context.

Its relation to the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is

$$
x = R \cos\phi
$$

where $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle measured from the $+\hat{x}$ direction, and $Z$ is vertical height with $z=Z$.

This coordinate is used with the corresponding y and vertical coordinates to locate the divertor target surface center in three-dimensional space. It provides the geometric reference point for describing target placement, plasma-wall interaction geometry, and line-of-sight or incidence-angle relationships without implying any particular method used to determine the geometry.

Typical magnitudes for divertor target surface centers are about 0.5-8 m in medium-size to large tokamaks. Values near the $\phi=0$ reference direction are positive and comparable to the local major radius, while targets at other toroidal angles can have smaller or negative x coordinates.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the divertor-target surface center lies on the $+\hat{x}$ side of the origin in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

NAMES.name: x_direction_unit_vector_of_camera
NAMES.short: X-axis projection of the unit vector defining the image-up orientation direction of a camera in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The X component of the camera's image-up direction unit vector specifies how much the camera's vertical image axis aligns with the $\hat{x}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. The image-up direction defines which way is "up" in the camera's recorded field of view and, together with the line-of-sight axis, fully characterizes the camera's rotational orientation in the machine frame.

The three Cartesian components $(u_x, u_y, u_z)$ of the image-up unit vector satisfy the normalization constraint:

$$
u_x^2 + u_y^2 + u_z^2 = 1
$$

where $u_x$ is this quantity and $u_y$ is the [Y component](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_camera). Because the vector is a unit vector by construction, the magnitude of each component is bounded between $-1$ and $+1$.

The components are established from the mechanical mounting geometry of the camera, typically determined during installation surveys or geometric calibration against surveyed reference targets. Knowing the image-up vector is essential for mapping pixel coordinates in the camera image to spatial directions in the machine frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the camera's image-up direction unit vector has a component pointing in the $+\hat{x}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_limiter
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Total xenon ion number density in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a limiter, summed over all positive charge states and excluding neutral xenon atoms.
NAMES.long:
Xenon density at a limiter is the total number density of xenon ions at the plasma-side near-sheath location where open magnetic field lines meet the limiter surface. The unqualified impurity ion density is summed over all positive xenon charge states; neutral xenon atoms are excluded. As a number density, its physical range is non-negative.

It is defined from charge-state-resolved xenon ion densities by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Xe,lim}} = \sum_{q=1}^{Z_{\mathrm{Xe}}} n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{q+},\mathrm{lim}}
$$

where $q$ is the integer positive charge state, $Z_{\mathrm{Xe}}=54$ is the xenon nuclear charge, and $n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{q+},\mathrm{lim}}$ is the local density of xenon ions with charge $+q e$ at the limiter, in m$^{-3}$. The summed density $n_{\mathrm{Xe,lim}}$ is also in m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from edge and limiter-region line emission together with collisional-radiative modeling, local electron temperature and electron density estimates, and boundary-plasma transport modeling. It is sensitive to local ionization and recombination, parallel transport along open field lines, xenon source strength, and recycling or retention at nearby plasma-facing material.

Typical values are highly scenario dependent. Trace xenon seeding near a limiter can give about $10^{12}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$, while strong localized injection or radiating-edge operation can produce local near-surface values of about $10^{16}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$; the value remains zero when no xenon ions are present.

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Y coordinate of the center of a diagnostic aperture in the camera right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame, measured from that frame's origin along its y axis.
NAMES.long:
The Y coordinate of a diagnostic aperture is the displacement of the aperture center along the $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ axis of the camera right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}, \hat{\mathbf{z}})$ frame. The frame origin is the point assigned coordinates $(0,0,0)$ by the calibrated camera geometry, so this coordinate is one component of the aperture-center position relative to that same origin.

The camera-frame aperture position and its Y component are related by projection onto the camera-frame basis:

$$
\mathbf{r}_{O_c\to\mathrm{ap}} = x_\mathrm{ap}\hat{\mathbf{x}} + y_\mathrm{ap}\hat{\mathbf{y}} + z_\mathrm{ap}\hat{\mathbf{z}}, \qquad y_\mathrm{ap} = \mathbf{r}_{O_c\to\mathrm{ap}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{y}}
$$

where $O_c$ is the camera-frame origin, $\mathbf{r}_{O_c\to\mathrm{ap}}$ is the vector from that origin to the aperture center, $x_\mathrm{ap}$, $y_\mathrm{ap}$, and $z_\mathrm{ap}$ are camera-frame Cartesian coordinates in meters, and the basis vectors are dimensionless unit vectors. The camera-frame $z_\mathrm{ap}$ component is distinct from vertical height unless the camera right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}, \hat{\mathbf{z}})$ frame is explicitly aligned with the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

This coordinate is determined from the calibrated geometry of the diagnostic aperture, using mechanical design information, optical-bench survey, photogrammetry, or in-vessel alignment measurements. Together with [x_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture) and the corresponding camera-frame $z$ component, it specifies the aperture-center position in the camera right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}, \hat{\mathbf{z}})$ frame; related geometric descriptions may instead use major_radius_of_diagnostic_aperture and [vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Typical numerical values are installation-specific because they depend on the chosen camera-frame origin and aperture mounting geometry. The coordinate is reported in meters and is normally fixed for a calibrated aperture unless the diagnostic is mechanically reconfigured or realigned.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture center is displaced in the $+\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ direction from the origin of the camera right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}, \hat{\mathbf{z}})$ frame.

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Cartesian Y coordinate of the divertor target surface center in the right-handed (x, y, z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The Y coordinate locates the center of the divertor target surface along the $\hat{y}$ axis of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame, where $\hat{z} = \hat{Z}$ is vertical and $\hat{x}$ is aligned with $\phi = 0$, with the toroidal angle $\phi$ increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$. This coordinate relates to the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ description of the same point by the standard transformation $y = R\sin\phi$, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle.

This coordinate is used alongside [x_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:x_coordinate_of_divertor_target) and [vertical_coordinate_of_divertor_target](name:vertical_coordinate_of_divertor_target) to fully specify the three-dimensional Cartesian position of the divertor target center in plasma-wall interaction modeling. It is obtained from engineering drawings of the divertor geometry or from geometric calibration of diagnostics such as infrared cameras that image the target surface.

The magnitude of $y$ is bounded by the major radius of the machine; for a target segment at toroidal angle $\phi$ and radial distance $R$ from the symmetry axis, $|y|$ spans zero to approximately $R$ depending on the toroidal location of the target.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the divertor target center is displaced in the $+\hat{y}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: y_direction_unit_vector_of_camera
NAMES.short: Y component of the camera's image-up unit vector in its local right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame. It is a dimensionless scalar giving the projection of the camera's image-up direction onto the local +y axis.
NAMES.long:
The y direction unit vector component of a camera is the y projection of the camera's image-up unit vector, which defines the physical direction appearing upward in the recorded image. It is resolved in the camera's local right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame and is a dimensionless scalar.

The component is the projection of the normalized up vector onto the local $\hat{y}$ basis direction:

$$
u_y = \mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{up}} \cdot \hat{y}
$$

where $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{up}} = (u_x, u_y, u_z)$ is the camera image-up unit vector with dimensionless components satisfying $u_x^2 + u_y^2 + u_z^2 = 1$.

The up vector is established from the camera mounting geometry and refined by optical calibration or an in-vessel surveyed reference direction, then normalized before its components are used. The y component alone does not fix the camera pose; the complete image-up axis requires all three components, and the full orientation additionally requires the viewing direction.

Values lie in the range $[-1, 1]$: near $+1$ the image-up direction is nearly aligned with $+\hat{y}$, near $-1$ with $-\hat{y}$, and near $0$ the up direction has little projection along $\hat{y}$.

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_conduction
NAMES.short: Conductive component of plasma power deposited on first-wall and divertor material surfaces. It represents heat carried by thermal conduction and excludes convected, radiated, recombination, and neutral-particle power channels.
NAMES.long:
Power at wall due to conduction is the component of the wall-deposited plasma energy flux carried by thermal conduction, primarily electron heat conduction along magnetic field lines in the scrape-off-layer and divertor plasma. It is distinct from particle enthalpy convection, radiation, recombination energy, and neutral-particle energy deposition.

The scalar power is defined by integrating the deposited conductive heat-flux density over the plasma-facing material surface:

$$
P_{\mathrm{wall,cond}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wall}}} q_{n,\mathrm{cond}}^{\mathrm{dep}} \, dA
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{wall,cond}}$ is the conducted wall power, $A_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the wetted first-wall and divertor material surface, $dA$ is a surface element in $\mathrm{m^2}$, and $q_{n,\mathrm{cond}}^{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the local conductive heat-flux density into the material in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. The upstream parallel conductive heat flux is often modeled as $q_{\parallel,\mathrm{cond}} = -\kappa_\parallel \nabla_\parallel T_e$, where $q_{\parallel,\mathrm{cond}}$ is in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $\kappa_\parallel$ is in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,eV^{-1}}$ when $T_e$ is expressed in eV, and $\nabla_\parallel T_e$ is in $\mathrm{eV\,m^{-1}}$. Mapping this upstream flux to $q_{n,\mathrm{cond}}^{\mathrm{dep}}$ includes magnetic incidence on the surface and may include a sheath heat-transmission factor, so the deposited conductive power is not simply the bare upstream parallel flux integrated over geometric wall area.

In practice this quantity is inferred from wall heat-flux measurements and edge-plasma modeling. Infrared thermography, calorimetry, embedded temperature sensors, Langmuir probes, and edge Thomson scattering can constrain the deposited heat flux, electron temperature gradients, and the partition between conductive and convective channels. Together with [power_at_wall_due_to_convection](name:power_at_wall_due_to_convection), this quantity forms the main kinetic thermal contribution to plasma_power_at_wall; it is also part of thermal_power_at_wall and the divertor-local thermal load described by [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor).

Typical magnitudes range from $10^5-10^7$ W in medium-size tokamak plasmas, can fall near zero in strongly detached or highly radiative conditions, and can reach $10^7-10^8$ W or more in high-power devices if a large fraction of scrape-off-layer power reaches material surfaces conductively.
NAMES.sign: Positive when conductive thermal energy is deposited from the plasma into first-wall or divertor material surfaces.

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_convection
NAMES.short: Power deposited on plasma-facing wall and divertor surfaces by convective particle energy flux from the scrape-off layer, including particle enthalpy and directed kinetic energy carried into the material surface.
NAMES.long:
Convective power at the wall is the surface-integrated rate at which plasma particles deposit energy on plasma-facing material surfaces by their motion into the surface. It includes thermal enthalpy and directed kinetic energy carried by particles from the scrape-off layer, and is distinct from conductive heat transport without net particle flow, represented by [power_at_wall_due_to_conduction](name:power_at_wall_due_to_conduction).

The deposited convective power is defined as the integral of the incident normal convective heat-flux density over the plasma-facing surface:

$$
P_\mathrm{conv} = \int_S q_{\mathrm{conv},\perp} \, dA, \qquad q_{\mathrm{conv},\perp}=\mathbf{q}_\mathrm{conv}\cdot\hat{n}_m
$$

where $S$ is the union of wall and divertor surfaces exposed to the plasma, $\mathbf{q}_\mathrm{conv}$ is the convective particle energy-flux vector, and $\hat{n}_m$ is the unit normal directed from the plasma into the material. With this convention $q_{\mathrm{conv},\perp}$ is positive for power incident on the component, consistent with the local flux-density quantity heat_flux_of_plasma_facing_component. In sheath-limited estimates, $q_{\mathrm{conv},\perp}\approx \sum_s \gamma_s n_s T_s c_s$, where $n_s$ is the sheath-entrance number density in m$^{-3}$, $T_s$ is the species temperature in joules per particle, $c_s$ is the characteristic sound speed in m s$^{-1}$, and $\gamma_s$ is a dimensionless sheath heat-transmission factor; if $T_s$ is supplied in eV it must be multiplied by the elementary charge to give SI power density.

In practice this quantity is obtained from edge-plasma transport or kinetic modeling with sheath boundary conditions, or inferred from integrated heat-load measurements combined with power-balance constraints. It contributes to the total thermal_power_at_wall, while [thermal_power_of_divertor](name:thermal_power_of_divertor) refers to the corresponding thermal power deposited on divertor surfaces only.

Typical integrated values are strongly scenario dependent. In attached divertor conditions they are commonly of order 0.01-1 MW in low-power experiments, 0.1-10 MW in medium and large tokamak plasmas, and can exceed 10 MW in high-power exhaust scenarios before strong detachment or radiative dissipation reduces the particle energy reaching material surfaces.

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation
NAMES.short: Total resistive Joule power converted to heat within conducting wall, plasma-facing, and vessel structures by induced, halo, or other plasma-wall currents.
NAMES.long:
Power at the wall due to ohmic dissipation is the total rate at which electrical energy is converted into heat inside conducting wall, plasma-facing, and vessel structures by currents associated with plasma-wall interaction. It includes resistive dissipation from eddy currents induced by changing magnetic fields and from halo or shared currents that pass through conducting structures.

The instantaneous Joule-heating power over the conducting material volume is

$$
P_\mathrm{ohm} = \int_V \eta(\mathbf{x},T)\, |\mathbf{j}(\mathbf{x})|^2 \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the conducting material volume, $\eta(\mathbf{x},T)$ is the electrical resistivity at position $\mathbf{x}$ and material temperature $T$ in $\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$, $\mathbf{j}$ is the local current density in $\mathrm{A}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}$, and $dV$ is a differential volume element in $\mathrm{m}^3$. For passive resistive materials, $\eta \ge 0$ and $|\mathbf{j}|^2 \ge 0$, so the integral is non-negative and represents heat production rather than a signed electromagnetic power flow.

This quantity is computed from electromagnetic circuit or field models of the conducting structures, often constrained by magnetic sensors, wall-current measurements, halo-current measurements, and material resistivity data. Thermal analysis or calorimetry can provide an independent constraint when other heat sources, such as particle impact, radiation, and recombination, are separated. The related [energy flux at wall due to eddy current](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_eddy_current) describes a local surface heat flux from eddy-current dissipation only; this quantity is a volume-integrated power and may also include halo-current dissipation.

Typical values are about 10^3-10^6 W during routine operation with slowly varying fields, and about 10^6-10^9 W during disruptions, vertical displacement events, or rapid current quenches in large devices. The magnitude depends on plasma current, magnetic-field ramp rate, wall geometry, material resistivity, and the electrical circuit paths that connect the plasma to surrounding conducting structures.

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_recombination
NAMES.short: Total power deposited on plasma-facing wall surfaces by all recombination processes, encompassing both plasma-ion recombination and surface recombination of incident neutral particles into molecules.
NAMES.long:
The total recombination power at the wall aggregates two distinct heat-load channels: the plasma-ion channel, in which ions arriving at the surface capture free electrons and release their recombination energy into the wall material, and the neutral surface-recombination channel, in which incident hydrogen-isotope atoms combine into diatomic molecules on the material surface and deposit the molecular binding energy as heat.

This quantity is the wall-surface component of the broader [power due to recombination](name:power_due_to_recombination), which encompasses volumetric recombination throughout the plasma volume. The two contributing channels are resolved separately: [plasma_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:plasma_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination) carries the ion-channel contribution and [neutral_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination) carries the neutral surface-recombination contribution, their sum giving:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}} = P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{ion}} + P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{neutral}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the integrated plasma-ion recombination power and $P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{neutral}}$ is the neutral surface-recombination power, both summed over all plasma-facing surfaces.

In edge plasma models, this quantity is evaluated from particle-balance calculations coupled to surface-interaction models, with each channel weighted by the recombination energy per event and the incident particle flux to the wall.

NAMES.name: neutral_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Power deposited on the plasma-facing wall by surface recombination of incident neutral particles, predominantly hydrogen-isotope atoms that combine into diatomic molecules and release their binding energy as heat in the wall material. It is distinct from the recombination power associated with incident plasma ions.
NAMES.long:
Neutral recombination power at the wall is the rate at which binding energy released by surface recombination of incident neutral particles is converted into heat in plasma-facing wall material. For hydrogenic plasmas the dominant channel is associative formation of H2, D2, T2, or mixed-isotope molecules from two adsorbed atoms, releasing the molecular formation enthalpy into the solid. This is the neutral-origin component of the total recombination wall power and is separate from the recombination heat carried by incident plasma ions.

The deposited power is obtained by integrating the local heat release over the plasma-facing surface:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rec},n} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wall}}} \Gamma_{n}(\mathbf{x})\, E_{\mathrm{rec}}(\mathbf{x})\, dA
$$

where $\Gamma_{n}$ is the local flux of incident neutral particles participating in surface recombination, in m^-2 s^-1, and $E_{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the effective heat deposited in the wall per participating particle, in J. If the molecular formation enthalpy $\Delta H_{\mathrm{mol}}$ is quoted per molecule, about 4.5 eV for one hydrogen-isotope molecule formed from two atoms, then the heat deposited per incident atom is approximately $\eta_{\mathrm{heat}}\,\Delta H_{\mathrm{mol}}/2$, where $\eta_{\mathrm{heat}}$ is the fraction of released energy retained in the solid rather than carried away by desorbed molecules.

In practice this quantity is estimated from modeled neutral fluxes to plasma-facing surfaces, surface recombination probabilities, and the effective accommodation of the released binding energy. It can be constrained by wall calorimetry, particle-balance analysis, spectroscopy, and neutral-transport modeling. The effective heat fraction depends on surface material, temperature, isotope, adsorbate coverage, and roughness.

Typical integrated values span roughly 10^2-10^5 W for main-chamber wall recycling in medium-sized devices, with larger values possible under high-recycling conditions and large neutral fluxes. This contribution is generally smaller than the total neutral power deposited on the wall but is relevant to detailed plasma-wall interaction power balances.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is deposited into the wall.

NAMES.name: plasma_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination
NAMES.short: Total power deposited on plasma-facing wall surfaces by recombination of plasma ions, constituting the ion-channel contribution to the overall recombination wall heat load integrated over all plasma-facing surfaces.
NAMES.long:
When plasma ions arrive at a plasma-facing wall surface, they undergo surface recombination, releasing energy equal to their ionization potential plus any residual kinetic energy carried to the surface. This quantity integrates that energy deposition rate over all plasma-facing wall surfaces and represents the plasma-ion species channel within the parent quantity [power_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:power_at_wall_due_to_recombination), which also includes neutral-particle contributions.

The deposited power is related to the local incident ion flux density by:

$$
P_\mathrm{rec} = \int_A \Gamma_\mathrm{ion}(\mathbf{r}) \, E_\mathrm{rec} \, dA
$$

where $\Gamma_\mathrm{ion}$ is the local ion particle flux density at the surface in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, $E_\mathrm{rec}$ is the mean energy released per recombination event (sum of ionization potential and residual kinetic energy, in J), and the integral extends over the total wetted plasma-facing area $A$.

This quantity excludes energy deposited by recombination of neutral particles into molecules at the surface, which is captured separately by [neutral_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination). The analogous quantity resolved at divertor strike surfaces is [plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination). It is estimated from edge plasma transport models constrained by incident ion-flux and particle-balance measurements at the boundary.

NAMES.name: power_density_at_wall
NAMES.short: Power flux density deposited on plasma-facing wall surfaces by all incident particle and radiation channels from the boundary plasma.
NAMES.long:
Power density at the wall quantifies the total thermal energy load per unit surface area delivered to plasma-facing components, aggregating contributions from charged particle impact, neutral atom bombardment, charge-exchange flux, and photon irradiation. It provides a spatially distributed measure of wall heating across the full plasma-facing geometry, in contrast to extremal statistics such as [peak_power_density_at_first_wall](name:peak_power_density_at_first_wall) or [peak_power_density_at_divertor_target](name:peak_power_density_at_divertor_target).

The local wall power density $q_w$ sums over all incident energy channels:

$$
q_w = \sum_s \Gamma_s \, E_s + q_{\mathrm{rad}}
$$

where $\Gamma_s$ is the incident particle flux density of species $s$, $E_s$ is the mean energy deposited per particle, and $q_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the radiative contribution represented by [energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_radiation](name:energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_radiation).

Spatially resolved wall heat loads are measured via calibrated infrared thermography or derived from boundary plasma transport simulations validated against bolometric total-power measurements. The [electron_energy_flux_at_wall](name:electron_energy_flux_at_wall) and ion contributions can be tracked separately as components of this total.

Typical steady-state values range from 0.1–1 MW/m² on the main first wall to 5–20 MW/m² at actively loaded divertor strike zones; transient power loads during edge-localized modes can transiently exceed these by an order of magnitude.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_beryllium_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of total beryllium ion number density to electron number density. It measures beryllium impurity abundance relative to the plasma electron population, with the beryllium ion density summed over charged ionization states.
NAMES.long:
The ratio of beryllium density to electron density is a dimensionless impurity abundance measuring how much beryllium ion population is present relative to the free electron population. The beryllium numerator is the total beryllium ion number density, summed over charged ionization states, and does not by itself weight the ions by charge.

The defining relation is:

$$
f_\mathrm{Be} = \frac{n_\mathrm{Be}}{n_e} = \frac{\sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}}{n_e}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Be}$ is the total beryllium ion number density, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in charge state $q$, and $n_e$ is the electron number density; all densities in the ratio have units of m$^{-3}$. In a quasi-neutral plasma, the charge-weighted impurity contribution enters the electron balance through terms of the form $q n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+}}$, so this ratio is closely related to fuel dilution but is not itself the charge fraction.

Beryllium impurities are commonly produced by plasma-wall interaction processes such as sputtering of beryllium-containing plasma-facing components, followed by transport and ionization in the edge and confined plasma. The ratio is inferred by combining beryllium spectroscopic measurements and collisional-radiative modeling with electron density measurements from diagnostics such as interferometry and Thomson scattering. Related beryllium density quantities include [volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density), [beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis), [beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [beryllium_density_at_limiter](name:beryllium_density_at_limiter).

Typical values in well-conditioned plasmas with beryllium plasma-facing surfaces are about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$, with many H-mode conditions lying near $10^{-3}$-$5 \times 10^{-3}$. Values can rise to several percent during strong wall source events, early conditioning phases, or after disruptions.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_carbon_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short: Ratio of total carbon number density, summed over neutral carbon and all carbon charge states, to electron number density.
NAMES.long:
The ratio of carbon density to electron density is a dimensionless impurity fraction expressing the abundance of carbon relative to the electron population. The carbon density is the total number density of carbon nuclei, including neutral carbon atoms and all ionized charge states from singly ionized to fully stripped carbon.

The ratio is defined by normalizing the summed carbon density to the electron density:

$$
f_C = \frac{n_C}{n_e}, \qquad n_C = \sum_{q=0}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C},q}
$$

where $f_C$ is the carbon fraction, $n_e$ is the electron number density in m$^{-3}$, $n_C$ is the total carbon number density in m$^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{C},0}$ is neutral atomic carbon, and $n_{\mathrm{C},q}$ for $q=1,\ldots,6$ are carbon ions with charge state $q+$.

In practice, $n_C$ may be inferred from spectroscopic measurements, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, edge and divertor line emission, or collisional-radiative modeling, often combined with an independently measured or reconstructed $n_e$. The numerator may correspond conceptually to a [volume-averaged carbon density](name:volume_averaged_carbon_density), a [line-averaged carbon density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density), or another physically specified carbon density measure, but the defining ratio is always formed with the corresponding electron density. Because neutral carbon contributes to $n_C$ but not directly to quasineutrality or $Z_\mathrm{eff}$, the ionization-state distribution matters when relating this fraction to charge-weighted impurity effects. In an otherwise deuterium plasma with fully stripped carbon, quasineutrality gives $Z_\mathrm{eff}=1+30 f_C$; partial ionization gives a smaller charge-weighted contribution for the same total carbon density.

Typical core or volume-averaged carbon fractions are about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ in low-carbon wall conditions and about $10^{-2}$-$5\times10^{-2}$ in carbon-wall or strong erosion conditions. Larger local values can occur near plasma-facing carbon sources, in the scrape-off layer, or in detached divertor regions.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_boron_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless global boron impurity fraction equal to the volume-averaged total boron number density divided by the volume-averaged electron number density.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a global measure of boron content in a plasma, expressed as the ratio of the volume-averaged total boron number density to the volume-averaged electron number density. The boron density includes boron nuclei in all ionization states represented in the plasma composition, so the ratio measures elemental boron abundance relative to electrons rather than a single charge state.

For a plasma volume $V$, the ratio is defined by

$$
f_B = \frac{\langle n_B \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}, \qquad \langle n \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V}\int_V n(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $n_B$ is the total boron number density, $n_e$ is the electron number density, and both averaged densities have units of m$^{-3}$. The ratio $f_B$ is dimensionless.

The value is commonly inferred from plasma composition analysis by combining measurements or modeling of impurity content with the electron density distribution used to form the same volume average. It is useful for comparing the global level of boron introduced by wall conditioning, erosion, or impurity transport independently of the absolute plasma density.

Typical values are non-negative and usually much smaller than unity when boron is a trace impurity. Values approaching unity would indicate that boron makes a major contribution to the plasma particle inventory and charge balance rather than acting as a minor impurity.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_oxygen_ion_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Ratio of volume-averaged total oxygen ion number density to volume-averaged electron density, expressing the global oxygen impurity concentration as a dimensionless plasma composition fraction.
NAMES.long:
The oxygen fraction $f_O$ measures the global oxygen impurity burden in a fusion plasma as the ratio of the volume-averaged oxygen ion density to the volume-averaged electron density, where both averages are taken over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface.

$$
f_O = \frac{\langle n_O \rangle}{\langle n_e \rangle}
$$

where $\langle n_O \rangle = \sum_{q=1}^{8} \langle n_{O^{q+}} \rangle$ is the volume-averaged oxygen ion number density summed over all ionization stages from $O^{1+}$ to $O^{8+}$, and $\langle n_e \rangle$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density).

The quantity is inferred from vacuum ultraviolet or soft X-ray spectroscopy of oxygen emission lines combined with collisional-radiative or coronal equilibrium modeling; it is the normalized complement to [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density), which carries the absolute density, while [line_averaged_oxygen_density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density) provides a routinely measured chord-integrated cross-check.

In clean, well-conditioned tokamak discharges $f_O$ remains below 0.01; values of several percent can occur during commissioning, after disruptions, or with intentional oxygen seeding. Because each fully-stripped oxygen ion contributes eight electrons, even modest $f_O$ values measurably dilute fuel ion density and enhance radiative power losses through oxygen line emission.

NAMES.name: reference_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Reference wavelength of an optical filter is the nominal center or peak wavelength of its passband, usually the wavelength at which the nominal transmission is maximal. It identifies the spectral location of the filter response, not the full passband shape or width.
NAMES.long:
Reference wavelength of a filter, $\lambda_\mathrm{ref}$, is the nominal spectral position assigned to an optical bandpass filter. For a single-peaked bandpass it is normally the wavelength at which the nominal spectral transmittance is largest; for asymmetric or structured responses it is a manufacturer- or calibration-defined reference point for the passband center.

For a peak-defined filter reference, the defining relation is

$$
\lambda_\mathrm{ref} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\lambda} T_\mathrm{nom}(\lambda)
$$

where $T_\mathrm{nom}(\lambda)$ is the nominal spectral transmittance as a function of wavelength $\lambda$.

The value is obtained from the filter specification or from laboratory spectral-transmission calibration. It is used together with the passband width and, when available, lower and upper wavelength bounds to describe the spectral region transmitted by the filter; the reference wavelength alone does not fully determine the filter response.

Typical values for visible and infrared plasma diagnostics are about $4\times10^{-7}$-$1.5\times10^{-5}$ m, with narrow line filters often centered near specific atomic or molecular emission wavelengths and thermal-infrared filters commonly in the micrometer range.

NAMES.name: angular_width_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Vertical angular span subtended by the effective Bragg crystal aperture at the X-ray source, along the Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is a geometric acceptance angle, distinct from the Bragg diffraction angle, the rocking-curve width, and the toroidal angular span.
NAMES.long:
The angular width of a Bragg crystal is the non-negative vertical angular span of the effective diffracting aperture as seen from the X-ray source or chosen source point. The vertical direction is the $Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, complementary to the toroidal $\phi$ angular span described by [toroidal_angle_of_bragg_crystal](name:toroidal_angle_of_bragg_crystal). This quantity is closely related to [angle_of_bragg_crystal](name:angular_width_of_bragg_crystal) when that name is used for the same vertical acceptance angle; it is not the Bragg diffraction angle $\theta_B$ that selects wavelength, and it is not the intrinsic rocking-curve width.

For a flat aperture centered on the line from source to crystal, the vertical angular width is the angle subtended by the effective vertical aperture height:

$$
\alpha_v = 2 \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{a_v}{2L}\right) \simeq \frac{a_v}{L}
$$

where $\alpha_v$ is the angular width in rad, $a_v$ is the effective vertical aperture height in meters, and $L$ is the distance from the source point to the crystal center in meters. The approximation applies when $a_v \ll L$.

In practice, the effective aperture may be set by the physical crystal height, masks, collimators, or the illuminated part of a curved focusing crystal. For curved or off-axis geometries, the same quantity is obtained from the angular envelope of rays from the source that intercept the active Bragg-diffracting surface, usually by geometric optics or ray tracing. Together with the toroidal angular span, it contributes to the collected solid angle and photon throughput, while spectral selection remains governed by Bragg diffraction.

Typical vertical angular widths in tokamak X-ray crystal spectrometers are about 0.001-0.05 rad. Compact or large-aperture systems can approach 0.1 rad, while high-resolution channels often use a few milliradians to a few tens of milliradians.

NAMES.name: bragg_crystal_width
NAMES.short: Full width of the Bragg crystal in an X-ray crystal spectrometer along the first transverse (X1) axis, applicable only for rectangular crystal geometry.
NAMES.long:
The Bragg crystal width specifies the physical extent of the diffracting crystal element along its first transverse coordinate axis (X1) in an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel. This dimension is only defined for rectangular crystal geometry; together with bragg_crystal_height along the orthogonal X2 axis and [thickness_of_bragg_crystal](name:thickness_of_bragg_crystal) through the crystal body, it fully parameterizes the three-dimensional rectangular crystal geometry required for solid-angle and acceptance calculations.

The X1 width governs the acceptance aperture along the meridional or sagittal direction depending on the crystal mount orientation. A larger width intercepts a greater solid angle of X-ray emission from the plasma source, increasing photon throughput, but can introduce geometric aberrations in curved-crystal focusing arrangements such as Johann or Johansson geometries. The bragg_wavelength separately characterizes the diffraction condition, linking crystal orientation to the photon energies that satisfy Bragg's law.

Typical crystal widths for fusion-diagnostic X-ray spectrometers range from a few millimeters to a few tens of millimeters, depending on crystal material and spectrometer geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the extent is measured as a physical length from one edge of the crystal to the other along the X1 transverse axis of the crystal coordinate frame.

NAMES.name: bremsstrahlung_power
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic power radiated by the plasma via bremsstrahlung, the continuum emission arising from electron deceleration in the Coulomb fields of plasma ions.
NAMES.long:
Bremsstrahlung (braking radiation) is continuum electromagnetic emission produced when free electrons are decelerated in the Coulomb fields of ions; this quantity is the plasma-volume-integrated total radiated power from that process, representing a global energy loss term in the plasma power balance.

The total bremsstrahlung power is defined by:

$$
P_\text{brem} = C_\text{brem} \int n_e^2(\mathbf{r})\, Z_\text{eff}(\mathbf{r})\, T_e^{1/2}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density in m$^{-3}$, $Z_\text{eff}$ is the mean effective ion charge, $T_e$ is the electron temperature in eV, and $C_\text{brem} \approx 5.34 \times 10^{-37}$ W m$^3$ eV$^{-1/2}$ is the free-free emission coefficient. The strong $n_e^2$ and $Z_\text{eff}$ dependence means impurity content significantly amplifies bremsstrahlung losses.

The global bremsstrahlung power is inferred from broadband bolometric measurements or by volumetrically integrating $n_e$, $T_e$, and $Z_\text{eff}$ profiles derived from Thomson scattering and spectroscopy. The local spectral counterpart [bremsstrahlung spectral radiance] additionally enables $Z_\text{eff}$ inference from visible continuum emission.

Together with [power due to line radiation](name:power_due_to_line_radiation) from bound-bound atomic transitions and [power due to synchrotron radiation](name:power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation) from relativistic electron gyration, bremsstrahlung emission is one of the principal radiative power loss channels. In present-generation tokamaks, total bremsstrahlung losses range from approximately 0.5-10 MW; in high-density, high-$Z_\text{eff}$ burning-plasma scenarios, losses can reach several tens of MW.

NAMES.name: brightness_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Photon radiance of soft X-ray emission received on a detector channel, integrated over the detector's energy acceptance band.
NAMES.long:
Soft X-ray (SXR) brightness is the number of soft-X-ray photons arriving at a detector channel per unit area, per unit time, and per unit solid angle, integrated over the instrument's energy acceptance band. The emission originates from free-free (bremsstrahlung), free-bound (recombination), and bound-bound (line radiation) contributions from electrons and impurity ions in the sub-keV to few-keV photon energy range.

The quantity is defined by the energy-band integral of the differential photon radiance:

$$
B = \int_{E_1}^{E_2} \frac{d^4 N}{dA \, dt \, d\Omega \, dE} \, dE
$$

where $E_1$ and $E_2$ are the lower and upper energy limits of the detector's acceptance band, $N$ is the photon count, $A$ is the detector active area, $t$ is time, and $\Omega$ is the solid angle subtended by the detection geometry.

SXR detectors are arranged in multi-channel arrays covering the plasma cross-section with fan-beam line-of-sight geometries. Individual channel signals are combined via tomographic inversion to reconstruct the local emissivity, enabling plasma tomography, detection of MHD modes such as sawteeth and neoclassical tearing modes, and tracking of impurity transport. The companion power-radiance quantity [spectral_radiance_of_soft_xray_detector](name:spectral_radiance_of_soft_xray_detector) weights each photon by its energy rather than counting it. For the analogous photon-count brightness in the hard X-ray regime, see [hard_xray_brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness).

NAMES.name: brightness_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short: Photon radiance measured by a visible-band camera channel, giving the number of photons collected per unit detector area, per unit time, and per unit solid angle along a line of sight.
NAMES.long:
Brightness of a visible camera is the photon radiance reaching the camera within its visible passband along a line of sight. It counts photons rather than radiant energy, normalized by collection area, observation time, and accepted solid angle, with the viewing-angle projection treated explicitly.

The photon radiance can be defined from the photons collected by a small detector element viewing a small solid angle:

$$
B_\mathrm{vis} = \frac{dN_\gamma}{dt\,dA\,\cos\alpha\,d\Omega}
$$

where $B_\mathrm{vis}$ has unit m^-2.s^-1.sr^-1, $dN_\gamma$ is the photon count with unit 1, $dt$ is the exposure or integration time in s, $dA$ is the unprojected physical detector area in m^2, $\alpha$ is the [alpha angle] in rad between the detector surface normal and the incoming ray, and $d\Omega$ is the accepted solid angle in sr. The factor $dA\cos\alpha$ is the projected detector area normal to the ray.

In practice this quantity is obtained from calibrated camera counts after dark-offset subtraction, flat-field and gain correction, detector quantum-efficiency calibration, exposure-time normalization, optical-transmission correction, and geometric calibration of the viewed solid angle. It can include visible line radiation, continuum bremsstrahlung, molecular-band emission, impurity radiation, and light from plasma-wall interactions within the camera response band.

Typical magnitudes vary widely with wavelength band, viewing geometry, and plasma conditions. Faint continuum or wall-background signals may be about 10^15-10^18 m^-2.s^-1.sr^-1, while bright edge or divertor line emission is often 10^18-10^22 m^-2.s^-1.sr^-1; intense transient or saturated views can exceed 10^22 m^-2.s^-1.sr^-1.

NAMES.name: calibration_factor_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short: Multiplicative calibration factor that converts a dark-corrected raw pixel count from a visible-band camera detector into absolute band-integrated photon radiance, expressed in inverse square meters per second per steradian. It aggregates relay optics transmission, detector quantum efficiency, electronic gain, pixel etendue, and exposure time, integrated over the camera's spectral bandpass, into a single per-pixel coefficient.
NAMES.long:
The calibration factor of a visible camera is the multiplicative coefficient that converts a dark-corrected raw pixel count into the absolute band-integrated photon radiance incident on that pixel. It encapsulates the full end-to-end sensitivity of the detection channel: relay optics transmission, detector quantum efficiency, electronic gain, pixel etendue, and exposure time, all combined into a single per-pixel value. The dark-corrected radiance follows the linear relation $L = C\,I$, where $I$ is the dark-subtracted count and $C$ is this factor.

Because $C$ inverts the detection chain, it equals the reciprocal of the channel throughput. For a pixel of area $A_\mathrm{pix}$ subtending solid angle $\Omega_\mathrm{pix}$, exposed for time $\tau$ with electronic gain $g$ and a bandpass-averaged product of quantum efficiency and optical transmission $\langle \eta T \rangle$:

$$
C = \frac{1}{A_\mathrm{pix}\,\Omega_\mathrm{pix}\,\tau\,g\,\langle \eta T \rangle}
$$

where $A_\mathrm{pix}$ is in m^2, $\Omega_\mathrm{pix}$ in sr, $\tau$ in s, and $g$ and $\langle \eta T \rangle$ are dimensionless. The denominator carries units of m^2 sr s, so $C$ has units of m^-2 s^-1 sr^-1, consistent with a band-integrated photon radiance per count. The factor therefore decreases as any element of the throughput increases: a more efficient optical path, higher quantum efficiency, or higher gain produces more counts per unit radiance and hence a smaller counts-to-radiance conversion factor.

The factor is determined by laboratory or in-situ calibration against a source of known absolute spectral radiance, such as an integrating sphere or a calibrated tungsten-halogen lamp, operated under the same optical, spectral-filter, and electronic configuration used during plasma discharges. Because sensitivity varies from pixel to pixel, the factor is resolved across the detector and implicitly absorbs flat-field and vignetting non-uniformities.

No universal value exists because $C$ depends strongly on the optics, detector type, gain setting, and spectral filter. For fast visible cameras on tokamaks, representative magnitudes span roughly $10^{10}$ to $10^{15}$ m^-2 s^-1 sr^-1 per count; these are illustrative only, and the applicable measured calibration must be used for quantitative work.

NAMES.name: count_at_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Detected photon count rate at a single pixel of an X-ray crystal spectrometer detector, giving the number of Bragg-diffracted X-ray photons registered at that pixel per unit time.
NAMES.long:
The photon count rate at a detector pixel quantifies how many X-ray photons diffracted by the crystal arrive at one pixel element per second during a spectrometer acquisition frame. Each pixel samples a narrow photon-energy interval determined by the Bragg diffraction geometry; the characteristic photon energy assigned to a pixel is given by [energy_of_detector_pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel), with spectral bounds defined by [lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).

The mapping from pixel position to photon wavelength follows the Bragg condition

$$
2d\sin\theta = \lambda
$$

where $d$ is the crystal plane spacing, $\theta$ is the local diffraction angle at the pixel, and $\lambda$ is the corresponding photon wavelength.

The count rate is recorded by solid-state detector arrays (CCDs, strip detectors, or pixel arrays) and constitutes the primary observable for X-ray crystal spectroscopy of highly charged impurity emission lines. The physical size of each pixel, relevant for geometric efficiency corrections, is described by [extent_of_detector_pixel](name:extent_of_detector_pixel). The count rate may be normalized to a reference value to form [normalized_count_at_detector_pixel](name:normalized_count_at_detector_pixel), and its temporal evolution is tracked by [time_derivative_of_count_at_detector_pixel](name:time_derivative_of_count_at_detector_pixel).

NAMES.name: curvature_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Radius of curvature of a diagnostic optical element surface, giving the signed distance from the surface vertex to its center of curvature and thereby determining the element's geometric focusing power.
NAMES.long:
The radius of curvature $R$ of an optical element surface is the signed distance from the surface vertex to its center of curvature, controlling how the element focuses or defocuses incident radiation. As a parent quantity, it generalizes over the multiple distinct surfaces and functional curvature geometries of a complete optical element, including reflective entry and exit surfaces and spectral image surfaces.

For a spherical surface, $R$ and the surface curvature $\kappa$ are related by:

$$
R = \frac{1}{\kappa}
$$

where $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) is the principal curvature at the surface vertex. Smaller $|R|$ implies stronger focusing power; a flat surface corresponds to $R \to \infty$. Specific variants include [back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element), which characterizes the rear-surface radius along the local X1 axis for cylindrical and toroidal geometries, and [spectral_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:spectral_surface_curvature_of_optical_element), which gives the Rowland-circle radius of the spectral image surface in spectrometer channels. The primary dispersing surface geometry is described by [surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:curvature_of_optical_element). Radii are determined by optical profilometry or interferometric metrology during element fabrication and calibration. Typical absolute values range from 0.1 m to a few meters for UV and X-ray spectrometer optics.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center of curvature lies on the same side as the incoming radiation (concave surface geometry).

NAMES.name: back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Radius of curvature of the rear surface of a diagnostic optical element along the local X1 axis, applicable to spherical, cylindrical, and toroidal surface geometries.
NAMES.long:
The back-surface X1 radius of curvature $R_{\mathrm{back},X1}$ describes the curvature of the exit face of a diagnostic optical element in the X1 direction of the local surface frame $(X1, X2, X3)$, where $X1$ and $X2$ span the optical surface and $X3$ is the outward surface normal. This parameter is required by ray-tracing and Gaussian-optics models to compute the wavefront transformation induced by the rear surface of lenses, windows, and mirrors used in visible and infrared camera systems and visible spectrometer diagnostics. A finite value applies only when the surface curvature type permits non-planar geometry in X1: specifically, spherical (type 2), cylindrical along X1 (type 4), and toroidal (type 5) surface types.

For a thick lens in air, the paraxial focal length $f$ is related to the front and back radii by the Lensmaker's equation:

$$
\frac{1}{f} = (n-1)\left[\frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{front},X1}} - \frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{back},X1}} + \frac{(n-1)d}{n\,R_{\mathrm{front},X1}\,R_{\mathrm{back},X1}}\right]
$$

where $n$ is the refractive index of the element material, $d$ is the axial thickness, and $R_{\mathrm{front},X1}$ is the front-surface radius of curvature given by front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element. For toroidal or cylindrical elements the orthogonal principal curvature in X2 is an independent parameter given by [vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element); for a spherical surface both principal radii are equal.

Absolute values range from a few millimeters for tightly curved condenser elements to hundreds of meters for near-flat windows and beam-splitters; a zero value conventionally represents an infinite radius (planar surface).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center of curvature of the back surface lies on the exit (transmitted-beam) side of the optical element.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions in a plasma fuel population, used locally or as the deuterium-density basis for line averages, volume averages, and isotope-density ratios. It represents absolute deuterium fuel content; any dimensionless abundance or ratio must state its normalization separately.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density is the species-resolved number density of deuterium ions in a plasma, conventionally denoted $n_D$. It counts ionized deuterium fuel particles per unit physical volume and is distinct from a deuterium fraction, concentration, or isotope ratio, which require an additional normalization. Local, chord-averaged, volume-averaged, and ratio quantities all derive from the same underlying $n_D$ field.

The local absolute density is defined by the particle count in an infinitesimal volume:

$$
n_D = \frac{dN_D}{dV}
$$

where $N_D$ is the number of deuterium ions in volume $V$; the absolute density has SI unit $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Neutral deuterium atoms and non-hydrogenic impurity ions are not included unless a more specific quantity states a different population.

In practice, $n_D$ is obtained from isotope-sensitive particle diagnostics, spectroscopic constraints, fusion-product information, and particle-balance or transport analysis. A [line-averaged deuterium density](name:line_averaged_deuterium_density) is the path average of $n_D$ along a diagnostic chord, while a [volume-averaged deuterium density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_density) is its average over the plasma volume. The [ratio of tritium density to deuterium density](name:ratio_of_tritium_density_to_deuterium_density) uses the same $n_D$ as the deuterium reference density in a dimensionless isotope-density ratio.

Typical local or averaged deuterium ion densities in magnetically confined fusion plasmas range from $10^{18}-10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, with core values in fueled tokamak plasmas often $10^{19}-10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. In nearly pure deuterium operation, $n_D$ can be close to the total hydrogenic ion density; in balanced deuterium-tritium mixtures, it is often of the same order as the tritium density.

NAMES.name: efficiency_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Dimensionless optical throughput of a spectrometer channel: the fraction of photons within the channel acceptance that are delivered to the active detector area after collection, transmission, reflection, dispersion, aperture, and window losses.
NAMES.long:
Efficiency of a spectrometer channel is the dimensionless probability that a photon within the channel acceptance reaches the active detector area. It represents optical throughput losses only, and is distinct from the geometrical or spectral acceptance described by spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel.

The channel efficiency can be defined as a ratio of photon fluxes:

$$
\eta_\mathrm{ch}(\lambda) = \frac{\Phi_\mathrm{det}(\lambda)}{\Phi_\mathrm{acc}(\lambda)}
$$

where $\Phi_\mathrm{det}(\lambda)$ is the photon flux delivered to the detector and $\Phi_\mathrm{acc}(\lambda)$ is the photon flux from the observed source that lies within the channel acceptance before optical losses. Both quantities must be expressed in the same units, such as photons s$^{-1}$ for band-integrated photon flux or photons s$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$ for wavelength-resolved photon flux.

In practice, this efficiency is obtained from radiometric calibration using calibrated lamps, integrating spheres, laser sources, or transfer-standard detectors. The calibration may include mirror reflectivity, lens or fiber transmission, slit throughput, grating efficiency, filter transmission, detector-window transmission, and alignment losses; detector quantum efficiency may be included only when the efficiency is intended to describe the full photon-to-signal response.

The physical range is $0 \leq \eta_\mathrm{ch} \leq 1$. Well-aligned visible spectroscopy channels commonly have efficiencies from about 0.01-0.8, depending on wavelength, optical coatings, fiber coupling, grating order, and aperture losses.

NAMES.name: emissivity_due_to_fusion
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of neutron production from thermonuclear fusion reactions, giving the spatial distribution of fusion neutron emission per unit volume at each point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The neutron emissivity due to fusion quantifies the number of fusion-born neutrons generated per unit volume per unit time at a given plasma location. This volumetric source term encodes the combined effect of local fuel-ion densities and the thermally-averaged fusion reactivity, and drives the global neutron field from which plasma performance is diagnosed.

For a binary fusion reaction between ion species $a$ and $b$, the emissivity is given by:

$$
\epsilon_{ab} = \frac{n_a \, n_b}{1 + \delta_{ab}} \langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab}
$$

where $n_a$ and $n_b$ are the number densities of the reacting ions, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab}$ is the fusion reactivity (velocity-averaged fusion cross-section) at the local ion temperature, and $\delta_{ab} = 1$ for identical-species reactions to avoid double-counting.

The emissivity profile is inferred from measurements by neutron camera arrays and collimated detector systems via Abel inversion or tomographic reconstruction. The two principal reaction channels are resolved as [deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), covering the neutron-emitting D-D branch, and [deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), which dominates in D-T operation due to the much larger fusion cross-section. Integrating this emissivity over the plasma volume and weighting by the per-reaction neutron energy connects to the [total_neutron_power](name:total_neutron_power).

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of neutron production from deuterium-deuterium fusion reactions, giving the spatial distribution of DD neutron emission per unit volume across the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-deuterium neutron emissivity $\varepsilon_{DD}$ is the local number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from D-D fusion reactions. Of the two equally probable D-D reaction branches, only the neutron-producing channel $^2\text{H} + ^2\text{H} \rightarrow {^3\text{He}} + n$ (releasing a 2.45 MeV neutron) contributes to this quantity; the proton-producing branch $^2\text{H} + ^2\text{H} \rightarrow T + p$ does not.

The emissivity is related to the local fuel conditions by:

$$
\varepsilon_{DD} = \frac{n_D^2}{2} \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}
$$

where $n_D$ is the local deuterium number density and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}$ is the velocity-averaged reaction rate coefficient for the neutron-producing branch; the factor $1/2$ prevents double-counting of identical reactants.

The spatial profile of $\varepsilon_{DD}$ is reconstructed from chord-integrated signals recorded by multiple neutron detectors distributed around the device, using tomographic inversion to recover the local distribution. Volume integration of $\varepsilon_{DD}$ yields the global neutron emission rate characterized by [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion) for the purely thermal component and includes beam-related contributions captured by [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion). The D-T plasma analog is [deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), and the corresponding local fusion power density from all D-D channels is [deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion).

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Neutron emissivity due to deuterium-tritium fusion reactions in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium-tritium fusion emissivity is the local volumetric rate at which neutrons are produced by deuterium-tritium fusion reactions. Each D-T reaction produces one neutron with energy near 14.1 MeV, so this quantity is equal to the D-T fusion reaction-rate density and is the source-rate counterpart of [deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion).

For a mixture of thermal and nonthermal deuterium and tritium populations, the total emissivity can be written as a sum over reacting population pairs:

$$
\epsilon_{DT} = \sum_{i,j} n_{D,i} n_{T,j} \langle \sigma v_{\mathrm{rel}} \rangle_{DT,ij}
$$

where $\epsilon_{DT}$ is the D-T neutron emissivity in $m^{-3}.s^{-1}$, $i$ and $j$ label thermal, beam, or other fast-ion populations, $n_{D,i}$ and $n_{T,j}$ are deuterium and tritium number densities in $m^{-3}$, and $\langle \sigma v_{\mathrm{rel}} \rangle_{DT,ij}$ is the D-T fusion reactivity for that pair in $m^3.s^{-1}$. For a thermal deuterium-thermal tritium pair, this factor is the thermally averaged D-T fusion reactivity.

In practice, this quantity is computed from ion densities, temperatures, and fast-ion distribution functions, or inferred from absolutely calibrated neutron measurements such as neutron counters, activation systems, neutron cameras, and spectrometers. Spatial reconstruction may use tomographic or model-constrained inversion. The total can be decomposed into thermal-thermal, beam/fast-thermal, thermal-fast, and fast-fast terms, corresponding to distinctions used for quantities such as [neutron_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion) and [deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion).

Typical values span many orders of magnitude: low-temperature or trace-tritium regions may be below $10^{14}$ $m^{-3}.s^{-1}$, while hot D-T cores in high-performance tokamak plasmas can reach about $10^{16}$-$10^{19}$ $m^{-3}.s^{-1}$. The rate rises steeply with ion temperature in the several-keV to tens-of-keV range and, for thermal reactants, scales approximately with the product of deuterium and tritium densities.

NAMES.name: energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Characteristic photon energy assigned to a detector pixel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer from the pixel's Bragg diffraction geometry.
NAMES.long:
The energy of a detector pixel is the central photon energy represented by that pixel's spectral channel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It is set by the pixel position relative to the diffracting crystal and detector surface, and is the energy counterpart of the pixel Bragg wavelength [wavelength_of_detector_pixel](name:wavelength_of_detector_pixel). The finite spectral acceptance of the pixel is bracketed by [lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).

For diffraction order $n$, the central pixel energy follows from Bragg's law and the photon relation $E = hc/\lambda$:

$$
E_\mathrm{pix} = \frac{n h c}{2 e d \sin\theta_\mathrm{pix}}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{pix}$ is the photon energy in eV, $n$ is the dimensionless positive integer diffraction order, $h$ is Planck's constant in J s, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum in m s^-1, $e$ is the elementary charge used to convert joules to electronvolts, $d$ is the crystal-plane spacing in meters, and $\theta_\mathrm{pix}$ is the Bragg angle for the pixel in radians.

The energy-to-pixel mapping is obtained from the spectrometer geometry by ray tracing, from an optical model of the crystal and detector, or by calibration against emission lines with well-known photon energies. In fusion applications these lines often come from highly ionized impurities, such as He-like or H-like argon, krypton, or other injected species.

Typical photon energies range from a few hundred eV for soft X-ray instruments to 5-20 keV for harder X-ray crystal spectrometers, depending on the chosen crystal spacing, diffraction order, viewing geometry, and target spectral lines.

NAMES.name: etendue_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Optical throughput factor for a spectrometer channel, expressed as a linear etendue: an effective entrance-aperture length multiplied by the channel collection solid angle. It is the m.sr reduced counterpart of full area etendue, which uses aperture area and has units m^2.sr.
NAMES.long:
Etendue of a spectrometer channel is the optical acceptance that determines how much radiation from an extended source can be delivered through that channel. In general optics, etendue is an area-solid-angle throughput; this quantity represents the linear or reduced form used for slit-like or channelized spectrometers, where the aperture area has been reduced to an effective linear entrance dimension. More specific quantities, such as [spectral etendue of a spectrometer channel](name:spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel), may include additional weighting by the spectral instrument function while retaining the same underlying throughput concept.

The linear spectrometer-channel etendue can be written as an acceptance-weighted integral over entrance position and collection direction:

$$
G_\ell = \int_\ell \int_\Omega W(\ell', \hat{s}) \, d\Omega \, d\ell'
$$

where $G_\ell$ is the linear etendue, $\ell'$ is position along the effective entrance aperture, $\hat{s}$ is a ray direction, $d\Omega$ is differential solid angle, and $W$ is a dimensionless acceptance weight including vignetting or other geometric acceptance effects. For uniform acceptance this reduces to the effective entrance length multiplied by the effective collection solid angle.
