It is usually computed from aperture dimensions, stops, fiber or slit geometry, optical magnification, and collection cone angle, often with ray tracing when the acceptance is not uniform. It can also be inferred experimentally by observing a calibrated extended radiance source and comparing the detected signal with the known source radiance and instrument response.

Typical values for narrow-slit or fiber-coupled fusion spectrometer channels are about $10^{-10}$-$10^{-5}$ m.sr, with large-aperture high-throughput channels reaching roughly $10^{-4}$ m.sr. The value is non-negative and decreases with smaller apertures, stronger vignetting, or narrower collection cones.

NAMES.name: exposure_time_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Duration of the detector integration window for a spectrometer channel, defining the temporal interval over which incident photons are accumulated to form a single spectral measurement frame.
NAMES.long:
The exposure time of a spectrometer channel is the duration of the detector integration window for a single spectral acquisition — the temporal interval during which incident photons are continuously accumulated by the detector to produce one spectral measurement. It directly controls the fundamental trade-off between temporal resolution and signal-to-noise ratio: shorter exposures resolve faster plasma dynamics, while longer exposures build up signal for weak emission lines at the cost of temporal averaging.

For an integrating detector, the accumulated signal count $N$ relates to the exposure time $t_\mathrm{exp}$ and the incident photon rate $\Phi$ as:

$$
N = \Phi \cdot t_\mathrm{exp}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the photon flux reaching the detector active area. For shot-noise-limited detection the signal-to-noise ratio scales as $\sqrt{N}$, so longer exposures are beneficial for faint spectral features.

The exposure time is set by the acquisition timing system and may be configured independently per channel in multi-channel or scanning spectrometer systems. It is selected based on the expected emission intensity, the saturation threshold of the detector, and the timescale of the plasma phenomenon under observation. The [spectral flux of spectrometer channel](name:spectral_flux_of_spectrometer_channel) gives the photon count rate accumulated within this integration window; together they determine the total count per frame.

Typical values span from a few microseconds for fast transient events such as disruptions or edge-localized modes to tens of milliseconds for quasi-steady emission measurements in ohmic or H-mode plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector is actively integrating the spectral signal over a valid acquisition interval.

NAMES.name: extent_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Physical linear span of a detector pixel footprint along a specified direction in the detector plane. It supports pixel-index to physical-position calibration, but is distinct from optical resolution and from pixel pitch when inactive gaps or non-square pixels are present.
NAMES.long:
Extent of a detector pixel is the linear span of one pixel footprint along a chosen detector-plane direction. The footprint may represent the active sensitive area for photon collection or the effective pixel cell used in a geometric calibration; it should not be confused with the center-to-center pitch unless neighboring pixels tile the detector plane without appreciable inactive gaps. For rectangular pixels, the horizontal and vertical extents are separate quantities; for square pixels they are equal.

The extent along one local detector-plane axis is defined by the coordinate bounds of the pixel footprint:

$$
d_a = a_+ - a_-
$$

where $a \in \{u,v\}$ selects a coordinate of the local detector-plane frame $(\hat{u},\hat{v})$ with coordinates $(u,v)$, $a_-$ and $a_+$ are the lower and upper footprint boundaries in meters, and the pixel center on that axis is $a_c=(a_-+a_+)/2$.

Values are obtained from sensor design data, detector metrology, or calibration images of a target with known spacing. For index-to-position mappings, the origin and the center-versus-edge convention must be specified independently: if $u_0$ is the lower edge of pixel $i=0$ in the local detector-plane frame $(\hat{u},\hat{v})$ and $p_u$ is the pitch, the center of pixel $i$ lies at $u_0+(i+1/2)p_u$; $p_u=d_u$ only for contiguous pixels with negligible gaps, with $u_0$, $p_u$, and $d_u$ expressed in meters.

Typical values are $5 \times 10^{-6}$-$2 \times 10^{-4}$ m. Infrared focal-plane sensors commonly use $1 \times 10^{-5}$-$5 \times 10^{-5}$ m pixel extents, while x-ray cameras and crystal-spectrometer detectors often use $1 \times 10^{-5}$-$1 \times 10^{-4}$ m depending on sensor technology and required sampling.

NAMES.name: extent_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Edge-to-edge active length of a soft X-ray detector measured along a specified in-plane detector axis, such as its horizontal or vertical sensitive direction. It describes the physical span that can register soft X-ray photons, excluding inactive borders or support structures.
NAMES.long:
The extent of a soft X-ray detector is the physical edge-to-edge length of the photon-sensitive active area along one specified axis in the detector plane, such as the horizontal or vertical sensitive direction. It is a geometric calibration quantity for converting detector position to viewing angle, crystal-dispersion coordinate, or image position, and it is distinct from the size of non-sensitive packaging, mounts, or camera housing.

If $u$ denotes distance along the measured detector-plane axis, the active extent is

$$
L_{\mathrm{det}} = u_{\max} - u_{\min}
$$

where $u_{\min}$ and $u_{\max}$ are the two active-edge coordinates of the photon-sensitive region in meters, and $L_{\mathrm{det}}$ is the detector extent along the same axis.

The extent is determined from detector specifications, mechanical metrology, calibration masks, or image-based edge calibration. For a contiguous detector with uniform pixels along the same measured axis, it may be computed as $L_{\mathrm{det}} \simeq N_{\mathrm{pix}}\,\Delta u_{\mathrm{pix}}$, where $N_{\mathrm{pix}}$ is the number of active pixels and $\Delta u_{\mathrm{pix}}$ is the pixel pitch along that same axis; this relation should not mix horizontal and vertical pixel pitches, and it must be modified when gaps, dead margins, binning, or nonuniform pixels are present. For a detector at distance $D$ from an aperture or reference point, the small-angle angular span along the same axis is approximately $L_{\mathrm{det}}/D$.

Typical active extents for soft X-ray cameras and crystal-spectrometer detectors are 0.005-0.3 m, with compact semiconductor sensors often near 0.005-0.05 m and larger spectroscopic imaging detectors commonly near 0.05-0.3 m.

NAMES.name: filter_window_width
NAMES.short: Filter window width is the full physical opening of a rectangular X-ray filter aperture measured along the X1 axis of the local right-handed aperture frame (X1, X2, X3), where X1 and X2 lie in the aperture plane and X3 is normal to the filter surface. It is the X1 counterpart of the aperture extent along X2 given by the filter window height.
NAMES.long:
Filter window width is the full linear extent of a rectangular filter window along the X1 axis of the local right-handed aperture frame (X1, X2, X3). The X1 and X2 axes lie in the aperture plane, X3 is the outward normal to the filter surface, and the orthogonal transverse extent along X2 is the [filter_window_height](name:filter_window_height).

The width is the span of the rectangular opening between its two edges along the X1 axis:

$$
w = x_{1,\mathrm{max}} - x_{1,\mathrm{min}}
$$

where $x_{1,\mathrm{min}}$ and $x_{1,\mathrm{max}}$ are the X1 coordinates of the opposing aperture edges, measured in the local aperture plane. Together with the height $h$ from [filter_window_height](name:filter_window_height), the width $w$ sets the geometric open area $A = w\,h$ (see [surface_area_of_filter](name:surface_area_of_filter)), which contributes to the diagnostic etendue, the product of collecting area and accepted solid angle.

The width is usually obtained from the mechanical design of the aperture, manufacturing drawings, or metrology of the filter holder. In transmission calculations it is used together with the filter material, angle of incidence, and [thickness_of_filter](name:thickness_of_filter) to determine the photon throughput and spectral response. It is the rectangular-geometry analog of the more general [width_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:width_of_diagnostic_aperture).

Typical values range from $1 \times 10^{-4}$-$5 \times 10^{-2}$ m, with sub-millimeter openings used for narrow slits or high-resolution views and centimeter-scale openings used where larger photon collection is required.

NAMES.name: flux_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.short: Total neutron emission rate from all thermal fusion channels in the plasma, integrating D-D, D-T, and T-T thermonuclear reactions driven by Maxwellian bulk ion velocity distributions.
NAMES.long:
The global thermal-fusion neutron emission rate is the total count of neutrons produced per unit time by thermonuclear reactions between fuel ions whose velocity distributions are Maxwellian at the local ion temperature. It aggregates all neutron-producing isotope-pair channels—D-D, D-T, and T-T—while excluding contributions from beam-target or beam-beam fast-ion reactions.

The total rate is the plasma-volume integral of the summed channel emissivities:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{th}} = \int_V \sum_{a,b} f_{ab}\, n_a\, n_b\, \langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab}(T_i) \, dV
$$

where $n_a$ and $n_b$ are the reacting species number densities, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab}(T_i)$ is the Maxwellian-averaged fusion reactivity at local ion temperature $T_i$, and $f_{ab} = 1/2$ for identical-species pairs to avoid double-counting. Channel-resolved contributions are provided by [deuterium-deuterium thermal flux](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion) and [tritium-tritium thermal flux](name:tritium_tritium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion); the D-T channel is described by [neutron flux due to thermal fusion](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion).

Measured using neutron detectors—activation foils, fission chambers, or scintillator arrays—positioned outside the vacuum vessel and absolutely calibrated with activation samples or time-of-flight spectrometry. The companion quantity [total neutron flux] includes non-thermal beam-target and beam-beam contributions in addition to this thermal channel.

In pure DD plasmas the rate is of order $10^{14}$–$10^{16}$ s$^{-1}$; in DT-burning reactor-scale plasmas the 14.1 MeV DT channel dominates and rates reach $10^{18}$–$10^{20}$ s$^{-1}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutrons are emitted from the plasma at a net outward rate.

NAMES.name: hard_xray_brightness
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short: Photon radiance of hard X-ray emission incident on a diagnostic channel, giving the photon flux per unit detector area and per unit solid angle, integrated over the channel energy band.
NAMES.long:
Hard X-ray brightness is the photon radiance of bremsstrahlung emission arriving at a diagnostic channel, quantifying the photon arrival rate per unit detector area and per unit solid angle. In tokamak plasmas, hard X-ray emission above a few tens of keV is generated predominantly by non-thermal bremsstrahlung from suprathermal electrons colliding with bulk plasma ions and impurity ions; the channel brightness therefore constrains the suprathermal electron energy distribution.

The photon radiance is defined as:

$$
L_\gamma = \frac{d^2 \dot{N}_\gamma}{dA \, d\Omega}
$$

where $\dot{N}_\gamma$ is the photon arrival rate at the detector surface element $dA$, and $d\Omega$ is the solid angle element subtended at the source. The power-equivalent counterpart of this photon radiance is given by [spectral_radiance_of_hard_xray_detector](name:spectral_radiance_of_hard_xray_detector), which relates to $L_\gamma$ via $L_P = \langle h\nu \rangle L_\gamma$, where $\langle h\nu \rangle$ is the mean photon energy in the detection band.

Hard X-ray diagnostic channels employ collimated scintillator or semiconductor detectors with defined energy bandpass filters. The brightness is obtained by dividing the measured photon count rate by the detector étendue (product of area and solid angle), and absolute calibration across multiple energy bands enables reconstruction of the suprathermal electron spectrum through bremsstrahlung inversion. The analogous photon-radiance quantity for the soft X-ray regime is [brightness_of_soft_xray_detector](name:brightness_of_soft_xray_detector), and the total integrated power over the channel acceptance is captured by hard_xray_power.

NAMES.name: hard_xray_emissivity
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short: Local photon emission rate per unit volume and per unit solid angle, integrated over a specified hard-X-ray energy band. It is mainly produced by bremsstrahlung from suprathermal or runaway electrons decelerating in the Coulomb fields of plasma ions, and is not a per-energy spectral quantity.
NAMES.long:
Hard-X-ray emissivity is the local rate at which photons are emitted into unit solid angle within a specified hard-X-ray energy interval. It is a non-negative, band-integrated bremsstrahlung quantity produced mainly by suprathermal or runaway electrons interacting with plasma ions. It differs from [bremsstrahlung_spectral_emissivity](name:bremsstrahlung_spectral_emissivity), which is resolved per photon energy.

The band-integrated emissivity is obtained by integrating the spectral photon emissivity over the selected photon-energy interval:

$$
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}(\mathbf{x}; E_1,E_2) = \int_{E_1}^{E_2} \varepsilon_E(\mathbf{x},E)\,dE
$$

where $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}$ is the hard-X-ray emissivity, $\varepsilon_E$ is the spectral photon emissivity per unit photon energy, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $E_1$ and $E_2$ define the analysis or detector energy band.

In an optically thin plasma, the corresponding photon-rate brightness is related by the line-of-sight integral $B_{\mathrm{HXR}} = \int_{\mathrm{LOS}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{HXR}}\,dl$ before instrumental effects are applied. In practice, emissivity is inferred from multi-channel hard-X-ray measurements using forward modeling or tomographic reconstruction, including detector efficiency, viewing geometry, attenuation, and the chosen energy response. It depends on the suprathermal electron distribution, ion density and charge state, and bremsstrahlung cross sections, so it should not be interpreted as directly proportional to suprathermal electron density without a kinetic emission model. The related hard_xray_power is a detector or radiated energy-rate quantity in watts and requires weighting photon rates by photon energy and instrument response.

Typical reconstructed band-integrated values range from near diagnostic background to about 10^10-10^15 m^-3.s^-1.sr^-1 for weak suprathermal tails, and can reach 10^15-10^18 m^-3.s^-1.sr^-1 during strong runaway-electron or intense hard-X-ray events. The magnitude depends strongly on the lower energy threshold, bandwidth, plasma density and composition, and the high-energy tail of the electron distribution.

NAMES.name: hard_xray_outer_width
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short: Outer half-width of the hard X-ray emissivity peak in normalized toroidal flux coordinate, defined as the radial distance from the peak to the half-maximum point on the separatrix-facing side.
NAMES.long:
The outer half-width of the hard X-ray emissivity peak measures the radial distance in normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{tor,norm}$ from the emissivity maximum to its half-maximum point on the side facing the separatrix. Hard X-ray emission in magnetized plasmas originates from bremsstrahlung of energetic non-thermal electrons — runaway and fast electrons — as they scatter off background plasma ions; a spatially localized emissivity peak therefore reflects a confined population of such electrons, and the outer half-width characterizes how far that population extends radially toward the plasma edge.

The outer half-width $\Delta\rho_{ext}$ is defined by:

$$
\Delta\rho_{ext} = \rho_{1/2,ext} - \rho_{peak}
$$

where $\rho_{peak}$ is the $\rho_{tor,norm}$ coordinate of the emissivity maximum, $\rho_{1/2,ext}$ is the outboard coordinate at which the emissivity falls to half its peak value, and $\rho_{tor,norm} = \sqrt{\Phi_{tor}/\Phi_{tor,\mathrm{LCFS}}}$ with $\Phi_{tor,\mathrm{LCFS}}$ the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the last-closed flux surface.

The emissivity radial distribution is inferred from multi-chord hard X-ray camera brightnesses via tomographic inversion under the assumption of toroidal symmetry. Comparing the outer half-width with the complementary hard_xray_inner_width reveals radial asymmetry in the non-thermal electron population; a larger outer value relative to the inner indicates that the fast electron distribution extends further toward the separatrix than toward the magnetic axis. Both quantities are expressed on the [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) scale.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outer half-maximum boundary lies at greater $\rho_{tor,norm}$ than the emissivity peak, in the direction of increasing normalized toroidal flux toward the separatrix.

NAMES.name: height_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Full physical extent of a hard X-ray detector aperture along the local X2 axis of the detector coordinate frame, applicable to rectangular aperture geometry.
NAMES.long:
The height of a hard X-ray detector is the full dimension of the detector aperture measured along the local X2 axis of the detector coordinate frame (X1, X2, X3), where X1 and X2 lie in the nominal aperture plane and X3 is normal to the detector surface. This geometric parameter is defined for rectangular aperture geometries and represents one of two orthogonal in-plane dimensions required to fully characterize the aperture opening.

Together with [width_of_hard_xray_detector](name:width_of_hard_xray_detector), which gives the X1 extent, the height defines the total aperture area $A = h \times w$, where $h$ is the X2 extent and $w$ is the X1 extent. The aperture area enters the étendue calculation that determines the photon collection efficiency of the diagnostic channel. The analogous X2 dimension for X-ray diagnostic filter windows is [filter_window_height](name:filter_window_height), which follows the same local-frame X2 convention.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture extent is measured in the direction of increasing X2 coordinate in the local detector frame.

NAMES.name: height_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Height of an optical element is the usable physical aperture extent measured along X2 in the right-handed local aperture frame (X1, X2, n), where X1 and X2 span the aperture plane and n is the surface normal. It applies to rectangular optical elements and is distinct from the X1 width.
NAMES.long:
Height of an optical element is the full usable clear-aperture dimension along $X_2$ in the right-handed local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, n)$, where $X_1$ and $X_2$ lie in the aperture plane and $n$ is the aperture normal. For a rectangular aperture it is the second transverse dimension of the element that can transmit, reflect, or otherwise accept radiation. It is distinct from [optical_element_width](name:optical_element_width), which is the corresponding $X_1$ dimension; the closely related [optical_element_height](name:height_of_optical_element) denotes the same physical $X_2$ extent with different standard-name wording.

If the usable aperture is represented by the set $\mathcal{A}$ of points on the element projected onto the local aperture plane, the height is the extent of their $X_2$ coordinates:

$$
h_\mathrm{opt} = \max_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{A}} X_2(\mathbf{p}) - \min_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{A}} X_2(\mathbf{p})
$$

where $X_2(\mathbf{p})$ is the coordinate of point $\mathbf{p}$ along the second transverse aperture axis. For an ideal centered rectangle this reduces to the rectangle side length along $X_2$.

In practice the value is obtained from mechanical design, metrology, or alignment surveys of mirrors, crystals, windows, filters, collimators, and camera apertures. It should represent the clear or illuminated usable extent that limits optical throughput and ray tracing, excluding opaque mounts, bevels, clamps, or damaged regions unless those regions are intentionally part of the aperture model.

Typical values range from 0.001-0.05 m for small x-ray crystals, pinholes, and collimating apertures, 0.01-0.3 m for infrared camera apertures and relay optics, and 0.1-1 m for large windows or mirrors. The value is non-negative and may be smaller than the manufactured part size when the clear aperture is limited by holders or masks.

NAMES.name: lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Minimum photon energy accepted by a detector pixel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It is the low-energy edge of that pixel's photon-energy bandpass.
NAMES.long:
The lower bound energy of a detector pixel is the minimum photon energy in the spectral interval accepted by that pixel. Together with the corresponding upper bound, it defines the pixel bandpass around the calibrated photon_energy coordinate.

For a crystal spectrometer calibrated by Bragg diffraction, the lower bound for pixel $p$ can be written as the minimum energy over the Bragg-angle interval accepted by that pixel:

$$
E_{\mathrm{lower},p} = \min_{\theta \in \Omega_p} \frac{n h c}{2 d \sin\theta\, e}
$$

where $\Omega_p$ is the accepted Bragg-angle interval of pixel $p$, $n$ is the positive integer diffraction order for the calibrated spectral branch, $d$ is the crystal lattice-plane spacing, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $e$ is the elementary charge converting joules to electronvolts. Equivalently, if $d$ is expressed in nm, $hc/e = 1239.841984\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$ gives $E$ directly in eV.

In practice this bound is obtained from the spectrometer geometry, crystal spacing and orientation, detector position, pixel aperture, and a wavelength or line-emission calibration. The finite pixel size and optical response determine the accepted angular interval, so the lower bound is the low-energy edge of the pixel response rather than merely the energy at its center.

Typical lower bounds for fusion X-ray crystal spectrometers are 500-20000 eV, with common impurity-line measurements in the 3000-8000 eV range and harder spectral branches extending to 10000-50000 eV. Adjacent-pixel energy intervals are often a few eV to tens of eV, depending on dispersion and pixel size.

NAMES.name: lower_photon_energy
NAMES.short: Minimum photon energy defining the low-energy edge of an X-ray detector, camera pixel, or energy-resolved emission band. Incident photons below this cutoff are rejected, not counted, or excluded from the corresponding photon-energy window.
NAMES.long:
Lower photon energy is the minimum photon energy admitted by a photon-counting or energy-selective X-ray measurement. Together with an upper cutoff such as [upper_photon_energy](name:upper_photon_energy), it defines the accepted photon-energy interval; for pixel-specific thresholds it is the lower-edge counterpart of [lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and is paired with [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).

Photon energy is related to radiation frequency and wavelength by:

$$
E_\gamma = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}
$$

where $E_\gamma$ is photon energy, $h$ is Planck's constant, $\nu$ is photon frequency, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\lambda$ is wavelength. The lower threshold $E_\mathrm{lower}$ selects photons satisfying $E_\gamma \ge E_\mathrm{lower}$, usually in combination with an upper threshold $E_\mathrm{upper}$.

In practice this threshold is set by detector absorption filters, scintillator or semiconductor response, electronic discrimination levels, pulse-height analysis, or analysis choices used to isolate an energy band for emissivity inference. Calibration with known radiation sources or modeled detector response functions is used to relate the threshold setting to photon energy.

Typical lower thresholds are about 100-1000 eV for soft X-ray measurements and about 1e3-1e5 eV for hard X-ray measurements, depending on detector material, filter stack, electronic noise floor, and the intended spectral band.

NAMES.name: neutron_energy
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Kinetic energy of a fusion-born neutron, used as the energy variable for neutron emission spectra, transport, and detector response calculations.
NAMES.long:
Neutron energy $E_n$ is the kinetic energy carried by a neutron emitted or transported in a fusion plasma. It is the spectral variable for neutron emission spectra and detector response functions, and it separates reaction channels such as DD and DT fusion by their characteristic birth energies. Broad distributions arise from ion thermal motion, energetic-ion reactions, scattering, and transport effects.

Detector response calculations often fold an incident neutron spectrum with an energy-dependent response over $E_n$:

$$
C_k = \int R_k(E_n)\, \frac{d\Phi_n}{dE_n}(E_n)\, dE_n
$$

where $C_k$ is the predicted signal in detector channel $k$, in counts for a fluence calculation or counts s$^{-1}$ for a flux calculation; $R_k(E_n)$ is the channel response, with units counts m$^2$ for this normalization; and $d\Phi_n/dE_n$ is the incident differential fluence spectrum in m$^{-2}$ eV$^{-1}$ or differential flux spectrum in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$.

The birth spectrum is computed from two-body fusion kinematics folded with reactant velocity distributions, then modified by scattering and transport before detection. Measurements infer the spectrum using time-of-flight systems, recoil-particle spectrometers, scintillators, activation thresholds, or other energy-sensitive diagnostics together with response-function unfolding. Energy-resolved neutron emission is represented by neutron_energy_spectrum, with reaction-specific fluxes such as [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion), deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion, and [deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion).

Typical diagnostic coverage is $1 \times 10^3$-$2 \times 10^7$ eV. Primary thermal DD neutrons occur near $2.45 \times 10^6$ eV, and primary thermal DT neutrons near $1.41 \times 10^7$ eV; thermal broadening is often $10^4$-$10^5$ eV, while energetic-ion populations can produce broader asymmetric tails.

NAMES.name: neutron_incident_fluence_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Incident neutron fluence at a neutron detector converter per neutron emitted by a toroidal ring source at a specified source position and neutron energy. It is a non-negative spatial-energy sensitivity kernel for converting source yield or source-rate distributions into converter fluence or fluence-rate responses.
NAMES.long:
Incident neutron fluence of a neutron detector converter is the number of source neutrons crossing unit area at the converter per neutron emitted by a specified toroidal ring source. The quantity depends on source-ring position and neutron energy and represents the transport, collimation, shielding, scattering, and geometric view factors between the plasma source and the converter.

The normalized per-unit-ring-source kernel may be defined as:

$$
K_\mathrm{conv}(s,E_n) = \frac{d\Phi_\mathrm{conv}(s,E_n)}{dN_\mathrm{ring}(s,E_n)}
$$

where $K_\mathrm{conv}$ is the incident converter fluence kernel, $s$ labels the source-ring position, $E_n$ is the neutron energy, $\Phi_\mathrm{conv}$ is the fluence accumulated at the converter, and $N_\mathrm{ring}$ is the total number of neutrons emitted by that ring over the time interval. The source weighting for this fluence quantity is therefore a time-integrated neutron yield; if the source description is an emissivity rate, convolution with the same kernel gives a fluence rate rather than a time-integrated fluence.

The kernel is normally computed with neutral-particle transport, Monte Carlo, or deterministic radiation-transport calculations using a unit toroidal ring source. Practical calculations include the viewing geometry, apertures, attenuation and scattering in surrounding structures, and energy-dependent neutron interactions before or in the converter; they may be checked against calibration measurements with known neutron sources.

The kernel is non-negative and is zero for source regions or neutron energies that cannot contribute to the converter response. Typical values span about $10^{-10}-10^{-3}$ m^-2 per emitted neutron in collimated fusion neutron systems, with larger values possible for close unshielded views and much smaller values for heavily shielded or out-of-view source regions.

NAMES.name: normalized_count_at_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Dimensionless detector-pixel signal formed by dividing the pixel photon count rate by a positive reference photon count rate associated with the same acquisition frame. A value of 1 means the pixel count rate equals the reference rate.
NAMES.long:
Normalized count at detector pixel is a relative photon count-rate signal for one detector pixel of an X-ray crystal spectrometer. The underlying detector signal is the photon count rate at that pixel, while the normalization reference is a positive count-rate scale applied consistently within the same acquisition frame.

The normalized value is defined by the ratio

$$
C_n(p) = \frac{\dot{N}(p)}{\dot{N}_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $C_n(p)$ is the dimensionless normalized count for detector pixel $p$, $\dot{N}(p)$ is the photon count rate at that pixel in $\mathrm{count}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference photon count rate for the same frame in $\mathrm{count}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The quantity is undefined if $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{ref}} = 0$.

In practice, $\dot{N}(p)$ is obtained from the detector counts after applying the relevant exposure-time and detector-response corrections used for the measurement. The same $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ must be used for all detector pixels that are compared within a frame; otherwise the relative scale changes. The spectral interpretation of pixel $p$ is set by its energy bandpass, bounded by the [lower-bound photon energy](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and [upper-bound photon energy](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).

Values are non-negative because both count rates are non-negative. A value of 0 indicates no detected photon count rate at that pixel after the applied corrections, a value of 1 indicates equality with the reference count rate, and values greater than 1 are possible when the pixel count rate exceeds the reference rate. The standard name specifies a relative count-rate ratio; it does not by itself imply total-frame, peak, or average-count normalization.

NAMES.name: nuclear_rate_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Volumetric nuclear-reaction response of a neutron detector converter to incident neutrons from a unit source. It gives the number of converter reactions per unit converter volume per emitted source neutron, so it becomes a physical rate density only after scaling by the source emission rate.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a local response kernel for neutron-induced nuclear reactions in a detector converter material. It represents reaction yield per converter volume for a unit neutron source, not a time rate by itself.

For an effective monoenergetic or spectrum-averaged response, the local kernel can be written as:

$$
k_R = n_t \, \sigma_\mathrm{eff} \, F_n
$$

where $k_R$ is the converter nuclear-reaction response per unit volume in $m^{-3}$, $n_t$ is the target-nucleus number density in $m^{-3}$ as represented by [nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter), $\sigma_\mathrm{eff}$ is the microscopic reaction cross-section averaged over the incident neutron energy spectrum in $m^2$, and $F_n$ is the incident neutron fluence per emitted source neutron in $m^{-2}$ as represented by incident_neutron_fluence_of_neutron_detector_converter. The emitted source neutron is a counting normalization, so the resulting unit is $m^{-3}$.

The kernel is usually computed by neutron transport from a unit source to the converter, followed by folding the local neutron fluence spectrum with the converter material composition and reaction cross-sections. To obtain a physical detector reaction rate, multiply the kernel by the neutron emission rate of the corresponding source element, integrate over the converter volume represented by [volume_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:volume_of_neutron_detector_converter), and then sum or integrate over all source elements contributing to the detector response.

Typical magnitudes vary by many orders of magnitude because they depend on source-converter distance, shielding, collimation, converter material, and reaction threshold. Values can range from less than $10^{-12}$ m^-3 in weakly coupled or heavily shielded views to about $10^{-1}$ m^-3 for strongly coupled converter regions per emitted source neutron.

NAMES.name: optical_element_width
NAMES.short: Full width of an optical-element aperture along X1 in the right-handed local element frame (X1, X2, X3), where X3 is normal to the aperture surface. It applies to rectangular aperture geometry.
NAMES.long:
Optical element width is the usable aperture extent along the first transverse axis $X_1$ of a right-handed local element frame $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$. The axes $X_1$ and $X_2$ span the aperture surface, while $X_3$ is normal to that surface; for a rectangular aperture this width is one side length, paired with [height_of_optical_element](name:height_of_optical_element) along $X_2$.

For an aperture bounded by minimum and maximum positions along $X_1$, the width is

$$
W = X_{1,\max} - X_{1,\min}
$$

where $W$ is the optical element width in meters, and $X_{1,\max}$ and $X_{1,\min}$ are the largest and smallest local $X_1$ positions of the usable aperture boundary, also in meters. The result is a non-negative geometric extent.

The width is obtained from the optical design, clear-aperture specification, or dimensional metrology of the fabricated element. Together with the $X_2$ height it determines the geometric aperture area $W H$ for an unobscured rectangle, which affects solid angle, photon throughput, and étendue; [width_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:width_of_diagnostic_aperture) is the analogous width for a diagnostic aperture not specifically tied to an optical element.

Typical values for X-ray crystal spectrometer reflectors and similar diagnostic optical elements are 0.001-0.1 m, with smaller widths favored for compact or high-resolution optics and larger widths used when photon throughput is limiting.

NAMES.name: power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.short: Local thermonuclear fusion energy release rate per unit volume, encompassing contributions from all fuel-ion reaction channels including deuterium-deuterium and deuterium-tritium.
NAMES.long:
Volumetric power density deposited by thermonuclear fusion reactions in the plasma, representing the total local energy released per unit volume per unit time across all contributing fuel-ion reaction channels. This parent quantity generalizes over channel-specific instances such as [deuterium-deuterium fusion power density](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion) and [deuterium-tritium fusion power density](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion).

The volumetric fusion power density for a reaction channel between species $i$ and $j$ is defined as:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fus},ij}(\mathbf{r}) = n_i(\mathbf{r})\, n_j(\mathbf{r})\, \langle \sigma v \rangle_{ij}(T)\, Q_{ij}
$$

where $n_i$ and $n_j$ are the reactant number densities in m$^{-3}$, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{ij}(T)$ is the thermally averaged reaction-rate coefficient at local ion temperature $T$, and $Q_{ij}$ is the total energy released per reaction. For DT reactions, $Q_{DT} = 17.6\;\text{MeV}$; for the two DD branches combined, the effective energy yield is approximately 3.65 MeV per reaction.

In practice this quantity is computed from local fuel-ion density and ion temperature profiles using tabulated reaction-rate coefficients, or inferred from neutron emission diagnostics combined with reaction-rate models. The particle-channel counterparts [deuterium-deuterium neutron emissivity] and [deuterium-tritium emissivity](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion) track neutron production rates rather than total energy release.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short: Local fusion energy release rate per unit volume from deuterium-deuterium reactions. It includes energy released through the neutron-emitting and proton-emitting D-D branches, expressed as a volumetric power density.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium-deuterium fusion power density is the local rate at which nuclear binding energy is released per unit plasma volume by reactions between deuterium ions. It is a source term for fusion product energy before any subsequent transport, slowing down, or wall losses. The quantity includes energy released in both principal D-D branches, not only the neutron-emitting branch.

Using a total D-D reactivity summed over the neutron-emitting and proton-emitting branches, the local power density is

$$
p_{DD} = \frac{1}{2} n_D^2 \langle\sigma v\rangle_{DD} E_{DD} = \epsilon_{n,DD}\frac{E_{DD}}{f_n}
$$

where $n_D$ is deuterium ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_{DD}$ is the velocity-distribution-averaged total D-D reactivity in $\mathrm{m}^3\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $E_{DD}$ is the branch-weighted reaction energy in joules. The factor $1/2$ avoids double counting pairs of identical deuterons. $\epsilon_{n,DD}$ is the neutron emissivity from the D-D neutron branch in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and $f_n$ is that branch's fraction of all D-D reactions, so neutron-branch emissivity is converted to total D-D power density by multiplying by $E_{DD}/f_n$. For nearly equal branch probabilities, $f_n \approx 0.5$; with branch energies of 3.27 MeV and 4.03 MeV, $E_{DD} \approx 3.65$ MeV = $5.85\times10^{-13}$ J per total D-D reaction, and $E_{DD}/f_n \approx 7.30$ MeV = $1.17\times10^{-12}$ J per emitted D-D neutron.

In practice, this quantity may be computed from deuterium density, ion velocity distributions, and nuclear reactivity data, or inferred from neutron measurements. Tomographic inversion estimates the local D-D neutron emissivity, after which branch fractions and reaction energies provide the conversion to total fusion power density. Absolute calibration, scattered-neutron corrections, viewing geometry, fuel dilution, and nonthermal deuterium populations can all affect the inferred value.

Typical core values in present deuterium plasmas range from 10-10^4 W m^-3 for thermal ion temperatures of a few to about 15 keV. Hotter plasmas or plasmas with strong fast-ion populations can reach 10^5-10^6 W m^-3 locally, while values near the cool plasma edge are often much smaller.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Local volumetric power density from deuterium-tritium thermonuclear reactions, with each reaction yielding 17.6 MeV distributed between the alpha particle (3.5 MeV) and the neutron (14.1 MeV).
NAMES.long:
The D-T fusion power density is the local rate at which deuterium-tritium reactions $D + T \rightarrow {}^4\mathrm{He} + n$ deposit energy per unit plasma volume, with each event releasing $Q_\mathrm{DT} = 17.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$, partitioned as 3.5 MeV to the alpha particle and 14.1 MeV to the 14.1 MeV neutron.

The volumetric power density is defined by:

$$
P_\mathrm{DT} = n_D \, n_T \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_\mathrm{DT} \, Q_\mathrm{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the local deuterium and tritium number densities, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_\mathrm{DT}$ is the velocity-averaged D-T fusion reactivity (maximized near ion temperature $T_i \approx 65\,\mathrm{keV}$), and $Q_\mathrm{DT} = 17.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$ is the total energy released per reaction.

The spatial distribution of $P_\mathrm{DT}$ is inferred from neutron emissivity tomography: multi-channel neutron detector signals are tomographically inverted to yield the [deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion) (volumetric reaction rate), which is then scaled by $Q_\mathrm{DT}$ to obtain the power density. In a balanced D-T fuel mixture at reactor-relevant temperatures of 10–20 keV, the D-T channel dominates the total [power_density_due_to_fusion](name:power_density_due_to_fusion), exceeding the [deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion) by roughly two orders of magnitude due to the much larger D-T reactivity at these temperatures. Peak on-axis values in near-ignition plasmas are expected to reach several MW m$^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: power_density_due_to_radiation
NAMES.short: Volumetric rate at which plasma thermal energy is converted into emitted electromagnetic radiation. It represents a local radiative loss term per unit volume in plasma power balance.
NAMES.long:
Power density due to radiation is the local rate per unit volume at which plasma thermal energy is converted into emitted electromagnetic radiation. It includes continuum emission, line radiation, recombination radiation, and radiation from intrinsic or injected impurities. It is the same physical loss density commonly denoted [radiative_power_density](name:power_density_due_to_radiation), while this name emphasizes its role as one term in plasma power balance alongside processes such as power_density_due_to_conduction.

The quantity is defined from a radiated power element by:

$$
p_\mathrm{rad} = \frac{dP_\mathrm{rad}}{dV}
$$

where $p_\mathrm{rad}$ is the local radiative power density, $dP_\mathrm{rad}$ is the photon power emitted from the volume element $dV$, and the resulting unit is W m$^{-3}$.

Experimentally it is inferred from bolometer signals, filtered cameras, spectroscopy, or tomographic reconstructions by converting measured photon brightness into local emissivity. In modeling and power-balance analysis it is often estimated with atomic cooling functions; for an optically thin plasma a common local form is $p_\mathrm{rad} \approx n_e \sum_z n_z L_z(T_e,n_e,\ldots)$, where $n_e$ is electron density in m$^{-3}$, $n_z$ is the density of radiating species or charge state $z$ in m$^{-3}$, $T_e$ is electron temperature, and $L_z$ has units W m$^3$.

Typical values span many orders of magnitude: hot-core bremsstrahlung and light-impurity emission are often 10^3-10^6 W m^-3, while radiating edge regions, impurity-seeded plasmas, or disruption-mitigation scenarios can reach 10^5-10^8 W m^-3 locally. Exact values depend strongly on density, temperature, impurity concentration, charge-state distribution, and optical thickness.
NAMES.sign: Positive when radiative emission removes energy from the plasma.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_line_radiation
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic power radiated by the plasma via line radiation, the discrete photon emission from bound-bound transitions in impurity and hydrogen ions.
NAMES.long:
Power due to line radiation is the volume-integrated electromagnetic power emitted in discrete spectral lines by bound-bound atomic transitions in neutral atoms and ions. It is a component of the total radiated power, distinct from continuum [bremsstrahlung_power](name:bremsstrahlung_power) and [power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation](name:power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation), and usually represents an energy-loss channel from the thermal plasma.

For optically thin plasma, a common collisional-radiative representation is:

$$
P_\mathrm{line} = \int_V n_e \sum_z n_z L_z(T_e,n_e) \, dV
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron density in m$^{-3}$, $n_z$ is the density in m$^{-3}$ of emitting ion population $z$, $L_z$ is the effective line-radiation cooling coefficient in W m$^3$, $T_e$ is the electron temperature, and $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$.

In practice, line-radiation power is inferred from absolutely calibrated spectroscopy, filtered imaging, bolometry with spectral separation, or tomographic reconstruction combined with atomic physics models. Computations require electron temperature, electron density, impurity concentrations, ionization balance, excitation rates, photon energies, and possible corrections for optical thickness in dense edge or divertor regions.

Typical values range from $10^4$-$10^5$ W in very clean low-power plasmas to $10^5$-$10^7$ W in present-day auxiliary-heated tokamaks, and can reach several $10^7$ W in impurity-seeded, detached, or strongly radiating scenarios. The emitted power contributes to plasma energy loss, while radiated_power_at_wall describes the surface-deposited radiative load after transport to surrounding structures.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic power emitted by the plasma through synchrotron radiation from relativistic electron gyro-motion in the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Synchrotron-radiation power is the total electromagnetic power emitted by electrons whose gyro-motion in the magnetic field is relativistic enough to radiate appreciably. It is a mechanism-specific contribution to the plasma radiative power balance and is non-negative, with zero corresponding to absent or negligible synchrotron emission.

For a plasma volume $V$, the emitted synchrotron power is defined by the volume integral of the local volumetric emissivity:

$$
P_{\mathrm{syn}} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{syn}}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{syn}}$ is the global power in W, $p_{\mathrm{syn}}$ is the local synchrotron emissivity in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, and $\mathbf{r}$ denotes position. The integration is over the emitting plasma volume.

The quantity denotes emitted synchrotron power. It is not necessarily the net power escaping the plasma-facing boundary: synchrotron photons may be reabsorbed in the plasma or reflected by surrounding structures. If a radiation-transport model is used, the emissivity in the integral should represent the chosen convention, such as gross emitted emissivity or net loss emissivity after absorption.

In practice, synchrotron power is usually computed from the electron distribution function, magnetic-field strength, plasma geometry, and an optical-depth or wall-reflection model; direct bolometric separation from other radiative mechanisms is generally difficult. For thermal plasmas the emission grows rapidly with electron temperature and magnetic-field strength and is also proportional to the number of radiating electrons, but quantitative values require the full emissivity model rather than a universal scaling law.

Typical global values span many orders of magnitude: effectively 0 W when relativistic-electron synchrotron emission is negligible or not modeled, up to kW-MW levels in hot high-field tokamak plasmas, with reactor-relevant scenarios potentially reaching the upper part of that range depending on absorption and reflection assumptions.

NAMES.name: power_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Radiative power received by a hard X-ray detector channel, integrated over its photon-energy acceptance band and serving as a direct measure of suprathermal electron bremsstrahlung emission.
NAMES.long:
Hard X-ray diagnostic power is the total electromagnetic power deposited on a detector channel by photons in the hard X-ray band, produced predominantly by suprathermal and runaway electrons decelerating in the Coulomb fields of plasma ions via bremsstrahlung.

The channel-integrated power relates to the photon power spectral density $d\Phi/dE$ at the detector face through:

$$
P = \int_{\Delta E} \frac{d\Phi}{dE} \, dE
$$

where $\Delta E$ is the channel's photon-energy acceptance interval and $d\Phi/dE$ is the power spectral density incident on the detector.

Measurement uses scintillator-based detectors (NaI(Tl), BGO, LaBr$_3$) or solid-state semiconductor detectors (CdTe, HPGe) operated in current mode or pulse-height analysis mode, with detector efficiency calibration applied to convert count rates to power. The hard X-ray power level is sensitive to the high-energy tail of the electron energy distribution, making this quantity a primary diagnostic indicator for runaway electron characterization and suprathermal electron beam measurements during disruptions and off-normal plasma events.

The spectrally resolved counterpart, expressed as power per detector area per steradian, is [spectral radiance of a hard X-ray detector channel](name:spectral_radiance_of_hard_xray_detector). The soft X-ray analog covering lower photon energies is [power_of_soft_xray_detector](name:power_of_soft_xray_detector). The total volumetric bremsstrahlung emission driving the detected signal is described by [bremsstrahlung_power](name:bremsstrahlung_power).

NAMES.name: power_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Radiative power received by a soft X-ray detector channel, integrated over its soft-X-ray photon-energy band.
NAMES.long:
Power of a soft X-ray detector is the total electromagnetic power delivered to one detector channel by plasma emission in the soft-X-ray photon-energy range. It is an energy-band-integrated received power, so it depends on both the plasma spectral emission along the viewing chord and the channel throughput over photon energy.

A common model expresses the received power as a photon-energy integral of the line-integrated directional spectral emissivity weighted by the detector étendue and spectral response:

$$
P_\mathrm{SXR} = \int R(E)\,\mathcal{G}(E)\left[\int_\mathrm{LOS} \varepsilon_E(\mathbf{r}(\ell),E)\,d\ell\right] dE
$$

where $E$ is photon energy, $R(E)$ is the dimensionless filter and detector response, $\mathcal{G}(E)$ is the channel étendue in m^2 sr, $\varepsilon_E$ is the directional spectral emissivity in W m^-3 sr^-1 J^-1 when $E$ is in joules, and $d\ell$ is a line element in meters along the line of sight. If photon energy is expressed in eV, $\varepsilon_E$ must instead be expressed per eV so that the integral remains in W. Equivalent formulations may use spectral radiance at the detector aperture in place of the bracketed line integral.

In practice this quantity is inferred from detector current, voltage, or photon-counting rate using calibration of the filter transmission, detector quantum efficiency, gain, aperture, and viewing geometry. It is used to compare soft-X-ray brightness between channels, constrain tomographic reconstructions, and monitor fast changes associated with MHD activity, impurity radiation, or core temperature variations.

Typical received powers are about $10^{-9}-10^{-5}$ W for strongly collimated or heavily filtered channels in medium-size tokamak plasmas, and may reach $10^{-4}-10^{-3}$ W for large-étendue channels or very bright soft-X-ray emission. The range depends strongly on plasma temperature, impurity content, filter thickness, detector area, and viewing chord.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_aperture
NAMES.short: Major radius R coordinate of the geometric center of a diagnostic aperture in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The major-radius $R$ coordinate of the geometric center of a diagnostic aperture locates the aperture centroid along the radial axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the machine toroidal symmetry axis measured outward. For spatially extended apertures, the representative point is the centroid of the aperture opening; the physical size of the aperture opening is separately characterized by [radius_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture).

This coordinate is established from mechanical survey data or optical alignment procedures performed during diagnostic installation and commissioning, and it enters line-of-sight geometry models that project plasma emission volumes onto detector arrays. It applies across a wide range of plasma diagnostics, including hard and soft X-ray cameras, visible and ultraviolet spectrometers, neutron detectors, and infrared imaging systems. The analogous coordinate for filter windows is given by [radial_coordinate_of_filter_window](name:radial_coordinate_of_filter_window), and the measurement-position counterpart used in equilibrium reconstruction is [radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position](name:radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position).

Typical values span roughly 0.5–10 m depending on device size and the radial placement of the diagnostic port.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture center lies at a positive major radius in the $+\hat{R}$ direction from the machine toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Major radius R of a single detector pixel, locating it along the radial direction from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial coordinate $R$ of a detector pixel gives the perpendicular distance from the machine's toroidal symmetry axis to the pixel center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate increasing outward from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

For X-ray crystal spectrometer diagnostics, pixel spatial coordinates are fixed by the mechanical geometry of the detector camera assembly — the crystal mount, focusing optics, and detector array — rather than by in-situ plasma measurements. Together with [vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel](name:vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel), this coordinate fully specifies the two-dimensional position of the pixel in the poloidal cross-section. The pixel radial position enters solid-angle and Bragg-diffraction geometry calculations that map spectral channels to plasma emission locations, and it is paired with [energy_of_detector_pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel) when constructing the spatial-to-spectral mapping for each pixel. The analogous quantity for a diagnostic aperture element is the [radial_coordinate_of_aperture](name:radial_coordinate_of_aperture).

Typical values range from approximately 1 m to 10 m, depending on machine size and spectrometer mounting location.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physical detector positions, as $R$ measures the outward distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short: Radial (R) position of the geometric center of a diagnostic filter window, giving its distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The coordinate $R$ gives the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the geometric center of a diagnostic filter window in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$ and $Z$ is the vertical height. Filter windows are thin absorbing foils or transmission elements placed in the optical path of X-ray and spectroscopic diagnostic channels; their precise spatial location is required for line-of-sight modeling, solid-angle weighting, and cross-channel spatial registration.

This coordinate is obtained from mechanical design specifications or optical metrology surveys of the installed diagnostic assembly. It pairs naturally with the aperture-dimension descriptors [filter_window_width](name:filter_window_width) and [filter_window_height](name:filter_window_height), which give the transverse extents of the filter aperture, and with [thickness_of_filter](name:thickness_of_filter), which governs photon attenuation through the filter material. The corresponding radial position of a diagnostic aperture element is given by [radial_coordinate_of_aperture](name:radial_coordinate_of_aperture).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the filter window center is displaced outward from the toroidal symmetry axis, consistent with $R \geq 0$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radiance_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Photon radiance of an identified spectral emission line: photon rate per unit area perpendicular to the viewing direction and per unit solid angle, integrated over the wavelength interval assigned to the line.
NAMES.long:
Radiance at a spectral line is the wavelength-integrated spectral photon radiance associated with one identified emission line. It characterizes photon number reaching an observer per unit area perpendicular to the viewing direction and per unit solid angle, not total emitted power or energy radiance.

Let $I_\lambda(\lambda)$ be the calibrated spectral photon radiance. The line radiance $L_\mathrm{line}$ is defined by integrating the continuum-subtracted spectral radiance over the wavelength window assigned to the line:

$$
L_\mathrm{line} = \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} \left[I_\lambda(\lambda) - I_{\lambda,\mathrm{bg}}(\lambda)\right] \, d\lambda
$$

where $L_\mathrm{line}$ has units m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$, $\lambda$ is wavelength in meters, $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are the endpoints of the integration window with $\Delta\lambda=\lambda_2-\lambda_1$ in meters, and $I_\lambda$ and $I_{\lambda,\mathrm{bg}}$ have units m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$. The window is chosen to contain the instrumental and physical line shape while excluding neighboring lines as far as possible; the background term represents continuum emission, stray light, dark signal, or other slowly varying contributions estimated from adjacent wavelengths or from a simultaneous fit. For a gross line integral, the same expression applies with $I_{\lambda,\mathrm{bg}}=0$.

In practice, line radiance is obtained from calibrated spectroscopic measurements. A [spectral calibration factor](name:spectral_calibration_factor_of_spectrometer) $K_\lambda(\lambda)$ converts wavelength-resolved detector signal $C_\lambda(\lambda)$, after subtraction of detector background $C_{\lambda,\mathrm{bg}}(\lambda)$, to spectral photon radiance; the corresponding practical relation is $L_\mathrm{line}=\int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} K_\lambda(\lambda)[C_\lambda(\lambda)-C_{\lambda,\mathrm{bg}}(\lambda)]\,d\lambda$ over the same line window. Grating spectrometers, filter spectrometers, and charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy systems use this quantity for emission-line strengths; inference of densities, effective charge, or radiated power requires additional atomic-physics and viewing-geometry modeling.

The wavelength-resolved quantity underlying the integral is related to [spectral flux], while [flux at spectral line](name:spectral_flux_of_spectrometer_channel) is the corresponding line-integrated photon-flux analog before radiance normalization or absolute radiance calibration. [Brightness of visible camera](name:brightness_of_visible_camera) is a broadband radiance analog integrated over a camera passband rather than over a single identified line.

Typical visible and near-ultraviolet line radiances in magnetically confined plasmas span about $10^{16}$-$10^{21}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$ for weak-to-strong steady emission. Bright edge events or active beam and charge-exchange lines can approach $10^{22}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$, with values depending strongly on species, charge state, electron temperature and density, path length, neutral-beam density for active measurements, and optical passband.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_krypton_number_density_to_maximum_electron_number_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of the volume-averaged total krypton number density to the maximum electron number density. It is a global scalar measure of krypton impurity concentration normalized to the peak electron number density.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total krypton number density averaged over the plasma volume, divided by the maximum electron number density in the same plasma. It measures the global krypton inventory relative to the peak electron-density scale, rather than a local krypton abundance at the position of peak density.

The ratio is defined using the volume average of the sum over krypton charge states:

$$
F_{\mathrm{Kr}} = \frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V}{\max_{\mathbf{x}\in V_p} n_e(\mathbf{x})}, \qquad \langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p}\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $V_p$ is the plasma volume, $n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}$ is the krypton number density in charge state $q$, $\sum_q n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}$ is the total krypton number density in m^-3, and $n_e$ is the electron number density in m^-3. The resulting ratio is dimensionless.

In practice, the krypton density is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, bolometry, soft-x-ray emission, and collisional-radiative modeling, combined with an equilibrium estimate of the plasma volume. The maximum electron number density is obtained from electron-density diagnostics such as interferometry, Thomson scattering, or reflectometry, depending on the available measurements and reconstruction method.

Typical values for krypton-seeded plasmas are about $10^{-6}-10^{-4}$ for trace impurity operation and may approach $10^{-3}$ when krypton radiation is intentionally strong. The value depends on fueling, impurity transport, charge-state distribution, plasma volume, and the degree of central density peaking.

NAMES.name: reference_calibration_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Zero-pixel wavelength intercept of the linear pixel-to-wavelength dispersion mapping used to calibrate a spectrometer channel.
NAMES.long:
This parameter defines the wavelength assigned to pixel index zero in the linear dispersion model for a spectrometer channel. The pixel-to-wavelength mapping takes the form:

$$
\lambda(k) = k \cdot g + \lambda_0
$$

where $\lambda(k)$ is the wavelength at pixel $k$, $g$ is the dispersion gain (wavelength increment per pixel), and $\lambda_0$ is this reference calibration wavelength — the zero-pixel intercept. Together with the gain, $\lambda_0$ fully specifies the linear wavelength axis, enabling conversion of raw detector pixel indices to physical wavelengths.

The offset is determined during spectrometer wavelength calibration by fitting the pixel positions of precisely known emission lines to the linear dispersion model; the intercept $\lambda_0$ is extracted from the resulting least-squares fit. This procedure applies to both UV and visible grating spectrometers used in plasma spectroscopy diagnostics.

Typical values lie in the range $1 \times 10^{-7}$ to $8 \times 10^{-7}$ m, spanning the UV-to-visible operational range of fusion spectroscopy systems. This intercept is the complement to the dispersion gain encoded in calibration_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel; together they constitute the complete linear wavelength calibration. Absolute photon spectral radiance is subsequently obtained using the [spectral_calibration_factor_of_spectrometer](name:spectral_calibration_factor_of_spectrometer).

NAMES.name: reference_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Reference wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the wavelength at which that channel's spectral instrument function has maximum response. It is a peak-position parameter of the channel response, distinct from a calibration reference wavelength and from the wavelength of a physical spectral line.
NAMES.long:
Reference wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the wavelength coordinate at which that channel's spectral instrument function reaches its maximum response. It is an instrument-response property for the channel, not the wavelength of an observed spectral line and not the reference wavelength used to define or check a wavelength calibration. As a wavelength, it is a non-negative spectral coordinate rather than a signed direction-dependent quantity.

Let $G_c(\lambda)$ denote the spectral instrument function of channel $c$ as a function of wavelength $\lambda$. The reference wavelength $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref},c}$ is the peak location:

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{ref},c} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\lambda} G_c(\lambda)
$$

where $G_c$ may be normalized or unnormalized, because the peak position is unchanged by an overall response scaling. If the response model has multiple local maxima, the reference wavelength denotes the designated principal response peak used to define the channel center.

In practice, $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref},c}$ is obtained from wavelength calibration measurements, an optical or diffraction geometry model, or spectral fitting of known features to a channel response model. For crystal X-ray spectrometers, the nominal wavelength is constrained by the Bragg relation $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta_B$, where $d$ is the lattice-plane spacing, $\theta_B$ is the Bragg angle, and $n$ is the diffraction order. The related [spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel](name:spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel) describes response broadening, while spectral_instrument_function_of_spectrometer_channel describes the full wavelength-dependent response shape.

This quantity should be distinguished from [reference_calibration_wavelength](name:reference_calibration_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel), which is a fiducial wavelength used to establish or validate a wavelength scale, and from [wavelength_of_spectral_line](name:wavelength_of_spectral_line), which is a physical photon wavelength associated with an atomic, molecular, or ionic transition.

Typical values depend on the spectral band: crystal X-ray spectrometer channels commonly lie in the range $10^{-11}$-$10^{-9}$ m, with many impurity-line measurements near $10^{-10}$-$10^{-9}$ m, while ultraviolet and visible spectrometer channels are typically about $10^{-7}$-$10^{-6}$ m.

NAMES.name: roughness_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Dimensionless surface-scattering parameter of a diagnostic optical element, where 0 represents ideal specular reflection and 1 represents ideal diffuse reflection.
NAMES.long:
Roughness of an optical element is a dimensionless phenomenological parameter describing how strongly the element redistributes incident radiation away from the ideal specular direction. It is not a length roughness such as an rms surface height; it is a scattering convention used to characterize optical behavior.

The admissible range and endpoint convention are

$$
0 \le r \le 1,\qquad r=0\ \text{for ideal specular reflection},\qquad r=1\ \text{for ideal diffuse reflection}
$$

where $r$ is the roughness parameter. Intermediate values represent increasing diffuse scattering; in optical models $r$ is often used as a weight between a specular bidirectional response and a diffuse bidirectional response, without requiring the diffuse component to be isotropic or Lambertian.

The parameter is estimated from optical scatter measurements such as bidirectional reflectance, bidirectional transmittance, or total integrated scatter, and may also be inferred from surface metrology combined with a wavelength-dependent scattering model. It generally depends on wavelength, incidence angle, polarization, coating condition, contamination, and radiation or plasma exposure history.

Typical values are 0-0.05 for highly polished diagnostic mirrors or windows with little measurable scatter, 0.05-0.3 for moderately rough or contaminated optical surfaces, and 0.5-1 for deliberately diffusing or severely degraded surfaces.

NAMES.name: spectral_absorptivity_of_filter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless wavelength-dependent probability that an incident photon is absorbed in a diagnostic filter material rather than transmitted or redirected by other loss channels. It ranges from 0 for no absorption to 1 for complete absorption at the specified wavelength.
NAMES.long:
Spectral absorptivity of a filter is the fraction of incident photons at wavelength $\lambda$ that are absorbed within the filter material. It is dimensionless, bounded by $0 \le A_\lambda \le 1$, and describes the wavelength dependence of filter attenuation rather than a wavelength-integrated response.

For a monochromatic photon population, the absorptivity can be written as a photon balance:

$$
A_\lambda = \frac{N_\mathrm{abs}(\lambda)}{N_\mathrm{inc}(\lambda)} = 1 - T_\lambda - R_\lambda - S_\lambda
$$

where $\lambda$ is wavelength in meters, $N_\mathrm{inc}$ and $N_\mathrm{abs}$ are the incident and absorbed photon counts, $T_\lambda$ is the transmitted photon fraction, $R_\lambda$ is the reflected fraction, and $S_\lambda$ represents other nonabsorbed losses such as scattering out of the accepted beam or escaping fluorescence. For a homogeneous slab of thickness $d$ in meters with linear attenuation coefficient $\mu(\lambda)$ in m$^{-1}$, the unscattered transmitted fraction is often approximated by $T_\lambda \simeq \exp[-\mu(\lambda)d]$; then $A_\lambda \simeq 1-\exp[-\mu(\lambda)d]$ only when reflection, scattering, and escaping secondary radiation are negligible or are intentionally included in the lost-photon category.

Spectral absorptivity is obtained from tabulated or measured optical constants, mass attenuation coefficients, material composition, layer thicknesses, and surface coatings, and may be verified by calibration with known photon spectra. It is defined only over the wavelength interval for which those material properties and calibration data are valid; outside that interval, extrapolated values should be treated as model assumptions rather than measured filter behavior. The corresponding transmission relation is $T_\lambda = 1 - A_\lambda - R_\lambda - S_\lambda$, reducing to $T_\lambda \simeq 1-A_\lambda$ only when the additional nonabsorbed loss channels are negligible.

Typical values span nearly the full range 0-1: thin filters may have absorptivity below 0.01 in their pass band, intermediate attenuation often gives 0.1-0.9, and wavelengths near strong absorption edges or below the filter cutoff can approach 1. Sharp spectral structure can occur near material absorption edges, so neighboring wavelengths may have substantially different absorptivity.

NAMES.name: spectral_calibration_factor_of_spectrometer
NAMES.short: Calibration factor converting a dark-corrected spectrometer count rate at a wavelength channel into absolute photon spectral radiance density per unit wavelength. It is wavelength-dependent and includes the effects of throughput, etendue, detector gain, spectral width, and optical efficiency.
NAMES.long:
Spectral calibration factor of a spectrometer is a wavelength-dependent coefficient that converts a dark-subtracted detector count rate, or an equivalent count-rate-normalized signal, into absolute photon spectral radiance density. The spectral coordinate $\lambda$ is wavelength in meters, and the normalization is per unit wavelength, not per unit frequency, wavenumber, photon energy, or integrated spectral channel. With photon counts treated as dimensionless, the factor has unit $m^{-3}\,sr^{-1}$ so that multiplication by a signal rate in $s^{-1}$ gives photon spectral radiance density in $m^{-3}\,s^{-1}\,sr^{-1}$.

For a wavelength sample $i$, the defining calibration relation is:

$$
L_\lambda(\lambda_i) = C_\lambda(\lambda_i)\,\dot{S}(\lambda_i)
$$

where $L_\lambda(\lambda_i)$ is the calibrated photon spectral radiance density in $m^{-3}\,s^{-1}\,sr^{-1}$, $C_\lambda(\lambda_i)$ is the spectral calibration factor in $m^{-3}\,sr^{-1}$, and $\dot{S}(\lambda_i)$ is the corrected detector signal rate in $s^{-1}$. If the measurement is recorded as integrated counts $N_i$ over an exposure time $\Delta t$, then $\dot{S}(\lambda_i)$ is obtained from $N_i/\Delta t$ after dark, background, gain, and linearity corrections. For a finite spectral channel, the radiance integrated over that channel is approximately $L_\lambda(\lambda_i)\Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{eff},i}$, linking this quantity to the [effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

The factor is determined by viewing a calibrated lamp, integrating sphere, monochromator, or line source with known spectral radiance under the same optical configuration used for plasma measurements. It includes the collection etendue_of_spectrometer_channel, wavelength-dependent transmission, grating or filter response, detector quantum efficiency, electronic gain, and the conversion from finite channel signal to per-wavelength radiance density. In grating systems it is normally assigned to each detector pixel or wavelength bin; in filter spectrometers it applies to the channel centered at the filter wavelength with its effective spectral width.

Typical values span many orders of magnitude because they scale approximately as the inverse of etendue, efficiency, and spectral width. Visible high-throughput systems commonly have factors around $10^{15}$-$10^{20}\ m^{-3}\,sr^{-1}$, while ultraviolet systems, narrow spectral bins, or low-throughput optical paths may require $10^{18}$-$10^{23}\ m^{-3}\,sr^{-1}$.

NAMES.name: spectral_efficiency_of_filter
NAMES.short: Wavelength-dependent probability, bounded from 0 to 1, that a photon incident on a diagnostic filter produces a registered detection event. It includes filter transmission, optical throughput, detector quantum efficiency, and other wavelength-dependent losses in the detection chain.
NAMES.long:
Spectral efficiency of a filter is the fraction of photons incident on the filter at a given wavelength that are ultimately registered as detection events. It is a dimensionless probability satisfying $0 \le \eta(\lambda) \le 1$ and represents the detected channel, not merely the optical transmission through the filter.

For a wavelength bin centered at $\lambda_i$, the efficiency is defined from incident photon rate and registered count rate over the same bin:

$$
\eta_i = \frac{S_i}{\Phi_i} = \frac{\int_{\Delta\lambda_i} S_\lambda(\lambda)\,d\lambda}{\int_{\Delta\lambda_i} \Phi_\lambda(\lambda)\,d\lambda}
$$

where $S_\lambda$ is the registered event-rate spectral density, in counts per second per wavelength unit, $\Phi_\lambda$ is the photon-rate spectral density incident on the filter, in photons per second per wavelength unit, and $\Delta\lambda_i$ is the wavelength bin. The continuous value $\eta(\lambda)$ is the narrow-bin limit or a calibrated interpolation of these bin-averaged probabilities.

Photons not registered may be absorbed in the filter, reflected or scattered out of the accepted optical path, redirected by interference-filter angle effects, transmitted but lost in later optics, or transmitted to the detector without producing an accepted event. Therefore spectral efficiency is related to, but not determined solely by, spectral absorptivity or transmittance; it also includes detector quantum efficiency, collection geometry, electronic thresholds, and wavelength-dependent optical losses.

In practice, spectral efficiency is measured with a calibrated monochromator, tunable laser, or lamp source whose photon rate at the filter is known, and by comparing the registered event rate with that incident photon rate for each wavelength bin. It may also be computed as a product of independently measured component responses, provided their angular, polarization, temperature, aging, and contamination dependencies are applicable to the same optical path.

Typical values range from less than $10^{-4}$ outside a filter passband to $0.01-0.9$ within the passband. Well matched visible detection chains often peak around $0.1-0.7$, while ultraviolet or infrared systems can be lower because of reduced optical throughput or detector quantum efficiency.

NAMES.name: spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Spectral etendue of a spectrometer channel is its area-solid-angle optical acceptance averaged over wavelength with a normalized channel spectral response. The normalization makes the spectral weighting integrate to unity, so the quantity retains units of m^2 sr.
NAMES.long:
Spectral etendue of a spectrometer channel is the effective optical throughput of that channel after accounting for its finite spectral acceptance. It represents the geometric area-solid-angle acceptance sampled by photons according to the channel spectral instrument function.

The spectral etendue $G_c$ for channel $c$ can be defined as a response-weighted average of the wavelength-dependent etendue:

$$
G_c = \int A\Omega(\lambda)\, w_c(\lambda)\, d\lambda, \qquad \int w_c(\lambda)\, d\lambda = 1
$$

where $A\Omega(\lambda)$ is the area-solid-angle throughput at wavelength $\lambda$, and $w_c(\lambda)$ is the normalized spectral weighting for the channel. If an unnormalized instrument response $S_c(\lambda)$ is used, then $w_c(\lambda)=S_c(\lambda)/\int S_c(\lambda)\,d\lambda$; consequently $w_c$ has inverse-wavelength units and $G_c$ keeps the same unit as etendue, $\mathrm{m^2\,sr}$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from optical modeling, ray tracing, aperture and solid-angle measurements, or radiometric calibration using a known spectral source. The spectral weighting is usually determined from monochromatic scans or from a characterized spectrometer line-spread function, then normalized before it is applied to the wavelength-dependent throughput.

No device-independent numerical range is implied: the value is set by aperture size, collection solid angle, optical transmission, vignetting, and the width and shape of the channel response. It should therefore be treated as an instrument calibration quantity rather than inferred from a generic tokamak or spectrometer scale.

NAMES.name: spectral_flux_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Uncalibrated photon-equivalent count rate registered by a spectrometer channel for a selected spectral line or wavelength passband. It is a detector count rate measured before conversion to absolute spectral radiance.
NAMES.long:
Spectral flux of a spectrometer channel is the photon-equivalent detection rate assigned to a selected spectral feature or wavelength passband. It is an instrumental count-rate quantity that represents how rapidly photons are registered by the detector for that feature, not an absolutely calibrated radiance or emissivity.

For a channel and a selected spectral feature or passband, the detected spectral flux is the photon-equivalent count accumulated over the feature divided by the integration time:

$$
\Phi = \frac{N}{\Delta t}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the spectral flux in s^-1, $N$ is the photon-equivalent detector count accumulated for the selected line or passband, and $\Delta t$ is the detector integration time in seconds.

In practice this quantity is obtained by summing or fitting the detector signal over the wavelength interval associated with an emission line or filter band, then dividing by the exposure time. Instrumental corrections such as detector gain, dark-signal subtraction, dead-time, and relative channel response may be applied so that channels can be compared, but absolute throughput calibration is deliberately not applied.
