Conversion to absolute spectral radiance requires multiplying or dividing by a calibration factor that bundles the collection etendue, optical transmission, detector quantum efficiency, and effective spectral width into a single throughput coefficient; that coefficient is carried by the calibration and channel instrument factors rather than by this count rate itself.

Typical values vary strongly with line brightness, optical throughput, detector gain, and integration time. Weak lines may produce roughly 10^2-10^4 s^-1 per channel, while bright visible or ultraviolet lines in fusion plasmas commonly give 10^5-10^8 s^-1 before detector saturation or nonlinear response becomes important.

NAMES.name: spectral_radiance
NAMES.short: Photon-number spectral radiance of observed plasma emission, equal to the photon flux per unit projected collector area, per unit solid angle, and per unit wavelength interval along a diagnostic line of sight.
NAMES.long:
Spectral radiance is the fundamental radiometric quantity expressing the intensity of plasma radiation along a line of sight, resolved simultaneously per unit projected collector area, per unit solid angle, and per unit wavelength interval. It is the primary photometric observable for absolute spectroscopic analysis of plasma emission processes including bremsstrahlung continuum, charge exchange recombination, and impurity line radiation.

The photon-number spectral radiance $L_\lambda$ at wavelength $\lambda$ is defined by:

$$
L_\lambda = \frac{d^2 \Phi_\gamma}{d\Omega \, dA_\perp \, d\lambda}
$$

where $\Phi_\gamma$ is the detected photon rate in s$^{-1}$, $\Omega$ is the solid angle subtended by the collecting aperture in sr, $A_\perp$ is the collecting area projected onto the plane perpendicular to the line of sight in m$^2$, and $\lambda$ is wavelength in m, giving $L_\lambda$ in m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$. The non-standard m$^{-3}$ dimension arises from combining the per-area factor (m$^{-2}$) with the per-wavelength factor (m$^{-1}$) on a photon-count basis.

Absolute calibration is performed by comparing raw detector signals to a source of known radiance, yielding a [spectral calibration factor](name:spectral_calibration_factor_of_spectrometer). The related bremsstrahlung_spectral_radiance specializes this quantity to the visible continuum component used for effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ inference, and the local volumetric emission analog is captured by [bremsstrahlung_spectral_emissivity](name:bremsstrahlung_spectral_emissivity). Measurements restricted to a discrete spectral line, such as the Stark-split beam emission described by [motional_stark_radiance](name:motional_stark_radiance_at_spectral_line), employ the same radiometric framework but integrated over a specific spectral feature.

NAMES.name: spectral_radiance_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Power radiance of hard X-ray emission received on a detector channel, equal to detected power per unit detector area per unit solid angle, resolved over one or more photon energy acceptance bands.
NAMES.long:
The spectral radiance of a hard X-ray detector channel is the detected radiative power normalized by the product of detector area and acceptance solid angle (the étendue), integrated within each photon energy band of the channel. Hard X-ray emission in fusion plasmas is generated predominantly by bremsstrahlung from suprathermal electrons and runaway electron populations, making this quantity a key diagnostic for characterizing the high-energy tail of the electron distribution.

The channel brightness $B$ is defined as:

$$
B = \frac{P}{A \cdot \Omega}
$$

where $P$ is the radiative power collected by the channel, $A$ is the effective detector area, and $\Omega$ is the solid angle subtended by the collection optics; their product $A \cdot \Omega$ is the étendue.

Unlike [hard_xray_brightness](name:hard_xray_brightness), which expresses photon flux per unit area and solid angle, this quantity is a power-based radiance, directly mirroring [spectral_radiance_of_soft_xray_detector](name:spectral_radiance_of_soft_xray_detector) for the hard X-ray energy range. Multi-channel measurements along varied lines of sight enable tomographic inversion to recover the spatially resolved hard X-ray emissivity profile, from which the energy distribution and confinement properties of suprathermal electron populations can be inferred.

NAMES.name: spectral_radiance_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Power radiance of soft X-ray emission incident on a detector channel, defined as detected power per unit area per unit solid angle and integrated over the detector energy band.
NAMES.long:
Soft X-ray spectral radiance is the detected electromagnetic power from plasma emission per unit detector area per unit solid angle, integrated over one or more energy bands defined by the detector channel's filter or spectral response. It quantifies the power flux delivered along a specific line of sight through the plasma and is distinct from photon radiance; the companion quantity [brightness_of_soft_xray_detector](name:brightness_of_soft_xray_detector) expresses the same measurement in photons per second rather than in power units.

The defining relation is:

$$
L = \frac{d^2 P}{dA \, d\Omega}
$$

where $P$ is the detected power, $dA$ is the active detector area element, and $d\Omega$ is the solid-angle element subtended by the field of view; integration over the detector energy passband is implicit in this band-integrated form.

Soft X-ray power radiance is measured with semiconductor photodiodes placed behind metallic foil filters that select an effective energy passband, commonly in the range 0.1–10 keV. Fan arrays of such channels enable tomographic inversion to recover the volumetric soft X-ray emissivity profile, supporting impurity transport studies, MHD mode tracking, and sawtooth monitoring. Multiplying by the detector étendue (area times solid angle) recovers the total channel power given by [power_of_soft_xray_detector](name:power_of_soft_xray_detector). The hard X-ray power radiance analog following the same spatial radiance definition at higher photon energies is [spectral_radiance_of_hard_xray_detector](name:spectral_radiance_of_hard_xray_detector).

NAMES.name: spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Wavelength-resolved ratio of the vacuum speed of light to the phase velocity in a diagnostic optical element material, capturing the spectral dispersion required for chromatic transmission and reflection modeling.
NAMES.long:
The spectral refractive index $n(\lambda)$ of an optical element quantifies how the phase velocity of light is reduced relative to vacuum as a function of wavelength $\lambda$. Its wavelength dependence, known as dispersion, governs chromatic aberration, wavelength-dependent Fresnel reflection coefficients, and the focusing and transmission characteristics of lenses, windows, and filters across a diagnostic spectral range.

The defining relation is:

$$
n(\lambda) = \frac{c}{v_\phi(\lambda)}
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum and $v_\phi(\lambda)$ is the phase velocity at wavelength $\lambda$. In practice, $n(\lambda)$ is well described by a Sellmeier dispersion relation, $n^2(\lambda) = 1 + \sum_i B_i \lambda^2 / (\lambda^2 - C_i)$, with empirically determined material coefficients $B_i$ and $C_i$ specific to the optical glass or crystal.

The spectral refractive index is evaluated on the same wavelength axis defined by [spectral_wavelength](name:spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element) and is typically sourced from manufacturer material specifications or measured by prism minimum-deviation refractometry or spectroscopic ellipsometry. For infrared optical elements, $n(\lambda)$ is paired with the extinction coefficient to fully characterize the complex optical response governing transmission and reflection. The full dispersion curve constitutes the spectral resolution of the broadband refractive_index_of_optical_element.

Typical values span $n \approx 1.45$–$1.47$ for fused silica in the UV-visible range, $n \approx 1.5$ for BK7 optical glass, and $n \approx 2.4$ for ZnSe at mid-infrared wavelengths. Compare with [parallel_refractive_index](name:parallel_refractive_index), which describes the refractive index projected along a wave beam directional axis in plasma wave-propagation contexts.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the phase velocity of light in the material is less than the speed of light in vacuum, as holds for all conventional dielectric and metallic optical elements used in fusion plasma diagnostics.

NAMES.name: spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Wavelength coordinate axis defining the spectral sampling grid at which the optical properties or instrument response of a diagnostic optical element are characterized.
NAMES.long:
This quantity specifies the set of photon wavelength values constituting the spectral axis used to sample the wavelength-resolved properties of a diagnostic optical element, such as its transmission, reflectivity, absorption, refractive index, or instrument response function. It applies across a wide range of diagnostic types, from crystal X-ray spectrometers and soft or hard X-ray filter windows to visible-band filter spectrometers, wherever the element's spectral behavior must be characterized on a defined wavelength grid.

The photon wavelength $\lambda$ relates to photon energy $E$ by

$$
\lambda = \frac{hc}{E}
$$

where $h$ is Planck's constant and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. For hard X-ray filter materials the grid spans roughly 0.001–0.1 nm; for soft X-ray diagnostics, 0.1–50 nm; for visible-band spectrometers, 380–780 nm.

This spectral coordinate is the companion axis to wavelength-resolved material properties such as [spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element](name:spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element) and feeds into the derivation of quantities like [effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel). For identifying individual spectral features resolved within this grid, the central rest-frame vacuum wavelength of a transition is given by [wavelength_of_spectral_line](name:wavelength_of_spectral_line).

NAMES.name: spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Spectral width of a spectrometer channel is the Gaussian standard deviation, expressed as a wavelength interval, of the channel response to monochromatic radiation. It describes instrumental broadening about the channel reference wavelength.
NAMES.long:
Spectral width of a spectrometer channel is the wavelength standard deviation of a Gaussian component of the channel response to monochromatic radiation. It represents the instrumental contribution to line-shape broadening about the [reference wavelength](name:reference_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel), separate from physical broadening in the emitting plasma. The valid physical domain is $\sigma_\lambda \ge 0$; $\sigma_\lambda = 0$ is the ideal limit of no spectral broadening by that component.

For a Gaussian component $G(\lambda)$ centered at $\lambda_0$, the width is equivalently the square root of the second central moment:

$$
\sigma_\lambda^2 = \frac{\int (\lambda - \lambda_0)^2 G(\lambda)\, d\lambda}{\int G(\lambda)\, d\lambda}
$$

where $\lambda$ and $\lambda_0$ are wavelengths in meters, $\lambda_0$ is the channel reference wavelength, and $G(\lambda)$ is the Gaussian response component expressed with the same amplitude units as the corresponding spectral instrument function. The normalization of $G$ cancels in the ratio, so $\sigma_\lambda$ has units of meters; the Gaussian full width at half maximum is $2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\,\sigma_\lambda$.

In practice, this width is estimated from calibration measurements with narrow spectral lines, from optical response modeling, or by fitting measured spectra while separating source broadening from instrumental broadening. Contributions can include crystal rocking curve, detector spatial resolution mapped into wavelength, aperture geometry, finite source extent, and alignment tolerances. Together with component amplitudes represented by the spectral_factor_of_spectrometer_channel and centers such as the reference wavelength, the widths define Gaussian terms that compose the spectral_instrument_function_of_spectrometer_channel or channel-level [instrument_function_of_spectrometer_channel](name:spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

Typical values range from $10^{-14}$-$10^{-12}$ m for high-resolution x-ray crystal spectrometer channels and $10^{-12}$-$10^{-10}$ m for lower-resolution optical or ultraviolet spectrometer channels. Values should be interpreted relative to the channel reference wavelength and the intrinsic source line width; instrumental widths comparable to or larger than the physical width dominate the measured broadening.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_filter
NAMES.short: Total true geometric area of the filter window surface that intercepts incoming radiation. For curved windows, this is the material surface area, not merely the planar projected aperture.
NAMES.long:
Surface area of a filter is the true geometric area of the filter-window face exposed to the accepted radiation beam. It describes the size of the intercepting surface and is distinct from [thickness_of_filter](name:thickness_of_filter), which governs attenuation through the material.

For an arbitrarily shaped or curved window, the surface area can be defined by integrating over the exposed surface:

$$
A = \int_U \left| \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial u} \times \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial v} \right|\,du\,dv
$$

where $A$ is the surface area in m^2, $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ is the position vector of the window surface in meters, and $u$ and $v$ are dimensionless surface parameters spanning the exposed region $U$. For a flat window this reduces to the planar aperture area; for a rectangular clear aperture with side lengths $a$ and $b$ in meters, the area is $ab$.

In practice, the value is obtained from mechanical design dimensions, aperture-mask geometry, optical or mechanical metrology, or a surface model of the installed window. For curved filter windows, the true surface area should be computed from the measured or specified curvature rather than from the projected outline alone. The area scales the intercepted photon rate for a given incident flux density, while the energy-dependent transmission is set primarily by material composition and filter thickness.

Typical values range from 10^{-6}-10^{-4} m^2 for small channel filters and from 10^{-4}-10^{-2} m^2 for larger camera or spectrometer filter windows.

NAMES.name: surface_roughness_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Dimensionless surface roughness parameter of an optical element that represents how microscopic surface texture changes reflection from specular to diffuse. A value of 0 corresponds to perfectly specular reflection, while a value of 1 corresponds to perfectly diffuse reflection.
NAMES.long:
Surface roughness of an optical element is a dimensionless parameter, denoted here by $r_s$, that characterizes the scattering effect of microscopic surface texture on reflected radiation. It is bounded by $0 \le r_s \le 1$, with $r_s = 0$ representing an ideal specular surface and $r_s = 1$ representing an ideal diffuse surface. The parameter describes optical scattering behavior rather than macroscopic element shape, which is characterized separately by quantities such as [front surface curvature] and [back surface curvature](name:back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element).

There is no universal governing equation for $r_s$ because its numerical value depends on the bidirectional reflectance distribution function or radiation-transport model in which it is used. In a specific model, $r_s$ may be derived from measured surface parameters such as RMS height variation $\sigma_h$ in meters, surface correlation length $\ell_c$ in meters, optical wavelength $\lambda$ in meters, and incidence angle $\alpha$ in radians. The mapping from those physical inputs to the bounded interval $[0,1]$ must be defined by the chosen optical scattering model.

The parameter is determined from surface metrology, angle-resolved scatter measurements, calibration measurements, or manufacturer specifications for mirrors, windows, lenses, filters, and diffuser elements. In diagnostic optical modeling it controls how much reflected power remains in the specular direction and how much is redistributed into a broader angular distribution.

Typical values span the full dimensionless interval 0-1. Polished diagnostic optics are usually assigned values close to 0, intentionally diffusing or strongly degraded surfaces values close to 1, and partially scattering surfaces intermediate values. Numerical thresholds for "polished," "degraded," or "diffuse" behavior are model dependent and should be interpreted consistently with the reflectance model being used.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Physical thickness of the Bragg crystal measured along its surface normal, controlling X-ray absorption and diffraction efficiency in a crystal spectrometer channel.
NAMES.long:
The thickness of a Bragg crystal is the dimension measured perpendicular to the diffracting crystal planes — along the crystal surface normal. It is a fundamental geometric parameter governing the trade-off between X-ray absorption within the crystal bulk and the integrated diffraction efficiency, and it directly sets the operating regime of the Bragg reflection.

For Bragg diffraction, crystal thickness $t$ determines whether the crystal operates in the dynamical (Darwin) regime ($t \gg \Lambda$, where $\Lambda$ is the X-ray extinction depth) with saturated peak reflectivity, or in the kinematical limit ($t \ll \Lambda$) where peak reflectivity scales as $t^2$. Bulk transmission through the crystal material follows Beer–Lambert attenuation:

$$
I = I_0 \exp(-\mu t)
$$

where $I_0$ is the incident X-ray intensity and $\mu$ is the linear attenuation coefficient of the crystal material at the relevant photon energy.

Crystal thickness is fixed at fabrication and can be verified by X-ray transmission measurements or optical profilometry. Typical values range from tens of micrometers for thin mica or silicon crystals to a few millimeters for bent-crystal focusing geometries used in fusion X-ray spectroscopy.

Together with [bragg_crystal_width](name:bragg_crystal_width) and height_of_bragg_crystal, the thickness fully characterizes the three-dimensional geometry of the crystal element.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_filter
NAMES.short: Physical thickness of a diagnostic filter window material, which governs the energy-dependent photon attenuation and the effective spectral passband of X-ray detector channels.
NAMES.long:
The filter window thickness is the geometric extent of the absorbing filter material measured along the direction normal to the filter surface, coinciding with the photon beam propagation path. Together with the material composition, it sets the Beer-Lambert transmission spectrum of the filter, controlling the low-energy photon cutoff and shaping the spectral sensitivity of the detector channel.

The photon transmission through a filter of thickness $d$ at photon energy $E$ follows:

$$
T(E) = \exp(-\mu(E)\, d)
$$

where $\mu(E)$ is the energy-dependent linear attenuation coefficient of the filter material in m$^{-1}$ and $d$ is the filter thickness. Increasing $d$ suppresses low-energy photons more strongly, raising the effective energy cutoff of the diagnostic.

The thickness is a fixed hardware parameter established at instrument construction and determined by the required spectral selection. In soft X-ray diagnostics, filter foils span from tens of nanometers to tens of micrometers; hard X-ray diagnostics may use material layers from tens of micrometers to millimeters. The wavelength-resolved photon absorption that results from this thickness is captured by [spectral absorptivity of the filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter), while the lateral extent of the filter opening is characterized by [radius_of_filter](name:radius_of_filter). The analogous geometric parameter for the dispersing element is [thickness_of_bragg_crystal](name:thickness_of_bragg_crystal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the filter material thickness is measured from the beam-entry face to the beam-exit face along the direction of photon propagation.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Physical thickness of an optical element is the perpendicular separation between its opposing optical surfaces. It is a non-negative geometric length of the element, normally defined along the element normal or another stated thickness reference.
NAMES.long:
The thickness of an optical element is the physical distance between its two opposing optical surfaces, measured perpendicular to the reference surface or along the specified element normal. It is a non-negative geometric length of the component itself, independent of the direction in which light is propagated. For curved, wedged, or nonparallel elements, the value corresponds to the stated thickness convention, such as center thickness, edge thickness, or local normal separation.

Thickness is obtained from mechanical design, metrology, or optical modeling. Common measurements include calipers or micrometers for accessible plane-parallel elements, coordinate measurement or profilometry for curved or wedged optics, and interferometry or ellipsometry for thin films. In optical calculations for a homogeneous element at normal incidence, $\mathrm{OPL}=n d$, where $\mathrm{OPL}$ is optical path length in meters, $d$ is thickness in meters, and $n$ is the dimensionless refractive index at the relevant wavelength; more general calculations also require surface curvatures, wedge, aperture, coatings, roughness, and refractive-index dispersion.

Representative order-of-magnitude values depend strongly on the component type: coatings and very thin filters may be about 10^-8-10^-5 m, filter plates and small windows about 10^-4-10^-2 m, and robust protective windows or large optical elements can be thicker. The appropriate value is set by material strength, absorption length, thermal loading, wavelength range, and optical design.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_bremsstrahlung_count_at_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Rate at which visible bremsstrahlung continuum photons produce photoelectron-equivalent counts in a single detector pixel. It is the time derivative of the accumulated bremsstrahlung count and represents a detected count rate, not a source photon emission rate.
NAMES.long:
The time derivative of bremsstrahlung count at a detector pixel is the detected photoelectron-equivalent count rate associated with visible bremsstrahlung continuum light incident on that pixel. The accumulated count is dimensionless; its time derivative has unit s^-1 and is distinct from the number of photons emitted by the plasma or the photon flux arriving at the detector, because it includes optical throughput, spectral response, quantum efficiency, and detector conversion to photoelectrons.

For detector pixel $p$, the rate is defined from the accumulated bremsstrahlung count $N_{\mathrm{brem},p}$ as

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{brem},p}(t) = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{brem},p}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{brem},p}$ is the dimensionless accumulated photoelectron-equivalent bremsstrahlung count in pixel $p$, $t$ is time in s, and $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{brem},p}$ is the detected count rate in s^-1. This quantity is conceptually the bremsstrahlung-specific form of tendency_of_count_at_detector_pixel and is closely related to [bremsstrahlung_rate](name:time_derivative_of_bremsstrahlung_count_at_detector_pixel).

In practice, the rate is inferred from camera, photodiode, or photomultiplier signals viewing a selected visible-continuum spectral band. Raw electronic signals are converted to photoelectron-equivalent counts using the detector gain, exposure time or sampling interval, dark and offset subtraction, relative channel calibration, and, when needed, corrections for background line radiation or stray light. The resulting calibrated rate describes detected photoelectrons attributable to bremsstrahlung; it is not the plasma emissivity itself, which additionally requires line-of-sight geometry, spectral bandwidth, transmission, detector efficiency, and plasma parameters such as electron density, electron temperature, and effective charge.

Typical calibrated count rates span about 10^3-10^8 s^-1 per pixel in visible bremsstrahlung systems. Edge or low-density views may be near 10^2-10^5 s^-1, while bright core views with large optical throughput can reach 10^7-10^9 s^-1 before detector saturation or pile-up effects become important.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_along_line_of_sight
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle coordinate of the second point used with a first point to define a diagnostic line of sight or pellet path in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It gives the point's azimuthal position about the toroidal symmetry axis, in radians.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the toroidal angle $\phi$ of the second point used, together with a corresponding first point, to define a diagnostic line of sight or an analogous pellet path. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in meters, $\phi$ is azimuthal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters. Angles differing by integer multiples of $2\pi$ represent the same physical azimuthal direction.

Relative to a right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ with coordinate values $(x,y,z)$, $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, and a chosen $\phi=0$ direction, the second-point coordinates satisfy:

$$
x = R\cos\phi,\quad y = R\sin\phi,\quad z = Z
$$

where $R$ and $Z$ are in meters and $\phi$ is in radians. Equivalently, $\phi$ is obtained from the transverse Cartesian coordinates by a two-argument arctangent, modulo $2\pi$.

The second point is normally determined from the designed geometry, survey, optical alignment, or trajectory setup. Paired with the corresponding first point, it fixes the direction of the line of sight or pellet path; intermediate positions along that line or path have coordinates derived from the defining-point geometry and should not be confused with this second-point coordinate. The companion coordinates needed to specify the same point are major_radius_of_along_line_of_sight and [vertical_coordinate_of_along_line_of_sight](name:vertical_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal).

Typical angular representatives span a full toroidal turn, such as $0-2\pi$ rad or $-\pi-\pi$ rad depending on the chosen wrap convention, while a particular port, viewing system, or pellet injector usually occupies a narrower sector. Comparisons of angle differences should account for periodic wrapping at multiples of $2\pi$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Angular span subtended by a Bragg diffracting crystal in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It defines the horizontal acceptance angle over which the crystal can intercept X-ray radiation for Bragg diffraction.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of a Bragg crystal is the angular extent of the crystal projection in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the horizontal acceptance arc over which a curved or cylindrical diffracting crystal can intercept X-ray radiation for Bragg diffraction.

The span is obtained from the crystal-edge toroidal coordinates in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame on a continuous angular branch:

$$
\Delta\phi_\mathrm{crystal} = \phi_{\max}^{\mathrm{unwrapped}} - \phi_{\min}^{\mathrm{unwrapped}}
$$

where $\phi_{\min}^{\mathrm{unwrapped}}$ and $\phi_{\max}^{\mathrm{unwrapped}}$ are the lower and upper toroidal edge angles in radians after placing both edges on the same continuous branch, with $\Delta\phi_\mathrm{crystal} \ge 0$. If the physical crystal crosses the $2\pi$ branch cut in $\phi$, one edge angle is shifted by an integer multiple of $2\pi$ before evaluating the difference.

During design or calibration, this quantity is computed from the known crystal edge locations, from the crystal arc length and [toroidal_curvature_of_bragg_crystal](name:toroidal_curvature_of_bragg_crystal), or from metrology of the mounted crystal. Together with radial_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal, [radius_of_bragg_crystal](name:radius_of_bragg_crystal), and [vertical_curvature_of_bragg_crystal](name:vertical_curvature_of_bragg_crystal), it helps determine the ray directions accepted by the crystal aperture and the range of Bragg incidence angles sampled at once.

Typical values are set by crystal size, curvature, and spectrometer layout; the definition itself only requires a non-negative span not exceeding a full turn. For finite curved-crystal X-ray spectrometers, representative engineering values are often about 0.001-0.1 rad, with high-resolution narrow-aperture designs generally toward the lower end.

NAMES.name: total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Total neutron production rate from thermonuclear reactions among Maxwellian bulk ions, summed over neutron-producing DD, DT, and TT branches. It excludes beam-target, beam-beam, fusion-product, radio-frequency-tail, and other fast-ion fusion contributions.
NAMES.long:
The total neutron source rate due to thermal fusion is the number of neutrons produced per unit time by fusion reactions between bulk ions whose velocity distributions are locally Maxwellian. It is the thermal component of [total neutron source rate due to fusion], made from neutron-producing D-D, D-T, and T-T reaction branches. Neutron multiplicity is counted, and non-Maxwellian fast-ion reactions are excluded.

The thermal source rate can be expressed as a volume integral of local Maxwellian reaction rates:

$$
S_n^{\mathrm{th}} = \int_V \sum_r \nu_{n,r}\,\frac{n_{a_r} n_{b_r}}{1+\delta_{a_r b_r}}\,\langle \sigma v \rangle_r(T_{a_r},T_{b_r})\,dV
$$

where $S_n^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the total thermal neutron source rate, $r$ labels neutron-producing reaction branches, $\nu_{n,r}$ is the number of neutrons emitted by branch $r$, $n_{a_r}$ and $n_{b_r}$ are reactant ion densities, $\delta_{a_r b_r}$ is one for identical reactants and zero otherwise, and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_r$ is the Maxwellian-averaged fusion reactivity. The denominator prevents double counting of identical ion pairs; for D-D fusion, the D(d,n)$^3\mathrm{He}$ branch is counted and the D(d,p)T branch is not.

In practice, this quantity is computed from reconstructed ion density, ion temperature, fuel composition, and plasma volume using tabulated or fitted Maxwellian reactivities. It is inferred experimentally from absolutely calibrated neutron measurements, such as fission chambers, activation systems, scintillators, or neutron cameras, with corrections for detector efficiency, attenuation, scattering, and viewing geometry. Separating the thermal component from fast-ion contributions generally requires kinetic modeling, neutron energy information, or comparison with beam and radio-frequency heating histories.

Typical values are below $10^{10}$ Hz in low-temperature or very low-density plasmas, about $10^{12}$-$10^{16}$ Hz in many deuterium plasmas, and $10^{17}$-$10^{20}$ Hz in high-performance D-T experiments; reactor-scale D-T plasmas can approach $10^{20}$-$10^{21}$ Hz. Because the reactivity rises steeply with ion temperature in the several-keV range and the source scales approximately with reacting density products such as $n_D n_T$, small changes in temperature, fuel mix, and dilution can change the rate by orders of magnitude.

NAMES.name: total_plasma_radiated_power
NAMES.short: Total radiated power from the entire plasma volume, integrated over all photon energies and emission mechanisms, representing the global electromagnetic radiative loss from the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Total plasma radiated power is the aggregate electromagnetic power emitted by the plasma and carried away by photons. It includes continuum and line radiation from all plasma regions included in the physical volume being considered, and is a global loss term in the plasma power balance.

If $\epsilon_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{r})$ is the spectral-integrated volumetric radiative emissivity, the total radiated power is

$$
P_\mathrm{rad} = \int_V \epsilon_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $V$ is the plasma volume, $\epsilon_\mathrm{rad}$ has units W m$^{-3}$, and $dV$ has units m$^3$.

In experiments, this quantity is commonly inferred from bolometric measurements by reconstructing the spatial emissivity distribution and integrating it over the plasma volume. It may also be computed from radiation models that combine impurity line radiation, recombination radiation, bremsstrahlung, and other relevant photon-emission processes. Related quantities may restrict the integration region, for example to the plasma inside the last closed flux surface, or isolate a specific contribution such as [bremsstrahlung_power](name:bremsstrahlung_power).

Typical values range from $10^4$-$10^6$ W in small or moderate plasmas and from $10^6$-$5 \times 10^7$ W in high-power tokamak plasmas. The radiated fraction of the injected or conducted heating power is often 20-80%, depending strongly on density, impurity content, edge conditions, and detachment state.

NAMES.name: tritium_density
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Local number density of tritium ions in the plasma, the foundational fuel-ion parameter underlying chord-averaged, volume-averaged, and isotopic ratio child quantities.
NAMES.long:
Tritium ion number density $n_T$ quantifies the local concentration of hydrogen-3 fuel ions in the plasma. It serves as the common physical basis for a family of derived quantities: the chord-integrated mean [line_averaged_tritium_density](name:line_averaged_tritium_density), the confined-volume mean [volume_averaged_tritium_density](name:volume_averaged_tritium_density), and dimensionless isotopic ratios such as [ratio_of_tritium_density_to_electron_density](name:ratio_of_tritium_density_to_electron_density) and [ratio_of_tritium_density_to_deuterium_density](name:ratio_of_tritium_density_to_deuterium_density).

In deuterium-tritium (DT) fusion plasmas the local volumetric reaction rate is:

$$
R_{DT} = n_T \, n_D \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}$ is the Maxwellian-averaged DT fusion reactivity. The combined DT fuel-ion purity relative to the electron population is tracked by [ratio_of_deuterium_tritium_density_to_electron_density](name:ratio_of_deuterium_tritium_density_to_electron_density).

Tritium density is inferred from active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, neutron emission measurements in DT plasmas, or pellet injection and fueling diagnostics.
NAMES.sign: Positive when tritium ions are present in the plasma.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_tritium_density_to_deuterium_density
NAMES.short: Ratio of local tritium ion number density to local deuterium ion number density in a deuterium-tritium plasma. It quantifies the isotopic fuel mix independently of the total ion density.
NAMES.long:
The ratio of tritium density to deuterium density is a dimensionless measure of the local deuterium-tritium fuel composition. It compares the number density of tritium ions with the number density of deuterium ions at the same location and time, and is defined only where the deuterium density is nonzero.

The ratio is defined by:

$$
r_{T/D} = \frac{n_T}{n_D}
$$

where $r_{T/D}$ has unit 1, $n_T$ is the tritium ion number density in $m^{-3}$, and $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density in $m^{-3}$. Values greater than 1 indicate tritium-rich fuel, values less than 1 indicate deuterium-rich fuel, and $r_{T/D}=1$ corresponds to equal tritium and deuterium ion densities.

In practice this ratio may be inferred from isotope-resolved particle measurements, charge-exchange or neutral-particle diagnostics, or from fusion-product and neutron-emission analysis combined with plasma composition and temperature information. Neutron emission alone primarily constrains the product $n_D n_T$ weighted by the fusion reactivity, so determining $n_T/n_D$ requires additional assumptions or independent constraints on the ion densities, ion temperature, fast-ion contribution, and diagnostic calibration.

Typical core deuterium-tritium operation aims for near-equimolar fuel, with $r_{T/D}$ often in the range 0.5-2. Larger or smaller values can occur during isotope-ratio control transients, fueling asymmetries, burnup, or experiments deliberately biased toward deuterium-rich or tritium-rich mixtures.

NAMES.name: upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: High-energy edge of the photon spectral acceptance interval for a detector pixel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It is the maximum photon energy included in that pixel's bandpass.
NAMES.long:
The upper bound energy of a detector pixel is the largest photon energy accepted within that pixel's spectral bandpass. In a dispersive X-ray crystal spectrometer it marks the high-energy edge of the interval over which photons diffracted by the crystal are assigned to that pixel, complementing the lower bound and bracketing the representative pixel energy.

For a crystal reflection, the high-energy edge is related to the Bragg angle at the corresponding edge of the pixel acceptance:

$$
E_{\mathrm{upper}} = \frac{n h c}{2 d \sin\theta_{\mathrm{upper}}}
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is in eV, $n$ is the dimensionless diffraction order, $h$ is Planck's constant in eV s, $c$ is the speed of light in $m\,s^{-1}$, $d$ is the lattice-plane spacing in meters, and $\theta_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is the Bragg angle in radians. Equivalently, $n\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}} = 2d\sin\theta_{\mathrm{upper}}$ with photon wavelength $\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}}$ in meters and $E_{\mathrm{upper}} = hc/\lambda_{\mathrm{upper}}$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from the calibrated mapping between detector position and photon energy, using the crystal spacing, diffraction order, spectrometer geometry, and detector pixel extent. Calibration may be refined with known spectral lines, and the resulting bound can include effects from finite pixel size, crystal rocking curve, source extent, alignment uncertainty, and the chosen definition of the pixel response threshold.

Typical upper-bound energies for fusion X-ray crystal spectrometers are 1000-20000 eV. The separation from the corresponding lower bound is often 1-50 eV in high-resolution line spectroscopy and can be larger for broad-band or lower-dispersion configurations.

NAMES.name: upper_bound_wavelength_of_camera
NAMES.short: Long-wavelength (red-side) cutoff of the spectral sensitivity band of a visible camera detector channel, above which photons fall outside the detector response.
NAMES.long:
The upper bound wavelength is the long-wavelength edge of the spectral acceptance band of a visible camera detector channel. Photons with wavelengths exceeding this value lie outside the detector's sensitivity range and do not contribute to the measured signal. Together with the lower-wavelength cutoff, it defines the complete bandpass window within which photon flux from the plasma is integrated.

The effective spectral bandwidth of the detection channel is

$$
\Delta\lambda = \lambda_{\mathrm{upper}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{lower}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the short-wavelength (blue-side) cutoff. The [calibration factor of the visible camera] converts counts integrated over this window to absolute photon radiance.

The spectral cutoff is governed by the photodetector material's quantum efficiency rolloff and any bandpass interference filters placed in the optical collection path. Narrow-band filtered channels constrain the upper bound to within a few nanometers above the center of a target plasma emission line, while broadband unfiltered channels are bounded by the sensor's intrinsic material response.

Typical upper bound values for silicon-based sensors range from approximately $6 \times 10^{-7}$ to $1.1 \times 10^{-6}$ m; channels targeting D-alpha (approximately $6.56 \times 10^{-7}$ m) or He-I (approximately $5.87 \times 10^{-7}$ m) emission use narrow bandpass filters with upper cutoffs placed a few nanometers above the respective line centers.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wavelength corresponds to a physically realizable electromagnetic wave, as all electromagnetic wavelengths are intrinsically positive-valued lengths.

NAMES.name: upper_photon_energy
NAMES.short: Upper photon energy bound defining the high-energy threshold of an X-ray detector channel spectral sensitivity window.
NAMES.long:
The upper photon energy bound marks the maximum photon energy at which a detector channel registers photon counts, defining the high-energy edge of the band over which photon flux is integrated. Together with [lower_photon_energy](name:lower_photon_energy), it fully specifies the energy band used for spectrally resolved X-ray bremsstrahlung measurements in both soft and hard X-ray diagnostics.

The photon energy $E_\gamma$ relates to radiation frequency $\nu$ and wavelength $\lambda$ through:

$$
E_\gamma = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}
$$

where $h \approx 4.136 \times 10^{-15}$ eV·s is Planck's constant and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

The upper energy limit is set by detector material properties, filter transmittance, and electronic discriminator thresholds in the pulse-height analyzer. Soft X-ray channel upper bounds span roughly 0.1–10 keV; hard X-ray diagnostic channels extend to tens to hundreds of keV depending on detector type. The analogous threshold for crystal spectrometer cameras is [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physical photon energies, as $E_\gamma = h\nu > 0$ for any non-zero photon frequency.

NAMES.name: vertical_angle_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Vertical viewing angle of a detector pixel, defined as the signed elevation offset of that pixel's line of sight from the camera optical axis. Together with the horizontal pixel angle, it specifies the ray direction within the camera field of view.
NAMES.long:
Vertical angle of a detector pixel is the signed elevation angle, denoted $\beta$, between the pixel line of sight and the camera optical axis, measured in the vertical direction of the camera image plane. Both $\beta$ and the related horizontal angle $\alpha$ are angular quantities expressed in radians; the horizontal counterpart is [alpha angle], and angular acceptance limits may be represented by an [upper bound angle].

In a camera-centered right-handed orthonormal basis $(\hat{h}, \hat{v}, \hat{o})$, where $\hat{o}$ points along the optical axis from the camera into the observed scene, $\hat{v}$ is the positive vertical direction in the image plane, and $\hat{h} \times \hat{v} = \hat{o}$, the vertical angular coordinate of a unit line-of-sight direction $\hat{\ell}$ can be written as:

$$
\beta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\hat{\ell}\cdot\hat{v},\,\hat{\ell}\cdot\hat{o}\right)
$$

where $\operatorname{atan2}$ preserves the sign of the vertical offset and returns the angle in radians. For optical systems with distortion or relay optics, this expression represents the equivalent calibrated angular coordinate of the ray rather than a simple linear detector-coordinate mapping.

The angle is obtained from optical calibration of the camera, including the lens model, detector geometry, alignment of the optical axis, and any mirrors or windows in the viewing path. It is used with the horizontal angle to reconstruct the three-dimensional line of sight for visible-light measurements and to relate each detector element to the observed plasma or wall region.

Typical values span about $-0.5$-$0.5$ rad for wide-angle views and about $-0.1$-$0.1$ rad for narrow views; adjacent detector pixels often differ by $10^{-5}$-$10^{-3}$ rad depending on focal length and detector pitch.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the line of sight is tilted from the optical axis toward $+\hat{v}$ in the camera-centered right-handed basis $(\hat{h}, \hat{v}, \hat{o})$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_bolometer
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the center of a bolometer detector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a bolometer is the $Z$ position of the detector center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The coordinate value is measured in meters relative to the device coordinate origin and locates the detector center above or below the reference midplane.

This coordinate is determined from the diagnostic geometry, typically using mechanical design data, metrology surveys, or alignment calibration. Together with the detector radial coordinate, toroidal angle, aperture position, and viewing direction, it contributes to the geometric definition of a bolometer line of sight or viewing cone, but does not by itself define the full chord geometry.

Typical values are device dependent. Detector centers are commonly near diagnostic ports or the vessel periphery, with $Z$ values of about -2 to 2 m in medium-sized tokamaks and up to roughly -10 to 10 m in large devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector center lies in the $+Z$ direction, vertically above the coordinate origin.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_camera
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the center of a camera in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates the geometric center of a camera — encompassing visible, X-ray, and UV imaging instruments — along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the height measured from the machine midplane with $Z$ increasing upward.

This coordinate is obtained from mechanical survey, laser tracker measurements, or design models of the diagnostic installation referenced to the machine coordinate origin. Together with $R$ and $\phi$, it fully specifies the three-dimensional position of the camera center in the tokamak geometry. The analogous vertical coordinate for general optical elements is given by [vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element](name:vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element), and for diagnostic apertures by [vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the camera center lies above the machine midplane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Vertical height Z of the center of a detector pixel in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It is an absolute machine-geometry coordinate of the pixel center, not a detector-local row index or the active-height span across pixels.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a detector pixel is the $Z$ coordinate of the geometric center of an individual pixel of a radiation-imaging detector (such as an X-ray camera or crystal spectrometer) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is an absolute machine-geometry coordinate measured from the $Z=0$ reference plane, distinct from any detector-local active-height coordinate, row index, or the full vertical extent of the pixel.

Together with the corresponding radial and toroidal coordinates of the same pixel center, this quantity fixes the spatial location of each sensing element, which in turn defines the viewing geometry used to relate detected radiation to its plasma source region.

Typical absolute values are set by the diagnostic installation height and commonly lie within $-2$ to $2$ m for medium-sized tokamaks, extending to several meters in larger devices. Differences in $Z$ between neighboring pixel centers are much smaller, of order $0.001$ to $0.1$ m, set by pixel pitch and detector orientation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pixel center lies above the $Z=0$ reference plane, displaced in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate, in meters, of the geometric center of a diagnostic filter window in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. Z is measured from the machine midplane and is positive upward along the vertical axis.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a filter window is the $Z$ position of the geometric center of the window that transmits selected radiation to a diagnostic. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height measured in meters from the machine midplane.

This coordinate is normally determined from the mechanical survey, engineering model, or installed diagnostic geometry. Together with the corresponding radial coordinate and toroidal angle, it locates the filter-window center for line-of-sight, aperture, and ray-tracing calculations. The related quantity [vertical_coordinate_of_filter](name:vertical_coordinate_of_filter_window) may denote the same center when the filter is represented by its window center rather than by a distinct body coordinate.

Typical values are device- and diagnostic-dependent, commonly ranging from -5-5 m in large tokamaks and from -1-1 m in smaller laboratory devices. Values near 0 m are close to the machine midplane, while positive and negative values identify windows mounted above and below that plane.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the filter-window center lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the geometric center of a soft X-ray detector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ specifies the height of the geometric center of a soft X-ray detector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ increases upward along the machine symmetry axis with $Z = 0$ at the machine midplane.

Together with the corresponding major-radius position, this coordinate fully determines the poloidal location of the detector center, which is required for computing line-of-sight geometry and for mapping chord-integrated soft X-ray signals onto the poloidal cross-section. The coordinate is obtained from engineering survey or CAD documentation of the diagnostic hardware rather than from in-situ plasma measurements.

Detectors distributed at varying $Z$ heights across one or more poloidal viewing fans enable Abel inversion or tomographic reconstruction of the soft X-ray emissivity distribution. The analogous vertical position coordinates for other diagnostic components follow the same geometric convention, as in [vertical_coordinate_of_bolometer](name:vertical_coordinate_of_bolometer) and [vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector center is located above the machine midplane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_curvature_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Radius of curvature of the Bragg crystal diffracting surface in the vertical, sagittal X2 direction of the local crystal-frame X1, X2, X3 basis. It is reported as a positive radius and characterizes the out-of-dispersion bending of doubly curved X-ray crystal optics.
NAMES.long:
Vertical curvature of a Bragg crystal is the radius of curvature of the diffracting surface along the vertical, sagittal surface direction of the local crystal-frame $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$ basis, where $X_1$ lies along the spectral dispersion direction on the surface, $X_2$ lies along the vertical, out-of-dispersion direction on the surface, and $X_3$ is the outward surface normal. It is a geometric radius of the bent substrate and is reported as a positive (non-negative) magnitude, with smaller values denoting tighter bending; it carries no orientation sign because it describes the shape of the surface rather than a directed vector.

Near a reference point on the diffracting surface, the displacement of the surface along the normal direction $X_3$ as a function of the vertical coordinate $X_2$ defines the vertical radius of curvature through the paraxial sag relation:

$$
z(X_2) \simeq \frac{X_2^{\,2}}{2 R_v}
$$

where $z$ is the surface sag along $X_3$ in meters, $X_2$ is the vertical, out-of-dispersion coordinate on the surface in meters, and $R_v$ is the vertical radius of curvature in meters. Equivalently $R_v$ is the inverse of the local surface curvature in the $X_2$ direction. In doubly curved geometries this vertical radius works together with the meridional (dispersion-plane) radius to set the focusing of the diffracting element, controlling how rays that diverge above and below the dispersion plane are collected toward the detector.

The value is fixed by the spectrometer optical design and is verified by mechanical or optical metrology of the crystal substrate or diffracting surface, for example surface profilometry, interferometry, or coordinate measurement, and may be cross-checked by ray-tracing against calibration spectra. It is a design and as-built geometric property of the optic, not a measured plasma quantity.

Typical vertical radii in fusion X-ray crystal spectrometers span roughly 0.1-5 m, with compact, strongly focusing instruments tending toward the lower end and weakly focusing or nearly flat sagittal profiles toward several meters. Very large values correspond to a nearly flat surface in the vertical direction and weak out-of-dispersion focusing.

NAMES.name: vertical_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Signed vertical principal radius of curvature of an optical element front surface in the local aperture frame (X1, X2, z), where X2 is the vertical aperture coordinate and z is the surface-normal or optical-axis coordinate. Although the name says curvature, the meter unit denotes a radius of curvature.
NAMES.long:
The vertical front surface curvature is the signed principal radius of curvature of the front, beam-entry surface of an optical element in the vertical aperture direction. It describes how the surface bends in the $X_2$ direction of the local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, z)$, where $X_1$ and $X_2$ span the aperture plane and $z$ is the surface-normal or optical-axis coordinate.

Near the surface vertex, the vertical section of the front-surface sag is represented to lowest order by:

$$
z_s(0, X_2) \simeq \frac{X_2^2}{2 R_2}, \qquad \kappa_2 = \frac{1}{R_2}
$$

where $z_s$ is the surface sag, $R_2$ is this signed radius of curvature, and $\kappa_2$ is the reciprocal curvature with units m^-1.

This quantity is meaningful for front-surface prescriptions that resolve curvature by aperture direction, including spherical, cylindrical, toroidal, and separably curved surfaces. For a spherical surface, the vertical radius equals the orthogonal front-surface radius; for a cylindrical surface one principal direction may be effectively flat; for toroidal or separably curved surfaces the $X_1$ and $X_2$ radii may differ. The related [vertical front surface radius](name:vertical_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element) denotes the same radius interpretation, while [x front surface curvature] gives the corresponding orthogonal aperture-direction quantity.

The value is normally obtained from the optical prescription or from surface metrology by fitting the measured front-surface sag to the chosen surface model. Representative absolute radii can span about 0.01-100 m in diagnostic optical systems, with very weakly curved or flat directions represented by much larger or effectively infinite radii.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center of curvature of the vertical front-surface section lies in the $+z$ direction from the surface vertex in the local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, z)$.

NAMES.name: vertical_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Signed radius of curvature of an optical element's front surface along the local X2 vertical direction of the aperture frame (X1, X2, z), where z is the local surface-normal or optical-axis coordinate. It applies to spherical, cylindrical, toroidal, and separably curved front surfaces whose vertical radius is specified independently.
NAMES.long:
The vertical front-surface radius of an optical element is the signed radius of curvature of the element's entrance or reflecting surface in the $X_2$ principal section of the local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, z)$. Here $X_1$ and $X_2$ span the local aperture or tangent plane, $X_2$ is the vertical transverse direction, and $z$ is the local surface-normal or optical-axis coordinate. This is a radius in meters, not the reciprocal curvature in m$^{-1}$.

Near the local vertex, after subtracting any planar tilt, the small-sag form of the front surface in the $X_2$ direction is

$$
z(x_2) - z(0) \simeq \frac{x_2^2}{2 R_2}
$$

where $x_2$ is displacement along $X_2$ in meters, $z$ is surface sag along the local $z$ coordinate in meters, and $R_2$ is this signed vertical front-surface radius in meters. The approximation assumes $|x_2| \ll |R_2|$ and a local tangent frame; an exactly circular principal section has this expression as its second-order expansion.

The value is usually obtained from optical design specifications, crystal-bending geometry, or surface metrology such as profilometry or interferometry. It determines vertical focusing in ray tracing and wave-optics calculations. For a spherical surface the $X_1$ and $X_2$ radii are equal; for cylindrical, toroidal, or separably curved surfaces the two transverse radii may differ and must be specified independently. The closely related [vertical_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:vertical_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element) uses the same vertical front-surface radius convention, while x_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element refers to the orthogonal $X_1$ direction and [vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element) to the rear surface.

Typical absolute values range from about 0.1-10 m for tightly bent X-ray crystal reflectors to 1-100 m for weakly focusing mirrors or grazing-incidence optics. A nearly flat surface is represented by a radius whose magnitude is much larger than the aperture size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center of curvature of the front surface in the $X_2$ principal section lies on the $+z$ side of the local tangent plane.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_spectrometer
NAMES.short: Uncalibrated detector-channel voltage from a visible-light filter spectrometer before dark/offset subtraction and radiometric calibration. It represents the readout potential difference produced by detector response and electronics, not an absolute photon flux or radiance.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a spectrometer is the raw electrical potential difference delivered by a visible-light filter spectrometer detector readout for a selected spectral passband. It includes detector gain, bias, dark signal, and electronic offset, and is not yet converted to detector photon rate, spectral radiance, or line-integrated flux.

The detector response can be modeled as an additive offset plus a wavelength-weighted response to photons arriving at the detector:

$$
V(t) = V_\mathrm{off}(t) + \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} R_V(\lambda,t)\,\dot{N}_{\lambda,\mathrm{det}}(\lambda,t)\,d\lambda
$$

where $V$ and $V_\mathrm{off}$ are voltages in V, $\lambda$ is wavelength in m, $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ bound the filter passband, $\dot{N}_{\lambda,\mathrm{det}}$ is the photon arrival-rate spectral density at the detector in photons s^-1 m^-1, and $R_V$ is the effective detector-and-electronics voltage responsivity in V s photon^-1. The offset term is retained in the raw voltage and must be estimated separately, for example from dark or blocked-light measurements.

In practice this signal is read from a photodiode, avalanche photodiode, photomultiplier, or similar detector chain. Subtracting $V_\mathrm{off}$ and applying detector responsivity calibration can infer a detector photon rate, while conversion to spectral radiance also requires optical etendue, transmission, filter-shape, window-loss, and collection-geometry calibration. The related [flux_at_spectral_line](name:spectral_flux_of_spectrometer_channel) is an uncalibrated photon flux integrated over a spectral line and should not be interpreted as an absolutely calibrated radiance or photon rate unless those calibrations have been applied.

Typical raw signals at the digitizer input range from 0.0001-10 V, with dark or bias offsets commonly 0.0001-0.1 V. Saturation is often set by detector electronics or digitizer limits, commonly near 1-10 V or by bipolar input ranges such as -10-10 V.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the spectrometer signal output terminal is at a higher electric potential than its reference terminal.

NAMES.name: requested_voltage_of_spectrometer
NAMES.short: Commanded setpoint voltage for a spectrometer high-voltage supply, giving the intended detector or electrode bias relative to the supply return/reference terminal rather than a measured signal output.
NAMES.long:
The requested voltage of a spectrometer is the commanded electrical potential difference for a spectrometer high-voltage supply. It represents the intended bias applied to a detector, multiplier, photocathode, anode, or other controlled electrode relative to the designated return/reference terminal.

When interpreted as an ideal voltage setpoint, the quantity is defined by the commanded potential difference:

$$
V_\mathrm{req} = \Phi_\mathrm{out,set} - \Phi_\mathrm{ref}
$$

where $\Phi_\mathrm{out,set}$ is the commanded electric potential of the controlled high-voltage output terminal or biased electrode, and $\Phi_\mathrm{ref}$ is the electric potential of the supply return/reference terminal.

The value is usually generated from an operator setting, diagnostic configuration, or automated scan used to control detector gain, charge collection, or particle/electron multiplication. It should be distinguished from a measured high-voltage supply readback, if one is available, and from voltage_of_spectrometer_channel, which denotes an uncalibrated electrical output signal from a spectrometer channel rather than the high-voltage supply setpoint.

Typical requested values range from 0-5000 V in magnitude, depending on detector technology and operating mode. Photomultiplier, microchannel-plate, and electron-multiplier systems commonly use 500-3000 V in magnitude; low-voltage bias or gating electrodes may use 10-200 V.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the commanded high-voltage output terminal or biased electrode is at a higher electric potential than its designated return/reference terminal.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Raw electrical output voltage from one spectrometer detector channel, measured relative to its electronics reference or baseline before radiometric calibration. It represents detector and front-end response in that spectral channel rather than a calibrated radiance, irradiance, photon flux, or optical power.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a spectrometer channel is the electrical potential difference produced by one detector channel and its readout electronics for a selected spectral channel or wavelength band. It is an uncalibrated detector signal and may include effects of detector responsivity, electronic gain, dark current, offsets, integration time, and bandwidth.

The channel voltage is defined relative to the applicable electronics reference or baseline:

$$
V_\mathrm{ch} = V_\mathrm{out,ch} - V_\mathrm{ref,ch}
$$

where $V_\mathrm{out,ch}$ is the detector-channel output potential and $V_\mathrm{ref,ch}$ is the channel reference potential, zero-light baseline, dark baseline, or digitizer reference used for that measurement.

In practice this voltage is measured by the detector front end, such as a photodiode, photomultiplier, avalanche photodiode, or camera readout channel followed by amplification and digitization. Conversion to radiometric quantities requires separate calibration for spectral response, optical throughput, detector gain, integration time, and any dark or background correction.

Typical unsaturated analog channel voltages range from 0.001-10 V, depending on detector type, amplifier gain, light level, and digitizer range. Baseline offsets are often 0.0001-0.1 V, while values near the acquisition limits, commonly 1-10 V, may indicate saturation or clipping rather than increased optical signal.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the channel output potential is higher than its electronics reference or baseline.

NAMES.name: width_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Full transverse width of a rectangular diagnostic aperture along X1 in its local aperture frame (X1, X2, X3), where X1 and X2 span the opening and X3 is normal to it. It defines one clear-opening dimension for line-of-sight collimation, aperture area, and étendue calculations.
NAMES.long:
Width of a diagnostic aperture is the full clear opening of a rectangular aperture measured along the $X_1$ direction of a local Cartesian aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$. The $X_1$ and $X_2$ axes span the aperture plane, while $X_3$ is normal to the aperture or aligned with the nominal line of sight. It is one of the two transverse dimensions that determine the finite acceptance of a collimating opening.

For an ideal rectangular opening, the clear aperture area is the product of the two transverse widths:

$$
A = w_1 w_2
$$

where $A$ is the open area in m$^2$, $w_1$ is this width along $X_1$ in m, and $w_2$ is the companion orthogonal width along $X_2$ in m. The geometric étendue for small-angle uniform acceptance scales approximately as $A\Omega$, where $\Omega$ is the accepted solid angle.

In practice, the width is taken from mechanical design models, engineering drawings, or as-built metrology at the limiting clear aperture, excluding masks, supports, bevels, or other structures that do not transmit the line of sight. The physical concept is the diagnostic counterpart of width_of_aperture, which describes the same full transverse opening dimension for non-diagnostic collimators. The orthogonal $X_2$ aperture width supplies the second rectangular dimension; [radius_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) is the corresponding size parameter for circular diagnostic openings, while [filter_window_width](name:filter_window_width) describes a transmitting window rather than the collimating aperture itself.

Typical values range from $1 \times 10^{-4}$-$5 \times 10^{-2}$ m. Fiber entrances and pinholes are often $1 \times 10^{-4}$-$2 \times 10^{-3}$ m, bolometer slits and small optical apertures are commonly $10^{-3}$-$10^{-2}$ m, and neutron or gamma-ray collimating apertures may reach several $10^{-2}$ m.

NAMES.name: width_of_filter
NAMES.short: Full wavelength extent of a diagnostic filter transmission passband, expressed as a positive scalar span between two defined passband-edge wavelengths.
NAMES.long:
Width of filter is the positive scalar extent of the wavelength interval transmitted by a diagnostic filter according to a specified passband-edge criterion. It abstracts the spectral passband span represented more specifically by [spectral width of filter](name:spectral_width_of_filter).

For a passband bounded by lower and upper edge wavelengths, the width is

$$
\Delta \lambda = \lambda_2 - \lambda_1
$$

where $\lambda_1 < \lambda_2$ are the two wavelengths defining the passband edges. The edge criterion may be a specified fraction of the peak transmission, such as the 90% level used for [spectral width of filter](name:spectral_width_of_filter).

In practice the width is obtained from a measured or manufacturer-specified filter transmission curve by locating the two wavelengths that satisfy the chosen edge criterion and taking their separation. It is used to characterize spectral selectivity, photon throughput, and the wavelength range contributing to a radiation measurement.

Typical values depend strongly on filter type and diagnostic band: narrow interference filters may have widths of 1e-10-1e-8 m, while broader optical or X-ray bandpass filters can have widths of 1e-8-1e-6 m.

NAMES.name: spectral_width_of_filter
NAMES.short: Full wavelength extent of the spectral passband of a diagnostic optical filter, measured between the pair of wavelengths at which the filter transmission falls to 90% of its peak value.
NAMES.long:
The spectral width of a diagnostic optical filter quantifies the range of wavelengths the filter transmits, defined as the wavelength interval between the long- and short-wavelength points at which transmission equals 90% of its peak value. This 90%-transmission convention provides a conservative estimate of the effective passband and distinguishes the quantity from a full-width-at-half-maximum measure. A narrower spectral width improves rejection of background continuum and neighboring spectral lines, while a broader passband increases photon throughput for faint emission features.

The passband full width at the 90%-transmission level is

$$
\Delta\lambda_{90} = \lambda_+ - \lambda_-
$$

where $\lambda_+$ is the long-wavelength 90%-transmission edge, reported independently as [upper_wavelength_of_filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), and $\lambda_-$ is the corresponding short-wavelength edge, reported as [lower_wavelength_of_filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter).

The spectral width is determined by calibrated laboratory transmission measurements using a monochromator, or taken directly from manufacturer filter specifications. It is conceptually distinct from the physical aperture dimension described by [width_of_filter](name:width_of_filter), which characterizes the geometric extent of the filter window rather than its wavelength selectivity.

Typical spectral widths range from less than 1 nm for narrow-line filters isolating specific plasma emission lines to several tens of nanometers for broadband infrared filters used in thermal imaging of plasma-facing components.

NAMES.name: width_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Full physical width of a hard X-ray detector aperture measured along the local X1 direction of the detector frame (X1, X2, X3). It is one rectangular-aperture dimension used with the orthogonal height.
NAMES.long:
Width of a hard X-ray detector is the full clear aperture extent along the local detector-frame axis $\hat{X}_1$ in the detector frame $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2, \hat{X}_3)$. Together with the orthogonal height along $\hat{X}_2$, it defines the rectangular detector opening used in geometric acceptance calculations. As a length, it is a non-negative scalar and does not encode the orientation sign of the local axis.

For two small, planar, mutually visible rectangular apertures separated in free space, the detector width enters the usual small-aperture etendue approximation through the detector area:

$$
G \simeq \frac{(w_\mathrm{det} h_\mathrm{det})(w_\mathrm{ap} h_\mathrm{ap})}{L^2}\cos\alpha_\mathrm{det}\cos\alpha_\mathrm{ap}
$$

where $G$ is the geometric etendue in m$^2$ sr, $w_\mathrm{det}$ is this detector width in m, $h_\mathrm{det}$ is the detector height in m, $w_\mathrm{ap}$ and $h_\mathrm{ap}$ are the corresponding opposing-aperture dimensions in m, $L$ is the center-to-center separation in m, and $\alpha_\mathrm{det}$ and $\alpha_\mathrm{ap}$ are the angles between each aperture normal and the connecting ray in radians. The approximation assumes aperture dimensions are small compared with $L$, the apertures are approximately planar, the centers and normals are sufficiently aligned that one representative separation and angle can be used, and vignetting or other obstructions are negligible.

In practice the value is taken from the mechanical design, metrology, or detector calibration geometry as the distance between the clear inner aperture edges projected onto $\hat{X}_1$. If edge chamfers, masks, or partial obstructions are present, the relevant value is the effective clear width used by the line-of-sight or acceptance model.

Typical hard-X-ray detector aperture widths are 0.001-0.05 m, with millimeter-scale values common for tightly collimated channels and centimeter-scale values used for larger scintillator or camera openings.

NAMES.name: width_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Full non-negative spatial extent of a rectangular optical element aperture along the X1 axis of its right-handed local optical-element frame (X1, X2, X3), where X3 is normal to the aperture plane. It defines one transverse dimension of the optical acceptance geometry.
NAMES.long:
Width of an optical element is the full geometric extent of a rectangular aperture along the $X_1$ direction in a right-handed local optical-element frame $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$. The $X_3$ axis is normal to the aperture plane, while $X_1$ and $X_2$ span the transverse opening.

For a rectangular aperture, the width is the difference between the upper and lower aperture limits along $X_1$:

$$
W = X_{1,\max} - X_{1,\min}
$$

where $W$ is the width, and $X_{1,\max}$ and $X_{1,\min}$ are the maximum and minimum coordinates of the open aperture along $X_1$, all in meters. The limits are ordered so that $W \ge 0$; zero represents a closed or degenerate aperture in this direction.

In practice, this quantity is obtained from mechanical design dimensions, optical metrology, or calibration of the limiting aperture or collimator. Together with the corresponding height $h$ along $X_2$ and an accepted solid angle $\Omega$, it contributes to the optical etendue, for example $G \approx W h \Omega$ for a uniformly illuminated rectangular aperture, where $W$ and $h$ are in meters, $\Omega$ is in sr, and $G$ is in m$^2$ sr.

Typical values range from 0.001-0.1 m, with smaller values for pinholes, narrow slits, or highly collimated systems and larger values for camera or spectrometer collection optics.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: X1 coordinate of a Bragg-crystal outline vertex, measured along the first axis of the crystal-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame. Together with the corresponding X2 coordinate, it defines the crystal cross-section boundary used in diffraction geometry.
NAMES.long:
The $x_1$ coordinate of a Bragg crystal is the signed scalar position of an outline vertex along the first axis of the crystal-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. Paired with the corresponding [x2 coordinate of a Bragg crystal](name:x2_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal), it identifies one vertex of the crystal cross-section boundary; consecutive paired vertices define the ordered polygonal outline of the crystal aperture.

For a vertex with position vector $\mathbf{r}$ in the crystal-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame, the coordinate is the projection of the displacement from the local origin onto the positive $X_1$ axis:

$$
x_1 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{X_1}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the local-frame origin and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{X_1}$ is the unit vector along the positive $X_1$ direction.

Crystal outline coordinates are usually obtained from mechanical design drawings, manufacturer specifications, or optical and coordinate-measuring metrology of the mounted crystal. The outline specifies the physical aperture and illuminated crystal extent in ray tracing or spectrometer geometry models, but it does not by itself determine whether the Bragg condition is satisfied; diffraction also depends on lattice spacing, incidence angle, diffraction order, and X-ray wavelength.

Typical coordinate magnitudes for Bragg-crystal spectrometers range from 0.001-0.10 m, with millimeter-scale values for small crystals and centimeter-scale values for larger analyzer crystals or extended mounts.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the local origin has a component along the positive $X_1$ axis of the crystal-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_filter
NAMES.short: X1 coordinate of a vertex or sampled point on a diagnostic filter boundary in the local planar (X1, X2) frame. It gives the projection of that boundary point along the first in-plane basis direction and is distinct from quantities that specifically name a separate filter-window component.
NAMES.long:
The $x_1$ coordinate of a filter is the signed in-plane position of a point on the boundary of the filtering element or its transmissive footprint, expressed in a local planar $(X_1, X_2)$ frame with basis $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$. It describes the filter boundary itself; [x1_coordinate_of_filter_window](name:x1_coordinate_of_filter_window) should be used when the intended object is a separately identified filter-window component.

For a boundary point at position $\mathbf{r}_v$ and a filter-frame origin at $\mathbf{r}_0$, the coordinate is the projection onto the first local basis direction:

$$
x_1 = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{X}_1
$$

where $\hat{X}_1$ is the first in-plane unit vector of the local planar $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. The origin is normally a defined reference point of the filter plane, such as a geometric center or mechanical fiducial, while $\hat{X}_1$ and $\hat{X}_2$ span the plane and are fixed by the diagnostic mechanical definition or calibration fiducials.

The coordinate is obtained from mechanical drawings, CAD geometry, survey metrology, or calibration of the filter aperture used in the X-ray diagnostic line of sight. Together with the corresponding [x2_coordinate_of_filter](name:x2_coordinate_of_filter), it defines a polygonal or sampled boundary used to compute geometric transmission, vignetting, and ray intersections through the filter.

Typical absolute coordinate excursions are about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ m for compact soft-X-ray filter apertures and can reach a few $10^{-2}$ m for larger spectrometer filter openings.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the boundary point lies in the $+\hat{X}_1$ direction from the origin of the local planar $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short: First-axis position of a filter-window outline vertex in the local (X1, X2) frame, specifying the aperture boundary geometry of an X-ray diagnostic filter.
NAMES.long:
The $X_1$ coordinate of a filter-window outline vertex is the signed displacement of that vertex along the first axis of the local planar $(X_1, X_2)$ frame of the filter window. Together with the corresponding $X_2$ coordinate, it specifies a point on the polygonal or piecewise-linear boundary of the filter aperture.
