For a vertex at position $\mathbf{r}$ in the filter plane relative to a local origin $\mathbf{r}_0$, the coordinate is the projection onto the first local basis direction:

$$
X_1 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{X_1}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{X_1}$ is the unit vector along the first axis of the local planar $(X_1, X_2)$ frame and $X_1$ is measured in meters.

The coordinate is usually determined from the mechanical design, metrology, or diagnostic geometry model of the filter assembly. The ordered set of vertices defined by paired $X_1$ and $X_2$ coordinates describes the clear aperture boundary that limits transmitted X-ray radiation.

Typical values are set by the physical size of the filter window: small pinhole or slit-like apertures may have vertex coordinates of about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ m, while larger camera filter windows commonly span about $10^{-2}$-$10^{-1}$ m from the local origin.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the local origin is in the $+X_1$ direction of the local planar $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: X1 coordinate of an optical element's outline vertices or fiber-center positions in the element-local two-dimensional Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
The X1 coordinate locates a point — such as an aperture outline vertex, a detector-face boundary vertex, or an optical fiber center — along the first axis of the element-local two-dimensional Cartesian (X1, X2) frame. This local frame is defined independently for each optical element, with its origin placed at a reference feature of the component (for example, a grating summit, a detector center, or a fiber bundle centroid) and its axes aligned with the element's principal directions.

Together with the companion X2 coordinate, the (X1, X2) pair describes the planar geometry of optical elements such as aperture boundaries, detector active areas, grating outlines, or fiber spatial layouts. Closed polygons formed from ordered (X1, X2) vertex pairs define the collimating or sensitive area used in etendue calculations and line-of-sight reconstruction. Analogous coordinates for other diagnostic components follow the same convention: [x1_coordinate_of_aperture](name:x1_coordinate_of_aperture) and [x1_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x1_coordinate_of_filter) describe collimating aperture outlines, while [x1_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector](name:x1_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector) covers detector-face vertices.

Typical values span the physical dimensions of the optical element, ranging from fractions of a millimeter for individual optical fiber cores to several centimeters for large detector faces or diffraction grating surfaces.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point lies in the positive X1 direction from the origin of the element-local (X1, X2) coordinate frame.

NAMES.name: x1_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: X1 coordinate of the soft X-ray detector outline vertices in the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame, used to define the polygonal detector boundary for etendue and line-of-sight calculations.
NAMES.long:
The X1 coordinate specifies the position of each vertex of the soft X-ray detector's polygonal outline along the first axis of the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame. Together with the companion [X2 coordinate](name:x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector), these vertex coordinates fully define the cross-sectional shape of the detector aperture. The complete outline is required to compute the etendue — the geometric throughput governing the detector's luminous acceptance — and to trace the lines of sight that determine what fraction of plasma soft X-ray emission reaches the channel.

For a polygonal detector with $N$ vertices, the outline is the ordered sequence of $(X1_i,\,X2_i)$ pairs for $i = 1,\ldots,N$, with the polygon closed by returning to the first vertex. The detector-local (X1, X2) axes are attached to the detector face; their orientation relative to the machine cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is defined by the detector's mounting geometry. Typical soft X-ray detector face dimensions range from a few millimeters to several centimeters. The analogous first-axis coordinate for a neutron detector is [x1_coordinate_of_neutron_detector](name:x1_coordinate_of_neutron_detector).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex is displaced in the positive X1 direction from the origin of the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate along the X2 axis of a Bragg-crystal outline vertex in the crystal-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame, parameterizing the cross-sectional boundary of the crystal element in an X-ray crystal spectrometer.
NAMES.long:
The X2 coordinate labels each vertex of the Bragg crystal's cross-sectional outline in the crystal-local Cartesian (X1, X2) plane, where X1 and X2 span the nominal crystal aperture surface and the X2 axis is the second transverse direction. A sequence of such vertices, paired with the corresponding [x1_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal](name:x1_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal) values, fully parameterizes the closed irregular boundary of the crystal element used for Bragg diffraction in an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel.

The outline geometry defines the active diffracting area and enters into calculations of the solid angle subtended by the crystal from the X-ray source, directly influencing photon collection efficiency. For rectangular crystals, the full width along the X1 axis is also captured by [bragg_crystal_width](name:bragg_crystal_width), while the angular acceptance from the source is characterized by [angular_width_of_bragg_crystal](name:angular_width_of_bragg_crystal).

Crystal outline coordinates are specified from engineering drawings or coordinate metrology of the spectrometer assembly and represent fixed hardware geometry. The same (X1, X2) local-frame convention is applied consistently across spectrometer components, as in [x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture) and [x2_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector](name:x2_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex lies in the positive X2 direction of the crystal-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: X2 coordinate of a diagnostic aperture outline vertex in the local aperture-plane (X1, X2) frame. Together with the X1 coordinate, it defines the transverse boundary used in sight-line, acceptance, and etendue geometry.
NAMES.long:
The $x_2$ coordinate of a diagnostic aperture is the signed position of an outline vertex along the second axis of the local aperture-plane $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. Paired with the corresponding $x_1$ coordinate, it specifies the transverse polygon or curved boundary that limits the rays accepted by an aperture, fiber entrance, detector face, or similar diagnostic opening.

For a polygonal aperture outline, the paired vertex coordinates determine the enclosed geometric area through the shoelace relation:

$$
A = \frac{1}{2}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(x_{1,i}x_{2,i+1} - x_{1,i+1}x_{2,i}\right)\right|
$$

where $N$ is the number of outline vertices, cyclic indexing is used so vertex $N+1$ is vertex $1$, and $x_{1,i}$ and $x_{2,i}$ are measured in meters. The resulting area $A$ is in square meters and is one input to aperture acceptance and etendue calculations.

In practice, $x_2$ values are obtained from mechanical drawings, optical design models, metrology of aperture plates or fiber bundles, or calibration of detector geometry. The coordinate is interpreted only relative to the local aperture-plane $(X_1, X_2)$ frame, whose origin and axis directions are defined by the diagnostic geometry.

Typical magnitudes range from $10^{-5}$-$10^{-1}$ m, from tens of micrometers for small fiber cores to millimeters or centimeters for pinholes, slits, detector faces, and camera apertures.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex is displaced in the $+X_2$ direction of the local aperture-plane $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_filter
NAMES.short: X2 coordinate of filter window outline vertices in the local orthogonal (X1, X2) plane frame, giving the second-axis positions that jointly define the filter aperture boundary shape.
NAMES.long:
The filter aperture boundary is represented as a closed polygon of vertices whose positions are specified in a local orthogonal 2D coordinate system $(X_1, X_2)$ attached to the filter element. The X2 coordinate provides the second-axis component of each boundary vertex, and together with [x1_coordinate_of_filter](name:x1_coordinate_of_filter), fully defines the transverse cross-sectional outline of the filter window. This planar boundary geometry is used to compute the étendue, solid angle, and angular acceptance of the associated X-ray diagnostic channel.

The local $(X_1, X_2)$ frame is defined in the plane of the filter element; both axes form a right-handed orthogonal pair with the origin fixed to the filter element mounting reference. Filter windows in X-ray diagnostics span dimensions from roughly 0.001–0.05 m, so outline vertex coordinates lie within that range of the local frame origin. The identical coordinate convention governs the aperture outline described by [x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture), while the closely related [x2_coordinate_of_filter_window](name:x2_coordinate_of_filter_window) applies the same scheme to a more narrowly scoped filter-window object.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex position lies in the positive $X_2$ direction from the local frame origin.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short: X2 coordinate of the filter window outline vertices in the local (X1, X2) frame, jointly defining the aperture boundary shape with the paired X1 vertex positions.
NAMES.long:
The X2 coordinate gives the positions of the filter window outline vertices along the second axis of the local two-dimensional $(X_1, X_2)$ coordinate frame attached to the filter window assembly. Together with the [X1 coordinate](name:x1_coordinate_of_filter_window), these vertex positions jointly specify the full irregular polygonal boundary of the filter aperture.

The outline is constructed from a set of $N$ vertex pairs $(x_{1,i},\, x_{2,i})$, $i = 1, \ldots, N$, connected sequentially to close the boundary polygon:

$$
\partial A = \{(x_{1,i},\, x_{2,i}) : i = 1, \ldots, N\}
$$

where each $(x_{1,i}, x_{2,i})$ is a vertex of the closed outline and $\partial A$ denotes the filter aperture boundary. This representation applies when the window shape is described as an irregular polygon; simpler geometries such as rectangles or circles may instead be parameterized by scalar width or radius descriptors.

The filter window geometry is characterized during instrument fabrication or calibration by direct dimensional measurement of the filter frame. For X-ray cameras and crystal spectrometers, the precise aperture shape determines the acceptance solid angle and enters etendue calculations that link measured count rates to source brightness, making accurate vertex coordinates essential for absolute photometric calibration. The analogous role for collimating apertures is served by [x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline vertex lies in the positive $X_2$ direction from the local coordinate origin of the filter window frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of a hard X-ray detector outline vertex along the X2 axis in the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
The X2 coordinate of a hard X-ray detector is the signed position of a detector-outline vertex along the second axis of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. Together with the companion x1_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector, it defines the detector outline in the local plane; the value is relative to the detector-local origin and axis orientation, not to an absolute machine position.

For a vertex displacement from the detector-local origin, the coordinate is the scalar projection onto the local X2 direction:

$$
x_2 = \Delta \mathbf{r}_v \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2
$$

where $x_2$ is the X2 coordinate in meters, $\Delta \mathbf{r}_v$ is the vector from the detector-local origin to the vertex in meters, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the positive X2 axis of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

In practice, X2 vertex coordinates are obtained from the detector mechanical design, survey information, or geometry model. Paired with X1 coordinates, they specify the polygonal detector outline used in geometric area, etendue, and sight-line acceptance calculations. The same local-outline concept is used for related diagnostic aperture and detector coordinates such as [x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture) and [x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector](name:x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector).

Typical magnitudes are set by the physical detector face and the chosen local origin. Compact hard-X-ray detector outlines are often millimeter-to-centimeter scale, with representative coordinate magnitudes around 0.001-0.1 m; exact values are device-specific and may be positive or negative within the local outline.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the detector-local origin has a component in the positive X2 direction of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Coordinate of a point on an optical element measured along the second axis of the element's local planar (X1, X2) frame. It is the signed in-plane displacement from the local origin resolved on the X2 basis direction.
NAMES.long:
The x2 coordinate of an optical element is the signed distance, within the element's local plane, from the element's local origin to a specified point resolved along the second local in-plane axis. The coordinate is defined in a local planar $(X_1,X_2)$ frame with origin $O$ and basis $(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2)$ attached to the optical element, rather than in a global laboratory frame.

For an orthonormal local planar basis, the coordinate is the projection of the point displacement onto the second basis direction:

$$
x_2 = (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_O) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{X}}_2
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of the point, $\mathbf{r}_O$ is the position vector of the local origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2$ is the unit vector along the local $X_2$ axis.

In practice, this coordinate is obtained from mechanical drawings, optical metrology, or calibration fits by expressing measured point positions in the element's local planar $(X_1,X_2)$ frame. The same definition applies whether the point represents a fiber center, an aperture-outline vertex, a detector-face point, or another geometrical feature of an optical component.

There is no universal physical range because the value is set by the transverse size of the particular optical element and by the chosen local origin. Meaningful values normally lie within the element's active or mechanical aperture; compact diagnostic optics may have absolute coordinates of order $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}$ m, while larger optical elements can extend beyond this range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the displacement from the local origin to the point has a component in the $+\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2$ direction of the optical element's local planar $(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2)$ basis.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate along the X2 axis of a vertex on the soft X-ray detector boundary in the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame. Together with the X1 coordinate, it defines the detector boundary used for line-of-sight acceptance and etendue calculations, distinct from any diagnostic aperture.
NAMES.long:
The $x_2$ coordinate of a soft X-ray detector is the signed in-plane position of a point on the detector boundary in the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame with orthonormal basis $(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_1, \hat{\mathbf{X}}_2)$. Together with the [soft-X-ray detector $x_1$ coordinate](name:x1_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector), it specifies the detector boundary; this detector surface is distinct from the diagnostic aperture boundary described, for example, by the [diagnostic-aperture $x_2$ coordinate](name:x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture).

The coordinate is the scalar projection of the detector-boundary point relative to the detector-local origin onto the local $X_2$ direction:

$$
x_2 = (\mathbf{r}_d - \mathbf{r}_{d,0}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{X}}_2
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_d$ is the detector-boundary point position vector in m, $\mathbf{r}_{d,0}$ is the detector-local origin position vector in m, and $\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2$ is a dimensionless unit vector.

Detector boundary coordinates are obtained from mechanical design, survey metrology, CAD models, or alignment calibration of the diagnostic head. In ray tracing and etendue calculations, the detector boundary defines the detector integration surface $A_d$, while the diagnostic aperture defines a separate aperture integration surface $A_a$; a common geometric etendue relation is $G = \int_{A_d}\int_{A_a} \cos\alpha_d\cos\alpha_a\, |\mathbf{r}_d-\mathbf{r}_a|^{-2}\, dA_d\, dA_a$, where $\mathbf{r}_d$ and $\mathbf{r}_a$ are detector and aperture surface-point position vectors in m, $dA_d$ and $dA_a$ are differential surface elements in m^2, and the cosine factors are dimensionless projections onto the two surface normals.

Typical signed coordinate values are about -0.01-0.01 m for compact diode or chip-scale soft X-ray detector elements and can extend to about -0.05-0.05 m for larger detector assemblies, depending on the chosen detector-local origin.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector-boundary point is displaced in the $+\hat{\mathbf{X}}_2$ direction of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Translational kinetic temperature of the low-energy neutral atom component, represented by the narrow Doppler-broadened contribution to visible spectral emission. It characterizes the cold population separately from hotter charge-exchange or beam-related neutrals.
NAMES.long:
Cold neutral temperature is the translational kinetic temperature of the low-energy neutral atom population contributing to an observed emission line. In two-component Doppler models it corresponds to the narrow Gaussian component, while the broad component is associated with hotter neutrals described by [hot_neutral_temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature). It is a component-resolved quantity and is distinct from a state- or population-averaged [neutral_state_temperature](name:neutral_state_temperature).

For a non-relativistic Maxwellian neutral distribution with isotropic velocity spread along the line of sight, the Doppler full width at half maximum of a spectral line is related to the cold neutral temperature by:

$$
T_\mathrm{cold} = \frac{m c^2}{8 \ln 2\, e}\left(\frac{\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{D,FWHM}}{\lambda_0}\right)^2
$$

where $m$ is the neutral atom mass, $c$ is the speed of light, $e$ is the elementary charge, $\lambda_0$ is the rest wavelength, and $\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{D,FWHM}$ is the Doppler contribution to the fitted narrow-line full width after other broadening mechanisms have been accounted for. The result is expressed in eV.

In practice this quantity is inferred by fitting visible emission-line shapes with one or more components. Instrumental resolution, fine-structure effects, Zeeman or Stark broadening, and line blending must be modeled or deconvolved so that the remaining narrow width represents neutral thermal motion. If the neutral distribution is non-Maxwellian, strongly anisotropic, or sufficiently energetic for relativistic corrections to matter, the fitted value should be interpreted as an effective cold-component temperature rather than a true thermodynamic temperature.

Typical cold neutral temperatures in edge and divertor spectroscopy are of order 0.1-10 eV, depending on recycling conditions, isotope mass, ionization mean free path, and local coupling to the plasma. Values much smaller than the associated [hot_neutral_temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature) indicate a clear separation between recycled thermal neutrals and hotter charge-exchange or beam-related populations.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight projected velocity of the cold neutral atom population inferred from an emission-line Doppler shift.
NAMES.long:
Cold neutral velocity is the scalar projection of the mean velocity of the cold neutral atom population along a specified spectrometer line of sight. The cold component is the relatively narrow, low-energy neutral emission component, complementary to [hot_neutral_velocity](name:hot_neutral_velocity), with the corresponding thermal width characterized by [cold_neutral_temperature](name:cold_neutral_temperature).

For nonrelativistic Doppler shifts, the line-of-sight velocity is determined from the signed centroid shift of the cold spectral component:

$$
v_\mathrm{los} = c\,\frac{\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{los}}{\lambda_0}
$$

where $v_\mathrm{los}$ is the line-of-sight velocity in m.s^-1, $\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{los}$ is the signed wavelength shift in meters after applying the line-of-sight orientation convention, $\lambda_0$ is the rest or central [wavelength_of_spectral_line](name:wavelength_of_spectral_line) in meters, and $c$ is the speed of light in m.s^-1. With this definition, $\Delta\lambda_\mathrm{los}>0$ corresponds to motion from the first line-of-sight point toward the second; depending on viewing geometry, this may correspond to either the measured redshift or its negative.

In practice this quantity is obtained from the calibrated centroid of the cold component of an atomic emission line. Spectral modeling separates this centroid shift from instrumental calibration offsets, line blending, thermal broadening, and any broader hot-neutral contribution; the result is only the velocity component projected along the observed line of sight, not the full neutral flow vector.

Typical magnitudes in edge and divertor neutral spectroscopy are of order 1,000-30,000 m.s^-1, with signed values near zero possible when the neutral flow is weak or nearly perpendicular to the line of sight.
NAMES.sign: Positive when cold neutral atoms move from the first defining point of the line of sight toward the second defining point.

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Kinetic temperature of the energetic (hot) component of the neutral atom population, inferred from the broad Doppler profile of visible spectral line emission.
NAMES.long:
The hot neutral temperature characterizes the energetic component of the neutral atom population in the plasma edge and scrape-off layer, distinguished from the thermal bulk described by [cold_neutral_temperature](name:cold_neutral_temperature). Hot neutrals arise primarily from charge exchange reactions between thermal ions and cold neutrals, or from energetic recycling at plasma-facing surfaces, producing a fast atom population carrying significantly more kinetic energy than the bulk.

The temperature is inferred by fitting the observed spectral emission line profile to a two-Gaussian model. The broad Gaussian component corresponds to the hot neutral sub-population, with its half-width governed by the Doppler broadening relation:

$$
\Delta\lambda_D = \frac{\lambda_0}{c}\sqrt{\frac{8\ln 2 \, k_B T_{\rm hot}}{m_n}}
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is the rest-frame line center wavelength of the emission transition, $c$ is the speed of light, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T_{\rm hot}$ is the hot neutral temperature, and $m_n$ is the neutral atom mass.

Measurements are obtained from visible spectrometer channels recording hydrogen isotope Balmer series emission, where spectral line fitting resolves the hot and cold sub-populations simultaneously. Polarization spectroscopy channels provide access to both the temperature and the line-of-sight Doppler shift, the latter captured in [hot_neutral_velocity](name:hot_neutral_velocity).

Typical values for the hot component span a few eV to approximately 50 eV in edge and scrape-off layer plasmas, substantially above the cold bulk neutral temperature of approximately 0.1–1 eV, and bounded above by the local ion temperature.

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight projected velocity of the energetic (hot) neutral atom population, inferred from the Doppler centroid shift of the broad emission component in visible polarization spectroscopy.
NAMES.long:
The hot neutral population consists of energetic neutral atoms — produced primarily by charge-exchange reactions between fast ions and cold neutrals or by beam-neutral interactions — whose velocity distribution yields a broad Doppler profile overlaid on the narrower thermal (cold) component. The line-of-sight component $v_\mathrm{hot}$ represents the bulk flow of this energetic neutral ensemble along the diagnostic chord, distinguishing it from [cold_neutral_velocity](name:cold_neutral_velocity) for the thermal population; the associated kinetic spread is captured by [hot_neutral_temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature).

The centroid velocity is extracted from the observed wavelength shift of the emission line:

$$
v_\mathrm{hot} = c \, \frac{\lambda_\mathrm{obs} - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0}
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light, $\lambda_\mathrm{obs}$ is the centroid wavelength of the hot neutral spectral component, and $\lambda_0$ is the rest wavelength of the observed line.

Measurement requires fitting the observed line profile from a visible polarization spectrometer with a multi-Gaussian model that separates the broad hot and narrow cold neutral contributions; the centroid shift of the broad component yields $v_\mathrm{hot}$. Hot neutrals sourced from fast-ion charge exchange carry line-of-sight velocities spanning tens to hundreds of km/s, substantially exceeding those of cold recycled neutrals.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the hot neutral atoms are moving from the first to the second point along the line of sight.

NAMES.name: neon_fraction
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Neon fraction is the ratio of the volume-averaged total neon particle density, summed over all ionization states, to the volume-averaged electron density. It is dimensionless and represents the plasma-wide neon concentration relative to electrons.
NAMES.long:
Neon fraction is a dimensionless impurity concentration measuring how much neon is present in the plasma relative to electrons. The neon density includes neutral and ionized neon populations summed over all charge states before the plasma-volume average is formed.

The volume-averaged neon fraction is defined by

$$
f_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \frac{\left\langle \sum_{q=0}^{10} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}} \right\rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}$ is the number density of neon in charge state $q$ in m^-3, $n_e$ is the electron density in m^-3, and $\langle \cdot \rangle_V = V^{-1}\int_V (\cdot)\,dV$ denotes a plasma-volume average over volume $V$. The numerator is the [volume-averaged neon density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density), and the denominator is the volume-averaged electron density.

In practice, neon fraction is inferred from plasma composition analysis using impurity spectroscopy, radiation measurements, charge-state balance modeling, and electron-density information. It should be interpreted as a global composition measure, not as a local impurity abundance at a particular radius or viewing chord.

Typical values are much less than unity. Background neon levels in plasmas without deliberate neon injection are often below $10^{-4}$-$10^{-3}$, while neon-seeded radiating plasmas can reach about $10^{-3}$-$10^{-2}$ depending on fueling, confinement, and exhaust conditions.

NAMES.name: neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Dimensionless fraction of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population component (cold recycled or hot charge-exchange neutrals) relative to the total neutral atom population.
NAMES.long:
The neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$ expressing the relative abundance of a defined component of the hydrogen-isotope neutral population. In the standard two-component neutral model, cold recycled neutrals and charge-exchange-born hot neutrals partition the neutral atom inventory, and their respective fractions sum to unity.

The fraction for a given component is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{component}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{component}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{component}}$ is the number density of the specified neutral component and $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$, $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ are the cold and hot neutral number densities respectively.

The component fractions are inferred from Doppler-broadening analysis of visible hydrogen-isotope spectral emission lines, in which the cold and hot neutral populations contribute distinct narrow and broad Gaussian components to the line shape. The [cold_neutral_fraction](name:cold_neutral_fraction) characterizes the low-energy recycled neutral component, while [hot_neutral_fraction](name:hot_neutral_fraction) gives the charge-exchange-born component; together they form a complete partition of the neutral population. The energy threshold separating the two components must be specified by the diagnostic or population model employed.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified neutral component density is greater than zero.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Cold neutral fraction is the dimensionless fraction of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population assigned to the low-energy neutral component. It is defined relative to the cold and hot neutral components used in the analysis; the cold/hot boundary must be specified by the diagnostic or population model.
NAMES.long:
The cold neutral fraction is the population fraction of neutral atoms of a specified hydrogen isotope that are classified as cold, meaning lower in kinetic energy than the corresponding hot neutral component. The classification boundary between cold and hot neutrals is not universal; it is set by the diagnostic interpretation, spectral decomposition, or population model used for the isotope being analyzed.

For a two-component cold/hot decomposition, the cold neutral fraction is

$$
f_\mathrm{cold} = \frac{n_\mathrm{cold}}{n_\mathrm{cold} + n_\mathrm{hot}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{cold}$ and $n_\mathrm{hot}$ are the cold and hot neutral number densities for the same isotope, typically in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$. For nonnegative densities this gives $0 \le f_\mathrm{cold} \le 1$. If additional neutral populations are treated separately or excluded from the decomposition, the fraction applies only to the cold-plus-hot population used in the denominator.

In visible spectroscopy, this fraction is commonly inferred by separating emission associated with low-energy recycled or thermal neutrals from emission associated with higher-energy neutrals, using line shapes, Doppler broadening, line ratios, and collisional-radiative modeling. The inferred value depends on the adopted cold/hot energy threshold and on corrections for atomic physics rates, viewing geometry, and instrument response.

Typical values can span the full range 0-1. Values near 1 indicate that the represented neutral population is dominated by low-energy recycled or thermal neutrals, while values near 0 indicate dominance by the hot neutral component, for example from energetic charge-exchange populations or beam-related neutrals.

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Fraction of charge-exchange-born hot neutral atoms in the total neutral population of a hydrogen isotope, assuming a two-component hot-plus-cold neutral partition. It is the hot neutral density divided by the sum of hot and cold neutral densities.
NAMES.long:
Hot neutral fraction is the dimensionless abundance of fast neutral atoms produced mainly by charge exchange relative to all neutral atoms of the same hydrogen isotope in a two-component neutral model. The complementary population is the cold neutral component, so the modeled total neutral density is the sum of hot and cold neutral densities.

The defining ratio is:

$$
f_\mathrm{hot} = \frac{n_\mathrm{hot}}{n_\mathrm{hot} + n_\mathrm{cold}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{hot}$ and $n_\mathrm{cold}$ are the hot and cold neutral number densities in $m^{-3}$ for the same isotope and physical region.

In visible spectroscopy, hot and cold neutral contributions may be inferred from line-shape components, such as Doppler-broadened charge-exchange emission and colder recycling or fueling emission. The measured component intensities are not density fractions by themselves; converting them to $f_\mathrm{hot}$ requires an emissivity or collisional-radiative model that accounts for excitation, charge exchange, ionization, neutral velocity distributions, instrument response, and line-of-sight integration.

By definition $0 \le f_\mathrm{hot} \le 1$. Values near 0 indicate a cold-neutral-dominated population, while values near 1 indicate a hot-neutral-dominated population; the realized value is strongly dependent on plasma conditions, neutral sources, charge-exchange rates, and the observation region.

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Total neutron emission rate from beam-beam fusion, summing the neutron-producing D(d,n) helium-3 branch, D-T reactions, and T-T reactions in which both reactants are energetic fast ions from neutral beam injection. The T-T contribution is a neutron count rate that includes its two-neutron final-state multiplicity.
NAMES.long:
Neutron flux due to beam-beam fusion is the global neutron emission count rate produced by fusion reactions between two energetic fast ions born from neutral beam injection. It includes the neutron-producing deuterium-deuterium branch $\mathrm{D(d,n)^3He}$, deuterium-tritium reactions, and tritium-tritium reactions; it excludes beam-thermal and thermal-thermal reactions. Because the unit is Hz, this quantity is a neutron production rate in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ rather than an areal particle flux.

The total beam-beam neutron emission rate is the sum of neutron count rates from the contributing fuel channels:

$$
\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{bb}} = \Gamma_{n,\mathrm{DD}(d,n),\mathrm{bb}} + \Gamma_{n,\mathrm{DT},\mathrm{bb}} + \Gamma_{n,\mathrm{TT},\mathrm{bb}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{bb}}$ is the total beam-beam neutron emission rate, $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{DD}(d,n),\mathrm{bb}}$ includes only the neutron-producing $\mathrm{D(d,n)^3He}$ branch of deuterium-deuterium fusion, $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{DT},\mathrm{bb}}$ is the deuterium-tritium neutron count rate, and $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{TT},\mathrm{bb}}$ is the tritium-tritium neutron count rate. The D-T channel produces one approximately 14 MeV neutron per reaction; the D-D neutron branch produces one approximately 2.45 MeV neutron per branch reaction; T-T fusion produces a continuum neutron spectrum and, for the dominant $\mathrm{T+T\to ^4He+2n}$ channel, contributes two emitted neutrons per reaction, so its neutron rate is a count rate rather than simply a reaction rate.

In practice this quantity is computed from fast-ion distribution functions and energy-dependent fusion reactivity kernels integrated over the two fast-ion populations. It can also be inferred by combining neutron diagnostics with modeling or subtraction of beam-thermal and thermal-thermal components. It is sensitive to neutral beam power, injection energy, fast-ion slowing down, pitch-angle distribution, isotope mix, and spatial overlap of the energetic ion populations.

Typical values are near 0 Hz when neutral beam injection is absent or when the relevant reacting isotope is absent. In neutral-beam-heated deuterium plasmas, beam-beam neutron rates are often in the range $10^{10}$-$10^{16}$ Hz; in high-power mixed deuterium-tritium or tritium-rich plasmas they can reach $10^{15}$-$10^{18}$ Hz, depending strongly on beam energy and fast-ion confinement.

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Beam-thermal neutron emission rate from fusion reactions between injected fast ions and thermal plasma ions, summed over DD, DT, and TT channels.
NAMES.long:
Neutron flux due to beam-thermal fusion is the volume-integrated neutron emission rate produced when fast neutral-beam ions fuse with thermal ions in the plasma. It excludes purely thermal-thermal and beam-beam reactions, and counts emitted neutrons rather than fusion events, so DD branching and TT neutron multiplicity are included.

A channel-resolved expression for the rate is:

$$
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{BT}} = \sum_{a,b\in\{D,T\}} \int_V dV \int d^3 v_a \int d^3 v_b\, f_a^{\mathrm{beam}}(\mathbf r,\mathbf v_a) f_b^{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf r,\mathbf v_b)\, \sigma_{ab}(v_{\mathrm{rel}})\, v_{\mathrm{rel}}\, Y_{ab}(v_{\mathrm{rel}})
$$

where $\Phi_n^{\mathrm{BT}}$ is the neutron emission rate in s$^{-1}$, equivalent to Hz; $a$ is the fast beam isotope and $b$ is the thermal target isotope; $f_a^{\mathrm{beam}}$ and $f_b^{\mathrm{th}}$ are velocity-space densities normalized to number density in m$^{-3}$; $\sigma_{ab}$ is the fusion cross-section in m$^2$; $v_{\mathrm{rel}}=|\mathbf v_a-\mathbf v_b|$ is the relative speed in m s$^{-1}$; and $Y_{ab}$ is the neutron yield per reaction. For DT, $Y_{DT}=1$; for TT, $Y_{TT}=2$ because two neutrons are emitted per reaction; for DD, $Y_{DD}$ is the energy-dependent branching fraction of the neutron-producing branch.

In practice this rate is computed from fast-ion distributions, thermal ion densities and temperatures, isotope composition, and fusion reactivity data. It is constrained experimentally by neutron monitors, activation systems, neutron cameras, and neutron spectroscopy, often using beam modulation or transport modeling to separate beam-thermal emission from [thermal_neutron_flux](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion) and other neutron-producing components. The channel-resolved components include [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion), [deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion), and the TT beam-thermal contribution; their sum contributes to total_neutron_flux.

Typical beam-thermal neutron emission rates are about $10^{12}$-$10^{16}$ Hz in deuterium neutral-beam plasmas, $10^{16}$-$10^{19}$ Hz in high-power mixed deuterium-tritium operation, and can approach $10^{20}$ Hz in large burning-plasma scenarios with strong auxiliary beams. Values scale strongly with injected power, fast-ion confinement, target density, isotope mix, and ion temperature.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_fraction
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged nitrogen concentration: the total nitrogen-particle density over all charge states divided by electron density.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen fraction is the dimensionless volume-averaged abundance of nitrogen relative to electrons in a plasma. It counts nitrogen nuclei in all ionization states, from neutral $\mathrm{N}^{0}$ through fully stripped $\mathrm{N}^{7+}$, and normalizes their total number density by the local electron density.

Using a volume average over the plasma volume, the fraction is defined as:

$$
f_\mathrm{N} = \left\langle \frac{\sum_{q=0}^{7} n_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}}}{n_e} \right\rangle_V
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{N}^{q+}}$ is the number density of nitrogen with charge state $q$, $q=0$ denotes neutral nitrogen, $q=7$ denotes fully stripped nitrogen, $n_e$ is electron density, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_V$ denotes volume averaging. Fully stripped nitrogen is $\mathrm{N}^{7+}$; there is no $\mathrm{N}^{8+}$ charge state for nitrogen.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from a combination of impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination measurements when available, bolometric radiation constraints, electron-density measurements, and collisional-radiative or transport modeling to complete the charge-state distribution. Neutral and fully stripped populations can be difficult to observe directly, so their contributions are often inferred from ionization-balance modeling rather than measured as isolated emission features.

Typical values are $10^{-4}$-$10^{-3}$ for trace background nitrogen and $10^{-3}$-$5\times10^{-2}$ during deliberate nitrogen seeding for radiative divertor or edge-cooling control. Larger fractions increase radiated power and fuel dilution and therefore strongly affect plasma performance.

NAMES.name: power_density_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Radiative power density from plasma soft X-ray emission received per unit active detector surface area, integrated over photon-energy bands transmitted by filters and windows and weighted by the detector spectral response.
NAMES.long:
Power density of a soft X-ray detector is the radiant power from plasma soft X-ray emission received per unit active detector surface area. The received power is limited to the photon-energy band or bands passed by the filter/window assembly and by the detector spectral response, so it is a band- and response-weighted irradiance rather than an intrinsic plasma emissivity.

The area-normalized received power is defined by

$$
q_\mathrm{SXR} = \frac{P_\mathrm{SXR}}{A_\mathrm{act}}
$$

where $q_\mathrm{SXR}$ is the detector power density in W m$^{-2}$, $P_\mathrm{SXR}$ is the response-weighted soft X-ray power in W accepted by the detector, and $A_\mathrm{act}$ is the active detector surface area in m$^2$. The energy integration implicit in $P_\mathrm{SXR}$ includes the selected photon-energy band, filter and window transmission, and detector spectral responsivity.

In practice this quantity is inferred from calibrated detector current, voltage, or count-rate signals after accounting for dark offsets, electronic gain, active area, and spectral responsivity. It is the active-area normalization of [power_of_soft_xray_detector](name:power_of_soft_xray_detector). Relations to [spectral_radiance_of_soft_xray_detector](name:spectral_radiance_of_soft_xray_detector) or [brightness_of_soft_xray_detector](name:brightness_of_soft_xray_detector) additionally require viewing geometry, etendue or solid angle, spectral transmission, and photon-energy weighting; solid-angle normalization alone is not sufficient. The incident direction is into the active detector surface from the plasma-facing side, and outward emission or reflection from the detector is not part of the received-power density.

Typical magnitudes vary strongly with aperture, filter thickness, line of sight, plasma temperature, and impurity content. Heavily filtered or edge-dominated channels may measure about 10^-6-10^-3 W m^-2, while core-viewing channels in hot tokamak plasmas commonly lie around 10^-3-10^1 W m^-2; intense transient events can approach 10^2 W m^-2 before detector saturation or attenuation limits are reached.

NAMES.name: radiated_power_density
NAMES.short: Local non-negative volumetric rate at which plasma emits electromagnetic radiation, representing radiated power per unit volume.
NAMES.long:
Radiated power density is the local, non-negative volumetric rate at which plasma thermal energy is converted to electromagnetic radiation. It includes continuum, line, recombination, and other photon emission processes that contribute to bolometric radiated power.

The total radiated power associated with a plasma volume is the volume integral of the local emission density:

$$
P_\mathrm{rad} = \int_V p_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_\mathrm{rad}$ is total radiated power in W, $p_\mathrm{rad}$ is radiated power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes spatial position, and $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$. For an axisymmetric reconstruction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height, the poloidal-plane volume element is $dV = 2\pi R\,dR\,dZ$; this reduction assumes toroidal symmetry of $p_\mathrm{rad}$.

Bolometer measurements infer this quantity from calibrated line-of-sight signals through an optically thin plasma. For channel $i$, the measured signal is commonly modeled as a path integral, $b_i \approx \int_{\ell_i} G_i(\mathbf{x})\,p_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{x})\,dl$, where $b_i$ is the calibrated channel response, $G_i$ is the geometric and instrumental response kernel, $\ell_i$ is the viewing chord, and $dl$ is path length in meters. Tomographic inversion combines many such chords, with regularization and uncertainty estimates, to recover the spatial emission distribution.

Typical local values are about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in relatively low-radiation core plasmas, $10^6$-$10^8$ W m$^{-3}$ in strongly radiating edge, divertor, or impurity-accumulation regions, and near zero outside the emitting plasma within measurement uncertainty.

NAMES.name: radius_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Radius of a circular Bragg-crystal aperture, defined as the distance from the aperture center to the circular edge of the active diffracting surface. It is an aperture-size radius characterizing the usable transverse extent of the crystal that participates in Bragg reflection, not a curvature radius of the crystal substrate.
NAMES.long:
The radius of a Bragg crystal is the geometric radius of the circular active diffracting aperture in an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel. It specifies the usable transverse size of the crystal face that participates in Bragg reflection, and it belongs to the same physical quantity class as [radius_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture). It is distinct from the substrate curvature radii and from the lattice spacing that fixes the diffraction angle.

For a circular aperture the radius is half the full diameter of the active diffracting area:

$$
r = \frac{D}{2}
$$

where $r$ is the aperture radius in meters and $D$ is the full diameter of the active circular surface in meters. The fully illuminated collecting area scales as $A = \pi r^2$, so the étendue and photon throughput of the channel increase with the square of this radius, subject to practical limits from focusing optics, angular acceptance, and edge vignetting.

This radius is determined from the crystal mount, aperture mask, or manufactured active area rather than from Bragg's law. It is independent of the toroidal and vertical curvature radii of the crystal substrate, which describe the shaping of a focusing crystal, and independent of the diffracting wavelength set by the crystal lattice.

Typical values range from about 0.002-0.05 m for compact high-resolution X-ray spectrometer crystals, with larger specialized crystals reaching roughly 0.1 m depending on optical layout and required photon collection.

NAMES.name: radius_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Radius of a circular diagnostic aperture, defined as the distance from the aperture center to its circular edge. It characterizes the opening size used to compute the corresponding aperture area.
NAMES.long:
The radius of a circular diagnostic aperture is the distance from the center of an idealized circular opening to its edge. It is the appropriate size parameter when the entrance aperture, collimating aperture, or sensitive circular region is modeled as a circle; non-circular apertures are characterized by quantities such as [width_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:width_of_diagnostic_aperture).

For an ideal circular aperture, the associated aperture area is

$$
A = \pi r^2
$$

where $r$ is the aperture radius in meters and $A$ is the area_of_diagnostic_aperture in square meters. The corresponding [diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture) is $d = 2r$, where $d$ is the full edge-to-edge distance through the aperture center.

The radius is obtained from mechanical drawings, dimensional metrology, optical inspection, or calibration of the fabricated diagnostic component. For a non-ideal or partially obscured circular opening, an effective radius may be chosen so that the ideal circular area matches the usable open area. The radius contributes to geometric throughput and solid-angle calculations together with the aperture position, orientation, and viewing geometry, but it does not by itself determine the full acceptance.

Representative engineering scales are device- and diagnostic-dependent. Small pinholes or tightly collimated openings may have radii of about 0.0001-0.001 m, while many optical, fiber, or detector apertures use millimeter- to centimeter-scale radii of about 0.001-0.01 m; larger values can occur in wide-aperture systems.

NAMES.name: radius_of_filter
NAMES.short: Radius of a circular diagnostic filter-window aperture, defined as the distance from the aperture center to its circular edge.
NAMES.long:
Radius of a circular filter-window aperture is the distance from the center of the clear opening to its circular edge. It is a purely geometric parameter that sets the size of the window through which photons pass in X-ray diagnostic channels, and applies only when the filter-window geometry is circular. It is distinct from the filter thickness, which governs energy-dependent attenuation, and from any radius of curvature of the filter surface.

The clear circular aperture area $A$ used in solid-angle and geometric throughput (etendue) calculations follows directly from the radius $r$:

$$
A = \pi r^2
$$

where $r$ is the aperture radius in meters and $A$ is the resulting clear aperture area in square meters.

The radius is typically taken from the mechanical design of the filter holder or determined by dimensional metrology, optical microscopy, or imaging of the aperture edge. When the filter window is itself the limiting circular aperture of a channel, this radius coincides with the radius of the diagnostic aperture.

Typical values range from about $1\times10^{-4}$ m to $5\times10^{-2}$ m, with sub-millimeter openings used for tightly collimated channels and millimeter-to-centimeter openings used for cameras or spectrometers with larger acceptance.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Photon wavelength assigned to each detector pixel of an X-ray crystal spectrometer by the Bragg diffraction geometry of the dispersing crystal.
NAMES.long:
In an X-ray crystal spectrometer, each detector pixel intercepts photons diffracted at a specific angle by the Bragg crystal, and this angle uniquely determines the photon wavelength. The wavelength varies primarily along the principal dispersion direction of the detector, with a secondary dependence across the orthogonal direction arising from the elliptical curvature of iso-wavelength surfaces produced by curved-crystal geometry.

The per-pixel wavelength follows Bragg's law:

$$
\lambda = \frac{2d\sin\theta}{n}
$$

where $d$ is the interplanar spacing of the diffracting crystal planes, $\theta$ is the local Bragg angle at the pixel position in the spectrometer focal plane, and $n$ is the integer diffraction order.

The wavelength map is computed from the spectrometer geometry — crystal curvature, crystal-to-detector distance, and pixel coordinates — and calibrated against known spectral emission lines; the reference diffraction wavelength at the nominal crystal orientation is described by bragg_wavelength. Pixel-by-pixel energy bounds on the spectral acceptance window are provided by [lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel). Typical wavelengths for fusion-relevant X-ray impurity emission lines (helium-like argon, titanium, or iron charge states) fall in the range 0.1–1 nm.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wavelength is assigned at a positive Bragg diffraction angle from the crystal surface, which is satisfied for all physically detected photons.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Spectral wavelength characterizing the passband of a diagnostic optical filter, encompassing the passband edge wavelengths and the nominal center or reference transmission wavelength.
NAMES.long:
Optical diagnostic filters define a spectral passband through which radiation passes to a detector. Several wavelengths characterize this passband: [lower_wavelength_of_filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter) marks the short-wavelength attenuation edge below which radiation is blocked, [upper_wavelength_of_filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter) marks the long-wavelength cutoff, and [reference_wavelength_of_filter](name:reference_wavelength_of_filter) identifies the nominal peak or center transmission wavelength.

The relationship between wavelength $\lambda$, photon frequency $\nu$, and the speed of light in vacuum $c$ is:

$$
\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}
$$

where $\nu$ is the photon oscillation frequency in Hz.

Passband center wavelengths in visible plasma spectroscopy typically fall in the 300-800 nm range, selected to coincide with prominent atomic or molecular emission features such as H$\alpha$ at 656.3 nm or He I at 587.6 nm. Interference filters and narrowband etalons achieve bandwidths from sub-nanometer to tens of nanometers. The [spectral_wavelength](name:spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element) describes the full spectral axis context, and [wavelength_of_spectral_line](name:wavelength_of_spectral_line) provides the rest-frame reference for targeted spectral lines.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wavelength is the spatial period of a forward-propagating electromagnetic wave in the transmission medium.

NAMES.name: lower_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Short-wavelength (high-photon-energy) edge of the transmission passband of a diagnostic filter or filter window. Radiation at shorter wavelengths than this nominal cutoff is attenuated below the specified transmission criterion.
NAMES.long:
The lower wavelength of a filter, denoted $\lambda_{\min}$, is the nominal short-wavelength edge of the filter or filter-window transmission passband. It is expressed in meters and corresponds to the highest photon energies intended to be transmitted by the filter; photons with $\lambda < \lambda_{\min}$ are attenuated below the applicable transmission criterion.

Photon energy is inversely related to wavelength:

$$
E_\gamma = \frac{hc}{\lambda}
$$

where $E_\gamma$ is photon energy, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\lambda$ is photon wavelength. A smaller $\lambda_{\min}$ therefore means that higher-energy photons are included in the nominal transmitted band.

In practice, $\lambda_{\min}$ is determined from a calibrated or manufacturer-specified spectral transmission curve $T(\lambda)$. The cutoff should correspond to an explicit attenuation or transmission threshold, such as the shortest wavelength at which $T(\lambda)$ rises above a chosen fraction of the in-band or peak transmission. Together with [upper_wavelength_of_filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), this quantity gives the nominal wavelength interval of the filter, but the detailed wavelength-dependent response is described by quantities such as [spectral_absorptivity_of_filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter).

Typical values depend strongly on the diagnostic spectral range: visible continuum filters often have lower wavelengths of about $3 \times 10^{-7}$-$8 \times 10^{-7}$ m, soft-X-ray filter windows about $10^{-10}$-$10^{-8}$ m, and hard-X-ray filter windows about $10^{-12}$-$10^{-10}$ m.

NAMES.name: upper_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Upper wavelength limit of the passband transmitted by a diagnostic filter window. It is the long-wavelength, low-photon-energy cutoff of the filter-window transmission band.
NAMES.long:
The upper wavelength of a filter is the long-wavelength boundary of the passband transmitted by a filter window. It is the largest wavelength included by the filter-window transmission criterion and therefore corresponds to the lowest photon energy admitted by that filter passband. Together with [lower_wavelength_of_filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter), it defines the wavelength interval of the transmitted band, normally with $\lambda_{\mathrm{lower}} \le \lambda_{\max}$.

The corresponding minimum photon energy is related to the cutoff wavelength by

$$
E_{\min} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{\max}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\max}$ is the upper wavelength cutoff in meters, $E_{\min}$ is the corresponding photon energy in joules, $h$ is Planck's constant in joule seconds, and $c$ is the speed of light in meters per second.

For a real filter window the spectral transmission edge is gradual rather than perfectly sharp, so the upper wavelength should be interpreted using the stated passband criterion, such as a specified transmission threshold or calibrated edge definition. It is obtained from the filter-window transmission curve, computed from material optical properties and thickness or measured by spectral transmission calibration.

Representative X-ray and soft-X-ray filter-window upper cutoffs are commonly in the range $10^{-11}$-$10^{-8}$ m, depending on filter material, thickness, and the selected transmission criterion. The wavelength-dependent attenuation within and outside the passband is described by [spectral_absorptivity_of_filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter).

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Central rest-frame vacuum wavelength of an atomic, ionic, molecular, or nuclear spectral emission or absorption line. It is set by the transition energy between quantum states and identifies the unshifted physical line.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of a spectral line is the central vacuum wavelength $\lambda_0$ of the photon associated with a transition between two quantum states, evaluated in the rest frame of the emitting or absorbing species. It is a property of the transition itself, separate from observed wavelength shifts, broadening, field-induced splitting, and instrumental response.

The rest wavelength is set by the transition energy:

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{h c}{|E_u - E_l|}
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is the vacuum wavelength in meters, $h$ is the Planck constant in joule seconds, $c$ is the speed of light in meters per second, and $E_u$ and $E_l$ are the upper- and lower-state energies in joules.

In spectroscopy, $\lambda_0$ is usually taken from evaluated atomic, molecular, or nuclear transition data, or from fitted line centers after wavelength calibration and correction to vacuum wavelength. For an observed line center $\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}$ in meters, the non-relativistic Doppler relation is $(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}-\lambda_0)/\lambda_0 \approx v_{\mathrm{los}}/c$ for $|v_{\mathrm{los}}| \ll c$, where $v_{\mathrm{los}}$ is in meters per second and is positive when the source recedes from the observer, increasing the observed wavelength. Thermal Doppler Gaussian width scales as $\sigma_\lambda/\lambda_0 \approx \sqrt{k_B T_s/(m_s c^2)}$, where $\sigma_\lambda$ is in meters, $T_s$ is the species temperature in kelvin, and $m_s$ is the particle mass in kilograms; equivalently use $\sqrt{T_s/(m_s c^2)}$ when $T_s$ is expressed as an energy.

The quantity is not limited to a particular spectral band. Lines used in plasma spectroscopy commonly span about $1\times10^{-11}$-$1\times10^{-5}$ m, including soft-x-ray lines near $1\times10^{-10}$-$1\times10^{-9}$ m, extreme-ultraviolet and ultraviolet lines near $1\times10^{-8}$-$4\times10^{-7}$ m, visible lines near $4\times10^{-7}$-$7\times10^{-7}$ m, and near-infrared lines near $7\times10^{-7}$-$1\times10^{-5}$ m; other atomic, molecular, or nuclear transitions can lie outside these ranges.

NAMES.name: area_of_first_wall
NAMES.short: Area of first wall is the total surface area of the material surface that forms the plasma-facing first wall, whether bare vessel surface or installed wall armor. It is a scalar geometric area used as a reference for wall-integrated heat, particle, and plasma-wall interaction quantities.
NAMES.long:
Area of first wall is the total area of the material surface classified as the first wall on the plasma-facing side of the vessel or wall armor. It is a true surface area, not a projected area, and is distinct from the area of the last closed flux surface because it follows the engineered wall geometry rather than a magnetic flux surface.

For a first-wall surface $\mathcal{S}_\mathrm{fw}$, the area is defined by the surface integral; for a surface axisymmetric about the $Z$ axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the same area can be reduced to an integral over its poloidal generating curve:

$$
A_\mathrm{fw} = \int_{\mathcal{S}_\mathrm{fw}} dA, \qquad A_\mathrm{fw} = 2\pi \int_{\Gamma_\mathrm{fw}} R\, ds
$$

where $A_\mathrm{fw}$ has unit m^2, $dA$ is the differential surface-area element with unit m^2, $\Gamma_\mathrm{fw}$ is the poloidal curve that generates the axisymmetric first-wall surface, $R$ is major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $ds$ is differential arc length along $\Gamma_\mathrm{fw}$.

In practice, this area is computed from engineering geometry or a surface mesh by summing the areas of all faces assigned to the first-wall boundary. Port openings and cut-outs contribute no material area, while recessed panels, limiter faces, baffles, or divertor-interface surfaces are included only when they are part of the physical first-wall surface being characterized; the same component scope should be used when normalizing wall quantities such as [plasma_deposited_power_at_wall](name:plasma_deposited_power_at_wall), total_incident_electron_particle_flux_at_wall, or energy_flux_at_first_wall.

Typical values are geometry-dependent: compact devices may have first-wall areas of a few to a few tens of m^2, while large tokamaks and reactor-scale designs may have tens to hundreds of m^2. For axisymmetric designs, the scaling is roughly set by the product of toroidal circumference and poloidal wall perimeter, with local armor shaping and penetrations modifying the exact value.

NAMES.name: coolant_pressure_at_cooling_circuit_inlet
NAMES.short: Absolute static pressure of the coolant at the entry point of a cooling circuit, providing the upstream pressure boundary condition for hydraulic, heat-transfer, and structural-load calculations.
NAMES.long:
Coolant pressure at a cooling-circuit inlet is the absolute static thermodynamic pressure of the fluid as it enters the hydraulically defined circuit or component. It sets the upstream pressure boundary condition for the momentum balance and influences coolant density, phase margin, pumping requirements, and pressure loading on the surrounding structure.

For a hydraulically equivalent circuit segment after any hydrostatic head correction, the inlet pressure is commonly related to outlet pressure by the Darcy-Weisbach loss relation:

$$
P_\mathrm{in} = P_\mathrm{out} + \Delta P = P_\mathrm{out} + \left(f\frac{L}{D_h} + \sum_i K_i\right)\frac{\rho v^2}{2}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{in}$ and $P_\mathrm{out}$ are absolute static inlet and outlet pressures in Pa, $\Delta P$ is the pressure loss in Pa, $f$ is the dimensionless Darcy friction factor, $L$ is the flow length in m, $D_h$ is the hydraulic diameter in m, $K_i$ are dimensionless local-loss coefficients, $\rho$ is coolant mass density in kg m^-3, and $v$ is mean coolant speed in m s^-1.

In practice, this pressure is measured with a static pressure tap and pressure transducer near the circuit entrance, or computed from pump, manifold, and hydraulic-resistance models. Its interpretation is closely tied to coolant_flow: the mass flow rate sets the mean speed through the flow area and therefore the frictional and local pressure losses. Thermal power removal is evaluated primarily from mass flow, [coolant_temperature_at_inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet), [coolant_temperature_at_outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet), and pressure-dependent coolant properties; inlet pressure alone does not determine the enthalpy rise or [net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

Typical inlet pressures for structural-component cooling circuits range from 10^5-2 x 10^7 Pa. Pressurized water and helium circuits commonly operate at 5 x 10^6-1.6 x 10^7 Pa, while lower-pressure liquid-metal or auxiliary coolant loops may operate near 10^5-10^6 Pa.

NAMES.name: coolant_volume_of_breeder_blanket
NAMES.short: Total volume occupied by lead-lithium (PbLi) coolant/breeder inside the whole breeder blanket. It is a geometric inventory quantity, distinct from a per-module volume and excluding external coolant loops or non-coolant materials.
NAMES.long:
Coolant volume of a breeder blanket is the total geometric volume occupied by the lead-lithium (PbLi) eutectic inside the whole blanket. Here PbLi is the coolant/breeder material being counted, not merely an example liquid metal. The quantity excludes solid structural material, purge gas, vacuum gaps, external coolant loops, tanks, and heat exchangers; a module-specific value would refer to one blanket module, whereas this whole-blanket value is the sum over all blanket modules or sectors.

The volume is the integral over the PbLi domain inside the breeder blanket:

$$
V_\mathrm{cool} = \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{PbLi} \cap \Omega_\mathrm{blanket}} dV
$$

where $V_\mathrm{cool}$ is the coolant volume in m^3, $\Omega_\mathrm{PbLi}$ is the region occupied by PbLi, $\Omega_\mathrm{blanket}$ is the whole breeder-blanket domain, and $dV$ is a differential volume element in m^3.

In design studies this volume is usually computed from engineering geometry by summing the PbLi-filled channels, manifolds, and breeder zones that lie within the blanket boundary. In operation it may be checked indirectly from fill level, drain volume, or mass inventory measurements together with the PbLi density at the relevant temperature.

The volume enters liquid-metal inventory estimates through $M_\mathrm{PbLi} = \rho_\mathrm{PbLi} V_\mathrm{cool}$ and residence-time estimates through $\tau \approx V_\mathrm{cool}/\dot{V} = \rho_\mathrm{PbLi} V_\mathrm{cool}/\dot{m}$, where $\rho_\mathrm{PbLi}$ is density, $\dot{V}$ is volumetric flow rate, and $\dot{m}$ is mass flow rate. For heat-removal sizing it is used together with flow distribution, allowable temperature rise, pressure drop, material limits, and [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket); it does not by itself determine mass flow rate or net thermal power, and blanket nuclear heating can include energy deposited in structural components as well as in coolant or breeder regions.

Typical values for reactor-scale liquid-metal breeder blankets are about 10-200 m^3 for the full blanket. Individual sectors, cassettes, or test blanket modules can contain much smaller volumes, commonly 0.01-10 m^3, and should not be confused with the whole-blanket total unless explicitly summed over the complete blanket.

NAMES.name: net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Net thermal power removed from a single breeder blanket module by its coolant. It equals the total coolant enthalpy increase summed across all coolant branches serving the module and combines nuclear energy deposition with the absorbed fraction of incident radiation that reaches the coolant.
NAMES.long:
Net thermal power of a breeder blanket module is the rate at which the module's coolant circuit carries thermal energy away from that module. It is an aggregate per-module power that combines thermal energy transferred to the coolant from neutron and gamma heating, decay heat when relevant, and the absorbed fraction of incident radiation, while excluding power generated or removed outside the module boundary.

For a steady coolant circuit, the defining calorimetric relation is the total coolant enthalpy rise across all coolant branches serving the module:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th,net}} = \sum_k \dot{m}_k \left(h_{\mathrm{out},k} - h_{\mathrm{in},k}\right)
$$

where $k$ labels coolant branches, $\dot{m}_k$ is the coolant mass flow rate in branch $k$ (kg/s), and $h_{\mathrm{in},k}$ and $h_{\mathrm{out},k}$ are the inlet and outlet specific enthalpies (J/kg). The common expression $\dot{m}\, c_p\, \Delta T$, with $c_p$ in J/(kg·K), is a constant-$c_p$ approximation to this enthalpy balance valid when pressure changes and the temperature dependence of the heat capacity are small.

This module-level power aggregates the nuclear deposition tracked by [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket) and its layer-resolved counterpart [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), and shares the same coolant enthalpy-balance formalism as [thermal_power_of_plant_component_port](name:thermal_power_of_plant_component_port). It feeds reactor-level power balance and tritium-breeding-efficiency assessments.

Typical values range from about $10^4$-$10^6$ W for small test blanket modules or low-power operating phases, and about $10^6$-$10^7$ W per module for reactor-relevant breeding blanket segments, depending on module size, neutron wall loading, coolant design, and plasma radiated power.
NAMES.sign: Positive when thermal energy is removed from the breeder blanket module by the coolant circuit.

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket
NAMES.short: Total nuclear heating power deposited in the breeder blanket by neutron and photon interactions, integrated over all blanket modules and constituent materials. It represents volumetric nuclear energy deposition and excludes separate plasma-facing surface heat loads.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket is the total rate at which fusion neutrons and secondary photons deposit energy inside the blanket volume. It includes volumetric energy deposition in breeder, multiplier, coolant, structural, and other internal materials, and excludes plasma radiation, charged-particle, neutral-particle, and other surface heat loads treated as boundary heating.

The blanket total is obtained by integrating the local nuclear heating power density over the blanket volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc,blanket}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{blanket}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{nuc,blanket}}$ is the integrated blanket nuclear heating power, $V_{\mathrm{blanket}}$ is the volume occupied by the breeder blanket, $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local volumetric nuclear heating power density in W m$^{-3}$, and $dV$ is a volume element.

In practice this quantity is computed with coupled neutron-photon transport calculations using the fusion neutron source, material compositions, geometry, and nuclear reaction data. The same total can be partitioned into module contributions such as [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) or material-layer contributions such as [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer); heating in associated shielding regions is described separately by [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield). The spatial distribution underlying the integral is represented by [nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module). Results may be checked against integral neutronics benchmarks, activation measurements, photon-heating detectors, or calorimetric measurements where available.

For reactor-scale D-T blankets with fusion power near $2 \times 10^9$ W, representative blanket nuclear heating powers are about $1.2$-$1.6 \times 10^9$ W. The value scales with neutron source strength, blanket coverage, material composition, and neutron energy multiplication, which is often in the range $1.1$-$1.3$ for power-producing blanket concepts; partial test blankets or lower-power sources can be orders of magnitude smaller.

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Total nuclear heating power deposited within one material layer of a breeding blanket by neutron and photon energy deposition in that layer.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket layer is the total rate at which fusion-born neutrons and secondary photons deposit energy in the material volume assigned to that layer. It includes local energy deposition from nuclear reactions and photon interactions in structural, breeder, multiplier, coolant-channel, or other functional materials that belong to the layer.

It is obtained by integrating the local nuclear heating power density over the layer volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{layer}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the layer nuclear heating power in W, $V_{\mathrm{layer}}$ is the physical volume of the layer in m$^3$, $dV$ is a differential volume element in m$^3$, and $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the local nuclear heating power density in W m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from coupled neutron-photon transport and nuclear data, usually by tallying heating over the material cells representing the layer. Gamma heating should be interpreted as energy deposited by photons produced by neutron interactions, activation, capture, inelastic scattering, or other photon sources represented in the transport model, not as a universal signature of a particular breeding reaction. If a module is decomposed into non-overlapping layers that completely partition the module volume, the sum of the layer heating powers equals the corresponding [module nuclear heating power](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module); otherwise gaps, overlaps, homogenization choices, and separately modeled components can make the sums differ.

Typical values for a single blanket-module layer range from about 10^3-10^6 W in reactor-relevant blanket designs, depending on neutron wall loading, layer volume, material composition, and radial position. Small test modules or weakly irradiated peripheral layers may be below this range, while large high-power modules or layers close to the plasma-facing side can exceed it.

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Total nuclear heating power deposited in a single breeder blanket module by neutron scattering, neutron capture, and secondary gamma radiation interactions with the module's structural and functional materials.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket module is the total rate at which neutron and photon radiation transfer energy to the structural and functional materials comprising that module. The dominant mechanisms are neutron elastic and inelastic scattering, exothermic neutron capture reactions (including lithium reactions that also breed tritium), and absorption of secondary gamma rays produced throughout the module volume.

The module-level heating power is the volume integral of the local nuclear heating power density $q_\text{nuc}(\mathbf{r})$ over the module volume $V$:

$$
P_\text{nuc} = \int_V q_\text{nuc}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $q_\text{nuc}$ is the volumetric energy deposition rate in W m$^{-3}$, as described by [nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module).

This quantity is obtained from neutron and photon transport simulations and feeds directly into thermal-hydraulic analyzes for coolant sizing and material temperature verification. It is more spatially resolved than [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket), which aggregates over all modules, and complements [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), which further resolves heating by material layer within the module. Unlike [total_neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), this quantity includes gamma-ray heating contributions and accounts only for energy absorbed rather than that generated within the module.

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield
NAMES.short: Nuclear heating power deposited in the breeding blanket shield by neutron and gamma radiation interactions with shield structural materials.
NAMES.long:
The breeder blanket shield absorbs residual neutron and gamma radiation that penetrates the breeding zone, converting particle energy to heat through neutron scattering, capture reactions, and Compton scattering of secondary photons. This thermal load determines the cooling circuit requirements for the shield structure and is a principal design constraint for protecting superconducting magnets from radiation-induced heating.

The total nuclear heating power is the volume integral of the local nuclear power density $q'''(\mathbf{r})$ over the shield volume $V_\mathrm{shield}$:

$$
P_\mathrm{shield} = \int_{V_\mathrm{shield}} q'''(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $q'''(\mathbf{r})$ is in W m$^{-3}$ and sums contributions from both neutron and secondary gamma interactions throughout the shield material.

This quantity is evaluated via neutron transport analysis using validated nuclear cross-section libraries for the shield material composition, benchmarked against integral activation experiments. It is the shield-level analog of the layer-resolved [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer) and the blanket-wide integral [nuclear heating power of the full breeding blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket); the volumetric counterpart [nuclear power density of a breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module) provides the spatially resolved distribution used in detailed thermal-hydraulic analyzes.

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Volumetric nuclear heating power density deposited in a single breeder blanket layer by neutron and gamma interactions. It is local heat generation per unit material volume, distinct from volume-integrated blanket power.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear power density of a breeder blanket layer is the local volumetric rate at which energy from neutron and gamma interactions is deposited as heat in the layer material. It is a material heat-source density for a particular layer, not the total power generated by that layer or by the blanket.

The local definition is the differential nuclear heating power per material volume:

$$
q'''_\mathrm{nuc}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{dP_\mathrm{nuc}}{dV}
$$

where $q'''_\mathrm{nuc}$ is the nuclear power density in W m$^{-3}$, $dP_\mathrm{nuc}$ is the incremental nuclear heating power in W deposited in the material volume element $dV$ in m$^3$, and $\mathbf{r}$ denotes position in the layer.
