NAMES.short: Total pressure of the suprathermal co-passing particle population, obtained by integrating both parallel and perpendicular kinetic energy contributions of the fast-particle distribution function over the co-passing velocity-space domain.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing fast particles are suprathermal guiding-center orbits that circulate toroidally in the same direction as the plasma current, covering the velocity-space region where the pitch-angle cosine $\xi = v_\parallel/v$ exceeds the magnetic trapping boundary. This quantity is the orbit-class-resolved scalar pressure component of the total fast_particle_pressure, complementing the [counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and [trapped_fast_particle_pressure](name:trapped_fast_particle_pressure) contributions that together partition the full fast-particle pressure.

The co-passing fast-particle pressure is defined as the second velocity moment of the fast-particle distribution function $f_\mathrm{fast}$ restricted to the co-passing domain $\Omega_\mathrm{co}$:

$$
P_\mathrm{co} = \frac{m}{3} \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{co}} v^2 \, f_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m$ is the particle mass, $v = |\mathbf{v}|$ is the speed, and $\Omega_\mathrm{co}$ denotes the co-passing region ($\xi > \xi_\mathrm{trap}$, with $\xi_\mathrm{trap}$ the trapping-boundary cosine). Equivalently, $P_\mathrm{co} = \tfrac{1}{3}(P_{\parallel,\mathrm{co}} + 2P_{\perp,\mathrm{co}})$, decomposing into the [parallel component](name:parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and the [perpendicular component](name:perpendicular_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure).

This quantity is computed from kinetic distribution-function solvers or Monte Carlo transport codes that resolve velocity-space orbit classes. Tangential neutral beam injection preferentially populates the co-passing orbit class, making this pressure component particularly prominent in NBI-heated plasmas where beam geometry and injection energy determine the co-passing fraction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when suprathermal particles occupy the co-passing orbit class with finite kinetic energy density.

NAMES.name: conductivity
NAMES.short: Diagonal elements of the electrical conductivity tensor in a magnetized plasma, giving the anisotropic Ohmic response of current density to the driving electric field in each geometric direction.
NAMES.long:
The electrical conductivity $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ is a second-rank tensor that relates the conducted current density vector $\mathbf{j}$ to the local electric field $\mathbf{E}$ through the generalized Ohm's law $\mathbf{j} = \boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \mathbf{E}$. In a magnetized plasma this tensor is strongly anisotropic: electrons stream nearly freely along the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ while the Lorentz force suppresses mobility in the perpendicular plane, producing diagonal components that differ by orders of magnitude depending on direction.

Each diagonal component $\sigma_{\alpha\alpha}$ satisfies

$$
j_\alpha = \sigma_{\alpha\alpha}\, E_\alpha
$$

where $\hat{\alpha}$ is a local coordinate direction, $j_\alpha$ is the conductive current density in that direction, and $E_\alpha$ is the co-directed electric field component; off-diagonal Hall and diamagnetic coupling terms are excluded from these diagonal entries.

The [parallel_conductivity](name:parallel_conductivity) along the local magnetic field direction is by far the largest component; in the Spitzer limit it scales as $\sigma_\parallel \propto T_e^{3/2} Z_\mathrm{eff}^{-1}$, where $T_e$ is the electron temperature and $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective ion charge. Neoclassical trapped-particle effects reduce the effective parallel conductivity below the collisional Spitzer value. The cross-field projections — [poloidal_conductivity](name:poloidal_conductivity), [radial_conductivity](name:radial_conductivity), [toroidal_conductivity](name:toroidal_conductivity), and [vertical_conductivity](name:vertical_conductivity) — characterize the Ohmic coupling in the respective flux or cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ coordinate directions. Contributions from diamagnetic drift are described separately by electrical_conductivity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift. Typical parallel conductivities in tokamak cores range from $10^6$ to $10^8$ m$^{-1}$\,\Omega$^{-1}$ across the 0.1–20 keV electron-temperature range, and decrease sharply at lower temperatures owing to the $T_e^{3/2}$ dependence.

NAMES.name: coulomb_logarithm
NAMES.short: Dimensionless logarithm of the ratio of the Debye screening length to the minimum Coulomb impact parameter, appearing as a multiplicative factor in all classical collision frequencies and resistivity expressions.
NAMES.long:
The Coulomb logarithm $\ln \Lambda$ is a dimensionless factor encoding the effective range of impact parameters that contribute to cumulative small-angle Coulomb scattering in a plasma. It arises because the Debye-shielded potential introduces a maximum effective impact parameter $b_{\max}$, while quantum or classical mechanics sets a minimum $b_{\min}$, producing a well-defined logarithmic ratio.

The defining expression is

$$
\ln \Lambda = \ln\!\left(\frac{b_{\max}}{b_{\min}}\right)
$$

where $b_{\max} = \lambda_D$ is the Debye screening length, and $b_{\min}$ is the larger of the classical distance of closest approach $e^2/(m_e v_e^2)$ and the thermal de Broglie wavelength $\hbar/(m_e v_e)$, with $e$ the elementary charge, $m_e$ the electron mass, and $v_e$ the electron thermal speed.

The collision frequency scales as $\nu \propto \ln \Lambda$ and the Spitzer resistivity as $\eta \propto \ln \Lambda \, T_e^{-3/2}$, where $T_e$ is the electron temperature. In tokamak core conditions ($T_e \sim 5$–$10$ keV, $n_e \sim 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$), $\ln \Lambda \approx 17$–$19$; in the cooler edge ($T_e \sim 10$–$100$ eV), values fall to approximately $10$–$14$. The pedestal-localized value is captured by [coulomb_logarithm_at_pedestal_top](name:coulomb_logarithm_at_pedestal_top).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the Debye length exceeds the minimum Coulomb impact parameter, a condition satisfied in all weakly coupled plasmas where $\Lambda > 1$.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_density
NAMES.short: Total number density of counter-passing particles — those whose guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the plasma current — including both thermal and suprathermal contributions from the distribution function.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing particles are those whose guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the local plasma current direction, giving them sufficient parallel energy to complete full poloidal orbits around the torus without being reflected by the magnetic mirror force. This density integrates both the thermal bulk and any suprathermal population over the counter-passing region of phase space, weighted solely by orbit topology.

The counter-passing number density is defined by the velocity-space integral of the guiding-center distribution function restricted to the counter-passing domain:

$$
n_\text{cpass}(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{\text{cpass}} f(\mathbf{r}, v_\parallel, v_\perp) \, 2\pi v_\perp \, dv_\parallel \, dv_\perp
$$

where $f(\mathbf{r}, v_\parallel, v_\perp)$ is the guiding-center distribution function and the integral extends over the phase-space region of particles that circulate counter to the plasma current without magnetic trapping.

This quantity is computed by kinetic Fokker-Planck solvers that evolve the guiding-center distribution function and classify phase-space trajectories by orbit topology. Together with [co-passing density](name:total_co_passing_particle_density) and [trapped density](name:total_trapped_particle_density), it provides a complete orbit-class decomposition of the total local particle number density; summing all three classes recovers the full population. The suprathermal subset of this orbit class is resolved separately by [counter_passing_fast_particle_density](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_density), and the pressure moment of the same orbit class is given by counter_passing_pressure. Asymmetry between the co-passing and counter-passing densities reflects net parallel momentum injection, for example from directed neutral beam injection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when counter-passing particles are present in the distribution function; particle number density is intrinsically non-negative.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.short: Scalar kinetic pressure moment of the suprathermal particle distribution restricted to counter-passing guiding-center orbits. It represents the counter-passing fast-particle contribution to pressure, evaluated locally or as a flux-surface average of the same orbit-selected moment.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast-particle pressure is the scalar trace pressure carried by suprathermal particles on passing guiding-center orbits whose transit direction is opposite to the plasma current. It is the fast-particle contribution to [counter-passing total particle pressure], complementary to [co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:co_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and [trapped fast-particle pressure](name:trapped_fast_particle_pressure). As a trace quantity it is consistent with the parallel and perpendicular tensor components for the same orbit class.

The local scalar trace pressure is defined by the second velocity moment over the counter-passing part of phase space:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cp,fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{3}\sum_s m_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},s}(\mathbf{x})} v^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_s$ is the particle mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is the particle speed in m s$^{-1}$, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the fast-particle distribution function, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},s}$ contains only passing orbits with parallel transit opposite to the plasma current. The result has units of Pa. The tensor trace relation is $P_{\mathrm{cp,fast}}=(P_{\parallel,\mathrm{cp,fast}}+2P_{\perp,\mathrm{cp,fast}})/3$ when [parallel](name:parallel_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and [perpendicular](name:perpendicular_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) components use the same orbit selection.

In practice this pressure is computed from fast-particle distribution functions obtained from orbit-following, Fokker-Planck, or Monte Carlo modeling, often constrained by energetic-particle diagnostics such as neutron emission, gamma emission, neutral-particle analysis, or fast-ion light emission. A flux-surface-averaged value is obtained by first forming the local orbit-selected pressure moment and then averaging that scalar over a surface of constant magnetic flux; the averaging does not change the counter-passing orbit definition or the pressure-tensor trace relation.

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. Values may be near 0 Pa where the counter-passing fast population is absent, around 10^2-10^4 Pa in modest auxiliary-heated plasmas, and up to order 10^5 Pa in strongly beam-heated or fusion-alpha-heated cores; the counter-passing subset is usually a fraction of the total fast-particle pressure.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport
NAMES.short: Vector current density generated by anomalous (turbulence-driven) transport in the plasma, representing the net electrical current per unit area beyond classical and neoclassical predictions.
NAMES.long:
Anomalous transport arises from plasma micro-instabilities and turbulence — such as ion-temperature-gradient and electron-temperature-gradient modes, drift waves, and interchange instabilities — that drive particle and momentum fluxes far exceeding classical collisional and neoclassical predictions. When these turbulent fluxes are charge-selective or carry net momentum, they produce a macroscopic current density $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{anom}$ distributed throughout the plasma volume.

In transport models, $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{anom}$ enters the generalized Ohm's law alongside neoclassical and inductively driven contributions. The full vector decomposes into components resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — including the [radial](name:radial_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport), [toroidal](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport), and [vertical](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport) projections — and a [parallel component](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport) along the local magnetic field direction $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$. This quantity is distinct from [current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), which captures a separate non-ideal MHD current source.

This quantity is evaluated in turbulent transport simulations using quasilinear or nonlinear models; the anomalous current density is derived self-consistently from charge-selective turbulent fluxes. Experimental inference requires subtracting neoclassical and inductive contributions from measured total current density profiles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net conventional current (positive charge displacement due to anomalous transport) flows in the $+\hat{R}$ (radially outward), $+\hat{\phi}$ (direction of increasing toroidal angle), or $+\hat{Z}$ (vertically upward) direction for the respective cylindrical component, or in the direction of $\hat{b}$ for the parallel component.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Vector current density produced by diamagnetic drift in a magnetized plasma, directed by the right-handed cross product of the magnetic field with the plasma pressure gradient and scaled by the squared magnetic-field magnitude. It is perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the pressure gradient.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic-drift current density is the perpendicular current produced by pressure gradients in a magnetized plasma. For an isotropic scalar pressure, it is directed along the ordered cross product of the magnetic field with the plasma pressure gradient, so that it contributes to the perpendicular current required for magnetohydrodynamic pressure balance.

For scalar pressure $p$, the diamagnetic current density is defined by

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic current density, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $B^2=\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{B}$, and $\nabla p$ is the plasma pressure gradient in Pa m^-1. With this ordering, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}} \times \mathbf{B}=\nabla p_\perp$ when the pressure gradient is perpendicular to the magnetic field, consistent with perpendicular force balance.

In practice this quantity is computed from reconstructed or modeled magnetic fields together with pressure gradients inferred from density and temperature measurements or transport calculations. Its radial and vertical projections in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame are related to [radial_diamagnetic_current_density](name:radial_diamagnetic_current_density) and [vertical_diamagnetic_current_density](name:vertical_diamagnetic_current_density).

Typical magnitudes in magnetically confined fusion plasmas are about 10^2-10^5 A m^-2 in the core and edge pedestal, with larger values occurring where pressure gradients are steep and the magnetic field is comparatively weak.
NAMES.sign: Positive when conventional positive charge flow is along $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p$.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short: Vector electric current density arising from heat-viscosity terms in the collisional plasma fluid closure, where the divergence of the heat-viscosity stress tensor drives net charge transport in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The heat-viscosity current density is the electric current density vector generated when heat-viscosity contributions in a collisional plasma fluid model (such as the Braginskii closure) induce net species motion that results in charge transport. In a magnetized plasma, the viscous stress tensor $\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\pi}$ contains a heat-viscosity part $\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\pi}_\mathrm{hv}$ that couples heat transport to bulk plasma momentum; the divergence of this tensor enters the fluid momentum equation for each species and drives flows carrying net electric current.

The heat-viscosity current density vector $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{hv}$ is expressed as:

$$
\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{hv} = \sum_s q_s n_s \mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{hv}}
$$

where $q_s$ is the charge of species $s$, $n_s$ is its number density, and $\mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{hv}}$ is the flow velocity component driven by heat-viscosity forces in the species momentum balance.

This vector is decomposed into geometric projections, including the [radial component](name:radial_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) along $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The companion quantity current_density_due_to_collisions captures the distinct inter-species collisional friction mechanism, while [radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) represents the analogous contribution from field-aligned (parallel) viscosity. Heat-viscosity current contributions are most significant in the edge plasma where the collisionality is high enough for fluid closures to remain valid.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net charge flow points in the direction of increasing coordinate of the respective projection axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_ion_inertia
NAMES.short: Vector current density arising from the inertial force terms of the ion fluid in the two-fluid plasma model, principally through the polarization drift generated by ion acceleration in the momentum equation.
NAMES.long:
The current density due to ion inertia represents the net electric current produced by the inertial acceleration terms in the ion fluid momentum equation. In a two-fluid plasma description, ions with finite mass contribute to net charge transport whenever they are accelerated — through flow convergence, curvature forces, or time-varying electric fields — giving rise to a polarization-type current that is absent in the massless-electron fluid.

The dominant contribution is the ion polarization drift current:

$$
\mathbf{J}_{inertia} = \frac{m_i n_i}{e B^2} \mathbf{B} \times \frac{d_i \mathbf{v}_{\perp i}}{dt}
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ is the ion number density, $e$ is the elementary charge, $B$ is the magnetic field magnitude, and $d_i/dt = \partial/\partial t + \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \nabla$ is the ion convective derivative applied to the perpendicular ion velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\perp i}$.

The divergence of this current feeds the vorticity equation and contributes to the radial current balance, making it particularly significant in edge and scrape-off-layer transport modeling where large ion flows develop. In multi-fluid transport codes, the vector is evaluated on generalized geometry grids and decomposed into cylindrical components — [radial_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), [toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), [vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia) — and a field-aligned component [parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia). The analogous turbulent contribution is given by [current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport).
NAMES.sign: Positive when each vector component points in the positive $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, or $\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, or along the local magnetic field direction for the parallel component.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction
NAMES.short: Electric current density vector driven by frictional momentum exchange between plasma ions and background neutral particles in a partially ionized plasma.
NAMES.long:
Ion-neutral-friction current density is the part of the electric current density attributable to collisional momentum exchange between plasma ions and neutral atoms or molecules. It is a full vector quantity; more specific names represent projections or components, such as [parallel current density due to ion-neutral friction](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), [radial current density due to ion-neutral friction](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and [poloidal current density due to ion-neutral friction](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction) in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

A complete vector definition is the charge-weighted velocity contribution induced by the ion-neutral friction term in the momentum balance:

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathrm{charged}} q_{\alpha} n_{\alpha} \, \delta \mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{(\mathrm{in})}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}}$ is this current density in A.m^-2, $\alpha$ labels charged species, $q_{\alpha}$ is species charge in C, $n_{\alpha}$ is number density in m^-3, and $\delta \mathbf{u}_{\alpha}^{(\mathrm{in})}$ is the mean-velocity contribution in m.s^-1 produced by ion-neutral friction. For an ion species $s$, the driving force density is often represented as $\mathbf{F}_{s n}=m_s n_s \nu_{s n}(\mathbf{u}_n-\mathbf{u}_s)$, where $m_s$ is ion mass in kg, $\nu_{s n}$ is an ion-neutral momentum-transfer frequency in s^-1, $\mathbf{u}_s$ and $\mathbf{u}_n$ are ion and neutral velocities in m.s^-1, and $\mathbf{F}_{s n}$ is in N.m^-3; this identifies the frictional source without imposing a perpendicular, parallel, or diamagnetic approximation.

In practice this quantity is computed by isolating the ion-neutral friction term in a fluid, drift-kinetic, or neutral-plasma momentum balance using ion and neutral densities, temperatures, flow velocities, and collision rates. It is usually inferred from modeling constrained by edge and divertor diagnostics rather than measured directly; radial, toroidal, and vertical projections use the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, while poloidal projections use an explicitly specified flux coordinate set such as $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

Typical magnitudes in partially ionized edge and divertor plasmas range from 1-10^4 A.m^-2. Values can be below 1 A.m^-2 where neutral density or momentum-transfer rate is small, while localized dense, cold divertor regions can reach 10^4-10^5 A.m^-2.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component points along its named positive direction, for example $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, or along the magnetic field for a parallel projection.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
NAMES.short: Full current density vector produced by the divergence of the field-aligned component of the plasma viscous stress tensor. It is the viscous drift current required to balance the parallel-viscous force density against the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Current density due to parallel viscosity is the vector current associated with the force density produced by spatial variation of the field-aligned part of the plasma viscous stress tensor. It is a viscous drift-current contribution to momentum balance, distinct from currents driven by pressure gradients, inertia, resistivity, or perpendicular viscous stress.

The defining force-balance form for this contribution is:

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel} = \frac{(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel) \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel}$ is the current density due to parallel viscosity, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the parallel viscous stress tensor in Pa, $\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the corresponding viscous force density in N m$^{-3}$, equivalently Pa m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, and $B=|\mathbf{B}|$. The cross product makes this contribution locally perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$.

This current is generally inferred rather than measured directly. It is evaluated from a magnetic-field estimate and a closure or model for the field-aligned viscous stress, with the divergence capturing spatial variation of parallel viscous momentum transport. When resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, its projections include [radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity). The total radial and toroidal viscous-current components combine these with perpendicular-viscosity contributions in [radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity) and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity); [parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) is the complementary field-aligned contribution driven by perpendicular viscous stress.

Typical magnitudes are closure- and regime-dependent. Components are often 10^-2-10^2 A.m^-2 in weakly viscous core regions and can reach 10^3-10^4 A.m^-2 in steep-gradient, strong-flow-shear, or edge regions, usually remaining below the main equilibrium current density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current density vector is directed as $(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel) \times \mathbf{B}$ according to the right-hand rule.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Full current density vector arising from the divergence of the perpendicular viscous stress tensor in magnetized plasma, driving drift currents transverse to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The current density vector $\mathbf{J}_{\pi_\perp}$ quantifies the electromagnetic current generated when the divergence of the perpendicular viscous stress tensor acts on the charged-particle fluid in a magnetized plasma. Perpendicular viscosity encompasses the components of the viscous stress tensor that act transverse to the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, coupling cross-field velocity shear to momentum transport across flux surfaces and producing a drift current that enters the overall current balance.

The defining relation follows from the perpendicular projection of the two-fluid momentum equation:

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\pi_\perp} = \frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}_\perp)}{B^2}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\pi}_\perp$ is the perpendicular viscous stress tensor and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the local magnetic field magnitude. This full vector subsumes the [diamagnetic-direction projection](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and all cylindrical components resolved in the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This current is most significant in the edge and scrape-off layer where velocity shear and density gradients are steep. It is computed from two-fluid transport models that carry the full viscous stress tensor and contributes, alongside [bootstrap current density], to non-inductive current closure in the plasma momentum balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial component points in the $+R$ direction away from the symmetry axis, the toroidal component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and the vertical component points in the $+Z$ direction, all defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_viscosity
NAMES.short: Full vector current density produced by viscous-stress terms in plasma momentum balance. It represents viscosity-driven charge transport before choosing any radial, poloidal, field-aligned, perpendicular, or diamagnetic projection.
NAMES.long:
Current density due to viscosity is the vector part of the electric current density associated with viscous-stress terms in plasma momentum balance. It represents charge transport caused by the divergence of the viscous stress tensor and is defined before selecting any particular component, projection, channel, or normalization.

A useful species decomposition defines the vector contribution as the charge-weighted sum of the velocity components generated by viscous forces:

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{visc}} = \sum_s q_s n_s \mathbf{u}_{s,\mathrm{visc}}
$$

where $s$ labels species, $q_s$ is species charge in C, $n_s$ is number density in m^-3, and $\mathbf{u}_{s,\mathrm{visc}}$ is the velocity contribution in m.s^-1 driven by the viscous force density $\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\pi}_s$ in the species momentum equation. This equation defines the current contribution; determining $\mathbf{u}_{s,\mathrm{visc}}$ requires a collisional, gyroviscous, neoclassical, or transport closure for the stress tensor $\boldsymbol{\pi}_s$.

This quantity is normally computed from fluid or transport momentum balance using plasma profiles, magnetic geometry, flow, and rotation constraints rather than measured directly. Specialized names are projections or channel separations of this parent: [radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity) resolves the vector along $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; [poloidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity) is its poloidal component; [parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and [diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) identify particular field-aligned or diamagnetic contributions.

No device-independent numerical range in A.m^-2 is meaningful for the parent quantity because it aggregates components and closures that can differ by regime, collisionality, gradients, and magnetic geometry. In applications, its magnitude is usually interpreted relative to other current-density contributions, with values near zero indicating negligible viscous charge transport and larger signed values indicating that viscous stress is important in the local momentum balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component of $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{visc}}$ points along the positive direction of the explicitly stated projection basis, such as increasing $R$ for a radial component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame or the selected local magnetic-field direction for a parallel component.

NAMES.name: current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive
NAMES.short: Net plasma current driven without inductive electric-field drive, excluding the ohmic transformer contribution.
NAMES.long:
Current due to non-inductive current drive is the net toroidal component of plasma current produced without relying on the inductive loop electric field. It includes self-generated bootstrap current and externally driven contributions from neutral beams and electromagnetic waves, including lower-hybrid, electron-cyclotron, ion-cyclotron, fast-wave, electron-Bernstein, and other wave-particle current-drive mechanisms. It excludes the ohmic current associated with transformer induction.

The total non-inductive current is the poloidal-cross-section integral of the non-inductive toroidal current density in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
I_\mathrm{NI} = \int_S j_{\mathrm{NI},\phi}(R,Z)\, dA
$$

where $I_\mathrm{NI}$ is the non-inductive current in A, $S$ is the plasma poloidal cross-section in m$^2$, $j_{\mathrm{NI},\phi}$ is the non-inductive toroidal current density in A m$^{-2}$, $R$ is major radius in m, $Z$ is vertical height in m, and $dA$ is an area element in m$^2$.

In practice this quantity is inferred by combining current-density source models with measurements that constrain the total current distribution. Bootstrap current is usually evaluated from neoclassical transport using pressure gradients, collisionality, and magnetic geometry; auxiliary driven current is estimated from beam deposition, RF or wave absorption, and kinetic response models, then checked against magnetic, motional-Stark-effect, polarimetric, or current-diffusion constraints.

Representative values range from 0 A in phases with negligible non-inductive drive to $10^4$-$10^6$ A in many auxiliary-heated plasmas, and can reach several $10^6$ A in high-bootstrap-fraction or steady-state scenarios. The signed value depends on whether the driven current is co-current or counter-current relative to the chosen toroidal direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the driven plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_due_to_ohmic_induction
NAMES.short: Electric current component produced by the Ohmic resistive response to an electric field induced by changing magnetic flux. It excludes bootstrap current and externally driven non-inductive current, which are distinct drive mechanisms.
NAMES.long:
Current due to ohmic induction is the component of electric current generated when changing magnetic flux induces an electric field and a conducting medium responds through finite resistivity. It is a drive-mechanism component, not the total current from all mechanisms: bootstrap current and externally applied non-inductive drive are separate contributions. A representative specialization is [plasma current due to ohmic induction](name:plasma_current_due_to_ohmic_induction).

The current can be defined from the Ohmic current-density component crossing an oriented surface that cuts the current channel:

$$
I_\mathrm{Ohm} = \int_S \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{Ohm}\cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $S$ is the oriented surface, $d\mathbf{A}$ is its vector area element, and $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{Ohm}$ is the current density produced by the inductive electric field. In toroidal-plasma applications, $S$ is typically a poloidal cross-section at fixed $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity is usually inferred rather than measured directly as an isolated signal. Transport and current-drive analysis estimate it from loop voltage or inductive electric field, conductivity or resistivity, and current diffusion; equilibrium reconstructions constrain the total current, while component balance separates Ohmic, bootstrap, and externally driven non-inductive contributions.

Typical magnitudes in tokamak plasmas range from $10^4$-$10^7$ A, depending on device size, temperature, effective charge, and loop voltage. The Ohmic contribution can be close to the total current in purely inductive discharges, but it can be much smaller or near 0 A during strongly non-inductive operation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the Ohmic current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Number density of a plasma constituent at the internal transport barrier reference radius, where reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep local particle density gradients to form.
NAMES.long:
The internal transport barrier (ITB) is a narrow region within the plasma volume where cross-field turbulent transport is locally suppressed, enabling steep radial gradients in density, temperature, and toroidal momentum to be sustained. This name abstracts over species-specific number densities $n_s(r_\mathrm{ITB})$ evaluated at the single flux-surface radius $r_\mathrm{ITB}$ assigned to the barrier in the chosen radial coordinate (commonly normalized toroidal-flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$), spanning electrons, fuel ions, and impurity species from low-$Z$ elements such as [boron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:boron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) to high-$Z$ species such as [krypton_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:krypton_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

The quantity is a local point value — the particle count per unit volume at $r_\mathrm{ITB}$ — not a width-averaged or volume-integrated quantity; for multi-charge-state impurities the density is summed over ionization states unless a charge-state-resolved child name is used. The [electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) are representative species-specific children; [total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) provides the sum over all ion populations at the same location.

Electron densities at an ITB range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in medium-to-large tokamaks; impurity densities are lower by factors of $10^{2}$–$10^{4}$ depending on atomic number. Species-dependent measurement approaches include Thomson scattering, interferometry, and reflectometry for electrons, and charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or line emission analysis for ions and impurities.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local number density of beryllium ions at the internal transport barrier reference radius, where reduced cross-field transport can produce steep impurity density gradients.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium density at an internal transport barrier is the local number density of beryllium ions on the flux surface selected as the barrier reference location. Unless a charge state is specified separately, it is an elemental impurity ion density summed over beryllium ionization states.

The local number density is defined as the differential beryllium ion count per plasma volume evaluated at the barrier location:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}}) = \left.\frac{dN_{\mathrm{Be}}}{dV}\right|_{r=r_{\mathrm{ITB}}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the number of beryllium ions in a small plasma volume $V$, and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ denotes the flux-surface label of the internal transport barrier reference radius.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements when available, and collisional-radiative modeling, often constrained by equilibrium and transport analysis. The barrier location is identified from the region of reduced turbulent transport or steep gradients, and the beryllium density is evaluated or interpolated on that flux surface.

Typical values are trace-impurity densities compared with the bulk ion density. In plasmas with beryllium plasma-facing components or measurable beryllium influx, representative internal-transport-barrier values are often about $10^{16}$-$10^{18}$ m^-3, depending on wall source strength, confinement, ionization balance, and impurity screening.

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Unweighted local number density of carbon ions at the internal-transport-barrier reference radius. It counts carbon ion particles per unit volume, summed over ionization states when charge-state-resolved densities are combined, and excludes neutral carbon and charge weighting.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at an internal transport barrier is the local unweighted number density of carbon ions on the radial surface selected as the barrier reference. It counts ion particles per unit volume and excludes neutral carbon; it is not an electric charge density or an effective-charge weighting. It is the carbon-species counterpart of [total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and can be compared with other impurity densities at the same location.

With a dimensional radial coordinate $r$ measured in meters, the compact definition is the carbon-ion density field evaluated at the prescribed internal-transport-barrier reference radius:

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,ion}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}}) = \sum_{q=1}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})
$$

where $q$ is the carbon ion charge state, $n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}$ is the number density of carbon ions in that charge state, and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the value of the same radial coordinate at the selected ITB reference surface. All number densities in this expression are particle number densities with unit m^-3; if carbon is represented as a single elemental ion species, $n_{\mathrm{C,ion}}$ denotes the same charge-state-summed carbon ion density.

In practice, the ITB reference surface is identified from measured or reconstructed kinetic and transport behavior, and the carbon-ion density is evaluated locally on that surface rather than averaged over the full barrier width. Carbon abundance may be inferred from impurity spectroscopy together with atomic population modeling or transport analysis, with the charge-state sum made explicitly when charge-state-resolved information is available.

Typical values are highly scenario dependent. For trace-carbon conditions in confined tokamak plasmas, ITB-local carbon ion densities are often of order $10^{16}-10^{18}$ m^-3; carbon-rich wall sources, impurity injection, or strong accumulation can move the value outside this range.

NAMES.name: density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Local particle number density of a plasma constituent evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic axis is the singular innermost flux surface where $\nabla\psi = 0$, with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux, located at coordinates $(R_{\rm axis}, Z_{\rm axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. On-axis number density captures the central concentration of a given species and, for the centrally peaked profiles characteristic of H-mode confinement, is typically the profile maximum.

The on-axis value is defined as

$$
n_s^{\rm axis} = n_s(R_{\rm axis}, Z_{\rm axis})
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of species $s$ in m$^{-3}$ evaluated at the magnetic-axis location. For ion and impurity species, this quantity is summed over ionization states unless a specific charge state is designated separately, as illustrated by [carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [argon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis).

On-axis density is inferred by evaluating a fitted radial density profile at the normalized flux-coordinate origin $\rho = 0$, drawing on Thomson scattering or interferometry for electrons and charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or spectroscopic line-ratio analysis for ions. Species-specific instances span fuel ions such as [deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [electron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:electron_density_at_magnetic_axis) to high-Z impurities; the aggregate summed over all ion species is given by [total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis).

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Number density of argon ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The argon ion number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis concentration of argon impurity ions, the species-specific realization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), evaluated at the point where $\nabla\psi = 0$ (with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux) at coordinates $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Neoclassical impurity transport tends to drive high-$Z$ species inward under collisional H-mode conditions, making this on-axis value a sensitive indicator of core argon accumulation relative to outer radii, distinct from the boundary concentration captured by [argon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:argon_density_at_plasma_boundary).

Argon is introduced into fusion plasmas for radiative power balance experiments, edge cooling, and disruption mitigation; the on-axis density reflects both the seeded impurity inventory and any neoclassical inward pinch, with the peaking factor $n_\mathrm{Ar}(0)/\langle n_\mathrm{Ar}\rangle$ serving as a quantitative measure of core accumulation. On-axis impurity concentrations are typically orders of magnitude below the bulk ion density under trace-seeding conditions, increasing substantially during massive-injection disruption mitigation.

This quantity is commonly inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy of argon charge-state line emission or from soft X-ray tomography, with the magnetic axis position supplied by equilibrium reconstruction. Comparing this value with [argon_density_at_pedestal](name:argon_density_at_pedestal) characterizes the radial impurity gradient between the core and the transport barrier. The analogous on-axis density for neon is [neon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:neon_density_at_magnetic_axis), governed by the same neoclassical transport physics but with different charge-dependent accumulation rates.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local number density of beryllium ions at the magnetic axis, summed over ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium density at the magnetic axis is the local number density of beryllium impurity nuclei on the magnetic axis. The magnetic axis is the innermost location of the nested magnetic-flux surfaces, where the poloidal magnetic flux has an extremum.

The charge-state-summed beryllium density at the magnetic axis is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be,axis}} = \sum_z n_{\mathrm{Be}^{z+}}(\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{z+}}$ is the number density of beryllium in ionization state $z$, and the sum runs over the beryllium ionization states included in the species balance. In axisymmetric geometry the axis location is commonly specified by $R_\mathrm{axis}$ and $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The on-axis value is inferred from core impurity measurements such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, beryllium line spectroscopy, soft X-ray or bolometric constraints, and impurity transport analysis constrained by those diagnostics. Compared with pedestal, boundary, line-averaged, and volume-averaged beryllium densities, it characterizes radial peaking of the beryllium distribution and helps quantify core fuel dilution and impurity radiation.

Typical on-axis beryllium densities in tokamak plasmas with beryllium sources are about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}$ m^-3, depending on wall source strength, impurity screening, accumulation, and transient impurity events.

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Number density of boron ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost flux-surface singular point of the confined plasma, summed over all boron ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Boron density at the magnetic axis is the local number density of boron ions on the innermost flux-surface singular point of a magnetically confined plasma. It is a charge-state-summed impurity density, representing the total population of ionized boron regardless of ionization stage.

The on-axis boron density can be written as the sum over boron ion charge states evaluated at the magnetic axis:

$$
n_{\mathrm{B,axis}} = \sum_q n_{\mathrm{B}^{q+}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}})
$$

where $q$ indexes boron ion charge states, $n_{\mathrm{B}^{q+}}$ is the number density of charge state $q$, and $(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}})$ locates the magnetic axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height. For an axisymmetric plasma the value is independent of toroidal angle $\phi$; in three-dimensional equilibria it refers to the value on the magnetic-axis curve.

In practice, the magnetic-axis location is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction, while boron densities are inferred from spectroscopic measurements, charge-exchange or line-emission analysis, and impurity transport or collisional-radiative modeling. Because different boron charge states radiate most strongly in different temperature ranges, the charge-state-summed density generally requires a model-based reconstruction rather than a single spectral line.

Typical on-axis boron densities in tokamak core plasmas are about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Values near the upper end can occur after boronization, boron injection, or strong plasma-wall interaction, and often correspond to roughly $10^{-5}$-$10^{-2}$ of the local electron density.

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Local number density of carbon ions at the magnetic axis, summed over carbon ion charge states rather than tied to a single ionization state. It is a point value at the plasma center, not a flux-surface, line, or volume average.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at the magnetic axis is the local elemental number density of the carbon ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis, the center of the nested closed magnetic flux surfaces. Because no charge state is specified, it denotes the sum over carbon ion charge states and is not the density of a single state such as fully stripped carbon unless all carbon ions are in that state.

The charge-state sum defining the local elemental carbon ion density is

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,axis}} = \sum_{q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{C}}} n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}$ is the local number density of carbon ions in charge state $q$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the set of carbon ion charge states included in the ion population, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the magnetic-axis position.

In practice this quantity is obtained by evaluating a reconstructed or modeled carbon density distribution at the magnetic axis. Spectroscopic constraints, charge-state balance, collisional-radiative modeling, and impurity transport calculations may all contribute to the inferred elemental density, but the standard name denotes the local axis value itself, not a flux-surface average, line-integrated value, or volume-averaged impurity content.

Typical values depend strongly on wall material, impurity sources, and plasma conditions. Core carbon densities of $10^{16}-10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ are common in low-impurity plasmas, while carbon-wall operation or enhanced impurity influx can produce values approaching $10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: deposited_power
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated power deposited into a particle distribution by a given source or sink, representing the total energy transfer rate to or from that population.
NAMES.long:
The deposited power is the net rate of kinetic energy transfer from a specified source or sink to a particle distribution function, integrated over the full plasma volume. It is the volume integral of the local energy source term in the kinetic (Fokker-Planck or bounce-averaged) equation and serves as the global power-balance scalar for a single source contribution.

The deposited power $P$ is defined by integrating the volumetric power density $s_p(\mathbf{r})$ over the plasma volume $V$:

$$
P = \int_V s_p(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $s_p$ is the local energy deposition rate per unit volume in W m$^{-3}$. The local volumetric counterpart is described by [particle deposited power density].

Population-resolved specializations include [electron deposited power](name:electron_deposited_power) for the electron channel and [plasma deposited power](name:plasma_deposited_power) for the combined plasma ensemble; [total plasma deposited power](name:total_plasma_deposited_power) aggregates contributions across all sources. The quantity is computed by kinetic transport solvers that handle wave-particle interaction, neutral beam injection, and fast-particle collisional slowing-down.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the source deposits net energy into the particle distribution; negative when the source extracts net energy from the distribution.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions evaluated at the radial position of the internal transport barrier, the flux surface where turbulent cross-field transport is locally suppressed and steep radial gradients can form.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium ion number density at the internal transport barrier (ITB) characterizes the local fuel-ion concentration at the barrier's reference flux surface, where cross-field turbulent diffusion is suppressed and steep radial density gradients can persist. Internal transport barriers form when $E \times B$ velocity shear or reversed magnetic shear quenches dominant drift-wave turbulence, creating a region of locally enhanced particle confinement.

The quantity is the deuterium ion density profile $n_D(\rho)$ evaluated at the ITB reference radius $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$:

$$
n_D^\mathrm{ITB} = n_D(\rho_\mathrm{ITB})
$$

where $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the ITB position in the chosen radial coordinate, such as the normalized toroidal flux radius, and corresponds to the surface where the transport suppression is most pronounced.

In practice, this value is inferred from Thomson scattering, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or reflectometry measurements resolved at the barrier location, combined with equilibrium reconstruction to map measurement positions to flux-surface coordinates.

The parent quantity [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) covers all constituent species using the same locus convention. The analogous fuel-ion siblings for hydrogen and tritium are [hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The pedestal counterpart for deuterium is [deuterium_density_at_pedestal](name:deuterium_density_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when deuterium ions are present; particle number density is an intrinsically non-negative quantity.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density at the magnetic axis is the local number density of ionized deuterium fuel at the center of the nested closed flux surfaces. It counts deuterium ions, normally fully ionized $D^+$ in the hot core, and excludes neutral deuterium atoms.

The quantity is the deuterium number-density field evaluated at the magnetic-axis point:

$$
n_{D,\mathrm{axis}} = n_D(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}) = \left.\frac{dN_D}{dV}\right|_{\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density, $N_D$ is the number of deuterium ions in an infinitesimal volume $V$, and $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}$ is the point where $\nabla\psi=0$ for the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$.

In practice this value is obtained by evaluating the deuterium density at the reconstructed magnetic axis. It may be constrained by isotope-resolved density measurements, neutron emission, particle-balance modeling, and quasineutrality using electron density, impurity content, and other ion-species densities. It is closely related to the full deuterium density distribution [deuterium_density](name:deuterium_density), the electron density on axis [electron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:electron_density_at_magnetic_axis), and the summed ion density on axis [total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis).

Typical on-axis values in tokamak plasmas are $0.1-5 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with lower values in low-density or weakly fueled discharges and higher values in dense deuterium or deuterium-tritium scenarios.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_flux
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short: Total neutron emission rate from deuterium-deuterium fusion through the neutron-producing D(d,n)He-3 branch. It includes thermal, beam-thermal, and beam-beam deuteron reactions; each counted reaction emits one 2.45 MeV neutron.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-deuterium neutron flux is the global rate at which neutrons are produced by the neutron branch of DD fusion, $\mathrm{D(d,n)^3He}$. It counts neutron-producing reactions from all relevant deuteron populations, including thermal bulk ions, beam ions reacting with thermal deuterons, and beam ions reacting with other fast deuterons.

The total DD neutron emission rate can be written as the sum of thermal, beam-thermal, and beam-beam contributions:

$$
S_{\mathrm{DD},n} = S_{\mathrm{th},n} + S_{\mathrm{bt},n} + S_{\mathrm{bb},n} = \int_V \left[\frac{1}{2} n_{\mathrm{D,th}}^2 \langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{DD},n}^{\mathrm{th}} + R_{\mathrm{bt},n} + R_{\mathrm{bb},n}\right] dV
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{DD},n}$ is the total neutron rate in Hz, $S_{\mathrm{th},n}$, $S_{\mathrm{bt},n}$, and $S_{\mathrm{bb},n}$ are the thermal, beam-thermal, and beam-beam parts, $n_{\mathrm{D,th}}$ is the thermal deuterium density, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{DD},n}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the branch reactivity for $\mathrm{D(d,n)^3He}$, and $R_{\mathrm{bt},n}$ and $R_{\mathrm{bb},n}$ are local volumetric neutron production rates from beam-thermal and beam-beam reactions. The factor $1/2$ avoids double counting identical thermal deuteron pairs.

Experimentally, this rate is inferred from absolutely calibrated neutron diagnostics such as fission chambers, activation systems, scintillators, or proportional counters, with corrections for detector efficiency, geometry, attenuation, and neutron energy response. In modeling and transport analysis, the thermal part corresponds to [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion), the beam-thermal part to [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion), and the beam-beam part to [deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion).

Typical DD neutron rates range from about $10^{10}$-$10^{14}$ Hz in low-power or ohmic deuterium plasmas, $10^{14}$-$10^{16}$ Hz in hotter medium-sized tokamak plasmas, and up to $10^{17}$-$10^{18}$ Hz when strong neutral-beam heating produces a large fast-deuteron population.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Ion number density of the fictitious combined deuterium-tritium fuel pseudo-species, equal to the sum of the local deuterium and tritium ion densities in transport models treating both isotopes as one effective ion.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-tritium density is the local ion count per unit volume belonging to the fictitious combined fuel pseudo-species formed by merging the deuterium and tritium populations into a single effective ion. This simplification reduces the fuel ion description to a single continuity equation and is employed in transport simulations that do not resolve D and T as separately evolved species.

The DT pseudo-species density $n_{DT}$ equals the sum of the individual isotope number densities:

$$
n_{DT} = n_D + n_T
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density and $n_T$ is the tritium ion number density.

The local density is inferred from neutron emission profiles, hydrogen isotope spectroscopy, or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with charge-state balance. In integrated modeling, it is evolved by a continuity equation incorporating ionization, recombination, and transport source terms. The volume average of this quantity is [volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density), and the on-axis value is [deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis). When D and T are resolved as separate species, the individual isotope densities are tracked by [volume_averaged_deuterium_density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_density) and [volume_averaged_tritium_density](name:volume_averaged_tritium_density).

Typical core values in DT burning plasmas range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, decreasing toward the edge and scrape-off layer.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Number density of the fictitious single-species deuterium-tritium fuel ion, with mass 2.5 amu, evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier. It is the local ITB value used when deuterium and tritium are modeled as one effective species.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-tritium density at the internal transport barrier is the number density of a fictitious fuel-ion species that combines deuterium and tritium into one effective constituent with mass 2.5 amu. It represents the density value at the radial location where an internal transport barrier produces a localized reduction of cross-field transport and can support steep gradients. This is a local radial evaluation of the DT density, not a volume average over the plasma or an average over the finite barrier width.

The ITB value is the DT density evaluated at the barrier radial label:

$$
n_{\mathrm{DT,ITB}} = n_{\mathrm{DT}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{DT,ITB}}$ is the DT density at the internal transport barrier in m$^{-3}$, $n_{\mathrm{DT}}(r)$ is the fictitious DT number density as a function of radial label $r$, and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the radial label of the internal transport barrier. The label may be a minor-radius-like radial coordinate in meters or a named flux coordinate such as normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$.

In practice, the barrier location is identified from kinetic measurements and transport analysis, for example by a localized steepening of density or temperature gradients, reduced turbulent transport, or strong shear in $\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}$ flow. The DT value is obtained by evaluating or interpolating $n_{\mathrm{DT}}$ at $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$; if $n_{\mathrm{DT}}$ represents a flux-surface-averaged radial density, then this quantity is the value of that average on the ITB flux surface rather than an additional average over the barrier width. Related quantities distinguish the same effective species at other landmarks, such as [deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis), from separate-isotope values such as [deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and from normalized fuel-content measures such as [ratio_of_deuterium_tritium_density_to_electron_density](name:ratio_of_deuterium_tritium_density_to_electron_density).

Representative modeled ITB-region values are typically of order $0.1-2 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in magnetically confined deuterium-tritium scenarios. The value depends on fueling, isotope mix, confinement regime, and whether the effective DT species is used instead of separate deuterium and tritium populations.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Number density of a fictitious single-species deuterium-tritium fuel ion mixture, representing equal deuterium and tritium number densities with mean atomic mass 2.5 amu, evaluated at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the ion number density at the magnetic axis for a fictitious single deuterium-tritium fuel species. The species represents an equimolar deuterium-tritium mixture, so the deuterium and tritium number densities are equal and the arithmetic-mean ion mass is about 2.5 atomic mass units. It is used in single-fluid transport descriptions where separate isotope densities are not evolved.

The axial value is the value of the fictitious deuterium-tritium density at the magnetic-axis position:

$$
n_{\mathrm{DT},0} = n_{\mathrm{DT}}(R_0, Z_0), \qquad n_{\mathrm{D}}(R_0, Z_0) = n_{\mathrm{T}}(R_0, Z_0) = \frac{1}{2} n_{\mathrm{DT},0}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{DT},0}$ is the axial fictitious-DT number density, $n_{\mathrm{DT}}$ is the local fictitious-DT fuel-ion density, $n_{\mathrm{D}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{T}}$ are the isotope-resolved densities implied by the equimolar mixture, and $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the magnetic-axis location in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The magnetic axis is the extremum of the poloidal magnetic flux, equivalently $\nabla\psi=0$ in the poloidal plane for an axisymmetric equilibrium.

In practice this quantity is obtained from transport modeling, equilibrium-constrained density reconstruction, or interpretive analysis combining fuel-composition information with total ion-density constraints. Neutron emission constrains the deuterium-tritium reaction rate and hence the product of deuterium and tritium densities, while charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, neutral-particle analysis, electron density, impurity content, and quasineutrality provide complementary constraints on the fuel-ion density and isotope mix.

Typical central values in reactor-relevant deuterium-tritium core simulations are $0.3-2 \times 10^{20}$ m^-3. Lower-density experiments or non-burning scenarios may have equivalent axial DT densities of $10^{18}-10^{19}$ m^-3, depending on fueling, confinement, dilution by impurities or helium ash, and operational density limits.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
NAMES.short: Signed scalar component, along the local diamagnetic direction, of the perpendicular current density generated by the divergence of the parallel viscous stress tensor. The diamagnetic direction is parallel to the magnetic field crossed with the pressure gradient.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic current density due to parallel viscosity is the signed scalar component, along the local diamagnetic direction, of the perpendicular current density driven by the divergence of the parallel viscous stress tensor. The diamagnetic direction is the unit vector parallel to $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field and $p$ is the plasma pressure.

The parallel viscous force density acts as a body force in the fluid momentum balance, and its perpendicular current response is projected onto the diamagnetic direction:

$$
j_{\pi_\parallel,\mathrm{dia}} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\frac{(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel)\times\mathbf{B}}{B^2},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p}{|\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p|}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the parallel viscous stress tensor (in Pa, equivalently N m^-2), $\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the associated viscous force density (in N m^-3), $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field (in T) with $B=|\mathbf{B}|$, $p$ is the plasma pressure (in Pa), and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic unit vector defined where $|\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p|$ is nonzero. The vector $(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel)\times\mathbf{B}/B^2$ is the full perpendicular current density associated with the force density, and the dot product retains only its diamagnetic component. Dimensionally this scales as force density divided by magnetic-field strength, $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}/\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$.

This quantity is computed rather than measured directly. The parallel viscous stress is obtained from kinetic, neoclassical, or fluid closures using plasma density, temperature, flow, collisionality, and magnetic-geometry gradients; its divergence is converted to a perpendicular current and projected onto $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}$. Diagnostic measurements constrain the equilibrium and kinetic inputs used in the calculation. The magnitude is largest where the parallel viscous stress and the pressure gradient are both strong, such as in edge and pedestal transport layers, and small in weak-gradient core regions.

This quantity is the diamagnetic projection of the parent vector [current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), which also admits other directional projections such as [radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity). Together with [diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and [diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) it forms the viscosity-channel decomposition that contributes to the total_diamagnetic_current_density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the parallel-viscosity-driven perpendicular current density has a component in the direction of $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p$.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Diamagnetic-direction component of the current density generated by perpendicular viscous stress. The direction is perpendicular to the magnetic field and the plasma pressure gradient, with orientation set by the local magnetic-field cross pressure-gradient basis.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic current density due to perpendicular viscosity is the scalar component of the current density driven by perpendicular viscous stress in the local diamagnetic direction. It represents the part of the viscosity-driven current that is aligned with the drift-like direction perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the plasma pressure gradient, rather than the poloidal, toroidal, or field-parallel directions.

The scalar projection is defined using the pressure-gradient diamagnetic unit vector:

$$
j_{\mathrm{dia},\pi_\perp}
=
\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\mathbf{j}_{\pi_\perp},
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}
=
\frac{\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p}{|\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p|}
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{dia},\pi_\perp}$ is in A m^-2, $\mathbf{j}_{\pi_\perp}$ is the vector current density contribution due to perpendicular viscous stress in A m^-2, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $p$ is the plasma pressure in Pa, and $\nabla p$ is the pressure gradient in Pa m^-1. In flux-surface descriptions where $p=p(\psi)$, the pressure gradient is collinear with the poloidal magnetic-flux gradient $\nabla\psi$; a basis written with $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla\psi$ therefore represents the same local diamagnetic direction up to the sign of $dp/d\psi$, while this definition fixes the scalar sign by the pressure-gradient diamagnetic basis.

This quantity is normally computed from a fluid or transport model that evaluates the divergence of the perpendicular viscous stress tensor and then projects the resulting current contribution onto $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}$. It is not usually measured directly; it is inferred from modeled momentum balance, magnetic geometry, and pressure-gradient information. Closely related projections of the same perpendicular-viscosity current are the poloidal, toroidal, and parallel components, while the diamagnetic component due to parallel viscosity isolates the same projection direction for a different viscous stress contribution.

Representative magnitudes are highly model- and regime-dependent. In weak-gradient regions the value is often close to 0 A m^-2, while transport calculations with strong pressure and flow-shear gradients may give order-of-magnitude values around 1-10000 A m^-2; this range is a practical scale for interpretation, not a universal bound.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vector current density due to perpendicular viscous stress projects along the local diamagnetic basis direction $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}=\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p/|\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p|$.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Effective charge Zeff of the plasma ion mixture evaluated at the internal transport barrier, defined as the charge-squared-weighted mean charge number over all ion species.
NAMES.long:
The effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ characterizes the ionic composition of a magnetically confined plasma by weighting each ion species by the square of its charge number relative to the first charge moment, yielding a single dimensionless index of impurity content.

The defining relation is

$$
Z_\text{eff} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{\sum_s n_s Z_s}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$ (summed over all charge states) and $Z_s$ is its charge number. A pure single-species hydrogenic plasma gives $Z_\text{eff} = 1$; the presence of higher-$Z$ impurities always raises $Z_\text{eff}$ above unity.

Evaluated at the internal transport barrier (ITB), this quantity captures the local effective charge where turbulent transport is suppressed and kinetic profile gradients are steep — the same reference location used by [electron density at the ITB](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [electron temperature at the ITB](name:electron_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier). Local impurity accumulation or expulsion near the ITB can shift the local $Z_\text{eff}$ considerably from its volume-averaged value.

The effective charge is inferred spectroscopically from the free-free bremsstrahlung continuum, whose radiated intensity scales as $n_e^2 Z_\text{eff} T_e^{-1/2}$ where $n_e$ is the electron number density and $T_e$ is the electron temperature, or from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy summed over resolved ion species. In clean deuterium discharges $Z_\text{eff}$ approaches 1.0, rising to 3–5 in high-impurity or metallic-wall scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when any ionized species populate the plasma, which is always the case in a magnetically confined discharge; the lower bound $Z_\text{eff} = 1$ is attained only for a hypothetically impurity-free single-species plasma.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Effective charge at the magnetic axis is the local density-weighted mean of squared ion charge numbers, summed over ion species or charge states and normalized by electron density. It quantifies how on-axis impurities increase collisionality relative to a pure hydrogen-isotope plasma.
NAMES.long:
Effective charge at the magnetic axis is the local value of [effective_charge](name:effective_charge) evaluated on the magnetic axis, the center of the nested magnetic flux surfaces. It is not the arithmetic mean ion charge; because the charge number is squared, highly charged impurity ions contribute disproportionately even at small density fractions.

For a plasma with local electron density and ion species or charge-state densities, the on-axis effective charge is defined as:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff,axis}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}) Z_s^2}{n_e(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}})}
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species or ionization states present at the magnetic axis, $n_s$ is the corresponding ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $Z_s$ is the positive ion charge number in units of the elementary charge, $n_e$ is the electron density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ denotes the magnetic-axis location. For a quasineutral plasma, $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$ locally, so the ratio has unit 1.

In practice the quantity is computed from a local estimate of plasma composition at the magnetic axis. That composition may be inferred from a combination of electron-density information, impurity measurements, radiation constraints, and transport or atomic-physics modeling; no single diagnostic defines it universally.

Representative on-axis values are $Z_{\mathrm{eff,axis}}=1$ for a pure hydrogen-isotope plasma and about 1-3 for many low-to-moderate impurity tokamak cores. Larger values indicate a stronger contribution from high-charge impurity ions or unusually impurity-rich conditions.

NAMES.name: effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Velocity-like transport coefficient that multiplies the local density of a transported species or quantity to yield the advective (pinch) contribution in a flux-surface-averaged plasma transport equation.
NAMES.long:
The effective convection velocity is the advective coefficient in flux-surface-averaged plasma transport equations; its product with the local density of the transported quantity (particle number, momentum, or energy density) gives the convective flux contribution through closed flux surfaces. It generalizes pinch velocity concepts, subsuming bulk plasma flow, neoclassical Ware pinch, and turbulence-driven advection into a single signed transport coefficient. Species- and channel-specific forms include [ion_charge_state_effective_convection_velocity](name:ion_charge_state_effective_convection_velocity) for charge-state-resolved particle transport, [momentum_effective_convection_velocity](name:momentum_effective_convection_velocity) for the ion momentum channel, and [neutral_state_effective_convection_velocity](name:neutral_state_effective_convection_velocity) for state-resolved neutral transport.

The convective flux $\Gamma_\text{conv}$ of the transported quantity is given by:

$$
\Gamma_\text{conv} = V_\text{eff} \, f
$$

where $f$ is the relevant local density (particle number density, momentum density, or energy density) and $V_\text{eff}$ is the effective convection velocity. This decomposition separates the advective (pinch) contribution from the diffusive term $-D \nabla f$ in standard flux-surface-averaged transport equations.

The coefficient is extracted by integrated transport analysis through fitting the advective term to experimentally observed profile evolution, or computed from turbulent flux models such as quasi-linear or nonlinear gyrokinetic calculations. The parent quantity convection_velocity defines the general family, and convected_velocity is the related pure advective velocity. Typical magnitudes in confined tokamak plasmas range from sub-meter-per-second values in the core to tens of meters per second near the pedestal, with sign encoding inward or outward advection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when directed radially outward, in the direction of increasing minor radius from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: electric_field
NAMES.short: Electric field vector giving the electric force per unit positive stationary test charge at a plasma location, excluding the magnetic part of the Lorentz force. It includes electrostatic contributions from scalar-potential gradients and inductive contributions from time-varying magnetic flux.
NAMES.long:
The electric field $\mathbf{E}$ is a vector field that gives the electric force per unit positive stationary test charge. It represents the electric part of electromagnetic interaction, distinct from the magnetic velocity-dependent force on a moving charge.
