where $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{DD}}^{\mathrm{bt}}$ is in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, numerically Hz; $f_{\mathrm{D,b}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{D,th}}$ are fast-beam and thermal-deuteron velocity-space densities with units $\mathrm{m}^{-3}(\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^{-3}$; $v_{\mathrm{rel}}=|\mathbf{v}_b-\mathbf{v}_t|$ is the relative speed in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$; $\sigma_n$ is the cross section in $\mathrm{m}^2$ for the neutron branch $\mathrm{D(d,n)^3He}$; $d^3v_b$ and $d^3v_t$ have units $(\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^3$; and $dV$ has units $\mathrm{m}^3$. No factor of $1/2$ appears because the fast and thermal populations are treated as distinct reactant classes; if a total DD fusion cross section is used instead of $\sigma_n$, it must be weighted by the energy-dependent neutron-branch fraction.

In practice this rate is computed from the overlap of the fast-deuteron distribution produced by neutral-beam deposition and slowing down with the thermal deuterium density and temperature. It is constrained by total neutron yield measurements, neutron cameras, activation systems, and models that decompose the DD neutron signal into thermonuclear, beam-thermal, and beam-beam components. The rate increases with beam power, fast-ion confinement, thermal deuterium density, and the fraction of fast ions in the DD fusion cross-section energy range.

Typical values are 0 Hz when either deuterium neutral-beam ions or thermal deuterium fuel are absent, about $10^{10}$-$10^{13}$ Hz in low-power or small-device deuterium-beam plasmas, $10^{13}$-$10^{16}$ Hz in many medium and large tokamak beam-heated deuterium plasmas, and up to about $10^{17}$ Hz in high-power scenarios with strong fast-ion confinement.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Neutron flux from deuterium-tritium fusion between neutral-beam fast ions and thermal plasma ions, expressed as the global neutron emission rate.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium-tritium beam-thermal neutron flux is the total neutron emission rate from D-T fusion reactions in which one reactant is a neutral-beam-injected fast ion and the other is a thermal plasma ion. It includes both fast deuterons reacting with thermal tritons and fast tritons reacting with thermal deuterons, and excludes beam-beam and thermal-thermal reactions. Because each D-T fusion reaction produces one neutron, the quantity is a volume-integrated reaction rate with unit Hz.

With velocity-space distribution functions normalized to physical density, the beam-thermal D-T neutron rate is

$$
\Phi_{n,DT}^{BT} = \int_V d^3x \int d^3v_b \int d^3v_t\, \sigma_{DT}(v_\mathrm{rel})\, v_\mathrm{rel}\, \left[ f_{D,b}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}_b) f_{T,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}_t) + f_{T,b}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}_b) f_{D,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}_t) \right]
$$

where $V$ is the emitting plasma volume, $\sigma_{DT}$ is the D-T fusion cross-section, $v_\mathrm{rel}=|\mathbf{v}_b-\mathbf{v}_t|$, $f_{D,b}$ and $f_{T,b}$ are fast-ion distributions from neutral-beam injection, and $f_{D,\mathrm{th}}$ and $f_{T,\mathrm{th}}$ are thermal-ion distributions. Each distribution is normalized by $\int f_{s,k}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v=n_{s,k}(\mathbf{x})$, so $f$ has units of density per velocity-space volume and the integral has units of s$^{-1}$. The two terms represent fast D on thermal T and fast T on thermal D; retaining the thermal velocity integral avoids reducing the expression to a cold-target approximation.

In practice this component is inferred from absolutely calibrated neutron measurements together with beam deposition, fast-ion transport, and thermal density and temperature information. Neutron spectra, time response, and spatial emissivity can help separate beam-thermal emission from beam-beam and thermal-thermal components. The reported value is the total source rate integrated over the emitting plasma volume, not a detector count rate or a neutron flux through a surface.

Typical values range from $10^{12}$-$10^{15}$ Hz in trace-tritium or low-power beam-heated experiments, $10^{15}$-$10^{17}$ Hz in present high-performance D-T tokamak discharges, and can approach or exceed $10^{18}$ Hz in reactor-scale beam-heated plasmas, depending on beam power, fast-ion confinement, fuel mix, and ion temperature.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions at the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of helium ions whose nuclei have mass number 3, evaluated at the barrier reference location. In the hot plasma core, helium-3 is usually fully ionized, so this counts ions rather than electron charge density. It is the isotope-resolved helium-3 counterpart of [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

For a barrier location labeled by normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, the value is defined by evaluating the helium-3 ion density at that location:

$$
n_{{}^3\mathrm{He},\mathrm{ITB}} = n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}\!\left(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm,ITB}}\right)
$$

where $n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}$ is the helium-3 ion number density field and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm,ITB}}$ is the internal-transport-barrier reference location expressed as normalized toroidal flux radius.

In practice, the helium-3 density is inferred by combining isotope-composition measurements, spectroscopy or neutral-particle information when available, particle-balance constraints, and transport analysis constrained by electron density and effective charge. The barrier location is identified from reduced cross-field transport or steep gradients in quantities such as temperature, density, or pressure, then mapped to the same radial label used for the density evaluation.

Typical values are about $10^{17}$-$10^{19}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ for trace or minority helium-3 populations. Dedicated helium-3-rich or minority-heating scenarios can reach $10^{19}$-$10^{20}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, depending on fueling, confinement, and dilution by other ion species.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost flux-surface center of the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 density at the magnetic axis is the number of helium-3 ions per unit volume at the innermost flux-surface center of the confined plasma. The magnetic axis is the location where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes; in an axisymmetric equilibrium it is specified by $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The on-axis density is the local helium-3 number density evaluated at the magnetic-axis position:

$$
n_{^{3}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{axis}} = n_{^{3}\mathrm{He}}(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $n_{^{3}\mathrm{He},\mathrm{axis}}$ and $n_{^{3}\mathrm{He}}$ are helium-3 ion number densities in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ gives the magnetic-axis location in the poloidal plane.

In practice this quantity is obtained by mapping isotope-resolved density information onto magnetic flux surfaces from an equilibrium reconstruction and taking the innermost value. Helium-3 densities may be inferred from neutral-particle analysis, spectroscopy, particle-balance modeling, fueling rates, and integrated transport analysis, depending on whether helium-3 is a trace species, a minority-heating species, or a fuel component.

Typical values are near zero in plasmas without intentional helium-3 fueling, about $10^{17}$-$10^{19}$ m^-3 in helium-3 minority experiments, and up to order $10^{20}$ m^-3 when helium-3 is a major fuel ion.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-4 ions, the principal ash product of deuterium-tritium fusion, evaluated at the radial position where the internal transport barrier suppresses cross-field turbulent transport.
NAMES.long:
Helium-4, with mass number 4 (two protons and two neutrons), is the dominant particle ash produced by deuterium-tritium reactions via $\mathrm{D} + \mathrm{T} \rightarrow {}^4\mathrm{He} + n$. This quantity gives the local particle number density of helium-4 ions at the flux-surface position of the internal transport barrier (ITB), a radial layer where turbulent cross-field heat and particle transport are locally suppressed and steep radial gradients in density, temperature, and rotation can be sustained.

The ITB-localized density is a point evaluation of the continuous radial helium-4 profile:

$$
n_{\mathrm{He4,ITB}} = n_{\mathrm{He4}}(\rho_\mathrm{ITB})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{He4}}(\rho)$ is the helium-4 density profile, $\rho$ is a normalized radial coordinate (typically the square root of normalized toroidal flux), and $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the barrier location, identified by a local minimum in the turbulent ion heat diffusivity.

Helium-4 density profiles are inferred via charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy on helium emission lines or through impurity transport modeling constrained by spectroscopic measurements. Elevated helium-4 density at the ITB can indicate reduced helium flushing from the core, relevant for assessing fuel dilution in burning plasmas. This quantity is the helium-4 analog of [helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and complements [helium_4_density_at_pedestal](name:helium_4_density_at_pedestal) and [helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary) in characterizing the radial helium-4 distribution. For the full species family at the ITB, see [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when helium-4 ions are present at the barrier location; this quantity is invariant under reversal of the toroidal magnetic field direction or plasma current orientation, as it represents a non-negative particle count per unit volume.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-4 ions — the primary ash product of deuterium-tritium fusion reactions — evaluated at the magnetic axis, where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Helium-4, the stable isotope with two protons and two neutrons, accumulates as fusion ash in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas as thermalized alpha particles reach thermal equilibrium with the bulk plasma. Its number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis value of the radial He-4 concentration profile, evaluated at the geometric center $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ of the nested flux-surface family in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — where $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height — at which the poloidal magnetic flux satisfies $\nabla\psi = 0$.

This quantity is the He-4 specialization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), directly analogous to [helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis) for the He-3 isotope. The ratio of this on-axis value to the on-axis electron density characterizes the degree of ash accumulation: elevated He-4 fractions dilute the D-T fuel and increase bremsstrahlung losses, degrading fusion performance. Comparing the on-axis value against [helium_4_density_at_pedestal](name:helium_4_density_at_pedestal) and [helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary) maps the radial He-4 concentration gradient that drives ash transport from the core toward the boundary.

The He-4 density profile is measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy targeting He-4 emission lines, or inferred from $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ spectroscopy combined with particle balance analysis. In deuterium-tritium burning plasmas the on-axis He-4 density can reach values on the order of a few percent of the electron density before ash dilution becomes performance-limiting.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Local number density of hydrogen (protium) ions in the plasma, giving the count of H+ particles per unit volume at a specified spatial position.
NAMES.long:
The hydrogen density quantifies the local concentration of protium ions ($^1$H$^+$, the lightest hydrogen isotope with mass number $A = 1$) at a point in the plasma. It is distinct from the neutral atomic hydrogen density and from the number densities of heavier hydrogenic isotopes such as deuterium ($^2$H) and tritium ($^3$H).

The number density $n_H$ at position $\mathbf{r}$ is defined as

$$
n_H(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{dN_H}{dV}
$$

where $N_H$ is the number of hydrogen ions within the infinitesimal volume element $dV$ centered at $\mathbf{r}$.

Spatially averaged forms provide experimentally accessible measures of the same quantity: [line_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:line_averaged_hydrogen_density) gives the path-length-normalized ion count along a spectroscopic or interferometric chord, while [volume_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_hydrogen_density) integrates the ion content over the full plasma volume. The isotopic composition of the hydrogenic fuel is tracked by [ratio_of_hydrogen_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density](name:ratio_of_hydrogen_density_to_total_hydrogenic_density), which expresses $n_H$ relative to the combined protium, deuterium, and tritium ion density. The aggregate over all three hydrogen isotopes is given by hydrogenic_density, and the full multi-species ion sum by [total_ion_density](name:total_ion_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when hydrogen ions are present at the specified location.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen ions at the radial location of the internal transport barrier, where suppressed turbulent transport enables steep particle density gradients to develop.
NAMES.long:
The hydrogen ion number density at the internal transport barrier quantifies the local concentration of hydrogen (protium, $^1$H) ions at the ITB radius — the radial position in the plasma core where cross-field turbulent transport is significantly reduced, allowing steep gradients in density and pressure to be sustained. As the lightest hydrogenic species, hydrogen may serve as the primary fuel ion or a minority constituent depending on the operational scenario, and its density at the ITB directly reflects the local particle transport balance between source, diffusion, and convection.

This quantity is the hydrogen ion number density profile $n_H(r)$ evaluated at $r_\mathrm{ITB}$, the barrier radius identified from a minimum in the local particle diffusivity or a maximum of the logarithmic pressure gradient. The parent quantity [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) defines this evaluation framework for any plasma constituent.

The hydrogen density at the ITB is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or from interferometric line-integrated density measurements combined with impurity-profile modeling. The analogous measurement for the dominant deuterium fuel species is [deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier); light and heavy impurity contributions at the same location are captured by [carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The hydrogen ion density at the plasma edge is separately characterized by [hydrogen_density_at_limiter](name:hydrogen_density_at_limiter).

NAMES.name: hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen (protium) ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The hydrogen ion number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis value of the radial hydrogen density profile, sampled at the geometric center $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — the innermost point of the nested flux-surface family where $\nabla\psi = 0$, with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux. This is a local point value and not a flux-surface average.

Under the quasi-neutrality constraint, the on-axis hydrogen ion density $n_H$ is linked to the electron number density $n_e$ and co-existing ion species densities $n_s$ of charge number $Z_s$ via:

$$
n_H = n_e - \sum_{s \neq H} Z_s \, n_s
$$

where the sum runs over all non-hydrogen ion species present.

In practice, this value is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or derived from the quasi-neutrality condition when electron and impurity densities are independently constrained by Thomson scattering and interferometry. It serves as the on-axis anchor of the radial hydrogen density profile, complementing the edge values captured by [hydrogen_density_at_pedestal](name:hydrogen_density_at_pedestal) and [hydrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:hydrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary). The species-analogous quantity for deuterium fuel ions is [deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis).

Typical on-axis hydrogen ion densities in tokamak plasmas range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on fueling scenario, plasma current, and auxiliary heating power.
NAMES.sign: Positive when hydrogen ions are present at the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: implicit_source_rate
NAMES.short: Linearization rate coefficient for the stiff portion of a plasma source term in transport equations, equal to the net implicit source contribution per unit of the local transported quantity.
NAMES.long:
In transport solvers that decompose source terms into explicit and implicit (stiff) contributions, the implicit source rate is the linearization coefficient for the quantity-dependent portion of the total source. This decomposition applies uniformly to particle, energy, and momentum transport channels, making this quantity a general concept spanning all transported scalar quantities in a plasma transport model.

The transport balance for a generic transported quantity $Q$ (particle number density, energy density, or momentum density) reads:

$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{\Gamma} = S_{\rm exp} + S_{\rm imp} \cdot Q
$$

where $\mathbf{\Gamma}$ is the associated transport flux and $S_{\rm exp}$ is the explicit (non-stiff) source contribution independent of $Q$. By isolating the $Q$-proportional component as $S_{\rm imp} \cdot Q$, implicit time-advancement schemes can invert this term analytically, avoiding the severe time-step restrictions imposed by fast atomic processes such as ionization and recombination.

Species- and channel-resolved forms include [electron_implicit_source_rate](name:electron_implicit_source_rate) for the electron particle channel and energy_implicit_source_rate for plasma energy transport. Values are derived from atomic physics databases and collision rate models; magnitudes span several orders of magnitude depending on local plasma density and temperature.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the implicit term acts as a net source that increases the transported quantity; negative when it acts as a net sink.

NAMES.name: electron_implicit_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Implicit (stiff) rate coefficient for the electron particle source in transport equations, multiplied by the local electron density to give the source contribution treated implicitly.
NAMES.long:
Electron implicit source rate is the coefficient that represents the stiff, density-proportional part of the electron particle source in a particle-balance transport equation. It converts the local electron density into an implicit source-density contribution, so its dimensions are inverse time rather than particles per volume per time.

The source decomposition can be written in unit-balanced form as:

$$
S_e = S_{e,\mathrm{exp}} + \gamma_{e,\mathrm{imp}} n_e
$$

where $S_e$ is the total electron particle source density, $S_{e,\mathrm{exp}}$ is the part advanced explicitly, $\gamma_{e,\mathrm{imp}}$ is the electron implicit source rate, and $n_e$ is the local electron density; $S_e$ and $S_{e,\mathrm{exp}}$ have units of m^-3 s^-1 when $n_e$ is in m^-3.

It is usually computed rather than measured directly. Atomic and molecular processes such as electron-impact ionization contribute positive density-proportional terms, while radiative and three-body recombination contribute negative terms; transport models may also include linearized fueling, recycling, or other external particle sources according to the numerical implicit-explicit split. It is the electron-particle counterpart of [electron_energy_implicit_source_rate](name:electron_energy_implicit_source_rate) and is coupled to ion source coefficients through ionization balance and quasineutrality.

Typical values are near zero for weakly sourced core regions, about 10^-3-10 s^-1 for particle replacement on confinement-time scales, and can reach 10^2-10^5 s^-1 in cold edge, recycling, or localized strong-source regions where atomic timescales are short. Negative values of similar magnitude can occur where recombination or net particle removal dominates.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the implicit term $\gamma_{e,\mathrm{imp}} n_e$ increases the electron number density.

NAMES.name: energy_implicit_source_rate
NAMES.short: Linearization rate coefficient for the stiff portion of a plasma energy source term in transport equations, equal to the net implicit energy source contribution per unit of local energy density.
NAMES.long:
In plasma transport solvers, source terms are decomposed into explicit and stiff (implicit) contributions to ensure numerical stability across disparate energy-exchange time scales. The energy implicit source rate is the linearization coefficient for the energy-density-dependent portion of the total volumetric energy source, and it has dimensions of inverse time.

The implicit energy source contribution is written as:

$$
S_E^{\rm impl} = \gamma_E \cdot \mathcal{E}
$$

where $\gamma_E$ is the energy implicit source rate and $\mathcal{E}$ is the local energy density (or temperature proxy, depending on solver convention) of the species. Stiff processes such as collisional thermalization, radiative cooling, or resonant wave heating are handled via this implicit decomposition to avoid prohibitively small time steps in the transport solver.

This rate applies to any plasma species energy channel: for the electron energy balance, see [electron_energy_implicit_source_rate](name:electron_energy_implicit_source_rate); for a single ion charge state, see [ion_state_energy_implicit_source_rate](name:ion_state_energy_implicit_source_rate). Both are specializations of the more general [implicit_source_rate](name:implicit_source_rate), which spans particle, energy, and momentum transport channels.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the implicit source term represents net energy gain (heating) for the species.

NAMES.name: electron_energy_implicit_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Implicit rate coefficient for the stiff part of an electron energy source term. Multiplying it by the local electron energy density gives the contribution treated implicitly in an electron energy balance or transport solver.
NAMES.long:
The electron energy implicit source rate is the linear coefficient used to represent the stiff part of an electron energy source or sink. It separates a source term into a part evaluated explicitly and a part proportional to the local electron energy density, improving numerical stability for rapidly responding physics.

A common local decomposition of the electron energy source is:

$$
Q_e = Q_{e,\mathrm{expl}} + S_{e,\mathrm{impl}}\,u_e
$$

where $Q_e$ is the total volumetric electron energy source, $Q_{e,\mathrm{expl}}$ is the explicit contribution, $S_{e,\mathrm{impl}}$ is the electron energy implicit source rate, and $u_e$ is the electron energy density. The product $S_{e,\mathrm{impl}}u_e$ has units of volumetric power density.

This coefficient is usually obtained from the linearization of heating, radiation, equilibration, ionization, recombination, or other source models with respect to the evolved electron energy variable. It is a numerical representation of local stiffness rather than a directly measured physical observable; experiments constrain it through the underlying source models and reconstructed electron density, temperature, and radiation or heating power.

Typical magnitudes are highly model dependent. Slowly varying heating or loss terms may have effective rates below 1 s^-1, while stiff collisional, atomic, or radiation terms commonly fall in the range 1-10^4 s^-1 and can be larger in cold or dense edge conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the implicit contribution adds energy to the electron population.

NAMES.name: ion_atomic_mass
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Atomic mass of an ion species expressed in unified atomic mass units. It identifies the isotope and sets the ion mass scale used in collisionality, inertia, gyroradius, and transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
Ion atomic mass is the isotope-specific mass assigned to an ion species, expressed relative to the unified atomic mass unit. It is primarily a species property: different isotopes of the same element have different atomic masses, while different ionization states of the same isotope have nearly the same mass for most plasma-transport purposes.

The ion mass used in transport calculations is commonly obtained from the atomic-mass parameter as:

$$
m_i = A_i m_u
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $A_i$ is the ion atomic mass expressed in unified atomic mass units, and $m_u$ is the unified atomic mass constant. Small corrections from removed bound electrons and ionization energies are usually negligible compared with the nuclear mass for fusion-plasma transport modeling.

The value is determined from the isotope composition of the ion species, using tabulated atomic masses or known fuel and impurity inventories. It enters calculations of thermal speed, gyrofrequency, gyroradius, collisional slowing down, diffusion, and neoclassical and turbulent transport coefficients.

Typical values are about 1.008 u for protium, 2.014 u for deuterium, 3.016 u for tritium, 4.003 u for helium-4, exactly 12 u for carbon-12 by definition of the atomic mass scale, and about 182-186 u for common tungsten isotopes. Fusion-plasma ion species typically span roughly 1-250 u.

NAMES.name: ion_atomic_number
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Nuclear charge number of the ion species, equal to the number of protons in the nucleus, serving as its invariant elemental identifier independent of ionization state.
NAMES.long:
The ion atomic number $Z_n$ is the number of protons in the nucleus of the ion species, an intrinsic nuclear property that is independent of ionization state and uniquely identifies the element. In fusion-relevant plasmas, common values include $Z_n = 1$ for hydrogen isotopes (deuterium, tritium), $Z_n = 2$ for helium, $Z_n = 6$ for carbon, $Z_n = 18$ for argon, and $Z_n = 74$ for tungsten.

The maximum realizable ionization charge for a fully stripped ion equals $Z_n$, making it the natural upper bound for ion_charge. The effective plasma charge $Z_\mathrm{eff} = \sum_i n_i Z_i^2 / n_e$, where $n_i$ is the number density of ion species $i$, $Z_i$ is its ionization charge state, and $n_e$ is the electron density, depends directly on $Z_n$ for fully ionized impurities.

As a fixed nuclear property, $Z_n$ is an invariant input to plasma transport modeling rather than a plasma-measurable quantity. Unlike ion_charge, which reflects the realized ionization state and varies with local temperature and density, $Z_n$ is immutable for a given element. The companion quantity [ion_atomic_mass](name:ion_atomic_mass) provides the nuclear mass, while [atomic_number](name:ion_atomic_number) covers the same concept without restricting to the ion population.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physical ion species, as $Z_n$ counts nuclear proton number and is never negative.

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion temperature averaged over all ion species, evaluated at the flux surface corresponding to the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The internal transport barrier is a region of strongly suppressed turbulent transport in the plasma core, identified by steep temperature and pressure gradients that separate it from the surrounding plasma. The species-averaged ion temperature at this location captures the characteristic thermal state of the combined ion population at the barrier, encompassing fuel ions, minority species, and impurity ions.

The density-weighted species average is defined as:

$$
T_i^{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s T_{i,s}}{\sum_s n_s}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density and $T_{i,s}$ is the temperature of ion species $s$, with the sum running over all ion populations. This density-weighted mean ensures numerically dominant species contribute most to the average and corresponds to the first moment of the combined ion distribution function.

The ITB ion temperature is inferred primarily from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, which extracts local ion thermal energy from the Doppler broadening of impurity emission lines. The ITB reference position is assigned to the flux surface of maximum transport-barrier strength, parameterized by a radial coordinate such as the normalized toroidal flux radius. The companion quantity [total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) provides the total ion density at the same surface; ion_average_temperature_at_plasma_boundary gives the analogous species-averaged temperature at the outer boundary. Typical ITB ion temperatures in advanced tokamak scenarios range from 2-15 keV, substantially exceeding pedestal-top values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the mean kinetic energy per degree of freedom of the ion population is above absolute zero.

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Density-weighted ion temperature averaged over all ion species and charge states, evaluated at the magnetic axis. It characterizes the central ion thermal energy, not necessarily the maximum temperature in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Ion average temperature at the magnetic axis is the local density-weighted mean temperature of the ion population, including all ion species and charge states represented in the plasma. The magnetic axis is the innermost closed flux surface, where the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux vanishes. This quantity is the on-axis counterpart of ion_average_temperature and should not be interpreted as a guaranteed global maximum, since off-axis heating, internal transport barriers, or hollow radial temperature structure can shift hotter ions away from the axis.

For resolved ion populations, the average is commonly defined as:

$$
T_{i,\mathrm{avg}}(\mathrm{axis}) = \frac{\sum_s \sum_\zeta n_{s,\zeta}(\mathrm{axis})\,T_{s,\zeta}(\mathrm{axis})}{\sum_s \sum_\zeta n_{s,\zeta}(\mathrm{axis})}
$$

where $s$ labels ion species, $\zeta$ labels charge state, $n_{s,\zeta}$ is the local ion density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $T_{s,\zeta}$ is the corresponding ion temperature in eV. The denominator is the local total ion density summed over the same species and charge states.

In practice, the on-axis value is obtained from core ion temperature measurements such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, neutron spectroscopy, or neutral-particle analysis, often combined with density composition estimates or transport reconstruction. If only a dominant ion species is measured, the reported average may approximate that dominant species temperature unless impurity or multiple-fuel-ion contributions are explicitly included.

Typical on-axis values are about 100-1000 eV in low-temperature or early-phase plasmas, 1000-10000 eV in many confined tokamak core plasmas, and 10000-25000 eV in high-performance reactor-relevant scenarios.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Effective particle diffusion coefficient for ions in a specified charge state, relating the diffusive particle flux to the negative number density gradient across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The ion charge-state particle diffusivity quantifies diffusive transport of ions in a given ionization state across magnetic flux surfaces. In the Fickian closure, the diffusive particle flux $\Gamma$ is related to the charge-state number density gradient by

$$
\Gamma = -D \nabla n_s
$$

where $n_s$ is the local number density of the specified ion charge state and $D$ is this diffusion coefficient. The coefficient captures combined contributions from neoclassical collisional diffusion, anomalous turbulence-driven transport, and any explicitly modeled processes within a given transport model.

This diffusivity is inferred by transport analysis that matches modeled charge-state density profiles to experimental measurements; for impurity ions, primary diagnostics include charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy and controlled impurity injection scans. The [radial ion-state diffusion coefficient](name:radial_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient) represents the same quantity resolved explicitly along the radial cross-flux-surface direction. The [ion charge-state energy diffusivity](name:ion_charge_state_energy_diffusivity) provides the thermal-energy-transport analog for the same ionization state, and [parallel ion charge-state momentum diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity) covers the field-aligned momentum channel.

Typical values in tokamak core plasmas span approximately $10^{-2}$–$1$ m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; neoclassical predictions are generally at the lower end, while anomalous turbulence-driven transport can elevate the effective coefficient by an order of magnitude or more in low-confinement conditions.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Effective particle convection velocity for a specified ion charge state in the radial particle transport equation on flux surfaces labeled by coordinates (r, theta, phi). It multiplies that charge-state density in the advective part of the particle flux decomposition.
NAMES.long:
Effective convection velocity for ion charge state $z$ is the radial advective transport coefficient that multiplies the density of ions in that charge state in a flux-surface-averaged particle balance. It is the charge-state-resolved counterpart of [ion_state_effective_convection_velocity](name:ion_charge_state_effective_convection_velocity) and is related to, but not necessarily identical with, [ion_state_particle_convection_velocity](name:ion_charge_state_effective_convection_velocity), because the effective coefficient can absorb pinch-like and off-diagonal transport contributions.

For a minor-radius-like radial flux-surface label $r$ in meters, where $r$ is the radial coordinate in flux coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$ and increases from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, a common defining decomposition of the charge-state-resolved radial particle flux is:

$$
\Gamma_z = -D_z \frac{\partial n_z}{\partial r} + v_z^{\mathrm{eff}} n_z
$$

where $\Gamma_z$ is the flux-surface-averaged radial particle flux density in m^-2.s^-1, $D_z$ is the associated effective particle diffusivity in m^2.s^-1, $n_z$ is the particle density of charge state $z$ in m^-3, and $\theta$ and $\phi$ are the poloidal and toroidal angles of the flux coordinate set. The product $v_z^{\mathrm{eff}} n_z$ is the advective part of the particle flux after the diffusive term proportional to the density gradient has been separated.

The coefficient is normally inferred rather than measured directly. Transport analysis combines charge-state-resolved density evolution, diagnostic constraints such as spectroscopic information, ionization and recombination balance, particle sources and sinks, and an assumed or fitted diffusive term to determine $v_z^{\mathrm{eff}}$; the separation between $D_z$ and $v_z^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is model-dependent unless the flux decomposition and radial label are fixed.

Typical core magnitudes for main ions and impurity charge states are 0.1-10 m.s^-1. In edge, pedestal, or transient conditions, effective velocities of 10-100 m.s^-1 can occur, with negative values corresponding to inward pinch-like convection under the sign convention below.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_z^{\mathrm{eff}} n_z$ is directed outward, from the magnetic axis toward increasing radial flux-surface label $r$ in flux coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Temperature of ions belonging to a specified ionization charge state, representing the random kinetic energy per particle after removal of bulk flow. It is the scalar temperature associated with the second central moment of that charge state's velocity distribution, expressed in eV.
NAMES.long:
Ion charge-state temperature is the kinetic temperature of ions of a given species in a specified ionization charge state. It quantifies the thermal velocity spread of that subpopulation, excluding directed bulk motion; for an anisotropic distribution, the scalar value corresponds to one third of the trace of the temperature tensor.

For a velocity distribution normalized to the charge-state density, the scalar temperature in eV is defined by the second central moment:

$$
T_{i,q} = \frac{m_i}{3 e\, n_{i,q}} \int \left|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{i,q}\right|^2 f_{i,q}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $T_{i,q}$ is the temperature of ion species $i$ in charge state $q$, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $e$ is the elementary charge, $n_{i,q}$ is the density of that charge state, $\mathbf{u}_{i,q}$ is its bulk flow velocity, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $f_{i,q}$ is the velocity distribution function.

In experiments, charge-state-resolved ion temperatures are commonly inferred from Doppler broadening of spectral lines, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, neutral particle measurements, or collisional-radiative analysis. When direct measurements are not available, they may be computed from transport energy balance, impurity evolution, and collisional equilibration with other ion and electron populations.

Typical values range from 1-10 eV in cold edge or detached divertor plasma, 10-1000 eV in the scrape-off layer and pedestal region, and 1000-20000 eV in hot confined plasma. Strong ion-ion collisions often make different charge states approach a common ion temperature, while low density, strong sources, radiation, or nonthermal populations can produce charge-state-dependent temperatures.

NAMES.name: ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Local number density of ions at a plasma point, counting ion particles per unit volume; specific instances are qualified by species, population (thermal or fast), or degree of aggregation over species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
Ion number density is the fundamental local plasma quantity giving the count of ionic particles per unit volume at a point in the plasma. In a multi-component plasma this general concept encompasses several specialized variants: species-specific densities such as oxygen_ion_density and xenon_ion_density, population-partitioned densities including [thermal_ion_density](name:thermal_ion_density) for the Maxwellian subpopulation and [fast_ion_density](name:fast_ion_density) for suprathermal ions, and aggregate totals such as [total_ion_density](name:total_ion_density), which sums contributions from all ion species and all charge states.

Local ion density enters the plasma quasi-neutrality condition through:

$$
n_e = \sum_s Z_s \, n_{i,s}
$$

where $n_e$ is the local electron number density, $n_{i,s}$ is the number density of ion species $s$, and $Z_s$ is the charge number of species $s$ in units of the elementary charge.

Ion number densities are measured using charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy for impurity species, neutron or proton emission diagnostics for hydrogenic fuel populations, or derived from integrated equilibrium and transport reconstruction. Spatial averages over the confined plasma volume are represented by [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density), while charge-state-resolved populations are tracked by [total_ion_state_density](name:total_ion_state_density).

Core ion densities in tokamak deuterium plasmas typically span $10^{19}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$; impurity species such as oxygen or xenon are generally present at one to several orders of magnitude lower concentrations.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Number density of fast (non-thermal) ions of a given species, summed over all ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Fast (non-thermal) ions constitute the suprathermal tail of the ion velocity distribution, with energies substantially exceeding the local thermal energy $k_B T_i$. This quantity is obtained by integrating the fast-ion distribution function over the suprathermal region of velocity space and summing over all ionization states of the given species, yielding the local concentration of energetic ions per unit volume. It forms the fast-ion component of [ion_density](name:ion_density), complementary to the thermal population described by [thermal_ion_density](name:thermal_ion_density).

The fast-ion number density is defined as:

$$
n_\mathrm{fast} = \int f_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{v})$ is the fast-ion distribution function restricted to the suprathermal velocity domain and $\mathbf{v}$ is the ion velocity. The charge-state-resolved counterpart [fast_ion_state_density](name:fast_ion_state_density) sums to $n_\mathrm{fast}$ over all ionization states $z$.

Fast ions arise primarily from neutral beam injection and ion cyclotron resonance heating, and also from fusion reactions producing energetic reaction products. The fast-ion density is inferred experimentally from neutral particle analyzers, fast-ion loss detectors, and charge-exchange spectroscopy at suprathermal energies, and is computed by Fokker-Planck or Monte Carlo orbit codes that evolve the fast-ion distribution. Typical values in heated tokamak discharges range from $10^{17}$ to a few times $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, representing a few percent to roughly 20% of the total ion density at high injected power.
NAMES.sign: Positive when fast ions occupy the volume element, as number density is a non-negative integral of a non-negative distribution function.

NAMES.name: ion_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Fickian diffusion coefficient for the total ion population relating diffusive ion particle flux to the spatial gradient of total ion number density, aggregated over all charge states and generalized over directional projections.
NAMES.long:
The ion diffusion coefficient $D_i$ characterizes irreversible Fickian particle transport of the total ion population in a magnetized plasma, summed over all charge states. It quantifies the proportionality between the diffusive ion particle flux density and the opposing gradient of total ion number density, without resolving a specific spatial direction.

The defining constitutive relation is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,\mathrm{diff}} = -D_i \nabla n_i
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive ion particle flux density and $n_i$ is the total ion number density summed over all charge states.

In magnetized plasma transport models, $D_i$ is strongly anisotropic due to the confining magnetic field. Directional components are resolved as separate projections: the [radial ion diffusion coefficient](name:radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient) governs cross-field particle transport across magnetic flux surfaces, while the [poloidal ion diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_diffusion_coefficient) describes transport along the poloidal direction. This quantity serves as the parent abstraction over those directional components, providing the shared physics reference for the Fickian ion particle transport channel.

This coefficient is typically inferred from transport modeling by matching simulated ion density profiles against measurements, or prescribed as a free parameter in fluid transport codes. It belongs to the broader diffusion_coefficient family, which encompasses energy and momentum transport channels alongside particle transport.

NAMES.name: ion_energy_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective scalar diffusivity for diffusive thermal-energy transport of the total ion population, summed over all ion species and charge states. It parameterizes the down-gradient part of ion energy flux after convective, advective, and source terms are treated separately.
NAMES.long:
Ion energy diffusivity $\chi_i$ is an effective scalar coefficient for diffusive transport of ion thermal energy. It applies to the total ion population aggregated over all ion species and charge states, unlike charge-state-resolved quantities such as [ion_state_energy_diffusivity](name:ion_state_energy_diffusivity).

A directional Fickian closure can be written for any dimensionless unit direction $\hat{\mathbf e}$ as

$$
\mathbf q_{i,\mathrm{diff}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf e} = -\chi_i\, \hat{\mathbf e} \cdot \nabla W_i
$$

where $\mathbf q_{i,\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive ion thermal-energy flux in W m$^{-2}$, $W_i$ is the total ion thermal energy density in J m$^{-3}$, $\nabla W_i$ is its spatial gradient in J m$^{-4}$, and $\chi_i$ is in m$^2$ s$^{-1}$. The minus sign states the down-gradient convention: for positive $\chi_i$, the projected diffusive energy flux is directed toward decreasing ion thermal energy density. When a temperature-gradient form is used instead, the driving term is usually proportional to $n_i\nabla T_i$ with $T_i$ expressed in joules; density-gradient, convective, and source terms must then be defined separately in the ion energy balance.

In practice, $\chi_i$ is inferred from ion energy-balance analysis using measured ion temperatures and densities together with heating, ion-electron exchange, atomic losses, and temporal storage terms. It may include neoclassical collisional transport and turbulence-induced mixing, and it is meaningful only within the chosen scalar diffusive closure. Direction-specific specializations include [poloidal_ion_energy_diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_energy_diffusivity), [radial_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient), and [radial_total_thermal_ion_energy_diffusivity_over_edge_region](name:radial_total_thermal_ion_energy_diffusivity_over_edge_region).

Order-of-magnitude effective values in magnetically confined plasmas commonly span 0.1-10 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ in core transport analyzes, with lower values near neoclassical expectations and larger values in turbulence-dominated or edge-region conditions. Apparent locally negative fitted values can occur when uncertainties, transients, or non-diffusive transport dominate; such cases indicate breakdown of a simple scalar diffusive interpretation rather than a physical negative diffusivity.

NAMES.name: ion_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion thermal energy flux density through an oriented surface, combining conductive heat transport and convective enthalpy flux summed over all ion species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
Ion energy flux is the signed surface-normal density of thermal energy transported by ions across an oriented surface. It combines conductive heat flow driven by ion-temperature gradients with convective enthalpy carried by the mean ion motion, with contributions summed over all ion species and charge states.

A common fluid closure expresses the scalar flux through a surface with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ as:

$$
q_i = \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \sum_s \left(-\boldsymbol{\kappa}_s \cdot \nabla T_s + \frac{5}{2} p_s \mathbf{v}_s\right)
$$

where $s$ labels ion species and charge states, $\boldsymbol{\kappa}_s$ is the ion thermal-conductivity tensor with components in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $T_s$ is the ion temperature in $\mathrm{K}$, $p_s$ is the ion pressure in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the mean ion velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. If temperature is represented in energy units, the conductive coefficient and gradient must be converted consistently so each term carries units of $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

In practice, ion energy flux is inferred from transport modeling, power-balance analysis, or fluid and kinetic reconstructions using measured ion temperature, density, pressure, and flow information. The conductive part depends strongly on collisionality and magnetic-field-aligned transport, while the convective enthalpy part becomes important where particle flows or recycling-driven ion sources are large.

Typical magnitudes range from about $10^4-10^6\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ in low-power scrape-off-layer and edge regions to $10^7-10^8\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ near strong exhaust channels or divertor strike regions. Core turbulent ion heat fluxes mapped to surface-normal components are often in the $10^4-10^6\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ range, depending on heating power, confinement regime, and plasma size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion thermal energy is transported through the oriented surface in the direction of its chosen unit normal.

NAMES.name: ion_kinetic_energy_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion kinetic energy density is the total kinetic energy per unit volume carried by all ion species, including both random thermal motion and directed bulk-flow motion. It is the sum of the corresponding species contributions over the complete ion population.
NAMES.long:
Ion kinetic energy density is the local kinetic-energy content of the complete ion population per unit volume. It includes the internal kinetic energy associated with random particle motion and the kinetic energy of directed bulk flow, summed over thermal ions, impurity ions, and fast-ion species when they are part of the ion population considered.

A pressure-and-flow decomposition for the total ion kinetic energy density is

$$
w_i = \sum_{s \in \mathrm{ions}} \left[ \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_s) + \frac{1}{2} m_s n_s |\mathbf{u}_s|^2 \right]
$$

where $w_i$ is the ion kinetic energy density in J m^-3, $\mathbf{P}_s$ is the pressure tensor of ion species $s$ in Pa, $m_s$ is the ion mass in kg, $n_s$ is the number density in m^-3, and $\mathbf{u}_s$ is the bulk velocity in m s^-1. For an isotropic scalar-pressure description, $\mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_s)/2 = 3p_s/2$; if temperature is used, $p_s = n_s T_s$ with $T_s$ expressed as energy per particle in J, or $p_s = n_s e T_s$ when $T_s$ is specified in eV.

In practice this quantity is computed from ion distribution functions or from fluid moments: densities, pressures or temperatures, and flow velocities for each ion species. The single-species contribution is [ion species kinetic energy density](name:ion_kinetic_energy_density). This quantity differs from [total plasma energy](name:total_plasma_energy), which is a volume-integrated thermal stored energy and does not include directed bulk-flow kinetic energy.

Typical values range from about 10-10^3 J m^-3 in cold scrape-off-layer or edge plasma, 10^4-10^6 J m^-3 in tokamak core plasma, and can exceed 10^6 J m^-3 in very high-pressure or fast-ion-rich regimes. The bulk-flow term is often smaller than the thermal term in the core, but it can be important in strongly rotating plasmas, edge flows, and populations with large directed velocity.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net momentum source density vector of the total ion population, summed over all ion charge states, representing the local directed rate at which physical processes inject momentum into the ion fluid per unit area.
NAMES.long:
The ion momentum source density is the net directed momentum input to the ion fluid per unit area, aggregated over all ion charge states of the plasma. Physical processes contributing to this source include charge exchange with neutrals, ionization, recombination, electromagnetic $\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$ body forces, and ion-neutral friction, all of which redistribute momentum between the ion, electron, and neutral populations in edge transport.

The source vector $\mathbf{S}_i^{\mathrm{mom}}$ appears on the right-hand side of the ion fluid momentum balance:

$$
\frac{\partial (m_i n_i \mathbf{v}_i)}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_i = \mathbf{S}_i^{\mathrm{mom}}
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ the total ion number density summed over all charge states, $\mathbf{v}_i$ the charge-state-averaged ion velocity, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_i$ the total ion stress tensor.

The vector decomposes into physically distinct projections: [toroidal_ion_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_momentum) drives toroidal rotation, [poloidal_ion_momentum](name:poloidal_ion_momentum) governs poloidal circulation, and [parallel_ion_momentum](name:parallel_ion_momentum) controls flow along magnetic field lines. This charge-state-summed source complements the charge-state-resolved [parallel_ion_state_momentum](name:parallel_ion_state_momentum) and is a species-specific component of the total plasma momentum source, which additionally includes neutral contributions such as those captured by [parallel_neutral_momentum](name:parallel_neutral_momentum).

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_diffusivity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective cross-field diffusion coefficient for radial transport of total ion momentum caused by diamagnetic drift. It aggregates the contribution over all ion charge states and is expressed in m^2 s^-1.
NAMES.long:
Ion momentum diffusivity due to diamagnetic drift is the effective coefficient multiplying the radial gradient of total ion momentum in the diamagnetic part of the diffusive momentum flux. It represents the ion aggregate over all charge states, rather than a charge-state-resolved coefficient, and has units of m^2 s^-1.

For a momentum component represented by the total ion momentum density $M_i$, the diffusive diamagnetic contribution to the radial momentum flux can be written as:

$$
\Gamma_{M_i}^{\mathrm{dia}} = -\chi_{M_i}^{\mathrm{dia}}\,\frac{\partial M_i}{\partial r}
$$

where $\Gamma_{M_i}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the radial flux of that ion momentum component in kg m^-1 s^-2 and is positive outward, $\chi_{M_i}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diffusivity in m^2 s^-1, $M_i$ is the total ion momentum density in kg m^-2 s^-1, and $r$ is an outward minor-radial distance in meters measured across flux surfaces from the magnetic-axis region toward the plasma boundary. The minus sign gives down-gradient diffusion: a positive outward gradient of $M_i$ produces an inward diffusive flux, and a negative outward gradient produces an outward diffusive flux.

The diamagnetic contribution is associated with pressure-gradient-driven drift motion perpendicular to the magnetic field and enters momentum-balance modeling as one part of the cross-field ion momentum transport. In practice it is obtained from transport analysis, neoclassical or gyrokinetic calculations, or reduced momentum-balance fits constrained by measurements of ion flow, density, temperature, and equilibrium geometry.

Typical effective values in tokamak core transport studies are about 0.01-10 m^2 s^-1. Values near zero indicate a negligible modeled diamagnetic diffusive contribution, while edge regions, transient phases, or strongly driven plasmas can give effective values of several tens of m^2 s^-1.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Source density of total-ion toroidal angular momentum produced by diamagnetic-drift transport, summed over all ion species and charge states. It is the signed contribution of ion pressure-gradient drift fluxes to the ion momentum balance.
NAMES.long:
Total-ion diamagnetic-drift momentum source density is the local rate per unit volume at which pressure-gradient-driven ion drift transport changes [toroidal_ion_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_momentum). It is an internal transport contribution, not an externally applied torque, and the sum includes all ion species and charge states. The toroidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Written as a conservative transport contribution, the source density is the negative divergence of the diamagnetic flux of ion toroidal angular momentum:

$$
S_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = -\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{L_\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = -\nabla \cdot \sum_{a\in\mathrm{ions}} \left(m_a n_a R v_{\phi,a}\right)\mathbf{v}_{D,a}
$$

where $S_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is in kg.m^-1.s^-2, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{L_\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the [ion diamagnetic momentum flux](name:ion_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) in kg.s^-2, $\nabla\cdot$ is the spatial divergence operator with components in m^-1, and $a$ indexes ion species and charge states. Here $m_a$ is ion mass in kg, $n_a$ is ion number density in m^-3, $R$ is major radius in meters in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $v_{\phi,a}$ is toroidal fluid velocity in m.s^-1, and $\mathbf{v}_{D,a}$ is diamagnetic drift velocity in m.s^-1 generated by the perpendicular ion pressure gradient.

In practice the term is computed by combining equilibrium geometry, ion pressure-gradient estimates, species composition, and toroidal-flow information to construct the charge-state-resolved diamagnetic momentum fluxes and then taking their divergence. It is usually inferred from momentum-balance and transport analyzes rather than measured directly; charge-state-resolved contributions correspond to [ion_state_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_state_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and the total plasma contribution is momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift. The related neutral contribution, when included in the same source decomposition, is [neutral_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:neutral_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

Typical absolute magnitudes are order $10^{-4}$-$10^1$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 in weak-gradient core regions and $10^1$-$10^4$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 locally in pedestal, edge, or scrape-off-layer regions with short pressure-gradient scale lengths. The value can change sign with the direction of toroidal flow, pressure-gradient orientation, magnetic geometry, and spatial convergence or divergence of the diamagnetic momentum flux.
NAMES.sign: Positive when convergence of the ion diamagnetic-drift momentum flux increases total-ion toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated rate of energy transfer to the ion population from all sources, summed over all ion species, covering wave absorption, fast-particle thermalization, and collisional exchange channels.
NAMES.long:
Ion power is the total rate at which energy is deposited into the ion channel of a plasma, obtained by integrating the local volumetric ion power density over the full confined plasma volume and summing over all ion species. It serves as the global ion-channel energy-balance quantity in transport analyzes, complementary to the electron power channel.

The total ion power $P_i$ is defined as:

$$
P_i = \int_V Q_i(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $Q_i(\mathbf{r})$ is the net volumetric power density deposited into all ion species at position $\mathbf{r}$, in units of W m$^{-3}$, and $V$ is the confined plasma volume.

In auxiliary-heated plasmas this quantity decomposes by population: [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power) captures direct wave energy absorbed by the suprathermal minority, while [thermal_ion_power](name:thermal_ion_power) quantifies bulk Maxwellian ion heating. The aggregate over all sources and species is given by [total_ion_power](name:total_ion_power), and the combined electron-plus-ion budget by total_plasma_deposited_power. Ion power is inferred from global power-balance analyzes, calorimetry of heating systems, and kinetic simulations benchmarked against measured ion temperature profiles.

Typical values range from a few hundred kilowatts in ohmic discharges to 10–30 MW during full neutral-beam or radio-frequency auxiliary heating in medium-to-large tokamak experiments.

NAMES.name: ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Isotropic kinetic pressure of the ion population at a plasma location, summed over all charge states and spanning thermal and non-thermal (fast-ion) contributions.
NAMES.long:
Ion pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure of the ion fluid, defined through the second velocity moment of the ion distribution function. It encompasses both the bulk thermal contribution from ions in local thermodynamic equilibrium and the non-thermal fast-ion contribution from suprathermal particles produced by auxiliary heating. The quantity is summed over all ion charge states present in the plasma.

The total ion pressure decomposes as:

$$
p_i = p_{i,\mathrm{thermal}} + p_{i,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $p_{i,\mathrm{thermal}}$ is the isotropic thermal pressure from random ion motion and $p_{i,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the contribution from the suprathermal ion distribution, both summed over all charge states.

The thermal component, [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure), is inferred from ion temperature and density profiles measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or Thomson scattering. The combined quantity [total_ion_pressure](name:total_ion_pressure) enters radial force balance, beta calculations, and pressure-driven instability analysis; the fast-ion fraction can be dominant during high-power neutral beam or ion cyclotron heating.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion population contributes outward pressure force on a bounding surface element, which holds for any plasma with finite ion thermal energy or non-thermal fast-ion content.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Fast-ion pressure is the non-thermal kinetic pressure carried by suprathermal ions, summed over ionization states. It may be expressed as an isotropic equivalent pressure, gyrotropic tensor components, or derivatives describing radial variation.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion pressure is the part of ion pressure carried by suprathermal ions rather than by the thermal Maxwellian ion population. It is summed over ionization states and describes the kinetic stress associated with fast-ion velocity spread. In magnetized plasmas it is often represented in the local right-handed field-aligned basis $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{b})$, with $\hat{e}_1 \times \hat{e}_2 = \hat{b}$ and $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, so that parallel and perpendicular components can be distinguished.

The pressure tensor is defined by the second central velocity moment of the fast-ion distribution function:

$$
\mathbf{P}_\mathrm{fast} = \sum_\alpha m_\alpha \int (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_\alpha) \otimes (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_\alpha)\, f_{\alpha,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $\alpha$ indexes the ion species and ionization states included in the suprathermal population, $m_\alpha$ is the ion mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $\mathbf{u}_\alpha$ is the fast-ion mean velocity, $f_{\alpha,\mathrm{fast}}$ is normalized so that its velocity-space integral gives number density, and $\otimes$ denotes the dyadic product. For a gyrotropic distribution, the scalar equivalent is $p_\mathrm{fast}=(p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast}}+2p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}})/3$, with specialized components represented by [parallel fast-ion pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure), [perpendicular fast-ion pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure), and [total fast-ion pressure](name:total_fast_ion_pressure).

In practice, fast-ion pressure is inferred by combining kinetic measurements and modeling of the suprathermal distribution, using constraints from diagnostics such as neutron emission, fast-ion loss measurements, neutral-particle analysis, fast-ion D-alpha emission, collective scattering, and equilibrium or transport reconstruction. Radial variation is represented by quantities such as the [radial derivative](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure) and [second radial derivative](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure), taken with respect to the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the normalized toroidal flux radius increasing from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary. Related evolution and state-resolved forms include [tendency of parallel fast-ion pressure](name:tendency_of_parallel_fast_ion_pressure) and [parallel fast-ion state pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure).

Typical values are strongly dependent on heating method, confinement, and fast-ion slowing-down physics. In purely Ohmic plasmas the value can be negligible, while in auxiliary-heated tokamak cores it is commonly about $10^3-10^5$ Pa. In high-performance regimes it can contribute roughly $0.01-0.3$ of the [total ion pressure](name:total_ion_pressure), with lower values toward the plasma edge as fast-ion density and energy decrease.

NAMES.name: ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Number density of ions of a specified element in a specific charge state, representing the bulk thermal population at a given plasma location without suprathermal contributions.
NAMES.long:
The ion state density $n_{i,z}$ quantifies the local particle count per unit volume for an ion of element $i$ in charge state $z$, forming the fundamental charge-state-resolved building block of multifluid and impurity transport models. In the absence of a population qualifier, this quantity represents the bulk thermal component, excluding fast or suprathermal ions; the all-population (thermal plus non-thermal) counterpart is [total_ion_state_density](name:total_ion_state_density), while the non-thermal portion alone is given by [fast_ion_state_density](name:fast_ion_state_density).

The charge-state densities enter the plasma quasineutrality constraint:

$$
n_e = \sum_{i,z} z \cdot n_{i,z}
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density and the sum runs over all ion species $i$ and charge states $z$.

Charge-state-resolved densities are inferred from passive or active spectroscopy, including charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy and line-integrated emission measurements combined with atomic physics models of ionization and recombination balance. Transport codes evolve $n_{i,z}$ through continuity equations incorporating cross-field diffusion, parallel transport, ionization, and recombination source terms.

For fully stripped main fuel ions in the core of a tokamak, $n_{i,z}$ ranges from $10^{19}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$; for high-$Z$ impurity ions, individual charge-state densities span many orders of magnitude depending on local temperature and ionization equilibrium.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions of the specified species and charge state are present in the plasma volume element.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Local number density of fast (non-thermal) ions resolved to a specific charge state, counting only ions whose velocity distribution departs significantly from a Maxwellian.
NAMES.long:
The fast ion state density is the number of suprathermal ions per unit volume occupying a specific ionic charge state $z$. Unlike the bulk thermal population, these fast ions carry energies well above the ambient plasma thermal energy and are described by a non-Maxwellian velocity distribution function.

The quantity is the zeroth velocity moment of the non-thermal ion distribution:

$$
n_\mathrm{fast}^{(z)} = \int f_\mathrm{fast}^{(z)}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_\mathrm{fast}^{(z)}(\mathbf{v})$ is the suprathermal velocity distribution function for ions in charge state $z$. The [ion_state_density](name:ion_state_density) of the same charge state equals the sum of this fast component and the [thermal_ion_state_density](name:thermal_ion_state_density) Maxwellian component, while [fast_ion_density](name:fast_ion_density) aggregates the present quantity over all charge states of a given species.

Fast ions are produced by neutral beam injection, ion cyclotron resonance heating, or thermonuclear fusion reactions, and thermalize through Coulomb collisions over the species-dependent slowing-down timescale. Charge-state-resolved profiles are determined by solving the fast-ion kinetic equation using Monte Carlo orbit-following codes, with experimental constraints from fast-ion charge-exchange emission diagnostics, gamma-ray spectroscopy, or neutron emission. In NBI-heated core plasmas, the total fast ion density reaches $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$; individual charge-state values span this range according to the dominant ionization stage populated.
NAMES.sign: Positive when fast ions occupy the specified charge state in the plasma volume.

NAMES.name: ion_state_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Particle diffusion coefficient for a specific ion charge state, relating the diffusive particle flux of that ionization state to its number density gradient, without specifying a spatial projection.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state particle diffusion coefficient $D$ quantifies Fickian diffusive transport of a specified ion charge state in the edge plasma, where particles of that ionization state are redistributed down their local number density gradient. Resolving by charge state allows edge transport models to capture ionization-state-dependent diffusivities that differ from the charge-state-averaged [poloidal_ion_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_diffusion_coefficient).

The defining Fickian relation for the diffusive particle flux density $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{s,\mathrm{diff}}$ of charge state $s$ is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{s,\mathrm{diff}} = -D \nabla n_s
$$

where $n_s$ is the local number density of the specified ion charge state.

This quantity is the direction-agnostic parent of two spatial projections: [radial_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient), governing cross-flux-surface particle transport, and [poloidal_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient), governing transport along poloidal arclength. In magnetized edge plasmas the radial and poloidal diffusivities are generally unequal, reflecting the anisotropy imposed by the magnetic geometry. The analogous coefficient for thermal energy transport of a single charge state is [poloidal_ion_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient). This name specializes the broader diffusion_coefficient to the ion-charge-state particle channel.

NAMES.name: ion_state_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Fickian particle diffusion tensor for a specific ion charge state in magnetized plasma, with directional components relating the diffusive particle flux of that charge state to the local charge-state density gradient.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state diffusivity is the Fickian diffusion tensor for a specified ion charge state in a magnetized plasma, with each directional component relating the diffusive particle flux of that charge state to its number-density gradient in the corresponding direction. Transport in magnetized edge plasma is strongly anisotropic: diffusion along magnetic field lines greatly exceeds cross-field transport, so the directional component is essential to characterize the physical process.

The defining Fick's-law relation along component direction $\alpha$ is:

$$
\Gamma_{i,\alpha} = -D_{i,\alpha} \frac{\partial n_i}{\partial x_\alpha}
$$

where $\Gamma_{i,\alpha}$ is the diffusive particle flux of charge state $i$ in direction $\alpha$, $D_{i,\alpha}$ is the component diffusivity, and $n_i$ is the charge-state number density in m$^{-3}$.

The cross-field [radial_ion_state_diffusivity](name:radial_ion_state_diffusivity) governs particle transport across flux surfaces in the edge plasma, driven primarily by turbulence and anomalous processes. The field-aligned component [parallel_ion_charge_state_diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_diffusivity) reflects collisional transport along magnetic field lines and can exceed the radial component by several orders of magnitude. Radial values in edge plasmas range from approximately 0.1 to 10 m^2 s^{-1}; parallel values can reach 10^3 to 10^6 m^2 s^{-1}. Components are inferred from particle balance modeling or impurity injection experiments, and the momentum analog is captured by [radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity).

NAMES.name: ion_state_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Effective velocity at which a specific ion charge state convects its thermal energy radially across flux surfaces in the charge-state-resolved energy transport equation.
NAMES.long:
In flux-surface-averaged radial transport models, the total radial energy flux of an ion charge state is decomposed into diffusive and convective contributions. The ion state energy convection velocity $v_E$ is the effective velocity parameterizing the convective part for a given charge state, providing finer charge-state resolution than the species-averaged ion_energy_convection_velocity.

The convective energy flux contribution $q_{\mathrm{conv}}$ for the charge state is:

$$
q_{\mathrm{conv}} = \frac{3}{2} n_s T_s v_E
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of the charge state in m$^{-3}$ and $T_s$ is its temperature in J.

This quantity is computed by transport codes that resolve the charge state distribution and is not directly measurable; it is inferred from energy balance analysis or prescribed within transport models. The particle-convection analog for the same charge state is ion_state_convection_velocity, and the analogous quantity for neutral states is [neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity](name:neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity). The charge-state-summed counterpart is total_ion_energy_convection_velocity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convective energy flux is directed outward, away from the magnetic axis in the direction of increasing normalized poloidal flux.

NAMES.name: ion_state_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Scalar energy-flux density component for a specified ion charge state, equal to the power per unit area crossing an oriented surface.
NAMES.long:
Ion state energy flux is the signed scalar component of the energy-flux density associated with one resolved ion charge state. It represents the net rate at which that charge state's energy crosses a unit area of an oriented surface, independent of any particular decomposition into convective, conductive, or exchange terms.

For an oriented surface with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, the scalar component is the projection of the charge-state energy-flux-density vector onto that normal:

$$
F_{E,z}^{(n)} = \mathbf{F}_{E,z} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $F_{E,z}^{(n)}$ is the scalar ion-state energy flux in W m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{F}_{E,z}$ is the vector energy-flux density of ion charge state $z$ in W m$^{-2}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is a dimensionless unit normal defining the positive crossing direction.

In transport analysis, this quantity is usually obtained from charge-state-resolved energy balance models or inferred from combinations of density, temperature, flow, heat-conduction, and collisional energy-exchange estimates. It is the charge-state-resolved counterpart of more aggregate quantities such as [energy_flux](name:radial_total_thermal_electron_energy_flux) and may be summed over charge states or species to form total ion energy-flux measures such as [radial_total_ion_energy_flux](name:radial_total_ion_energy_flux). Direction-specific and related charge-state transport quantities include [radial_ion_charge_state_energy_flux](name:radial_ion_state_energy_flux) and [parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux).

Typical magnitudes span about 10$^1$-10$^5$ W m$^{-2}$ in relatively diffuse edge plasma and can reach 10$^5$-10$^8$ W m$^{-2}$ in scrape-off-layer and divertor heat-transport regions, depending on density, temperature, flow speed, gradients, and ionization balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy carried by the specified ion charge state crosses the oriented surface in the direction of the chosen positive normal.

NAMES.name: ion_state_implicit_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Linearization coefficient for the stiff portion of the ion charge state particle source term in transport solvers, equal to the net implicit particle source per unit local ion charge state density.
NAMES.long:
In transport solvers that split particle source terms into explicit and implicit (stiff) contributions, the ion charge state density continuity equation retains an implicit term proportional to the local density $n_{i,z}$. This quantity is the proportionality coefficient $\lambda_\mathrm{imp}$ that multiplies $n_{i,z}$ on the right-hand side of the particle balance equation, allowing stiff density-coupled source processes to be advanced semi-implicitly without the prohibitively small time steps required by fully explicit treatment.

The coefficient is defined as the stiff Jacobian element of the total particle source:

$$
\lambda_\mathrm{imp} = \left.\frac{\partial S_{i,z}}{\partial n_{i,z}}\right|_{\mathrm{stiff}}
$$

where $S_{i,z}$ is the total volumetric particle source for the ion charge state and $n_{i,z}$ is its number density. The full source decomposes as $S_{i,z} = S_\mathrm{exp} + \lambda_\mathrm{imp}\,n_{i,z}$, with $S_\mathrm{exp}$ the explicit (density-independent) remainder; together these two terms recover the total [ion_state_source_rate](name:ion_state_source_rate) used in the non-decomposed continuity equation.

This coefficient is computed by source modeling routines and supplied to the transport solver; it is not a directly measured diagnostic quantity. The analogous implicit coefficient for the electron particle channel is [electron_implicit_source_rate](name:electron_implicit_source_rate), and the corresponding coefficient for the ion charge state energy transport equation is [ion_state_energy_implicit_source_rate](name:ion_state_energy_implicit_source_rate), applying the same decomposition pattern across transport channels.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the implicit term acts as a net local particle source per unit ion charge state density, representing a tendency toward density growth.

NAMES.name: ion_state_lower_bound_charge
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Minimum ionization charge number (Z_min) of an ion charge-state bundle, defining the lower bound of the charge state range grouped together for a given ion species.
NAMES.long:
