In multi-fluid plasma models, ion species can be represented not as individual charge states but as bundles spanning a contiguous range of ionization states. This quantity is the lower bound of that range — the least-ionized state included in the bundle — identified by its integer charge number $Z_\mathrm{min}$.

The bundle is fully defined by the pair $(Z_\mathrm{min}, Z_\mathrm{max})$, where the upper bound is stored as [ion_state_upper_bound_charge](name:ion_state_upper_bound_charge). When no bundling is applied — that is, when the ion is represented as a single charge state — $Z_\mathrm{min} = Z_\mathrm{max}$. For neutral species the value is zero. Typical integer values range from 0 (neutral) up to the atomic number of the element for fully stripped ions.

This integer field appears wherever bundled charge-state groups are used: in transport, source, wave-heating, and wall interaction models. It is set by the model configuration and identifies which atomic data apply to the grouped ion population. The concentration-weighted mean charge of the bundle, relevant for transport calculations, is tracked separately by ion_state_average_charge, which coincides with $Z_\mathrm{min}$ in the single-state (no-bundling) limit.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion carries a net positive electric charge; equals zero for neutral species.

NAMES.name: ion_state_momentum
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Vector momentum source density for a single ion charge state, giving the area-normalized rate of directional momentum transfer via ionization, recombination, and charge exchange in edge plasma multi-fluid models.
NAMES.long:
The ion charge-state momentum source density quantifies the net rate of directed linear momentum added to or removed from a specified ion fluid per unit area through atomic and collisional processes, including ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and frictional coupling to other species. In multi-fluid edge plasma transport models, this vector source term appears in the per-charge-state momentum conservation equation, coupling individual ionic populations to the broader plasma through mass, momentum, and energy exchange channels.

The quantity is resolved along the principal axes of the magnetic geometry. The field-aligned component [parallel_ion_state_momentum](name:parallel_ion_state_momentum) governs momentum exchange along the local magnetic field direction $\hat{b}$; poloidal and toroidal projections resolve contributions in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; and the radial component captures cross-field momentum deposition, which is related to quantities such as [radial_edge_ion_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_momentum_flux_over_edge_region). Summation of the per-charge-state contributions over all ionic species and ionization states recovers the aggregate ion momentum source density.

This source term is evaluated from atomic rate coefficients (for ionization, recombination, and charge exchange) combined with local plasma density and temperature profiles in edge transport solvers that resolve charge-state-resolved ion fluid equations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the source transfers momentum to the ion charge state in the positive direction of the respective geometric coordinate.

NAMES.name: ion_state_power
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic wave power absorbed by an ion charge state, equal to the sum of contributions from the thermal bulk and fast suprathermal ion populations, volume-integrated over the plasma and excluding collisional energy exchange between populations.
NAMES.long:
The ion state power represents the total wave-absorbed power for a specified ion charge state, encompassing both the bulk Maxwellian and suprathermal ion contributions. It is obtained by volume-integrating the local energy deposition rate over the confined plasma and excludes power transferred between populations via Coulomb collisions, thereby isolating the direct wave-particle interaction channel for the charge state.

The total power decomposes as:

$$
P_{\text{state}} = P_{\text{thermal,state}} + P_{\text{fast,state}}
$$

where $P_{\text{thermal,state}}$ is the power absorbed by the thermal bulk ion population at the given charge state, captured by [thermal_ion_state_power](name:thermal_ion_state_power), and $P_{\text{fast,state}}$ is the power absorbed by the suprathermal population, captured by [fast_ion_state_power](name:fast_ion_state_power), both in watts.

This quantity is computed from wave-plasma interaction models that resolve the energy partition between thermal and fast ion populations. The partition depends on the heating scheme: ion cyclotron resonance heating preferentially deposits energy into a resonant minority species, generating a suprathermal tail, while the thermal background absorbs through collisional damping of the wave. For charge-state-summed analogs that aggregate over all states of the respective populations, see [thermal_ion_power](name:thermal_ion_power) and [fast_ion_power](name:fast_ion_power).

NAMES.name: ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Pressure of a specified ion charge state, which may represent the thermal Maxwellian contribution, the non-thermal fast-particle contribution, or their sum as the total charge-state pressure.
NAMES.long:
Ion charge state pressure characterizes the kinetic pressure associated with ions occupying a single ionization state, resolving the multi-species plasma composition down to the charge-state level. Depending on the physical population under consideration, this quantity may represent the [thermal component](name:thermal_ion_state_pressure) arising from Maxwellian random motion and excluded from non-thermal contributions, the fast suprathermal component from an energetic ion distribution, or the [total pressure](name:total_ion_state_pressure) combining both thermal and non-thermal contributions.

For the Maxwellian thermal component, the defining relation is:

$$
p_s = n_s k_B T_s
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ions in charge state $s$ and $T_s$ is the ion temperature of that charge state expressed in energy units; the fast-particle contribution adds the non-thermal pressure from energetic ions resolved as the second velocity moment of the suprathermal distribution.

The charge-state pressure appears in charge-state-resolved momentum and energy balance equations within multi-fluid and kinetic transport models. Radial structure is encoded by [the first radial derivative](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, and by [the second radial derivative](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure) giving the local radial profile curvature. The underlying thermal kinetic energy is captured by [ion_charge_state_temperature](name:ion_charge_state_temperature), while the aggregate thermal pressure summed over charge states is given by [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge state exerts kinetic pressure on surrounding fluid elements, consistent with the non-negative definiteness of the pressure tensor as the second moment of the velocity distribution.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Anisotropic pressure tensor of fast (suprathermal) ions for a specific charge state, encapsulating both the stress along and perpendicular to the local magnetic field as the second velocity moment of the nonthermal ion distribution.
NAMES.long:
Fast (suprathermal) ions in a magnetized plasma develop an anisotropic pressure because the Lorentz force couples particle motion differently along and perpendicular to the local magnetic field direction $\hat{b}$. For a specific ion charge state, the fast-ion pressure tensor decomposes into two scalar projections:

$$
\mathbf{P}_f = p_{f,\parallel}\,\hat{b}\hat{b} + p_{f,\perp}\,(\mathbf{I} - \hat{b}\hat{b})
$$

where $p_{f,\parallel}$ is the [parallel fast-ion state pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure), $p_{f,\perp}$ is the [perpendicular fast-ion state pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure), and $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity tensor. This quantity is the parent abstraction that unifies those projections together with their radial derivatives such as [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_pressure).

Unlike the thermal [ion_state_pressure](name:ion_state_pressure), which characterizes a near-Maxwellian ion population, the fast-ion pressure originates from a non-Maxwellian slowing-down distribution produced by neutral beam injection, ion cyclotron resonance heating, or fusion reactions. The resulting pressure anisotropy $p_{f,\parallel} - p_{f,\perp}$ can drive kinetic instabilities such as Alfvén eigenmodes. Charge-state-summed analogs are available as [parallel_fast_ion_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure) and [perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure).

Fast-ion pressure profiles are computed from kinetic models — including Monte Carlo slowing-down simulations and Fokker-Planck solvers — applied to beam-injected or fusion-born particle populations. In neutral beam injection scenarios, the suprathermal pressure can be comparable to or exceed the bulk ion thermal pressure in the beam deposition region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion population for the charge state carries non-negative kinetic pressure, consistent with the non-negativity of the second velocity moment of the distribution function.

NAMES.name: ion_state_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Net volumetric particle source rate for a specific ion charge state, entering the charge-state-resolved continuity equation as a creation or destruction term.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state source rate is the net volumetric rate at which particles of a specified ionic charge state are created or destroyed within a plasma volume element, serving as the source term in the charge-state-resolved particle continuity equation. Processes contributing to this rate include electron-impact ionization, radiative and dielectronic recombination, and charge exchange with neutral species.

The governing charge-state continuity equation is:

$$
\frac{\partial n_z}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z = S_z
$$

where $n_z$ is the number density of charge state $z$ in m$^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z$ is the associated particle flux in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $S_z$ is this source rate. Transport solvers may decompose $S_z$ into an explicit part added directly to the right-hand side and an implicit part proportional to $n_z$; the latter is captured separately as the [implicit ion particle source rate].

This quantity is computed by coupling atomic physics rate coefficients for ionization and recombination to local electron temperature and density profiles, and may incorporate contributions from neutral beam injection or pellet injection. Summing over all ionization states yields the total [ion source rate]; the analogous quantity for neutral charge states is the [neutral state source rate](name:neutral_state_source_rate).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified charge state experiences a net local particle gain; negative when ionization from below or recombination from above causes a net depletion of that state.

NAMES.name: ion_state_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Scalar temperature of ions in a specified ionization state, defined from the random kinetic energy associated with the second central moment of that charge-state-resolved ion velocity distribution after removal of its bulk flow.
NAMES.long:
Ion state temperature is the scalar thermodynamic temperature assigned to ions of one chemical species in a specified ionization state. It characterizes the random part of their kinetic energy, not the kinetic energy of any mean flow of that charge-state population.

For an ion species of mass $m_i$ in ionization state $s$, with velocity distribution $f_{i,s}(\mathbf{v})$, the temperature in electronvolts is defined by the second central moment:

$$
T_{i,s} = \frac{m_i}{3 e}\,\frac{\int |\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{i,s}|^2 f_{i,s}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v}{\int f_{i,s}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v}
$$

where $e$ is the elementary charge, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m/s, $\mathbf{u}_{i,s}$ is the bulk velocity of that ionization-state population in m/s, and $f_{i,s}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{i,s}\,d^3v$ gives the ion density in m^-3. The factor $1/e$ converts the random kinetic energy per particle from joules to electronvolts, so that a Maxwellian population has mean random kinetic energy $(3/2)eT_{i,s}$.

Ion state temperature is inferred from charge-state-resolved diagnostics such as Doppler broadening of spectral lines, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or from kinetic and transport modeling. When the velocity distribution is anisotropic or non-Maxwellian, this scalar represents the isotropic temperature associated with the trace of the pressure tensor for the selected ionization state.

Typical values range from 10-500 eV in edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas, 0.5-20 keV in the confined core of tokamaks, and may be lower for cold neutral or weakly ionized populations treated as ion states in edge modeling.

NAMES.name: ion_state_upper_bound_charge
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Maximum ionization charge number (Z_max) of an ion charge-state bundle; equals the lower-bound charge when the bundle contains only a single resolved charge state.
NAMES.long:
The upper-bound charge number specifies the highest ionization state included in an ion charge-state bundle, where the ionization charge $Z$ counts the number of electrons removed from the neutral atom. In multi-fluid plasma models, consecutive ionization states of the same ion species are often grouped into bundles to reduce computational expense; this quantity gives the ceiling $Z_\mathrm{max}$ of the charge range $[Z_\mathrm{min}, Z_\mathrm{max}]$ spanned by the bundle.

When a bundle encloses only a single charge state, $Z_\mathrm{max}$ equals the corresponding [lower-bound charge]. For multi-state bundles the interval width $Z_\mathrm{max} - Z_\mathrm{min} \geq 1$, and the [concentration-weighted average charge] or [mean charge] provides a representative effective charge for transport and source-term calculations.

Charge-state values are non-negative integers bounded above by the nuclear charge number $Z_n$ of the species: for hydrogen $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 1$, for carbon $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 6$, and for heavy impurities such as tungsten $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 74$. The bundle definition is set at model initialization and does not vary with plasma conditions at a given time step.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion carries net positive charge, corresponding to the removal of one or more electrons from the neutral atom.

NAMES.name: ion_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Bulk fluid velocity vector of an ion species in a specified ionization charge state, defined as the first velocity moment of the charge-state distribution function normalized by the local charge-state number density.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state velocity is the mean flow velocity of ions belonging to a single resolved ionization charge state, representing the hydrodynamic drift of that charge-state fluid within the plasma. In a multi-fluid treatment, each charge state $z$ of a given ion species carries its own velocity field, which couples to neighboring charge states through ionization, recombination, and Coulomb friction between the constituent fluids.

The velocity vector is the first moment of the charge-state-resolved distribution function $f_z(\mathbf{v})$:

$$
\mathbf{u}_z = \frac{1}{n_z} \int \mathbf{v} \, f_z(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $n_z = \int f_z(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$ (in m$^{-3}$) and $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity.

The vector components are defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is the vertical height. The magnetic-field-aligned projection is [parallel_ion_state_velocity](name:parallel_ion_state_velocity), which is experimentally accessible via Doppler shifts from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. The charge-state-averaged parallel flow is captured by [parallel_ion_velocity](name:parallel_ion_velocity), while [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) provides the electron-fluid counterpart entering Ohm's law. Full vector components are computed self-consistently in multi-fluid edge transport codes that evolve separate momentum equations per charge state.

Typical parallel ion-state flow speeds range from sub-km/s in the low-flow core to near-sonic values of order $10^4$ m/s approaching the divertor target.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flow is directed in the positive direction of the respective basis vectors $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Charge-state-averaged bulk fluid velocity vector of the ion population, giving the mean directed ion motion at each plasma location.
NAMES.long:
The ion velocity is the bulk fluid velocity of the ion population at a given plasma location, averaged over all charge states weighted by their local number densities. It represents the mean directed motion of the composite ion fluid and is the first moment of the charge-state-summed ion distribution function normalized by the total ion number density.

The charge-state-averaged ion fluid velocity is defined as:

$$
\mathbf{v}_i = \frac{\sum_z n_{i,z}\, \mathbf{v}_{i,z}}{\sum_z n_{i,z}}
$$

where $n_{i,z}$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$ and $\mathbf{v}_{i,z}$ is the bulk velocity of that charge state. In practice the sum is dominated by the most abundant charge state for a given ion species.

The vector decomposes into directional projections: [parallel_ion_velocity](name:parallel_ion_velocity) gives the field-aligned component, [toroidal_ion_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) and poloidal_ion_velocity give the azimuthal and poloidal flow components, and [radial_ion_velocity](name:radial_ion_velocity) gives the major-radius component. The full ion velocity vector is distinct from [center_of_mass_velocity](name:center_of_mass_velocity), which weights each plasma species by mass rather than number density.

Ion flow velocities are measured through charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, which resolves Doppler shifts of emission lines to infer toroidal and poloidal components; Mach probes provide local measurements in the scrape-off layer. Typical toroidal flow speeds in H-mode plasmas range from a few to ~100 km/s; poloidal flows are generally an order of magnitude smaller, and parallel flows in the scrape-off layer can approach the local ion acoustic speed.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion fluid velocity vector has a positive projection onto the respective coordinate axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, or onto the local magnetic field direction $\hat{B}$ for the parallel component.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Number density of iron ions at the radial location of the internal transport barrier, where suppressed turbulent transport enables steep impurity density gradients to develop.
NAMES.long:
Iron (Fe, atomic number $Z = 26$) is a high-Z metallic impurity that enters fusion plasmas through sputtering or erosion of plasma-facing components. An internal transport barrier (ITB) is a radially localized region where turbulent cross-field transport is strongly suppressed, enabling steep radial gradients in density and temperature to develop and persist. This quantity is the total iron ion number density — summed over all ionization charge states — evaluated at the single reference radius assigned to the ITB in the chosen flux coordinate.

The ITB-local iron density is defined as:

$$
n_{\rm Fe}^{\rm ITB} = \sum_{z=1}^{26} n_{{\rm Fe},z}(r_{\rm ITB})
$$

where $n_{{\rm Fe},z}$ is the number density of iron ions in charge state $z$ and $r_{\rm ITB}$ is the ITB reference radius in the chosen flux coordinate.

This quantity is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy targeting iron spectral lines, or from impurity transport modeling constrained by soft X-ray tomography and bolometry data. The ITB reference radius is identified from regions of steep gradient in the ion or electron temperature profile, as described under [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier). Analogous quantities for other impurity species include [carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), [argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [oxygen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:oxygen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier); the companion electron density is [electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when iron ions are present at the internal transport barrier location.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Number density of iron ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Iron ($\mathrm{Fe}$, atomic number 26) is a high-$Z$ metallic impurity that enters the plasma primarily through physical sputtering of iron-containing plasma-facing components. At the magnetic axis — the point $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $\nabla\psi = 0$ — this density gives the on-axis value of the iron impurity radial profile and is the primary indicator of core impurity accumulation.

The total iron number density summed over all ionization states is:

$$
n_\mathrm{Fe}(R_\mathrm{axis}) = \sum_{z=1}^{26} n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{z+}}(R_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $z$ is the charge state ranging from singly-ionized $\mathrm{Fe}^{1+}$ to fully-stripped $\mathrm{Fe}^{26+}$, and $n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{z+}}$ is the partial density in m$^{-3}$.

Elevated on-axis values signal core impurity accumulation, which develops when the neoclassical inward pinch of high-$Z$ impurities exceeds outward turbulent transport. This quantity is inferred by combining line-integrated spectroscopic measurements — soft X-ray tomography, vacuum ultraviolet spectroscopy, or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy — with Abel inversion or impurity transport modeling. Core iron concentrations $n_\mathrm{Fe}/n_e$ typically span $10^{-5}$–$10^{-3}$ in tokamaks with iron-containing plasma-facing components. The [iron_density_at_pedestal](name:iron_density_at_pedestal) and [volume_averaged_iron_density](name:volume_averaged_iron_density) provide complementary pedestal-top and global characterizations of the same species; [nitrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:nitrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis) is the analogous on-axis density for nitrogen and follows the same localized [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis) structure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when iron ions are present; the number density is zero only in the complete absence of iron impurities and otherwise strictly positive.

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Number density of krypton ions evaluated at the radial position of the internal transport barrier, where locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport sustains steep impurity density gradients within the confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
Krypton (atomic number $Z = 36$) is a noble-gas impurity that is seeded into fusion plasmas for divertor heat-load mitigation and radiative power exhaust control. This quantity is the total number of krypton particles per unit volume, aggregated over all charge states present, evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier (ITB) — a localized zone where cross-field turbulent transport is strongly suppressed, allowing steep radial gradients in both temperature and impurity density to persist.

The krypton density at the ITB reflects the competition between the neoclassical inward pinch, which tends to accumulate impurities in the plasma core, and turbulent outward diffusion, which is reduced at the barrier; the resulting impurity peaking makes this quantity a sensitive indicator of barrier strength and confinement quality. It is a species-specific instance of [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier), directly analogous to [xenon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:xenon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:argon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) for heavier and lighter noble-gas impurities, respectively.

In practice the value is inferred from vacuum ultraviolet or soft X-ray spectroscopy of krypton line emission, or from impurity transport modeling constrained by measured radial profiles. Combining this quantity with [electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) enables estimates of the local krypton impurity fraction and its contribution to the effective charge $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ at the barrier. The krypton density at other radial locations is given by [krypton_density_at_pedestal](name:krypton_density_at_pedestal), [krypton_density_at_limiter](name:krypton_density_at_limiter), and [krypton_density_at_divertor_target](name:krypton_density_at_divertor_target).

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Number density of krypton ions evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Krypton ($Z = 36$) is a noble-gas impurity that can be seeded into confined plasmas for radiative power exhaust management or employed as a spectroscopic tracer. The krypton number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis value of the impurity concentration profile at the innermost nested flux surface, located at coordinates $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $\nabla\psi = 0$, with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux. It is the krypton-species instance of the [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis) family.

The on-axis krypton density is inferred from spectrally resolved line-emission diagnostics — such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy — combined with atomic data for the krypton charge-state distribution, and serves as the inner boundary value of the impurity concentration profile in radial transport analyzes.

Comparing this on-axis value with [krypton_density_at_pedestal](name:krypton_density_at_pedestal) and [krypton_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:krypton_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) characterizes the radial accumulation pattern: central peaking indicates the neoclassical inward pinch dominates over turbulent outward diffusion, while a hollow profile signals the reverse. The analogous on-axis density for boron is given by [boron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:boron_density_at_magnetic_axis).

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Lithium ion number density evaluated at the representative radial location of an internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Lithium ion number density at the internal transport barrier is the local number of lithium ions per unit volume at the representative radial location of an ITB. The ITB is a localized region of reduced radial transport within the confined plasma, so impurity densities can vary strongly across the barrier.

Using the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ (normalized toroidal flux radius), the point value is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Li,ITB}} = n_{\mathrm{Li}}\!\left(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm,ITB}}\right)
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Li,ITB}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{Li}}$ are lithium ion number densities in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm,ITB}}$ is the dimensionless value of the normalized toroidal flux radius selected to represent the ITB. If the barrier has finite radial width, the representative point is commonly chosen as the barrier center, the location of strongest local gradient, or the same ITB location used for related quantities such as [total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

The value is obtained by identifying the ITB location from the radial variation of transport-sensitive plasma quantities and evaluating a lithium-specific density estimate at that location. Lithium density is typically inferred from species-sensitive impurity measurements combined with atomic-physics or transport analysis, and it should be interpreted together with neighboring-location quantities such as [lithium_density_at_pedestal](name:lithium_density_at_pedestal) and [lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis).

Typical trace-to-minor lithium impurity densities in confined tokamak plasmas are about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$, usually well below the local total ion density. Values outside this order-of-magnitude range can occur depending on lithium source strength, confinement, and diagnostic sensitivity.

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Local number density of lithium ions evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The lithium ion number density at the magnetic axis gives the on-axis value of the lithium impurity concentration, summing contributions from all ionization charge states ($\mathrm{Li}^{1+}$, $\mathrm{Li}^{2+}$, and $\mathrm{Li}^{3+}$). As a specialization of the [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis) parent, it is evaluated at the coordinates $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height — at the unique interior point where $\nabla\psi = 0$.

The on-axis lithium density is defined as:

$$
n_\mathrm{Li,axis} = n_\mathrm{Li}(R_\mathrm{axis},\, Z_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Li}$ is the total lithium ion number density summed over charge states and $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ is the location satisfying $\nabla\psi = 0$ inside the confined plasma.

Elevated on-axis lithium density signals impurity accumulation in the plasma core, which dilutes the fuel species and reduces fusion reactivity; this contrasts with the pedestal and edge environments characterized by [lithium_density_at_pedestal](name:lithium_density_at_pedestal) and [lithium_density_at_limiter](name:lithium_density_at_limiter). The quantity is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or passive impurity spectroscopy combined with radial profile reconstruction that extrapolates to the axis. The [line_averaged_lithium_density](name:line_averaged_lithium_density) provides a complementary chord-integrated measure, while [lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) characterizes barrier-region impurity content.
NAMES.sign: Positive when lithium ions are present at the magnetic axis; this scalar number density is invariant under reversal of the toroidal magnetic field or plasma current direction.

NAMES.name: loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Toroidal electromotive force integrated around the last closed flux surface, measuring the net inductive and resistive voltage driving ohmic plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The loop voltage at the plasma boundary is the line integral of the total electric field around a toroidal contour lying on the last closed flux surface (LCFS), equal to the time rate of change of the total poloidal magnetic flux threading that boundary.

The defining relation is:

$$
V_{loop} = -\frac{d\Psi_b}{dt}
$$

where $\Psi_b$ is the total poloidal magnetic flux enclosed by the LCFS. In a resistive plasma at quasi-steady state this balances as $V_{loop} \approx R_p I_p$, where $R_p$ is the total parallel plasma resistance and $I_p$ is the plasma current; during ramp phases the inductive term $L_p dI_p/dt$ adds significantly. This quantity therefore characterizes both ohmic flux consumption and the resistive state of the plasma column.

It is inferred from voltage loops or flux loops positioned outside the plasma, after subtracting time derivatives of external coil fluxes. The externally driven component alone is captured by [external_loop_voltage](name:external_loop_voltage), and the [toroidal_electric_field](name:toroidal_electric_field) profile provides the radially resolved field from which boundary values are extracted.

Typical magnitudes are 0.1–5 V during the current flat-top in medium-to-large tokamaks, rising to 10–20 V during rapid current ramp-up.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electromotive force drives plasma current in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short: Vector field whose curl gives the magnetic induction, gage-dependent but physically central to canonical momentum, gyrokinetic, and magnetohydrodynamic formulations of magnetized plasmas.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ is a gage-dependent vector field characterizing the electromagnetic state of a plasma. It enters fundamental physics through the canonical particle momentum $\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v} + q\mathbf{A}$, where $m$ is particle mass and $q$ is particle charge, and it governs inductive electromagnetic effects in both equilibrium and perturbed plasma states.

The defining relation connecting $\mathbf{A}$ to the magnetic induction $\mathbf{B}$ is:

$$
\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic induction. Only the curl of $\mathbf{A}$ is directly physical; the vector potential itself is gage dependent. Its time derivative contributes to the inductive electric field via $\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{ind} = -\partial\mathbf{A}/\partial t$, which is central to Faraday's law in electromagnetic plasma models.

Specific projections serve distinct physical roles. The field-aligned component $A_\parallel = \mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{b}$, where $\hat{b}$ is the equilibrium field unit vector, governs Alfvénic dynamics and is the component retained in gyrokinetic and reduced-MHD formulations; [its normalized perturbed amplitude](name:parallel_normalized_perturbed_magnetic_vector_potential_amplitude) is used in eigenmode studies. Cylindrical components in the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — radial, toroidal, and vertical — are natural for equilibrium and MHD calculations, while the poloidal projection in flux coordinates $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$ arises in neoclassical transport analyzes. In vacuum regions, $\mathbf{A}$ is generated solely by external coil currents, with no plasma-current contribution.

NAMES.name: mass_density
NAMES.short: Total mass per unit volume of the plasma fluid, dominated by ion species contributions since individual ion masses greatly exceed the electron mass.
NAMES.long:
Mass density $\rho$ quantifies the inertial content of the plasma per unit volume and is the fundamental quantity linking fluid momentum density to bulk flow velocity in single-fluid and multi-fluid magnetohydrodynamic descriptions. It governs the inertial term in the momentum equation and sets the characteristic scale for Alfvén wave propagation, $v_A = B/\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}$, where $B$ is the magnetic field strength and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space.

The defining relation sums contributions from all particle species:

$$
\rho = \sum_s n_s m_s
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of species $s$ and $m_s$ is the corresponding particle mass. Because the electron-to-proton mass ratio is approximately $5.5 \times 10^{-4}$, the electron contribution is negligible and $\rho$ is determined almost entirely by the ion populations, with each species weighted by its [atomic mass](name:atomic_mass).

Mass density is computed from measured ion density profiles combined with species-specific atomic masses, summed over all ion species and charge states. In equilibrium analyzes it appears as a radial profile parameterized by the poloidal flux coordinate; in edge and MHD models it is resolved on general geometry grid subsets. For a pure deuterium plasma with core density $n_D \approx 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, the core mass density is approximately $3 \times 10^{-7}$ kg m$^{-3}$; scrape-off-layer values are often two to three orders of magnitude lower. The [center of mass velocity](name:center_of_mass_velocity) of the bulk plasma flow is obtained by dividing the total momentum density by $\rho$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local plasma region contains material with finite mass per unit volume.

NAMES.name: momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Effective velocity-like coefficient for the advective, non-diffusive part of momentum transport in a plasma or neutral fluid. More specific names define the transported momentum population, species, charge state, component, projection, or physical contribution.
NAMES.long:
Momentum convection velocity is an effective transport coefficient that parameterizes the advective part of a momentum flux. It is not necessarily the bulk flow velocity of a single species; it may represent a closure velocity for total, ion, neutral, toroidal, diamagnetic, species-resolved, or state-resolved momentum transport.

For a resolved momentum density component or projection, the common flux decomposition writes the convective contribution as

$$
\Gamma_M^{\mathrm{conv}} = V_M M
$$

where $M$ is the selected momentum density, $\Gamma_M^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is its non-diffusive convective flux through the chosen direction or surface, and $V_M$ is the corresponding momentum convection velocity. Vector or tensor momentum-flux closures apply the same idea component-wise, with the more specific quantity defining the transported momentum and direction; examples include [toroidal_momentum_convection_velocity](name:toroidal_momentum_convection_velocity), [ion_momentum_convection_velocity](name:ion_momentum_convection_velocity), and [neutral_momentum_convection_velocity](name:neutral_momentum_convection_velocity).

This coefficient is usually inferred from momentum balance analysis, transport modeling, or closure relations rather than measured directly. It can include contributions from turbulence, neoclassical pinches, diamagnetic drifts, neutral flow, charge exchange, ionization, and source-driven redistribution, depending on the specific child quantity.

Typical magnitudes range from 0.1-100 m.s^-1 for weak core momentum pinches and can reach 10^2-10^4 m.s^-1 in edge, scrape-off-layer, or neutral-momentum applications. The value can be either sign because it represents a directed component or projection of an effective advective transport velocity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the resolved velocity component or projection is directed along the positive direction defined by the corresponding specific quantity, such as $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, or along the specified oriented surface normal for a flux projection.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Effective convection velocity for radial toroidal momentum transport arising from the diamagnetic drift, parameterizing the diamagnetic contribution to the convective momentum flux across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic momentum convection velocity is the effective radial velocity at which toroidal angular momentum is transported by the diamagnetic drift mechanism across magnetic flux surfaces. In a magnetized plasma, pressure gradients sustain a diamagnetic drift that contributes a convective term to the radial momentum transport equation, driving a net momentum flux even in the absence of turbulent fluctuations.

The diamagnetic convection velocity $V_{dia}$ appears in the radial transport equation for toroidal angular momentum density $L_\phi$:

$$
\frac{\partial L_\phi}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{V'}\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\left(V' V_{dia} L_\phi\right) = S_\phi
$$

where $\rho$ is a radial flux coordinate, $V' = dV/d\rho$ is the derivative of enclosed plasma volume with respect to $\rho$, and $S_\phi$ collects all toroidal torque-density sources.

This velocity is derived from transport models that parameterize neoclassical and anomalous diamagnetic contributions to momentum convection. Species-resolved forms are given by [ion_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity) and its charge-state-resolved counterpart [ion_state_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity](name:ion_state_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity); the parent [momentum_convection_velocity](name:momentum_convection_velocity) aggregates all convective mechanisms acting on toroidal momentum.
NAMES.sign: Positive when directed radially outward, in the direction of increasing minor radius.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective convection velocity for ion momentum transport in a plasma.
NAMES.long:
Ion momentum convection velocity is an effective velocity that advects ion momentum density in momentum-transport equations for plasma ions. It represents the convective or pinch contribution to the ion momentum flux, separate from diffusive viscosity, residual stress, and explicit momentum sources, and it is not generally identical to the bulk ion fluid velocity.

The convective flux density of a chosen ion-momentum component is represented by:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{conv}}_{p_{i,a}} = p_{i,a}\,\mathbf{V}_{i,\mathrm{mom,conv}}
$$

where $p_{i,a}=n_i m_i u_{i,a}$ is the ion momentum density associated with ion flow component $u_{i,a}$, $n_i$ is the ion density, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $a$ labels the momentum component being transported, and $\mathbf{V}_{i,\mathrm{mom,conv}}$ is this effective convection velocity.

In practice, the quantity is computed or inferred from momentum-balance analysis, fluid closures, neoclassical theory, or turbulence calculations by isolating the part of the ion momentum flux proportional to local momentum density. Component-specific quantities specify the projection direction: [parallel ion momentum convection velocity](name:parallel_ion_momentum_convection_velocity) is along the magnetic field, while [vertical ion momentum convection velocity](name:vertical_ion_momentum_convection_velocity) is the $Z$ projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height. Related scalar projections such as [radial ion momentum effective convection velocity](name:radial_ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity), [parallel momentum effective convection velocity](name:parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity), and [poloidal momentum effective convection velocity](name:poloidal_momentum_effective_convection_velocity) use the same coefficient concept after projection onto their stated directions.

Representative magnitudes are strongly projection dependent. Cross-field effective pinch velocities are often 0.1-100 m.s^-1, vertical edge convection terms are often 1-1000 m.s^-1, and field-aligned effective convection can reach 10^2-10^5 m.s^-1 when it is comparable to parallel ion flows.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a component of the vector points in the positive direction of the named coordinate or projection basis used for that component, such as the $+Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame or the direction of the magnetic field for a parallel projection.

NAMES.name: ion_state_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Charge-state-resolved diamagnetic effective convection velocity for cross-flux-surface transport of toroidal ion momentum. It is the velocity coefficient associated with the diamagnetic contribution for a specified ionization state of an ion species.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic momentum convection velocity for a single ionization state is the effective velocity that, multiplied by the toroidal-momentum density of that charge state, reproduces the diamagnetic part of the cross-flux-surface flux of toroidal ion momentum. It provides finer resolution than the species-level [ion_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity) and the fully aggregated [diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity), allowing distinct ionization stages of the same species to carry different pressure-gradient-driven momentum-convection responses.

The coefficient is defined as the ratio of the diamagnetic toroidal-momentum flux density to the toroidal-momentum density of the charge state:

$$
v_{\mathrm{dia}}^{(z)} = \frac{\Gamma_{\mathrm{mom,dia}}^{(z)}}{m_i \, n_{i,z} \, u_{\phi,i,z}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{mom,dia}}^{(z)}$ is the diamagnetic contribution to the cross-flux-surface flux density of toroidal momentum (kg m^-1 s^-2), $m_i$ is the ion mass (kg), $n_{i,z}$ is the number density of the ionization state $z$ (m^-3), and $u_{\phi,i,z}$ is its toroidal flow velocity (m s^-1). The diamagnetic label denotes the part of the transport associated with the charge-state pressure gradient; the underlying local diamagnetic drift scale is $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia}}^{(z)} = \mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_{i,z} / (q_{i,z} \, n_{i,z} \, B^2)$, with $p_{i,z} = n_{i,z} k_B T_{i,z}$ the partial pressure, $q_{i,z} = Z_z e$ the charge-state charge, and $\mathbf{B}$ the magnetic field.

In practice the coefficient is obtained from transport modeling or from interpretation of the momentum balance using reconstructed densities, temperatures, charge-state fractions, flows, and magnetic geometry. Flux-surface averaging and the chosen closure determine how the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic contribution is represented as a single scalar convection velocity for each charge state. The analogous flux quantity is [ion_charge_state_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

Typical effective magnitudes in core plasmas are of order a few m s^-1, with larger values possible in steep-gradient or low-density regions; the value may be inward or outward and can differ markedly between ionization states.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective diamagnetic convection of toroidal ion momentum for the charge state is directed outward across flux surfaces, toward increasing normalized minor radius.

NAMES.name: ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Effective velocity coefficient for non-diffusive convection of momentum carried by a specified ion species in a specified ionization state. A concrete qualifier may identify the transport direction or the transported momentum component, so related names are not necessarily projections of one geometric velocity vector.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state momentum convection velocity is the effective advective coefficient multiplying the momentum density of an ion species in a specified charge state in a multi-fluid momentum balance. It represents the non-diffusive part of momentum transport; in concrete names, the qualifier may refer to the direction of transport, as in [radial ion-state momentum convection velocity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity), or to the momentum component being transported, as in [toroidal ion-state momentum convection velocity](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity).

A common reduced form for the convective flux of an ion-state momentum component is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{mom,conv}}_{i,q,\alpha} = \boldsymbol{V}^{\mathrm{mom,conv}}_{i,q,\alpha}\, M_{i,q,\alpha}
$$

where $M_{i,q,\alpha}$ is the density of momentum component $\alpha$ carried by ion species $i$ in ionization state $q$, $\boldsymbol{V}^{\mathrm{mom,conv}}_{i,q,\alpha}$ is the effective convection velocity, and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{mom,conv}}_{i,q,\alpha}$ is the corresponding convective momentum flux. In reduced transport equations, this velocity may be represented by its signed component along the relevant transport direction rather than by a full spatial vector.

In practice, this quantity is obtained from charge-state-resolved transport analysis or fluid modeling by separating advective momentum flux from diffusive viscosity, external torque, collisional exchange, ionization, recombination, and neutral-interaction source terms. It may represent turbulent or neoclassical momentum pinch effects, bulk plasma advection, scrape-off-layer flows, or effective closure terms chosen to reproduce measured rotation and flow evolution.

Typical cross-field effective convection velocities are about 0.01-100 m.s^-1 in confined-plasma transport analysis, while field-aligned or scrape-off-layer momentum advection can reach 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1 depending on temperature, collisionality, and connection length. The value can be positive or negative because the coefficient describes directed transport rather than a speed magnitude.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convection is along the positive transport direction associated with the corresponding momentum-transport term: outward toward increasing flux-surface label such as $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ for radial transport, toward increasing $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ for poloidal transport, toward $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame for vertical transport, or along the declared positive field-aligned direction for parallel transport.

NAMES.name: momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.short: Effective inverse relaxation time for loss of ordered fluid momentum through collisional friction and neoclassical viscosity; the general structural parent for species-, charge-state-, and projection-resolved momentum damping rates.
NAMES.long:
The momentum damping rate $\nu_D$ is the reciprocal relaxation time that quantifies how rapidly ordered fluid momentum is dissipated within a plasma population through inter-species collisional friction and neoclassical viscous stresses. It enters the fluid momentum balance as a linear loss coefficient applied to the local momentum density, capturing the collective effect of Coulomb collisions and drift-driven viscosity acting on any directed flow component.

The defining relation for a fluid momentum component $p$ subject to damping is:

$$
\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}\bigg|_{\rm damp} = -\nu_D \, p
$$

where $\nu_D$ is the damping rate and $p$ is the local fluid momentum density. The magnitude of $\nu_D$ depends on plasma collisionality, species masses and charges, and the local magnetic geometry.

This name is the structural parent for species- and projection-resolved variants. In transport models, $\nu_D$ is derived analytically from neoclassical friction-force coefficients or from velocity-space integrals of the collision operator evaluated at the local plasma parameters. Ion-population values are provided by [ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:ion_momentum_damping_rate); charge-state-resolved counterparts are given by [ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:ion_state_momentum_damping_rate). Directional projections include [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), [toroidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), [parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), and [radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate).

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective inverse relaxation time for collisional and neoclassical dissipation of bulk ion fluid momentum, expressed as a vector whose components each quantify the damping rate along a distinct geometric projection of the ion velocity.
NAMES.long:
The ion momentum damping rate is the effective inverse relaxation timescale at which ordered bulk ion fluid momentum is dissipated through Coulomb collisions and neoclassical viscous stresses. As a vector, it encodes the geometric anisotropy of momentum loss in a magnetized plasma, where the field-aligned and toroidal projections relax through distinct mechanisms compared with the poloidal or radial projections.

In the ion fluid momentum balance the damping contribution enters as:

$$\frac{\partial \mathbf{p}_i}{\partial t}\bigg|_{\rm damp} = -\boldsymbol{\nu}_D^{\,i} \cdot \mathbf{p}_i$$

where $\mathbf{p}_i = m_i n_i \mathbf{v}_i$ is the ion momentum density, with $m_i$ the ion mass, $n_i$ the number density, and $\mathbf{v}_i$ the bulk ion fluid velocity. The rate $\boldsymbol{\nu}_D^{\,i}$ is applied component-wise and aggregates contributions from all ion charge states.

Component-resolved scalar rates are [radial_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:radial_ion_momentum_damping_rate), [toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate), [poloidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate), and [parallel_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:parallel_ion_momentum_damping_rate). These are computed from neoclassical transport theory or turbulent-momentum-transport models. This quantity serves as the ion-species-level structural parent described by [momentum_damping_rate](name:momentum_damping_rate), which covers the general multi-species case.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the rate coefficient reduces the magnitude of the corresponding ion momentum component, producing exponential relaxation toward zero ordered flow.

NAMES.name: ion_state_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Vector inverse relaxation time for collisional and neoclassical dissipation of ordered fluid momentum of a specific ion charge state, resolved along the parallel, poloidal, radial, and toroidal directions.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state momentum damping rate is the component-resolved inverse relaxation time quantifying how rapidly ordered fluid momentum of an ion in a specified charge state is dissipated through Coulomb collisional friction and neoclassical viscous stresses in a toroidally confined plasma. As a vector quantity, each directional projection enters the corresponding component of the ion fluid momentum equation as a linear damping coefficient, relating the rate of momentum loss to the local ion fluid velocity for that charge state.

The defining relation for each projection $\alpha$ (parallel, poloidal, radial, or toroidal) is:

$$
\left.\frac{\partial u_\alpha}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{damp}} = -\nu_{D,\alpha}\, u_\alpha
$$

where $\nu_{D,\alpha}$ is the damping rate component for projection $\alpha$ and $u_\alpha$ is the corresponding ion fluid velocity component for the given charge state.

The four directional components are [parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate) for the field-aligned direction, [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate) for the meridional surface-tangential direction, [radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), and [toroidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate) for the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Charge-state-aggregated analogs include [parallel_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:parallel_ion_momentum_damping_rate) and [radial_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:radial_ion_momentum_damping_rate), while pressure-gradient-driven contributions are captured by ion_state_momentum_diamagnetic_damping_rate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the momentum damping rate component points in the positive direction of the respective projection axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.short: Vector of directional kinematic diffusivities relating diffusive momentum flux density to the local flow-velocity gradient for plasma or neutral species in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The momentum diffusion coefficient is a vector transport coefficient whose components quantify diffusive redistribution of fluid momentum along distinct geometric directions in a magnetized plasma. Each component acts as a kinematic diffusivity, coupling the local diffusive momentum flux density to the spatial gradient of the corresponding flow-velocity component.

The defining Fickian relation for the diffusive momentum flux density along direction $i$ is

$$
\Pi_i^{\rm diff} = -\rho \, D_i \, \frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_i}
$$

where $\rho$ is the local mass density in kg m$^{-3}$, $u_i$ is the fluid velocity component, and $D_i$ is the momentum diffusion coefficient in that direction.

Magnetized plasmas are strongly anisotropic: the component parallel to the local magnetic field typically exceeds cross-field components by several orders of magnitude due to Lorentz-force suppression of perpendicular transport, as quantified by [parallel_edge_plasma_momentum_diffusivity](name:parallel_edge_plasma_momentum_diffusivity). Toroidal and poloidal projections — such as toroidal_plasma_momentum_diffusivity and [poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity](name:poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity) — are distinct both in magnitude and in the collisional or turbulent mechanisms that drive them. In edge and divertor regions, charge-exchange coupling between ions and neutrals transfers momentum between species, making the neutral-particle components physically significant alongside the plasma components captured by plasma_momentum_diffusivity. Inference relies on momentum-balance analysis of measured flow profiles, supplemented by fluid or gyrokinetic modeling of turbulent and collisional contributions.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Vector of directional diffusion coefficients governing diffusive transport of bulk-ion momentum in a magnetized plasma, with distinct radial, poloidal, and toroidal components forming the diagonal of the ion momentum diffusivity tensor.
NAMES.long:
The ion momentum diffusion coefficient vector collects the anisotropic diagonal components of the bulk-ion momentum diffusivity tensor, each relating the diffusive flux of bulk-ion momentum along a given geometric direction to the local gradient of ion momentum density in that direction. In a gradient-diffusion closure, each directional component $\chi_{\rm mom}$ satisfies the constitutive relation:

$$
\Gamma_{\rm mom} = -\chi_{\rm mom}\,\nabla(m_i n_i v_i)
$$

where $\Gamma_{\rm mom}$ is the diffusive ion momentum flux density, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ is the ion number density, and $v_i$ is the bulk ion flow velocity component in the corresponding direction. The three projections are [radial_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient), governing cross-flux-surface momentum mixing; [poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient), governing transport along the poloidal direction tangent to flux surfaces; and [toroidal_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient), governing diffusion of toroidal angular momentum. The radial component is the confinement-relevant quantity and is inferred from toroidal momentum balance analyzes or gyrokinetic and fluid turbulence simulations. The scalar analog [ion_momentum_diffusivity](name:ion_momentum_diffusivity) represents the same physical concept without directional decomposition, while plasma_momentum_diffusivity extends the concept to the full plasma mixture.

NAMES.name: ion_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Effective directional momentum diffusion coefficient for a specified ion charge state, giving the diagonal diffusivities that relate diffusive momentum flux density to the local ion velocity gradient along each geometric direction.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state momentum diffusion coefficient encodes the anisotropic diagonal momentum diffusivities for a resolved ion charge state, characterizing how collisional, neoclassical, or turbulent processes scatter that ion population's momentum along the radial, poloidal, and toroidal directions of the device.

In the diffusive closure, the momentum flux density for charge state $s$ along direction $i$ is defined by

$$
\Pi_i^s = -\chi_i^s \, m_s n_s \, \frac{\partial u_i^s}{\partial x_i}
$$

where $m_s$ is the ion mass, $n_s$ is the number density of that charge state, $u_i^s$ is the flow velocity component along direction $i$, and $\chi_i^s$ is the corresponding momentum diffusivity. Positive values of $\chi_i^s$ indicate down-gradient momentum transport; negative values can arise when turbulent momentum redistribution drives an up-gradient pinch contribution.

The vector form assembles these directional components: the [radial ion-state momentum diffusion coefficient](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) governs cross-field transport through flux surfaces, capturing neoclassical viscosity and turbulent Reynolds-stress contributions; the [poloidal ion-state momentum diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) quantifies momentum relaxation along flux surfaces in the poloidal direction. These diffusivities are inferred from global transport analysis, neoclassical theory, or gyrokinetic simulation; typical core values span 0.1–10 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ in tokamak plasmas. The parent [momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:momentum_diffusion_coefficient) describes the analogous quantity for bulk plasma without charge-state resolution, and plasma_momentum_diffusivity provides a bulk-plasma effective diffusivity for comparison.

NAMES.name: momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.short: Vector Fick's-law transport coefficient relating the diffusive momentum flux to the local momentum-density gradient, abstracting over plasma species, neutral populations, charge states, and directional projections in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
Momentum diffusivity is the proportionality coefficient between the diffusive momentum flux and the negative local gradient of momentum density, following a Fick's-law closure for the fluid momentum balance. Physically, it encapsulates contributions from collisional viscosity, turbulent mixing, charge-exchange friction, and diamagnetic drifts. As a vector quantity, its radial, poloidal, toroidal, parallel, and vertical components capture the strongly anisotropic transport characteristic of magnetized plasma, where diffusivity along magnetic field lines greatly exceeds cross-field values.

The diffusive momentum flux density component along direction $\hat{e}_i$ is

$$
\Gamma_{m,i} = -D_{m,i} \frac{\partial (m n v_i)}{\partial x_i}
$$

where $D_{m,i}$ is the momentum diffusivity component, $m$ is particle mass, $n$ is number density, and $v_i$ is the fluid velocity component along $\hat{e}_i$, making $m n v_i$ the local momentum density.

This parent name abstracts over species-resolved and process-attributed children including plasma_momentum_diffusivity for the total plasma and analogous neutral-population variants; the [radial_plasma_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_plasma_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) is the cross-field specialization and [parallel_edge_plasma_momentum_diffusivity](name:parallel_edge_plasma_momentum_diffusivity) is the field-aligned form. Values are inferred from fluid transport simulations by computing the diffusive momentum flux relative to the local momentum-density gradient, or estimated analytically from neoclassical and turbulence theory.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.short: Effective cross-field diffusion coefficient for the diamagnetic contribution to plasma momentum transport, arising from pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic drifts rather than collisional viscosity.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic momentum diffusivity is the effective cross-field diffusion coefficient that characterizes how pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic drifts contribute to plasma momentum transport across flux surfaces, independently of collisional viscosity mechanisms. In a magnetized plasma, a spatial pressure gradient $\nabla p$ drives guiding-center drifts perpendicular to both $\nabla p$ and the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$; this non-dissipative diamagnetic drift carries momentum radially in a diffusion-like manner that is captured as an effective coefficient.

The diamagnetic contribution to the radial momentum flux density is expressed as:

$$
\Gamma_\mathrm{mom}^\mathrm{dia} = -D_\mathrm{dia} \, \nabla(m n v)
$$

where $D_\mathrm{dia}$ is the diamagnetic momentum diffusivity, $m$ is the particle mass, $n$ the number density, and $v$ the relevant fluid velocity component.

This quantity is the structural parent of [ion_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity](name:ion_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity), which aggregates the diamagnetic momentum diffusivity over all ion charge states, and [ion_state_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity](name:ion_state_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity), which resolves it for a single specified charge state. The closely related [diamagnetic_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:ion_momentum_diffusivity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [momentum_diffusivity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_momentum_diffusivity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) are peer names encoding the same physical mechanism. Within the broader [momentum_diffusivity](name:momentum_diffusivity) framework, the diamagnetic component is especially significant in edge and pedestal regions where steep pressure gradients amplify the drift-driven momentum flux.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Kinematic diffusion coefficient for the momentum of ions in a specified ionization state, relating the diffusive momentum flux in each geometric direction to the local momentum density gradient via a Fick-law closure.
NAMES.long:
Momentum diffusivity for an ion charge state is the transport coefficient appearing in the diffusive closure of the charge-state-resolved momentum equation, quantifying how neoclassical and turbulent processes redistribute the momentum of ions at a given ionization level. It is the momentum analog of thermal diffusivity, with the diffusive flux proportional to the local gradient of the corresponding momentum density component.

The diffusive momentum flux for charge state $s$ in direction $\alpha$ is:

$$
\Pi_{s,\alpha}^{\rm diff} = -m_s n_s \chi_{s,\alpha} \frac{\partial v_{s,\alpha}}{\partial x_\alpha}
$$

where $m_s$ is the ion mass, $n_s$ is the number density of charge state $s$, $v_{s,\alpha}$ is the flow velocity component in direction $\alpha$, and $\chi_{s,\alpha}$ is this momentum diffusivity.

The directional components resolve distinct transport channels: [radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity) governs cross-field transport through flux surfaces; [parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity) covers field-aligned diffusion along the magnetic field; [toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity) and [poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity) address the azimuthal projections. The charge-state-summed analog for the bulk plasma is plasma_momentum_diffusivity.

Typical values range from 0.1–10 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ in the plasma core, with larger values toward the edge and scrape-off layer where turbulent transport dominates over neoclassical diffusion.

NAMES.name: ion_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective cross-field diffusivity for the diamagnetic contribution to ion momentum transport, summed over all charge states of the ion species.
NAMES.long:
Ion diamagnetic momentum diffusivity is an effective transport coefficient for the diffusive part of ion momentum flux associated with diamagnetic drift dynamics. It represents the charge-state-summed response of an ion species, rather than the contribution of a single ionization state.

A common local closure relates the diamagnetic contribution to the radial flux of ion momentum to the radial gradient of ion momentum density:

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{dia}}_i(r) = -D^{\mathrm{dia}}_{\Pi,i}(r)\,\frac{\partial \mathcal{P}_i}{\partial r}
$$

where $\Pi^{\mathrm{dia}}_i$ is the diamagnetic contribution to the cross-flux-surface ion momentum flux, taken positive toward larger $r$, $D^{\mathrm{dia}}_{\Pi,i}$ is the ion diamagnetic momentum diffusivity, and $\mathcal{P}_i = \sum_z \mathcal{P}_{i,z}$ is the ion momentum density summed over charge states $z$ of the ion species. The coordinate $r$ is a minor-radius-like flux-surface label in the flux-coordinate set $(r,\theta,\phi)$, measured in meters and increasing outward from the magnetic axis; $\theta$ is poloidal angle and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. The minus sign gives the down-gradient diffusive convention, so a positive coefficient drives outward momentum transport when $\mathcal{P}_i$ decreases outward.

Diamagnetic drift flows arise from cross-field ion pressure gradients in a magnetized plasma, so this coefficient is typically evaluated from momentum-balance modeling using measured or simulated rotation, density, temperature, pressure-gradient, and magnetic-geometry information. As an effective closure coefficient, it may include unresolved turbulent, neoclassical, and modeling residual effects assigned to the diamagnetic momentum-transport channel.

Typical modeled values are 0.01-10 m^2 s^-1 in confined-core conditions, while steep-gradient edge regions or strongly turbulent phases can give effective values of 10-100 m^2 s^-1. Local fitted values outside these ranges, including negative values, usually indicate that the chosen diffusive term is absorbing residual convective or up-gradient momentum flux rather than representing a purely diffusive process.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Diffusion coefficient relating the diffusive ion momentum flux to the local ion momentum density gradient, expressing the rate at which diffusive processes redistribute momentum within the total ion population summed over charge states.
NAMES.long:
The ion momentum diffusivity $D_{\mathrm{mom}}^i$ is the effective diffusion coefficient characterizing how diffusive processes redistribute momentum within the total ion population across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the species-summed, charge-state-integrated scalar counterpart of [ion_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:ion_state_momentum_diffusivity), which resolves the same quantity by charge state, and represents the effective-scalar form of the full tensor [momentum_diffusivity](name:momentum_diffusivity).

The diffusive component of the ion momentum flux density $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{mom},i}$ satisfies:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{mom},i} = -n_i m_i D_{\mathrm{mom}}^i \nabla v_i
$$

where $n_i$ is the ion number density, $m_i$ is the ion mass, and $v_i$ is the mean ion fluid velocity.

The ion momentum diffusivity is inferred by fitting a transport model to measured ion rotation profiles, obtained via charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. Comparing $D_{\mathrm{mom}}^i$ with the ion thermal diffusivity yields the ion-channel Prandtl number, a key indicator of whether momentum and heat are transported by the same underlying turbulent mechanism.

In tokamak core plasmas, values fall in the range 0.1–10 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, comparable in magnitude to the ion thermal diffusivity under turbulence-dominated conditions and smaller when neoclassical processes dominate. The radial projection is separately quantified by [radial_momentum_diffusivity](name:radial_momentum_diffusivity), while the diamagnetic-drift-driven contribution is captured by [ion_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity](name:ion_diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity).

NAMES.name: ion_state_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: State-resolved scalar diffusion coefficient for directed ion momentum. It parameterizes down-gradient viscous redistribution of momentum for a specified ion species and ionization state; directional specializations supply the chosen component.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state momentum diffusivity is an effective scalar transport coefficient for the directed momentum density of a specified ion species and ionization state. It represents a diagonal diffusive response for a chosen direction or projection, so the parent concept covers field-aligned, radial, poloidal, toroidal, and vertical momentum diffusion without selecting one of them.

For a selected component $\alpha$, a Fickian diffusive closure can be written as:

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}_{s,\alpha} = -D^{(m)}_{s,\alpha}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial \ell_\alpha}\left(n_s m_s u_{s,\alpha}\right)
$$

where $\Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}_{s,\alpha}$ is the diffusive flux of the directed momentum density, $D^{(m)}_{s,\alpha}$ is the momentum diffusivity, $n_s$ is the ion charge-state density, $m_s$ is the ion mass, $u_{s,\alpha}$ is the directed ion flow velocity, and $\ell_\alpha$ is distance along the selected transport direction. For nonnegative $D^{(m)}_{s,\alpha}$, the minus sign makes the diffusive momentum flux oppose gradients of momentum density and smooth velocity shear.

In practice this coefficient is inferred from transport analysis using ion velocity measurements, charge-state densities, momentum sources, and reconstructed or modeled momentum fluxes. It may combine collisional viscosity, neoclassical transport, and turbulent anomalous transport. Directional quantities such as [parallel ion-state momentum diffusivity](name:parallel_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity) and [radial ion-state momentum diffusivity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_diffusivity) specify the relevant projection; toroidal and vertical specializations use the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Typical effective values in magnetically confined plasmas are about 0.01-10 m^2.s^-1 in core transport analyzes and can reach 10-100 m^2.s^-1 in edge or strongly turbulent regions. The value depends on collisionality, turbulence level, ionization state, and the selected direction; a purely diffusive coefficient is nonnegative.

NAMES.name: momentum_due_to_hot_tail
NAMES.short: Momentum-space scale associated with suprathermal electrons produced by the hot-tail mechanism during rapid plasma cooling. It represents electron momentum relevant to the retained hot-tail population, with more specific names defining particular characteristic values or thresholds.
NAMES.long:
Hot-tail momentum is the scalar magnitude of electron momentum associated with the suprathermal part of an electron distribution that does not immediately rethermalize during a rapid temperature collapse. It identifies a characteristic location in momentum space for the hot-tail population and may be specialized to particular values such as the [critical momentum due to hot tail](name:critical_momentum_due_to_hot_tail).

The electron momentum magnitude is related to speed by:

$$
p = \gamma m_e v = \frac{m_e v}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}
$$

where $p$ is the momentum magnitude, $m_e$ is the electron rest mass, $v$ is the electron speed, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\gamma$ is the Lorentz factor. The non-relativistic approximation $p \approx m_e v$ applies only for slow electrons; hot-tail and runaway-seed calculations commonly use the relativistic form because the relevant tail can reach a substantial fraction of $c$.

In practice, hot-tail momentum scales are computed from kinetic or reduced-kinetic descriptions of the electron distribution during a thermal quench. They are governed by the competition between collisional slowing down, rapid cooling of the thermal bulk, and any accelerating electric field, and are inferred from quantities such as the electron temperature history, density, effective charge, and distribution-function evolution.

Typical values are often quoted as normalized momentum $p/(m_e c)$. Hot-tail seed and threshold scales commonly lie around $p/(m_e c)=0.1-10$, spanning mildly suprathermal electrons to MeV-scale runaway seeds; the value tends to be lower for faster cooling and higher when collisional drag remains strong.

NAMES.name: momentum_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Velocity-like coefficient in the flux-surface-averaged ion momentum transport equation that, when multiplied by the local ion momentum density, gives the convective pinch flux of that momentum component across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The momentum effective convection velocity is the vector transport coefficient governing advective (pinch) transport of ion momentum across magnetic flux surfaces in the flux-surface-averaged radial transport description. Unlike the bulk ion flow velocity, it is an off-diagonal kinetic or fluid transport coefficient that encodes contributions from neoclassical, turbulent, and diamagnetic drift mechanisms, and is in general distinct for each momentum projection (toroidal, poloidal, parallel).

In the radial momentum transport model, the convective momentum flux through a flux surface takes the form:

$$
\Gamma_{\rm mom}^{\rm conv} = V_{\rm eff}^{\rm mom} \cdot \langle \rho_m u \rangle
$$

where $V_{\rm eff}^{\rm mom}$ is this effective convection velocity, $\rho_m$ is the local ion mass density, and $u$ is the momentum component being transported. The species-aggregated form is given by [ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity](name:ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity), which sums contributions across all ion charge states. This quantity is the momentum-specific specialization of the parent [effective_convection_velocity](name:effective_convection_velocity), which applies the same pinch-coefficient role to density, energy, and other transported quantities.

The coefficient is not directly measurable; it is inferred from transport model fits to experimentally reconstructed plasma rotation profiles, or computed from gyrokinetic and neoclassical calculations that resolve flux-surface-averaged cross-field momentum fluxes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective advection is directed outward across flux surfaces, away from the magnetic axis in the direction of increasing minor radius.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_momentum_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Charge-state-aggregated diamagnetic effective convection velocity for radial ion momentum transport. It is the velocity coefficient that, multiplied by the total ion momentum density, reproduces the summed charge-state diamagnetic convective momentum flux across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
