Diamagnetic momentum effective convection velocity is the scalar velocity coefficient that condenses the charge-state-aggregated diamagnetic convective contribution to radial ion momentum transport into a single effective velocity. It multiplies the total ion momentum density to reproduce the summed diamagnetic convective momentum flux from all ion charge states.

For ion charge states indexed by $z$, it is defined as the ratio of the summed diamagnetic momentum flux to the summed momentum density on a magnetic flux surface:

$$
V_{\pi,\mathrm{eff}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{\sum_z \langle \Gamma_{\pi,z}^{\mathrm{dia}} \rangle}{\sum_z \langle \pi_z \rangle}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\pi,z}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the radial diamagnetic flux of ion momentum for charge state $z$ (units of momentum density times m.s^-1, i.e. kg.m^-1.s^-2 or Pa for linear momentum density), $\pi_z$ is the corresponding momentum density, and $\langle A \rangle$ denotes the average of $A$ over a magnetic flux surface labeled by the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. Equivalently, given charge-state velocities $V_{\pi,z}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ with a common convention, $V_{\pi,\mathrm{eff}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = \sum_z \langle \pi_z \rangle V_{\pi,z}^{\mathrm{dia}} / \sum_z \langle \pi_z \rangle$, provided the denominator is nonzero.

This is the charge-state-aggregated counterpart of the ion-resolved ion_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity and the per-state [ion_state_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity](name:ion_state_diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity); it carries the effective qualifier relative to [diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_convection_velocity) to indicate the density-weighted aggregation over charge states. It is not usually a directly measured velocity but is inferred from reconstructed equilibrium geometry, kinetic profiles, rotation measurements, and the transport model used to separate the diamagnetic component from other momentum-flux channels.

Typical magnitudes are 0.1-10 m.s^-1 in core transport analyzes and can reach 10-100 m.s^-1 in steep-gradient regions or during strong momentum redistribution. The value may be either inward or outward and should be interpreted together with the chosen momentum density and the full momentum-flux decomposition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the charge-state-aggregated diamagnetic convective flux of ion momentum is directed toward increasing normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective cross-field velocity coefficient in ion momentum transport: it multiplies a selected ion momentum component to represent advective radial flux across magnetic flux surfaces. Its specializations refer to the ion momentum component being transported, not to projections of one common velocity vector.
NAMES.long:
An ion momentum effective convection velocity is an effective cross-field advective coefficient in a flux-surface-averaged ion momentum balance. It represents the velocity multiplying a chosen signed component of ion momentum to form the convective part of that component's radial momentum flux. The labels in [parallel](name:parallel_ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity), [poloidal](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity), and [radial](name:radial_ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity) forms identify which ion momentum component appears in the balance; they are not spatial projections of a single velocity vector.

For a momentum component $k$, the convective contribution to the flux-surface-averaged radial momentum flux is commonly written as:

$$
\Pi_k^{\mathrm{conv}} = V_{k,\mathrm{eff}} M_k
$$

where $\Pi_k^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective radial flux of ion momentum component $k$, $M_k$ is the flux-surface-averaged density of that signed ion momentum component, and $V_{k,\mathrm{eff}}$ is the corresponding effective convection velocity.

This coefficient is not generally a directly measured fluid velocity. It is inferred from momentum transport analysis or kinetic modeling by separating the total radial flux of a chosen ion momentum component into diffusive, convective, residual-stress, and source-driven contributions. Depending on the model, it can combine turbulent, neoclassical, finite-orbit-width, and geometry effects into one effective pinch or outward convection coefficient.

Typical core values in tokamak momentum-transport modeling are often about -20-20 m.s^-1, while strong rotation shear, edge pedestals, or transient phases can give larger effective values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convection velocity points outward across magnetic flux surfaces, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, in the direction of increasing $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: momentum_flux
NAMES.short: Rate of transport of linear momentum per unit area across an oriented surface in the plasma, combining convective, isotropic pressure, and viscous stress contributions from any species or population.
NAMES.long:
The momentum flux describes the rate at which linear momentum crosses a unit area of an oriented surface in the plasma. It encompasses the convective ram-pressure term, the isotropic thermal pressure, and viscous or turbulent stress contributions, and appears as the divergence term in the plasma fluid momentum-balance equation.

The momentum-flux tensor for a single plasma fluid is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Pi} = \rho \mathbf{v}\mathbf{v} + p\,\mathbf{I} + \boldsymbol{\pi}
$$

where $\rho$ is the mass density, $\mathbf{v}$ the bulk flow velocity, $p$ the scalar pressure, $\mathbf{I}$ the identity tensor, and $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ the viscous stress tensor. The momentum current through a surface with outward unit normal $\hat{n}$ is $\boldsymbol{\Pi}\cdot\hat{n}$.

This name is the structural parent for species- and direction-resolved forms. Species-specific instances include [ion momentum flux](name:ion_momentum_flux), [neutral momentum flux](name:neutral_momentum_flux), and [plasma momentum flux](name:plasma_momentum_flux), each summed over the relevant population. Directional projections such as [parallel momentum flux] isolate field-aligned transport, while [poloidal momentum flux](name:poloidal_momentum_flux) captures cross-field transport through toroidally symmetric surfaces. The complementary volume source density entering the momentum balance is given by [volumetric plasma momentum source].

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Vector of linear-momentum transport rate per unit area for ions in a specific charge state, with directional projections characterizing charge-state-resolved momentum transport across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The ion charge-state momentum flux is the vector flux density of linear momentum carried by ions in a single ionization state $z$, combining convective transport from bulk flow and non-convective contributions from pressure and viscous stress. It appears in the charge-state-resolved momentum-balance equation as the flux term whose divergence governs local momentum redistribution across flux surfaces and couples to electromagnetic forces, inter-species friction, and anomalous transport terms.

The component form of the momentum-flux tensor for charge state $z$ is:

$$
\Pi_{z,ij} = m_i n_z v_{z,i} v_{z,j} + p_z \delta_{ij} + \pi_{z,ij}
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_z$ is the number density of charge state $z$, $v_{z,i}$ and $v_{z,j}$ are fluid velocity components, $p_z$ is the scalar pressure, $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta, and $\pi_{z,ij}$ is the viscous stress tensor for that charge state.

Scalar projections onto coordinate axes are resolved in the component names: [radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux) for outward transport across flux surfaces, [toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux) and [poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux) for the respective in-surface momentum components, and [parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux) for field-aligned transport. Summing over all ionization stages recovers the total ion [momentum_flux](name:momentum_flux).
NAMES.sign: Positive when momentum is transported in the direction of increasing $R$ for the radial component, in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ for the toroidal component, and along the local magnetic field direction $\hat{b}$ for the parallel component.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Vector rate of linear momentum transport per unit area for the total ion population, summed over all ion species and charge states, encompassing convective, pressure, and viscous stress contributions.
NAMES.long:
The ion momentum flux represents the rate at which the total ion population transports linear momentum through a unit area, summed over all ion species and charge states. It combines convective bulk-flow momentum, scalar pressure (isotropic kinetic stress), and viscous or turbulent off-diagonal stress contributions. Its divergence appears in the ion momentum balance equation, governing the forces that drive and redistribute plasma rotation and bulk flows; this quantity is the ion-specific instance of the general [momentum_flux](name:momentum_flux).

The total ion momentum flux density is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\mathrm{ion} = \sum_s \left( m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s \mathbf{v}_s + p_s \mathbf{I} + \boldsymbol{\pi}_s \right)
$$

where $m_s$ is the ion species mass, $n_s$ is the number density, $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the mean fluid velocity, $p_s$ is the scalar pressure, $\mathbf{I}$ is the unit tensor, and $\boldsymbol{\pi}_s$ is the viscous stress tensor for species $s$, with the sum running over all ion species.

Specific resolved components isolate distinct transport channels: [toroidal_ion_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_flux) quantifies the radial flux of toroidal momentum relevant to rotation drive, [parallel_ion_momentum_flux](name:parallel_ion_momentum_flux) captures transport along the magnetic field, and [poloidal_ion_momentum_flux](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_flux) resolves the poloidal channel. The convective contribution can be parameterized through the [radial_ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion momentum is transported in the positive direction of the resolved projection axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with outward (increasing $R$) as positive for radial projections.

NAMES.name: ion_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Full momentum-flux vector for ions in a specified ionization state, giving the charge-state-resolved rate of linear-momentum transport per unit area across all directional projections.
NAMES.long:
The ion state momentum flux is the complete vector describing the rate of transport of linear momentum per unit area by ions in a specified charge (ionization) state in a multi-species edge plasma. Its directional projections along axes of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame partition momentum transfer via convection, partial pressure, and viscous stress contributions specific to a single ionization level; the named scalar projections are the radial, toroidal, poloidal, vertical, and field-aligned components.

The general element of the momentum flux tensor for ion state $s$ is:

$$
\Pi_{ij}^{(s)} = m_s n_s v_{s,i} v_{s,j} + p_s \delta_{ij} + \pi_{s,ij}
$$

where $m_s$ is the ion mass, $n_s$ is the number density, $v_{s,i}$ and $v_{s,j}$ are velocity components in directions $i$ and $j$, $p_s$ is the partial pressure of the ion state, and $\pi_{s,ij}$ is the viscous stress tensor contribution. The divergence of this tensor drives local redistribution of ion flow momentum in the charge-state momentum balance of multi-fluid edge transport models.

This quantity is evaluated in edge transport codes that resolve individual ion charge states; its scalar projections characterize anisotropic momentum transport across the scrape-off layer and edge region. Analogous quantities labeled by `ion_charge_state` include [toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux) and [parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux). The effective convection velocity for radial momentum transport is given by [radial_ion_state_effective_momentum_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net momentum transport is directed along the positive $R$, $\phi$, or $Z$ axis for the radial, toroidal, or vertical projections, respectively, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Signed scalar density of momentum transport assigned to the diamagnetic-drift contribution in a transport decomposition. It generalizes ion, ion-charge-state, and neutral-state entries without assuming a particular species, momentum component, or surface orientation.
NAMES.long:
Momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift is the signed scalar contribution to momentum transport that a transport decomposition attributes to the diamagnetic-drift term. It is a flux density of a specified momentum component through an oriented surface, with the physical dimensions of stress or pressure.

For magnetized charged species, such as [ion momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:ion_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [ion charge-state momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), the term is associated with pressure-gradient-driven cross-field drift physics. For [neutral-state momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:neutral_state_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), it denotes the neutral-state contribution assigned to the same decomposition channel and should not be interpreted as a literal Lorentz-force diamagnetic drift of neutral particles.

In practice this quantity is inferred from momentum balance or transport modeling rather than measured directly as an isolated flux. Calculations may use constituent densities, flows, temperatures, pressure gradients $\nabla p$, magnetic-field information, collisional exchange, and source or sink terms; the charged-particle diamagnetic drift may enter explicitly, while neutral entries generally depend on the adopted multi-fluid or kinetic closure.

Typical signed values in edge and pedestal transport studies can range from $10^{-2}$-$10^{3}$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, with larger magnitudes possible in strong-gradient core or transient regions. Neutral-state contributions are often smaller where neutral density is low, but can become important near material boundaries or fueling regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic contribution carries the referenced momentum component through the oriented transport surface in the positive surface-normal direction.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Diamagnetic-drift contribution to the outward radial flux of toroidal linear momentum for one ion charge state. It transports the charge state's signed toroidal momentum through the drift driven by the magnetic field crossed with that charge state's partial-pressure gradient.
NAMES.long:
The ion charge state momentum flux due to diamagnetic drift is the radial flux of toroidal linear momentum carried by one ionization state of an ion species. The transported momentum is the toroidal component, not radial momentum; the radial direction is the outward normal to magnetic flux surfaces in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\rho$ increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

A common local definition is the toroidal momentum density multiplied by the radial component of the diamagnetic drift velocity:

$$
\Pi_{\phi,s}^{\mathrm{dia}} = m_i n_s u_{\phi,s}\left[\frac{\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p_s}{Z_s e\,n_s B^2}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\rho\right]
$$

where $\Pi_{\phi,s}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic contribution to the radial flux of toroidal momentum for charge state $s$, $m_i$ is the ion mass in kg, $n_s$ is the charge-state density in m$^{-3}$, $u_{\phi,s}$ is the toroidal flow velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $p_s$ is the charge-state partial pressure in Pa, $Z_s e$ is the positive ion charge in C, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $B=|\mathbf{B}|$, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\rho$ is the outward unit normal to a flux surface. The toroidal velocity component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

In practice this term is computed as one contribution to the ion momentum balance from charge-state density, temperature or pressure, pressure gradients, magnetic geometry, charge number, and toroidal flow. Charge-state-resolved inputs are commonly constrained by spectroscopy, particle-balance analysis, and collisional-radiative modeling, then combined with fluid or transport closures; the diamagnetic flux itself is usually not measured as an isolated diagnostic observable.

Typical signed magnitudes in tokamak transport analyzes are about 10^-4-1 kg m^-1 s^-2, with values up to about 10 kg m^-1 s^-2 possible in steep pressure-gradient regions or plasmas with strong toroidal rotation. The value may be small when the diamagnetic drift has little projection along the outward flux-surface normal.
NAMES.sign: Positive when positive toroidal momentum, defined by motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, is transported toward increasing flux-surface radius $\rho$.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Local number density of neon ions at the internal transport barrier reference radius, where reduced cross-field turbulent transport can produce steep impurity-density gradients.
NAMES.long:
Neon density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of ionized neon nuclei on the flux surface used to mark the internal transport barrier. It represents the neon impurity concentration at the radius where cross-field turbulent transport is reduced and temperature, density, or impurity gradients can become steep.

For a fully resolved charge-state description, the total ionized neon density at the barrier is

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ne}}(\rho_{\mathrm{ITB}}) = \sum_{q=1}^{10} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}(\rho_{\mathrm{ITB}})
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the chosen flux-surface label for the internal transport barrier, such as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, and $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}$ is the local density of neon ions with charge state $q$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, soft-x-ray or extreme-ultraviolet line emission, charge-exchange measurements where available, and collisional-radiative modeling constrained by the local electron temperature and density. Transport analysis evaluates the result on the barrier flux surface identified from steep gradients or reduced inferred diffusivity.

Typical values range from $10^{15}$-$10^{18}$ m^-3 for trace or weakly seeded neon and can approach $10^{19}$ m^-3 during strong neon seeding or impurity accumulation near the barrier. The value is normally much smaller than the electron density but can strongly affect radiation, dilution, and effective charge.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Number density of neon ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Neon is a noble-gas impurity commonly introduced into tokamak plasmas for radiative cooling, divertor protection, and impurity transport studies. The on-axis value $n_\mathrm{Ne}$ gives the innermost point of the radial neon density profile, evaluated at the location where $\nabla\psi = 0$, with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux. At this point $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the interplay of the neoclassical inward pinch and anomalous transport governs whether neon accumulates centrally or develops a hollow profile, making $n_\mathrm{Ne,axis}$ a key indicator of impurity accumulation behavior.

This quantity is the neon-specific realization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), and it can be compared against the same-species profile at other flux surfaces via [neon_density_at_pedestal](name:neon_density_at_pedestal) and [neon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:neon_density_at_plasma_boundary). On-axis densities of other noble-gas impurities are cataloged as [argon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis), enabling multi-species accumulation comparisons.

Neon ion densities at the magnetic axis are inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy of neon line emission, or from impurity transport modeling constrained by radiated power profiles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neon ions are present at the magnetic axis location $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$, as particle number density is a non-negative quantity.

NAMES.name: neutral_density
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Local number density of electrically neutral particles (atoms or molecules) at a plasma point, encompassing thermal, suprathermal, and ion-associated neutral populations.
NAMES.long:
Neutral particles are electrically neutral atoms or molecules present throughout the plasma volume as a result of recycling at material surfaces, gas injection, and incomplete ionization. The neutral density quantifies the number of such particles per unit volume at a local plasma point, and serves as the generic concept abstracting over population-specific, species-specific, and thermodynamic-state-resolved forms.

The neutral population decomposes into thermally equilibrated and suprathermal contributions:

$$
n_0 = n_{0,\mathrm{th}} + n_{0,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $n_{0,\mathrm{th}}$ is the [thermal neutral density](name:thermal_neutral_density), describing neutrals whose velocity distribution follows a local Maxwellian, and $n_{0,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [fast neutral density](name:fast_neutral_density), the suprathermal population generated primarily by charge-exchange reactions between energetic ions and cold neutrals. The [total neutral density](name:total_neutral_density) sums both populations over all atomic and molecular species and resolved internal quantum states, while the [ion neutral density] tracks the neutral subpopulation associated with a specific parent ion species.

Neutral densities are measured through spectroscopic emission diagnostics, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and neutral-particle analyzer data, or are computed by Monte Carlo neutral transport modeling coupled to plasma fluid solutions. The neutral population is most concentrated near recycling surfaces such as divertor targets and limiters.

Typical values range from $10^{14}$ m$^{-3}$ in the plasma core to $10^{18}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in the divertor and scrape-off layer of current tokamaks.

NAMES.name: fast_neutral_density
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Suprathermal (non-Maxwellian) neutral particle number density at a point in the plasma, summed over all internal quantum states of the neutral species. It represents the neutral population not described by the local thermal neutral distribution.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutral density is the number of neutral atoms or molecules per unit volume belonging to a suprathermal, non-Maxwellian population of a specified neutral species. It excludes the locally thermalized neutral component and is summed over internal quantum states such as excitation levels when those states are not resolved.

At a spatial point $\mathbf{x}$, it is the zeroth velocity moment of the fast component of the neutral distribution function:

$$
n_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_\alpha \int f_{\alpha,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\alpha$ labels internal quantum states, $f_{\alpha,\mathrm{fast}}$ has units of m$^{-6}$ s$^{3}$ when velocity is in m s$^{-1}$, and the integral is over the velocity distribution assigned to the suprathermal component. The fast component is not defined by a universal sharp cutoff at the local thermal speed; it is the non-Maxwellian part separated from the locally thermal neutral distribution by the physics model or diagnostic interpretation.

In practice, fast neutral density is inferred or computed from neutral transport, beam attenuation, recycling, and charge-exchange source models, often constrained by spectroscopic emission or charge-exchange measurements. The operational separation from [thermal_neutral_density](name:thermal_neutral_density) is based on whether the neutral population is locally equilibrated with the background gas or plasma-neutral environment; beam neutrals, halo neutrals, and energetic charge-exchange neutrals are typical contributors to the fast component.

Typical values vary strongly with fueling, beam power, wall recycling, and plasma opacity. Hot confined plasmas may have local fast neutral densities around $10^{12}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$, while intense neutral-beam paths, edge, or scrape-off-layer charge-exchange regions can reach about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$; the value is generally less than or comparable to the [total_neutral_density](name:total_neutral_density).

NAMES.name: neutral_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Fickian diffusion coefficient for neutral particle transport in edge plasma, relating the diffusive neutral particle flux to the local neutral density gradient without specification of a particular transport direction.
NAMES.long:
The neutral diffusion coefficient quantifies the proportionality between the diffusive flux of neutral particles and the spatial gradient of their number density, abstracting over the directional components that resolve transport along specific geometric axes of the torus. In the strongly anisotropic environment of magnetized edge plasmas, neutral particles interact with the background plasma primarily through charge exchange and ionization, making the effective diffusivity a key parameter governing recycling and fueling dynamics.

The constitutive (Fick's law) relation for the diffusive neutral particle flux density $\Gamma_n$ in a given spatial direction is:

$$
\Gamma_n = -D_n \, \nabla n_n
$$

where $D_n$ is the neutral diffusion coefficient and $n_n$ is the local neutral particle number density. The directional components [poloidal_neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_diffusion_coefficient) and [radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient) specialize this relation along the poloidal and radial directions respectively, reflecting the geometric anisotropy of the edge region.

Values of $D_n$ are computed from fluid or kinetic neutral transport models that account for charge-exchange mean free paths and collisional momentum transfer with background ions. The analogous energy transport coefficient is described by [poloidal_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient), and the charge-state-resolved counterpart appears in [poloidal_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient).

NAMES.name: neutral_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Effective scalar diffusion coefficient for neutral particle transport. It closes the diffusive neutral flux through Fick's law, relating the flux to the negative gradient of neutral density as a single direction-averaged coefficient.
NAMES.long:
Neutral diffusivity is the effective scalar coefficient that parameterizes the spatial spreading of neutral particles by random motion, elastic collisions, charge exchange, and related atomic processes. It applies when the neutral particle flux can be represented by an isotropic or direction-averaged diffusion closure rather than by a fully kinetic description.

The Fick's-law closure relates the diffusive neutral particle flux to the neutral density gradient:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{n}^{\mathrm{diff}} = - D_n \nabla n_n
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{n}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive neutral particle flux in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, $D_n$ is the neutral diffusivity, and $n_n$ is the neutral density in m$^{-3}$ (so $\nabla n_n$ is in m$^{-4}$). The leading minus sign carries neutral particles down the neutral density gradient for positive $D_n$.

Neutral diffusivity is not measured directly; it is inferred from neutral density evolution, particle-balance constraints, and comparisons with kinetic or Monte Carlo neutral transport calculations. For an isotropic random walk a useful estimate is $D_n \sim v_n \lambda_n / 3$, where $v_n$ is a representative neutral speed and $\lambda_n$ is an effective mean free path including elastic scattering, charge exchange, ionization, dissociation, and wall recycling effects.

This scalar form collapses the anisotropic diffusion tensor into a single effective value and is the isotropic counterpart of the direction-resolved coefficients [radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient), [poloidal_neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_diffusion_coefficient), toroidal_neutral_diffusion_coefficient, parallel_neutral_diffusion_coefficient, and perpendicular_neutral_diffusion_coefficient; it is the neutral analog of the charged-species particle_diffusivity.

Typical effective values are 0.1-100 m^2.s^-1 for cold, collisional edge or divertor neutrals and 100-1000 m^2.s^-1 for hotter or more weakly collisional neutrals with longer mean free paths.

NAMES.name: neutral_energy_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Effective scalar diffusivity for the diffusive transport of thermal energy carried by thermal neutral atoms and molecules. It is the local aggregate coefficient used when neutral excited states and directional transport components are not resolved separately.
NAMES.long:
Neutral energy diffusivity is an effective scalar transport coefficient for the diffusive redistribution of thermal energy carried by thermal neutral atoms and molecules. It captures the part of neutral heat transport that is proportional to a local gradient of neutral thermal-energy density, aggregating the underlying neutral-kinetic processes into a single isotropic coefficient when individual neutral states and directional transport channels are not resolved.

In a scalar Fickian closure, the diffusive neutral thermal-energy flux is written as the product of the diffusivity and the local energy-density gradient:

$$
q_{E,n} = - \chi_{E,n} \, \nabla u_{E,n}
$$

where $q_{E,n}$ is the diffusive thermal-energy flux density in W m^-2, $\chi_{E,n}$ is the neutral energy diffusivity, and $u_{E,n}$ is the neutral thermal-energy density in J m^-3. For a monatomic translational neutral temperature the energy density is commonly formed from $(3/2)\, n_n T_n$ per species, where $n_n$ is in m^-3 and $T_n$ is expressed as energy per particle (use $k_B T_n$ if a kelvin temperature is supplied).

This coefficient is a scalar aggregate: it represents an isotropic or direction-averaged local coefficient and does not by itself carry tensor anisotropy. Where directional resolution is required, the component coefficients tangent and normal to flux surfaces are described separately by [poloidal_neutral_energy_diffusivity](name:poloidal_neutral_energy_diffusivity) and [radial_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_energy_diffusion_coefficient); the present scalar should be understood as their effective combined replacement when those channels are not modeled individually.

The diffusivity is not directly observable. It is typically inferred from kinetic-neutral or fluid-neutral transport calculations, or from transport analyzes constrained by neutral pressure, spectroscopy, and energy-balance observations. Admissible physical values are non-negative, with $\chi_{E,n}=0$ representing no diffusive thermal-energy transport in the closure; magnitudes scale with neutral mean free path and are largest where neutrals stream over long collisionless distances.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diffusive thermal-energy flux is directed from regions of larger to smaller neutral thermal-energy density.

NAMES.name: neutral_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Neutral energy flux is the signed component of energy flux density carried by neutral atoms and molecules across an oriented area or along a specified direction. It is summed over neutral species and includes convective enthalpy, bulk-flow kinetic energy, and conductive heat transport.
NAMES.long:
Neutral energy flux is the scalar projection of the vector energy flux density carried by neutral particles. It represents the rate at which neutral atoms and molecules transport energy through a unit oriented area, summed over neutral species and states, rather than the magnitude of the full vector flux.

A common fluid expression for the component along a unit direction $\hat{e}$ is:

$$
q_{E,n}^{(\hat{e})} = \hat{e} \cdot \sum_s \left[n_s \mathbf{v}_s \left(h_s + \frac{1}{2} m_s |\mathbf{v}_s|^2\right) - \boldsymbol{\kappa}_s \cdot \nabla T_s \right]
$$

where $q_{E,n}^{(\hat{e})}$ has units W m$^{-2}$, $s$ indexes neutral species or states, $n_s$ is number density in m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the neutral flow velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $h_s$ is thermal enthalpy per particle in J, $m_s$ is particle mass in kg, $T_s$ is temperature, and $\boldsymbol{\kappa}_s$ is the neutral thermal-conductivity tensor. For a monatomic ideal gas, $h_s = 5 k_B T_s/2$ when $T_s$ is in K; if temperature is represented in eV, the corresponding conversion to joules is included in $h_s$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from neutral fluid moments or kinetic distribution functions, constrained by measurements such as spectroscopy, pressure diagnostics, and calorimetry. The projection direction is specified by the more specific component: for example, [parallel neutral energy flux](name:parallel_neutral_energy_flux) is along the local magnetic field, while [radial neutral energy flux](name:radial_neutral_energy_flux) is along an outward-increasing flux-surface label in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. Geometric positions may be described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Typical magnitudes in tokamak edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas range from $10^2$-$10^5$ W m$^{-2}$ in weakly neutral regions to $10^5$-$10^7$ W m$^{-2}$ near strong recycling zones, gas puffing locations, and divertor targets. Local transient values can be higher when neutral pressure, temperature gradients, or recycling sources are large.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral energy is transported in the positive direction of the specified component or, for a surface flux, through the surface in the direction of its oriented normal.

NAMES.name: neutral_momentum
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Area-normalized momentum source density vector for the neutral species population, giving the net force per unit area from plasma-neutral atomic processes and boundary exchange, summed over all neutral states.
NAMES.long:
The neutral momentum source density vector encodes the net area-normalized rate of momentum transfer to the aggregate neutral particle population from plasma-neutral interactions in the edge region, summed over all neutral charge states. It enters the neutral fluid momentum balance as the distributed body-force term that couples neutral dynamics to the surrounding plasma.

Dominant exchange mechanisms include charge exchange (which redistributes directed momentum between ions and neutrals), ionization (which removes momentum from the neutral population), recombination (which deposits ion momentum onto newly formed neutrals), and elastic collisions. The total source aggregates state-resolved contributions:

$$
\mathbf{S}_n = \sum_s \mathbf{S}_{n,s}
$$

where $s$ indexes individual neutral states and each $\mathbf{S}_{n,s}$ combines reactive, collisional, and boundary-flux terms per unit area.

This vector is evaluated on general-geometry computational meshes covering the scrape-off layer and divertor, where neutral dynamics strongly influence plasma exhaust and plasma-wall interaction modeling. Directional projections include [parallel_neutral_momentum](name:parallel_neutral_momentum), which isolates the component along the local magnetic-field direction, and [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum) for the state-resolved toroidal contribution. The analogous source term resolved for the full plasma system is represented component-wise by parallel_momentum.

NAMES.name: neutral_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Effective vector velocity at which neutral particle momentum is advectively transported in edge-plasma fluid models, aggregated over all neutral species and excited states as a transport closure coefficient distinct from the actual neutral particle flow velocity.
NAMES.long:
The neutral momentum convection velocity is the effective bulk vector velocity appearing in the non-diffusive, advective contribution to neutral momentum transport in edge-plasma and scrape-off-layer fluid models. It encapsulates the net effect of charge-exchange, ionization, and recombination reactions on the aggregate neutral momentum balance across all neutral species and excited states, serving as a transport closure coefficient rather than the physical flow speed of any individual neutral population.

In multi-fluid edge-plasma transport frameworks, the total neutral momentum flux is decomposed into a diffusive part proportional to the local momentum-density gradient and a convective (pinch-like) part proportional to the momentum density:

$$
\mathbf{F}_p = -D_p \nabla p_n + \mathbf{V}_c \, p_n
$$

where $D_p$ is the neutral momentum diffusivity and $p_n$ is the neutral momentum density. The convection velocity $\mathbf{V}_c$ (this quantity) drives advective momentum transport independently of the local gradient, functioning as a neutral momentum pinch.

The quantity is computed in fluid neutral transport solvers as a closure derived from atomic physics rate coefficients and the local plasma state. Its directional projections include the radial_neutral_momentum_convection_velocity ($R$ component) and the [vertical_neutral_momentum_convection_velocity](name:vertical_neutral_momentum_convection_velocity) ($Z$ component) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The analogous charge-state-resolved quantity is [radial_neutral_state_effective_momentum_convection_velocity](name:radial_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity). The parent [momentum_convection_velocity](name:momentum_convection_velocity) establishes the general momentum-flux decomposition framework from which this neutral-species specialization is derived.
NAMES.sign: Positive radial, toroidal, and vertical components correspond to velocity directed in the $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, and $+\hat{Z}$ directions of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, respectively.

NAMES.name: neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Vector diffusion coefficient governing diffusive transport of momentum in the neutral particle population, with directional components representing anisotropic momentum diffusivities along the radial, poloidal, and toroidal directions.
NAMES.long:
The neutral momentum diffusion coefficient quantifies the effective diffusivity that drives collisional and turbulent spreading of neutral-particle momentum down local velocity gradients. As a vector quantity, its components represent the diagonal entries of the momentum diffusion tensor for neutrals in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, capturing anisotropy across the radial, poloidal, and toroidal directions independently.

The diffusive neutral momentum flux density along direction $\hat{e}_i$ is governed by:

$$
\Pi_{\mathrm{diff},i} = -\rho_n \, D_{\mathrm{mom},i} \, \frac{\partial u_{n,i}}{\partial x_i}
$$

where $\rho_n$ is the neutral mass density, $u_{n,i}$ is the neutral flow velocity component along $\hat{e}_i$, and $D_{\mathrm{mom},i}$ is the corresponding directional component of this coefficient.

In edge plasma modeling, the dominant physical mechanisms determining this diffusivity are charge-exchange with background ions, neutral-neutral collisions, and elastic scattering; the resulting coefficient is strongly anisotropic in realistic magnetic geometries. The [radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) gives the cross-field component driving transport across magnetic flux surfaces. For comparison, the analogous momentum diffusivity for the bulk plasma is captured by plasma_momentum_diffusivity, and the toroidal ion channel counterpart is described by toroidal_momentum_diffusivity.

NAMES.name: neutral_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Vector diffusion coefficient for bulk neutral-particle momentum, governing anisotropic diffusive redistribution driven by neutral-neutral viscosity and charge-exchange collisions in edge and divertor plasma.
NAMES.long:
Neutral momentum diffusivity is the direction-dependent transport coefficient that relates the diffusive neutral-fluid momentum flux in each spatial direction to the local gradient of neutral momentum density, forming the neutral-particle analog of plasma_momentum_diffusivity. As a vector quantity it encompasses distinct directional components — including [parallel_neutral_momentum_diffusivity](name:parallel_neutral_momentum_diffusivity), [poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity](name:poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity), [toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity), and [vertical_neutral_momentum_diffusivity](name:vertical_neutral_momentum_diffusivity) — reflecting the anisotropy imposed by the magnetic geometry and the varying collisional regimes of edge and divertor regions.

The component $\chi_{n,\mathrm{mom}}$ along a direction $\hat{e}$ enters the neutral fluid momentum balance through the diffusive flux:

$$
\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{mom}} = -\chi_{n,\mathrm{mom}} \, \nabla_{\hat{e}}(m_n n_n u_n)
$$

where $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $n_n$ is the neutral number density, and $u_n$ is the neutral fluid velocity component along $\hat{e}$.

The dominant physical mechanisms contributing to neutral momentum diffusivity are neutral-neutral viscous collisions and charge-exchange interactions with background ions; the latter can transfer substantial momentum between the neutral and ion populations and are especially significant in dense regions where charge-exchange mean-free paths are short. This coefficient is computed within fluid-neutral transport models that solve the neutral momentum equation self-consistently alongside the plasma fluid equations.

NAMES.name: neutral_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Rate per unit area at which neutral atoms and molecules transport linear momentum across an oriented surface in the edge plasma, combining convective and isotropic-pressure contributions summed over all neutral species and internal states.
NAMES.long:
The neutral momentum flux describes the rate at which the collective neutral population transports linear momentum across a unit area of an oriented surface in the edge plasma. It captures both the directed convective flow of neutral particles and the isotropic thermal pressure of the neutral gas, aggregated over all neutral species and their internal quantum states.

The neutral momentum-flux tensor $\overleftrightarrow{\Pi}_n$ is:

$$
\overleftrightarrow{\Pi}_n = m_n n_n \mathbf{v}_n \mathbf{v}_n + p_n \mathbf{I}
$$

where $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $n_n$ is the neutral number density, $\mathbf{v}_n$ is the bulk neutral velocity, $p_n = n_n k_B T_n$ is the neutral thermal pressure with $T_n$ the neutral temperature, and $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity tensor. The divergence of this tensor drives the neutral momentum balance equation and couples neutral dynamics to the ion fluid through charge-exchange and elastic collisions.

This quantity is evaluated within edge fluid or kinetic neutral transport models rather than measured directly. Directional projections include [toroidal_neutral_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_flux), [poloidal_neutral_momentum_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_momentum_flux), [vertical_neutral_momentum_flux](name:vertical_neutral_momentum_flux), and [parallel_neutral_momentum_flux](name:parallel_neutral_momentum_flux) along the local magnetic-field direction. The analogous ion-fluid momentum transport rate is [radial_edge_ion_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_momentum_flux_over_edge_region), while the effective convective transport coefficient for neutral momentum is radial_neutral_effective_momentum_convection_velocity.

NAMES.name: neutral_source_rate
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Net volumetric production rate of neutral particles, equal to creation minus loss processes per unit volume. It enters the neutral particle density balance as a source term, with positive values representing a net gain of neutral particles.
NAMES.long:
Neutral source rate is the local net rate at which neutral particles of a given species are produced or removed by atomic, molecular, and plasma interaction processes. It represents creation minus loss per unit physical volume and directly changes the neutral number density.

A common local neutral continuity equation is

$$
\frac{\partial n_n}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left(n_n \mathbf{u}_n\right) = S_n
$$

where $n_n$ is the neutral number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\mathbf{u}_n$ is the neutral flow velocity in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $S_n$ is the neutral source rate in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The equation is coordinate independent; when expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $S_n$ is the net rate per physical volume at position $(R, \phi, Z)$.

In practice, $S_n$ is computed from neutral transport and collisional-radiative models using rates for ionization, recombination, charge exchange, molecular dissociation, recycling, gas fueling, pellet ablation, and neutral beam deposition when relevant. It can also be constrained indirectly by particle balance, spectroscopy, pressure gages, and neutral particle diagnostics, with volume or flux-surface averaging applied only after the local volumetric rate has been defined.

Typical magnitudes vary strongly with plasma region and fueling conditions: core values with weak neutral penetration may be $10^{16}$-$10^{20}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, edge and scrape-off-layer recycling regions are commonly $10^{20}$-$10^{23}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and highly localized pellet, gas-puff, or beam-related sources can locally exceed $10^{24}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net processes add neutral particles to the neutral population, increasing the neutral number density.

NAMES.name: neutral_species_atomic_mass
NAMES.subject: neutral_species
NAMES.short: Atomic mass of a neutral species expressed in unified atomic mass units. It identifies the isotope or elemental composition and sets the particle inertia used in mass density, momentum, energy, and transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
Neutral species atomic mass is the rest mass assigned to one neutral atom or isotope, expressed in unified atomic mass units. It is independent of the local plasma state and characterizes the inertia of the neutral constituent used in fluid and kinetic transport quantities.

The particle mass is related to its numerical atomic mass by:

$$
m_s = A_s u
$$

where $m_s$ is the mass of one neutral particle of species $s$, $A_s$ is the numerical atomic mass, and $u$ is the unified atomic mass unit, equal to one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom in its ground state. In practical calculations $1\,u = 1.66053906660 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ may be used for conversion to SI mass.

Atomic masses are normally taken from isotope or elemental reference tables rather than measured as a plasma diagnostic quantity. For isotope-resolved species the tabulated isotope mass is used; for an element without isotope resolution, an abundance-weighted elemental atomic mass may be appropriate. The value enters conversions such as number density to mass density and influences neutral thermal speeds, momentum exchange, source deposition, and transport time scales.

Typical values are about 1.008 u for protium, 2.014 u for deuterium, 3.016 u for tritium, 4.003 u for helium-4, 12 u for carbon-12, 20.18 u for neon, 39.95 u for argon, and 183.84 u for tungsten. Fusion fuel and helium ash are usually in the 1-4 u range, while impurity neutrals can range from about 12-184 u depending on the species.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: State-resolved convection velocity for neutral particle transport across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the advective drift coefficient multiplying the density of a specified neutral state in a flux-surface-averaged radial particle flux law.
NAMES.long:
Neutral-state convection velocity is the effective radial advective velocity for particles belonging to a specified neutral state. It represents the part of the cross-flux-surface particle flux proportional to the neutral-state density, distinct from diffusive transport driven by a density gradient.

For the radial flux coordinate $r_\mathrm{eff}$ (effective minor radius, in meters) increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, a local flux-surface-averaged closure can be written as:

$$
\Gamma_{n,k,r} = -D_{n,k}\frac{\partial n_{n,k}}{\partial r_\mathrm{eff}} + v_{n,k} n_{n,k}
$$

where $k$ labels the neutral state, $\Gamma_{n,k,r}$ is the particle flux per unit area across a surface of constant $r_\mathrm{eff}$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $D_{n,k}$ is the particle diffusivity in $\mathrm{m}^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $n_{n,k}$ is the neutral-state density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $v_{n,k}$ is the convection velocity in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. If a normalized radial flux coordinate $\rho$ is used instead, the gradient term requires the appropriate length or metric factor, such as replacing $\partial/\partial r_\mathrm{eff}$ by $(1/L_\rho)\partial/\partial\rho$, to preserve these units.

The coefficient is usually inferred rather than measured directly, using particle-balance analysis, neutral-transport modeling, or fitted transport closures that separate gradient-driven and advective contributions to the state-resolved neutral flux. The aggregate neutral_convection_velocity describes an effective coefficient for the summed neutral population; it is not generally the arithmetic mean of the state-resolved velocities and becomes a simple density-weighted combination only under additional assumptions about diffusivities and density gradients.

Representative effective values range from -1000-1000 m.s^-1. Core values are often near zero to tens of m.s^-1, while edge or source-dominated neutral transport closures can require hundreds to thousands of m.s^-1 depending on ionization, charge exchange, recycling, and the chosen radial coordinate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convective contribution $v_{n,k} n_{n,k}$ carries neutral particles toward increasing radial flux coordinate $r_\mathrm{eff}$, outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_density
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Number density of neutral particles occupying a specified internal quantum state, covering both thermal and suprathermal velocity populations within that state.
NAMES.long:
The state-resolved neutral density quantifies the number of neutral particles per unit volume that occupy a particular internal quantum state of the neutral species — such as an electronic, vibrational, or rotational level. This parent quantity abstracts over the velocity-population decomposition: its children [fast_neutral_state_density](name:fast_neutral_state_density) and [thermal_neutral_state_density](name:thermal_neutral_state_density) divide the same state-resolved population into its suprathermal and Maxwellian contributions respectively, while [total_neutral_state_density](name:total_neutral_state_density) combines both populations within the given quantum state.

The state population $n_0(s)$ for quantum state $s$ satisfies the closure relation:

$$
n_{0,\mathrm{total}} = \sum_s n_0(s)
$$

where $n_{0,\mathrm{total}}$ is the total neutral density summed over all internal states, recoverable as [total_neutral_density](name:total_neutral_density) when the sum spans all quantum states of all neutral species.

State-resolved neutral densities are essential inputs to collisional-radiative models that compute line emission rates, ionization source terms, and charge-exchange reaction rates in edge and divertor plasmas. Ground-state neutral densities in tokamak divertor regions typically range from $10^{14}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, while excited-state populations are orders of magnitude lower and are inferred from optical emission spectroscopy of atomic line series such as the Balmer and Lyman series for hydrogen isotopes.

NAMES.name: fast_neutral_state_density
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Number density of fast (non-thermal) neutral particles occupying a specified internal quantum state of the neutral species.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutral state density is the number of neutral particles per unit volume in a specified internal quantum state that belong to the fast, non-thermal part of the neutral population. It distinguishes energetic neutrals, such as charge-exchange atoms, beam neutrals, or wall-reflected neutrals, from the bulk thermal neutral gas while retaining the state identity needed for excitation, ionization, and radiation modeling.

A common kinetic definition is the velocity-space integral of the state-resolved neutral distribution above a chosen fast-particle energy threshold:

$$
n_i^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{E(\mathbf{v}) \ge E_{\mathrm{th}}} f_i(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3 v
$$

where $n_i^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast density of internal state $i$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $f_i$ is the state-resolved neutral velocity distribution in units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$ when integrated over velocity, $E(\mathbf{v})$ is kinetic energy in J, and $E_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the fast-particle threshold energy in J. In applications that use eV for neutral kinetic energy, $E$ and $E_{\mathrm{th}}$ must be converted consistently.

In practice this quantity is computed with kinetic neutral transport or collisional-radiative models, often constrained by diagnostics sensitive to energetic neutrals such as neutral particle analyzers, charge-exchange measurements, or line emission from state-selective transitions. The separation between thermal and fast neutrals depends on the modeled distribution and on the selected energy threshold or non-thermal component definition.

Typical values span a wide range: about $10^{10}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$ in hot confined plasma regions, and about $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in edge, scrape-off-layer, divertor, or source-adjacent regions where recycling, neutral beams, or wall reflection can create stronger fast-neutral populations.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Particle diffusivity for neutral atoms or molecules in a specified internal state, relating the diffusive neutral flux to the local neutral density gradient via a Fick-law constitutive relation.
NAMES.long:
The neutral-state diffusion coefficient characterizes irreversible particle transport of neutral atoms or molecules occupying a specified internal state — electronic, vibrational, or charge-resolved — through the edge plasma, where neutral recycling, plasma fueling, and impurity sourcing drive steep density gradients.

The diffusive flux of neutrals in state $s$ obeys the Fick-law constitutive relation:

$$
\mathbf{J}_{n,s} = -D_{n,s} \, \nabla n_{n,s}
$$

where $n_{n,s}$ is the number density of neutrals in state $s$ and $D_{n,s}$ is the state-resolved diffusion coefficient.

This quantity is the direction-agnostic parent of its directional projections: the [poloidal neutral-state diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient) governs transport along the poloidal direction, and the [poloidal neutral diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_diffusion_coefficient) provides an analogous coefficient aggregated over all neutral states. In edge-plasma fluid and kinetic models, $D_{n,s}$ is evaluated on unstructured geometry grids covering the scrape-off layer and divertor region; values are obtained from neutral Monte Carlo transport calculations or prescribed as free parameters in reduced fluid formulations.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Scalar Fickian diffusion coefficient for a specified neutral species state. It relates the neutral-state particle flux density to the gradient of the neutral-state number density without decomposing the transport into a particular direction.
NAMES.long:
Neutral-state diffusivity is an effective scalar coefficient describing how particles in a specified neutral species state spread because of spatial gradients in their number density. It represents the isotropic or direction-averaged Fickian part of neutral transport, without selecting radial, parallel, or other directional components.

For neutral state $s$, the Fickian particle flux density is commonly written as

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s = -D_s \nabla n_s
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s$ is the neutral-state particle flux density, $D_s$ is the neutral-state diffusivity in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $n_s$ is the neutral-state number density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, and $\nabla n_s$ is its spatial gradient in $\mathrm{m^{-4}}$. The minus sign expresses down-gradient transport: for positive $D_s$, particles flow from higher neutral-state density toward lower neutral-state density.

In practice, this coefficient may be inferred by fitting neutral-density and particle-flux estimates from spectroscopy, pressure measurements, gas-balance analysis, or fueling-response experiments. It may also be computed or prescribed in neutral transport models using kinetic, Monte Carlo, Boltzmann, or fluid closures, where collisions, charge exchange, ionization losses, wall interactions, and molecular processes can all affect the effective value.

Typical effective values are highly regime dependent: molecular or cold-gas diffusion can be about $10^{-5}$-$10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, collisional neutral transport in edge-plasma modeling often uses about $10^{-2}$-$10^2\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and weakly collisional fast-neutral transport can correspond to $10^2$-$10^4\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$ when represented by a local diffusion approximation.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Effective radial convection velocity of a neutral species in a specified internal state across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the advective coefficient multiplying the state-resolved neutral density in the neutral particle continuity equation, including model-effective advective contributions beyond the bare convected velocity.
NAMES.long:
Neutral-state effective convection velocity is the effective advective speed normal to magnetic flux surfaces for a neutral species in a specified internal state. It is expressed for transport across flux surfaces in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ is a radial flux label, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. It differs from [neutral_state_convected_velocity](name:neutral_state_convected_velocity) by including effective advective or pinch-like contributions introduced by the transport closure, not only the bare convected motion of the neutral state.

The radial particle flux density of neutral state $s$ is commonly written in a convection-plus-diffusion form using a physical distance coordinate $r_\perp$ measured locally normal to the flux surfaces:

$$
\Gamma_s = V_{s,\mathrm{eff}} n_s - D_{s,\mathrm{eff}} \frac{\partial n_s}{\partial r_\perp}
$$

where $\Gamma_s$ is the outward particle flux density in m^-2.s^-1, $V_{s,\mathrm{eff}}$ is the neutral-state effective convection velocity in m.s^-1, $n_s$ is the neutral-state density in m^-3, $D_{s,\mathrm{eff}}$ is the corresponding effective diffusion coefficient in m^2.s^-1, and $r_\perp$ is a physical normal distance in m. If a normalized flux label $\rho$ is used, the density gradient is converted to this physical-gradient form through the metric factor relating $\rho$ to $r_\perp$, so the velocity retains units of m.s^-1.

The coefficient is obtained from state-resolved neutral particle balance or transport modeling after separating effective diffusive, advective, and source/sink contributions. It is closely related to [neutral_state_convection_velocity](name:neutral_state_convection_velocity), the non-effective state-resolved convection coefficient, to [neutral_convection_velocity](name:radial_electron_convection_velocity), which is not resolved by internal state, and to [particle_effective_convection_velocity](name:neutral_state_effective_convection_velocity), the more general particle effective-convection concept.

Typical magnitudes are highly model- and region-dependent. Representative effective neutral-state convection velocities in transport analyzes are often of order 0.1-1000 m.s^-1, with values near zero when the inferred radial flux is mainly diffusive and larger magnitudes in edge or recycling-influenced regions. The value may be positive or negative because it is a signed transport coefficient, not a speed magnitude.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convective contribution to the neutral-state particle flux is directed outward across magnetic flux surfaces, from the magnetic axis toward increasing radial flux label $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Effective velocity for convective transport of energy by a neutral particle species in a specified internal state, serving as the signed coefficient multiplying that state's energy density in the convective energy flux.
NAMES.long:
The neutral state energy convection velocity is the effective transport coefficient for the convective energy flux carried by a single neutral species in a specific internal state. It appears in neutral particle energy transport at the plasma boundary and represents how rapidly energy associated with that neutral state is advected along a given spatial direction, distinct from the actual mean fluid velocity of the neutral population.

The convective energy flux for the neutral state is expressed as:

$$
q_{\rm conv} = v_{\rm energy} \cdot \varepsilon_{\rm state}
$$

where $v_{\rm energy}$ is this convection velocity and $\varepsilon_{\rm state}$ is the energy density of the neutral species state in J m$^{-3}$.

This quantity is decomposed into directional projections in transport models: the [radial component](name:radial_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity) acts along the major-radius direction $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the [poloidal component](name:poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity) acts along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, and the [parallel component](name:parallel_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity) is evaluated as a flux-surface average along the magnetic field direction. The analogous coefficient for neutral particle transport is [neutral_state_effective_convection_velocity](name:neutral_state_effective_convection_velocity), and the corresponding quantity for ion energy transport is [radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity). This quantity specializes the general [energy_convection_velocity](name:energy_convection_velocity) concept to the charge-state-resolved neutral species level.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is convected in the direction of increasing coordinate value for the respective spatial component.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Signed energy flux density carried by neutrals in a specified quantum state, including directed transport of particle, thermal, kinetic, and internal-state energy.
NAMES.long:
Neutral state energy flux is the signed energy flux density carried by neutral particles belonging to a specified quantum state. It represents the normal component of the total neutral-state energy-flow vector through an oriented surface, including energy transported by particle motion and by non-convective heat flow.

A kinetic definition for the flux through a surface with unit normal $\hat{n}$ is:

$$
\Phi_{E,n,s} = \hat{n} \cdot \int E_s(\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{v}\,f_{n,s}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\Phi_{E,n,s}$ is the neutral energy flux density for state $s$, $f_{n,s}$ is the neutral velocity distribution function, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $E_s(\mathbf{v})$ is the energy carried by one neutral in that state, including translational kinetic energy and any internal excitation energy relevant to the state definition. In fluid descriptions this same quantity is commonly represented as the sum of a convective energy flux and a conductive or diffusive heat-flux contribution.

In practice it is obtained from neutral transport modeling, kinetic Monte Carlo calculations, moment equations, or diagnostic inference combined with an energy balance. The value depends strongly on neutral density, temperature or energy distribution, drift or streaming velocity, ionization and charge-exchange rates, and wall or recycling sources.

Typical magnitudes in edge and divertor plasmas range from 10^2-10^6 W m^-2, with localized high-recycling or beam-like neutral populations reaching about 10^7 W m^-2.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy carried by the neutral state crosses the oriented surface in the direction of the positive surface normal.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_momentum
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Area-normalized vector source of linear momentum for a specified neutral species charge state, representing net momentum transfer from charge exchange, ionization, recombination, elastic scattering, and related collisions.
NAMES.long:
Neutral state momentum is the vector source of linear momentum transferred to a specified neutral species charge state, normalized by the area through which the transfer is represented. It has pressure-like dimensions while retaining the direction of the net impulse acting on the neutral population, and it contributes to the neutral momentum balance together with advection, pressure, and momentum-flux terms.

When the area-normalized source is obtained by integrating a local collisional force density over a representative length, a generic balance for state $s$ can be written as:

$$
\mathbf{M}_s = \int_{\Delta \ell} \left[ m_s n_s \sum_j \nu^{\mathrm{cx}}_{sj}(\mathbf{u}_j-\mathbf{u}_s) + \sum_{\alpha \in \mathcal{B}_s} R_\alpha \Delta\mathbf{p}_{\alpha\to s} - \sum_{\beta \in \mathcal{L}_s} R_\beta \Delta\mathbf{p}_{s\to\beta} + \mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{el}}_s \right] d\ell
$$

where $\mathbf{M}_s$ is the area-normalized momentum source vector, $d\ell$ is a length element in m, and the bracketed term is a local force density. The mass $m_s$ is in kg, $n_s$ is the neutral-state density in m^-3, $\nu^{\mathrm{cx}}_{sj}$ is an effective charge-exchange frequency with collision partner $j$ in s^-1, and $\mathbf{u}_s$ and $\mathbf{u}_j$ are species mean velocities in m s^-1. The sets $\mathcal{B}_s$ and $\mathcal{L}_s$ contain reactions that create and remove state $s$, $R_\alpha$ and $R_\beta$ are volumetric reaction rates in m^-3 s^-1, $\Delta\mathbf{p}$ is the event-averaged momentum increment or removal in kg m s^-1, and $\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{el}}_s$ is the elastic-scattering force density in kg m^-2 s^-2.

In practice, this quantity is evaluated from plasma and neutral densities, temperatures, species flow velocities, distribution functions, and atomic or molecular rate coefficients. Charge exchange transfers directed momentum between ion and neutral populations while conserving the momentum of the interacting pair, ionization removes the momentum carried by neutrals leaving the state, recombination and molecular channels add product momentum, and elastic scattering redistributes momentum among existing particles. Direct measurement is uncommon; spectroscopy, neutral pressure gages, particle balance, and plasma momentum balance provide indirect constraints.

Projected components may be taken along radial, toroidal, poloidal, or magnetic-field-parallel directions. Related projected quantities include [poloidal_neutral_state_momentum](name:poloidal_neutral_state_momentum), [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum), and [parallel_neutral_momentum](name:parallel_neutral_momentum), while momentum-flux analogs such as [parallel_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:parallel_neutral_state_momentum_flux) and [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux) describe transport of neutral-state momentum rather than a local source.

Representative modeled magnitudes are highly regime dependent: 10^-6-10^-2 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in weakly recycling or low-neutral-density edge regions, 10^-2-10^2 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in scrape-off-layer and divertor conditions, and up to about 10^3 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in localized high-recycling, detachment-front, or gas-injection regions. Values may be near zero where the neutral density is small or interacting flows are nearly equilibrated.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component of the net momentum transfer to the neutral state acts along the positive direction of its basis vector; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, this is $+\hat{R}$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, or $+\hat{Z}$, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Effective convection velocity vector governing advective momentum transport for a single resolved neutral species state in edge plasma fluid models.
NAMES.long:
The neutral state momentum convection velocity $\mathbf{V}_\mathrm{conv}$ is the full-vector effective velocity that multiplies the local neutral momentum density in the non-diffusive term of the fluid momentum transport equation, acting as a species-resolved momentum pinch velocity that redistributes momentum independently of local density gradients.

In fluid edge-plasma transport models, the total vectorial momentum flux of a neutral state with mass $m_n$, number density $n_n$, and bulk fluid velocity $\mathbf{v}_n$ is decomposed into diffusive and convective parts:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{mom} = -D_\mathrm{mom} \nabla (m_n n_n \mathbf{v}_n) + \mathbf{V}_\mathrm{conv}\,(m_n n_n \mathbf{v}_n)
$$

where $D_\mathrm{mom}$ is the momentum diffusivity. The effective convection velocity encodes non-diffusive transport mechanisms — including drift contributions and neutral-plasma friction effects — specific to the given neutral state population.

This vector is resolved through its geometric projections in practice. The [radial component](name:radial_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity) determines cross-field momentum pinch, and the [parallel component](name:parallel_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity) governs field-aligned momentum advection; poloidal, toroidal, and vertical projections complete the decomposition in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The present quantity is the neutral-state-resolved instance of [momentum_convection_velocity](name:momentum_convection_velocity), and radial_neutral_effective_momentum_convection_velocity provides the corresponding scalar effective radial counterpart.
NAMES.sign: Positive when each vector component points in the positive direction of its corresponding coordinate axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Anisotropic momentum diffusion coefficient for neutral particles in a specified internal quantum state, decomposed into radial, poloidal, and toroidal directional components encoding the geometric anisotropy of cross-field and field-aligned transport in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The neutral-state momentum diffusion coefficient is the effective Fickian diffusivity, resolved by internal (electronic or vibrational) quantum state, that relates the diffusive momentum flux density of neutral particles to the local gradient of their bulk flow velocity. State resolution is physically significant when internal-state-dependent collision cross-sections alter momentum exchange rates between specific neutral populations and the background plasma, as occurs in recycling-dominated edge and divertor regions where excited-state neutrals may carry distinct transport properties.

For geometric direction $i$ and neutral internal state $s$, the diffusive momentum flux density $\Pi^{(s)}_{\mathrm{diff},i}$ satisfies:

$$
\Pi^{(s)}_{\mathrm{diff},i} = -\rho^{(s)}_n \, D^{(s)}_{\mathrm{mom},i} \, \nabla_i u^{(s)}_{n,i}
$$

where $\rho^{(s)}_n$ is the neutral mass density of state $s$, $D^{(s)}_{\mathrm{mom},i}$ is the momentum diffusion coefficient for that state in direction $i$, and $u^{(s)}_{n,i}$ is the corresponding neutral flow velocity component.

The vector decomposes into the [radial component](name:radial_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient), the [poloidal component](name:poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient), and the [toroidal component](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient), each capturing diffusive momentum transport along the respective geometric direction of the magnetic equilibrium. The state-summed toroidal analog without internal-state resolution is [toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity). The parent [momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:momentum_diffusion_coefficient) provides the generalized form for plasma species. State-resolved coefficients are derived from collisional-radiative neutral models using state-specific atomic collision data.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: State-resolved vector diffusion coefficient governing diffusive transport of neutral-particle momentum within a specified neutral species internal state, relating local momentum density gradients to diffusive fluxes along each spatial direction.
NAMES.long:
Neutral-state momentum diffusivity is the state-resolved, directionally decomposed diffusion coefficient that quantifies diffusive redistribution of momentum carried by neutral particles occupying a specified quantum or excitation state of a neutral species. It is the neutral-species counterpart of the plasma [momentum_diffusivity](name:momentum_diffusivity), generalized to individual internal states so that distinct momentum exchange pathways — for example, between ground-state and vibrationally excited neutrals — can be tracked separately in edge and divertor transport models.

The diffusive closure relates the neutral momentum flux $\Pi_{n,s,\alpha}$ for neutral state $s$ in spatial direction $\hat{e}_\alpha$ to the local momentum density gradient:

$$
\Pi_{n,s,\alpha} = -\rho_{n,s} \, D_{m,s,\alpha} \, \frac{\partial v_{n,s,\alpha}}{\partial x_\alpha}
$$

where $\rho_{n,s}$ is the neutral mass density in state $s$, $v_{n,s,\alpha}$ is the corresponding fluid velocity component, and $D_{m,s,\alpha}$ is the state-resolved diffusivity component in direction $\alpha$.

The directional projections of this vector quantity are [parallel_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:parallel_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity) along magnetic field lines, [poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity) in the poloidal direction, and [vertical_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:vertical_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity) along the $Z$-axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This state-by-state resolution distinguishes the quantity from [toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity), which aggregates over all neutral states, and from [toroidal_neutral_state_diffusivity](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity), which governs particle rather than momentum transport for the same state.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Momentum flux density vector of neutral particles in a specified atomic, molecular, charge, or excitation state that gives the rate at which that population transports linear momentum per unit area across any orientation-defined transport surface.
NAMES.long:
The neutral-state momentum flux density is the second-rank momentum transport tensor for neutral particles occupying a specified internal state — including atomic, molecular, charge, or excitation states — whose projections onto chosen transport directions yield the scalar directional flux components. It quantifies how each resolved neutral population redistributes linear momentum through convective and pressure-driven effects, and enters the state-resolved neutral species momentum-balance equation in edge plasma transport models.

For state $s$ the convective-plus-pressure contribution to the momentum flux density tensor is:

$$
\Pi_{ij}^{(s)} = m_s n_s v_{s,i}\, v_{s,j} + p_s\, \delta_{ij}
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass, $n_s$ is the number density of state $s$, $v_{s,i}$ is the $i$-th component of the mean fluid velocity $\mathbf{v}_s$, $p_s$ is the scalar pressure of state $s$, and $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta. The divergence $\partial_j \Pi_{ij}^{(s)}$ gives the local momentum source density coupling state $s$ to neighboring neutral states and to the plasma.
