N = \int f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3x \, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the spatial coordinate and $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity. As the [ratio_of_particle_count_to_simulated_particle_count](name:ratio_of_particle_count_to_simulated_particle_count), the same concept appears in Monte Carlo and particle-following kinetic codes as the statistical weight assigned to each computational marker, i.e., how many real physical particles a single marker represents. Both variants are dimensionless: the total count is a pure integer-valued integral over phase space, while the ratio is a weighting factor that scales marker populations to physical particle numbers. In Monte Carlo simulations, the marker weight can range from order unity (for small-domain test cases) to $10^{10}$ or more for bulk ion populations in reactor-scale devices, depending on the number of computational markers and the total confined particle inventory.

NAMES.name: particle_density
NAMES.short: Zeroth velocity-space moment of the particle distribution function, giving the local number density integrated over all energy populations and guiding-center orbit classes.
NAMES.long:
Particle density is the zeroth moment of the phase-space distribution function $f(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v})$ obtained by integrating over all particle velocities:

$$
n(\mathbf{r}) = \int f(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $n$ is the local number density and $f$ is the full distribution function encompassing both thermal and suprathermal populations at position $\mathbf{r}$. This quantity makes no restriction on particle energy or orbital topology, so it includes contributions from all guiding-center orbit classes (trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing) as well as from fast and thermal sub-populations simultaneously.

Decomposing by orbital topology recovers component quantities such as [trapped_density](name:total_trapped_particle_density) and [co_passing_density](name:total_co_passing_particle_density); summing over all particle species (electrons, ions, and neutrals) yields the total_particle_density. For the combined species total on a general-geometry grid, see also total_electron_ion_neutral_particle_number_density.

Computed in kinetic and Monte Carlo models by numerically integrating $f$ over velocity space on a spatial or flux-surface grid. Experimental estimates of orbit-class-resolved components rely on fast-ion diagnostics such as neutral particle analyzers or collective Thomson scattering.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physical particle distributions, as number density is a non-negative definite quantity by construction.

NAMES.name: fast_particle_density
NAMES.short: Number density of suprathermal particles, defined as the zeroth velocity moment of the fast-particle distribution function and summed over trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing orbit classes.
NAMES.long:
Fast-particle density is the local number density of non-thermal particles whose energies are substantially above the bulk thermal population. It includes particles produced by auxiliary heating, such as neutral beam injection or ion cyclotron resonance heating, and fusion-born products such as alpha particles. When orbit classes form a complete non-overlapping partition of fast-particle phase space, the total density is the sum of the trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing contributions.

The density is the zeroth velocity moment of the fast-particle distribution function:

$$
n_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} f_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v = \sum_{\alpha} n_{\mathrm{fast},\alpha}(\mathbf{r})
$$

where $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-particle density, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $f_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-particle distribution function, and $\alpha$ labels mutually exclusive orbit-class contributions such as [trapped_fast_particle_density](name:trapped_fast_particle_density), [co_passing_fast_particle_density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_density), and [counter_passing_fast_particle_density](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_density). The integral is over all velocity space and gives units of m^-3.

In practice, fast-particle density is computed from kinetic distribution functions obtained with slowing-down, Fokker-Planck, drift-kinetic, gyrokinetic, Monte Carlo, or orbit-following models. It can be constrained experimentally by diagnostics sensitive to energetic particles, including neutron measurements, neutral particle analyzers, fast-ion charge-exchange methods, and fast-ion light emission. The related [fast_ion_density](name:fast_ion_density) is the ion-specific analog, while fast_particle_pressure and [fast_ion_pressure](name:fast_ion_pressure) quantify the pressure carried by these energetic populations relative to the bulk [particle_density](name:particle_density).

Typical values in magnetically confined plasmas are about 10^16-10^19 m^-3 for auxiliary-heated fast-particle populations, with local values approaching 10^20 m^-3 in strongly heated or fusion-product-rich regimes. Although usually smaller than the bulk particle density, the fast-particle density can make a significant contribution to pressure, current drive, wave-particle interaction, and stability because the particles have high energy.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_particle_density
NAMES.short: Number density of suprathermal particles in the co-passing orbit class, from the fast-particle distribution function restricted to the co-passing region of velocity space.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing fast particle density is the number of non-thermal particles per unit physical volume whose guiding-center orbits are passing and belong to the co-passing branch. It is a partial zeroth moment of the fast-particle distribution function, complementary to the counter-passing and trapped fast-particle contributions.

The density at position $\mathbf{x}$ is defined by integrating the fast-particle distribution over the co-passing velocity-space domain:

$$
n_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x})} f_{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the suprathermal distribution function with units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the subset of velocity space corresponding to co-passing orbits. The trapped-passing boundary is set by magnetic geometry and particle invariants such as energy and magnetic moment; in pitch coordinates it should be treated as the local trapped-passing separatrix rather than a universal pitch cutoff.

In practice, this quantity is computed by applying an orbit-classification operator to a kinetic fast-particle distribution and taking the partial zeroth moment over the co-passing domain. The same definition applies whether the distribution is expressed in Cartesian velocity, energy-pitch, or guiding-center variables, provided the appropriate velocity-space Jacobian is included. When the orbit classes form a complete disjoint partition, the total fast-particle density is the sum of the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped contributions.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent because fast-particle populations are set by sources, slowing-down, redistribution, and loss processes. Representative values can range from below $10^{14}$ m$^{-3}$ in weak suprathermal populations to $10^{17}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in strongly heated or fusion-product-rich plasmas, usually remaining below the bulk thermal particle density.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_particle_density
NAMES.short: Number density of fast (suprathermal) particles in the counter-passing orbit class, where guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the bulk plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast particles are suprathermal ions or electrons whose guiding-center parallel velocity is anti-parallel to the bulk plasma current, executing closed toroidal orbits without magnetic mirror reflection. They are distinct from trapped particles, which undergo mirror reflection on the low-field side of the torus, and from [co_passing_fast_particle_density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_density) particles, which travel parallel to the current.

The counter-passing fast-particle density is the velocity-space integral of the fast-particle distribution function $f_\text{fast}$ restricted to counter-passing orbits:

$$
n_\text{fast,cp}(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{v_\parallel < 0} f_\text{fast}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $v_\parallel$ is the guiding-center parallel velocity and the integration domain covers orbits with $v_\parallel$ anti-parallel to the plasma current direction.

Together with [co_passing_fast_particle_density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_density), this quantity partitions the passing component of [fast_particle_density](name:fast_particle_density) by orbit class. The counter-passing population has opposite radial drift-orbit displacement from co-passing particles due to gradient and curvature drifts in the inhomogeneous tokamak field, making this decomposition essential for toroidal momentum balance, fast-particle orbit-loss studies, and neoclassical transport analyzes. The related [counter_passing_density](name:counter_passing_density) covers both thermal and suprathermal counter-passing particles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when counter-passing fast particles are present, with counter-passing defined as guiding-center parallel velocity anti-parallel to the plasma current direction.

NAMES.name: particle_flux
NAMES.short: Directed number of particles crossing a unit oriented surface per unit area per unit time, the general particle-transport flux spanning all species, charge states, and internal states.
NAMES.long:
Particle flux quantifies the directed flow of any plasma or neutral constituent across an oriented reference surface, capturing contributions from bulk convection, diffusion, drift motions, and turbulence. It is the fundamental quantity in the particle continuity equation and applies equally to electrons, ions at any charge state, and neutral atoms or molecules.

For a fluid element with number density $n$ and mean fluid velocity $\mathbf{v}$, the particle flux vector is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma} = n \mathbf{v}
$$

where the surface-normal projection $\Gamma = \boldsymbol{\Gamma} \cdot \hat{n}$ satisfies the continuity equation $\partial n / \partial t + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma} = S$, with $S$ the local particle source rate density. In kinetic descriptions, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is the first velocity moment of the distribution function $f(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}, t)$ integrated over all velocities.

Species-resolved specializations include [electron_particle_flux](name:electron_particle_flux) for the electron population, [ion_particle_flux](name:ion_particle_flux) for ions summed over charge states, and [neutral_particle_flux](name:neutral_particle_flux) for neutral atoms and molecules. The net outward particle flux integrated over a closed surface determines the temporal rate of change of [particle_count](name:particle_count) within the enclosed volume.

Particle flux is measured directly by electrostatic probes in the scrape-off layer and inferred from density profile gradients combined with transport modeling across the confined plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when particles flow in the direction of the outward surface normal, away from the enclosed plasma volume.

NAMES.name: electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron particle flux is the signed number of electrons crossing a unit area per unit time through an oriented surface. It is the surface-normal component of electron particle transport due to flow, drifts, diffusion, or turbulence.
NAMES.long:
Electron particle flux is the signed rate at which electrons cross unit area of an oriented surface. It is the surface-normal component of the electron particle-flux density vector, combining transport from bulk motion, drifts, collisional diffusion, and turbulent fluctuations.

The flux through a surface with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is commonly decomposed into convective and nonconvective contributions:

$$
\Gamma_e = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \left(n_e \mathbf{u}_e + \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,\mathrm{diff}} + \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,\mathrm{drift}} + \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{e,\mathrm{turb}}\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e$ is the electron particle-flux density vector, $n_e$ is electron density, $\mathbf{u}_e$ is the mean electron velocity, and the remaining terms represent diffusive, drift, and turbulent particle transport contributions.

In practice, electron particle flux is obtained from particle balance, kinetic or fluid transport calculations, or experimental inference using density, flow, and particle-source measurements. Diffusive closures often make the diffusive contribution proportional to $-\nabla n_e$, while turbulent transport is usually inferred from fluctuation measurements or from balance between sources, sinks, and changes in density.

Typical magnitudes range from $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ m^-2.s^-1 for cross-field transport in confined or scrape-off-layer plasmas, and can reach $10^{22}$-$10^{24}$ m^-2.s^-1 for strong parallel flows to material surfaces in high-density divertor conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net electron particle flow crosses the oriented surface in the direction of its positive normal.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Full particle flux vector of ions in a specified ionization charge state, giving the directed number flow per unit area per unit time for that charge state resolved independently from all other ionization stages.
NAMES.long:
The ion charge state particle flux vector characterizes the directed flow of ions in a specific ionization stage $z$ through a unit surface per unit time, treating each charge state as a distinct species in charge-state-resolved multi-fluid transport models. This per-stage resolution is essential for modeling impurity accumulation and fuel-ion evolution in confined plasmas, where ionization and recombination continuously couple adjacent charge states.

The flux vector is defined as the first velocity moment of the charge-state population:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z = n_z \mathbf{v}_z
$$

where $n_z$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$ and $\mathbf{v}_z$ is the mean fluid velocity of that charge-state population.

Directional projections of this vector yield [radial_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:radial_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) for cross-field transport across magnetic flux surfaces, [poloidal_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) for poloidal flow asymmetries, and [parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) for field-aligned streaming. The scalar surface-normal analog [ion_state_particle_flux](name:ion_state_particle_flux) represents a single-surface projection used in one-dimensional transport approximations.

Charge-state-resolved fluxes are computed in multi-fluid or kinetic transport codes using ionization and recombination rate coefficients from atomic databases. Core plasma values span approximately $10^{18}$–$10^{21}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, while fluxes near plasma-facing components and divertor targets can exceed $10^{22}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$.

NAMES.name: ion_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net oriented number flux of ions through a unit area per unit time, summed over all charge states of an ion species. It is the scalar particle-transport flux used in the ion continuity balance.
NAMES.long:
Ion particle flux is the net transport rate of ions across an oriented unit area, summed over all ion charge states of a given species. It represents the scalar projection of the ion particle-flux vector onto the relevant transport direction or surface normal, so it can be positive or negative depending on the direction of net ion motion.

Total ion particle conservation is commonly expressed by the continuity balance:

$$
\frac{\partial n_i}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i = S_i
$$

where $n_i$ is the total ion number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i$ is the ion particle-flux vector in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $S_i$ is the net ion particle source density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ from ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and imposed sources or sinks. The scalar flux is the oriented component of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i$, equivalently $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}$ for positive surface normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$.

In experiments and transport analysis, ion particle flux is inferred from density evolution, atomic source estimates, flow measurements, and transport closures for diffusive, convective, neoclassical, turbulent, and field-parallel motion. The charge-state-resolved counterpart is [ion_state_particle_flux](name:ion_state_particle_flux); [parallel_ion_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_particle_flux) and [parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) describe field-aligned transport, while [electron_particle_flux](name:electron_particle_flux) is the analogous electron quantity entering ambipolar particle balance.

Typical absolute magnitudes vary widely with plasma region and operating regime. Edge and scrape-off-layer transport values often span $10^{18}$-$10^{22}\ \mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and directed fluxes near strongly recycling divertor targets can approach $10^{23}\ \mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$; core cross-field values are often lower and more sensitive to fueling and confinement.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net ion flow is in the direction of the chosen positive normal to the surface through which the flux is evaluated.

NAMES.name: ion_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Signed scalar particle flux of ions in a specified ionization charge state through an oriented unit surface. It is the surface-normal projection of the charge-state ion particle flux, including convective, diffusive, drift, and turbulent transport contributions.
NAMES.long:
Ion state particle flux is the signed number rate per unit area at which ions of a given element and ionization charge state cross an oriented surface. It is a scalar surface-normal projection, so it can describe crossing of a magnetic flux surface, a material boundary, or a control-volume face, rather than the magnitude of the full particle-flux vector. In charge-state-resolved particle continuity equations it transports the density of that charge state between neighboring regions and across boundaries.

A common decomposition of the scalar normal flux is

$$
\Gamma_{a,z,n} = \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{a,z} = n_{a,z} u_{a,z,n} - D_{a,z}\,\nabla_n n_{a,z} + \Gamma_{a,z,n}^{\mathrm{drift}} + \Gamma_{a,z,n}^{\mathrm{turb}}
$$

where $a$ labels the ion species, $z$ labels the ionization charge state, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen unit normal to the surface, $\Gamma_{a,z,n}$ is in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, $n_{a,z}$ is the charge-state density, $u_{a,z,n}$ is the normal convective velocity, $D_{a,z}$ is an effective diffusion coefficient, $\nabla_n n_{a,z}$ is the density gradient along the normal direction, and the final terms represent drift and turbulent contributions when they are retained.

In practice this flux is computed from fluid or kinetic transport models, inferred from particle balance, or constrained by measurements of density, flow, ionization, recombination, and boundary loss rates. Diagnostics such as spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements, and probes can constrain pieces of the balance, but the charge-state-resolved flux usually requires a transport model because ionization and recombination couple neighboring charge states.

Typical main-ion cross-field values in confined and edge transport are about $10^{19}$-$10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, while parallel exhaust or sheath-adjacent values can reach $10^{22}$-$10^{24}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. Trace impurity charge-state fluxes scale with abundance and ionization stage and may be much smaller, commonly $10^{15}$-$10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net particle flow of the specified ionization charge state is in the direction of the chosen oriented surface normal.

NAMES.name: neutral_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Neutral particle flux is the species- and state-integrated net number flux density of neutral atoms and molecules crossing a unit oriented surface per unit time. It is the general parent quantity for directional components such as parallel, poloidal, and radial neutral particle flux.
NAMES.long:
Neutral particle flux is the net number flux density of all neutral atoms and molecules, integrated over neutral species and internal states. It describes how many neutral particles cross a unit oriented area per unit time and is used as the general quantity underlying component fluxes such as [parallel neutral particle flux](name:parallel_neutral_particle_flux), [poloidal neutral particle flux](name:poloidal_neutral_particle_flux), and [radial neutral particle flux](name:radial_neutral_particle_flux).

The flux enters the neutral-particle continuity equation:

$$
\frac{\partial n_0}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0 = S_0
$$

where $n_0$ is the species-integrated neutral density in $m^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_0$ is the neutral particle flux density vector, and $S_0$ is the net volumetric source rate in $m^{-3}\,s^{-1}$, positive for net production of neutrals and negative for net loss. Sources and sinks may include ionization, recombination, molecular reactions, wall recycling, and external fueling.

In practice, neutral particle flux is computed from neutral kinetic or fluid descriptions as the velocity moment of the neutral distribution function, or equivalently from neutral density and mean velocity after summing over species and states. It is usually inferred indirectly from edge and divertor diagnostics, gas-balance analysis, recycling measurements, spectroscopy, and coupled plasma-neutral transport modeling. The density appearing in the balance is related to [total neutral density](name:total_neutral_density).

Typical edge and divertor values are about 10^20-10^23 m^-2 s^-1, with lower values in weakly fueled scrape-off-layer regions and larger values near strong recycling surfaces, gas injection, or transient fueling events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral-particle flux vector crosses the unit area in the direction of the oriented surface-element normal.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Signed number flux of neutral particles in a specified internal state through an oriented surface, per unit area and per unit time. It is the surface-normal component of state-resolved neutral particle transport.
NAMES.long:
Neutral-state particle flux is the signed surface-normal number flux of neutral atoms or molecules belonging to a specified internal state. For a closed control surface, choosing the normal outward from the control volume makes positive values represent neutral particles leaving that volume; choosing the opposite normal reverses the sign.

For an oriented surface with unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, the scalar flux is the projection of the vector particle flux:

$$
\Gamma_s = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $\Gamma_s$ is the scalar neutral-state particle flux in $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s$ is the vector number flux of neutrals in internal state $s$ in $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal to the surface. In a local particle balance it enters through $\partial n_s/\partial t + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s = S_s$, where $n_s$ is the state-resolved neutral density in $m^{-3}$ and $S_s$ is the net volumetric source in $m^{-3}\,s^{-1}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from neutral kinetic or fluid transport models as a velocity moment of the state-resolved distribution, or from a particle crossing rate divided by the corresponding surface area. Experimental constraints are usually indirect, using spectroscopy, pressure measurements, gas balance, and recycling observations to infer the state-resolved neutral population and its transport.

Typical magnitudes span about $10^{17}$-$10^{22}$ $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$ in low-density or weakly recycling regions and can reach $10^{22}$-$10^{24}$ $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$ near strong gas, recycling, or divertor sources. Fluxes for excited internal states are often smaller than ground-state neutral fluxes because excited-state populations are shorter lived.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles in the specified internal state cross the oriented surface in the direction of the chosen unit normal.

NAMES.name: parallel_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Field-aligned component of the electron particle flux vector, obtained by projecting the electron particle flux onto the local magnetic-field direction.
NAMES.long:
Parallel electron particle flux is the component of the [electron particle flux](name:electron_particle_flux) along the local magnetic-field direction. It describes the signed rate at which electrons cross a unit area whose normal is parallel to the field, and is a key measure of field-aligned particle transport in magnetized plasmas.

The field-aligned component is defined by projecting the electron particle flux vector onto the magnetic-field unit vector:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,e} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} = n_e\,\mathbf{u}_e \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\parallel,e}$ is the parallel electron particle flux, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e$ is the electron particle flux vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field, $n_e$ is the electron density, and $\mathbf{u}_e$ is the electron fluid velocity.

In transport modeling this quantity is computed from electron density and parallel velocity moments, or from the full particle flux vector by projection onto $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$. In experiments it is constrained indirectly through particle balance, edge and divertor diagnostics, Langmuir probe measurements where applicable, and comparison with inferred parallel flows and target particle fluxes.

Typical magnitudes vary strongly with confinement regime and location: core parallel electron particle fluxes may be near zero in the plasma frame or up to 10^21-10^23 m^-2.s^-1 when driven by flows, while edge and scrape-off-layer values commonly reach 10^22-10^25 m^-2.s^-1 near open field lines and divertor targets.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron particle flux is directed along the local magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Particle flux density of ions in a specified charge state projected onto the local magnetic-field direction. It is the signed rate at which that charge-state population streams along the field per unit area.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion charge-state particle flux is the signed particle flux density of ions in one ionization stage resolved along the local magnetic field direction. It describes field-aligned streaming of that charge-state population and is a charge-state-resolved contribution to [parallel_ion_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_particle_flux).

For charge state $z$, the common fluid definition is:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,z} = n_z v_{\parallel,z}
$$

where $n_z$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$ in $m^{-3}$, and $v_{\parallel,z}$ is their mean velocity component along $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ in $m\,s^{-1}$. The product has units of particle flux density, $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$.

In charge-state particle balance, this quantity enters through the field-aligned divergence term, commonly written inline as $\nabla \cdot (\Gamma_{\parallel,z}\hat{b})$, together with perpendicular transport and sources or sinks from ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and external fueling. It is usually computed from kinetic distribution moments or fluid density and flow variables, and may be constrained indirectly using spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements, and transport reconstruction.

Typical magnitudes vary widely with species, charge state, confinement region, and collisionality. Trace impurity charge states in the confined plasma may be below $10^{18}$ m^-2.s^-1, while edge, scrape-off-layer, and divertor charge states with strong field-aligned flows commonly reach $10^{20}-10^{24}$ m^-2.s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions in the specified charge state flow in the direction of the local magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$, equivalently along $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the total ion particle flux density along the local magnetic field direction, aggregated over all charge states of the ion species.
NAMES.long:
The parallel ion particle flux $\Gamma_{\parallel,i}$ quantifies the net flow of ions per unit area per unit time along the local magnetic field direction $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, summed over all charge states of the ion species. It enters the ion density continuity equation as the divergence term governing parallel transport, and is the dominant particle transport channel along open magnetic field lines in the scrape-off layer and divertor regions.

The defining relation is:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,i} = n_i \, v_{\parallel,i}
$$

where $n_i$ is the ion number density and $v_{\parallel,i}$ is the component of the ion fluid velocity parallel to $\mathbf{B}$.

This quantity is computed in edge and plasma transport models from the fluid momentum balance or by integrating the ion distribution function over the parallel velocity dimension. For charge-state-resolved transport, the counterpart [parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) provides per-charge-state resolution. The analogous quantities for other plasma components are [parallel_electron_particle_flux](name:parallel_electron_particle_flux) and [parallel_neutral_particle_flux](name:parallel_neutral_particle_flux).

Typical magnitudes in the scrape-off layer range from $10^{20}$ to $10^{22}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, with values increasing toward divertor target plates as parallel flow accelerates toward the Bohm condition at the magnetic presheath entrance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion particle flow is co-directed with the magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Net number flux of neutral atoms and molecules per unit area along the local magnetic field direction, integrated over all neutral species and atomic or molecular states.
NAMES.long:
The parallel neutral particle flux is the component of the neutral particle flux density projected along the local magnetic field direction $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$. Defined as the species-integrated quantity over all neutral atoms and molecules and their internal states, it characterizes the dominant transport channel for neutrals along field lines in the edge and scrape-off-layer plasma. Together with [poloidal_neutral_particle_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_particle_flux), it spans the principal directional decomposition of edge neutral transport.

The neutral continuity equation couples this flux to the local neutral number density $n_0$:

$$
\frac{\partial n_0}{\partial t} + \nabla_\parallel \Gamma_\parallel^{0} + \nabla_\perp \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\perp^{0} = S_0
$$

where $\nabla_\parallel = \hat{b} \cdot \nabla$ is the derivative along the magnetic field line, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\perp^{0}$ is the cross-field neutral flux, and $S_0$ is the net volumetric source rate accounting for ionization, recombination, and charge-exchange reactions.

This quantity is computed by edge plasma transport codes solving neutral fluid or kinetic equations in complex scrape-off-layer and divertor geometry. Results can be validated indirectly against neutral pressure gage measurements and visible spectroscopy of charge-exchange and recycling emission. The state-resolved energy counterpart [parallel_neutral_state_energy_flux](name:parallel_neutral_state_energy_flux) tracks energy transport per individual neutral state, while [parallel_ion_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_state_particle_flux) provides the analogous parallel ion particle channel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles flow in the direction of the local magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the particle flux for neutral atoms or molecules in a specified internal state, resolved along the magnetic field direction in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The parallel neutral-state particle flux quantifies the number of neutral atoms or molecules occupying a specified internal quantum state (electronic, vibrational, or rotational) that cross a unit area per unit time along the direction parallel to the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. Resolving the flux by internal state is essential in edge plasma models because reaction rates for ionization, charge exchange, and dissociation depend critically on which state the neutral population occupies.

The flux is defined as:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,s} = n_s \, v_{\parallel,s}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of neutrals in internal state $s$ and $v_{\parallel,s}$ is their mean velocity component parallel to $\mathbf{B}$.

This quantity is distinct from [parallel_neutral_particle_flux](name:parallel_neutral_particle_flux), which integrates over all internal states. The complementary poloidal projection is [poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux), and the energy transport carried by the same state-resolved neutral population is described by [parallel_neutral_state_energy_flux](name:parallel_neutral_state_energy_flux). The ion analog, resolved by charge state, is [parallel_ion_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_state_particle_flux). In the edge and divertor regions, typical magnitudes range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{22}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, with peak values occurring near the divertor target plates where neutral recycling is strongest.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles in the specified state flow in the direction of the local magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: particle_pressure
NAMES.short: Kinetic pressure of a particle population obtained from the second velocity-space moment of the distribution function, encompassing thermal and nonthermal contributions across all orbit classes and perturbation states.
NAMES.long:
Particle pressure is the scalar mechanical pressure carried by a specified particle population, computed directly from the kinetic distribution function rather than from a fluid closure assumption. It is the parent quantity for orbit-class-resolved and perturbation-resolved variants of kinetic pressure derived from the second moment of the distribution.

The scalar pressure combines the parallel and perpendicular kinetic stress components:

$$
P = \frac{P_\parallel + 2P_\perp}{3} = \frac{1}{3}\int m\,|\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}|^2\,f(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $m$ is the particle mass, $\mathbf{u}$ is the mean fluid velocity, $f(\mathbf{v})$ is the distribution function, and $P_\parallel$, $P_\perp$ are the pressure components parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field. Restricting the velocity-space integral to the co-passing trajectory domain yields [co_passing_particle_pressure](name:co_passing_particle_pressure); evaluating only the fluctuating part of $f$ yields the perturbed variant relevant to turbulence analysis. In kinetic and gyrokinetic transport codes, particle pressure is obtained by numerical quadrature over the phase-space distribution; for Maxwellian populations the expression reduces to $P = nkT$, where $n$ is number density and $T$ is temperature. The fast-particle analog [co_passing_fast_particle_pressure](name:co_passing_fast_particle_pressure) illustrates how orbit-class and population restrictions combine within this hierarchy.

NAMES.name: particle_source_rate
NAMES.short: Net volumetric rate of particle production or loss from a distribution function source, serving as the source term in the particle-density transport equation.
NAMES.long:
The particle source rate $S_n$ is the net rate per unit volume at which particles are created or destroyed by processes described through a distribution function, such as neutral beam injection ionization, thermonuclear fusion birth, or pellet ablation.

It enters the particle continuity equation as:

$$
\frac{\partial n}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma} = S_n
$$

where $n$ is the number density and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is the directed particle flux. Positive values indicate net particle production; negative values indicate a net particle sink from the distribution source.

This quantity is computed from Fokker-Planck or kinetic solvers that track the birth and thermalization of fast particles on a flux-surface-averaged radial grid, and it is used as direct input to particle transport equations in integrated modeling workflows. The [thermal_particle_source_rate](name:thermal_particle_source_rate) isolates the thermal-population contribution, while ion_source_rate and [electron_source_rate](name:electron_source_rate) provide species-resolved counterparts. For neutral particles, the analogous quantity is [neutral_source_rate](name:neutral_source_rate).

Typical values in NBI-heated tokamak core plasmas span $10^{18}$–$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$, depending on injected power, beam energy, and local plasma density.

NAMES.name: ion_particle_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated net ion particle source rate inside an enclosing flux surface, summed over all ion species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
Ion particle source rate is the cumulative net rate at which ion particles are produced, injected, or removed within the volume bounded by a flux surface. It is summed over all ion species and charge states, so it represents the total-ion particle balance rather than a single species or charge-state channel. Positive contributions add ions to the enclosed plasma volume, while negative contributions remove ions.

Using a monotonic radial flux-surface label $\rho$, the cumulative rate is defined by the volume integral of the local net total-ion source density:

$$
\Gamma_i(\rho,t) = \int_{V(\rho)} S_i(\mathbf{x},t)\,dV
$$

where $\Gamma_i$ is the ion particle source rate, $V(\rho)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the flux surface labeled by $\rho$, and $S_i(\mathbf{x},t)$ is the local net volumetric total-ion source density in m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$. The integrand corresponds to the local [total_ion_source_rate](name:total_ion_source_rate), not to a flux-surface-averaged quantity; if a flux-surface average is used in computation, it must be combined with the appropriate differential volume element to reproduce the same volume integral.

In practice this quantity is computed from transport and source modeling constrained by diagnostics and actuator information. The net local source may include ionization, recombination, charge-exchange contributions to the total-ion balance, neutral fueling, pellet deposition, neutral-beam particle deposition, and explicit particle removal or exhaust. Contributions that only redistribute population among ion charge states cancel when summed over all ion species and charge states.

Typical magnitudes are $10^{19}$-$10^{22}$ s$^{-1}$ in small to medium tokamak plasmas and can reach $10^{22}$-$10^{23}$ s$^{-1}$ in high-density, strongly fueled, or reactor-scale plasmas. The enclosed rate approaches zero near the magnetic axis with the enclosed volume and gives the net total-ion source for the confined plasma at the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.short: Perpendicular component of the species-summed fast-particle pressure tensor for co-passing orbits, produced by velocity components transverse to the local magnetic field. Co-passing denotes passing guiding-center motion with the same toroidal sense as the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressure is the perpendicular component of the fast-particle pressure tensor after restricting the distribution to co-passing passing orbits and summing over the included fast species. It represents kinetic stress from velocity components orthogonal to the local magnetic field. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, co-passing denotes passing guiding-center orbits whose toroidal motion is in the same sense as the plasma current.

The species-summed kinetic moment is

$$
P_{\perp,\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co},s}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v_\perp^2 f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $s$ labels the included fast-particle species, $m_s$ is the species mass in kg, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $t$ is time in s, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $v_\perp$ is the speed perpendicular to the local magnetic field in m s$^{-1}$, $f_s$ is the fast-particle distribution function in s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element in m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The domain $\Omega_{\mathrm{co},s}$ is the passing part of velocity space whose guiding-center orbit has bounce-averaged toroidal velocity $R\dot{\phi}$, in the same $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, in the same sense as the plasma current; trapped and counter-passing orbits are excluded. For common heating and fusion-product applications the fast species are usually energetic ions, but the definition applies to any suprathermal species included in the sum.

This quantity is computed as a second velocity moment of an orbit-class-resolved fast-particle distribution, typically after classifying particles by pitch, constants of motion, or guiding-center trajectories. It is not usually measured directly as a local tensor component; instead it is inferred through kinetic modeling constrained by diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal particles. Together with [parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure](name:parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure), it describes pressure anisotropy of the co-passing fast population, while [perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure) includes the corresponding perpendicular contributions from all fast-particle orbit classes.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. As an order-of-magnitude guide, auxiliary-heated tokamak cores can have perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressures of about $10^2$-$5\times10^4$ Pa, with much smaller values in weakly heated regions or where the co-passing fast-particle population is depleted.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.short: Perpendicular pressure carried by fast particles on counter-passing guiding-center orbits. It is the perpendicular second velocity moment of the counter-passing part of the suprathermal distribution function.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular counter-passing fast-particle pressure is the perpendicular component of the kinetic pressure tensor contributed by suprathermal particles whose guiding-center orbits are passing and whose parallel motion is opposite to the plasma-current direction. It represents the part of the anisotropic fast-particle pressure associated with the counter-passing region of velocity space; for an unqualified fast-particle population it is summed over all included fast species.

For a gyrotropic distribution, the perpendicular pressure is the second perpendicular velocity moment of the counter-passing fast-particle distribution:

$$
P_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{counter}} = \sum_s \int_{\mathrm{counter}} \frac{m_s v_\perp^2}{2}\, f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $s$ indexes fast-particle species, $m_s$ is particle mass, $v_\perp$ is speed perpendicular to the local magnetic field, $f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-particle distribution function, and the integration domain is restricted to counter-passing orbits. The factor $m_s v_\perp^2/2$ is the perpendicular kinetic energy associated with gyromotion, so this pressure component is non-negative for a non-negative distribution function.

In practice this quantity is obtained from kinetic fast-particle modeling, reduced distribution functions, or reconstruction constrained by diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal ions or electrons, such as neutron emission, fast-ion loss measurements, charge-exchange measurements, or energetic-particle radiation. It is commonly compared with the corresponding [parallel counter-passing fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) to characterize pressure anisotropy, and with co-passing and trapped perpendicular components to decompose the fast-particle pressure by orbit class.

Typical values range from $10^2$-$10^5$ Pa in present-day auxiliary-heated plasmas, with localized values approaching $10^6$ Pa in high-power neutral-beam or radio-frequency-heated scenarios. The relative size of this component depends on injection geometry, wave-particle resonance, collisional slowing down, pitch-angle scattering, and orbit losses.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Perpendicular fast electron pressure is the gyrotropic pressure moment of the suprathermal electron distribution associated with velocity components perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular fast electron pressure, denoted $p_{\perp,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}$, is the component of the fast-electron pressure tensor in either direction perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction. It describes the perpendicular kinetic energy density of the non-thermal electron population and is distinct from the parallel component $p_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}$.

For a gyrotropic fast-electron distribution, the local perpendicular pressure is the second velocity moment

$$
p_{\perp,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int \frac{1}{2} m_e v_\perp^2 f_e^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v_\perp$ is the speed perpendicular to the local magnetic field, and $f_e^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-electron distribution function. For a gyrotropic pressure tensor, the scalar fast electron pressure is related by $p_e^{\mathrm{fast}} = (p_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}} + 2p_{\perp,e}^{\mathrm{fast}})/3$.

The quantity is computed from kinetic distribution functions, reduced fast-electron models, or inferred from diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal electrons such as electron cyclotron emission, hard x-ray emission, or bremsstrahlung. The unqualified quantity is local; when a flux-surface average is used for transport or equilibrium analysis, the average is applied after forming this local velocity-space moment and should be stated explicitly by the averaged quantity.

Typical values are near zero when no significant fast-electron population is present, about 10^2-10^4 Pa in strongly wave-heated core plasmas, and often 1-10^2 Pa in edge or scrape-off-layer conditions. Large anisotropy between $p_{\perp,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ and $p_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ can affect wave absorption, transport, and kinetic stability.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Perpendicular component of the fast ion pressure for the ion species considered, summed over ionization states. It represents the kinetic pressure associated with suprathermal ion velocity components transverse to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular fast ion pressure is the component of the suprathermal ion pressure tensor associated with motion across the local magnetic field. For a given ion species it is summed over ionization states and complements the parallel component [parallel_fast_ion_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure); equality of the perpendicular and parallel components corresponds to an isotropic fast-ion pressure contribution.

A kinetic definition is the second velocity moment of the fast-ion distribution perpendicular to the magnetic field:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast},\perp} = \sum_q \int \frac{1}{2} m_i v_\perp^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},q}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $q$ labels ionization state, $f_{\mathrm{fast},q}$ is the fast-ion distribution function normalized so that its velocity integral gives density, and $v_\perp$ is the magnitude of the particle velocity component perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction. The factor $1/2$ accounts for the two perpendicular degrees of freedom in the pressure tensor moment.

In practice this quantity is computed from modeled or reconstructed fast-ion distribution functions, including source, slowing-down, orbit, and wave-particle effects. It may be constrained by diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal ions, such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, fast-ion D-alpha emission, collective Thomson scattering, or gamma-ray measurements, depending on ion species and energy range.

Typical values range from near zero in weakly heated or edge regions to about 10-10^4 Pa in many auxiliary-heated plasmas, and can reach 10^4-10^5 Pa where energetic neutral-beam ions, radio-frequency-accelerated ions, or fusion-born alpha particles contribute strongly.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Perpendicular pressure contributed by non-thermal ions in a specified charge state, equal to the transverse diagonal pressure-tensor component relative to the local magnetic field. It is the charge-state-resolved fast-ion contribution to pressure anisotropy.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular fast-ion-state pressure is the transverse diagonal component of the kinetic pressure tensor for non-thermal ions in a single charge state. It measures the kinetic stress associated with fast-ion motion perpendicular to the local magnetic field and can differ from the corresponding parallel component for beam ions, fusion products, and radio-frequency-accelerated ion tails.

For an ion charge state $q$, the perpendicular component is defined from the fast-ion velocity distribution as:

$$
P_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}^{(q)} = \frac{m_i}{2} \int \left|\mathbf{v} - v_\parallel \hat{\mathbf{b}}\right|^2 f_{\mathrm{fast}}^{(q)}(\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $f_{\mathrm{fast}}^{(q)}$ is the non-thermal distribution function for charge state $q$, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field, and $v_\parallel=\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}$. The factor $1/2$ converts the total squared speed in the two perpendicular velocity directions into one transverse diagonal pressure component; equivalently, for a gyrotropic distribution it is the pressure associated with either perpendicular velocity component.

This quantity is usually computed by integrating a charge-state-resolved fast-ion distribution from kinetic, Fokker-Planck, orbit-following, bounce-averaged, or Monte Carlo transport modeling. It may be constrained indirectly by fast-ion diagnostics such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, gamma-ray emission, collective scattering, or fast-ion charge-exchange measurements, but the pressure itself is a velocity-space moment rather than a directly measured signal.

Typical core values in neutral-beam-heated or radio-frequency-heated tokamak plasmas are about $10^2$-$10^4$ Pa per important charge state, with lower values near the edge and possible values approaching $10^5$ Pa in high-power scenarios with strong fast-ion confinement. The value should be compared with [parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure) to quantify charge-state-resolved anisotropy, with [perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure) for the sum over charge states, and with perpendicular_plasma_pressure for the corresponding total plasma pressure component.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_neutral_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Perpendicular kinetic pressure of suprathermal neutral particles in a specified internal quantum or excitation state, arising from velocity components perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular fast neutral state pressure is the component of the kinetic pressure tensor of suprathermal (non-thermal) neutral particles associated with motions perpendicular to the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, resolved by the particle's internal quantum or excitation state $s$. It is the state-resolved analog of [perpendicular_fast_neutral_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_neutral_pressure) and represents a perpendicular projection of [fast_neutral_state_pressure](name:fast_neutral_state_pressure), capturing how individual internal states contribute to the total perpendicular fast-neutral pressure.

The defining relation is the second velocity moment of the state-specific fast neutral distribution restricted to the perpendicular velocity plane:

$$
P_{\perp,\mathrm{fast},s} = \frac{m_n}{2} \int f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{v})\, v_\perp^2 \, d^3v
$$

where $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{v})$ is the velocity distribution function of fast neutrals in internal state $s$, and $v_\perp$ is the speed component perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$.

This quantity is relevant wherever fast neutrals generated by charge-exchange reactions or dissociation events carry significant perpendicular energy, particularly in edge and scrape-off layer plasmas. Values are computed by kinetic neutral transport codes that resolve internal-state populations across the fast neutral velocity distribution, or estimated from state-specific spectroscopic measurements combined with velocity distribution models. The [neutral_state_particle_flux](name:neutral_state_particle_flux) provides complementary state-resolved information on the associated particle transport.
NAMES.sign: Positive when fast neutral particles in state $s$ carry net kinetic energy in the plane perpendicular to the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.short: Kinetic scalar gyrotropic perpendicular pressure of the suprathermal particle population, summed over species. It is the one-half trace of the fast-particle pressure tensor over the plane transverse to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular fast-particle pressure is the scalar pressure component associated with suprathermal particle motion transverse to the local magnetic field. It is the half-trace of the fast-particle pressure tensor over the plane normal to the field, summed over all fast-particle species, and is distinct from the field-aligned parallel component.

For a gyrotropic projection of a fast-particle distribution, the local kinetic moment is

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},\perp}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_s \int \frac{1}{2} m_s v_{\perp,s}^2 f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $s$ indexes particle species, $m_s$ is the particle mass in kg, $v_{\perp,s}$ is the perpendicular peculiar speed relative to the local magnetic field in m s$^{-1}$, $f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-particle phase-space distribution with units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element with units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The corresponding [parallel_fast_particle_pressure](name:parallel_fast_particle_pressure) is the projection of the same tensor along the local magnetic field; the scalar trace pressure satisfies $p_{\mathrm{fast}}=(2P_{\mathrm{fast},\perp}+P_{\mathrm{fast},\parallel})/3$.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by integrating a modeled or inferred fast-particle distribution over velocity space and summing the included suprathermal species. Thermal bulk pressure is excluded, and no specific diagnostic or computational method is part of the definition.

Representative magnitudes are scenario dependent. The value is 0 Pa when no suprathermal population is present; for order-of-magnitude estimates, $P_{\mathrm{fast},\perp}\sim n_{\mathrm{fast}}E_\perp$, so $n_{\mathrm{fast}}=10^{16}-10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ with perpendicular energies of 10-1000 keV corresponds roughly to 10-10$^5$ Pa.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Effective velocity of directed runaway-electron transport across magnetic flux surfaces. It represents the convective contribution to perpendicular particle transport, distinct from diffusive spreading driven by density gradients.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular runaway-electron convection velocity is the effective directed velocity that advects the runaway-electron population across magnetic flux surfaces. It describes the convective part of cross-field particle transport, separate from gradient-driven spreading represented by [perpendicular runaway electron diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity). In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels nested magnetic flux surfaces and increases outward, the perpendicular direction is the local flux-surface normal.

In a flux-surface-averaged particle balance, the [perpendicular runaway electron particle flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux) is commonly decomposed into diffusive and convective terms:

$$
\Gamma_{RE,\perp} = -D_{\perp,RE}\frac{\partial n_{RE}}{\partial r_\psi} + v_{\perp,RE} n_{RE}
$$

where $\Gamma_{RE,\perp}$ is the perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux, $D_{\perp,RE}$ is the perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity, $n_{RE}$ is the runaway-electron number density, $r_\psi$ is an effective radial flux-surface coordinate in meters that increases outward, and $v_{\perp,RE}$ is the convection velocity. The same transport decomposition is the runaway-electron-specific counterpart of the more general [electron convection velocity].

This velocity is usually inferred rather than measured directly. It is obtained from transport modeling, kinetic simulations, or constrained particle-balance analysis using diagnostics sensitive to runaway-electron density and losses, and it is interpreted together with source terms such as the [volume-averaged runaway electron source rate](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate). Physical contributions can include radial electric-field effects, externally applied magnetic perturbations, stochastic magnetic fields, and orbit-averaged drift losses acting on the runaway population.

Typical inferred effective values are highly scenario dependent: magnitudes below 1 m s^-1 are consistent with weak directed cross-field drift, 1-100 m s^-1 is typical of moderate convective loss modeling, and transient values of 10^2-10^4 m s^-1 may be used to represent rapid losses during strong perturbations or disruption-mitigation phases.
NAMES.sign: Positive when directed outward along the flux-surface normal, from smaller to larger radial flux-surface label toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Cross-field diffusion coefficient governing the perpendicular spread of runaway electrons across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular diffusivity $D_\perp$ of runaway electrons quantifies how rapidly the runaway electron population spreads across magnetic flux surfaces due to stochastic magnetic field perturbations, collisional pitch-angle scattering, and turbulent transport processes. It is the perpendicular projection of the full runaway_electron_diffusivity tensor, characterizing the diffusive part of cross-field transport for this suprathermal population.

The diffusive contribution to the perpendicular particle flux is defined as:

$$
\Gamma_{\perp}^{\text{diff}} = -D_\perp \nabla_\perp n_r
$$

where $n_r$ is the [runaway electron number density](name:runaway_electron_density). Combined with the convective contribution from [perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity), this constitutes the net [perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux).

The value of $D_\perp$ is inferred from runaway electron density evolution measurements or prescribed in disruption transport models based on the estimated level of magnetic field stochasticity. During disruptions with significant stochastic magnetic field perturbations, $D_\perp$ can reach $10^{-2}$–$1\;\text{m}^2\,\text{s}^{-1}$; under quiescent magnetohydrodynamic conditions cross-field stochasticity is substantially weaker. Larger values of $D_\perp$ enhance runaway electron losses to the first wall and suppress the growth of the post-disruption runaway current.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Scalar component of runaway-electron particle flux across magnetic flux surfaces, projected onto the outward flux-surface normal.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux is the scalar flux of runaway electrons crossing magnetic flux surfaces. It is the normal component of the runaway-electron particle-flux vector and describes cross-field transport, distinct from particle motion along the local magnetic-field direction as represented by parallel particle-flux components such as [parallel_electron_particle_flux](name:parallel_electron_particle_flux) and [parallel_ion_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_particle_flux).

The projection defining the scalar perpendicular flux is

$$
\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{out}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron particle-flux vector in m^-2.s^-1 and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the dimensionless unit normal to the magnetic flux surface, oriented from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary. The scalar $\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}}$ has units m^-2.s^-1.

In transport modeling this quantity may be computed from the continuity balance for [runaway_electron_density](name:runaway_electron_density) or represented with an effective convection-diffusion closure along a local flux-surface-normal coordinate $r_\perp$ in meters. A common form is $\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}} = -D_\perp\,\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}/\partial r_\perp + V_\perp n_{\mathrm{RE}}$, where $D_\perp$ is [perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity) in m^2.s^-1, $V_\perp$ is [perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity) in m.s^-1, $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is runaway-electron density in m^-3, and $\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}/\partial r_\perp$ has units m^-4. This closure is a modeling representation; the physical quantity itself is the normal projection of the particle flux.

The flux is generally inferred rather than measured directly, using reconstructed or modeled runaway-electron density evolution together with transport assumptions. No device-independent numerical range is implied by the standard name; representative magnitudes should be assessed from the scale $|\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}}| \sim D_\perp n_{\mathrm{RE}}/L_\perp + |V_\perp| n_{\mathrm{RE}}$, where $L_\perp$ is the characteristic density-gradient length in meters.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net flux is directed along the outward flux-surface normal from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: pfirsch_schlueter_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: pfirsch_schlueter
NAMES.short: Pfirsch-Schlueter return current density arising from diamagnetic drift, the neoclassical current that enforces divergence-free total current flow by compensating the poloidally varying perpendicular diamagnetic current on toroidal flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The Pfirsch-Schlueter current is the field-aligned neoclassical return current that arises because the perpendicular diamagnetic drift current varies along a flux surface in toroidal geometry, producing a non-zero poloidal divergence that must be canceled to satisfy $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} = 0$. It is a constituent of the broader [current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and is sustained entirely by the plasma pressure gradient without requiring a direct parallel electric field.

The defining condition is obtained by integrating the current-continuity equation along field lines:

$$
\nabla_{\parallel} J_\text{PS} = -\nabla \cdot \left(\frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{B^2}\right)
$$

where $p$ is the total isotropic plasma pressure in Pa and $B$ is the magnetic field magnitude in T. For a tokamak with safety factor $q$, the characteristic magnitude scales as $|J_\text{PS}| \sim 2q|\nabla p|/B$, growing with $q$ because higher safety factor means a longer field-line path over which the return current must be distributed.

The Pfirsch-Schlueter current is computed from equilibrium reconstructions or neoclassical transport models once the pressure profile and flux-surface geometry are known. Its parallel projection is available as [parallel_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:parallel_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), while the poloidal and radial projections of the parent diamagnetic current are described by [poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [radial_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the Pfirsch-Schlueter current flows in the direction of the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: pfirsch_schlueter
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the Pfirsch-Schlueter return current driven by diamagnetic drift. It is the signed field-aligned current density that closes the divergence of pressure-gradient-driven perpendicular diamagnetic current on a toroidal flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The parallel Pfirsch-Schlueter current density due to diamagnetic drift is the field-aligned part of the neoclassical return current associated with perpendicular diamagnetic current. It appears because pressure-gradient-driven perpendicular currents in a torus generally have nonzero divergence and must be balanced by a current flowing along magnetic field lines.

In magnetostatic current continuity, the diamagnetic Pfirsch-Schlueter contribution satisfies

$$
\nabla \cdot \left(j_{\parallel,\mathrm{PS}}^{\mathrm{dia}}\mathbf{b}\right) = -\nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}_{\perp,\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{PS}}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the signed parallel current density in A m^-2, $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{B}/B$ is the dimensionless magnetic-field unit vector, and $\mathbf{j}_{\perp,\mathrm{dia}}$ is the perpendicular diamagnetic current density in A m^-2, so both sides have units A m^-3. In single-fluid pressure balance, $\mathbf{j}_{\perp,\mathrm{dia}}$ is commonly evaluated as $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p/B^2$, where $p$ is pressure in Pa and $B$ is magnetic-field strength in T.

This quantity is usually computed from reconstructed magnetic geometry and measured kinetic pressure gradients rather than measured directly. A flux-surface solution of the field-line continuity equation gives the local variation of the return current; the Pfirsch-Schlueter part is separated from net parallel-current contributions such as inductive or bootstrap current.

Typical magnitudes are about 10^3-10^5 A m^-2 in weak-gradient core regions and can reach 10^5-10^6 A m^-2 where pressure gradients, magnetic-field inhomogeneity, or flux-surface shaping are large. The value can change sign around a flux surface because it is a return current that redistributes charge along magnetic field lines.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current density flows in the direction of the magnetic-field unit vector $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{B}/B$.

NAMES.name: plasma_current_due_to_ohmic_induction
NAMES.short: Total toroidal plasma current produced by inductive loop-voltage drive through the plasma's collisional ohmic response, excluding non-inductive current-drive contributions.
NAMES.long:
Plasma current due to ohmic induction is the toroidal part of the plasma current produced by an inductive electric field and the plasma's collisional resistive response. It is the inductively driven contribution to the net plasma current, distinct from bootstrap current and externally driven non-inductive contributions such as [current due to non-inductive current drive](name:current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive). Here toroidal refers to the $\phi$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The total ohmic contribution is obtained by projecting the parallel ohmic current density onto the toroidal direction and integrating it over a poloidal cross-section:

$$
I_\mathrm{Ohm} = \int_S j_{\phi,\mathrm{Ohm}}\, dA, \qquad j_{\phi,\mathrm{Ohm}} \simeq \frac{B_\phi}{B}\,\frac{E_\parallel}{\eta}
$$

where $S$ is a poloidal cross-section at fixed $\phi$, $j_{\phi,\mathrm{Ohm}}$ is the toroidal ohmic current density, $dA$ is the cross-section area element in m$^2$, $B_\phi/B$ is the projection from the magnetic-field-aligned direction to the toroidal direction, $E_\parallel$ is the parallel electric field in V m$^{-1}$, and $\eta$ is the plasma resistivity in ohm m. The local relation is the resistive parallel Ohm's-law limit; kinetic, neoclassical, and transient corrections can modify the detailed current distribution.

In practice this quantity is computed from the inductive loop voltage or the time derivative of poloidal magnetic flux together with an electrical conductivity or current-diffusion model. It may also be inferred as the portion of the measured total plasma current remaining after subtracting modeled non-inductive current sources, with magnetic diagnostics constraining the net current and equilibrium geometry.

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent: $10^4$-$10^5$ A in small tokamaks, $10^5$-$2 \times 10^6$ A in medium-sized tokamaks, and up to about $10^7$-$1.5 \times 10^7$ A in large inductive tokamak plasmas. In high-bootstrap or externally driven scenarios the ohmic contribution can be much smaller than the total plasma current and can approach zero.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal current crossing a poloidal cross-section flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: plasma_deposited_power
NAMES.short: Power delivered to the plasma particle distribution by heating and energy transfer mechanisms, representing the plasma-specific component of the total deposited power budget.
NAMES.long:
Plasma deposited power quantifies the net rate at which energy is transferred to the confined plasma particle distribution — electrons and ions collectively — from all active heating and generation mechanisms. Sources include ohmic dissipation, neutral beam injection, radio-frequency heating, and thermalization of energetic fusion products, partially offset by non-plasma sinks such as charge-exchange losses and ionization energy costs.

The volume-integrated form, [total_plasma_deposited_power](name:total_plasma_deposited_power), is obtained by integrating the local volumetric power density $p_\mathrm{dep}$ over the confined plasma volume $V$:

$$
P_\mathrm{dep} = \int_V p_\mathrm{dep}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $p_\mathrm{dep}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local deposited power density in W m$^{-3}$ at position $\mathbf{r}$ inside the plasma boundary.

In steady state, the plasma deposited power must balance the sum of thermal conduction, convection, and radiation losses; in transient phases it drives changes in stored energy. It is inferred from calorimetric measurements of individual heating systems corrected for transmission and shine-through losses, and cross-checked against bolometric radiated-power estimates to close the global energy budget. In current medium-scale tokamak experiments auxiliary deposited power typically ranges from 1-30 MW; in burning plasma scenarios fusion alpha-particle deposition alone would contribute a comparable or larger contribution to the total.

NAMES.name: plasma_energy
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated internal kinetic energy stored in the confined plasma, encompassing contributions from thermal and fast-particle populations and excluding electromagnetic-field and bulk plasma flow energies.
NAMES.long:
Plasma energy is the global stored internal kinetic energy of a magnetically confined plasma, obtained by integrating the total kinetic pressure over the plasma volume. It serves as the primary scalar confinement metric; children [thermal_plasma_energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy) and [total_plasma_energy](name:total_plasma_energy) resolve whether the integral is restricted to thermal populations or extended to include fast-particle contributions.

The defining relation is:

$$
W = \frac{3}{2} \int p \, dV
$$

where $p$ is the kinetic pressure (thermal only or summed over all electron and ion populations including fast particles) and the integral is taken over the confined plasma volume.

Experimentally, plasma energy is inferred from diamagnetic-loop measurements, which respond to the total perpendicular pressure integrated around the torus, or reconstructed by combining electron temperature and density profiles from Thomson scattering with ion temperature profiles from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. The related quantity stored_thermal_electron_energy isolates the electron thermal contribution, while total_plasma_stored_energy represents a closely analogous global integral.

Typical stored energies range from a few kilojoules in small tokamaks to 10–30 MJ in large devices at high performance. The ratio $\tau_E = W / P_{\rm heat}$, where $P_{\rm heat}$ is the net absorbed heating power, defines the global energy confinement time and is the central figure of merit for assessing transport losses.

NAMES.name: poloidal_center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the plasma center-of-mass velocity, computed as the mass-weighted mean of all contributing species fluid velocities projected onto the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long:
The center-of-mass velocity describes the bulk fluid motion of the plasma as a whole, accounting for all ionic, electronic, and neutral particle species weighted by their mass density. The poloidal component $v_{\theta,\mathrm{cm}}$ characterizes the net poloidal circulation of this composite fluid, which governs neoclassical poloidal rotation and enters the radial force balance that determines the radial electric field.

The defining relation is:

$$
v_{\theta,\mathrm{cm}} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s v_{\theta,s}}{\sum_s m_s n_s}
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$, $n_s$ its number density, and $v_{\theta,s}$ its individual poloidal fluid velocity, with the sum running over all plasma species.

The poloidal component complements [toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity) to describe the bulk plasma flow in the poloidal plane; poloidal_ion_velocity and [poloidal_neutral_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_velocity) give the individual species contributions. This quantity is inferred from multi-species charge exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with momentum-balance constraints in fluid transport modeling.

Poloidal rotation speeds in tokamak plasmas are typically small relative to toroidal rotation, with values in the range 0.1-5 km/s in the plasma core and potentially higher magnitudes near internal transport barriers and the separatrix.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the bulk plasma flow is directed in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_conductivity
NAMES.short: Poloidal projection of the electrical conductivity tensor in a flux coordinate system (rho, theta, phi). It is the local diagonal coefficient relating poloidal current density to poloidal electric field.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal conductivity is the poloidal projection of the electrical conductivity tensor in a flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels magnetic surfaces, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. It represents the local diagonal response of the poloidal current-density projection to the poloidal electric-field projection.

For the diagonal projection used by this quantity, the local Ohm-law relation is

$$
J_\theta = \sigma_\theta E_\theta
$$

where $J_\theta = \mathbf{J}\cdot\hat{e}_\theta$ is the current-density projection along the unit direction $\hat{e}_\theta$ tangent to increasing $\theta$, in A m$^{-2}$; $E_\theta = \mathbf{E}\cdot\hat{e}_\theta$ is the electric-field projection in V m$^{-1}$; and $\sigma_\theta$ is the poloidal conductivity in ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$. This scalar is the $\theta\theta$ diagonal/projection coefficient; off-diagonal tensor terms, Hall response, and couplings to radial or toroidal electric fields are not included in it.

In practice, poloidal conductivity is specified by a transport model, obtained by projecting a full conductivity tensor onto $\hat{e}_\theta$, or inferred from reconstructed current densities and electric fields when a local diagonal relation is adequate. It may represent classical collisional, neoclassical, or effective anomalous transport, so it depends on plasma temperature, density, collisionality, magnetic geometry, and turbulence assumptions.

Typical effective values are highly model-dependent and can span about $10^{-2}$-$10^{8}$ ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$. Hot, weakly collisional core plasmas usually have larger projected conductivities, while cold edge regions or cross-field-dominated effective models can be much smaller.

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.short: Poloidal component, along increasing poloidal angle theta in the flux coordinate system (psi, theta, phi), of the electric current density driven by collisional momentum exchange between plasma particle populations. In partially ionized edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas this contribution is commonly dominated by ion-neutral friction.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal current density due to collisions is the component of the collision-driven electric current density tangent to a magnetic flux surface in the poloidal direction, represented by the unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$. In an axisymmetric plasma this direction lies in the meridional plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The poloidal component is the projection of the collision-driven charged-particle current onto $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$:

$$
