j_{\mathrm{coll},\theta} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta \cdot \sum_s q_s n_s \mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{coll}}
$$

where $q_s$ is the charge of species $s$ in C, $n_s$ is its number density in m$^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{coll}}$ is the part of its mean velocity in m.s$^{-1}$ produced by collisional momentum balance. These velocities follow from collisional friction force densities entering the species momentum equations; in partially ionized edge plasmas the ion-neutral friction $\mathbf{R}_{in}=m_i n_i \nu_{in}(\mathbf{v}_n-\mathbf{v}_i)$ is commonly the dominant such term.

This quantity is inferred rather than measured directly. Transport and edge-plasma analyzes compute it from charged-particle densities and flows, neutral density and flow estimates, collision frequencies, electromagnetic fields, and momentum-balance closures, then project the resulting current onto $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$. Probes, spectroscopy, interferometry, and charge-exchange measurements constrain the inputs, especially in the edge, divertor, and scrape-off layer.

Magnitudes are negligible in hot, weakly neutral core plasma. In the edge and scrape-off layer modeled values commonly span roughly 1-10$^4$ A.m$^{-2}$, and localized divertor or detached-plasma regions can reach higher values where neutral density and relative ion-neutral velocity are large.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collision-driven current density points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\psi, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
NAMES.short: Poloidal current density produced by the divergence of the field-aligned viscous stress tensor.
NAMES.long:
Parallel-viscosity-driven poloidal current density is the component of electric current density along the poloidal direction generated by divergence of the field-aligned viscous stress tensor in a magnetized plasma. The poloidal direction is the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in a magnetic-flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It is the parallel-viscosity part of [poloidal current density due to viscosity](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity), distinct from [perpendicular-viscosity](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and [heat-viscosity](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) contributions.

The current-density contribution associated with parallel viscous stress is obtained from the magnetized-fluid momentum balance:

$$
\mathbf{j} = \frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}_\parallel)}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}$ denotes only the contribution from parallel viscosity, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $B$ is its magnitude, and $\boldsymbol{\pi}_\parallel$ is the field-aligned viscous stress tensor. This standard name denotes the projection of this contribution along the unit direction of increasing $\theta$ in the magnetic-flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

In practice this quantity is computed in transport or neoclassical modeling from the divergence of the parallel viscous stress, using plasma flow, collisionality, temperature, density, and magnetic-geometry information. It is usually inferred rather than measured directly, and is constrained through consistency with momentum balance and current transport.

Typical magnitudes are highly regime dependent, often 10^-1-10^4 A.m^-2 in confined-plasma transport calculations, with localized steep-gradient edge regions sometimes approaching 10^5 A.m^-2.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the magnetic-flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity
NAMES.short: Poloidal current-density contribution from viscosity, equal to the sum of the parallel-, perpendicular-, and heat-viscosity contributions resolved along increasing theta in the flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
Poloidal current density due to viscosity is the component, along the poloidal direction of the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, of the current generated by viscous forces in the plasma momentum balance. It is the additive viscous contribution obtained from the parallel-viscosity, perpendicular-viscosity, and heat-viscosity stress channels, with the poloidal direction defined by increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ on a magnetic flux surface.

When the viscous force density is written as the negative divergence of the viscous stress tensor, the associated magnetized-plasma drift current and its poloidal projection are

$$
j_{\theta}^{\mathrm{visc}} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}\cdot\left(\frac{\mathbf{F}_{\Pi}\times\mathbf{B}}{B^2}\right),\qquad \mathbf{F}_{\Pi}=-\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi},\qquad j_{\theta}^{\mathrm{visc}}=j_{\theta}^{\parallel\mathrm{visc}}+j_{\theta}^{\perp\mathrm{visc}}+j_{\theta}^{\mathrm{heat\,visc}}
$$

where $j_{\theta}^{\mathrm{visc}}$ is this quantity in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\theta$, $\mathbf{F}_{\Pi}$ is the viscous force density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in $\mathrm{T}$ with $B=|\mathbf{B}|$, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}$ is the total viscous stress tensor in $\mathrm{Pa}$. The three additive terms are the poloidal current-density contributions from the parallel-, perpendicular-, and heat-viscosity parts of the stress model; no particular closure is implied.

In practice this quantity is computed in transport modeling or interpretive analysis by evaluating the divergence of the selected viscous stress tensor, forming the corresponding current-density contribution, and projecting it onto the poloidal direction of $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It is usually inferred from a momentum-balance or neoclassical/transport calculation rather than measured directly.

Representative magnitudes are strongly regime and closure dependent. Core values are often about $10^{-2}$-$10^{3}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, while localized edge, pedestal, or strong-gradient regions can reach $10^{4}$-$10^{5}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the viscous current-density contribution points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the effective electron particle convection velocity, the advective coefficient multiplying electron density in a particle-transport flux law.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal electron convection velocity is the effective advective velocity component for electron particle transport in the poloidal direction of a flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. It is a transport coefficient rather than necessarily the microscopic electron fluid velocity, representing directed electron particle transport tangent to magnetic flux surfaces after diffusive density-gradient transport is separated.

The poloidal electron particle flux is commonly decomposed into diffusive and convective contributions:

$$
\Gamma_{e,\theta} = -D_{e,\theta}\frac{1}{h_\theta}\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial \theta} + n_e v_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\theta}$ is the [poloidal electron particle flux](name:poloidal_electron_particle_flux), $D_{e,\theta}$ is the poloidal electron particle diffusivity, $n_e$ is the electron number density, $v_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the poloidal electron convection velocity, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $h_\theta$ converts angular variation into distance along the poloidal coordinate line.

This quantity is usually inferred as an effective coefficient in transport analysis or computed in fluid, drift-fluid, gyrofluid, or reduced transport models. It can include the modeled effects of drifts, parallel flows projected onto poloidal transport, turbulent pinch terms, sources and sinks, and closure assumptions, so it should not be interpreted automatically as a directly measured electron flow speed.

Typical modeled values are approximately -1000 to 1000 m.s^-1 in edge and scrape-off-layer transport studies, while core effective poloidal convection coefficients are often closer to -100 to 100 m.s^-1 depending on magnetic geometry, collisionality, turbulence, and source localization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron particle convection is directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the electron particle diffusion coefficient. It is the poloidal-poloidal diagonal tensor component that relates the diffusive electron particle flux to the electron density gradient along the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal electron diffusion coefficient is the electron particle diffusivity acting along the poloidal direction, tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ on a magnetic flux surface in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. In an anisotropic transport tensor it is the poloidal-poloidal diagonal component, distinct from radial or toroidal diffusion and from off-diagonal cross-couplings.

For a Fickian closure of the diffusive part of the poloidal electron particle flux, it is defined by

$$
\Gamma^{e}_{\mathrm{pol,diff}} = -D^{e}_{\mathrm{pol}}\,\nabla_{\mathrm{pol}} n_e
$$

where $\Gamma^{e}_{\mathrm{pol,diff}}$ is the diffusive contribution to the [poloidal_electron_particle_flux](name:poloidal_electron_particle_flux) in m^-2 s^-1, $D^{e}_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal electron diffusion coefficient in m^2 s^-1, $n_e$ is the electron density in m^-3, and $\nabla_{\mathrm{pol}} n_e$ is the density gradient per unit poloidal length in m^-4. The minus sign states the down-gradient convention: positive $D^{e}_{\mathrm{pol}}$ drives diffusive electron particle flux from higher toward lower electron density.

In transport modeling this coefficient may represent neoclassical, turbulent, or empirical particle transport in the poloidal direction. It is usually prescribed, fitted from particle-balance constraints and density measurements, or obtained from reduced transport closures; the related [electron_diffusion_coefficient](name:electron_diffusion_coefficient) describes the corresponding radial or aggregate electron particle diffusivity used in many models.

Typical effective values are strongly model- and region-dependent. Edge and scrape-off-layer applications often use order-of-magnitude values around 0.01-10 m^2 s^-1, with larger localized values possible when the coefficient represents unresolved turbulent mixing rather than a microscopic collisional diffusivity.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Poloidal electron energy diffusion coefficient is the coefficient of the local electron-temperature gradient in the poloidal conductive heat-flux closure. It quantifies effective diffusive electron thermal-energy transport along the poloidal direction in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
The poloidal electron energy diffusion coefficient quantifies effective diffusive transport of electron thermal energy in the poloidal direction of flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It is the coefficient multiplying the local electron-temperature gradient in the conductive heat-flux closure; larger values imply faster poloidal smoothing of electron-temperature perturbations.

The local Fick-law form for the diffusive poloidal electron heat flux is:

$$
q_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{diff}} = - n_e D_{e,\theta}^{E} \nabla_\theta T_e
$$

where $q_{e,\theta}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the heat-flux component in the direction of increasing $\theta$ in W.m^-2, $n_e$ is electron number density in m^-3, $D_{e,\theta}^{E}$ is the poloidal electron energy diffusion coefficient in m^2.s^-1, and $\nabla_\theta T_e$ is the electron-temperature gradient per unit length along increasing $\theta$ in J.m^-1. The minus sign means that a positive coefficient produces down-gradient heat flow; if $T_e$ is expressed in eV, the temperature gradient must be multiplied by the elementary charge to obtain SI heat flux.

This coefficient is not measured directly. It is obtained or constrained through transport analysis by matching electron-temperature evolution, heat-flux balances, perturbative heat-pulse propagation, or comparisons with neoclassical and turbulence-based estimates. It is closely related to [poloidal_electron_energy_diffusivity](name:poloidal_electron_energy_diffusivity) and is the electron-energy counterpart of particle-transport quantities such as [poloidal_electron_diffusivity](name:poloidal_electron_diffusivity).

Representative effective values are highly model and region dependent. Values used in transport studies are commonly of order 0.01-10 m^2.s^-1, while localized fitted coefficients may be smaller or larger depending on plasma regime and the chosen transport closure.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Poloidal electron energy flux is the component of the electron thermal energy flux vector along increasing theta in flux coordinates (psi, theta, phi), where theta is the poloidal angle. It represents directed electron energy transport per unit area in the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal electron energy flux is the directed flux of electron thermal energy and enthalpy per unit area along the poloidal direction. In flux coordinates $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$, with $\psi$ labeling magnetic-flux surfaces, $\theta$ the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ the toroidal angle, it is the projection of [electron_energy_flux](name:electron_energy_flux) onto the local unit vector tangent to increasing $\theta$ at fixed $\psi$ and $\phi$.

The defining projection, shown with a common collisional-fluid decomposition of the total electron energy flux, is

$$
q_{e,\theta} = \mathbf{q}_e \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \left(\frac{5}{2} n_e T_e \mathbf{v}_e - \kappa_{e,\parallel}\hat{\mathbf{b}}\,\nabla_\parallel T_e - \kappa_{e,\perp}\nabla_\perp T_e\right)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
$$

where $q_{e,\theta}$ and $\mathbf{q}_e$ are in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $n_e$ is electron density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $T_e$ is electron temperature expressed as particle energy in joules, or as eV with the elementary-charge conversion applied in $n_eT_e$, $\mathbf{v}_e$ is electron fluid velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\kappa_{e,\parallel}$ and $\kappa_{e,\perp}$ are thermal conductivities with units such that each conductive term is in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ is the unit vector toward increasing $\theta$.

In practice, this quantity is computed from magnetic geometry, electron density and temperature, flow or particle-flux information, and a chosen electron heat-transport closure, or inferred by inverting the electron energy balance. Edge diagnostics such as temperature, density, spectroscopic, probe, and calorimetric measurements can constrain the terms, but the poloidal projection requires the local metric of the flux coordinates $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$. Together with [radial_electron_energy_flux](name:radial_electron_energy_flux) and [parallel_electron_energy_flux](name:parallel_electron_energy_flux), it describes the directional anisotropy of electron energy transport.

Typical absolute magnitudes in tokamak edge and scrape-off-layer transport are $10^4$-$10^7\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, with high-power divertor or near-separatrix conditions reaching about $10^8\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. Values can be much smaller near stagnation points or where opposing convective and conductive contributions nearly cancel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron energy flux vector has a component toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the electron particle flux vector in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi): the signed rate at which electrons cross a unit area whose normal is the local tangent to increasing theta. It is a particle flux, not an electric current.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal electron particle flux is the component of the electron particle flux vector along the local poloidal direction in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It represents the signed number of electrons crossing a unit area per unit time whose normal is the unit tangent to increasing $\theta$, at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$. It is a particle flux, so the electron charge sign is not included.

The component is defined by projecting the total electron particle flux vector onto the poloidal unit direction:

$$
\Gamma_{e,\theta} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{e}}_\theta
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\theta}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e$ have units of $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{e}}_\theta$ is the dimensionless unit vector tangent to increasing $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. Electron particle balance involves the divergence of the full flux vector through $\partial n_e/\partial t + \nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e = S_e$, where $n_e$ is electron density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ and $S_e$ is the net electron particle source in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

The quantity is usually inferred from density evolution, flow measurements, fluctuation measurements, and transport modeling rather than measured as an isolated component. In a fluid moment description an advective contribution may be written inline as $n_e V_{e,\theta}$, where $V_{e,\theta}$ is the electron flow component in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$; diffusive, collisional, and turbulent contributions are closure-dependent and are included in $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e$ before the projection is taken.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^{18}$-$10^{22}$ m^-2.s^-1 in confined-plasma transport analyzes. In edge, pedestal, and scrape-off-layer conditions, strong drifts, recycling, or turbulence can give local magnitudes of $10^{22}$-$10^{24}$ m^-2.s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron particle flux vector points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the electron bulk flow velocity.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal electron velocity $v_{\theta,e}$ is the component of the electron fluid bulk velocity tangent to magnetic flux surfaces in the poloidal direction. In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, it measures electron flow along increasing or decreasing poloidal angle $\theta$, distinct from the radial component across flux surfaces and the toroidal component around the symmetry axis. It is the electron analog of poloidal_ion_velocity and complements [radial_electron_velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity), [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity), and [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity).

The poloidal component is the projection of the electron fluid mean velocity onto the poloidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\theta,e} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta \cdot \mathbf{u}_e, \qquad \mathbf{u}_e = \frac{1}{n_e}\int \mathbf{v}\, f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\theta$, $\mathbf{u}_e$ and $v_{\theta,e}$ are in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m.s^-1, $f_e$ is the electron velocity-space distribution such that $\int f_e\,d^3v=n_e$, and $n_e$ is the electron density in m^-3.

In practice, $v_{\theta,e}$ is computed from kinetic or fluid models by projecting the electron mean flow onto the poloidal basis, or inferred from force-balance and transport constraints using measured density, temperature, electric-field, and current information. In the edge and scrape-off layer it may also be constrained by probe-based flow measurements and by decomposing parallel flow into poloidal and toroidal projections.

Typical magnitudes are commonly in the range 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1, depending on collisionality, pressure gradients, electric fields, magnetic geometry, and proximity to the separatrix.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron fluid poloidal flow is directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Diagonal coefficient that relates the diffusive flux of poloidal momentum for a specified ion ionization state to the local gradient of that state's poloidal flow velocity. It quantifies collisional and turbulent mixing of poloidal flow, not diffusion of the full momentum-density gradient.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion charge-state momentum diffusivity is the diagonal coefficient for diffusive transport of the poloidal momentum carried by one ion ionization state. It multiplies the local gradient of that charge state's poloidal flow velocity, not the gradient of the full momentum density. The poloidal component is tangent to a magnetic surface in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

Locally, the diffusive outward flux of poloidal momentum for ion charge state $z$ can be written as

$$
\Pi_{\rho\theta,z}^{\mathrm{diff}} = - m_i n_z D_{\theta,z}\,\frac{\partial u_{\theta,z}}{\partial r_\perp}
$$

where $\Pi_{\rho\theta,z}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the outward normal flux of poloidal momentum in Pa, $m_i$ is the ion mass in kg, $n_z$ is the density of charge state $z$ in m$^{-3}$, $D_{\theta,z}$ is this diffusivity in m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, $u_{\theta,z}$ is the poloidal flow velocity component in m s$^{-1}$, and $r_\perp$ is outward distance normal to the magnetic surface in m. The minus sign expresses relaxation of poloidal-flow shear: the diffusive contribution is directed down the local velocity gradient.

This coefficient is usually inferred rather than measured directly. It is estimated from momentum-balance analysis using measured ion flows, temperatures, densities, and sources, or from neoclassical and turbulence-based transport models; charge-state resolution additionally requires information on the population and flow of the selected ionization state.

Typical effective values are about 0.01-10 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ in the confined core of tokamak plasmas, with edge, pedestal, or transient conditions sometimes reaching 10-100 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$. Very small collisional estimates can be below 0.01 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, while strong turbulence can make the effective diffusivity comparable to other anomalous momentum diffusivities.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged radial flux of poloidal, theta-directed ion momentum for a single charge state in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi), with rho increasing outward from the magnetic axis. It is the net poloidal momentum transported across a flux surface per unit area.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion charge-state momentum flux is the flux-surface average of the radial transport of poloidal momentum for ions in a specified charge state. The transported momentum is along the poloidal direction in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, while the transport direction is normal to surfaces of constant $\rho$, with $\rho$ increasing from the magnetic axis toward the last closed flux surface. The toroidal angle $\phi$ is the angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, a general flux-surface-averaged definition is:

$$
\Gamma_{\theta,\zeta}(\rho) = \frac{1}{A(\rho)} \int_{0}^{2\pi}\!\int_{0}^{2\pi} J_S(\rho,\theta,\phi)\, \hat{\mathbf{n}}_\rho \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_{i\zeta} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta \, d\theta\, d\phi
$$

where $\Gamma_{\theta,\zeta}$ is the poloidal momentum flux for ion charge state $\zeta$ in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $A(\rho)$ is the flux-surface area in m$^2$, $J_S$ is the surface-area Jacobian with $dA=J_S d\theta d\phi$, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\rho$ is the outward unit normal, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing poloidal angle, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{i\zeta}$ is the total momentum-flux tensor in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$. Its convective part is $m_i n_{i\zeta}\mathbf{v}_{i\zeta}\mathbf{v}_{i\zeta}$, where $m_i$ is ion mass in kg, $n_{i\zeta}$ is charge-state density in m$^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{v}_{i\zeta}$ is velocity in m s$^{-1}$; turbulent Reynolds stress and collisional viscous stress may also contribute.

This quantity is usually inferred rather than measured directly. It is computed from charge-state-resolved momentum balance using measured or modeled density, temperature, rotation, electric-field, fluctuation, and collisionality information, and it is used as the flux-divergence term governing redistribution of poloidal flow for each ionization state.

Representative magnitudes vary widely with species abundance and confinement regime. Main-ion charge-state values in core transport analyzes are often $10^{-4}$-$1$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, trace impurity charge states may be $10^{-6}$-$10^{-3}$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, and steep edge gradients or strong momentum input can produce values of order $1$-$10$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when positive poloidal momentum, directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, is transported outward toward increasing $\rho$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_charge_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Signed particle flux of ions in ionization charge state z along the poloidal direction in a flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi), equal to the number crossing unit area perpendicular to that direction per unit time.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion charge-state particle flux is the component of the ion particle-flux vector for a specified ionization charge state along the poloidal direction in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. It gives the signed rate at which ions of that charge state cross a unit area whose normal is the local poloidal direction.

The local component is the projection of the charge-state particle-flux vector onto the poloidal unit direction:

$$
\Gamma_{\theta,z} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{e}}_\theta = n_z v_{\theta,z}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\theta,z}$ is the poloidal ion charge-state particle flux in $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z$ is the particle-flux vector for charge-state population $z$ in $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$, $n_z$ is the density of ions in ionization charge state $z$ in $m^{-3}$, $v_{\theta,z}$ is their mean poloidal velocity in $m\,s^{-1}$, and $z$ is the dimensionless charge-state label, with ion charge $+z e$.

In charge-state continuity balances, this flux contributes through the divergence of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_z$ together with ionization, recombination, charge-exchange, and particle-source terms. It may be computed from velocity moments of kinetic distribution functions, from fluid particle balances using measured or modeled densities and mean flows, or inferred indirectly from spectroscopy combined with charge-state population modeling.

Typical magnitudes are strongly species- and regime-dependent. Abundant ion charge states in edge plasmas commonly have magnitudes around $10^{20}$-$10^{24}\ m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$ for $n_z \sim 10^{18}$-$10^{20}\ m^{-3}$ and $v_{\theta,z} \sim 10^2$-$10^4\ m\,s^{-1}$, while trace impurity charge states may be much smaller, about $10^{14}$-$10^{21}\ m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions in charge state $z$ flow in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Poloidal ion diffusion coefficient is the aggregate coefficient relating diffusive ion particle flux in the poloidal direction to the gradient of total ion number density. It represents species- and charge-state-summed ion particle transport when resolved ion-state coefficients are not used.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion diffusion coefficient $D_{i,\mathrm{pol}}$ is the effective particle diffusivity for the aggregate ion population in the poloidal direction on a magnetic surface. It describes species- and charge-state-summed ion particle transport, distinct from resolved ion-state diffusion coefficients and from energy or momentum diffusion coefficients.

For a Fickian diffusive closure, it relates the diffusive part of the [poloidal_ion_particle_flux](name:poloidal_ion_particle_flux) to the poloidal gradient of total ion number density:

$$
\Gamma_{i,\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{i,\mathrm{pol}}\,\nabla_{\mathrm{pol}} n_i
$$

where $\Gamma_{i,\mathrm{pol}}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the poloidal diffusive ion particle flux, $D_{i,\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal ion diffusion coefficient, $\nabla_{\mathrm{pol}} n_i$ is the poloidal component of the gradient of total ion number density, and $n_i$ is the summed ion number density. The minus sign indicates that a positive diffusivity drives diffusive particle flux down the density gradient.

This coefficient is the poloidal directional component of the parent [ion_diffusion_coefficient](name:ion_diffusion_coefficient). When transport is resolved by charge state, the corresponding species-resolved quantity is [poloidal_ion_state_diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_state_diffusivity); when the transported quantity is ion momentum rather than particle number, the related coefficient is [poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient). The thermal-energy counterpart is [poloidal_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient), and the electron particle analog is [poloidal_electron_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_electron_diffusion_coefficient).

In practice, $D_{i,\mathrm{pol}}$ is usually an effective transport coefficient prescribed in edge or plasma transport models, inferred from particle-balance analysis, or adjusted to reproduce measured ion density evolution together with sources, sinks, convection, ionization, and recombination. For a physically diffusive closure it is non-negative; negative inferred values generally indicate that non-diffusive or up-gradient effects have been forced into a purely Fickian representation.

Typical effective values range from 0.01-10 m^2.s^-1 in edge and scrape-off-layer transport modeling, with smaller values possible for weak transport and larger values used to represent strong turbulence or enhanced cross-field mixing.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_momentum
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Poloidal component, along theta in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi), of the net area-normalized momentum source acting on ions and summed over all ion charge states. It is a force per unit area, not a volumetric force density.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion momentum is the poloidal component of the net area-normalized momentum source acting on the ion fluid, summed over all ion charge states. It represents transfer of momentum along $\theta$ in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ by external sources, atomic processes, and interspecies interactions. The quantity has the dimensions of force per unit area; it is not a local volumetric force density.

With a common area normalization for all charge states, the total ion source is the charge-state sum:

$$
M_{i,\theta} = \sum_z M_{i,z,\theta}
$$

where $M_{i,\theta}$ is the net poloidal ion momentum source in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $M_{i,z,\theta}$ is the corresponding area-normalized source for charge-state index $z$ in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, and the sum includes all ion charge states. A volumetric force density $f_{i,\theta}$ would instead have units kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-2}$; it must be volume-integrated and divided by the chosen normalization area before it represents $M_{i,\theta}$.

In practice, this quantity is computed by projecting momentum-transfer terms onto the poloidal direction in the same flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ and applying the area normalization used for the transport balance. Contributions may include neutral-particle interactions, wave momentum deposition, ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and collisional friction, and they can also be inferred from ion momentum balance using measured flows and pressure gradients.

Typical values are strongly dependent on plasma regime and normalization area. Core values are often near zero or in the range $10^{-4}$-$10$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, while localized edge, neutral-interaction, or wave-driven sources can reach $10$-$10^{3}$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the area-normalized force transfers poloidal momentum to ions in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Rate coefficient for relaxation of the bulk ion fluid momentum component along the poloidal-angle direction θ on magnetic flux surfaces in flux coordinates (ρ, θ, φ).
NAMES.long:
The poloidal ion momentum damping rate is the coefficient for collisional or neoclassical relaxation of the bulk ion fluid momentum component tangent to a magnetic surface in the poloidal-angle direction. The direction is the increasing $\theta$ direction in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. This bulk-ion quantity describes the ion population as a whole, rather than one charge state.

A linear damping contribution to the poloidal momentum density may be written as

$$
\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(n_i m_i u_{\theta,i}\right)\right|_{\mathrm{damp}} = -\nu_{\theta,i}\, n_i m_i u_{\theta,i}
$$

where $n_i$ is the ion number density, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $u_{\theta,i}$ is the bulk ion velocity component along increasing $\theta$, and $\nu_{\theta,i}$ is the poloidal ion momentum damping rate. The displayed term represents only the local linear relaxation part of a full momentum balance; sources, stresses, inertia, and radial transport can also contribute.

The rate is usually obtained from neoclassical transport theory, reduced momentum-balance modeling, or fits constrained by measured ion rotation and plasma profiles. It depends on collisionality, magnetic geometry, trapped-particle fraction, species composition, temperature, density, and the reference flow about which the momentum perturbation is damped. The charge-state-resolved counterpart is [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate); related component rates are [toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate) and [radial_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:radial_ion_momentum_damping_rate).

Representative values in core tokamak transport applications are about 10^2-10^6 s^-1, with lower values typical of hotter, weakly collisional regions and higher values possible in colder or more collisional regions. The range is order-of-magnitude only and should be interpreted relative to local collision, transit, and transport timescales.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the linear term acts to relax, rather than amplify, a perturbation of the poloidal bulk ion momentum.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective advective, or pinch, velocity for radial transport of the poloidal component of ion momentum across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the velocity-like convective coefficient multiplying flux-surface-averaged poloidal ion momentum density in an ion momentum balance.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion momentum effective convection velocity is the velocity-like coefficient that represents advective radial transport of the ion poloidal momentum density across magnetic flux surfaces. The poloidal component is tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho$ is an outward-increasing radial flux coordinate and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; in that frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The coefficient $V_{p_{\theta i}}$ is defined by the convective term in a local flux-gradient decomposition of the radial poloidal-ion-momentum flux:

$$
\Gamma_{p_{\theta i}} = -D_{p_{\theta i}} \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\left\langle m_i n_i u_{i,\theta} \right\rangle + V_{p_{\theta i}} \left\langle m_i n_i u_{i,\theta} \right\rangle
$$

where $\Gamma_{p_{\theta i}}$ is the flux of poloidal ion momentum across magnetic surfaces toward increasing $\rho$, $\rho$ is a length-like outward-increasing flux-surface label, $D_{p_{\theta i}}$ is the [poloidal ion momentum diffusivity](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusivity), $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes a flux-surface average, $m_i$ is ion mass, $n_i$ is ion density, and $u_{i,\theta}$ is the ion fluid velocity component along increasing $\theta$. Here $\theta$ is the poloidal coordinate label in $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, not a unit; if a dimensionless normalized flux label is used instead of a length-like $\rho$, the corresponding metric factors are included in the effective coefficients.

Effective values are obtained by separating radial ion momentum flux into diffusive and convective contributions after flux-surface averaging and after accounting for explicitly modeled sources, sinks, and residual stresses. In practice they may be inferred from the evolution of poloidal flows and ion density, from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or other ion-flow diagnostics coupled to transport analysis, or predicted by neoclassical, gyrokinetic, or reduced turbulent-transport models.

Typical core values in tokamak transport studies are of order -10 to 10 m.s^-1, with fitted values in strong-gradient or edge regions sometimes reaching -50 to 50 m.s^-1. The magnitude is often comparable to a momentum diffusivity divided by a radial scale length, so it depends sensitively on collisionality, turbulence drive, magnetic geometry, and momentum sources.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convective term carries positive flux-surface-averaged poloidal ion momentum density toward increasing $\rho$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged radial transport flux density of poloidal ion linear momentum across a magnetic flux surface, summed over all ion charge states. It is the total-ion counterpart of charge-state-resolved poloidal ion momentum flux and has the dimensions of stress.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion momentum flux is the flux-surface-averaged radial flux density of ion linear momentum in the poloidal direction, evaluated across magnetic flux surfaces labeled by an outward-increasing radial coordinate in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It is not a flux directed poloidally; the transported momentum component is poloidal, while the transport direction is normal to the flux surface. It is the charge-state sum of [poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux).

For a fluid representation, the flux-surface-averaged radial-poloidal stress component is

$$
\Pi_{i,\theta}^{\rho} = \left\langle \sum_s \left( m_s n_s v_{s,\rho} v_{s,\theta} + \pi_{s,\rho\theta} \right) \right\rangle_{\rho}
$$

where $\Pi_{i,\theta}^{\rho}$ is the poloidal ion momentum flux in kg.m^-1.s^-2, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rho}$ denotes an average over the magnetic flux surface $\rho=\mathrm{constant}$, and $s$ indexes ion charge states. Here $m_s$ is ion mass in kg, $n_s$ is ion number density in m^-3, $v_{s,\rho}$ is the physical velocity normal to the flux surface in m.s^-1, $v_{s,\theta}$ is the physical poloidal velocity in m.s^-1, and $\pi_{s,\rho\theta}$ is the non-convective radial-poloidal stress in kg.m^-1.s^-2, including viscous or turbulent contributions as appropriate.

In practice this flux is inferred from ion momentum balance or transport closure rather than measured directly. Local radial-poloidal stress densities may be evaluated from density, charge-state composition, radial particle transport, poloidal flow, and stress models, then averaged over a constant-$\rho$ surface in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ to obtain the flux-surface scalar; the analogous radial flux of toroidal ion momentum is [toroidal_ion_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_flux).

Representative magnitudes span broad ranges: about 10^-5-10^-1 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in the core and 10^-3-10 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in edge or scrape-off-layer conditions with strong flows and steep gradients. Values are typically much smaller than the thermal pressure because they measure correlations between radial transport and poloidal momentum or off-diagonal stress, not the scalar pressure itself.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net flux through a magnetic flux surface of constant $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ transports ion linear momentum in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ toward increasing $\rho$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the net ion particle-flux density, giving the number of ions crossing unit area per unit time in the poloidal direction. It is summed over all ion charge states for the ion population considered.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion particle flux is the signed component of the net ion particle-flux density along the unit vector tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It represents particle transport around a magnetic flux surface, through a surface whose normal is poloidal, after summing over all charge states of the ion population considered.

For charge-state-resolved ion fluxes, the poloidal component is the projection of the summed particle-flux density onto the poloidal direction:

$$
\Gamma_{i,\mathrm{pol}} = \sum_z \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,z}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta = \sum_z n_{i,z}\,\mathbf{v}_{i,z}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta = n_i\,\bar{\mathbf{v}}_i\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $z$ labels ion charge state, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector toward increasing $\theta$, $\Gamma_{i,\mathrm{pol}}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,z}$ are in m^-2 s^-1, $n_{i,z}$ and $n_i$ are in m^-3, $\mathbf{v}_{i,z}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{v}}_i$ are in m s^-1, $n_i=\sum_z n_{i,z}$, and $\bar{\mathbf{v}}_i$ is the density-weighted mean ion velocity over charge states.

In practice this quantity is inferred from ion density and flow measurements together with transport analysis, or computed in fluid, kinetic, or hybrid plasma models from the ion continuity and momentum balance. Charge-state-resolved contributions may be obtained from collisional-radiative or impurity-transport modeling and then summed to form the net ion particle flux.

Typical absolute magnitudes are about 10^19-10^21 m^-2 s^-1 in weakly flowing core regions, 10^21-10^23 m^-2 s^-1 near the pedestal or scrape-off layer, and can approach 10^24 m^-2 s^-1 in strong divertor or transient flows.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net charge-state-summed ion particle flux is directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the effective convection velocity for a specified ion charge state in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi). Multiplied by the charge-state density, it gives the advective contribution to that charge state's poloidal particle flux.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal ion state convection velocity is the component of an effective particle-convection velocity tangent to a magnetic surface in the direction of varying poloidal angle for a specified ion charge state. In a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ is a radial flux label, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, it characterizes advection of that charge state's density along the $\theta$ direction. It is an effective transport coefficient and may include drift, neoclassical, collisional, and turbulent contributions rather than only the mean fluid flow.

The advective contribution to the poloidal particle flux is defined by:

$$
\Gamma_{\theta,z}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_z V_{\theta,z}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\theta,z}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective poloidal particle flux of charge state $z$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $n_z$ is the charge-state density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $V_{\theta,z}$ is the poloidal ion state convection velocity in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Diffusive fluxes and ionization, recombination, or charge-exchange source terms enter separately in the charge-state continuity balance.

In practice this coefficient is obtained from charge-state-resolved transport modeling or inferred by matching measured density, spectroscopy, and particle-source evolution with continuity equations. It depends on local magnetic geometry, electric-field and pressure-gradient drifts, collisional friction with background species, ionization and recombination balance, and turbulent transport closures. The analogous coefficient for advecting thermal energy of the same charge state is [poloidal_ion_state_energy_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_energy_convection_velocity), and the charge-state-summed species coefficient is poloidal_ion_convection_velocity.

Typical effective poloidal convection speeds are 0.1-100 m.s^-1 in core transport analyzes and 10^2-10^4 m.s^-1 in edge, scrape-off-layer, or divertor conditions where drifts and projected parallel flow can produce strong poloidal asymmetries. Values near zero indicate negligible net poloidal advection of the charge state.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convection velocity is directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal particle diffusivity, also called a diffusion coefficient, for a specified ion charge state in edge plasma. It relates the diffusive particle flux along poloidal arclength to the charge-state density gradient.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion-state diffusion coefficient is the scalar transport coefficient for density-gradient-driven particle diffusion of a specified ion species in a specified charge state along the poloidal direction. It represents the diffusive part of particle mixing around magnetic flux surfaces and is distinct from convective, source, sink, or radial transport terms.

The Fickian contribution to the poloidal particle flux is commonly written:

$$
\Gamma_{\theta,i,q}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\theta,i,q}\,\frac{\partial n_{i,q}}{\partial l_\theta}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\theta,i,q}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the poloidal diffusive particle flux of ion species $i$ in charge state $q$ in $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, $D_{\theta,i,q}$ is the poloidal diffusion coefficient in $m^2\,s^{-1}$, $n_{i,q}$ is the charge-state density in $m^{-3}$, and $l_\theta$ is poloidal arclength in meters. The leading minus sign means that a positive diffusivity drives particles from higher density toward lower density along the poloidal path.

In practice this coefficient is inferred or prescribed in edge transport modeling from particle balance, impurity or main-ion density evolution, comparison with spectroscopic and probe measurements, or reduced descriptions of turbulent and collisional cross-field mixing. It is often an effective coefficient that may combine unresolved turbulent transport with collisional contributions for the selected charge state.

Typical effective edge and scrape-off-layer values are about 0.1-10 m^2.s^-1, with smaller values possible for nearly neoclassical transport and larger values in strongly turbulent or transient boundary-plasma conditions. As a scalar diffusivity it is normally non-negative; fitted negative values usually indicate limitations of a reduced transport model or missing off-diagonal transport terms rather than physical diffusion.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component, in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi), of the effective convection velocity used in energy transport for a specified ion charge state. It represents advective heat transport associated with that state, separate from conductive or diffusive energy fluxes.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion state energy convection velocity is the poloidal component of an effective velocity coefficient for thermal-energy transport of one ion charge state. It is defined in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. Unlike the particle [poloidal_ion_state_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_convection_velocity), this quantity multiplies the thermal or enthalpy content assigned to the ion state in the energy balance.

When the poloidal energy flux is separated into conductive and convective parts, the coefficient may be defined by the ratio of convective energy flux density to the chosen thermodynamic energy density:

$$
v_{\varepsilon,\theta,z} = \frac{q^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\theta,z}}{H_z}
$$

where $v_{\varepsilon,\theta,z}$ is this velocity, $q^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\theta,z}$ is the poloidal convective energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$ for charge state $z$, and $H_z$ is the corresponding energy or enthalpy density in J m$^{-3}$. For an ideal-ion closure, $H_z$ is often proportional to $n_z T_z$; if $T_z$ is specified in eV, it must be converted to joules when forming an SI-consistent density.

The value is usually obtained from transport analysis, fluid or kinetic modeling, or heat-flux inference after conductive and source terms have been separated. It can represent effects of drifts, collisional coupling, turbulence, parallel dynamics projected onto the poloidal direction, and charge-state-resolved sources or sinks.

Typical effective magnitudes are about 1-1000 m.s^-1 in core and edge transport modeling. In steep-gradient edge regions or strongly drift-dominated conditions, values of 1000-10000 m.s^-1 can occur, while near stagnation points the coefficient may pass through zero and change sign.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convective energy transport is directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the energy-flux density vector for ions of a specified species and ionization charge state, defined along increasing poloidal angle in a flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion state energy flux is the component of the ion energy-flux density vector tangent to the poloidal direction for a specified ion species and ionization charge state. The poloidal direction lies in the $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and follows increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in a chosen flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. This signed scalar represents the net power carried by that charge-state population across unit area normal to the local poloidal direction.

The component is defined by projecting the ion-state energy-flux density vector onto the local poloidal unit vector:

$$
q_{\theta,i,z} = \mathbf{q}_{i,z} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $q_{\theta,i,z}$ is the poloidal ion-state energy flux in W m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{q}_{i,z}$ is the total energy-flux density vector for ion species $i$ and ionization charge state $z$ in W m$^{-2}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\theta$.

It is computed from kinetic moments or fluid energy-balance models for the selected ion state, including the modeled transport of thermal and flow energy. It is closely related to the corresponding [poloidal ion state velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity), [poloidal ion state particle flux](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_particle_flux), [poloidal ion state momentum flux](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_flux), and transport-coefficient quantities such as the [poloidal ion state momentum diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient). Radial, toroidal, and field-aligned projections are represented by [radial ion state energy flux](name:radial_ion_state_energy_flux), [toroidal ion state energy flux], and [parallel ion state energy flux](name:parallel_ion_state_energy_flux).

Typical absolute magnitudes are highly device-, region-, and model-dependent. Local transport calculations often span about $10^2$-$10^7$ W m$^{-2}$, with values near zero where poloidal transport is weak and larger values in steep-gradient edge, scrape-off-layer, or divertor regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy flows in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_momentum
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Area-normalized poloidal momentum source term for a single ion charge state, equal to force per unit area projected onto the local poloidal tangent. It is the charge-state-resolved contribution that sums to the total poloidal ion momentum source.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion state momentum is the area-normalized source term for the poloidal component of momentum of one ion species in one charge state. It represents a force per unit area acting on that charge-state population and is the charge-state-resolved specialization of the summed ion quantity [poloidal_ion_momentum](name:poloidal_ion_momentum) in a flux-surface transport framework.

The source contribution to the charge-state-resolved poloidal momentum balance can be written as

$$
S_{\theta,a,z} = \left(\frac{\partial P_{\theta,a,z}}{\partial t}\right)_\mathrm{sources} = \mathbf{S}_{a,z}\cdot\hat{\theta}
$$

where $S_{\theta,a,z}$ is this quantity in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $P_{\theta,a,z}$ is area-normalized poloidal momentum in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$, $t$ is time in $\mathrm{s}$, $\mathbf{S}_{a,z}$ is the area-normalized momentum-source vector for ion species $a$ and charge state $z$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, and $\hat{\theta}$ is the dimensionless unit tangent toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. The unit therefore denotes force per unit area; a volume force density would have different dimensions.

In practice this quantity is computed by projecting process-specific momentum inputs onto the local poloidal tangent and retaining the contribution for a single charge state. Relevant processes can include atomic ionization and recombination recoil, charge-exchange and elastic collisions, wave-particle momentum deposition, particle fueling, and collisional momentum exchange with other species or charge states. Summing over charge states gives the corresponding total ion poloidal momentum source.

Typical magnitudes are often small or sign-changing compared with toroidal momentum sources, with core values commonly around $10^{-4}-10^{1}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$. Strongly localized edge, charge-exchange, ionization, or externally driven regions can reach about $10^{2}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, depending on density, flow speed, reaction rate, and source geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the source adds momentum in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Effective poloidal convection velocity for ion charge-state momentum transport in a flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
The poloidal ion-state momentum convection velocity is the component along the poloidal coordinate $\theta$ of an effective advective velocity for momentum transport of ion species $s$ in charge state $z$. It is defined in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. It transports the poloidal momentum density associated with that charge state and may differ from the particle or energy convection velocity.

In a convective-diffusive momentum balance, the poloidal convective flux of poloidal momentum for ion state $(s,z)$ can be written as:

$$
\Pi_{\theta\theta,s,z}^{\mathrm{conv}} = v_{\theta,s,z}^{\mathrm{mom,conv}}\, m_s n_{s,z} u_{\theta,s,z}
$$

where $\Pi_{\theta\theta,s,z}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the flux of poloidal momentum in the poloidal direction with units kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $v_{\theta,s,z}^{\mathrm{mom,conv}}$ is this convection velocity, $m_s$ is the ion mass, $n_{s,z}$ is the charge-state number density, and $u_{\theta,s,z}$ is the mean poloidal fluid velocity. The product $m_s n_{s,z} u_{\theta,s,z}$ is the poloidal momentum density, with units kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$.

This quantity is normally an effective transport coefficient rather than a directly measured flow. It is inferred or prescribed within a chosen momentum-transport decomposition using constraints from ion flow measurements, charge-state densities, momentum sources and sinks, viscosity, orbit effects, and turbulence closures. Related quantities include [poloidal_ion_momentum_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_effective_convection_velocity) for the charge-state-summed ion analog, [toroidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity) for the toroidal component, and [radial_ion_state_effective_momentum_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity) for radial effective momentum convection.

Representative magnitudes are 0.1-100 m.s^-1 for many core and pedestal momentum-transport applications. Larger or smaller fitted values can occur when the effective coefficient absorbs localized sources, sinks, or viscous terms, so comparisons are most meaningful within the same transport decomposition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convection velocity points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Reciprocal of the relaxation time for collisional or neoclassical damping of the poloidal momentum of a specified ion species and charge state. The poloidal component is tangent to a magnetic flux surface in the meridional plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system and points along increasing theta in explicit flux coordinates such as (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion-state momentum damping rate is the reciprocal of the relaxation time over which the poloidal momentum of a specified ion species and charge state is dissipated. The poloidal component is tangent to a magnetic flux surface in the meridional $(R, Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; equivalently it is the component along increasing $\theta$ in an explicitly specified flux coordinate system such as $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$.

In a local momentum-density balance, the damping contribution is represented as a linear relaxation term:

$$
\left(\frac{\partial p_{\theta,a}}{\partial t}\right)_\mathrm{damp} = -\nu_{\theta,a}\, p_{\theta,a}
$$

where $a$ labels the ion charge state, $\nu_{\theta,a}$ is the damping rate, and $p_{\theta,a} = m_a n_a V_{\theta,a}$ is the poloidal momentum density with $m_a$ in kg, $n_a$ in m$^{-3}$, and $V_{\theta,a}$ in m s$^{-1}$. The minus sign makes the term dissipative: a non-negative $\nu_{\theta,a}$ relaxes the existing poloidal momentum toward zero regardless of its sign.

This rate is typically obtained from collisional and neoclassical momentum-balance models, or inferred by fitting observed poloidal-flow relaxation to such a balance. It depends on charge state, ion mass and charge, density, temperature, magnetic geometry, collisionality, and coupling to other species through Coulomb friction and poloidal viscous stresses. Charge-state resolution matters for impurity species occupying several ionization stages simultaneously, each carrying a distinct damping coefficient; the species-summed counterpart is the poloidal ion momentum damping rate.

As an order-of-magnitude guide, hot, weakly collisional core conditions tend to give values near $10^2$-$10^5$ s$^{-1}$, while cooler, denser, more collisional edge conditions and high-charge states can reach $10^5$-$10^7$ s$^{-1}$; these ranges are contextual rather than canonical.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Radial flux density of poloidal linear momentum carried by ions in a specified ionization state through a magnetic flux surface. It is the charge-state-resolved stress component for outward transport of poloidal momentum.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion state momentum flux is the radial transport flux of poloidal linear momentum for ions in a specified ionization state. It is the radial-poloidal component of the momentum-flux tensor in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ increases outward across nested magnetic flux surfaces and $\theta$ labels the poloidal direction. It is not the flux moving in the poloidal direction; it is the amount of poloidal momentum crossing a flux surface per unit area and per unit time.

For ion species $i$ and ionization state $s$, a common decomposition is

$$
\Pi_{\theta\rho}^{(i,s)} = m_i n_{i,s} v_{\theta,i,s} v_{\rho,i,s} + \pi_{\theta\rho}^{(i,s)}
$$

where $\Pi_{\theta\rho}^{(i,s)}$ is the flux of poloidal momentum across the outward radial direction, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_{i,s}$ is the number density of that ionization state, $v_{\theta,i,s}$ is its poloidal velocity component, $v_{\rho,i,s}$ is its outward radial velocity component, and $\pi_{\theta\rho}^{(i,s)}$ is the nonconvective stress contribution, including viscous, collisional, turbulent, or fluctuation-correlated terms as appropriate.

In practice this quantity is obtained from transport analysis or kinetic/fluid modeling by projecting the charge-state-resolved momentum-flux tensor onto the poloidal momentum direction and the outward radial surface normal. Experimental estimates combine ionization-state densities, flow velocities inferred from spectroscopic or probe-based diagnostics when available, and modeled nonconvective stress terms; direct measurement of the full tensor component is uncommon.

Typical magnitudes are often 10^-4-1 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in core transport analyzes and 0.01-100 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in edge or scrape-off-layer conditions, depending strongly on ion mass, charge-state density, radial particle transport, poloidal flow shear, and turbulent stress. The value may be positive or negative because it is a signed tensor component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion momentum in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ is transported outward, toward increasing $\rho$, across a magnetic flux surface.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the bulk fluid velocity for ions in a specified ionization charge state, projecting the charge-state-resolved mean flow onto the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal component $v_{\theta,z}$ of the mean fluid velocity for ions in a resolved ionization charge state $z$, obtained by projecting the full [ion_state_velocity](name:ion_state_velocity) vector onto the poloidal direction. In a multi-fluid plasma model, each charge state of an ion species carries its own independent velocity field; the poloidal component can differ substantially between charge states owing to neoclassical friction, charge-dependent transport forces, and orbit effects at the plasma edge.

The poloidal velocity of charge state $z$ enters the radial force balance:

$$
E_r = \frac{1}{Z_z e n_z} \frac{\partial p_z}{\partial r} - v_{\theta,z} B_\phi + v_{\phi,z} B_\theta
$$

where $E_r$ is the radial electric field, $Z_z$ is the ion charge number, $e$ is the elementary charge, $n_z$ is the number density of charge state $z$, $p_z$ is its pressure, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic field, $B_\theta$ is the poloidal magnetic field, and $v_{\phi,z}$ is the [toroidal_ion_state_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity). This coupling links poloidal rotation to measurable pressure gradients and toroidal flow for each charge state.

Poloidal ion velocities are measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), resolving Doppler shifts of charge-exchange emission lines in the poloidal viewing direction. The charge-state-averaged counterpart is poloidal_ion_velocity. Typical magnitudes range from tens of meters per second to tens of kilometers per second, depending on ion species, charge state, and radial location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux at the internal transport barrier is the value of the equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux function on the flux surface identified with the barrier. It locates the barrier relative to the magnetic-axis and plasma-boundary flux references.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the internal transport barrier is the equilibrium flux-function value $\psi_\mathrm{ITB}$ on the flux surface associated with an internal transport barrier. An internal transport barrier is a core or mid-radius region of reduced turbulent transport, commonly identified by locally steep gradients in temperature, density, rotation, or related transport indicators.

A common normalized location for the same barrier is obtained from the magnetic-axis and plasma-boundary flux references:

$$
\psi_{N,\mathrm{ITB}} = \frac{\psi_\mathrm{ITB} - \psi_\mathrm{axis}}{\psi_\mathrm{boundary} - \psi_\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $\psi_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the internal transport barrier, $\psi_\mathrm{axis}$ is the [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and $\psi_\mathrm{boundary}$ is the [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary). All three flux values are expressed in Wb and must be taken from the same equilibrium flux convention.

In practice, the barrier position is inferred from measured or reconstructed kinetic and rotation profiles, for example from changes in local gradients or inferred effective diffusivities. The corresponding value of $\psi_\mathrm{ITB}$ is then read from the magnetic-equilibrium flux function on the flux surface passing through that radial location.

The absolute value in Wb is device- and equilibrium-dependent; the physically relevant placement is usually its position within the interval spanned by the magnetic-axis and plasma-boundary flux values. Internal transport barriers are generally core or intermediate-radius features, distinct from edge pedestal locations such as [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_pedestal](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux function is positive on the internal-transport-barrier flux surface.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short: Physical poloidal projection of the magnetic vector potential in the flux-coordinate system (psi, theta, phi), along the unit tangent in the direction of increasing poloidal angle theta. It is gage dependent; only the magnetic induction obtained from its curl is directly physical.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic vector potential is the physical component of the magnetic vector potential along the poloidal coordinate-line tangent in the flux-coordinate system $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$, where $\psi$ is a flux label, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. It is a gage-dependent potential component, not a direct observable, and it is distinct from the covariant coefficient multiplying $\nabla\theta$ in a coordinate-basis expansion.

The component is defined by projection onto the poloidal unit tangent:

$$
A_{\hat{\theta}} = \mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}, \qquad
\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta} =
\frac{\left.\partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\theta\right|_{\psi,\phi}}
{\left|\left.\partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\theta\right|_{\psi,\phi}\right|}
$$

where $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic vector potential, $\mathbf{x}(\psi,\theta,\phi)$ is the position vector in meters, and $A_{\hat{\theta}}$ has unit $T\,m$. The covariant tangent component $\mathbf{A}\cdot(\partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\theta)_{\psi,\phi}$ instead has an additional metric factor, $h_\theta = |(\partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\theta)_{\psi,\phi}|$, and is not the quantity defined here.

The magnetic induction is recovered from $\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}$. In the flux-coordinate system $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$, this curl is evaluated with the coordinate Jacobian and metric; derivatives of the metric-weighted poloidal projection with respect to $\psi$ and $\phi$ contribute to toroidal and flux-radial components of $\mathbf{B}$ together with derivatives of the other vector-potential components. A gage transformation $\mathbf{A}\rightarrow\mathbf{A}+\nabla\chi$ can change $A_{\hat{\theta}}$ while leaving $\mathbf{B}$ unchanged, so this component cannot by itself specify the magnetic field.

This quantity is not measured directly. It is computed after choosing a gage and coordinate mapping, usually from an equilibrium or electromagnetic-field model constrained by magnetic measurements, plasma current, boundary conditions, and, for time-dependent studies, inductive electric-field information. Comparisons of $A_{\hat{\theta}}$ are meaningful only when the same gage convention and the same definition of $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$ are used.

Because the quantity is gage dependent, there is no device-independent typical range. In a fixed gage, equilibrium-scale magnitudes often scale as $|A_{\hat{\theta}}|\sim B L$; for magnetic fields of 1-10 T and length scales of 0.1-5 m this corresponds roughly to 0.1-50 T m, while perturbative components can be much smaller.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathbf{A}$ projects along the unit tangent in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\psi$ and $\phi$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_momentum_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Effective radial convection velocity for transport of aggregate ion poloidal momentum across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the velocity-like coefficient of the convective, or pinch, term rather than the poloidal flow speed itself.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal momentum effective convection velocity is the velocity-like coefficient that represents radial advection of aggregate ion poloidal momentum across magnetic flux surfaces. It is a transport coefficient in the momentum balance, not the poloidal flow speed itself, and no additional moment-arm or angular-momentum normalization is implied.

The coefficient is defined by the convective term in a diffusion-convection decomposition of the radial flux of poloidal ion momentum:

$$
\Pi_{\theta,r} = -D_\theta \frac{\partial (m_i n_i v_\theta)}{\partial r} + V_\theta^{\mathrm{eff}} m_i n_i v_\theta
$$

where $V_\theta^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is this quantity in $m.s^{-1}$, $\Pi_{\theta,r}$ is the radial flux of poloidal momentum in $kg.m^{-1}.s^{-2}$, $D_\theta$ is the poloidal momentum diffusivity in $m^2.s^{-1}$, $m_i$ is ion mass in $kg$, $n_i$ is ion number density in $m^{-3}$, $v_\theta$ is poloidal flow speed in $m.s^{-1}$, and $r$ is a minor-radius-like radial label in meters increasing outward across the flux surfaces. The component $\theta$ is the poloidal direction in flux coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$, where $\theta$ is poloidal angle and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. For multiple ion species or charge states, $m_i n_i v_\theta$ denotes the aggregate ion poloidal momentum density used in the balance.

In practice, this coefficient is specified by a transport closure or inferred by fitting an evaluated radial poloidal-momentum flux to a chosen diffusive-convective form. The split between diffusion and convection is meaningful only after the transported momentum density, radial label, and diffusivity convention have been fixed. This aggregate-ion quantity has the same physical role as poloidal_ion_momentum_convection_velocity, while [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity) denotes the corresponding charge-state-resolved coefficient; related component analogs include toroidal_ion_momentum_convection_velocity and [parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity](name:parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity).

Representative magnitudes are strongly model- and regime-dependent. In core momentum-transport studies the magnitude is often of order 0-10 m.s^-1, while fitted edge, pedestal, or transient coefficients can reach several tens of m.s^-1; either sign is possible depending on whether the effective convective transport is outward or inward.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convective transport of poloidal momentum is radially outward, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: poloidal_momentum_flux
NAMES.short: Poloidal momentum flux is the flux density of the poloidal linear-momentum component through a transport surface in the surface's positive-normal direction. In flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi), "poloidal" denotes the theta-directed momentum being transported, not a poloidal surface normal.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal momentum flux is the component of the momentum-flux density that transports poloidal linear momentum through a transport surface. In flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, the adjective poloidal refers to the $\theta$-directed momentum component; the flux direction is the positive normal of the transport surface, commonly toward increasing radial flux coordinate $\rho$ for magnetic-flux-surface transport.

The scalar flux of poloidal momentum through a transport surface is obtained by projecting the momentum-flux density tensor onto the transported component and the surface normal:

$$
\Gamma_{p_\theta} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_\rho
$$

where $\Gamma_{p_\theta}$ is the poloidal momentum flux, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector tangent to increasing $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\rho$ is the unit normal of the transport surface toward increasing $\rho$, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}$ is the momentum-flux density tensor. $\Gamma_{p_\theta}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}$ have unit kg m^-1 s^-2; both unit vectors are dimensionless. In a common single-fluid decomposition, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}=\varrho\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}+p\mathbf{I}+\boldsymbol{\pi}$, with $\varrho$ mass density in kg m^-3, $\mathbf{v}$ velocity in m s^-1, $p$ isotropic pressure in kg m^-1 s^-2, $\mathbf{I}$ the dimensionless identity tensor, and $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ the viscous stress tensor in kg m^-1 s^-2.

This quantity is generally computed rather than measured directly, using reconstructed density, temperature, flow, and fluctuation information together with a fluid, neoclassical, kinetic, or turbulence-transport closure. Species- and state-resolved quantities such as [poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:poloidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux) use the same transport-surface-normal projection for a selected population. Quantities such as [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux) change the transported momentum component while retaining the same distinction between transported component and flux direction.

Typical signed magnitudes in transport calculations are often 10^-4-10^2 kg m^-1 s^-2, with values near zero where poloidal flow shear or turbulent stress changes sign. Strongly driven edge or scrape-off-layer flows can produce larger local magnitudes, approaching 10^3 kg m^-1 s^-2 in high-density, high-flow conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when poloidal linear momentum in the increasing-$\theta$ direction is transported through the transport surface along its positive normal, toward increasing $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the energy flux density carried by neutral particles, resolved along poloidal angle theta in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi). It quantifies net neutral energy transport per unit area per unit time.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral energy flux is the scalar physical component of the neutral-particle energy flux density in the poloidal direction of flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It describes energy carried by neutral atoms or molecules across a unit area per unit time, including whatever neutral kinetic, internal, or thermal energy content is represented by the neutral model.

The component is defined by projecting the neutral energy-flux-density vector onto the local poloidal unit direction:

$$
q_{\mathrm{pol},n} = \mathbf{q}_n \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_n$ is the neutral energy-flux-density vector and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

In practice, $\mathbf{q}_n$ is obtained from neutral kinetic calculations, fluid neutral closures, or moment calculations over neutral states; experimental constraints are usually indirect, from spectroscopy, pressure measurements, bolometry, calorimetry, and particle balance. Depending on the closure, the same vector may be represented as bulk convective transport plus thermal or conductive transport, or as a direct moment of the neutral distribution. Recycling at material surfaces, followed by ionization, charge exchange, dissociation, or recombination, creates particle and heat or energy source terms that can drive or relax the gradients associated with this flux.

Typical magnitudes in edge and scrape-off-layer neutral transport are about $10^1$-$10^6$ W m^-2, with localized divertor recycling regions occasionally reaching $10^7$ W m^-2. Values depend strongly on neutral density, wall recycling, plasma temperature, collisionality, and divertor detachment state.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral energy is transported in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_momentum
NAMES.subject: neutral
