NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the area-normalized neutral momentum source density, summed over neutral states.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral momentum is the poloidal component of the net area-normalized momentum source density acting on electrically neutral atomic and molecular populations. The poloidal direction lies in the meridional $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, tangent to the local flux surface direction associated with the poloidal angle in a flux coordinate system such as $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. Charged ion populations are not included.

The state-summed quantity is obtained by adding the corresponding contribution from each neutral state:

$$
M_{n,\theta} = \sum_s M_{n,s,\theta}
$$

where $M_{n,\theta}$ is the summed poloidal neutral momentum source density and $M_{n,s,\theta}$ is the contribution from neutral state $s$; both are expressed in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$. The per-state terms correspond to quantities such as [poloidal_neutral_state_momentum](name:poloidal_neutral_state_momentum), while the summed component contributes to the total [poloidal_momentum](name:poloidal_momentum) balance.

In practice this quantity is evaluated from neutral kinetic or fluid transport calculations, or inferred as part of a momentum balance using neutral densities, velocities, and interaction rates. It represents the local poloidal force per unit area transferred to the neutral population after all neutral states have been combined.

Typical magnitudes are strongly regime dependent: values may be near zero in regions with very low neutral density, while edge and divertor source regions commonly span about $10^{-5}-10^{1}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ depending on neutral pressure, flow speed, and coupling to the plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral momentum source projects in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Diagonal poloidal component of the neutral momentum-flux tensor, formed from the poloidal projection on a magnetic surface in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi). For an ideal neutral fluid it combines advective transport of poloidal momentum with isotropic neutral pressure.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral momentum flux is the poloidal-poloidal component of the neutral momentum-flux tensor for a neutral particle population. The poloidal projection is taken along the tangent to a magnetic flux surface in the increasing $\theta$ direction of flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, and $Z$ is vertical height. This is a diagonal stress-like quantity, not the signed particle flux associated with [poloidal neutral velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_velocity).

For a kinetic neutral distribution, the ideal-fluid contribution is the second moment of the poloidal particle velocity:

$$
\Pi_{n,\mathrm{pol}} = m_n \int v_{\mathrm{pol}}^2 f_n(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \simeq m_n n_n u_{n,\mathrm{pol}}^2 + p_n
$$

where $\Pi_{n,\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal neutral momentum flux, $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass in kg, $f_n$ is the velocity distribution with integral $n_n$ in m^-3, $v_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the particle velocity projection in m s^-1, $u_{n,\mathrm{pol}}$ is the mean poloidal neutral velocity in m s^-1, and $p_n$ is the isotropic neutral pressure in kg m^-1 s^-2. For an isotropic neutral fluid the displayed closure is exact; the squared velocity term and pressure term are unchanged by reversing the orientation chosen for $\theta$.

In practice this quantity is usually computed from neutral fluid variables or as a velocity-space moment of a kinetic neutral distribution. It may be constrained indirectly using neutral density, temperature, and flow estimates from spectroscopy, pressure measurements, and transport modeling, but it is not usually measured as a standalone observable.

Typical magnitudes in edge and scrape-off-layer neutral transport are about 10^-5-10 kg m^-1 s^-2. Dense divertor or gas-injection regions can reach 10^2 kg m^-1 s^-2, while very rarefied neutral populations may be below 10^-6 kg m^-1 s^-2.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the total neutral particle flux density, summed over all neutral species and internal states, giving the net number of neutrals crossing a unit surface area per unit time in the poloidal direction in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral particle flux density is the poloidal projection of the total [neutral_particle_flux](name:neutral_particle_flux) vector, integrated over all neutral species and internal atomic or molecular states. It quantifies the net flow of neutral atoms and molecules per unit area per unit time along the poloidal direction, and is the species-integrated counterpart to [poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux), which resolves the same quantity for a single specified neutral internal state.

The quantity appears in the neutral particle continuity equation:

$$
\frac{\partial n_n}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_n = S_n
$$

where $n_n$ is the neutral number density, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_n$ is the neutral particle flux vector, and $S_n$ is the net source density from ionization, recombination, and charge exchange. The poloidal component $\Gamma_{n,\theta} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_n \cdot \hat{e}_\theta$ drives neutral transport along the poloidal angle $\theta$.

In the edge plasma, strong poloidal neutral flows arise from recycling at plasma-facing components, charge-exchange momentum transfer with ions, and ionization sinks near the target plates. This flux component is computed within neutral fluid or kinetic transport models covering the scrape-off layer and divertor. The companion quantity [poloidal_neutral_momentum_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_momentum_flux) captures poloidal transport of momentum carried by the same neutral population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutrals flow in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the effective convection velocity for particle transport of a specified neutral atomic or molecular state. It is the signed advective speed along the poloidal angle in the flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi), distinct from species-summed neutral convection and from radial transport.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral state convection velocity is the state-resolved advective speed that multiplies the density of one neutral atomic or molecular state in the poloidal particle flux. It describes directed transport along the poloidal coordinate $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, separate from radial transport and from the species-summed [poloidal neutral species convection velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_convection_velocity). The corresponding energy-transport quantity is [poloidal neutral state energy convection velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity).

The convective contribution to the poloidal particle flux density is defined by:

$$
\Gamma_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}} = n_a\,v_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $a$ labels the specified neutral state, $\Gamma_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective poloidal particle flux density in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $n_a$ is the neutral-state number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $v_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the poloidal convection velocity in $\mathrm{m.s}^{-1}$.

In transport modeling, this velocity is usually an effective coefficient inferred from the ratio of poloidal advective particle flux to state density after separating diffusive, source, and sink contributions. It may be constrained by neutral density, emission, and particle-balance measurements, or computed from kinetic or fluid neutral-transport closures; it should not be interpreted automatically as the ballistic speed of individual neutral particles.

Representative modeled magnitudes are strongly regime- and closure-dependent. Values may be close to 0 m.s^-1 where poloidal neutral advection is weak, while effective coefficients of order 1-100 m.s^-1 are common scales used to characterize modest poloidal redistribution; larger local values should be checked against the defining flux-to-density ratio rather than treated as universal typical behavior.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\theta,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$ in the flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal particle diffusivity for neutral particles in a specified atomic or molecular state, such as ground, metastable, excited, or molecular. In flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi), it is projected along the theta direction tangent to a magnetic flux surface and relates down-gradient diffusive flux to the state-resolved neutral density gradient.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral state diffusion coefficient is the particle diffusivity of neutral atoms or molecules in a specified internal state along the poloidal direction on a magnetic flux surface. In flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho$ is a radial flux coordinate, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle, the poloidal direction is tangent to the surface in the direction of increasing $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$. A neutral state denotes a resolved atomic or molecular population, such as a ground, metastable, excited electronic, vibrational, rotational, or molecular state, so this coefficient can differ between state populations of the same species.

The Fickian closure for the poloidal diffusive particle flux is:

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{pol},s}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\mathrm{pol},s}^{(n)} \frac{1}{h_\theta}\frac{\partial n_s^{(n)}}{\partial \theta}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{pol},s}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive neutral particle flux component along increasing poloidal angle, $D_{\mathrm{pol},s}^{(n)}$ is this coefficient, $n_s^{(n)}$ is the density of neutral state $s$, and $h_\theta = |\partial \mathbf{x}/\partial \theta|$ is the metric factor converting poloidal-angle variation to arclength at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$. The minus sign gives the gradient convention: for a positive diffusion coefficient, the diffusive flux is directed toward lower state-resolved neutral density.

In practice, this coefficient is usually supplied by a transport model or inferred by matching neutral density, spectroscopic emission, recycling, or pressure observations with kinetic or fluid neutral-transport calculations. It is the state-resolved counterpart of the species-aggregated [poloidal_neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_diffusion_coefficient), the neutral analog of [poloidal_particle_diffusivity](name:poloidal_particle_diffusivity), and the particle-transport counterpart of [poloidal_neutral_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient). It may depend on the internal state, local collisionality, neutral temperature, ionization, recombination, excitation, charge-exchange processes, and flux-surface geometry.

Typical effective values are model dependent. Fluid neutral closures in the edge plasma and scrape-off layer commonly use 0.01-100 m^2.s^-1, while weakly collisional or fast-neutral effective descriptions can require 100-10000 m^2.s^-1. Values near zero represent negligible poloidal mixing for that neutral state; negative fitted values would indicate a non-Fickian or anti-diffusive effective closure rather than ordinary diffusion.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Physical poloidal component, along increasing theta in the flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi), of the effective energy convection velocity for a specific neutral species state.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral state energy convection velocity is the physical velocity component that advects thermal energy of a specific neutral species state in the poloidal direction. It is the metric velocity along increasing $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, not the angular coordinate rate $d\theta/dt$.

In a state-resolved neutral energy balance, the convective contribution to the poloidal energy flux density is represented by

$$
Q_\theta^{\mathrm{conv}} = v_{E,\theta}\,\mathcal{E}
$$

where $Q_\theta^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the physical poloidal convective energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $v_{E,\theta}$ is this energy convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $\mathcal{E}$ is the thermal-energy density of the neutral state in J m$^{-3}$.

The quantity is usually obtained from neutral transport modeling or from balance analysis that separates particle, momentum, and energy transport channels. It is distinct from the particle-transport velocity [poloidal_neutral_state_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_convection_velocity), because energy convection weights the motion by the transported thermal energy rather than by particle number alone.

Representative effective magnitudes in edge and divertor neutral-transport applications are often about $10^2$-$10^4$ m s$^{-1}$, but the value is strongly model dependent and may differ from the microscopic thermal speed when sources, sinks, charge exchange, ionization, recombination, and state-to-state energy redistribution are included.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the physical velocity component points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the energy flux density carried by neutral particles in a specified internal state, along increasing theta in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral state energy flux is the signed component of the energy-flux density of neutral particles in a specified internal quantum state along the poloidal direction in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. It is the state-resolved contribution to [poloidal_neutral_energy_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_energy_flux) and includes advected thermal enthalpy, directed bulk kinetic energy, internal-state energy, and non-advective heat flow.

A common fluid decomposition for state $s$ writes the poloidal component $Q_{\theta,s}$ as:

$$
Q_{\theta,s} = h_s\Gamma_{\theta,s} + \frac{1}{2}m_s|\mathbf{v}_s|^2\Gamma_{\theta,s} + \epsilon_s\Gamma_{\theta,s} + q_{\theta,s}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\theta,s}=n_s v_{\theta,s}$ is the [poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux) in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, $n_s$ is number density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $v_{\theta,s}$ is the poloidal bulk velocity component in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the bulk velocity vector in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $m_s$ is particle mass in kg, $h_s$ is thermal enthalpy per neutral particle in joules, $\epsilon_s$ is the internal energy assigned to state $s$ in joules, and $q_{\theta,s}$ is the non-advective heat-flux component along $\theta$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. The kinetic-energy factor uses the total bulk speed; the poloidal projection enters through $\Gamma_{\theta,s}$. Each term on the right-hand side has units of $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

This quantity is usually inferred from transport analysis rather than measured directly. Neutral fluid, kinetic, or Monte Carlo descriptions compute it from state-resolved density, temperature or enthalpy, velocity, internal-state population energy, and a heat-flow closure; spectroscopy, neutral pressure measurements, calorimetry, and recycling or charge-exchange constraints can provide input information. It is used with [poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity) to distinguish advective energy transport from the total flux including heat flow.

Typical absolute values in tokamak edge and divertor neutral populations are about $10^0-10^7\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. Cold, diffuse neutral gas often lies near the lower end, while recycling, charge-exchange, or fast molecular and atomic populations in high-power edge regions can approach the upper end.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral-state energy is transported in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_momentum
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the area-normalized momentum source for one neutral state, representing transfer of directed neutral momentum between that state and the surrounding plasma or other neutrals.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral-state momentum is the component of the momentum source for a single neutral state along the poloidal direction, tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. The poloidal direction lies in the cross-section spanned by $R$ and $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the source represents the rate at which directed momentum is added to or removed from that neutral state per unit area.

The state-resolved projection and its aggregation over neutral states are defined by:

$$
S_{\theta,n}^{(a)} = \mathbf{S}_{n}^{(a)} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}, \qquad S_{\theta,n} = \sum_a S_{\theta,n}^{(a)}
$$

where $S_{\theta,n}^{(a)}$ is the poloidal momentum source for neutral state $a$ in kg.m^-1.s^-2, $\mathbf{S}_{n}^{(a)}$ is the area-normalized neutral momentum-source vector for that state in kg.m^-1.s^-2, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\theta$, and $S_{\theta,n}$ is the aggregate poloidal neutral momentum source obtained by summing over neutral states.

In practice this quantity is evaluated from moment integrals of neutral kinetic or fluid source terms, including momentum exchange associated with ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and elastic scattering. It is usually constrained indirectly through neutral-particle diagnostics, spectroscopy, plasma flow measurements, and particle-balance modeling rather than by a direct local measurement of neutral momentum transfer.

Typical magnitudes are close to zero in neutral-poor core regions, about 10^-4-10 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in edge and scrape-off-layer conditions, and can reach 10-10^3 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in dense divertor, recycling, or fueling regions. The signed value depends on whether the net interaction accelerates the neutral state with or against the local poloidal direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the area-normalized momentum source for the neutral state points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: State-resolved kinematic coefficient for poloidal diffusion of neutral-particle flow momentum, in the direction of increasing poloidal angle theta in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi). It relates the diffusive poloidal momentum flux of neutrals occupying a specified internal state to the local gradient of their poloidal flow velocity.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral-state momentum diffusion coefficient is the state-resolved kinematic transport coefficient for redistribution of poloidal bulk-flow momentum carried by neutral particles. It applies to neutrals in a specified internal electronic, vibrational, or metastable state and represents the effective spreading of their poloidal flow by collisions, charge exchange, and closure approximations. The positive poloidal direction is the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

A local Fickian closure for the diffusive flux of poloidal momentum can be written as:

$$
\Pi_{\theta,\alpha}^{\mathrm{diff}} = - m_\alpha n_\alpha D_{\theta,\alpha}^{\mathrm{mom}} \nabla_\theta u_{\theta,\alpha}
$$

where $\alpha$ labels the neutral internal state, $D_{\theta,\alpha}^{\mathrm{mom}}$ is this coefficient in m^2.s^-1, $m_\alpha$ is the particle mass in kg, $n_\alpha$ is the state density in m^-3, $u_{\theta,\alpha}$ is the poloidal flow velocity in m.s^-1, $\nabla_\theta$ is the derivative per meter along increasing $\theta$, and $\Pi_{\theta,\alpha}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the corresponding momentum flux. For slowly varying density, a positive coefficient smooths the poloidal momentum density $m_\alpha n_\alpha u_{\theta,\alpha}$ by driving flux from larger toward smaller poloidal flow velocity. It is the poloidal counterpart of the [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) and the state-resolved analog of the species-summed [poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusivity).

This coefficient is usually obtained from neutral transport modeling rather than measured directly. It may be estimated from kinetic or fluid neutral calculations using elastic scattering, charge-exchange, ionization, and state-changing collision rates, or adjusted as an effective closure parameter to reproduce observed neutral flows and momentum exchange.

Typical effective values are 0.01-10 m^2.s^-1 for cold, highly collisional edge or divertor neutrals, 10-1000 m^2.s^-1 for warmer charge-exchange-coupled neutrals in the scrape-off layer, and can exceed 1000 m^2.s^-1 when long-mean-free-path neutral motion is represented by a diffusive closure. Values may be near zero where the population of the specified neutral state is negligible.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a positive gradient of the neutral-state poloidal flow velocity along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ produces a diffusive poloidal momentum flux in the negative poloidal direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Transport-surface-normal flux density of the poloidal component of linear momentum carried by neutral particles in a specified internal state, in flux-surface coordinates (rho, theta, phi). The flux direction is the positive transport-surface normal; this is not a poloidal-direction projection of the momentum-flux vector.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral-state momentum flux is the transport-surface-normal flux density of the poloidal component of linear momentum carried by neutral particles in a specified internal state. In flux-surface coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, the surface is a constant-$\rho$ transport surface and the momentum component is associated with motion in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$; the flux direction is the positive transport-surface normal, not the poloidal direction.

A common fluid decomposition separates convective momentum transport from non-convective stress transport:

$$
F_{n,s}^{\perp\theta} = m_n n_{n,s} v_{n,s,\perp} v_{n,s,\theta} + \pi_{n,s}^{\perp\theta}
$$

where $F_{n,s}^{\perp\theta}$ is the poloidal momentum flux of neutral state $s$, $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $n_{n,s}$ is the state-resolved neutral density, $v_{n,s,\perp}$ is the velocity component normal to the transport surface and positive toward increasing $\rho$, $v_{n,s,\theta}$ is the poloidal velocity component, and $\pi_{n,s}^{\perp\theta}$ is the pressure-tensor or viscous-stress contribution transporting poloidal momentum across the surface.

In kinetic neutral descriptions, this quantity is computed as the velocity-space moment of the state-resolved neutral distribution weighted by surface-normal velocity and poloidal momentum. In fluid or reduced transport descriptions, it is evaluated from neutral density, mean flow, and stress closures; direct experimental inference is usually indirect and constrained by neutral density, temperature, flow, charge-exchange, ionization, recombination, and recycling information.

Typical magnitudes vary strongly with neutral density and flow anisotropy. Core-penetrating neutral contributions can be below $10^{-8}$-$10^{-5}$ kg.m^-1.s^-2, edge and scrape-off-layer values are often $10^{-5}$-$10^{-1}$ kg.m^-1.s^-2, and dense divertor or recycling regions can reach $10^{-1}$-$10$ kg.m^-1.s^-2.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net flux evaluated through a constant-$\rho$ transport surface in flux-surface coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, using the positive surface normal, carries poloidal momentum in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the particle flux density of neutral particles in a specified internal state. It is the signed number of those neutrals crossing unit area per unit time along the poloidal direction in a chosen flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral-state particle flux is the physical poloidal component of the number-flux-density vector for neutral atoms or molecules in a specified internal state. It counts, with sign, how many such neutrals cross a unit area per unit time through surfaces normal to the poloidal direction, and excludes neutrals in other internal states.

The component is the projection of the state-resolved neutral particle flux vector onto the unit vector tangent to increasing poloidal angle in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, where $\rho$ labels magnetic surfaces, $\theta$ is poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle:

$$
\Gamma_{0,s,\theta} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{0,s}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{e}}_\theta
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{0,s}$ is the number flux density of neutral species in internal state $s$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{e}}_\theta$ is the local poloidal unit vector, and $\Gamma_{0,s,\theta}$ is the signed poloidal component. In a state-resolved particle balance it enters through the divergence of the total flux, for example $\partial n_{0,s}/\partial t + \nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{0,s} = S_{0,s}$, where $n_{0,s}$ is the neutral density and $S_{0,s}$ contains ionization, recombination, charge-exchange, wall, and internal-state transition sources and sinks.

This quantity is usually inferred rather than measured directly. It is computed from kinetic or fluid neutral transport models constrained by diagnostics such as spectroscopy, neutral pressure measurements, and particle source estimates; the state population may require a collisional-radiative model for electronic, vibrational, rotational, or metastable levels.

Typical magnitudes in edge and divertor neutral populations are $10^{18}$-$10^{23}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. Weakly populated excited states or well-shielded core regions can be below $10^{16}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, while ground-state recycling fluxes near strong divertor or wall sources can approach $10^{24}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux is directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the bulk fluid velocity for neutral particles in a specified internal quantum or energy state.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral state velocity is the projection of the [neutral_state_velocity](name:neutral_state_velocity) onto the poloidal direction, giving the mean poloidal convective motion of neutral particles occupying a specific internal quantum, excitation, or energy state. As a fluid moment of the state-resolved neutral distribution function, it captures directed poloidal transport for that neutral population rather than random thermal speeds.

The quantity is defined by projecting the state-resolved neutral bulk flow vector $\mathbf{v}_s$ onto the poloidal unit vector $\hat{\theta}$:

$$
v_{\theta,s} = \mathbf{v}_s \cdot \hat{\theta}
$$

where $s$ labels the internal quantum or energy state and $\hat{\theta}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

State-resolved poloidal velocities are particularly relevant in edge and divertor plasma modeling, where neutrals in distinct quantum or energy states participate in charge-exchange, ionization, and momentum-exchange processes at state-specific rates, producing different effective flow velocities for each state. The species-summed analog [poloidal_neutral_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_velocity) integrates over all neutral states, while [poloidal_ion_state_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity) provides the equivalent charge-state-resolved quantity for ions. The related [poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity) captures the effective advective velocity governing momentum transport for the same state.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\theta,s}$ is directed in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the bulk neutral particle fluid velocity. It is the projection of the neutral mean flow onto the poloidal direction on a magnetic surface.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral velocity is the component of the bulk mean velocity of neutral particles along the poloidal direction, i.e. tangent to a magnetic surface in a meridional plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is one component of the full [neutral velocity](name:neutral_velocity), complementary to the [radial neutral velocity](name:radial_neutral_velocity) and toroidal neutral velocity.

The component is defined by projecting the neutral mean-flow vector onto the local poloidal unit direction:

$$
v_{\theta,n} = \mathbf{v}_n \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_n$ is the neutral bulk velocity, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ on the magnetic surface, and $v_{\theta,n}$ is the signed poloidal neutral velocity.

In kinetic terms, the neutral bulk velocity is the first velocity moment of the neutral distribution function divided by the neutral density; in fluid or transport modeling it is obtained from the neutral momentum balance. Experimentally it is inferred indirectly from neutral-particle diagnostics, spectroscopy, or constrained plasma-edge modeling, because neutrals are not tied to magnetic field lines and can have strongly nonlocal sources from recycling, charge exchange, and ionization.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^2-10^4$ m.s$^{-1}$ in edge and divertor regions, with larger values possible where charge-exchange sources, strong pressure gradients, or rapid recycling flows dominate. In the confined core, neutral densities are usually low and the corresponding mean velocity may be poorly constrained.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral mean flow is in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ on the magnetic surface in the right-handed flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $\phi$ increasing in the same sense as the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: power_density
NAMES.short: Net local rate of energy transfer per unit volume into the electron population; it is the source-minus-sink term that drives the electron energy transport balance.
NAMES.long:
Power density is the volumetric source term for the electron energy balance. It represents the net local rate at which all included mechanisms add energy to, or remove energy from, the electron population per unit volume.

A common local form of the electron energy balance is:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac{3}{2} n_e T_e\right) + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}_e = P_e
$$

where $n_e$ is electron density in $m^{-3}$, $T_e$ is electron temperature expressed as an energy in joules, $\mathbf{q}_e$ is electron energy flux in $W\,m^{-2}$, and $P_e$ is the power density in $W\,m^{-3}$. If $T_e$ is given in eV, it must be converted to joules in this equation.

In practice, power density is obtained from transport analysis by combining measured or reconstructed electron density and temperature evolution with the divergence of the electron energy flux and with modeled or inferred heating and loss terms. It is distinct from source-rate coefficients such as [electron_implicit_source_rate](name:electron_implicit_source_rate), which parameterize how a numerical source depends on an evolving state variable; power density is the resulting energy transfer rate per volume.

Typical tokamak electron-channel values are about $10^3-10^6\ W\,m^{-3}$ for broad core heating or loss terms, can reach $10^6-10^8\ W\,m^{-3}$ in strongly localized deposition or edge-loss regions, and may be close to zero where sources and sinks nearly balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred into the electron population.

NAMES.name: co_passing_power_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged volumetric rate at which kinetic energy is added to or removed from the co-passing orbit population. It is the energy moment of the source term for passing particles moving on the co-current branch.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing power density is the flux-surface-averaged volumetric source rate of kinetic energy for passing particles whose parallel motion is on the co-current orbit branch. It separates energy exchange with the co-passing population from corresponding exchange with counter-passing and trapped particles.

The local energy moment of the phase-space source term gives the flux-surface-averaged power density:

$$
p_{\mathrm{co}}(\rho) = \left\langle \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}} \frac{1}{2} m v^2\, S_f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v \right\rangle_{\rho}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing power density, $\rho$ labels the magnetic flux surface, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rho}$ is the flux-surface average, $\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing region of velocity or invariant space, $m$ is particle mass, $v$ is speed, $S_f$ is the source contribution to the distribution-function evolution per unit spatial volume and per unit time, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element.

In practice this quantity is computed by orbit-classifying the kinetic distribution and integrating the energy moment of source operators over the co-passing domain. The source term may come from wave-particle interactions, neutral-particle injection, external fueling, collisional operators, or modeled loss mechanisms; constraints from global power balance and fast-particle or radiation diagnostics are often used to validate the inferred deposition or removal.

Typical magnitudes are $10^3-10^6\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, with strongly localized wave or neutral-beam deposition reaching $10^7\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$. Values close to zero indicate weak net coupling to the co-passing population, while negative values of comparable magnitude occur where the modeled process removes kinetic energy.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the modeled source process increases the kinetic energy of the co-passing orbit population per unit volume.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_power_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged volumetric energy source rate for the counter-passing orbit population. It is the local power density transferred to or from that population by wave-particle interactions, collisions, or particle sources.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing power density is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which kinetic energy is added to the counter-passing orbit population per unit physical volume. Counter-passing refers to the passing part of velocity space whose guiding-center motion is opposite to the co-passing direction; it excludes trapped orbits.

A kinetic definition is the energy moment of the net source operator over the counter-passing velocity-space domain, followed by a flux-surface average:

$$
S_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\varepsilon}(\rho,t) = \left\langle \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v^2\, \mathcal{S}_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v \right\rangle_{\rho}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\varepsilon}$ has units W m$^{-3}$, $\rho$ is a radial flux-surface label in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing velocity-space domain, $m_s$ is the species mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed in m s$^{-1}$, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The operator $\mathcal{S}_s$ is the net time rate of change of the distribution function from sources, collisions, and wave interactions; if $\int f_s d^3v$ is a number density in m$^{-3}$, then $\mathcal{S}_s$ has units s$^2$ m$^{-6}$. The notation $\langle A\rangle_{\rho}$ denotes the flux-surface average at fixed $\rho$, equivalently the surface integral of $A$ weighted by $1/|\nabla\rho|$ divided by the corresponding weighted surface area.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic or Fokker-Planck models by taking the velocity-space energy moment of the relevant collision, external source, and wave-particle operators over the counter-passing domain. It is constrained indirectly by deposited heating, fast-particle measurements, loss measurements, and power-balance analysis. Together with [co_passing_power_density](name:co_passing_power_density) and [trapped_power_density](name:trapped_power_density), it partitions the orbit-integrated [power_density](name:electron_power_density).

Typical magnitudes are 10$^3$-10$^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, with localized radio-frequency or neutral-beam deposition reaching about 10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$. Weakly driven regions can be near zero, and collisional drag or loss terms can give negative values with comparable magnitudes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the counter-passing orbit population gains kinetic energy from the net source operator.

NAMES.name: electron_power_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Signed volumetric source term in the electron energy transport equation that captures net power deposition into or removal from the electron population per unit plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The electron power density $Q_e$ is the aggregate signed volumetric source in the electron energy balance, capturing all mechanisms that exchange power with the electron population — including ohmic heating, wave absorption, collisional energy exchange with ions and neutrals, ionization, and radiation losses — per unit plasma volume.

The principal defining relation is the electron energy transport equation:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\!\left(\frac{3}{2} n_e T_e\right) + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}_e = Q_e
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density, $T_e$ is the electron temperature in energy units, and $\mathbf{q}_e$ is the electron heat flux vector.

The total $Q_e$ aggregates all power channels acting on electrons. It can be decomposed into sub-contributions such as [fast_electron_power_density](name:fast_electron_power_density) for the suprathermal electron component and [thermal_electron_power_density](name:thermal_electron_power_density) for the bulk electron channel. The complementary species-level source terms are [ion_power_density](name:total_ion_power_density) and [neutral_power_density](name:neutral_state_power_density). Core heating sources typically fall in the range $10^4$–$10^7$ W m$^{-3}$; negative values arise when electrons transfer energy to ions via Coulomb collisions or lose energy through radiation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is deposited into the electron population (net electron heating); negative when the electron channel is a net donor of energy to other populations or loss mechanisms.

NAMES.name: ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net non-transport volumetric energy source rate for the ion thermal channel, giving the local power per unit volume deposited into or removed from ions by heating, collisional exchange, atomic, nuclear, and other local source or sink processes.
NAMES.long:
Ion power density is the signed local rate per unit volume at which non-transport processes add energy to the ion thermal channel. It is a source term in the ion energy balance and excludes the divergence of conductive, convective, turbulent, neoclassical, or other spatial transport fluxes, which are separate balance terms.

A compact local ion energy balance can be written with transport separated from the source term:

$$
P_i = \frac{\partial w_i}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}_{E,i}
$$

where $P_i$ is the ion power density in W m$^{-3}$, $w_i$ is the ion thermal energy density in J m$^{-3}$, $t$ is time in s, and $\mathbf{q}_{E,i}$ is the transported ion energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$. In this form, $P_i$ contains only local non-transport sources and sinks, while $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}_{E,i}$ accounts for spatial redistribution of ion energy.

Ion power density is usually inferred from power-balance or transport analysis rather than measured directly. Inputs can include ion temperature and density measurements, external heating deposition models, collisional electron-ion energy exchange, fusion-product heating, charge-exchange and atomic loss estimates, and constraints from the reconstructed energy flux.

Typical magnitudes in magnetically confined fusion plasmas are about $10^2$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ for core ion-channel sources in low- to high-power discharges. Strongly localized heating or loss regions can reach $10^6$-$10^7$ W m$^{-3}$, and net sink terms have the same units with negative values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net non-transport processes deposit energy into the ion thermal channel.

NAMES.name: ion_state_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total net volumetric power source for a specified ion charge state, giving the local rate at which that population gains or loses energy through non-transport interactions.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state power density is the signed local rate of energy gain per unit plasma volume for ions belonging to one specified species and charge state. It is the total non-transport source term for that charge-state population, including effects such as external heating, atomic energy exchange, charge exchange with neutrals, and Coulomb energy exchange with electrons or other ion populations.

The local definition is the source part of the energy-density balance:

$$
P_{a\zeta} = \left.\frac{\partial \mathcal{E}_{a\zeta}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{sources}}
$$

where $P_{a\zeta}$ is the ion-state power density for ion species $a$ and charge state $\zeta$, in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$; $\mathcal{E}_{a\zeta}$ is the corresponding energy density, in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$; and the subscript indicates that only local source and sink processes are included, not advective or conductive energy transport. Integrating $P_{a\zeta}$ over a plasma volume gives the net power delivered to that charge-state population in that volume.

In practice, this quantity is computed from a combination of heating deposition, atomic and molecular rate coefficients, neutral and impurity populations, charge-exchange rates, and Coulomb collisional energy-exchange rates. It may also be inferred indirectly by balancing the measured or reconstructed time evolution of charge-state-resolved energy density against transport and known external power inputs.

Typical absolute magnitudes are about $10^3$-$10^6\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ in the main confined plasma. Localized heating regions, dense edge plasma, or divertor plasma can reach $10^6$-$10^8\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$, while weak trace charge states may have much smaller values.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified ion charge state gains energy.

NAMES.name: neutral_state_power_density
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric rate at which energy density is added to or removed from a specific neutral species quantum state by atomic and collisional processes. It is the state-resolved neutral energy source term, with positive values denoting net energy gain by that state.
NAMES.long:
Neutral-state power density is the net source rate of energy density for a single neutral species quantum state. The resolved state can represent an electronic excitation, vibrational or rotational level, molecular state, isotope-specific neutral, or another quantum configuration used in the neutral population model. It is the energy-balance analog of [neutral_state_source_rate](name:neutral_state_source_rate) and is used together with state thermodynamic quantities such as [total_neutral_state_density](name:total_neutral_state_density) and [total_neutral_state_pressure](name:total_neutral_state_pressure).

A compact reaction-sum definition is

$$
P_s = \sum_r \mathcal{R}_{s,r} \, \Delta E_{s,r}
$$

where $P_s$ is the neutral-state power density for state $s$ in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathcal{R}_{s,r}$ is the event-rate density for process $r$ affecting state $s$ in m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$, and $\Delta E_{s,r}$ is the net energy gained by state $s$ per event in J. The indices $s$ and $r$ are labels and have no units. Included process terms may represent ionization, recombination, charge exchange, excitation, de-excitation, elastic heating or cooling by electrons and ions, radiative coupling, or molecular reactions; for continuous energy exchange, $\mathcal{R}_{s,r}\Delta E_{s,r}$ denotes the equivalent volumetric energy-transfer rate.

This quantity is usually computed rather than measured directly. Collisional-radiative, fluid, or kinetic neutral models evaluate it from neutral-state populations, electron and ion densities and temperatures, relative velocities, reaction-rate coefficients, and the energy accounting used for internal states. Summing over neutral states gives a species-level contribution such as [neutral_power_density](name:neutral_state_power_density), while [neutral_state_energy_flux_at_wall](name:neutral_state_energy_flux_at_wall) describes energy transported to a material surface rather than a local volumetric source.

Typical magnitudes are strongly localized and model dependent. Values can be near 0 W m$^{-3}$ where the neutral population is negligible, about $10^0$-$10^5$ W m$^{-3}$ in weak neutral source regions, and $10^5$-$10^8$ W m$^{-3}$ in strong edge, divertor, fueling, or recycling regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified neutral quantum state gains energy density from the included processes.

NAMES.name: power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.short: Signed local volumetric power density exchanged by a plasma population through Coulomb collisions, positive when the population gains energy from its collision partners and negative when it loses energy to them.
NAMES.long:
Coulomb collisions between plasma populations — electrons, thermal ions, suprathermal fast ions, and neutral-beam-injected particles — continuously redistribute kinetic energy at a rate determined by local density, temperature, and the Coulomb logarithm. This quantity expresses that energy exchange as a signed volumetric power density for a given population: positive when the population absorbs energy from its collision partners, and negative when it transfers energy outward to them.

For two Maxwellian populations $a$ and $b$, the energy exchange rate density takes the form:

$$
Q_{ab} = \nu_{ab}^{E} \, n_a \, (T_b - T_a)
$$

where $\nu_{ab}^{E}$ is the energy equilibration rate coefficient, $n_a$ is the number density of species $a$, and $T_a$, $T_b$ are the temperatures in energy units. The net collisional power density for any population sums contributions from all collision partners, including both thermal and suprathermal populations.

This term enters the energy transport equations of multi-fluid and gyrokinetic models, where it is derived by applying the Coulomb collision operator to the species distribution function. The [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) specializes this concept to resolved fast-ion charge states. For the volume-integrated energy balance across all populations, see total_plasma_deposited_power.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified plasma population gains energy from Coulomb collisions with other plasma populations.

NAMES.name: electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Total Coulomb-collisional power density for the electron population, aggregating energy exchange with all plasma species across both the bulk thermal and suprathermal fast-electron sub-populations.
NAMES.long:
The electron Coulomb-collisional power density is the local volumetric rate at which the electron population as a whole gains or loses energy through pairwise Coulomb interactions with all other plasma species, integrating over the full electron distribution without restricting to a single population class.

It appears as a source term $Q_e$ in the electron energy-balance equation alongside convective and conductive heat fluxes:

$$
Q_e = \sum_{s \neq e} Q_{e \leftarrow s}
$$

where $Q_{e \leftarrow s}$ is the power density transferred from species $s$ (ions or distinct particle populations) to the electrons, and $e$ denotes the electron population. This total decomposes into a bulk thermal channel described by [thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) and a suprathermal channel described by [fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions); the sum of these two sub-components equals this quantity when no other electron population classes are resolved. The term is evaluated from velocity-space integrals of the Coulomb collision operator weighted by particle kinetic energy, typically within neoclassical or kinetic transport frameworks. The parent quantity [power_density_due_to_collisions](name:power_density_due_to_collisions) generalizes this concept to any named plasma species or charge state.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron population gains net energy from Coulomb collisions with other species.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Coulomb-collisional power density received by the fast electron population. It is the volumetric rate of kinetic-energy exchange between suprathermal electrons and other plasma species.
NAMES.long:
Fast-electron collisional power density is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the suprathermal electron population. It represents the fast-electron channel of electron collisional energy exchange; together with the thermal-electron channel it forms the total electron collisional power density.

The quantity is the kinetic-energy moment of the Fokker-Planck collision operator for the fast-electron distribution:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_s \int \frac{1}{2} m_e v^2\, C_{es}[f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}, f_s](\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where the sum is over collision partners $s$, $f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}\,d^3v$ gives the fast-electron density, $f_s$ is the distribution of species $s$, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed in m/s, and $C_{es}$ has units of $f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ per second. With these definitions the integral has units of W m^-3. For relativistic fast electrons, the kinetic-energy weight is replaced by the appropriate relativistic kinetic energy.

In practice this quantity is computed by applying a Coulomb collision operator to a modeled or reconstructed fast-electron distribution and integrating over velocity space. If the fast population is partitioned by orbit class, the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped components sum to this quantity when the same collision model and phase-space partition are used.

Typical local absolute magnitudes are scenario dependent: about 10^2-10^5 W m^-3 for weak suprathermal tails, 10^5-10^7 W m^-3 in strongly driven electron-heating or current-drive cases, and up to 10^8 W m^-3 or more in localized runaway-electron regimes. During ordinary slowing down, the value is often negative because fast electrons transfer energy to the thermal plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the fast electron population.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional power transferred to fast electrons from co-passing fast particles. It is the local kinetic-energy exchange rate for the fast-electron target population due to that source orbit class.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing fast electron power density due to collisions is the local volumetric rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the target fast-electron population from co-passing source fast particles. The co-passing qualifier labels the source fast-particle orbit class; it does not mean that the target fast-electron velocity integral is restricted to co-passing electrons.

Using a collision-operator convention in which $C_{e_f\leftarrow \mathrm{co}}$ denotes the contribution to $\partial f_{e_f}/\partial t$ for target fast electrons caused by collisions with the co-passing fast-particle source distribution, the power density is the target kinetic-energy moment:

$$
P_{e_f\leftarrow \mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\Omega_{e_f}} \frac{1}{2} m_e v^2 \, C_{e_f\leftarrow \mathrm{co}}\!\left[f_{e_f}, f_{\mathrm{co}}\right](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\Omega_{e_f}$ is the target fast-electron velocity-space domain, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $v$ is the target electron speed in m s$^{-1}$, $f_{e_f}$ and $f_{\mathrm{co}}$ are distribution functions with units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, and $C_{e_f\leftarrow \mathrm{co}}$ has units s$^2$ m$^{-6}$. Integrations over the source-particle velocity variables and the restriction to the co-passing source orbit class are part of the collision operator.

In practice this term is evaluated from kinetic collision operators in Fokker-Planck, Monte Carlo, orbit-following, or reduced transport calculations that resolve the source orbit class and the target fast-electron energy range. It is constrained indirectly by measurements that determine the fast-particle and fast-electron populations; it is not a directly measured diagnostic signal. The [counter-passing counterpart](name:counter_passing_fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) uses the counter-passing source branch, while [co-passing thermal-electron power density](name:co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) changes the target population; sums over orbit classes or target species connect to [fast-electron collisional power density](name:fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) and [co-passing fast-particle collisional power density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Representative local magnitudes are scenario dependent; in regions where nonthermal populations overlap, modeling values often span roughly $10^2$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$, while values may be near 0 W m$^{-3}$ where the co-passing source density is small. The term may be negative when the same collisional channel removes kinetic energy from the fast-electron target population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the co-passing fast-particle source population to the target fast-electron population.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local signed Coulomb-collisional power density contributed by the counter-passing part of the fast-electron distribution to the fast-electron energy balance. Positive values represent net collisional energy deposition into fast electrons; negative values represent collisional energy loss from them.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions change the kinetic energy of the fast-electron population, retaining only the contribution associated with the counter-passing part of fast-electron phase space. Fast electrons are suprathermal electrons, and counter-passing states are passing guiding-center orbits whose toroidal transit is opposite to the plasma-current circulation.

The kinetic definition is the energy moment of the collisional Fokker-Planck operator over the counter-passing domain:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},e}^{\mathrm{coll,cp}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}} \frac{1}{2} m_e v^2 \, C_e^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_{\mathrm{fast},e}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast},e}^{\mathrm{coll,cp}}$ is in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is the electron speed in m s$^{-1}$, $f_{\mathrm{fast},e}$ is the fast-electron distribution function with units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, $C_e^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_{\mathrm{fast},e}]$ is its collisional time derivative with units s$^2$ m$^{-6}$, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The domain $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the passing part of velocity space on the counter-passing side of the trapped-passing boundary; equivalently, for a pitch variable $\xi=v_\parallel/v$, it is the interval outside the trapped region whose bounce-averaged toroidal angular velocity $\langle\dot{\phi}\rangle$ is opposite to the plasma-current circulation in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height.

In practice this term is computed in kinetic, Fokker-Planck, or Monte Carlo fast-electron transport calculations by applying the Coulomb collision operator to the fast-electron distribution and integrating over the counter-passing orbit class. It is not measured directly; it is inferred from modeled fast-electron phase-space distributions constrained by diagnostics, equilibrium information, and background plasma quantities such as density, temperature, and effective charge. Summing the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped orbit-class contributions gives the total [fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions); the corresponding co-passing contribution is [co_passing_fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions), and an analogous counter-passing term for thermal electrons is [counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions).

No device-independent numerical range is meaningful for this local signed source term, because it scales with the local fast-electron density, energy, pitch-angle asymmetry, and collisional slowing-down rate. Values are typically interpreted relative to the total fast-electron collisional power density; the term is near 0 W m$^{-3}$ where the counter-passing fast-electron population is negligible and may have either sign where collisions exchange energy between fast electrons and the background plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions deposit kinetic energy into the fast-electron population through the counter-passing contribution.

NAMES.name: ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net local volumetric power density transferred to the combined ion population through Coulomb collisions, summing fast-ion and thermal-ion exchange channels over all species, charge states, and orbit classes.
NAMES.long:
Ion collisional power density is the aggregate local volumetric rate at which the entire ion population—both suprathermal fast ions and Maxwellian thermal ions—gains or loses energy through pairwise Coulomb interactions with electrons and other plasma constituents. It is the ion component of the more general [power_density_due_to_collisions](name:power_density_due_to_collisions) and resolves into two physically distinct sub-channels.

The total decomposes as:

$$
Q_\mathrm{ion}^\mathrm{coll} = Q_\mathrm{fast\,ion}^\mathrm{coll} + Q_\mathrm{th\,ion}^\mathrm{coll}
$$

where $Q_\mathrm{fast\,ion}^\mathrm{coll}$ is the [fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions), aggregated over co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped orbit classes, and $Q_\mathrm{th\,ion}^\mathrm{coll}$ is the [thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions), representing Coulomb heating of the bulk Maxwellian ion distribution by non-thermal particles.

This quantity is evaluated from kinetic or orbit-averaged transport models that apply the Fokker–Planck collision operator to the ion distribution function. In scenarios driven by neutral beam injection or ion-cyclotron resonance heating, the fast-ion collisional channel dominates near the power deposition zone, while electron–ion equipartition governs the thermal-ion channel in the core.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion population gains energy through Coulomb collisions.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net volumetric rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the fast-ion population, summed over orbit classes such as co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped ions.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion power density due to collisions is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the fast-ion population per unit volume. It is a signed energy source term for the selected fast-ion population and represents the orbit-class-summed counterpart of orbit-resolved quantities such as [counter-passing fast-ion collisional power density](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions).

For one fast-ion species, the collisional power density is the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator acting on the fast-ion distribution:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast,coll}} = \int \frac{1}{2} m_i v^2\, C_{\mathrm{coll}}[f_{\mathrm{fast}}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the fast-ion mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is the particle speed in m/s, $f_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-ion distribution function, $C_{\mathrm{coll}}[f_{\mathrm{fast}}]$ is the Coulomb collision operator with units of particles per volume per time per velocity-space volume, and $d^3v$ has units $(\mathrm{m/s})^3$. The velocity-space integral converts the collision-induced change of the distribution into an energy transfer rate per unit volume, with units W m$^{-3}$; contributions from multiple fast-ion species are summed when the quantity represents a combined fast-ion population.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic descriptions of the fast ions, for example by taking the energy moment of a Fokker-Planck collision operator, by accumulating collisional energy changes of Monte Carlo markers, or by post-processing a reconstructed fast-ion distribution. The co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped orbit-class contributions add algebraically to this total, and the corresponding volume integral gives [fast-ion power due to collisions](name:fast_ion_power_due_to_collisions).

Typical local magnitudes are about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in many heated tokamak core plasmas and can reach $10^7$-$10^8$ W m$^{-3}$ near strong neutral-beam, radio-frequency, or fusion-alpha sources. During slowing down, the term is often negative for the fast-ion population because energy is transferred from fast ions to thermal electrons and ions; positive values can occur when collisions transfer energy into the selected fast-ion population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic energy of the fast-ion population.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Local volumetric Coulomb collisional energy transfer rate to fast ions belonging to the co-passing orbit class, which circulate poloidally in the same direction as the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The co-passing orbit class consists of fast ions whose guiding-center trajectories complete full poloidal circuits in the same direction as the plasma current, as opposed to trapped particles (which bounce between magnetic mirror points) and counter-passing ions. This quantity isolates the co-passing contribution to the total fast-ion collisional power density, enabling orbit-resolved energy-balance analysis of suprathermal ion populations.

The collisional power density is the energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator restricted to the co-passing velocity-space domain:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cp}} = \int_{\mathrm{co\text{-}passing}} \tfrac{1}{2} m_i v^2 \, C[f_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{cp}}] \, d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the fast-ion mass in kg, $v$ is the particle speed in m s$^{-1}$, and $C[f_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{cp}}]$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the co-passing portion of the fast-ion distribution function.

Orbit-resolving Fokker-Planck or Monte Carlo kinetic codes evaluate this quantity by partitioning velocity space into co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped regions. Summing these three orbit-class components recovers [fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions), the total fast-ion collisional power density. The symmetric companion for the counter-circulating population is [counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions); asymmetry between the two arises from anisotropic fast-ion sources such as co-injected neutral beams.
NAMES.sign: Positive when co-passing fast ions gain kinetic energy through Coulomb collisions with background plasma species.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to fast ions on counter-passing guiding-center orbits. Counter-passing ions move parallel to the magnetic field opposite to the plasma-current direction.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast-ion power density due to collisions is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the counter-passing part of the fast-ion distribution. Counter-passing refers to passing guiding-center orbits whose parallel velocity is opposite to the plasma-current direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

It is the energy moment of the collision operator restricted to the counter-passing region of velocity space:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{s,b} \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v^2\, C_{sb}[f_s,f_b](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the counter-passing fast-ion collisional power density at spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, $s$ indexes fast-ion species or charge states, $b$ indexes background plasma species, $m_s$ is the fast-ion mass, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$, $f_s$ and $f_b$ are distribution functions, $C_{sb}$ is the collision operator acting on fast ions of class $s$ due to collisions with species $b$, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing domain. With a pitch variable $\xi=v_\parallel/v$ and positive $v_\parallel$ chosen along the plasma current, $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}$ corresponds to $\xi<0$. The resulting unit is W m$^{-3}$.

This quantity is usually obtained from kinetic fast-ion calculations, Fokker-Planck or Monte Carlo collision operators, or reduced transport models using the reconstructed magnetic geometry and fast-ion distribution. For suprathermal fast ions in a cooler plasma it is often negative because Coulomb drag removes kinetic energy from the fast-ion population; it can be positive where collisions heat the selected counter-passing fast ions.

Typical magnitudes are $10^2$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in regions with appreciable fast-ion pressure and can reach about $10^7$ W m$^{-3}$ in strongly heated cores. Values approach zero where the counter-passing fast-ion density is small or collisional energy exchange is weak.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic energy of the counter-passing fast-ion population.

NAMES.name: ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of Coulomb-collisional energy exchange for a specified ion charge state, positive for net energy gain and negative for net energy loss to other plasma populations.
NAMES.long:
Ion-state collisional power density is the net volumetric power deposited into or extracted from a single ionic charge state by Coulomb collisions with all other plasma populations — electrons, bulk ions of other charge states, and fast particles. It is the charge-state-resolved component of [power_density_due_to_collisions](name:power_density_due_to_collisions) in the plasma energy balance, and being pairwise-conservative, power removed from one charge state appears as a gain for its collision partner, so the sum over all populations vanishes identically.

The quantity is defined as the energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator for charge state $z$:

$$
P_\mathrm{coll}^{(z)} = \int \frac{m v^2}{2} \, \mathcal{C}^{(z)}\!\left[f^{(z)}\right] d^3v
$$

where $m$ is the ion mass, $v$ is particle speed, and $\mathcal{C}^{(z)}$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the distribution function $f^{(z)}$ of charge state $z$. Summing over all charge states of a species recovers the total ion collisional power density.

This term enters as a source or sink in the charge-state energy equation and is evaluated in kinetic or fluid transport codes from the second velocity moment of the collision operator. No direct experimental diagnostic resolves it per charge state; values are inferred from impurity transport modeling constrained by spectroscopic line-emission measurements.

Orbit-class-resolved subsets are tracked separately as [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) for suprathermal ions and [thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) for bulk thermal ions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer net energy into the specified ion charge state.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Coulomb collisional power density for fast ions in a specified charge state, giving the local energy exchange rate per volume between that fast-ion population and the background plasma. It is positive when collisions add kinetic energy to the selected fast-ion state and negative when they remove it.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion state collisional power density is the local kinetic-energy exchange rate per unit volume between fast ions in a specified charge state and the surrounding plasma due to Coulomb collisions. It is a signed scalar source term in the fast-ion energy balance, resolved by charge state rather than summed over all charge states.

The quantity is defined as the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb Fokker-Planck collision operator acting on the fast-ion distribution for charge state $q$:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast},q}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int \frac{1}{2} m_q v^2\, C_q^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_{\mathrm{fast},q}, f_{\mathrm{bg}}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fast},q}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ has units of W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is velocity, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ in m s$^{-1}$, $m_q$ is the ion mass in kg, $f_{\mathrm{fast},q}$ is the fast-ion velocity distribution for charge state $q$, $f_{\mathrm{bg}}$ represents the background electron and ion distributions, and $C_q^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the Coulomb Fokker-Planck collision operator with units of distribution function per second. For fast-ion slowing-down calculations this operator is commonly treated as a linearized test-particle operator with drag and diffusion coefficients expressible through Rosenbluth potentials.

In practice this term is inferred from kinetic modeling constrained by measurements of the fast-ion population and by background density, temperature, and composition, which determine the Coulomb collision frequencies. Volume integration gives [fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions), summing over charge states gives [fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions), and orbit-topology partitions give [co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), [counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), and [trapped_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:trapped_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical absolute magnitudes are about 10$^{3}$-10$^{7}$ W m$^{-3}$ in beam-heated, radio-frequency-heated, or fusion-alpha-heated tokamak plasmas. Values can be much smaller in weak-source or edge regions and larger locally in compact, high-power deposition regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the selected fast-ion charge-state population.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional kinetic-energy transfer rate for a specified fast-ion charge state, restricted to co-passing particles that circulate poloidally in the same direction as the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The co-passing fast-ion-state collisional power density is the local volumetric rate of kinetic-energy exchange between fast ions of a specified charge state in the co-passing orbit class and the surrounding plasma, driven by Coulomb collisions. Co-passing particles follow closed toroidal orbits and circulate poloidally in the same sense as the plasma current, occupying a distinct region of velocity space that is separate from the trapped and counter-passing populations.

The quantity is computed as the velocity-space integral of the Coulomb collision operator weighted by kinetic energy, restricted to the co-passing velocity-space domain for a single ion charge state $s$:

$$
P_\text{co-pass}^{\text{fast},s} = \int_{\Omega_\text{co-pass}} \frac{m_i v^2}{2} \, C[f_\text{fast}^s] \, d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $v$ is the particle speed, $C[f_\text{fast}^s]$ is the Fokker-Planck collision operator for the fast-ion distribution function $f_\text{fast}^s$ of charge state $s$, and $\Omega_\text{co-pass}$ denotes the co-passing region of velocity space.

This quantity is obtained from kinetic transport simulations that resolve the full distribution function over orbit class, such as Fokker-Planck or Monte Carlo codes, where velocity-space integrals are performed separately over co-passing trajectories for each ion charge state. Summing co-passing and [counter-passing](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) contributions recovers the orbit-class-integrated quantity [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions). The charge-state-summed co-passing analog is [co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions deliver net kinetic energy to the co-passing fast ions of the specified charge state.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional kinetic-energy transfer rate for a specified fast-ion charge state, restricted to counter-passing particles. Positive values mean that charge state gains kinetic energy from collisions; negative values mean it loses kinetic energy.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast ion state power density due to collisions is the local collisional source term in the kinetic-energy balance of a specified fast-ion charge state, evaluated only over the counter-passing part of velocity space. Counter-passing fast ions have guiding-center parallel motion whose toroidal circulation is opposite to the plasma-current direction. The charge-state label denotes one resolved ionization state of the fast-ion species.

The quantity is the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator over the counter-passing velocity-space domain:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}} = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}} \mathcal{E}_z(\mathbf{v})\, C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}](\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing collisional power density for charge state $z$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing region of velocity space, $\mathcal{E}_z$ is the particle kinetic energy in joules, and $C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}]$ is the collisional part of the time derivative of the local fast-ion distribution function for that charge state. If $f_{\mathrm{fast},z}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{\mathrm{fast},z}\,d^3v$ is the number density, then $C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}]$ has units of number density per time per velocity-space volume, and $d^3v$ has units $(\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^3$, giving $P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}}$ in W m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from a kinetic fast-ion distribution and a Coulomb collision operator, often constrained by measurements such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, fast-ion loss signals, charge-exchange spectroscopy, or gamma-ray diagnostics. Orbit classification partitions the distribution into trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing domains; summing the orbit components gives [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), while summing over charge states gives [counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions). The complementary counter-current decomposition is [co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), and a thermal-ion analog is [counter_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical magnitudes are highly regime dependent: orbit- and charge-state-resolved values can be below 1 W m$^{-3}$ in weakly populated regions, 10$^2$-10$^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in auxiliary-heated core plasmas, and locally approach 10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$ in strongly driven fast-ion populations. Negative values occur where collisions remove kinetic energy from the specified fast-ion charge state and transfer it to other species or charge states.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic energy density of the specified fast-ion charge state.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated net power transferred to a plasma particle population through Coulomb collisions, abstracting over all source and receiving population combinations without prescribing which species serve as donor or receiver.
NAMES.long:
