Coulomb collisions mediate energy exchange between plasma populations — electrons, thermal ions, fast particles, impurity ions, and neutrals — converting differential kinetic energy into thermal energy of the receiving species. This abstract parent captures the general concept of volume-integrated collisional power transfer without specifying which populations participate; every concrete child quantity carries explicit population labels to identify the donor and receiver.

The volume-integrated collisional power is defined as:

$$
P_{\rm coll} = \int_V Q_{\rm coll}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $Q_{\rm coll}$ is the local collisional power exchange density and the integral extends over the plasma volume $V$.

Concrete population-resolved instances of this quantity include [ion_power_due_to_collisions](name:ion_power_due_to_collisions), which covers the total ion population summed over all species and charge states, and [ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:ion_state_power_due_to_collisions), which resolves this to a specified ionization state. Source-resolved variants such as [fast_particle_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_particle_power_due_to_collisions), [thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions), and [thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions) additionally identify the donating population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net energy is deposited into the specified receiving population (net collisional heating); negative when the receiving population loses energy to others (net collisional cooling).

NAMES.name: ion_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb collisional power transferred to the total ion population, aggregating both thermal and fast ion sub-populations over all ion species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the volume-integrated net rate of energy transfer into the complete ion population from Coulomb scattering interactions with all colliding plasma constituents. It is the all-ion aggregate of [power_due_to_collisions](name:power_due_to_collisions) and decomposes into two population-resolved contributions: [fast_ion_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_due_to_collisions) for energy received by the non-Maxwellian fast-ion component and [thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions) for the bulk Maxwellian ion population.

The collisional power density transferred from donor population $b$ to ion population $a$ is:

$$
q_{b \to a} = \nu_{ba}^{E}\, n_a\,(T_b - T_a)
$$

where $\nu_{ba}^{E}$ is the energy exchange frequency between populations $b$ and $a$, $n_a$ is the ion number density, and $T_a$, $T_b$ are the respective temperatures in energy units. This quantity is the volume integral of the sum $\sum_{b} q_{b \to a}$ over all ion species and charge states.

In practice it is evaluated from collisional transport models or Fokker-Planck solvers tracking fast-ion slow-down and bulk ion–electron temperature equilibration. Charge-state-resolved contributions are accessible via [fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions) and [thermal_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when collisions deposit net energy into the ion population.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb collisional power transferred from background ions to the total fast ion population. It is summed over all fast ion species and charge states represented in that population.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion power due to collisions is the net rate at which Coulomb collisions with background ions change the kinetic energy of the total fast-ion population. The total includes all represented fast-ion species and charge states, so state-resolved contributions add to this population-integrated quantity.

A kinetic definition is the energy moment of the fast-ion collision operator associated with background ions:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fi}\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_{a\in\mathrm{FI}} \int_V \int \frac{1}{2} m_a v^2\, C_{a\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_a,\{f_i\}]\, d^3v\, dV
$$

where $a$ labels fast-ion species or charge states, $m_a$ is the particle mass, $v$ is particle speed, $f_a$ is the fast-ion distribution, $\{f_i\}$ denotes the background-ion distributions, $C_{a\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the part of the collision operator that changes $f_a$ through collisions with background ions, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

In practice this quantity is computed by taking the collisional energy moment of a kinetic fast-ion distribution and integrating over velocity space and plasma volume. Equivalently, it is the volume integral of the corresponding fast-ion collisional power density. For the same interacting populations and volume, energy conservation gives the reciprocal balance $P_{\mathrm{fi}\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}} + P_{i\leftarrow\mathrm{fi}}^{\mathrm{coll}} \simeq 0$, where the second term is the matching contribution to thermal-ion power due to collisions, apart from numerical error or additional species partitions.

Typical magnitudes range from 10^3-10^7 W in present-day auxiliary-heated experiments and can reach 10^7-10^8 W in reactor-scale plasmas. The signed value is often negative when energetic ions slow down on cooler background ions, because energy is then transferred from fast ions to the thermal-ion population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the background ion population to the fast-ion population.

NAMES.name: ion_state_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb-collisional power transferred to a specified ion species and charge state, abstracting over whether the recipient ion population is thermal or fast.
NAMES.long:
This quantity captures the net rate of energy exchange via Coulomb collisions between all plasma populations and a specific ion species resolved by charge state, integrated over the confined plasma volume. It serves as a structural abstraction encompassing both [thermal_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions), which covers Maxwellian-distributed thermal ion states, and [fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions), which covers non-Maxwellian suprathermal ion states.

The collisional power for ion state $s$ integrates the local collisional energy-transfer rate density $Q_s$ over the plasma volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{coll},s} = \int_V Q_s(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $Q_s$ is the net power density received by state $s$ from all collisional partners — electrons, thermal ions, and fast particles — via Coulomb interactions.

A positive value indicates net collisional heating of the ion state; a negative value indicates net energy loss, as occurs when a fast-ion state undergoes collisional slowing-down. This quantity contributes to the total ion energy channel within [power_due_to_collisions](name:power_due_to_collisions) when summed across all ion states and species. It is computed from integrated transport models or kinetic solvers that resolve ion distribution functions and species-resolved collisional energy-exchange rates.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb-collisional power transferred to the fast, non-Maxwellian ion population of a specified species and charge state. It is positive for collisional energy gain by that fast-ion state and negative for net slowing-down loss.
NAMES.long:
Fast ion state power due to collisions is the total rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the non-Maxwellian fast-ion population of one ion species and charge state. It is the volume integral of [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) and forms the fast-component counterpart to [thermal_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions) within the state-resolved collisional power balance.

For species $a$ and charge state $z$, a kinetic definition is the volume integral of the kinetic-energy moment of the collision term assigned to energy transfer into the fast distribution:

$$
P^{\mathrm{coll}}_{\mathrm{fast},a,z} = \int_V d^3x \int d^3v\, \frac{1}{2} m_a v^2\, \mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{field}}_{\mathrm{fast},a,z}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})
$$

where $m_a$ is the ion mass, $v = |\mathbf{v}|$, and $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{field}}_{\mathrm{fast},a,z}$ is the field-particle Coulomb-collision term acting on the fast-ion distribution for species $a$ in charge state $z$, summed over the relevant collision partners. The velocity-space kinetic-energy moment in the inner integral has units W m$^{-3}$ before volume integration, and the outer integral gives W.

In practice this quantity is inferred from kinetic modeling of non-Maxwellian fast-ion populations, such as those produced by neutral beam injection, ion-cyclotron heating, fusion reactions, or other energetic-particle sources. It is computed by evaluating the collisional energy moment locally and integrating over the plasma volume; summing over charge states and fast-ion species gives the corresponding aggregate [fast_particle_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_particle_power_due_to_collisions), while comparison with [ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:ion_state_power_due_to_collisions) separates fast and thermal contributions.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^3$-$10^7$ W in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, depending on heating power, fast-ion density, slowing-down time, and the selected species and charge state. Values for weak minority states can be below $10^3$ W, while high-power beam or radio-frequency heated fast-ion populations can reach several $10^6$-$10^7$ W; for ordinary slowing down, the value is often negative because collisions remove energy from the fast population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer net kinetic energy into the specified fast-ion species and charge state.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_neutral_beam_shinethrough
NAMES.short: Power carried by neutral beam particles that traverse the plasma without being ionized or otherwise stopped and leave the far plasma boundary. It represents the unabsorbed fraction of launched neutral beam power that is deposited on plasma-facing surfaces rather than in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Neutral beam shinethrough power is the portion of injected neutral beam power that remains in fast neutral particles after crossing the confined plasma and exits the far side without being absorbed. It is distinct from prompt fast-ion orbit loss after ionization and from power lost before the beam enters the plasma; the absorbed plasma-heating counterpart is power_due_to_neutral_beam_injection.

For beamlets or beam energy components treated independently, a survival-probability model is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{sh}} = \sum_b P_{b,0}\exp\!\left[-\int_{\ell_b} n_e(\ell)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{eff},b}(\ell)\,d\ell\right]
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{sh}}$ is the shinethrough power, $b$ indexes beamlets or beam energy components, $P_{b,0}$ is the launched neutral-beam power contribution for $b$ whose sum is related to [total_power_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:total_power_of_neutral_beam_injector), $\ell$ is distance along the neutral trajectory in m, $n_e(\ell)$ is electron density in m^-3, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{eff},b}(\ell)$ is the effective stopping cross-section in m^2 including ionization and charge-exchange removal of beam neutrals. The exponential factor is the neutral survival probability, so shinethrough decreases rapidly as the line-integrated density or stopping cross-section increases.

In practice, this quantity is computed by tracing neutral beamlets through reconstructed plasma density, temperature, and impurity distributions and integrating the corresponding attenuation along each path. Experimental constraints can come from calorimetry or thermography of shine-through armor, together with accounting of launched and plasma-deposited neutral beam power.

Typical values in high-density heating plasmas are $10^4-10^6$ W for multi-megawatt injectors, often less than 1-5% of launched power. Low-density startup, current ramp-up, very high beam energy, or long tangency paths can raise values to $10^6-10^7$ W, about 10-50% of launched power in unfavorable cases.

NAMES.name: radial_center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the plasma center-of-mass (barycentric) flow velocity, projected along the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial center-of-mass velocity is the projection of the barycentric bulk-flow velocity of the multispecies plasma onto the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis. It is the radial component of [center_of_mass_velocity](name:center_of_mass_velocity), which equals total plasma momentum density divided by total mass density.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
v_{R,\text{cm}} = \hat{R} \cdot \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\sum_s m_s n_s}
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$, $n_s$ is its number density, and $\mathbf{v}_s$ is its bulk fluid velocity.

Radial flows transport particles and energy across magnetic flux surfaces and are central to cross-field transport in the plasma edge and divertor. In multi-fluid transport models this component is computed directly from the species momentum equations; spectroscopic Doppler measurements of [radial_ion_velocity](name:radial_ion_velocity) and [radial_neutral_velocity](name:radial_neutral_velocity) for individual species, weighted by their respective mass densities, can provide an observational approximation. The analogous projection along the local magnetic field direction is [parallel_center_of_mass_velocity](name:parallel_center_of_mass_velocity).

Typical magnitudes in the plasma edge range from 10 to 1000 m/s, with larger transient values near the separatrix during particle-loss events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flow is directed in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, outward toward increasing major radius.

NAMES.name: radial_conductivity
NAMES.short: Radial conductivity is the diagonal radial component of the electrical conductivity tensor. In the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, it gives the scalar coefficient multiplying the radial electric-field component to form the radial Ohmic current-density contribution, excluding off-diagonal tensor couplings.
NAMES.long:
Radial conductivity is the radial diagonal component $\sigma_R \equiv \sigma_{RR}$ of the electrical conductivity tensor in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the local radial Ohmic response to the radial electric-field component, not the full tensor response of the plasma.

For the diagonal scalar component, the local constitutive relation is

$$
J_R = \sigma_R E_R
$$

where $J_R$ is the radial current density in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $E_R$ is the radial electric field in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $\sigma_R$ is the radial conductivity in $\Omega^{-1}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Off-diagonal tensor contributions such as $\sigma_{R\phi}E_\phi$ or $\sigma_{RZ}E_Z$ are separate conductivity components and are not included in this scalar coefficient.

In practice, radial conductivity is usually a modeled or inferred transport coefficient rather than a directly measured material property. It may be obtained from collisional, neoclassical, turbulent, or edge-closure transport models, or inferred from radial current balance when the radial electric field and non-Ohmic current contributions are independently constrained.

Typical effective values are highly model dependent because cross-field electrical conduction in a magnetized plasma is strongly suppressed compared with parallel conduction. Representative core-to-edge modeling values can span about $10^{-8}$-$10^{2}\ \Omega^{-1}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, with edge, scrape-off-layer, or numerical closure values sometimes lying outside this range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a positive radial electric-field component $E_R$ in the $+R$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system produces a radial current-density component $J_R$ in the $+R$ direction.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport
NAMES.short: Radial component of the electrical current density driven by anomalous transport processes, directed along the major-radius direction across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial component of the anomalous current density, $j_{r,\rm anom}$, is the projection of the anomalous current density vector onto the outward major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Anomalous transport refers to turbulence-driven processes that produce charge transport exceeding classical and neoclassical predictions, arising from fluctuating electric fields and density perturbations in the plasma.

The defining projection is

$$
j_{r,\rm anom} = \mathbf{j}_{\rm anom} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\rm anom}$ is the full [current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport) vector and $\hat{R}$ is the outward unit vector in the major-radius direction.

This radial current component is computed from turbulent transport simulations or anomalous transport models and is relevant primarily in the edge plasma where anomalous transport dominates. It contributes to the ambipolarity constraint and the radial electric field balance, complementing other radial current contributions such as [radial_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the anomalous current flows in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ (radially outward from the magnetic axis).

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Radial current density due to diamagnetic drift is the major-radius component of the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic current in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents current associated with species diamagnetic drifts, not radial bulk particle flow.
NAMES.long:
Radial current density due to diamagnetic drift is the $\hat{R}$ projection of the macroscopic diamagnetic current density caused by cross-field gradients of total scalar plasma pressure. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ increases counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity describes an electrical current associated with opposing ion and electron diamagnetic drifts, not a center-of-mass radial plasma velocity.

The defining relation for a scalar-pressure plasma description is:

$$
j_{\mathrm{dia},R} = \hat{R} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{|\mathbf{B}|^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude, $p = \sum_s p_s$ is the total scalar plasma pressure summed over species in Pa, $\nabla p$ is the pressure gradient in Pa m$^{-1}$, and $j_{\mathrm{dia},R}$ is the radial diamagnetic current density in A m$^{-2}$. If a pressure tensor rather than scalar pressure is retained, this scalar expression represents the isotropic-pressure limit.

In practice, this component is evaluated from reconstructed or modeled magnetic fields and pressure gradients, followed by projection onto $\hat{R}$. It is closely related to [radial_diamagnetic_current_density](name:radial_diamagnetic_current_density); [vertical_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) is the corresponding projection along $+\hat{Z}$.

Representative magnitudes are strongly device- and regime-dependent because $|\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia}|$ scales approximately as $|\nabla p|/|\mathbf{B}|$. Order-of-magnitude radial components can be below 1 A m$^{-2}$ in weak-gradient regions and can reach 10$^2$-10$^5$ A m$^{-2}$ where pressure gradients are steep; the radial projection may be much smaller than the full diamagnetic current density if the current is nearly tangential to flux surfaces.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic drift current density has a component in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the heat-viscosity-driven current density, projected onto the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the contribution to the plasma current density arising from heat-viscosity terms in fluid transport theory.
NAMES.long:
Radial current density due to heat viscosity is the major-radius component of the current-density contribution generated by heat-viscosity terms in plasma fluid transport theory. The heat-viscosity contribution is the current density associated with the heat-viscosity part of the stress closure in the fluid-moment equations; this quantity is its projection onto the radial direction.

The radial component is obtained by projecting the heat-viscosity current-density contribution onto the major-radius unit vector:

$$
j_{R,\mathrm{hv}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $j_{R,\mathrm{hv}}$ is the radial current density due to heat viscosity, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}$ is the [heat-viscosity current-density contribution](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is evaluated in transport or fluid-moment modeling from the chosen heat-viscosity closure and the local plasma state, then projected along $\hat{R}$. It is not measured directly; estimates are inferred by combining equilibrium geometry with density, temperature, flow, and current-balance information. It is the radial counterpart of the [parallel](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), [toroidal](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and [vertical](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) components of the same heat-viscosity current density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the heat-viscosity current-density contribution points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction
NAMES.short: Radial component, along increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the electric current density associated with ion-neutral friction.
NAMES.long:
Radial current density due to ion-neutral friction is the major-radius component of the electric current density contribution associated with collisional momentum exchange between plasma ions and neutral atoms or molecules. It describes charge transport produced by ion-neutral drag and the resulting ion momentum balance, not the ion-neutral friction force density itself.

The component is defined by projecting the ion-neutral-friction current-density vector onto the radial unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
j_{R,\mathrm{in}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $j_{R,\mathrm{in}}$ is the radial current density in A.m^-2, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the electric current density contribution due to ion-neutral friction in A.m^-2, and $\hat{R}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $R$.

In practice this quantity is computed from fluid or kinetic transport models that include ion momentum balance, charge conservation, ion-neutral collision rates, neutral densities, and ion-neutral relative flows. Experimental constraints commonly come from combinations of plasma density and temperature measurements, spectroscopy of neutral and ion populations, and magnetic or electrostatic constraints on current closure.

Typical magnitudes are often about 0.01-100 A.m^-2 in weakly neutral, magnetized edge plasma regions, and can reach 100-10000 A.m^-2 locally in cold, dense, partially ionized boundary or divertor conditions. The value is sensitive to neutral density, ion-neutral collision frequency, plasma magnetization, and the current-closure path.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current density contribution due to ion-neutral friction points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the current density due to perpendicular viscous stress, projected along the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial current density due to perpendicular viscosity is the $\hat{R}$ projection of the plasma current-density contribution associated with the divergence of the perpendicular viscous stress tensor. It represents the part of that viscosity-driven current flowing along increasing or decreasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis.

A component-level definition is

$$
j_R^{(\Pi_\perp)} = \hat{R}\cdot\mathbf{j}^{(\Pi_\perp)}, \qquad (\mathbf{j}^{(\Pi_\perp)}\times\mathbf{B})_\perp \simeq -\left(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\perp\right)_\perp
$$

where $j_R^{(\Pi_\perp)}$ is this radial component in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{j}^{(\Pi_\perp)}$ is the current-density contribution attributed to perpendicular viscosity, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\perp$ is the perpendicular viscous stress tensor whose divergence is a force density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. The force-balance relation identifies the part of the current constrained by the perpendicular Lorentz balance; any field-aligned contribution associated with the same stress source is treated separately, for example by [parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity).

This quantity is usually computed from a transport or edge-plasma model using a closure for perpendicular viscosity, the magnetic equilibrium, and spatial gradients of flow and pressure. It is not normally measured directly; it is inferred as one term in current balance and can be compared with [radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity), [radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), and other contributions to [radial_current_density](name:radial_total_current_density). The related [poloidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) describes the projection of the same viscosity-driven current onto a poloidal direction.

Representative magnitudes are highly regime- and closure-dependent, so there is no universal device-independent range in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. The value is expected to be near zero where perpendicular viscous stress gradients are weak and can become localized in edge, scrape-off-layer, or strongly sheared-flow regions; interpretation is usually made relative to the total radial current density and to the other modeled current-density channels in the same calculation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, outward from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: First derivative of electron pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius. It gives the signed outward variation of electron pressure across nested magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of electron pressure is the rate of change of the electron pressure $p_e$ with the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. It describes how the flux-surface-labeled electron pressure varies from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary and provides the scalar flux-coordinate gradient used in transport balance terms.

The derivative is defined by

$$
\frac{d p_e}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $p_e$ is the electron pressure in pascals and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless, with $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=1$ at the boundary reference surface. Because the radial coordinate is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as pressure, Pa.

In practice this quantity is computed by forming a smooth electron-pressure function on nested flux surfaces and differentiating it with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. If pressure is formed from electron density and temperature, use $p_e=n_e T_e$ when $T_e$ is in joules, or equivalently $p_e=e n_e T_e$ when $T_e$ is reported in electronvolts, where $e$ converts electronvolts to joules. The corresponding physical vector gradient is $\nabla p_e = (d p_e/d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}})\nabla\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, so conversion to a spatial gradient depends on the flux-coordinate metric.

Typical absolute magnitudes are about $10^3$-$10^5$ Pa in the core of medium-sized tokamaks and can reach $10^5$-$10^6$ Pa in steep pedestals or internal transport barriers. Values depend strongly on density, temperature, confinement regime, and the radial width over which the pressure changes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron pressure increases with increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, i.e., outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial derivative of fast-electron perpendicular pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius. It measures how the suprathermal electron pressure component perpendicular to the magnetic field changes from the magnetic axis toward the last-closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Radial derivative of fast-electron perpendicular pressure is the first derivative of the suprathermal electron pressure component perpendicular to the magnetic field with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate. The radial variable is $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ in flux coordinates $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$, with $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=1$ at the last-closed flux surface. It is not a derivative with respect to the major radius $R$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The derivative is defined as:

$$
G_{p_{\mathrm{fast},e,\perp}}}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}) = \frac{\partial p_{\mathrm{fast},e,\perp}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fast},e,\perp}$ is the fast-electron perpendicular pressure and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless, so the derivative has the same unit as pressure. A conversion to a gradient per meter requires the metric factor relating $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ to physical distance along the chosen radial direction.

In practice this quantity is computed by differentiating an inferred or modeled fast-electron perpendicular pressure distribution on flux surfaces. The pressure may be constrained by kinetic modeling and diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal electrons, and the derivative is often regularized or smoothed because differentiation amplifies local uncertainty. It enters gradient-driven transport terms and closures involving anisotropic fast-electron pressure.

Typical absolute magnitudes are near 0 Pa when the suprathermal electron population is negligible, about 10-10^4 Pa in many heating or current-drive scenarios, and can reach 10^5 Pa or more in localized regions with strong energetic-electron pressure gradients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-electron perpendicular pressure increases with increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ from the magnetic axis toward the last-closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First derivative of the fast (non-thermal) ion number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, summed over all ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of fast ion density quantifies how rapidly the non-thermal ion population varies across nested flux surfaces, expressed as the first derivative of [fast_ion_density](name:fast_ion_density) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, which runs from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface. The density is summed over all charge states of the fast ion population, consistent with its parent quantity.

The defining relation is:

$$
\frac{d n_\mathrm{fast}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the total fast ion number density aggregated over charge states and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, so the derivative carries the same unit as the density itself.

This gradient appears directly in transport flux expressions and is required by numerical transport solvers to evaluate radial diffusion and convection terms without recomputing the derivative from raw profiles. For core-peaked fast ion distributions, as typically arise from neutral beam injection or fusion-born alpha deposition, the gradient is negative through most of the plasma interior and steepens near the deposition region. The [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density) captures the curvature of the same profile, while [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_density) provides the equivalent gradient resolved per charge state.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast ion density increases in the direction of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First derivative of the scalar, charge-state-averaged fast-ion pressure with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius rho_tor,norm. It quantifies how the nonthermal ion pressure changes from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of fast-ion pressure is the gradient of the scalar fast-ion pressure with respect to the flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, the normalized toroidal flux radius that increases from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary. The pressure is the charge-state-averaged nonthermal ion pressure; it is not specifically the parallel or perpendicular pressure component of an anisotropic pressure tensor.

The quantity is defined as

$$
G_{\mathrm{fast}}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}) = \frac{\partial p_{\mathrm{fast}}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the scalar fast-ion pressure and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless. Because the differentiation coordinate is dimensionless, $G_{\mathrm{fast}}$ has the same unit as pressure, Pa.

In practice, $p_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is obtained from a fast-ion distribution function or pressure moment, often constrained by equilibrium reconstruction and energetic-particle diagnostics such as neutron emission, fast-ion D-alpha emission, gamma-ray measurements, or neutral-particle analysis. The derivative is usually computed after radial smoothing or fitting, because direct finite differences of reconstructed fast-ion pressure can amplify noise.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^3-10^5$ Pa in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas and can approach $10^6$ Pa where the fast-ion pressure changes over a narrow radial interval. The value is often negative in the core-to-edge direction because fast-ion pressure commonly decreases outward, but positive values can occur near localized sources or redistribution regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the scalar fast-ion pressure increases with increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: First derivative of the fast (non-thermal) ion number density for a specified charge state with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius rho_tor,norm.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of fast-ion state density is the change of the number density of non-thermal ions in a specified charge state with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. It is the radial-gradient counterpart of [fast_ion_state_density](name:fast_ion_state_density) and is distinct from the charge-state-summed [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density).

It is defined by differentiating the charge-state-resolved fast-ion density with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$:

$$
g_s(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}) = \frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{fast},s}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $g_s$ is the radial derivative, $n_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the fast-ion state density for charge state $s$ in m$^{-3}$, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux radius, with $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=1$ at the plasma boundary.

In practice this derivative is computed numerically from charge-state-resolved fast-ion density estimates obtained from fast-ion modeling, transport analysis, or diagnostic-constrained reconstruction. Finite-difference, spline, or other differentiation methods may be used, so the value is sensitive to radial grid resolution, smoothing, and boundary treatment, especially near localized sources, loss regions, or steep transport barriers. It enters gradient-driven transport terms, for example diffusive particle flux contributions proportional to $-D_s\,\partial n_{\mathrm{fast},s}/\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, where $D_s$ is an effective diffusivity for charge state $s$.

Typical absolute magnitudes are often $10^{16}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in neutral-beam- or radio-frequency-heated tokamak plasmas, with values approaching $10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ in sharply localized deposition, ionization, or loss regions. Weakly heated or nearly flat fast-ion populations can have gradients close to zero.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion density of the specified charge state increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of charge-state-resolved fast ion pressure with respect to the flux coordinate rho_tor,norm (normalized toroidal flux radius).
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of fast ion state pressure is the first derivative of the pressure carried by the nonthermal fast-ion population in a specified ion charge state with respect to the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ (normalized toroidal flux radius). It describes the radial pressure-gradient drive associated with one ionization state, distinct from the charge-state-summed quantity [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure).

For charge state $q$, the derivative is defined by:

$$
G_{p,\mathrm{fast},q}(\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}) = \frac{\partial p_{\mathrm{fast},q}}{\partial \rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $G_{p,\mathrm{fast},q}$ is the radial derivative, $p_{\mathrm{fast},q}$ is the fast ion pressure of charge state $q$ in Pa, and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, with 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface. Because the differentiation coordinate is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as pressure.

In transport modeling, this quantity is computed by evaluating the charge-state-resolved fast ion pressure from the fast-ion distribution or moment equations and differentiating it along $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. It is the fast-ion counterpart of [radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure), and it is used together with related gradients such as [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_density); radial curvature is described by second-derivative quantities such as [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure) and [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_state_pressure).

Typical absolute values range from 10^2-10^5 Pa in present tokamak plasmas, depending on heating power, charge-state population, confinement, and how rapidly the fast-ion pressure changes across the plasma radius. Larger values can occur in strongly heated plasmas or near localized fast-ion pressure gradients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast ion state pressure increases as $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ increases from the magnetic axis toward the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of total ion pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux coordinate, summed over all ion charge states.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of total [ion_pressure](name:ion_pressure) quantifies how the aggregate ion pressure $P_i$, summed over all charge states, varies across nested flux surfaces. This pressure gradient drives neoclassical and anomalous transport fluxes, contributes to the radial force balance, and appears as a source term in the ion energy transport equation.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{dP_i}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $P_i$ is the total ion pressure in Pa and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the separatrix.

In transport solvers, this derivative is evaluated numerically from the ion pressure profile and used in the discretization of the radial transport equations. The [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure) complements this quantity for higher-order finite-difference stencils. For charge-state-resolved calculations, the analogous quantity is [radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure); the electron counterpart is [radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure).

In typical H-mode plasmas the ion pressure peaks at the core and decreases toward the edge, so this derivative takes negative values throughout most of the profile, with the largest magnitudes occurring in the steep pedestal region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion pressure increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, that is, in the outward direction from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of the thermal pressure of a specified ion charge state with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, providing the charge-state-resolved pressure gradient for transport equations.
NAMES.long:
The radial pressure gradient of a single ion charge state, quantifying how the charge-state-resolved thermal pressure changes across nested flux surfaces parametrized by the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$, which runs from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{\partial p_{i,s}}{\partial \rho_{\rm tor,norm}}
$$

where $p_{i,s}$ is the [ion_state_pressure](name:ion_state_pressure) (thermal pressure of ion charge state $s$) and $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, so the derivative retains the unit of pressure.

This gradient is evaluated numerically by transport solvers discretizing the radial transport equations for each ion charge state. The charge-state-summed counterpart, integrating over all ionization levels of the ion species, is [radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure), and the second-order radial derivative at the charge-state level is [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_pressure). The analogous electron quantity is [radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure). In typical confined plasmas, pressure decreases from core to edge, so this derivative is negative over most of the profile, with steeper magnitudes in pedestal and internal transport barrier regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge state pressure increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of the temperature of a specified ion charge state with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, giving the local temperature gradient driving ion energy transport.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of [ion_charge_state_temperature](name:ion_charge_state_temperature) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ quantifies how steeply the temperature of a specified ion charge state varies across nested flux surfaces. This gradient enters directly into the thermodynamic force terms of the ion energy transport equation, driving both neoclassical and turbulent heat fluxes in the ion channel and controlling the local power balance for that charge state.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{dT_{i,z}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $T_{i,z}$ is the temperature of ions in charge state $z$ and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to zero at the magnetic axis and unity at the last closed flux surface.

This derivative is computed from the charge-state-resolved ion temperature profile within transport solver numerics. The companion quantity [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_state_temperature) provides the profile curvature; [radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature) gives the charge-state-averaged analog. Steep gradients are characteristic of internal transport barriers and the pedestal region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $T_{i,z}$ increases in the direction of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Rate of change of poloidal electron fluid velocity with normalized toroidal flux radius. It represents the radial shear of electron poloidal flow.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of poloidal electron velocity is the change of the electron fluid velocity component in the poloidal direction with normalized toroidal flux radius. It quantifies outward shear of the electron poloidal flow and is used in transport and momentum-balance terms that depend on flow gradients.

Using flux coordinates $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$, the first radial derivative is defined by

$$
G_{v_{\theta,e}} = \left.\frac{\partial v_{\theta,e}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}\right|_{t,\theta,\phi}
$$

where $v_{\theta,e}$ is the poloidal electron fluid velocity in m.s^-1, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux radius, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The partial-derivative notation means that time and angular coordinates are held fixed; when $v_{\theta,e}$ is represented as a flux-surface quantity, this reduces to the ordinary derivative of that radial function with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. Because $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as velocity.

In practice this quantity is computed by differentiating an inferred or modeled electron poloidal flow with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. The underlying flow may be obtained from force-balance analysis, electric-field constraints, spectroscopy, reflectometry, or kinetic transport modeling; smoothing or regularized differentiation is commonly needed because radial derivatives amplify measurement noise.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^2$-$10^4$ m.s^-1 in the core and can reach $10^4$-$10^5$ m.s^-1 in regions with strong flow shear, such as pedestal or internal-transport-barrier regions. The sign distinguishes outward increase from outward decrease of the signed poloidal electron velocity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron fluid velocity component in the $+\theta$ direction of flux coordinates $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$ increases as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Radial derivative of the poloidal velocity of a specified ion species and charge state with respect to the outward normalized toroidal flux radius in flux coordinates (rho_tor_norm, theta, phi). It measures the charge-state-resolved radial shear of poloidal ion flow across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of [poloidal_ion_state_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity) quantifies how the poloidal flow of ion species $s$ in charge state $k$ changes with outward normalized toroidal flux radius. It is a charge-state-resolved measure of poloidal flow shear in flux coordinates $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=1$ at the plasma boundary used for the normalization.

For ion species $s$ and charge-state index $k$, the quantity is defined by differentiation at fixed poloidal angle, toroidal angle, and time:

$$
D_\rho v_{\theta,s,k} = \left(\frac{\partial v_{\theta,s,k}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}\right)_{\theta,\phi,t}
$$

where $v_{\theta,s,k}$ is the poloidal velocity component along increasing $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$. The species label $s$ identifies the ion species, such as a fuel isotope or impurity element, and the charge-state label $k$ identifies its ionization stage. Because $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as velocity.

In practice this derivative is obtained by differentiating the charge-state-resolved poloidal velocity as a function of $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, using finite-difference, finite-volume, spline, or spectral methods, or from a momentum-balance calculation that directly evaluates radial gradient terms. It enters charge-state-resolved momentum transport through viscous, inertial, and inter-state coupling terms.

The related [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_velocity) is the ion-species counterpart after combining charge states. If the bulk ion poloidal velocity is density-weighted, $v_{\theta,s} = \sum_k n_{s,k} v_{\theta,s,k}/\sum_k n_{s,k}$, then its radial derivative contains both the density-weighted sum over $k$ of $D_\rho v_{\theta,s,k}$ and additional terms from radial variation of the charge-state densities $n_{s,k}$; it is therefore not generally a simple unweighted sum of charge-state derivatives.

Typical magnitudes range from 10-10000 m.s^-1, depending on collisionality, impurity content, rotation drive, and how sharply the charge-state flow varies across neighboring flux surfaces.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\theta,s,k}$, defined along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$, increases with increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ at fixed $\theta$ and $\phi$.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of the poloidal ion bulk-flow velocity with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, averaged over ion charge states.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of the poloidal ion velocity quantifies how sharply the poloidal component of the ion bulk flow changes along the minor-radial direction at a given flux surface. It is the charge-state-averaged quantity; the charge-state-resolved counterpart is [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_state_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_state_velocity). This gradient enters the ion momentum transport equation through viscous stress and flow-shear terms, and transport solvers require it to close the discretized radial momentum balance.

The quantity is defined as

$$
\frac{d v_{\mathrm{pol,ion}}}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $v_{\mathrm{pol,ion}}$ is the poloidal component of the charge-state-averaged ion bulk velocity (the parent quantity poloidal_ion_velocity) and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} \in [0,1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless, the derivative carries the same unit as the velocity itself.

This quantity is computed numerically within transport solver frameworks from the radial profile of the poloidal ion velocity. It is used together with [second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_velocity) to build finite-difference or spectral representations of the momentum equation. The analogous electron-fluid quantity is [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\mathrm{pol,ion}}$ increases with increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, i.e., when the poloidal ion bulk flow has a positive outward radial gradient.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: First derivative, with respect to the outward normalized toroidal flux radius, of the toroidal velocity component of a specified ion charge state. It measures the radial shear of charge-state toroidal rotation across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of toroidal ion state velocity is the local rate of change of the toroidal velocity component for a specified ion charge state with respect to the outward normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. It quantifies charge-state-resolved toroidal rotation shear across nested magnetic flux surfaces.

The defining derivative is

$$
\frac{d v_\phi}{d \rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $v_\phi$ is the [toroidal ion state velocity](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity) in m.s^-1, taken along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height. The coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last-closed flux surface, so the derivative also has unit m.s^-1.

In practice this quantity is obtained by differentiating a measured, reconstructed, or modeled radial dependence of charge-state toroidal velocity after mapping the velocity to $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. It is used in momentum-transport analysis to represent local toroidal rotation shear for a particular charge state; the charge-state-averaged analog is [radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity), the poloidal analog is [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_state_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_ion_state_velocity), and curvature of the same radial dependence is represented by [second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_state_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_state_velocity).

Typical absolute values are about 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1 in many core-plasma rotation-shear regions, and can reach several 10^5-10^6 m.s^-1 where toroidal velocity changes rapidly over a narrow interval of $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. The sign and magnitude can differ between ion charge states when collisional coupling, sources, or impurity transport produce distinct rotation behavior.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the component of the ion charge-state velocity along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame becomes more positive with increasing outward normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$.

NAMES.name: radial_electric_field
NAMES.short: Major-radius component of the plasma electric field in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R points outward from the toroidal symmetry axis. It enters the radial force balance and sets the local E cross B drift.
NAMES.long:
The radial electric field is the projection of the plasma electric-field vector onto the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ increases outward from the toroidal symmetry axis. It is a central quantity in radial force balance and governs the radial structure of the $\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}$ flow.

The component is defined by projection onto the radial basis vector:

$$
E_R = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing major radius $R$. In the electrostatic approximation it reduces to $E_R = -\partial \Phi / \partial R$, the negative radial gradient of the electrostatic potential $\Phi$; inductive contributions can arise when the magnetic vector potential varies in time.

The radial electric field is commonly inferred from radial force balance using measured pressure gradients and flow velocities of a tracked ion species, from Doppler reflectometry via the measured perpendicular rotation near the cutoff layer, or from local potential-gradient measurements in the plasma edge. Interpretation depends on the magnetic geometry, because the observed $\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}$ velocity combines the electric field with the local magnetic-field direction.

Magnitudes are typically of order $10^2$-$10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ across much of the core plasma and can reach $10^4$-$10^5$ V m$^{-1}$ or larger in steep-gradient edge pedestals and transport barriers; the sign and magnitude vary strongly with radius, confinement regime, plasma rotation, and pressure-gradient strength.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric-field vector has a component in the $+R$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, outward from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial component of the electron particle diffusion coefficient, relating the cross-field electron density flux to the local radial density gradient normal to magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The radial electron diffusion coefficient $D_{e,r}$ characterizes Fickian diffusive transport of electron particle density in the direction perpendicular to magnetic flux surfaces. It is the cross-field particle diffusivity for the electron species, distinct from the thermal energy diffusivity captured by [radial_electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient).

The coefficient enters the electron continuity equation through Fick's first law:

$$
\Gamma_{e,r} = -D_{e,r} \frac{\partial n_e}{\partial r}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,r}$ is the outward radial electron particle flux, $n_e$ is the electron number density, and $r$ is the coordinate normal to the local flux surface.

In edge-plasma transport simulations, $D_{e,r}$ encodes the net cross-field diffusion from both neoclassical and anomalous (turbulence-driven) mechanisms; in practice the anomalous contribution from drift-wave and interchange turbulence dominates by one or more orders of magnitude over the classical collisional value. The coefficient is an input or output of fluid transport solvers employing unstructured grid descriptions of the edge and scrape-off-layer regions. The ion-species analog is [radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient), and the neutral-particle counterpart is [radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_diffusion_coefficient).

Typical values in the edge plasma and scrape-off layer range from 0.01 to 1 m²·s⁻¹, with anomalously enhanced values of 0.1–1 m²·s⁻¹ common across L-mode and H-mode regimes.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial component of the effective diffusion coefficient governing cross-field diffusive transport of electron thermal energy, relating the outward heat flux to the negative radial electron temperature gradient.
NAMES.long:
The radial electron energy diffusion coefficient is the radial projection of the effective thermal diffusivity for the electron energy channel, quantifying how efficiently electron heat is transported across magnetic flux surfaces by diffusion along the flux-surface-normal direction. It aggregates contributions from collisional, neoclassical, and turbulent mechanisms into a single scalar coefficient specific to the radial transport direction.

The defining Fickian closure for the radial diffusive electron conductive heat flux $q_{e,r}$ is:

$$
q_{e,r} = -n_e \chi_{e,r} \, \nabla_r T_e
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density, $T_e$ is the electron temperature, $\nabla_r T_e$ is its radial gradient, and $\chi_{e,r}$ is this radial energy diffusion coefficient. Unlike the orientation-independent [electron_energy_diffusivity](name:electron_energy_diffusivity), this coefficient is restricted to the cross-field radial direction and thus enters directly into 1D radial transport models.

The coefficient is inferred from radial power balance by combining electron temperature profiles obtained from Thomson scattering or electron cyclotron emission diagnostics with modeled electron heat deposition from external heating and radiation accounting. Typical core values in H-mode tokamak discharges range from 0.3 to 3 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, with elevated values in L-mode reaching 5–10 m$^2$ s$^{-1}$. The corresponding ion-channel quantity is [radial_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_ion_energy_diffusion_coefficient), and the radial electron particle transport coefficient is [radial_electron_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_electron_diffusion_coefficient).

NAMES.name: radial_electron_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial component of the net electron energy flux density crossing magnetic flux surfaces, representing electron energy transported per unit area per unit time.
NAMES.long:
Radial electron energy flux is the outward-normal component of the electron energy-flux density across magnetic flux surfaces. It represents net cross-field transport of electron energy, independent of the particular closure used to separate diffusive, convective, or other contributions.

For a radial flux coordinate $\rho$ in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\rho$ increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, the radial component is

$$
q_{e,r} = \mathbf{q}_e \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_\rho
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_e$ is the electron energy-flux density in W m$^{-2}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\rho = \nabla\rho / |\nabla\rho|$ is the unit normal to surfaces of constant $\rho$ in the direction of increasing $\rho$.

In transport analysis this quantity is inferred from the electron energy balance, using sources and sinks such as auxiliary heating, collisional exchange with ions, radiation, particle sources, and the time variation of electron thermal energy. Modeling may parameterize it with effective diffusion and effective energy-convection coefficients, but those coefficients describe a chosen transport closure rather than the definition of the flux itself.

Typical magnitudes range from about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-2}$ in magnetically confined plasmas, depending on heating power, confinement regime, radius, and edge gradients. Larger transient values can occur during rapid profile changes or near strong localized power deposition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron energy is transported toward increasing radial flux coordinate $\rho$, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Net number of electrons crossing a unit area oriented perpendicular to the radial direction per unit time, combining diffusive and convective cross-field transport contributions in the electron density continuity equation.
NAMES.long:
The radial electron particle flux $\Gamma_{e,r}$ is the projection of the electron particle-flux density vector onto the radial direction, quantifying the net cross-field electron transport per unit area per unit time. It combines contributions from collisional diffusion, bulk convective flow, and turbulent fluctuations, and enters directly into the electron continuity equation governing the evolution of the electron density profile.

In 1D transport modeling, the flux is commonly decomposed into diffusive and convective components:

$$
\Gamma_{e,r} = -D_e \frac{\partial n_e}{\partial r} + V_e n_e
$$

where $D_e$ is the radial electron particle diffusion coefficient, $V_e$ is the effective convection velocity (see [radial_electron_convection_velocity](name:radial_electron_convection_velocity)), and $n_e$ is the local electron number density.

This quantity is computed by transport models incorporating measured electron density profiles together with reconstructed or modeled diffusion and convection coefficients. The radial integral of $\Gamma_{e,r}$ must close the global particle balance, including ionization sources and wall recycling. The analogous quantity for individual ion charge states is given by [radial_ion_state_particle_flux](name:radial_ion_state_particle_flux).
NAMES.sign: Positive when electrons flow radially outward, away from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Projection of the electron fluid bulk flow velocity onto the major-radius direction, giving the net electron flow toward or away from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial electron velocity $v_{e,R}$ is the component of the electron bulk fluid velocity resolved along the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is measured from the machine symmetry axis. It governs cross-field electron mass transport in the poloidal plane and enters the electron continuity equation through the divergence of the radial particle flux $n_e v_{e,R}$. It is one component of the parent vector [electron_velocity](name:electron_velocity).

The quantity is defined as the first velocity-space moment of the electron distribution function $f_e$ projected onto $\hat{R}$:

$$
v_{e,R} = \frac{1}{n_e} \int v_R \, f_e(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $n_e$ is the local electron number density and $v_R$ is the $\hat{R}$-component of a particle velocity $\mathbf{v}$.

Radial electron flow is generally much smaller in magnitude than [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) but is significant for cross-field particle transport, particularly in the edge and scrape-off layer. It is most often inferred from transport analysis using measured density profiles and particle source rates, or derived from fluid simulations. The sibling components [poloidal_electron_velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity) and [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity) complete the cylindrical decomposition; the ion analog is [radial_ion_velocity](name:radial_ion_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron fluid flows in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, i.e., radially outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radial_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Effective radial convection velocity for thermal energy transport in the edge plasma. It is the major-radius component of the effective velocity that advects enthalpy in the convective part of the energy flux, and should not be read as the bulk plasma flow speed.
NAMES.long:
Radial energy convection velocity is the major-radius component, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, of an effective velocity that represents the convective (advective) part of the thermal energy flux. It is a transport descriptor rather than a measured flow: it packages the radial enthalpy advection into an equivalent velocity that, when multiplied by a pressure-like normalization, reproduces the convective energy flux. The orthogonal poloidal projection is given by [poloidal_energy_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_energy_convection_velocity).

The effective velocity is defined by dividing the radial convective energy flux density by an enthalpy normalization. For a single non-relativistic monatomic thermal population this takes the form

$$
v_R = \frac{q_R^{\mathrm{conv}}}{\tfrac{5}{2}\, p}
$$

where $v_R$ is the radial energy convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $q_R^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial convective energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $p$ is the thermal pressure in Pa (with $p = n k_B T$), and the factor $5/2$ is the dimensionless enthalpy coefficient. This $\tfrac{5}{2} p v_R$ relation is the standard enthalpy-flux normalization; other decompositions of the total energy flux may select a different convective coefficient, so the precise value depends on how the flux is split into convective, conductive, and source contributions.

In transport analysis this quantity is obtained by separating the modeled or reconstructed radial energy flux into convective and conductive parts and assigning the convective part to an effective velocity at each grid location. Working on a generalized geometry grid allows the quantity to be represented across the edge, scrape-off layer, and divertor, where nested flux-surface coordinates lose regularity. Species- and population-resolved counterparts describe electron, ion, and neutral energy convection separately.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convective transport of energy is directed toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Radial ion charge-state momentum diffusivity is the cross-flux-surface transport coefficient for momentum density carried by ions in a specified ionization state. It relates the diffusive radial momentum-density flux to the radial gradient of that same momentum density.
NAMES.long:
Radial ion charge-state momentum diffusivity is an effective scalar coefficient for diffusive transport of momentum density carried by ions in a specified ionization state across magnetic flux surfaces. It applies to the momentum density associated with the flow component being modeled and separates Fickian diffusion from convective momentum pinch, external torque, and collisional exchange terms. Larger values imply faster flattening of the charge-state momentum-density distribution.

Using a radial flux-surface label $r$ that increases from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, the diffusive radial flux of momentum density for charge state $k$ is written as:

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{p,k,r}
= -D_{p,k,r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}
\left(m_i n_{i,k} u_{i,k}\right)
$$

where $D_{p,k,r}$ is the radial ion charge-state momentum diffusivity in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $\Gamma^{\mathrm{diff}}_{p,k,r}$ is the diffusive radial flux of momentum density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ and is positive toward increasing $r$, $m_i$ is the ion mass in kg, $n_{i,k}$ is the number density of charge state $k$ in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $u_{i,k}$ is the relevant flow-velocity component in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $m_i n_{i,k}u_{i,k}$ is the corresponding momentum density.

In practice this coefficient is inferred from momentum-balance analysis or calculated by neoclassical and turbulent transport models using charge-state-resolved density, flow, source, torque, and collision information. Charge-state resolution is important for impurity transport because ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and interspecies friction can change which ions carry the momentum and how rapidly it is redistributed.

Typical effective values in magnetically confined plasmas are 0.05-10 m^2.s^-1 in the confined plasma core, with values below 0.1 m^2.s^-1 possible for weakly turbulent or neoclassical transport and values of 10-50 m^2.s^-1 possible near steep-gradient regions or during strong turbulence. Heavy impurity charge states can differ from main ions because collisionality and charge-exchange sources modify their momentum relaxation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diffusive radial flux of ion charge-state momentum density is opposite to the radial gradient of that momentum density.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Radial component of the momentum flux for ions in a specified ionization state, giving the signed net transport rate of radial linear momentum per unit area across surfaces of constant rho in flux coordinates (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
Radial ion charge state momentum flux is the charge-state-resolved ion contribution to radial momentum transport across surfaces of constant $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$. It represents the signed net rate at which radial linear momentum is transported through unit area, and therefore has the dimensions of pressure.

A compact definition is the oriented flux density of radial linear momentum:

$$
\Gamma_{\rho p_\rho}^{i,z} = \frac{dP_\rho^{i,z}}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $i$ labels the ion species, $z$ labels the ionization state, $dP_\rho^{i,z}$ is the signed radial linear momentum transported across the oriented surface element $dA$ in time interval $dt$, $P_\rho^{i,z}$ has unit kg m s^-1, $dA$ has unit m^2, and $\Gamma_{\rho p_\rho}^{i,z}$ has unit kg.m^-1.s^-2.

In fluid or kinetic moment descriptions, this net flux can be decomposed into convective transport of radial momentum by radial motion and stress-like contributions. A common interpretation is a term proportional to $m_i n_{i,z} u_\rho^2$, with $m_i$ the ion mass, $n_{i,z}$ the charge-state density, and $u_\rho$ the radial flow speed, plus pressure, viscous, collisional, or turbulent stress terms according to the closure being used. The standard name denotes the total radial component, not any particular closure or decomposition.

This quantity is usually obtained from transport modeling, moment equations, or momentum-balance analysis using charge-state densities, flows, gradients, and momentum sources. Summing over ionization states gives the aggregate [radial_ion_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_momentum_flux_over_edge_region); adding non-ion and field contributions gives the total [radial_momentum_flux](name:radial_magnetic_vector_potential). The corresponding source term in the balance equation is [radial_ion_charge_state_momentum_source](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_flux), and the neutral-state analog is [radial_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:radial_neutral_state_momentum_flux).

Typical magnitudes are strongly regime and closure dependent. For deuterium-like ions with $n_{i,z}=10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3 and radial flows $u_\rho=1$-$10^3$ m s^-1, the convective scaling $m_i n_{i,z} u_\rho^2$ spans roughly $10^{-8}$-$10^{-1}$ kg.m^-1.s^-2; stress and turbulent transport terms may be smaller or larger and are often compared with the local charge-state pressure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net radial momentum flux crosses a surface of constant $\rho$ in the direction of increasing $\rho$.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_charge_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged radial particle flux of ions in a specified charge state, giving the net number crossing a magnetic flux surface per unit area and time.
NAMES.long:
Radial ion charge state particle flux is the flux-surface-averaged radial number flux of an ion species $i$ in charge state $q$. It counts particles rather than electric charge and represents the net transport of that charge state across a magnetic flux surface, including both outward and inward contributions.

For a magnetic flux surface labeled by an outward dimensionless radial flux coordinate $\rho$ and, when useful, by an effective minor radius $r_\mathrm{eff}$, the flux is the surface average of the normal projection of the particle-flux density:

$$
\Gamma_{i,q}^{r_\mathrm{eff}} = \left\langle \mathbf{F}_{i,q}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{r_\mathrm{eff}} \right\rangle_\mathrm{fs}
$$

where $\Gamma_{i,q}^{r_\mathrm{eff}}$ has units m^-2 s^-1, $\mathbf{F}_{i,q}$ is the vector particle-flux density for species $i$ and charge state $q$ with units m^-2 s^-1, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{r_\mathrm{eff}}$ is the outward unit normal to surfaces of increasing $r_\mathrm{eff}$, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_\mathrm{fs}$ denotes a flux-surface average. The coordinate $\rho$ has unit 1 and $r_\mathrm{eff}$ is in meters. A common diffusive-convective representation is $\Gamma_{i,q}^{r_\mathrm{eff}}=-D_{i,q}\,\partial n_{i,q}/\partial r_\mathrm{eff}+V_{i,q}n_{i,q}$, where $D_{i,q}$ has units m^2 s^-1, $V_{i,q}$ has units m s^-1, and $n_{i,q}$ has units m^-3.

In a charge-state-resolved continuity balance, this flux enters through the radial divergence term: $\partial n_{i,q}/\partial t = -\mathcal{V}'^{-1}\partial(\mathcal{V}'\Gamma_{i,q}^{r_\mathrm{eff}})/\partial r_\mathrm{eff}+S_{i,q}$, where $\mathcal{V}'=d\mathcal{V}/dr_\mathrm{eff}$ has units m^2 and $S_{i,q}$ is the net source density from ionization, recombination, charge exchange, external fueling, and loss processes with units m^-3 s^-1. The flux is usually derived in transport analysis from density evolution, atomic source and sink rates, and prescribed or predicted transport coefficients rather than measured directly as a local diagnostic signal.

The charge-state-summed ion counterpart is [radial_ion_particle_flux](name:radial_ion_particle_flux), while [ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:ion_charge_state_particle_flux) denotes the corresponding vector flux before radial projection. Neutral particle transport is described by [radial_neutral_particle_flux](name:radial_neutral_particle_flux) or, when internal neutral states are resolved, [radial_neutral_state_particle_flux](name:radial_neutral_state_particle_flux). The analogous charge-state-resolved energy transport quantity is [radial_ion_charge_state_energy_flux](name:radial_ion_state_energy_flux).

Typical values are reported in m^-2 s^-1 and are strongly case-dependent because the flux scales with density gradients, source localization, impurity concentration, and charge-state coupling. No device-independent numerical range is implied by the standard name; different charge states of the same element can have different magnitudes and even opposite directions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions in the specified charge state cross a magnetic flux surface outward, from smaller to larger enclosed plasma volume in the direction of increasing $\rho$.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_diffusion_coefficient
