The leading minus sign converts the fast-particle energy-loss rate into thermal-ion heating; for fast-particle slowing down on ions, the operator moment is negative and this power is positive.

In practice, this power is inferred rather than measured directly. It is obtained from kinetic fast-particle modeling or power-balance analysis using the fast-particle distribution, thermal ion densities, charge states, temperatures, and Coulomb logarithm; the local collisional energy-transfer rate is then integrated over the plasma volume and summed over thermal ion states. It is commonly considered together with [thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions) to partition fast-particle slowing-down power between ions and electrons.

Typical values range from near 0 W when no appreciable fast population is present to 10^3-10^6 W in small or weakly heated plasmas, 10^6-10^7 W in auxiliary-heated tokamaks, and 10^7-10^8 W in burning-plasma scenarios.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Isotropic kinetic pressure from random thermal motion of all thermal ion species and ionization states. It is the aggregate of charge-state-resolved thermal ion pressures and excludes fast or suprathermal ion contributions.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure carried by the bulk thermal ion population. It is summed over all thermal ion species and ionization states, so it is the aggregate counterpart of [thermal_ion_state_pressure](name:thermal_ion_state_pressure), and it excludes pressure from fast or suprathermal ions.

For a plasma with multiple thermal ion species or charge states, the defining relation is:

$$
p_{i,\mathrm{th}} = \sum_s p_{i,s,\mathrm{th}} = \sum_s n_s k_B T_s
$$

where $p_{i,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal ion pressure, $p_{i,s,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal pressure of ion state $s$, $n_s$ is its number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $T_s$ is its thermodynamic temperature in kelvin, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant. If ion temperature is expressed in electronvolts, the factor $k_B T_s$ is replaced by $e T_s$, where $e$ is the elementary charge. When all thermal ions share a common temperature, this reduces to the total thermal ion density multiplied by the common thermal energy per ion.

In practice, thermal ion pressure is computed from ion density and ion temperature estimates for each relevant species or charge state, using kinetic diagnostics and consistency constraints such as quasineutrality. It is combined with [thermal_electron_pressure](name:thermal_electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash) to form the dominant bulk thermal pressure contribution, and is conceptually related to [total_ion_pressure](name:total_ion_pressure) when total ion pressure is decomposed into thermal and nonthermal parts.

Representative values vary widely with confinement regime and radius: cool edge or scrape-off-layer plasma can be below 1 Pa to about 10^3 Pa, while confined hot plasma is commonly in the 10^3-10^5 Pa range and can reach a few 10^5 Pa in high-performance conditions.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Derivative of total thermal ion pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius. Because that radial flux coordinate is dimensionless, the derivative retains units of pressure.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) is the rate of change of total thermal ion pressure with respect to the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the normalized toroidal flux radius. It quantifies the outward pressure gradient across nested magnetic flux surfaces and provides a pressure-gradient drive term for ion energy transport.

The defining derivative is

$$
G_{p_i}(\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}) = \frac{\partial p_{i,\mathrm{th}}}{\partial \rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $G_{p_i}$ is the radial derivative, $p_{i,\mathrm{th}}$ is the total thermal ion pressure summed over the thermal ion species being modeled, and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ ranges from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface. Since $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as pressure, Pa.

In practice, this quantity is computed by differentiating the radial dependence of thermal ion pressure inferred from ion density and temperature measurements, or from a transport calculation. Smoothing, fitted basis functions, or conservative finite differences are commonly used to reduce noise before differentiation. The related [radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure) is the analogous derivative for the corresponding ion pressure quantity, [second_radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure) gives the associated curvature, and [radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature](name:radial_derivative_of_ion_temperature) is often used with density gradients to decompose the pressure gradient.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^3$-$10^5$ Pa in broad core regions and can reach $10^5$-$10^6$ Pa in steep pedestal or edge-gradient regions, depending on density, ion temperature, plasma size, and confinement regime. In many confined plasmas the value is negative over much of the radius because thermal ion pressure is largest near the magnetic axis.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total thermal ion pressure increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, outward from the magnetic axis toward the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative of total thermal ion pressure with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius, quantifying the local radial curvature of the thermal ion pressure profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of thermal ion pressure quantifies the curvature of the [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) profile along the normalized toroidal flux radius. Negative values indicate a concave-down pressure profile, characteristic of the plasma core where pressure is peaked, while positive values indicate concave-up curvature, which can arise near internal transport barriers or in pedestal-like structures.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{\partial^2 p_i^{th}}{\partial \rho_{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $p_i^{th}$ is the total thermal ion pressure and $\rho_{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius running from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, the resulting derivative carries the same unit as the pressure.

This quantity is evaluated numerically by transport solvers, where it enters the spatial discretization of diffusive terms in the radial ion heat and momentum transport equations. It is the second-order companion to the first-order [radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_thermal_ion_pressure), and it is structurally analogous to the [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_pressure) for the fast ion population and to [second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_ion_pressure) for the total (thermal plus fast) ion pressure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the thermal ion pressure profile is concave upward with respect to increasing $\rho_{tor,norm}$.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Number density of thermalized (Maxwellian) ions of a specified atomic species and ionization state, excluding suprathermal and fast-ion populations.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion state density is the local number of ions per unit volume in the bulk Maxwellian population for one atomic species and one ionization state. The species identifies the nucleus or isotope, and the state is identified by charge number or an equivalent ionization-state label, such as neutral, singly ionized, or fully stripped. Suprathermal beam ions, fusion products, RF-heated tails, and other fast-ion populations are not included.

The kinetic definition is the zeroth velocity moment of the thermal part of the distribution function:

$$
n_{a,q}^{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x},t) = \int f_{a,q}^{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $a$ labels the atomic species, $q$ labels the ionization state, $f_{a,q}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the Maxwellian thermal component of the distribution function, $\mathbf{x}$ is the local plasma position, and $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity. At the same species and state, [total_ion_state_density](name:total_ion_state_density) is partitioned into this thermal contribution and [fast_ion_state_density](name:fast_ion_state_density); summing this quantity over ionization states gives [thermal_ion_density](name:thermal_ion_density) for the species.

In practice, thermal ion state density is obtained from transport or collisional-radiative models that evolve charge-state populations, or inferred from spectroscopic measurements of line emission and charge-exchange recombination combined with atomic-rate coefficients. Main-ion densities are often constrained by electron density and quasi-neutrality, while impurity charge-state densities are constrained by measured radiation, ionization balance, and transport assumptions.

Typical main-fuel thermal charge-state densities in the confined plasma are about $10^{19}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$. Individual impurity charge-state densities commonly span $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on concentration, ionization balance, and radial location; neutral or weakly ionized states can be much larger in cold edge or detached plasma regions and much smaller in the hot core.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional power density transferred from a fast or non-Maxwellian particle distribution to bulk thermal ions in one specified ionic charge state. Positive values represent heating of that charge-state population.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion state power density due to collisions is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy between a fast or non-Maxwellian particle distribution and the bulk thermal ions in one specified ionic charge-state population. It is a state-resolved ion energy source term; summing over ionic charge states gives the corresponding state-summed thermal-ion collisional power density.

A kinetic definition is the energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator acting on the thermal ion state:

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},i,\zeta}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} E_i(\mathbf{v})\, C_{i,\zeta \leftarrow f}^{\mathrm{Coul}}[f_{i,\zeta}, f_f](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},i,\zeta}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $E_i(\mathbf{v})=m_i|\mathbf{v}|^2/2$ is thermal-ion kinetic energy in J, $m_i$ is ion mass in kg, and $\zeta$ labels the ionic charge state. The operator $C_{i,\zeta \leftarrow f}^{\mathrm{Coul}}$ is the Coulomb-collision contribution to the time derivative of the thermal-ion-state distribution caused by the fast distribution $f_f$; for distributions normalized so that $\int f\,d^3v$ gives density in m$^{-3}$, $f$ has units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, $C$ has units s$^2$ m$^{-6}$, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from collisional slowing-down or Fokker-Planck operators using the fast-particle distribution, the thermal ion density and temperature of the selected charge state, ion charge and mass, and the Coulomb logarithm. It is usually inferred through transport or power-balance modeling rather than measured directly; fast-particle diagnostics, thermal-ion temperature evolution, and total heating constraints provide consistency checks. If an orbit-class decomposition is used, the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped contributions add to this state-resolved value.

Typical magnitudes in auxiliary-heated or alpha-heated tokamak cores are 10$^3$-10$^6$ W m$^{-3}$ for dominant fuel-ion charge states. Edge regions, weak fast-particle populations, or trace impurity charge states often have 10$^{-2}$-10$^3$ W m$^{-3}$, with the exact value scaling strongly with fast-particle density, energy, background temperature, charge state, and local composition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the fast-particle distribution to the specified thermal ion charge-state population.

NAMES.name: co_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional power density transferred to thermal ions in a specified charge state from the co-passing component of a fast-particle distribution.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions deposit kinetic energy in thermal ions of a specified charge state, considering only the co-passing orbit component of the fast-particle distribution. The co-passing qualifier selects passing fast particles moving in the co-current direction, and the charge-state qualifier resolves which thermal ion population receives the energy.

It is commonly defined as the negative kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator acting on the co-passing fast-particle distribution due to collisions with the specified thermal ion charge state:

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},z}^{\mathrm{co,coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = -\int \frac{1}{2} m_f v^2\, C_{fz}^{\mathrm{coll}}\!\left[f_{\mathrm{co}}, f_{\mathrm{th},z}\right](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},z}^{\mathrm{co,coll}}$ is in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $m_f$ is the fast-particle mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed in m s$^{-1}$, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. If $f_{\mathrm{co}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{th},z}$ are normalized so that $\int f\,d^3v$ gives number density in m$^{-3}$, then they have units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$ and the operator $C_{fz}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ has units of phase-space density per second, s$^2$ m$^{-6}$. The minus sign converts the fast-particle collisional energy loss into heating of the thermal ion charge state $z$.

In practice this power density is computed from a kinetic or reduced distribution-function model by applying a Coulomb or Fokker-Planck collision operator to the co-passing part of the fast-particle distribution and taking its energy moment. The local scalar value is independent of coordinate basis; when a spatial label is needed, it may be given in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. Summing over charge states gives [co_passing_thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions), while comparison with [co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) checks energy conservation between the fast and thermal populations.

Typical magnitudes are 10$^2$-10$^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in the heated core of neutral-beam, ion-cyclotron, or fusion-alpha scenarios, with peaks approaching 10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$ in compact high-power plasmas. Values can be much smaller for trace ion charge states, weak fast-particle populations, or radial regions with little co-passing fast-particle density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the co-passing fast-particle distribution to the specified thermal ion charge state.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional power density transferred from the counter-passing component of a non-Maxwellian particle distribution to thermal ions of a specified charge state. Counter-passing identifies the donor particles whose guiding-center parallel motion is opposite to the plasma current, not an orbit class of the receiving thermal ions.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local rate of collisional energy transfer per unit volume from counter-passing non-Maxwellian particles to a thermal ion population in a specified charge state. The counter-passing qualifier applies to the donor fast-particle component; the receiving thermal ions are the bulk Maxwellian ions of the selected ion charge state.

A kinetic definition is the energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator for the donor particles restricted to the counter-passing orbit class:

$$
p_{i_s}^{\mathrm{cp}\to\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x}) = -\int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}} \frac{1}{2} m_f v^2\, C_{f i_s}[f_f,f_{i_s}^{\mathrm{th}}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $p_{i_s}^{\mathrm{cp}\to\mathrm{th}}$ is the power density in W m$^{-3}$, $i_s$ denotes the receiving thermal ion charge state, $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing part of donor velocity space, $m_f$ is the donor-particle mass in kg, $v$ is speed in m s$^{-1}$, $f_f$ is the non-Maxwellian donor distribution, $f_{i_s}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal ion distribution for the selected charge state, and $C_{f i_s}$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the donor distribution due to that thermal ion state. The minus sign makes energy lost by the donor component appear as heating of the thermal ion state.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic distribution functions or transport calculations by evaluating collisional slowing-down and energy-exchange terms separately for counter-passing donor particles and for each receiving ion charge state. It may also be inferred in integrated modeling by partitioning total collisional ion heating according to orbit class, species, and charge-state-resolved collision partners.

Typical values span a wide range: about 10^2-10^5 W m$^{-3}$ for weak fast-ion tails or peripheral regions, 10^5-10^7 W m$^{-3}$ in strongly heated tokamak cores, and locally higher values during intense neutral-beam injection or radio-frequency acceleration. The value can be negative if collisions transfer net thermal-ion energy back to the counter-passing non-Maxwellian component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when collisional energy transfer is from the counter-passing non-Maxwellian donor particles to the specified thermal ion charge state.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb collisional power transferred from a fast particle distribution to the thermal population of a specified ion species charge state.
NAMES.long:
The quantity gives the total rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from a fast (non-Maxwellian) particle population into the thermal ion population of a specified ion species $a$ at charge state $z$, integrated over the plasma volume $V$.

$$
P_{\mathrm{th}}^{(a,z)} = \int_V Q_{\mathrm{coll}}^{(a,z)}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $Q_{\mathrm{coll}}^{(a,z)}$ is the local volumetric Coulomb collisional power density deposited into thermal ions of species $a$ at charge state $z$, evaluated from the fast particle kinetic distribution via Fokker–Planck collision integrals.

This is the charge-state-resolved component of [thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions), which sums over all ionization states of the species. The fast-population analog at the same charge-state resolution is [fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions), while [thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions) provides the corresponding electron channel. The local power density form appears in [trapped_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:trapped_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions) for orbit-class-resolved analyzes. This quantity enters collisional energy-balance equations for impurity heating and fast-ion thermalization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net kinetic energy flows from the fast particle distribution into the thermal ion charge-state population.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Isotropic thermal pressure of a specific ion charge state arising from random thermal motion, excluding fast-particle contributions.
NAMES.long:
The thermal pressure of an ion charge state is the isotropic scalar pressure contributed by ions in a particular ionization state through their random thermal motions. It is the thermal component of the full [ion_state_pressure](name:ion_state_pressure) and explicitly excludes fast (non-thermal) particle contributions, which are tracked separately in parallel and perpendicular fast-pressure quantities.

The defining relation is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th},s} = n_s \, k_B \, T_s
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ions in charge state $s$, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $T_s$ is the thermal temperature of that charge state. Summing $P_{\mathrm{th},s}$ over all charge states of a given ion species recovers the species-level [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure). Adding the fast-particle pressure contributions yields the [total_ion_state_pressure](name:total_ion_state_pressure) for the same charge state.

This quantity is derived from charge-state-resolved ion density and temperature profiles, obtained through charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, collisional-radiative modeling, or kinetic equilibrium reconstruction. It is defined across both the core and edge plasma regions, where the charge-state distribution varies significantly with local temperature and density through the ionization balance. The analogous quantity for neutral species in a specific internal state is [thermal_neutral_state_pressure](name:thermal_neutral_state_pressure).

Typical values range from a few Pa in the scrape-off layer to $10^3$–$10^5$ Pa in the core of high-performance tokamak discharges, depending on the charge state density and temperature.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any non-zero thermal ion population in the given charge state.

NAMES.name: thermal_neutral_density
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Local number density of thermal (Maxwellian) neutral particles, summed over all internal quantum states of the neutral species.
NAMES.long:
Thermal neutral density is the local volumetric concentration of neutral atoms or molecules with a Maxwellian velocity distribution, summed over all internal quantum states of the neutral species. It represents the equilibrium-thermalized component of the neutral population, distinct from fast non-Maxwellian neutrals generated by charge exchange with energetic ions or neutral beam interactions.

The quantity $n_{\rm th,neutral}$ is defined as the zeroth velocity moment of the Maxwellian distribution summed over internal states $s$:

$$
n_{\rm th,neutral} = \sum_s \int f_{{\rm th},s}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_{{\rm th},s}(\mathbf{v})$ is the Maxwellian velocity distribution function for internal state $s$. The state-resolved quantity [thermal_neutral_state_density](name:thermal_neutral_state_density) gives the contribution from each individual quantum level; summing over all such states recovers $n_{\rm th,neutral}$.

This population arises principally from plasma recycling at plasma-facing surfaces, radiative recombination, and molecular dissociation in the edge and scrape-off layer. Densities in this thermal component are inferred from Balmer-series and Lyman-series emission spectroscopy or neutral pressure gages, and computed by edge plasma transport codes coupling fluid or kinetic neutral solvers with atomic physics databases.

Typical values range from $10^{16}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in the scrape-off layer and divertor to below $10^{15}$ m$^{-3}$ in the core of a fusion-grade tokamak plasma. The complementary non-Maxwellian neutral population is described by [fast_neutral_density](name:fast_neutral_density); their sum constitutes the full [neutral_density](name:neutral_density).

NAMES.name: thermal_neutral_state_density
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Number density of thermal (Maxwellian) neutral particles occupying a specific internal quantum state, excluding the suprathermal neutral population within that state.
NAMES.long:
The thermal neutral state density gives the number density of neutral particles whose velocity distribution approximates a Maxwellian at the local neutral temperature, resolved for a single internal quantum state (electronic, vibrational, or rotational level) of the neutral species. Separating thermal from suprathermal neutrals within each state is essential for accurate modeling of atomic processes — ionization, recombination, and charge exchange — whose rate coefficients depend on the neutral velocity distribution.

The total neutral density for internal state $s$ decomposes as:

$$
n_{\mathrm{neutral},s} = n_{{\mathrm{thermal}},s} + n_{{\mathrm{fast}},s}
$$

where $n_{{\mathrm{thermal}},s}$ is this quantity and $n_{{\mathrm{fast}},s}$ is the [fast neutral state density](name:fast_neutral_state_density). Summing over all internal states $s$ recovers the state-summed [thermal_neutral_density](name:thermal_neutral_density), while the combined thermal-plus-fast population for a single state is tracked by [total_neutral_state_density](name:total_neutral_state_density).

This quantity is computed from neutral kinetic transport models that evolve Maxwellian and suprathermal populations separately, and can be constrained by spectroscopic measurements such as Balmer-series line intensities analyzed through collisional-radiative models. In the ionization-dominated plasma core, thermal neutral densities fall below $10^{12}$ m$^{-3}$; in the edge and scrape-off layer they range from $10^{14}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on recycling intensity, wall geometry, and neutral penetration depth.

NAMES.name: thermal_neutral_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Isotropic pressure of a neutral population in a specified internal quantum or excitation state arising from random thermal motion about the mean flow velocity. It excludes dynamic pressure from directed bulk flow and anisotropic fast-neutral contributions.
NAMES.long:
Thermal neutral state pressure is the scalar, isotropic pressure of neutral particles in one specified internal atomic, molecular, quantum, or excitation state. It is the part of the state-resolved neutral pressure associated with random thermal motion about the mean flow velocity, not with directed flow or anisotropic fast-neutral stress.

For a state-resolved velocity distribution, the scalar thermal pressure is one third of the trace of the random kinetic stress:

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},s} = \frac{1}{3} m_s \int |\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_s|^2 f_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},s}$ is the thermal pressure of state $s$ in Pa, $m_s$ is the particle mass in kg, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{u}_s$ is the mean flow velocity of that state in m s$^{-1}$, and $f_s$ is normalized so that $n_s=\int f_s\,d^3v$ is the state density in m$^{-3}$. For a Maxwellian state population this reduces to $p_{\mathrm{th},s}=n_s k_B T_s$ when $T_s$ is a thermodynamic temperature in K, or equivalently $p_{\mathrm{th},s}=e\,n_s T_s$ when $T_s$ is expressed in eV, with $e$ the elementary charge in J eV$^{-1}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from state-resolved neutral fluid or kinetic transport models, either by taking the velocity moment of the distribution function or by using the Maxwellian product of state density and thermal temperature. Experimental constraints are usually indirect: state densities may be inferred from line emission, absorption, or neutral-particle diagnostics with collisional-radiative modeling, while thermal temperatures may be constrained by Doppler broadening or by transport-model closure assumptions.

Representative values vary strongly with neutral density, excitation state, and local ionization and charge-exchange balance. Edge, scrape-off-layer, and divertor neutral states commonly span about $10^{-6}$-$10$ Pa; excited states are often toward the lower end because their populations are smaller. As a scale estimate, $n_s=10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$ and $T_s=1$ eV gives $p_{\mathrm{th},s}\approx 1.6\times10^{-3}$ Pa.

Summing this quantity over internal states gives [thermal_neutral_pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure). The total [neutral_state_pressure](name:neutral_state_pressure) may also include non-thermal or directed-flow contributions, while anisotropic fast-neutral state stresses are represented by [parallel_fast_neutral_state_pressure](name:parallel_fast_neutral_state_pressure) and [perpendicular_fast_neutral_state_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_neutral_state_pressure). The charged-particle analog for ions is [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure).

NAMES.name: thermal_particle_power_density_due_to_thermalization
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate at which fast, non-thermal particles transfer kinetic energy to the thermal particle population through Coulomb thermalization. Positive values denote heating of the thermal particles.
NAMES.long:
Thermal particle power density due to thermalization is the local energy source rate deposited into the background thermal particle population by fast particles as they slow down through Coulomb collisions. It represents collisional conversion of suprathermal kinetic energy, such as from neutral-beam ions or fusion-born alpha particles, into thermal plasma heat.

A kinetic definition is obtained from the energy moment of the fast-particle slowing-down operator:

$$
p_\mathrm{th}(\mathbf{x}) = -\sum_s \int \dot{\varepsilon}_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, f_s^\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $p_\mathrm{th}$ is the thermalization power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $s$ indexes fast-particle species, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $\dot{\varepsilon}_s$ is the collisional rate of change of fast-particle kinetic energy in W per fast particle, $f_s^\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-particle distribution in particles m$^{-3}$ (m s$^{-1}$)$^{-3}$, and $d^3v$ has units (m s$^{-1}$)$^3$. The minus sign converts fast-particle energy loss during slowing down into thermal-particle heating.

This quantity is usually computed from fast-particle kinetic or Fokker-Planck modeling constrained by heating sources and fast-particle diagnostics. It enters the thermal energy balance as a volumetric source term; integration over the confined plasma volume gives the related [thermal_particle_power_due_to_thermalization](name:thermal_particle_power_due_to_thermalization).

Typical core values in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas are about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$, with localized values approaching $10^7$ W m$^{-3}$ for strong neutral-beam or alpha-particle heating. Values are small where the fast-particle density is low or where collisional slowing-down power is weak.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from fast particles to the thermal particle population.

NAMES.name: thermal_particle_power_due_to_thermalization
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated rate at which energy is deposited in the bulk thermal particle population as fast particles thermalize through Coulomb collisions. Positive values denote heating of the thermal particles.
NAMES.long:
Thermal particle power due to thermalization is the net power delivered to the bulk thermal particle population when suprathermal particles slow down and become part of the thermal background. It represents collisional energy transfer from the fast-particle population to the thermal population as a whole.

The volume-integrated power is obtained by integrating the local thermalization power density over the plasma volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{th,therm}}(t) = \int_V q_{\mathrm{th,therm}}(\mathbf{x}, t)\, dV
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{th,therm}}$ is the local rate of energy transfer to thermal particles in W m^-3, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which the thermalization source is evaluated.

In practice this quantity is computed from a fast-particle distribution or slowing-down model by evaluating the Coulomb collisional energy-loss rate from suprathermal particles to the thermal background and integrating it over volume. It can also enter power-balance analyzes as the part of neutral-beam, radio-frequency, fusion-alpha, or other fast-particle energy that is ultimately deposited into the bulk thermal population.

Typical values range from 0 W when no confined suprathermal population is present or when thermalization is negligible, up to the fast-particle source power that remains confined long enough to thermalize. The scale is therefore scenario-specific and is set by the available fast-particle power and confinement, rather than by a universal numerical range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from fast particles to the bulk thermal particle population.

NAMES.name: thermal_particle_source_rate
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged volumetric net rate at which particles enter or leave the thermal population, summed over orbit populations.
NAMES.long:
The thermal particle source rate is the net local rate per unit volume at which particles are transferred into or out of the thermal background distribution. It includes the orbit-population-summed contribution of processes such as slowing-down thermalization of suprathermal particles, acceleration of thermal particles into nonthermal populations, and other modeled Fokker-Planck particle exchange terms.

It enters the thermal particle balance as the source term in the continuity equation:

$$
\frac{\partial n_{\rm th}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\rm th} = S_{\rm th}
$$

where $n_{\rm th}$ is the thermal particle density, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\rm th}$ is the thermal particle flux density, and $S_{\rm th}$ is the thermal particle source rate.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic, Fokker-Planck, or Monte Carlo descriptions of particle distributions coupled to a thermal background, often after averaging over a magnetic flux surface. It is the orbit-summed counterpart of orbit-resolved components such as [co-passing](name:co_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate), [counter-passing](name:counter_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate), and [trapped](name:trapped_thermal_particle_source_rate) thermal particle source rates, and is closely related to the associated energy-transfer quantity [thermal particle power density due to thermalization](name:thermal_particle_power_density_due_to_thermalization).

Typical magnitudes in magnetically confined fusion plasmas range from about 10^18-10^22 m^-3.s^-1, depending on density, heating power, fast-particle content, fueling, and loss processes. Values near zero indicate approximate local balance between transfer into and out of the thermal population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when particles are added to the thermal population and negative when particles are removed from it.

NAMES.name: co_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged volumetric source rate of thermal particle density for the co-passing orbit population. It represents the net rate at which particles are added to or removed from that orbit class.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing thermal particle source rate is the rate per unit volume at which thermal particles enter or leave the co-passing passing-orbit population after averaging over a magnetic flux surface. Co-passing denotes the passing orbit class whose guiding-center motion is aligned with the reference plasma-current direction, complementary to counter-passing and trapped orbit classes.

It is the source term in the flux-surface-averaged particle balance for the co-passing population:

$$
\frac{\partial \langle n_{\mathrm{cp}}\rangle_\rho}{\partial t}
+ \frac{1}{V'}\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\left(V'\left\langle \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{cp}}\cdot\nabla\rho\right\rangle_\rho\right)
= \langle S_{\mathrm{cp}}\rangle_\rho
$$

where $\langle\cdot\rangle_\rho$ denotes an average over the magnetic flux surface labeled by the dimensionless radial flux coordinate $\rho$, $V'=dV/d\rho$ is the differential volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, $n_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the co-passing thermal-particle density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the particle flux density in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and $S_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the volumetric source rate in $\mathrm{m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from kinetic or transport modeling by integrating the modeled collisional, wave-particle, and orbit-class transition terms over the co-passing part of velocity space and over the flux surface. It may also be inferred as the residual source required by a particle balance when the co-passing density evolution and radial particle flux are known.

No device-independent typical magnitude follows from the definition alone, because the value depends on species, radial location, distribution function, wave fields, collision rates, and the chosen separation between passing and trapped orbit classes. A useful scale is the particle replacement time $\tau_{\mathrm{cp}}=\langle n_{\mathrm{cp}}\rangle_\rho/|\langle S_{\mathrm{cp}}\rangle_\rho|$; for example, $10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$ changes a $10^{19}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ co-passing population on a 0.1 s time scale.
NAMES.sign: Positive when local processes add thermal particles to the co-passing orbit population.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged net volumetric rate at which thermal particles enter or leave the counter-passing orbit class, whose dominant toroidal circulation opposes the plasma current. It is the counter-passing contribution to the orbit-class decomposition of the total thermal particle source.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing thermal particle source rate is the orbit-class contribution to the thermal particle balance for passing guiding-center orbits that circulate toroidally opposite to the plasma current. Counter-passing particles form a distinct phase-space population from co-passing and trapped particles, and together these three classes constitute the orbit-resolved decomposition of the thermal particle source. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height, counter-passing means the net toroidal guiding-center drift opposes the direction of plasma current flow.

The source rate enters the flux-surface-averaged particle continuity equation for the counter-passing population, where it balances the density evolution and the net particle outflow:

$$
\frac{\partial \langle n_\mathrm{cp} \rangle}{\partial t} = \langle S_\mathrm{cp} \rangle - \left\langle \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{cp} \right\rangle
$$

where $\langle n_\mathrm{cp} \rangle$ is the flux-surface-averaged counter-passing thermal particle density in m^-3, $\langle S_\mathrm{cp} \rangle$ is this source rate in m^-3.s^-1, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{cp}$ is the particle flux of the population, $t$ is time, and angle brackets denote a flux-surface average. A positive flux divergence represents net outflow and reduces the local density, while $\langle S_\mathrm{cp} \rangle$ acts as a volumetric injection or removal term independent of transport.

In practice this quantity is computed by integrating kinetic or transport source operators over the thermal-energy range and the counter-passing pitch-angle domain, then applying a flux-surface average. Contributing processes include ionization, recombination, charge exchange, neutral-beam thermalization, pellet or gas fueling, imposed particle sinks, and collisional pitch-angle scattering that transfers particles across the trapped-passing boundary. Summing this rate with [co_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate](name:co_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate) and [trapped_thermal_particle_source_rate](name:trapped_thermal_particle_source_rate) recovers the total [thermal_particle_source_rate](name:thermal_particle_source_rate). It describes particle-number balance and is distinct from [counter_passing_power_density](name:counter_passing_power_density), which describes energy transfer for the same population.

Magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. Core source or sink levels in present-day tokamaks are commonly of order 10^19-10^21 m^-3.s^-1, with localized edge fueling, pellet, or beam-deposition regions reaching higher transient values. Values near zero occur where fueling, loss, and orbit-class transfer terms nearly cancel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when particles are added to the counter-passing thermal population.

NAMES.name: thermal_plasma_energy
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated stored thermal energy of the confined plasma, equal to 3/2 times the volume integral of the total thermal pressure; the thermal component of total stored plasma energy excluding fast-particle and electromagnetic-field contributions.
NAMES.long:
Thermal plasma energy $W_{th}$ is the total internal kinetic energy stored in the thermal particle species of the confined plasma, comprising electron and ion contributions integrated over the plasma volume. It is the thermal component of the total [plasma_energy](name:plasma_energy), distinguished from fast-particle stored energy and electromagnetic-field energy.

The defining relation is:

$$
W_{th} = \frac{3}{2} \int p_{th} \, dV
$$

where $p_{th} = p_e + p_i$ is the sum of electron and ion thermal pressures and the integral spans the confined plasma volume $V$.

In practice, $W_{th}$ is inferred by integrating the pressure profile derived from Thomson scattering, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and equilibrium reconstruction. Diamagnetic flux loop measurements provide an independent global estimate that is directly sensitive to the perpendicular pressure stored in the plasma.

Typical stored thermal energies range from ~100 kJ in small research devices to tens of MJ in large tokamaks under strong auxiliary heating. The energy confinement time $\tau_E = W_{th} / P_{loss}$, where $P_{loss}$ is the total power loss from the plasma, is the primary global confinement figure of merit. The quantity $W_{th}$ appears as the stored-energy tendency in the power balance, captured by [difference_of_total_plasma_deposited_power_and_tendency_of_total_plasma_stored_energy](name:difference_of_total_plasma_deposited_power_and_tendency_of_total_plasma_stored_energy), and its time derivative determines the net heating requirement at any given plasma state.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Pressure-equivalent time-evolution term for total electron pressure at a fixed dimensionless radial flux-surface label. Dividing by the associated time interval gives the physical pressure rate of change.
NAMES.long:
The time derivative of electron pressure is the pressure-equivalent accumulation term for total electron pressure at a fixed radial flux-surface label. Because this quantity has unit Pa, it represents the pressure change associated with a time interval; division by that interval gives the true time derivative in Pa s$^{-1}$.

The relation to the physical rate of change is:

$$
\Delta p_e(\chi; t, \Delta t) = p_e(\chi,t+\Delta t)-p_e(\chi,t) \simeq \Delta t \left.\frac{\partial p_e}{\partial t}\right|_{\chi}
$$

where $\chi$ is a dimensionless radial flux-surface label such as normalized toroidal flux radius, $t$ is time in seconds, $\Delta t$ is the associated time interval in seconds, and $\Delta p_e$ is the Pa-valued quantity. The electron pressure is $p_e=n_e k_B T_e$ when $T_e$ is in kelvin, with $n_e$ the electron number density and $k_B$ the Boltzmann constant; equivalently $p_e=n_e e T_e$ when $T_e$ is expressed in electronvolts, with $e$ the elementary charge.

This term enters the local electron pressure transport balance as the temporal accumulation term at fixed $\chi$. It is usually evaluated from time-resolved electron density and temperature evolution, or from the residual of a pressure transport equation balancing radial transport, volumetric heating, radiation, collisional exchange, and particle-source effects. It is the temporal counterpart of [radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure) and [second_radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure](name:second_radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure), and is analogous to ion-state pressure tendency quantities such as tendency_of_ion_state_pressure.

The magnitude scales as $|\partial p_e/\partial t|\Delta t$. For core electron pressures of about 10^3-10^5 Pa and evolution times from 10^-3-1 s, representative pressure-equivalent increments are often about 1-10^4 Pa; near steady state they can be much smaller, while rapid transients can produce changes that are a sizable fraction of the local electron pressure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron pressure at the fixed flux-surface label increases over the associated time interval.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Finite-time pressure change produced by the local temporal evolution of total ion pressure at a fixed radial flux-surface label. The pressure includes thermal and fast-ion contributions summed over the ionization states of the represented ion population, not a thermal-only ion sum.
NAMES.long:
The time derivative of ion pressure is the pressure increment associated with temporal evolution of total ion pressure at a fixed radial flux-surface label $\chi$. The pressure is the [total_ion_pressure](name:total_ion_pressure) for the represented ion population, including thermal and fast-ion components over its ionization states; the related [total_thermal_ion_pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure) and [tendency_of_thermal_ion_pressure](name:tendency_of_thermal_ion_pressure) refer to thermal-ion pressure only.

Because this quantity has the pressure unit, it represents the derivative integrated over an evolution interval rather than the instantaneous rate:

$$
\Delta_t p_i(\chi) = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \left.\frac{\partial p_i(\chi,t)}{\partial t}\right|_{\chi} \, dt
$$

where $\Delta_t p_i$ is in Pa, $p_i$ is the total ion pressure in Pa, $t$ is time in s, and $\chi$ is a fixed scalar label attached to a magnetic flux surface, such as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. For a species-resolved representation, $p_i$ may be written as $\sum_\zeta (p_{i,\zeta}^{\mathrm{th}} + p_{i,\zeta}^{\mathrm{fast}})$, where $\zeta$ indexes ionization states of the represented ion species; dividing $\Delta_t p_i$ by $t_1-t_0$ gives an average rate in Pa s$^{-1}$.

In practice, this increment is inferred from time-resolved pressure reconstructions or from the pressure part of an ion energy balance. Thermal contributions are obtained from ion density and temperature, while fast-ion contributions require information about the fast-ion distribution; mapping each time slice to the same $\chi$ separates temporal pressure evolution from motion of the flux surfaces.

Typical magnitudes depend strongly on the interval length and plasma regime. In tokamak transport analyzes, interval-integrated changes are often 10^2-10^4 Pa in the core over millisecond-scale evolution and 1-10^3 Pa near the edge, with values approaching 10^5 Pa during rapid heating, relaxation, or loss events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total ion pressure at fixed $\chi$ increases over the evolution interval.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_parallel_fast_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Temporal change of the fast (non-thermal) electron pressure component parallel to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed pressure increment associated with temporal evolution of the fast (non-thermal) electron pressure component along the local magnetic field. The fast electron population is suprathermal and can have an anisotropic pressure tensor with distinct parallel and perpendicular components. The base pressure is [parallel_fast_electron_pressure](name:parallel_fast_electron_pressure); related perpendicular quantities are [perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure) and [time_derivative_of_perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure](name:time_derivative_of_perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure).

The pressure increment is obtained by integrating the instantaneous pressure rate over the interval:

$$
\Delta_t p_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}(t;\Delta t) = p_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}(t+\Delta t) - p_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}(t) = \int_t^{t+\Delta t} \dot{p}_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}(t') \, dt'
$$

where $\Delta_t p_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ and $p_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ are pressures in Pa, $\dot{p}_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}} = \partial p_{\parallel,e}^{\mathrm{fast}}/\partial t$ is the instantaneous pressure rate in Pa s$^{-1}$, and $t'$, $t$, and $\Delta t$ are times or time intervals in s. Thus the quantity represented here is the interval-integrated contribution of the instantaneous time derivative, with dimensions of pressure.

The underlying parallel fast-electron pressure can be evaluated from the second velocity moment of the fast-electron distribution along the magnetic-field direction. Its temporal increment is modeled from pressure-balance contributions such as wave or beam energy transfer to electrons, collisional slowing-down into the thermal bulk, pitch-angle scattering, radial transport, orbit losses, and wave-particle interactions. Experimental constraints are usually indirect, using diagnostics sensitive to non-thermal electrons such as hard-x-ray bremsstrahlung, electron-cyclotron emission, synchrotron radiation, and current-drive response.

Typical magnitudes over millisecond-scale evolution intervals range from 1-10^3 Pa in moderate auxiliary-heating conditions and can reach 10^3-10^5 Pa for strong wave-current-drive or runaway-electron populations. The magnitude scales with the length of the evolution interval for a given instantaneous pressure rate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the parallel fast-electron pressure increases over the evolution interval.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Temporal tendency, expressed in pressure units, of the parallel fast-ion pressure for a specified ion charge state. It describes the charge-state-resolved evolution of the non-thermal ion pressure moment along the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The time derivative of parallel fast-ion state pressure is the pressure-unit tendency term associated with temporal evolution of the parallel pressure of a fast, non-thermal ion population in charge state $s$. The underlying pressure is the second velocity moment parallel to the local magnetic field, so this quantity tracks how the anisotropic fast-ion energy content along the field changes in time.

A pressure-unit representation of the temporal derivative contribution over an evolution interval $\Delta t$ is

$$
D_t P_{\mathrm{fast},\parallel,s} = \Delta t\,\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int m_i\,c_\parallel^2\,f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $D_t P_{\mathrm{fast},\parallel,s}$ denotes the pressure-equivalent time-derivative contribution, $P_{\mathrm{fast},\parallel,s}$ is [parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure), $\Delta t$ is the evolution interval in seconds, $m_i$ is the ion mass in kg, $c_\parallel$ is the particle velocity relative to the local mean flow projected along the magnetic field in m s$^{-1}$, and $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the fast-ion distribution function with units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$.

In practice this term is obtained from kinetic fast-ion calculations, moment equations, or time-differenced reconstructions of anisotropic fast-ion pressure. It is driven by the balance of external heating and fast-ion birth, collisional energy exchange with thermal species, pitch-angle scattering that transfers energy between parallel and perpendicular moments, radial transport, charge-state evolution, charge exchange, orbit losses, and other loss mechanisms.

Typical values are most meaningful relative to the local fast-ion pressure scale. In quasi-steady phases the value is often close to 0 Pa, while during heating turn-on, redistribution, or rapid loss events it can become a significant fraction of the local [parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure) over the evolution interval.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the parallel fast-ion pressure for charge state $s$ increases over the evolution interval.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Velocity-dimension temporal increment obtained by integrating the time derivative of the electron bulk-flow component along increasing poloidal angle in flux coordinates rho_tor_norm, theta, phi. Dividing by the elapsed time gives the corresponding poloidal electron acceleration.
NAMES.long:
Time derivative of poloidal electron velocity is the velocity-dimension temporal increment associated with the electron bulk-flow component $v_{\theta,e}$ along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinates $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$. It is the time-integrated change of [poloidal_electron_velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity) over a specified interval, so it has the same dimension as velocity rather than acceleration.

The velocity-dimension temporal increment at fixed normalized toroidal-flux radius is defined by integrating the physical time derivative over the interval:

$$
\Delta_t v_{\theta,e}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}; t_0,t_1)
= \int_{t_0}^{t_1}
\left.\frac{\partial v_{\theta,e}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}},t)}{\partial t}\right|_{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
\, dt
= v_{\theta,e}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}},t_1)-v_{\theta,e}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}},t_0)
$$

where $\Delta_t v_{\theta,e}$ is in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $v_{\theta,e}$ is the poloidal electron velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $t_0$, $t_1$, and $t$ are times in seconds, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal-flux radius. The angles $\theta$ and $\phi$ are angular coordinates in radians, and the interval-averaged physical acceleration is $\Delta_t v_{\theta,e}/(t_1-t_0)$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from time-resolved evaluations of the same electron poloidal flow component at the same $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, or by integrating the poloidal component of an electron momentum balance over the time interval. Holding the same radial flux label separates temporal evolution from radial variation; related radial variation of the parent flow is described by [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity) and [second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity).

Typical magnitudes are interval dependent because $|\Delta_t v_{\theta,e}|$ scales approximately as the local poloidal electron acceleration multiplied by $t_1-t_0$. For a well-resolved transport evolution, the increment is usually interpreted relative to the local magnitude of [poloidal_electron_velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity); values comparable to the full flow speed indicate rapid evolution or a long elapsed interval.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\theta,e}(t_1)$ exceeds $v_{\theta,e}(t_0)$, with positive $v_{\theta,e}$ directed toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux coordinates $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_argon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the argon ion bulk flow velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system at the radial location of an internal transport barrier, a localized region of strongly reduced radial heat and particle transport.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal argon velocity at an internal transport barrier is the component of the bulk flow velocity of argon ions along the toroidal direction at the barrier location. The right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system is used, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. An internal transport barrier is a localized region inside the confined plasma where radial heat and particle transport are strongly reduced, often accompanied by steep gradients in temperature, density, or rotation.

The toroidal component is defined by projecting the argon ion bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar}} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol e}_{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the argon toroidal velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the argon ion bulk velocity, and $\hat{\boldsymbol e}_{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

In practice this quantity may be inferred from spectroscopic measurements of argon emission or charge-exchange light when available, or computed from transport analysis constrained by measurements of impurity rotation. The internal-transport-barrier location is identified from local transport reduction and associated steep radial gradients, and the velocity is evaluated for the argon ion population represented by the measurement or model.

Typical core impurity toroidal velocities near internal transport barriers are of order $10^3$-$10^5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, depending on heating, external torque, collisionality, plasma rotation, and the argon charge states contributing to the observed signal.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the argon ion bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: toroidal_argon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the argon impurity ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal argon velocity at the magnetic axis quantifies the net bulk fluid motion of argon impurity ions projected onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ at the singular point of the flux-surface geometry where $\nabla\psi = 0$. Because the magnetic axis sits on the innermost nested flux surface, this quantity captures the core impurity rotation, which couples to the bulk plasma rotation through collisional momentum exchange and radial force balance.

The toroidal component is defined as:

$$
v_\phi^{\mathrm{Ar}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the fluid mean velocity of the argon ion population and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice, toroidal argon velocities are inferred from Doppler shifts of charge exchange recombination spectroscopy emission lines produced during neutral beam injection, with line-of-sight contributions deconvolved to recover the local ion velocity. Radial profiles of argon rotation can be compared with the pedestal value [toroidal_argon_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_pedestal), the barrier value [toroidal_argon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), and the boundary value [toroidal_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_argon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). Analogous on-axis quantities for other impurity species are [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).

Core toroidal impurity velocities in neutral-beam-heated tokamaks span roughly $-10^5$ to $+3 \times 10^5$ m/s, with sign and magnitude determined by beam injection geometry and intrinsic rotation drive.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the argon ion bulk velocity is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the beryllium impurity ion bulk flow velocity at the flux surface assigned to the internal transport barrier, resolved along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal beryllium velocity at the internal transport barrier is the toroidal component of the beryllium impurity ion bulk-flow velocity evaluated on the flux surface that characterizes the barrier location. The internal transport barrier is a localized region of reduced cross-field transport, so the toroidal impurity flow there is often closely connected to rotation shear, radial electric field structure, and momentum transport.

Using the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the toroidal projection is defined by

$$
v_{\phi}^{\mathrm{Be}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Be}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Be}}$ is the beryllium impurity ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

In practice this quantity is commonly inferred from Doppler shifts of beryllium line emission, especially by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy using a neutral beam and tangential or multi-chord viewing geometry. Passive spectroscopy can also constrain impurity rotation when suitable emission and geometric information are available. Comparison with related quantities such as [toroidal beryllium velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), [toroidal beryllium velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_pedestal), and [toroidal nitrogen velocity at the internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) helps separate radial variation from impurity-species effects.

Typical toroidal impurity velocities at an internal transport barrier are about $10^4$-$10^5$ m s$^{-1}$ in beam-heated tokamak plasmas, with the magnitude and sign depending on applied torque, collisional coupling, neoclassical damping, and the radial electric field.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Be}} \cdot \hat{\phi} > 0$, with $\hat{\phi}$ pointing in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the beryllium impurity ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal fluid velocity of beryllium impurity ions at the magnetic axis is the projection of the beryllium ion bulk flow onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$, evaluated at the point where the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ attains its extremum and $\nabla\psi = 0$.

The defining relation is:

$$
v_\phi^\mathrm{Be} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Be} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Be}$ is the beryllium ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This on-axis value anchors the beryllium rotation profile and can be compared with analogs at outer flux surfaces: [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_pedestal), [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). The corresponding on-axis quantity for helium-4 ions is [toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).

Toroidal impurity rotation is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, where the Doppler shift of a beryllium emission line yields the line-of-sight velocity component, which is decomposed into toroidal and poloidal contributions. In neutral-beam-heated tokamaks, core toroidal rotation can range from a few km/s to ~100 km/s depending on injected torque and plasma current; ohmic plasmas rotate more slowly.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi^\mathrm{Be}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of carbon ion flow velocity at the internal transport barrier, evaluated in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component of carbon ion flow velocity at the internal transport barrier (ITB) characterizes the plasma rotation of carbon impurity ions at a localized region of suppressed anomalous transport in the plasma core. ITBs form near flux surfaces of low magnetic shear or low-order rational safety factors, where reduced turbulent transport produces steep radial gradients in temperature and density profiles.

Carbon ion rotation is connected to the local radial electric field through the ion radial force balance. For carbon ions with charge state $Z_C$, pressure $p_C$, and number density $n_C$:

$$
E_r = v_\phi^C B_\theta - v_\theta^C B_\phi + \frac{1}{Z_C e n_C} \frac{dp_C}{dr}
$$

where $v_\phi^C$ is the toroidal carbon velocity, $v_\theta^C$ is the poloidal carbon velocity, $B_\theta$ and $B_\phi$ are the poloidal and toroidal magnetic-field components, $r$ is the minor-radial coordinate, and $e$ is the elementary charge.

This velocity is measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), where Doppler shifts of carbon emission lines yield the local ion rotation; the ITB position is identified from the profile gradient structure. Comparing with [toroidal hydrogen velocity at the ITB](name:toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), [toroidal nitrogen velocity at the ITB](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [toroidal krypton velocity at the ITB](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) supports cross-species momentum balance analysis. The [carbon ion density at the ITB](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) together with this velocity characterizes the carbon particle flux at the barrier, while [toroidal carbon velocity at the pedestal top](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_pedestal_top) plays an analogous role at the edge transport barrier.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the carbon ion velocity points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the local bulk velocity of carbon impurity ions at the magnetic axis, resolved along +phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is an on-axis rotation quantity, not a flux-surface average.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal carbon velocity at the magnetic axis is the local toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity of carbon impurity ions at the magnetic axis. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This is a local on-axis quantity and is not a flux-surface average.

The on-axis toroidal component is defined by projecting the carbon bulk velocity onto the toroidal basis direction at the magnetic axis:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{C},0} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}}(R_0, \phi, Z_0) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{C},0}$ is the on-axis toroidal carbon velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon impurity ion bulk velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the magnetic-axis position with $R_0$ and $Z_0$ in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$.

It is typically inferred from impurity spectroscopy, especially charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy when available, together with an equilibrium reconstruction used to locate the magnetic axis and project measured line-of-sight velocities onto the toroidal direction. The value constrains core rotation and momentum transport; with poloidal impurity flow, pressure gradients, and magnetic-field components, it also contributes to impurity radial force balance and estimates of the core radial electric field.

Representative magnitudes in tokamak cores are often of order $10^3$-$10^5$ m s$^{-1}$, depending on external torque, intrinsic rotation, collisional coupling, and plasma regime. Values may be close to zero when toroidal momentum input is weak or when opposing torque contributions balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the carbon impurity ion bulk flow at the magnetic axis is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short: Toroidal projection of the plasma center-of-mass velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height. It is the mass-weighted mean toroidal speed of all plasma species treated as a single bulk fluid.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal center-of-mass velocity $v_\phi^\mathrm{cm}$ is the component of the multispecies barycentric plasma velocity along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the net toroidal rotation of the plasma treated as one bulk fluid, with each species weighted by its mass density.

The species mass-weighted projection is

$$
v_\phi^\mathrm{cm} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s v_{\phi,s}}{\sum_s m_s n_s}
$$

where $s$ indexes plasma species, $m_s$ is the particle mass, $n_s$ is the number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $v_{\phi,s}$ is the species toroidal velocity in $\mathrm{m.s}^{-1}$, and the denominator is the total plasma mass density. Because electron mass is much smaller than ion masses, this quantity is usually dominated by the main ions and any sufficiently dense heavy impurities.

In practice, toroidal center-of-mass velocity is computed from species densities and toroidal velocities in fluid or kinetic transport calculations. Experimentally, ion toroidal rotation is commonly inferred from Doppler shifts of charge-exchange or passive line emission, with corrections when impurity rotation is used as a proxy for main-ion rotation.

Typical magnitudes in confined tokamak plasmas are about $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s^-1. Neutral-beam-heated plasmas often lie toward the upper end of this range, while intrinsic or ohmic rotation is commonly $10^3$-$10^4$ m.s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi^\mathrm{cm}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_co_passing_fast_current_density
NAMES.short: Toroidal current density from co-passing fast (non-thermal) particles, excluding back-current contributions from thermal electrons and ions.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal co-passing fast current density $J_{\phi,\text{fast,co-pass}}$ quantifies the toroidal component of current density carried exclusively by fast (suprathermal) particles occupying co-passing orbits — trajectories that circulate around the torus without being magnetically trapped, in the direction aligned with the magnetic field.

The quantity is obtained by integrating the product of the toroidal velocity $v_\phi$ and the fast-particle distribution function $f_\text{fast}$ over the co-passing region $\Omega_\text{co-pass}$ of velocity space:

$$
J_{\phi,\text{fast,co-pass}} = q_s \int_{\Omega_\text{co-pass}} v_\phi \, f_\text{fast}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $q_s$ is the particle charge. Back-currents induced in the thermal electron and ion populations by Coulomb drag on the fast particles are explicitly excluded, distinguishing this quantity from [toroidal_co_passing_current_density](name:toroidal_co_passing_current_density), which retains the thermal back-current.

The quantity is computed from fast-particle distribution functions generated by Fokker-Planck solvers or Monte Carlo codes tracking the suprathermal population separately from the bulk plasma. In neutral beam injection scenarios, co-passing fast ions typically dominate the net fast-particle current drive because co-passing orbits carry a net toroidal drift preferentially aligned with the injection geometry. The complementary counter-passing contribution is given by [toroidal_counter_passing_fast_current_density](name:toroidal_counter_passing_fast_current_density), the trapped-particle contribution by [toroidal_trapped_fast_current_density](name:toroidal_trapped_fast_current_density), and the orbit-class sum by toroidal_fast_current_density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-particle current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_co_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Collisional source density of toroidal angular momentum transferred to co-passing fast electrons by Coulomb scattering. The toroidal direction is the increasing phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame; co-passing denotes passing orbits in the plasma-current toroidal direction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the torque per unit volume acting on the co-passing fast-electron population through Coulomb collisions, expressed as a source of toroidal angular momentum. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. Co-passing electrons are the passing part of the fast-electron population whose toroidal motion is in the same direction as the plasma current.

For a local kinetic description, the collisional toroidal torque density is the first toroidal momentum moment of the collision operator multiplied by major radius:

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{fe}}^{\mathrm{co,coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = R \int m_e v_\phi\, C_{\mathrm{coll}}\!\left[f_{\mathrm{fe}}^{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\right] \, d^3v
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{fe}}^{\mathrm{co,coll}}$ has units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $R$ is in meters, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kilograms, $v_\phi$ is the velocity component along increasing $\phi$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $f_{\mathrm{fe}}^{\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing fast-electron distribution, and $C_{\mathrm{coll}}[f]$ is its collisional time derivative with units of $f$ per second. If $f$ is normalized so that $\int f\,d^3v$ is a number density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, then $C_{\mathrm{coll}}[f]$ has units $\mathrm{s^2\,m^{-6}}$ and $d^3v$ has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-3}}$, giving the torque-density unit $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic or guiding-center distributions using Coulomb slowing-down, energy diffusion, and pitch-angle scattering operators. It appears in fast-electron toroidal angular-momentum balance and represents the collisional drag or acceleration of the co-passing population relative to the surrounding plasma.

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent: weak suprathermal electron tails may give $10^{-7}$-$10^{-3}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, while intense runaway-electron or strongly collisional fast-electron populations can reach $10^{-3}$-$1\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$. Values approach zero where the co-passing fast-electron density is negligible or where opposing collisional contributions nearly cancel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the co-passing fast-electron toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_co_passing_fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular-momentum source per unit volume transferred by Coulomb collisions to co-passing fast ions in a specified fast-ion charge state. It is the moment about the symmetry axis of the toroidal collisional force density in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the state-resolved toroidal torque density applied by Coulomb collisions to the co-passing part of a fast-ion population. It represents a local source of toroidal angular momentum for fast ions in charge state $q$, not the $\hat{\phi}$ projection of a torque-density vector; it is the moment about the symmetry axis associated with the toroidal collisional force in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The defining relation is the moment of the toroidal collisional force density about the symmetry axis:

$$
\mathcal{T}_{\phi,q}^{\mathrm{co,fast}} = R\,F_{\phi,q}^{\mathrm{coll}\rightarrow\mathrm{co,fast}}
$$

where $R$ is the major radius in meters in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $F_{\phi,q}^{\mathrm{coll}\rightarrow\mathrm{co,fast}}$ is the toroidal component of the collisional force density on co-passing fast ions in charge state $q$ in N m$^{-3}$, and $\mathcal{T}_{\phi,q}^{\mathrm{co,fast}}$ is the resulting toroidal torque density in N m$^{-2}$. The charge-state label $q$ is dimensionless.

In practice, the collisional force density is computed as a velocity-space momentum moment of the Coulomb collision operator acting on the co-passing fast-ion distribution. The state index refers to the receiving fast-ion charge state; summing this quantity over the resolved fast-ion charge states gives [toroidal_co_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions). Additional sums over orbit classes, where available, connect this co-passing contribution with corresponding trapped or total fast-ion torque-density quantities.

No universal numerical range is intrinsic to this state-resolved exchange term. Its magnitude and sign depend on the fast-ion distribution, collisional drag, background plasma composition, and the partition of particles among charge states; it may be much smaller than the charge-state-summed co-passing fast-ion torque density and can pass through zero where competing collisional momentum-transfer contributions balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional force on the co-passing fast ions has a toroidal component in the direction of increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_co_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Collisional source density of toroidal angular momentum carried by co-passing fast ions, resolved along the phi direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents Coulomb-collision transfer of toroidal torque between background plasma species and this orbit class.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal co-passing fast-ion torque density due to collisions is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer toroidal angular momentum to the co-passing fast-ion population per unit volume.
