The toroidal direction is the $\phi$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height; co-passing denotes passing fast-ion orbits moving in the co-current toroidal sense, distinct from trapped and counter-passing orbit classes.

A kinetic expression for the collisional torque density is

$$
\tau_{\phi}^{\mathrm{co},f,\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = R \sum_b \int m_f v_{\phi}\, C_{fb}\!\left[f_f^{\mathrm{co}},f_b\right](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $\tau_{\phi}^{\mathrm{co},f,\mathrm{coll}}$ has unit $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $R$ is the major radius in m, the sum is over collision partners $b$, $m_f$ is the fast-ion mass in kg, $v_{\phi}$ is the toroidal velocity component in m/s, $C_{fb}$ is the Coulomb-collision operator giving the rate of change of the co-passing fast-ion distribution due to species $b$, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element in $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-3}}$. The factor $R$ converts toroidal momentum exchange into angular-momentum torque density about the symmetry axis.

In practice this quantity is computed from a fast-ion distribution function and collisional slowing-down, pitch-angle-scattering, and energy-diffusion operators for electrons and ion species. It is often inferred within transport or orbit-kinetic modeling constrained by heating geometry and fast-ion diagnostics; charge-state- or species-resolved contributions add linearly to the total collisional torque density. Complementary orbit-channel quantities include [toroidal_counter_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_counter_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and [toroidal_trapped_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_trapped_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions), while [toroidal_co_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) describes the analogous thermal-ion channel.

Typical local magnitudes are about $10^{-4}$-$1\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas. Values can approach a few $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ in strongly beam-driven regions and are near zero when the co-passing fast-ion population or collisional momentum exchange is weak.
NAMES.sign: Positive when collisions increase the toroidal angular momentum of co-passing fast ions associated with motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_co_passing_thermal_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal torque density in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame transferred to a specified thermal ion charge state by Coulomb collisions with co-passing energetic particles. It is the local source of that charge state's toroidal angular momentum per unit plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal co-passing thermal ion state torque density due to collisions is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer toroidal angular momentum from the co-passing energetic-particle population to a specified thermal ion charge state. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing $c6$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The co-passing qualifier refers to the energetic-particle orbit class involved in the exchange, not to the orbit class of the recipient thermal ions.

It is related to the toroidal collisional force density on the recipient ion state by

$$
\tau_{\phi}^{\mathrm{th},z \leftarrow \mathrm{co}} = R\,S_{p,\phi}^{\mathrm{th},z \leftarrow \mathrm{co}}
$$

where $R$ is major radius and $S_{p,\phi}^{\mathrm{th},z \leftarrow \mathrm{co}}$ is the toroidal component of the collisional momentum source density acting on thermal ion charge state $z$ due to collisions with co-passing energetic particles. In kinetic treatments, $S_{p,\phi}$ is obtained as the toroidal velocity moment of the appropriate Coulomb collision operator; multiplying by $R$ converts toroidal force density to the source of angular momentum about the symmetry axis.

The quantity is computed in kinetic and transport modeling by separating the energetic-particle distribution into orbit classes, evaluating the collisional momentum exchange with each thermal ion charge state, and retaining the toroidal angular-momentum component. Summing over thermal ion charge states gives [toroidal_co_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions), while summing over energetic-particle orbit classes gives [toroidal_thermal_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions). The counter-passing and trapped orbit-class counterparts describe the same recipient thermal ion state acted on by different energetic-particle orbit populations.

Typical local magnitudes are about $10^{-4}$-$10$ N m^-2 in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, depending on energetic-particle density, slowing-down rate, major radius, and collisional coupling to the selected charge state. Values may be much smaller when energetic-particle momentum input is weak or nearly balanced between orbit classes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional transfer accelerates the specified thermal ion charge state in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_co_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular-momentum source density in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, transferred by Coulomb collisions from the co-passing fast-particle population to the bulk thermal-ion population.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the toroidal torque per unit volume imparted to thermal ions by Coulomb collisions with the co-passing part of a fast-particle distribution. The toroidal direction is the $\phi$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. Here co-passing labels the fast-particle source population; charge-state-resolved thermal-ion variants partition the receiving thermal ions into specific ion states.

For a receiving thermal ion species $i$, the local collisional toroidal torque density is the velocity-space moment of the collision operator weighted by the toroidal angular momentum per particle:

$$
T_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{th}\leftarrow\mathrm{co}} = R\,m_i \int v_\phi\, C_{i\leftarrow\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $T_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{th}\leftarrow\mathrm{co}}$ has unit $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $R$ is major radius in meters, $m_i$ is the ion mass in kilograms, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component in meters per second, $C_{i\leftarrow\mathrm{co}}$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on receiving thermal ions due to the co-passing fast-particle population with units of distribution function per second, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The factor $m_i\int v_\phi C_{i\leftarrow\mathrm{co}}d^3v$ is a toroidal force density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$; multiplication by $R$ converts it to torque density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.

It is usually computed from kinetic or transport modeling by evaluating the collisional friction moment between the co-passing fast-particle distribution and the receiving thermal-ion population. If ion species or charge states are resolved separately, the bulk thermal-ion torque is obtained by summing the corresponding receiver classes, while the charge-state-resolved sibling represents one such partition.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^{-3}$-$1\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ in auxiliary-heated core plasmas and can reach $1$-$10\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ locally near strong fast-ion deposition or large fast-ion pressure gradients. Values are small when the co-passing fast-particle population is weak or when counter-passing contributions nearly cancel the net collisional angular-momentum transfer.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional force on the receiving thermal ions is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_co_passing_torque_density
NAMES.short: Toroidal torque density contributed by the co-passing particle population. It is the local source rate of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume for that orbit class, distinct from counter-passing and trapped contributions.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal co-passing torque density is the local rate at which toroidal angular momentum is added to, or removed from, particles in the co-passing passing-orbit class. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the quantity refers to the toroidal component of angular momentum associated with that coordinate convention.

A kinetic source moment for one or more represented species can be written as

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \int_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{co}}} m_s R v_\phi S_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing toroidal torque density, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing region of velocity space, $s$ labels the included species, $m_s$ is particle mass in kg, $R$ is major radius in meters, $v_\phi$ is toroidal velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $S_s = \partial f_s/\partial t|_\mathrm{src}$ is the distribution-function source rate. Equivalently, it is the source part of $\partial \ell_{\phi,\mathrm{co}}/\partial t$, where $\ell_{\phi,\mathrm{co}} = \sum_s \int_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{co}}} m_s R v_\phi f_s d^3v$ has units kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$; therefore $\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{co}}$ has units N m$^{-2}$.

In practice this quantity is computed by taking the toroidal angular-momentum moment of kinetic or transport source terms over the co-passing orbit class. It is combined with related orbit-class contributions such as [toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density](name:toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density) and [toroidal_trapped_torque_density](name:toroidal_trapped_torque_density); force-resolved components such as [toroidal_co_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force](name:toroidal_co_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force) represent specific physical mechanisms within the same co-passing momentum balance.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent because this is a local source term tied to momentum deposition, collisional exchange, and electromagnetic forces. It is often close to 0 N m$^{-2}$ outside active source or sink regions, and its magnitude is best interpreted relative to the local toroidal_plasma_momentum and momentum transport time.
NAMES.sign: Positive when toroidal angular momentum is added to the co-passing population in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: toroidal_co_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular-momentum source per unit volume produced by the J×B force from flux-surface-normal current carried by co-passing particles. It is the co-passing orbit-class contribution to toroidal torque density from radial-current interactions with the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal co-passing torque density due to the Lorentz force is the toroidal angular-momentum source per unit volume produced by the flux-surface-normal current associated with co-passing particles in a magnetized plasma. Co-passing particles are passing guiding-center orbits whose parallel motion is in the plasma-current direction; they are not mirrored into trapped bounce motion.

For transport quantities the relevant scalar is commonly the flux-surface average of the toroidal moment of the Lorentz force density:

$$
\left\langle \tau_\phi^{\mathrm{co}} \right\rangle_\psi = \left\langle R\,\left[(\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{rad}} \times \mathbf{B})\cdot\hat{\phi}\right]_{\mathrm{co}} \right\rangle_\psi
$$

where $\tau_\phi^{\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing J×B toroidal torque density, $R$ is major radius, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the current-density component normal to magnetic flux surfaces, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_\psi$ denotes averaging on a surface of constant poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$. The square-bracket subscript $\mathrm{co}$ means retaining only the contribution of co-passing particles to the flux-surface-normal current. For a local value before averaging, the integrand inside $\langle\cdot\rangle_\psi$ is the corresponding torque density.

This quantity is computed by classifying the co-passing part of a kinetic particle distribution, taking the charge-weighted moment that gives its flux-surface-normal current, and contracting that current with the magnetic field. In toroidal momentum balance it is one orbit-class source term; adding the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped contributions gives [toroidal_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force](name:toroidal_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force), while [toroidal_co_passing_torque_density](name:toroidal_co_passing_torque_density) includes co-passing toroidal torque density from all mechanisms.

No universal typical range is assigned to this orbit-resolved source because it scales with the scenario-dependent product of major radius, radial current density, and poloidal magnetic-field strength. It is often interpreted relative to other toroidal momentum sources and becomes most important where fast-particle orbit losses, strong gradients, or nonambipolar transport produce appreciable flux-surface-normal current.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal component of the $\mathbf{J}\times\mathbf{B}$ torque on the co-passing population acts in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_conductivity
NAMES.short: Toroidal conductivity is the phi-phi diagonal component of the electrical conductivity tensor, relating toroidal conductive current density to toroidal electric field along +phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal conductivity is the $\phi\phi$ diagonal component of the electrical conductivity tensor in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the local linear response of conductive current density to electric field along the toroidal basis direction $+\hat{\phi}$.

In a local tensor Ohm's law, conductive current density components are related to electric-field components by

$$
J_i = \sum_{j \in \{R,\phi,Z\}} \sigma_{ij} E_j
$$

where $J_i$ is a conductive current-density component, $E_j$ is an electric-field component, and $\sigma_{ij}$ is the conductivity tensor. The toroidal conductivity is only $\sigma_{\phi\phi}$; off-diagonal contributions such as $\sigma_{\phi R}E_R$ and $\sigma_{\phi Z}E_Z$ to $J_\phi$ are separate tensor couplings and are not included. When those off-diagonal terms are neglected, the diagonal toroidal contribution is $J_\phi^{(\mathrm{diag})}=\sigma_{\phi\phi}E_\phi$.

It is computed in transport models from collisional, neoclassical, turbulent, or prescribed resistivity models and can be constrained experimentally from Ohmic power balance, loop-voltage analysis, current-density reconstruction, or driven-current response. For a gyrotropic tensor aligned with the magnetic field, the diagonal toroidal component is approximately $\sigma_\parallel b_\phi^2 + \sigma_\perp(1-b_\phi^2)$, with $b_\phi=B_\phi/|B|$; it approaches the parallel Spitzer conductivity only when the toroidal magnetic field dominates the poloidal field, perpendicular and Hall/off-diagonal terms are small, and the electric field and current are mainly field-aligned.

Typical values are highly regime dependent: 10^3-10^6 m^-1.ohm^-1 in cool edge or scrape-off-layer plasma, 10^7-10^9 m^-1.ohm^-1 in hot tokamak cores, and lower effective values when anomalous momentum loss, radiation, partial ionization, or prescribed turbulent resistivity dominates.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_current_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density from the counter-passing orbit class, encompassing contributions from all particle populations and including back-current drag from thermal electrons and ions.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing particles complete full poloidal circuits in the direction opposing the plasma current and contribute a net toroidal current density whose sign is generally opposite to the driven current. This quantity captures the $\hat{\phi}$ projection of that current, integrated over the full counter-passing portion of the distribution function and flux-surface averaged, including the back-current response of thermal electrons and ions to collisional momentum exchange. The companion quantity [toroidal_counter_passing_fast_current_density](name:toroidal_counter_passing_fast_current_density) isolates the fast-particle contribution alone and excludes these back-current terms.

The flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density is defined as:

$$
\langle J_\phi^{\mathrm{cp}} \rangle = \left\langle \int_{\mathrm{cp}} \sum_s q_s\, v_\phi\, f_s(\mathbf{v})\, d^3v \right\rangle_{\!\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $q_s$ is the charge of species $s$, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component, $f_s$ is the distribution function restricted to the counter-passing orbit domain, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes the flux-surface average.

This quantity is evaluated in kinetic transport simulations that classify particle orbits by guiding-center topology. Together with co-passing and [toroidal_trapped_current_density](name:toroidal_trapped_current_density) contributions, it provides a complete orbit-class decomposition of the total driven toroidal current density. It is the toroidal projection of the full vector counter_passing_current_density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_fast_current_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density carried by the counter-passing fraction of the fast (non-thermal) particle distribution, excluding thermal back-current contributions from electrons and thermal ions.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast particles complete unobstructed poloidal transits with drift motion opposing the reference toroidal direction, and their collective motion produces a net toroidal current density distinct from both the trapped population and the thermal bulk. This quantity isolates the direct toroidal current contribution of those orbits, with the drag-induced return currents carried by thermal electrons and ions explicitly excluded.

The current density is obtained by integrating the fast-particle distribution function $f_\mathrm{fast}$ over the counter-passing region of velocity space:

$$
J_{\phi,\mathrm{cp,fast}} = q \int_{\mathrm{cp}} v_\phi \, f_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $q$ is the particle charge, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component, and the integration domain is restricted to orbits satisfying $\lambda = v_\parallel/v < -\lambda_\mathrm{trap}$, with $\lambda_\mathrm{trap}$ the pitch-angle trapping boundary separating passing from trapped orbits.

This quantity is computed from Fokker-Planck solvers or Monte Carlo transport codes that resolve the fast-particle distribution function by orbit class. It is central to current drive analysis, where the balance between co-passing and counter-passing fast particle contributions determines the net directed toroidal current drive efficiency.

To form the total fast-particle toroidal current density, this term is summed with [toroidal_co_passing_fast_current_density](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_current_density) and [toroidal_trapped_fast_current_density](name:toroidal_trapped_fast_current_density); their combined contribution is toroidal_fast_current_density. The counter-passing current integrated over all particle populations, including thermal species, is given by [toroidal_counter_passing_current_density](name:toroidal_counter_passing_current_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $J_{\phi,\mathrm{cp,fast}}$ is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Toroidal torque density about the symmetry axis transferred by Coulomb collisions to counter-passing fast electrons, whose guiding-center parallel motion is opposite to the toroidal plasma current. In the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame it is major radius times the phi-directed collisional force density.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal counter-passing fast electron collisional torque density is the rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer toroidal angular momentum about the symmetry axis to the counter-passing subset of the fast electron population. Counter-passing fast electrons are suprathermal electrons whose guiding-center parallel motion is opposite to the toroidal plasma current. The toroidal direction is the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

It is the major radius multiplied by the $\phi$-directed collisional force density on that orbit class:

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{tor},e}^{\mathrm{fast,cp}} = R F_{\phi,e}^{\mathrm{coll,fast,cp}} = R \int_{\mathrm{cp}} m_e v_\phi \, C_e^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_e^{\mathrm{fast}}] \, d^3v
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{tor},e}^{\mathrm{fast,cp}}$ has units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $R$ is the major radius at the point of evaluation, $F_{\phi,e}^{\mathrm{coll,fast,cp}}$ is the collisional force density in the $\hat{\phi}$ direction, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v_\phi$ is the velocity component along $\hat{\phi}$, $C_e^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_e^{\mathrm{fast}}]$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the fast-electron distribution function, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and the integral is restricted to the counter-passing phase-space domain.

This quantity is normally computed rather than measured directly. Kinetic modeling supplies the fast-electron distribution, classifies guiding-center orbits by passing direction, evaluates the collisional momentum moment, and multiplies by $R$ to obtain torque density about the symmetry axis. The counter-passing contribution combines with the [co-passing](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and [trapped](name:toroidal_trapped_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) contributions to form the total [toroidal fast electron collisional torque density](name:toroidal_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions); analogous counter-passing species contributions are defined for [thermal electrons](name:toroidal_counter_passing_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and [fast ions](name:toroidal_counter_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent. Interpretive fast-electron transport calculations commonly give $10^{-6}$-$1$ $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ for weakly driven suprathermal electron populations, while localized current-drive or runaway-electron cases can reach $1$-$100$ $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$; either sign is possible depending on the direction of the collisional momentum transfer.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the $\phi$-directed collisional force density on counter-passing fast electrons points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Local toroidal torque density, in N m^-2, transferred by Coulomb collisions with a specified ion charge state to fast ions in the counter-passing orbit class. It is the toroidal angular-momentum deposition rate per unit volume about the symmetry axis and includes the major-radius lever arm.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal counter-passing fast-ion state torque density due to collisions is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer toroidal angular momentum to the counter-passing subset of the fast-ion distribution through interactions with a specified ion charge state. The quantity has units $N\,m^{-2}$, equivalent to torque per unit volume, $(N\,m)\,m^{-3}$. The counter-passing label identifies the fast-ion orbit class contributing to the moment, not an additional collision partner.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, a kinetic definition for ion charge state $a$ is:

$$
\tau_{\phi,a}^{\mathrm{cp}}(\mathbf{x}) = R \int m_f v_\phi\, \mathcal{C}_{fa}\!\left[f_f^{\mathrm{cp}}, f_a\right](\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $R$ is the major radius in m, $m_f$ is the fast-ion mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the physical toroidal velocity component in m s$^{-1}$, $f_f^{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing fast-ion distribution, $f_a$ is the distribution of ions in charge state $a$, and $\mathcal{C}_{fa}$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on $f_f^{\mathrm{cp}}$ due to that state. If $f$ is normalized so that $\int f\,d^3v$ is number density in m$^{-3}$, then $\mathcal{C}_{fa}$ has units s$^2$ m$^{-6}$; the velocity moment before multiplication by $R$ is a toroidal force density in N m$^{-3}$, and the lever arm $R$ converts it to a torque density in N m$^{-2}$.

In practice the value is computed from a fast-ion distribution and background plasma state by evaluating the collisional part of the kinetic equation and taking this velocity moment over the counter-passing region of phase space. It may also be inferred indirectly in integrated momentum-balance analyzes, using rotation, density, temperature, and fast-ion measurements to constrain the distribution and collisional slowing-down rates.

Typical absolute magnitudes are $10^{-5}$-$10^{-2}$ N m$^{-2}$ for weak fast-ion momentum exchange, $10^{-3}$-$1$ N m$^{-2}$ in many beam-heated tokamak plasmas, and up to $1$-$10$ N m$^{-2}$ near strongly localized fast-ion momentum deposition. The signed value depends on the direction of the collisional toroidal momentum transfer for the selected counter-passing orbit branch.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional toroidal force transferred to the counter-passing fast ions points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, so that $R m_f v_\phi$ increases.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal collisional torque density delivered to fast ions on counter-passing orbits, equal to the collisional source of their toroidal angular momentum per unit volume.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal counter-passing fast-ion torque density due to collisions is the rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions change the toroidal angular momentum of fast ions on counter-passing passing orbits. It is an orbit-class-resolved collisional momentum source; together with the corresponding [co-passing](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and [trapped](name:toroidal_trapped_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) contributions, it forms the collisional fast-ion toroidal torque density.

For a local value, the torque density is the major-radius-weighted toroidal collisional force density:

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{fast,cp}}(\mathbf{x}) = R \sum_a m_a \int v_\phi\, C_{a,\mathrm{coll}}\!\left[f_a^{\mathrm{fast,cp}}\right](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $R$ is the major radius and $v_\phi=\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal velocity component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, $a$ labels fast-ion species, and $m_a$ is the species mass. The distribution function $f_a^{\mathrm{fast,cp}}$ has units $\mathrm{m}^{-3}(\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^{-3}$, and the Coulomb collision operator $C_{a,\mathrm{coll}}[f]$ has units $\mathrm{m}^{-3}(\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The velocity integral gives a toroidal force density; multiplication by $R$ converts it to a toroidal angular-momentum source density with units $\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from a kinetic fast-ion distribution classified by orbit type, using a Coulomb or Fokker-Planck collision operator and integrating the resulting toroidal momentum source over velocity space and relevant fast-ion species. It is often used in toroidal angular-momentum balance to separate collisional exchange involving counter-passing fast ions from the co-passing and trapped orbit-class contributions.

Typical magnitudes in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas are about 0.01-10 $\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}$, with localized high-power neutral-beam cases reaching several tens of $\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}$. The signed value may be either positive or negative depending on whether collisions accelerate or brake the counter-passing fast ions in the positive toroidal sense.
NAMES.sign: Positive when collisions exert a toroidal force on the counter-passing fast ions in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Toroidal torque per unit volume transferred to thermal electrons by Coulomb collisions with counter-passing fast particles. It is the local rate of toroidal angular-momentum exchange about the symmetry axis, signed along increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the counter-passing fast-particle contribution to the collisional toroidal torque density acting on thermal electrons. Counter-passing fast particles have passing guiding-center orbits whose parallel motion is opposite to the plasma-current direction; through Coulomb friction they transfer toroidal angular momentum to the thermal electron population about the symmetry axis.

The quantity can be represented as the major-radius moment of the collisional toroidal force density in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{ctr}}^{\mathrm{th,e}}(R,Z) = R\,m_e \int v_\phi\, C_{\mathrm{e}\leftarrow\mathrm{fp,ctr}}[f_{\mathrm{th,e}}, f_{\mathrm{fp,ctr}}] \, d^3v
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v_\phi$ is the thermal-electron toroidal velocity component in m/s, $C_{\mathrm{e}\leftarrow\mathrm{fp,ctr}}$ is the Coulomb collision operator contribution to the time derivative of the thermal-electron distribution due to counter-passing fast particles, with units of phase-space density per second, and $d^3v$ is the thermal-electron velocity-space volume element in $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^3$. The integral multiplied by $m_e$ gives toroidal force density, and the factor $R$ converts it to torque per unit plasma volume.

It is usually computed from kinetic or reduced-kinetic fast-particle calculations by evaluating the electron collision operator separately for the counter-passing orbit class. It is not normally measured directly; experimental constraints enter through fast-particle diagnostics, electron profiles, and momentum-balance analysis.

Typical local magnitudes are highly scenario dependent. Core values in transport calculations are often $10^{-4}-1\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, while strong fast-particle sources can produce localized peaks of $1-10\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$; near cancelation with co-passing or trapped contributions can make the net thermal-electron collisional torque density much smaller.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional transfer of toroidal angular momentum to the thermal electron population is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_thermal_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Rate of toroidal angular momentum transfer per unit volume from Coulomb collisions to a specified thermal ion charge state by counter-passing fast particles. It equals the toroidal collisional force density on the recipient state multiplied by the major-radius lever arm, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal counter-passing thermal-ion-state torque density due to collisions is the rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer toroidal angular momentum from the counter-passing part of a fast-particle distribution to thermal ions in a specified charge state. The charge-state index identifies the recipient ionization state, and the toroidal direction is the $\phi$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This is a torque density rather than a force density: the local toroidal force density is multiplied by the major-radius lever arm to give the rate of toroidal angular-momentum transfer per unit volume.

The local torque density is the major-radius lever arm times the collisional toroidal force density on the recipient thermal-ion state:

$$
\mathcal{T}_{\phi} = R\,F_{\phi}
$$

where $\mathcal{T}_{\phi}$ is the torque density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $R$ is the major radius in meters, and $F_{\phi}$ is the toroidal collisional force density on the recipient thermal ion charge state in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. The force density $F_{\phi}$ is itself the toroidal momentum moment of the Coulomb collision term coupling the counter-passing fast particles to that thermal-ion state, so that toroidal momentum lost by the counter-passing fast particles is gained by the recipient thermal ions.

This quantity is usually computed rather than measured directly. It is obtained by taking toroidal momentum moments of Coulomb collision terms in kinetic, Fokker-Planck, Monte Carlo, or reduced transport calculations, using the local geometry to supply the lever arm $R$ and separating the fast-particle population by orbit class. Experimental constraints typically enter through measurements of fast-particle sources and losses, ion composition, temperature, density, and toroidal rotation.

Typical magnitudes are highly source and device dependent. Values of $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ are common for weak fast-particle populations or broad slowing-down torque, while localized neutral-beam-driven regions can reach $0.1$-$10\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional toroidal force on the recipient thermal ion charge state points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, so that the state gains positive toroidal angular momentum.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal torque per unit volume transferred to bulk thermal ions by Coulomb collisions with the counter-passing fast-particle population in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the toroidal torque density acting on bulk thermal ions due to Coulomb collisions with the counter-passing component of a fast-particle population. It is the local rate of transfer of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume to the recipient thermal ions, with the toroidal direction defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Counter-passing particles have guiding-center parallel motion opposite to the plasma-current direction, so this channel can contribute with the opposite sign to the corresponding co-passing channel.

The torque density can be written as the toroidal moment of the collision term acting on the thermal-ion distribution:

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{cp}} = R \sum_i m_i \int v_\phi\, C_{i\leftarrow\mathrm{cp}}[f_i, f_{\mathrm{cp}}] \, d^3v
$$

where $i$ labels recipient thermal-ion species, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $v_\phi = \mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal velocity component, $f_i$ is the thermal-ion distribution, $f_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing fast-particle distribution, and $C_{i\leftarrow\mathrm{cp}}$ is the Coulomb collision operator contribution transferring momentum from that fast-particle subset to species $i$. For the same binary collisions, momentum conservation gives the equal-and-opposite reaction torque on the counter-passing fast-particle population.

This quantity is usually computed from kinetic fast-particle transport or slowing-down calculations that resolve passing-orbit topology and evaluate collisional momentum exchange with the thermal plasma. It enters the thermal-ion toroidal momentum balance together with the co-passing and trapped orbit-class contributions, and its volume integral contributes to the aggregate thermal torque due to collisions. Rotation measurements and fast-particle diagnostics can constrain the models used to infer it, but the torque density itself is generally a computed momentum-source term rather than a directly measured observable.

Typical local magnitudes in beam-heated tokamak plasmas are about $10^{-4}-1\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, with smaller values in weak fast-particle populations and larger localized values possible near strong tangential beam deposition or during transient redistribution. In common neutral-beam scenarios the counter-passing contribution often has the opposite sign to the dominant co-passing torque because the two orbit classes carry opposite toroidal angular momentum.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions with counter-passing fast particles transfer toroidal angular momentum to thermal ions in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density
NAMES.short: Local source rate of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume acting on counter-passing particles, whose guiding-center parallel velocity is opposite to the plasma current. It includes the major-radius lever arm and is summed over particle species and momentum-exchange mechanisms.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal counter-passing torque density is the source rate of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume applied to the counter-passing orbit-class population. Counter-passing particles are passing guiding centers whose parallel velocity is opposite to the plasma-current direction; trapped particles are excluded. The aggregate includes the major-radius lever arm and sums over particle species and momentum-exchange mechanisms.

At a point with major radius \(R\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame, where \(R\) is major radius, \(\phi\) is toroidal angle, and \(Z\) is vertical height, the defining velocity-space moment is

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{cp}} = \sum_a \sum_k R \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},a}} m_a\, v_\phi\, S_{a,k}[f_a] \, d^3v
$$

where \(\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{cp}}\) is the torque density in N m^-2, \(a\) indexes particle species, \(k\) indexes momentum-exchange mechanisms, \(R\) is in m, \(m_a\) is the particle mass in kg, \(v_\phi\) is the toroidal component of guiding-center velocity along \(\hat{\phi}\) in m s^-1, \(S_{a,k}[f_a]\) is the rate of change of the distribution function due to mechanism \(k\) in s^2 m^-6 when \(f_a\) has units s^3 m^-6, and \(d^3v\) is the velocity-space volume element in m^3 s^-3. The domain \(\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},a}\) is the counter-passing part of velocity space outside the trapped region, and the factor \(R\) converts a toroidal force-density moment into an angular-momentum source rate per unit volume.

In practice this quantity is computed by orbit-classifying kinetic distribution functions and taking the same moment of collisional, wave-particle, electromagnetic, and external-source operators over the counter-passing domain. It can also be inferred indirectly from toroidal momentum balance when the other transport and source terms are constrained. Together with [toroidal_co_passing_torque_density](name:toroidal_co_passing_torque_density) and [toroidal_trapped_torque_density](name:toroidal_trapped_torque_density), it partitions the total orbit-class torque density; [toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force](name:toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force) is a mechanism-specific contribution.

Typical orbit-class-resolved values in tokamak transport analyzes are about 10^-3-10 N m^-2, while localized strong external momentum input can produce values of 10-100 N m^-2. The value is zero when there is no net angular-momentum exchange with the counter-passing population or when positive and negative mechanism contributions cancel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the summed source increases toroidal angular momentum corresponding to motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle \(\phi\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal torque density exerted on counter-passing particles by the J cross B force arising from the current component normal to the flux surface. Counter-passing particles are those whose guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal counter-passing torque density due to the $J\times B$ force is the rate of change of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume assigned to the orbit class whose guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the plasma current. The toroidal direction is the $\phi$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and this quantity retains only the Lorentz-force contribution produced by the current component normal to the flux surface. It is interpreted as the flux-surface-averaged toroidal angular-momentum source for the counter-passing population.

The flux-surface-averaged source may be written as

$$
T_{\phi,\mathrm{cp}}^{J\times B}=\left\langle R\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\cdot\left(J_{\perp,\mathrm{cp}}\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\times\mathbf{B}\right)\right\rangle
$$

where $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes the flux-surface average, $R$ is major radius in m, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the outward unit normal to the flux surface, $J_{\perp,\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing current density along that normal in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T. The relevant current component is the one normal to the flux surface; this coincides with the cylindrical radial direction $\hat{R}$ only in the special case of circular, concentric surfaces, and in general differs from it once the equilibrium is shaped, so the two should not be treated as identical.

The quantity is obtained from kinetic or Fokker-Planck transport models that partition the particle distribution by orbit class, retaining only the counter-passing segment when forming the current and the associated $J\times B$ force. Together with the [co-passing](name:toroidal_co_passing_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force) and [trapped](name:toroidal_trapped_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force) orbit-class contributions, it decomposes the [total toroidal J cross B torque density](name:toroidal_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force); summing the orbit classes recovers that aggregate. It is the mechanism-specific counterpart of the broader [counter-passing toroidal torque density](name:toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density).

Magnitudes scale with the local fast-particle current and the magnetic field, and are largest where radial current or fast-particle gradients are strong; the sign and amplitude depend on scenario, beam geometry, and orbit-class cancelation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the $J\times B$ force from the flux-surface-normal current component drives counter-passing toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport
NAMES.short: Toroidal projection of the current density vector due to anomalous transport onto the direction of increasing toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component $j_\phi^{\rm ano}$ is the projection of the anomalous current density vector $\mathbf{j}_{\rm ano}$ onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It quantifies the electrical current per unit cross-sectional area driven in the toroidal direction by turbulence-induced transport processes.

The projection is given by

$$
j_\phi^{\rm ano} = \mathbf{j}_{\rm ano} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\rm ano}$ (in $\text{A} \cdot \text{m}^{-2}$) is the full anomalous current density vector and $\hat{\phi}$ (dimensionless) is the unit vector pointing in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

This quantity is typically obtained from the anomalous current density vector computed by gyrokinetic or fluid turbulence simulations, or from reduced transport models, by evaluating the dot product with the toroidal unit vector at each point.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $j_\phi^{\rm ano}$ flows in the direction of increasing $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from $+Z$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Toroidal projection of the plasma current density carried by the diamagnetic drift, arising from cross-field pressure gradients acting on magnetized plasma species.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic drift gives rise to a plasma current density flowing perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the plasma pressure gradient; this quantity is the scalar projection of that current density vector along the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The toroidal diamagnetic current density is given by:

$$
j_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{B^2}\right) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $p$ is the total plasma pressure, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field vector, and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$.

This is the toroidal projection of the parent [current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) vector; the analogous poloidal component is described by [poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). It is computed from kinetic pressure profiles combined with magnetic equilibrium geometry, and enters the current budget in MHD force-balance and edge-transport models, with greatest importance in steep-gradient regions such as the H-mode pedestal and internal transport barriers.

Typical magnitudes span $10^4$–$10^7$ A m$^{-2}$ in fusion-relevant pedestal and transport-barrier regions where pressure gradients are steepest.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal diamagnetic current density is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short: Toroidal projection of the heat-viscosity-driven current density, taken along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents the electric current-density contribution associated with heat-flow-related viscous stress in a plasma.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal current density due to heat viscosity is the component of electric current density associated with the heat-flow-dependent part of viscous stress in a magnetized plasma. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, it is the projection along $\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle. It is one contribution to [toroidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and is distinct from current-density terms due to parallel or perpendicular viscosity.

The toroidal component is defined by projecting the heat-viscosity current-density vector onto the toroidal basis direction:

$$
j_{{\rm hv},\phi} = \mathbf{j}_{\rm hv} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $j_{{\rm hv},\phi}$ is the toroidal current density due to heat viscosity in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{j}_{\rm hv}$ is the heat-viscosity contribution to current density in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. The vector $\mathbf{j}_{\rm hv}$ represents the current response associated with heat-flow-related viscous stress; the detailed constitutive closure is model-dependent.

In transport analysis this quantity is usually computed from the heat-viscosity term in a momentum-balance or generalized-Ohm-law closure and then projected onto $\hat{\phi}$. It is normally inferred from plasma state variables and transport-model terms rather than measured as an independent diagnostic signal. Related resolved quantities include [poloidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), [parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and the heat-current counterpart [parallel_heat_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity).

Representative magnitudes are strongly closure- and scenario-dependent. Values may be near 0 A.m^-2 when heat-viscosity stress is weak or omitted, while local corrections of order 10^2-10^5 A.m^-2 can occur in steep-gradient transport calculations; these are scale estimates rather than hard bounds and should be interpreted relative to the local total toroidal current-density budget.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the heat-viscosity-driven current density has a toroidal component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia
NAMES.short: Toroidal component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame with phi increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above, of the current density arising from ion inertia in the plasma momentum balance.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal projection of the current density due to ion inertia, taken along the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$. The inertial current is the perpendicular current that must flow to balance the ion inertial force (the time variation and advection of the ion fluid momentum) against the Lorentz force in the momentum equation.

The inertial current density is obtained by crossing the ion inertial force density with the magnetic field:

$$
j_{\phi} = \left[ \frac{\rho_i}{B^2}\, \mathbf{B} \times \frac{d\mathbf{v}_i}{dt} \right] \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\rho_i$ is the ion mass density in kg m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the ion fluid velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, and $d\mathbf{v}_i/dt = \partial \mathbf{v}_i/\partial t + (\mathbf{v}_i \cdot \nabla)\mathbf{v}_i$ is the convective acceleration. This is the fluid analog of the polarization current and is dimensionally a current density (A m$^{-2}$).

This quantity is evaluated within fluid or multi-fluid transport models rather than measured directly; it can be reconstructed from modeled ion flow, density, and magnetic field profiles using the relation above. Together with the [radial](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), [poloidal](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), [vertical](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), and [parallel](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia) projections it fully specifies the vector [current density due to ion inertia](name:current_density_due_to_ion_inertia).

The inertial current is generally a small correction to the total toroidal current density, becoming appreciable where ion flows are strong and rapidly varying, such as during transients or in regions of steep velocity gradients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal inertial current density points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the electric current density driven by frictional momentum exchange between plasma ions and neutral particles. In the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, positive values correspond to current flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle phi.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal current density due to ion-neutral friction is the component along the toroidal direction of the electric current density associated with momentum exchange between ions and neutral particles. It describes how neutral drag on ion motion contributes to charge-current flow around the torus in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The toroidal component is defined by projecting the ion-neutral-friction current-density contribution onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
j_{\phi,\mathrm{in}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $j_{\phi,\mathrm{in}}$ is the toroidal current density due to ion-neutral friction in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the corresponding vector current-density contribution in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In fluid models, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}}$ is computed from the ion-neutral friction force density that enters the ion momentum balance; a common estimate uses $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{in}} \approx m_i n_i \nu_{in}(\mathbf{u}_n-\mathbf{u}_i)$, where $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{in}}$ is force density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$, $m_i$ is ion mass in $\mathrm{kg}$, $n_i$ is ion density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $\mathbf{u}_i$ and $\mathbf{u}_n$ are ion and neutral velocities in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $\nu_{in}$ is the ion-neutral momentum-transfer collision frequency in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

This quantity is usually inferred rather than measured directly, using plasma density, temperature, flow, and neutral population estimates in edge-transport or momentum-balance calculations. The toroidal and poloidal components are geometric projections in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, while a parallel component is a projection along the magnetic-field direction and a diamagnetic contribution is associated with pressure-gradient and magnetization physics; these related quantities should not be interpreted as a single complete set of independent orthogonal components.

Typical modeled magnitudes are near zero where the neutral density is negligible, often $1-10^3\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$ in partially ionized scrape-off-layer and divertor plasma, and can locally approach $10^4\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$ in cold, dense, strongly recycling regions. The sign and magnitude depend on neutral density, ion-neutral collision frequency, relative ion-neutral flow, plasma collisionality, and magnetic geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current density due to ion-neutral friction points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the current density driven by perpendicular viscous stress in the plasma fluid, projected along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal current density due to perpendicular viscosity is the toroidal component of the current density associated with perpendicular viscous stress in a magnetized plasma. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity is the toroidal projection of [current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and complements the radial, poloidal, and field-aligned projections of the same physical contribution.

The component is defined by projecting the perpendicular-viscosity-driven current-density vector onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
j_{\perp\mathrm{visc},\phi} = \mathbf{j}_{\perp\mathrm{visc}} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\perp\mathrm{visc}}$ is the current density due to perpendicular viscous stress, measured in A m$^{-2}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$, and $j_{\perp\mathrm{visc},\phi}$ is the toroidal component, also measured in A m$^{-2}$.

This contribution is usually computed rather than measured directly. It is obtained from the perpendicular viscous stress tensor used in a fluid, drift-kinetic, or transport model, inserted into the momentum and charge-balance relations that define viscosity-driven current, and then projected onto $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$. It contributes alongside other viscous-current terms, such as [toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), to [toroidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity).

Typical magnitudes are strongly regime dependent. Core values may be below 1 A m$^{-2}$ when perpendicular viscous forces are weak or symmetry cancels the toroidal projection, while edge, pedestal, and scrape-off-layer calculations commonly span 1-10^4 A m$^{-2}$, with larger localized values possible in steep-gradient or strongly sheared flows.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perpendicular-viscosity-driven current density has a component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity of the effective deuterium-tritium fuel-ion species at the internal transport barrier. The species is a fictitious single ion with atomic mass 2.5 amu, and the component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal deuterium-tritium velocity at the internal transport barrier (ITB) is the $\hat{\phi}$ component of the bulk flow velocity of an effective fuel-ion fluid at the ITB location. The effective deuterium-tritium species represents deuterium and tritium as a single fictitious ion species with atomic mass 2.5 amu; resolved-isotope counterparts are [toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier). The component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The toroidal component is the projection of the effective deuterium-tritium bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi,DT} = \mathbf{v}_{DT} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{DT}$ is the bulk velocity of the effective deuterium-tritium species and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$.

In experiments, toroidal ion rotation near the ITB is commonly inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy using Doppler shifts of impurity emission, then related to the main-ion or effective fuel-ion rotation through modeling assumptions or collisional corrections. In transport calculations that combine deuterium and tritium, this quantity is the toroidal velocity of the combined fuel-ion momentum variable at the ITB. Related effective-DT values at other reference locations are [toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal).

Typical ITB toroidal velocities in rotating H-mode plasmas are about $1\times10^4$-$3\times10^5$ m s$^{-1}$, with lower values in low-torque plasmas. Strong radial shear of this velocity across the ITB is often important for turbulence suppression and transport-barrier formation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective deuterium-tritium bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity of the fictitious deuterium-tritium single-species (atomic mass 2.5 amu) evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal deuterium-tritium velocity at the magnetic axis is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the bulk flow velocity of a fictitious single-ion species representing the DT fuel mixture, evaluated at the location where $\nabla\psi = 0$. The effective DT species carries an atomic mass of 2.5 amu — the arithmetic mean of deuterium (2 amu) and tritium (3 amu) — allowing transport simulations to model the combined fuel population as a single fluid without separately resolving each isotope.

The toroidal projection is defined as:

$$
v_\phi = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{DT} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{DT}$ is the bulk flow velocity of the fictitious DT species and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In experiment, ion toroidal rotation near the magnetic axis is inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy via the Doppler shift of fuel-ion or impurity emission lines; the fictitious DT value at the axis is then extracted through transport modeling or extrapolation. The on-axis velocity sets the innermost boundary condition for the toroidal momentum transport equation. Analogous quantities at other radial positions are captured by [toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_deuterium_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier); the single-isotope deuterium counterpart at the same location is [toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the deuterium ion flow velocity evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal deuterium velocity at the internal transport barrier (ITB) is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the bulk deuterium ion flow vector sampled at the ITB — a region of reduced turbulent transport in the plasma interior, characterized by steep gradients in temperature, density, and rotation velocity, often associated with reversed or weak magnetic shear.

The quantity is defined by the projection:

$$
v_\phi^D = \mathbf{v}_D \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate.

Toroidal ion flow at the ITB is measured primarily by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), where the Doppler shift of emission lines from reactions between injected neutral beam atoms and plasma deuterium ions yields the local bulk velocity. Rotation velocities in ITB plasmas range from a few km/s to several tens of km/s depending on plasma current, heating power, and barrier strength. Velocity shear at the ITB location is closely linked to radial electric field structure and plays a central role in turbulence suppression. For toroidal velocities of other species at the same location, see [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_deuterium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk deuterium ion flow velocity at the magnetic axis, taken along the phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal deuterium velocity at the magnetic axis is the central value of the deuterium ion bulk flow projected onto the toroidal direction. It characterizes rotation of the deuterium population at the radial center of the nested magnetic flux surfaces, not a full radial variation of the flow.

The quantity is defined by projecting the deuterium bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector at the magnetic-axis location:

$$
v_{\phi,D,\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{v}_D(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi,D,\mathrm{axis}}$ is in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{v}_D$ is the deuterium ion bulk velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}$ is a point on the magnetic-axis curve, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

In practice, this value is obtained from central ion-flow measurements when available, or inferred from nearby core measurements together with equilibrium geometry and transport or momentum-balance constraints. Such estimates should be interpreted as contextual determinations of the magnetic-axis value rather than as part of the definition.

Representative magnitudes are device- and scenario-dependent, commonly about $10^3$-$10^5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in low-torque plasmas and up to a few $10^5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ when strong external momentum input is present.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the deuterium bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_electric_field
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the electric field in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the signed projection of the electric field along increasing toroidal angle phi.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal electric field is the component of the electric-field vector along the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. In tokamak plasmas it is the component most directly associated with inductive electron acceleration, plasma initiation, toroidal current drive, and ohmic dissipation.

The component is defined by projection onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
E_\phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $E_\phi$ is the toroidal electric field in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

In practice, $E_\phi$ is inferred from loop-voltage measurements, magnetic-flux evolution, transport analysis, or local electric-field estimates. For an axisymmetric field that is approximately uniform along a circular contour of major radius $R$ in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the local relation is commonly interpreted as $E_\phi \approx V_\mathrm{loop}/(2\pi R)$, where $V_\mathrm{loop}$ is the voltage around that contour in volts and $R$ is in meters; this approximation should not be treated as a general pointwise equality when the field varies poloidally or toroidally. During plasma initiation, $E_\phi$ is considered together with [prefill pressure] and [perpendicular magnetic field] because these affect ionization avalanche and electron confinement. During ohmic operation, the product of toroidal electric field and toroidal current density contributes to Joule heating and is related to [plasma resistance].

Representative magnitudes are typically about $0.01-0.2\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ during established ohmic current sustainment, and about $0.1-10\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ during startup, breakdown, or rapid current ramp phases. The value depends on device size, applied loop voltage, plasma resistivity, gas conditions, and magnetic-field error levels.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric-field component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the electron bulk fluid velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal electron velocity is the projection of the electron bulk fluid velocity onto the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the mean electron flow around the torus and is a signed component of the electron momentum balance.

For an electron distribution function, the toroidal bulk velocity is the first velocity moment projected onto $\hat{\phi}$:

$$
v_{e,\phi} = \mathbf{v}_e \cdot \hat{\phi} = \frac{1}{n_e}\int v_\phi f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_e$ is the electron bulk velocity, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, $v_\phi$ is the particle velocity component along $\hat{\phi}$, $f_e$ is the electron distribution function, and $n_e$ is the electron density.

In practice, toroidal electron velocity may be inferred from momentum-balance modeling, kinetic measurements, charge and current balance, or transport calculations. Because electrons carry much of the toroidal current response, this velocity is closely related to the electron contribution to toroidal current density, while remaining distinct from the ion counterpart [toroidal_ion_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) and from radial, poloidal, or field-parallel electron flow components.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent: magnitudes of 1e3-1e5 m.s^-1 are common in magnetically confined plasmas, while low-density edge regions, strong current drive, or transient conditions can produce values of several 1e5 m.s^-1 or more.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Radial derivative of the signed toroidal electron fluid velocity, the phi component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius rho_tor,norm.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the flux-coordinate derivative of the signed toroidal component of the electron fluid velocity in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It describes how the toroidal electron flow changes between neighboring magnetic surfaces as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases from the magnetic axis toward the last closed flux surface.

The derivative is defined by differentiating the toroidal electron velocity with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$:

$$
\frac{\partial v_{\phi,e}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $v_{\phi,e}$ is the [toroidal electron velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity) in m.s^-1 and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is a dimensionless flux coordinate equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface. Because the differentiation coordinate is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as the velocity.

In practice the quantity is obtained from the radial dependence of $v_{\phi,e}$ on magnetic surfaces, using a smooth fitted representation or local numerical differentiation with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. It is the first-derivative counterpart of [second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity), and uses the same flux-coordinate differentiation concept as [radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure](name:radial_derivative_of_electron_pressure).

Representative magnitudes in tokamak transport analysis are often of order 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1 per unit $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, with values near zero where the toroidal electron velocity is radially flat. Larger local magnitudes can occur where the signed electron flow changes rapidly over a narrow interval in $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the signed toroidal electron velocity component $v_{\phi,e}$, taken positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, increases as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases from the magnetic axis toward the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Second derivative of the toroidal electron fluid velocity with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius, quantifying the radial curvature of the electron toroidal rotation profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of the toroidal electron velocity quantifies the curvature of the $v_{e,\phi}$ profile along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, where $v_{e,\phi}$ is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the electron bulk fluid velocity as defined in [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity). A nonzero curvature indicates that the first-order radial shear [radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_toroidal_electron_velocity) is itself varying radially, which is physically significant near transport barriers and velocity inflection layers.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d^2 v_{e,\phi}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, dimensionless and ranging from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the separatrix. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, the second derivative retains the same unit as the velocity itself.

This higher-order derivative is used in numerical transport solvers for spatial discretization of the electron momentum equation. The analogous ion quantity is [second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity), and the poloidal counterpart is [second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_poloidal_electron_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $d^2 v_{e,\phi}/d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2 > 0$, inheriting the convention that $v_{e,\phi}$ is positive when the electron fluid flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Toroidal fast-electron torque density due to Coulomb collisions is the rate of toroidal angular-momentum transfer per unit volume to fast electrons from thermal electrons. It equals major radius times the phi-directed collisional force density in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal fast-electron torque density due to collisions is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions with thermal electrons transfer toroidal angular momentum to the fast-electron population per unit volume. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. This is an angular torque density, so it includes the major-radius lever arm multiplying the toroidal force density.

For a kinetic fast-electron distribution, the quantity is the toroidal velocity moment of the collision operator multiplied by $R$:

$$
\tau^{\mathrm{coll}}_{\phi,\mathrm{fe}}(R,Z) = R \int m_e v_\phi\, C^{\mathrm{coll}}_{\mathrm{fe}\leftarrow e}[f_\mathrm{fe},f_e] \, d^3v
$$

where $\tau^{\mathrm{coll}}_{\phi,\mathrm{fe}}$ is in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $R$ is in m, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the particle velocity component along $+\hat{\phi}$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $C^{\mathrm{coll}}_{\mathrm{fe}\leftarrow e}$ is the Coulomb collision operator giving the rate of change of the fast-electron distribution $f_\mathrm{fe}$ due to thermal electrons with distribution $f_e$. The velocity integral gives the collisional toroidal force density on fast electrons in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$; multiplication by $R$ gives angular torque density.

This quantity is usually computed from a kinetic or reduced fast-electron transport model by taking the toroidal moment of the electron-electron collision term, and may then be volume-integrated to obtain [toroidal_fast_electron_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_electron_torque_due_to_collisions). Orbit-resolved contributions such as [toroidal_trapped_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_trapped_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and [toroidal_co_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) separate the same collisional momentum exchange by fast-electron orbit class. It is distinct from a total fast-particle collisional torque density because only the fast-electron population and its collisions with thermal electrons are included.

Typical signed magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent: values of $10^{-4}$-$10^{1}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ are common in modeled fast-electron current-drive or weak runaway-electron conditions, while localized relaxation of dense fast-electron populations can reach $10^{2}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ or more.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions exert a toroidal force on the fast electrons in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_electron_torque_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated toroidal torque transferred to the fast (non-thermal) electron population through Coulomb collisions with the thermal background plasma.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the total toroidal angular momentum per unit time exchanged between the fast (non-thermal) electron population and the thermal plasma constituents via Coulomb collisions, integrated over the entire plasma volume.
