It measures the net collisional momentum transfer that modifies the toroidal rotation of the fast-electron distribution function.

The volume-integrated toroidal torque is obtained from the angular-momentum moment of the Coulomb collision operator acting on the fast electron distribution:

$$
T_\phi = \int m_e R \, v_\phi \, C[f_{\rm fast}] \, d^3v \, dV
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $R$ is the major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component, $C$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the fast electron distribution function $f_{\rm fast}$, and the integral is taken over both velocity space $d^3v$ and the plasma volume $dV$.

This quantity is evaluated from kinetic modeling of the fast electron distribution function using Fokker-Planck or bounce-averaged solvers. The complementary torque on the thermal electron sub-population is given by [toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions), while [toroidal_fast_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_torque_due_to_collisions) aggregates collisional torque over all fast particle species. The orbit-resolved local torque density for co-passing fast electrons is available as [toroidal_co_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net toroidal torque on fast electrons is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Collisional toroidal torque density transferred to fast ions in a specified charge state by Coulomb collisions with background particles. It is the toroidal angular-momentum source per unit volume, summed over all fast-ion orbit topologies.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal fast-ion state torque density due to collisions is the Coulomb-collisional source of mechanical toroidal angular momentum for fast ions in a specified charge state, expressed per unit plasma volume. It is summed over all fast-ion orbit topologies and is associated with the $\phi$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The local kinetic form is the toroidal angular-momentum moment of the collisional operator:

$$
\mathcal{T}_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{(q)} = R\,m_q \int v_\phi \left[\sum_b C_{qb}(f_q, f_b)\right] \, d^3v
$$

where $\mathcal{T}_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{(q)}$ is this torque density for charge state $q$ in N m$^{-2}$, $R$ is major radius in m, $m_q$ is the fast-ion mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the particle velocity component in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction in m s$^{-1}$, $f_q$ and $f_b$ are fast-ion and background distribution functions normalized to number density with units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, $C_{qb}$ is the Coulomb collision operator for interactions with background population $b$ with units of $f_q$ per second, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The integral without $R$ is a toroidal force density in N m$^{-3}$; multiplying by $R$ gives torque per unit volume in N m$^{-2}$.

In practice the quantity is computed by applying Fokker-Planck, Monte Carlo, orbit-following, or transport collision operators to the fast-ion distribution and then taking the toroidal velocity moment for the selected charge state. Experimental analyzes infer it indirectly from fast-ion distribution modeling and toroidal momentum balance, constrained by diagnostics such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, gamma-ray emission, charge exchange, or collective scattering. Conceptually, it is the toroidal component of fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions; summing over charge states gives [toroidal_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions), volume integration gives [toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions), and the trapped-orbit contribution is [toroidal_trapped_fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical core magnitudes in beam-heated tokamak plasmas are $10^{-2}$-$10$ N m$^{-2}$. Strongly localized slowing-down or pitch-angle-scattering regions can approach $10$-$100$ N m$^{-2}$, while weak fast-ion populations or outer-plasma regions may be below $10^{-3}$ N m$^{-2}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional torque accelerates the fast-ion charge-state population in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated torque about the symmetry axis transferred by Coulomb collisions from background plasma species to fast ions in a selected ion charge state.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal fast-ion state torque due to collisions is the rate at which Coulomb collisions change the toroidal angular momentum of the fast-ion population in a specified ion species and charge state. It is integrated over the plasma volume and represents collisional exchange with background plasma species, not externally applied torque.

A convenient kinetic definition is the major-radius moment of the collisional toroidal force density:

$$
N_{\phi,sq}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \int_V R \left[\sum_b \int m_s v_\phi C_{sq,b}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v\right] dV
$$

where $s,q$ identify the selected fast-ion species and charge state, $R$ is major radius in meters in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $m_s$ is the ion mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the physical toroidal velocity component in m s$^{-1}$, and $C_{sq,b}$ is the Coulomb collision-operator contribution from background species or charge state $b$. The velocity integral gives toroidal force density in N m$^{-3}$, multiplication by $R$ gives torque density in N m$^{-2}$, and the volume integral gives torque in N m, equivalent to m.N. The sum over $b$ includes all background collisional partners represented for this state; a total fast-ion collisional torque is obtained by summing the corresponding state-resolved contributions.

This quantity is usually computed from a fast-ion distribution function and a collisional slowing-down, pitch-angle-scattering, or full Fokker-Planck collision operator, using the reconstructed magnetic geometry to supply $R$ and the volume element. It is not measured directly, but is inferred from transport or orbit-kinetic modeling constrained by diagnostics sensitive to the fast-ion population and background plasma conditions.

Typical absolute magnitudes for state-resolved fast-ion collisional torques are about 0.001-10 m.N in medium-sized tokamak analyzes, and can reach 10-100 m.N in large or high-power cases. Values near zero indicate little net collisional exchange of toroidal angular momentum for the selected fast-ion charge state, while the sign distinguishes co-current from counter-current exchange according to the convention below.
NAMES.sign: Positive when collisions increase the toroidal angular momentum $R m_s v_\phi$ of the selected fast-ion charge state, with $v_\phi$ in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Rate per unit plasma volume at which Coulomb collisions with background ion species transfer toroidal angular momentum to the fast-ion population, taken about the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It aggregates contributions over fast-ion orbit classes and over the background ion species included in the collision model.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal fast-ion torque density due to collisions is the local rate per unit plasma volume at which Coulomb collisions with background ion species change the toroidal angular momentum of the fast-ion population. The toroidal direction is $\hat{\phi}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Unless a more resolved quantity is specified, it represents the aggregate over fast-ion orbit classes and over the background ion species retained in the collision operator; collisional momentum exchange with electrons is excluded.

The quantity is the toroidal moment of the collisional force density acting on the fast ions:

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{fast\ ion}}(\mathbf{x}) = R \sum_{a \in \mathrm{fast\ ions}} \sum_{b \in \mathrm{ions}} \hat{\phi} \cdot \int m_a\,\mathbf{v}\, C_{ab}[f_a,f_b](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{fast\ ion}}$ is the torque density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $R$ is the toroidal moment arm in meters, $a$ indexes fast-ion populations, $b$ indexes background ion species or charge states, $m_a$ is the fast-ion mass in kg, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $f_a$ and $f_b$ are distribution functions, and $C_{ab}$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on $f_a$ due to species $b$. The velocity-space integral is a toroidal force density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$; multiplication by $R$ converts it to a torque per unit volume.

This quantity is normally computed from kinetic fast-ion distributions using Fokker-Planck, orbit-following, or slowing-down collision models constrained by energetic-particle diagnostics and equilibrium information. Charge-state-resolved ion contributions are the local constituents of [toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions). It is distinct from the all-background-species aggregate [toroidal_fast_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_torque_due_to_collisions), which sums collisional torque from both thermal ions and electrons; the present quantity retains only the ion-collision contribution.

Magnitudes vary widely with heating power, fast-ion content, and background rotation, and can be positive, negative, or near zero across the radius depending on the fast-ion distribution, collisional slowing-down, and pitch-angle scattering. The largest local values arise in strongly neutral-beam- or energetic-ion-heated regimes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional force on the fast ions has a $+\hat{\phi}$ component, increasing their toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_particle_torque_due_to_j_cross_b_force
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated toroidal fast-particle torque from the Lorentz force associated with radial fast-particle current. It is the major-radius moment arm times the force component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This scalar is the total toroidal torque on the fast-particle population produced by the Lorentz force from its radial current. It represents a volume-integrated source of toroidal angular momentum, with the toroidal direction defined by increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The torque is the major-radius moment of the toroidal component of the Lorentz force density:

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}} = \int_V R\,\hat{\phi}\cdot\left(\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{fast,rad}}\times\mathbf{B}\right)\,dV
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the integrated torque in N m, $R$ is major radius in m, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{fast,rad}}$ is the radial fast-particle current density in A m^-2, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic flux density in T, $dV$ is the volume element in m^3, and $V$ is the integration volume.

In practice this quantity is computed from a fast-particle distribution function or reduced energetic-particle model by forming the radial current moment, combining it with the magnetic field, and integrating the resulting torque density over the plasma volume. It is commonly compared with other toroidal momentum sources and sinks such as collisional fast-particle torque and thermalization torque.

No device-independent numerical range is implied for this integrated torque; its magnitude scales with fast-particle radial current, magnetic geometry, and plasma volume. The physically relevant scale is usually established by comparison with other integrated torques in the same momentum balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net torque acts in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_torque_due_to_collisions
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated toroidal torque transferred to the fast particle population by Coulomb collisions with all background plasma species, including electrons and every thermal ion species or charge state.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal fast-particle torque due to collisions is the volume-integrated rate at which Coulomb collisions transfer toroidal angular momentum to the fast particle population. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This aggregate includes collisions with electrons and all thermal ion species and charge states, not only a single ion species.

The aggregate torque can be written as the plasma-volume integral of the toroidal collisional force density weighted by the lever arm $R$:

$$
T_\phi^{\mathrm{fast}} = \int_V R \sum_{j \in \{e,\,\mathrm{thermal\ ion\ species\ and\ charge\ states}\}} f_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow j}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $T_\phi^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the total collisional torque on fast particles in $\mathrm{N\,m}$, $V$ is the plasma volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, $R$ is major radius in $\mathrm{m}$, $dV$ is a differential volume element in $\mathrm{m^3}$, and $f_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}\leftarrow j}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the toroidal component of the collisional force density exerted on fast particles by background species $j$ in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. The summation over $j$ includes electrons and every thermal ion species and charge state.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic or transport calculations by taking the toroidal momentum moment of the Coulomb collision operator for the fast-particle distribution, or it is constrained indirectly from global momentum balance. Species-resolved contributions from [toroidal_fast_electron_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_electron_torque_due_to_collisions) and [toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions) sum to this aggregate; with consistent fast-thermal momentum accounting, the corresponding reaction appears in [toroidal_thermal_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_due_to_collisions).

Typical absolute magnitudes are near 0-0.1 N m for nearly isotropic fast-particle populations or balanced heating, 0.1-50 N m in medium-size beam-heated plasmas, and can reach 10-200 N m in large high-power neutral-beam scenarios. The signed value may be either polarity depending on the direction of the fast-particle toroidal momentum relative to the background plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when collisions exert a net toroidal force on fast particles in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Toroidal velocity of helium-3 ions at the radial location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal helium-3 velocity at an internal transport barrier is the component of the helium-3 ion mean fluid velocity along the toroidal direction, evaluated at the radial location of the barrier. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, this is the velocity component parallel to $\hat{\phi}$, describing motion around the machine symmetry axis.

The quantity is the local helium-3 toroidal velocity sampled at the barrier location:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{ITB}}^{(^3\mathrm{He})} = v_{\phi}^{(^3\mathrm{He})}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})
$$

where $v_{\phi}^{(^3\mathrm{He})}$ is the helium-3 toroidal velocity in m/s and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the radial coordinate of the internal transport barrier, for example a minor-radius coordinate or an explicitly named flux coordinate such as normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$.

In practice, this velocity may be inferred from Doppler shifts of helium-3 spectral lines, charge-exchange spectroscopy when suitable transitions are available, or transport analysis constrained by momentum balance. The internal transport barrier location is usually identified from steep gradients or reduced transport in temperature, density, rotation, or related transport coefficients, and the local velocity is obtained by interpolation or fitting at that radial position.

Typical absolute values of toroidal ion rotation at internal transport barriers are about $10^3-10^5$ m/s, depending on momentum input, collisionality, magnetic configuration, and radial electric-field shear.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-3 toroidal velocity is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the helium-3 ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, resolved along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal helium-3 velocity at the magnetic axis is the bulk flow velocity of helium-3 ions projected onto the toroidal direction at the innermost equilibrium location of the confined plasma. The toroidal direction is the $\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The magnetic axis is the location where the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.

The component is defined by projecting the helium-3 bulk velocity onto the toroidal basis vector at the magnetic axis:

$$
v_{\phi,\,^3\mathrm{He}}^{\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{u}_{^3\mathrm{He}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{u}_{^3\mathrm{He}}$ is the helium-3 ion bulk velocity, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, and $(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}})$ is the magnetic-axis position in the poloidal plane.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from ion flow measurements such as Doppler spectroscopy or charge-exchange recombination measurements when helium-3 emission is available, or from multi-ion transport analysis constrained by related measurements. The magnetic-axis value is obtained by evaluating the reconstructed or fitted radial variation of helium-3 toroidal flow at the axis.

Typical core values range from about $-2 \times 10^5$ to $2 \times 10^5$ m.s^-1 in tokamak plasmas. Helium-3 that is well coupled collisionally to the main ions often rotates at comparable speed, while minority helium-3 populations influenced by radio-frequency heating or strong momentum sources can deviate from the main-ion toroidal flow.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-3 bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Toroidal velocity of helium-4 ions at the internal transport barrier, taken along increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the species-specific helium-4 form of the bulk toroidal rotation evaluated on the flux surface representing the barrier location.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal helium-4 velocity at the internal transport barrier is the component of the bulk $^{4}\mathrm{He}$ ion flow along the toroidal direction, evaluated on the flux surface chosen to represent the barrier location. The internal transport barrier is a region of locally suppressed turbulent transport identified by steepened pressure or temperature gradients. This species-resolved rotation can differ from main-ion, electron, or other impurity rotation because sources, collisional coupling, and radial electric-field effects are species dependent.

The quantity is the projection of the helium-4 bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector at the barrier flux surface:

$$
v_{\phi}^{(^{4}\mathrm{He})} = \mathbf{v}^{(^{4}\mathrm{He})} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}^{(^{4}\mathrm{He})}$ is the helium-4 bulk ion velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

The value is commonly inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy through the Doppler shift of helium charge-exchange emission lines, with the line-of-sight velocity converted to the toroidal component using viewing geometry and magnetic-equilibrium information. The barrier radius is identified from the steepening of electron or ion temperature gradient profiles in the equilibrium reconstruction.

Typical magnitudes range from near zero in weakly rotating plasmas up to about $2 \times 10^{5}$ m.s^-1 in strongly heated, neutral-beam-driven discharges, with either sign possible depending on momentum input, intrinsic rotation, and local transport.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-4 bulk flow points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Toroidal hydrogen ion flow velocity evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal hydrogen ion velocity at an internal transport barrier is the component of the hydrogen ion bulk flow parallel to the toroidal basis direction, evaluated at the radial position where the barrier is identified. It describes the local hydrogen rotation associated with the barrier and is a signed velocity component, not a speed magnitude.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the component is defined by projecting the hydrogen ion flow velocity onto the toroidal unit vector at the internal-transport-barrier location:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{H},\mathrm{ITB}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{H}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the hydrogen ion bulk flow velocity, $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is a radial label for the barrier location, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

This quantity is commonly obtained from Doppler spectroscopy of hydrogen-related emission, often with charge-exchange or beam-assisted interpretation, and may also be constrained through transport analysis using species force balance. In such analyzes it is coupled to poloidal flow, pressure gradients, and magnetic-field components in determining the radial electric field and flow shear near the barrier.

Typical magnitudes in core tokamak plasmas are often $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s^-1, depending on external momentum input, collisional coupling to other ion species, neutral-beam geometry, and the strength of the internal transport barrier. Values near zero or sign reversals can occur in weakly rotating or counter-rotating conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the hydrogen ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_hydrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the hydrogen ion fluid velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal hydrogen velocity at the magnetic axis quantifies the bulk fluid flow of hydrogen ions along the $\hat{\phi}$ direction at the plasma center, where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ vanishes. On-axis toroidal rotation reflects the integrated effect of plasma momentum transport driven by neutral beam injection, intrinsic torques, and wave-driven momentum deposition.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as the projection onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{H}} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{H} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{H}$ is the hydrogen ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), which derives the ion flow velocity from the Doppler shift of hydrogen emission lines when a neutral beam intersects the plasma; the on-axis value corresponds to the innermost resolvable CXRS channel. Typical on-axis values range from a few km/s in Ohmic discharges to 100–300 km/s in strongly beam-heated plasmas. Analogous on-axis velocities for other ion species — including [toroidal helium-4 velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [toroidal helium-3 velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), and [toroidal tungsten velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) — follow the same definition and enable cross-species rotation comparisons that constrain radial electric field profiles and neoclassical transport models.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\phi,\mathrm{H}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Momentum diffusivity for ions in a specified charge state associated with the toroidal direction phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, quantifying diffusive radial transport of their toroidal momentum.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion charge-state momentum diffusivity is the kinematic diffusion coefficient for toroidal momentum carried by ions in a selected charge state. It represents collisional, neoclassical, and turbulent mixing of toroidal momentum between neighboring flux surfaces. The toroidal direction is $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

A common local transport closure defines the diffusive part of the radial toroidal-momentum flux density by

$$
\Pi_{\phi,i}^{(c),\mathrm{diff}} = -\chi_{\phi,i}^{(c)} \frac{\partial p_{\phi,i}^{(c)}}{\partial r}
$$

where $\chi_{\phi,i}^{(c)}$ is this diffusivity, $p_{\phi,i}^{(c)}$ is the toroidal momentum density of ion charge state $c$, and $\Pi_{\phi,i}^{(c),\mathrm{diff}}$ is the radial flux density of that toroidal momentum. The coordinate $r$ is an outward-increasing scalar radial coordinate labeling nested flux surfaces, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary; it is distinct from the major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The leading minus sign states that diffusive transport is down the outward radial gradient: if $p_{\phi,i}^{(c)}$ decreases outward, the diffusive flux is outward.

This coefficient is inferred by fitting toroidal momentum balance using measurements of ion rotation, density, temperature, and applied torque, together with estimates of neoclassical viscosity and turbulent momentum transport. Charge-state resolution is most relevant for impurity ions or partially ionized edge populations, where different charge states can experience different collisionality, sources, and radial localization.

Typical inferred values are 0.01-10 m^2.s^-1 in many confined tokamak plasmas. Low-turbulence or nearly neoclassical regions can be below 0.01 m^2.s^-1, while edge layers or strongly turbulent conditions can reach 10-100 m^2.s^-1.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_momentum
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the area-normalized momentum source for the total ion population, summed over all ion charge states in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents force per unit area that changes ion toroidal momentum in plasma transport.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion momentum is the toroidal component of the area-normalized momentum source acting on the total ion population. It represents the force per unit area that adds, removes, or redistributes ion momentum along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The component is defined by projecting the charge-state-summed vector [ion_momentum](name:ion_momentum) onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
M_{\phi i} = \hat{\phi} \cdot \mathbf{M}_i = \sum_{a \in \mathrm{ion\ states}} \hat{\phi} \cdot \mathbf{M}_{i,a}
$$

where $M_{\phi i}$ is the toroidal ion momentum source, $\mathbf{M}_i$ is the total area-normalized ion momentum source vector, $a$ indexes ion species and charge states, $\mathbf{M}_{i,a}$ is the area-normalized momentum source for state $a$, and $\hat{\phi}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The state-resolved terms correspond to [toroidal_ion_state_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum). Contributions commonly arise from ion-neutral charge exchange and friction, ionization and recombination recoil, externally supplied particles and momentum, viscous momentum transfer, and the toroidal component of electromagnetic forces. Direct measurement of a local momentum source is uncommon; it is usually inferred from ion flow evolution, momentum-flux divergence, and force-balance constraints. The neutral counterpart is [toroidal_neutral_momentum](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum), and advective representations are related to [toroidal_momentum_convection_velocity](name:toroidal_momentum_convection_velocity).

Typical absolute magnitudes are about $10^{-4}$-$10^{1}$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 in weakly driven scrape-off-layer or edge transport regions, and can reach $10^{2}$-$10^{3}$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 in localized recycling, charge-exchange, divertor, or strong external momentum-input regions. Values may be close to zero where opposing toroidal drives and damping terms nearly cancel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal momentum source acts in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Inverse relaxation time for damping the bulk ion momentum component along the toroidal phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It quantifies how rapidly toroidal ion rotation is relaxed by collisional, neoclassical, neutral, or modeled transport processes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal ion momentum damping rate is an inverse timescale for relaxation of the bulk ion momentum density associated with velocity along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is a rate coefficient: larger values imply faster loss of organized toroidal ion rotation to collisional, neoclassical, neutral, or other modeled momentum sinks.

A common local relaxation representation defines the damping contribution to the toroidal momentum source density as

$$
S_{\phi,\mathrm{damp}} = -m_i n_i \nu_{\phi,i}\left(u_{\phi,i}-u_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right)
$$

where $S_{\phi,\mathrm{damp}}$ is the damping part of the toroidal ion momentum source density in kg m^-2 s^-2, $m_i$ is the ion mass in kg, $n_i$ is the ion density in m^-3, $\nu_{\phi,i}$ is the toroidal ion momentum damping rate in s^-1, and $u_{\phi,i}$ and $u_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{ref}}$ are toroidal ion velocities in m s^-1 along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. If the full momentum balance uses $S_\phi$ for a total toroidal momentum source density, $S_\phi$ has the same units. For a damping term $\nu_{\phi,i}$ is non-negative and reduces the velocity relative to the reference rotation; a negative fitted coefficient represents anti-damping or drive rather than damping.

The rate is usually inferred rather than measured directly. It can be estimated from ion momentum-balance analysis using toroidal rotation measurements, ion density and temperature, neutral interaction estimates, and equilibrium geometry, or computed from neoclassical and kinetic transport models that represent collisional viscosity, trapped-particle effects, charge-exchange with neutrals, applied three-dimensional magnetic perturbations, and other effective momentum sinks. Transient spin-up or spin-down observations constrain it through the observed exponential relaxation time of toroidal ion rotation.

Typical effective values in confined tokamak core conditions are about 0.1-100 s^-1, corresponding to relaxation times of 10 ms-10 s. Neutral-rich edge plasmas, high-collisionality regimes, or strong applied non-axisymmetric magnetic perturbations can give modeled local values of 10^2-10^4 s^-1, while weakly damped core conditions may be below 0.1 s^-1.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Radial flux density across magnetic flux surfaces of the toroidal component of ion linear momentum in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It includes convective and ion pressure-stress contributions and has the dimensions of a stress.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion momentum flux is the scalar flux-surface-normal transport rate of the toroidal component of ion linear momentum per unit area. The toroidal component is defined along the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This quantity is a momentum-flux density, not a full vector; its dimensions are those of stress.

For a magnetic flux surface labeled by a radial flux coordinate $\rho$ increasing outward from the magnetic axis, a local scalar definition is

$$
\Pi_{i,\phi}^{\rho} = \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\rho} \cdot \left(n_i m_i \mathbf{v}_i \mathbf{v}_i + \mathbf{P}_i\right) \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\rho}$ is the outward unit normal to the flux surface, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $n_i$ is ion number density, $m_i$ is ion mass, $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the ion bulk velocity, and $\mathbf{P}_i$ is the ion pressure-stress tensor including thermal, viscous, and turbulent stress contributions as appropriate. The dyadic term $n_i m_i \mathbf{v}_i \mathbf{v}_i$ gives the convective transport of toroidal momentum.

In practice this flux is inferred from ion momentum balance, from transport models using measured or calculated rotation, density, temperature, torque, and stress terms, or from kinetic and fluid calculations of turbulent and neoclassical momentum transport. Related component and species resolutions include [radial_ion_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_momentum_flux_over_edge_region), [toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux), and [toroidal_total_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_total_momentum_flux).

Typical magnitudes are often $10^{-3}-10$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 in confined tokamak plasmas, with values approaching $10-100$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 in regions with strong rotation shear, strong external torque, or large edge stresses.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion linear momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is transported outward, from lower to higher radial flux coordinate $\rho$, across a magnetic flux surface.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_momentum_implicit_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Rate coefficient for the implicit source proportional to ion momentum in the toroidal phi direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. Its magnitude is an inverse time scale; its sign distinguishes proportional drive from damping.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion momentum implicit source rate is the scalar coefficient multiplying the existing ion toroidal momentum density in a linearized momentum-balance source term. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The linearized implicit contribution to the toroidal ion momentum source density is represented as:

$$
S_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}} = \gamma_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}\,p_\phi
$$

where $\gamma_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}$ is this rate coefficient with unit $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $p_\phi$ is the toroidal ion angular-momentum density with unit $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$, and $S_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}$ is the corresponding toroidal ion angular-momentum source density with unit $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

This coefficient is normally obtained by linearizing momentum-source and momentum-sink models about the current plasma state rather than by direct measurement as an independent diagnostic observable. It is used to treat source terms proportional to the existing toroidal flow, such as viscous relaxation, collisional or neutral drag, and wave-particle momentum exchange; non-proportional applied torque is represented separately by [toroidal_ion_torque](name:toroidal_ion_torque). Closely related rate or coefficient names are [toroidal_ion_momentum_coefficient](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_implicit_source_rate), [toroidal_ion_implicit_source_rate](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_implicit_source_rate), and the more general ion_momentum_implicit_source_rate.

There is no device-independent typical range because the value depends on the chosen linearization, species, collisionality, and local plasma conditions. Its magnitude is best interpreted as an inverse relaxation time: $|\gamma_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}|=1\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ corresponds to a 1 s proportional time scale, while $|\gamma_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}|=10^3\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ corresponds to a 1 ms stiff time scale; zero means no implicit proportional contribution is included.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $S_{\phi,\mathrm{impl}}$ has the same sign as $p_\phi$, so the implicit contribution amplifies the existing toroidal ion momentum.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_rotation_frequency
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular rotation frequency of an ion species, averaged over charge states, defined as the toroidal velocity divided by the local major radius.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal rotation frequency $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ characterizes the bulk angular rotation of an ion species about the machine symmetry axis in the toroidal direction, with contributions from all charge states combined into a single effective frequency. It is the primary scalar measure of ion toroidal rotation used in momentum transport analysis and serves as a profile quantity spanning core to edge plasma regions.

The defining relation connects $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ to the toroidal fluid velocity $v_\mathrm{tor}$ and the local major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
\Omega_\mathrm{tor} = \frac{v_\mathrm{tor}}{R}
$$

where $v_\mathrm{tor}$ is the toroidal component of the ion mass-flow velocity, and $R$ is the major radius at the evaluation point. When multiple charge states are present, this frequency is the charge-state-averaged value, weighted by respective particle densities. The charge-state-resolved counterpart is [toroidal ion state rotation frequency](name:toroidal_ion_state_rotation_frequency), which distinguishes contributions from individual ionization levels.

Toroidal rotation is routinely inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, which measures the Doppler shift of impurity emission lines to obtain $v_\mathrm{tor}$; $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ then follows by dividing by the local $R$. The closely related quantity [toroidal ion velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) gives the same physical flow in velocity units. In NBI-heated core plasmas, $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ typically spans $10^3$–$10^5$ rad/s, with co-current rotation being predominant during tangential beam injection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ions rotate in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Effective across-flux-surface convection velocity for radial transport of toroidal momentum carried by a specified ion charge state. The toroidal label identifies the transported momentum component, not the direction of this velocity.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion-state momentum convection velocity is the effective radial velocity coefficient for the non-diffusive transport of toroidal momentum carried by ions of a specified species and charge state. The toroidal momentum component is defined along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the coefficient itself describes transport across magnetic flux surfaces labeled by a radial flux coordinate such as $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$.

In a local flux-surface-averaged momentum balance, the convective contribution to the radial flux of toroidal ion-state momentum can be written as

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\phi,i,z} = V_{\phi,i,z} p_{\phi,i,z}
$$

where $\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\phi,i,z}$ is the convective radial flux density of toroidal momentum for ion species $i$ in charge state $z$ in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $V_{\phi,i,z}$ is this convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $p_{\phi,i,z}$ is the toroidal momentum density in kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. The density is often represented as $p_{\phi,i,z}=m_i n_{i,z} u_{\phi,i,z}$, with $m_i$ the ion mass in kg, $n_{i,z}$ the charge-state density in m$^{-3}$, and $u_{\phi,i,z}$ the ion flow component along $\hat{\phi}$ in m s$^{-1}$. The total radial momentum flux may also contain a diffusive term proportional to the radial gradient of toroidal momentum; this quantity represents the pinch-like or outward non-diffusive part.

It is not usually measured directly. It is inferred from momentum-balance analysis using rotation measurements, ion densities, momentum sources and sinks, collisional exchange, and neoclassical or turbulent transport modeling; charge-state-resolved values are most relevant when impurity transport, partial ionization, or state-dependent momentum exchange is important.

Typical inferred core values are about -20-20 m s$^{-1}$ in tokamak transport analyzes, with strong momentum-pinch, edge, or barrier conditions occasionally giving magnitudes of 50-100 m s$^{-1}$. Values near zero indicate that non-diffusive convection is small compared with diffusive transport and applied momentum sources.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a positive toroidal momentum density, with ion flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, produces a convective flux directed toward increasing radial flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Rate coefficient for collisional or neoclassical damping of the toroidal phi component of fluid momentum for a specified ion charge state in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal ion state momentum damping rate is a charge-state-resolved effective relaxation coefficient for the toroidal component of ion fluid momentum. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. In radial transport balances it is normally an effective flux-surface-averaged coefficient for the selected ion charge state, not a microscopic point-particle collision frequency.

A common defining use is as the coefficient multiplying the toroidal momentum density in a radial flux-surface momentum balance written with a minor-radius-like flux-surface label $r$ measured in meters:

$$
\frac{\partial P_{\phi,q}}{\partial t}
+ \frac{1}{V'}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(V'\Gamma_{\phi,q}^{r}\right)
= S_{\phi,q} - \nu_{\phi,q} P_{\phi,q}
$$

where $\nu_{\phi,q}$ is the toroidal ion state momentum damping rate, $q$ labels the ion charge state, $P_{\phi,q}=m_i n_{i,q} v_{\phi,i,q}$ is the toroidal linear momentum density in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $m_i$ is ion mass in $\mathrm{kg}$, $n_{i,q}$ is charge-state density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $v_{\phi,i,q}$ is toroidal fluid velocity in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Also, $V'=dV/dr$ is differential plasma volume per unit $r$ in $\mathrm{m}^{2}$, $\Gamma_{\phi,q}^{r}$ is the radial flux of toroidal momentum in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$, and $S_{\phi,q}$ represents non-damping sources of toroidal momentum density in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. A dissipative damping model has $\nu_{\phi,q}\ge 0$; a negative value would represent an effective toroidal momentum drive rather than damping.

The rate is usually inferred or prescribed in transport modeling rather than measured directly. It may be computed from Coulomb collision operators, neoclassical viscosity closures, charge-state-resolved impurity momentum exchange, or reduced relaxation models. It is the toroidal component of [ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), the charge-state-resolved counterpart of [toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_damping_rate), and is analogous to [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), [radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate), and [parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate). The corresponding electron momentum concept is represented by toroidal_electron_momentum_damping_rate.

Typical effective values are highly model and regime dependent. In core tokamak transport studies they may range from near 0 to about $10^5$ s^-1; edge, impurity-rich, or strongly collisional cases, and models with different closure assumptions, can lie outside this broad range.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Flux density of the toroidal component of linear momentum for ions in a specified ion state, with the toroidal direction given by increasing phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It includes convective cross-surface transport and non-convective stress contributions.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion-state momentum flux is the cross-surface flux density of the toroidal component of linear momentum carried by ions in a specified state. The toroidal component is defined along the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity includes both convective transport by flow normal to the transport surface and non-convective transport by stresses.

For a transport surface with outward unit normal $\hat{n}$, the flux can be decomposed into convective and non-convective parts:

$$
F_{\phi,s} = m_s n_s u_{\phi,s} u_{n,s} + \Pi^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n\phi,s}
$$

where $F_{\phi,s}$ is the toroidal momentum flux for ion state $s$, $m_s$ is the ion mass, $n_s$ is the state density, $u_{\phi,s}=\mathbf{u}_s\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal flow velocity, $u_{n,s}=\mathbf{u}_s\cdot\hat{n}$ is the outward-normal flow velocity, and $\Pi^{\mathrm{nc}}_{n\phi,s}$ is the non-convective normal flux of toroidal momentum. The non-convective term represents viscous, turbulent, collisional, or kinetic stress transport as a flux contribution; it is not a separate scalar pressure term.

In practice this quantity is obtained from state-resolved momentum balance in fluid, gyrofluid, or kinetic transport calculations. The convective part uses density and flow estimates for the selected ion state, while the non-convective part is inferred from stress closures, fluctuation correlations, collisional transport models, or constraints from spectroscopic measurements of ion flows and temperatures. Related quantities include the total-ion [toroidal_ion_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_flux), the charge-state variant [toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_ion_charge_state_momentum_flux), and directional ion-state components such as [radial_ion_state_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_flux), [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_flux](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_flux), parallel_ion_state_momentum_flux, and [vertical_ion_state_momentum_flux](name:vertical_ion_state_momentum_flux).

Order-of-magnitude estimates follow from the convective scale $m_s n_s |u_{\phi,s}u_{n,s}|$ together with the modeled stress contribution. For edge and scrape-off-layer conditions with $n_s=10^{18}-10^{20}$ m^-3, $|u_{\phi,s}|=10^3-10^5$ m s^-1, and $|u_{n,s}|=0.1-10^2$ m s^-1, representative convective magnitudes are about 10^-7-1 kg m^-1 s^-2; strong rotation, steep shear, or intermittent turbulence can give larger local stress-like fluxes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when toroidal momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is transported along the outward normal of the transport surface.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_rotation_frequency
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular rotation frequency of a specific ion charge state, equal to the toroidal bulk velocity divided by the local major radius.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal rotation frequency of an ion charge state quantifies the angular velocity at which ions belonging to a given ionization level revolve around the machine symmetry axis. It characterizes the toroidal spin of a charge-state-resolved ion population, providing finer kinetic detail than species-averaged quantities.

The defining relation is:

$$
\Omega_\mathrm{tor} = \frac{v_\mathrm{tor}}{R}
$$

where $v_\mathrm{tor}$ is the bulk toroidal velocity of the charge-state population and $R$ is the local major radius measured from the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This charge-state-resolved quantity distinguishes specific ionization levels of an ion species, in contrast to [toroidal_ion_rotation_frequency](name:toroidal_ion_rotation_frequency), which averages over all charge states. Different ionization states can rotate at distinct rates owing to their differing charge-to-mass ratios, neoclassical poloidal asymmetries, and differential collisional coupling to the bulk plasma. The corresponding linear velocity is [toroidal_ion_state_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity), related by $v_\mathrm{tor} = \Omega_\mathrm{tor} R$.

Toroidal rotation is measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, which resolves Doppler-shifted emission from specific charge states and, combined with the local major-radius profile, yields $\Omega_\mathrm{tor}$ directly. In tokamak H-mode core plasmas, values typically range from $10^3$ to a few times $10^5$ rad/s, with impurity charge states occasionally showing rotation rates distinct from the hydrogenic bulk.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge state rotates in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_state_torque_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Major-radius-weighted toroidal angular-momentum source density for a specified ion species and ionization state. It is the net torque per unit volume acting on that charge state, not merely a linear toroidal momentum source.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion-state torque density is the local rate at which mechanical toroidal angular momentum is added to, or removed from, a specified ion species in a specified ionization state. The toroidal direction is defined by the toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity is the major-radius-weighted source acting on the charge-state angular momentum about the symmetry axis.

The source density for ion species $a$ and ionization state $q$ can be defined through the source part of the local angular-momentum balance:

$$
\tau_{\phi,a,q} = \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(R\,m_a\,n_{a,q}\,u_{\phi,a,q}\right)\right|_{\mathrm{sources}}
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,a,q}$ is the torque density in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $R$ is in meters, $m_a$ is the ion mass in kg, $n_{a,q}$ is the charge-state density in m$^{-3}$, and $u_{\phi,a,q}$ is the toroidal flow velocity in m s$^{-1}$. The factor $R$ distinguishes this angular-momentum source density from a linear toroidal momentum source density, which has different dimensions.

In practice it is evaluated by summing source and sink mechanisms assigned to the specified charge state. Examples include neutral-beam momentum deposition after ionization, radio-frequency wave momentum input, collisional friction, charge exchange with neutrals, and transfer of particles and momentum between ionization states by ionization and recombination. State-changing terms should conserve the appropriate total angular momentum when summed over all charge states, apart from externally applied inputs and losses to neutrals, material surfaces, or other reservoirs.

Typical local magnitudes are strongly device and scenario dependent. Weakly driven or trace charge states may have magnitudes of 10$^{-5}$-10$^{-2}$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, broad driven regions often fall around 10$^{-3}$-1 kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, and localized beam, wave, or edge-neutral interaction regions can reach 1-10 kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the source increases $R\,m_a n_{a,q}u_{\phi,a,q}$ for toroidal flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_torque
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal ion torque is the volume-integrated rate at which explicit sources add toroidal angular momentum to the total ion population, summed over charge states. It has torque units and is distinct from toroidal ion torque density, the local source per unit volume.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion torque is the integrated angular-momentum source acting on the total ion population, summed over ion charge states. It represents the explicit, non-stiff part of a decomposed toroidal momentum source: the part not proportional to the instantaneous ion toroidal angular momentum.

With $L_{\phi,i}$ denoting total ion toroidal angular momentum, the source decomposition can be written as

$$
T_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{tot}} = T_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{explicit}} + C_{\phi,i} L_{\phi,i}, \qquad T_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{tot}} = \int_V \tau_{\phi,i}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $T_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{explicit}}$ is the explicit toroidal ion torque in kg.m^2.s^-2, $T_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total integrated ion torque, $C_{\phi,i}$ is the [toroidal ion momentum coefficient](name:toroidal_ion_momentum_implicit_source_rate) in s^-1, $L_{\phi,i}$ is in kg.m^2.s^-1, and $\tau_{\phi,i}$ is the [toroidal ion torque density](name:toroidal_ion_torque_density) in kg.m^-1.s^-2 integrated over volume $V$. This unit balance distinguishes the integrated torque from a volumetric torque density.

In transport modeling, this quantity is computed by summing momentum-input channels such as neutral-beam injection, wave-particle momentum transfer, collisional exchange, and externally imposed forces over the relevant plasma volume and over ion charge states. Contributions represented by a coefficient multiplying the current ion toroidal angular momentum belong to the implicit term, while remaining angular-momentum input belongs to this explicit torque.

Typical magnitudes are strongly device- and actuator-dependent. Weakly driven or nearly torque-balanced plasmas can have values below 0.1 kg.m^2.s^-2, medium-size plasmas with tangential auxiliary heating often give 0.1-10 kg.m^2.s^-2, and large high-power injection cases can reach 10-100 kg.m^2.s^-2.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the source adds ion toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_torque_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Local source rate of ion angular momentum about the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, including the major-radius moment arm. It is summed over ion species and charge states; internal ion-ion exchanges cancel, leaving net torque from sources outside that sum.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion torque density is the local rate per unit volume at which toroidal angular momentum about the symmetry axis is transferred to the total ion population. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the relevant moment arm is the major radius $R$, so this quantity is a torque density rather than a linear toroidal force density. The total ion population means the sum over all ion species and charge states.

A local toroidal angular-momentum balance may be written as:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\sum_{\alpha \in \mathrm{ions}} m_\alpha n_\alpha R v_{\phi,\alpha}\right) + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\ell_\phi,i} = \tau_{\phi,i}
$$

where $\alpha$ labels ion species and charge states, $m_\alpha$ is ion mass in kg, $n_\alpha$ is ion number density in m^-3, $R$ is major radius in m, $v_{\phi,\alpha}$ is the toroidal ion fluid velocity in m.s^-1 along $\hat{\phi}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\ell_\phi,i}$ is the flux of toroidal ion angular momentum in kg.s^-2, and $\tau_{\phi,i}$ is the toroidal ion torque density in kg.m^-1.s^-2. The quantity inside the time derivative is the ion contribution to [toroidal total plasma angular momentum density].

In transport analysis, $\tau_{\phi,i}$ is computed from net sources that transfer toroidal angular momentum to ions, such as neutral-beam fast-ion slowing down, wave momentum absorption, electromagnetic torques, ion-neutral charge exchange or friction, and exchange with electrons or other populations not included in the summed ion set. Collisions among ion species or charge states within the summed ion population redistribute toroidal angular momentum internally and do not contribute to the total-ion torque density; such effects are represented only in state-resolved quantities such as [toroidal ion state torque density](name:toroidal_ion_state_torque_density) or collisional state-source terms.

Typical volume-averaged magnitudes in present magnetic-confinement plasmas are about $10^{-4}-10^{-1}$ kg.m^-1.s^-2, while localized beam, wave, or edge momentum deposition can approach $1$ kg.m^-1.s^-2. Low-torque or nearly intrinsic-rotation scenarios can have values close to zero after summing over the full ion population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the torque transfers angular momentum to ions in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the charge-state-averaged ion fluid velocity, quantifying the bulk ion flow along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal ion velocity is the $\phi$-component of the mean ion fluid velocity vector, obtained by projecting [ion_velocity](name:ion_velocity) onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. When multiple charge states are present, it represents the charge-state-averaged bulk flow and is the dominant rotation component governing toroidal angular momentum transport and confinement.

The toroidal component is defined as:

$$
v_\phi^{(i)} = \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the charge-state-averaged ion fluid velocity vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The toroidal ion velocity is measured experimentally through charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), where Doppler shifts of emission lines from impurity ions yield the local ion flow velocity along the line of sight. Neoclassical transport models and multi-fluid solvers additionally compute this quantity from the radial force balance on the ion fluid, connecting it to the radial electric field and pressure gradient.

Typical magnitudes range from a few km/s in ohmic discharges to 100–300 km/s in neutral-beam-heated H-mode plasmas. Its radial gradient drives the [radial_edge_ion_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_momentum_flux_over_edge_region) and the effective convection characterized by radial_ion_effective_momentum_convection_velocity. The related [toroidal_plasma_velocity](name:toroidal_impurity_ion_velocity_at_measurement_position) captures whole-plasma toroidal rotation inferred from X-ray spectroscopy, while [toroidal_ion_state_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_state_momentum) provides the charge-state-resolved toroidal momentum source in edge transport equations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of the charge-state-averaged toroidal ion velocity with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius, quantifying local shear in ion toroidal rotation.
NAMES.long:
Radial derivative of toroidal ion velocity is the derivative of the charge-state-averaged ion fluid velocity in the toroidal direction with respect to $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ (normalized toroidal flux radius). It measures radial shear of ion toroidal rotation on magnetic flux surfaces. The signed velocity component $v_{\phi,i}$ is along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The derivative is defined by differentiating the charge-state-averaged toroidal ion velocity with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius:

$$
G_{\phi,i}(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}) = \frac{\partial v_{\phi,i}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $G_{\phi,i}$ denotes this derivative, $v_{\phi,i}$ is the charge-state-averaged toroidal ion fluid velocity, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless, increasing from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary. Because $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless, $G_{\phi,i}$ has the same physical dimension as velocity.

It is obtained by differentiating a smooth representation of toroidal ion rotation versus $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. The underlying velocity may be inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, Doppler spectroscopy, or momentum-balance analysis with magnetic-equilibrium mapping; for multiple ion charge states, the charge-state average is formed before the radial derivative is taken.

Typical magnitudes in tokamak core plasmas are $10^3$-$10^5$ m s$^{-1}$; sharp rotation shear near transport barriers, pedestals, or localized momentum input can reach $10^5$-$10^6$ m s$^{-1}$. Values near zero indicate weak radial variation of toroidal rotation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the signed toroidal ion velocity $v_{\phi,i}$ increases as $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative, with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius rho_tor_norm, of the charge-state-averaged ion velocity component along the phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of toroidal ion velocity is the curvature of the charge-state-averaged ion toroidal velocity with respect to the flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ (normalized toroidal flux radius). The velocity component is along the $\phi$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface.

It is defined by differentiating the signed toroidal ion velocity twice with respect to the dimensionless radial flux coordinate:

$$
D_{\rho\rho} v_{i,\phi} = \frac{\partial^2 v_{i,\phi}}{\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}^2}
$$

where $D_{\rho\rho} v_{i,\phi}$ is this second derivative, $v_{i,\phi}$ is the charge-state-averaged toroidal ion velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is dimensionless. The derivative has units of m s$^{-1}$ because the differentiating coordinate is dimensionless.

In practice it is obtained by fitting, reconstructing, or modeling the radial dependence of [toroidal_ion_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) as a function of $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ and differentiating the smooth representation. This derivative is the second-order counterpart of [radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity](name:radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_velocity); it differs from [second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_state_velocity](name:second_radial_derivative_of_toroidal_ion_state_velocity), which is resolved by ion charge state. Because second derivatives amplify noise and localized features, smoothing or regularization is commonly needed when inferring it from measured rotation.

Typical absolute magnitudes are broad: 10^3-10^5 m s^-1 for slowly varying core rotation, 10^5-10^6 m s^-1 where momentum sources, transport barriers, or edge rotation shear produce stronger curvature, and near zero where the velocity varies almost linearly with $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$. Values can be positive or negative.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\partial^2 v_{i,\phi}/\partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}^2 > 0$ for increasing $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, with $v_{i,\phi}$ positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_iron_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the iron ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the single flux-surface radius assigned to the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component $v_\phi^\mathrm{Fe}$ of the iron ion bulk flow velocity is a point value evaluated at the single flux-surface radius assigned to the internal transport barrier (ITB). The ITB is a localized region of suppressed turbulent transport characterized by steep radial gradients in temperature, density, and rotation, making this velocity sensitive to the local momentum balance and the radial electric field.

The iron impurity flow at the ITB is linked to the radial electric field $E_r$ through the impurity force balance:

$$
E_r = v_\phi^\mathrm{Fe} B_\theta - v_\theta^\mathrm{Fe} B_\phi + \frac{1}{Z_\mathrm{Fe}\, e\, n_\mathrm{Fe}} \frac{\partial p_\mathrm{Fe}}{\partial r}
$$

where $B_\theta$ and $B_\phi$ are the poloidal and toroidal magnetic field components, $Z_\mathrm{Fe}$ is the relevant iron charge state, $e$ is the elementary charge, $n_\mathrm{Fe}$ is the local [iron number density at the ITB](name:iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and $\partial p_\mathrm{Fe}/\partial r$ is the radial iron pressure gradient.

This velocity is measured principally by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), where Doppler-shifted spectral emission from iron is decomposed into toroidal and poloidal components. Comparison with [toroidal nitrogen velocity at the internal transport barrier](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) provides multi-species momentum balance checks, and [toroidal iron velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_iron_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) supplies the outer boundary reference for the radial iron rotation profile.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the iron ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_iron_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the iron impurity ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost confined point where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal iron velocity at the magnetic axis is the $\hat{\phi}$-projected bulk fluid velocity of iron (Fe) impurity ions at the innermost confined plasma point, where the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ satisfies $\nabla\psi = 0$ at the position $(R_{\rm axis}, Z_{\rm axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The quantity is defined as the toroidal projection of the iron fluid velocity vector evaluated at the magnetic axis:

$$
v_\phi^{\rm Fe}\big|_{\rm axis} = \mathbf{v}^{\rm Fe} \cdot \hat{\phi}\big|_{\nabla\psi=0}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle and the evaluation is restricted to the magnetic axis position.

Iron impurity toroidal velocities are measured through charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), which resolves Doppler shifts of iron line emission following charge exchange with injected neutral beam atoms. The on-axis value is inferred by fitting the radial velocity profile across multiple CXRS channels and extrapolating to the magnetic axis radius.

Iron toroidal velocities in confined tokamak plasmas range from approximately $-10^5$ to $+10^5$ m/s, set by the balance between external toroidal momentum input and neoclassical and anomalous transport. The companion quantity [toroidal iron velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_iron_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) provides the outer boundary value; [toroidal nitrogen velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal oxygen velocity at the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) are analogous quantities for lighter impurity species at the same location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the iron ion bulk flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the krypton ion bulk-flow velocity at the radial location of an internal transport barrier, resolved along the +phi direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal krypton velocity at an internal transport barrier is the toroidal component of the bulk flow velocity of krypton ions evaluated at the barrier location. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters. An internal transport barrier is an interior region where turbulent transport is reduced and gradients or rotation shear can become steep.

The component is defined by projection of the krypton bulk velocity onto the toroidal basis vector at the internal-transport-barrier location:

$$
v_{\mathrm{Kr},\phi}^{\mathrm{ITB}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Kr}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ITB}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the krypton ion bulk-flow velocity, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ denotes the physical location or flux surface identified as the internal transport barrier, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, and $v_{\mathrm{Kr},\phi}^{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is expressed in m s$^{-1}$.

In practice, the barrier location is identified from measured or reconstructed gradients, transport indicators, or rotation shear, and the krypton toroidal flow is then evaluated at that location. When suitable krypton line emission is available, local spectroscopic Doppler measurements can constrain the flow after accounting for viewing geometry; otherwise the value may be inferred from physically constrained impurity-flow analysis. The same krypton toroidal velocity component at other radial landmarks is described by [toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_pedestal), and [toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

Representative signed values in tokamak core and internal-barrier regions commonly range from $-2 \times 10^5$ to $+2 \times 10^5$ m s$^{-1}$, with magnitudes set by external torque, intrinsic rotation, collisional coupling to the main ions, and local momentum transport. Weakly rotating plasmas may have values close to zero, while strong neutral-beam-driven or high-performance regimes can approach the upper end of this range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the krypton ion bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Toroidal component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the krypton velocity at the magnetic axis, where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal krypton velocity at the magnetic axis is the scalar component of the krypton species velocity along the toroidal direction at the center of the nested closed flux surfaces. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the magnetic axis is the location where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes.

The toroidal component is defined by projecting the krypton velocity vector onto the toroidal unit vector at the magnetic-axis position:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Kr},0} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Kr}(R_0, \phi, Z_0) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Kr},0}$ is the toroidal krypton velocity at the magnetic axis in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Kr}$ is the krypton species velocity vector in m.s^-1, $R_0$ is the magnetic-axis major radius in meters, $Z_0$ is the magnetic-axis vertical position in meters, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in radians, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the dimensionless unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$.

In practice this quantity is obtained by evaluating the inferred or modeled krypton velocity field at the magnetic-axis location. The velocity may be constrained by spectroscopic Doppler measurements of krypton emission or by impurity momentum-balance modeling, with interpolation to the magnetic axis performed consistently with the reconstructed flux-surface geometry.

Typical signed core impurity toroidal velocities are highly scenario dependent: values may be near 0 m.s^-1 in weakly rotating plasmas and can reach order 10^4-10^5 m.s^-1 in strongly rotating cores.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the krypton velocity component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the lithium impurity ion fluid velocity evaluated at the representative radial location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component of the lithium impurity ion fluid velocity, evaluated at the representative radial location of the internal transport barrier (ITB), a localized region of reduced turbulent cross-field transport identified by steep radial gradients in ion temperature, density, and rotation.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as

$$
v_\phi = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Li} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Li}$ is the lithium ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) with a neutral beam is the primary measurement method, resolving the Doppler shift of lithium emission lines to yield the toroidal velocity at each radial position. Toroidal rotation at the ITB is coupled to the local radial electric field $E_r$ via ion force balance, and strong $E \times B$ shear at the ITB is associated with turbulence suppression. For the same quantity at other radial positions, see [toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_pedestal); analogous ITB velocities for other impurity species include [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_beryllium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier). The corresponding local lithium ion density is given by [lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:lithium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lithium ion velocity is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the lithium impurity ion fluid velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Li}}$ of the lithium ion fluid velocity at the magnetic axis quantifies the on-axis toroidal rotation speed of lithium impurity ions, driven by momentum sources such as neutral beam injection and shaped by neoclassical and turbulent transport processes. The magnetic axis is the locus inside the confined plasma where $\nabla\psi = 0$, i.e., where the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ reaches its extremum.

The defining projection onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ is:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Li}} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Li} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Li}$ is the lithium ion fluid velocity vector and $\hat{\phi}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is inferred from Doppler-shift analysis of charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) emission lines of lithium ions, with the measurement position mapped to the magnetic axis through equilibrium reconstruction.
