On-axis impurity toroidal velocities in tokamak plasmas range from a few km/s to about 100 km/s depending on heating power and plasma conditions. The companion pedestal value is [toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_lithium_velocity_at_pedestal), the analogous oxygen-impurity quantity at the axis is [toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), and the on-axis lithium number density is [lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:lithium_density_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lithium ion flow points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_mhd_mode_number
NAMES.short: Dimensionless integer Fourier harmonic that labels the toroidal periodicity of an MHD perturbation eigenmode, counting complete oscillation cycles per full toroidal circuit of the device.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal MHD mode number $n$ is the integer Fourier index that characterizes the toroidal periodicity of a linear magnetohydrodynamic perturbation eigenmode. It forms the toroidal projection of the mhd_mode_number set of quantum numbers, uniquely identifying the harmonic content of a non-axisymmetric perturbation.

For a first-order MHD perturbation $\delta f$, the toroidal dependence takes the form:

$$
\delta f \propto \exp(i n \phi)
$$

where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The integer $n$ counts complete oscillation periods per toroidal transit; $n = 0$ denotes an axisymmetric perturbation. Together with the poloidal mode number $m$, the index $n$ identifies resonant flux surfaces through $q = m/n$, where $q$ is the safety factor. The companion [radial_mode_number](name:radial_mode_number) counts radial nodes of the eigenfunction between axis and boundary.

In linear stability analysis, unstable modes span $|n| = 1$ for kink and external-kink modes, $n = 1$–5 for neoclassical tearing modes, and $n \gg 1$ for high-$n$ ballooning instabilities. The per_toroidal_mode_perturbed_energy gives the energy assigned to each $n$, and linear_mhd_mode_frequency_real_part gives the associated eigenfrequency.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perturbation phase advances in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the effective convection velocity for momentum transport, governing the pinch-like non-diffusive radial flux of toroidal momentum independent of local momentum-density gradients.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal momentum convection velocity is the toroidal projection of the effective convection vector $\mathbf{v}^{\rm conv}$ that enters the diffusion-convection decomposition of the radial momentum flux. It quantifies all non-diffusive contributions to toroidal momentum transport — including intrinsic rotation, Coriolis pinch, and turbulence-driven parallel velocity pinch effects — that produce a net radial momentum flux even in the absence of a local momentum-density gradient.

In the standard flux-gradient framework, the radial flux of toroidal momentum $\Gamma_{p_\phi}$ is decomposed as:

$$
\Gamma_{p_\phi} = -D_\phi \frac{\partial (m_i n_i v_\phi)}{\partial r} + v_\phi^{\rm conv} \cdot m_i n_i v_\phi
$$

where $D_\phi$ is the toroidal momentum diffusivity, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ is the number density, and $v_\phi$ is the toroidal fluid velocity. The convection velocity $v_\phi^{\rm conv}$ is the quantity documented here.

This coefficient is derived from turbulent transport simulations or neoclassical calculations and is central to predicting toroidal rotation profiles in the plasma edge and core regions. It is the toroidal projection of [momentum_convection_velocity](name:momentum_convection_velocity); the corresponding poloidal projection is poloidal_momentum_convection_velocity. Species-resolved neutral variants are [toroidal_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity](name:toroidal_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity) and [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity). The closely related [toroidal_momentum_velocity](name:toroidal_momentum_convection_velocity) captures the same pinch physics for the radial grid formulation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convection velocity is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ axis).

NAMES.name: toroidal_momentum_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the effective convection velocity for cross-surface transport of aggregate ion toroidal momentum. It is the net coefficient multiplying the local toroidal momentum density to give the convective (non-diffusive) part of the radial momentum flux in a flux-surface-averaged transport model.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal momentum effective convection velocity is the toroidal component of the effective convection (pinch) velocity that advects aggregate ion toroidal momentum across nested magnetic flux surfaces. The toroidal momentum is associated with motion in the $\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the cross-surface direction follows a flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho$ is a radial flux label increasing from the magnetic axis to the boundary.

In a flux-surface-averaged toroidal momentum balance, the convective part of the cross-surface flux is written as the product of this velocity and the local momentum density:

$$
\Gamma_\phi^{\mathrm{conv}} = v_{\phi,\mathrm{eff}} \, p_\phi
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective convection velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $p_\phi$ is the local aggregate ion toroidal momentum density in kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $\Gamma_\phi^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective flux of toroidal momentum across the flux surface in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$. The adjective "effective" denotes a net coefficient that lumps together every term in the chosen transport decomposition that is proportional to $p_\phi$, after the diffusive contribution and explicitly non-proportional terms such as residual stress or applied torque density have been separated.

This coefficient is not the toroidal rotation speed and is usually not measured directly. It is inferred by solving or fitting the momentum balance using measured ion toroidal rotation, often from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, together with ion density and temperature, magnetic geometry, and estimates of external torque and diffusive transport. It can incorporate turbulent and neoclassical momentum-pinch contributions and flux-surface-averaging geometry effects when these are represented as proportional to the momentum density.

Inferred magnitudes in tokamak core momentum transport analyzes are typically of order a few to a few tens of meters per second, with the sign indicating the direction of cross-surface convection rather than the sign of the toroidal momentum itself.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convection velocity points toward increasing $\rho$, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the neon ion flow velocity evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal neon velocity at the internal transport barrier (ITB) is the $\hat{\phi}$-directed component of neon ion bulk flow at the plasma radius where localized suppression of turbulent transport creates steep gradients in temperature, density, and rotation.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as

$$
v_\phi^{\mathrm{Ne}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ne}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the neon ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is inferred from the Doppler shift of neon emission lines in charge exchange recombination spectroscopy measurements, with the ITB radius identified from the peak of the temperature or rotation gradient. For a complete impurity transport characterization at the ITB, this velocity pairs naturally with [neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:neon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The same projection at adjacent confinement locations is given by [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal); the analogous nitrogen impurity quantity is [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier).

In neutral-beam-heated ITB discharges, neon toroidal velocities at the ITB span approximately 10,000–200,000 m s$^{-1}$, with the sign and magnitude reflecting the net torque input and intrinsic rotation drive at the barrier.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi^{\mathrm{Ne}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the neon ion flow velocity at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component of the neon ion bulk flow velocity at the magnetic axis characterizes the on-axis toroidal rotation of the plasma as traced by the neon impurity. In tokamak equilibria with approximate toroidal symmetry, the toroidal rotation is nearly constant on flux surfaces, so this on-axis value parameterizes the core rigid-body rotation.

The quantity is the projection of the neon ion velocity onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ evaluated at the magnetic axis, the point where $\nabla\psi = 0$:

$$
v_\phi^\mathrm{Ne} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{Ne} \cdot \hat{\phi} \Big|_{\nabla\psi = 0}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux.

Neon toroidal velocity at the magnetic axis is measured via charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), exploiting the Doppler shift of neon impurity emission lines excited by a neutral beam. The on-axis value may require radial extrapolation of the measured CXRS profile toward the magnetic axis. In NBI-heated plasmas, core impurity toroidal velocities range from $10^4$ to $10^5$ m/s; in ohmically heated plasmas the rotation is smaller and may reverse sign depending on the momentum balance.

The complementary location-resolved variants include [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal), [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). The analogous on-axis quantity for nitrogen is [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neon ions flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the torus along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Effective velocity coefficient for radial or flux-surface-normal convection of toroidal neutral momentum density. The toroidal momentum component is defined along increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame; the coefficient need not equal the neutral bulk toroidal flow.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal neutral momentum convection velocity is the effective advective velocity that multiplies the toroidal component of neutral momentum density in a momentum-transport closure. Here toroidal identifies the momentum component, defined along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, while the associated transport is normally radial or across flux surfaces, for example toward increasing $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$. It is not a flux through a surface whose normal is $\hat{\phi}$, and it need not be equal to the neutral bulk toroidal velocity.

With an outward radial or flux-surface-normal convention, the convective contribution to the flux of toroidal neutral momentum density is commonly written as:

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\perp,p_{\phi n}} = p_{\phi n}\, V_{c,p_{\phi n}}
$$

where $\Pi^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\perp,p_{\phi n}}$ is the convective flux of toroidal neutral momentum density across the chosen radial or flux-surface-normal direction, $p_{\phi n}$ is the toroidal neutral momentum density, and $V_{c,p_{\phi n}}$ is this convection velocity. The sign of $p_{\phi n}$ is set by the neutral toroidal flow direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice this quantity is obtained from neutral fluid or kinetic transport models by separating the toroidal neutral momentum flux into convective, diffusive, and residual contributions. It is closely related to [toroidal_neutral_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_flux), but represents only the velocity-like coefficient of the convective part. Comparison with [toroidal_neutral_velocity](name:toroidal_neutral_momentum_convection_velocity) is useful, but ionization, charge exchange, sources, sinks, and closure assumptions can make the effective convection velocity differ from the neutral bulk toroidal flow.

Typical magnitudes in edge and scrape-off-layer neutral transport closures range from 10-10^4 m.s^-1, with values near zero in weakly convective regions and larger values where neutral sources, recycling, charge exchange, or strong gradients dominate the momentum balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when positive toroidal neutral momentum, whose velocity component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, is convected toward increasing radial coordinate $\rho$ in flux coordinates $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_species
NAMES.short: Convection velocity for cross-flux-surface transport of toroidal momentum carried by neutrals of one chemical species, aggregated over its neutral states. The toroidal label identifies the transported momentum component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, not a velocity directed toroidally.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal neutral species momentum convection velocity is the flux-surface-normal convection coefficient that multiplies the toroidal momentum density carried by neutrals of one chemical species. The toroidal momentum component is defined by the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the coefficient itself is not a velocity along $\hat{\phi}$. The species aggregation is over neutral states of that chemical species, not over different chemical species.

The defining relation is preservation of the total convective flux of toroidal momentum across a magnetic flux surface:

$$
\Gamma_{\phi,a}^{\mathrm{conv}} = P_{\phi,a} V_{\phi,a}^{\mathrm{conv}} = \sum_{s \in a} P_{\phi,s} V_{\phi,s}^{\mathrm{conv}}
$$

where $a$ denotes one neutral chemical species, $s$ runs over the neutral states of that species, $P_{\phi,s}$ is the signed toroidal momentum density of state $s$, $V_{\phi,s}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the state-resolved coefficient [toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity), and $P_{\phi,a}$ and $\Gamma_{\phi,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ are the corresponding species-summed momentum density and convective momentum flux. When $P_{\phi,a}$ is nonzero, this equation makes $V_{\phi,a}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ the momentum-density-weighted state average, so the aggregate preserves the total convective momentum flux.

This coefficient is usually computed in neutral transport or reduced momentum-balance models rather than measured directly. It is constrained by neutral source and sink physics, recycling and fueling, ionization, charge exchange with ions, elastic collisions, and closures for the neutral velocity distribution. Spectroscopy, neutral pressure measurements, and charge-exchange observations can help validate the neutral populations and flows used to infer it.

Typical effective magnitudes are highly model dependent. They are often negligible where neutral density is negligible in the confined core, while edge and scrape-off-layer models commonly use or infer 1-10^3 m.s^-1 and can reach several 10^3 m.s^-1 near strong recycling or directed neutral sources.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux-surface-normal convection is outward, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Effective convection velocity that advects the toroidal component of momentum of a single neutral state (a specific charge or excitation state of a neutral species) across flux surfaces. The "toroidal" label identifies the transported momentum component, not the direction of the velocity, which is directed normal to flux surfaces in the radial transport sense.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal neutral-state momentum convection velocity is the effective convection velocity used to model the advective (convective) transport of the toroidal component of momentum belonging to one neutral state. A neutral state denotes a specific charge or excitation level of a neutral species. The word "toroidal" here labels which component of momentum is being carried, namely the toroidal momentum $m_a n_a v_{\phi,a}$; the convection velocity itself is directed across flux surfaces (the radial transport channel), not along the toroidal angle.

The advective flux of toroidal momentum carried by the convective channel for neutral state $a$ is written as the product of the toroidal momentum density and this effective convection velocity:

$$
\Gamma^{\mathrm{conv}}_{\phi,a} = m_a \, n_a \, v_{\phi,a} \, v_{\mathrm{conv},a}
$$

where $m_a$ is the neutral particle mass, $n_a$ is the number density of neutral state $a$, $v_{\phi,a}$ is the toroidal velocity of that state, and $v_{\mathrm{conv},a}$ is the effective convection velocity that transports this toroidal momentum across flux surfaces. The convection velocity is an across-flux-surface (radial) quantity, distinct from the local toroidal flow speed of the neutrals.

In edge and scrape-off-layer transport modeling, this effective velocity is obtained from the neutral momentum balance or from a reduced closure fitted to kinetic-neutral behavior, alongside a diffusive contribution. Charge exchange, ionization, recombination, elastic collisions, wall recycling, and molecular dissociation all influence its value and sign. The state-summed counterpart, aggregated over all neutral charge states of the same species, is the toroidal neutral-species momentum convection velocity.

Typical signed magnitudes in edge-neutral transport range from about -10000 to 10000 m.s^-1, with cold recycled neutrals usually below 1000 m.s^-1 and charge-exchange or fast molecular-fragment neutrals reaching several 10000 m.s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convection velocity is directed outward across flux surfaces, away from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Flux density of toroidal linear momentum carried by neutral particles in a specified atomic, molecular, or excitation state. Toroidal refers to the direction of increasing phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame; the flux direction is the positive transport-surface normal.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal neutral-state momentum flux is the scalar component of the kinetic momentum-flux tensor for a neutral particle population in a specified atomic, molecular, or excitation state. The transported momentum component is toroidal linear momentum in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, while the flux direction is the separately defined positive normal or transport direction. It is a linear-momentum flux density, so no factor of major radius $R$ is included.

For neutral state $a$, the kinetic definition across a surface with positive normal $\hat{n}$ is

$$
\Pi_{n\phi}^{(a)}(\mathbf{x}) = \int m_a\, v_n\, v_\phi\, f_a(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $m_a$ is the particle mass in kg, $v_\phi = \mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal velocity component in m s$^{-1}$, $v_n = \mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{n}$ is the velocity component along the positive flux direction in m s$^{-1}$, $f_a$ is the velocity distribution in m$^{-3}$(m s$^{-1}$)$^{-3}$, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The first tensor index denotes the flux direction and the second denotes the transported momentum direction; a fluid decomposition would contain both convective and random-motion contributions.

This quantity is usually computed from kinetic or moment-based neutral transport models by integrating the state-resolved velocity distribution. Experimental constraints come indirectly from measurements sensitive to neutral density, temperature, and flow, such as spectroscopy, neutral-particle analysis, gas pressure measurements, and atomic or molecular state-population modeling.

Typical absolute magnitudes vary strongly with neutral density and flow anisotropy. Values are often $10^{-8}$-$10^{-4}$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ where neutral populations are weak, $10^{-4}$-$1$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ in edge, divertor, recycling, or beam-influenced regions, and can approach $1$-$10$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ in localized high-density or fast-neutral sources.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_n v_\phi > 0$, where $v_\phi$ is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and $v_n$ is along the positive normal of the transport surface.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_state_torque_density
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal torque per unit volume exerted by neutral particles in a specified species state on the plasma about the machine symmetry axis. Summed over all represented neutral internal states it yields the aggregate neutral toroidal torque density.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal neutral state torque density is the volumetric torque about the machine symmetry axis exerted by neutral particles in a specified species state on the surrounding plasma. It is a torque per unit volume, not a linear-momentum source density, and it represents the state-resolved contribution to the toroidal angular-momentum exchange between neutrals and the plasma through charge exchange, ionization, recombination, elastic scattering, and molecular processes. The toroidal direction is the direction of increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The state-resolved torque density is obtained by applying the major-radius moment arm to the corresponding toroidal linear-momentum exchange density for that neutral state:

$$
\tau_{\phi,n}^{(a)} = R\,S_{\phi,n}^{(a)}
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,n}^{(a)}$ is the torque density exerted on the plasma by neutral state $a$ in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $R$ is major radius in meters, and $S_{\phi,n}^{(a)}$ is the toroidal linear-momentum exchange density for that state in kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-2}$. The aggregate neutral toroidal torque density is the state sum $\tau_{\phi,n}=\sum_a \tau_{\phi,n}^{(a)}$ over all represented neutral species states, equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the torque the plasma exerts on those neutrals.

This quantity is usually computed from velocity-space moments of neutral source and collision operators rather than measured directly. It is constrained through modeling informed by diagnostics of density, temperature, rotation, neutral pressure, radiation, and particle sources. The value is meaningful only for the neutral states included in the model, so omitted states or simplified atomic physics can change both the state-resolved partition and the summed torque.

Typical local magnitudes range from roughly $10^{-5}$ to $1$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ in edge, scrape-off-layer, and neutral-source regions, and may reach $1$-$10$ kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ in highly localized beam, charge-exchange, or divertor interaction zones. Values near zero are common where neutral density or toroidal momentum exchange is weak, and opposite-sign contributions from different states can partially cancel in the aggregate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral state exerts a torque on the plasma that drives plasma angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_torque_density
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Toroidal neutral torque density is the signed source rate of plasma toroidal angular momentum per unit volume caused by momentum exchange with neutral particles. It is aggregated over all neutral internal states and refers to the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal neutral torque density is the local rate at which neutral particles add to or remove from the plasma's toroidal angular momentum per unit volume. It represents the aggregated contribution of all neutral internal states, including atomic, molecular, and fragment populations, and is associated with the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

When the neutral-plasma momentum exchange for internal state $\alpha$ is represented by a force density $\mathbf{S}^{\mathrm{mom}}_{\alpha}$ acting on the plasma, the total neutral torque density is

$$
\tau_{\phi,n} = R \sum_{\alpha \in n} \mathbf{S}^{\mathrm{mom}}_{\alpha} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and the sum includes all neutral internal states $\alpha$. The factor $R$ converts toroidal force density into a source of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume.

In practice this quantity is computed from neutral transport and plasma-source models by summing momentum exchange from charge exchange, ionization, recombination, elastic collisions, molecular breakup, and neutral recycling. It is usually inferred indirectly through toroidal momentum balance, rotation measurements, spectroscopy, and constrained transport modeling rather than measured as a standalone local observable. The state-resolved contribution corresponds to [toroidal_neutral_state_torque_density](name:toroidal_neutral_state_torque_density), and comparison with charged-particle sources uses [toroidal_ion_torque_density](name:toroidal_ion_torque_density).

Typical magnitudes in confined-plasma transport studies are about 0.01-10 kg.m^-1.s^-2 for beam-fueled or core neutral momentum exchange, while localized edge and divertor charge-exchange or recycling regions can reach 0.1-100 kg.m^-1.s^-2. Volume-averaged values may be much smaller because positive and negative local contributions can cancel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral interactions add toroidal angular momentum to the plasma in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the nitrogen ion flow velocity at an internal transport barrier, a localized region of reduced radial transport and steep plasma gradients.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal nitrogen velocity at an internal transport barrier is the component of the nitrogen ion fluid velocity tangent to the toroidal direction at the barrier location. It characterizes impurity rotation where radial heat and particle transport are reduced and local gradients are steep, with respect to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

In a local flux-surface coordinate set $(r,\theta,\phi)$, with $r$ an outward radial distance, $\theta$ a poloidal angle, and $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the nitrogen toroidal velocity is commonly related to radial force balance by:

$$
E_r = \frac{1}{Z_N e n_N}\frac{\partial p_N}{\partial r} - v_{\theta,N} B_\phi + v_{\phi,N} B_\theta
$$

where $v_{\phi,N}$ is the toroidal nitrogen velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $v_{\theta,N}$ is the poloidal nitrogen velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $E_r$ is the radial electric field in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $Z_N$ is the nitrogen ion charge state, $e$ is the elementary charge in C, $n_N$ is the nitrogen ion density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $p_N$ is the nitrogen pressure in Pa, $r$ is in m, and $B_\phi$ and $B_\theta$ are the toroidal and poloidal magnetic-field components in T.

The value is usually determined by fitting Doppler shifts of nitrogen charge-exchange recombination line emission and assigning the measurement to the barrier position identified from steep temperature, density, pressure, or rotation gradients. When direct nitrogen spectra are unavailable, it may be estimated from impurity rotation models or from radial-force-balance analysis constrained by measured magnetic field, pressure gradients, and electric field.

Typical signed values in tokamak internal transport barriers are about $-5\times10^4$ to $5\times10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; absolute speeds of a few $10^3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ are common, while strong torque input can produce values approaching $1\times10^5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when nitrogen ions flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the nitrogen impurity ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal nitrogen velocity at the magnetic axis quantifies the azimuthal ($\hat{\phi}$) component of the bulk flow velocity of nitrogen impurity ions at the innermost equilibrium point of the plasma, where $\nabla\psi = 0$ and flux surfaces degenerate to a single point.

The quantity is formally defined as:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{N}} = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{N} \cdot \hat{\phi}\Big|_{\mathrm{magnetic\,axis}}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{N}$ is the nitrogen ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

Nitrogen toroidal velocity profiles are measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), which resolves the Doppler shift of emission lines from nitrogen ions following charge exchange with injected neutral beam atoms; the on-axis value is inferred from radial profiles extrapolated to $r = 0$ or from channels viewing near the magnetic axis.

Typical on-axis impurity toroidal velocities in tokamak plasmas range from a few hundred to tens of thousands of m/s depending on heating power, momentum injection, and intrinsic rotation mechanisms. Analogous quantities for other impurity species at the magnetic axis include [toroidal neon velocity](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal carbon velocity](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis); the same nitrogen species evaluated at the plasma boundary is given by [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_{\phi,\mathrm{N}}$ is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the oxygen ion bulk flow velocity at the radial location of an internal transport barrier, expressed along the phi direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal oxygen velocity at an internal transport barrier is the component of the bulk flow velocity of oxygen ions tangent to the toroidal direction at the barrier radius. It characterizes impurity rotation in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The internal-transport-barrier location is commonly identified by the normalized toroidal-flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, and this quantity is evaluated at that radial position.

The toroidal component is the projection of the oxygen ion bulk velocity onto the toroidal basis direction:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{O}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{O}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{O}}$ is the oxygen ion bulk flow velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

In practice, this velocity is usually inferred from Doppler shifts of oxygen impurity emission, for example using active charge-exchange or passive spectroscopy, and then mapped to the internal-transport-barrier radius. The barrier radius may be identified from sharp changes or extrema in temperature, density, pressure, rotation, or inferred transport as functions of $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$.

Typical magnitudes in tokamak plasmas range from $10^3$-$2\times10^5$ m.s^-1, with the largest values often occurring in strongly heated or momentum-driven plasmas. Values near an internal transport barrier can differ substantially from core or edge rotation because steep pressure gradients, radial electric fields, and momentum transport all affect impurity flow.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the oxygen ion bulk flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk oxygen impurity ion flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost confined-plasma point where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity of oxygen impurity ions at the magnetic axis characterizes the azimuthal rotation of this impurity species at the plasma core. Oxygen co-rotates with the bulk plasma to leading order, with departures driven by neoclassical poloidal friction, charge-exchange coupling to neutrals, and momentum-transport processes that create radial gradients between the axis and the boundary.

The toroidal component is the projection of the oxygen ion fluid velocity onto the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{O}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{O}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{O}}$ is the oxygen ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

The primary measurement technique is charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, where the Doppler shift of an oxygen emission line is used to infer the ion flow velocity along the diagnostic line of sight; decomposition to the toroidal component requires knowledge of the viewing geometry. The on-axis value represents the innermost point of the rotation profile and is related to but distinct from [toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_oxygen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), with the radial structure governed by momentum transport. Analogous on-axis toroidal velocities for other impurity species are [toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the oxygen ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, which is counter-clockwise when viewed from the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

NAMES.name: toroidal_plasma_momentum_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Total toroidal component of plasma linear momentum at the magnetic axis, summed over electrons and all ion species. It is the magnetic-axis endpoint of the radial total toroidal momentum quantity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, not a local toroidal angular-momentum density.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal plasma momentum at the magnetic axis is the value at the magnetic axis of the total toroidal component of plasma linear momentum, including electrons and all ion species. The toroidal component is taken along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and the magnetic axis is the innermost closed-flux-surface locus. Because the unit is kg m s^-1, this quantity is distinct from angular-momentum-density quantities such as toroidal_plasma_angular_momentum_density or toroidal_total_plasma_angular_momentum_density.

The magnetic-axis value is defined as the inner endpoint of the same radial total quantity represented by [toroidal_total_plasma_momentum](name:toroidal_total_plasma_momentum):

$$
P_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}} = \lim_{\rho \to 0} P_\phi(\rho)
$$

where $P_\phi(\rho)$ is the total toroidal plasma momentum in kg m s^-1 at normalized radial flux coordinate $\rho$ in a flux-coordinate labeling $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, summed over all ion species and electrons, and $\rho=0$ labels the magnetic axis. This definition keeps the dimensions of total linear momentum and does not introduce the major-radius factor $R$ that appears in toroidal angular momentum.

In practice the value is obtained from radial reconstructions of species density, composition, mass, and toroidal flow velocity, with the magnetic axis identified from an equilibrium reconstruction. Spectroscopic rotation measurements, charge-exchange measurements for ions, and transport modeling may contribute to the species-summed value; the outer reference counterpart is [toroidal_total_plasma_momentum_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_total_plasma_momentum_at_plasma_boundary).

Typical absolute magnitudes are device- and analysis-dependent because this is a total quantity rather than a density. Present-day tokamak values are often order 10^-2-10^1 kg m s^-1, with larger or rapidly rotating plasmas reaching tens of kg m s^-1, and weak or canceling toroidal flows giving values near 0 kg m s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total toroidal plasma momentum points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_rotation_frequency_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular rotation frequency of the species-independent E-cross-B drift, expressed using the velocity-divided-by-local-major-radius convention. It equals minus the derivative of the flux-surface-averaged electrostatic potential with respect to poloidal magnetic flux, making it identical for all particle species on a given flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal rotation frequency due to the E-cross-B drift is the angular frequency of the toroidal part of the electrostatic drift motion. Because it is driven purely by the radial electric field acting through the equilibrium magnetic field, it is identical for all particle species on a given flux surface, distinguishing it from rotation components that carry species-dependent diamagnetic or centrifugal contributions. It is expressed using the same convention as a toroidal velocity divided by the local major radius.

The defining flux-surface angular frequency is

$$
\Omega_E(\psi) = -\frac{d\langle\Phi\rangle}{d\psi}
$$

where $\langle\Phi\rangle$ is the flux-surface-averaged electrostatic potential in volts and $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux in webers. Since $1\ \mathrm{V}/\mathrm{Wb} = 1\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$, the derivative has units of angular frequency.

The underlying drift velocity is $\mathbf{v}_{E} = (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B})/B^2$, where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field in volts per meter and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in tesla. In the velocity-over-major-radius convention this frequency corresponds to $\Omega_E = v_{E,\phi}/R$, where $v_{E,\phi}$ is the toroidal component of the E-cross-B drift velocity (in meters per second) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and $R$ is the local major radius (in meters).

In practice this quantity is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction together with an inferred or modeled electrostatic potential, by differentiating $\langle\Phi\rangle$ with respect to $\psi$. The radial electric field that sets the potential gradient is commonly inferred from the radial force balance on impurity ions or from edge electrostatic probes.

The value can pass through zero where the flux-surface-averaged electrostatic potential has a local extremum as a function of poloidal magnetic flux, and its magnitude is largest in regions of strong radial electric-field shear such as the pedestal.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal component of the E-cross-B drift gives angular rotation in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric toroidal collisional source of angular momentum deposited in the bulk thermal electron population through Coulomb collisions with a fast particle distribution. It is the local rate of transfer of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume to thermal electrons, projected onto the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal thermal electron torque density due to collisions is the rate per unit volume at which toroidal angular momentum is transferred to the bulk (near-Maxwellian) thermal electron population by Coulomb collisions with a fast particle distribution. The toroidal direction is the $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. When guiding-center orbit topology is resolved, this quantity is the sum of the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped contributions to the thermal electrons.

In a kinetic formulation, the local collisional torque density is the first toroidal moment of the collision operator weighted by major radius:

$$
\tau_{e,\phi}^{\mathrm{coll}}(R,Z) = R \int m_e\, v_\phi\, \mathcal{C}[f_e, f_{\mathrm{fast}}] \, d^3v
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass (kg), $v_\phi$ is the thermal-electron velocity component along $\hat{\phi}$ (m s$^{-1}$), $f_e$ and $f_{\mathrm{fast}}$ are the thermal-electron and fast-particle distribution functions (s$^3$ m$^{-6}$), $\mathcal{C}$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on $f_e$ due to $f_{\mathrm{fast}}$ (s$^2$ m$^{-6}$), and $R$ is the major radius (m). The velocity integral yields the toroidal collisional force density on thermal electrons (N m$^{-3}$); multiplying by $R$ converts it to torque density with unit N m$^{-2}$.

This quantity is generally computed from a kinetic distribution and a Coulomb collision operator using bounce-averaged or kinetic-fluid Fokker-Planck solvers rather than measured directly. It enters the electron toroidal angular-momentum balance as a local source term, and its volume integral gives the corresponding net toroidal torque on the thermal electron population. Momentum conservation implies an equal and opposite collisional torque on the interacting fast population, apart from approximations in the collision model.

Magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent and vary by orders of magnitude with the strength and localization of the fast population; representative values are not well constrained by a single reference and should be taken from the specific equilibrium and source model under consideration. The value can be positive or negative depending on the direction of the toroidal momentum transferred to the thermal electrons.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional torque transfers toroidal angular momentum to thermal electrons in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated toroidal torque transferred to the bulk thermal electron population through Coulomb collisions with fast (non-Maxwellian) particles in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal collisional torque on thermal electrons is the volume integral of the toroidal component of the Coulomb drag force that the fast particle distribution exerts on the bulk electron population. It quantifies the rate at which non-Maxwellian fast particles deposit toroidal angular momentum into the thermal electron fluid, coupling the kinetic fast-particle physics to bulk electron momentum balance.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
T_{\phi,e}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \int_V R \, \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{coll},e} \cdot \hat{\phi} \, dV
$$

where $R$ is the major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{coll},e}$ is the Coulomb collisional friction force per unit volume on the thermal electron population from the fast particle distribution, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

This torque is computed from kinetic modeling of the fast particle distribution by evaluating Coulomb collision operators to extract the momentum exchange rate with the thermal electron component. Because the electron rest mass is far smaller than typical fast ion masses, the coupling of toroidal angular momentum from fast ions to thermal electrons is generally weaker than the corresponding ion channel, though fast electron sources such as those from wave-driven current drive can produce substantial contributions.

The local torque density counterpart is [toroidal thermal electron torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions). The species-summed analog over all thermal particles is [toroidal thermal torque due to collisions], and the complementary quantity deposited into the fast electron population is [toroidal fast electron torque due to collisions](name:toroidal_fast_electron_torque_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net Coulomb friction on thermal electrons acts in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_thermal_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular-momentum source density delivered by Coulomb collisions to thermal ions in a specified ionization state, equal to the major-radius lever arm times the phi-directed collisional force density in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local toroidal angular-momentum transfer rate per unit plasma volume received by thermal ions in a specified ionization state through Coulomb collisions. It is charge-state-resolved; summing over ionization states gives the total thermal-ion collisional toroidal torque density. The toroidal direction is the $\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining relation is the major-radius lever arm times the local toroidal force density:

$$
\tau_{\phi,q}^{\mathrm{th,coll}} = R f_{\phi,q}^{\mathrm{th,coll}}
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,q}^{\mathrm{th,coll}}$ is the torque density on thermal ions in ionization state $q$, $R$ is the major radius, and $f_{\phi,q}^{\mathrm{th,coll}}$ is the $\hat{\phi}$ component of the collisional force density acting on that thermal ion state. The product has units of N m$^{-2}$, consistent with torque per unit volume.

This quantity is normally computed rather than measured directly, by taking the toroidal momentum moment of Coulomb collision operators in kinetic, hybrid, or transport calculations. It represents momentum exchange between the selected thermal ion charge state and other particle populations, such as energetic ions or electrons, and the sum over all interacting populations obeys total momentum conservation apart from externally imposed sources, sinks, and boundary losses. The volume integral gives [toroidal_thermal_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions), while summing over ionization states gives [toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions); orbit-class-resolved counterparts include trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing thermal-ion state torque densities.

Representative local magnitudes are often $10^{-3}$-$10^{1}$ N m$^{-2}$ in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas and may approach $10^{2}$ N m$^{-2}$ where fast-ion momentum exchange is strongly localized. Values can be much smaller in weakly driven or nearly momentum-balanced conditions, and they scale with major radius, charge-state density, collisional coupling strength, and the toroidal momentum imbalance of the interacting populations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional toroidal angular-momentum transfer to the thermal ion state is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_thermal_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated toroidal torque transferred to the thermal ion population of a specific charge state via Coulomb collisions with fast particles, quantifying the toroidal angular momentum deposited into that ion state by the suprathermal distribution.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the net toroidal component of the angular momentum transferred from a fast-particle distribution to thermal ions of a specific charge state through Coulomb collisions, integrated over the entire plasma volume. It is a global scalar that resolves momentum deposition at the level of individual ion charge states, providing a detailed accounting of how suprathermal particles (e.g., from neutral beam injection or fusion reactions) slow down and transfer toroidal angular momentum to each ionization stage of main or impurity ions.

The defining relation is:

$$\tau_\phi^{\mathrm{th},Z} = \int_V C_\phi^{\mathrm{fast}\to\mathrm{th},Z}(\mathbf{r})\, dV$$

where $C_\phi^{\mathrm{fast}\to\mathrm{th},Z}$ is the toroidal component of the Coulomb-collision momentum-transfer rate density from the fast-particle distribution to the thermal ions of charge state $Z$, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

This quantity is computed from kinetic modeling that solves for the fast-particle distribution function and evaluates the linearized Coulomb collision operator against the thermal ion background. Resolving contributions per charge state allows momentum deposition to be tracked separately for each ionization level, which is essential for impurity transport and toroidal momentum balance modeling.

Summing over all thermal ion charge states and adding the electron contribution from [toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions) recovers the total thermal-particle collisional torque in toroidal_thermal_torque_due_to_collisions. The complementary momentum received by the fast-ion charge state is given by [toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional momentum transfer acts in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net collisional toroidal torque density transferred to thermal ions by Coulomb collisions with fast-particle source populations. It sums the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped fast-particle source-orbit contributions and is signed along phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal thermal-ion torque density due to collisions is the local torque per unit volume transferred to the bulk thermal ion population by Coulomb collisions with fast particles. It represents toroidal angular-momentum deposition by fast-particle source populations, summed over co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped source-orbit classes. The toroidal direction is $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining kinetic moment includes the major-radius lever arm that converts toroidal force density to torque density:

$$
\tau_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{th}} = R\,m_i \int v_\phi\, C_i^{\mathrm{fp}\rightarrow\mathrm{th}}[f_{\mathrm{fast}},f_{\mathrm{th},i}]\, d^3v
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the torque density transferred to thermal ions of species $i$ in N m$^{-2}$, $R$ is the major radius in m, $m_i$ is the ion mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the velocity component along $\hat{\phi}$ in m s$^{-1}$, and $C_i^{\mathrm{fp}\rightarrow\mathrm{th}}$ is the Coulomb collision-operator term for momentum transfer from co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped fast-particle source distributions to the thermal ion distribution. With the normalization $\int f\,d^3v=n$, $f_{\mathrm{fast}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{th},i}$ have units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, $C_i^{\mathrm{fp}\rightarrow\mathrm{th}}$ has units s$^2$ m$^{-6}$, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$.

In practice, this quantity is computed from kinetic collision operators, orbit-following models, or transport calculations that evaluate collisional slowing-down and pitch-angle scattering of fast particles. The source-orbit components are the co-passing [toroidal_co_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions), counter-passing [toroidal_counter_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_counter_passing_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions), and trapped [toroidal_trapped_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_trapped_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) contributions; their sum gives this total thermal-ion torque density. Volume integration gives [toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_due_to_collisions), while the corresponding collisional angular-momentum change of the fast-ion population is related to [toroidal_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent because they scale with fast-particle density, slowing-down rate, pitch distribution, and major radius. The value is 0 N m$^{-2}$ when no fast-particle collisional momentum source is present; in beam- or alpha-heated tokamak cores, local magnitudes are often of order $10^{-3}$-$10^1$ N m$^{-2}$, with either sign possible depending on the direction of deposited toroidal angular momentum.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the torque transfers toroidal angular momentum to thermal ions in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, equivalent to increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated toroidal angular-momentum source deposited in the bulk thermal-ion population by Coulomb collisions with fast particles, summed over all thermal-ion charge states. In the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, it is the torque about the symmetry axis associated with the phi-directed collisional force.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal thermal-ion torque due to collisions is the net rate at which Coulomb collisions with fast particles transfer toroidal angular momentum to the bulk thermal-ion population. It is summed over all thermal-ion charge states and excludes electron and neutral-particle momentum channels. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, it is the moment about the symmetry axis produced by the toroidal component of the collisional force on thermal ions.

The volume-integrated torque can be written as the charge-state sum of the toroidal force moment:

$$
T_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_q \int_V R\,F_{\phi,i_q}^{\mathrm{coll}}(R,\phi,Z)\,dV
$$

where $T_{\phi,i}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is in N m, $q$ labels thermal-ion charge states, $V$ is the plasma volume, $R$ is in m, $F_{\phi,i_q}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the $\phi$ component of the collisional force density on thermal ions in charge state $q$ in N m^-3 in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $dV$ is in m^3. The charge-state-resolved counterpart is [toroidal_thermal_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_state_torque_due_to_collisions); the broader thermal charged-particle torque including non-ion thermal species is [toroidal_thermal_torque_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_due_to_collisions).

This quantity is usually computed from the Coulomb collision operator or equivalent friction terms in kinetic and transport analyzes of fast particles interacting with the thermal plasma. The local momentum-exchange rate density is evaluated for each thermal-ion charge state and integrated over the confined plasma volume using the magnetic-equilibrium geometry; experimentally it is inferred from modeling constrained by fast-particle diagnostics and plasma density, temperature, and rotation measurements rather than measured directly.

Typical absolute values are 0.01-10 N m in present medium-size tokamaks with appreciable fast-ion populations and can reach several tens of N m in high-power neutral-beam-heated plasmas. Values are near zero when the fast-particle population is weak, nearly toroidally balanced, or transfers little net toroidal momentum to thermal ions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional force on the thermal-ion population is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_torque_density
NAMES.short: Local source rate of angular momentum about the symmetry axis per unit volume in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where phi is the toroidal angle.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal torque density is the local source rate of angular momentum about the symmetry axis per unit volume in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the volumetric source term for [toroidal plasma momentum]; integrating it over a plasma volume gives a total [toroidal torque] or net [toroidal plasma torque].

In a toroidal angular-momentum balance, the source term is represented by:

$$
\frac{\partial L_\phi}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{L_\phi} = \tau_\phi
$$

where $\tau_\phi$ is the toroidal torque density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $L_\phi$ is the toroidal angular-momentum density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$, and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{L_\phi}$ is the flux of toroidal angular momentum. For the mechanical particle contribution, $L_\phi$ includes the lever arm $R$, for example $L_\phi = \sum_s m_s n_s R v_{\phi,s}$, where $m_s$, $n_s$, and $v_{\phi,s}$ are the mass, number density, and toroidal velocity of species $s$.

This quantity is computed from momentum deposition by particle sources, wave-particle interactions, fusion products, electromagnetic forces, and collisional exchange, and it may also be inferred from momentum-balance analysis constrained by rotation measurements. Flux-surface averaging changes the spatial representation but not the unit: it remains torque per unit volume, not a volume-integrated torque.

Typical absolute values in magnetically confined plasmas are about $10^{-3}$-$1\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ for broadly deposited auxiliary-heating sources, with localized fast-particle or wave-driven deposition sometimes reaching $1$-$10\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the source deposits angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal torque density exerted on a specified particle population by the J×B Lorentz force acting on current normal to magnetic flux surfaces. The toroidal direction is the phi direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. The associated current includes radial fast-particle currents and the quasi-neutrality-preserving return current.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal torque density due to the $\mathbf{J}\times\mathbf{B}$ force is the flux-surface-averaged rate of toroidal angular momentum transfer per unit volume to a specified particle population. The relevant current is the component normal to magnetic flux surfaces, comprising radial fast-particle currents and the quasi-neutrality-preserving return current, so the quantity is population scoped and does not by itself represent the whole plasma.

For a magnetic surface labeled by a radial flux coordinate $\rho$, it is defined as

$$
\tau_\phi(\rho) = \left\langle R\,\left(\mathbf{J}_\perp \times \mathbf{B}\right)\cdot\hat{\phi}\right\rangle_{\rho}
$$

where $R$ is major radius in m, $\mathbf{J}_\perp$ is the current density normal to the magnetic surface in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic flux density in T, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\langle\cdots\rangle_{\rho}$ denotes the average over that magnetic surface.

It is computed from kinetic or guiding-center estimates of nonambipolar radial currents, charge-conserving return currents, and reconstructed magnetic geometry. The total torque on the same population follows from volume integration, $T_\phi = \int \tau_\phi\,dV$; when the population is fast particles this integral corresponds to [toroidal_fast_torque_due_to_j_cross_b_force](name:toroidal_fast_particle_torque_due_to_j_cross_b_force), while a whole-plasma torque requires summing all population torque densities and other momentum sources.

Magnitudes are strongly device and scenario dependent. For neutral-beam-driven fast-ion nonambipolar current, flux-surface-averaged values are often $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}$ N m$^{-2}$ in weak-torque regions and can reach $1$-$10$ N m$^{-2}$ in localized strong-ripple or loss regions; the sign may change with radius as current direction and magnetic geometry vary.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R(\mathbf{J}_\perp \times \mathbf{B})\cdot\hat{\phi}$ drives toroidal motion in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_torque_due_to_neutral_beam_shinethrough
NAMES.short: Signed torque about the symmetry axis, in the phi direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, carried away by neutral beam particles that traverse the plasma without ionization. It is the rate at which their beam angular momentum is not transferred to the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal torque due to neutral beam shinethrough is the signed rate at which mechanical angular momentum about the symmetry axis is carried away by injected neutral particles that cross the plasma without ionization. It describes the unabsorbed angular-momentum flux of the neutral beam; when forming a plasma momentum balance, this carried-away amount is subtracted from the beam angular momentum that could otherwise be deposited.

The contribution from a distribution of surviving beam particles can be written as a rate-weighted sum over the shinethrough population:

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{st}} = \int_{\Lambda_{\mathrm{st}}} \dot N_{\mathrm{st}}(\lambda)\, m_b(\lambda)\, R(\lambda)\, v_b(\lambda)\, \hat{\mathbf b}(\lambda)\cdot\hat{\phi}\, d\lambda
$$

where $\lambda$ labels beamlets, species, energy components, launch positions, and directions; $\dot N_{\mathrm{st}}(\lambda)d\lambda$ is the surviving neutral particle rate in s$^{-1}$; $m_b$ is the beam-particle mass in kg; $v_b$ is the neutral speed along the injected trajectory in m s$^{-1}$; $R$ is major radius in m; and $\hat{\mathbf b}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal projection of the beam direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The geometric factor $R\hat{\mathbf b}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the signed toroidal impact parameter, commonly specified through the beamline tangency radius and injection angle. The velocity component is the neutral beam particle velocity projection, not the local plasma toroidal flow velocity, and the resulting torque is in N m.

In practice this quantity is computed from the neutral beam species, energy fractions, particle rates, beamlet geometry, and attenuation through the plasma. Ray tracing or Monte Carlo neutral transport determines which injected particles survive to the far side without ionization, and their rate-weighted toroidal angular momentum is summed. Direct constraints can come from measurements of unabsorbed beam power on beam dumps or first-wall components, but the torque sign and angular-momentum lever arm are set primarily by beamline geometry.

Typical magnitudes are 0.001-1 N m during well-fueled heating phases where the shinethrough fraction is small. Values can reach 1-10 N m in low-density startup, high-energy injection, or weakly attenuating plasmas, where shinethrough can be a significant correction to the neutral-beam momentum budget.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the shinethrough neutral particles carry angular momentum about the symmetry axis with toroidal velocity component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_total_plasma_momentum
NAMES.short: Total toroidal linear momentum of the plasma, formed by integrating the local phi-directed momentum density over a flux-surface-bounded plasma volume and summing ions and electrons. It is a total linear-momentum component, not a local toroidal angular-momentum density.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal total plasma momentum is the volume-integrated scalar component of plasma kinetic momentum along the local $\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is summed over all ion species and electrons and contains no extra factor of major radius $R$; therefore it represents total toroidal linear momentum rather than toroidal angular momentum density.

For a volume $V(\rho)$ enclosed by a closed magnetic flux surface labeled by radial coordinate $\rho$, the total toroidal plasma momentum is

$$
P_\phi(\rho) = \int_{V(\rho)} \sum_s m_s n_s(\mathbf{x}) v_{\phi,s}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species and electrons, $m_s$ is particle mass in kg, $n_s$ is number density in m$^{-3}$, $v_{\phi,s}$ is the local toroidal velocity component in m s$^{-1}$, and $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$. The integrand has units kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and the volume integral has units kg m s$^{-1}$.

In flux-surface analyzes this quantity is computed by integrating local toroidal momentum density over nested flux-surface shells; the value at the plasma boundary is the total toroidal linear momentum contained in the confined plasma. It may be inferred from charge-exchange spectroscopy, impurity and main-ion rotation measurements, density and composition estimates, and equilibrium geometry; the electron contribution is normally small because of the electron mass but is included in the species sum.

Typical absolute values range from about 0.01-10 kg m s$^{-1}$ in small and medium tokamaks and can reach 1-100 kg m s$^{-1}$ in large, dense, strongly rotating plasmas. Values near zero occur when toroidal flows are weak or when co- and counter-directed momentum contributions nearly cancel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net toroidal particle momentum is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_total_runaway_electron_current
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Total toroidal electric current carried by the runaway electron population in the plasma. It is the runaway-electron contribution to the net toroidal plasma current and is a key quantity for characterizing post-disruption runaway beams.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal total runaway electron current is the net conventional electric current due to the runaway electron population through a poloidal plasma cross-section, taken along the toroidal direction. It is the runaway-electron contribution to the [toroidal_total_plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current) and coincides with the global toroidal runaway current denoted by [runaway_electron_current](name:toroidal_total_runaway_electron_current).

Using the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the current is the integral of the toroidal component of the runaway-electron current density over the poloidal plasma cross-section:

$$
I_{\mathrm{RE},\phi} = \int_{A_p} \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{RE}} \cdot \hat{\phi} \, dA
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, $dA$ is a poloidal cross-sectional area element in m$^2$, and $A_p$ is the plasma poloidal cross-section.

In practice this quantity is obtained by integrating a modeled or inferred runaway-electron current-density component over the confined plasma cross-section. It is the integrated counterpart of the local quantity [parallel_runaway_electron_current_density](name:parallel_runaway_electron_current_density), and its largest value attained over a pulse is tracked separately by runaway_electron_maximum_current.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the conventional runaway-electron current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_current_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density associated with the trapped part of a particle distribution. It includes the fast-particle contribution and the accompanying thermal electron and ion drag back-current.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped current density is the flux-surface average of the toroidal component of current associated with particles classified as trapped in the magnetic field. It represents the total trapped-sector contribution in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The total trapped contribution is decomposed into the direct fast-particle moment and the thermal drag-current response:

$$
\langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}} \rangle = \langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{fast}} \rangle + \langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{drag},e} \rangle + \langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{drag},i} \rangle
$$

where $\langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}} \rangle$, $\langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{fast}} \rangle$, $\langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{drag},e} \rangle$, and $\langle J_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{drag},i} \rangle$ are flux-surface-averaged toroidal current densities in A.m^-2. The full passing/trapped decomposition also includes the co-passing and counter-passing toroidal current-density contributions.

In practice, this quantity is computed from kinetic distribution functions by identifying trapped phase-space orbits, taking the charge-weighted toroidal-velocity moment of the fast species, and adding the collisional momentum-balance response of thermal electrons and ions. It is usually constrained indirectly by magnetic-equilibrium information, total-current measurements, and fast-particle diagnostics rather than measured as an isolated component.

Typical magnitudes are 10^3-10^5 A.m^-2 in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas and can approach 10^6 A.m^-2 in strongly driven regions. The signed total may be much smaller than the direct fast-particle term when electron and ion drag-current contributions partially cancel it.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $J_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_fast_current_density
NAMES.short: Toroidal component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height, of the current density carried by trapped fast nonthermal particles. It excludes electron and thermal-ion return-current contributions.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped fast current density is the $\phi$ component, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, of the electrical current density carried by nonthermal particles whose guiding-center orbits are trapped between mirror points. It represents only the fast-particle contribution from the trapped region of phase space and excludes compensating currents carried by electrons and thermal ions.

A local kinetic definition is the charge-weighted toroidal velocity moment of the trapped fast distribution:

$$
j_{\phi,\mathrm{fast,tr}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_s q_s \int_{\mathcal{T}} v_\phi\, f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $s$ labels fast particle species, $q_s$ is the signed particle charge, $v_\phi$ is the velocity component along $\hat{\phi}$, $f_{s,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the nonthermal distribution function, and $\mathcal{T}$ denotes the part of velocity space corresponding to trapped orbits. The same moment may be averaged over a flux surface when a radially resolved scalar current density is required.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic distribution functions obtained from Fokker-Planck, Monte Carlo, or orbit-following models, with the trapped population identified from pitch angle, magnetic moment, and bounce motion. It may be constrained indirectly by fast-particle diagnostics and by current-balance analysis, but it is not the total plasma current density because return currents and thermal species are excluded.

Typical magnitudes range from 10^2-10^5 A.m^-2 in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas and may approach 10^6 A.m^-2 locally in strong current-drive scenarios. The trapped contribution is often smaller than the passing fast-particle toroidal current density because trapped guiding-center orbits have limited net toroidal streaming.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the trapped fast-particle current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Toroidal (phi) component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the Coulomb-collisional torque density transferred to trapped fast electrons. It is the local rate of toroidal momentum exchange per unit volume for the trapped fast-electron population.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped fast-electron collisional torque density is the $\hat{\phi}$ component, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, of the torque density transferred to trapped fast electrons by Coulomb collisions. It describes the local rate per unit volume at which collisions change the toroidal mechanical angular momentum of fast electrons whose pitch angles keep them on magnetically trapped bounce orbits.

The local torque density can be written as the toroidal angular-momentum moment of the collisional kinetic operator over the trapped part of phase space:

$$
T_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{fe,tr}} = \int_{\Gamma_\mathrm{tr}} m_e R v_\phi\, C_\mathrm{coll}[f_\mathrm{fe}]\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma_\mathrm{tr}
$$

where $T_{\phi,\mathrm{coll}}^{\mathrm{fe,tr}}$ has unit N m^-2, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $R$ is major radius in m, $v_\phi$ is the particle velocity component along $+\hat{\phi}$ in m s^-1, $f_\mathrm{fe}$ is the fast-electron distribution, and $C_\mathrm{coll}[f_\mathrm{fe}]$ is its Coulomb-collisional rate of change with units of $f_\mathrm{fe}$ s^-1. The measure $\mathrm{d}\Gamma_\mathrm{tr}$ denotes the trapped-region phase-space measure: in a local velocity-space representation it is $\mathrm{d}^3v$ restricted to trapped pitch angles, while in a bounce- or orbit-averaged representation it includes the appropriate trapped-orbit Jacobian and bounce-time weighting, normalized so that $\int_{\Gamma_\mathrm{tr}} f_\mathrm{fe}\,\mathrm{d}\Gamma_\mathrm{tr}$ has unit m^-3.

In practice, this quantity is computed from kinetic Fokker-Planck, guiding-center, or bounce-averaged fast-electron models by applying the relevant Coulomb collision operator to the trapped part of the distribution and taking the toroidal momentum moment. It is usually inferred through modeling constrained by equilibrium, current, radiation, and fast-electron diagnostics rather than measured directly. The sum of this trapped contribution and the corresponding [passing fast-electron contribution] gives the [total fast-electron collisional toroidal torque density](name:toroidal_fast_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical absolute magnitudes are strongly scenario dependent: auxiliary-heated fast-electron tails often give $10^{-5}$-$10^{-1}$ N m^-2, while runaway-electron or strongly driven current-relaxation cases can reach $10^{-1}$-$10$ N m^-2 locally. Values may be near zero or change sign where collisional friction balances sources or where trapped-particle phase-space gradients reverse.
NAMES.sign: Positive when collisions transfer toroidal momentum to the trapped fast-electron population in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_fast_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Collisional torque density is the rate per unit plasma volume at which Coulomb collisions with all background plasma species change the toroidal angular momentum of trapped fast ions. The sign refers to angular momentum about the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle phi.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped fast-ion torque density due to collisions is the local rate per unit plasma volume at which Coulomb collisions with the background plasma change the toroidal angular momentum of fast ions on trapped, banana-like guiding-center orbits. The collision term sums contributions from all background charged species included in the kinetic collision operator (thermal ions and electrons), and the quantity is restricted to the trapped part of the fast-ion distribution.

The quantity is the toroidal-angular-momentum moment of the full collision operator integrated over the trapped region of velocity space:

$$
T_{\phi,\mathrm{tr}}^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = m_f R \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbf{x})} v_\phi \sum_b C_b[f_f](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$
