where $m_f$ is the fast-ion mass, $R$ is the major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $v_\phi$ is the velocity component in the $\hat{\phi}$ direction, $C_b[f_f]$ is the Coulomb collision operator acting on the fast-ion distribution $f_f$ due to background species $b$ (summed over thermal ions and electrons), and $\Omega_{\mathrm{tr}}$ is the trapped part of velocity space. In an axisymmetric field the trapped partition is identified from the pitch condition $\xi^2 < 1 - B/B_{\max}$ along the orbit, where $\xi = v_\parallel/v$ is the pitch cosine and $B_{\max}$ is the maximum magnetic-field strength encountered on that orbit.

This quantity is usually computed from a fast-ion distribution function and a collisional Fokker-Planck operator rather than measured directly. Transport and orbit-following analyzes infer it by combining fast-ion source information, slowing-down and pitch-angle-scattering physics, magnetic geometry, and diagnostic constraints on the fast-ion population; the result gives the collisional exchange of toroidal angular momentum between the background plasma and the trapped fast-ion population.

Typical magnitudes vary strongly with heating power, fast-ion density, collisionality, and trapped-particle fraction. Absolute values are often about $10^{-4}-10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ in weakly driven plasmas and $10^{-2}-1\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ in neutral-beam-heated plasmas, with localized values of several $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ possible near strong fast-ion sources or steep distribution gradients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions impart net toroidal angular momentum to trapped fast ions in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular-momentum torque density transferred by collisions to the trapped-orbit part of the thermal electron population. It equals the major-radius lever arm times the collisional toroidal force density in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped thermal electron torque density is the collisional source of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume for thermal electrons whose guiding-center orbits are trapped. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, it is the major-radius lever arm multiplying the toroidal collisional force density acting on that receiving population. The word trapped identifies the orbit class of the thermal electrons receiving the momentum source, not a separate restriction on the collision partner.

The torque density is obtained from the toroidal momentum moment of the collision operator with the toroidal lever arm included:

$$
\tau_{\phi,e,\mathrm{th,tr}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(R,Z) = R\,m_e \int v_\phi\, C_{e,\mathrm{th,tr}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{v};R,Z)\, d^3v
$$

where $R$ is major radius in m, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component in m s$^{-1}$, and $C_{e,\mathrm{th,tr}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collision-operator contribution for trapped thermal electrons in units of distribution function per second when $n_e=\int f\,d^3v$. The velocity integral gives a toroidal force density in N m$^{-3}$; multiplication by $R$ gives a torque density in N m$^{-2}$.

In kinetic or drift-kinetic calculations, this quantity is computed by integrating the collisional momentum exchange over the trapped region of velocity and pitch-angle space. Together with [toroidal co-passing thermal electron torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_co_passing_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and [toroidal counter-passing thermal electron torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_counter_passing_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions), it contributes to the orbit-class decomposition of [toroidal thermal electron torque density due to collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical absolute magnitudes in thermal-electron momentum balance are often 10^-6-1 N m^-2 in the core and can reach 1-100 N m^-2 in edge regions or strongly driven plasmas, depending on density, collisionality, major radius, and toroidal flow shear.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional toroidal force on trapped thermal electrons acts in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_thermal_electron_torque_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_electrons
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric toroidal torque density on trapped thermal electrons produced by electron-electron Coulomb collisions. It is the major-radius lever-arm times the collisional toroidal force density in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped thermal electron torque density due to Coulomb collisions with electrons is the rate of change of trapped-electron toroidal angular momentum per unit volume caused only by electron-electron Coulomb scattering. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height, and excludes electromagnetic, turbulent, neutral, and electron-ion momentum sources.

For a local distribution function, the collisional torque density can be written as the major-radius lever arm multiplying the toroidal collisional force density:

$$
\tau_{e,\mathrm{tr},\phi}^{(ee)}(\mathbf{x}) = R\,m_e \int_{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})} v_\phi\, C_{ee}[f_e,f_e](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component, $C_{ee}[f_e,f_e]$ is the electron-electron Coulomb collision operator giving the collisional time derivative of the thermal electron distribution due to electron collision partners, and $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})$ is the trapped region of velocity space at position $\mathbf{x}$. The factor $R$ converts toroidal force density to torque density about the symmetry axis, giving units of $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.

In practice this term is computed from kinetic or neoclassical models by evaluating the electron-electron collision operator and integrating only over particle orbits classified as trapped, usually according to invariants such as magnetic moment, energy, and bounce accessibility. For a complete electron population, self-collisions conserve total electron momentum, but the trapped-subpopulation contribution can be nonzero because collisions exchange momentum between trapped and passing regions of velocity space.

Typical magnitudes are strongly regime dependent and may range from near zero in weakly collisional, nearly momentum-conserving cases to about $10^{-3}$-$10^{2}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ in edge, pedestal, or strongly anisotropic thermal electron distributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional toroidal force on trapped thermal electrons is in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, corresponding to angular-momentum transfer in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_thermal_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Toroidal collisional torque density transferred from the trapped-particle distribution to thermal ions of a specified ion charge state. It is the local rate of toroidal angular-momentum exchange per unit volume due to Coulomb collisions.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal trapped thermal ion state torque density due to collisions is the toroidal component of collisional torque per unit volume deposited in thermal ions of a specified ion charge state by the trapped portion of a particle distribution. The toroidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The charge-state index labels the receiving thermal-ion population.

A local kinetic definition is obtained by taking the toroidal angular-momentum moment of the Coulomb-collision term acting on the receiving thermal-ion charge state:

$$
\tau_{\phi,z}^{\mathrm{trap}\rightarrow\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x}) = R\,m_z \int v_\phi\, C_z^{\mathrm{trap}\rightarrow\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,z}^{\mathrm{trap}\rightarrow\mathrm{th}}$ is the torque density in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, $z$ labels the receiving ion charge state, $R$ is major radius in $\mathrm{m}$, $m_z$ is the mass in $\mathrm{kg}$ of that ion population, $v_\phi$ is toroidal velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $C_z^{\mathrm{trap}\rightarrow\mathrm{th}}$ is the Coulomb-collision contribution to the time derivative of the receiving thermal-ion distribution caused by trapped particles with units $\mathrm{m^{-3}(m\,s^{-1})^{-3}s^{-1}}$, and $d^3v$ has units $\mathrm{(m\,s^{-1})^3}$. The factor $R$ converts toroidal force density into torque density about the symmetry axis.

This quantity is usually computed from kinetic or reduced transport models by separating the trapped-orbit part of the source distribution, evaluating the collisional momentum-transfer operator, and projecting the result onto the toroidal direction. Summing over receiving ion charge states gives the total trapped-to-thermal-ion collisional torque density; related quantities distinguish all-orbit, fast-ion, electron, and counter-passing contributions.

Typical absolute values in tokamak transport calculations are about $10^{-6}$-$1\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, with larger local values up to $10\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ possible near strong sources, steep distribution-function gradients, or high collisionality. Values can be close to zero when trapped and thermal populations are near collisional momentum balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional torque deposited in the receiving thermal-ion charge state increases its toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Collisional toroidal torque density transferred to trapped thermal ions by Coulomb collisions with charged particles included in the kinetic collision operator. It is the rate of toroidal angular-momentum deposition per unit volume on the trapped bulk-ion orbit class in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped thermal ion torque density due to collisions is the collisional source of toroidal angular momentum per unit volume deposited in bulk thermal ions whose guiding-center orbits are trapped. It is an internal Coulomb-friction term: collisions transfer angular momentum between the trapped thermal-ion population and the charged partner populations retained in the kinetic description, without representing neutral, wave, or externally applied torques. The aggregate thermal-ion value is the sum over thermal-ion species or charge states; the corresponding resolved contribution is [toroidal_trapped_thermal_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_trapped_thermal_ion_state_torque_density_due_to_collisions).

A local kinetic definition is the trapped-orbit moment of the Coulomb collision operator over the target thermal-ion populations:

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{trap}}^{\mathrm{th,i}} = \sum_{a\in \mathrm{th\,i}} \sum_b \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{trap},a}} R\,m_a\,v_\phi\,C_{ab}[f_a,f_b] \, d^3v
$$

where $a$ labels thermal-ion species or charge states, $b$ labels the charged collision-partner populations included in the collisional model, $f_a$ and $f_b$ are distribution functions, and $C_{ab}$ is the Coulomb collision operator giving the rate of change of the target distribution $f_a$ due to collisions with $b$. $R$ is major radius in meters, $m_a$ is particle mass in kg, $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component in m s$^{-1}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{trap},a}$ is the trapped part of velocity space for population $a$. The integral has the canonical unit N m$^{-2}$, equivalent to torque per unit volume.

This quantity is usually computed from kinetic or neoclassical collisional models after classifying particle motion into trapped and passing orbit classes. It is not measured directly; it is inferred from distribution-function calculations constrained by density, temperature, composition, magnetic geometry, and rotation measurements. Because Coulomb collisions conserve total angular momentum across all interacting charged populations, a nonzero value represents redistribution of toroidal angular momentum into the trapped thermal-ion component, while related orbit or species components carry the compensating exchange.

Typical magnitudes are highly scenario- and model-dependent, so no universal numerical range should be assigned without specifying the plasma conditions and collision partners included in the calculation. The signed value is commonly interpreted relative to [toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_collisions) and to charge-state-resolved trapped thermal-ion components; it may be near zero when collisional exchanges balance and can become important where trapped-particle fraction, collisionality, or differential toroidal rotation is large.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collisional toroidal torque on trapped thermal ions acts in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_torque_density
NAMES.short: Toroidal trapped torque density is the local rate at which toroidal angular momentum about the symmetry axis is deposited per unit volume in trapped particles of a kinetic distribution. It is the trapped-orbit contribution to torque deposition from wave, beam, or collisional source processes.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped torque density is the torque per unit volume acting on the trapped-particle part of a kinetic distribution. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, it represents the source rate of mechanical toroidal angular momentum about the symmetry axis. Trapped particles have pitch angles such that magnetic mirroring prevents a full poloidal transit, so they bounce between turning points and follow banana-like guiding-center orbits.

For a kinetic particle source, the torque density can be written as the trapped velocity-space moment of the source rate density:

$$
\tau_\phi^{\mathrm{trap}}(R,Z) = m R \int_{\mathrm{trap}} v_\phi\, S(\mathbf{v};R,Z)\, d^3v
$$

where $m$ is particle mass, $R$ converts toroidal force density to angular torque density about the symmetry axis, $v_\phi$ is the velocity component along $+\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $S(\mathbf{v};R,Z)$ is a particle source rate density in velocity space, so $S\,d^3v$ is the number of particles added per unit physical volume per unit time. The integration domain is the trapped region of velocity space, whose boundary is set by the particle pitch and the magnetic-field variation along the orbit.

This quantity is computed from kinetic source operators in Fokker-Planck, quasilinear wave-particle, neutral-beam, orbit-following, or collisional transport calculations that resolve orbit class. The trapped contribution is commonly compared with the [co-passing](name:toroidal_co_passing_torque_density) and [counter-passing](name:toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density) contributions; their sum gives the total [toroidal_torque_density](name:toroidal_torque_density) for the distribution.

Typical absolute local values are often $10^{-4}$-$1$ N m$^{-2}$ in present-day auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, with localized high-power beam or wave deposition reaching $1$-$10$ N m$^{-2}$. Much smaller values can occur in weakly driven plasmas or where the net trapped-particle torque nearly cancels after pitch-angle scattering and collisional redistribution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when trapped particles receive toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_trapped_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal angular-momentum source density exerted on trapped particles by the Lorentz force arising from the trapped-particle current normal to the flux surface crossing the poloidal magnetic field. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the trapped-particle orbit-class contribution to the J cross B toroidal momentum balance.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal trapped torque density due to the Lorentz force is the flux-surface-averaged toroidal angular-momentum source per unit volume acting on the trapped portion of the particle distribution when the trapped-particle current normal to the flux surface interacts with the poloidal magnetic field. Trapped particles are those whose parallel motion is mirror-confined between banana-orbit bounce points, so they execute periodic poloidal reversals rather than completing full poloidal transits. The toroidal direction is the $\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters.

The flux-surface-averaged contribution from the trapped-particle current normal to the flux surface is

$$
\mathcal{T}_{\phi}^{\mathrm{tr}} = \left\langle R\, \hat{\phi} \cdot \left( \mathbf{j}_{\perp}^{\mathrm{tr}} \times \mathbf{B}_{p} \right) \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\perp}^{\mathrm{tr}}$ is the trapped-particle current density normal to the flux surface (in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$), $\mathbf{B}_{p}$ is the poloidal magnetic field lying in the $(R, Z)$ plane (in $\mathrm{T}$), $R$ is the major-radius moment arm (in $\mathrm{m}$), and $\langle \cdot \rangle_{\psi}$ denotes the flux-surface average. Only the poloidal field enters because the cross product of a surface-normal current with the toroidal field has no toroidal projection; the major-radius factor converts the toroidal force density into an angular-momentum source density, giving units of $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.

This quantity is typically obtained from kinetic or orbit-following calculations that decompose the distribution function into trapped and passing orbit classes, evaluate the surface-normal current carried by the trapped population, and combine it with the reconstructed equilibrium magnetic field. It can also be constrained indirectly through toroidal momentum balance when rotation, equilibrium, and current profiles are known. The trapped contribution partitions the total toroidal $\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}$ torque density together with the co-passing and counter-passing orbit-class contributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the trapped-particle Lorentz force transfers toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal flow velocity of tritium ions evaluated at the reference flux-surface radius of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The internal transport barrier (ITB) is a localized region of strongly reduced turbulent cross-field transport, identified by steep radial gradients in kinetic profiles. The toroidal velocity of tritium ions at the ITB characterizes the azimuthal rotation of this fuel species at the barrier radius, which influences momentum transport and $E \times B$ flow shear stabilization of turbulence.

The toroidal velocity component is the projection of the tritium ion bulk-flow velocity onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
v_{\phi,T} = \mathbf{v}_T \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_T$ is the tritium ion fluid velocity.

This quantity is inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), in which the Doppler shift of emission lines from tritium ions provides the ion velocity component along the diagnostic line of sight, resolved onto the toroidal direction. Typical toroidal ion velocities in ITB plasmas range from tens to a few hundred km/s, with velocity shear at the ITB foot often correlated with barrier formation. The local tritium ion density at this same location is given by [tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). Analogous toroidal tritium velocities at other radial positions are [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal), and [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). The corresponding toroidal flow of helium-3 at the ITB is [toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the tritium ion flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ axis).

NAMES.name: toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the tritium ion fluid velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal tritium ion fluid velocity at the magnetic axis quantifies the bulk rotation of the tritium fuel-ion population at the plasma core in the $\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The magnetic axis is the singular locus where $\nabla\psi = 0$, marking the deepest nested flux surface of the equilibrium.

The toroidal velocity component $v_\phi$ is related to the toroidal angular rotation frequency $\omega_\phi$ by:

$$
v_\phi = R_\mathrm{axis}\,\omega_\phi
$$

where $R_\mathrm{axis}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis.

This quantity is measured using charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS), where the Doppler shift of emission lines from tritium ions following charge-exchange reactions with injected fast neutrals yields the line-of-sight velocity. In neutral-beam-heated deuterium-tritium plasmas, on-axis toroidal rotation velocities range from $10^3$ to a few $\times 10^5$ m/s depending on heating power and momentum input.

The on-axis value anchors the core of the toroidal rotation profile; the evolution toward the edge can be assessed via [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_tritium_velocity_at_plasma_boundary). The analogous core rotation for $^3$He is given by [toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis), while the tritium ion number density at the same location is [tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the tritium ion fluid flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the mean flow velocity of tungsten impurity ions at the reference radial location of an internal transport barrier. In the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, it represents rotation of the tungsten population around the torus.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal tungsten velocity at an internal transport barrier is the component of the mean tungsten impurity-ion flow along the toroidal $\hat{\phi}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. An internal transport barrier is a localized core region of reduced cross-field turbulent transport, so impurity rotation and density gradients can be steep near that radius.

In local force-balance analysis, this velocity is related to the radial electric field through the tungsten ion radial momentum balance in a right-handed flux-surface coordinate system $(r, \theta, \phi)$, with $r$ increasing outward and $\phi$ the toroidal angle:

$$
E_r = v_{\phi,W} B_\theta - v_{\theta,W} B_\phi + \frac{1}{Z_W e n_W}\frac{\partial p_W}{\partial r}
$$

where $E_r$ is the electric-field component along $r$, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, $B_\theta$ and $B_\phi$ are the poloidal and toroidal magnetic-field components, $v_{\theta,W}$ is the poloidal tungsten velocity, $n_W$ is the local [tungsten ion number density](name:tungsten_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), $p_W$ is the tungsten pressure, $Z_W$ is the charge number of the tungsten ion population, and $e$ is the elementary charge.

It is measured or inferred from Doppler shifts of tungsten line radiation using charge-exchange or passive impurity spectroscopy, with viewing geometry projected onto the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The internal-transport-barrier location is identified from localized extrema or steep gradients in reconstructed temperature, density, rotation, or transport indicators, and the velocity is evaluated at that reference radial point.

Typical magnitudes in tokamak plasmas with internal transport barriers are $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s^-1, depending on momentum input, plasma current, collisionality, and tungsten charge state. The signed value may be in either toroidal direction and can pass through zero near rotation shear layers.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the tungsten ion flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the tungsten impurity ion fluid velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity of tungsten impurity ions at the magnetic axis is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the W ion fluid velocity evaluated at the innermost flux surface, where $\nabla\psi = 0$ with $\psi$ the poloidal magnetic flux. Core impurity rotation couples to the bulk plasma rotation through collisional momentum exchange and neoclassical forces, making this quantity a key boundary condition for impurity transport modeling.

The velocity component is defined as:

$$
v_\phi^W = \mathbf{v}_W \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_W$ is the tungsten ion fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

This quantity is obtained primarily from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) using the Doppler shift of tungsten emission lines, or inferred by combining impurity transport modeling with equilibrium reconstruction. Toroidal impurity rotation velocities at the magnetic axis in current devices span a few km/s to roughly 100 km/s depending on the tangential neutral-beam momentum deposition. The sibling quantities [toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_tungsten_velocity_at_plasma_boundary) characterize the outer-region rotation of the same species, while [toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_helium_4_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) provides the analogous on-axis quantity for helium-4.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi^W$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ axis).

NAMES.name: toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the xenon ion bulk flow velocity at the radial location of an internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal xenon velocity at an internal transport barrier is the $\phi$ component of the bulk flow velocity of xenon ions evaluated at the radial position of the barrier. The component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It characterizes local impurity rotation in the steep-gradient region associated with reduced core transport.

The local value is defined by evaluating the xenon ion velocity field at the barrier location and projecting onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Xe}}^{\mathrm{ITB}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Xe}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Xe}}^{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Xe}}$ is the xenon ion bulk velocity in m.s^-1, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the radial label of the internal transport barrier. The radial label may be a minor-radius-like coordinate in meters or an explicitly named flux coordinate such as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, which is dimensionless.

In practice this quantity is obtained by resolving measured or reconstructed xenon ion flow onto the toroidal direction and interpolating that value to the internal-transport-barrier location. Spectroscopic Doppler information from suitable xenon charge states, together with equilibrium geometry and profile analysis, can be used when available; the quantity represents directed bulk flow, not thermal speed.

Typical values in magnetically confined plasmas are of order $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s^-1. Values near zero can occur in weakly rotating plasmas, while the sign and magnitude depend on applied torque, intrinsic rotation, collisional coupling, and local pressure-gradient and electric-field balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when xenon ions flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the xenon ion bulk flow velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal xenon velocity at the magnetic axis is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the xenon ion fluid velocity at the innermost point of the confined plasma, where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient $\nabla\psi = 0$. As a heavy high-$Z$ impurity, xenon ions carry toroidal momentum coupled to the main-ion fluid through Coulomb collisions and viscous stress, making this quantity a sensitive probe of core momentum transport and impurity transport physics.

The toroidal velocity component is defined as:

$$
v_{\phi,\,\mathrm{Xe}}^{\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Xe}} \cdot \hat{\phi}\big|_{\mathrm{magnetic\;axis}}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and the magnetic axis position is identified by the equilibrium condition $\nabla\psi = 0$.

This quantity is obtained from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) by measuring the Doppler shift of xenon emission lines, either by directly observing the magnetic axis or by extrapolating a radial rotation profile inward. Companion measurements at other radial locations are captured by [toroidal xenon velocity at the pedestal](name:toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_pedestal) and [toroidal xenon velocity at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_xenon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary), enabling characterization of the full core-to-edge rotation profile. The analogous quantity for krypton is [toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_krypton_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the xenon ion bulk flow is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: total_co_passing_particle_density
NAMES.short: Number density of co-passing particles integrated over all populations — thermal and suprathermal alike — where co-passing orbits have guiding-center parallel velocity directed along the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing particles are those whose guiding-center parallel velocity component is aligned with the plasma current direction, a subset of non-trapped (passing) orbits. The total aggregation sums contributions from both the thermal bulk and any suprathermal (fast) minority populations, yielding the complete co-passing contribution to local number density. This orbit-class-resolved density is distinct from the full particle density, which also includes trapped and counter-passing orbit contributions.

The quantity is defined by integrating the complete particle distribution function over the co-passing partition of velocity space:

$$
n_\text{co} = \int_{\mathcal{D}_\text{co}} f(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f$ is the distribution function, $\mathbf{r}$ is the spatial position, $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity, and $\mathcal{D}_\text{co}$ restricts integration to orbits with $v_\parallel$ in the plasma-current direction.

This quantity is evaluated from kinetic or drift-kinetic models that resolve $f$ explicitly, available either as a flux-surface-averaged radial profile or as a full poloidal-plane distribution that reveals orbit-class density asymmetries.

Core values in deuterium plasmas lie in the $10^{19}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ range, with the co-passing fraction depending on collisionality and the trapped-particle fraction determined by local magnetic geometry.

The suprathermal subset alone is captured by [co_passing_fast_particle_density](name:co_passing_fast_particle_density), and the counter-directed analog is [counter_passing_density](name:counter_passing_density). The corresponding pressure moment follows the same decomposition as total_co_passing_particle_pressure, and [co_passing_density](name:total_co_passing_particle_density) is a closely related name for the same aggregate quantity with less explicit notation.

NAMES.name: total_electron_deposited_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated deposited power for the electron population from a specified source or sink. It is the net rate at which that term transfers energy to or from electrons over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Total electron deposited power is the volume-integrated rate at which a specified source or sink transfers energy to the electron population. It is a source-resolved global term in the electron energy balance and can represent either net heating or net cooling.

The volume-integrated deposited power is defined by integrating the electron power-deposition density over the confined plasma volume:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{dep}} = \int_V q_{e,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $q_{e,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local deposited power density assigned to electrons in W m^-3, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position, and $V$ is the confined plasma volume.

In practice this quantity is computed from modeled or inferred source terms in the electron energy equation, using the part of each source or sink assigned to electrons. It is closely related to [electron_deposited_power](name:total_electron_deposited_power) as another integrated electron deposition quantity, and it contributes to broader energy-budget quantities such as [total_electron_power](name:total_electron_deposited_power), total_plasma_deposited_power, and [total_plasma_particle_deposited_power](name:total_plasma_particle_deposited_power).

Typical magnitudes are strongly source- and device-dependent. Weak source or sink terms may be in the 10^3-10^5 W range, while dominant electron-heating contributions in high-power plasmas are commonly in the 10^6-10^7 W range and can reach tens of megawatts in large devices or reactor scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified source term transfers energy to the electron population and negative when it removes energy from the electron population.

NAMES.name: total_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Isotropic kinetic pressure of the entire electron population, summing the thermal Maxwellian bulk contribution and any non-thermal fast electron contribution.
NAMES.long:
Total electron pressure is the complete isotropic mechanical stress exerted by the electron population, encompassing contributions from both the thermal Maxwellian bulk and any non-thermal (fast or suprathermal) electrons. It enters the plasma momentum equation through the pressure-gradient force $-\nabla p_e$, driving parallel and cross-field transport throughout the plasma.

The total electron pressure decomposes as:

$$
p_e = p_{e,\mathrm{th}} + p_{e,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} k_B T_e$ is the thermal component with $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ the thermal electron number density and $T_e$ the electron temperature, and $p_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the non-thermal contribution from fast or suprathermal electrons.

The thermal component dominates in most regimes and is inferred from combined electron density and temperature measurements; the fast-electron contribution gains importance during electron cyclotron or lower hybrid heating. The total is obtained by summing both components, typically from transport modeling constrained by kinetic profile data.

Core values in H-mode tokamak discharges range from a few to tens of kilopascals, while scrape-off layer values fall below 1 kPa. The analogous quantity for ions is [total_ion_pressure](name:total_ion_pressure); the purely thermal contribution summed over all species is given by thermal_pressure. The parent quantity [electron_pressure](name:electron_pressure) defines the general Maxwellian pressure-gradient context.
NAMES.sign: Positive throughout any physical plasma; as a positive-definite thermodynamic scalar, this quantity does not change sign when the plasma current or toroidal field direction is reversed, unlike directional electromagnetic quantities.

NAMES.name: total_electron_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Net electron particle source rate integrated over the full plasma volume, aggregating contributions from all electron-production and -removal processes such as ionization, recombination, and neutral beam injection.
NAMES.long:
The total electron source rate is the volume integral of the local [electron_source_rate](name:electron_source_rate), which represents the signed net production or removal of free electrons per unit volume due to all active particle processes. Integrating over the plasma volume converts this local source density into a global balance quantity directly characterizing the net rate of change of the total electron inventory.

$$
S_e^{\rm tot} = \int_V s_e(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $s_e(\mathbf{r})$ is the local electron source rate density and $V$ is the plasma volume.

Dominant contributions include ionization of neutral hydrogen and impurity atoms, electron-ion recombination, neutral beam injection, pellet injection, and gas puffing. This integral is computed from local source profiles derived from atomic physics rate coefficients and neutral transport models. It is the electron-species counterpart to total_ion_particle_source_rate and [total_particle_source_rate](name:total_thermal_particle_source_rate), which provide analogous global rates for ion species and general particle distribution sources respectively.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net electron creation exceeds net removal across the plasma volume.

NAMES.name: total_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Gyrotropic pressure tensor of the suprathermal ion population summed over all charge states, characterized by independent components parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The total fast-ion pressure represents the full gyrotropic kinetic stress of the suprathermal ion population, summed over all charge states, as a contribution to the plasma pressure balance. Fast ions — including fusion-born alpha particles, neutral-beam-injected ions, and radio-frequency-accelerated ions — retain pressure anisotropy with $P_\parallel \neq P_\perp$ relative to the local magnetic field because their pitch-angle scattering rate is slow compared with their energy transfer rate to the bulk plasma. The anisotropic structure is fully captured by the two independent scalar components [parallel total fast-ion pressure](name:parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure) and [perpendicular total fast-ion pressure](name:perpendicular_total_fast_ion_pressure).

For a gyrotropic fast-ion distribution, the pressure tensor is:

$$
\overleftrightarrow{P}_\text{fast} = P_{\perp}\,\overleftrightarrow{I} + (P_{\parallel} - P_{\perp})\,\hat{b}\hat{b}
$$

where $P_{\parallel}$ and $P_{\perp}$ are the parallel and perpendicular scalar pressure components, $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, and $\overleftrightarrow{I}$ is the identity tensor.

Fast-ion pressure profiles are obtained from kinetic particle-following or Fokker-Planck solvers that evolve the suprathermal distribution function under collisional slowing-down and pitch-angle scattering. The anisotropic fast-ion stress enters the MHD force balance and can drive pressure-anisotropy-driven instabilities when $P_{\parallel}/P_{\perp}$ departs significantly from unity. The parent quantity [fast_ion_pressure](name:fast_ion_pressure) provides per-charge-state resolution.

In high-performance discharges with strong neutral beam or ion cyclotron resonance heating, fast-ion pressure can reach 10–50% of the total plasma pressure in the core, with anisotropy ratios $P_{\parallel}/P_{\perp}$ ranging from near unity for isotropized distributions to several for strongly beam-like distributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion population exerts compressive kinetic pressure, consistent with the second velocity moment of a non-negative distribution function being positive.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total fast-ion parallel pressure is the fast (suprathermal) ion pressure in the direction parallel to the local magnetic field, summed over all fast-ion species and charge states. It is the parallel component of the gyrotropic fast-ion pressure tensor and differs from the perpendicular component when the fast-ion distribution is anisotropic.
NAMES.long:
Parallel total fast-ion pressure is the field-aligned component of the gyrotropic pressure tensor for non-thermal ions, summed over all fast-ion species and charge states. It is the total counterpart of [parallel_fast_ion_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure) and [parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure), and it complements [perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure) and [perpendicular_total_fast_ion_pressure](name:perpendicular_total_fast_ion_pressure) in describing fast-ion pressure anisotropy.

The kinetic definition is the parallel second central velocity moment of the fast-ion distribution functions:

$$
P_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast,total}} = \sum_s m_s \int \left(v_\parallel - u_{\parallel,s}\right)^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $s$ indexes fast-ion species, $m_s$ is the ion mass, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the fast-ion distribution function, $v_\parallel = \mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{b}$ is the velocity component along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$, and $u_{\parallel,s}$ is the species mean parallel flow velocity. For a gyrotropic pressure tensor, this quantity and the perpendicular pressure determine the trace-equivalent scalar fast-ion pressure through the inline relation $p_\mathrm{fast} = (P_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast,total}} + 2P_{\perp,\mathrm{fast,total}})/3$.

In practice it is computed from fast-ion distribution functions inferred from diagnostics such as neutron emission, gamma-ray emission, neutral-particle analysis, fast-ion D-alpha spectroscopy, or collective Thomson scattering, often combined with orbit-following, Fokker-Planck, or Monte Carlo transport calculations. Strong neutral-beam injection, ion-cyclotron heating, or fusion-born alpha populations can make the parallel and perpendicular components substantially different before pitch-angle scattering and slowing down reduce the anisotropy.

Typical values in magnetically confined fusion plasmas are about 10^2-10^6 Pa. Values near the upper end occur in high-power beam-heated or alpha-heated core regions, while weakly heated regions or locations with little confined fast-ion population can be much lower.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_total_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total fast-ion perpendicular pressure, summed over all species, is the component of the suprathermal ion gyrotropic pressure tensor associated with ion motion perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular total fast-ion pressure $P_{\perp,\text{fast}}$ is the principal perpendicular component of the gyrotropic pressure tensor of suprathermal ions, summed over all ion species and charge states. It quantifies the kinetic energy of fast ions stored in the two velocity degrees of freedom transverse to the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. Together with [parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure](name:parallel_total_fast_ion_pressure), it fully characterizes the pressure anisotropy of the fast-ion population described by the parent [total_fast_ion_pressure](name:total_fast_ion_pressure) tensor.

The perpendicular pressure is the second velocity moment of the fast-ion distribution function in the plane perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$:

$$
P_{\perp,\text{fast}} = \sum_s \frac{m_s}{2} \int v_\perp^2 \, f_{\text{fast},s}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the ion mass for species $s$, $v_\perp$ is the particle speed in the plane perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$, and $f_{\text{fast},s}$ is the fast-ion velocity distribution function for species $s$, with the sum running over all fast-ion species.

This quantity is computed from guiding-center kinetic models or Fokker-Planck solvers that evolve the fast-ion distribution function. Preferential perpendicular energization by ion cyclotron resonance heating drives $P_{\perp,\text{fast}} \gg P_{\parallel,\text{fast}}$, while neutral beam injection at oblique angles produces more moderate anisotropy. The charge-state-resolved analog is [perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure), and the thermal-ion counterpart is [total_thermal_ion_pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion population carries nonzero kinetic energy in degrees of freedom perpendicular to the local magnetic field; this quantity is non-negative for all physically realizable fast-ion distributions.

NAMES.name: total_fast_particle_count
NAMES.short: Total number of suprathermal fast particles in the distribution, integrated over the plasma volume and summed over fast-particle species and orbit classes.
NAMES.long:
Total fast-particle count is the population of suprathermal particles confined in the plasma. It is the volume integral of the local [fast_particle_density](name:fast_particle_density), and is the fast-particle contribution to [total_particle_count](name:total_particle_count) when both are defined for the same plasma volume and species set. It is distinct from [total_count](name:total_particle_count), which is an unqualified count and does not by itself specify a plasma-particle population.

The defining volume integral is

$$
N_{\mathrm{fast}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{plasma}}} n_{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is a dimensionless particle count, $V_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the confined plasma volume, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, and $n_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-particle number density in m$^{-3}$. The integrand $n_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the zeroth velocity moment of the fast-particle distribution function, summed over included particle species and orbit classes; equivalently, $n_{\mathrm{fast}} = \sum_{s,o}\int f_{\mathrm{fast},s,o}\,d^3v$, with $f_{\mathrm{fast},s,o}$ in m$^{-3}$(m s$^{-1}$)$^{-3}$.

In practice, this count is computed by integrating a reconstructed or modeled fast-particle density over the confined plasma volume. The density may be constrained by kinetic modeling together with measurements sensitive to suprathermal populations, such as neutron emission, gamma emission, neutral-particle analysis, collective Thomson scattering, or fast-ion loss diagnostics.

Typical magnitudes range from about $10^{17}$ to $10^{21}$ particles in present magnetic-confinement experiments, depending on heating power, fast-particle source rate, slowing-down time, plasma volume, and loss processes. Larger reactor-scale plasmas can approach or exceed the upper part of this range when alpha-particle confinement is strong.

NAMES.name: total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total ion number density at a local plasma point, summed over all ion species and charge states and including both thermal and non-thermal ion populations. It represents the aggregate ion population, not the density of one selected species or ionization state.
NAMES.long:
Total ion density is the aggregate number density of ions at a plasma point, obtained by summing the densities of all ion species, all resolved charge states, and both thermal and non-thermal ion populations. It is distinct from a species-resolved ion density or a single charge-state density.

The total may be expressed as a sum over species, charge states, and population components:

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{total}} = \sum_s \sum_q \left(n^{\mathrm{th}}_{s,q} + n^{\mathrm{nth}}_{s,q}\right)
$$

where $s$ labels ion species, $q$ labels charge state, $n^{\mathrm{th}}_{s,q}$ is the thermal density of that species and charge state, and $n^{\mathrm{nth}}_{s,q}$ is the corresponding non-thermal density. Equivalently, it is the sum of [total ion state density](name:total_ion_state_density) over all resolved species and charge states; [total thermal ion density](name:total_thermal_ion_density) is the thermal part of this aggregate.

In experiments and simulations, total ion density is usually inferred by combining composition measurements, charge-state balance, impurity diagnostics, neutral-beam or fast-ion modeling, and quasineutrality constraints. In a nearly pure deuterium-tritium plasma with singly charged main ions, it is close to the electron density, while in plasmas with significant impurities or multiple ionization states it differs because each ion contributes one particle to $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ regardless of charge.

Typical values range from about $10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3 in the edge and scrape-off-layer plasma and about $0.1$-$2 \times 10^{20}$ m^-3 in the confined core of medium to large tokamaks. Non-thermal ion populations are often a small correction to the total density but can be important in plasmas with strong auxiliary heating or energetic fusion products.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: First-order radial derivative of total ion number density (thermal plus non-thermal, summed over all charge states) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate.
NAMES.long:
The first radial derivative of [total_ion_density](name:total_ion_density) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ characterizes the spatial variation of the total ion particle inventory across nested flux surfaces. The total ion population encompasses both thermal and non-thermal (fast) ions, aggregated over all charge states.

The defining expression is:

$$
\frac{d n_i^\mathrm{tot}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $n_i^\mathrm{tot}$ is the total ion number density (in m$^{-3}$, thermal plus non-thermal, summed over charge states) and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, with $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 1$ at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, this derivative carries the same unit as the density itself.

This quantity is evaluated numerically within transport solver frameworks as part of diffusion-advection flux computation for the ion particle transport equation. It enters the diffusive ion particle flux as $\Gamma_i \sim -D_i \, dn_i^\mathrm{tot}/d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, where $D_i$ is the ion diffusion coefficient. The [second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density) is its higher-order companion used in more accurate discretization schemes. For charge-state-resolved calculations, [radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density) provides per-state gradients, while [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density) isolates the non-thermal contribution alone.
NAMES.sign: Positive when total ion density increases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, directed toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_total_ion_density_to_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of total ion number density to electron number density. The total ion density is the sum over all positive ion species and charge states, including thermal and nonthermal populations, and the ratio is used to check species bookkeeping and quasineutrality consistency.
NAMES.long:
The ratio of total ion density to electron density compares the total count of positive ions with the electron population at the same physical location and time. Total ion density is the sum over all ion species and positive charge states, including thermal and nonthermal ions, while neutral atoms are excluded.

The defining relation is:

$$
\frac{n_{i,\mathrm{tot}}}{n_e} = \frac{\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{Z \ge 1} n_{\alpha,Z}}{n_e}
$$

where $n_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total positive-ion number density, $n_e$ is the electron number density, and $n_{\alpha,Z}$ is the number density of ion species $\alpha$ in charge state $Z$. This is a number-density ratio, not a charge-weighted neutrality condition; quasineutrality instead compares $n_e$ with $\sum_{\alpha,Z} Z n_{\alpha,Z}$.

In practice the numerator is computed by summing the modeled or inferred densities of all included ion populations, using consistent species definitions and charge-state bookkeeping. The denominator is obtained from the electron density used in the same physical state, often constrained by density diagnostics and transport or equilibrium reconstruction. Deviations from the expected range are useful indicators of inconsistent impurity content, missing fast-ion contributions, interpolation errors, or numerical conservation errors.

Typical values are close to 1 for plasmas dominated by singly charged hydrogen isotopes, about 0.8-1.0 when helium ash or modest impurity content is present, and lower in impurity-rich or highly ionized mixtures because one ion can contribute more than one electron. Values significantly above 1 in a quasineutral plasma usually indicate inconsistent density definitions or missing electron density contributions.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Second derivative of total ion number density (thermal plus non-thermal, summed over all charge states) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, quantifying the radial curvature of the ion density profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of total ion density describes the curvature of the ion density profile along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. The total ion density $n_i$ encompasses both thermal and non-thermal (fast) ion contributions, summed over all charge states, providing a complete representation of the ion population's radial structure as required by 1D transport equations.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{d^2 n_i}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $n_i$ is the total ion density and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, with $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 1$ at the last closed flux surface. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, this second derivative carries the same unit as the density itself.

This curvature term arises in second-order spatial discretization of radial ion transport equations, where both first- and second-order derivatives are needed to evaluate diffusive flux terms accurately. It is computed numerically from the total ion density profile during transport solver iterations, complementing the [first radial derivative of total ion density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density). Analogous second-derivative quantities are defined for the fast-ion sub-population in [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density) and for individual charge states in [second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total ion density profile is concave upward as a function of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., when the local profile curvature $d^2 n_i / d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2 > 0$.

NAMES.name: total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total ion density at an internal transport barrier is the local unweighted number-density sum over all ion populations present there, including fuel, minority, impurity, and non-thermal ions when they are part of the ion inventory. It excludes neutral particles and is not charge weighted.
NAMES.long:
Total ion density at an internal transport barrier (ITB) is the local ion number density obtained by adding the number densities of all ion populations at the barrier. The sum includes thermal and, when represented, non-thermal ion populations for fuel, minority, and impurity ions; neutral particles are excluded. It is an unweighted particle count, not a charge density, mass density, or pressure.

The local total is defined by the population sum evaluated at the ITB location:

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{total}}(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{ITB}) = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathrm{ions}} n_\alpha(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{ITB})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the position of the internal transport barrier and $\alpha$ labels an ion population, which may distinguish chemical species, charge state, and thermal or non-thermal component. Both $n_\alpha$ and $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ are number densities in m^-3. If charge states are resolved, each charge-state population contributes its own number density term; the charge $Z_\alpha$ is not used as a weight in this sum.

In practice this quantity is obtained by combining local density and composition information at the identified ITB location. Electron-density measurements constrain the charge-weighted ion inventory through quasineutrality, while spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination measurements, neutron or neutral-particle information, and transport analysis may constrain selected ion species or energetic-ion components. The total ion number density is then computed from the inferred population densities and composition model by applying the unweighted sum above.

Typical local values in tokamak plasmas with internal transport barriers are of order 1 x 10^19-1 x 10^20 m^-3. This range is an order-of-magnitude guide rather than a device-independent bound, because the value depends on the local electron density, impurity content, fuel mix, and any non-thermal ion population included in the ion inventory.

NAMES.name: total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total number density summed over all ion species, evaluated at the magnetic axis where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The total ion density at the magnetic axis $n_{i,\mathrm{total}}$ is the sum of local number densities of all ion species — fuel ions, impurity ions, and minority ion species — at the innermost point of the confined plasma, the magnetic axis defined by $\nabla\psi = 0$. Neutral particles are excluded from this sum by convention.

The defining relation is:

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{total}} = \sum_s n_s
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$ in m$^{-3}$, with the sum running over all ion species present in the plasma.

This on-axis value is obtained from Thomson scattering, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or multi-chord interferometry, with the magnetic-axis location determined from equilibrium reconstruction. Combined with [electron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:electron_density_at_magnetic_axis), it constrains the quasi-neutrality condition $n_e = \sum_s Z_s n_s$, where $Z_s$ is the charge number of species $s$. Analogous values at the boundary and pedestal are provided by [total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:total_ion_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [total_ion_density_at_pedestal](name:total_ion_density_at_pedestal). Typical on-axis values in tokamak discharges span $10^{19}$–$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$, increasing toward the upper bound in high-density pellet-fueled scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion particles are present at the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: total_ion_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net local ion energy flux density vector carried by all ion species and charge states. It sums conductive heat flow and convective enthalpy transport by bulk ion motion, giving the rate and direction of ion thermal-energy transport per unit area.
NAMES.long:
Total ion energy flux is the local vector flux density of thermal energy carried by the combined ion population, including main fuel ions and impurities in all charge states. It represents transport per unit area by both random thermal conduction and directed ion-fluid motion; it is not a flux-surface-averaged or area-integrated power. The vector is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a multi-species plasma it is the sum of conductive heat flux and convective enthalpy flux over all ion species:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_i^{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_{s \in \mathrm{ions}} \left( \mathbf{q}_s + \frac{5}{2} p_s \mathbf{v}_s \right)
$$

where $\mathbf{Q}_i^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total ion energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{q}_s$ is the conductive heat-flux contribution of ion species $s$ in W m$^{-2}$, $p_s$ is the scalar ion pressure of species $s$ in Pa, and $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the mean ion flow velocity of species $s$ in m s$^{-1}$. The factor $5/2$ gives the ideal monatomic-plasma enthalpy flux; if temperatures are represented in electron-volts, the pressure uses the corresponding energy conversion.

In transport modeling and interpretive power balance this quantity is computed from ion density, temperature, and velocity profiles together with heat-transport closure models, or inferred indirectly from diagnostic constraints on profiles and power flows. The [radial_total_ion_energy_flux](name:radial_total_ion_energy_flux), poloidal_total_ion_energy_flux, and [parallel_total_ion_energy_flux](name:parallel_total_ion_energy_flux) are projections of this local vector onto chosen geometry axes, and ion_energy_convection_velocity parameterizes its convective contribution. The closely related [total_thermal_ion_heat_flux](name:total_thermal_ion_heat_flux) describes the same ion thermal-energy channel, while [total_energy_flux](name:total_thermal_ion_heat_flux) aggregates the full energy balance across plasma species.

Typical magnitudes in scrape-off-layer and edge-plasma conditions are $10^4$-$10^7$ W m$^{-2}$, depending on heating power, density, temperature gradients, connection length, and divertor geometry; core conductive fluxes are generally lower. Cross-field components tend toward the lower end of this range, while field-aligned components carrying energy toward material surfaces can be substantially larger.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the normal component carries ion energy through an oriented surface in the direction of that surface's positive normal.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_ion_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Component of the total ion energy flux along the local magnetic field direction, equal to the net thermal power per unit area transported field-aligned by all ion species combined.
NAMES.long:
The parallel total ion energy flux is the projection of the [total_ion_energy_flux](name:total_ion_energy_flux) vector onto the local magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$. It captures both conductive heat transport and convective enthalpy flux, summed over all ion species in the plasma.

The defining relation is:

$$
q_{\parallel,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{total}} = \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{total}} \cdot \hat{b}
$$

where $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{total}}$ is the total ion energy flux vector and $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector aligned with the local magnetic field. Summing over all ion species distinguishes this quantity from [parallel_ion_state_energy_flux](name:parallel_ion_state_energy_flux), which resolves the flux per individual charge state. In the scrape-off layer and divertor, parallel transport far exceeds cross-field transport, making this flux the primary determinant of plasma-facing component heat loads. Typical magnitudes along SOL field lines range from $10^7$–$10^9$ W m$^{-2}$ depending on plasma power exhaust conditions and field-line connection length. The corresponding electron contribution is described by [parallel_electron_energy_flux](name:parallel_electron_energy_flux).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the energy flux is directed along the magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: radial_total_ion_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Radial component of the total ion thermal energy flux density, combining conductive heat transport and convective enthalpy flux summed over all ion species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
The radial total ion energy flux is the projection of the [total_ion_energy_flux](name:total_ion_energy_flux) vector onto the radial coordinate direction, quantifying the net rate of thermal energy transport per unit area by the combined ion population. It encompasses both conductive heat transport and convective enthalpy carried by radial ion fluid motion, and is summed over all ion species and charge states present in the plasma.

For a multi-species ion plasma, the defining expression is:

$$
Q_{r,\text{ion}}^{\text{tot}} = \sum_s \left( q_{r,s} + \frac{5}{2}\, n_s T_s u_{r,s} \right)
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species, $q_{r,s}$ is the radial conductive heat flux of species $s$, $n_s$ is the number density, $T_s$ is the ion temperature, and $u_{r,s}$ is the radial fluid velocity of species $s$.

This quantity appears in the radial ion energy conservation equation and is evaluated by edge and core transport solvers. The [radial_total_ion_effective_energy_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity) represents the effective convection velocity derived from this flux normalized by the local ion pressure, while [radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_energy_convection_velocity) captures the convective component for individual ion species. Typical values in the edge plasma and scrape-off layer range from $10^5$ to $10^7$ W m$^{-2}$, increasing near the separatrix in high-power scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion energy is transported in the outward radial direction, away from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: total_ion_heating_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net rate of energy deposition in all ion species from all heating sources, integrated over the full volume of the confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
Total ion heating power is the rate at which energy from all coupled sources — ohmic heating, neutral beam injection, ion cyclotron resonance, fusion-product slowing-down, and collisional equilibration from electrons — is deposited in the combined ion population of the confined plasma, summed over all ion species and charge states.

The quantity is defined as the volume integral of the total ion energy source density $S_\text{ion}(\mathbf{r})$ over the plasma volume $V$ enclosed by the last closed flux surface:

$$
P_\text{ion} = \int_V S_\text{ion}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $S_\text{ion}$ aggregates contributions from every heating and equilibration process across all ion species. Individual contributions such as [total power due to ion cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating) are subsets of this integral.

In transport analysis this global value is obtained as the boundary limit of the cumulative radial heating profile; the radially resolved representation that tracks the enclosed power as a function of flux surface is given by [total ion heating power at inside flux surface](name:total_ion_heating_power_at_inside_flux_surface). The thermal-ion subset of this power is accessible via [thermal ion power at inside flux surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface) evaluated at the plasma boundary. Experimentally the quantity is constrained by calorimetric accounting of individual heating systems combined with measured radiation and charge-exchange energy losses.

Whole-plasma values range from about 1 MW in ohmically heated discharges to 10-50 MW in high-power auxiliary-heated H-mode scenarios on large tokamaks.

NAMES.name: total_ion_power
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net rate of energy transfer from a specified source to the ion population, summed over all ion species and integrated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Total ion power is the volume-integrated contribution of a specified source to the ion energy balance. It includes the net energy coupled to all ion species and excludes power coupled directly to electrons, which is represented separately by quantities such as [total_electron_power](name:total_electron_deposited_power).

For ion species indexed by $a$, the total ion power is the volume integral of the local ion power density summed over species:

$$
P_{\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_a \int_V p_a(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $p_a$ is the net power density coupled to ion species $a$ in W m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is the plasma volume element, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which the source contribution is evaluated.

In practice this quantity is computed from source modeling or diagnostic inference by integrating the spatial distribution of ion heating or cooling and summing over thermal and fast ion species as appropriate. It is the ion-channel contribution to the source power balance; adding the corresponding electron-channel contribution gives the total plasma power from the same source when no other channels are included.

Typical values range from 0 W for an absent or inactive source to $10^3$-$10^6$ W for weak source terms, and up to $10^6$-$5 \times 10^7$ W for strong auxiliary ion heating in medium to large tokamak plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred from the source to the ion population.

NAMES.name: total_ion_power_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net volumetric power density deposited into the ion channel, aggregated over all ion species and charge states, representing the total energy source term in the ion energy transport equation.
NAMES.long:
The total ion power density is the net volumetric rate of energy deposition into the combined ion population, summed across all ion species and charge states. It serves as the source term on the right-hand side of the ion energy transport equation, balancing all energy gains and losses to the ion channel from simultaneously active processes in the plasma.

The governing ion energy balance takes the form:

$$
\frac{\partial W_i^{\rm tot}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{q}_i = P_{\rm ion}^{\rm tot}
$$

where $W_i^{\rm tot}$ is the total ion thermal energy density in J m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{q}_i$ is the total ion heat flux in W m$^{-2}$, and $P_{\rm ion}^{\rm tot}$ is the volumetric source density accumulated from neutral beam injection, ion-cyclotron heating, fusion product thermalization, charge exchange, and collisional energy transfer from electrons.

This quantity is obtained by summing energy source contributions across all ion species and ionization states, making it the aggregate counterpart to the per-charge-state [ion_state_power_density](name:ion_state_power_density) and the complementary electron-channel quantity [electron_power_density](name:electron_power_density). The related [ion_power_density](name:total_ion_power_density) similarly represents a species-summed ion power density; the `total_` qualifier here explicitly emphasizes aggregation over all charge states as well as species. The corresponding particle source is described by [total_ion_source_rate](name:total_ion_source_rate).
NAMES.sign: Positive when net energy flows into the ion channel, representing a volumetric energy gain by the total ion population.

NAMES.name: total_ion_pressure
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Total isotropic scalar pressure of the ion fluid at a plasma location, summing thermal and fast (non-thermal) contributions over all charge states of a given ion species.
NAMES.long:
The total ion pressure is the isotropic scalar pressure of the entire ion fluid at a given point in the plasma, combining the Maxwellian thermal bulk and suprathermal fast-ion contributions summed over all charge states of the species. It represents the physically complete ion kinetic pressure entering force-balance and energy-transport equations in multi-fluid and magnetohydrodynamic models.

The total ion pressure decomposes additively as:

$$
P_i = P_{i,\mathrm{th}} + P_{i,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $P_{i,\mathrm{th}}$ is the [thermal ion pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) from the Maxwellian bulk, satisfying $P_{i,\mathrm{th}} = n_i k_B T_i$ with $n_i$ the ion number density and $T_i$ the ion temperature, and $P_{i,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the suprathermal fast-ion contribution. The [total thermal ion pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure) isolates the bulk-only term; the [total ion state pressure](name:total_ion_state_pressure) provides per-charge-state resolution.

Together with [total electron pressure](name:total_electron_pressure), the total ion pressure contributes to the full plasma pressure $P = P_e + P_i$ appearing in the MHD force-balance $\nabla P = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$. Fast-ion contributions can become comparable to or exceed the thermal term during neutral beam injection or ion cyclotron resonance heating. The quantity is inferred by combining ion temperature and density profile diagnostics with energetic-particle measurements and fast-ion transport modeling.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion population has nonzero kinetic energy, which holds for all physical ion populations; scalar ion pressure is an intrinsically non-negative quantity.

NAMES.name: total_ion_source_rate
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Net volumetric source term for total ion particle density, summed over all ion species and charge states. It includes ionization, recombination, charge exchange, fueling, and external particle injection or removal processes.
NAMES.long:
Total ion source rate is the net local rate at which processes create or remove ion particles per unit volume, after summing over all ion species and charge states. It is the species-summed particle source term corresponding to ion_source_rate, and is distinct from energy deposition quantities such as [total_ion_power_density](name:total_ion_power_density).

In a local particle balance, the total ion source rate $S_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ enters the continuity equation:

$$
\frac{\partial n_{i,\mathrm{tot}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,\mathrm{tot}} = S_{i,\mathrm{tot}}
$$

where $n_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total ion particle density in m$^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total ion particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $S_{i,\mathrm{tot}}$ is in m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$. The divergence is evaluated in physical space; for example, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. In flux-surface-averaged transport, the same balance is interpreted after averaging on surfaces labeled by an explicitly named flux coordinate, for example $(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}, \theta, \phi)$.

In practice, this quantity is computed from particle balance using models or measurements of ionization, recombination, charge exchange with neutrals, neutral beam fueling, gas puffing, pellet ablation, and other particle exchange processes. It may also be inferred from density evolution and particle flux estimates when the transport divergence term is known.

Typical core and edge magnitudes are about $10^{18}$-$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ in magnetically confined plasmas, with larger local values possible near strong fueling, pellet deposition, or intense recycling regions. Negative values occur where recombination, charge exchange, or outward particle exchange removes ions faster than they are created.
NAMES.sign: Positive when local processes produce a net increase in the total ion particle density.

NAMES.name: total_ion_state_density
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Total particle number density of a specific ion charge state, summing both thermal and non-thermal (fast) ion contributions at a given plasma location.
NAMES.long:
The total ion charge-state density $n_{i,z}^{\rm tot}$ quantifies the number of particles per unit volume for ion species $i$ in charge state $z$, aggregating both the Maxwellian thermal bulk and any non-thermal (fast) population occupying that charge state. This distinguishes it from the thermal-only [ion_state_density](name:ion_state_density), which excludes suprathermal contributions, making this quantity the appropriate building block for transport models that account for neutral beam injection or fast-particle thermalization.

The total density decomposes as:

$$
n_{i,z}^{\rm tot} = n_{i,z}^{\rm thermal} + n_{i,z}^{\rm fast}
$$

where $n_{i,z}^{\rm thermal}$ is the thermal (Maxwellian) component and $n_{i,z}^{\rm fast}$ is the non-thermal component for species $i$ in charge state $z$.

This quantity is computed from multispecies fluid or kinetic transport codes resolving individual charge states, and is inferred observationally by combining charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy with fast-ion population modeling. Its radial gradient drives diffusive particle fluxes encoded in [radial_ion_state_particle_flux](name:radial_ion_state_particle_flux), and its radial e-folding decay in the scrape-off layer is characterized by [total_ion_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:total_ion_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer).

Typical values range from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ for main-ion charge states in the edge plasma, with trace impurity charge states several orders of magnitude lower depending on species and plasma conditions.
