where $\Pi_{ZZ}^{(i,\zeta)}$ is the vertical momentum flux in kg m^-1 s^-2, $i$ identifies the ion species, $\zeta$ identifies the ionization state, $P_Z^{(i,\zeta)}$ is signed $Z$-directed linear momentum in kg m s^-1, $dA_Z$ is an area element with normal $+\hat{Z}$ in m^2, and $dt$ is the time interval in s.

In practice, this quantity is calculated from charge-state-resolved kinetic or fluid momentum balance. Kinetic treatments evaluate the corresponding second velocity moment of the selected ionization-state distribution, while reduced transport models may include mean-flow advection and stress terms from collisions and fluctuations without requiring a unique pressure-viscous decomposition. Experimental constraints usually come indirectly from ion density, temperature, and flow measurements combined with momentum-balance analysis.

Typical absolute magnitudes are strongly regime and species dependent. For individual ionization states, modeled transport components often lie in the 0.01-10000 kg m^-1 s^-2 range; full main-ion kinetic normal-stress components in hot cores can be 100-100000 kg m^-1 s^-2, while trace impurity states are usually reduced roughly in proportion to their density fraction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $+\hat{Z}$-directed momentum of ions in the specified ionization state is transported through a surface with normal $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_ion_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z-axis) projection of the mean flow velocity for ions in a specified ionization charge state, capturing the net upward or downward hydrodynamic drift of that charge-state fluid within the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The vertical ion state velocity is the $Z$-component of the bulk fluid velocity of an ion species in a single resolved ionization charge state, representing the upward or downward hydrodynamic drift of that charge-state fluid. It is the vertical projection of the parent vector [ion_state_velocity](name:ion_state_velocity), resolving the multi-fluid flow field of charge-state-resolved ions along the $Z$-axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The quantity is the $Z$-projection of the first velocity moment of the charge-state distribution function normalized by the local number density:

$$
u_Z = \frac{1}{n_{i,z}} \int v_Z \, f_{i,z}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $u_Z$ is the $Z$-component of the charge-state fluid velocity, $v_Z$ is the microscopic particle velocity along $Z$, $n_{i,z}$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$, and $f_{i,z}(\mathbf{v})$ is the corresponding velocity distribution function.

This component is relevant in the edge and divertor regions, where vertical flows contribute to poloidal circulation, ion–neutral momentum exchange, and impurity transport between the midplane and divertor targets. It is computed from multi-fluid or kinetic plasma boundary simulations on unstructured grids. The charge-state-averaged ion counterpart is [vertical_ion_velocity](name:vertical_ion_velocity), and the analogous quantity for neutrals in a specified quantum state is [vertical_neutral_state_velocity](name:vertical_neutral_state_velocity). The resulting momentum transport in this direction is described by [vertical_ion_state_momentum_flux](name:vertical_ion_state_momentum_flux).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge-state fluid flows in the $+Z$ direction (vertically upward) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Z component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic drift velocity of a specified ion charge state. It is perpendicular to the local magnetic field and that charge state's pressure gradient.
NAMES.long:
The vertical ion-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift is the $Z$ component of the ion charge-state diamagnetic drift velocity in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The corresponding vector quantity is [ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift); together with [radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), this component describes the projection of that drift onto the cylindrical basis.

For an ion species and charge state $(i,k)$ with isotropic pressure, the vertical component is defined by the pressure-gradient drift formula:

$$
v_{\mathrm{dia},Z}^{i,k} =
\frac{\left(\nabla p_{i,k} \times \mathbf{B}\right)\cdot \hat{Z}}
{\mathcal{Z}_{i,k} e\, n_{i,k}\, |\mathbf{B}|^2}
$$

where $p_{i,k}$ is the charge-state pressure in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $\nabla p_{i,k}$ is its spatial gradient in $\mathrm{Pa\,m^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in $\mathrm{T}$, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude in $\mathrm{T}$, $n_{i,k}$ is the charge-state density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $\mathcal{Z}_{i,k}$ is the dimensionless positive ion charge number, $e$ is the elementary charge in $\mathrm{C}$, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is generally evaluated from measured, reconstructed, or calculated pressure and magnetic-field information rather than measured as an independent flow component. The pressure may be obtained from charge-state density and temperature, using $p_{i,k}=n_{i,k}T_{i,k}$ when $T_{i,k}$ is expressed as energy per particle with consistent conversion to $\mathrm{Pa}$. It represents the pressure-gradient part of the perpendicular fluid drift and is physically distinct from the electric-field-driven [vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) and from parallel flow.

Typical absolute values in magnetized edge plasmas are 100-10000 m.s^-1, depending on pressure-gradient scale length, magnetic-field strength, density, and charge state. The vertical component can be smaller in regions where the projection of $\nabla p_{i,k} \times \mathbf{B}$ onto $\hat{Z}$ is weak, and it can change sign across pressure extrema or where the local magnetic geometry changes the projected drift direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic drift velocity component points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) component of the E×B guiding-center drift velocity for magnetized ions in a specified charge state, evaluated in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The E×B guiding-center drift arises when a magnetized ion experiences an electric field perpendicular to the confining magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. Because the drift $\mathbf{v}_{E\times B} = \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B} / B^2$ is independent of particle mass and charge sign, every ion charge state at the same spatial location shares the same drift velocity vector; this quantity isolates the vertical $Z$ projection of that vector for a charge-state-resolved ion population.

The vertical component is given by:

$$
v_Z^{E\times B} = \frac{(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B})_Z}{B^2} = \frac{E_R B_\phi - E_\phi B_R}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric field, $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic field magnitude, and $R$, $\phi$, $Z$ are the major-radial, toroidal, and vertical coordinates of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This component is computed from the electrostatic potential gradient and the magnetic field distribution in edge plasma transport simulations that resolve the charge-state composition of the ion population. Combining this vertical projection with the radial and toroidal projections recovers the full drift vector [ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift). The analogous quantity for neutral particles is [vertical_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:vertical_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift), and the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic counterpart for ions is [vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the E×B drift velocity points in the $+Z$ direction (upward along the machine symmetry axis).

NAMES.name: vertical_ion_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) projection of the charge-state-averaged ion bulk fluid velocity, capturing the mean ion flow component along the height axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical component of the ion bulk fluid velocity, $v_{i,Z}$, is the projection of the charge-state-averaged mean ion flow velocity $\mathbf{v}_i$ onto the $\hat{Z}$ axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ coordinate frame, where $Z$ is the height measured along the machine symmetry axis. It quantifies the net vertical directed motion of the ion fluid at each plasma location and is a component of the parent [ion_velocity](name:ion_velocity) vector.

The quantity arises as the $\hat{Z}$-projection of the first velocity-space moment of the ion distribution function $f_i$:

$$
v_{i,Z} = \frac{1}{n_i} \int v_Z \, f_i(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $n_i$ is the local ion number density and $v_Z$ is the particle velocity component along $\hat{Z}$.

In tokamak edge and divertor plasmas, vertical ion flows arise from the poloidal component of $E \times B$ and diamagnetic drifts, poloidal rotation, and parallel transport projected onto $\hat{Z}$ by the local magnetic-field geometry. This component is particularly relevant in diverted configurations where poloidal field lines carry ion flow toward or away from the divertor targets. The convective contribution to vertical ion momentum transport is captured by [vertical_ion_momentum_convection_velocity](name:vertical_ion_momentum_convection_velocity), and the charge-state-resolved analog is [vertical_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:vertical_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion bulk flow is directed in the $+Z$ direction, upward along the machine height axis.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Vertical neutral momentum diffusivity is the aggregate-neutral diffusivity coefficient for diffusive momentum transport along the Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. The vertical qualifier identifies the flux and gradient direction, not the component of momentum being transported.
NAMES.long:
Vertical neutral momentum diffusivity is the coefficient that relates a vertical gradient of aggregate neutral momentum density to down-gradient diffusive momentum transport along $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes neutral momentum transport summed over the neutral population represented by the aggregate neutral momentum equation; state-resolved transport is described by [vertical_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity](name:vertical_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity).

For a diagonal Fick's-law closure, the diffusive flux along $Z$ of a neutral momentum-density component $P_{n,\alpha}$ is

$$
\Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}_{n,\alpha Z} = -D^{(n)}_{m,Z}\,\frac{\partial P_{n,\alpha}}{\partial Z}
$$

where $\alpha$ labels the transported momentum component, $\Pi^{\mathrm{diff}}_{n,\alpha Z}$ is the diffusive flux of that momentum component along $Z$ in kg m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $P_{n,\alpha}$ is the aggregate neutral momentum density in kg m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, $Z$ is vertical height in m, and $D^{(n)}_{m,Z}$ is the vertical neutral momentum diffusivity in m$^2$ s$^{-1}$. The minus sign indicates down-gradient diffusion: for positive diffusivity, momentum is transported from larger to smaller momentum density along the vertical direction.

This coefficient is usually computed from a neutral transport closure rather than measured directly. It may be derived from kinetic-neutral calculations, estimated from neutral viscosity and collision frequencies, or used as an effective parameter in fluid models; neutral-neutral collisions, charge exchange with ions, ionization, recombination, and wall recycling can all influence the appropriate value. It is the diffusive counterpart to [vertical_neutral_momentum_convection_velocity](name:vertical_neutral_momentum_convection_velocity) and contributes to vertical neutral momentum fluxes, including state-resolved quantities such as [vertical_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:vertical_neutral_state_momentum_flux).

Typical effective values are strongly model and regime dependent. Edge and divertor neutral-fluid closures commonly use values of order 0.01-100 m^2 s^-1, with lower values associated with dense, highly collisional regions and larger effective values associated with longer mean-free-path or deliberately broadened reduced closures. The coefficient should be interpreted as a transport-closure parameter, not as a universal material constant.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Vertical neutral momentum flux is the projection of the aggregate neutral momentum-flux density vector onto the +Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It sums contributions from all represented neutral species and internal states, unlike a state-resolved neutral momentum flux.
NAMES.long:
Vertical neutral momentum flux is the vertical component of the aggregate momentum-flux density carried by neutral atoms and molecules. It represents transport of neutral linear momentum across surfaces by neutral motion and by collisional or closure terms, summed over all represented neutral species and internal states. It differs from a state-resolved neutral momentum flux, which retains one neutral species, molecule, or internal state as a separate contribution.

The scalar projection is defined from the aggregate neutral momentum-flux density vector:

$$
\mathcal{F}_{p,n,Z} = \boldsymbol{\mathcal{F}}_{p,n} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathcal{F}_{p,n,Z}$ is the vertical neutral momentum flux in kg.m^-1.s^-2, $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{F}}_{p,n}$ is the aggregate neutral momentum-flux density vector in kg.m^-1.s^-2, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, and $Z$ vertical height. If neutral populations are resolved, $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{F}}_{p,n}$ is the sum of their individual contributions, $\sum_s \boldsymbol{\mathcal{F}}_{p,n,s}$, in the same unit. This is a coordinate projection onto $\hat{Z}$; parallel neutral momentum flux is instead a projection along the local magnetic-field direction and is not a component of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice, vertical neutral momentum flux is computed from neutral kinetic distribution-function moments or from neutral fluid moment equations, including convective transport and model-dependent diffusive or viscous closures. It is strongly affected by recycling at material surfaces, gas fueling, molecular dissociation, ionization, charge exchange with ions, and elastic collisions. Direct measurement is uncommon; experiments usually constrain it indirectly through neutral pressure measurements, spectroscopy, imaging, and plasma-edge measurements interpreted with neutral transport modeling.

Typical magnitudes are highly source- and geometry-dependent: about 10^-6-10^-3 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in weakly neutral core-edge regions, 10^-3-1 kg.m^-1.s^-2 in scrape-off-layer or private-flux regions, and 1-10^2 kg.m^-1.s^-2 locally near strong recycling surfaces, gas injection, or detached divertor fronts. Because the scalar is signed, quoted magnitude ranges refer to $|\mathcal{F}_{p,n,Z}|$; the signed value can be near zero, positive, or negative depending on the net vertical transport direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aggregate neutral momentum-flux density vector has a component in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction, toward increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_species_center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_species
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-component of the mass-weighted mean velocity of a neutral plasma species, representing the bulk vertical drift of the neutral fluid in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The center-of-mass velocity of a neutral species is the momentum density divided by the total mass density, summed over all constituent neutral states of the species, yielding the bulk fluid velocity of the neutral population. Its vertical component $v_Z^{\rm cm}$ quantifies neutral drift along the $Z$-axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate and $Z$ is the vertical height above the geometric midplane.

$$
v_Z^{\rm cm} = \frac{\sum_k m_k n_k v_{Z,k}}{\sum_k m_k n_k}
$$

where $m_k$ is the particle mass, $n_k$ is the number density, and $v_{Z,k}$ is the vertical velocity of neutral state $k$ of the species.

This quantity represents the true fluid-frame convection velocity of the neutral species mixture and is conceptually distinct from the [vertical neutral species momentum convection velocity](name:vertical_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity), which enters the divergence of the neutral momentum flux tensor and may incorporate higher-order multi-fluid closure terms. In divertor and scrape-off-layer regions, vertical neutral drifts contribute to recycling dynamics and cross-field momentum exchange between the neutral and charged-particle populations. The [center_of_mass_velocity](name:center_of_mass_velocity) of the full plasma-neutral mixture is the analogous many-species generalization obtained when the mass-density-weighted sum is extended over all species.

Neutral velocities are inferred from Doppler-shift spectroscopy of atomic or molecular line emission, from neutral particle analyzers, or from edge neutral transport calculations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center-of-mass velocity of the neutral species is directed in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_species_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_species
NAMES.short: Local vertical component, along Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the neutral bulk convection velocity for one species after summing over its resolved neutral states. It is not a flux-surface average unless an averaging operation is specified.
NAMES.long:
Vertical neutral-species momentum-convection velocity is the local $Z$ component of the bulk neutral velocity for one atomic or molecular species after combining the resolved neutral states of that species. It is the velocity component that convects vertical momentum in neutral-fluid transport, with $Z$ the vertical coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This is a local quantity, not a flux-surface average unless a separate averaging operation is applied.

When state-resolved neutral populations are combined into a species-level bulk velocity, the vertical component is the density-weighted moment of the state velocities:

$$
v_{Z,s} = \frac{\sum_\alpha n_{s,\alpha} v_{Z,s,\alpha}}{\sum_\alpha n_{s,\alpha}}
$$

where $s$ labels the neutral species, $\alpha$ labels a resolved neutral state, $n_{s,\alpha}$ is the state number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $v_{Z,s,\alpha}$ is the state vertical velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$, and $\sum_\alpha n_{s,\alpha}$ is the total neutral density of species $s$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$. For one species, an equivalent mass-density weighting gives the same result because the resolved neutral states have the same particle mass.

In practice this quantity is computed in neutral transport or multi-fluid models from the first velocity moment of the neutral distribution, or by combining state-resolved fluid velocities with their densities. Recycling, gas fueling, ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and wall or divertor geometry can all set the local direction and magnitude of the vertical component.

Because this is a signed local component rather than a speed magnitude, there is no universal device-independent typical value. Useful scale estimates are set by neutral thermal or injection speeds: for deuterium neutrals at 1-10 eV, thermal-speed scales are about $10^4$-$3 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$, while the vertical component may be near zero or much smaller when the flow is mainly radial or toroidal.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral species bulk flow is directed toward increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Effective vertical Z-component of the convection velocity governing momentum advection for a specified neutral state in an edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
Vertical neutral-state momentum convection velocity is the component along vertical height $Z$ of the effective velocity that advects momentum carried by a specified neutral population state. It describes whether the modeled neutral momentum transport is directed upward or downward in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scalar component is defined by projecting the effective neutral-state momentum convection velocity onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
v_{c,Z}^{(n,s)} = \hat{Z} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{c}^{(n,s)}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{c}^{(n,s)}$ is the effective momentum convection velocity for neutral species $n$ in state $s$, $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector, and $v_{c,Z}^{(n,s)}$ has unit m.s^-1.

This quantity is usually computed from neutral fluid or kinetic-neutral transport models rather than measured directly. It may represent resolved neutral flow, drift terms, or an effective closure for advective momentum transport, including the influence of recycling, ionization, charge exchange, elastic collisions, and boundary sources.

Typical modeled values in scrape-off-layer and divertor conditions range from about -10^4 to 10^4 m.s^-1. Weakly convective regions may have magnitudes below 10^2 m.s^-1, while strongly directed recycling or source-driven neutral flows can approach 10^5 m.s^-1 locally.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective momentum convection velocity for the neutral state has a component in the $+Z$ direction, upward in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_state_momentum_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Vertical neutral-state momentum diffusivity is the Z-direction component of state-resolved neutral momentum diffusivity, relating vertical gradients of neutral-state momentum density to down-gradient diffusive transport in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical neutral-state momentum diffusivity is the transport coefficient for diffusive redistribution of neutral momentum along the $Z$ direction for one resolved neutral state. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The state label $s$ is a discrete neutral-population identifier, such as an atomic, molecular, or excited-state population, rather than a continuous coordinate.

A common down-gradient closure for the diffusive vertical momentum flux of neutral state $s$ is

$$
\Pi_{Z,\mathrm{diff}}^s = -D_Z^s \frac{\partial p_Z^s}{\partial Z}
$$

where $D_Z^s$ is the vertical neutral-state momentum diffusivity, $p_Z^s = \rho^s v_Z^s$ is the vertical momentum density of that neutral state, $\rho^s$ is its mass density, $v_Z^s$ is its mean vertical velocity, and $\Pi_{Z,\mathrm{diff}}^s$ is the corresponding diffusive momentum flux density. The minus sign expresses ordinary down-gradient diffusion: a positive vertical gradient of $p_Z^s$ drives diffusive momentum transport toward lower $p_Z^s$.

This coefficient is usually specified, inferred, or evolved in neutral-transport and multi-fluid plasma-boundary models from collision rates, mean free paths, turbulent mixing assumptions, or calibration to neutral-flow and momentum-flux observations. Kinetic estimates often scale as $D \sim v_\mathrm{th}\lambda/3$, where $v_\mathrm{th}$ is a neutral thermal speed and $\lambda$ is an effective mean free path. The associated diffusive flux is represented by [vertical_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:vertical_neutral_state_momentum_flux), while advective transport is represented separately by [vertical_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:vertical_neutral_state_momentum_convection_velocity); removing the state resolution gives [vertical_neutral_momentum_diffusivity](name:vertical_neutral_momentum_diffusivity).

Typical effective values are strongly model dependent: 0.01-10 m^2 s^-1 for collisional neutral diffusion in dense edge or divertor conditions, 1-100 m^2 s^-1 when long mean-free-path neutrals or turbulent mixing dominate, and values above 100 m^2 s^-1 may be used as effective closures in weakly collisional boundary plasmas. Larger values imply faster vertical smoothing of neutral-state momentum density.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_state_momentum_flux
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Vertical component of the neutral-state momentum-flux density vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It represents momentum carried by neutrals in a specified charge or excitation state and transported per unit area and time along the vertical Z direction.
NAMES.long:
Vertical neutral-state momentum flux is the $Z$ projection of the neutral-state momentum-flux density vector for a specified neutral charge or excitation state. The direction $Z$ is vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $\phi$ is toroidal angle; the component label identifies the direction of the flux vector, not a chosen radial or flux-surface-normal transport direction. It is a component of [neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:neutral_state_momentum_flux), alongside related projections such as [radial_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:radial_neutral_state_momentum_flux), [poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:poloidal_neutral_state_momentum_flux), and [parallel_neutral_state_momentum_flux](name:parallel_neutral_state_momentum_flux).

A kinetic moment representation for a transported momentum variable carried by neutral state $a$ is

$$
\Phi_{Z,a} = \int p_a(\mathbf{v})\, v_Z\, f_a(\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $\Phi_{Z,a}$ is the vertical momentum-flux density component, $p_a(\mathbf{v})$ is the particle momentum associated with the neutral-state momentum balance in kg m s^-1, $v_Z = \mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{Z}$ is the vertical particle velocity in m s^-1, and $f_a$ is the velocity-space distribution function normalized so that $\int f_a\,d^3v$ is number density in m^-3. This gives units of kg m^-1 s^-2; the use of $v_Z$ expresses the vertical projection of the flux vector and does not introduce a radial surface normal.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic neutral distributions or from neutral-fluid moment equations, including convective transport and pressure or stress contributions. It is usually inferred through transport modeling constrained by neutral-density, flow, radiation, and charge-exchange information rather than measured directly as a local flux. The value can change sign when the net neutral momentum transport changes from upward to downward.

Typical magnitudes are strongly region- and model-dependent because they scale with neutral density, neutral temperature, and directed neutral flow. In edge and divertor conditions, absolute values commonly span about 10^-6-10^2 kg.m^-1.s^-2, while symmetry or weak vertical flow can make the signed component close to zero.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral-state momentum flux has a component in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_state_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Local Z component of the state-resolved neutral bulk velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the density-weighted mean convective velocity of neutral particles in a specified quantum or energy state.
NAMES.long:
Vertical neutral-state velocity is the local component of the bulk velocity of neutral particles in a specified quantum or energy state along the vertical coordinate $Z$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The bulk velocity is the density-weighted first velocity moment of that state-resolved neutral population, so this quantity describes upward or downward convection rather than random thermal motion.

The vertical component is defined by projecting the state-resolved bulk velocity onto $\hat{Z}$, equivalently by taking the corresponding first moment of the distribution function:

$$
v_Z^{(\alpha)}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{u}^{(\alpha)}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{Z} = \frac{1}{n^{(\alpha)}(\mathbf{x})}\int v_Z f^{(\alpha)}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\alpha$ labels the neutral state, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $\mathbf{u}^{(\alpha)}$ is the state-resolved neutral bulk velocity, $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector, $f^{(\alpha)}$ is the state-resolved neutral distribution function, $n^{(\alpha)} = \int f^{(\alpha)} d^3v$ is the neutral density for that state, and $v_Z = \mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{Z}$. The moment is physically meaningful where $n^{(\alpha)}$ is nonzero.

In practice this velocity is obtained from neutral transport or collisional-radiative calculations by forming the first velocity moment of each neutral state, or inferred indirectly from state-selective spectroscopic Doppler shifts when sufficient signal is available. It is a local mean velocity and is not a flux-surface, volume, or time average unless an averaging operation is explicitly specified.

Typical edge recycling or thermal-neutral convective components are about 10-500 m.s^-1, while strongly directed neutral sources, charge-exchange populations, or beam-related neutrals can produce components of $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s^-1. Values become poorly constrained when the local density of the specified neutral state is very small.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the state-resolved neutral bulk velocity points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, toward increasing vertical height.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Vertical component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame of the E×B drift velocity contribution assigned to a neutral particle species in a specified quantum state.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the $Z$ component, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, of the [neutral-state E×B drift velocity](name:neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift). The neutral state is an identifier for a particular internal atomic or molecular state population, such as a ground, excited, metastable, or molecular state; it is not a charge state. Because an isolated neutral particle has zero charge, this term denotes the state-resolved advective velocity contribution associated with an E×B transport decomposition, not direct Lorentz acceleration of a neutral particle.

The associated E×B drift velocity is defined from the electric and magnetic fields by

$$
\mathbf{v}_{E\times B} = \frac{\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{E\times B}$ is in m.s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field in V.m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude. The vertical component is the projection $\mathbf{v}_{E\times B}\cdot\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice this component is computed from reconstructed or measured electric and magnetic fields and then projected onto $\hat{Z}$ for the selected neutral-state population. The electric field may be inferred from electrostatic potential gradients, radial force balance, probes, spectroscopy, or transport modeling, while the magnetic field is taken from the magnetic equilibrium or field model.

The characteristic speed scale is $|\mathbf{E}|/|\mathbf{B}|$. In tokamak edge and scrape-off-layer conditions, vertical components are commonly 0-10000 m.s$^{-1}$, while strong edge electric fields or transient conditions can give components of order 10000-100000 m.s$^{-1}$; the signed value depends on the local field geometry and projection onto $\hat{Z}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the E×B drift velocity contribution has a positive projection along $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Vertical component of the neutral species bulk fluid velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, averaged over all neutral quantum and energy states.
NAMES.long:
Vertical neutral velocity is the component of the neutral-species bulk fluid velocity along the vertical $Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the density-weighted mean motion of the neutral population after averaging over neutral quantum and energy states, distinct from the state-resolved quantity [vertical_neutral_state_velocity](name:vertical_neutral_state_velocity).

The vertical component is defined by projecting the neutral bulk velocity onto the vertical basis vector:

$$
v_{n,Z} = \mathbf{v}_n \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $v_{n,Z}$ is the vertical neutral velocity in m.s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{v}_n$ is the neutral bulk velocity in m.s$^{-1}$ averaged over the neutral population, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice this velocity may be obtained as the first velocity moment of a neutral distribution function, from neutral fluid or kinetic transport calculations, or inferred from Doppler shifts of neutral emission when the viewing geometry constrains the vertical component. It is useful for describing neutral penetration, recycling flows, gas fueling, and vertical momentum exchange with ions and electrons.

Typical values in tokamak edge and divertor plasmas are $10^2-10^4$ m.s$^{-1}$ for thermal or recycling neutrals. Directed gas sources, strong recycling flows, or fast-neutral dominated regions can produce vertical components of order $10^4-10^5$ m.s$^{-1}$, with either sign depending on the flow direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral bulk velocity has a component in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_argon_density
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume average of the local argon ion number density over the confined plasma region. Unless a charge state is specified, argon density includes ions in all ionization stages summed over charge state.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged argon density is the spatial average of the local argon ion number density over the confined plasma volume. It represents a global concentration measure, distinct from the total argon inventory, which would be this average multiplied by the plasma volume. Unless a charge state is specified, $n_\mathrm{Ar}$ includes all ionization stages of argon summed over charge state.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{Ar} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_\mathrm{Ar}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $V_p$ is the confined plasma volume in m$^3$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, $n_\mathrm{Ar}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local argon ion number density in m$^{-3}$, and $\langle n_\mathrm{Ar} \rangle_V$ is in m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity spectroscopy, radiation modeling, charge-state balance calculations, or impurity transport modeling, then integrated over the reconstructed confined plasma volume. It is complementary to local measures such as argon density at the magnetic axis and at the plasma boundary, and to line-integrated or line-averaged measurements. Its relation to effective charge and radiated power depends on the argon charge-state distribution, electron temperature, electron density, and atomic rate coefficients, not on the volume-averaged density alone.

Typical volume-averaged values are about $10^{14}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$ for trace diagnostic argon injections and $10^{16}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ for deliberate argon seeding in tokamak plasmas. Values near or above $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ correspond to substantial impurity concentrations for plasmas with electron density of order $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged number density of the combined deuterium-tritium fuel ion pseudo-species.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged deuterium-tritium density is the spatial average of the number density of a combined fuel ion pseudo-species representing deuterium and tritium together. This pseudo-species is often used when the two hydrogenic isotopes are modeled as a single effective ion population rather than as separate deuterium and tritium densities.

For a plasma volume $V$, the volume average is

$$
\langle n_{DT} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V}\int_V n_{DT}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $\langle n_{DT} \rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged deuterium-tritium density in $m^{-3}$, $n_{DT}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local deuterium-tritium pseudo-species number density in $m^{-3}$, $dV$ is a volume element in $m^3$, and $V$ is the averaging volume in $m^3$. The corresponding total deuterium-tritium fuel inventory is $\int_V n_{DT}\,dV$ and is a particle count, not a density.

In practice this quantity is computed from an inferred or simulated spatial density distribution and an associated plasma volume. It is distinct from a line-averaged deuterium-tritium density, which averages along a viewing chord or path rather than over the plasma volume, and from the deuterium-tritium density at the magnetic axis, which samples the central value.

Typical core-fueling and transport studies use volume-averaged deuterium-tritium densities of order $10^{19}-10^{20}\ m^{-3}$, with lower values in startup or low-density scenarios and higher values in high-performance burning-plasma regimes.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_hydrogen_density
NAMES.subject: hydrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of hydrogen (protium) ions averaged over the total plasma volume, providing a single global scalar measure of hydrogen particle content independent of ionization state.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged hydrogen density is the spatial mean of the local hydrogen number density over the entire confined plasma volume, aggregating contributions from all charge states and both thermal and non-thermal hydrogen populations. It collapses the profile dependence of [hydrogen_density](name:hydrogen_density) into a single global scalar characterizing the total hydrogen fuel inventory.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_H \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_H(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_H(\mathbf{r})$ is the local hydrogen number density and $V$ is the total confined plasma volume.

This aggregate is computed by integrating radially resolved hydrogen density profiles — obtained from diagnostics such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, beam-emission spectroscopy, or visible Balmer-line spectroscopy — over the plasma volume using differential volume elements from equilibrium reconstruction. The [line_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:line_averaged_hydrogen_density) is a chord-path counterpart that directly represents interferometric line-of-sight measurements rather than a full volume integral.

Typical values range from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on plasma density regime and device size. In mixed hydrogen-deuterium plasmas, the hydrogen fraction relative to total hydrogenic density is tracked by hydrogen_fraction, and the analogous volume average for deuterium is [volume_averaged_deuterium_density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_density).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_ion_charge
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged charge number of the dominant ionization state for a given ion species, representing the global mean ionization level integrated over the confined plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged ion charge $\langle Z_\mathrm{ion} \rangle$ is the spatial mean of the dominant-state charge number for a given ion species across the confined plasma volume. It is the volume-averaging transformation of ion_charge, compressing a spatially varying ionization profile into a single global scalar that tracks the mean ionization level of each species.

$$
\langle Z_\mathrm{ion} \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int Z_\mathrm{ion}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the confined plasma volume and $Z_\mathrm{ion}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local dominant-state ion charge number of the species at position $\mathbf{r}$.

This quantity is particularly relevant during plasma initiation and current ramp-up, when gas breakdown and ionization fronts cause the mean charge state to evolve dynamically from near-neutral to partially or fully ionized conditions. The volume average captures this global ionization progression as a single time-evolving scalar for each species present.

Unlike ion_species_charge, which is the density-weighted average over all occupied charge states of a species, this quantity reflects only the dominant ionization state. For the density-weighted mean-squared charge relevant to resistivity and impurity transport, see [effective_charge](name:effective_charge); the corresponding volumetric ion number density is given by [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion carries net positive electric charge, as holds for all ionized plasma species with at least one electron removed.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged number density of a specific ion species computed over the confined plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged ion density $\langle n_i \rangle$ is the spatial mean of the local number density $n_i(\mathbf{r})$ for a designated ion species, integrated over the plasma volume $V$ bounded by the last closed flux surface. As a single global scalar it encapsulates the ion inventory of that species in the confined plasma, complementing the full radial profile given by [ion_density](name:ion_density) and distinguished from [volume_averaged_total_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_density), which sums contributions from all ion species simultaneously.

The defining volume average is:

$$
\langle n_i \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_i(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface and $n_i$ is the local number density of the designated ion species, summed over all its ionization states.

This quantity is obtained from radial ion density profiles derived via charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or impurity transport modeling, with the volume integral carried out using flux-surface geometry from equilibrium reconstruction. It pairs with [volume_averaged_ion_temperature](name:volume_averaged_ion_temperature) for species-resolved energy-balance assessments and is linked to [volume_averaged_electron_density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) through the quasi-neutrality constraint relating the sum of all ion charge densities to the electron density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the designated ion species has a nonzero particle inventory within the confined plasma volume.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_ion_state_average_charge_number
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged mean charge number of an ion charge-state bundle, obtained by integrating the local concentration-weighted charge average over the confined plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged ion state average charge number is the global scalar form of [ion_state_average_charge_number](name:ion_state_average_charge_number), representing the ionization level of a charge-state bundle condensed into a single plasma-wide value rather than a radial profile. It characterizes the mean effective charge of the bundle across the entire confined plasma, making it useful for global impurity transport monitoring and multi-species plasma bookkeeping.

The quantity is defined by integrating the local concentration-weighted mean charge over the confined plasma volume:

$$
\langle Z \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V} \int_V \sum_z Z \cdot x_z \, dV
$$

where $Z$ is the integer charge number of charge state $z$, $x_z$ is its fractional concentration within the bundle satisfying $\sum_z x_z = 1$, and $V$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last-closed flux surface.

This global scalar is inferred by combining spectroscopic charge-state fraction measurements with equilibrium flux-surface geometry to perform the volume integral, or computed directly from transport or atomic physics models that resolve charge-state populations. It is distinct from [volume_averaged_effective_charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge) ($Z_\mathrm{eff}$), which weights charge contributions by $Z^2$ relative to electron density, and from [volume_averaged_ion_charge](name:volume_averaged_ion_charge), which captures the dominant single ionization state rather than the bundle-averaged mean. Typical values range from 1 for singly ionized species to the full nuclear charge number of the element (e.g., 6 for fully stripped carbon, 18 for fully stripped argon), with intermediate values arising from partial ionization in cooler plasma regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge-state bundle contains ionized states with charge number $Z \geq 1$, following the convention that charge numbers count elementary positive charges removed from a neutral atom.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_neon_density
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Mean elemental number density of neon averaged over the plasma volume, where the local neon density is the sum over all ionization states from neutral neon to fully stripped neon.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged neon density is the plasma-volume mean of the total elemental neon number density. The local elemental neon density includes all charge states of neon, from neutral atoms to fully stripped ions, so it measures neon content rather than any single neon ionization state.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Ne}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V}\int_V \left(\sum_{q=0}^{10} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x})\right)\,dV
$$

where $V$ is the plasma volume in m$^3$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$ of neon with charge state $q$, and $q=0$ denotes neutral neon while $q=10$ denotes fully stripped neon.

In practice, this quantity is inferred by combining impurity diagnostics and plasma modeling that relate neon line radiation, charge-state balance, transport, and ionization-recombination physics to an elemental neon density distribution. The volume average provides a single bulk measure of neon impurity inventory, useful for comparing seeding level, dilution, and radiative impurity content across plasma scenarios.

Representative values are highly scenario dependent. Trace neon concentrations may give volume-averaged densities around $10^{15}$-$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$, while deliberate neon seeding for radiation control can produce values of order $10^{17}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on plasma density, confinement, and impurity source strength.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Volume average of the local runaway electron number density over the confined plasma. It is a nonnegative global measure of the runaway population produced and depleted by generation, transport, and slowing-down processes.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged runaway electron density is the runaway-electron number per unit confined plasma volume after averaging the local [runaway_electron_density](name:runaway_electron_density) over that volume. It condenses a spatially varying runaway population into a single global density while retaining the dimensions of a number density.

The volume average is defined by integrating the local runaway electron density over the confined plasma volume:

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{RE} \rangle = \frac{1}{V_\mathrm{p}} \int_{V_\mathrm{p}} n_\mathrm{RE}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $n_\mathrm{RE}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local runaway electron density at position $\mathbf{r}$, $V_\mathrm{p}$ is the confined plasma volume, and $dV$ is the volume element.

The quantity is computed from kinetic or fluid runaway-electron models by integrating the local density over the confined plasma volume, or inferred indirectly by combining diagnostics such as hard-X-ray bremsstrahlung, synchrotron radiation, and constraints on current carried by relativistic electrons with forward modeling. Its time evolution follows a volume-integrated particle balance: generation terms contribute through the [volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate), while radial transport out of the confined volume, impacts on material surfaces, and collisional slowing or scattering that returns particles below the runaway threshold reduce it.

Representative values are highly scenario dependent. The value is effectively zero when no runaway population is present, may lie around $10^{12}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$ for weak seed populations, and can reach $10^{16}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in disruption or post-disruption runaway-plateau scenarios in large tokamaks. The [volume_averaged_energy_density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density) provides a complementary global measure of the kinetic energy carried by the same population.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_total_ion_density
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume average of the total ion number density summed over all ion species, providing a single global measure of ion particle content in the confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged total ion density is a global parameter obtained by averaging the local total ion number density — summed over all ion species and charge states, and including both thermal and non-thermal populations — over the confined plasma volume enclosed by the last-closed flux surface.

The defining volume average is:

$$
\langle n_i^{\text{tot}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_i^{\text{tot}}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_i^{\text{tot}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local [total_ion_density](name:total_ion_density) at position $\mathbf{r}$, summed over all ion species and charge states, and $V$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last-closed flux surface.

This quantity characterizes overall plasma fueling efficiency and is widely used in confinement scaling studies and comparisons with the Greenwald density limit. It can be derived from chord-integrated measurements such as interferometry after appropriate geometric weighting, or by integrating charge-state-resolved kinetic density profiles over flux surfaces. It differs from [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density), which tracks a single species rather than the multi-species aggregate, and from [line_averaged_density](name:line_averaged_total_ion_density), which performs a chord-weighted rather than volumetric average.

Typical values range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ in tokamak operation, with reactor-relevant high-density H-mode scenarios approaching the upper end.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net ion particles are present in the confined volume, as ion number density is intrinsically non-negative.

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Xenon ion number density at the radial reference location of an internal transport barrier, where reduced cross-field transport allows steep radial gradients to form. Represents the local concentration of xenon impurity ions, summed over ionization states unless a charge-state-resolved quantity is specified.
NAMES.long:
Xenon ion number density at the radial reference location of an internal transport barrier (ITB). An ITB is a region inside the confined plasma where turbulent cross-field transport is locally reduced, allowing steep radial gradients to form; this quantity is the local xenon ion density evaluated at the radial reference surface associated with that barrier.

The quantity is the local value of the xenon density profile sampled at the barrier reference radius:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Xe,ITB}} = n_{\mathrm{Xe}}(r_{\mathrm{ITB}})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Xe}}$ is the xenon ion number density and $r_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the radial reference location of the barrier, expressed in a flux-surface label such as the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$.

Xenon is a high-$Z$ impurity, so its local density is typically a small fraction of the main-ion density and depends strongly on fueling, edge screening, ionization balance, and transport across the barrier. Lighter impurity densities at the same location are given by [carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [oxygen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:oxygen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and the total ion density at the same reference surface is [total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Xenon ion number density evaluated at the magnetic axis, where poloidal magnetic flux has an extremum and its spatial gradient vanishes. Unless a charge state is specified separately, it is the total xenon ion density summed over ionization states present in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Xenon density at the magnetic axis is the local number density of xenon ions on the magnetic axis, the reference curve around which nested magnetic flux surfaces close and where [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) has an extremum with vanishing spatial gradient. Unless a charge state is specified separately, this quantity aggregates xenon ions over all ionization states present in the plasma. Neutral xenon atoms are not included, and the resulting number density is non-negative.

The on-axis value can be written as a charge-state sum evaluated at the magnetic-axis location:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Xe,axis}} = \sum_{q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{Xe}}} n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{q+}}(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Xe}^{q+}}$ is the local number density of xenon ions with charge state $q$, and $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{Xe}}$ is the set of xenon ionization states present or included in the diagnostic or modeling interpretation. The set is not assumed to contain every formal charge state $q=1,\ldots,54$. The position $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ is the magnetic-axis location in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, and $Z$ vertical height; all densities have units of m$^{-3}$.

Xenon is a high-atomic-number noble-gas impurity used in radiative power-exhaust studies, so its on-axis density is a sensitive indicator of impurity screening, accumulation, and inward transport. It is inferred from spectroscopic measurements of xenon charge states, such as soft-X-ray or X-ray crystal spectroscopy and, where applicable, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, together with ionization-balance and impurity-transport modeling constrained by equilibrium reconstruction. Comparisons with [xenon_density_at_pedestal](name:xenon_density_at_pedestal) and [xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary) distinguish edge retention from penetration to the core.

Typical on-axis xenon ion densities are much smaller than the main-ion and electron densities. In deliberate seeding experiments, representative core values are about $10^{16}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$; in unseeded or strongly screened plasmas they may be below $10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$ or below diagnostic sensitivity.

NAMES.name: bulk_plasma_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Bulk-fluid diamagnetic drift velocity of the thermal plasma, driven by the pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field. It is a center-of-mass flow contribution perpendicular to both the pressure gradient and the magnetic field, not an individual-particle drift.
NAMES.long:
Bulk plasma velocity due to diamagnetic drift is the center-of-mass thermal-plasma flow contribution associated with the pressure-gradient term in the perpendicular fluid momentum balance. It is perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the pressure gradient and represents a collective fluid drift rather than transport by individual particle orbits. This is the same physical vector as bulk_plasma_diamagnetic_drift_velocity; the present name emphasizes its role as one contribution to the bulk plasma velocity.

For a species-resolved description, the bulk vector is obtained as a mass-density-weighted average of the included thermal-species diamagnetic drift velocities:

$$
\mathbf{v}_{*,\mathrm{bulk}} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_{*s}}{\sum_s m_s n_s}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_{*s} = \frac{\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p_s}{q_s n_s B^2}
$$

where $s$ labels a thermal plasma species, $m_s$ is the particle mass in kg, $n_s$ is the density in m^-3, $q_s$ is the charge in C, $p_s$ is the scalar pressure in Pa, $\nabla p_s$ is in Pa m^-1, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$. The resulting vector has unit m.s^-1.

In practice this velocity is computed from reconstructed magnetic-field geometry together with measured or modeled density and temperature profiles used to form species pressure gradients. It is commonly resolved into components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Typical component magnitudes are about 10^2-10^4 m.s^-1 in tokamak cores and can reach 10^4-10^5 m.s^-1 in steep-gradient edge or pedestal regions. The value decreases where pressure gradients are weak or where the magnetic-field magnitude is large.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved velocity component points along the positive direction of its corresponding basis vector, for example $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short: Total neutron emission rate from deuterium-deuterium thermonuclear reactions driven by the Maxwellian thermal velocity distribution of bulk deuterium ions, excluding beam-target and beam-beam fast-ion contributions.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium-deuterium flux due to thermal fusion is the total rate at which neutrons are produced by the neutron branch of thermal D-D fusion in the bulk plasma. It is a scalar source rate for the emitting plasma volume, not an area-normalized particle flux, and it excludes D-D reactions involving nonthermal deuterons such as neutral-beam ions.

The rate is the volume integral of the local thermal D-D neutron emissivity:

$$
R_{DD,n}^{\mathrm{th}} = \int_V \epsilon_{DD,n}^{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV = \int_V \frac{1}{2} n_D^2(\mathbf{x})\,\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}(T_i(\mathbf{x}))\,dV
$$

where $R_{DD,n}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is this neutron emission rate, $V$ is the emitting plasma volume, $\epsilon_{DD,n}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the local [deuterium-deuterium neutron emissivity], $n_D$ is the thermal deuterium ion density, $T_i$ is the thermal ion temperature, and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}$ is the Maxwellian reactivity for the neutron-producing D-D branch. The factor $1/2$ avoids double-counting identical deuteron pairs.

In practice this rate is inferred from calibrated neutron diagnostics, such as fission chambers, activation systems, scintillators, or neutron cameras, and is compared with calculations using measured density, ion temperature, fuel dilution, and reconstructed plasma volume. Separation from fast-ion contributions requires modeling or diagnostic discrimination of beam-target and beam-beam channels; together with those channels it contributes to the branch-resolved [deuterium_deuterium_flux](name:deuterium_deuterium_flux), while summing corresponding thermal rates across fusion reactions contributes to [flux_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:flux_due_to_thermal_fusion).

Typical thermal D-D neutron rates range from below 1e10 Hz in cold or dilute deuterium plasmas to 1e12-1e15 Hz in strongly heated tokamak plasmas, and may approach 1e16-1e17 Hz in large high-performance deuterium discharges. The thermal component becomes significant for ion temperatures of about 5-20 keV, and each neutron from the D-D neutron branch has an energy near 2.45 MeV before spectral broadening by ion thermal motion and bulk plasma rotation.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_current_density
NAMES.short: Current density driven by the cross product of the magnetic field and the plasma pressure gradient, flowing perpendicular to both, arising from the differential gyration drifts of ions and electrons in an inhomogeneous magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic current density is the electric current that flows perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the local plasma pressure gradient in a magnetized plasma. It originates from the asymmetry between ion and electron guiding-center drifts in an inhomogeneous pressure field, producing a net charge flux that closes within flux surfaces without requiring net particle transport along field lines. As a parent quantity it abstracts over all directional projections and serves as the shared physical basis for component forms such as [parallel_diamagnetic_current_density](name:parallel_diamagnetic_current_density) along the field line and [toroidal_diamagnetic_current_density](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) along the toroidal direction, as well as radial, poloidal, and vertical projections in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The defining relation in magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium is:

$$
\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} = \frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field vector, $\nabla p$ is the gradient of the total scalar plasma pressure, and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the field magnitude.

This current is obtained from fluid or MHD equilibrium calculations that supply both the pressure profile and the magnetic geometry. Experimentally, the integrated effect of diamagnetic currents is detected through diamagnetic loop measurements that sense the associated magnetization signal. The heat-viscosity-driven contribution is separately cataloged as [diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current component points in the positive direction of its resolved projection axis, consistent with $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p$ being positive when projected onto that axis.

NAMES.name: poloidal_diamagnetic_current_density
NAMES.short: Projection of the diamagnetic current density onto the poloidal direction in a flux-coordinate system (rho, theta, phi). It arises from the cross product of the magnetic field with the plasma pressure gradient in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal diamagnetic current density is the projection of the full [diamagnetic_current_density](name:diamagnetic_current_density) onto the poloidal basis direction $\hat{\theta}$ of a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ on magnetic surfaces. It represents the part of the guiding-center diamagnetic-drift current that circulates poloidally, complementing the toroidal_diamagnetic_current_density and [parallel_diamagnetic_current_density](name:parallel_diamagnetic_current_density) projections.

For an isotropic scalar pressure, the defining relation is

$$
j_{\mathrm{dia},\theta} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\hat{\theta} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p}{B^2}\right)\cdot\hat{\theta}
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{dia},\theta}$ is the poloidal component, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field with magnitude $B$ in T, $p$ is the plasma pressure in Pa, and $\nabla p$ is in Pa m$^{-1}$. The flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ uses the toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height; the result is in A m$^{-2}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction and kinetic-pressure information by evaluating the pressure gradient, forming $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p/B^2$, and projecting the result onto $\hat{\theta}$. Direct measurement of this component in isolation is uncommon; uncertainties are usually dominated by pressure-gradient resolution, magnetic-field geometry, and the definition of the poloidal basis near separatrices or strongly shaped flux surfaces.

Typical magnitudes are about $10^3-10^5$ A m$^{-2}$ in moderate-gradient core plasmas and can reach $10^5-10^6$ A m$^{-2}$ in steep edge or pedestal regions. The signed component may pass through zero where the pressure gradient, magnetic geometry, or projection onto the poloidal direction changes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projection of $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is in the $+\hat{\theta}$ direction of the flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_diamagnetic_current_density
NAMES.short: Radial component of the diamagnetic current density, driven by the cross product of the magnetic field and the plasma pressure gradient projected onto the major-radius direction.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic current density arises in magnetized plasmas wherever a pressure gradient exists perpendicular to the magnetic field, producing a drift current perpendicular to both $\mathbf{B}$ and $\nabla p$. The radial component $j_{\mathrm{dia},R} = \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} \cdot \hat{R}$ is the projection of the full [diamagnetic current density](name:diamagnetic_current_density) vector onto the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The defining expression for the diamagnetic current density vector is:

$$
\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} = \frac{\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic field vector and $p$ is the total plasma pressure. The radial projection isolates the component crossing magnetic surfaces in the $\hat{R}$ direction, which enters the radial current balance and — through ambipolarity constraints — can influence the radial electric field and plasma rotation.

This component is computed from pressure gradient and magnetic field geometry profiles. In edge and scrape-off-layer regions with steep pressure gradients and complex magnetic geometry, it can be comparable to or larger than the radial ohmic or [radial_current_density](name:radial_total_current_density). The complementary decomposition of the same vector yields toroidal_diamagnetic_current_density and [parallel_diamagnetic_current_density](name:parallel_diamagnetic_current_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic current flows in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: vertical_diamagnetic_current_density
NAMES.short: Vertical component of diamagnetic current density in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, driven by the magnetic field crossed with the plasma pressure gradient.
NAMES.long:
Vertical diamagnetic current density is the projection of the diamagnetic current density vector onto the vertical basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the pressure-gradient-driven perpendicular current associated with species diamagnetic drifts in a magnetized plasma.

For scalar total pressure $p$, the vertical projection is defined from the diamagnetic current density vector by

$$
j_{\mathrm{dia},Z} = \frac{(\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p) \cdot \hat{Z}}{|\mathbf{B}|^2}
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{dia},Z}$ is the vertical component, $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic field in tesla, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude, $p$ is the total plasma pressure in pascals, $\nabla p$ is the pressure gradient in pascals per meter, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector. Any part of $\nabla p$ parallel to $\mathbf{B}$ does not contribute to the cross product.

In practice, $j_{\mathrm{dia},Z}$ is usually inferred rather than measured directly. Spatially resolved density and temperature measurements provide the pressure, magnetic diagnostics or equilibrium reconstruction provide $\mathbf{B}$, and numerical differentiation provides $\nabla p$ before taking the vector product and vertical projection. The full vector is [diamagnetic_current_density](name:diamagnetic_current_density); directional counterparts include [radial_diamagnetic_current_density](name:radial_diamagnetic_current_density) and [poloidal_diamagnetic_current_density](name:poloidal_diamagnetic_current_density). The closely related [vertical_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) represents the same pressure-gradient current in a drift-velocity decomposition when total scalar pressure is used, while [diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) denotes a distinct current driven by viscous stress.

Typical component magnitudes are order $10^2$-$10^6$ A m$^{-2}$ in many confined-plasma regions and can approach order $10^7$ A m$^{-2}$ in localized steep-gradient edge layers. The scale is set by the perpendicular pressure-gradient magnitude divided by magnetic-field strength, and the vertical component can be small or change sign when local field and pressure-gradient geometry rotate the diamagnetic current away from $\hat{Z}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic current density points in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction, toward increasing vertical height $Z$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local number density of the suprathermal (non-thermal) electron population, forming the fast-electron fraction of the total electron density and distinct from the bulk thermal electron component.
NAMES.long:
The fast electron density $n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ quantifies the number of suprathermal electrons per unit volume — electrons whose energies lie substantially above the bulk Maxwellian distribution. Fast electrons arise through wave-particle interactions during electron cyclotron or lower hybrid heating, inductive electric field acceleration, or rapid MHD events such as sawtooth crashes that eject energetic electrons from the core region.

The total [electron density](name:electron_density) $n_e$ decomposes as:

$$
n_e = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} + n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal electron number density and $n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is this quantity.

The fast electron population is inferred from hard X-ray bremsstrahlung emission diagnostics, suprathermal electron cyclotron emission radiometry, or kinetic transport models that resolve the non-Maxwellian high-energy tail of the electron distribution function. In edge and scrape-off layer plasmas, fast electrons transported from the core contribute to energy deposition on plasma-facing components. The [runaway electron density](name:runaway_electron_density) is a distinct sub-population of fast electrons continuously accelerated by the parallel inductive electric field and represents an extreme tail of this quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when suprathermal electrons are present in the plasma volume element; as a number density this quantity is non-negative everywhere.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: First-order radial derivative of the fast (non-thermal) electron number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of fast electron density quantifies how the suprathermal (non-thermal) electron number density $n_\mathrm{fast}$ varies with the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, which parameterizes nested flux surfaces from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the separatrix. This gradient characterizes the spatial structure of the non-thermal electron population as distinct from the bulk thermal electrons.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{dn_\mathrm{fast}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the [fast electron density](name:fast_electron_density) and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius ranging from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the last closed flux surface.

This derivative is evaluated numerically within transport solvers from the radial distribution of fast electron density, serving as input to the discretized transport equations governing non-thermal electron evolution. The [second radial derivative of fast electron density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density) provides higher-order curvature information for the same population. The analogous gradient for the total electron population is [radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density), and for non-thermal ions, [radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_ion_density) provides a direct parallel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast electron density $n_\mathrm{fast}$ increases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, corresponding to a suprathermal electron population concentrated toward the plasma boundary rather than the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Second derivative of the fast, nonthermal electron number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius rho_tor_norm. It quantifies the radial curvature of the fast-electron density in flux space.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of fast-electron density is the curvature of the nonthermal electron number density as a function of the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. It characterizes how rapidly the radial gradient of [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density) changes between neighboring flux surfaces, helping distinguish hollow, peaked, or flattened fast-electron distributions.

The derivative is defined by the local centered-curvature limit:

$$
\frac{\partial^2 n_\mathrm{fast}}{\partial \rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}(\rho) = \lim_{\Delta\rho \to 0} \frac{n_\mathrm{fast}(\rho + \Delta\rho) - 2 n_\mathrm{fast}(\rho) + n_\mathrm{fast}(\rho - \Delta\rho)}{(\Delta\rho)^2}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-electron number density, $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux radius, and $\Delta\rho$ is an increment in that coordinate. Because the radial coordinate is dimensionless, the derivative has the same unit as density.

In practice, $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is inferred from diagnostics sensitive to nonthermal electrons, such as hard-X-ray, synchrotron, microwave, or electron-cyclotron emission, or from kinetic and transport modeling constrained by such measurements. The second derivative is usually computed from a fitted or regularized radial dependence, since direct differencing of noisy density estimates strongly amplifies measurement noise.

Typical absolute magnitudes are highly scenario dependent. Broad fast-electron populations with $n_\mathrm{fast}$ around $10^{15}$-$10^{18}$ m^-3 and radial scale lengths $\Delta\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ of 0.3-1 give about $10^{15}$-$10^{19}$ m^-3; localized deposition, avalanching, or sharp transport barriers can produce $10^{20}$ m^-3 or larger.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-electron density is locally concave upward as a function of $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, so its radial slope increases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_fast_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local temporal rate-of-change contribution to the fast, non-thermal electron number density, expressed as a density change over the chosen time interval. It quantifies growth or depletion of the suprathermal electron population.
NAMES.long:
The time derivative of fast electron density is the density-valued change in the fast, non-thermal electron number density associated with temporal evolution over a specified interval. It represents the local growth or depletion of the suprathermal electron population rather than an instantaneous rate per unit time.

For an interval from $t_0$ to $t_1$, the density-valued contribution is the time integral of the instantaneous tendency:

$$
\Delta_t n_\mathrm{fast} = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \frac{\partial n_\mathrm{fast}}{\partial t}(t)\,dt = \Delta t\,\overline{\frac{\partial n_\mathrm{fast}}{\partial t}}
$$

where $\Delta_t n_\mathrm{fast}$ is this quantity, $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density), $\Delta t=t_1-t_0$, and the overbar denotes the interval-averaged instantaneous tendency. The instantaneous tendency has units of density per time, while its time integral has units of density.

This quantity is usually inferred from time-resolved density estimates or evaluated in transport and kinetic modeling from the balance of fast-electron sources, collisional thermalization into the bulk electron population, and particle transport. It is the fast-electron counterpart of [time_derivative_of_total_electron_density](name:time_derivative_of_total_electron_density) and is analogous to [time_derivative_of_fast_ion_density](name:time_derivative_of_fast_ion_density); spatial-gradient effects are related to [radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density).

Typical magnitudes are strongly scenario- and interval-dependent. In slowly evolving phases the contribution is often a small fraction of the local fast-electron density, about 10^12-10^16 m^-3 over a transport interval, while strong heating, current-drive, runaway growth, or rapid loss events can produce contributions of 10^16-10^19 m^-3 or larger.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-electron density increases over the chosen time interval.

NAMES.name: fast_neutral_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Gyrotropic kinetic pressure of the suprathermal (fast) neutral particle population, decomposing into components parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field direction, summed over all internal quantum states of the neutral species.
NAMES.long:
