The sign and magnitude depend jointly on the local concavity of the flux profile and on the orientation convention inherited from $\psi$ itself; values change sign where the radial variation of $d\psi/d\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ switches between increasing and decreasing.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial derivative $d\psi/d\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ increases with increasing toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Number density of the bulk thermal (Maxwellian) electron population, excluding fast and suprathermal electron contributions.
NAMES.long:
The thermal electron density $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the number of thermal (Maxwellian) electrons per unit volume, representing the bulk electron component whose velocity distribution is described by a Maxwellian at the local electron temperature. It is the dominant electron population in most quiescent plasma conditions and is the relevant density for transport equations, pressure balance, and quasineutrality constraints.

The total [electron_density](name:electron_density) partitions into thermal and fast contributions:

$$
n_e = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} + n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [fast electron density]. In the absence of significant suprathermal populations this fast term is negligible and $n_{e,\mathrm{th}} \approx n_e$.

Thomson scattering and microwave reflectometry measure the electron density profile; where the fast electron population is negligible, the inferred $n_e$ directly approximates $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$. During electron cyclotron current drive or lower hybrid heating scenarios the fast electron contribution becomes appreciable and the two populations must be tracked separately.

Typical core values range from $1 \times 10^{19}$ to $2 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in tokamak plasmas, falling to $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in the scrape-off layer. The thermal electron density enters the electron thermal pressure $p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} T_e$ and the charge-neutrality relation, and is the electron-species analog of [thermal_ion_density](name:thermal_ion_density).

NAMES.name: thermal_neutral_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Isotropic kinetic pressure of the thermal neutral population due to random thermal motion about the mean flow velocity. For a neutral species, it is aggregated over neutral internal states unless an explicitly state-resolved pressure is specified.
NAMES.long:
Thermal neutral pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure carried by neutral particles in the thermal part of the velocity distribution. It represents the isotropic contribution from random motion relative to the mean neutral flow, excluding directed ram pressure and distinct fast-neutral components. For a neutral species, this quantity is aggregated over neutral internal quantum, excitation, or molecular states unless a state-resolved pressure is specified.

For a Maxwellian neutral population, the thermal pressure is

$$
p_{\mathrm{th},n} = n_n k_B T_n
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th},n}$ is the thermal neutral pressure, $n_n$ is the neutral number density in m^-3, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $T_n$ is the thermodynamic neutral temperature in K. If the neutral temperature is expressed as an energy per particle, the equivalent relation is $p_{\mathrm{th},n}=n_n T_{n,E}$ with $T_{n,E}$ in joules, or $p_{\mathrm{th},n}=n_n e T_{n,\mathrm{eV}}$ when the temperature is given in eV.

Thermal neutral pressure is inferred from neutral density and temperature estimates obtained from kinetic neutral transport modeling, gas-balance analysis, spectroscopy, pressure gages, or coupled plasma-neutral simulations. In non-Maxwellian cases it corresponds to one third of the trace of the random-velocity pressure tensor for the thermal neutral population, after separating any mean-flow contribution.

Typical values span a wide range: about 1e-4-1 Pa in hot core regions where neutral density is very low, 0.01-100 Pa in edge and scrape-off-layer conditions, and higher local values can occur in cold, dense divertor or gas-puff regions depending on neutral density and temperature.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local temporal tendency of electron temperature at a fixed spatial label, represented as the temperature change implied by the rate over a 1 s reference interval. Positive values indicate heating and negative values indicate cooling.
NAMES.long:
The time derivative of electron temperature quantifies the local temporal tendency of the electron thermal energy scale at a fixed spatial label. In the eV-valued representation used for this quantity, the physical derivative is multiplied by a 1 s reference duration, so the value is a signed temperature increment that preserves the sign and relative magnitude of the underlying rate.

The eV-valued tendency can be defined from the physical derivative as:

$$
D_{T_e} = \tau_0 \left.\frac{\partial T_e}{\partial t}\right|_{\xi}, \qquad \tau_0 = 1\,\mathrm{s}
$$

where $D_{T_e}$ is this quantity, $T_e$ is electron temperature in eV, $t$ is time in seconds, and $\xi$ is the spatial label held fixed during differentiation. The corresponding physical rate is $D_{T_e}/\tau_0$ in eV s$^{-1}$.

This quantity is usually inferred rather than directly measured by a single diagnostic. It can be estimated from time-resolved electron-temperature measurements after mapping them to the same spatial label, or computed from an electron energy balance including heat-flux divergence, collisional energy exchange with ions, radiative losses, and externally deposited electron heating.

Representative magnitudes are strongly scenario-dependent. Quasi-stationary regions are near 0 eV, slow transport evolution often gives magnitudes of about 10-1000 eV, and rapid heating, cooling pulses, or edge transients can reach 10000-100000 eV locally in this 1 s-normalized representation; for example, a 100 eV temperature change over 10 ms corresponds to 10000 eV.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron temperature increases with increasing time at the evaluation point.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_flux_surface_averaged_metric
NAMES.short: Time derivative, at fixed dimensional toroidal flux radius, of the derivative of enclosed plasma volume with respect to that radius. It measures how the flux-surface volume metric changes as equilibrium geometry evolves.
NAMES.long:
The time derivative of the flux-surface averaged metric is the rate of change, at fixed toroidal flux radius, of the radial derivative of enclosed plasma volume. The underlying metric is the geometric weight flux_surface_averaged_metric used when conservation laws are written in flux coordinates $(\rho_\mathrm{tor}, \theta, \phi)$.

Using the dimensional toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$, the quantity is defined as

$$
\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\right|_{\rho_\mathrm{tor}} \left( \frac{\partial V}{\partial \rho_\mathrm{tor}} \right)
$$

where $V(\rho_\mathrm{tor},t)$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the flux surface in $m^3$, $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is in meters, and $t$ is time in seconds. Thus $\partial V/\partial \rho_\mathrm{tor}$ has units $m^2$, and its time derivative has units $m^2.s^{-1}$.

In practice this quantity is obtained by differentiating the flux-surface volume metric in time at the same toroidal flux radius, using a time sequence of consistent equilibrium geometries. It accounts for the expansion or contraction of flux-surface volume elements in radial transport equations. The poloidal-coordinate counterpart is related to poloidal_flux_surface_averaged_metric; transformations involving poloidal flux use [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux), and time-dependent flux relabeling is closely related to [time_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_constant_toroidal_flux](name:time_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux).

The value is zero for a time-independent equilibrium geometry, positive where the local volume metric increases with time, and negative where it decreases. No universal numerical range is machine independent; its magnitude scales with the local metric and with the inverse timescale of equilibrium evolution, so it is typically interpreted relative to $\partial V/\partial \rho_\mathrm{tor}$ and the relevant transport timescale.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Time rate of change of the poloidal magnetic flux at a fixed flux-surface label, governing the resistive evolution of the current density profile via the flux diffusion equation.
NAMES.long:
The partial time derivative $\partial\psi/\partial t$ of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) $\psi$ quantifies how rapidly the flux profile changes at each flux-surface label as the plasma current profile evolves. It is the central time-advance term in the poloidal flux diffusion equation, governing the resistive-timescale evolution of the current density and safety-factor profile. Because $\psi$ depends on the chosen radial flux coordinate, the partial time derivative is strictly defined only with that coordinate held fixed; the sibling [time_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_constant_toroidal_flux](name:time_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux) makes this explicit by constraining differentiation to constant toroidal flux $\Phi$.

By Faraday's law, $\partial\psi/\partial t$ equals the negative circulation of the toroidal electric field around the corresponding flux contour:

$$
\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t} = -\oint_C \mathbf{E}\cdot d\boldsymbol{\ell}
$$

where $C$ is the closed toroidal circuit at flux-surface label $r$ and $d\boldsymbol{\ell}$ is oriented in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. In resistive MHD, this loop electromotive force is balanced by the parallel resistive response and non-inductive current-drive source terms, yielding the parabolic flux diffusion equation that self-consistently evolves the current profile alongside the [radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:radial_derivative_of_poloidal_magnetic_flux).

This quantity is computed numerically within transport solvers by finite-differencing $\psi$ between successive time steps at fixed grid points in the chosen radial coordinate. Typical magnitudes range from $\sim 10^{-3}$ V during quasi-steady operation to $\sim 1$ V during current ramp-up phases.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ increases with time at the given flux-surface label.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_radius_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Radial flux-surface coordinate equal to the square root of the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux divided by pi times the reference toroidal field, evaluated at the location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux radius at the internal transport barrier (ITB) locates the ITB on the flux-surface coordinate $\rho_\text{tor}$. An ITB is a region of strongly suppressed turbulent transport in the plasma interior that produces steep radial gradients in temperature, density, or toroidal rotation profiles, typically arising under reversed or relaxed magnetic shear conditions.

$$
\rho_\text{tor} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_\text{tor}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\Phi_\text{tor}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the flux surface and $B_0$ is the reference vacuum toroidal field at the geometric center. This coordinate increases monotonically from zero at the magnetic axis — see [toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis) — to its value at the last closed flux surface, making it a well-ordered radial label for all confined flux surfaces.

The ITB position is determined by identifying the peak logarithmic gradient in a measured kinetic profile — for instance from Thomson scattering or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy — and converting the physical location to $\rho_\text{tor}$ via equilibrium reconstruction. The analogous quantity for edge transport barriers is [toroidal_flux_radius_at_pedestal_top](name:toroidal_flux_radius_at_pedestal_top), while the underlying dimensionless radial coordinate is [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux $\Phi_\text{tor}$ threads the flux surface in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, yielding $\rho_\text{tor} \geq 0$ for all physically confined flux surfaces.

NAMES.name: toroidal_vorticity
NAMES.short: The toroidal (phi-direction) component of the plasma vorticity vector, equal to the projection of the curl of the plasma flow velocity onto the toroidal unit vector.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal vorticity is the $\hat{\phi}$-component of the plasma vorticity vector $\boldsymbol{\omega} = \nabla \times \mathbf{v}$, where $\mathbf{v}$ is the bulk plasma flow velocity. It captures the rotational structure of the plasma flow field in the toroidal direction and is a key quantity in MHD and two-fluid transport models describing momentum transport in magnetically confined plasmas.

The toroidal component is defined as:

$$
\omega_\phi = (\nabla \times \mathbf{v}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis.

This quantity is computed from the plasma velocity field resolved on a generalized grid and enters the vorticity transport equation governing toroidally and poloidally asymmetric flows. The related scalar ratio_of_plasma_vorticity_to_major_radius represents $\omega_\phi / R$ and appears naturally in the cylindrical form of the toroidal vorticity equation. The full vorticity vector is also decomposed into [radial_vorticity](name:radial_vorticity), [poloidal_vorticity](name:poloidal_vorticity), and [parallel_vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity) components, together forming a complete representation of the plasma rotational flow structure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $(\nabla \times \mathbf{v}) \cdot \hat{\phi}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: total_current_density
NAMES.short: Net electric current density summing all current-carrying mechanisms — ohmic, bootstrap, and externally driven contributions — over all plasma species, before specialization to any geometric or magnetic-field projection direction.
NAMES.long:
Total current density is the net conventional charge flux per unit area at a plasma point, formed by aggregating all current-carrying processes — ohmic induction, bootstrap, and externally driven currents — over all resolved species and charge states. It generalizes [current_density](name:current_density) to represent the full sum of current mechanisms appearing in transport and edge-plasma models, serving as the common physical basis for directional projections.

The aggregate satisfies:

$$
J_\mathrm{total} = J_\mathrm{ohmic} + J_\mathrm{bootstrap} + J_\mathrm{drive}
$$

where $J_\mathrm{ohmic}$ is the ohmic inductive contribution driven by loop voltage, $J_\mathrm{bootstrap}$ is the pressure-gradient-driven neoclassical component, and $J_\mathrm{drive}$ collects all external current-drive sources, each in A m$^{-2}$.

Directional projections specialize this parent for specific transport and edge modeling contexts: the field-aligned (parallel) component governs current balance in transport equations, while poloidal, radial, and vertical projections appear in edge models where cross-field charge transport matters — the radial projection is particularly relevant alongside other edge transport quantities such as [radial_plasma_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_plasma_momentum_diffusion_coefficient). Vertical and toroidal components are resolved along $\hat{Z}$ and $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.
NAMES.sign: Positive when conventional current flows in the positive direction of the chosen projection coordinate — in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ for toroidal projections, along $+\hat{Z}$ for vertical projections, outward along the flux-surface normal for radial projections, or aligned with the reference magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ for the parallel projection.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_current_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged parallel total current density, defined by the total current density projected on the magnetic field and normalized by the signed reference toroidal magnetic field. It is the net field-aligned current density used in transport current-balance physics.
NAMES.long:
Parallel total current density is a signed scalar measure of the net total current flowing along the magnetic field, expressed with the flux-surface-averaged, reference-field-normalized convention used in transport physics. It combines all physical mechanisms contributing to the total current before evaluating the field-aligned component.

The defining convention is the flux-surface average of the magnetic-field projection of the total current density divided by the signed reference toroidal magnetic field:

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{tot}} = \frac{\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle}{B_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $B_0$ is the signed reference toroidal magnetic field in T, and $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes an average over a magnetic flux surface.

In practice, the quantity is computed by forming the total current density, taking its scalar product with the magnetic field, applying the flux-surface average, and dividing by $B_0$. Magnetic-equilibrium constraints determine the current distribution, while kinetic and current-drive physics may determine how individual contributions add to the total; this quantity is the summed total after applying the same convention.

Representative magnitudes in tokamak transport analyzes are commonly $10^4$-$10^7$ A m$^{-2}$, depending on plasma current, cross-sectional area, magnetic geometry, and non-inductive current drive.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle$ has the same sign as the signed reference toroidal magnetic field $B_0$; $B_0$ is positive when the reference toroidal field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: total_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Total number density of free electrons per unit volume, equal to the sum of thermal and non-thermal electron populations.
NAMES.long:
Total electron density is the number of free electrons per unit volume, including both the Maxwellian thermal population and any non-thermal or fast-electron population. It is the population-resolved form of [electron_density](name:electron_density) when the total is explicitly distinguished from [thermal_electron_density](name:thermal_electron_density) and [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density).

The total density is defined by summing the thermal and fast electron contributions:

$$
n_e^{\rm tot} = n_e^{\rm th} + n_e^{\rm fast}
$$

where $n_e^{\rm tot}$ is the total electron density, $n_e^{\rm th}$ is the thermal electron density, and $n_e^{\rm fast}$ is the fast-electron density. In quasineutral plasma regions it is constrained approximately by $n_e^{\rm tot} \simeq \sum_i Z_i n_i$, where $Z_i$ and $n_i$ are the charge state and density of ion species $i$.

Total electron density is inferred from diagnostics sensitive to electron number, such as interferometry, reflectometry, Thomson scattering, and spectroscopy, often combined with equilibrium or transport modeling. Thermal diagnostics usually dominate the estimate in the confined plasma, while fast-electron contributions may be important during strong auxiliary heating, current drive, runaway-electron production, or energetic-electron transport into the edge and scrape-off layer. Together with electron temperature and population composition, it contributes to quantities such as [total_electron_pressure](name:total_electron_pressure).

Typical values are about $0.1-2 \times 10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ in many confined tokamak plasmas, rising to several $10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ in high-density regimes. Edge and scrape-off-layer values commonly span $10^{17}-10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, depending on fueling, recycling, detachment, and distance from the last closed flux surface.

NAMES.name: radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: First radial derivative of the total (thermal plus non-thermal) electron number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, used to evaluate electron density gradient terms in particle transport equations.
NAMES.long:
The radial derivative of [total_electron_density](name:total_electron_density) quantifies how rapidly the combined thermal and non-thermal electron density changes along the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, where $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 1$ at the last closed flux surface.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\frac{dn_e^\mathrm{tot}}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}}
$$

where $n_e^\mathrm{tot}$ is the total electron number density (thermal plus non-thermal contributions, in m$^{-3}$) and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is the dimensionless normalized toroidal flux coordinate.

This gradient term enters directly into the discretized radial particle transport equation for electrons and is evaluated numerically from the density profile during transport solver iterations. The [second_radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density) provides the curvature term needed for higher-order discretization schemes. The corresponding quantity for the non-thermal electron sub-population is [radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density](name:radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density), while the ion-species analog is [radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_ion_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when total electron density increases in the direction of increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: second_radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Second derivative of total electron number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, quantifying the radial curvature of the electron density profile.
NAMES.long:
The second radial derivative of total electron density characterizes the curvature of the electron density profile along the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$. The total electron density $n_e$ encompasses both thermal and non-thermal (fast) electron sub-populations, making this derivative applicable across all plasma regimes where both contribute — consistent with [total_electron_density](name:total_electron_density).

The quantity is formally defined as:

$$
\frac{\partial^2 n_e}{\partial \rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}^2}
$$

where $n_e$ is the total electron number density and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} \in [0, 1]$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, with $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm} = 1$ at the last-closed flux surface. Because $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$ is dimensionless, this second derivative carries the same units as the density itself.

This derivative is computed numerically within transport solver discretizations, where second-order spatial operators appear in the diffusion terms of the radial transport equations. It complements the first-order [radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density](name:radial_derivative_of_total_electron_density), together providing both the gradient and curvature information needed for higher-order numerical schemes. The corresponding quantity for the fast electron sub-population is [second_radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_fast_electron_density), and the analogous ion-state quantity is [second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density](name:second_radial_derivative_of_total_ion_state_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total electron density profile is concave upward with respect to increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, i.e., when the outward radial gradient of $n_e$ increases with increasing normalized toroidal flux.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_total_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Temporal rate of change of total electron number density, including thermal and nonthermal electrons. It is positive for local electron accumulation and negative for depletion.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the local temporal rate of change of [total_electron_density](name:total_electron_density), where total electron density includes both [thermal_electron_density](name:thermal_electron_density) and [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density). It represents electron accumulation or depletion at a point or on a flux surface, rather than the volume-averaged tendency represented by [time_derivative_of_volume_averaged_electron_density](name:time_derivative_of_volume_averaged_electron_density).

The compact definition is:

$$
\dot{n}_e^{\mathrm{tot}} \equiv \frac{\partial n_e^{\mathrm{tot}}}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(n_{e,\mathrm{th}} + n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}\right)
$$

where $n_e^{\mathrm{tot}}$ is total electron density, $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is thermal electron density, $n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is fast-electron density, and $t$ is time. As a time derivative of number density, the physical units are $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ when time is measured in seconds.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from time-resolved density measurements, kinetic reconstructions, or transport analysis by differentiating the total electron density with respect to time. In a flux-surface-averaged particle balance using flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\rho$ increasing from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary, it is determined by net volumetric electron sources and sinks together with the divergence of electron particle flux; positive outward flux is directed toward larger $\rho$.

Typical absolute values are near zero during stationary phases, often below $10^{18}-10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ within experimental and modeling uncertainty. Density ramps, gas fueling, pellet injection, or rapid edge transients can produce local rates of $10^{19}-10^{21}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, with still larger short-lived values possible in disruptions or very localized events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total electron density increases with increasing time.

NAMES.name: total_neutral_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Total kinetic pressure of neutral particles, summing both thermal and non-thermal (fast) contributions across all internal states of the neutral species.
NAMES.long:
Total neutral pressure is the combined kinetic pressure of the neutral particle population, comprising isotropic thermal pressure from neutrals near local thermodynamic equilibrium and non-thermal pressure from suprathermal (fast) neutrals, aggregated across all internal quantum states of the species.

The total pressure decomposes as:

$$
p_\mathrm{neutral} = p_\mathrm{th} + p_\mathrm{fast}
$$

where $p_\mathrm{th} = n_\mathrm{th}\,k_B\,T_\mathrm{neutral}$ is the thermal contribution, $n_\mathrm{th}$ is the thermal neutral number density, $T_\mathrm{neutral}$ is the neutral temperature, and $p_\mathrm{fast}$ is the non-thermal pressure from suprathermal neutrals, computed as one-third of the second velocity moment of the fast neutral distribution function.

In plasma transport modeling, the neutral pressure profile is computed from coupled fluid or kinetic neutral models in which charge exchange and ionization redistribute momentum between the neutral and plasma populations. This quantity enters plasma momentum and energy balance equations as a source term and governs neutral penetration depth into the confined plasma.

In core plasma regions, strong ionization screens neutral penetration and total neutral pressures remain well below 1 Pa. In the edge plasma and scrape-off layer, values range from 0.01–10 Pa under standard recycling conditions; near divertor strike points during high-recycling operation, values can approach tens of Pa. The state-resolved counterpart is [total_neutral_state_pressure](name:total_neutral_state_pressure); the thermal-only contribution is described by [thermal_neutral_pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure); and the analogous ion quantity is [total_ion_state_pressure](name:total_ion_state_pressure). The parent quantity [neutral_pressure](name:neutral_pressure) describes gage measurements of bulk neutral gas pressure in the vacuum vessel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles exert an outward kinetic pressure on an enclosing surface element, consistent with pressure as a non-negative second-order moment of the neutral velocity distribution.

NAMES.name: total_plasma_mass_density
NAMES.short: Total plasma mass density is the local plasma mass per unit volume, formed by summing the particle mass times number density over all charged plasma species: electrons, main ion isotopes, and impurity charge states. Neutral atoms and molecules are excluded.
NAMES.long:
Total plasma mass density is the local mass of the charged plasma constituents per unit volume. It is the scalar inertial density of the multi-species mixture, set by the particle populations present at a given location.

The defining relation is the species mass sum:

$$
\rho = \sum_s m_s n_s
$$

where $\rho$ is the total plasma mass density (in kg.m^-3), $s$ indexes the plasma species, $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$ (in kg), and $n_s$ is its local number density (in m^-3). The sum runs over electrons and every charged ion or impurity charge state in the plasma composition; the electron term $m_e n_e$ is typically negligible because ion masses exceed the electron mass by a factor of roughly 1836 or more. Neutral atoms and molecules are not included here, in contrast to the separately defined density summed over electrons, ions, and neutrals.

In practice the total plasma mass density is reconstructed from measured or inferred species densities and composition: electron density measurements, quasineutrality, isotope fractions, impurity concentrations, and charge-state information constrain the individual terms in the sum. In single-fluid plasma descriptions it is the coefficient multiplying the material acceleration in the momentum balance and it sets the Alfven speed $v_A = B / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}$.

In confined deuterium or deuterium-tritium plasmas with particle densities near $10^{19}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3, typical values are about $3 \times 10^{-8}$-$3 \times 10^{-7}$ kg.m^-3. Lower-density edge or scrape-off-layer regions can fall to $10^{-10}$-$10^{-8}$ kg.m^-3, while high-density detached edge regions may approach core values.

NAMES.name: tritium_tritium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: tritium_tritium
NAMES.short: Global neutron count rate from thermonuclear tritium-tritium fusion reactions between thermal tritons. It is the thermal-plasma TT-channel contribution to the aggregate thermal-fusion neutron emission rate and excludes beam-thermal and beam-beam fusion.
NAMES.long:
Tritium-tritium flux due to thermal fusion is the globally integrated neutron emission rate from TT reactions between Maxwellian thermal tritons. Here flux denotes a count rate with unit hertz, not a surface flux density. It is the TT-channel contribution to [thermal_neutron_flux](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), while [tritium_tritium_flux](name:tritium_tritium_flux) is the total TT neutron rate including thermal-thermal, beam-thermal, and beam-beam contributions when those populations are present.

The thermal TT neutron count rate is the volume integral of the local neutron source density:

$$
\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{TT}}^{\mathrm{th}} = \int_V \nu_n\,\frac{n_T^2}{2}\,\langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{TT}}(T_T)\,dV
$$

where $\nu_n$ is the neutron multiplicity per TT fusion reaction, normally 2 for the $\mathrm{T}+\mathrm{T}\rightarrow\alpha+2n$ channel, $n_T$ is the thermal triton density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{TT}}$ is the Maxwellian-averaged TT reactivity in $\mathrm{m}^3\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ at thermal triton temperature $T_T$, and $dV$ is a volume element in $\mathrm{m}^3$. The result has unit $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, equivalent to hertz; the TT neutron energies form a continuum rather than a monoenergetic line.

In practice this rate is computed from thermal tritium density, ion temperature, and plasma volume using evaluated fusion-reactivity fits. It may be constrained by neutron diagnostics such as fission chambers, activation systems, scintillators, or spectrometers, provided the TT thermal contribution can be separated from DD, DT, beam-driven, and background neutron sources.

Typical values range from below $10^{10}$ Hz in trace-tritium or low-temperature plasmas to $10^{15}$-$10^{18}$ Hz in high-temperature plasmas with an appreciable thermal tritium population. The rate scales approximately with $n_T^2$, plasma volume, and the strongly temperature-dependent TT reactivity.

NAMES.name: vertical_current_density
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-component of the electric current density vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, giving the net conventional charge flux per unit area directed along the Z-axis.
NAMES.long:
The vertical component of the [current_density](name:current_density) vector quantifies the net conventional charge flux per unit area flowing along the vertical $Z$-axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining projection is:

$$
j_Z = \mathbf{j} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}$ is the full plasma current density vector satisfying Ampere's law $\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}$, with $\mathbf{B}$ the magnetic field and $\mu_0$ the permeability of free space.

In the plasma core, $j_Z$ is typically small relative to the dominant toroidal component, but becomes significant near X-points, the divertor, and throughout the edge and scrape-off layer where poloidal and vertical current structures develop. This base quantity carries no aggregation qualifier; the [vertical_total_current_density](name:vertical_total_current_density) sums contributions from all physical mechanisms, vertical_inertial_current_density isolates the polarization (inertial) contribution, and [vertical_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) captures the viscous channel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing $Z$ (upward) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_vorticity
NAMES.short: Vertical vorticity is the projection of the plasma vorticity vector onto the vertical Z direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is the Z-component of the curl of the plasma fluid velocity and measures signed local rotation in the R-φ plane.
NAMES.long:
Vertical vorticity is the component of the plasma-fluid [vorticity](name:vorticity) vector along the vertical axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$. It measures the signed local angular shear of the velocity field associated with circulation about the vertical direction. The complementary cylindrical components are [radial_vorticity](name:radial_vorticity) and [toroidal_vorticity](name:toroidal_vorticity); related magnetic-geometry projections include [poloidal_vorticity](name:poloidal_vorticity) and [parallel_vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity).

For a plasma fluid velocity $\mathbf{v}$ with cylindrical components $v_R$ and $v_\phi$, the vertical component of the curl is

$$
\omega_Z = (\nabla \times \mathbf{v})\cdot\hat{Z} = \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial (R v_\phi)}{\partial R} - \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial v_R}{\partial \phi}
$$

where derivatives are taken in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and $\omega_Z$ has unit s^-1. In axisymmetric conditions the toroidal-derivative term is absent, so vertical vorticity is mainly the radial shear of $R v_\phi$; in non-axisymmetric or turbulent flows, toroidal variation of the radial velocity can also contribute.

Vertical vorticity is computed by differentiating measured or modeled velocity fields. In experiments the required velocity components can be inferred from flow diagnostics and from reconstructed $E\times B$, diamagnetic, or parallel-flow contributions; in transport and turbulence modeling it is obtained directly from the simulated plasma velocity field or from drift-reduced stream-function formulations.

Typical magnitudes are 10^3-10^5 s^-1 for slowly varying core rotation shear, 10^4-10^6 s^-1 in edge transport barriers and scrape-off-layer turbulence, and up to 10^6-10^7 s^-1 during rapid transient or small-scale shear events. The signed value may change across shear layers, vortices, and turbulent eddies.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $(\nabla \times \mathbf{v})$ points in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_beryllium_density
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Volume average of the beryllium ion number density over the confined plasma volume, yielding a single global scalar measure of beryllium impurity content in a discharge.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged beryllium ion number density is a global integral summary of the beryllium impurity content within the confined plasma. It collapses the spatially varying local [beryllium_density](name:beryllium_density) profile into a single representative value by integrating over the total plasma volume.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{Be} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_\mathrm{Be}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Be}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local beryllium ion number density summed over all ionization states and $V$ is the total confined plasma volume.

This quantity is obtained by integrating beryllium impurity density profiles — inferred from vacuum ultraviolet spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or impurity transport modeling — against the volume element derived from equilibrium reconstruction. The complementary chord-averaged measure is [line_averaged_beryllium_density](name:line_averaged_beryllium_density), which is directly accessible from line-integrated spectroscopic diagnostics without requiring a full volume integration. The normalized impurity content is captured by [ratio_of_beryllium_density_to_electron_density](name:ratio_of_beryllium_density_to_electron_density).

Beryllium (atomic number $Z = 4$) is a low-Z impurity whose volume-averaged density is several orders of magnitude below the electron density. For typical electron densities of $10^{19}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, beryllium impurity fractions of $10^{-3}$–$10^{-2}$ correspond to absolute values of order $10^{16}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when beryllium ions are present within the confined plasma volume.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_boron_density
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Volume average of the total boron number density over the plasma volume. The density includes neutral boron and all boron ionization states, giving a global measure of elemental boron impurity content.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged boron density is the total elemental boron number density averaged over the confined plasma volume bounded by the last-closed flux surface. It includes neutral boron and all ionization states of boron, so it represents the abundance of boron nuclei rather than the density of a single charge state.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle n_B \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_B(\mathbf{x})\,dV,\qquad n_B = \sum_{q=0}^{5} n_{\mathrm{B}^{q+}}
$$

where $V_p$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last-closed flux surface, $n_B(\mathbf{x})$ is the local total boron number density, and $n_{\mathrm{B}^{q+}}$ is the density of boron in charge state $q$, with $q=0$ denoting neutral boron and $q=5$ fully stripped boron. All number densities are in m^-3 and $V_p$ is in m^3.

In practice, this quantity is inferred from impurity diagnostics and plasma modeling that constrain the boron charge-state distribution, spatial distribution, and neutral contribution. Spectroscopic measurements, charge-state-resolved impurity analysis, and transport or collisional-radiative modeling may be combined to estimate the local $n_B$ before integration over the last-closed-flux-surface volume.

Typical values are trace-impurity densities relative to the main plasma density, often about 10^15-10^18 m^-3 in boron-conditioned tokamak plasmas, with larger values possible during active boron injection, strong wall sources, or transient impurity influx events.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_carbon_density
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume mean of the total carbon number density, summed over all charge states from neutral to fully stripped carbon.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged carbon density is the spatial mean of the total carbon particle number density over the confined plasma volume, aggregating contributions from all ionization states. It serves as a single global scalar monitor of the total carbon impurity inventory in the confined plasma, applied in impurity transport analysis and energy-balance accounting.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_C \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V \sum_{z=0}^{6} n_{C,z}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_{C,z}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local number density of carbon in ionization state $z$ (from neutral $z=0$ through fully stripped $z=6$), and $V$ is the plasma volume bounded by the last-closed flux surface. This quantity is the volume-averaging transformation applied to [carbon_density](name:carbon_density).

In practice it is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy of carbon emission lines, ultraviolet spectroscopy, or impurity transport modeling integrated over the full plasma cross-section.

Typical values range from $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in low-impurity plasmas with conditioned walls, rising toward $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in carbon-wall machines with significant recycling. The companion [line_averaged_carbon_density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density) provides a chord-weighted rather than volume-weighted mean; the two quantities differ in the presence of radial density gradients. Analogous volume-averaged impurity densities for other light species are [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) and [volume_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density), which follow the same transformation-subject-base grammar pattern.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_deuterium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Deuterium ion number density averaged over the total plasma volume, providing a global scalar measure of the deuterium fuel inventory normalized to the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged deuterium ion number density is the spatial mean of the local deuterium ion density over the entire confined plasma volume. It collapses the full radial and poloidal density profile into a single global figure of merit for fuel inventory monitoring, complementing local point values such as [deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis) at the plasma center or [deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:deuterium_density_at_plasma_boundary) at the edge.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_D \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_D(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_D(\mathbf{r})$ is the local deuterium ion number density at position $\mathbf{r}$ and $V$ is the total confined plasma volume.

In practice, this quantity is derived by integrating radial density profiles — obtained from Thomson scattering, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or reflectometry — over the plasma volume element from equilibrium reconstruction. It differs from [line_averaged_deuterium_density](name:line_averaged_deuterium_density), which represents a chord-weighted average along an interferometry line of sight rather than a true volume integral. The analogous quantity for hydrogen fuel ions is [volume_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_hydrogen_density).

Typical values in deuterium-fueled tokamak plasmas range from $0.5 \times 10^{19}$ to $1 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on the fueling scenario, density operational point, and proximity to the Greenwald density limit.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_effective_charge
NAMES.short: The volume average of the effective ionic charge Zeff over the plasma, providing a single global scalar characterization of bulk impurity content.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged effective charge is the plasma-volume mean of the local effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$, a dimensionless parameter quantifying how multi-charged impurity species elevate the mean-square ionic charge above the pure-hydrogen baseline. It is derived from the local [effective_charge](name:effective_charge) profile by integrating over the confined plasma volume $V$.

The local effective charge is defined by the ionic-density-weighted charge ratio

$$
Z_\text{eff}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\sum_i n_i(\mathbf{r}) \, Z_i^2}{n_e(\mathbf{r})}
$$

where $n_i$ is the number density of the $i$-th ion species, $Z_i$ is the corresponding atomic charge number, and $n_e = \sum_i n_i Z_i$ is the electron density imposed by quasi-neutrality. The volume-averaged quantity integrates this local value over the confined plasma volume.

This global scalar is inferred from continuum bremsstrahlung spectroscopy, where radiated power scales as $P_\text{brem} \propto n_e^2 Z_\text{eff} T_e^{1/2}$, or from impurity density profiles measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. The [line_averaged_effective_charge](name:line_averaged_effective_charge) provides an alternative single-chord diagnostic proxy, while [effective_charge_at_limiter](name:effective_charge_at_limiter) gives the boundary value. A pure deuterium plasma has $Z_\text{eff} = 1$; moderate impurity levels in tokamak operation yield values in the range 1.2–4, with values above 3 indicating substantial high-$Z$ contamination.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any physical plasma composition, since all ion densities $n_i$ and charge numbers $Z_i$ entering the defining sum are non-negative.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density averaged over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, providing the primary global scalar for discharge density characterization and density feedback control.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged electron density $\langle n_e \rangle$ is the mean of the local electron number density integrated over the plasma volume $V$ bounded by the last closed flux surface (LCFS). It compresses the full radial electron density profile into a single global scalar that quantifies the total electron content of the discharge, serving as a primary parameter in confinement characterization and fueling control.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_e \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_e(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_e(\mathbf{r})$ is the local [electron density] and $V$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the LCFS.

Multi-channel interferometry estimates $\langle n_e \rangle$ directly by combining line-integrated electron density measurements from multiple viewing chords spanning different minor-radius positions. Profile diagnostics such as Thomson scattering and reflectometry constrain the spatial distribution, while equilibrium reconstruction provides the LCFS boundary geometry that defines $V$.

Representative values in H-mode tokamak discharges span $0.3$–$1.5 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with the volume average lying below the on-axis peak for centrally-peaked profiles. Together with [volume_averaged_electron_temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature) and [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density), it forms the set of global scalar parameters entering energy confinement scaling laws and Greenwald density-limit assessments.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electrons are present within the plasma volume.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Time derivative of the electron number density averaged over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. It quantifies how the mean free-electron density changes as the plasma gains or loses particles and as the averaging volume evolves.
NAMES.long:
Time derivative of volume-averaged electron density is the temporal rate of change of the free-electron number density averaged over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. It describes accumulation or depletion of electrons in the volume-mean density, independent of the diagnostic or reconstruction method used to infer the density.

For an instantaneous averaging volume $V(t)$, the defining derivative is

$$
\frac{d\langle n_e \rangle_V}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left[\frac{1}{V(t)}\int_{V(t)} n_e(\mathbf{x},t)\,dV\right]
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density in m^-3, $V(t)$ is the averaging volume in m^3, $t$ is time in s, and $d\langle n_e \rangle_V/dt$ has unit m^-3.s^-1. The simplified fixed-volume relation $d\langle n_e \rangle_V/dt = (1/V)\int_V \partial n_e/\partial t\,dV$ is exact only when the averaging volume is not changing; for a last-closed-flux-surface-bounded volume that evolves in time, boundary motion and the changing normalization also contribute.

In practice, this quantity is obtained by differentiating a reconstructed or fitted time trace of [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density). The density estimate may combine line-integrated interferometry, Thomson scattering, reflectometry, or other electron-density measurements constrained by the plasma equilibrium; smoothing, fitting, or physics-based filtering is commonly used because time differentiation amplifies measurement noise. In particle-balance interpretation, $V\,d\langle n_e \rangle_V/dt$ represents the fixed-volume rate of change of free-electron content and is compared with ionization, recombination, fueling, recycling, and particle flux through the plasma boundary.

Typical values are near 0 m^-3.s^-1 during density flat-top phases, with slow ramps often in the range 1e18-1e20 m^-3.s^-1. Strong gas fueling, pellet injection, rapid pump-out, disruptions, or termination phases can produce transient magnitudes of 1e20-1e22 m^-3.s^-1, depending on plasma size and confinement conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the volume-averaged electron density increases with time.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron temperature averaged over the plasma volume inside the last closed flux surface. It is a global scalar measure of the bulk electron thermal state for confinement and thermal energy balance studies.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged electron temperature is the electron temperature averaged with equal weight over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. It is a non-negative scalar that represents the bulk electron thermal state, distinct from a central, line-averaged, or density-weighted temperature. Because it is a volume integral of the local temperature, it depends on the spatial distribution of $T_e$ within the closed-field-line region.

The volume average is defined by integrating the local electron temperature over the enclosed plasma volume:

$$
\langle T_e \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} \int_{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} T_e(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $\langle T_e \rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged electron temperature in eV, $T_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local electron temperature in eV at position $\mathbf{x}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, and $V_\mathrm{LCFS}$ is the plasma volume inside the last closed flux surface in m^3.

In practice it is computed by combining measurements or model estimates of the electron temperature distribution with the reconstructed plasma geometry. Thomson scattering, electron cyclotron emission, spectroscopy, and transport modeling can contribute to the local temperature estimate; interpolation and flux-surface mapping are commonly needed to cover the full closed plasma volume.

Typical values range from about 1-100 eV during early plasma formation, 100-1000 eV in cold or low-power discharges, and 1000-10000 eV in well-heated tokamak plasmas, with higher values possible in high-performance regimes.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_helium_3_density
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged helium-3 ion density over the full confined plasma volume. It is the mean number density of charged helium-3 ions, summed over singly ionized and fully stripped states and excluding neutral atoms.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged helium-3 density is the plasma-volume mean of the helium-3 ion number density. It includes only charged helium-3 ionization states, $^3\mathrm{He}^{1+}$ and $^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}$, and excludes neutral helium-3 atoms.

The volume average is obtained by integrating the ion-state-summed local density over the confined plasma volume and dividing by that volume:

$$
\langle n_{^3\mathrm{He}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p}\left(\sum_{q=1}^{2} n_{^3\mathrm{He}^{q+}}(\mathbf{r})\right)\,dV
$$

where $\langle n_{^3\mathrm{He}} \rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged helium-3 ion density in m^-3, $V_p$ is the confined plasma volume in m^3, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, $\mathbf{r}$ denotes position in the plasma, $q$ is the ion charge state, and $n_{^3\mathrm{He}^{q+}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local density in m^-3 of helium-3 ions with charge $q+$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from particle-balance analysis or minority-species transport modeling constrained by spectroscopic measurements, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy when applicable, and other diagnostics sensitive to helium isotope content. It is the volume-average counterpart of [line_averaged_helium_3_density](name:line_averaged_helium_3_density); local quantities such as [helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis) describe where the helium-3 ions are concentrated, while [volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density) is the analogous volume mean for the neighboring isotope.

Typical values range from near zero in plasmas without helium-3 fueling to 10^16-10^19 m^-3 for minority-ion heating scenarios, and can reach 10^19-10^20 m^-3 in plasmas where helium-3 is a significant fuel component.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_helium_3_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Ratio of the volume-averaged helium-3 ion number density to the volume-averaged electron number density, where each density is independently averaged over the confined plasma volume before division.
NAMES.long:
The ratio $\langle n_\mathrm{He3} \rangle_V / \langle n_e \rangle_V$ quantifies the helium-3 contribution to plasma composition relative to the total electron population. Averaging each density independently over the confined plasma volume before forming the ratio makes this quantity mathematically distinct from the volume average of the local density ratio $\langle n_\mathrm{He3} / n_e \rangle_V$; the two coincide only when the $^3$He and electron density profiles are strictly proportional.

$$
f_{\mathrm{He3}} = \frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{He3}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $\langle n_{\mathrm{He3}} \rangle_V$ and $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ are the volume-averaged helium-3 ion and electron number densities in m$^{-3}$.

The numerator is inferred from spectroscopic impurity analysis or particle balance combined with transport modeling, while the denominator is obtained from line-integrated interferometric measurements. In minority-heating schemes, values range from 0.03 to 0.10; in advanced D-$^3$He fuel-cycle studies, the ratio can reach 0.5. The closely related [helium_3_fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_helium_3_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density) encodes the same global composition metric; this explicit form removes any ambiguity about whether averaging precedes or follows the ratio operation. The [volume_averaged_helium_3_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_3_density) provides the numerator separately, and the analogous helium-4 composition metric is given by [fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_helium_4_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_helium_4_density
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Mean number density of helium-4 ions obtained by integrating the local density over the total confined plasma volume, providing a single global measure of fusion-ash accumulation in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged helium-4 density is the spatial mean of the local [helium_4_density](name:helium_4_density) over the entire confined plasma volume. As the primary thermonuclear ash product of deuterium-tritium reactions, helium-4 accumulates as alpha particles born near 3.5 MeV slow down and thermalize; the steady-state level is set by the balance between thermonuclear production and helium exhaust through the divertor.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_{{}^4\text{He}} \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_{{}^4\text{He}}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the local helium-4 ion number density and $V$ is the total confined plasma volume.

This quantity is inferred by integrating a reconstructed helium density profile over the plasma volume; input profiles are commonly obtained from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy targeting He$^{2+}$ emission or from integrated transport modeling. The [line_averaged_helium_4_density](name:line_averaged_helium_4_density) offers a related chord-integrated measure that diverges from the volume average when the density profile is strongly peaked or hollow. Companion volume-averaged densities for lighter species include [volume_averaged_helium_3_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_3_density) and [volume_averaged_hydrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_hydrogen_density).

In high-performance D-T discharges, the tolerable helium ash fraction relative to electron density is a few percent, corresponding to volume-averaged helium-4 densities of order $10^{18}$–$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ for typical electron densities near $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when helium-4 ions are present within the confined plasma volume.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_helium_4_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of the confined-volume-averaged helium-4 ion number density to the confined-volume-averaged electron number density, with the two averages evaluated independently before division.
NAMES.long:
This ratio is the quotient of the confined-volume average helium-4 ion number density and the confined-volume average electron number density. It is a global helium-4 concentration measure, not the volume average of the local pointwise ratio. In a fully ionized plasma, twice this value approximates the fraction of electron charge balance supplied by helium-4 ions.

The ratio is defined from independent volume averages over the confined plasma volume:

$$
f_{{}^4\mathrm{He},e}^{V} = \frac{\langle n_{{}^4\mathrm{He}}\rangle_V}{\langle n_e\rangle_V}, \qquad \langle n_s\rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_\mathrm{conf}} \int_{V_\mathrm{conf}} n_s(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $n_{{}^4\mathrm{He}}$ and $n_e$ are local helium-4 ion and electron number densities in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $dV$ is a volume element in $\mathrm{m}^3$, $V_\mathrm{conf}$ is the confined plasma volume in $\mathrm{m}^3$, and $\langle n_s\rangle_V$ has units of $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$. The resulting ratio is dimensionless.

It is computed by combining an equilibrium-based confined volume with spatially resolved or model-constrained density estimates. Electron density is commonly constrained by interferometry, polarimetry, reflectometry, or Thomson scattering, while helium-4 content may be inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, passive helium spectroscopy, neutral-particle measurements, or particle-transport analysis.

Typical values are about $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$ in trace-helium experiments and about $0.01$-$0.05$ in burning deuterium-tritium plasmas with controlled helium ash removal. Sustained values approaching $0.1$ indicate substantial helium dilution of the fuel mixture.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_ion_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged ion temperature for a specific ion species, integrated over the confined plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged ion temperature $\langle T_i \rangle$ is a global scalar derived from the local [ion_temperature](name:ion_temperature) profile by integrating over the entire confined plasma volume up to the last closed flux surface, providing a single aggregate measure of the thermal energy content for a given ion species.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle T_i \rangle = \frac{1}{V_{\rm LCFS}} \int_0^{V_{\rm LCFS}} T_i(V') \, dV'
$$

where $T_i(V')$ is the local ion temperature at volume coordinate $V'$ and $V_{\rm LCFS}$ is the total plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface.

In practice, $\langle T_i \rangle$ is evaluated by summing $T_i \, dV$ over nested flux surfaces, where the differential volume element $dV = 2\pi R \, dR \, dZ$ is computed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Local ion temperatures feeding into the profile are commonly obtained from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy on impurity or fuel ion emission lines.

Typical values range from 1–5 keV in standard L-mode plasmas to 5–20 keV in high-confinement H-mode or advanced scenarios on medium-to-large tokamaks. The species-summed counterpart is [volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature), while [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density) provides the analogous species-resolved density average. The ratio of on-axis to volume-averaged temperature, characterizing profile peaking, is given by ratio_of_ion_temperature_to_volume_averaged_ion_temperature.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_iron_density
NAMES.subject: iron
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged iron density is the total number density of ionized iron, summed over Fe charge states and averaged over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged iron density is the plasma-volume mean of the elemental iron ion number density. It includes all ionized charge states of iron and is non-negative because it is an average of number densities.

The volume average is defined by integrating the charge-state-summed iron density over the plasma volume:

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{Fe} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p} \int_{V_p} \left(\sum_{q=1}^{26} n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}(\mathbf{r})\right)\, dV
$$

where $V_p$ is the plasma volume in m$^3$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, $q$ is the ion charge-state index from singly ionized iron to fully stripped iron, and $n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{q+}}$ is the local number density of charge state $q$ in m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is inferred from impurity diagnostics and modeling that estimate the spatial distribution and charge-state balance of iron, then integrate over the confined plasma volume. It is complementary to local quantities such as [iron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:iron_density_at_magnetic_axis), chord-integrated measurements such as [line_averaged_iron_density](name:line_averaged_iron_density), and the normalized impurity content represented by iron_fraction.

Typical values are strongly device- and scenario-dependent because iron sources depend on plasma-facing materials, sputtering, erosion, transport, and core accumulation. In magnetically confined plasmas iron is usually a trace impurity, commonly interpreted through its fraction of the electron density; broad representative volume averages can range from about $10^{13}$-$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on operating conditions.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_krypton_density
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume average of the total local krypton number density, including all ionization states from neutral krypton through fully stripped krypton.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged krypton density is the total krypton particle content per unit plasma volume. It includes every krypton charge state, so it measures elemental krypton abundance rather than the density of one particular ionization stage.

The volume average is defined from the local total krypton density over the plasma volume:

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p}\left(\sum_{z=0}^{36} n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{z+}}(\mathbf{x})\right)\,dV
$$

where $\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged krypton density in m^-3, $V_p$ is the plasma volume in m^3, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, $n_{\mathrm{Kr}^{z+}}$ is the local number density of krypton charge state $z$ in m^-3, and $z=0$ denotes neutral krypton while $z=36$ denotes fully stripped krypton.

In practice this quantity is inferred by combining impurity transport modeling with spectroscopic measurements of selected krypton charge states, radiated-power constraints, gas-injection accounting, and charge-state balance calculations. It is closely related to line-averaged krypton density, but weights the local krypton density by plasma volume rather than by a diagnostic chord.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. Trace krypton concentrations may correspond to about 10^13-10^15 m^-3, while deliberate krypton seeding for radiation control can produce volume-averaged elemental densities of about 10^15-10^17 m^-3 in present tokamak plasmas, depending on electron density, confinement, and exhaust conditions.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_lithium_density
NAMES.subject: lithium
NAMES.short: Volume average of the lithium ion number density within the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. It provides a global measure of lithium impurity content per unit confined volume.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged lithium density is the confined-plasma volume average of the local lithium ion number density. It is the lithium-species analog of [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density) and quantifies the global lithium impurity content inside the last closed flux surface.

The volume average is defined by integrating the local lithium density over the confined plasma volume:

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Li}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}}\int_{V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}} n_{\mathrm{Li}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Li}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local lithium ion number density, $V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, and $dV$ is the physical volume element.

In practice this quantity is computed from a reconstructed lithium density distribution and the corresponding confined plasma volume. Lithium density may be inferred from spectroscopic measurements with collisional-radiative modeling, from impurity transport analysis, or from integrated plasma simulations constrained by diagnostics.

Typical values are about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ for trace lithium impurity content in tokamak plasmas, with strongly lithium-conditioned or actively lithium-injected plasmas occasionally reaching $10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume mean of the total nitrogen number density, summed over all ionization states from neutral to fully stripped nitrogen.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged nitrogen density $\langle n_N \rangle$ is the spatial mean of the local nitrogen number density over the entire plasma volume, with contributions from all charge states between neutral $N^0$ and fully stripped $N^{7+}$. It condenses the spatially varying impurity field into a single scalar that represents the total nitrogen inventory of the discharge, complementing the local [nitrogen_density](name:nitrogen_density) profiles resolved in space.

The defining spatial average is:

$$
\langle n_N \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_N(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the confined plasma volume and $n_N(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nitrogen number density at position $\mathbf{r}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, aggregated across all ionization states.

Nitrogen is deliberately seeded in fusion devices to radiate power in the divertor and scrape-off layer, reducing heat loads on plasma-facing components. The volume-averaged density is inferred from spectroscopic measurements of nitrogen line emission or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with global particle-balance analysis.

In nitrogen-seeded H-mode discharges, values range from $10^{17}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, a small fraction of the total electron density yet radiatively significant. For a chord-integrated counterpart, see [line_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density); [nitrogen_fraction](name:nitrogen_fraction) normalizes this density to the local electron density. The analogous quantity for neon impurity seeding is [volume_averaged_neon_density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_oxygen_density
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Volume average of the oxygen ion number density over the confined plasma volume inside the last closed flux surface, summed over oxygen ion charge states and excluding neutral oxygen.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged oxygen density is the spatial mean number density of oxygen ions in the confined plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface. It represents the total oxygen-ion inventory per unit plasma volume, summed over ion charge states rather than describing any single charge state or neutral oxygen population.

The average over the confined plasma volume is defined by:

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{O} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} \int_{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} n_\mathrm{O}(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $V_\mathrm{LCFS}$ is the volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, $dV$ is a volume element, and $n_\mathrm{O}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local oxygen ion density, conventionally summed over oxygen ion charge states from $\mathrm{O}^{+}$ through fully stripped $\mathrm{O}^{8+}$.

In practice this quantity is computed by combining an equilibrium-derived plasma volume with reconstructed oxygen ion density distributions from impurity transport analysis, charge-exchange measurements, and visible, vacuum-ultraviolet, or extreme-ultraviolet spectroscopy interpreted with collisional-radiative modeling. It is closely related to [line_averaged_oxygen_density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density), but a line average can differ from the true volume mean when the oxygen distribution is centrally peaked, hollow, or localized near the plasma edge.

Typical values are about $10^{15}$-$10^{17}$ m^-3 in low-oxygen tokamak plasmas and can reach $10^{18}$ m^-3 during oxygen-rich wall conditions, impurity accumulation, or strong recycling events. For representative volume-averaged electron densities of $10^{19}$-$10^{20}$ m^-3, these values correspond to oxygen fractions of roughly $10^{-4}$-$10^{-2}$, as captured by [oxygen_fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_oxygen_ion_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density). Oxygen contributes to radiative power losses and to the effective plasma charge, so comparison with [volume_averaged_total_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_density) and other impurity densities is useful for global particle and power balance.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Density-weighted effective temperature of the total thermal ion population — all species and charge states combined — averaged over the confined plasma volume, serving as a single global scalar measure of ion confinement performance.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged total ion temperature $\langle T_{i,\text{tot}} \rangle_V$ is the density-weighted mean thermal energy per ion, summed over all thermal ion species and charge states and integrated over the entire confined plasma volume. It reduces the full [total_ion_temperature](name:total_ion_temperature) radial profile to a single global scalar, making it a primary metric for comparing ion energy confinement across discharges and devices.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle T_{i,\text{tot}} \rangle_V = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_s \int n_s(\mathbf{r})\, T_s(\mathbf{r})\, dV}{\displaystyle\sum_s \int n_s(\mathbf{r})\, dV}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$, $T_s$ is its local temperature, and the integration extends over the plasma volume bounded by the last-closed flux surface.

This quantity is estimated by combining spatially resolved ion temperature profiles — measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy — with equilibrium-reconstructed volume elements, or inferred from stored ion thermal energy divided by total ion particle content. Typical values range from 2–10 keV in H-mode tokamak discharges and 0.5–3 keV in L-mode operation. For the species-resolved volume average see [volume_averaged_ion_temperature](name:volume_averaged_ion_temperature); the corresponding global pressure is [total_thermal_ion_pressure](name:total_thermal_ion_pressure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the thermal ion population carries non-zero kinetic energy; as a thermodynamic temperature this quantity is intrinsically non-negative.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_tritium_density
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged number density of tritium ions in the confined plasma. It is the confined-volume mean of the local tritium ion density and provides a global measure of hydrogen-3 fuel content.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged tritium ion density is the confined-plasma-volume mean of the local tritium ion number density. It reduces the spatial distribution of hydrogen-3 fuel ions to a single scalar representing the global tritium content of the main plasma.

The volume average is defined by integrating the local density over the confined plasma volume and dividing by that volume:

$$
\langle n_T \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p} \int_{V_p} n_T(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_T(\mathbf{r})$ is the local [tritium_density](name:tritium_density) in m^-3, $dV$ is a volume element, and $V_p$ is the confined plasma volume in m^3.

In practice, this quantity is computed by combining isotope-resolved tritium density information with the reconstructed confined plasma volume. The density information may come from charge-exchange spectroscopy, neutral-particle analysis, neutron-emission constraints in deuterium-tritium plasmas, or transport modeling constrained by measurements. It is distinct from [line_averaged_tritium_density](name:line_averaged_tritium_density), which weights density along a sightline, and complements location-specific quantities such as [tritium_density_at_pedestal](name:tritium_density_at_pedestal), [tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis), [tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:tritium_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [tritium_density_at_divertor_target](name:tritium_density_at_divertor_target).

Typical values are near zero in plasmas without tritium fueling, about $10^{18}$-$5 \times 10^{19}$ m^-3 in tritium or deuterium-tritium experiments, and can approach $10^{20}$ m^-3 in high-density burning-plasma scenarios depending on fueling, confinement, and isotope mix.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_tungsten_density
NAMES.subject: tungsten
NAMES.short: Mean number density of tungsten ions within the last closed flux surface, summed over all tungsten ionization states. It equals the total confined tungsten ion count divided by the enclosed plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged tungsten density is the mean number density of tungsten ions inside the last closed flux surface. It includes all ionic charge states of tungsten and represents the total confined tungsten ion population divided by the plasma volume enclosed by that surface.

The volume average over the last-closed-flux-surface volume is defined by:

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{W} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} \int_{V_\mathrm{LCFS}} n_\mathrm{W}(\mathbf{x}) \, dV
$$

where $n_\mathrm{W}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_q n_{\mathrm{W}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local [tungsten_density](name:tungsten_density) summed over ionization states, $V_\mathrm{LCFS}$ is the volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, and $dV$ is the volume element. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $dV = R\,dR\,d\phi\,dZ$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The integral gives the total number of confined tungsten ions, so division by $V_\mathrm{LCFS}$ gives units of m^-3.

In practice, this quantity is computed by reconstructing the tungsten density distribution from spectroscopic measurements, radiation modeling, charge-state balance calculations, and impurity transport analysis, then integrating it over the closed-flux-surface volume. It complements aggregate ion-density measures such as [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density) and [volume_averaged_total_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_density), and it provides a global impurity-load measure distinct from location-specific values such as [tungsten_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:tungsten_density_at_magnetic_axis) or [tungsten_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:tungsten_density_at_plasma_boundary).

Typical volume-averaged tungsten densities in present tokamaks with tungsten plasma-facing components are roughly $10^{13}$-$10^{16}$ m^-3, depending on tungsten source strength, edge screening, transport, central accumulation, and heating conditions. These values are trace impurity densities, many orders of magnitude below the main-ion and electron densities, but they can strongly affect radiative power balance because tungsten is a high-atomic-number impurity.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_xenon_density
NAMES.subject: xenon
NAMES.short: Volume average of the elemental xenon ion number density over the full plasma volume. The local elemental density is summed over xenon ionization states, giving a single global measure of xenon impurity content.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged xenon density is the plasma-volume average of the local elemental xenon ion number density. The elemental xenon ion density is the sum of all xenon ionic charge-state densities, from singly ionized xenon through fully stripped xenon, and does not distinguish how the xenon population is distributed among charge states.

The volume average is defined by integrating the local elemental xenon ion density over the plasma volume:

$$
